Research: Resources

  • “Sometimes Mr. Spitzer wondered if he had ever really slept”: Mr. Spitzer doubts he has ever truly slept, or died. In his dream a river of fire and a river of ice run past arctic animals in opulent rooms, until all the rivers seem one great river of reality, with “a burning star in the frozen cloud” above the ice pinnacles.
  • “brilliant as five-pointed Arcturus”: Arcturus is the brightest star in the northern constellation of Bootes. “Canst thou guide Arcturus with his sons?” (Job 38:32, KJV). See Astronomy and The Bible.
  • “old walruses sitting upon gilded chairs of the fin de siecle period”: Fin de siècle, “end of the century,” names the 1890s, with their sense of an age ending in elegance and decay. Compare the Walrus of Lewis Carroll’s “The Walrus and the Carpenter” (Through the Looking-Glass, 1871).
  • “glass harmonicas”: Benjamin Franklin invented the glass armonica in 1761, a row of nested glass bowls turning on a spindle and played with wet fingers; Mozart wrote for it in 1791. See Music and Instruments.
  • “for this was his swan song, his silent song, the swan being mute”: The mute swan is not truly mute; it hisses, snorts, and grunts. See the swan song in the Chapter 61 resources. See Birds.
  • “there were great fiddler crabs following the boats”: The male fiddler crab has one enormous claw, which he waves like a fiddler’s bow to court females and warn off rivals. See The Sea and Water.
  • “there was far away a viola da gamba faintly singing, preceding the violoncello”: The viola da gamba is a bowed, fretted string instrument that was popular during the Renaissance and Baroque periods and is held between the legs. It belongs to the viol family, is distinct from the cello, and typically has six or seven strings tuned in fourths with a major third in the middle. Key features include frets on the fingerboard to aid intonation, a softer and brighter sound than a cello, and a flat back with sloping shoulders.
    • Violoncello (or cello) is a large, bowed string instrument in the violin family, played sitting down with the instrument held between the knees.
    • See the viola da gamba in the Chapter 60 resources.
  • “flying naiads”: In Greek mythology, the naiads, sometimes also hydriads, are a type of female spirit, or nymph, presiding over fountains, wells, springs, streams, brooks and other bodies of fresh water. See Greek Mythology.
  • “piccolos and hautboys”: The piccolo is a type of small, shrill woodwind instrument. The instrument is a small version of a flute played an octave higher.
    • The hautboy is an oboe or similar treble double reed instrument.
  • “running coach dogs running silently”: The Dalmatian was the coach dog, bred to trot beside or beneath carriages and guard the horses; fire engines kept the custom. See Dogs and Horses and Carriages.
  • “Hyperborean bees”: Hyperborean means a member of a people in Greek mythology who lived in perpetual sunshine. The Hyperboreans lived “beyond the North Wind,” Boreas. See Greek Mythology.
  • “many golden cockerels flapping their wings and crowing on singing weathervanes”: Compare Rimsky-Korsakov’s opera The Golden Cockerel (first performed 1909), whose golden bird crows warnings from its perch. See Music and Composers and Birds.
  • “phaeton shells”: Phaëton was the son of the sun god Helios (or Phoebus) in Greek mythology. He asked to prove his parentage by driving his father’s sun chariot, but his lack of skill caused the horses to run wild, burning the earth and creating deserts. Zeus eventually struck him with a thunderbolt to stop him. Horse-drawn light, open, four-wheeled carriage popular in the 18th and 19th centuries. It was owner-driven (no outside driver’s seat) and often had a folding top. An open-style car without fixed weather protection, similar to its horse-drawn predecessor. See Greek Mythology.
  • “the faded music of the harpsichord”: The harpsichord is a keyboard instrument that produces sound by plucking strings with a plectrum when a key is pressed, unlike the piano which strikes strings with hammers. It was a dominant keyboard instrument during the Renaissance and Baroque eras and is known for its distinctive sound. See the harpsichord in the Chapter 60 resources.
  • “the large-eyed squids staring at the paraselene”: A paraselene, moon dog, or mock moon is an atmospheric optical phenomenon which consists of a bright spot on one or both sides of a full moon.
    • Giant and colossal squids have the largest eyes of any animal, as big as dinner plates. See The Sea and Water.
  • “he was the great conductor conducting the water music”: Handel’s Water Music was first played on a barge on the Thames in July 1717, for King George I, who had it repeated three times. See Music and Composers.
  • “like an osculating star he crossed the face of the moon”: When the moon passes in front of a star, astronomers call it an occultation; Young’s “osculating” means kissing. See Astronomy.
  • “his largo”: Largo is an Italian term that means “slow and broad” and indicates a very slow tempo.
  • “his barcarolle which was his elegy”: A barcarolle is a folk song of Venetian gondoliers, which is imitated in classical music to create a gently rocking rhythm, often in 6/8 or 12/8 time. The most famous examples are Jacques Offenbach’s “Barcarolle” from the opera The Tales of Hoffmann and Frédéric Chopin’s Barcarolle, Op. 60 for solo piano. See On the barcarolle and Music and Composers.
  • “his body should be draped in the American flag though he had never fought in any war”: In the United States the custom of covering a soldier’s coffin with the flag spread during the Civil War; the government still gives a burial flag to veterans. See The Civil War.
  • “instructions not to deliver the Boston Transcript”: The Boston Evening Transcript was a daily afternoon newspaper in Boston, Massachusetts, published from 1830 to 1941. It is no longer in publication, with its final issue printed on April 30, 1941.
    • T. S. Eliot satirized its readers in “The Boston Evening Transcript” (1915): “The readers of the Boston Evening Transcript / Sway in the wind like a field of ripe corn.” See American Writers.
  • “The International Stamp Collector”: “The International Stamp Collector” and “The Society of Interplanetary Butterfly Lovers” appear to be Young’s inventions, gently comic versions of the hobby journals and collectors’ societies that flourished in the early twentieth century. Stamp collecting and butterfly collecting were both popular pastimes of the era, and both suit Mr. Spitzer’s habit of preserving fragile, fading things.
  • “the secretive egg of some great bird like the sea gannet”: The sea gannet is a large seabird, most commonly referring to the Northern Gannet, known for its spectacular plunge-diving to catch fish. These birds are white with black and gold markings and spend their lives at sea, only coming to land to nest. See Birds.
  • “two quarts of Pasteurized milk”: Pasteurized milk is milk that has been heated to kill harmful bacteria and other pathogens, making it safe to drink without risk of serious illness from harmful microbes. This process, named after Louis Pasteur, involves heating milk to a specific temperature for a set time, such as 145 degrees for 30 minutes or 161 degrees for 15 seconds, before cooling it down and packaging it. Pasteurization significantly extends shelf life and is the gold standard for milk safety, with most commercially available milk being pasteurized.
  • “the Pledge of Allegiance”: The Pledge of Allegiance is a patriotic recited verse that promises allegiance to the flag of the United States and the republic of the United States. The first version was written in 1885 by Captain George Thatcher Balch, a Union army officer in the Civil War who later authored a book on how to teach patriotism to children in public schools. In 1892, Francis Bellamy revised Balch’s verse as part of a magazine promotion surrounding the World’s Columbian Exposition, which celebrated the 400th anniversary of Christopher Columbus’ arrival in the Americas. Bellamy, the circulation manager for The Youth’s Companion magazine, helped persuade then-president Benjamin Harrison to institute Columbus Day as a national holiday and lobbied Congress for a national school celebration of the day. The magazine sent leaflets containing part of Bellamy’s Pledge of Allegiance to schools across the country and on October 21, 1892, over 10,000 children recited the verse together. Bellamy’s version of the pledge is largely the same as the one formally adopted by Congress 50 years later, in 1942. The official name of The Pledge of Allegiance was adopted in 1945. The most recent alteration of its wording came on Flag Day (June 14) in 1954, when the words “under God” were added. However, Bellamy’s authorship has been contested, as evidence has come out contradicting his claim. Several countries have a form of national pledge or oath, though the practice of daily, mandatory recitation in schools (as commonly associated with the US) is unusual by international standards. In many nations, oaths are typically reserved for specific occasions like citizenship ceremonies or for public officials.
  • “author of the music of the spheres”: See Pythagoras and the Music of the Spheres.
  • “dance of the golden cock-of-the-rock”: The cock-of-the-rock is a real bird of South American cloud forests; the brilliant orange males gather at leks, where they dance and display to win the females. See Birds.
    • The Andean cock-of-the-rock, the national bird of Peru, is a brilliant orange bird whose males gather to dance and display for the females.
  • “graduate of the New England Conservatory of Music”: The New England Conservatory of Music (NEC) was founded in Boston, Massachusetts, in 1867 by Eben Tourjée, making it the oldest independent music school in the United States. From its beginnings in a few rented rooms above the Boston Music Hall, the conservatory grew into a major music institution with a celebrated venue, Jordan Hall, which was granted National Historic Landmark status jointly with the NEC in 1994. Over its history, NEC has become a global leader in music education, known for its innovative approach and for attracting influential musicians as faculty and students.
  • “North, Northwest of the Great Bear”: Northwest of Ursa Major, the Great Bear, is the constellation Camelopardalis. Camelopardalis is a large, faint constellation that borders the northwestern part of the Great Bear. See Astronomy.
  • “his brother’s milky blue stone ring and ticking jeweled wrist watch”: The right hand that signs the lawyer’s will wears Peron’s ring and Peron’s ticking watch, while the left hand signs as the musician; the twins divide Mr. Spitzer’s body between them. See Twins and Doubles.
  • “Harvard graduate magna cum laude”: Harvard University’s history began in 1636 when the Massachusetts Bay Colony founded it as New College to train clergy. It was renamed Harvard College in 1639 after its first major benefactor, clergyman John Harvard, and has since grown into the oldest institution of higher learning in the United States, renowned for its academic prestige, wealth, and influence.
    • At Harvard, graduating magna cum laude is a distinction awarded to students with “great distinction,” typically those in the top 15% of their class. It is a Latin honor determined by a combination of departmental recommendations for High or Highest Honors and college-wide GPA cutoffs, which are set annually.
  • “never seen at a Pop concert in the Great Shell”: The Great Shell may be the Edward A. Hatch Memorial Shell, commonly called the Hatch Shell, an outdoor concert venue on the Charles River Esplanade in the Back Bay section of Boston, Massachusetts. Built in 1939-1940, it is one of the city’s prominent examples of Art Deco architecture. The Hatch Shell is best known for hosting the Boston Pops annually for the Boston Fourth of July celebration, but is also used for free concerts most weekends and many weeknights during the summer months. The grass pavilion in front of the stage has no permanent seating. There is a memorial nearby to Arthur Fiedler, first permanent conductor of the Pops.
    • Arthur Fiedler began the free Esplanade concerts in 1929 in an earlier wooden shell.
  • “the pack rat who lined his papery nest”: The pack rat, or wood rat, is also called the trade rat, because it often drops what it is carrying to pick up something shinier, seeming to leave a fair exchange. See The Pack Rat.
  • “greater than Haydn’s Creation”: Haydn’s Creation or The Creation is an oratorio written by Haydn and considered to be one of his masterpieces. It is a celebration of the creation of the world as in the Book of Genesis. See Genesis.
  • “Johann Strauss’s Boston Dreams”: Johann Strauss’s Boston Dreams may refer to 1872 when Strauss visited America and Boston built a stadium that sat 100,000 people.
    • The 1872 event was Patrick Gilmore’s World’s Peace Jubilee, whose Coliseum was said to hold 100,000; Strauss conducted “The Blue Danube” there with an orchestra of more than a thousand.
  • “Gustave Pick’s Fiacre Song”: Gustave Pick’s Fiacre Song may refer to Gustav Pick’s Fiakerlied which is a Viennese song. Pick wrote it in 1885, the song of a Viennese cab driver proud of his horses.
  • “old trot, trot sheet music”: The “trot, trot” is the cab horse’s gait in Pick’s Fiakerlied, the song of a Viennese fiacre driver. See Horses and Carriages.
    • “old trot, trot sheet music” may refer to Trot, an old-style Korean pop music genre that emerged in the early 1900s, characterized by a repetitive, simple beat and ornamented, emotive vocals. It was influenced by Western dance styles like the foxtrot, Japanese enka, and Korean folk melodies, blending them into a unique style that expresses emotions like sadness, endurance, and hope.
  • “songs for the gondolieri”: Gondolieri is the Italian word for the gondola boatmen of Venice.
    • Compare Gilbert and Sullivan’s The Gondoliers (1889).
  • “he was that poor skeleton sleeping in the oyster bed”: See the skeleton with a missing rib in the Chapter 59 resources.
  • “without expectations of emoluments”: Emoluments are a salary, fee, or profit from employment or office.
  • “given unto the generations”: The public domain consists of all the creative work to which no exclusive intellectual property rights apply. Those rights may have expired, been forfeited, expressly waived, or may be inapplicable. There has been recent criticism of the current copyright laws in the US in that they do not help the public as they were meant to do but stifle creativity and scientific progress. One of the most famous examples is the copyrighted song Happy Birthday to You which a US Judge ruled invalid in 2015 (after 1964).
  • “given by his mortmain, his dead hand”: Mortmain, French for “dead hand,” is a legal concept referring to the perpetual, inalienable ownership of land by a corporation, such as a church or charity. Historically, this practice was disfavored because it removed land from the feudal system and deprived lords of valuable feudal incidents. To curb this, Statutes of Mortmain were enacted to regulate or prohibit the transfer of land to corporations without a license. See On mortmain.
  • “the constellation Orion”: Orion is a constellation visible globally and features the famous Orion’s Belt. The Orion Nebula, a stellar nursery within it, is one of the brightest in the sky. In Greek myth, Orion was a giant and mighty hunter. His death story varies, but most legends involve his death by the bow of Artemis or a scorpion’s sting, after which he was placed in the heavens. See On Orion, Taurus, the Pleiades, the Hyades, Astronomy, and Greek Mythology.
    • Taurus: In astrology, Taurus (April 20-May 20) is the second sign of the zodiac, representing the bull and associated with being grounded, practical, and sensual. As a constellation, it’s one of the oldest and most recognizable in the night sky, visible in the Northern Hemisphere and home to the Pleiades and Hyades star clusters.
    • The Pleiades, also known as the Seven Sisters, refers to both a prominent star cluster in the constellation Taurus and the seven daughters of Atlas and Pleione in Greek mythology. The star cluster is about 100 million years old and consists of thousands of stars, with six or seven visible to the naked eye. Its bright blue stars and visibility in the winter night sky have made it a significant feature in cultures around the world for centuries.
    • The Hyades, mythological sisters, were associated with rain, and after their brother Hyas died, they were transformed into the star cluster, which also became known as “the Rainy Ones.” The star cluster is the closest one to Earth, appears as a V-shape that forms the face of Taurus, and includes the bright star Aldebaran (though Aldebaran is not a true member).
    • See the Pleiades in the Chapter 60 resources.
  • “east of almighty Taurus like a great wentletrap”: Wentletraps are small, often white, very high-spired, predatory or ectoparasitic sea snails, marine gastropod mollusks in the family Epitoniidae. The word wentletrap originated in Dutch, and it means spiral staircase. These snails are sometimes also called “staircase shells,” and “ladder shells.” Precious wentletraps once sold for great sums, and Chinese counterfeits are said to have been molded from rice paste. See The Sea and Water.
  • “pearl-bordered fritillaries”: Fritillaries are a type of butterfly and a genus of flowering plants known for their checkered patterns. See Butterflies and Moths.
  • “his coronachs”: A coronach is a song or hymn of mourning composed or performed as a memorial to a dead person.
    • “He is gone on the mountain, / He is lost to the forest” (Sir Walter Scott, “Coronach,” The Lady of the Lake, 1810). See Romantic Poets.
  • “screaming coradicorns”: Young’s “coradicorns” are likely the Coraciiformes, the order of rollers, kingfishers, bee-eaters, and motmots, in which hornbills and hoopoes were also long classed. See Birds.
    • Coradicorn may refer to a cormorant, which is an aquatic bird.
  • “hornbills, hoopoes, motmots”: The hoopoe leads the birds on their pilgrimage in Attar’s Conference of the Birds (1177), and in Aristophanes’s The Birds it is the transformed king Tereus. See Cloudcuckooland in the Chapter 61 resources. See Birds.
  • “maps of wandering Cocytus”: Cocytus is the river of wailing in the underworld in Greek mythology. In Dante’s Inferno it is a lake of ice holding the traitors (Cantos 32-34). See Dante and Greek Mythology.
  • “old Polish kings who had been deposed”: The line of Polish kings spans from the first crowned king, Bolesław I the Brave, in 1025, to the last elected king of the Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth. Key dynasties include the Piast dynasty, which ruled from the kingdom’s founding until 1370, followed by the Jagiellonian dynasty after 1386. A significant aspect of Polish monarchy was the elective monarchy, where kings were chosen by the nobility, a unique system in Europe from the 16th to the 18th centuries.
  • “old Laplander emperors”: There is no historical record of “Laplander emperors” because Lapland (Sápmi) was never an independent empire with its own emperors. The term “Laplander” is outdated, and the indigenous Sámi people are historically part of the regions now known as Finland, Sweden, Norway, and Russia. Historically, the region was loosely governed by various authorities, and as part of larger empires like Sweden and Russia, its administration was managed by those states.
  • “old Siberian kings”: There was no unified “Siberian monarchy” or single line of “Siberian kings” in the modern sense. Instead, Siberian rulers were organized into various khanates, with the most prominent being the Khanate of Sibir, ruled by competing dynasties like the Taibugids and Shaybanids. The most famous “Siberian king” in this context was Khan Kuchum, the last ruler of the Khanate of Sibir, who was defeated by the Cossack Yermak Timofeyevich, leading to the Russian conquest of the region. The House of Sibirsky was the foremost of many Genghisid families formerly living in Russia. It traced its descent from Kuchum, the last of the Siberian khans. Kuchum’s sons were captured by Yermak’s Cossacks and brought to Muscovy, where they were settled in Yaroslavl and other towns and were authorized to style themselves Tsarevichs of Siberia. Kuchum’s grandson Alp-Arslan was even installed as a puppet khan of Kasimov between 1614 and 1627. In 1591, the son of Kuchum, Abul Khayir was the first of his dynasty to convert to Christianity. His conversion was followed by the conversion of his entire family who eventually assimilated into the Russian nobility. In 1686, the tsar decreed that the dynasties of the king of Imeretia in the Caucasus along with the princes of Siberia and Kasimov were to be entered into the Genealogical Book of the Russian nobility. The tsarevichs married into the best Russian families. One of their princesses was the wife of Peter the Great’s maternal uncle, another married a son of the Georgian king.
  • “Queen Victoria in her youth”: Queen Victoria’s youth was marked by a highly isolated upbringing under the “Kensington System,” a set of strict rules designed to keep her under the control of her mother and her advisor, Sir John Conroy. Born in 1819, she lived at Kensington Palace, had few companions her own age, and was not allowed to be alone. Despite her controlled childhood, she pursued hobbies like painting, drawing, writing in her diary, and singing.
    • The Penny Black, the first postage stamp (1840), bore Victoria’s profile as a girl, and British stamps kept that young head until her death in 1901.
    • “The great Consort in his age” is Prince Albert, who died in 1861 at forty-two.
  • “the Leaning Tower of Pisa”: Construction started in 1173 on the bell tower for the Pisa Cathedral. It began to lean by 1178 after the third floor was completed, due to a weak, shallow foundation on soft, sandy soil. Construction halted for nearly a century, a delay that allowed the soil to settle and prevented its early collapse. The tower was completed in 1372 after architects attempted to compensate for the lean by making the upper floors taller on one side. Modern efforts in the 1990s stabilized the tower and reduced its tilt to about 4 degrees, a lean that is now intentionally preserved.
  • “several Russian Imperials and Kolokol”: “Russian Imperials” refers to the Russian Empire, a vast Eurasian state that existed from 1721 to 1917, ruled by autocratic emperors known as “czars” or “tsars.” It was the third-largest empire in history and encompassed a wide array of ethnicities, religions, and cultures, governed by a system that often maintained a degree of local autonomy under a centralized bureaucracy. The empire’s history is defined by significant expansion, internal reforms, and eventual collapse during the Russian Revolution of 1917, which was exacerbated by its participation in World War I.
    • “Kolokol” is a Russian word for “bell” and can refer to several things, including the historical newspaper Kolokol edited by Alexander Herzen, the Kolokol Group of volcanoes in Russia’s Kuril Islands, the Tsar Bell (also called Tsar Kolokol) in the Moscow Kremlin, or an incapacitating agent known as Kolokol-1. (The incapacitating agent is after 1964.)
  • “crowned griffins”: “Crowned griffins” may refer to a symbol of power in heraldry and art, an emblem used for regions like Kashubia, or a creature with a crown in a specific context like a game or a piece of jewelry. The griffin itself is a mythical beast with the body of a lion and the head and wings of an eagle, symbolizing majesty and strength, which is then further emphasized by the addition of a crown. See Greek Mythology.
  • “the first flight of the Wright brothers”: The Wright brothers made the first controlled, sustained flight of a powered, heavier-than-air aircraft on December 17, 1903, at Kill Devil Hills near Kitty Hawk, North Carolina. The first flight, piloted by Orville, lasted 12 seconds and covered 120 feet, while the longest flight of the day (piloted by Wilbur) lasted 59 seconds and traveled 852 feet. This event, achieved after four years of research and trials, is considered the birth of the aviation age.
  • “a Greek drachma of the period of Theseus”: The drachma was the official currency of modern Greece from 1832 until the launch of the euro in 2001. The ancient silver drachma was struck from the sixth century BC; Theseus, a hero of legend, is older than any coin, which is Young’s joke. See Greek Mythology.
  • “a coin of the Guelf”: The coin of the Guelf may refer to the first coin of its type introduced in Florence AD 1252 during the turbulent period of clashes between Guelphs and Ghibellines in the Italian city-states of central and northern Italy.
  • “several cordobas”: The córdoba is the currency of Nicaragua, created in 1912 in the honour of Francisco Hernández de Córdoba, one of the Spanish captains who conquered those lands.
  • “American dimes with the head of the Liberty girl”: The Liberty girl dime may refer to the Mercury dime or Winged Liberty Head dime used between 1916 and 1945.
  • “all the way from here to Concord”: Concord may refer to Concord, Massachusetts, a historic town famous for being the site of the first battle of the American Revolutionary War.
  • “He had sprinkled the paper with dust almost as brilliant as mica”: Mica is a group of silicate minerals. It is known for its ability to be split into thin, flexible, and elastic sheets and is used in various industries, including electronics and makeup. Mica powder is a shimmer-producing powder used in cosmetics, crafts, and other products.
    • Before blotting paper, writers dried wet ink by shaking fine sand, called pounce, from a sander over the page.
  • “entries and double entries”: Double-entry bookkeeping, in which every sum is entered twice so the books balance, was first set out in print by Luca Pacioli in 1494.
  • “He could not count on his abacus”: An abacus is a manual calculator with beads that slide on rods, used for performing arithmetic calculations. It has been used for centuries and comes in various forms, including the classic Chinese Suan-Pan and a version designed for blind users. While largely replaced by electronic calculators, it is still used today for educational purposes, teaching children math, and is favored by some experts for its speed.
  • “had not many great composers written their works with visual patterns none could play”: Compare eye music, written to be seen rather than heard: Baude Cordier’s chanson “Belle, bonne, sage” (c. 1400) is written in the shape of a heart, and Renaissance composers blackened their notes for words of night and death. See Music and Composers.
  • “drifting mackerel clouds”: A mackerel sky is dappled with small clouds like the markings of a mackerel; “Mackerel sky and mares’ tails / Make lofty ships carry low sails.”
  • “the street music of the dead cities”: Nineveh was a major ancient city and the capital of the Neo-Assyrian Empire, located on the eastern bank of the Tigris River, across from modern-day Mosul, Iraq. It was a significant cultural and political center, known for its development of public squares, parks, and botanical gardens, and is also famous from biblical accounts in the Book of Jonah. The city flourished under kings like Sennacherib, who made it the capital around 705 B.C., but was ultimately destroyed in 612 B.C. by a coalition of Babylonians and Medes.
    • Tyre is a city in Lebanon, and one of the oldest continuously inhabited cities in the world. It was one of the earliest Phoenician metropolises and the legendary birthplace of Europa, her brothers Cadmus and Phoenix, and Carthage’s founder Dido.
    • Ur of the Chaldees refers to the ancient Sumerian city of Ur, located near the Euphrates River in modern-day southern Iraq, which is identified as the birthplace of Abraham in the Bible. The name “Chaldees” is a reference to the Chaldeans, a people who later became influential in the region and are linked to this city in the biblical text. The site was extensively excavated by Sir Leonard Woolley in the early 20th century, revealing a prosperous city with advanced culture, architecture, and a famous ziggurat. Woolley dug up the city between 1922 and 1934. “And they went forth with them from Ur of the Chaldees” (Genesis 11:31, KJV).
    • Carthage was the ancient Punic city and empire in North Africa that was Rome’s rival and is now a UNESCO World Heritage site. The ancient city was a major power in the ancient Mediterranean that ultimately clashed with Rome during the Punic Wars.
    • “Lo, all our pomp of yesterday / Is one with Nineveh and Tyre!” (Rudyard Kipling, “Recessional,” 1897).
    • See Babylon, Nineveh, and Tyre in the Chapter 61 resources.
  • “cities under the frozen sand of the Great Gobi Desert”: The Great Gobi Desert of Outer Mongolia refers to the Gobi Desert, a large desert and semi-desert region in southern Mongolia and northern China that is home to extreme temperatures, diverse landscapes, and unique wildlife. It is not entirely a sandy desert but features mountains, steppes, and former lakes, and is surprisingly rich in biodiversity, including the critically endangered wild Bactrian camel and Gobi bear. Historically, it was part of the Mongol Empire and a key route on the Silk Road, and today it is known for its significant dinosaur fossil discoveries.
    • Pyotr Kozlov found the ruined city of Khara-Khoto in the Gobi in 1908, and Roy Chapman Andrews’s expeditions of the 1920s found dinosaur eggs there.
  • “the echoic ivory maiden Galatea”: In Greek mythology, Galatea was the name of the following figures: 1) a Nereid who loved the shepherd Acis, and was loved by the cyclops Polyphemus. 2) the post-antiquity name given to the statue of a woman created by Pygmalion and brought to life by Aphrodite. 3) daughter of Eurytius, son of Sparton. She married a man of good family but poor, Lamprus. When she became pregnant, Lamprus wished to have a son and told her to expose the child if it turned out to be a girl. Galatea gave birth to a girl while Lamprus was away, so she, with the advice of seers and her own dreams, told Lamprus that the baby was male, and named her Leucippus. As Leucippus grew older, her true sex became harder and harder to conceal, so Galatea went to the sanctuary of Leto and prayed to the goddess to change her daughter into a man. Leto took pity on mother and daughter and made Leucippus an actual man. See Greek Mythology.
  • “From all his musical rags, future musicians must stitch together a musical coat”: Compare the philosophy of clothes in Thomas Carlyle’s Sartor Resartus (1831), “the tailor retailored.” See The Great Tailor and Clothing, Hats, and Skirts.
  • “Surely, however, he should not be discouraged by his failures”: This long paragraph conveys a powerful meditation on the persistence of creative spirit and identity beyond loss and failure. Mr. Spitzer’s music, though complex, fragmented, and often unheard, represents an eternal, multifaceted expression of life, death, and memory. His struggle is both deeply personal and cosmic, entwined with the universal rhythms of nature and time.
  • “the sentinel dolphin dying”: See Byron’s dying dolphin in the Chapter 56 resources. See Romantic Poets.
  • “wild screamings of stormy petrels”: Sailors named the storm petrel for Saint Peter, because it seems to walk on the water as it feeds (Matthew 14:29). See Birds.
  • “common measures and alia breves”: Alla breve is a time signature indicating 2 or 4 half-note beats in a bar.
    • An appoggiatura is a musical embellishment that is approached by a leap and resolved by a step to a consonant pitch. It creates temporary tension by being dissonant against the underlying harmony and is typically played on a strong beat, before resolving to the main, or “principal,” note. Unlike the very quick acciaccatura, the appoggiatura steals a significant portion of the main note’s duration, often taking about half the value.
  • “dreams of fishes sleeping in anemones like birds in nests”: Clownfish live among the stinging tentacles of sea anemones, protected by a coat of mucus. See The Sea and Water.
  • “forfended by other music”: To forfend is to avert, keep away, prevent, or protect.
  • “there was quinquevalent music”: Quinquevalent music is a rare or specialized term, with several interpretations: 1) in a theoretical or philosophical context, it has been mentioned in discussions about musical multiplicity, specifically as “music of five roads” or “five ways.” This suggests a conceptual framework for music that explores five different paths or dimensions, likely within a specific, non-mainstream musical theory or artistic project. 2) a more general interpretation relates to the prefix “quinquevalent” (meaning having a valence of five) and the musical term “quintet” (a group of five musicians or a piece of music for five performers). 3) the term “quinquevalent” itself is primarily used in chemistry and medicine (referring to a valence of five or a vaccine with five components). It is not standard music terminology.
  • “if all times were simultaneities of all times”: Compare T. S. Eliot: “Time present and time past / Are both perhaps present in time future” (“Burnt Norton,” 1936). See Time and American Writers.
  • “loon soul crying as the light faded”: The common loon’s wailing night call carries for miles across northern lakes. See Birds.
  • “add to his music of aubade and serenade his nocturne”: Aubade is a song or poem that greets the dawn, traditionally a morning love song about lovers parting at daybreak. The term, from the Old Occitan word auba meaning “dawn,” can also refer to morning music or a song sung outdoors at dawn as a compliment. The concept has been used in literature for centuries, notably in medieval France, and also appears as a subject for visual art, like the Picasso painting The Aubade. “It was the nightingale, and not the lark” (William Shakespeare, Romeo and Juliet, 3.5). See On the aubade and Shakespeare.
    • The piano nocturne was invented by John Field in 1812 and perfected by Chopin.
  • “pagoda umbrellas”: See The Umbrella.
  • “signs of alchemic gold”: The alchemists wrote their metals in signs: gold the sun, silver the moon, quicksilver Mercury, lead Saturn. See Astrology, Alchemy, and Esoterica.
  • “sign of Uranus and sign of Pluto”: Uranus is the seventh planet from the Sun, a tilted “ice giant” with at least 28 moons and faint rings. It is a cold, blue-green planet primarily composed of water, ammonia, and methane, and is known for its extreme axial tilt which causes long periods of continuous daylight and darkness at its poles. In mythology, Uranus was the Greek god of the sky. William Herschel, an oboist and composer before he was an astronomer, discovered it in 1781.
    • Pluto, a dwarf planet in the Kuiper Belt, was reclassified from a planet in 2006 because it did not meet all the criteria for a full-sized planet. It was the first Kuiper Belt object discovered, and NASA’s New Horizons mission provided the first close-up images in 2015. (2006 is after 1964.) Clyde Tombaugh discovered Pluto in 1930.
  • “sign of Sagittarius the Golden Archer”: Sagittarius, the Golden Archer, is the ninth astrological sign, associated with those born between approximately November 22 and December 21. Ruled by the planet Jupiter, it is a Fire sign represented by the Archer, or a centaur, who is often depicted aiming a bow and arrow. People born under this sign are known for being adventurous, optimistic, honest, and freedom-loving, though they can sometimes be impatient and blunt. See Astrology, Alchemy, and Esoterica.
  • “sign of the Southern Cross”: The Southern Cross is an asterism of the Crux constellation, made up of four or five bright stars that form a distinctive cross shape. It is a key navigational tool for finding the direction south and is prominently featured on the flags of several southern hemisphere countries, including Australia and New Zealand. It is one of the smallest and most easily recognized constellations in the southern night sky. See Astronomy.
  • “fugacious as flowers falling soon after blooming”: Fugacious means tending to disappear; fleeting.
  • “clouds of dogtooth violets”: The dogtooth violet is a bulbous herbaceous perennial flowering plant in the family Liliaceae, growing to 25 cm. It is native to central and southern Europe from Portugal to Ukraine. It is the only naturally occurring species of Erythronium in Europe.
    • America’s dogtooth violet is the trout lily (Erythronium americanum), named for its mottled leaves.
  • “music of his checkrein”: A checkrein, or bearing rein, is a piece of horse tack that controls the horse’s head position.
    • Anna Sewell’s Black Beauty (1877) was written partly to end the cruelty of the bearing rein, which held a horse’s head painfully high. See Horses and Carriages.
  • “flying notes of caprioles”: The capriole is a movement performed in classical riding, in which the horse leaps from the ground and kicks out with its hind legs.
    • The Lipizzaner stallions of Vienna’s Spanish Riding School still perform the capriole.
  • “song of the clew lines”: Clew lines are ropes used to haul the clews (the corners) of a square sail up to the yard, which is necessary for furling and reefing it. They run from the clews, often through blocks and fairleads, to the deck, allowing the crew to pull the sail up from below.
  • “apivorous birds”: Apivorous is an adjective that means “feeding on bees.” It describes animals, particularly birds, that eat bees as a food source. Bee-eaters and the honey buzzard are among them. See Birds.
  • “Pavanne for a Dead Lady”: Compare Maurice Ravel’s Pavane pour une infante défunte, “Pavane for a Dead Princess” (1899). See Music and Composers.
  • “Elegy for a Frog Eating a Firefly”: The polar bear and butterfly symbolize dormancy and rebirth, the iceberg music the hidden depths of experience, and the celestial notes the universal and eternal dimensions of art and memory.
    • See the frog’s funeral in the Chapter 61 resources. See Fireflies.
  • “Note to Aldebaran”: Aldebaran is the red eye of Taurus the bull, near the Hyades. See Astronomy.
  • “Small Burden for a Pack Rat”: A burden is the refrain of a song. See The Pack Rat.
  • “the great wind horn, water horn, submarine flower winding around his neck”: Compare the helicon and the sousaphone, brass basses that wrap around the player’s body. See Music and Instruments.
  • “until death did them part”: “Till death us do part,” from the marriage service of the Book of Common Prayer. See Weddings and Funerals.
  • “had given him tuberculosis of the lungs”: Tuberculosis, the “white plague,” killed about one in seven of all people in nineteenth-century Europe and America; streptomycin, the first drug to cure it, came in 1943.
  • “Blow on, horn-blower, blow on!”: Compare Tennyson: “Blow, bugle, blow, set the wild echoes flying, / Blow, bugle; answer, echoes, dying, dying, dying” (The Princess, 1850). See Romantic Poets.
  • “He knew a clarinetist who had committed suicide”: This paragraph uses the story of the clarinetist to illustrate themes of alienation, the quest for perfection, the impact of internal fears, and the possibility of transcendence through art or death. The kaleidoscopic imagery and the layering of real and symbolic witnesses enrich the text’s meditation on existence, while the clarinetist’s tragic end embodies the human longing for harmony and the fear of being “out of tune” in the grand symphony of life. See On the clarinetist’s greater orchestra and Suicide in History and Literature.
  • “the dormer roof of a Gloucester boarding house”: Gloucester, Massachusetts, is the old fishing port of Rudyard Kipling’s Captains Courageous (1897).
  • “even as the manifest dream concealed that hidden dream”: Freud distinguished the manifest content of a dream, what the dreamer remembers, from its latent content, the hidden wish it disguises (The Interpretation of Dreams, 1899). See Freud and Jung.
  • “star coral”: Star coral can refer to several types of reef-building stony corals, such as the mountainous, lobed, or boulder star corals, or to other less common corals like the ORA Asterospicularia or Northern Star Coral. These corals form large, complex colonies with star-shaped polyps and are found in various reef environments, with many species now facing threats from climate change.
    • The dogwinkle, dog whelk, dogwhelk, or Atlantic dogwinkle is a species of predatory sea snail, a carnivorous marine gastropod in the family Muricidae, the rock snails. Nucella lapillus was originally described by Carl Linnaeus in his landmark 1758 10th edition of Systema Naturae as Buccinum lapillus.
    • The scallop shell is the traditional emblem of St. James the Great, one of the apostles of Jesus and the patron saint of Spain and pilgrims. In medieval times, pilgrims who completed the journey to the shrine of St. James at the Cathedral of Santiago de Compostela in Galicia, Spain, would collect a scallop shell from the coast as a souvenir and proof of their accomplishment. They would wear the shell on their hat or cloak. The scallop shell is widely used today as a wayfinding symbol along the Camino de Santiago routes, often painted in yellow on a blue background on milestones and signs to guide pilgrims to their destination. The shell’s grooves, all converging at a central point, are seen as a metaphor for the many different paths pilgrims take from all over the world, all leading to the single destination of St. James’ tomb. The shell was also used by pilgrims as a practical utensil for gathering water to drink or as a makeshift bowl for food, which they might request from homes along the way. The red cross often painted on the shell is the Cross of Saint James (Cruz de Santiago), which is linked to medieval crusaders and Spanish military orders. The shell itself is a universal symbol for “weary travelers” and the “crusaders of the Order of St. James.”
  • “like the fringes of a fringe-topped surrey”: Compare “The Surrey with the Fringe on Top,” from Rodgers and Hammerstein’s Oklahoma! (1943).
  • “sand dollars as big as dinner plates”: See the sand dollar in the Chapter 60 resources.
  • “anything which was worth happening at all was worth happening twice”: Compare Nietzsche’s eternal recurrence, the thought that this very life must be lived again innumerable times (The Gay Science, 341, 1882). See Nietzsche.

  • “he had stood on the Library steps and had watched that old violinist”: Library steps may refer to the Library Company of Philadelphia, founded by Benjamin Franklin in 1731 as America’s first successful lending library, and the Free Library of Philadelphia, chartered in 1891, with its central branch opening in 1927.
    • If Mr. Spitzer is in Boston, as he learns in Louisburg Square, the steps may be those of the Boston Public Library on Copley Square (1895).
    • See The Old Violinist and the Chapter 58 resources.
  • “four horse hairs drawn from the tail of a white Siberian horse”: A violin bow is strung with 150 to 200 hairs from the tails of white stallions, the best long held to come from Siberia and Mongolia. See Music and Instruments.
  • “planets singing together”: “When the morning stars sang together, and all the sons of God shouted for joy” (Job 38:7, KJV). See The Bible.
  • “a member of the Philadelphia Symphony”: The Philadelphia Orchestra was founded in 1900 by Fritz Scheel, evolving into one of America’s most prominent symphony orchestras. Key figures in its history include conductors Leopold Stokowski and Eugene Ormandy, who shaped its sound and recorded extensively. The orchestra is known for its history of innovation, including being a leader in orchestral recordings and tours, and for forging a close relationship with composer Sergei Rachmaninoff. See On the Philadelphia Orchestra and Music and Composers.
  • “even as an Ishmael among men”: Ishmael was the son of Abraham and his concubine, Hagar, born before Abraham’s son Isaac with his wife Sarah. He is a significant figure in the Hebrew Bible, where his descendants are said to be numerous, and he is traditionally seen as the patriarch of the Arab people. Key events in his life include being the son whose birth was prophesied to Hagar and Abraham, being sent away with his mother, and later helping to bury his father, Abraham.
    • “He will be a wild man; his hand will be against every man, and every man’s hand against him” (Genesis 16:12, KJV). Melville’s outcast narrator begins, “Call me Ishmael” (Moby-Dick, 1851). See Genesis and American Writers.
  • “The death’s-head smiling, inviting pity for the moth”: The death’s-head hawkmoth carries a skull on its back and squeaks when handled. See Butterflies and Moths.
  • “cubes and cubes and cubes”: See Cubism in the Chapter 60 resources.
  • “the tailor who sat cross-legged in the door of the moon”: See The Great Tailor.
  • “crossing Louisburg Square”: Louisburg Square is a street in the Beacon Hill neighborhood of Boston, Massachusetts, bisected by a small private park. The park is bounded by Pinckney Street to the north and Mount Vernon Street to the south.
    • Louisa May Alcott spent her last years at No. 10, and William Dean Howells lived at No. 4. See American Writers.
  • “My God! I thought I was in Philadelphia”:
    • Compare W. C. Fields’s mock epitaph, “On the whole, I’d rather be in Philadelphia” (Vanity Fair, 1925).

Chapter 26

← Chapter 25 · Home · Chapter 27 →

Content note: Vera’s mother, Catherine Cartwheel, is addicted to opium.

Summary

Mr. Spitzer’s field of law is the dead: wills, deeds, archives, and lost heirs. One case involves two Boston spinsters, each believing she is Cleopatra. One left her fortune to her Siamese cats under his supervision, and the cats seem likely to live forever. He relives the hour he identified his twin in a city morgue, and the day Catherine refused his hand for the last time. He asks what Peron would have done had their places been reversed. He concludes that Peron would never have been faithful to Catherine’s bedside, but would have dragged her into the living sunlight even if it killed her. He reflects that to reach the upper world one must first travel through the lower.

Characters present

Joachim Spitzer · Peron Spitzer · Catherine Cartwheel · Vera Cartwheel

Concepts present

Themes: Death and Mortality · Duality and Doubles · Grief, Loss, and Mourning · Guilt, Innocence, and Justice · Illusion and Reality · Memory and the Past · Music, Sound, and Silence · Society, Class, and Race · Women, Gender, and Marriage

Symbols: Horses and Carriages · Roses and Flowers · Twins and Doubles

Philosophy: Heraclitus and Flux · Hinduism · Pythagoras and the Music of the Spheres · Schopenhauer

Allusions: Alice in Wonderland · American Writers · Ancient Egypt · Astronomy · Dante · Edgar Allan Poe · Fairy Tales and Folklore · Genesis · Greek Mythology · Music and Composers · Romantic Poets · Shakespeare · Suicide in History and Literature · The Bible · The Book of Job · The History of Opium

Key passages

From the research

  • Early in the chapter, Mr. Spitzer’s role is described as one dealing with “the dead,” wills, deeds, secret archives, and old houses haunted by ghosts: both literal and metaphorical. He has encountered many baffling situations, such as lost heirs and numerous wills designed to confuse even the most conscientious attorney. This has led him to doubt the very idea of inheritance and continuity through generations, extending even to physical traits like hair and eyes, which he likens to “properties… of a dream” that fade while observed. This passage underscores the theme of uncertainty and the fragile, illusory nature of identity and legacy.
  • Mr. Spitzer recalls an eccentric case of an old Boston lady who believed herself the reincarnation of Cleopatra and left her house and garden to her numerous Siamese cats, with the caretaker to live in the house as long as the cats lived. The cats are described almost mystically, with “nine lives,” prowling the house and garden as if they owned it, playing piano keys, and embodying a kind of magical, surreal presence. This passage conveys a haunting atmosphere and illustrates Mr. Spitzer’s encounters with the bizarre and uncanny elements of death and legacy. It also reflects his cautious and conservative approach to administering such an unusual estate.
  • This is a deeply poignant section where Mr. Spitzer recalls the shock of identifying his dead brother in a morgue among the homeless and faceless corpses. He reflects on how his life has since been shadowed by this event, feeling as if he lives his brother’s life and dies his brother’s death. The passage reveals Mr. Spitzer’s internal struggle with grief, memory, and the passing of time. It also illuminates the contrast between the brothers: Mr. Spitzer’s “cosmic serenity” versus his brother’s impatience, competition, and instability. This reflection on personal loss and identity is central to the chapter’s emotional core.
  • Mr. Spitzer expresses a belief in a future beyond the law and human institutions, a future of “silent music” and “heavenly harmonies” is fixed beyond time’s fluctuations. He contemplates the idea that perfect life should be perfect death, where there is no rivalry, no immortal derangement, but complete oblivion rather than memory. This is contrasted with Catherine’s opium-induced desire for complete memory. These meditations reveal Mr. Spitzer’s somber, even nihilistic, outlook on existence, death, and what, if anything, lies beyond.
  • The chapter contrasts Mr. Spitzer’s faithful, solemn devotion to Catherine and the dead with his brother Peron’s impetuous love of life, fear of death, and competitive nature. Mr. Spitzer doubts that his brother would have been so faithful or so enduring in grief, emphasizing Peron’s preference for the “great crowds of Derby Day” and his inability to face death or prolonged farewell. This contrast highlights different ways of confronting mortality and loss, and the complex dynamics of family loyalty and love.
  • Mr. Spitzer contemplates Catherine’s opium-induced visions and her tendency to “narcotize” her memory to avoid facing reality, creating an opaque inner world filled with imaginary beings. He serves as a guardian of her property and life, yet his presence is often ignored or rejected, and he is caught in a paradox of faithfulness and absence. This passage captures the theme of elusive truth, memory, and perception, and the isolating burden of care and love.
  • Toward the end, Mr. Spitzer reflects that to reach the upper world (perhaps a metaphor for peace, truth, or heaven), one must first pass through the lower world: the streets and alleys inhabited by thieves and painted street women. This metaphor suggests a journey through all aspects of life, including its sordid or painful parts, before reaching any transcendence. It ties into the chapter’s exploration of death, memory, and the complexity of existence.

Questions and observations

Reading closely

  • “His department was that of the dead.” How has the law shaped what Mr. Spitzer believes about inheritance?
  • The cats “seemed to know they owned the place.” Who owns whom in this house?
  • “Perfect life should be perfect death.” What kind of heaven does Mr. Spitzer want?

Characters

  • Catherine wants “a complete memory,” and Mr. Spitzer wants “a complete oblivion.” Why does she drug her memory, then?
  • Would Peron “have endured my mother’s pleasure in ignoring him”? What does Joachim’s faithfulness cost him?
  • Catherine “held it against him that he did not rescue her.” What would rescue mean for her?

Connections

  • Catherine’s canary “had died already many times without her knowledge” (Chapter 2). How do the immortal cats echo it?
  • In Chapter 25, Mr. Spitzer did not believe in heaven “except as a state of mind.” How does he describe it here?
  • One must “travel through the lower world” to reach the upper. Where has Vera’s own journey gone downward?

Reflection

  • Should the dead control the living through what they leave behind?
  • Is faithfulness without hope a virtue?
  • Would you choose a complete memory or a complete oblivion?

Research: Characters

Joachim Spitzer (Peron’s twin brother)

  • Family lawyer, guardian of the dead’s legacy.
  • Scrupulous, conservative, somber, introspective.
  • Struggles with the paradox of his profession and personal grief over his twin brother. He is caught between duty and emotional turmoil.
  • Believes in a final peace beyond life and law, emphasizing oblivion rather than memory after death.
  • His work involves dealing with the hidden past, dusty archives, and eccentric clients, many of whom create baffling legal puzzles through multiple wills or lost heirs.
  • This career, entered reluctantly, “only because of his father’s wishes,” keeps him continually close to death and the mysteries of inheritance.
  • A notable case in Mr. Spitzer’s youth involved an elderly Boston lady who believed she was Cleopatra reincarnated. She left her house and garden to her innumerable Siamese cats, with the ancient caretaker to live there and draw an income as long as the cats lived, and Mr. Spitzer to supervise. The cats are described almost as immortal beings, with a mysterious presence that haunts the house, symbolizing the blurred lines between life and death, reality and illusion.
  • He also considers Catherine’s narcotic-induced oblivion as a form of escape from reality, pondering the value of memory and oblivion in death.
  • Mr. Spitzer philosophizes on the necessity of traveling through the “lower world” (a metaphorical space of moral and social darkness) before reaching the “upper world” or enlightenment. This journey includes encountering thieves, street women, and the underbelly of life, suggesting his awareness of the complex layers of existence beyond his legal profession.
  • He identified his brother at “the morgue of a great city… among homeless men and fallen women and faceless creatures,” and his life has not been entirely his own since.
  • He proposed to Catherine, and when she refused “for the last fickle and unconstant time” his “passive hand,” he “turned so silently away.”
  • He hires the servants, pays her “astronomical bills,” and pays Peron’s debts “with every new day of his life.”

Peron Spitzer (Joachim’s twin brother)

  • Impulsive, competitive, impetuous, and restless.
  • His and Joachim’s lives and deaths intertwine; Peron’s death haunts Joachim.
  • He distrusted the law and wanted only “a crooked lawyer,” one who “would fix the witness and the judge,” and he often tried to fix his brother.
  • He preferred “the great crowds of Derby Day” to any dream, and “had been afraid of death.”
  • Represents the chaotic, fleeting nature of life and human memory.
  • He would have swept Catherine “into the living sunlight,” even if the sunlight were her death.

Catherine Cartwheel (Vera’s mother)

  • Bedridden and addicted to opium.
  • Mr. Spitzer handles her estate.
  • Represents illusions of grandeur and the persistence of the past into the present.
  • Central to Mr. Spitzer’s personal life, her illness and narcotic use create a complex emotional dynamic.
  • Embodies memory, oblivion, and the tension between awareness and escape.
  • Mr. Spitzer believes she drugs herself “so that she should not see him, this old family lawyer with his brother’s face.”

Research: Themes

Mortality and the Legacy of the Dead

See: Death and Mortality

  • The chapter explores how death shapes the living through legal, emotional, and mystical legacies. The dead control the living via wills and memories, but these connections are uncertain and fraught with paradox.

Memory versus Oblivion

See: Memory and the Past

  • Mr. Spitzer contrasts Catherine’s desire for memory with his own preference for oblivion after death, questioning what form of afterlife or peace is truly desirable.

Illusion and Reality

See: Illusion and Reality

  • The recurring motif of illusions, reincarnations, the cats’ seeming immortality, and fragmented memories highlights the fragile, dream-like quality of existence. This is similar to Catherine’s canary, which “had died already many times without her knowledge” (Chapter 2).

The Law and Its Limits

See: Guilt, Innocence, and Justice

  • The law is portrayed as an imperfect, sometimes arbitrary system that tries to impose order on the chaos of life and death. Mr. Spitzer hopes for a future beyond law, where harmony replaces discord.

Duality of Human Nature

See: Duality and Doubles · Twins and Doubles

  • Through the contrast between Joachim and his twin brother Peron, the duality of restraint versus impulsiveness, order versus chaos, and life versus death is examined.

Research: Symbols and Imagery

The Siamese Cats

See: Ancient Egypt

  • Symbolize mystery, immortality, and the blurred boundary between life and death. Their dominance in the Boston lady’s house reflects ongoing life amid death.

The Pyramid and the Sphinx

See: Ancient Egypt · Greek Mythology

  • Represent ancient legacies, riddles of existence, and the enigmatic nature of identity and memory.
  • These are Egyptian sphinxes, built in rival Boston gardens by two old women who each believed she was the reincarnation of Cleopatra.

The Dead Brother

See: Twins and Doubles · Peron Spitzer

  • A symbol of lost potential, memory, and the haunting presence of the past in the present.

Opium and Narcotics

See: The History of Opium

  • Reflect escape, oblivion, and the tension between retaining memory or seeking peace through forgetfulness.

The Upper and Lower Worlds

See: Dante · Greek Mythology

  • Mr. Spitzer’s lower world of “the thief who had stolen bright jewels” and “the painted street woman leering under a lamp” must be crossed to reach the upper, a journey “endless like some of those journeys taken by my mother.”

Research: Resources

  • “those who were poor and imagined they were rich and dwelled in many castles of illusion”: “Castles in Spain,” castles in the air, are in print in the Roman de la Rose (c. 1230) as chastiaus en Espaigne.
  • “handed down in golden perpetuity through the generations of the dead who thus controlled the living”: In the US, property can be passed down through generations in perpetuity, ensuring a lasting legacy. Promoting Inequality: A significant critique of inherited wealth is that it exacerbates economic inequality, enabling wealth acquisition without labor and hindering social mobility. Critics say perpetual trusts are “truly creating an American aristocracy” (Ray Madoff, New York Times, July 2010, as reported in the ABA Journal). Unrestricted perpetual trusts can hold wealth indefinitely, and could lead to the concentration of wealth in the hands of a few families, potentially creating a privileged class. Inheriting wealth without earning it can undermine a sense of accomplishment and make inheritors feel like mere placeholders for future generations. The US has a history of enacting estate and gift taxes, though their reach and rates have fluctuated over time, often tied to war financing or efforts to curb wealth concentration. There is ongoing debate about the role and impact of these taxes, with some advocating for their repeal and others for their reform. Traditional legal principles like the Rule Against Perpetuities, which began in the Duke of Norfolk’s Case (1682) to limit the “dead hand” of the grave over property, aimed to prevent perpetual trusts, but many states have modified or abolished this rule, leading to renewed debate about the implications of trusts that can last indefinitely. Other viewpoints have called for the complete abolition of inheritance, asserting that it is incompatible with a fair and equitable society.
  • “so many lost heirs, so many lost heiresses”: Salic law barred women from inheriting the French throne, and English succession preferred sons over elder daughters until 2013.
  • “There had been heirs who had been heiresses, heiresses who had been heirs”: Women’s property rights have expanded over time in the United States, but they have been restricted by gender stereotypes and laws. Under the English common law of coverture, a married woman’s property passed to her husband. In 1718, Pennsylvania’s Feme Sole Traders Act let the wives of absent mariners run businesses in their own names. In 1848, New York passed the Married Women’s Property Act, which allowed women to keep their property when they married. By the end of the Civil War, 29 states had passed some version of a Married Women’s Property Act, yet as late as 1887 a third of the states still did not let married women control their own earnings. (Wikipedia) Enslaved women could own nothing, not even themselves, and free women of color were often shut out of these rights in practice. Gender stereotypes and ideologies have historically been barriers to women’s property rights. See Women, Gender, and Marriage and the Chapter 23 resources.
  • “the reincarnation of Cleopatra”: Cleopatra VII (69-30 BC), the last ruler of Ptolemaic Egypt and Mark Antony’s lover. Belief in reincarnation runs through Hinduism, and through Theosophy, founded in New York in 1875. See Ancient Egypt and Hinduism.
  • “a Sphinx in her garden… a greater pyramid than her neighbor could afford”: The Great Sphinx and the Great Pyramid of Khufu at Giza. Egyptian Revival garden ornaments were a fashion after Napoleon’s expedition to Egypt (1798). See Ancient Egypt.
  • “leaving her house and garden to her innumerable Siamese cats”: Siamese cats came from Siam (Thailand). The first known in America was sent to Lucy Hayes at the White House in 1878.
    • There were cases of pets and animals inheriting estates, though some are legends. Gunther VI, a German Shepherd, descends from a dog said to have inherited $80 million from Countess Karlotta Liebenstein in 1992. The Times of London called it “a ruse concocted by the scion of an Italian pharmaceutical company,” Maurizio Mian, and the Countess apparently never existed (Netflix, Gunther’s Millions, 2023). The poodle said to have inherited a fortune from New York heiress Ella Wendel in 1931 is an urban legend: Time reported in 1933 that her poodle Tobey “was not even mentioned in the will.” Blackie, a cat, inherited Ben Rea’s £7 million fortune in 1988 and was named the wealthiest cat by Guinness World Records (Guinness World Records, “International Cat Day,” 2017).
  • “Egyptian securities, and New England shipping”: Egypt’s foreign debts led to the Anglo-French Dual Control (1876) and the British occupation of 1882. Egyptian bonds were a favorite of cautious Victorian investors. See Ancient Egypt.
  • “each having nine lives”: “A woman hath nine lives like a cat” (John Heywood, 1546). See Fairy Tales and Folklore.
  • “the windy garden where no birds sang”: “The sedge has withered from the lake, / And no birds sing” (Keats, “La Belle Dame sans Merci,” 1819). See Romantic Poets.
  • “eating from golden dishes fit for the dead pharaohs”: In ancient Egypt, cats were sacred to the goddess Bastet and were mummified by the hundreds of thousands. See Ancient Egypt.
  • “he had hesitantly called to leave his engraved calling card, to pay, in fact, his respects to the new owners”: Leaving an engraved calling card was the ritual of a nineteenth-century social call. See Society, Class, and Race.
  • “cats walking about like flower-faced sibyls”: The Sibyls were the prophetesses of the ancient world, among them the Cumaean Sibyl who guides Aeneas into the underworld. See Greek Mythology.
  • “less fearful than the raven might have been”: Poe’s “The Raven” (1845), perched “upon a bust of Pallas just above my chamber door.” See Edgar Allan Poe.
  • “A cat had walked up and down on the piano keys, playing a little tune from the works of one of the more obscure eighteenth-century musical composers”: Domenico Scarlatti’s Sonata in G minor, K. 30, has been called “The Cat’s Fugue” since the nineteenth century, after the story that his cat walked across the keyboard. See Music and Composers.
  • “like an old mummified pharaoh wrapped in his body which was his boat”: Pharaohs were buried with boats to carry them through the afterlife. Khufu’s cedar ship was found beside the Great Pyramid in 1954. See Ancient Egypt.
  • “this old family lawyer with the sombre, weedy look”: “Weeds,” from Old English wǣd, “garment,” survives in “widow’s weeds,” the black dress of mourning. See Grief, Loss, and Mourning.
  • “the attitude of a perpetual grief”: This may refer to the philosophy of Arthur Schopenhauer, who believed that death is a natural part of life and a return to a state of non-existence that existed before birth. He thought that individual consciousness is impermanent and that the life of an individual is meaningless. His key ideas are will-to-live (the driving force behind our attachment to life and our fear of death), knowledge (shows the meaninglessness of life and the worthlessness of living), suicide (pointless because it affirms the will-to-live, though it destroys the individual), palingenesis (the will, not the individual mind or soul, is reborn in new beings), redemption (that death is an opportunity for redemption through the negation of the will). The portrayal of Mr. Spitzer’s lifelong sorrow, his recognition of life as a series of losses and unfulfilled desires, and his contemplation of the illusory nature of reality all echo Schopenhauerian themes. The passage reflects a worldview where grief and suffering are continuous and intrinsic to life. His fullest statement is in The World as Will and Representation, vol. 2 (1844), chapter 41, “On Death and Its Relation to the Indestructibility of Our Inner Nature.” See Schopenhauer and Suicide in History and Literature.
  • “only his elegiac music”: An elegy is a song or poem of mourning. Mr. Spitzer’s “elegiac music” is music he has written “only for himself or for no mortal ear.” See Music, Sound, and Silence and the Chapter 25 resources.
  • “the heavenly harmonies forever fixed above the floods of time, dark time, those unmoving golden spheres”: “Musica universalis,” the music of the spheres: Boethius, in De institutione musica (c. 500), divided music into musica mundana (the music of the spheres), humana, and instrumentalis. The idea goes back to Pythagoras. Mr. Spitzer imagines “the silent music which requires neither instruments nor voices.” Mr. Spitzer, a semi-retired lawyer and composer of “silent music,” is attuned to the music of the spheres, the eternal, silent harmonies beyond earthly sounds. See Pythagoras and the Music of the Spheres, Astronomy, and Music, Sound, and Silence.
  • “He could believe in probably no hell more than this present individual life”: Mephistophilis in Marlowe’s Doctor Faustus (c. 1592), 1.3: “Why, this is hell, nor am I out of it.”
  • “a state of mind”: In Chapter 25, Mr. Spitzer did not believe in Heaven “except as a state of mind.” Here it is a state “when we should have completely forgotten who we were.” See the Chapter 25 resources.
  • “when we should have put off this mortal clay”: “Thou hast made me as the clay; and wilt thou bring me into dust again?” (Job 10:9), and Hamlet’s “When we have shuffled off this mortal coil” (3.1). See The Book of Job and Shakespeare.
  • “united in heavenly mansions”: “In my Father’s house are many mansions” (John 14:2). See The Bible.
  • “by the opium doses, by the needle points”: The hypodermic syringe (Alexander Wood, 1853) brought injected morphine into nineteenth-century medicine and addiction. See The History of Opium.
  • “sleeping car porters with golden roosters on their heads”: Pullman sleeping-car porters were Black men, many of them formerly enslaved, hired by the Pullman Company from 1867 for low wages and long hours, and passengers called every one of them “George.” The Brotherhood of Sleeping Car Porters, led by A. Philip Randolph, was founded in 1925. See Society, Class, and Race.
  • “and headless horsemen”: Washington Irving’s “The Legend of Sleepy Hollow” (1820). See American Writers and Fairy Tales and Folklore.
  • “all horses should come in first”: The Dodo’s verdict on the Caucus-race: “Everybody has won, and all must have prizes” (Alice’s Adventures in Wonderland, 1865). See Alice in Wonderland.
  • “he had lost his life, or he had gained his life through death”: “He that findeth his life shall lose it: and he that loseth his life for my sake shall find it” (Matthew 10:39). See The Bible and Suicide in History and Literature.
  • “a bouquet of winter violets”: Ophelia’s “I would give you some violets, but they withered all when my father died” (Hamlet 4.5). Violets were a flower of faithfulness. See Shakespeare and Roses and Flowers.
  • “turning to dust and ashes”: “For dust thou art, and unto dust shalt thou return” (Genesis 3:19), and the burial service’s “earth to earth, ashes to ashes, dust to dust” (Book of Common Prayer, 1549). See Genesis.
  • “the great crowds of Derby Day”: The Derby at Epsom, run since 1780. William Powell Frith painted its crowds in “The Derby Day” (1858). See Horses and Carriages and Peron Spitzer.
  • “His brother would not have sat up all night with any corpse”: The wake, the old custom of keeping watch over the dead until burial. See Grief, Loss, and Mourning.
  • “held it against him that he did not rescue her, carry her away as Peron might have done”: Catherine is expecting a man to save her, which is the damsel in distress. This is a narrative device in which one or more men must rescue a woman who has been kidnapped or placed in other peril. The “damsel” is often portrayed as beautiful, popular, and of high social status; she is usually depicted as a princess in works with fantasy or fairy tale settings. Kinship, love, lust or a combination of those motivate the male protagonist to initiate the narrative. Critics have linked the helplessness of these women to societal views that women as a group need to be taken care of by men and treated nicely. Throughout the history of the trope, the role of the woman as the victim in need of a male savior has remained constant, but her attackers have changed to suit the tastes and collective fears of the period: “monsters, mad scientists, Nazis, hippies, bikers, aliens…” (Wikipedia) See Fairy Tales and Folklore and Women, Gender, and Marriage.
  • “wandering through the intricate streets of a dark city in perhaps the underworld”: Dis, the walled city of Hell in Dante’s Inferno (cantos 8-9). See Dante.
  • “in order to reach the upper world, one must first travel through the lower world”: Mr. Spitzer’s belief that people need to travel through the lower world to reach the upper world mirrors The Pilgrim’s Progress (1678) and/or Dante’s writings. Purgatory has seven terraces for the seven deadly sins, and there are seven virtues. Hell has nine circles and Heaven has nine spheres: the Moon, Mercury, Venus, Sun, Mars, Jupiter, Saturn, the fixed stars, and the primum mobile. According to Dante the cosmos depends on God, who exists in the Empyrean, an immaterial heaven beyond space and time. The Empyrean is made up of God’s love and light, and is home to angels, the blessed, and the souls of the faithful. Interesting note that the woman with the Siamese cats believes she was the reincarnation of Cleopatra and Dante meets Cleopatra in the circle of Hell called Lust (“Cleopatràs lussurïosa,” Inferno 5.63). Virgil wrote “Facilis descensus Averno,” “the descent to Avernus is easy… but to retrace one’s steps and climb back to the upper air, that is the task, that is the labor” (Aeneid 6.126-129), and Heraclitus, “The way up and the way down are one and the same.” See Dante, Heraclitus and Flux, and Greek Mythology.

chapter-02:
Chapter 2

← Chapter 1 · Home · Chapter 3 →

Content note: Vera’s mother, Catherine Cartwheel, is addicted to opium.

Summary

Vera describes her mother, Catherine. She is an opium addict who has lain in bed for years among jewels and phantoms and treats her hallucinations as more real than the world. The chapter traces how she came to this. There was a brief marriage to Jock Cartwheel, and a love triangle with twin brothers: Catherine loved Peron Spitzer, who did not love her, while his brother Joachim loved Catherine without return. Joachim, Mr. Spitzer, is the family lawyer and visits her bedside every evening. An Egyptian sailor arrives looking for the dead Peron and mistakes Joachim for him, and Catherine gives the sailor elaborate directions through her labyrinthine house. There is also the vanished chauffeur, James, who long ago made off with her automobile and who, in her visions, drives her endlessly toward Alaska. Whenever her canary dies, Mr. Spitzer secretly replaces it. The chapter ends when a canary escapes into a thunderstorm. Catherine calmly accepts that she must now live forever and dismisses its distant twittering as another dream.

Characters present

Catherine Cartwheel · Joachim Spitzer · James the Chauffeur · The Egyptian Sailor · Mr. Res Tacamah · Mr. Chandelier · Vera Cartwheel · Peron Spitzer · Madge Capehorn · Jock Cartwheel

Concepts present

Themes: Death and Mortality · Illusion and Reality · Isolation and Connection · Madness and Sanity · Memory and the Past · Society, Class, and Race

Symbols: Birds · Clocks and Watches · Eyes and Blindness · Keys, Doors, and Locks · Pearls and Jewels · Pregnancy, Birth, and Children · The House · The Sea and Water · Twins and Doubles

Philosophy: Astrology, Alchemy, and Esoterica · Augustine and Christian Theology · Descartes and Dualism · Empiricism (Locke, Berkeley, Hume) · Epicureanism · Nietzsche · Plato and Platonism · Taoism and Zhuangzi · The Problem of Universals · Time, Physics, and Chaos Theory

Allusions: American Writers · Ancient Egypt · Astronomy · Dante · Edgar Allan Poe · Exploration and the Poles · Fairy Tales and Folklore · Genesis · Greek Mythology · Homer’s Epics · Milton · Revelation and the Apocalypse · Romantic Poets · Shakespeare · The Bible · The History of Opium · Women’s Suffrage

Key passages

From the research

  • The chapter opens with a vivid description of Catherine’s detachment from reality, her retreat into a world of dreams, phantoms, and visions. She sleeps in a stately bed, surrounded by jewels and illusions, her body horizontal and still but her mind endlessly active in a twilight realm where days and nights blur into one. This passage establishes her condition as one suspended between life and death, reality and fantasy, and introduces her as a luminous, ethereal figure whose identity is intertwined with opium dreams and spectral visitors like dead kings, angels, and movie stars. The birthmark she conceals and the shadowed cheek symbolize her hidden imperfections and her withdrawal from the world.
  • This chapter explains the complex, tragic backstory of Catherine’s life, including her failed marriage to Jock Cartwheel, a reckless sportsman who disappeared in the Alps, the social humiliations she endured, and the inheritance that burdened her. It also reveals her denial of her father’s strict domination and orthodox faith, and her agnostic stance despite the angels in her opium paradise. It deepens the understanding of her motivations for retreating into this dreamlike existence and the loss and abandonment she suffered.
  • The relationship between Catherine and Mr. Spitzer, a semi-retired lawyer who visits her faithfully every evening, is a crucial element. He is portrayed as a somewhat hapless, absent-minded man broken by his brother’s death, yet devoted to Catherine. Their interactions mix reality and fantasy, with Catherine often tormenting him with her elusive remarks and suggestions of invisible presences, while he tries to maintain order and reason. This dynamic illustrates the tension between her dream world and his grasp on reality, as well as her complex feelings of resentment and fondness toward him.
  • This chapter emphasizes Catherine’s uncanny knowledge of Mr. Spitzer’s movements and minor details of his life which he himself forgets. It raises the question of whether she is truly alive or already dead, and whether Mr. Spitzer even exists as she perceives him. Her world is one of illusions and ghostly realities, where distinctions between life and death, real and unreal, blur. The servants’ superstitions about her nocturnal wanderings and mysterious occurrences in the house add to the enigmatic aura.
  • A significant episode is the arrival of a gold-turbaned Egyptian sailor who claims to have come looking for Mr. Spitzer’s dead twin brother. Catherine insists on the Egyptian sailor’s reality, giving him detailed instructions to navigate the labyrinthine house, while Mr. Spitzer tries, even by a legal argument, to convince the Egyptian sailor that the man he seeks, Mr. Spitzer’s twin brother Peron, is dead, and that this is a case of mistaken identity. This episode symbolizes the permeable boundary between the worlds of the living and the dead, and Catherine’s role as a mediator or gatekeeper of these overlapping realities.
  • Here Catherine expresses a worldview in which the dream is the only reality worth accepting, because the real world is inevitably disappointing and unrealized. She sees life as a vast deception, and the dreams as protective and expansive, allowing a multiplicity of experiences and visions that transcend strict physical reality. This philosophical stance encapsulates the chapter’s major theme which is the tension between illusion and reality and the necessity of dreams to sustain life.
  • Catherine’s only faithful companion is a little yellow canary, kept in a gilded cage and drugged, Vera supposes, by the poisonous atmosphere of the room itself, perhaps by the opium in the gilded coffee cup where it perches. The bird symbolizes the tenuous thread of life sustaining her, and the careful subterfuge to replace the canary when it dies illustrates the fragile illusions that maintain her dream world and her existence. Mr. Spitzer’s role in maintaining this secret further highlights the delicate balance between reality and fantasy that defines her life.
  • Catherine imagines herself endlessly riding with James, her ex-chauffeur, toward Alaska, a place she never reaches despite years of travel. This endless, repetitive journey through an endless city symbolizes her trapped state between worlds, the impossibility of escape or arrival, and the persistence of memory and illusion. James’s dark intentions and her helplessness add a note of impending danger to this surreal journey.

Questions and observations

Reading closely

  • Catherine “presumed always that things were not what they seemed, that all forms must change their shapes.” How does the chapter itself keep changing shape as it moves from her bed to Mr. Spitzer’s walks, the Egyptian, James, and the canary?
  • The dreams “had begotten her, and she was their creation. She had not created the dreams, for they had created her.” What does it mean for a person to be made by her own dreams?
  • Catherine gives the Egyptian directions through a house where “there were rooms between the rooms, and now the doors had changed their places.” How is the house a map of her mind?
