    • Admiral Robert Peary was an American explorer and US Navy officer who made several expeditions to the Arctic. He claimed to have reached the North Pole in April 1909, a claim still disputed. See Exploration and the Poles.
    • Sir Ernest Shackleton was an Anglo-Irish Antarctic explorer, born in County Kildare in 1874. When his ship Endurance was crushed by the ice in 1915, he led all twenty-eight of his men to safety.
    • Dante Alighieri was an Italian poet who wrote the Divine Comedy. See Dante.
  • “a hurricane blowing off the Canary Islands”: The Canary Islands, off the northwest coast of Africa, were not named for the birds. The Roman writer Pliny the Elder said the name came from the Latin canis, “dog,” for the large dogs found there, and the birds were later named for the islands.

Vocabulary

Abscond
To leave secretly and in a hurry, often to escape the law or to make off with something.
Abstruse
Hard to understand; obscure.
Adagio
In music, a slow, leisurely tempo, or a piece played that way.
Adventitious
Happening by chance; not essential or built in.
Ambivalently
With mixed or contradictory feelings or meanings.
Apparition
A ghost, or a ghostlike image of a person.
Arabesque
An ornament of intertwined flowing lines, leaves, and tendrils.
Athwart
Across, from side to side; also, against.
Attaché case
A slim, hard-sided briefcase.
Augury
A sign or omen of what is to come, or the art of reading such signs.
Auk
A diving seabird of northern seas. The great auk, a large flightless species, became extinct in 1844.
Balloon fish
A pufferfish, which swallows water to swell its body into a spiny ball when threatened.
Bang-tail
Slang for a racehorse, from the custom of cutting a horse’s tail straight across.
Barometer
An instrument that measures air pressure, used to forecast the weather.
Bellrope
A rope pulled to ring a bell, such as one that summons a servant.
Burro
A small donkey.
Camphor

chapter-31:
Chapter 31

← Chapter 30 · Home · Chapter 32 →

Summary

Catherine and Mr. Spitzer admire Cousin Hannah, whose great deeds made their own lives seem unfulfilled. Her secret grief is circled but never named: the mirrors of her house draped in black, her failed battle to rescue Catherine from opium, her indifference to both Spitzer brothers. She sent not one flower to Peron’s grave and ignored Joachim “as if it were he who had died.” Mr. Spitzer remembers his long faithfulness to her, knocking at a door that never opened. He struggles to write her epitaph, drafting and discarding version after version.

Characters present

Joachim Spitzer · Catherine Cartwheel · Cousin Hannah · Peron Spitzer · Vera Cartwheel

Concepts present

Themes: Death and Mortality · Grief, Loss, and Mourning · Illusion and Reality · Love · Memory and the Past · Women, Gender, and Marriage

Symbols: Butterflies and Moths · Dogs · Eyes and Blindness · Moon and Stars · Mountains · The House

Philosophy: Existentialism

Allusions: American Writers · Ecclesiastes · Exploration and the Poles · Fairy Tales and Folklore · Gambling and Playing Cards · Genesis · Judaism · Shakespeare · The Bible · The Book of Job · Women’s Suffrage

Key passages

From the research

  • Mr. Spitzer indulges Catherine’s moods as long as they are not of reality, believing reality would kill her as it had killed her canary, which she imagined flying over the waves. This suggests a delicate balance between fantasy and harsh reality in her life.
  • Their mutual admiration for Peron (who gambled his life away) and Cousin Hannah, an adventurer whose own life made their adventures seem unfulfilled, hints at the complex relationships and ideals binding these characters.
  • Cousin Hannah is described as direct, fierce, and adventurously restless, having fought losing battles with shadows and enduring harsh physical and emotional challenges, including suffrage campaigns and desert treks. She embodies “forlorn romance” and is portrayed as a great captain metaphorically armored by suffrage and armed with swords of ice and fire.
  • Her refusal to marry and the whispered secret of her life shadowed by grief add mystery and depth to her character. Her life is marked by dramatic adventures and a stoic endurance of suffering.
  • Despite her strength and battles, she could not “rescue herself,” and her death is framed as a “domestic war,” contrasting with the grand battles she fought. This passage suggests a tragic dimension to her life and death.
  • She sought to “carry” Vera’s mother away from opium dreams, fighting her losing battle with shadows, showing her as a protective but ultimately tragic figure.
  • She ignored Joachim, the lawyer, after Peron’s death, refusing any recognition or mourning, which underscores her complex relations and possibly her disdain for what she considered weak or insubstantial men. Also Mr. Spitzer may not be who he seems to be.
  • Mr. Spitzer’s persistent but unanswered visits to Cousin Hannah’s empty house symbolize a futile effort to maintain connection and control over the past. His rituals of knocking, leaving calling cards, and bringing important papers contrast with the silence and absence inside, emphasizing themes of loss and the elusiveness of presence.
  • Cousin Hannah’s adventures in deserts and mountains serve as metaphors for her restless spirit and unattainable quests, with imagery of desert storms, Islamic kingdoms, and un-climbable alpine peaks creating a mythical aura around her.
  • The desert beauty’s mirror she brought is a symbol of the transience of human life, reinforcing the chapter’s meditation on mortality.
  • Mr. Spitzer’s efforts to compose an epitaph for Cousin Hannah, his hesitation and inability to decide on words reflect his sorrow and the difficulty of capturing a complex life and character in simple terms. His proposed epitaphs evoke her warrior spirit, her suffering, and her ultimate solitude and death at home rather than on a battlefield.
  • The meditation on death and memory adds philosophical depth to the narrative.
  • His own uncertain status between life and death, as suggested by bureaucratic errors listing him dead, parallels the ambiguous boundary between presence and absence that permeates this chapter.
  • Cousin Hannah’s scorn for Vera’s mother’s love for a “shadow,” a fleeting and unsubstantial man, contrasts with Catherine’s belief that death is necessary to her love. This conflict highlights different understandings of love, reality, and illusion.
  • Cousin Hannah’s rejection of the external man and her suspicion of phantoms as rivals underscore the chapter’s theme of the elusive and often illusory nature of relationships and human connections.
  • The repeated imagery of knocking on doors, peering through keyholes, and the sensation of being watched by hidden eyes evokes a haunting atmosphere, symbolizing the barriers between people, the mysteries of identity, and the unseen presences that linger in memory and imagination.

Questions and observations

Reading closely

  • Mr. Spitzer indulges Catherine’s moods “so long as they were not of reality.” Why would reality kill her?
  • Why does Mr. Spitzer knock only when “he knew she was absent”?
  • “Here lies one who… could not rescue herself.” Which of his epitaphs is truest?

Characters

  • Cousin Hannah judged both brothers: “It was Hobson’s choice… a choice between death and death.” Do you agree?
  • Catherine asks “when had she ever seen a man on earth?” What does she love instead?
  • Mr. Spitzer chooses “the charity of his inaccuracy,” a headstone with no dates. Why?

Connections

  • The canary “she thought was flying over the waves” first appeared in Chapter 2. What else in this house dies without Catherine knowing?
  • A clerk listed Mr. Spitzer “among the dead” in Chapter 25, and here it happens again. What does the record know that he doesn’t?
  • Cousin Hannah’s secret grief is “a body covered by the snow.” How does it mirror Catherine’s lost husband in the Alps (Chapter 30)?

Reflection

  • Is “each one who lives… shrunken by another’s death”?
  • Can you mourn someone who ignored you?
  • What would your epitaph leave out?

Research: Characters

Mr. Spitzer

  • A legal figure who serves as a connection between the living and the dead.
  • Indulges Catherine’s moods but is deeply affected by the passing of Cousin Hannah.
  • Exhibits profound grief, ritualistically visiting Cousin Hannah’s empty house and attempting to maintain legal and emotional ties.
  • His character embodies persistence, melancholy, and a struggle to reconcile presence and absence.
  • While Cousin Hannah was alive but away on her travels, Mr. Spitzer visited her empty mansion, knocking at the door and slipping his calling card through the slot “so that she would know that he had come during her absence.”
  • His visits symbolize the persistence of memory and the difficulty of accepting loss.
  • He contemplates an epitaph and memorial for Hannah, reflecting on her life as a warrior and adventurer.
  • He was “the only mourner” at her grave, “for the simple reason that most people thought she had died years before she had died.”

Catherine Cartwheel

  • A dreamer, living between reality and opium dreams.
  • Holds a love for a “shadow,” a dead or unreal man, rather than a concrete person.
  • Her relationship with reality is tenuous; she is entwined with mystical and illusory elements.
  • She and Mr. Spitzer share mutual admiration for Cousin Hannah and Peron.
  • Catherine’s love is for an elusive, intangible presence rather than a real man.
  • The metaphor of man as a shadow driven by the wind highlights themes of impermanence and spiritual longing.

Cousin Hannah

  • A formidable, adventurous woman, a “great captain” with a suffrage warrior’s spirit.
  • Known for her directness, fiery temper, and refusal to accept illusions or evasion.
  • Lived a nomadic life filled with symbolic and literal journeys across deserts, mountains, and forbidden cities.
  • She opposed Catherine’s love for the shadow, believing in facing harsh realities.
  • After death, she remains a spectral presence, her memory both revered and shrouded in secrecy.
  • Despite her public life and campaigns, she kept a secret of sorrow, which others hesitate to speak of.
  • Cousin Hannah disapproves of Catherine’s dreams and love for the “shadow.” Their conflict is ideological: directness and confrontation versus evasion and mystical longing.
  • She is portrayed as a mythic figure battling external foes and internal demons.
  • Her life and death symbolize the struggle between illusion and reality, love and loss.
  • The chapter describes her as a figure who fought battles greater than those recorded, with imagery of deserts, storms, and crusades.
  • She sent not one flower to Peron’s grave, neither a horseshoe of roses nor “two dice cubes in a lucky throw,” and ignored Joachim “as if it were he who had died.”
  • She called both brothers “equally insecure, as unsubstantial as flame and water.”

Research: Themes

Reality versus Illusion

See: Illusion and Reality

  • The novel contrasts characters’ perceptions of reality with their dreams, delusions, or mystical experiences.

Death and Immortality

See: Death and Mortality

  • The chapter explores how death affects memory, love, and legacy, particularly through Cousin Hannah and Vera’s mother.

Love and Shadows

See: Love

  • Catherine’s love is portrayed as a love for a shadow, a phantom rather than a living man.

Memory and Legacy

See: Memory and the Past

  • Mr. Spitzer’s grief and his attempts to memorialize Cousin Hannah illustrate struggles with remembering and forgetting.
  • “She had said that my mother was in love with no man on earth but with a fleeting shadow…” Emphasizes the theme of elusive love and the tension between reality and illusion.

Research: Symbols and Imagery

The Empty Mansion

See: The House

  • The empty house, the broken lanterns, the snow-covered garden, and the silent rooms evoke a ghostly atmosphere of abandonment and mourning.
  • The Empty Mansion represents absence, memory, and the passage of time. The desolation and decay of the mansion mirror Cousin Hannah’s death and the fading of her presence.

The Desert and the Alps

See: Mountains · Exploration and the Poles

  • The Desert and the Alps symbolize harsh trials, isolation, and spiritual quests. Cousin Hannah’s travels through these landscapes symbolize her restless spirit and adventurous life.

Eyes and the Keyhole

See: Eyes and Blindness

  • “…he would be overwhelmed by the increasing certainty that there was another great, rounded eye staring at him…” The imagery of eyes symbolizes observation, mystery, and the interplay between seen and unseen forces.

Flame and Water

See: Illusion and Reality

  • “…the flame evaporates the water. The water extinguishes the flame.” Symbolizes the mutual destruction or futility of opposing forces, reflecting on the men in Catherine’s life.

The Butterfly Card

See: Butterflies and Moths

  • The “great eye” of the planet, the “butterfly” symbol of resurrection, and references to historical and exotic locations enhance the dreamlike and timeless atmosphere.

Storms, Deserts, Snow, and Stars

See: Moon and Stars

  • Storms, deserts, snow, castles, veils, horses, swords, and stars.
  • These images underscore the mystical, elusive, and epic qualities of the characters’ inner lives.

The Great Water Eye

See: Moon and Stars

  • The “Great Water Eye” of the planet is a recurring symbolic image that links the characters’ personal dramas to the vastness of the universe.

Research: Resources

  • “as it had killed her canary which she thought was flying over the waves”: In Chapter 2 the canary “had died already many times without her knowledge.” Here she still thinks it is “flying over the waves.” See the Chapter 2 resources.
  • “her journeys into forbidden Mecca or Medinah or Fez”: Mecca and Medina are forbidden to non-Muslims. Richard Burton entered both in disguise in 1853.
    • Mecca is Islam’s holiest city in Saudi Arabia.
    • Medinah is the second holiest city in Islam.
    • Fez is an important city in Morocco.
  • “cutting like a two-edged sword”: “Sharper than any twoedged sword” (Hebrews 4:12). See The Bible.
  • “plucked up into the bosom of Abraham”: “The beggar died, and was carried by the angels into Abraham’s bosom” (Luke 16:22). See The Bible.
  • “saying that it should reveal the transience of human life”: The transience of human life is a philosophical concept emphasizing the impermanence and fleeting nature of existence, encourages mindfulness, acceptance of change, and a deeper appreciation for the present moment. In Buddhism, impermanence (anicca) is one of the three marks of existence.
  • “bearded human lions in their dens”: Daniel in the lions’ den (Daniel 6), and Scott’s “to beard the lion in his den” (Marmion, 1808). See The Bible.
  • “in love with no man on earth but with a fleeting shadow, the mere shadow of a man”: Shadows in scripture and Shakespeare. See The Bible, Ecclesiastes, The Book of Job, Shakespeare, and Love.
    • “Man is like to vanity: his days are as a shadow that passeth away” (Psalm 144:4).
    • Ecclesiastes 6:12 speaks of “all the days of his vain life which he spendeth as a shadow.”
    • “He cometh forth like a flower, and is cut down: he fleeth also as a shadow, and continueth not” (Job 14:2).
    • “For the law having a shadow of good things to come, and not the very image of the things” (Hebrews 10:1).
    • “Which are a shadow of things to come; but the body is of Christ” (Colossians 2:17).
    • “Life’s but a walking shadow” is a line from William Shakespeare’s Macbeth (5.5).
  • “girding her loins with suffrage like that iron girdle worn by a great Crusader’s wife”: “Gird up now thy loins like a man” (Job 38:3). The chastity belt of Crusaders’ wives is largely a legend of later centuries. See The Book of Job and Women’s Suffrage.
  • “not one horseshoe of the red and white roses… two dice cubes in a lucky throw, seven and eleven”: Floral horseshoes and dice were set on gamblers’ graves. Seven and eleven are winning throws in craps. See Gambling and Playing Cards and Peron Spitzer.
  • “each one who lives is shrunken by another’s death”: “Any man’s death diminishes me, because I am involved in mankind” (John Donne, Devotions upon Emergent Occasions, Meditation 17, 1624).
  • “forbidden cities of brides, those who were held in thralldom by a cruel bridegroom”: It recalls Perrault’s “Bluebeard” (1697), whose dead brides hang in the forbidden room. See Fairy Tales and Folklore.
  • “those who would never be awakened by the kiss of any living man or love”: The Sleeping Beauty of Chapter 29. See the Chapter 29 resources.
  • “the old St. Bernard”: The monks of the Great St. Bernard Hospice bred their dogs to find travelers lost in Alpine snow. Barry (1800-1814) is said to have saved forty lives. The brandy cask was the invention of the painter Edwin Landseer (1820). See Dogs.
  • “the latticed shutters in those mysterious Oriental cities where the secret women look out”: The mashrabiya, a carved wooden lattice that lets women see without being seen.
  • “Or he might imagine that his veiled wife was beautiful”: Veiling and wearing a veil of clothing or hanging cloth has a long history in many societies across the world. It is intended to cover some part of the head or face, or an object of some significance. The practice has been prominent in different forms in Judaism, Christianity, and Islam. The practice of veiling is especially associated with women and sacred objects, though in some cultures, it is men, rather than women, who are expected to wear a veil. Besides its enduring religious significance, veiling continues to play a role in some modern secular contexts, such as wedding customs. One view is that as a religious item, it is intended to honor a person, object or space. The actual sociocultural, psychological, and sociosexual functions of veils have not been studied extensively but most likely include the maintenance of social distance and the communication of social status and cultural identity. A veil also has symbolic interpretations, as something partially concealing, disguising, or obscuring. (Wikipedia) In Young’s sentence the veil may conceal “the visage of the naked skull.”
  • “draped by veils of black chiffon in memory of some earlier death”: Mirrors were covered in houses of mourning, in Victorian custom and in the Jewish shiva. See Grief, Loss, and Mourning and Judaism.
  • “for what were earthly riches, great castles and lonely towers”: Luke 12:16-21, the Parable of the Rich Fool, shows how wealth can be a distraction from the true purpose of life. “Thou fool, this night thy soul shall be required of thee: then whose shall those things be, which thou hast provided?” (Luke 12:20). Mr. Spitzer’s reflections echo the parable’s warning against greed and misplaced security. See The Bible.
  • “Often he had seen the lunar rainbow”: A Lunar rainbow or Moonbow is a rainbow produced by moonlight rather than direct sunlight. See the Chapter 29 resources.
  • “his calling card embossed with the butterfly which was his sign of resurrection”: Mr. Spitzer’s calling card. See Butterflies and Moths and the Chapter 26 resources.
  • “the old State Street Bank and Trust”: Boston’s State Street Bank, founded in 1792 as the Union Bank.
  • “Here lies that great Crusader who rode against the Saracens”: Mr. Spitzer’s epitaphs put Cousin Hannah on both sides of the Crusades: she rode against the Saracens, and “She has gone over to the Islamites.” Women did fight and rule on both sides.
    • Women played significant roles in the Crusades, either by leading armies, influencing political decisions, or promoting the cause: Eleanor of Aquitaine, Matilda of Tuscany, Melisende, Queen of Jerusalem, Margaret of Provence, Queen consort of France, Sibyl, Queen of Jerusalem, and Margaret of Beverly, who fought in the defense of Jerusalem against Saladin (1187). Ida of Austria led her own army in the Crusade of 1101, and the legendary Florine of Burgundy was said to have died fighting beside Sweyn of Denmark in 1097.
    • Women resisted during the Crusades: Shajar al-Durr, who ruled Egypt and organized its defense against the Seventh Crusade (1249-50), Anna Comnena, and the women of the Baltic Crusades. Ismat ad-Din Khatun, regent of Damascus, negotiated the end of the Crusader siege of Banias in 1174, and William of Tyre credited her with “courage beyond that of most women” (A History of Deeds Done Beyond the Sea, 20.31). At Shaizar, in Syria, when Assassins stormed the citadel in 1114, during the Crusade years though not by Crusaders, Usama ibn Munqidh’s mother armed the women, and an old servant, Funun, “covered herself with her veil, took up a sword and went into battle” (Usama ibn Munqidh, The Book of Contemplation, trans. Paul M. Cobb, 2008). Khawla bint al-Azwar, the most famous Arab woman warrior, fought the Byzantines at Yarmouk (636), five centuries before the Crusades.
  • “She raided the Etruscan towns”: Etruscan towns were a collection of independent city-states in central Italy, united by a shared culture and language. They thrived in the regions of Tuscany, Umbria, and Northern Lazio between the 7th and 2nd centuries BC. Important Etruscan cities include Tarquinia, Vulci, Populonia, Cerveteri, Volterra, and Chiusi. Many of these cities still have archaeological sites, necropolises, and museums that showcase their Etruscan heritage. (Wikipedia)
  • “Here lies one who searched all her life for her dead love, a body covered by the snow”: Young told Studs Terkel that Cousin Hannah came partly from an Alpine story in which two bloomer girls shed their skirts at a summit, and the younger, going back for hers, was lost: “the lady lost her life for a skirt.” She also drew on Margaret Fuller, who drowned off Fire Island in 1850 within reach of a sandbar (Marguerite Young, interview with Studs Terkel, WFMT radio, 1965). See the Chapter 30 resources. See Cousin Hannah and Women’s Suffrage.
  • “Here lies one who shared our common lot of mortal frailty”: Heidegger’s “being-towards-death,” from Being and Time (1927), is a fundamental aspect of human existence, highlighting the finite nature of our being and the importance of confronting mortality to live authentically. Heidegger distinguishes between authentic and inauthentic ways of living: authentic living confronts the inevitability of death and makes choices that are meaningful to oneself, while inauthentic living is swept along by what “they” say and do (das Man). Mr. Spitzer’s epitaph names the common condition Heidegger describes: one who “shared our common lot of mortal frailty.” See Existentialism.
  • “She was not fallen in a foreign field”: “If I should die, think only this of me: / That there’s some corner of a foreign field / That is for ever England” (Rupert Brooke, “The Soldier,” 1914).
  • “She has gone over to the Islamites”: In the Islamic tradition burial is a sacred practice. Cremation is strictly forbidden. The body is buried as soon as possible after death, ideally within 24 hours, in a simple shroud, facing Mecca and without a coffin. There are no elaborate markers; simple flat markers are used instead. There is a ritual washing and prayer, and mourners each place three handfuls of soil. Post-mortem examinations are avoided. The general mourning period is three days; a widow mourns four months and ten days (Qur’an 2:234), and many Muslim communities also mark the fortieth day. (Wikipedia)
  • “The rose of Sharon is growing in a desert place”: “I am the rose of Sharon” (Song of Solomon 2:1), and “the desert shall… blossom as the rose” (Isaiah 35:1). See The Bible and the Chapter 28 resources.
  • “Death snatched away her beautiful bride”: Young’s other source for Cousin Hannah was a story told by Charles Studin, a founder of the NAACP, about a suffragist “battle-axe” who fought men all her life, “one of the original bloomer girls,” yet for forty years brought home sealed trunks that proved at her death to hold “a complete bridal trousseau” each. “She had a dream too” (Marguerite Young, interview with Studs Terkel, WFMT radio, 1965). In another telling the lawyer found “fifty wedding gowns,” and Young added that she “had read the histories of mountain climbers, of suffragette captains, of travelers to the Middle East” (Ellen G. Friedman and Miriam Fuchs, “A Conversation with Marguerite Young,” Review of Contemporary Fiction 23, no. 1, Spring 2003 (1989 original)). See Cousin Hannah and Women, Gender, and Marriage.
  • “he had listed Mr. Spitzer’s name among the dead”: The clerk of Chapter 25. See the Chapter 25 resources.
  • “for Joachim, though he pretended to be so true, was weak as water”: “Unstable as water, thou shalt not excel” (Genesis 49:4). See Genesis.
  • “It was six of one and half a dozen of the other”: The phrase is in print in Captain Marryat’s The Pirate (1836).
  • “It was Hobson’s choice”: Hobson’s choice is a free choice in which only one thing is actually offered and is used to mean an illusion of choice. Thomas Hobson (d. 1631), a Cambridge stable keeper, made each customer take the horse nearest the door.
  • “worth a candle’s flame in the headlong wind”: From the French proverb le jeu ne vaut pas la chandelle, “the game is not worth the candle,” from card players who paid for the candles they played by. See Gambling and Playing Cards.
  • “her search for the external man”: “Though our outward man perish, yet the inward man is renewed day by day” (2 Corinthians 4:16). See The Bible.
    • Internalism and externalism are two opposite ways of integration of explaining various subjects in several areas of philosophy. These include human motivation, knowledge, justification, meaning, and truth. The distinction arises in many areas of debate with similar but distinct meanings. Internalism is the thesis that no fact about the world can provide reasons for action independently of desires and beliefs. Externalism is the thesis that reasons are to be identified with objective features of the world. (Wikipedia)
  • “The external man, there was no doubt, had been Cousin Hannah’s foe”: Cousin Hannah had scoffed at Catherine’s “search for the external man,” asking “was it flesh which made the man,” his weight, his measure, his girth. Against the outward man stands the inward one (2 Corinthians 4:16).
  • “to the sound of muffled drums”: “Our hearts, though stout and brave, / Still, like muffled drums, are beating / Funeral marches to the grave” (Longfellow, “A Psalm of Life,” 1838). See American Writers.

Chapter 38

← Chapter 37 · Home · Chapter 39 →

Content note: Vera’s mother, Catherine Cartwheel, is addicted to opium.

Summary

Catherine’s memories of Cousin Hannah are clouded by opium and by her dream of an immortal love, and Mr. Spitzer, being as one dead, must be prodded to remember anything at all. Catherine thought the lonely cause of suffrage unworthy of Hannah’s adventurous spirit and a waste of time. She would have been happy, she insists, if only Peron had lived, and she explains his neglect as a love too great to express: “This dead love which never was and never would be real was the one undying love.” Hannah had invited her to Egypt to show that a woman could be both beautiful and independent of man, and Catherine imagines the life she might have had, picketing Buckingham Palace, sleeping in silken tents, escaping from moated castles. She remembers Hannah’s sharp, masculine virtues with envy and guilt, wonders whom Hannah had loved, and is sorry that Hannah was not a knight or a Prince Charming come to wake her. Mr. Spitzer observes that most people are disoriented as to time, place, and person, and Vera calls the house what it has become, “this loony bin.”

Characters present

Cousin Hannah · Catherine Cartwheel · Joachim Spitzer · Vera Cartwheel · Peron Spitzer

Concepts present

Themes: Death and Mortality · Dreams and Imagination · Grief, Loss, and Mourning · Illusion and Reality · Love · Madness and Sanity · Memory and the Past

Symbols: Angels, Devils, and Myth · Clouds and Storms · Keys, Doors, and Locks · Moon and Stars · Mountains · Music and Instruments · Pearls and Jewels · Snow, Ice, and Winter

Philosophy: Aristotle · Astrology, Alchemy, and Esoterica · Augustine and Christian Theology · Heraclitus and Flux · Hinduism · Plato and Platonism · Pythagoras and the Music of the Spheres · Schopenhauer · Spiritualism and the Occult · Taoism and Zhuangzi

Allusions: Alice in Wonderland · Astronomy · Dante · Fairy Tales and Folklore · Genesis · Greek Mythology · Homer’s Epics · Judaism · Music and Composers · Revelation and the Apocalypse · Romantic Poets · Shakespeare · The Bible · The History of Opium · Women’s Suffrage

Key passages

From the research

  • The chapter opens by portraying Cousin Hannah as a formidable, almost mythic figure who never reconciled with life and whose identity remains blurred in memory. This passage sets the tone for the chapter’s exploration of memory, identity, and legacy. It emphasizes Hannah’s singularity and the elusive nature of her life and spirit, framing her as a person who lived on the outermost edges of experience.
  • Catherine is described as indefinite, clouded by dreams of immortal love and escape, living in a world of opium-induced fantasies and unawakened romance, in contrast to Cousin Hannah’s stark reality and fiery spirit. This contrast highlights two modes of existence: one engaged with harsh realities and causes (Hannah), and the other retreating into beautiful but unreal dreams (Catherine).
  • The chapter repeatedly emphasizes Cousin Hannah’s adventurous spirit and her sacrifices for the suffrage movement, portraying these efforts as both heroic and, from Catherine’s perspective, somewhat futile or unworthy of Hannah’s potential. This passage reveals Catherine’s ambivalence (envy mixed with guilt) as she reflects on Hannah’s committed activism versus her own life of dreams and withdrawal.
  • Catherine’s reflections on love are poignant and laden with sorrow. She imagines a love greater than any realized affection, a “dead love which never was and never would be real,” expressed in silence and absence rather than presence. She interprets Peron’s neglect as a form of love out of fear of her power, suggesting a profound but unspoken emotional tension. This theme of unattainable love permeates the chapter.
  • There are vivid passages describing Catherine’s dreams of travel and escape to exotic places (Egypt, Italy, the land of the Kurds) and her missed opportunities for a different life. These passages symbolize longing, regret, and the tension between the dream of freedom and the reality of confinement, both physical and psychological.
  • Catherine’s mind is portrayed as wandering and unreliable, filled with illusions and shifting memories. The narrative suggests that her dreams, though inaccurate, might hold a deeper truth than conventional reality. This raises philosophical questions about the nature of truth, memory, and perception.
  • Cousin Hannah is depicted as “sharp-witted, dashing and wild and reckless,” a figure of masculine virtues and relentless energy, “like a finely tempered blade” who never stopped despite adversity. This passage celebrates her fortitude and contrasts it with Catherine’s frailty and passivity.
  • The chapter discusses mysterious, mystical elements: the whisperings of the dead, the music of the spheres, and spectral visions, suggesting a world where life and death intermingle and where memory and existence are fluid. Cousin Hannah’s belief that the dead are silent and that her battles were with the living underscores the existential tension between life’s visible struggles and the ineffable beyond.
  • Despite her admiration for Cousin Hannah’s strength and purpose, Catherine is disappointed that Hannah is not the romantic hero she imagined, a knight or prince who could awaken her from her dreams. This passage reflects Catherine’s deep yearning for connection and meaning, mingled with a sense of loss.
  • The chapter closes with reflections on the instability of time and identity, suggesting that even the most certain facts of time, place, person may be illusions or dreams. Mr. Spitzer’s observations about disorientation and the blurring of reality and illusion reinforce the chapter’s overarching meditation on perception.

Questions and observations

Reading closely

  • Catherine believes “this dead love which never was and never would be real was the one undying love.” Why would an unreal love outlast a real one?
  • “Whichever one had lived, she would have missed the absent one.” What does Catherine need absence for?
  • “Perhaps it was that great captain who was weak, my mother who was strong.” Could Vera be right?

Characters

  • Hannah invited Catherine to Egypt to show “that one could be both beautiful and independent of man.” Why does Catherine refuse?
  • Hannah “had wept if she heard a skirt whirling, rustling in the wind.” What is she mourning?
  • Mr. Spitzer must be “prodded and forced to remember.” What does he gain by forgetting?

Connections

  • In Chapter 34 Hannah wore “iron keys” at her belt. Here she rattles them while “fighting a mirror with her jeweled sword.” What is she fighting?
  • Catherine wished Hannah were “the Prince Charming to awaken this Sleeping Beauty.” Who else in the novel waits to be awakened?
  • Mr. Spitzer asks whether he is “a man or a butterfly.” How does this echo the dreamer of Chapter 37?

Reflection

  • Is action “no necessary criterion or measure of life”?
  • Can a life lived for a cause be lived “in only one dimension”?
  • Who in the story is the sane one in “this loony bin”?

Research: Characters

Cousin Hannah

  • Described as a “great captain of extremes,” a resolute and brave suffragette who sacrificed much for her cause.
  • Adventurous and daring, having traveled “to the outermost reaches of space,” symbolizing exploration beyond physical and societal boundaries.
  • Exhibits masculine virtues: sharp, shrewd, incisive, relentless and compared to a “finely tempered blade.”
  • Seen as singularly devoted to her cause, seemingly indifferent to love or personal attachments.
  • Her presence is associated with powerful imagery: whistling sounds, iron keys, jeweled swords, and snow storms.
  • A figure of mystery and paradox; she weeps for subtle reasons (e.g., a snowflake touching her hand), showing a hidden emotional depth.
  • Her life is characterized by perpetual motion and battle, never fully reconciled with peace or rest.
  • Represents strength, fortitude, and the harsh realities of activism and sacrifice.
  • Catherine remembers her greeting, “Babylon is fallen,” but Vera says “it was not to be believed”: her mother “undoubtedly misunderstood as to time, place, person.”
  • She invited Catherine to Egypt “to show… that one could join her movement for reasons other than being ugly and old, that one could be both beautiful and independent of man.”
  • “She had burned like a live coal. Snow buried many cities but did not bury her.”
  • She wept “if she heard a skirt whirling, rustling in the wind.”

Catherine Cartwheel (Vera’s mother)

  • Portrayed as dreamy, opium-addicted, lost in illusions and fantasies of an “immortal love” and lost romances.
  • She envies Cousin Hannah’s adventures but remains passive, bound to memories and dreams rather than action.
  • Her mind is clouded, veiled by dreams that are as much about escape as about longing.
  • She imagines herself as a great courtesan with many imaginary lovers, embodying a spectral beauty trapped in time.
  • Her love life is described as unfulfilled, marked by silence and absence, especially with Peron.
  • She greeted Hannah, “Hello, traveller! And where do you come from now?”
  • “Oh, how happy, happy, happy my mother would have been… if only the great gambler had lived.”
  • She dreamed “she had found a stairway to heaven,” by which she could “over-hear the decrees and whisperings of the dead.”
  • Her eyes were “blurred, cobwebbed by her predisposed illusions, by nightshade and bella donna.”
  • She distorts reality, unable to fully grasp or engage with the present moment.
  • She has a sense of guilt about her withdrawal and dreams, contrasted with Cousin Hannah’s active life.
  • Her life is marked by isolation and a yearning for an “unearthly romance” free from mortal change.
  • Represents passivity, longing, and the desire for transcendence.

Mr. Spitzer

  • His mind is clouded and dwells on abstract, cosmic music and metaphysical concepts.
  • Symbolizes a detached intellectual or mystical observer, contrasting with the passionate activism of Cousin Hannah and the dreamy passivity of Catherine.
  • His perspective reflects on the limitations of human understanding and the ineffability of life’s mysteries.
  • “Being as one dead,” he “must be prodded and forced to remember.”
  • He is “writing now his nocturne in memory of her.”
  • Most people, he observes, “were at some level disoriented, unaware of the existing situation with reference to such apparently clear matters as time, place, identity of persons.”

Peron Spitzer

  • He was “this man of great wit but little brain—no legal knowledge in his head, no intellectual pretensions whatever.”
  • Catherine believes “he had expressed his love by his silence, his distance.”
  • “Sometimes she thought that only he lived.”

Research: Themes

Memory and Reality

See: Illusion and Reality · Memory and the Past

  • The chapter blurs the lines between memory, dream, and reality.
  • Catherine’s recollections are described as “inaccurate,” “clouded,” and “untrustworthy,” reflecting the elusive nature of truth.
  • The narrative questions the reliability of memory and whether dreams may contain a deeper accuracy than factual truth.
  • Time is fluid, with events and identities slipping and merging, e.g., Catherine confusing visitors or historical periods.

Love and Absence

See: Love · Grief, Loss, and Mourning

  • Love is portrayed as an unfulfilled, silent, and distant force.
  • Catherine loves an absent, dead man whose love, she believes, was expressed through silence and neglect rather than conventional gestures.
  • Peron’s love is described as “his love greater than his hatred” but unexpressed, a “dead love which never was and never would be real,” paradoxically eternal.
  • Cousin Hannah is described as never having loved, or only loving the “image of the dead,” though she weeps at a snowflake or a rustling skirt.

Sacrifice and Activism

See: Women’s Suffrage

  • Cousin Hannah embodies sacrifice for a cause, dedicating her life to suffrage and battling societal “ogres.”
  • Her life is one of relentless struggle and fortitude, marked by physical and emotional trials.
  • Catherine contrasts this with her own withdrawal and guilt for not engaging in such struggles.

Escapism and Fantasy

See: Illusion and Reality · Dreams and Imagination

  • Catherine lives largely in fantasy, opium dreams, and romanticized illusions.
  • Catherine imagines exotic travels, lost loves, and mystical experiences that contrast sharply with her sedentary reality.
  • Cousin Hannah’s life, though real and harsh, also contains elements of myth and legend, as perceived by Catherine.

Death and Immortality

See: Death and Mortality

  • Death is omnipresent but paradoxically intertwined with immortality in the narrative.
  • Catherine and Cousin Hannah seem caught between life and death, reality and dream.
  • The chapter references the “perennial dead” and the idea that death does not end mystery or existence.
  • The dead’s silence contrasts with the living’s whisperings, with Cousin Hannah focusing on the living and Catherine on the dead.

Research: Symbols and Imagery

Whistling Sound and Snow

See: Snow, Ice, and Winter

  • Cousin Hannah’s entrances marked by whistling and snowstorms symbolize her power and otherworldly nature.

Iron Keys and Jeweled Sword

See: Pearls and Jewels · Keys, Doors, and Locks

  • Represent authority, battle, and mystery. Hannah walked back and forth, “rattling great iron keys, striking against a stone wall, striking against the empty air, or fighting a mirror with her jeweled sword.”

Clouds, Whirlwinds, and Stars

See: Moon and Stars · Clouds and Storms

  • Reflect the fluidity of time, memory, and identity; also Catherine’s dreamlike mental state.

Frozen Beauty and Marble

See: Snow, Ice, and Winter

  • Catherine is “this beautiful and unawakened corpse, the cold and frigid beauty of the past,” symbolizing her emotional and physical stasis. Mr. Spitzer prefers “the cold and marble face, the unremembered face of an ideal love.”

Music of the Spheres

See: Moon and Stars · Music and Instruments · Pythagoras and the Music of the Spheres

  • Mr. Spitzer’s cosmic music imagery symbolizes the ineffable and eternal aspects of existence beyond human comprehension.

Centaur and Stone Huntsmen

See: Angels, Devils, and Myth

  • Mythical figures representing the intersection of past and present, reality and dream.

Church Bells and Tolling

See: Music and Instruments

  • Represent time’s passage, memory, and the inescapable presence of death.

Labyrinthine Streets and Changing Signs

See: Madness and Sanity

  • Symbolize confusion about identity and reality.

Research: Resources

  • “the beautiful music of the spheres”: Musica Universalis (music of the spheres) concept incorporates the metaphysical principle that mathematical relationships express qualities or “tones” of energy that manifests in numbers, visual angles, shapes and sounds which are all connected within a pattern of proportion. This has been explored by Pythagoras, Plato, Aristotle (he rejected the idea), Boethius developed three categories of music (musica mundana, musica humana, and musica quae in quibusdam constituta est instrumentis), Kepler expounded the idea in Harmonices Mundi (1619). Boethius’s writings were later illustrated, and Young may have taken inspiration from these illustrations for the novel. See the Character Hubs. See Pythagoras and the Music of the Spheres, Plato and Platonism, and Aristotle.
  • “its sound as of the human will”: Human Will or Free Will is the capacity of humans to make choices and decisions independently of external forces. Philosophy has debated the existence and nature of free will with arguments for and against. Determinism is the opposite of free will. Religions grapple with the concept of free will and attempt to reconcile it with divine sovereignty and predestination. Free will is closely linked with moral responsibility which is used to hold individuals accountable for their actions. Miss MacIntosh’s view of the human will is in the Chapter 3 resources.
    • Schopenhauer made music the direct image of the will: it “is as immediate an objectification and copy of the whole will as the world itself” (Arthur Schopenhauer, The World as Will and Idea 1.52, 1819, trans. R. B. Haldane and J. Kemp, 1883). See Schopenhauer.
    • Augustine defended the freedom of the will against predestination’s critics in On Free Choice of the Will (388-395). See Augustine and Christian Theology.
  • “seven deathless eternities”: “Seven deathless eternities” may recall Dante’s Divine Comedy, where the seven terraces of Purgatory purge the seven deadly sins. Seven heavens are found in Judaism and Islam, and Hindu cosmology has seven upper worlds, the lokas. The seven virtues join the four cardinal virtues of Greek philosophy to the three theological virtues of Paul (1 Corinthians 13:13). See Dante, Judaism, and Hinduism.
  • “the seven-stringed harp”: The seven-stringed harp is the lyre, which the poet Terpander was said to have given seven strings. See Greek Mythology.
    • The seven strings bearing “soul and spirit and astral body” recall Theosophy’s seven principles of man, which include the astral body (H. P. Blavatsky, The Key to Theosophy, 1889). See Spiritualism and the Occult.
  • “polar lights accompanied by strong sounds”: Northern peoples and Arctic travellers have long reported that the aurora crackles, hisses, and whistles, a sound scientists long doubted. See Astronomy.
  • “The lonely cause of suffrage had seemed to my mother to be quite unworthy”: Catherine does not believe in suffrage, and that was common among rich, white women from elite social and political backgrounds at the time. They argued that it would disrupt gender roles and the family structure, doubted women’s political capacity, and opposed broader progressive reforms such as prohibition. Racism drove them too, for they feared the vote would spread to women of color. They argued that it would simply double the size of the electorate without adding any new value or perspective. Opposition also came from business and industry since it may lead to increased regulation and reforms that would hurt their profits. See Women’s Suffrage.
    • The National Association Opposed to Woman Suffrage was founded in 1911 by Josephine Dodge.
  • “Babylon is fallen”: “Babylon the great is fallen, is fallen” (Revelation 18:2). See Revelation and the Apocalypse.
    • “Babylon is fallen, is fallen” (Isaiah 21:9). See The Bible.
  • “an Alpine crystal-hunter who had cut great steps in ice”: Crystal hunters, the Strahler of the Swiss Alps, have climbed for rock crystal since the Middle Ages. See Mountains.
  • “the heavenly bridegroom none should see”: “Behold, the bridegroom cometh; go ye out to meet him” (Matthew 25:6). See the Chapter 33 resources and The Bible.
  • “this great courtesan with a snow pompadour”: The pompadour, hair swept high off the forehead, is named for Madame de Pompadour (1721-1764), mistress of Louis XV.
  • “death’s dateless night”: “For precious friends hid in death’s dateless night” (Shakespeare, Sonnet 30). See Shakespeare.
  • “Yet though there was no time, though all were immortal”: Parmenides and the paradox of motion: Parmenides, an ancient Greek philosopher, argued that change and motion are illusions and that reality is unchanging and indivisible.
  • “the cloud-capped towers”: See the Chapter 35 resources and Shakespeare.
  • “picketed Buckingham Palace”: Buckingham Palace is the monarch’s official London residence and a working royal palace.
    • On May 21, 1914, Emmeline Pankhurst was arrested at the palace gates as suffragettes tried to bring a petition to King George V. See Women’s Suffrage.
  • “the land of the somnolent Kurds”: Kurds or Kurdish people are an Iranian ethnic group native to the mountainous region of Kurdistan.
  • “like the greatest escape artist”: The greatest escape artist was Harry Houdini (1874-1926), who escaped from handcuffs, straitjackets, and his Chinese Water Torture Cell.
  • “lived all her life in Italy”: Italy’s history has influenced the world with its art, architecture, and legal systems: Roman Empire, Catholic Church, Renaissance, Art and Architecture, Culture.
  • “There were jeweled daggers and poisoned cups”: The poisoned cups recall the Borgias, Pope Alexander VI and his son Cesare, whose enemies were said to die of poison.
  • “easeful dreams of a lost romance”: “I have been half in love with easeful Death” (John Keats, “Ode to a Nightingale,” 1819). See Romantic Poets.
  • “a funeral gondola black as a blackbird”: Franz Liszt wrote La lugubre gondola, “the funeral gondola,” in Venice in 1882, and the next year a gondola carried Wagner’s coffin down the Grand Canal. See Music and Composers.
  • “donjons and walls and angle towers”: Donjon is the great tower or innermost keep of a castle.
  • “that great cavalier servente”: In eighteenth-century Italy a cavalier servente, or cicisbeo, was a married woman’s acknowledged escort. Byron describes the custom in Beppo (1818). See Romantic Poets.
  • “all base metals were transmuted by time into finest gold”: The alchemists sought to transmute base metals into gold. See Astrology, Alchemy, and Esoterica.
  • “the aqua fortis of memory”: Aqua fortis is an archaic term for nitric acid.
    • Aqua fortis, “strong water,” dissolves silver but not gold, so assayers used it to part the two. See Astrology, Alchemy, and Esoterica.
  • “Life contained death as a cloud contained a passing star”: Zeno’s paradoxes: the finite can contain the infinite. Aristotle reports Zeno’s argument “that that which is in locomotion must arrive at the half-way stage before it arrives at the goal” (Aristotle, Physics 6.9, trans. R. P. Hardie and R. K. Gaye, 1930). Neil deGrasse Tyson explains that the halves, “even though there’s an infinite number of them,” sum “to a finite answer in a finite amount of time”: “Yes, the finite can contain the infinite, and indeed it does” (Neil deGrasse Tyson with Chuck Nice, “Cosmic Queries – In a Zeptosecond,” StarTalk Radio, September 3, 2024). See Aristotle.
  • “She had wept if she heard a skirt whirling”: Young told Studs Terkel that Cousin Hannah came partly from an Alpine story in which two bloomer girls shed their skirts at a summit, and the younger, going back for hers, was lost: “the lady lost her life for a skirt” (Marguerite Young, interview with Studs Terkel, WFMT radio, 1965). See the Chapter 31 resources. See Cousin Hannah.
  • “never oblique, never obtuse”: Catherine is described as obtuse (“But she was obtuse”), but Cousin Hannah is described as the opposite, acute. These descriptions are called “masculine virtues.” Catherine could not help admiring these traits, though she could not compete with them. The contrast between obtuse and acute highlights the difference between Catherine and Mr. Spitzer’s more passive, bewildered, or dreamlike states on the one hand, and Cousin Hannah’s active, clear-headed, and vigorous character on the other.
  • “a widely netted seine catching only the biggest star or fish”: There have been numerous studies on human memory with conclusions that it is very accurate or very inaccurate. They suggest although people don’t recall a large fraction of what they experience, what they do remember is accurate at least for a few days (Nicholas B. Diamond, Michael J. Armson, and Brian Levine, “The Truth Is Out There: Accuracy in Recall of Verifiable Real-World Events,” Psychological Science 31, no. 12, 2020).
  • “Not even when trains were stopped, buried by snow”: In the Great Blizzard of March 1888, trains were stranded in drifts from New York to New England. See Snow, Ice, and Winter.
  • “her grand idée fixe”: An idée fixe is an obsession. Berlioz gave the name to the melody that haunts his Symphonie fantastique (1830). See Music and Composers.
  • “the rescue of pale ladies held by one-eyed ogres”: See the Polyphemus entry in the Chapter 36 resources. See Homer’s Epics.
  • “Mr. Spitzer writing now his nocturne in memory of her”: The nocturne, a night piece for piano, was invented by John Field in 1812 and perfected by Chopin. See Music and Composers.
  • “she had found a stairway to heaven”: “And he dreamed, and behold a ladder set up on the earth, and the top of it reached to heaven: and behold the angels of God ascending and descending on it” (Genesis 28:12). See Genesis.
  • “Cousin Hannah must have believed that the dead were silent”: “The dead praise not the LORD, neither any that go down into silence” (Psalm 115:17). See The Bible.
  • “being never twice the same”: Heraclitus and the flux: he emphasized the constant state of flux and change in the universe, implying that perpetual motion is also a metaphor for the ever-changing nature of reality. See Heraclitus and Flux.
    • “Heracleitus is supposed to say that all things are in motion and nothing at rest; he compares them to the stream of a river, and says that you cannot go into the same water twice” (Plato, Cratylus 402a, trans. Benjamin Jowett). See Plato and Platonism.
  • “the word perpetual was that which had always frightened my mother”: A perpetual motion machine, one that runs forever without a source of energy, is impossible under the first and second laws of thermodynamics. The earliest known design is the overbalanced wheel of the Indian mathematician Bhāskara II (Siddhānta Shiromani, about 1150); Villard de Honnecourt drew another about 1230. (Wikipedia)
  • “action was no necessary criterion or measure of life”: Those that take action, do things, and are preoccupied with accomplishments are rewarded. The mid-western, Protestant work ethic is set in these standards. The Protestant work ethic is implicitly reflected through the character of Miss MacIntosh and her attitudes toward life, labor, and morality (Max Weber, The Protestant Ethic and the Spirit of Capitalism, 1905). In 2021 young people in China began “lying flat” (Elsie Chen, “These Chinese Millennials Are ‘Chilling,’ and Beijing Isn’t Happy,” New York Times, July 3, 2021). It recalls Diogenes the Cynic, a Greek philosopher, who lived in a large storage jar in Athens, often called a barrel, scorning comfort and convention. Work is considered “a false idol” and people instead rest, exercise, and relax as a form of “resistance.” See Miss MacIntosh.
  • “these irrational, mystical, four-faced doorways”: Janus, the Roman god of doorways, had two faces, and Janus Quadrifrons, the four-faced Janus, had a temple with four doors. See Greek Mythology.
  • “Clovis or Cuthbert or Crispin or Charles the Mad or the Beloved or the Bold”: Clovis I (about 466-511) united the Franks. Saint Cuthbert (died 687) was the monk-bishop of Lindisfarne, and Saint Crispin, patron of shoemakers, gave his name to the day of Agincourt in Henry V. Charles VI of France (1368-1422) was called both the Beloved and the Mad, and Charles the Bold (1433-1477) was the last Valois duke of Burgundy.
    • Clovis was the first king of the Franks to unite all of the Frankish tribes under one ruler.
    • Cuthbert was an Anglo-Saxon saint in the Celtic tradition.
    • Crispin is the patron Saint of cobblers, curriers, tanners, and leather workers.
    • Charles the Mad was king of France. He is known for his mental illness and psychotic episodes. He was also called Charles the Beloved. He at times believed that he was made of glass.
    • Charles the Bold was the Duke of Burgundy.
  • “sans peur et sans reproche”: Sans peur et sans reproche means without fear and beyond reproach.
    • The phrase was the epithet of Pierre Terrail, seigneur de Bayard (1476-1524), “le chevalier sans peur et sans reproche.”
  • “a French chevalier who had travelled great distances”: French chevalier is a French title originally equivalent to the English knight.
  • “a Red Cross knight”: Catherine is sorry that Hannah “was not a French chevalier… or a Red Cross knight.” The Redcrosse Knight of Edmund Spenser’s The Faerie Queene (1590) stands for holiness. With Una he slays the dragon that has imprisoned her parents.
  • “Richard Coeur de Leon”: Richard Coeur de Leon, Richard the Lionheart, was King of England. He had the reputation for being a great military leader and warrior.
  • “the early French kings carrying their oriflammes”: The oriflamme was the battle standard of the kings of France in the Middle Ages, kept at the abbey of Saint-Denis.
  • “some old Rinaldo riding”: Rinaldo is a legendary knight in medieval France.
    • He is Renaud de Montauban, a paladin of Charlemagne, and the Rinaldo of Boiardo’s Orlando Innamorato (1483) and Ariosto’s Orlando Furioso (1516).
  • “his bayard, his wonderful bay steed”: Bayard is a magic bay horse ridden by Rinaldo. It had the magic ability to adjust its size to fit the rider.
    • It could stretch to carry all four sons of Aymon at once.
  • “the Prince Charming to awaken this Sleeping Beauty”: In Perrault’s “Sleeping Beauty” (1697) the whole household sleeps for a hundred years with the princess, until the prince comes. See Fairy Tales and Folklore.
  • “the life-sized chessmen”: In Through the Looking-Glass (1871) Alice finds the chessmen alive and walks into a life-sized game of chess. See Alice in Wonderland.
  • “whether he was a man or a butterfly”: Zhuangzi’s butterfly dream. See the Chapter 37 resources and Taoism and Zhuangzi.
  • “a lost psyche drifting down the wind”: In Greek psyche means both soul and butterfly. Apuleius tells the story of Psyche and Cupid in The Golden Ass. See Greek Mythology.
  • “most people, it had been Mr. Spitzer’s unfortunate observation, were at some level disoriented”: Doctors still test whether a patient is “oriented” to person, place, and time, the same three matters Mr. Spitzer names. See Madness and Sanity.
  • “by nightshade and bella donna”: Deadly nightshade, Atropa belladonna, enlarges the pupils and blurs the sight. Italian women are said to have used it to make their eyes beautiful, hence bella donna, “beautiful lady.” See The History of Opium.
  • “Lunacy reigned supreme”: Lunacy comes from the Latin luna, the moon, which was long believed to cause madness. See Moon and Stars and Madness and Sanity.
