Chapter 55

← Chapter 54 · Home · Chapter 56 →

Content note: This chapter mentions the suicide of Mr. Spitzer’s twin brother, Peron.

Summary

Mr. Spitzer imagines the life he would have led if his brother had died first: his theoretical music, his butterflies and postage stamps, safe investments in sunken ships and dead Russian bonds, and a tenth symphony that would begin where other composers had ended their lives. He remembers the twin house he designed so that each brother had his half, every portrait, garden, and mirror repeated, and how Peron mocked it, moved the furniture, forged Joachim’s checks, and never did him a single favor. Since Peron’s death his eyes see double, the small things large and the great things small; he sleeps with his eyes open and wakes in the wrong carriage, the wrong passenger behind a skeleton coachman. Peron lived by carpe diem, Joachim by hoc opus, hic labor est. The walls of the twin house have been knocked down, and Mr. Spitzer, broken by the funeral and its debts, lives in an old beach-comber’s house, “still wondering whose funeral it was.”

Characters present

Joachim Spitzer · Peron Spitzer

Concepts present

Themes: Death and Mortality · Duality and Doubles · Identity and the Self · Isolation and Connection · Memory and the Past · Order, Chaos, and Discipline · Society, Class, and Race

Symbols: Butterflies and Moths · Clouds and Storms · Eyes and Blindness · Horses and Carriages · Lamps, Candles, and Light · Mirrors and Reflections · Music and Instruments · Silence and Deafness · The House · Twins and Doubles

Philosophy: Aristotle · Astrology, Alchemy, and Esoterica · Augustine and Christian Theology · Plato and Platonism · Pythagoras and the Music of the Spheres · Spinoza

Allusions: Alice in Wonderland · American Writers · Ancient Egypt · Astronomy · Exploration and the Poles · Gambling and Playing Cards · Greek Mythology · Iowa, Indiana, and the Midwest · Music and Composers · Romantic Poets · Shakespeare · The Bible

Key passages

From the research

  • Mr. Spitzer contemplates how he might have lived had his brother died earlier. It describes his orderly, carefully planned life dedicated to music, philately, and collecting rare artifacts. It shows his desire for certainty, order, and a calm pursuit of immortality through art, contrasting with the chaos brought by his brother. This sets up the fundamental tension between the brothers’ lives and personalities.
  • Mr. Spitzer’s conservative financial choices are described in detail. This symbolizes his attempt to secure an immutable future for his music and life, despite the apparent futility, reflecting his cautious and meticulous nature opposed to his brother’s recklessness.
  • The contrast between Joachim (Mr. Spitzer) and Peron are deeply explored as to their opposing characters. Joachim is altruistic, restrained, careful, and Peron was egotistical, reckless, and dismissive of Joachim’s order and sacrifices. It highlights Peron’s irresponsibility, including borrowing and forging checks in Joachim’s name, which caused Joachim’s financial ruin. The passage reveals Joachim’s feelings of invisibility, neglect, and resentment toward Peron, who never acknowledged or appreciated him.
  • The detailed description of the house, its symmetrical twin halves, and the doubled portraits and artifacts symbolize the intertwined yet opposed lives of the brothers. The house, with its precise architectural layout and mirrored rooms, reflects Joachim’s desire for balance and control, while Peron’s disregard for these arrangements symbolizes chaos and disruption. This metaphor extends to their personalities and fates.
  • Mr. Spitzer’s impaired perception and mental state is described as well as his physical and mental fragility. His difficulty distinguishing reality from hallucination or dream highlights his profound grief and alienation. His inability to fully “awaken” or “sleep” reflects his liminal, haunted existence after his brother’s death.
  • Mr. Spitzer’s wandering through memories and dreams, confusion over past and present, and his search for meaning in his fragmented life are poignantly rendered as an existential reflection on time, memory, and identity. He struggles with questions of identity, the passage of time as a fluid concept, and the absence of harmony connecting his life’s beginning and end. His experience of living “only at the end of time” and being lost between reality and illusion underscores the theme of existential disorientation.
  • The image of Mr. Spitzer unknowingly traveling in the wrong carriage, as the wrong passenger, driven by a skeletal coachman through unfamiliar landscapes, symbolizes his loss of control and direction in life. This haunting metaphor emphasizes his disconnection from reality and his brother’s lingering presence or shadow in his life.
  • The chapter contrasts Peron’s carefree motto “carpe diem” (seize the day) with Joachim’s solemn motto “hoc opus, hic labor est” (this is the work, this is the labor). This highlights their fundamental differences between Peron’s reckless enjoyment of the moment versus Joachim’s dedication to a difficult, serious artistic mission. It underscores the tragedy of their opposing paths and the sacrifices Joachim made for a legacy unappreciated by Peron.
  • The closing passage reflects Mr. Spitzer’s sense of isolation, the fading of the twin house and the life he once had, his confusion about his own identity, and his unresolved mourning for Peron who never mourned him. It is a reflection on loss, survival, and unresolved grief. It also evokes the futility and purposelessness he feels, despite his efforts to maintain order and shelter from life’s storms. The passage is a powerful summation of the chapter’s themes of loss, memory, and the fragile persistence of life.

Questions and observations

Reading closely

  • “If his brother had died, Mr. Spitzer would have lived.” What life does he imagine, and why does Young begin with a life that never happened?
  • “Silence was more beautiful than music, for the echo was more beautiful than the sound.” Why would a composer prefer silence?
  • “The morning had been the dream, and the night had been real.” What did the long winter night do to Mr. Spitzer?

Characters

  • Peron mocked “the mad man’s dream of absolute equality.” Why does the twin house offend him?
  • The bank teller “insisted that there was only one brother.” Was the teller wrong?
  • Peron lived by carpe diem and Joachim by hoc opus, hic labor est. Which motto does Mr. Spitzer live by now?

Connections

  • Mr. Spitzer wakes “in the wrong carriage” as “the wrong passenger.” How does his journey echo Vera’s bus ride?
  • “Could not the recording angel have made, also, a grand mistake?” Where else in the novel do ledgers, wills, and debts try to measure a life?
  • “After Peron’s death, he had dreamed he was two brothers, and one was dead.” Where else does one character carry another inside?

Reflection

  • “He had gone on when he could not go on.” What keeps a person going?
  • “If his goal had been realized, even for a moment, it would have ceased to be the object of his quest.” Is a goal worth more unreached?
  • Without Peron’s chaos “there would have been such perfect justice that there would have been a frozen world and nothing moving.” Does life need chance?

Research: Characters

Mr. Spitzer (Joachim)

  • A man of order, methodical, cautious, and devoted to a grand musical project he calls his “opus” or “dirge.”
  • Represents stability, intellectual rigor, and a desire for certainty in an uncertain world.
  • Lives a life of sacrifice, burdened by his brother’s recklessness and debts.
  • Suffers from physical and mental impairments, including distorted vision and a fragile body, symbolic of his fragile mental state.
  • Haunted by his brother’s absence and the loss of a shared past, struggling with identity and reality.
  • Symbolizes the rational, structured side of human nature, trying to impose order on chaos.

Peron (Mr. Spitzer’s Brother)

  • A gambler, extrovert, and embodiment of chaos, risk, and unpredictability.
  • Lives a life of abandon, irresponsibility, and indifference to consequence.
  • His death leaves Joachim to bear the burdens and debts he left behind.
  • Represents the impulsive, irrational, and destructive forces in life, contrasting sharply with Joachim’s order.
  • His laughter and ghostly presence continue to haunt Joachim.

Research: Themes

Duality and Mirror Imagery

See: Duality and Doubles

  • The chapter repeatedly emphasizes twins, mirrors, and reflections: twin portraits, twin gardens, twin portraits of historical figures, and the divided house.
  • Symbolizes the split between order (Joachim) and chaos (Peron), reason and passion, life and death.
  • The mirroring extends to the psychological level where the brothers are halves of one whole, each incomplete without the other.

Memory and Identity

See: Memory and the Past · Identity and the Self

  • Joachim’s identity is fragmented; his memory is unreliable, altered by grief and loss.
  • He questions whether he is himself or his brother, and whether he is awake or dreaming.
  • His life is a continuous search for meaning in the past and the present, often blurred and confused.

Order versus Chaos

See: Order, Chaos, and Discipline

  • Joachim’s life is governed by plans, maps, and precise arrangements designed to exclude chance and disorder.
  • Peron’s life is the antithesis: reckless, chaotic, and unpredictable.
  • The tension between these forces creates conflict and tragedy, illustrating the human struggle to balance these aspects.

Mortality and Immortality

See: Death and Mortality

  • Joachim views his music as a tomb, an immortal legacy that will outlive his physical existence.
  • Peron’s death and presumed freedom contrast with Joachim’s struggle to survive and find meaning.
  • The chapter meditates on death, mourning, and the desire for lasting significance.

Alienation and Isolation

See: Isolation and Connection

  • Joachim feels alienated from himself, others, and reality.
  • His impaired vision and mental confusion symbolize his estrangement from the world.
  • He lives in a liminal state, neither fully awake nor fully asleep, caught between life and death.

Research: Symbols and Imagery

The Twin House and Mirroring Rooms

See: Mirrors and Reflections · The House · Twins and Doubles

  • Symbolize the divided self and fractured identity; also the attempt to impose order on life’s chaos.

Music and Silence

See: Music and Instruments · Silence and Deafness

  • Music is both a creative act and a tomb; silence and echo represent memory and death.

The Butterfly Collection and Stamps

See: Butterflies and Moths

  • Represent delicate beauty, memory, and past achievements, threatened by Peron’s recklessness.

The Coach and Horses

See: Horses and Carriages

  • Symbolize the journey of life and death; Joachim often finds himself in the wrong carriage, lost in time and space.

The Candle Flames and Snuffers

See: Lamps, Candles, and Light

  • Represent life and death, consciousness and oblivion; the snuffer putting out stars is a metaphor for fading life.

Visual Impairments

See: Eyes and Blindness

  • Joachim’s double vision and shifting perspectives symbolize his mental confusion and the instability of perception.

Research: Resources

  • “such a thing as a non-aural music”: Pythagoras taught that the planets make a music by their motion that human ears cannot hear. Boethius divided music into three kinds, the music of the world, the music of the human being, and the music of instruments, and only the last can be heard (Boethius, De institutione musica 1.2, about 510). See Pythagoras and the Music of the Spheres.
  • “his great emperors and queens, his pearl-bordered moths”: Young’s collection is made of real butterflies and moths: the purple emperor, the queen, the pearl-bordered fritillary, the pebble prominent, the marbled white, and the mourning cloak, which the English call the Camberwell beauty. See The mourning cloak butterfly hibernating and Butterflies and Moths.
  • “his china shepherdesses for his twin marble chimney pieces”: may refer to the China shepherdesses that were popular for the wealthy in the nineteenth century and were often found on fictional mantels and compared in looks to the beauty of a female character.
    • Porcelain shepherdesses were made in pairs to stand at the two ends of a mantelpiece, by Meissen from the 1740s and by Chelsea, Derby, and Staffordshire potters into the nineteenth century.
  • “for he had been a great philatelist”: A philatelist is a person who collects and studies postage stamps, a practice also known as philately. The term combines the Greek roots “phil-“ (loving) and “ateleia” (tax-exemption), referring to the freedom from charges granted by a stamp. A philatelist may focus on the historical or artistic value of stamps, organizing their collections thematically or by country. The French collector Georges Herpin coined the word in 1864.
  • “a remarkable collection of triangles, monuments, commemoratives”: Collectors sort stamps by subject. The Cape of Good Hope triangulars of 1853 were the first triangular stamps, and the first United States commemoratives were the Columbian issue of 1893, marking four hundred years since Columbus’s first voyage.
  • “that the oldest coachman will stop and take on another passenger”: “Because I could not stop for Death – / He kindly stopped for me – / The Carriage held but just Ourselves – / And Immortality” (Emily Dickinson, “Because I could not stop for Death,” about 1862, published 1890). See The Black Coachman and American Writers.
  • “never have consulted Blackstone”: Sir William Blackstone’s Commentaries on the Laws of England (four volumes, 1765-1769) was the standard guide to the common law in England and America; Abraham Lincoln taught himself law from it.
  • “The other great composers had written only their ninth symphonies”: Curse of the ninth is a superstition connected with classical music. It is the belief that the ninth symphony is destined to be the composer’s last. After finishing it the composer is fated to die before finishing a tenth. Beethoven, Dvořák, and Bruckner each died with nine numbered symphonies, and Gustav Mahler, who feared the curse, left his Tenth unfinished at his death in 1911. See On the curse of the ninth and Music and Composers.
  • “as dead as Grand Russian Imperials today”: Imperial Russian government bonds, sold widely in France and abroad before 1917, became worthless when the Soviet government repudiated the tsarist debts in 1918. See the Grand Russian Imperial stocks and bonds in the Chapter 54 resources.
  • “the iron bells of old Czar Kolokol”: The Tsar Bell, also known as the Tsarsky Kolokol, Tsar Kolokol III, or Royal Bell, is a bell on display on the grounds of the Moscow Kremlin. The bell was commissioned by Empress Anna Ivanovna, niece of Peter the Great. It has never been in working order, suspended, nor rung. It was cast in bronze in 1733-1735 and cracked in the Kremlin fire of 1737, when an eleven-ton piece broke off. (Wikipedia)
  • “some old watered bond issues of the Lost Atlantis”: “Lost Atlantis” is a mythical island civilization described by Plato in his dialogues as a powerful, technologically advanced society that was destroyed by earthquakes and sank beneath the sea. While the story is a well-known myth and has inspired theories about real locations and even modern technological advancements, most historians and scientists believe Atlantis was a philosophical allegory created by Plato to serve as a cautionary tale against hubris. See Plato and Platonism. Watered stock is stock issued for far more than the company’s assets are worth, after the drovers said to have fed their cattle salt and let them drink before they were weighed for sale.
  • “sunken Roman galleys, Phoenician traders, Etruscan skills, Etruscan boatmen”: “Roman galleys” A galley is a type of ship optimised for propulsion by oars. Galleys were historically used for warfare, trade, and piracy mostly in the seas surrounding Europe. It developed in the Mediterranean world during antiquity and continued to exist in various forms until the early 19th century. Galleys were the primary warships used by the ancient Mediterranean naval powers, including the Phoenicians, Greeks and Romans. (Wikipedia)
    • “Phoenician traders” were ancient Mediterranean seafarers who established an extensive trade network from about 1550 to 300 B.C.E., exchanging goods like Tyrian purple dye, textiles, metalwork, and glass for raw materials such as copper, tin, ivory, and silver. They were skilled in navigation, shipbuilding, and craft production, establishing colonies and trading posts across the Mediterranean, from the Levant to Iberia and North Africa. Their innovations included the development of the alphabet and early forms of complex trading mechanisms like written contracts, weights, and even coins.
    • “Etruscan skiffs” is a general term used for the smaller, likely less complex boats associated with the Etruscan civilization, contrasted with their larger warships and merchant vessels. Evidence for these types of smaller boats comes from tomb paintings, like those in the Tomb of the Ship in Tarquinia, and clay models, though direct archaeological finds of Etruscan-specific small craft are scarce. These smaller vessels likely served for activities such as fishing, local transport, and possibly supporting larger ships.
    • “Etruscan boatman,” known as Charun or Charu, was a demon of the dead who ferried souls across a boundary to the afterlife, similar to the Greek Charon. Etruscan Charun was distinctively depicted with a hooked nose, hammer, and sometimes animal features like wings, and his presence on tombstones and funerary urns indicated the soul’s journey to the underworld ruled by Aita.
  • “the muted murmur of the paper nautilus”: The paper nautilus, or argonaut, is an octopus whose female makes a thin, paper-white shell to carry her eggs; Aristotle and Pliny believed she raised two arms as sails and sailed the sea in it. See Aristotle.
  • “The golden fleece would have turned to a grey beard”: Jason and the Argonauts sailed to Colchis for the Golden Fleece, the fleece of the winged ram, guarded by a dragon. See Greek Mythology.
  • “Should the alteration recognize that it was altered?”: Young turns Shakespeare’s “Love is not love / Which alters when it alteration finds” (William Shakespeare, Sonnet 116, 1609). See Shakespeare.
  • “leaving Joachim to face the music, pay the piper”: To pay the piper is to bear the cost, as in the proverb “he who pays the piper calls the tune.” The Pied Piper of Hamelin, cheated of his fee for ridding the town of rats, piped its children away.
  • “poor as a Skid Row bum”: See Skid Row in the Chapter 52 resources.
  • “a dead cue-ball artist”: See the billiards legend of Louis Fox in the Chapter 53 resources. See Gambling and Playing Cards.
  • “twirled the bare-ribbed bird-cages”: In chuck-a-luck, also called birdcage, three dice tumble in an hourglass-shaped wire cage, and players bet on the numbers that come up. See Gambling and Playing Cards.
  • “as if it were a sea of glass which had no end”: “And before the throne there was a sea of glass like unto crystal” (Revelation 4:6, KJV). See The Bible.
  • “all money was counterfeit even like the sun, moon, stars turned out at the great Mint”: Money, though officially minted, is worth what people agree it is worth, and Young sends the sun, moon, and stars to the same great Mint.
    • Before coins came barter and commodity money: cattle from about 9000 BC, and from about 1200 BC cowrie shells, the most widely and longest used currency in history, especially in Asia and Africa. Standard weights of gold and silver were used in Egypt and Mesopotamia by the third millennium BC. Lydia struck the first stamped coins of electrum about 650-600 BC, while Chinese mints cast coins shaped like spades and knives. Chinese merchants used paper receipts called “flying money,” and the Song government issued the first official paper currency in the 1020s; Sweden issued Europe’s first banknotes in 1661. In the nineteenth and early twentieth centuries governments tied paper money to gold. (Wikipedia)
    • The first minting facility, or mint, was likely established by the Lydians in the 7th century BC for coining precious metals, a practice that spread to Greece, Rome, and beyond, with modern countries often operating one national mint. Coinage spread from Lydia to the Aegean Islands, Italy, Persia, and India, with Romans developing modern minting techniques by the 4th century BC. The first national mint in the United States was established by the Coinage Act of 1792 in Philadelphia.
    • Counterfeit money is currency produced outside of the legal sanction of a state or government, usually in a deliberate attempt to imitate that currency and so as to deceive its recipient. Producing or using counterfeit money is a form of fraud or forgery, and is illegal in all jurisdictions of the world. The business of counterfeiting money is nearly as old as money itself: plated copies (known as Fourrées) have been found of Lydian coins, which are thought to be among the first Western coins. Before the introduction of paper money, the most prevalent method of counterfeiting involved mixing base metals with pure gold or silver. During World War II, the Nazis forged British pounds and American dollars. Traditionally, anti-counterfeiting measures involved including fine detail with raised intaglio printing on bills which allows non-experts to easily spot forgeries. On coins, milled or reeded (marked with parallel grooves) edges are used to show that none of the valuable metal has been scraped off. (Wikipedia)
  • “could certainly never have employed a Seeing Eye bookkeeper”: The Seeing Eye, the first guide dog school in the United States, was founded in 1929 by Dorothy Harrison Eustis, who had trained German shepherds for the Swiss army and police; it moved to Morristown, New Jersey, in 1931. See Eyes and Blindness.
  • “could not the recording angel have made, also, a grand mistake”: In Laurence Sterne’s Tristram Shandy, a book Young named among her influences, Uncle Toby swears an oath out of pity for the dying Le Fever, and “the ACCUSING SPIRIT, which flew up to heaven’s chancery with the oath, blush’d as he gave it in;—and the RECORDING ANGEL, as he wrote it down, dropp’d a tear upon the word, and blotted it out for ever” (Laurence Sterne, Tristram Shandy, vol. 6, ch. 8, 1762).
  • “from vastly towering cumulo-nimbus to darkening alto-stratus”: Cumulonimbus are the towering thunderheads; altostratus is the grey sheet of mid-level cloud that comes before steady rain or snow. The Latin cloud names go back to Luke Howard’s Essay on the Modifications of Clouds (1803). See Clouds and Storms.
  • “the long streamers of Aurora Borealis”: See the northern and southern lights in the Chapter 54 resources. See Astronomy and Exploration and the Poles.
  • “an old croupier, perhaps at the wrong wheel”: A croupier is the person in charge of a gaming table, gathering in and paying out money or tokens. See Gambling and Playing Cards.
  • “Gilts and Estates”: A gilt is a British government bond, called “gilt-edged” for its safety, since the government has never missed a payment. An estate is everything a person owns and owes at death, distributed by will or, without one, by law.
  • “Last Bequests”: a bequest is a gift of property, money, or other assets made from an estate to a specific individual, organization, or trust through a will or other estate planning document. It is essentially a legacy designated to be distributed after the estate owner’s death. Bequests are a flexible way to support loved ones and charitable causes, with different types including specific gifts of particular items, general cash amounts, or a percentage of the remaining estate.
  • “Progress of Probate”: involves filing the will and petition with the court, identifying and appraising assets, notifying interested parties, paying debts and taxes, and finally distributing the remaining property to beneficiaries. The timeline for this process varies by state and the complexity of the estate, typically ranging from several months to over a year, with complications like will contests or estate taxes extending the duration.
  • “Authenticity of Will”: A will’s authenticity is established by confirming the testator’s intent and capacity at the time of creation, and by verifying the proper execution under state law, which generally requires a written document signed by the testator and two witnesses (unless it’s a handwritten “holographic will,” which is valid in many states without witnesses). A self-proving affidavit, signed by the testator, witnesses, and a notary, simplifies probate by attaching the will to the affidavit, making the process easier and saving time and money.
  • “Will of the Dead”: may refer to a legal will and testament, a legally binding document that specifies how a person’s property should be distributed after their death. In a spiritual or metaphorical context, it could refer to the concept of the deceased having continued influence or wishes, such as in Jesus’s “let the dead bury their dead” (Matthew 8:22), which turns attention to the living. In the New Testament the covenant is a will that takes effect at a death: “For where a testament is, there must also of necessity be the death of the testator” (Hebrews 9:16).
  • “Cases in Chancery”: are legal matters handled by a type of court, originally established in England, that focuses on fairness and equity rather than strictly applying common law rules. These courts typically address issues like trusts and estates, corporate and partnership disputes, real estate and mortgage foreclosures, adoptions and guardianships, and requests for equitable remedies such as injunctions and specific performance of contracts. Unlike criminal cases, chancery courts resolve civil disputes, and they often involve complex personal, financial, and familial relationships.
  • “Laws Governing New England Fishing”: the regulation of New England fishing was a fragmented mix of international treaties, state-level rules, and early federal actions that lacked comprehensive conservation measures. The period was defined by escalating conflicts, increasing fishing efficiency, and a growing understanding of resource depletion, all of which would eventually necessitate stronger federal oversight in the 1970s.
  • “Laws Governing Whaling”: Whaling was a largely unregulated industry until the start of loose agreements in the 1930s and culminating in the formation of the International Whaling Commission (IWC) in 1946. These laws attempted to manage whale stocks but struggled with enforcement and compliance.
  • “that the man who found the whale was its owner”: Young reverses the whalemen’s own law. In Moby-Dick, “A Fast-Fish belongs to the party fast to it,” and “A Loose-Fish is fair game for anybody who can soonest catch it” (Herman Melville, Moby-Dick, ch. 89, “Fast-Fish and Loose-Fish,” 1851). In Swift v. Gifford (1872), a Massachusetts federal court held that a whale belonged to the ship whose harpoon first struck it, not to the ship whose crew later killed and took it. See American Writers.
  • “The Musical Sensibilities of the King Walrus”: may refer to Lewis Carroll’s poem “The Walrus and the Carpenter” which first appeared in 1871. Its rhythmic narrative has been set to music multiple times over the decades, including the 1951 Walt Disney film Alice in Wonderland. There it is sung by J. Pat O’Malley in a vaudeville style, and the charming Walrus eats the oysters.
  • “Burke’s Peerage in the Penguin World”: may refer to Burke’s Peerage Limited, a British genealogical publisher, considered an authority on the order of precedence of noble families and information on the lesser nobility of the United Kingdom. It was founded in 1826, when the Anglo-Irish genealogist John Burke began releasing books devoted to the ancestry and heraldry of the peerage, baronetage, knightage and landed gentry of Great Britain and Ireland. His first publication, a Genealogical and Heraldic Dictionary of the Peerage and Baronetage of the United Kingdom, was updated sporadically until 1847, when the company began publishing new editions every year as Burke’s Peerage, Baronetage and Knightage (often shortened and known as Burke’s Peerage). Other books followed, including Burke’s Landed Gentry, Burke’s Colonial Gentry, and Burke’s General Armory. In addition to its peerage publications, the Burke’s publishing company produced books on Royal families of Europe and Latin America, ruling families of Africa and the Middle East, distinguished families of the United States and historical families of Ireland. (Wikipedia)
  • “New England Mortality Rates”: Historically, New England mortality rates were characterized by significant changes over time, from periods of exceptionally high colonial-era life expectancy to high urban death rates in the 19th century, before undergoing a sharp decline in the early 20th century. Contrary to popular belief, 17th-century New England colonists enjoyed a long life expectancy, averaging 65 to 70 years. This was 15 to 20 years longer than in England at the time and was attributed to the healthy climate and spaced-out communities. Studies of early New England towns show surprisingly high child survival rates. For example, in Andover, Massachusetts, between 1640 and 1669, 87% to 91% of children survived to age 20 (Philip J. Greven Jr., Four Generations: Population, Land, and Family in Colonial Andover, Massachusetts, 1970). These long lifespans were frequently interrupted by devastating epidemics, such as outbreaks of smallpox, measles, and influenza. Because of low population density and less frequent exposure, community immunity would wane, leading to cyclic, highly destructive epidemics when a new disease was introduced. Europeans brought diseases like smallpox, measles, and cholera, to which Native Americans had no immunity. These outbreaks killed up to 90% of the Indigenous population in parts of New England. While overall U.S. mortality was low compared to Western Europe, urban areas saw a significant “mortality penalty.” By the early 1900s, the life expectancy for white people in New England’s urban areas was 46 years, compared to 54.7 years in rural areas. As towns grew, infectious diseases spread rapidly due to poor sanitation and crowded living conditions. As the leading cause of death in the 19th century, tuberculosis was a scourge in New England, affecting multiple members and generations of families. Diphtheria, scarlet fever, and whooping cough were major threats to children, contributing to high infant and child mortality rates. Cholera and typhoid fever also emerged as epidemic threats, particularly impacting port cities like Boston. The early 20th century saw a dramatic decline in mortality, largely due to public health measures and improved living standards, rather than new medical interventions.
  • “Actuarial Statistics”: is the application of statistical theory and probability analysis to evaluate and manage financial and other risks for organizations, particularly in the insurance, finance, and healthcare industries. Actuaries use statistical models and mathematical tools to quantify the likelihood and financial impact of uncertain events, enabling businesses to forecast outcomes, price products, manage capital, and allocate funds to cover potential losses.
  • “The Habits of the Night-Crowned Kingfisher”: “The Habits of the Night-Crowned Kingfisher” is an invented title. It may blend the kingfisher with the black-crowned night heron, a nocturnal fishing bird whose Latin name, Nycticorax, means night raven, for its harsh, crow-like call.
  • “The Life of the Sphinx Moth”: The life of a sphinx moth involves four stages: egg, larva (caterpillar), pupa, and adult. After mating, the adult female lays eggs on a host plant, which hatch into ravenous caterpillars that feed and grow, molting multiple times. Once fully grown, the caterpillar burrows into the soil or leaf litter to form a pupa, overwintering in this stage. The following spring, or later if delayed, the pupa transforms into an adult moth, which emerges, feeds on nectar using its proboscis, mates, and then lays eggs to begin the cycle anew.
  • “the seraph with his wings folded across his eyes”: “Above it stood the seraphims: each one had six wings; with twain he covered his face, and with twain he covered his feet, and with twain he did fly” (Isaiah 6:2, KJV). See The Bible.
  • “his tortoise harp with the gut string stretched inside its empty shell”: The baby Hermes made the first lyre from a tortoise shell strung with gut, then gave it to Apollo (Homeric Hymn to Hermes). See Greek Mythology.
  • “each with its blind boy cupid”: See blind Cupid in the Chapter 52 resources. See Greek Mythology.
  • “twin Corinthian columns and black and white parterres”: “Corinthian columns” are the most ornate of the three classical Greek orders, distinguished by their slender, fluted shafts and elaborate, bell-shaped capitals adorned with two rows of stylized acanthus leaves and scrolls. Named after the ancient city of Corinth, these columns are considered the most refined and elegant, often signifying wealth and prestige through their intricate, decorative design.
    • “parterres” is a level space in a garden or yard occupied by an ornamental arrangement of flower beds or in North America a part of the ground floor of an auditorium in the rear and on the sides, especially the part beneath the balcony.
  • “two pale cavaliers riding two pale horses”: “And I looked, and behold a pale horse: and his name that sat on him was Death, and Hell followed with him” (Revelation 6:8, KJV). See The Bible.
  • “the twin Lady Hamiltons”: “Lady Hamiltons” Dame Emma Hamilton, known upon moving to London as Emma Hart, and upon marriage as Lady Hamilton, was an English maid, model, dancer and actress. She began her career in London’s demi-monde, becoming the mistress of a series of wealthy men, culminating in the naval hero Lord Nelson, and was the favourite model and muse of the portraitist George Romney. In 1791, at the age of 26, she married Sir William Hamilton, British ambassador to the Kingdom of Naples, where she was a success at court, befriending the queen who was a sister of Marie Antoinette, and meeting Nelson. (Wikipedia)
  • “the twin George Washingtons fording the twin Delawares”: “George Washingtons fording the twin Delawares” Washington Crossing the Delaware is the title of three 1851 oil-on-canvas paintings by the German-American artist Emanuel Leutze depicting General George Washington’s crossing of the Delaware River with the Continental Army on the night of December 25-26, 1776, during the American Revolutionary War. Washington’s covert crossing the Delaware River that night was the first of several moves, leading to a surprise attack and victory against Hessian forces at the Battle of Trenton in New Jersey on the morning of December 26. The original, in the Kunsthalle in Bremen, was destroyed by bombing in 1942; another version hangs in the Metropolitan Museum of Art in New York. (Wikipedia)
  • “the twin Duchesses of Devon ascending the twin high-wheelers”: “Duchesses of Devon” There have been many Duchesses of Devonshire throughout history, including Georgiana Cavendish (1757-1806), a famous socialite and political activist known for her style and charisma, and Deborah Cavendish (1920-2014), a member of the well-known Mitford family and a writer and socialite. Other notable Duchesses include Mary Cavendish (1895-1988), who served as Mistress of the Robes to Queen Elizabeth II, and Amanda Cavendish (born 1944), the current wife of the 12th Duke. Flag: after 1964, the later duchesses.
    • Gainsborough’s portrait of Georgiana, Duchess of Devonshire, was stolen from Agnew’s gallery in London in 1876 by the thief Adam Worth and not recovered until 1901.
    • The high-wheeler, or penny-farthing, was the bicycle of the 1870s and 1880s, long after Georgiana’s death in 1806.
  • “the twin President Monroes, each signing the Monroe Doctrine”: “President Monroes” James Monroe (1758-1831), the last Founding Father to be president, served as the fifth president from 1817 to 1825, the Era of Good Feelings. He signed the Missouri Compromise, which admitted Missouri as a slave state, and in 1823 announced the Monroe Doctrine, opposing European intervention in the newly independent countries of the Americas. He belonged to the American Colonization Society, which sent freed Black Americans to Africa, and Liberia’s capital, Monrovia, is named for him. He died on July 4, 1831. (Wikipedia)
    • “Monroe Doctrine” was a U.S. foreign policy statement in 1823 by President James Monroe that opposed European colonialism and interference in the Western Hemisphere. It essentially divided the world into two spheres of influence: Europe and the Americas, with the U.S. pledging not to interfere in European affairs in exchange for European powers staying out of the newly independent nations of the Western Hemisphere. While initially not taken seriously by Europe, it evolved into a cornerstone of American foreign policy and was later extended by Theodore Roosevelt’s Corollary to justify U.S. intervention in Latin America.
    • Monroe did not sign a doctrine. He announced it in his annual message to Congress on 2 December 1823, in words largely drafted by his Secretary of State, John Quincy Adams.
  • “the twin British Red Coats”: “British Red Coats” refers to soldiers of the British Army, particularly those who wore distinctive red coats, primarily during the 17th to the early 20th centuries. The term gained notoriety in the United States due to their role as the opposing force during the American Revolution. While the red coat is strongly associated with the British, it was also adopted by other armies and has a history tied to practicality and symbolism.
  • “the twin belles of old New York”: may refer to The Dolly Sisters. Hungarian-American identical twins Rosie and Jenny Dolly were well-known dancers, singers, and actresses in New York City’s vaudeville and theater scene in the 1910s and ‘20s. They were famously successful on Broadway and became international celebrities. Their lives were later turned into the 1945 film The Dolly Sisters. There is also a popular Greenwich Village legend that tells the story of two feuding twin sisters who were the original inhabitants of the twin antebellum houses at 39 and 41 Commerce Street. According to the story, a sea captain built the identical houses for his twin daughters, giving them a shared garden but few windows facing each other to keep them apart. This version of the houses’ history is not supported by evidence. The houses were actually built in the 1830s by a New Jersey milkman as an investment property.
  • “the twin President Garfields”: “twin President Garfields” James Abram Garfield (1831-1881), born in a log cabin in Ohio, was a preacher, a Union general, and a congressman before he became the 20th president in March 1881. He published his own proof of the Pythagorean theorem (1876) and spoke for civil rights for African Americans and civil service reform. Charles J. Guiteau shot him on July 2, 1881, and he died on September 19, of infection caused by his doctors’ unsanitary methods. (Wikipedia)
  • “the twin Roman senators addressing the twin Roman senates”: “Roman senators” In the 3rd century BCE, Roman senators were members of a life-long, elite body that held significant power by advising magistrates and the Roman people. Membership was exclusive, initially consisting of patricians but later expanding to include plebeians who had held senior magistracies. The Senate’s authority stemmed from the collective prestige of its members, who were typically from wealthy, landowning families, and the Senate’s advisories (senatus consulta) were often followed in practice. The senate then numbered around 300 members. Famous Roman senators of the 3rd century BC include Marcus Claudius Marcellus, a renowned general and consul, and Cato the Elder, a staunch conservative statesman and military leader. Another key figure was Gaius Flaminius, a consul and politician known for his land reforms and his death at the Battle of Lake Trasimene.
  • “the twin St. Bernard dogs”: “St. Bernard dogs” became famous for rescuing alpine travelers by working with monks at the Great St. Bernard Hospice in the Alps, where they were bred for their strength, endurance, and keen sense of smell to find people buried under snow and avalanches. Working in pairs, one dog would locate and provide warmth and comfort to the stranded individual while the other returned to the hospice to alert the monks. The most famous of these dogs was Barry, credited with saving over 40 lives, with his preserved body now at the Natural History Museum of Bern.
  • “the twin Queen Isabellas of Spain bidding farewell to Christopher Columbus”: “Queen Isabellas of Spain” Isabella I of Castile (1451-1504), with her husband Ferdinand of Aragon, united Spain as the Catholic Monarchs. In 1492 they took Granada, ending Muslim rule in Spain, issued the Alhambra Decree expelling the Jews, and financed Columbus’s voyage; they also began the Spanish Inquisition. (Wikipedia)
    • “Christopher Columbus” was an Italian explorer and navigator, sponsored by the Spanish monarchs, who led four transatlantic voyages between 1492 and 1504, opening the door for widespread European colonization of the Americas. His expeditions began a new era of European exploration, but also brought disease and conquest to the Indigenous populations of the Americas.
    • The legend that Columbus died a pauper is not true. He died in Valladolid in 1506 with an income from the Indies, though still petitioning the crown for the titles and share he had been promised, and still believing he had reached Asia.
  • “had never seen the Chrysler Building”: “Chrysler Building” is a 1,046-foot Art Deco skyscraper at Lexington Avenue and 42nd Street in Manhattan, commissioned by Walter Chrysler. When it was completed in 1930 it was the tallest building in the world, for eleven months, until the Empire State Building. (Wikipedia)
  • “the old Flatiron Building”: “old Flatiron Building,” originally the Fuller Building, is a 22-story triangular skyscraper at Fifth Avenue, Broadway, and 23rd Street in Manhattan, designed by Daniel Burnham and opened in 1902. Its name comes from its shape, like a cast-iron clothes iron, and it anchors the south end of Madison Square. (Wikipedia)
  • “the old Fishback Building”: “old Fishback Building” may refer to the building in Indianapolis it was the start of Frank Fishback’s coffee roasting business in the late 1880s and by the 1910s it also sold Virginia Sweet brand foods. The company closed in the 1930s. The Fishback family is a family in America that can be traced back to John Fishback, an immigrant from Germany in 1714 who settled in Virginia with Governor Spottswood’s colony. Extensive genealogical records, including the 1914 book Genealogy of the Fishback Family in America, document the family’s history and its descendants’ migration across the United States, with significant populations historically in Kentucky and other states. See the Fishback Building in the Chapter 54 resources. See Iowa, Indiana, and the Midwest.
  • “had never seen Boston Common”: “Boston Common” is a public park in downtown Boston, Massachusetts. It is the oldest city park in the United States. Boston Common consists of 50 acres of land bounded by five major Boston streets: Tremont Street, Park Street, Beacon Street, Charles Street, and Boylston Street. The Common is part of the Emerald Necklace of parks and parkways that extend from the Common south to Franklin Park in Jamaica Plain, Roxbury, and Dorchester. The visitors’ center for the city of Boston is located on the Tremont Street side of the park. The Central Burying Ground is on the Boylston Street side of Boston Common and contains the graves of artist Gilbert Stuart and composer William Billings. Also buried there are Samuel Sprague and his son Charles Sprague, one of America’s earliest poets. Samuel Sprague was a participant in the Boston Tea Party and fought in the Revolutionary War. The Common was designated as a Boston Landmark by the Boston Landmarks Commission in 1977. (Wikipedia)
  • “the old Third Avenue El”: “old Third Avenue El” may refer to the now defunct IRT Third Avenue Line. The IRT Third Avenue Line, commonly known as the Third Avenue Elevated, Third Avenue El, or Bronx El, was an elevated railway in Manhattan and the Bronx, New York City. Originally operated by the New York Elevated Railway, an independent railway company, it was acquired by the Interborough Rapid Transit Company (IRT) and eventually became part of the New York City Subway system. The first segment of the line, with service at most stations, opened from South Ferry to Grand Central Depot on August 26, 1878. Service was extended to Harlem in Manhattan on December 30. In 1881 this line already began 24/7 service. Service in Manhattan closed on May 12, 1955, and it was the last elevated line in Manhattan to run, a frequent backdrop for movies. (Wikipedia)
  • “mystical laundry signs of old Chinatown”: “Chinatown” U.S. Chinatowns were ethnic enclaves, primarily in the West, established in the mid-19th century by immigrants drawn by the Gold Rush and railroad jobs, but were devastated by the 1882 Chinese Exclusion Act which banned further immigration and caused populations to decline. By the early 20th century, Chinatowns were predominantly male-dominated communities centered on social societies, gambling, and opium dens, but after the 1943 Magnuson Act repealed the exclusion laws, populations began to rise again, leading to changes in the established communities.
    • Shut out of most work by law and prejudice, many Chinese immigrants ran hand laundries, whose painted signs in Chinese characters Young calls mystical. See Society, Class, and Race.
  • “received a shower of ticker tape”: New York’s first ticker-tape parade, on 28 October 1886, celebrated the dedication of the Statue of Liberty, when office workers on Wall Street threw stock-ticker tape from their windows.
  • “the old-time Hoboken ferry boats”: “Old-time Hoboken ferry boats” may refer to the Hoboken Ferry Company, which began operations in 1822 as one of several ferry lines across the Hudson River. The Hoboken Ferry operated until 1967 and saw significant developments like the 1907 opening of the Delaware, Lackawanna & Western Railroad’s Hoboken Terminal, which the ferry served, and the introduction of various ferryboats like the double-ended, vehicle-carrying Binghamton in 1905. The ferries carried thousands of commuters daily until the Hudson and Manhattan Railroad tubes under the river opened in 1908 and took much of their trade. Flag: after 1964, the closing of 1967.
    • Here the Jersey shore is the New Jersey bank of the Hudson River, where the ferries left Hoboken for Manhattan, not the resort coast called the Jersey Shore.
  • “many mementos moris of Joachim’s life”: Memento mori is an artistic or symbolic trope acting as a reminder of the inevitability of death.
  • “The divine Melba sings”: The divine Melba sings may refer to Dame Nellie Melba who was an operatic soprano. See Music and Composers.
  • “Jenny Lind will sing tonight”: Jenny Lind may refer to Johanna Maria “Jenny” Lind who was a Swedish opera singer. P. T. Barnum brought her to America for a tour that opened at Castle Garden, New York, in September 1850. See Music and Composers.
  • “First American performance of Ole Bull”: Ole Bull may refer to Ole Bornemann Bull who was a Norwegian virtuoso violinist and composer. He first toured America in 1843 and in 1852 founded Oleana, a short-lived Norwegian colony in Pennsylvania. See Music and Composers.
  • “Boston debut of the Swiss bell-ringers”: “Swiss bell ringers” refers to both a popular form of American entertainment in the 19th and early 20th centuries, featuring musical performances with handbells and cowbells, and the generic term for handbell choirs that became popular as a result of these shows. These performing groups, which were not necessarily actually from Switzerland, brought a unique sound and visual spectacle to audiences, contributing to a lasting tradition of handbell music. In the 1840s Swiss bell-ringing acts, likely featuring family troupes, gained popularity in the United States after appearing in larger entertainment shows, like P.T. Barnum’s American Museum. Groups like the Spaulding Brothers’ Swiss Bell Ringers and the Peak Family Swiss Bell Ringers created elaborate performances, often including other musical instruments and vocalists. The name “Swiss” added a touch of exotic charm and a connection to the romanticized imagery of the Swiss Alps, influencing their popularity. Mr. Spitzer has a good ear: the first “Swiss” bell ringers to tour America, under P. T. Barnum in the 1840s, were English handbell ringers from Lancashire.
  • “the hitching posts which were little black boys with golden turbans”: “little black boys with golden turbans” The earliest versions of lawn jockeys, used as hitching posts, were created in the 1850s or early 1860s. There are several legends about the black lawn jockeys. The Jim Crow Museum of Racist Memorabilia writes that “there is very little, if any, primary source material for the claim that lawn jockeys were used as signaling devices for escaping slaves on the Underground Railroad.” It is featured in two stories: Raymond Chandler’s 1942 Philip Marlowe novel, The High Window, and a short story by Flannery O’Connor in 1955, The Artificial Nigger. The story suggests that people are not intrinsically racist: rather, racist views are handed down from generation to generation because some people stand to profit from racism. O’Connor said that it was her favorite story she had written. See Society, Class, and Race.
  • “His memory was become like an Aeolian harp”: “Aeolian harp” (also wind harp) is a musical instrument that is played by the wind. Named after Aeolus, the ancient Greek god of the wind, the traditional Aeolian harp is essentially a wooden box including a sounding board, with strings stretched lengthwise across two bridges. It is often placed in a slightly opened window where the wind can blow across the strings to produce sounds. The strings can be made of different materials (or thicknesses) and all be tuned to the same pitch, or identical strings can be tuned to different pitches. Besides being the only string instrument played solely by the wind, the Aeolian harp is also the only string instrument that plays solely harmonic frequencies. They are recognizable by the sound which is a result of this property, which has been described as eerie and ethereal. The Aeolian harp, already known in the ancient world, was first described by Athanasius Kircher (1602-1680) in his books. It became popular as a household instrument during the Romantic era, and Aeolian harps are still hand-crafted today. Some are now made in the form of monumental metal sound sculptures located on the roofs of buildings and windy hilltops. (Wikipedia) Coleridge’s “The Eolian Harp” (1795) made it the Romantic emblem of a mind played on by nature. See Romantic Poets.
  • “could not and never had been able to distinguish between two spots and three spots”: The spots are the pips on dice and playing cards. See Gambling and Playing Cards.
  • “He suffered from retinal rivalry”: In binocular, or retinal, rivalry, when each eye sees a different image the brain does not fuse them but switches back and forth between them; Charles Wheatstone described it in 1838. See Eyes and Blindness.
    • Mr. Spitzer is describing several maladies: tinnitus, diplopia, micro/macropsia (Alice in Wonderland syndrome) that can be caused by different things, including psychological. See Alice in Wonderland.
  • “to be semper fidelis, semper idem, semper paratus”: Semper fidelis is Latin for always faithful or loyal. It is the motto of the US Marine Corp.
    • Semper idem is Latin for always the same; Elizabeth I took the feminine form, semper eadem, as her motto.
    • Semper paratus is Latin for always ready. It is used by different organizations including the US Coast Guard.
    • There are now three different mottos hinting at three different personalities in this chapter. Peron is carpe diem; seize the day. Joachim is hoc opus, hic labor est; this is the task, this is the labor. Mr. Spitzer’s is semper fidelis, semper idem, semper paratus; always faithful, always the same, always ready.
  • “life in the midst of death, death in the midst of life”: “In the midst of life we are in death” (The Book of Common Prayer, 1662, The Burial of the Dead).
  • “or was he the tailor retailored”: Sartor Resartus is Latin for “the tailor retailored.” Thomas Carlyle’s book of that name (1833-1834) is a philosophy of clothes, and Young said she took Carlyle as her master when she turned from poetry to prose. See Young’s Interviews Analyzed.
  • “sub specie aeternitatis”: Sub specie aeternitatis is Latin for under the aspect of eternity or that which is universally and eternally true. See Spinoza.
    • “sub specie aeternitatis, under the aspect of eternity, in its essential or universal form” Mr. Spitzer asks whether he is “the tailor retailored,” seen from eternity rather than as one man bound by time.
    • It is an honorific expression denoting what is considered to be universally and eternally true, without any reference to or dependence upon temporal facets of reality. The Latin phrase can be rendered in English as “from the perspective of the eternal.” More loosely, it is commonly used to refer to an objective (or theoretically possible alternative) point of view. Spinoza’s “eternal” perspective is reflected in his Ethics (Part V, Prop. XXIII, Scholium), where he applies Euclid’s method (with the use of geometry) to philosophical inquiry, starting with God and nature, before moving to human emotions and the human intellect to reach an understanding of moral philosophy. By proceeding sub specie aeternitatis, Spinoza sought to arrive at an ethical theory that is as precise as Euclid’s Elements. In the history of philosophy, this way of proceeding may be contrasted with Aristotle’s. Aristotle’s methodological differentiations in his “philosophy of human affairs” and his natural philosophy are grounded in the distinction between what is “better known to us” and things “better known in themselves,” or what is “first for us” and what is “first by nature,” a distinction that is deliberately discarded by Spinoza, and also by other modern philosophers. (Wikipedia)
  • “the Newport polka”: No piece called the Newport polka turned up. Newport’s grand hotels had their own dance music in the 1850s, among them the Fillmore House Polka and Carl Bergmann’s Ocean House Polka Redowa, played by the Germania Musical Society (Historic Music of Newport, “The Music of the Grand Hotels of Newport”). The term can also refer to notated music sheets or other polka compositions from or related to Newport.
  • “He had never danced the schottische, the polka, or the minuet”: “schottische” is a 19th-century German partnered country dance, similar to a slower polka, that involves sidesteps and a slow turn, or sometimes a hop. Also known as the “Scottish dance,” it originated in Bohemia and became a popular European and American folk dance, influencing various regional styles and music like Argentina’s chotis and Finland’s jenkka. It is typically performed to music in 4/4 time and is still a part of folk dance traditions worldwide.
    • “polka” is a lively, 19th-century Bohemian (Czech) dance and dance music genre characterized by couples dancing to music in 2/4 time with a basic pattern of quick steps and a hop. Popularized across Europe and the Americas, the name likely derives from the Czech word “půlka,” meaning “half-step,” though it has also been mistakenly linked to Polish women due to the similar-sounding Czech word.
    • “minuet” is a social dance of French origin for two people, usually written in 3/4 time. The English word was adapted from the Italian minuetto and the French minuet. The term also describes the musical form that accompanies the dance, which subsequently developed more fully, often with a longer musical form called the minuet and trio, and was much used as a movement in the early classical symphony. While often stylized in instrumental forms, composers of the period would have been familiar with the popular dance. (Wikipedia)
  • “a little mother-of-pearl Venus comb”: “mother-of-pearl Venus comb” is a species of large predatory sea snail, a marine gastropod mollusk in the family Muricidae, the rock snails or murex snails. The shell of this Indo-Pacific species has a very long siphonal canal and numerous spines. Perfect specimens of the shell are not easily found because of the fragility of the numerous long spines.
  • “cast off, as he would say, these mortal coils”: “When we have shuffled off this mortal coil, / Must give us pause” (William Shakespeare, Hamlet, 3.1). See Shakespeare.
  • “the theft of the great carbuncle from the rajah’s crown”: See the carbuncle from a maharajah’s crown in the Chapter 54 resources. Nathaniel Hawthorne’s tale “The Great Carbuncle” (Twice-Told Tales, 1837) follows seekers who waste their lives hunting a legendary gem in the White Mountains of New Hampshire. See American Writers.
  • “when he had found himself talking to Mozart”: “Mozart” Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart was a prolific and influential composer of the Classical period. Despite his short life, his rapid pace of composition and proficiency from an early age resulted in more than 800 works representing virtually every Western classical genre of his time. (Wikipedia) Born in Salzburg in 1756, he played keyboard and violin and composed by the age of five, and toured Europe as a child with his father, Leopold, and his sister, Nannerl. In Vienna from 1781 he wrote The Marriage of Figaro, Don Giovanni, Così fan tutte, The Magic Flute, the Jupiter Symphony, and many piano concertos, and he died at 35 in 1791, leaving his Requiem unfinished. Nannerl was a celebrated keyboard prodigy whose touring career ended at 17, when she was kept at home; she later taught and performed in Salzburg. She is known to have composed works of music, though no manuscripts survive. In her later years she contributed to the biographical study of her late brother. (Wikipedia) See Music and Composers.
  • “a mere hieroglyph which had dropped from the alphabet of heaven”: “hieroglyph” a stylized picture of an object representing a word, syllable, or sound, as found in ancient Egyptian and other writing systems. See Ancient Egypt.
  • “For what was time?”: Augustine asked the same question: “What then is time? If no one asks me, I know: if I wish to explain it to one that asketh, I know not” (Augustine, Confessions 11.14, trans. E. B. Pusey, 1838). See Augustine and Christian Theology.
  • “old-fashioned Maxwell autos”: Maxwell autos may refer to Maxwell Motor Company which ran from 1904 to 1925 and which later became Chrysler. See the Maxwell automobile in the Chapter 54 resources.
  • “siste viator”: is a Latin phrase meaning “Stop, traveler,” commonly used as an inscription on Roman roadside tombs. The phrase itself is an epitaph, a warning to passersby, encouraging them to pause and consider mortality and their own inevitable end. It invokes themes of mortality, transience, and the universality of death, a common motif in Roman funerary practices.
  • “He had gone on when he could not go on”: Compare the last words of Samuel Beckett’s The Unnamable (1953): “you must go on, I can’t go on, I’ll go on.”
  • “his caput mortuum”: Caput mortuum, dead head, was the alchemists’ name for the worthless residue left in the flask after distillation; painters also gave the name to a dark violet iron-oxide pigment. See Astrology, Alchemy, and Esoterica.
  • “carpe diem”: Peron’s motto was carpe diem. Carpe diem is Latin for seize the day. The phrase is from Horace: “carpe diem, quam minimum credula postero,” seize the day, trusting as little as possible in tomorrow (Horace, Odes 1.11, 23 BC).
  • “hoc opus, hic labor est”: Hoc opus, hic labor est is Latin for “this is the task, this is the labor.” In Virgil’s Aeneid the Sibyl tells Aeneas that the descent to the underworld is easy, but to retrace one’s steps and escape to the upper air, this is the task, this is the labor (Virgil, Aeneid 6.126-129).
    • There are now three different mottos hinting at three different personalities in this chapter. Peron is carpe diem; seize the day. Joachim is hoc opus, hic labor est; this is the task, this is the labor. Mr. Spitzer’s is semper fidelis, semper idem, semper paratus; always faithful, always the same, always ready.
  • “his little salts and peppers winging through the mist”: The peppered moth is speckled black and white like salt and pepper; in sooty industrial England a black form all but replaced it, a famous case of natural selection. See Butterflies and Moths.
  • “In every gambler’s make-up”: Gambling or betting or gaming is the wagering of something of value on an event with an uncertain outcome with the intent of winning something else of value. Gambling dates back to the Paleolithic period, before written history. Financial Investments are generally not considered gambling when they meet certain criteria. Studies show that though many people participate in gambling as a form of recreation or to earn an income, gambling, like any behavior involving variation in brain chemistry, can become a behavioral addiction. Behavioral addiction can occur with all the negative consequences in a person’s life minus the physical issues faced by people who compulsively engage in drug and alcohol abuse. Problem gambling has multiple symptoms. Gamblers often gamble to try to win back money they have lost, and some gamble to relieve feelings of helplessness and anxiety. Gamblers may exhibit a number of cognitive and motivational biases that distort the perceived odds of events and that influence their preferences for gambles. Addiction by Design by Natasha Dow Schull shows how the manipulation of gambling pulls players into a trancelike state in which daily worries, social demands, and even bodily awareness fade away. Once in the zone, gambling addicts play not to win but simply to keep playing, for as long as possible, even at the cost of physical and economic exhaustion. Gamblers seek to lose themselves while the gambling industry seeks profit. Schull describes how the industry designs systems to profit from the maximum amount from gamblers and manipulates human psychology. Flag: after 1964, Natasha Dow Schüll’s Addiction by Design (2012). See Gambling and Playing Cards.
  • “alack and a day”: is an archaic interjection used to express sorrow, regret, grief, or a sense of misfortune, essentially meaning “woe to the day!” or “shame to the day!” the event occurred. It’s a longer form of the word “alack,” which itself functions similarly to “alas.”
  • “playing the bones”: Dice were first made of bone, so gamblers still call them bones; to play or roll the bones is to shoot dice. See Gambling and Playing Cards.
  • “coming when the groundhog came not”: On Groundhog Day, 2 February, the groundhog is said to come out of its burrow; if it sees its shadow, there will be six more weeks of winter. Punxsutawney, Pennsylvania, has kept the day since 1887.
  • “crazy as the old bank-teller or parimutuel man”: Parimutuel is a betting system in which all bets of a particular type are placed together in a pool; taxes and the house-take, or vigorish, are deducted, and payoff odds are calculated by sharing the pool among all winning bets. In some countries it is known as the tote after the totalisator, which calculates and displays bets already made. The parimutuel system is used in gambling on horse racing, greyhound racing, jai alai, and other sporting events of relatively short duration in which participants finish in a ranked order. A modified parimutuel system is also used in some lottery games. Parimutuel betting differs from fixed-odds betting in that the final payout is not determined until the pool is closed, in fixed-odds betting, the payout is agreed at the time the bet is made. Parimutuel gambling is frequently state-regulated, and it is offered in many places where gambling is otherwise illegal. Parimutuel gambling is often also offered at off-track facilities, where players may bet on the events without actually being present to observe them in person. (Wikipedia) The Paris entrepreneur Joseph Oller invented it in 1867. See Gambling and Playing Cards.
