Chapter 24

← Chapter 23 · Home · Chapter 25 →

Content note: Vera’s mother, Catherine Cartwheel, is addicted to opium.

Summary

Vera’s thoughts move through the household. The servants have absorbed Catherine’s dreams so completely that they argue whether it is Roman in the morning and Greek in the afternoon, and assign rooms to famous phantom guests. Catherine plans her own funeral, calls Athens on a telephone wired only to the servants’ quarters, and tries to reach Cousin Hannah on a number long disconnected. Mr. Spitzer will come again in the evening with his vague certainties about heaven. The servants see the black coachman and the white horses, an old valet waits on Wellington, and a gardener believes he is Potiphar’s wife. Mr. Spitzer, in Catherine’s eyes, is a roundhouse for trains that run no more, a ghost ship with the captain’s table set for two. Vera asks herself to whom she can turn with her questions about love, marriage, birth, and death, and finds no one.

Characters present

Catherine Cartwheel · Miss MacIntosh · Joachim Spitzer · Vera Cartwheel · Cousin Hannah · The Black Coachman

Concepts present

Themes: Death and Mortality · Illusion and Reality · Isolation and Connection · Madness and Sanity · Music, Sound, and Silence · Society, Class, and Race · Time

Symbols: Horses and Carriages · Moon and Stars · Roses and Flowers

Philosophy: Augustine and Christian Theology · Plato and Platonism · Spinoza

Allusions: Astronomy · Exploration and the Poles · Genesis · Music and Composers · Napoleon and Wellington · Shakespeare · The History of Opium

Key passages

From the research

  • The servants in the household are described as deeply immersed in the dream-like atmosphere created by Vera’s mother. They engage in elaborate fantasies, imagining themselves serving imaginary guests: historic figures, fictional personages, and legendary characters. This passage illustrates how the servants reflect and perpetuate Catherine’s opium-induced dreams, blurring the line between reality and illusion. For example, the old valet believes he serves Wellington, and the gardener imagines himself the spouse of Potiphar, while the Irish housemaid speaks only to herself to avoid confusion. The servants’ acceptance of this unreal environment underscores the theme of escapism and how the household is trapped in a timeless, surreal bubble.
  • The descriptions of the house being filled with imaginary guests sleeping “tier above tier” according to rank and station, the lighting of fires for guests who will never arrive, and the arrangement of Renaissance chairs for intimate conversation depict a grand but empty social world. This passage powerfully conveys Catherine’s craving for social connection and grandeur, yet it is all sustained by illusion. The “mad lady retouching her make-up” and the drunken second butler stumbling over her train amplify the eerie, ghostly quality of the household’s existence.
  • Catherine is obsessed with planning her own funeral and other grand events involving the dead returning to life, a motif that symbolically represents her preoccupation with mortality and the afterlife. Her social secretaries, invitations to ambassadors of Heaven and Hell, and the presence of fashionable dogs highlight her attempt to impose order and meaning on a world that is inherently chaotic and illusory. This passage reveals her complex psychology of wanting to be in control, her detachment from reality, and her engagement with the fantastic.
  • Catherine’s attempts to communicate by telephone with historical figures, relatives, and distant acquaintances only bring frustration and confusion. She calls Athens but reaches Rome, leaves messages for Emperor Hadrian who is never there, and receives only “a cackle of old hen voices” when calling Boston. The telephone is later revealed to be connected only to the servants’ quarters, emphasizing the isolation and breakdown of real connection. This passage poignantly illustrates Catherine’s alienation and the futility of her attempts to reach beyond her own dream-world.
  • Mr. Spitzer, described as a “roundhouse of the trains which run no more” and a “ghost ship with broken mainmasts,” symbolizes the unreliability and futility of seeking certainty or solace in Catherine’s world. He is a poor companion to her “eternal illness,” representing the failure of rationality or conventional comfort in the face of her decaying mental state. His presence contrasts with Vera’s desire for answers about life, love, and death, highlighting the gap between illusion and reality.
  • The chapter ends with Vera contemplating to whom she might turn for answers or to profound personal questions. This passage captures the existential uncertainty and search for meaning that underpin the narrative, emphasizing that even amidst the surreal, Vera seeks some grounding or truth.
  • “My mother herself might be, of course, the only genuine unbeliever, as everyone recognized, for she was very clever. My mother placed her faith only in the unreal.”

Questions and observations

Reading closely

  • “Just to hear the servants talk, anyone might have thought they were all real… especially when they were unreal.” What does Vera mean by “especially”?
  • Catherine’s telephone “was connected only with the servants’ quarters.” Who answers her?
  • “How else should they keep their jobs?” What do the servants gain by believing?

Characters

  • Catherine is “the only genuine unbeliever.” How can the dreamer be the one who doesn’t believe?
  • Mr. Spitzer is “a ghost ship… the captain’s table set for two, none aboard.” What does Catherine see in him?
  • Vera sets Miss MacIntosh, “coarse-grained and ruddy,” against Catherine’s illusions, yet still asks, “To whom should I have turned”? Why not to her?

Connections

  • The empty ship of Chapter 22 had “the captain’s table still set for two or three or four.” Why does the image return here?
  • In Chapter 14, Catherine said the white horses were her will and the coachman her conscience. What are the servants seeing?
  • Catherine calls the Bishop of Hippo and Hadrian, and Miss MacIntosh scolded Hadrian and Constantine (Chapter 22). What do the two women share?

Reflection

  • Can a household share a dream?
  • What does it cost to keep one’s job by believing?
  • To whom do we turn with the questions that matter most?

Research: Characters

Catherine Cartwheel (Vera’s mother)

  • Central figure, caught in opium dreams, presiding over an imaginary world filled with historical, mythological, and invented guests.
  • She is fully immersed in her visionary, dream-like state, discussing grand affairs and social invitations as if real.
  • She is aware of her illusionary world but maintains a clever detachment, placing faith only in the unreal.
  • Her attempts to reach historical or imaginary figures and the failure of these calls reveal her isolation and the limits of her dream world.

Miss MacIntosh

  • Practical, grounded, and coarse-grained, she offers contrast to Catherine and the servants’ fantastical world.
  • She is a companion to Vera and represents the voice of reality amidst chaos.

The Servants

  • Immersed in Catherine’s dreams, they adopt roles and beliefs reflecting the surreal environment.
  • Some believe they serve historical figures (e.g., Wellington), others think they live in impossible settings (a forest of cuckoo clocks).
  • They maintain the household’s illusion by preparing for imaginary guests and engaging in conversations about impossible events.
  • The servants’ conversation about imaginary guests and their roles within the dream world encapsulates the blending of fantasy and reality.

Mr. Spitzer

  • A mysterious and somewhat unsatisfactory companion to Catherine, embodying confusion and lost memories.
  • He represents uncertainty about earthly matters while espousing nebulous spiritual certainties about an ultimate Heaven.
  • His characterization as uncertain, evasive, and disconnected from his own memories contrasts with Catherine’s intense visionary life, highlighting themes of memory and reality.

Research: Themes

Reality versus Illusion

See: Illusion and Reality

  • The chapter immerses the reader in a world where the boundaries between real and imaginary are fluid. Catherine’s opium dreams populate the house with imaginary guests, servants who believe in elaborate fantasies, and environments that shift unpredictably.
  • The servants interact with these illusions as if real, discussing imaginary dignitaries, polishing imaginary shoes, and setting places for guests who never arrive. This highlights how illusion can become a shared reality in certain states of mind.

Madness and Sanity

See: Madness and Sanity

  • The novel delves into how prolonged exposure to Catherine’s dreams affects the servants, leading some to lose their grip on reality and adopt bizarre identities or behaviors (e.g., thinking they serve Wellington or living among cuckoo clocks).
  • This theme raises questions about the fragile line between sanity and madness in a closed, surreal environment.

Time and Space Distortion

See: Time

  • The house is timeless and spaceless in a conventional sense, populated by figures from different centuries, places, and mythologies simultaneously.
  • Imaginary guests from various epochs co-exist, and the servants debate the time of day as Roman or Greek, reflecting a dislocation from normal temporal experience.

Isolation and Communication

See: Isolation and Connection · Music, Sound, and Silence

  • Catherine attempts to communicate with distant or deceased figures through a telephone that only connects to the servants’ quarters, symbolizing her isolation and failed attempts at meaningful contact.
  • This motif underscores the theme of disconnection between Catherine’s inner world and external reality.

Death and the Afterlife

See: Death and Mortality

  • Catherine’s dreams include discussions about her own funeral rites and arrangements for the dead returning to life, blending death with ongoing social rituals.
  • The presence of flowers associated with death and the continual reference to the “dead horses” and “black coachman” suggest a liminal space between life and death.

Research: Symbols and Imagery

Imaginary Guests

See: Illusion and Reality

  • Imaginary guests and historical figures represent the blending of past, present, and fantasy, showing how Catherine’s mind holds vast, impossible histories simultaneously.

Black and White Horses and Coachman

See: Horses and Carriages · The Black Coachman

  • Black and white horses and coachman symbolize the passage between realms, possibly life and death, or reality and illusion. Earlier (Chapter 14) Catherine said the white horses were her will and the coachman was her conscience.

The Telephone

See: Isolation and Connection

  • The telephone is a device meant for communication but only connecting to servants’ quarters, symbolizing failed outreach and isolation.

Bronze Chrysanthemums

See: Death and Mortality

  • Bronze chrysanthemums are flowers for the dead, symbolizing mourning and death’s persistent presence.

Cuckoo Clocks and Elephants

See: Time

  • Cuckoo clocks and elephants represent distorted time and impossible realities within the servants’ transformed perceptions.

Snow Crystals and Halos

See: Moon and Stars

  • Snow crystals and halos are visual symbols of the dreamlike, kaleidoscopic nature of Catherine’s world, with multiple suns, moons, and shapes reinforcing the surreal atmosphere.

Research: Resources

  • “the servants in the servants’ quarters”: In the 1800s, servants were an essential part of households, performing a variety of tasks, including cooking, cleaning, and caring for children. They were often treated poorly, with low wages and long hours. In the early 1900s, servants worked in large households of wealthy families, performing a variety of tasks. They were expected to follow strict rules and hierarchies, and had little personal freedom. In Chicago, domestic work meant “long hours, low status, lack of freedom, and close supervision”; a reporter working undercover in 1901 toiled 15 hours a day for $2.75 a week plus room and board. By the late 1800s the work fell increasingly to Irish, German, Scandinavian, and Polish women, and in 1900 Black women, 4 percent of the city’s wage-earning women, were 30 percent of its domestic workers (Encyclopedia of Chicago).
  • “the life-sized chessmen moving across parterres of black and white”: Alice becomes a pawn on a living chessboard in Lewis Carroll’s Through the Looking-Glass (1871).
  • “old Beau Brummells coming to life in a crystal ballroom”: Beau Brummell (1778-1840) is a Regency Era figure who later became associated as a dandy, with fashion, and anything of good quality.
  • “one who had discovered a new planet, one who believed he dwelled on Uranus”: William Herschel discovered Uranus in 1781, the first planet found with a telescope. See Astronomy.
  • “Some had seen the black coachman”: The coachman and the white horses of Chapter 14. See The Black Coachman, Horses and Carriages, and the Chapter 14 resources.
  • “my mother’s opium dreams”: Before 1900, the typical opiate addict in America was an upper-class or middle-class white woman. As long as the opium user was a sick old lady there was no push to punish users. See The History of Opium.
  • “seemed to think that he was waiting on Wellington”: Duke of Wellington was a leading figure in 19th-century Britain, victor over Napoleon at Waterloo (1815). See Napoleon and Wellington.
  • “he lived in a forest of cuckoo clocks”: The cuckoo clock came from the Black Forest of Germany in the eighteenth century. See Time.
  • “Hannibal driving the elephants over the Alps”: Hannibal of Carthage crossed the Alps with his army and elephants in 218 BC to invade Italy.
  • “Admiral Peary was to be put into the blue room”: Admiral Robert Peary. See Exploration and the Poles and the Chapter 2 resources.
  • “which was already occupied by Plato’s boat”: Plato’s boat might refer to the Ship of State by Plato (Republic, Book 6). It is a metaphor comparing governing a city-state to being the captain of a ship and only philosopher kings should rule. See Plato and Platonism.
  • “Sir Christopher Wren and Jenny Lind were to be put into the rose”: Sir Christopher Wren was a highly acclaimed English architect, astronomer, and mathematician, the builder of St Paul’s Cathedral (1675-1710). Jenny Lind, “the Swedish Nightingale,” was a Swedish opera singer of the 19th century who toured America for P. T. Barnum in 1850-52. See Music and Composers.
  • “Spinoza and Shakespeare and Mrs. Sydington were already in the green”: Spinoza was a Dutch philosopher, author of the Ethics (1677). Shakespeare was a famous British playwright. See Spinoza and Shakespeare.
  • “Or was she a unicorn wearing a necklace?”: In the Lady and the Unicorn tapestries (c. 1500), the lady lays her necklace in a casket beneath the words “À mon seul désir.”
  • “believed he was the spouse to Potiphar, the Egyptian captain”: Potiphar’s wife tried to seduce Joseph and then accused him (Genesis 39). The gardener believes he is the wife. See Genesis.
  • “the bronze-colored chrysanthemums which are the flowers for the dead”: In France and Italy, chrysanthemums are laid on graves on All Saints’ Day. See Death and Mortality and Roses and Flowers.
  • “a sea change, a transformation”: “Nothing of him that doth fade, / But doth suffer a sea-change / Into something rich and strange” (The Tempest 1.2). See Shakespeare.
  • “Some were lions with wings”: The winged lion of St. Mark, as in Chapter 16. See the Chapter 16 resources.
  • “many mock suns and moons”: Sun dogs (parhelia) and moon dogs are bright spots beside the sun or moon, made by light bending through ice crystals, often on a halo. See Astronomy.
  • “The horizontal lady”: Catherine’s name for herself in Chapter 19. See Catherine Cartwheel and the Chapter 19 resources.
  • “some antiquated copy of the Boston or Philadelphia telephone directory… circa 1905”: The first telephone directory, a single card of fifty names, was printed in New Haven in 1878.
  • “She had called the Bishop of Hippo”: Bishop of Hippo is Saint Augustine who was also a theologian and philosopher. See Augustine and Christian Theology.
  • “She had left her messages for the Emperor Hadrian”: Emperor Hadrian was a Roman emperor from 117 to 138. See the Chapter 22 resources.
  • “King Canute had gone on a long voyage”: King Canute or Cnut the Great was King of England, Denmark, and Norway. See the Chapter 22 resources.
  • “How did it happen she never found the Lowells or the Saltonstalls at home”: The Boston Brahmins: “And this is good old Boston, / The home of the bean and the cod, / Where the Lowells talk only to Cabots, / And the Cabots talk only to God” (John Collins Bossidy, 1910).
  • “Why had Cousin Hannah never called”: Cousin Hannah. See Cousin Hannah.
  • “The Duchess of Spode had gone to a watering place”: The Duchess of Spode may refer to an English brand of pottery: Josiah Spode’s works at Stoke-on-Trent, founded in 1770.
  • “she should send her gold-turbaned blackamoor”: “Blackamoor” figures, carved and gilded Black servants in turbans, were a fashion of European decorative art. They turned enslaved people into ornaments. See Society, Class, and Race.
  • “Mr. Spitzer was a roundhouse of the trains which run no more”: In Dickens’s “The Signal-Man” (1866), a railway signalman is haunted by a ghost and a red danger light before a fatal crash, which fits Young’s “the red where there should be the green.” See Joachim Spitzer.
  • “a ghost ship with broken mainmasts and torn sails, the captain’s table set for two, none aboard”: The Mary Celeste was found adrift and abandoned in 1872, her crew gone. The empty ship of Chapter 22 had its table set “for two or three or four.” See the Chapter 22 resources.

Vocabulary

Blackamoor
An old term for a Black African or any dark-skinned person, common in European art and in decorative figures of Black servants. It is now considered offensive.
Celestial
Heavenly; of the sky.
Certitude
Certainty.
Chandelier
A branched hanging light.
Chimera
A monster of Greek myth, part lion, part goat, part serpent; any wild, impossible fancy.
Comme il faut
French for “as it should be”; proper, correct.
Concatenation
A linked series.
Conch
A large sea snail with a spiraled shell that can be blown like a horn. Held to the ear, it seems to hold the sound of the sea.
Cormorant
A large black diving seabird.
Emir
A commander or prince in the Islamic world.
Emissary
A messenger or agent.
Euphemistic
Using a mild word in place of a harsh one.
Halo
A ring of light around the sun or moon, caused by ice crystals high in thin clouds. In art, a ring of light around the head of a saint.
Mandarin
A high-ranking official of imperial China.
Medusa
A jellyfish in its free-swimming, bell-shaped stage, named for the Gorgon of Greek myth whose hair was snakes.
Obsequies
Funeral rites.
Parterre
An ornamental garden of flower beds laid out in a pattern. A parterred floor is inlaid in patterned sections.
Porte-cochere
A covered entrance where a carriage stops to let passengers out.
Roundhouse
A circular building for storing and turning locomotives.
Taffeta
A crisp, shiny silk.
Trackwalker
A railway worker who walks the line to inspect it.
chapter-11:
Chapter 11

← Chapter 10 · Home · Chapter 12 →

Summary

In this short chapter, Vera wonders how she will bear her isolation. She cannot live on illusion as her mother does, and she trusts herself to know where the dream ends and reality begins, as Miss MacIntosh taught her. She imagines how far her mother has traveled through her opium dream, which runs by the alphabet. The P’s must be past by now. The Q’s are hard company: the Queen Charlotte Islands, and the Queen Maud Mountains, who visits as a frigid, silent house guest in a lace skirt five hundred miles long. The R’s are the charming ones, guests who never met in life: Mr. Res Tacamah, the drug bottle; a pharaoh who unwraps into Rameses I, II, and III; Roland, Rimski-Korsakov, Sir Joshua Reynolds, Rhadamanthus, and Sir Walter Raleigh, who takes off his head with his plumed hat. Mr. Spitzer has missed them all, and Catherine will tell him so.

Characters present

Vera Cartwheel · Catherine Cartwheel · Joachim Spitzer · Miss MacIntosh · Mr. Res Tacamah

Concepts present

Themes: Dreams and Imagination · Grief, Loss, and Mourning · Identity and the Self · Illusion and Reality · Isolation and Connection · Memory and the Past · Society, Class, and Race

Symbols: Birds · Mountains · Opium · Snow, Ice, and Winter · The Bus and the Journey · The Sea and Water

Philosophy: Astrology, Alchemy, and Esoterica

Allusions: Ancient Egypt · Astronomy · Dante · Exploration and the Poles · Fairy Tales and Folklore · Genesis · Greek Mythology · Homer’s Epics · Music and Composers · Romantic Poets · Shakespeare · Sir Walter Raleigh · The History of Opium

Key passages

From the research

  • Everything Catherine sees in this chapter is Vera’s guess. “She must have reached,” “Perhaps my mother had already passed on.” Vera, who prides herself on knowing where the dream ends, spends the chapter dreaming her mother’s dream for her.
  • The chapter opens with Vera pondering how to endure isolation, recognizing that unlike her mother Catherine, mere illusions are insufficient. She is aware of the boundary between dream and reality, a lesson imparted by Miss MacIntosh, who denies the existence of what does not exist. This sets the thematic framework of the chapter, highlighting the tension between illusion and reality, and the difficulty of coping with solitude without resorting to self-deception.
  • Catherine is described as being in a “wakeful coma,” journeying through an opiate-induced voyage through various symbolic “places” starting with the letter P (Pericles, Penelope’s web, the Pleiades, penguins) and moving onto the Q’s and R’s. This voyage represents a surreal and metaphorical experience, suggesting that Catherine’s consciousness moves through layers of history, mythology, geography, and fantasy. These symbolic names imply a vast, intricate mental landscape, blending real and imagined elements.
  • The Q’s include the Queen Charlotte Islands, Queen Maud Mountains, and a naval battle, each representing different aspects of isolation, coldness, and distance. Queen Maud Mountains, in particular, is portrayed as an imperious, frigid visitor to Catherine’s bedroom, embodying a chilling and overwhelming presence that silences and immobilizes. The description of her skirt as “five hundred miles long and made of pure Brussels lace” evokes a surreal and vast majesty, emphasizing Catherine’s awe and envy.
  • Catherine’s mental journey perhaps continues to the R’s, a group connected by “silken relationships” despite never having met in reality. This assembly includes historical, mythical, and symbolic figures such as Mr. Res Tacamah (a drug bottle), the Egyptian pharaoh Rameses I, II, III (representing fragmented selves and layered identities), runes, royal masts, Roland, Rimski-Korsakov, Sir Joshua Reynolds, and others. The richness of this imagery suggests a complex and paradoxical inner world where time, space, and identity blur.
  • Mr. Spitzer appears as a figure who perpetually misses Catherine’s gatherings of extraordinary company, including great composers, painters, and mythological judges like Rhadamanthus. There is a tone of irony and loss here, as Mr. Spitzer is condemned for forgotten crimes and fails to witness Catherine’s vibrant and mysterious social realm, underscoring themes of absence and missed connection.
  • Among the remarkable guests, Sir Walter Raleigh stands out, described in a lavish white satin suit and associated with a society devoted to atheistic propositions, such as man existing before Adam and God being an idea or even “dog spelled backward.” This philosophical and irreverent note introduces questions about belief, existence, and the nature of divinity, adding a layer of intellectual challenge to Catherine’s dreamlike world.

Questions and observations

Reading closely

  • Catherine’s calculations admit “no theory of loss in the universe where all things were lost.” Who is right, Catherine or Vera?
  • Queen Maud Mountains hides her face behind a parasol “which happened to be my mother’s.” What does Catherine see when she looks at her guest?
  • The pharaoh learns he “had been partitioned into many selves without his knowing it.” Who else in the novel has been divided this way?

Characters

  • Vera says no “mere illusion would suffice me,” then imagines her mother’s dream in detail. How sure is she of the line between them?
  • Catherine is “this great hostess who was in exile.” What is she exiled from?
  • Rhadamanthus finds Mr. Spitzer “guilty of many forgotten crimes.” What crime might Catherine charge him with?

Connections

  • Mr. Res Tacamah was “the drug bottle with ears” in Chapter 2. What has changed in him?
  • Mr. Spitzer’s silent music in Chapter 2 meets Rimski-Korsakov’s music “which was not altogether silent.” Why does Catherine compare them?
  • Raleigh asks to be called “Ocean or Water.” How does the sea keep entering Catherine’s closed room?

Reflection

  • Is there a kind of loneliness that imagination makes worse rather than better?
  • Catherine never leaves her bed, so the mountain comes to her. What is gained and lost by living this way?
  • Can a person know where her own dreams end?

Research: Characters

Vera Cartwheel

  • Reflects on isolation and the difficulty of enduring it without resorting to illusions.
  • Maintains a clear boundary between dream and reality.

Catherine Cartwheel (Vera’s Mother)

  • Existing in a semi-conscious, dreamlike coma.
  • Her mental state is depicted as a voyage through symbolic landscapes and figures.
  • Acts as a hostess to a surreal assembly of historical, mythological, and symbolic guests.
  • Denies loss, existing in a universe where things are lost but preserved in other forms.

Mr. Spitzer

  • Absent from every gathering; Catherine will remind him afterward of all he missed.
  • Tied to legal errands and earthly concerns, contrasted with Catherine’s ethereal dream world.
  • Judged by Rhadamanthus in the dream for forgotten crimes, symbolizing guilt and judgment.

Miss MacIntosh

  • Her denial of “those things which did not exist” is the lesson Vera leans on to tell dream from reality.

Research: Themes

Isolation and Endurance

See: Isolation and Connection

  • Vera contemplates how to endure isolation, contrasting herself with her mother, who copes differently through dreams and illusions.
  • Vera is grounded in reality, aware of the dividing line between dream and reality, unlike her mother who dwells in a liminal, dreamlike state.

Dream versus Reality

See: Illusion and Reality · Dreams and Imagination

  • Catherine inhabits a dream world where places and people symbolize different stages or elements of her mental and emotional journey.
  • Her dream is a voyage through alphabetic symbolic “stations” (P’s, Q’s, R’s), each representing complex ideas, places, or characters.
  • Catherine’s dream reflects a universe where loss is denied or transformed rather than accepted.

Memory and Loss

See: Memory and the Past · Grief, Loss, and Mourning

  • Catherine’s dream denies loss, imagining a universe where things are lost but not lost forever.
  • This suggests a coping mechanism for dealing with grief or fading consciousness.

Identity and Multiplicity

See: Identity and the Self

  • Catherine’s dream involves figures like Rameses I, II, and III, representing fragmented selves and layered identities.
  • The dream hints at disjointed time and space, and the coexistence of past and present selves.

Research: Symbols and Imagery

Alphabetical Journey (P’s, Q’s, R’s)

See: The Bus and the Journey

  • Represents a symbolic progression or mental voyage.
  • P’s include Pericles, Admiral Peary, Penelope’s web, the Pleiades, and formal penguins.
  • Q’s include Queen Charlotte Islands, Queen Maud Mountains, and a naval battle.
  • R’s include a wide array of figures and concepts: Mr. Res Tacamah (a drug bottle, Catherine’s opium/laudanum), Egyptian pharaohs (Rameses I-III), runes, roulades, rubrics, royal masts, rose windows, Roman numerals, riddles, red-caps in Grand Central Station, Roland, Rimski-Korsakov, Sir Joshua Reynolds, the Great Ram constellation, Rhadamanthus, Sir Walter Raleigh, and more.

Queen Maud Mountains

See: Mountains

  • Personified as a cold, snobbish, imperious houseguest, symbolizing perhaps a harsh, distant presence.
  • The detail of her five-hundred-mile-long Brussels lace skirt evokes grandeur, coldness, and isolation.

Mr. Res Tacamah

See: Mr. Res Tacamah · Opium

  • A symbolic figure representing a drug bottle and shifting identities, suggesting notions of altered consciousness or dependency.

Rameses I, II, III

See: Ancient Egypt

  • Symbolize fragmented identities and the confusion of time within the dream.
  • The pharaoh unwrapping himself reveals the layered nature of self and memory.

Sir Walter Raleigh

See: Sir Walter Raleigh

  • Imagined with a white satin suit embroidered with pearls and gems.
  • His decapitation and request to be called “Ocean or Water” suggest themes of transformation, fluidity, and martyrdom or sacrifice.
  • Raleigh was beheaded in 1618.
  • Represents atheistic propositions and philosophical skepticism within the dream.

Research: Resources

  • “entertaining the P’s, the Q’s, the R’s”: “Mind your P’s and Q’s,” the old warning to watch one’s manners, suits a hostess who greets every guest by letter.
  • “her opiate voyage through nowhere”: Thomas De Quincey’s opium dreams in Confessions of an English Opium-Eater (1821) carried him to Egypt and the East: “I was buried, for a thousand years, in stone coffins, with mummies and sphinxes.” See Opium, The History of Opium, and the Chapter 4 resources.
  • “Pericles”: Pericles (c. 495-429 BC) led Athens in its golden age and had the Parthenon built. See Shakespeare.
    • Shakespeare’s Pericles, Prince of Tyre (c. 1608) is a voyage play. Its hero loses his wife, buried at sea in a chest, and his daughter, and finds both again.
  • “Admiral Peary”: Robert E. Peary claimed the North Pole in 1909 and was made a rear admiral in 1911. Matthew Henson, the Black explorer beside him, by his own account reached the spot first and got little credit for decades. In 1897 Peary brought six Inuit from Greenland to New York for the American Museum of Natural History, and four died within months. The museum staged a fake burial for the boy Minik while it kept his father Qisuk’s skeleton. See Exploration and the Poles, Society, Class, and Race, and the Chapter 2 resources.
  • “Penelope’s web”: In the Odyssey, Penelope weaves a shroud for Laertes by day and unravels it by night to hold off the suitors. See Homer’s Epics and the Chapter 5 resources.
  • “the Pleiades”: The Pleiades are the seven daughters of Atlas, set in the sky as a star cluster in Taurus. They return at the end of the chapter in Ronsard’s Pléiade. See Astronomy and Greek Mythology.
  • “a naval battle, an island, and a continent”: The battle is never named. Quiberon Bay (1759) is the famous Q: Admiral Hawke chased the French fleet into a rocky bay off Brittany in a November gale.
  • “Queen Charlotte Islands”: The Queen Charlotte Islands, off the Pacific coast of Canada, were named in 1787 for the ship Queen Charlotte, which was named for George III’s queen. They are the home of the Haida and are now called Haida Gwaii. See Birds.
    • The gyrfalcon is the largest of the falcons, a bird of the Arctic. White gyrfalcons were gifts for kings, and Catherine kept falconer’s gloves in Chapter 2.
    • Goldeneyes are diving ducks called “whistlers” for the sound of their wings in flight.
  • “a wild swan absent, one wild swan more”: In Andersen’s “The Wild Swans” (1838), eleven brothers are turned into swans, and their sister weaves nettle shirts to free them. The last shirt is unfinished, and the youngest is left with a swan’s wing. See Fairy Tales and Folklore and Birds.
  • “the proud, cold, utterly snobbish Queen Maud Mountains”: The Queen Maud Mountains rise at the head of the Ross Ice Shelf, on the south edge of the Ross Sea. Roald Amundsen found them in 1911 on his way to the South Pole and named them for Queen Maud of Norway, a daughter of King Edward VII of England. Queen Maud Land is a different region of Antarctica, claimed by Norway. See Exploration and the Poles, Mountains, and Snow, Ice, and Winter.
    • The Ross Sea, a deep bay of the Southern Ocean, is named for James Clark Ross, who sailed into it in 1841.
  • “colder than Boston society”: John Collins Bossidy’s toast (1910): “And this is good old Boston, / The home of the bean and the cod, / Where the Lowells talk only to Cabots, / And the Cabots talk only to God.” See Society, Class, and Race.
  • “coming like the mountain to Mahomet”: The proverb comes from Francis Bacon’s essay “Of Boldness” (1625). Mahomet called a hill to come to him, and when it would not, he said, “If the hill will not come to Mahomet, Mahomet will go to the hill.” Here the mountain comes to Catherine, who never leaves her bed. See Mountains.
  • “made of pure Brussels lace”: Brussels lace is well known for its delicacy and beauty. Originally it was only made from the finest spun linen thread, which was spun in dark damp rooms to keep the thread from becoming too brittle. Only one ray of light was allowed into the room, and it was arranged so that it fell upon the thread. (Wikipedia) See Clothing, Hats, and Skirts.
  • “pyramid-shaped ices”: Ices were molded into shapes for grand dinners. The pyramids Catherine serves come just before the pharaoh arrives. See Ancient Egypt.
  • “Mr. Res Tacamah who was the drug bottle”: His name may join Rx to tacamahac. Rx stands for the Latin recipe, “take,” at the head of a prescription, and tacamahac is an aromatic resin used in ointments and incense. In Chapter 2 he was “the drug bottle with ears to hear her ravings.” See Mr. Res Tacamah, Opium, and the Chapter 2 resources.
  • “Rameses I, II, III”: The royal mummies were found in 1881 in a hidden tomb at Deir el-Bahri, where priests had moved and rewrapped them, some in other kings’ coffins. Shelley’s “Ozymandias” (1818) takes its name from the Greek form of Ramesses II’s throne name, User-maat-re. See Ancient Egypt, Romantic Poets, and the Chapter 2 resources.
    • Menpehtyre Ramesses I (or Ramses) was the founding pharaoh of ancient Egypt’s 19th Dynasty. The dates for his short reign are not completely known but the timeline of late 1292-1290 BC is frequently cited as well as 1295-1294 BC. While Ramesses I was the founder of the 19th Dynasty, his brief reign mainly serves to mark the transition between the reign of Horemheb, who had stabilized Egypt in the late 18th Dynasty, and the rule of the powerful pharaohs of his own dynasty, in particular his son Seti I, and grandson Ramesses II. (Wikipedia)
    • Ramesses II, commonly known as Ramesses the Great, was an Egyptian pharaoh. He was the third ruler of the Nineteenth Dynasty. Along with Thutmose III of the Eighteenth Dynasty, he is often regarded as the greatest, most celebrated, and most powerful pharaoh of the New Kingdom, which itself was the most powerful period of ancient Egypt. (Wikipedia)
    • Usermaatre Meryamun Ramesses III was the second pharaoh of the Twentieth Dynasty in ancient Egypt. Some scholars date his reign from 26 March 1186 to 15 April 1155 BC, and he is considered the last pharaoh of the New Kingdom to have wielded substantial power. (Wikipedia) He took Ramesses II’s throne name and modeled his temple at Medinet Habu on Ramesses II’s, one king dreaming another’s dreams.
  • “partitioned into many selves without his knowing it”: The Egyptians held that a person was made of many parts: the ka, the life force; the ba, the soul that flies from the tomb; the name; the shadow; and the heart, weighed at judgment. See Ancient Egypt and Identity and the Self.
  • “runes, roulades, rubrics, royal masts, rose windows, Roman numerals, many riddles, many red-caps in the Grand Central Station”: Catherine’s R’s run from letters and songs to ships, churches, and numbers.
    • Runes are letters from ancient Germanic alphabets, also called runic alphabets or futharks, which were used primarily to write Germanic languages before the adoption of the Roman alphabet. They are also recognized as symbols with mysterious or magical significance, often used in divination and fortune-telling. Runes were typically carved into wood, stone, or bone.
    • A roulade is an elaborate embellishment of several notes sung to one syllable.
    • A rubric is a word or text written in red ink for emphasis. In the Book of Common Prayer, the rubrics are the instructions printed in red, the stage directions of the services in Chapter 10.
    • A royal mast is the topmost section of a sailing ship’s mast, above the topgallant.
    • A rose window is a round window of stained glass found in churches and cathedrals.
    • Roman numerals are a numeric system created by ancient Romans. They number Rameses I, II, III.
    • A red-cap is a railroad porter. Grand Central’s red caps were mostly Black men from 1909 on. The terminal did not pay them, and they lived on tips until the 1940s. In 1937 red caps organized the International Brotherhood of Red Caps.
    • Grand Central, officially Grand Central Terminal (1913), stands at 42nd Street and Park Avenue in Midtown Manhattan.
  • “Roland who was killed at Roncevalles”: Roland was a military leader under Charlemagne who died at the Battle of Roncevaux Pass in 778, when Basques ambushed Charlemagne’s rear guard. The Song of Roland (c. 1100) turns them into Saracens and has Roland blow his horn too late. In Dante’s Divine Comedy, Roland is named Orlando and placed in the Heaven of Mars with others who fought for the faith (Paradiso 18). See Dante.
  • “Rimski-Korsakov who never came except in Mr. Spitzer’s absence”: Rimski-Korsakov was a prominent Russian composer, a member of the Mighty Handful, five composers who drew on Russian folk music, and a significant figure in shaping Russian classical music. He is known for his operas, orchestral pieces like Scheherazade (1888), named for the bride who tells a tale night after night to stay alive, and Capriccio Espagnol. He sailed around the world as a young naval officer. See Music and Composers and Fairy Tales and Folklore.
    • “music which was not altogether silent”: Mr. Spitzer has written “only silent music, that which, for many years now, no one else had ever heard” (Chapter 2).
  • “Sir Joshua Reynolds”: Sir Joshua Reynolds (1723-1792) was an English painter who specialized in portraits. He promoted the “Grand Style” in painting, which depended on idealization of the imperfect. He was a founder and first president of the Royal Academy of Arts and was knighted by George III in 1769. (Wikipedia)
  • “the constellation known as the Great Ram”: The Great Ram is Aries, the first sign of the zodiac, the golden ram whose fleece Jason sought. See Astronomy and Greek Mythology.
  • “Raphael’s tomb”: Raphael (1483-1520), the Italian painter, is buried in the Pantheon in Rome. Pietro Bembo’s epitaph reads, “Here lies Raphael, by whom Nature feared to be outdone while he lived, and when he died, feared that she herself would die.”
  • “the songs of Ronsard”: Ronsard was a prominent French Renaissance poet, born in 1524. He was often called the “prince of poets” and was influential in developing the French sonnet and other poetic forms. Ronsard, with his friend Joachim du Bellay, founded the group of poets known as La Pléiade, which aimed to elevate the French language through poetry inspired by classical works. His most famous works include Les Odes (1550) and Les Amours (1552), which helped establish him as a leading poet. His sonnets are particularly admired, with “Mignonne, allons voir si la rose” being one of his most famous poems. He is credited with perfecting the 12-syllable Alexandrine line of French verse and is known for his rich imagery, classical references, and exploration of themes like love, beauty, and the fleeting nature of life. Ronsard also served as a poet and chaplain to King Charles IX and was a major literary figure during the French Renaissance. He continued to revise and publish his works throughout his life. The group took its name from the Pleiades, the seven stars among Catherine’s P’s. Ronsard wrote his poems to be sung, and composers set them in his lifetime.
  • “Tracing a lost heir to no property”: Mr. Spitzer has “practiced law in only the most desultory fashion, often without fee, preferring the lost causes” (Chapter 2). See Joachim Spitzer and the Chapter 2 resources.
  • “Rhadamanthus”: Rhadamanthus, son of Zeus and Europa and brother of Minos, was a king of Crete who became a judge of the dead. In Virgil’s Aeneid (Book 6), he forces the dead to confess the crimes they hid on earth, as he finds Mr. Spitzer “guilty of many forgotten crimes.” He returns in Chapter 14. See Greek Mythology.
  • “the sister ravens, the brother doves”: The Grimms’ “The Seven Ravens” and Giambattista Basile’s “The Seven Doves” (1634-36) both tell of brothers changed into birds and a sister who saves them. Young makes the ravens sisters. See Fairy Tales and Folklore and Birds.
  • “Sir Walter Raleigh in his marvelous white satin suit embroidered with seed pearls”: Sir Walter Raleigh (c. 1552-1618) was an English statesman, soldier, spy, writer, poet, and explorer. (Wikipedia) He was famous at Elizabeth’s court for the pearls and jewels on his clothes, even his shoes. See Sir Walter Raleigh and Exploration and the Poles.
    • Raleigh’s poetry is known as the plain style. His writing contains strong personal treatments of themes such as love, loss, beauty, and time. Most of his poems are short lyrics that were inspired by actual events. In poems Raleigh expresses a contempt-of-the-world attitude more characteristic of the Middle Ages than of the dawning era of humanistic optimism. But his lesser-known long poem, The Ocean’s Love to Cynthia, expresses a melancholy sense of history. The poem was written during his imprisonment in the Tower of London. (Wikipedia) Raleigh answered Christopher Marlowe’s “The Passionate Shepherd to His Love” with “The Nymph’s Reply to the Shepherd.” Raleigh gives an almost line-for-line refutation of Marlowe’s sentiments. Centuries later, William Carlos Williams added “Raleigh Was Right” (1940) to the conversation. It begins, “We cannot go to the country / for the country will bring us / no peace.”
  • “when he removed his white plumed hat, removed also his head”: Raleigh was beheaded at Westminster on October 29, 1618. Of the axe he said, “This is sharp medicine, but it is a physician for all diseases.” His widow kept his embalmed head for the rest of her life. The poem he wrote the night before begins, “Even such is Time, that takes in trust / Our youth, our joys, our all we have, / And pays us but with earth and dust.” See Sir Walter Raleigh.
  • “his intimate name, Ocean or Water”: Elizabeth called him “Water.” Spenser named him “the Shepherd of the Ocean” in Colin Clouts Come Home Againe (1595), and Raleigh wrote The Ocean’s Love to Cynthia, with the Queen as the moon who rules the tides. See Sir Walter Raleigh and The Sea and Water.
  • “a society of night devoted exclusively to atheistic propositions”: “The school of night” comes from Love’s Labour’s Lost (4.3): “Black is the badge of hell, / The hue of dungeons and the school of night.” The phrase became a name for Raleigh’s circle with Thomas Harriot and Christopher Marlowe, men accused of doubting Genesis and God. In 1594 an inquiry at Cerne Abbas examined charges of atheism against Raleigh’s circle. See Sir Walter Raleigh, Shakespeare, and Genesis.
    • “man had existed before Adam”: The Baines note (1593) charged Marlowe with saying that ancient authors “have assuredly written of above 16 thousand years agone whereas Adam is proved to have lived within 6 thousand years.” See the Chapter 9 resources on pre-Adamites.
    • “God is dog spelled backward”: The word read backward is the last of the R’s “many riddles.”

Vocabulary

Atheistic
Denying the existence of God.
Bellrope
A rope pulled to ring a bell, such as one that summons a servant.
Brussels lace
Fine lace made by hand in Brussels, Belgium, from linen thread.
Congealed
Thickened or stiffened, as with cold.
Courtier
An attendant at a royal court.
Frigid
Very cold; stiffly unfriendly.

Chapter 12

← Chapter 11 · Home · Chapter 13 →

Summary

It is past ten at night. Vera lies awake beside the Big Ben alarm clock, the one reliable clock in a house of clocks stopped one by one as Catherine withdrew to her bed. Wanting human company, she sets out for Miss MacIntosh’s bedroom. On the way she crosses the garden of the blind, planted by her grandfather for his blind wife to be touched and smelled rather than seen, and she feels a joy she will not know again: this first clear vision of the world will also be her last. She looks back on the child she was at seven, who bayed at the moon, heard the dead through a wireless in her head, and believed she was Chopin reborn, and on Miss MacIntosh, who brought her to her senses with a plain creed of daylight and duty. There were signs Vera did not read: Miss MacIntosh’s short breath, her blue lips, her threats to retire. The chapter closes on Catherine’s suspicion that Mr. Spitzer sometimes imagines himself to be his dead brother, betting on dark horses.

Characters present

Vera Cartwheel · Miss MacIntosh · Catherine Cartwheel · Joachim Spitzer · Peron Spitzer · The Black Coachman

Concepts present

Themes: Death and Mortality · Dreams and Imagination · Faith, God, and the Supernatural · Freedom and Escape · Guilt, Innocence, and Justice · Illusion and Reality · Isolation and Connection · Love · Memory and the Past · Order, Chaos, and Discipline · The Search for Meaning · Time

Symbols: Birds · Clocks and Watches · Eyes and Blindness · Fog and Mist · Hair, Wig, and Baldness · Horses and Carriages · Keys, Doors, and Locks · Lamps, Candles, and Light · Moon and Stars · Roses and Flowers · Shadows · Twins and Doubles

Philosophy: Plato and Platonism · Spiritualism and the Occult

Allusions: Fairy Tales and Folklore · Genesis · Music and Composers · Shakespeare · The Bible

Key passages

From the research

  • The chapter opens with a meditation on time, describing the Big Ben alarm clock as “Old Reliable,” contrasted with other clocks in the house that have stopped at different hours, symbolizing a suspended or fragmented perception of time, linked with Catherine’s gradual withdrawal from the world. This sets the objective measurement of time (servants’ clocks) against subjective experience (stopped clocks), reflecting how personal grief or change distorts time.
  • Vera’s unplanned visit to Miss MacIntosh’s bedroom is described as a sporadic, almost dreamlike moment that is “blurred” in memory and “told only through a veil of oblivion,” emphasizing the elusive nature of memory and how absence reveals what is hidden. This passage sets the tone for the exploration of consciousness and the limits of human understanding.
  • A long, lyrical reflection on the human senses and the body’s design celebrates the unity and beauty of nature. The eye is described as the organ of sight placed perfectly in the skull, with hair acting as a protective and sensory element, and the skin as a “drum of all our senses.” This passage praises the human body as a masterpiece of nature and highlights the interconnectedness of all living things.
  • Vera finds herself in a garden created for a blind person, her grandmother. She insists the place “could surely in no way have influenced” her own clarity of vision, yet she wonders, “what is the influence of place?” The garden is full of sensory experience beyond sight: textures, smells, and forms without color. This metaphor illustrates the theme of perception beyond the visible, and the coexistence of joy and sorrow, as the garden’s sadness contrasts with Vera’s boundless happiness.
  • Vera contemplates how her earlier dreams and visions experienced as musical discourses with ghosts, reincarnations, and fantastical experiences contrast with the harsh reality taught by Miss MacIntosh. The nursemaid’s admonition to accept that “nothing had happened” and that mortals are not omniscient introduces a sobering perspective. This tension between dream and reality, imagination and practicality, is a central philosophical conflict in the chapter.
  • Miss MacIntosh represents a grounded, no-nonsense worldview where she emphasizes moral clarity, the distinction between what is real and unreal, and the rejection of dreaming. Her views on love are practical, seeing it as “greatest love which could see another’s face in daylight and hear another’s voice.” She embodies endurance, frugality, and a refusal to indulge in illusions, contrasting with Vera’s imaginative tendencies.
  • Near the end, Vera sets out Miss MacIntosh’s creed in the face of divine mystery: the world is a flawed creation, and God has “been filled with the greatest remorse” over its imperfections. Humans should attend to their own lives and not “meddle in His remote business,” highlighting themes of humility and acceptance of the unknowable.
  • The long passage on hair (“The most beautiful ladies of history had been noted for their hair”) and the warning that “the first vision would also be the last” both prepare for Chapter 17, when Vera finds Miss MacIntosh bald.

Questions and observations

Reading closely

  • “Though time was an illusion, it was not the illusion of servants.” Who can afford to stop the clocks?
  • The details come “through a veil of oblivion which is itself a medium of memory.” How can forgetting be a way of remembering?
  • “Without eyelids, one would stare at the face of one’s love, even as one stares at death.” Why does Vera join love and death here?

Characters

  • The blind grandmother is “the most immediate of persons,” with no fancy at all. Why is the garden of the blind planted for her, of all people?
  • Miss MacIntosh “held my attention by yelling louder than the dead, louder than the waves.” What did she save Vera from, and what did it cost?
  • She “had not two faces.” Is that true of anyone in this novel?

Connections

  • Miss MacIntosh’s prophecy that Vera might be “a poor little shoemaker’s humble wife” (Chapter 9) now has her as a “wooden wife.” What has changed?
  • The thimble carved “Juliet, 1899” returns to the Romeo and Juliet dream of Chapter 6. Who was Juliet?
  • The twelve white swans recall Chapter 11’s “one wild swan more.” Why do bewitched brothers keep appearing?

Reflection

  • “What is the influence of place?” Are there places that hold sorrow?
  • Was Vera at seven, who preferred the dream to “the cause and effect sequences of the waking life,” wrong?
  • Is happiness more fragile when it cannot see what is coming?

Research: Characters

Vera Cartwheel

  • Reflective, imaginative, and sensitive.
  • Struggles between embracing imagination and dreams and confronting reality.
  • Experiences moments of joy and freedom but also faces the harsh truths of life and mortality.
  • At seven she bayed like a dog, dug for bones, heard the dead, and believed she was Chopin reborn, until Miss MacIntosh “restored me to my senses.”

Miss MacIntosh

  • The practical, no-nonsense caretaker who keeps the “Old Reliable” clock.
  • Represents pragmatism, moral clarity, and a grounded worldview.
  • Cautions against illusion and flight of fancy; emphasizes duty and reality.
  • Her perspective contrasts with Vera’s imaginative nature.
  • Her short breath, blue lips, and stone-grey skin are signs Vera does not yet read.
  • She threatens to retire, taps Vera with a silver thimble carved “Juliet, 1899,” and saves soap coupons “to exchange for crockery.”

Catherine Cartwheel

  • Catherine is mentioned as retiring slowly from the world, symbolized by the stopped clocks.
  • She suspects Mr. Spitzer sometimes imagines himself to be his dead brother.

Vera’s Grandfather and Grandmother

  • The grandfather who planted the garden for his blind wife represents the effort to create a world accessible through other senses.
  • The grandmother’s blindness and her practical nature are contrasted with Vera’s imaginative vision.
  • The grandmother argued with “her voluble black coachman” about the clouds, and touched the stone faces only once she was blind. See The Black Coachman.

Mr. Spitzer

  • A figure with an ambiguous nature and identity.
  • Catherine suspects he sometimes imagines himself to be his dead brother (Peron), blurring reality and fantasy.
  • Catherine once danced with “pigeon-toed, ambiguous Mr. Spitzer, perhaps with two Mr. Spitzers, one who had died, one who had lived.”

Research: Themes

The Illusion and Reality of Time

See: Illusion and Reality · Time

  • Vera reflects on time as both a practical necessity and an illusion.
  • The Big Ben alarm clock symbolizes reliable, practical time, set for servants who must rise at certain hours.
  • Other clocks in the house are stopped at different times, symbolizing frozen moments or hesitation in the past, especially linked to Catherine’s retreat from the world.

The Life of the Imagination versus Reality

See: Illusion and Reality · Dreams and Imagination

  • Vera contrasts a “life of the imagination” with the waking world, pondering the significance of dreams and whether they hold more truth than reality.
  • Dreams are described as limitless and bridging life and death, whereas waking life is governed by cause and effect.
  • Miss MacIntosh’s pragmatic attitude opposes Vera’s dreamy perspective, emphasizing practical reality and cautioning against illusions.

The Role and Limits of the Senses

See: Eyes and Blindness · The Search for Meaning

  • There is an extended meditation on the human senses (sight, hearing, taste, smell, and touch) as the means by which humans experience reality.
  • Vera highlights the design and function of eyes, eyelashes, eyelids, and hair as protective and sensory mechanisms.
  • The garden of the blind symbolizes a world without vision, emphasizing other ways of perceiving such as touch (Braille, texture), and questioning how place and perception influence sorrow and happiness.

Freedom, Innocence, and Joy

See: Guilt, Innocence, and Justice · Freedom and Escape

  • There is a moment of profound joy and freedom as Vera walks out into the night, celebrating the beauty and unity of nature.
  • This freedom is described as innocence and clarity of vision, untainted by past sorrow or fear.
  • Vera feels connected to the natural world, sensing stars, flowers, and animals as real and meaningful.

The Limits of Human Understanding and Divine Mystery

See: Faith, God, and the Supernatural · The Search for Meaning

  • Vera reflects on the limitations of human knowledge, emphasizing that humans are not omniscient and should not try to tamper with God’s mysteries.
  • God is portrayed as remorseful over creation’s imperfections, but humans are advised to focus on their own lives rather than cosmic mysteries.

Love and Human Relationships

See: Isolation and Connection · Love

  • Miss MacIntosh’s perspective on love is pragmatic and grounded; love is about seeing and hearing another in daylight and tested by harsh experience.
  • She is portrayed as a plain and practical woman, devoid of romantic illusions or flights of fancy.

Research: Symbols and Imagery

Clocks and Time

See: Clocks and Watches · Keys, Doors, and Locks

  • Clocks stopped at different hours symbolize frozen moments, hesitation, or the past lingering in the present.
  • The Big Ben, “Old Reliable,” wound daily by Miss MacIntosh, stands against the stopped clocks of Catherine’s retreat.

The Garden of the Blind

See: Eyes and Blindness

  • Represents a sensory world without sight, emphasizing the importance and limitations of perception.

Eyes and Eyelashes

See: Eyes and Blindness

  • Represent the function and fragility of vision and perception; Vera meditates on their biological and symbolic significance.

Moonlight and Mist

See: Fog and Mist · Moon and Stars · Lamps, Candles, and Light

  • The pregnant moonlight and mist create an atmosphere of mystery, illumination, and ambiguity.

Hair

See: Hair, Wig, and Baldness

  • Symbolic of protection and sensitivity; also connected to historical and biblical references.
  • The meditation on hair foreshadows Miss MacIntosh’s baldness in Chapter 17.

Flowers

See: Roses and Flowers

  • Sensual, tactile flowers in the garden illustrate the blending of senses and the threshold between perception and imagination.

Research: Resources

  • “As I had missed my birthday party”: The birthday party that never happened in Chapter 10, where “we had not even cut the birthday cake.” See the Chapter 10 resources.
  • “the Big Ben alarm clock”: The Big Ben was the Western Clock Company’s alarm clock, sold from 1909 and the first alarm clock advertised across the country (1910). It takes its name from the great bell in London. See Clocks and Watches and Time.
    • Big Ben is the nickname for the Great Bell of the Great Clock of Westminster, and, by extension, for the clock tower itself, which stands at the north end of the Palace of Westminster in London, England. The clock is a striking clock with five bells. (Wikipedia)
  • “for our rising up and for our lying down”: “When thou liest down, and when thou risest up” (Deuteronomy 6:7). See The Bible.
  • “no Tritons dreaming around the clock, no ladies weeping over dead birds, no sporting cupids”: French mantel clocks were crowded with gilded sea gods, nymphs, and cupids. Triton, son of Poseidon, blows a conch shell. See Clocks and Watches and Greek Mythology.
    • Jean-Baptiste Greuze’s painting Girl Weeping over Her Dead Bird (1765).
    • Catullus wrote of his beloved Lesbia’s dead sparrow: “Mourn, O Venuses and Cupids.”
  • “It did not repeat the hours”: Repeater clocks and watches chime the last hour again at the pull of a cord or the press of a button, so the hour can be heard in the dark. See Clocks and Watches.
  • “though time was an illusion, it was not the illusion of servants”: Einstein wrote in 1955 that the distinction between past, present, and future “is only a stubbornly persistent illusion.” Servants still had to rise on time. See Time.
  • “each clock having been stopped at a different hour”: In Dickens’s Great Expectations (1861), Miss Havisham stops every clock at twenty minutes to nine, the hour she was jilted, and never leaves her room. Mourners once stopped the clocks at a death. See Clocks and Watches, Memory and the Past, and the Chapter 4 resources.
  • “Drink Coca-Cola”: Cardboard advertising fans printed with “Drink Coca-Cola” were handed out in churches and stores, especially in the South. See the Chapter 1 resources.
  • “that we are not as shadows”: “What shadows we are, and what shadows we pursue” (Edmund Burke, 1780), and “our days upon earth are a shadow” (Job 8:9). See Shadows and Plato and Platonism.
    • Prospero: “the great globe itself… shall dissolve, / And, like this insubstantial pageant faded, / Leave not a rack behind. We are such stuff / As dreams are made on” (The Tempest 4.1).
    • The theme of shadows runs through the novel. It brings to mind Plato’s work, The Allegory of the Cave, or Plato’s Cave. It is an allegory presented by the Greek philosopher Plato in his work, Republic. The Cave describes a group of people who have lived chained to the wall of a cave all their lives, facing a blank wall. The people watch shadows projected on the wall from objects passing in front of a fire behind them and give names to these shadows. The shadows are the prisoners’ reality, but are not accurate representations of the real world. The shadows represent the fragment of reality that can normally be perceived through the senses, while the objects under the sun represent the true forms of objects that can only be perceived through reason. The philosopher is like a prisoner who is freed from the cave and comes to understand that the shadows on the wall are actually not the direct source of the images seen. A philosopher aims to understand and perceive the higher levels of reality. However, the other inmates of the cave do not even desire to leave their prison, for they know no better life. (Wikipedia) See the Chapter 3 resources.
  • “The eyeball was made to see with”: William Paley’s Natural Theology (1802) made the eye his proof of design: “there is precisely the same proof that the eye was made for vision, as there is that the telescope was made for assisting it.” The book opens with a watch found on a heath. See Eyes and Blindness.
    • Darwin admitted that the evolution of the eye “seems, I freely confess, absurd in the highest possible degree,” then showed how it could arise by small steps (On the Origin of Species, 1859). See the Chapter 3 resources.
  • “the spot on a peacock’s tail”: Juno set the hundred eyes of the slain watchman Argus in the peacock’s tail (Ovid, Metamorphoses 1). See Greek Mythology, Birds, and the Chapter 5 resources.
  • “the hole through the needle”: “It is easier for a camel to go through the eye of a needle, than for a rich man to enter into the kingdom of God” (Matthew 19:24). See the Chapter 3 resources.
  • “the brain was but the infoldings of the skin”: In the embryo, brain and skin both grow from the same outer layer, the ectoderm, which folds inward to form the neural tube.
  • “we were the masterpieces of nature”: “What a piece of work is a man! … the beauty of the world, the paragon of animals!” (Hamlet 2.2). See Shakespeare.
  • “the hair raising to warn us of our mortal danger”: “Then a spirit passed before my face; the hair of my flesh stood up” (Job 4:15). See Hair, Wig, and Baldness and The Bible.
  • “The most beautiful ladies of history had been noted for their hair”: Queen Berenice gave her hair to the gods for her husband’s safe return, and it was set among the stars as Coma Berenices. See Hair, Wig, and Baldness, Miss MacIntosh, and the Chapter 9 resources.
  • “Absalom was caught among the apple boughs and hanged by his hair”: In 2 Samuel 18:9, Absalom’s “head caught hold of the oak.” Vera makes it an apple tree. His heavy hair was cut once a year (2 Samuel 14:26). See Hair, Wig, and Baldness, The Bible, and the Chapter 5 resources.
  • “walks in the eye of the wind”: A sailor’s phrase for heading straight into the wind.
  • “dead men are usually found with their eyes open”: “Joseph shall put his hand upon thine eyes” (Genesis 46:4). The living close the eyes of the dead and once weighted them with coins. See Death and Mortality and Eyes and Blindness.
  • “Leonardo had forgotten to give eyebrows to his Mona Lisa”: The Mona Lisa (c. 1503-1519) is a half-length portrait by Leonardo da Vinci. (Wikipedia) The painting shows no eyebrows or lashes, though Giorgio Vasari (1550) praised its eyebrows, “the manner in which the hairs spring from the flesh.” See Eyes and Blindness and Hair, Wig, and Baldness.
  • “the garden of the blind”: Fragrance gardens for the blind were planted to be touched and smelled. The Brooklyn Botanic Garden opened one in 1955. Vera and Miss MacIntosh walk through this garden in Chapter 3. See Eyes and Blindness, Roses and Flowers, and the Chapter 3 resources.
  • “what is the influence of place?”: The Romans spoke of the genius loci, the spirit of a place. John Ruskin named the “pathetic fallacy” (1856), the habit of lending human feeling to nature.
    • “making the stones cry out”: “I tell you that, if these should hold their peace, the stones would immediately cry out” (Luke 19:40).
  • “the stumbling stone to the blind”: “Thou shalt not curse the deaf, nor put a stumblingblock before the blind” (Leviticus 19:14). See Eyes and Blindness and The Bible.
  • “the Braille texture of flowers”: Louis Braille, blinded as a child, published his raised-dot alphabet in 1829. See Eyes and Blindness.
  • “darkness moved on the face of the deep”: “And darkness was upon the face of the deep. And the Spirit of God moved upon the face of the waters” (Genesis 1:2). See Genesis.
  • “sweet william, cosmos, rose geranium, phlox, nasturtium, nicotiana”: Scented garden flowers. Rose geranium gives off its scent at a touch, and nicotiana, flowering tobacco, opens and perfumes the air at night. See Roses and Flowers.
  • “flowers of the old Jerusalem, flowers of the new Jerusalem”: “I am the rose of Sharon, and the lily of the valleys” (Song of Solomon 2:1), and the holy city, new Jerusalem, coming down “as a bride adorned for her husband” (Revelation 21:2). See Roses and Flowers and The Bible.
  • “the first vision would also be the last”: Foreshadowing of Chapter 17, when Vera finds Miss MacIntosh bald. See Miss MacIntosh.
  • “the beauty of that horror more beautiful than life”: “For beauty is nothing but the beginning of terror” (Rilke, Duino Elegies, 1923).
  • “Mr. Chandelier or Mr. Chanticleer”: Chanticleer is the proud rooster of Chaucer’s “The Nun’s Priest’s Tale” and the fables of Reynard the Fox. Mr. Chandelier is Catherine’s companion from Chapter 2. See Mr. Chandelier, Birds, and the Chapter 2 resources.
  • “a place for everything”: “A place for everything, and everything in its place,” the old household rule. See Order, Chaos, and Discipline.
  • “her lips turned blue and her skin lost its natural color, turning to saffron”: Blue lips and short breath are signs of a failing heart or lungs, a warning Vera does not read. See Miss MacIntosh.
  • “saving even the soap coupons to exchange for crockery”: Companies such as the Larkin Soap Company gave coupons that buyers traded for dishes and furniture.
  • “a poor little shoemaker’s wooden wife”: Miss MacIntosh’s prophecy in Chapter 9 was “a poor little shoemaker’s humble wife.” See the Chapter 9 resources.
  • “Juliet, 1899”: Maude Adams played Juliet at the Empire Theatre in New York in May 1899, opposite William Faversham. A dream in Chapter 6 has “She was Juliet, and I was Romeo.” See Shakespeare and the Chapter 6 resources.
  • “baying like a dog at the moon”: “I had rather be a dog, and bay the moon, / Than such a Roman” (Julius Caesar 4.3). See Shakespeare and Moon and Stars.
  • “a rooster crowing when there was no rooster”: “Before the cock crow, thou shalt deny me thrice” (Matthew 26:34). See The Bible and Birds.
  • “a wireless was attached to my head so that I might hear the voices of the dead”: In 1920 Thomas Edison told interviewers he was working on a machine to speak with the dead. See Spiritualism and the Occult.
  • “the reincarnation of Chopin”: Chopin wrote some sixty mazurkas, the Polish dance. The polka is Czech, and he wrote none. See Music and Composers and the Chapter 10 resources.
  • “perhaps with two Mr. Spitzers, one who had died, one who had lived”: Joachim and Peron Spitzer, the twins. See Peron Spitzer and Twins and Doubles.
  • “twelve white swans like brothers or suitors bewitched”: Andersen’s eleven brothers turned into swans, and the bewitched swan maidens of Tchaikovsky’s Swan Lake (1877). See Fairy Tales and Folklore, Birds, and the Chapter 11 resources.
  • “should stir no feather in the air”: Lear holds a feather to Cordelia’s lips: “This feather stirs; she lives!” (King Lear 5.3). See Shakespeare, Death and Mortality, and the Chapter 5 resources.
  • “to be nothing but an old humbug”: “Death, thou shalt die” (John Donne, Holy Sonnet 10, “Death, be not proud”). See Death and Mortality.
  • “headless horsemen ride about in purple fog”: Washington Irving’s “The Legend of Sleepy Hollow” (1820). See Fairy Tales and Folklore and the Chapter 2 resources.
  • “filled with the greatest remorse”: “And it repented the Lord that he had made man on the earth, and it grieved him at his heart” (Genesis 6:6). See Genesis and Faith, God, and the Supernatural.
  • “attend to our own knitting”: “Mind your own knitting,” the old way of saying mind your own business. “Study to be quiet, and to do your own business” (1 Thessalonians 4:11). See The Bible.
  • “The wisest man was a fool in God’s eyes, and there was a fool bound in the heart of every child”: 1 Corinthians 3:19 reads, “For the wisdom of this world is foolishness with God,” and Proverbs 22:15, “Foolishness is bound in the heart of a child; but the rod of correction shall drive it far from him.” The phrase captures the paradox of human existence: the striving for knowledge and meaning amid inherent limitations, and the acceptance that all are bound to folly in the grander cosmic scheme. See The Bible.
  • “We could not command the waters to stand still”: The waters of the Jordan “stood and rose up upon an heap” for Joshua (Joshua 3:16), and he commanded, “Sun, stand thou still” (Joshua 10:12). See The Bible.
  • “They were already moving”: Galileo is said to have muttered “And yet it moves” of the earth after he was forced to recant (1633).
  • “rather to endure ourselves than to test God”: “Ye shall not tempt the Lord your God” (Deuteronomy 6:16). See The Bible.
  • “the honest man was he who walked upright”: “He that walketh uprightly, and worketh righteousness, and speaketh the truth in his heart” (Psalm 15:2). See The Bible.
    • Diogenes is said to have walked Athens by day with a lamp, looking for an honest man.
  • “Love was undoubtedly greatest love which could see another’s face in daylight”: “For now we see through a glass, darkly; but then face to face” (1 Corinthians 13:12). See the Chapter 10 resources on “One who could know us and yet love us.”
  • “her face was not, it was simply not her fortune”: The nursery rhyme’s milkmaid: “My face is my fortune, sir, she said.” See Fairy Tales and Folklore and the Chapter 10 resources.
  • “perhaps it was we who passed through time”: Austin Dobson, “The Paradox of Time” (1877): “Time goes, you say? Ah no! / Alas, Time stays, we go.” See Time.
  • “She could not soar upward on wings of words to heaven”: Claudius: “My words fly up, my thoughts remain below: / Words without thoughts never to heaven go” (Hamlet 3.3). See Shakespeare.
  • “she was a middle brow”: The word was coined in Punch in 1925, between highbrow and lowbrow. See the Chapter 3 resources.
  • “She had not two faces”: Janus, the Roman god of doorways and beginnings, looks two ways at once. See Twins and Doubles.
  • “put his bet on the dark horse”: The phrase comes from Disraeli’s The Young Duke (1831): “a dark horse, which had never been thought of.” See Horses and Carriages and Peron Spitzer.
  • “those of the tramontane regions”: Tramontane, from the Latin transmontanus, means “beyond the mountains,” here the lands beyond the Alps. It is also the name of a cold north wind.

Content note: This chapter mentions the suicide of Mr. Spitzer’s twin brother, Peron.

Summary

After death, Catherine still travels, and she insists that only a hair’s breadth lies between life and death. Her selves leave her body on errands in the void, and she counts her pearls, afraid that when she has counted them all she will be lost. She walks naked through warm snow among footprints that may be hers or a gopher’s, and she is lost for years inside her own ear, a continent of stairways, echoes, and grand pianos, crying, “Let me out of my ear!” The house moves in the night. She takes the night train from Boston to New York through the Alps and the Gobi, followed by brigands, and returns as if she had never gone. She believes she commands winds, tides, and stars, yet she cannot walk. Mr. Spitzer keeps his sorrow alive, and Catherine thinks him less tragic than Peron, who leapt to his death. She remembers that Hannah paid a price for her lack of sorrow, and now, with Hannah dead, she keeps up their rivalry alone. Things left by imaginary visitors, a purple feather fan, riding gloves, an emperor’s white umbrella, prove to her that someone came.
