Chapter 43

← Chapter 42 · Home · Chapter 44 →

Summary

In silk hat and black cape, Mr. Spitzer keeps watch at Cousin Hannah’s deathbed, unsure whether he himself is living or dead. Hannah’s dying becomes a dance of death. She raves through deserts, mountains, and snow, asks whether the lid of the sky is raising or lowering, and speaks to the Emperor Tiberius, a blacksmith, a golden archer, and the Black Moor she calls her love, asking whether she is the anvil or the hammer. The suffrage captain who scorned feminine frivolity longs now for silk skirts, gold-fringed parasols, and her mirror, and Mr. Spitzer wonders whether she had always been “this pale Don Juan beneath her mask.” She searches for “my nymph, my lovely girl,” “my wild swan girl,” and Mr. Spitzer sees her going down like an old ship that no calker can mend. At the end she cries for “my skirt I lost so long ago” and asks, “should love be extinguished by death?”

Characters present

Joachim Spitzer · Cousin Hannah

Concepts present

Themes: Death and Mortality · Decay and Ruin · Grief, Loss, and Mourning · Identity and the Self · Illusion and Reality · Love · Memory and the Past · Women, Gender, and Marriage

Symbols: Clothing, Hats, and Skirts · Clouds and Storms · Fireflies · Lamps, Candles, and Light · Mirrors and Reflections · Moon and Stars · Mountains · Music and Instruments · Snow, Ice, and Winter · The Sea and Water

Philosophy: Augustine and Christian Theology · Buddhism · Freud and Jung · Hinduism · Marguerite Young on Her Craft · Time, Physics, and Chaos Theory

Allusions: Ancient Egypt · Astronomy · Fairy Tales and Folklore · Genesis · Greek Mythology · Music and Composers · Shakespeare · The Bible · Women’s Suffrage

Key passages

From the research

  • The chapter opens with vivid descriptions of Cousin Hannah’s struggle through dreamlike, stormy landscapes symbolizing her life’s battles and approaching death. The imagery of crossing deserts, climbing mountains, and clouds emphasizes the arduous journey of life and death, and the suffragette’s wild screams indicate confusion and loss of self-identity near death.
  • It is revealed that even this great lady “wept if a wandering snowflake touched her hand” and was “fragile as were all mortal things,” prone to “wild dreams, visions, fantasies, presentiments, forebodings, fears of the unknown.” This humanizes her, showing vulnerability despite her public strength and ideals.
  • Mr. Spitzer himself is uncertain of his own state, “not sure who he was, whether living or dead,” and reflects on the confusion about who is dying and the nature of death. His belief that “the dead cast no vote” and his abstention from voting reflect his detachment from worldly affairs.
  • The narrative explores death as both an ending and a beginning, a “great crucible” where opposites meet, and where “death was that which blew us all along.” It describes Cousin Hannah’s cries and visions as part of a larger metaphysical process, suggesting death is not peace but a storm or dance of contradictory forces.
  • Cousin Hannah speaks to various mythic and historical figures like the Emperor Tiberius, a blacksmith, a golden archer, a blackamoor, asking profound questions about identity and fate (“Am I the anvil which is struck or the hammer which strikes?”). This symbolizes her grappling with agency, power, and the unknown as life fades.
  • The blackamoor, a mysterious figure she calls her love, and the “great lamp-lighter” who might light her way, appear repeatedly in her delirium. This imagery suggests a guide or companion in the transition from life to death, blending cultural and mystical symbols.
  • Mr. Spitzer reflects on how Cousin Hannah’s ravings mix ancient history, myth, and personal memories, with cities, armies, and landscapes blending into a timeless dreamscape. There is uncertainty whether these are real memories, dreams, or hallucinations, emphasizing the blurred boundary between life and death, past and present.

Questions and observations

Reading closely

  • Cousin Hannah cannot decide “whether the lid was lowering or raising.” What does the chapter gain by leaving the direction of the lid unresolved, and how does the question change when the lid becomes the lid of the sky?
  • Hannah asks the blacksmith, “Am I the anvil which is struck or the hammer which strikes?” In what ways has the suffrage captain been both over her life? Which does she seem to be at the end?
  • Hannah’s visions travel to Ur, Nineveh, Crete, and Babylon. Mr. Spitzer prefers that she speak of the remote past, things “made safe by their remoteness,” rather than of tomorrow’s weather or the next election. Why might the far past feel safer than the near future at a deathbed?
  • Near its end the chapter turns to the image of an old ship coming apart, and Mr. Spitzer thinks that “not even the greatest calker could calk her now.” How does this sinking ship compare with Hannah’s own question, “Where’s my figurehead?” and with Catherine’s figurehead in Chapter 40?

Characters

  • Mr. Spitzer keeps his “attitudes of dignity, remorse, patience” because “someone must maintain spiritual equilibrium.” Is his calm a gift to the dying woman, a defense for himself, or both?
  • Mr. Spitzer admits he is “perhaps not the best of all possible witnesses to death-bed scenes” and has “a tendency to keep things alive after they were gone.” How does an uncertain witness change the weight of Hannah’s last words?
  • Mr. Spitzer suspects the Black Moor “might be a man and not a woman,” and Hannah searches for “my nymph, my lovely girl.” What does the chapter suggest about the love Hannah denied, and why might it surface only at the end?
  • Mr. Spitzer notices “pawn figures moving not only from dream to dream of the dreamer but from dreamer to dreamer,” so that the Black Moor resembles the black coachman of Catherine’s opium dreams. What would it mean for dreams to be shared, and how does this connect to his sense that “no one could simply be himself”?

Connections

  • Hannah spent her life refusing feminine frivolities, yet she cries for the skirt “which I took off so long ago.” How does the skirt work as a symbol of the self she set aside for the cause? Does the chapter mourn that choice or honor it?
  • In Hannah’s heaven “the white hen crows,” and “none shall stop her.” How does this reversal of the barnyard order echo the work of the suffrage movement? See Women’s Suffrage.
  • Hannah says, “Then put out the light,” and asks whether the turban-winder has come to strangle her. If she is casting herself as Desdemona, what does that reveal about how she has understood love and the men she fought against? See Shakespeare.
  • The chapter is titled “The Dance of Death” in the reading guide. How does Hannah’s “mad dance” on “a lonely mountain top” compare with the medieval dance of death, in which Death leads every rank of person to the grave? See On the danse macabre (Ch 43).

Reflection

  • Mr. Spitzer calls vanity “that which took longest dying” and finds it “in woman’s heart as in man’s heart” and perhaps “in the heart of God.” Is Hannah’s cry for her mirror and her skirt a betrayal of her cause, a last joke, or simply a human frailty the chapter refuses to blame her for?
  • Mr. Spitzer’s understanding “always came too late,” arriving “like a gift freely given to one who could not express his appreciation.” When does understanding arrive too late in ordinary life, and is it still worth having?
  • “When nothing was possible, all things were made possible.” In what situations does the loss of every option open something new?

Research: Characters

Mr. Spitzer

  • A somber, enigmatic figure who carries a high silk hat and black cape, symbolic of mourning and ritual.
  • He is both witness and participant in the suffragette’s dying experience.
  • Reflects deeply on life, death, identity, and the nature of existence.
  • Struggles with his own sense of being alive or dead, voting or not voting, and the meaning of his presence.
  • His observations are philosophical, often pondering the illusions of life and the mysteries beyond death.

Cousin Hannah

  • A once powerful figure, now fragile and approaching death.
  • Engaged in a fierce, chaotic battle against death, manifested in vivid, surreal visions.
  • Experiences wild dreams, hallucinations, and shifting identities in her final hours.
  • Struggles with recognition of self and the meaning of life and death.
  • Exhibits vanity, fear, ecstasy, confusion, and moments of clarity.
  • Her final moments are a “dance of death,” a paradoxical mix of seriousness and frivolity.
  • Young called her “Cousin Hannah, the alter ego of the opium lady if she had been set loose in the world” (Ellen G. Friedman and Miriam Fuchs, “A Conversation with Marguerite Young,” Review of Contemporary Fiction 23, no. 1, Spring 2003 (1989 original)). See Marguerite Young on Her Craft.

Research: Themes

Life, Death, and the Transition Between

See: Death and Mortality

  • Death is depicted not as an end but a complex transformation, a journey through storm, cloud, snow, and desert.
  • The suffragette’s battle with death is fierce and confusing; death is both a closing and an opening (“Oh, is the lid raising, lowering?”).
  • The ambiguity of death and existence is central, with Mr. Spitzer unsure if he or the suffragette is alive or dead.
  • Death is associated with loss, revelation, and paradox, often blending into life’s experiences.

Memory, Identity, and Illusion

See: Illusion and Reality · Memory and the Past · Identity and the Self

  • The suffragette’s past is fragmented and elusive, mixing real and imagined events.
  • Both characters wrestle with who they are and who others have been.
  • Dreams and memories flow outside of linear time, suggesting the permeability of identity.
  • Reality and illusion are intertwined; the suffragette’s visions may be symbolic rather than literal truth.

Vanity and Human Frailty

See: Decay and Ruin

  • Despite the gravity of death, vanity persists (“vanity of silken skirts,” “great parasols fringed by gold”).
  • The suffragette clings to images of beauty and love even as she fades.
  • The fragility of human existence is highlighted, especially in the face of death.

Love and Loss

See: Love · Grief, Loss, and Mourning

  • The suffragette expresses deep, eternal love in her delirium, though the identity of lover and beloved is unclear.
  • Love and death blur together, raising the question of whether death extinguishes love or transforms it. Her last whispered words ask, “should love be extinguished by death?”
  • The paradox of love’s endurance beyond death is a poignant motif.

The Role of the Observer

  • Mr. Spitzer’s role as witness is complicated by his own uncertain status.
  • He balances grief with detachment and observation with participation.
  • He questions the reliability of memory and perception, acknowledging possible error.

Research: Symbols and Imagery

High Silk Hat & Black Cape (Mr. Spitzer)

See: Clothing, Hats, and Skirts

  • Symbols of mourning, ritual, and his ambiguous status between life and death.

Storm, Snow, Desert, Mountains

See: Snow, Ice, and Winter · Mountains · Clouds and Storms

  • Represent the suffragette’s internal struggle and the vast unknown of death.

Skirt of Clouds and Waters

See: The Sea and Water · Clothing, Hats, and Skirts · Clouds and Storms

  • Symbolizes beauty, identity, and the suffragette’s fading presence.

Black Moor / Blackamoor

See: Shakespeare · The Black Coachman

  • A mysterious figure, possibly a lover or phantom, representing the suffragette’s complex relationships and desires.

Crystal Casket / Mirror

See: Mirrors and Reflections

  • Symbols of self-reflection, identity, and the enigma of existence; the mirror is sought but elusive.

Music (Lute, Harp, Bells)

See: Music and Instruments

  • Represents the ethereal, transcendent aspects of life and death; the music continues even as life fades.

Firefly Light / Star

See: Fireflies · Moon and Stars · Lamps, Candles, and Light

  • Symbolizes hope, guidance, and the fragile spark of life amid darkness.

Bellrope / Bells

See: Music and Instruments

  • Represent the passage of time, calling, and the inevitability of death.

Iceberg / Frozen Elements

See: Snow, Ice, and Winter

  • Emphasize coldness, isolation, and the slow crumbling of life.

Further notes from the text

  • Mr. Spitzer carries his high silk hat, “almost his only God,” and keeps watch unable to help, since he is as one already dead.
  • He wonders whether Hannah’s sudden longing for feminine frivolities is a last great joke, a parody of life at the moment life is fading. See Comedy in Chapter 43.
  • He had supposed that bodily death and real death would come together. Watching her, he begins to doubt it, and wonders whether the person dying now is someone he has not really seen since his forgotten youth.
  • Hannah’s delirium crosses the ancient world, Ur of the Chaldees, Nineveh, Crete, Babylon, and asks for her little boat and her figurehead, linking her dying to Catherine’s image of the figurehead in Chapter 40.
  • She cries out to the Black Moor, “beloved of woman,” the figure Mr. Spitzer later connects with the black coachman of Catherine’s dreams.
  • Her ravings repeat a paradox that sums up the novel’s method: look not into the things that are, to see the things that are not.
  • Near the end he pictures her going down like a ship in a whirlpool, and he is certain he will be on the other shore, not where the wreckage lands. The chapter closes on her whisper that death might be “her life, her love,” and her question, “should love be extinguished by death?”

Research: Resources

  • “that high silk hat which was almost his only God”: The high silk hat used to be a clear symbol of authority and status in society. It represented wealth and prestige. Culturally it also represented capitalism, enterprise, and ambition. The first top hats were made of beaver fur felt. From the 1840s silk plush replaced beaver, which gave the silk hat its name. For Mr. Spitzer the hat is “almost his only God.” See Clothing, Hats, and Skirts.
  • “this great emir of suffrage”: Emir comes from the Arabic amir, meaning commander or prince. It was the title of military leaders and rulers across the Islamic world. Calling Hannah an emir makes her a desert commander, which fits the armies, tents, and camel bells of her deathbed visions.
  • “the dead cast no vote”: Padding the rolls with the names of the dead, the “graveyard vote,” was an old charge against city machines such as Tammany Hall. Mr. Spitzer’s brother believed otherwise, and Mr. Spitzer, who has not “been inside a ballot box for years,” sits at the deathbed of a suffrage captain. See Women’s Suffrage.
  • “Oh, I am lost! I am saved!”: “I once was lost, but now am found” (John Newton, “Amazing Grace,” Olney Hymns, 1779).
  • “Oh, is that you, great lamp-lighter?”: Before electric street lights, a lamplighter walked the streets at dusk with a long pole, lighting each gas lamp, and came back at dawn to put them out. Hannah greets Mr. Spitzer this way when he arrives, and later asks whether “the great lamp-lighter” has come “to light her way through worlds of darkness.” Mr. Spitzer, who has “always tapped at every lamp-post” on his walks, becomes a guide for the dying, yet “not even the great lamp-bearer could light this darkness.” See The lamp-lighter (Ch 29) and On the lamplighter and The Little Prince (Ch 48).
  • “So like a palmer she had wandered through this world”: A palmer was a medieval pilgrim who had traveled to the Holy Land and carried back a palm frond as proof. Some palmers had no home and spent their lives traveling between holy sites. The word suits Hannah, whose great cause kept her always on the road and never settled.
  • “the auk’s egg”: The great auk was a large flightless seabird of the North Atlantic. Hunters killed the last confirmed pair on the island of Eldey, off Iceland, in June 1844. After its extinction, its eggs became prized collector’s items that sold for large sums at Victorian auctions. Placing the egg among Hannah’s vanities joins beauty to extinction. The Iceland connection also ties it to Mt. Hekla, which appears later in the chapter.
  • “the glass barouche”: A barouche was a fashionable four-wheeled carriage of the nineteenth century. It had a folding half-hood and two double seats facing each other, and it was built for being seen in. A barouche made of glass could not exist, which puts it among the vanities that veil and display at once.
  • “something almost spontaneously starting up outside of the scheme of time, whether future or past”: Eternalism (philosophy of time) is an approach to the ontological nature of time, which takes the view that all existence in time is equally real, as opposed to presentism or the growing block universe theory of time, in which at least the future is not the same as any other time. Some forms of eternalism give time a similar ontology to that of space, as a dimension, with different times being as real as different places, and future events are “already there” in the same sense other places are already there, and that there is no objective flow of time. It is sometimes referred to as the “block time” or “block universe” theory due to its description of space-time as an unchanging four-dimensional “block,” as opposed to the view of the world as a three-dimensional space modulated by the passage of time (Wikipedia). Mr. Spitzer half suspects that Hannah’s past is not memory at all but a time outside time, and that “one life might contain all.”
    • Hermann Minkowski declared in 1908 that “henceforth space by itself, and time by itself, are doomed to fade away into mere shadows.” When his friend Michele Besso died in 1955, Einstein wrote to Besso’s family, “People like us, who believe in physics, know that the distinction between past, present, and future is only a stubbornly persistent illusion” (Albert Einstein, letter of March 21, 1955). See Time, Physics, and Chaos Theory.
  • “this pale Don Juan beneath her mask”: Don Juan is a legendary, fictional Spanish literature character. He first appeared in a 1630 play, Tirso de Molina’s The Trickster of Seville, and probably most famously in the opera Don Giovanni by Mozart. He was a libertine, womanizer, arrogant, unrepentant, and was punished for these sins. Mr. Spitzer wonders whether Hannah had always been “this pale Don Juan beneath her mask,” the great seducer hidden inside the woman who refused love. See The Pale Don Juan and Music and Composers.
    • Molière’s Dom Juan (1665) and Byron’s unfinished Don Juan (1819-1824), in which the seducer is more often seduced, carried the figure on.
  • “the next horse race at Churchill Downs when the track was muddy”: Churchill Downs is the racetrack in Louisville, Kentucky, that opened in 1875 and has hosted the Kentucky Derby ever since. A muddy track favors certain horses and upsets the odds, which is exactly the uncertainty that drew Mr. Spitzer’s gambling brother. Mr. Spitzer judges that this talk of the future would be tactless at a deathbed. See On the Kentucky Derby and Black Jockeys (Ch 80).
  • “join the vast majority, just as the Romans said”: The Romans used the phrase “abiit ad plures,” meaning “he has gone to the many,” as a polite way to say someone had died. It appears in Petronius’s Satyricon. The English poet Edward Young used the same idea in his 1721 play The Revenge: “Death joins us to the great majority.” Mr. Spitzer turns the saying around and thinks the city of the dead might be “a smaller city.”
  • “Watchman, what hour?”: This is a version of Isaiah 21:11, “Watchman, what of the night?” In the prophecy, someone calls out from the darkness asking how long the night will last, and the watchman answers that “the morning cometh, and also the night.” The verse inspired John Bowring’s 1825 hymn “Watchman, Tell Us of the Night.” Hannah asks it as an old clock strikes, as if the hour of her death were a question someone on the wall could answer.
  • “Are they the hooded thirteen apostles?”: The twelve apostles included Judas Iscariot, who betrayed Jesus. Matthias was chosen to take his place (Acts 1:26), and Paul, who came later, is often called the thirteenth apostle. Jesus and the twelve made thirteen at the Last Supper, one root of the old superstition that thirteen at table is unlucky, and Hannah’s “hooded thirteen apostles” picketing the town clock carry that ominous number. In the Eastern tradition there may have been as many as seventy apostles, the seventy whom Jesus “sent them two and two before his face” (Luke 10:1). See The Bible.
  • “Is that the black knight?”: In Scott’s Ivanhoe (1819), the Black Knight, “Le Noir Fainéant,” is Richard the Lionheart in disguise. Hannah’s phantoms, too, hide one identity inside another.
  • “Did she lift her veil embroidered with the stars”: The veiled goddess of Sais declared, “I am all that has been, and is, and shall be, and my robe no mortal has yet uncovered” (Plutarch, On Isis and Osiris 9, trans. Frank Cole Babbitt, 1936). See Ancient Egypt.
  • “speaking to a blacksmith who was shoeing her wild horse”: In ancient Greece Hephaestus was the god of blacksmiths and was disabled either at birth or because of his fall from Mount Olympus. Zeus hurled him from Olympus, and he fell all day until he landed on Lemnos (Iliad 1.590-594). See Greek Mythology.
  • “Am I the anvil which is struck or the hammer which strikes?”: In Isaiah 41:7 the craftsmen are encouraged with a job well done when the hammer and anvil work together to make an object. In context the object is an idol, and the prophet is mocking people who build their own gods. Elsewhere the hammer both makes and destroys: “Is not my word like as a fire? saith the LORD; and like a hammer that breaketh the rock in pieces?” (Jeremiah 23:29), and Jael kills Sisera with a hammer and a tent nail (Judges 4:21). See The Bible.
    • Goethe’s second Cophtic Song ends with the choice: rule or serve, suffer or triumph, “Amboß oder Hammer sein,” “be anvil or hammer” (Johann Wolfgang von Goethe, “Kophtisches Lied, Ein Anderes”).
  • “the golden archer turning in windy heavens”: Sagittarius, the archer of the zodiac, aims his arrow at the heart of the Scorpion, the red star Antares. See Astronomy.
  • “winding, unwinding your turban, the turban moon in the cloud”: A turban is a long cloth wound around the head. Turbans have been worn since around 2350 B.C. (Wikipedia). Hannah sees the moon itself as a turban wound and unwound in the clouds.
  • “Is that the rooster crowing?”: “Before the cock crow, thou shalt deny me thrice” (Matthew 26:34). Hannah, who denied her love, hears the rooster at the end. See The Bible.
  • “what lazar demanding alms”: A lazar is a beggar with a disease, especially leprosy. The word comes from Lazarus, the beggar covered with sores in Luke 16, and it gave its name to the lazaretto, a hospital for contagious diseases. Lazarus of Bethany, who was raised from the dead, also haunts Mr. Spitzer’s world of the living dead. See Lazarus of Bethany (Ch 4).
  • “gardens of beautiful odalisques”: An odalisque was a servant woman in an Ottoman harem. The word comes from the Turkish odalık, meaning chambermaid. European painters turned the odalisque into a fantasy of the reclining, veiled woman, most famously in Ingres’s Grande Odalisque of 1814. These are women no man sees “unless he died,” hidden the way Hannah has hidden herself.
  • “Mt. Hecla, the iceberg burning with inner fire”: Mt. Hecla or Mt. Hekla is a stratovolcano in Iceland. In medieval Europe it was known as the gateway to Hell, as the Cistercian Herbert of Clairvaux wrote about 1180 in his book of miracles. Mr. Spitzer calls it “the iceberg burning with inner fire” and thinks Hannah was always nearer to it than to “the burning desert sand,” fire hidden under ice.
  • “came but with the neap tide”: A neap tide happens twice a month, when the sun and moon pull at right angles to each other at the first and third quarter moon. Neap tides have the smallest difference between high and low water. Young reverses this: Hannah’s “highest tide” arrives with the weakest tide of the month, and her life follows its own rhythm, “harnessed to no moon.”
  • “the spokes of the wheel”: Young described the characters in this book as the spokes of a wheel coming out from Miss MacIntosh in the center of the story: “I always thought of Miss MacIntosh as the center of the wheel, the hub,” with the other characters as “the spokes” (Ellen G. Friedman and Miriam Fuchs, “A Conversation with Marguerite Young,” Review of Contemporary Fiction 23, no. 1, Spring 2003 (1989 original)). In this chapter Mr. Spitzer lets “the spokes of the wheel” extend as far as possible before they reach “the clouded rim of doubt.” See The Wheel and the Spokes and Marguerite Young on Her Craft.
  • “the Emperor Tiberius with his trailing purple robes”: Emperor Tiberius or Tiberius Caesar Augustus was the second Roman emperor. He ruled from A.D. 14 to 37, Jesus was crucified during his reign, and he spent his last years withdrawn on the island of Capri. Hannah sees him in “his trailing purple robes,” the color reserved for emperors.
  • “Ur of the Chaldees glittering there”: Ur of the Chaldees or Ur Kasdim is a city mentioned in the Bible as the birthplace of Abraham. It stood in southern Mesopotamia, in what is now Iraq. Unlike the cities Mr. Spitzer imagines “buried under the desert sand and never exhumed,” Ur was dug up: the archaeologist Leonard Woolley excavated it between 1922 and 1934 and found its royal tombs. Terah “went forth with them from Ur of the Chaldees, to go into the land of Canaan” (Genesis 11:31). See Genesis.
    • Nineveh was an ancient Assyrian city of Mesopotamia and the capital of the Assyrian Empire. In the Bible, God sends Jonah to preach there: “Arise, go to Nineveh, that great city” (Jonah 1:2). It was destroyed in 612 B.C.
    • Crete is the largest and most populous of the Greek islands. It was the home of the Minoan civilization, and in Greek myth it held the labyrinth of the Minotaur. See Greek Mythology.
    • Babylon was the capital of the Babylonian Empire. It was said to hold the Hanging Gardens, it is linked with the Tower of Babel, and the people of Judah were carried there in exile in the 500s B.C.
  • “ram’s horn”: The shofar is a trumpet made from a ram’s horn and blown in Jewish worship, especially at Rosh Hashanah. In Joshua 6, priests blow seven ram’s horns and the walls of Jericho fall. Hannah’s “great angel blowing his horn upon a lonely mountain top” also recalls the angels with trumpets in Revelation 8, who announce the end of the world. See On the Battle of Jericho (Ch 59).
  • “Was she the burning phoenix or the star?”: The phoenix is the mythical bird that lives for centuries, burns itself on a pyre, and rises again from its own ashes. Herodotus wrote that the Egyptians said it came to Heliopolis every five hundred years. Christians later took it as a symbol of resurrection. For Hannah, who believed in no future life, the question of rising again stays open.
  • “Then put out the light”: This echoes Othello, Act 5, Scene 2, where Othello stands over the sleeping Desdemona and says “Put out the light, and then put out the light,” before smothering her in her bed. Several things in Cousin Hannah’s deathbed cries point to the play: she calls to a “Black Moor, beloved of woman,” she asks whether the turban-winder has come “to strangle me so that I cannot cry out,” and she lies in a bed that has become a deathbed. The suffrage captain, who spent her life refusing the role of wife, casts herself at the end as Shakespeare’s most famous murdered wife. See Shakespeare.
  • “None should see the face of love and live”: This echoes Exodus 33:20, where God tells Moses, “Thou canst not see my face: for there shall no man see me, and live.” Hannah replaces God with love, which suggests that for her, love was the force too great to look at directly.
  • “Comes he not to the dying king?”: In 1 Samuel 16:23, the young David plays the harp for King Saul, and the troubling spirit leaves the king. Hannah calls for her court musician to come with “great gold harp strings,” which places her in the role of a tormented king in need of music. Mr. Spitzer, the musician who hears “the music of the dead,” sits beside her unrecognized.
  • “Who blows this great Triton’s shell?”: Triton is a god of the sea in Greek mythology, the son of Poseidon. He blows a conch shell to calm or raise the waves, which is why Hannah asks, “Who blows this great Triton’s shell?” See Triton’s conch in the Chapter 42 resources. See Greek Mythology.
    • Triton shells are a marine mollusk. They are large sea snails named for the god, and their shells have long been blown as trumpets.
  • “is it the month of Ramadan?”: Ramadan is the ninth month of the Islamic calendar and a Muslim month of fasting, prayer, and reflection.
  • “Is it Shiraz or the sandalwood”: Shiraz is a dark-skinned grape used to produce red wine. Shiraz is also a city in southern Iran, long celebrated as the city of poets, roses, and gardens. The great Persian poets Hafez and Saadi are buried there, which suits Cousin Hannah’s “Shiraz or the sandalwood and the jewel and the incense of a dream.” See Shiraz.
    • Despite the legend that the grape came from Shiraz, DNA testing at the University of California, Davis, in 1998 showed that it is French, a cross of Dureza and Mondeuse Blanche.
  • “Or is it the third eye?”: Cousin Hannah asks whether the jewel gleaming in her love’s forehead is “the third eye.” Third eye is a mystical and esoteric concept of a speculative invisible eye on the forehead which provides perception beyond ordinary sight (Wikipedia). In Hindu tradition the god Shiva has a third eye in the center of his forehead, and when it opens it destroys. In one story Shiva burns Kama, the god of love, to ash with it. The forehead point is also the ajna chakra, the seat of inner sight, which the bindi marks. The question ties her lost love to both vision and destruction. See Hinduism.
  • “the eighth day of the week”: Eighth day of the week may refer to Burmese Theravada Buddhism where the week has eight days. Wednesday is divided into two parts. Early Christian writers also called the resurrection the “eighth day,” the day after the seven days of creation, and Augustine ends The City of God with the seventh day of rest leading into “the eighth and eternal day.” It is a time outside ordinary time. See Augustine and Christian Theology and Buddhism.
  • “the thirteenth month of the year”: The thirteenth month of the year may refer to the International Fixed Calendar that has thirteen months of 28 days each and the day of the week is constant. A thirteenth month also exists in lunar calendars that add a leap month to catch up with the solar year, such as the second month of Adar in the Hebrew calendar. Like the eighth day, it is a time outside ordinary time.
    • Moses Cotsworth proposed the International Fixed Calendar in 1902, and George Eastman kept the books of the Eastman Kodak Company by it from 1928 to 1989.
  • “great dancer in the infinite”: Shiva as Nataraja, Lord of the Dance, dances the universe through creation and destruction within a ring of fire (Ananda K. Coomaraswamy, “The Dance of Shiva,” 1918). See the third eye entry below. See Hinduism.
  • “Ah, Black Moor, beloved of woman”: Moors was a term first used by European Christians to designate the Muslim inhabitants of Maghreb, Iberian Peninsula, Malta, and Sicily during the Middle Ages (Wikipedia). Othello is “the Moor of Venice.” The Black Moor becomes a black rooster. See Shakespeare.
  • “In heaven the black rooster lays the egg, and the white hen crows”: An old proverb says “A whistling woman and a crowing hen are neither fit for God nor men.” It was used against women who spoke out of their expected place, which makes a crowing hen a fitting image for a suffragette. A rooster laying an egg was considered unnatural and dangerous. Medieval legend held that a rooster’s egg hatched the basilisk, and in Basel in 1474 a rooster accused of laying an egg was tried and burned (E. P. Evans, The Criminal Prosecution and Capital Punishment of Animals, 1906). Hannah’s heaven reverses the order of the barnyard. The hen crows, “and none shall stop her.” See Women’s Suffrage.
  • “Forbidden East”: Forbidden East may refer to the Forbidden City in Beijing, the palace of the emperors of imperial China, built in the early 1400s.
  • “the men wore skirts, and the ladies wore trousers or bloomers”: The oldest known trousers, found in the Yanghai cemetery in western China, were worn by horse riders some 3,000 years ago (Ulrike Beck et al., “The invention of trousers and its likely affiliation with horseback riding and mobility,” Quaternary International 348, 2014). The Scythian horse riders of the steppes, women as well as men, wore them later, and the Greeks thought trousers fit only for barbarians. Mr. Spitzer’s “forbidden east,” where the men wear skirts and the ladies wear trousers, turns the customs of his own country upside down.
    • Bloomers are divided women’s garments for the lower body. They were developed in the 19th century as a healthful and comfortable alternative to the heavy, constricting dresses worn by American women (Wikipedia). They take their name from their best-known advocate, the women’s rights activist Amelia Bloomer. It became a symbol of women’s rights in the early 1850s. See Amelia Bloomer in the Chapter 42 resources. See Women’s Suffrage and Clothing, Hats, and Skirts.
  • “pawn figures moving not only from dream to dream of the dreamer but from dreamer to dreamer”: Carl Jung believed that dreams reveal more than they conceal: dreams are “a part of nature, which harbors no intention to deceive, but expresses something as best it can” (C. G. Jung, Memories, Dreams, Reflections, 1962). They are a natural expression of the imagination and speak in the most straightforward language the mind has: mythic narratives. The parts of a person’s mythic life keep a similar structure across the whole lifespan. His collective unconscious is “identical in all men and thus constitutes a common psychic substrate of a suprapersonal nature which is present in every one of us” (C. G. Jung, The Archetypes and the Collective Unconscious, Collected Works 9, part 1, trans. R. F. C. Hull, 1959). It refers to the psychological constants shared by all societies, such as rites of passage into womanhood, or the growing fascination with death after middle age. Mr. Spitzer’s sense that the same figures pass from one dreamer to another is close to Jung’s collective unconscious. See Freud and Jung.
  • “Is there no meeting place, place where two parallel lines meet?”: Euclid’s fifth postulate held that parallel lines never meet. In the nineteenth century, mathematicians such as Lobachevsky and Riemann built non-Euclidean geometries in which that rule no longer holds, and in projective geometry parallel lines meet at a point at infinity. Hannah’s question asks whether two lives that ran side by side without touching, like hers and her lost love’s, can meet at the end.
  • “walk like the cripple healed by some great, sudden miracle”: In John 5, Jesus tells a man who had been unable to walk for thirty-eight years, “Rise, take up thy bed, and walk,” and in Acts 3 Peter heals a man lame from birth at the temple gate. Mr. Spitzer half expects Hannah, who never gave up a fight, to rise from her deathbed the same way, but “she lay prone as an everlasting horizon.”
  • “Is that the tent-maker? Is that the tent?”: The name of the Persian poet Omar Khayyam means “tentmaker.” Edward FitzGerald’s 1859 translation of his Rubáiyát made him famous in English as a poet of mortality, and in one quatrain the body is “but a Tent where takes his one day’s rest / A Sultan to the realm of Death addrest.” The apostle Paul was also a tentmaker by trade (Acts 18:3), and he called the body “our earthly house of this tabernacle,” a tent that will be taken down (2 Corinthians 5:1). Hannah, whose visions are full of desert tents, asks where the tent-maker sets his tent “upon what star or cloud” as her own tent is being struck.
  • “Look not into the things that are to see the things that are not”: This inverts 2 Corinthians 4:18, “While we look not at the things which are seen, but at the things which are not seen: for the things which are seen are temporal; but the things which are not seen are eternal.” Paul is urging faith. Hannah, who believed in no afterlife, is giving a warning.
  • “you like Mr. Chandelier moving through clouds”: Mr. Chandelier comes from Catherine Cartwheel’s opium dreams in Chapter 2, the chandelier imagined as her companion with “seven lighted candles in his seven crystal hands.” Hannah’s calling on him is another dream figure passing “from dreamer to dreamer.” See Mr. Chandelier.
  • “my wild swan girl”: In folklore the swan maiden sheds her feathered robe to become a woman, and whoever steals the robe can keep her. Tchaikovsky’s Swan Lake (1877) gives the story its best-known form. See Fairy Tales and Folklore and Music and Composers.
  • “Bacchus and his crew of satyrs crowned by flowers”: Bacchus, the Roman name for the Greek god Dionysus, is the god of the grape-harvest, winemaking and wine, fertility and orchards (Wikipedia). Hannah asks whether it is “Bacchus and his crew of satyrs crowned by flowers.” See Greek Mythology.
    • Satyrs in Greek mythology are male nature spirits, part goat or horse, who follow Dionysus.
    • Nymphs in Greek folklore are minor female nature deities (Wikipedia).
  • “Are those the music-makers”: “We are the music makers, / And we are the dreamers of dreams” (Arthur O’Shaughnessy, “Ode,” 1873). See Music and Composers.
  • “somersaultings like Pierrot”: Pierrot is a stock character of pantomime and comedy in the late seventeenth-century Italian troupe of players performing in Paris (Wikipedia). He is the sad clown, with a whitened face and loose white clothes, forever lovesick, usually for Columbine, who leaves him for Harlequin. The mime Jean-Gaspard Deburau made Pierrot famous in Paris in the 1820s and 1830s. Mr. Spitzer sees in Hannah’s “somersaultings like Pierrot” a lovesick clown hidden under the warrior.
    • Marcel Carné’s film Les Enfants du Paradis (1945) made Deburau its hero, the Pierrot who loves silently and loses.
  • “not even the greatest calker could calk her now”: A calker, now usually spelled caulker, forces fibers soaked in pitch or tar into the seams between a wooden ship’s planks to make it watertight. Mr. Spitzer’s “maritime memories derived from a remote forefather” turn Hannah’s dying body into an old ship coming apart at its seams.
  • “If the Southern Cross should be missing”: Southern Cross or Crux is a constellation of the southern sky that has four bright stars in a cross-shape (Wikipedia). See Astronomy.
  • “the Northern Cross should be missing”: Northern Cross is an astronomical asterism in the northern hemisphere of the celestial sphere and is much larger than the Southern Cross (Wikipedia). It is part of the constellation Cygnus, the Swan. See Astronomy.
  • “if this earth were totally abandoned, would not a bee zoom in a meadow of wild flowers . . . a leaf fall?”: If a tree falls in the forest does anyone hear it? The riddle was in print by 1883, in the magazine The Chautauquan. The question challenges the notion that perception is essential for reality. Some philosophers argue that the sound requires a conscious observer because it is a form of perception. Others argue that sound is an objective physical phenomenon that exists independently of perception. It can also suggest that life goes on without humans there to witness it, which decenters the human point of view.
    • George Berkeley held that for things of sense “their esse is percipi,” to be is to be perceived (A Treatise Concerning the Principles of Human Knowledge, 1710).
  • “was there not the white of edelweiss embroidered upon the hem?”: Edelweiss appears as a detail embroidered on the hem of the white skirt Cousin Hannah cries for. It is an alpine flower that grows in high-altitude habitats, and it carries a good deal of symbolism. It has been associated with courage and bravery, resilience and survival, nobility and purity, luck and good fortune. It grows on high, dangerous cliffs, and climbers risked their lives to gather it, which is why it came to stand for courage, a fitting emblem for Hannah.
  • “fields of asphodel”: Asphodel may refer to the Asphodel Meadows. It is a section of the underworld in Greek mythology where ordinary souls are sent to live after death (Wikipedia). See the meadow of asphodel in the Chapter 42 resources. See Greek Mythology.
  • “thin as Pleiades”: Pleiades, also known as The Seven Sisters or Messier 45, is an open star cluster in the night sky visible in virtually every part of the globe (Wikipedia). See Astronomy.
    • One of the seven sisters is said to hide her face, the lost Pleiad, for shame at marrying a mortal (Ovid, Fasti 4.169-178). See Greek Mythology.
  • “I see a light upon the other shore”: In Buddhism, awakening is the other shore. The Heart Sutra ends with the mantra “Gate gate pāragate pārasaṃgate bodhi svāhā,” “Gone, gone, gone beyond, gone altogether beyond, awakening, hail.” Mr. Spitzer, too, “would be upon the other shore.” See Buddhism.
  • “Is it the will-o’-the-wisp”: A will-o’-the-wisp is a ghostly light seen at night over marshes and bogs. It is also called ignis fatuus, Latin for “foolish fire.” In folklore it leads travelers off safe paths and into the swamp. It is now thought to come from burning marsh gases. Hannah asks, “must I follow her who followed me?” The question makes her lost love a light that is both a guide and a lure.
  • “Do I come again to that dark tower? Is that the winding horn?”: These questions recall Robert Browning’s 1855 poem “Childe Roland to the Dark Tower Came,” whose title comes from a line Edgar speaks in King Lear. Roland crosses a ruined wasteland to the dark tower where all the knights before him were lost, and the poem ends as he raises his horn: “Dauntless the slug-horn to my lips I set, / And blew.” Hannah, too, has come to the end of a long quest where others fell. See Childe Roland to the Dark Tower.
  • “Shall I put on this body and this love?”: “For this corruptible must put on incorruption, and this mortal must put on immortality” (1 Corinthians 15:53). See The Bible.
  • “Is that my love, my skirt moving through clouds”: Skirt has long been slang for a woman, as in “a bit of skirt.” The skirt Hannah lost “so long ago” may be both the garment she gave up for the cause and the woman she lost. See Young’s account of the bridal trousseaus under “a secret woman, a bride” in the Chapter 42 resources. See Women, Gender, and Marriage and Clothing, Hats, and Skirts.
  • “Oh, is she in the shadowed valley”: “Yea, though I walk through the valley of the shadow of death, I will fear no evil” (Psalm 23:4). See The Bible.
  • “Does he come to my bed?”: The goat with gold eyes and a beard recalls Pan, the goat-footed god of the wild, who pursued the nymph Syrinx until she was turned into reeds (Ovid, Metamorphoses 1.689-712). See Greek Mythology.

Vocabulary

Acclimatized
Grown used to a new climate, place, or situation.
Acme
The highest point of something; the peak.
Adventitious
Happening by chance; not essential or built in.
Ambrosial
Divinely fragrant or delicious. From ambrosia, the food of the Greek gods, which gave them immortality.
Amorphous
Without a clear shape or form.
Amphitheatre
A round or oval open-air arena with rising tiers of seats around a central space, used in ancient Rome for gladiator contests and public spectacles.
Anvil
The heavy iron block on which a blacksmith hammers hot metal into shape.
Apparition
A ghost, or a ghostlike image of a person.
Arcanum
A mysterious or specialized knowledge, language, or information accessible or possessed only by the initiate. From the Latin arcanus, hidden or closed. Plural: arcana.
Armorer
A maker or repairer of armor and weapons.
Astral
Having to do with the stars.
Auk
A diving seabird of northern seas. The great auk, a large flightless species, became extinct in 1844. More under Resources.
Balloon fish
A pufferfish, which swallows water to swell its body into a spiny ball when threatened.
Barnacled
Crusted with barnacles, small shelled sea creatures that cling to rocks, pilings, and the hulls of ships.
Barouche
A fashionable four-wheeled carriage with a folding half-hood and two seats facing each other. More under Resources.
Blackamoor
An old term for a Black African or any dark-skinned person, common in European art and in decorative figures of Black servants. It is now considered offensive.
Breastplate
A piece of armor covering the chest.
Caliph
The title of the chief Muslim ruler, understood as a successor to the Prophet Muhammad.
Calker
Also caulker. A worker who seals the seams of a wooden ship to make it watertight. More under Resources.
Carousel
A merry-go-round. Earlier, a tournament in which horsemen performed exercises and displays.
Casket
A small, often ornate box for jewels or valuables. In American usage, also a coffin, so Young’s “casket containing no jewel” carries both meanings.
Centaur
In Greek mythology, a creature with the head and upper body of a man and the body and legs of a horse.
Centurion
An officer in the Roman army who commanded about a hundred soldiers.
Chimerical
Imaginary, fanciful, or wildly unrealistic. From the Chimera, the fire-breathing monster of Greek myth made of a lion, a goat, and a serpent.
Citadel
A fortress, usually on high ground, that protects a city.
Clapper
The hanging metal tongue inside a bell that strikes it to make it ring.
Cockle
A small saltwater clam with a ribbed, heart-shaped shell. A cockleshell boat is a small, flimsy one.
Colonnade
A row of columns, usually holding up a roof.
Combers
A nautical term for long, curling waves that roll in and break on a beach or reef.
Conch
A large sea snail with a spiraled shell that can be blown like a horn. Held to the ear, it seems to hold the sound of the sea.
Consummation
The completion or fulfillment of something.
Cosmography
A description or map of the whole universe, both heavens and earth.
Crow’s-nest
A lookout platform high on a ship’s mast.
Crucible
A heat-resistant pot for melting metals. Figuratively, a severe test that changes a person.
Crusader
A soldier in the Crusades, the Christian military campaigns to take the Holy Land, fought between 1096 and 1291.
Crystal-gazer
A fortune-teller who looks into a crystal ball to see the future.
Crystal-hunter
A prospector in the Alps who climbs into rock clefts to find quartz crystals.
Cup-bearer
A servant who poured and served wine to a king, a position of great trust. Nehemiah was cup-bearer to the Persian king Artaxerxes, and in Greek myth the youth Ganymede was cup-bearer to Zeus.
Dance of death
Also danse macabre. A medieval image of Death leading people of every rank, from pope and king to child and beggar, in a dance to the grave. See On the danse macabre (Ch 43).
Deference
Polite respect, or yielding to someone else’s wishes or judgment.
Disembodiment
Separation from the body; existing as a spirit without a body.
Dopester
A person who predicts the outcome of horse races, elections, or other contests from inside information, or “dope.”
Emir
A commander or prince in the Islamic world. More under Resources.
Empearled
Adorned with pearls, or having a pearly sheen.
Enigma
A mystery or puzzle; a person or thing that is hard to understand.
Eunuch
A man who has been castrated. Eunuchs were employed for centuries to guard harems and to serve as officials in royal courts in the Middle East, China, and Byzantium. See The eunuch (Ch 35).
Fallacy
A mistaken belief, or a flaw in reasoning that makes an argument unsound.
Figurehead
A carved figure, often a woman, mounted on the bow of a sailing ship. See On the figurehead and intuition (Ch 40).
Firmament
The sky or the heavens, imagined as a solid dome overhead, as in Genesis 1.
Flounced
Trimmed with flounces, wide strips of gathered or pleated fabric sewn to a skirt or dress.
Forebodings
Feelings that something bad is about to happen.
Forecastle
The forward part of a ship below the deck, where the crew lived. Pronounced “FOHK-sul.”
Frivolities
Silly, trivial, or lighthearted things.
Gondolier
The boatman who rows a Venetian gondola, standing at the stern with a single oar.
Halcyon
Calm and peaceful. From the halcyon, a mythical bird said to calm the sea while it nested on the waves in winter.
Halo
A ring of light around the sun or moon, caused by ice crystals high in thin clouds. In art, a ring of light around the head of a saint.
Hanging gardens
The Hanging Gardens of Babylon, one of the Seven Wonders of the Ancient World: terraced gardens said to have been built by King Nebuchadnezzar II. No trace of them has ever been found.
Helm
The wheel or tiller that steers a ship.
Ibis
A long-legged wading bird with a downward-curved bill, sacred in ancient Egypt to Thoth, god of writing and wisdom.
Immured
Shut in or imprisoned, as if walled up.
Imponderable
Something that cannot be measured, weighed, or judged.
Inscrutable
Impossible to understand or interpret.
Inveterate
Long settled in a habit and unlikely to change, as in “inveterate gambler.”
Keel and list
To keel over is to capsize, with the keel, the ship’s backbone along the bottom, turning upward. To list is to lean to one side, usually from water taken on.
Lagoon
A stretch of shallow water separated from the sea by a reef or sandbar.
Lazar
A diseased beggar, especially one with leprosy. More under Resources.
Lethargy
Sluggishness, drowsiness, a lack of energy.
Livid
Bluish-gray, the color of a bruise. Also furiously angry.
Lunar month
The time from one new moon to the next, about 29.5 days.
Lute
A plucked string instrument with a rounded back shaped like half a pear, popular in Europe from the Middle Ages through the 1700s.
Maharajah
A great king or prince in India. From the Sanskrit for “great king.”
Mandarin
A high-ranking official of imperial China.
Medusa
A jellyfish in its free-swimming, bell-shaped stage, named for the Gorgon of Greek myth whose hair was snakes.
Mercurial
Quick and changeable in mood. From the swift Roman messenger god Mercury and the liquid metal named for him.
Metamorphic
Having to do with a change of form. In geology, rock that heat and pressure have changed.
Mica
A mineral that splits into thin, shiny, nearly transparent sheets and makes rock glitter.
Minaret
A tall, slender tower of a mosque, from which the call to prayer is given.
Mirage
An optical illusion, common in deserts, in which hot air bends light so that distant water or cities seem to appear.
Monsoon
A seasonal wind in South Asia that brings months of heavy rain.
Mosaic
A picture or pattern made by setting small pieces of colored stone, glass, or tile together.
Nag
An old or worn-out horse.
Neap tide
The tide with the smallest difference between high and low water, twice a month at the quarter moons. More under Resources.
Negligee
A woman’s light, flowing dressing gown.
Nepenthe
In Homer’s Odyssey, a drug from Egypt that Helen puts in the wine to banish grief and sorrow. Anything that brings forgetfulness of pain. See On Nepenthe (Ch 82).
Odalisque
A servant woman or concubine in a Turkish harem. More under Resources.
Pagoda
An Asian tiered tower with multiple eaves, usually a Buddhist temple or shrine.
Palmer
A medieval pilgrim who brought back a palm frond from the Holy Land. More under Resources.
Paradox
A statement or situation that seems to contradict itself and yet may be true.
Parasol
A light umbrella carried for shade from the sun.
Parterre
An ornamental garden of flower beds laid out in a pattern. A parterred floor is inlaid in patterned sections.
Perambulations
Walks or strolls, especially leisurely ones.
Peregrinations
A journey, especially a long or meandering one.
Phantasmal
Ghostly; like a phantom or an illusion.
Pinnacle
The highest point; a tall, pointed mountain peak or the slender spire on a building.
Portfolio
A flat case for carrying loose papers and documents.
Presentiment
An intuitive feeling that something is about to happen.
Principality
A territory ruled by a prince.
Prism
A clear piece of glass with flat sides that splits light into the colors of the rainbow.
Promontory
A high point of land jutting out into the sea.
Roseate
Rose-colored. Also hopeful or overly optimistic.
Rubicon
A small river in northern Italy. Julius Caesar crossed it with his army in 49 BC, starting a civil war, so “crossing the Rubicon” means passing a point of no return. See Crossing the Rubicon (Ch 23).
Sandalwood
A fragrant wood from India and the Pacific, burned as incense and used in perfume.
Sartorial
Having to do with clothing, tailoring, or style of dress.
Seer
A person who sees the future; a prophet.
Shah
The title of the king of Persia, now Iran.
Shell game
A swindle in which a pea is hidden under one of three shells or cups and shuffled, and bettors guess where it is. The operator usually palms the pea, so no one can win.
Skiff
A small, light boat for rowing or sailing. Young’s “skiff moon” is a crescent shaped like one.
Spar
A pole used as a ship’s mast, boom, or yard.
Steeplechase
A horse race over fences, ditches, and water jumps, first run cross-country from one church steeple to another.
Suffragette
A woman who campaigned for women’s right to vote. The word was coined by a London newspaper in 1906 for militant British activists. Most American activists called themselves suffragists. See Women’s Suffrage.
Sultanate
A country ruled by a sultan.
Supernumerary
Extra; more than the number needed. In the theater, an extra with no lines.
Surrey
A light four-wheeled horse-drawn carriage with two seats, often with a fringed canopy on top.
Testimonial
A formal statement given as evidence or proof of something.
Tonnage
The size or carrying capacity of a ship.
Torpor
A sluggish, heavy, half-asleep state.
Touch
Slang for asking someone for money, especially a small loan. To “make a touch” is to borrow or beg cash.
Transact
To carry out or carry through. Young uses it for crossing a distance, as in “transacted the gulf between two worlds.”
Transmutation
A change from one form or substance into another, especially the alchemists’ dream of turning base metal into gold.
Turret
A small tower on a building or castle.
Untenable
Impossible to defend, hold, or live in.
Vigil
A period of staying awake to keep watch, especially at the bedside of someone sick or dying.

Chapter 33

← Chapter 32 · Home · Chapter 34 →

Content note: Vera’s mother, Catherine Cartwheel, is addicted to opium.

Summary

A Boston newspaper once called Catherine “the late Mrs. Catherine Cartwheel,” widow of Jock, and Mr. Spitzer never told her. The same paper reported Peron seen on Benevolent Street, and Mr. Spitzer walked there the next evening. Catherine cannot reconstruct her wedding. Her bridegroom was a white camel, a church steeple, a key, the wind, perhaps Death while she slept. Mr. Spitzer cannot remember the wedding at all. He writes harp music to imitate the wind in a bridge’s cables, and day after day he asks the post office to trace a blank letter he mailed to himself years ago. He decides her dreaming is no farther from reality than the lives of those who punch time clocks: “They, too, could live only while they dreamed.” When she tells someone to open the door and a human-sized blackbird answers that it is already open, Mr. Spitzer gets up and opens it.

Characters present

Catherine Cartwheel · Joachim Spitzer · Jock Cartwheel · Peron Spitzer · The Black Coachman · Vera Cartwheel

Concepts present

Themes: Death and Mortality · Illusion and Reality · Isolation and Connection · Madness and Sanity · Memory and the Past · Music, Sound, and Silence · Time

Symbols: Birds · Dogs · Horses and Carriages · Keys, Doors, and Locks · Moon and Stars · Music and Instruments · Twins and Doubles · Weddings and Funerals

Philosophy: Marguerite Young on Her Craft

Allusions: American Writers · Astronomy · Edgar Allan Poe · Exploration and the Poles · Genesis · Greek Mythology · Judaism · Music and Composers · Romantic Poets · Shakespeare · The Bible

Key passages

From the research

  • Early in the chapter, it is revealed that a Boston newspaper mistakenly referred to Vera’s mother as deceased, calling her “the late Mrs. Catherine Cartwheel” despite her still being alive. Mr. Spitzer chooses not to correct this error, believing it “unimportant and possibly trivial,” as Catherine lives in a realm of “starry illusions” due to her opium addiction.
  • Catherine sometimes thinks she was never married, or was married to strangers “as often as an erroneous clock struck,” and she “would swear, of course, that she had never married Mr. Spitzer.” Her preference for imagining multiple, shifting, and fantastical bridegrooms underscores her dissociation from reality and her embrace of poetic, surreal identities.
  • Catherine’s fragmented and vague recollection of her wedding, surrounded by “spirits in the air,” “glassy pebbles rolling on the shore,” “swords of fire, swords of ice,” and “wild, ethereal wedding music,” creates a surreal, almost otherworldly atmosphere.
  • Mr. Spitzer’s role as the observer and caretaker is critical. He reflects on Catherine’s addiction, her detachment from time, and her illusory world, concluding that she is “probably no more enslaved than others were by their predisposition toward illusion.” His philosophical musings on consciousness, unconsciousness, and the nature of life and death add depth to the narrative, portraying a compassionate understanding of human frailty and the necessity of illusions. His own struggle with reality, his brother’s ruin, and his meticulous attempts to grasp the elusive, mirror Catherine’s own fragmented existence.
  • A striking passage describes Catherine talking to invisible or imagined persons, showing her living in a world where the usual distinctions between presence and absence, reality and fantasy, are dissolved. Mr. Spitzer’s rising to open the door, which the blackbird says is already open, demonstrates his gentle indulgence of her illusions and the poignancy of her condition.
  • References to the “dead lute-player in the garden,” “formal king penguins,” “melancholy seals,” and “tinkling duchesses” contribute to the surreal and symbolic texture of the chapter. These images reinforce the theme of a world where music, memory, and myth intermingle, and reality is perceived through a kaleidoscope of unusual and poetic visions.
  • Mr. Spitzer writes harp music as “the exact imitation of the wind playing through the strings and cables of a bridge,” and day after day he asks the post office to trace a dead letter he mailed to himself, “an envelope containing a piece of blank paper.” His music and his letter are both waiting for something that does not arrive.

Questions and observations

Reading closely

  • Mr. Spitzer leaves the error alone because “some day this Boston newspaper… would probably be right, having merely mistaken the time.” Is an early obituary a lie?
  • “She would often say that she was the kind of woman who could love only the man she had never married.” Why?
  • Mr. Spitzer mails himself “a piece of blank paper” and asks the post office to trace it. What is he waiting to receive?

Characters

  • Mr. Spitzer “could never remember this wedding,” expressing “his seething belligerence by his blank passivity.” Where else does his politeness hide anger?
  • He fears his unconsciousness “as he feared death.” Why does Catherine’s unconsciousness seem to him “a greater freedom”?
  • The paper reports Peron “walking along Benevolent Street.” Which brother is the newspaper wrong about?

Connections

  • In Chapter 32 Catherine married “a phantom.” Here “the bride had been a door. The bridegroom had been a key.” How do the two weddings differ?
  • Mr. Spitzer’s music imitates “the wind playing through the strings and cables of a bridge.” How does it echo the harp at Catherine’s wedding?
  • In Chapter 14 Catherine said “the coachman was her conscience.” Who drives her carriage here?

Reflection

  • Is anyone ever “quite awake”?
  • Would you correct a friend’s comforting mistake?
  • What would you mail to yourself?

Research: Characters

Catherine Cartwheel (Vera’s mother)

  • A once-famous beauty and socialite who has long been out of public view.
  • A complex figure, described as living in illusions and opium-induced dreams.
  • Her memories, especially of her wedding(s), are fragmented, poetic, and unreliable.
  • She is not told that a newspaper reported her death, and she sometimes thinks she was never married at all, though her husband was Jock, who “had disappeared when the mountains moved like waves.”
  • She interacts with imaginary figures and experiences reality as a blend of dream and fact.

Mr. Spitzer

  • A close, faithful friend of Catherine.
  • He understands her illusions and indulges them, choosing not to correct her perceptions.
  • He is practical but also philosophical, contrasting his own conscious precision with Catherine’s dreamlike state.
  • He is involved in artistic creation like writing harp music inspired by the wind and bridges.
  • Carries a burden of familial and financial complications (his brother’s debts), “vicarious debts, those he could never hope to pay to creditors he did not know.”
  • He represents a grounding figure, yet he is also caught in Catherine’s world of illusion.
  • Mr. Spitzer’s thoughts include existential questions about reality, illusion, death, and time.
  • He goes to the post office day after day to trace a letter he mailed to himself, “an envelope containing a piece of blank paper.”
  • Catherine rejected “the altogether different life she might have lived had she accepted his invitation to live in a secluded place and listen to his future music, that which had been as yet unwritten.”
  • He believes her conscious states “were probably like the unconscious states of other people.”

Peron Spitzer

  • The Boston newspaper reports him “seen recently walking along Benevolent Street, peering into old doorways.”

Jock Cartwheel

  • “The fashionable dog fancier, the fabulous yachtsman, the great mountain-climber who had disappeared when the mountains moved like waves.”

The Black Coachman

  • At the wedding Catherine saw “his silver buttons, his white gloves,” and sometimes heard “the coachman’s cries to his horses” without seeing him.

Research: Themes

Memory and Illusion

See: Illusion and Reality · Memory and the Past

  • Catherine’s memories are described as “beautifully inaccurate,” blending fact with fantasy.
  • She often confuses time, place, and people, exemplifying the fragility of human memory.
  • Memories of her wedding are surreal, involving images like bats, owls, icy landscapes, and ambiguous bridegrooms.
  • The narrative suggests memory as a form of dream or illusion that can persist beyond life.

Death and Existence

See: Death and Mortality

  • Catherine is reported dead by a Boston newspaper but is alive in her own dream world.
  • Death is portrayed ambiguously, sometimes as a wedding to Death itself or as slipping into an eternal unconsciousness.
  • The boundary between life and death is blurred, raising questions about what it means truly to live or die.

Time and Reality

See: Illusion and Reality · Time

  • Time is fluid and unreliable in Catherine’s experience; she confuses noon and midnight, beginnings and endings.
  • Mr. Spitzer attempts to keep time (symbolized by his brother’s watch) as a measure of reality, but even he is caught between illusion and fact.
  • The novel questions the nature of reality itself and how much is defined by perception.

Music and Sound

See: Music, Sound, and Silence

  • Mr. Spitzer’s harp music inspired by wind and bridge cables symbolizes the blending of natural forces and artistic creation.
  • Music serves as a metaphor for the ephemeral, invisible forces shaping human experience and memory.

Isolation and Companionship

See: Isolation and Connection

  • Despite Catherine’s isolation in her illusions, Mr. Spitzer remains a constant companion, albeit one often rejected by her.
  • Their relationship is marked by a tension between reality and fantasy, presence and absence.

Research: Symbols and Imagery

The Wedding and Bridegroom(s)

See: Weddings and Funerals · Keys, Doors, and Locks

  • Catherine’s ambiguous wedding(s) symbolize transitions, possibly to death or between states of consciousness.
  • The multiple, shifting bridegrooms (white camel, church steeple, wind) reflect the fluidity of identity and reality.

The Black Coachman and Carriage

See: Horses and Carriages

  • Symbolize passage, possibly death or transition.
  • The carriage on the streets of Boston, after years of absence, signals a disruption of normal order.
  • In Chapter 14 Catherine said her body was the carriage and “the coachman was her conscience.”

The Blackbird and the Door

See: Birds · Keys, Doors, and Locks

  • She tells someone to open the door, and the voice answers that it is already open, though the door is closed. She is talking to a human-sized blackbird.
  • These images portray the overlap of the real and the imaginary.

Stars and Celestial Imagery

See: Moon and Stars

  • Stars and heavens often represent unreachable or eternal realms.
  • Catherine refuses to marry Mr. Spitzer “not while the stars shone in the glassy heavens,” linking love and fate to cosmic forces.

The Newspaper Mistake

See: Illusion and Reality

  • The misreporting of Catherine’s death and Mr. Spitzer’s decision not to correct it sets the tone for the chapter’s exploration of truth versus illusion.

The Wedding Memories

See: Weddings and Funerals

  • Catherine’s hazy, fantastical memories of her wedding illustrate the blurred line between reality and fantasy.

Mr. Spitzer’s Harp Music

See: Music and Instruments

  • His artistic endeavor is inspired by natural sounds and symbolizes the attempt to impose order or meaning on chaos.

Catherine’s Conversations with Invisible Figures

See: Madness and Sanity

  • Demonstrates her detachment from consensus reality.
  • Mr. Spitzer could not hear the answer she heard, “though apparently what the other person said was quite rational.”

Research: Resources

  • “the fashionable dog fancier”: A dog fancier breeds and shows pedigree dogs. The Westminster Kennel Club held its first show in New York in 1877. See Dogs.
  • “great kings wrapped in canvas shrouds”: In burial at sea, the dead were sewn into canvas weighted with shot, the last stitch by tradition through the nose. See Death and Mortality.
  • “she was still entertaining Chinese mandarins”: Weissenbach, the real opium lady, “dreamed about… mandarins and… a human-sized black bird standing in the hallway” (Marguerite Young, interview with Charles Ruas, WBAI radio, New York). See the blackbird at the end of the chapter and Catherine Cartwheel.
  • “great balloon ascensionists who long ago had descended to earth, dragging their shrouds and cords”: Salomon Andrée set out by balloon for the North Pole in 1897 and vanished. The bodies and diaries of his party were found on White Island in 1930. See Exploration and the Poles.
  • “the mistake of a printer’s devil”: A printer’s devil was a young apprentice in a printing establishment who performed a number of tasks, such as mixing tubs of ink and fetching type. Notable writers including Ambrose Bierce, Benjamin Franklin, Walt Whitman, and Mark Twain served as printer’s devils in their youth.
  • “what ghostly hand had guided the great printer’s devil”: “In the same hour came forth fingers of a man’s hand, and wrote over against the candlestick upon the plaister of the wall” (Daniel 5:5), the writing at Belshazzar’s feast. See The Bible.
  • “just when the lamp-lighters were lighting the lamps”: Boston’s Beacon Hill is still lit by gas street lamps, once lit each evening by lamplighters.
  • “like the sobbing of the rain upon the river Styx”: The Styx is the river of the underworld, and the gods swore their oaths by it. See Greek Mythology.
  • “even her funeral, as he remembered his”: Mr. Spitzer remembers his own funeral because he buried his twin. Young said, “Grief was so great that he thought the wrong brother died” (Marguerite Young, interview with Studs Terkel, WFMT radio, 1965). See Twins and Doubles and Peron Spitzer.
  • “The bride had been a door. The bridegroom had been a key”: Christ says “I am the door” (John 10:9) and holds “the key of David” (Revelation 3:7), and the Church is “the bride, the Lamb’s wife” (Revelation 21:9). See The Bible.
  • “though she seemed to remember that he had been at her wedding”: “He that hath the bride is the bridegroom: but the friend of the bridegroom, which standeth and heareth him, rejoiceth greatly because of the bridegroom’s voice: this my joy therefore is fulfilled” (John 3:29). Mr. Spitzer is the friend at the wedding. See The Bible.
  • “swords of fire, swords of ice”: At the gate of Eden God placed “a flaming sword which turned every way” (Genesis 3:24). See Genesis.
  • “her powers of ratiocination were not good”: Poe called his Dupin detective stories, beginning with “The Murders in the Rue Morgue” (1841), “tales of ratiocination.” See Edgar Allan Poe.
  • “that she had been married to Death while she was sleeping”: Death and the Maiden, a theme of Renaissance painting and of Schubert’s song “Der Tod und das Mädchen” (1817), in which Death comes to a girl as a gentle lover: “Thou shalt sleep softly in my arms.” See Death and Mortality.
  • “Near-sighted bats flitting by on leathern wings”: “Save where the weak-ey’d bat, / With short shrill shriek flits by on leathern wing” (William Collins, “Ode to Evening,” 1747). Bats are not near-sighted. They see well and also hunt by echolocation. See Romantic Poets.
  • “Owls, great horned owls hooting above the lonely church steeples”: “From yonder ivy-mantled tow’r / The moping owl does to the moon complain” (Thomas Gray, “Elegy Written in a Country Churchyard,” 1751). Young named Gray’s Elegy as a model for Angel in the Forest (Marguerite Young, interview with Charles Ruas and Joan Schwartz, WBAI radio, New York). See Birds.
  • “the withered harp strings played upon by nothing but the fingers of the invisible wind”: At Yaddo, Truman Capote occupied Katrina Trask’s tower, where a harp played when the door opened, and Young said, “I used that harp in my description of the Opium Lady” (Charles Ruas, Conversations with American Writers, Knopf, 1985). See Catherine Cartwheel and Music and Instruments.
    • A harp played by the wind is an Aeolian harp, named for Aeolus, keeper of the winds. In Coleridge’s “The Eolian Harp” (1795) it is “that simplest Lute, / Placed length-ways in the clasping casement.” See Romantic Poets.
  • “The sere stars shook like autumn leaves”: “My way of life / Is fall’n into the sear, the yellow leaf” (Macbeth 5.3). See Shakespeare.
  • “the dead lute-player in the garden, his pear-shaped body, his long, twisted neck”: The lute has a pear-shaped body and a pegbox bent back from its neck. “He was this man who was this musical instrument.” See Music and Instruments.
  • “a great many formal king penguins, a great many melancholy seals”: King penguins live only in the far south, and seals in both polar seas, so “the bipolar illusion” means of both poles. See Exploration and the Poles.
  • “these dream fugues, these polyphonic compositions”: A fugue is a composition in which voices enter one after another on the same theme, as in Bach’s The Art of Fugue. In psychiatry a fugue is also a flight from one’s own identity. See Music and Composers.
    • “Palestrina” may refer to Giovanni Pierluigi da Palestrina (c. 1525-1594), the Italian composer of late Renaissance sacred music, best known for his Masses for the Roman Catholic Church.
    • Felix Mendelssohn placed him in the pantheon of the greatest musicians, writing, “I always get upset when some praise only Beethoven, others only Palestrina and still others only Mozart or Bach. All four of them, I say, or none at all.” (Wikipedia)
  • “differentiate between black and white, green and yellow and red”: Colors are the brain’s interpretation of different wavelengths of light. Human eyes have three kinds of color receptors, most sensitive to red, green, and blue, as Thomas Young proposed in 1802.
  • “Suppose there was no escort from here to there”: The damsel in distress is a romance trope dating from ancient times. It is a recurring narrative device in which one or more men must rescue a woman who has either been kidnapped or placed in general peril. Kinship, love, lust or a combination of those gives the male protagonist the motivation or compulsion to initiate the narrative. The female character herself may be competent, but still finds herself in this type of situation. The helplessness of these fictional females, according to some critics, is linked to views outside of fiction that women as a group need to be taken care of by men. The evolution of the trope throughout history has been described as: what changes through the decades isn’t the woman since she is always the weak victim in need of the male savior, it’s the attacker. The faces of the attacker in popular media are legion, whichever group best meets the collective fears of a culture is used (Wikipedia). Whether it’s Joachim Spitzer whom Catherine rejected or Cousin Hannah to remove men altogether as a savior figure, Catherine is not going to be saved by anyone.
  • “the tonnage of wind pressure against cables”: The Tacoma Narrows Bridge, “Galloping Gertie,” twisted in the wind and fell into Puget Sound on November 7, 1940.
  • “to inquire for a dead letter”: The Dead Letter Office received mail that could not be delivered. In Melville’s “Bartleby, the Scrivener” (1853), Bartleby had been a clerk there: “Dead letters! does it not sound like dead men?” See American Writers.
  • “Perhaps it was in the lunar Apennines”: The Apennines are a mountain chain in Italy. The lunar Apennines, the Montes Apenninus, were named by Johannes Hevelius in 1647 after the Italian range. See Astronomy.
  • “those who must punch time-clocks in great factories, those who must turn great wheels”: Willard Bundy patented the time clock in 1888. Chaplin’s Modern Times (1936) opens on workers at the time clock and swallows Charlie in the great wheels. Young said, “Charlie Chaplin has influenced every book I’ve ever written” (Marguerite Young, interview with Kay Bonetti, American Audio Prose Library, May 1983). See Marguerite Young on Her Craft.
  • “never to join in the chorus of this dumb-show”: A dumb-show, also known as a pantomime or mime, is a dramatic performance using gestures and body movements without words, often used to summarize, supplement, or comment on the main action of a play. Hamlet’s players perform a dumb-show before The Murder of Gonzago (3.2). (Wikipedia) See Shakespeare.
  • “none for this web of causality”: Causality is an influence by which one event, process, state, or object (a cause) contributes to the production of another event, process, state, or object (an effect) where the cause is partly responsible for the effect, and the effect is partly dependent on the cause. In general, a process has many causes, which are also said to be causal factors for it, and all lie in its past. An effect can in turn be a cause of, or causal factor for, many other effects, which all lie in its future. Some writers have held that causality is metaphysically prior to notions of time and space. Causality is an abstraction that indicates how the world progresses, so basic a concept that it is more apt as an explanation of other concepts of progression than as something to be explained by others more basic. The concept is like those of agency and efficacy. For this reason, a leap of intuition may be needed to grasp it. Accordingly, causality is implicit in the logic and structure of ordinary language. The topic of causality remains a staple in contemporary philosophy (Wikipedia).
  • “none for the place, none for the person”: Doctors test whether a patient is “oriented to person, place, and time.” See Madness and Sanity.
  • “except that the door was closed”: The Parable of the Ten Virgins (Matthew 25:1-13). It symbolizes spiritual readiness, and those that are able to enter the wedding feast. This imagery is rooted in Jewish wedding customs, where the bridegroom’s arrival was a central event, and the bride and her attendants would go out to meet him. The bridegroom came, “and the door was shut” (Matthew 25:10). “Watch therefore, for ye know neither the day nor the hour wherein the Son of man cometh” (Matthew 25:13). See The Bible and Judaism.
  • “she was talking to a human-sized blackbird”: This was Weissenbach’s: “a human-sized black bird standing in the hallway” (Marguerite Young, interview with Charles Ruas, WBAI radio, New York). See the entry on Chinese mandarins and Catherine Cartwheel.
