Chapter 22

← Chapter 21 · Home · Chapter 23 →

Summary

At a breakfast table laid, for no reason anyone names, with Haviland china, silver, and a bowl of white roses, Vera sits scratched, bruised, and aching, “seethingly irritated” that Miss MacIntosh never asks how she passed the night. Miss MacIntosh reads the water-stained newspaper aloud, a Brazilian rebellion, a needle-workers’ strike, gold to be drained from the sea, a famine in China, a new star, and steers the household like a ship (“All hands to the ropes!”). She scolds Vera about dust and unmatched socks and fires the old questions at her: the days of creation, which she counts from Sunday because Constantine “got us all off on the wrong day of the week,” and the world’s islands, mountains, boxers, and stars. Twice Vera asks whether the party dress was thrown away as a punishment, and twice she is answered with more questions. Miss MacIntosh scoffs at phantoms (“Who ever saw the ghost of his father?”), says she has not looked into a mirror in years, and mutters, almost asleep, “Baldness is no cure for sorrow, my dear.” Vera thinks of the two Mr. Spitzers, of the wreckage the sea casts up, and of her mother, who mistakes everything she sees for something else. “Was she all others? I wondered.”

Characters present

Vera Cartwheel · Miss MacIntosh · Richard MacIntosh · Catherine Cartwheel · Joachim Spitzer · Peron Spitzer · The Old Clam Digger · Solomon the Turtle · Mr. Chandelier · Mr. Res Tacamah · The Old Blind Sheep Dog

Concepts present

Themes: Death and Mortality · Decay and Ruin · Illusion and Reality · Isolation and Connection · Love · Memory and the Past · Order, Chaos, and Discipline · Society, Class, and Race · Time · Women, Gender, and Marriage

Symbols: Dogs · Eyes and Blindness · Hair, Wig, and Baldness · Horses and Carriages · Mirrors and Reflections · Roses and Flowers · The House · The Sea and Water · The Umbrella

Philosophy: Augustine and Christian Theology · Empiricism (Locke, Berkeley, Hume) · Freud and Jung · Marguerite Young on Her Craft · Nietzsche

Allusions: American Religious Movements · Ancient Egypt · Astronomy · Exploration and the Poles · Fairy Tales and Folklore · Genesis · Greek Mythology · Homer’s Epics · Iowa, Indiana, and the Midwest · Judaism · Milton · Revelation and the Apocalypse · Romantic Poets · Shakespeare · The Bible · The Book of Job · The History of Opium

Key passages

From the research

  • The chapter opens with Vera’s seething irritation and physical discomfort, describing scratches, aches, and a nameless fatigue that suggests both physical and spiritual malaise. This sets the tone of discontent and existential questioning that permeates the chapter. The sea is described as a mysterious, almost otherworldly presence, “an astral light as of some other planet.”
  • Vera’s feeling of disconnection from the usual routine and Miss MacIntosh’s cheerful insistence on continuing the day’s affairs despite Vera’s obvious distress highlight a fundamental tension between resignation and rebellion.
  • Miss MacIntosh reads aloud the morning newspaper, which is water-stained and blurred, symbolizing the blurred and unstable condition of the world and their lives. The newspaper covers a wide range of topics from international politics and economic troubles to mundane notices like shipments of coconuts and sports scores, reflecting the chaotic and fragmentary nature of modern life.
  • Her manner is repetitive and insistent on routine knowledge and memorization of things such as: biblical creation days, current events, and housekeeping duties. This shows her belief in order and discipline as a defense against chaos and despair.
  • The sea is a recurring symbol representing memory, oblivion, and the unknown. Miss MacIntosh doubts that the sea has memory, questioning “What does the sea remember when it swallows the ship?” This reflects Vera’s own questioning of existence and loss.
  • The house is depicted as a decaying, almost haunted place filled with relics, broken items, and ghosts of the past. The chapter describes the house’s vast but unused wealth (silver services, fine china) and its gradual ruination, symbolizing the decay of old values and failed dreams.
  • Miss MacIntosh is portrayed as brusque, pragmatic, and somewhat harsh, focused on housekeeping, moral discipline, and maintaining order. She criticizes Vera’s laziness and failure to perform her duties, insisting on sewing, cleaning, and learning practical skills for any future husband.
  • Her voice is described as grating and rasping, likened to rusted hinges and drowning sounds, emphasizing her toughness and weariness but also her refusal to indulge in illusions or sentimentalities.
  • The chapter is punctuated by Miss MacIntosh’s rapid-fire questions about the creation days, geography, history, sports, and the meaning of life and death. These questions serve as a kind of catechism, an attempt to impose order and knowledge on a world that feels chaotic and uncertain to Vera.
  • Vera reflects on the futility of these lessons and the disconnection between the external facts of the world and her internal sorrow and longing.
  • While Miss MacIntosh insists on routine and practical concerns, Vera is lost in a dreamlike state, haunted by memories, illusions, and phantasms. There is a growing sense of alienation and sorrow, Vera’s desire for “perfect happiness” contrasting with Miss MacIntosh’s grounded, if harsh, realism.
  • Miss MacIntosh’s dismissal of ghosts and phantoms as nonsense, and her readiness to confront any imaginary specter with her black umbrella, shows the rejection of fantasy she professes, though Young saw the umbrella as “a kind of canopy between her and reality” (Marguerite Young, interview with Studs Terkel, WFMT radio, 1965).
  • “‘Baldness is no cure for sorrow, my dear,’ she muttered sleepily, her voice like the continuation of a dream I had almost forgotten.” This is the only time Miss MacIntosh comes near the night.
  • “For many years now, she had never looked into a looking glass. She could not remember the last time she had seen herself.”

Questions and observations

Reading closely

  • The table is laid “as if for some special occasion, the nature of which I could hardly imagine.” What is the occasion?
  • “There is no news today that was not yesterday.” Why does Miss MacIntosh read the news at all?
  • “Baldness is no cure for sorrow.” Whose sorrow?

Characters

  • Vera asks twice about the party dress and is twice answered with questions. What is Miss MacIntosh evading?
  • Miss MacIntosh “had never been to sea” but talks “as if we were far out at sea.” Why?
  • “Was she all others?” What has Vera begun to see?

Connections

  • Chapter 18’s dawn quiz returns: Skagerrak and Shiloh then, James Bay and Fingal’s Cave now. What has changed between the two quizzes?
  • In Chapter 18 she “had never seen it herself except in a mirror.” Here she “had never looked into a looking glass” for years. Which is true?
  • Catherine mistakes a fan for a door and Mr. Spitzer for an umbrella stand. How is Miss MacIntosh’s blindness different?

Reflection

  • What do we ask questions to avoid answering?
  • “It takes more than clothes to make the man.” What does it take?
  • Is a routine a comfort or a hiding place?

Research: Characters

Vera Cartwheel

  • Tired, disillusioned, and inwardly restless, she struggles with a profound sense of sorrow and alienation.
  • She questions the value of the tasks imposed on her and longs for a life beyond repetitive lessons and duties.
  • She asks twice, “Did you throw away my party dress for a punishment?” and declares, “I shall dance again, even with my own shadow.”

Miss MacIntosh

  • A forthright, practical woman with a strong sense of duty, she is Vera’s caretaker and disciplinarian.
  • She is resistant to illusions and ghosts, skeptical of sentimentality, and focused on maintaining order.
  • Despite her harshness, she harbors her own doubts and vulnerabilities, reflected in her philosophical musings and physical frailty.
  • She counts the days of creation from Sunday, works every day of the week, and blames the Emperor Constantine for the Christian Sunday.
  • Her “old dollar watch… was given to her by her dead love.”

Richard, Miss MacIntosh’s brother (Mentioned)

  • A missionary who disappeared among the islands of Oceania, where he went to live among the head-hunters and was either eaten by them or converted by them (told in a later chapter). Here she asks only, “Where is my brother Richard? Some said I looked like him. His hair was red.”

Research: Themes

Routine versus Inner Turmoil

See: Order, Chaos, and Discipline

  • Vera experiences deep emotional fatigue and existential questioning, feeling trapped in repetitive, meaningless tasks imposed by Miss MacIntosh’s rigid routine. The contrast highlights the human struggle between external order and internal chaos.

Memory and Forgetfulness

See: Memory and the Past · The Sea and Water

  • The sea, a recurring motif, is described as both full of “wrinkles” and yet possibly without memory. This paradox symbolizes the blurred lines between remembering and forgetting, life and oblivion.

Illusion versus Reality

See: Illusion and Reality

  • Miss MacIntosh dismisses phantoms and ghosts as nonsense, emphasizing the importance of facing reality and practicality, whereas Vera’s experience is haunted by memories, dreams, and elusive presences.

Mortality and Loss

See: Death and Mortality

  • References to death, the “angel of death,” and shipwrecks evoke the fragility of life and the inevitability of decay. Miss MacIntosh speaks of the absence of new life (“we shall have no baby of our own”) and the presence of old, broken things, symbolizing lost hopes.

Knowledge and Education

See: Order, Chaos, and Discipline

  • The insistence on memorizing Biblical genealogies, current events, geography, and sports reflects a traditional, perhaps oppressive, approach to learning as a way to impose order and meaning in a chaotic world.

Isolation and Connection

See: Isolation and Connection

  • Vera feels isolated, disconnected from the external world and even from Miss MacIntosh, who seems unable to perceive Vera’s sorrow. There is a tension between their companionship and emotional distance.

Research: Symbols and Imagery

The Sea

See: The Sea and Water

  • Represents memory, oblivion, and the passage of time. It is both a life source and a graveyard, swallowing ships and memories alike.

The Breakfast Table

See: The House

  • The ornately set table contrasts with the characters’ modest lives, symbolizing lost grandeur or unrealized potential.

Phantoms and Ghosts

See: Illusion and Reality

  • Symbolizes Vera’s inner fears and the past’s haunting presence. Miss MacIntosh’s dismissal of them reflects a pragmatic worldview.

Broken and Sunken Objects

See: Decay and Ruin

  • Shipwrecks, broken crockery, and old estate remnants symbolize decay, loss, and the impermanence of human endeavors.

Black Umbrella

See: The Umbrella

  • Miss MacIntosh’s protective and practical tool, symbolizing her grounded nature and defense against both literal and figurative storms.

Technique

See: Marguerite Young on Her Craft

  • Symbolism: The chapter abounds with symbolic references to ships, storms, and phantoms, enhancing themes of memory and loss.
  • Stream of Consciousness: Vera’s thoughts flow freely between observation, memory, and philosophical reflection, emphasizing her inner turmoil. Young said both things about the method. She told Studs Terkel, “This is not a stream of consciousness novel. It’s a very controlled, rather realistic treatment of that kind of attitude” (Marguerite Young, interview with Studs Terkel, WFMT radio, 1965), and in 1983, asked whether the stream of consciousness was the method of the novel, she answered, “Yes, the stream of consciousness” (Marguerite Young, interview with Kay Bonetti, American Audio Prose Library, May 1983).
  • Allusion: Biblical references to creation days, historical figures (Emperor Constantine, King Canute), and biblical figures (Jeremiah) deepen thematic complexity.
  • Contrast: Between Vera’s emotional state and Miss MacIntosh’s external cheerfulness and routine.

Research: Resources

  • “her morning newspaper”: In the lists of events and things there appear to be two time periods being dealt with: one paragraph is the 1800s and the other the early 1900s.
  • “a Brazilian rebellion”: Brazil’s revolts within Miss MacIntosh’s memory include the Naval Revolt (1893-94), the war at Canudos (1896-97), the Revolt of the Lash (1910), when Black sailors mutinied against flogging, and the Revolution of 1930.
  • “a needle-workers’ strike or a new garment union”: In the “Uprising of the 20,000” (1909), shirtwaist makers in New York, most of them young immigrant women, struck for months. The International Ladies’ Garment Workers’ Union was founded in 1900. See Women, Gender, and Marriage and Society, Class, and Race.
  • “the instability of islands”: The Pacific islands came under colonial rule, foreign intervention, and control. Eventually the unstable conditions in the Pacific began to draw in European governments, all of which acknowledged some responsibility for the protection of their nationals and their property.
  • “the recent visit of a British prime minister”: This may be Ramsay MacDonald, who in 1929 became the first sitting British prime minister to visit the United States.
  • “the tonnage of water falling each day over Niagara Falls where was a honeymooners’ paradise”: Niagara Falls has a rich history as a honeymoon destination, beginning, by local tradition, with Theodosia Burr and Joseph Alston’s bridal tour in 1801. It was initially considered a destination for the wealthy, but became more accessible to a wider range of couples with the opening of the Erie Canal and the growth of railroads. The iconic Maid of the Mist boat tour, which takes visitors close to the base of the falls, has run since 1846 (Niagara Falls USA, “How Niagara Falls Became the Honeymoon Capital of the World”).
  • “a great drouth in the sheep-raising lands of Western Alberta”: The 1920s and 1930s drought in Western Canada, particularly in areas of Alberta, was not solely a “Dust Bowl” event in the same way as the US Great Plains. While conditions were harsh, with severe droughts and dust storms, the period also saw a significant economic downturn related to agricultural challenges. The drought of 1929 to 1937 devastated a quarter of Canada’s arable land and left 13,900 farms abandoned (The Canadian Encyclopedia, “Drought in Palliser’s Triangle”).
  • “a fall in sea island cotton”: Sea Island cotton, a long-staple variety cultivated on coastal islands of South Carolina and Georgia, was intimately linked to the institution of slavery. Its high quality and demand made it a lucrative crop, but its production relied entirely on the forced labor of enslaved Africans. The Sea Island cotton industry thrived from the late 1700s to the late 19th century, fueled by the brutal exploitation of enslaved people. The cultivation, harvesting, and processing of Sea Island cotton were entirely dependent on the labor of enslaved Africans. The Civil War ended slavery, but not the crop. Sea Island cotton was grown by freedpeople and others until it was “no longer economically viable by the 1910s,” and the boll weevil, arriving in the 1910s and 1920s, dealt the “final blow” (South Carolina Encyclopedia, “Cotton”). See Society, Class, and Race.
  • “a project for draining gold out of the sea”: Humans have known that gold exists in the ocean since at least 1872, when British chemist Edward Sonstadt discovered it. People have been captivated by the idea of extracting gold from the ocean for over 100 years. In the 1890s, New England pastor Prescott Ford Jernegan claimed to have invented a device that could extract gold from seawater using mercury and electricity. His Electrolytic Marine Salts Company at Lubec, Maine (1897-98) was a swindle, and he fled with investors’ money. The ocean contains around 20 million tons of dissolved gold (Atlas Obscura, “There Is Gold in Seawater, But We Can’t Get at It”), but there is only about one gram of gold for every 100 million metric tons of ocean water (NOAA Ocean Service, “Is there gold in the ocean?”). There is also undissolved gold in and on the seafloor, encased in rock “a mile or two underwater” (NOAA). Getting gold from seawater is very difficult, so it is not expected to happen anytime soon. Scientists have also tracked the amount of gold in the ocean over the last 3.5 billion years (Ross R. Large and others, “Gold in the oceans through time,” Earth and Planetary Science Letters, 2015).
  • “the lost regatta”: Throughout the 1800s, hundreds of professional and amateur boat clubs were established in the United States. A select few remain intact today, a few merged with other clubs, and others had brief but interesting lives. It gives a snapshot into what life was like in America as society’s elite established these clubs not just for athletics, but to build and maintain their social status, wealth, and political clout. Things weren’t so glamorous outside these boathouses in the US at that time (Rachel Freedman, “1800s: While White Men of Privilege Were Establishing Boat Clubs,” Rowsource).
    • The Henley Royal Regatta barred “mechanics, artisans, or labourers” until 1937. In 1920 it refused the American sculler John B. Kelly, a bricklayer.
  • “a shipment of cocoanuts”: DNA analysis of more than 1,300 coconuts from around the world reveals that the coconut was brought under cultivation in two separate locations, one in the Pacific basin and the other in the Indian Ocean basin (Gunn, Baudouin, and Olsen, PLoS ONE, 2011).
  • “the deposition of another Balkan king”: Serbia’s King Alexander Obrenović was murdered by his own officers in 1903. Greece deposed Constantine I in 1917 and declared a republic in 1924. Alexander I of Yugoslavia was assassinated in 1934, and Albania’s King Zog fled in 1939.
  • “the sea is full of wrinkles, though it has neither age nor grey hairs”: “Time writes no wrinkle on thine azure brow: / Such as creation’s dawn beheld, thou rollest now” (Byron, Childe Harold’s Pilgrimage IV, 1818). See Romantic Poets and The Sea and Water.
  • “the jeremiads”: A jeremiad, from Jeremiah’s name, is “a prolonged lamentation or complaint” and also “a cautionary or angry harangue” (Merriam-Webster). He was called the “weeping prophet” and was one of the major prophets of the Hebrew Bible.
  • “Commonwealth Edison was doing very well”: Samuel Insull’s utility empire, with Commonwealth Edison of Chicago at its head, collapsed in 1932. This news dates from before the crash, and it bears on the “two time periods” of the newspaper.
  • “Hong Kong funds were frozen, and the British were rank imperialists”: Britain took Hong Kong in the First Opium War, fought to force the opium trade on China (Treaty of Nanking, 1842). See The History of Opium.
  • “there was a great famine in China”: The North China famine of 1876-79 killed some nine to thirteen million people, and famines came again in 1920-21, 1928-30, and 1942-43.
  • “A younger brother had been assassinated in Java”: The sultans of Yogyakarta:
    • Hamengkubuwono IV died suddenly, perhaps by poison.
    • Hamengkubuwono V was killed by one of his wives.
  • “A new star had been discovered in the Northern Hemisphere”: T Coronae Borealis may refer to the New Star that is seen every 80 years. “It was first discovered in an outburst in 1866 by John Birmingham, though it had been observed earlier as a 10th magnitude star. It may have been observed in 1217 and in 1787 as well. In February 1946 a 15-year-old schoolboy from Wales named Michael Woodman observed a flare up, subsequently writing to the Astronomer Royal and leading to the theory that the star flares each 80 years” (Wikipedia).
  • “Mr. Spitzer’s close-mouthed old houseman with his clam buckets and his seine”: The old clam digger. See The Old Clam Digger.
  • “We loved no graven image”: “Thou shalt not make unto thee any graven image” (Exodus 20:4). See The Bible.
  • “we were using the Haviland china”: Haviland & Co. was founded at Limoges, France, by the American importer David Haviland in 1842.
  • “cabbage roses such as grew, if not in What Cheer, Iowa”: Miss MacIntosh’s hometown. See Iowa, Indiana, and the Midwest and Roses and Flowers.
  • “The first was to have begun what He could not finish”: Because creation is incomplete, the characters, particularly Miss MacIntosh, emphasize the importance of practical, honest living in the present world rather than dreaming of distant, perfect worlds or afterlives. The unfinished world demands human effort and self-discipline, and moral clarity, rather than escapism or fantasy.
    • The 8th day of creation is often used symbolically to represent a new beginning, a time of renewal or a significant event beyond the initial creation narrative, often associated with the covenant with Abraham and the practice of circumcision on the 8th day after birth, signifying a new life within the covenant with God. Some Christians interpret the 8th day as a reference to Jesus’ resurrection. “He that is eight days old shall be circumcised among you” (Genesis 17:12), and the Epistle of Barnabas (15) speaks of “a beginning of the eighth day, that is, a beginning of another world… we keep the eighth day with joyfulness, the day also on which Jesus rose again from the dead.”
  • “no monsters guarding the waves at the edge of the world”: Old maps put sea monsters at the edges of the known world. The Hunt-Lenox Globe (c. 1510) is marked “HC SVNT DRACONES,” “here are dragons.”
  • “pheasants’ tongues served by imaginary servants”: Suetonius says the emperor Vitellius was served “the livers of pike, the brains of pheasants and peacocks, the tongues of flamingos” (Vitellius 13).
  • “triple-crowned griffins with gold eggs between their gilded paws”: Herodotus tells of griffins guarding gold in the far north (Histories 3.116). See Greek Mythology.
  • “My mother always insisted that the hotel entertained many dead men”: Catherine’s dead guests. See Catherine Cartwheel.
  • “what God had created on Wednesday”: “And God made two great lights; the greater light to rule the day, and the lesser light to rule the night: he made the stars also” (Genesis 1:16). See Genesis.
  • “the Emperor Constantine’s having changed the calendar”: On March 7, 321, Constantine ordered that “on the venerable day of the Sun” magistrates and city people should rest. The Seventh-day Adventists and Seventh Day Baptists teach that Rome changed the Sabbath to Sunday, and Miss MacIntosh’s quarrel with Constantine is theirs. See American Religious Movements and Augustine and Christian Theology.
    • Miss MacIntosh’s quarrel is with the seven-day week and its day of rest. She counts from Sunday, works every day, and says God should have “created the world in seven days and rested on the eighth.” Young may be telling us that we are out of balance with nature, the seasons, and the natural order. The early Roman calendar followed the seasons more closely. It reinforces Miss MacIntosh’s advocacy for common sense and living within the realities of the present moment, acknowledging the limitations imposed by time and mortality.
    • The Roman calendar was used by the Roman Kingdom and Roman Republic. The earliest Roman calendars were lunar calendars that tracked the moon’s 29.5 day cycle. It also had an eight-day week, with a market day every eight days.
    • The Julian calendar was a reform of the Roman calendar that was based on the Egyptian solar calendar. It had 365.25 days in a year, with leap days added every four years. It was replaced by the Gregorian calendar in 1582.
    • The Romans were generally pagans for more than a thousand years. Paganism is a term used to describe people who worship multiple gods and nature, rather than one god as in monotheistic religions. The Roman Empire eventually became a Christian majority state, and pagans were persecuted. In February 391 Emperor Theodosius “prohibited sacrifices and the visiting of temples,” and in November 392 he forbade the worship of the pagan gods altogether (Encyclopaedia Britannica).
  • “Men did not live so long as in the past time”: The patriarchs of Chapter 20. See the Chapter 20 resources.
  • “were created on Thursday last. I think it must have been around four o’clock in the afternoon”: “And God created great whales” (Genesis 1:21). Vera’s mock precision recalls Archbishop James Ussher, who dated the creation to the evening before October 23, 4004 BC (Annales Veteris Testamenti, 1650). See Genesis.
  • “How does the other half live?”: Jacob Riis, How the Other Half Lives (1890). The conservative opinion in the Wikipedia article, that immigrants chose to live in slums as a stepping stone to living in America, is ludicrous. It is very convenient that slum lords would argue we need slums. Any conservative minority has been paid to have that conservative opinion in the US, from history up to the present. Riis’s autobiography, The Making of an American (1901), shows the nuance: he may have had prejudices against certain ethnicities, as racism has always been a thing, but that doesn’t explain that slums are necessary for the working class. See Society, Class, and Race.
    • Jacob Riis: “A particularly important effort by Riis was his exposure of the condition of New York’s water supply. His five-column story “Some Things We Drink,” in the August 21, 1891, edition of the “New York Evening Sun,” included six photographs (later lost). Riis wrote: “I took my camera and went up in the watershed photographing my evidence wherever I found it. Populous towns sewered directly into our drinking water. I went to the doctors and asked how many days a vigorous cholera bacillus may live and multiply in running water. About seven, they said. My case was made.” The story resulted in the purchase by New York City of areas around the New Croton Reservoir, and may well have saved New Yorkers from an epidemic of cholera. Riis tried hard to have the slums around Five Points demolished and replaced with a park. His writings resulted in the Drexel Committee investigation of unsafe tenements; this resulted in the Small Park Act of 1887. Riis was not invited to the eventual opening of the park on June 15, 1897, but went all the same, together with Lincoln Steffens. In the last speech, the street cleaning commissioner credited Riis for the park and led the public in giving him three cheers of “Hooray, Jacob Riis!” Other parks also were created, and Riis was popularly credited with them as well” (Wikipedia).
  • “every woman’s privilege and duty”: Women’s unpaid labor is the work that women do without financial compensation, such as cooking, cleaning, and caring for children. It’s often undervalued and underappreciated. Globally, women spend 2.5 times as many hours on unpaid care work as men (UN Women, “Care work keeps the world running”). Unpaid labor limits women’s time for paid work and can lead to longer hours. Unpaid labor can have negative emotional, mental, and physical health impacts on women. See Women, Gender, and Marriage.
  • “Solomon’s tub should be changed”: Solomon, the turtle Catherine gave Vera on her twelfth birthday (Chapter 9). See Solomon the Turtle and the Chapter 9 resources.
  • “The mill workers were striking”: In the Lawrence textile strike of 1912, the “Bread and Roses” strike, women and children of more than twenty nationalities walked out of the mills. See Society, Class, and Race.
  • “by the sweat of my brow”: “In the sweat of thy face shalt thou eat bread” (Genesis 3:19). See Genesis.
  • “a baseball autographed by a dead St. Louis Cardinal”: Young mentioned the St. Louis Cardinals and the Cardinals/Dodgers rivalry and this mention seems to be through the lens of racism. During this period, after the 1942 season, Branch Rickey, who had built up the Cardinals farm system as their general manager, moved to become the Dodgers’ general manager. In 1947, after Rickey broke the color line by signing Jackie Robinson to the Dodgers, there were rumors that southerners playing for the Cardinals were planning to boycott games against the Dodgers, although the players later denied it. In general, the Cardinals were latecomers to integration. Front-office executive Bing Devine said the owner from 1947 to 1953, Fred Saigh, refused to sign black players. There was a widespread belief that St. Louis was, in many ways, a Southern city. In the mid-1950s many of its stores and restaurants refused to serve black customers. The Cardinals, with baseball’s largest radio network blanketing the Midwest and South, had cultivated white Southern fans. Their ballpark was also the last in the majors to abolish segregated seating. Because of their lack of black players, the Cardinals’ play suffered on the field tremendously in the 1950s. Meanwhile, with the success of Robinson, the Dodgers doubled down on the opportunity to sign players of color from the Negro leagues. In the subsequent years after their pennant-winning season in 1947, they would sign Don Newcombe, Roy Campanella, and Jim Gilliam from the Negro leagues, adding to an already tremendous team. The Dodgers made the World Series in 1949, 1952, 1953, 1955, 1956, and 1959 (winning championships in 1955 and 1959) and were a historic pennant race away from making it in 1951, in part because they were the first to accept African American players. The 1951 season included a 14-game winning streak for the Dodgers against the Cardinals, the longest such streak in the rivalry. (Wikipedia) See Society, Class, and Race.
  • “the best baseball player in little old What Cheer”: Women have been playing baseball as long as men have. Their long connection with the game began in the 1860s and has continued through the efforts of individual pioneers like Amanda Clement, Jackie Mitchell, Toni Stone, Maria Pepe, and Ila Borders (American Girls Baseball, “The History of Women in Baseball”). The All-American Girls Professional Baseball League played from 1943 to 1954. See Women, Gender, and Marriage.
    • “Georgia had run faster than any of them”: her first name, Georgia, the G on her shirts in Chapter 9. See the Chapter 9 resources.
  • “the Islands of the Blessed or the Islands of the Dead”: Arnold Böcklin’s painting Isle of the Dead (1880) inspired Rachmaninoff’s tone poem (1909). See Greek Mythology and Fairy Tales and Folklore.
    • Islands of the Blessed may refer to the Islands in Greek mythology which were a semi-legendary place in the western ocean where the souls of heroes and worthy people went after death. They were also known as the Fortunate Isles or Elysian Fields.
    • Islands of the Dead may refer to a concept from pre-Christian Europe of an island to the west where souls went after death. It is reported as being part of Celtic belief by several Roman historians, and evidence for this belief is also found in Welsh folklore. It also existed in ancient Germanic traditions where the British Isles were sometimes depicted as the isles to the west that the dead inhabited. (Wikipedia)
  • “Take time by the forelock!”: The saying means to act quickly and decisively, especially to take advantage of an opportunity. It comes from the Greek Kairos, Opportunity, carved by Lysippus with a forelock in front and bald behind, so that he can be seized only as he comes. The Roman fabulist Phaedrus tells it of Occasio (Fables 5.8). See Hair, Wig, and Baldness.
  • “the firmament in the midst of the waters to divide the waters from the waters”: “Let there be a firmament in the midst of the waters, and let it divide the waters from the waters” (Genesis 1:6-7). See Genesis.
  • “It’s a heavy sea running”: A nautical phrase meaning there are large, powerful waves crashing against a ship, indicating rough and dangerous sea conditions. Its origin lies in the literal description of a turbulent ocean with large waves, commonly used by sailors to convey the severity of a storm at sea. Webster’s defines a “heavy sea” as “a sea in which the waves run high” (Webster’s Revised Unabridged Dictionary, 1913).
  • “The longer the orbit, the longer the planetary year”: Kepler’s third law (Harmonices Mundi, 1619) is that the square of a planet’s orbital period is directly proportional to the cube of the semi-major axis of its orbit, meaning a larger orbit leads to a longer orbital period. See Astronomy.
  • “Time was circled in a single week”: Nietzsche’s eternal recurrence (The Gay Science 341, 1882): “This life as you now live it and have lived it, you will have to live once more and innumerable times more.” See Nietzsche and Time.
    • The block universe is usually traced to Hermann Minkowski’s lecture “Space and Time” (1908): “Henceforth space by itself, and time by itself, are doomed to fade away into mere shadows, and only a kind of union of the two will preserve an independent reality.” It describes the universe as a four-dimensional block that contains every event that has ever happened, past, present, and future all equally real. The growing block version of the theory states that the past and present are real, but the future is unreal. As future events become present, they are added to the growing block of reality.
  • “Siberian wheat”: Mennonites from the Russian steppes brought “Turkey Red” winter wheat to Kansas in 1874, and the USDA’s Mark Carleton brought more Russian hard wheats around 1900.
  • “The American divorces were increasing”: American divorce rates peaked around 1980 (National Center for Family and Marriage Research, Bowling Green State University). In American history, divorce was initially very difficult to obtain, primarily restricted to cases of adultery and was heavily regulated by religious and legal authorities during the colonial era. By the mid-19th century, divorce rates began to rise significantly as states enacted more lenient laws allowing for broader grounds like cruelty, desertion, and habitual drunkenness, leading to a major surge in divorce rates during the 20th century (“no-fault” divorce laws).
  • “it was a wise child who knew his own father”: “It is a wise father that knows his own child” (The Merchant of Venice 2.2). Telemachus says, “My mother says I am his son; but I know not, for no man knows his own father” (Odyssey 1). See Shakespeare and Homer’s Epics.
  • “God created man on Friday, the sixth day”: “And the evening and the morning were the sixth day” (Genesis 1:31). See Genesis.
  • “Man is man’s wolf”: Homo homini lupus, “man is a wolf to man.” Young’s “Homo hominy lupus” puns on hominy, the corn grits of the Midwest. The source is Plautus, “Lupus est homo homini” (Asinaria 495), and Hobbes repeats it in the dedication of De Cive (1642). It implies that without social order or moral restraint, humans naturally act in their own self-interest, often to the detriment of others.
  • “I know no Greek, less Latin, less Hebrew”: Ben Jonson said Shakespeare had “small Latine, and lesse Greeke” (First Folio, 1623). See Shakespeare.
  • “The sheep cannot guard the sheep against the thief”: “He that entereth not by the door into the sheepfold, but climbeth up some other way, the same is a thief and a robber” (John 10:1). See The Bible.
  • “An old dog barks at nothing”: This turns around the proverb of Chapter 15, “An old dog barks not in vain.” See The Old Blind Sheep Dog, Dogs, Fairy Tales and Folklore, and the Chapter 15 resources.
  • “a confusion of tongues, the very Tower of Babel”: “Therefore is the name of it called Babel; because the Lord did there confound the language of all the earth” (Genesis 11:9). See Genesis.
  • “We must catch the old Devil by the tail”: The French “tirer le diable par la queue,” to pull the devil by the tail, means to be struggling or barely scraping by with limited financial resources.
  • “He sat next to God, and he thought that he was smarter than God”: Lucifer of Chapter 21. See the Chapter 21 resources.
  • “The first thrashing had its origin, I have no doubt, in heaven, and one fell”: “And there was war in heaven… and the great dragon was cast out” (Revelation 12:7-9). The dragon’s “tail drew the third part of the stars of heaven” (Revelation 12:4), as he goes “dragging the stars with him.” See Revelation and the Apocalypse.
  • “He was fallen from morning until seven o’clock, from evening until morning”: Milton’s fallen angel Mulciber: “from Morn / To Noon he fell, from Noon to dewy Eve, / A Summer’s day” (Paradise Lost 1.742-744). Luke has Satan fall “as lightning from heaven” (Luke 10:18). See Milton.
  • “Which state of the Union is named for its green mountains?”: Vermont, from the French vert mont, “green mountain,” and Nevada, Spanish for “snow-covered.”
  • “has won the famous steeplechase at Aintree where is the dreaded water-jump”: Master Robert, who had once pulled a plow, won the Grand National at Aintree in 1924. See Horses and Carriages.
  • “Here’s a horse of a different color”: “My purpose is, indeed, a horse of that colour” (Twelfth Night 2.3). See Shakespeare.
  • “Here were the names of some very interesting horses”: Miss MacIntosh’s racing news.
    • Flamingo was a British Thoroughbred racehorse and sire. In 1927 he was one of the best two-year-old colts in England when he won three of his five races including the National Breeders’ Produce Stakes.
    • Pericles’ Pride may refer to Pericles, a Greek statesman and general during the Golden Age of Athens. As the Wikipedia article on Pericles puts it, “Pericles marked a whole era and inspired conflicting judgments about his significant decisions. The fact that he was at the same time a vigorous statesman, general and orator only tends to make an objective assessment of his actions more difficult.” Pericles’ most visible legacy can be found in the literary and artistic works of the Golden Age, much of which survive to this day. In politics, Victor L. Ehrenberg (From Solon to Socrates, 1968) argues that a basic element of Pericles’ legacy is Athenian imperialism, which denies true democracy and freedom to the people of all but the ruling state. The promotion of such an arrogant imperialism is said to have ruined Athens. Pericles and his “expansionary” policies have been at the center of arguments promoting democracy in oppressed countries. Other analysts maintain an Athenian humanism illustrated in the Golden Age. The freedom of expression is regarded as the lasting legacy deriving from this period. Pericles is lauded as “the ideal type of the perfect statesman in ancient Greece” and his Funeral Oration is nowadays synonymous with the struggle for participatory democracy and civic pride. His Funeral Oration, especially this part (Thucydides, History of the Peloponnesian War 2.37, translation adapted from Benjamin Jowett, 1881): “Our form of government does not enter into rivalry with the institutions of others. Our government does not copy our neighbors’, but is an example to them. It is true that we are called a democracy, for the administration is in the hands of the many and not of the few. But while there exists equal justice to all and alike in their private disputes, the claim of excellence is also recognized; and when a citizen is in any way distinguished, he is preferred to the public service, not as a matter of privilege, but as the reward of merit. Neither is poverty an obstacle, but a man may benefit his country whatever the obscurity of his condition.”
    • No racehorse by the name Thine and Mine has been found, but when you flip the words there are two famous poems with the title that this may refer to: Mine and Thine by William Morris (1889) and Florence Van Leer Earle Coates (1904).
    • Trinitarian means relating to the Trinity, the Christian doctrine that God is one being with three aspects. Trinitarians believe that the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are co-equal and co-eternal.
  • “Here was a race-track at Pimlico”: Pimlico Race Course is in Baltimore, Maryland and hosts the Preakness Stakes.
  • “the kind of thing which should interest the late departed Mr. Spitzer”: Peron, the gambler of the race-tracks, “sometimes… seen double, standing in two places at once.” See Peron Spitzer and the Chapter 14 resources.
  • “Dog races in Heaven as on earth”: “Thy will be done in earth, as it is in heaven” (Matthew 6:10). See The Bible.
  • “What is the correct Chicago time?”: The railroads’ standard time began on November 18, 1883. Until then Chicago, like every city, kept its own local time.
  • “If a ship sinks and no one sees it sinking”: This seems to be a rephrasing of “If a tree falls in the woods…” This is a philosophical question that explores the idea of whether a sound exists if no one is there to perceive it, essentially questioning the nature of perception and reality itself. (Wikipedia) See Empiricism (Locke, Berkeley, Hume).
    • Berkeley’s “to be is to be perceived” (1710) lies behind the riddle. George Berkeley was an Anglo-Irish philosopher, writer, and clergyman who is regarded as the founder of “immaterialism,” a philosophical theory he developed which was later referred to as “subjective idealism” by others. He was an influence on Kant and Hume. Berkeley, California and the University of California, Berkeley are named after him. (Wikipedia)
  • “What is a man?”: “What is man, that thou art mindful of him?” (Psalm 8:4), pondering the value and nature of human beings. This question is a reflection on human fragility and insignificance compared to God’s power, yet also highlights the special attention God gives to humanity.
  • “shirts going in job lots, slightly damaged by fire and flood”: May refer to the Triangle Shirtwaist Factory fire in 1911 in New York City which killed 146 workers because a door to one stairway was locked, and the fire escape collapsed. Firefighters’ ladders couldn’t reach the upper floors. Workers, mostly all women, jumped to their deaths. The tragedy led to New York’s Factory Investigating Commission and its safety laws (1911-15). See Women, Gender, and Marriage and Society, Class, and Race.
  • “The evening primrose will soon be out”: This is another clue as to the time period of this chapter which is early summer to early fall.
  • “The neap tide is the least in the lunar month”: A neap tide occurs during the first and third quarter phases of the moon.
  • “the best which Bond Street could offer”: Bond Street is in London, England famous for its luxury shopping and is considered one of the most expensive streets in the world.
  • “Old-fashioned celluloid collars were going two for a nickel”: The separable (paper) collar was introduced in the early 1800s as a way of allowing men of more modest means to look sufficiently presentable when the occasion warranted it. Wealthier folks could have their entire shirts laundered after every wearing, but such services were largely out of reach to those with less money, such as laborers, farmers, clerks, or ordinary storekeepers. Laundering in the era before washing machines and modern fabrics was far more labor-intensive than today. The new style collar made it possible for much larger numbers of people to present themselves in church, courts, offices, and stores without bringing embarrassment or revealing their more modest status. (Wikipedia) Celluloid collars came in the 1870s.
  • “a recipe for gooseberry tart made of sea gooseberries”: The sea gooseberry is a comb jelly, a small transparent sea creature. A tart of comb jellies can only be a joke.
  • “those who fall in love are always blind”: “But love is blind, and lovers cannot see” (The Merchant of Venice 2.6). See Shakespeare and Love.
  • “Did you throw away my party dress for a punishment?”: The dress of Chapter 21. See the Chapter 21 resources.
  • “two stars in the Great Bear, the lines which joined them pointing nearly toward the North star”: The Pointers, Dubhe and Merak, at the bowl’s edge of the Big Dipper. See Astronomy.
  • “these poor tenements of clay”: The “houses of clay” of Job 4:19, as in Chapter 18. See The Book of Job and the Chapter 18 resources.
  • “I shall dance again, even with my own shadow”: The dancing of Chapter 21. See the Chapter 21 resources.
  • “Where are those towers of gold which God created before creation officially began? Where is that sea of jasper and of light?”: “A sea of glass like unto crystal” (Revelation 4:6), and “the building of the wall of it was of jasper” (Revelation 21:18). See Revelation and the Apocalypse.
  • “Describe that heaven which is filled with mares’-tails”: Luke Howard named the clouds cirrus, cumulus, and stratus in his Essay on the Modifications of Clouds (1803). The sailors’ rhyme runs, “Mackerel sky and mares’ tails / Make lofty ships carry low sails.”
    • A mackerel sky is a cloud formation that resembles fish scales. It’s made up of rows of altocumulus or cirrocumulus clouds that ripple across the sky.
  • “Where is James Bay?”: James Bay is located on the southern end of the Hudson Bay in Canada.
  • “Where is the Sea of Azov?”: The Sea of Azov is a small body of water between Russia and Ukraine.
  • “Where is the Coral Sea?”: The Coral Sea is off the northeast coast of Australia.
  • “Where is the Sargasso Sea”: The Sargasso Sea is a region of the Atlantic Ocean bounded by four currents forming an ocean gyre. Columbus crossed it in 1492.
  • “Where are the Gilbert Islands”: The Gilbert Islands are a chain of sixteen atolls and coral islands in the Pacific Ocean.
    • The Falkland Islands are an archipelago in the South Atlantic Ocean.
    • The Shetland Islands are a subarctic archipelago in the Northern Isles of Scotland.
    • Coronation Island is in Alaska off the northwest coast of Prince of Wales Island. Beside Henrietta Island and Bay Marguerite, this is more likely Coronation Island in the South Orkneys, named in 1821 for George IV’s coronation.
    • Henrietta Island is a small glacier-capped island in the East Siberian Sea. It was discovered in 1881 by De Long’s ill-fated Jeannette expedition.
    • Bay Marguerite is on the west side of the Antarctic Peninsula. Jean-Baptiste Charcot named it in 1909 for his wife, Marguerite. Young shares the name.
    • Port Royal is in southeastern Jamaica. Much of the town sank into the sea in the earthquake of 1692.
    • The Suez Canal is an artificial sea-level waterway in Egypt.
  • “Where is Fingal’s Cave?”: Fingal’s Cave is a sea cave on the uninhabited island of Staffa of Scotland. It inspired Mendelssohn’s Hebrides Overture (1830).
  • “Where is Victoria Station?”: Victoria Station is a railway station in Westminster, London, UK.
  • “Where is Charing Cross?”: Charing Cross is one of the medieval Eleanor crosses in Charing, Westminster, London, UK.
  • “Where is Trajan’s Column?”: Trajan’s Column is a Roman triumphal column in Rome, Italy.
  • “Where is Cleopatra’s Needle?”: Cleopatra’s Needle is the popular name for each of a pair of ancient Egyptian obelisks re-erected in London and New York City during the nineteenth century. See Ancient Egypt.
  • “Where is Mt. Pisgah, my dear?”: The mountain from which Moses saw the promised land: “And Moses went up… to the top of Pisgah” (Deuteronomy 34:1). See The Bible and the Chapter 20 resources.
  • “Where is Mt. Ararat”: “The ark rested… upon the mountains of Ararat” (Genesis 8:4). See Genesis.
  • “Where is Pike’s Peak?”: Pikes Peak (14,115 feet), in Colorado’s Front Range, was named for Zebulon Pike (1806). It lent its name to the “Pikes Peak or Bust” gold rush of 1859 and inspired “America the Beautiful” (1893). The highest summit of the Rockies is Mount Elbert.
  • “Where’s old Jessup Land, far to the North?”: The Arctic Jesup Land, named for Morris K. Jesup, president of the Peary Arctic Club, like Cape Morris Jesup in Greenland. See Exploration and the Poles.
  • “Sometimes in the glacier there’s a tidal crack”: Tidal cracks are formed in glaciers because of the movement of the tide underneath. Something that looks solid, like a sheet of ice or glacier, can be split open by the tide.
  • “Where’s Herbert Island?”: Herbert Island lies off northwest Greenland, near Thule, a walrus-hunting ground. See Exploration and the Poles.
  • “Where’s Cape Albert Edward?”: Cape Albert Edward is in Canada.
  • “Where is Queen Maud Mountains”: Roald Amundsen named them in 1911, on his way to the South Pole, for Queen Maud of Norway. See Exploration and the Poles.
  • “Where grows the winter cherry”: Winter cherry, the Chinese lantern plant, is a plant in Southern Europe and Asia.
  • “the Kirtland’s warbler”: The Kirtland’s warbler nests in young jack pine in the northern Lower Peninsula of Michigan, not the Upper Peninsula, as Miss MacIntosh says. It was long one of the rarest birds in North America.
  • “What dead king lies on the balcony at Elsinore?”: Hamlet’s father, whose ghost walks the platform at Elsinore (Hamlet 1.1). At the end Fortinbras orders the bodies “high on a stage be placed to the view” (5.2). See Shakespeare.
  • “In what tower are the ravens the guardians of the dead?”: Ravens are kept at the Tower of London, and legend says that if they leave, the kingdom will fall.
  • “What Greek city prided itself that it had no wall?”: Sparta. Lycurgus said, “That city is well fortified which has a wall of men instead of brick” (Plutarch, Life of Lycurgus 19). See the Chapter 20 resources.
  • “Who gave a sop to Cerebus?”: Cerberus is the hound of Hades. A sop to Cerberus is an idiom meaning giving something to appease. Young spells it “Cerebus.” The Sibyl throws Cerberus a honeyed, drugged cake so that Aeneas can pass (Aeneid 6). See Greek Mythology.
  • “Who was King Canute?”: King Canute was the king of England, Denmark, and Norway. He died in 1035, about forty years old. Henry of Huntingdon tells how he set his throne at the shore and commanded the tide to stop, to show his courtiers that the waves obey no king.
  • “Where is New South Wales?”: New South Wales is a state on the east coast of Australia.
  • “Where is my brother Richard?”: Miss MacIntosh’s red-haired brother. See Richard MacIntosh.
  • “Where are the Easter Islands, the Barents Sea, the Sandwich group, Shackleton Shelf, Enderby Land, Keeling Islands?”: Easter Island is in the Pacific Ocean and belongs to Chile. See the Chapter 18 resources.
    • The Barents Sea is where temperate and cold waters meet off the coast of Norway and Russia. It is named for Willem Barentsz (1596).
    • Sandwich group may refer to a British Territory in the southern Atlantic Ocean. These are probably the South Sandwich Islands, named by Cook in 1775. Cook also named the Hawaiian islands the Sandwich Islands (1778).
    • The Shackleton Shelf is in East Antarctica. It was charted by Mawson’s expedition (1912) and named for Shackleton.
    • Enderby Land is in Antarctica, discovered by John Biscoe in 1831.
    • The Keeling Islands are an Australian territory in the Indian Ocean. Darwin visited in 1836 and worked out his theory of coral atolls there.
  • “Where is the angel of death?”: May refer to Azrael, the angel of death in Islamic and later Jewish tradition. The hooded figure with a scythe comes from medieval European art. Jean Delville published the poem “Azraël” in his collection Les Horizons hantés (1892). It is about the Angel of Death appearing to King Solomon. In the poem, Azrael conjures the afterlife for Solomon. Delville’s drawing L’Allégorie de l’Enfer, also called Azrael (c. 1890), goes with the poem (Wikimedia Commons). The passage evokes the tension between acceptance and fear, the known and the unknown, life and death, which permeates the narrative. The angel of death is not simply a figure to be found or confronted but a symbol of the profound mystery and inevitability that shapes human existence. Longfellow’s “Azrael” (Tales of a Wayside Inn, 1873) also tells of King Solomon and the angel of death.
  • “Where are the Antilles”: The Antilles are an archipelago by the Caribbean Sea.
    • The Antipodes Islands are in the subantarctic waters near New Zealand.
  • “Where is the Giants’ Causeway?”: The Giants’ Causeway is an area of basalt columns in Northern Ireland. In legend, Finn McCool (Fingal) built it, and it is said to run under the sea to Fingal’s Cave. See Fairy Tales and Folklore.
  • “Where is the Golden Gate?”: The Golden Gate is a strait that connects San Francisco Bay and the Pacific Ocean.
  • “Where is Brooklyn Bridge?”: The Brooklyn Bridge is a hybrid cable-stayed/suspension bridge in New York City.
  • “Where is the Grand Central Station?”: Grand Central Terminal (1913), popularly Grand Central Station, is a commuter rail terminal in New York City.
  • “Whose dog did not bark in the night?”: May refer to a Sherlock Holmes story Silver Blaze, by Sir Arthur Conan Doyle, where the fact that a dog did not bark during the night when a race horse was removed from a stable was an important clue to solve the mystery of who removed the horse from the stable. Young said in an interview how much she loved murder mysteries, and she minored in criminology at Butler University (EBSCO Research Starters, “Marguerite Young”). It encapsulates a meditation on missed warnings, silent tragedies, and the profound isolation felt by characters like Vera and Miss MacIntosh as they navigate a world filled with unseen dangers and unspoken sorrows. See The Old Blind Sheep Dog.
  • “when there are only two ninepins left, one at each outermost edge”: A split. In tenpins, the 7-10 split, one pin at each back corner, is the hardest spare in bowling.
  • “Had you been in the crowds at Parker’s Arena on Parker’s Island”: Labor Day, the first Monday of September, became a federal holiday in 1894. No Parker’s Arena of 1900 has been found.
  • “the Sunday punch”: This is a powerful, devastating punch. See the Chapter 17 resources.
  • “Who is the umpire whom all men despise?”: May refer to the umpire Bill Klem.
  • “Who fought with John L. Sullivan, the victor until his last fight?”: John L. Sullivan was an American boxer who was the first heavyweight champion of gloved boxing. He was also the last heavyweight champion of bare-knuckle boxing and the first boxing superstar. (Wikipedia) James J. Corbett beat him in New Orleans in 1892.
  • “Who was Hercules?”: Hercules is famous in Roman and Greek mythology for his strength and his numerous far-ranging adventures. See Greek Mythology.
  • “the laws governing glove sports in the British Isles and in America”: The Queensberry rules (1867) were written by John Graham Chambers and published under the sponsorship of the Marquess of Queensberry. See the Chapter 17 resources.
  • “What sport was named after the Earl of Derby?”: The Earls of Derby have given their name to a number of sporting events. The Epsom Derby, first run in 1780, was named for the 12th Earl.
  • “Who ever saw one if he was in his senses?”: The meaning of the phrase is a pointed expression of rational disbelief in the supernatural or illusory visions that other characters might accept or experience.
  • “Who ever saw the ghost of his father?”: Hamlet’s father’s ghost (Hamlet 1.1-1.5). See Shakespeare.
  • “We are always the thing we see”: May refer to “We don’t see things as they are, we see things as we are,” which is commonly attributed to Anaïs Nin. The line appears in Nin’s Seduction of the Minotaur (1961), credited to the Talmud.
  • “It takes more than clothes to make the man”: It means that a person’s character, personality, and true worth cannot be judged solely by their appearance or what they wear. A person’s inner qualities and actions are what truly define them, not just their outward appearance. This saying directly contradicts the proverb “clothes make the man.” Polonius: “the apparel oft proclaims the man” (Hamlet 1.3). See Shakespeare.
  • “disturbing the even tenor of our days”: Gray: “They kept the noiseless tenor of their way” (Elegy Written in a Country Churchyard, 1751). It is a contemplative poem that meditates on the universality of death, particularly focusing on the lives and deaths of ordinary people buried in a rural churchyard.
  • “Moody’s Bibles”: The hotel Bible of Chapter 19. See the Chapter 19 resources.
  • “the old clam-digger had mistaken at first for a man”: The store window dummy Mr. Spitzer introduced to Catherine. See The Old Clam Digger and Joachim Spitzer.
  • “an old Jew’s pawn shop under the sign of the three golden balls”: The three golden balls were the sign of a pawnbroker. They come from the arms of the Medici and the legend of St. Nicholas’s three bags of gold. Young’s “old Jew’s pawn shop” draws on an old antisemitic stereotype. Medieval Christian law barred Jews from most trades and left them moneylending, and then despised them for it. See Society, Class, and Race.
  • “For many years now, she had never looked into a looking glass”: In Chapter 18 she “had never seen it herself except in a mirror.” See Mirrors and Reflections and the Chapter 18 resources.
  • “Emperor Hadrian, indeed! Who stole the mosaics off his tomb?”: Hadrian’s tomb is the Castel Sant’Angelo in Rome, stripped of its marble over the centuries. His deathbed poem begins “Animula vagula blandula,” “little soul, wandering, charming.”
  • “Mr. Chandelier, Mr. Res Tacamah”: Catherine’s companions, Mr. Res Tacamah “who was the drug bottle.” See Mr. Chandelier, Mr. Res Tacamah, The History of Opium, and the Chapter 2 resources.
  • “She would rather sow the whirlwind and reap it”: “For they have sown the wind, and they shall reap the whirlwind” (Hosea 8:7). See The Bible.
  • “nothing was sadder than the wisdom which did not help the wise”: Tiresias: “Alas, how dreadful to have wisdom where it profits not the wise!” (Sophocles, Oedipus the King 316-317, translated by R. C. Jebb).
  • “Baldness is no cure for sorrow”: Cicero tells the philosopher Bion’s joke about the king who tore out his hair in grief, “as though baldness were a cure for sorrow” (Tusculan Disputations 3.62). See Hair, Wig, and Baldness.
  • “her old dollar watch which was given to her by her dead love”: The silver-dollar watch of Chapter 19. See Love and the Chapter 19 resources.
  • “the inner man was all that counted”: “Though our outward man perish, yet the inward man is renewed day by day” (2 Corinthians 4:16). See The Bible.
  • “My mother saw everything but mistook everything she saw for something else”: What Vera describes resembles visual agnosia, a term Freud coined in On Aphasia (1891). See Catherine Cartwheel and Freud and Jung.
  • “My mother’s mother’s blindness had been only physical”: The blind grandmother of Chapter 12. See Eyes and Blindness and the Chapter 12 resources.
  • “What cared she for Issachar, Aaron, Absalom, Togarmah?”: The significance of these names is to situate the novel’s meditation on mortality, loss, and the passing of time within a biblical and mythic framework, underscoring the themes of decay and the search for meaning in the face of inevitable death. See Judaism.
    • Issachar: The Talmud argues that Issachar’s description in the Blessing of Jacob (“Issachar is a strong ass couching down between two burdens: and he saw that rest was good, and the land that it was pleasant; and bowed his shoulder to bear, and became a servant unto tribute,” Genesis 49:14-15) is a reference to the religious scholarship of the tribe of Issachar, though scholars feel that it may more simply be a literal interpretation of Issachar’s name. (Wikipedia)
    • Aaron: The rabbis particularly praise the brotherly sentiment between Aaron and Moses. When Moses was appointed ruler and Aaron high priest, neither betrayed any jealousy; instead they rejoiced in each other’s greatness. When Moses at first declined to go to Pharaoh, saying: “O my Lord, send, I pray, by the hand of him whom you will send” (Exodus 4:13), he was unwilling to deprive Aaron of the high position the latter had held for so many years; but the Lord reassured him, saying: “Behold, when he sees you, he will be glad in his heart” (Exodus 4:14). Indeed, Aaron was to find his reward, says Shimon bar Yochai; for that heart which had leaped with joy over his younger brother’s rise to glory greater than his was decorated with the Urim and Thummim, which were to “be upon Aaron’s heart when he goeth in before the Lord” (Exodus 28:30). Moses and Aaron met in gladness of heart, kissing each other as true brothers, and of them it is written: “Behold how good and how pleasant [it is] for brethren to dwell together in unity!” (Psalm 133:1) Of them it is said: “Mercy and truth are met together; righteousness and peace have kissed [each other]” (Psalm 85:10); for Moses stood for righteousness and Aaron for peace. Again, mercy was personified in Aaron, according to Deuteronomy 33:8, and truth in Moses, according to Numbers 12:7 (Kaufmann Kohler, “Aaron,” Jewish Encyclopedia, 1906).
    • Absalom: “He was a prince who could have had almost anything. The only things he wanted were things he could not have… Wealth is not determined by possessions but by mindset. In his mind, Absalom was a pauper. He only looked at what he did not have.” (Wikipedia) Absalom had erected a monument near Jerusalem to perpetuate his name: “Now Absalom in his lifetime had taken and reared up for himself a pillar, which is in the king’s dale: for he said, I have no son to keep my name in remembrance: and he called the pillar after his own name: and it is called unto this day, Absalom’s place” (2 Samuel 18:18). He wanted his father’s throne and led a revolt against David (2 Samuel 15-18). It was his half-brother Amnon who lusted after their sister Tamar, and Absalom killed Amnon for it (2 Samuel 13).
    • Togarmah “is a figure in the Generations of Noah in the Book of Genesis that represents the peoples known to the Hebrews. Togarmah is among the descendants of Japheth and is thought to represent some people located in Anatolia. Medieval sources claimed that Togarmah was the legendary ancestor of several ethnic groups in the Caucasus, including Armenians and Georgians” (Wikipedia, “Togarmah”). He was believed to have 10 sons.
  • “What cared she for any translation of the Word of God and flatteries to earthly kings”: The King James Version of Chapter 21. See the Chapter 21 resources.
  • “whose garments smelled of myrrh and aloes and cassia”: “All thy garments smell of myrrh, and aloes, and cassia, out of the ivory palaces” (Psalm 45:8). Young adds “of the dead.” King Ahab built “the ivory house” (1 Kings 22:39). See The Bible.
  • “or even the Baptists or even the Free Methodists”: The Free Methodist Church was founded in 1860. See American Religious Movements.

Vocabulary

A departure from what is normal or expected.

A Mediterranean plant whose deeply cut leaves are carved as ornament, especially on Corinthian columns.

A fragrant resin or wood used in perfume.

Before the Flood; very old.

Having to do with the stars.

Nonsense.

Heavy material, such as stones, carried low in a ship to keep it steady.

Crusted with barnacles, small shelled sea creatures that cling to rocks, pilings, and the hulls of ships.

The lead sheep of a flock, which wears a bell.
Brusque

Calker
Also caulker. A worker who seals the seams of a wooden ship to make it watertight.
Camisole
A woman’s light undergarment for the upper body. The text has “camesoles.”
Candelabra
A branched candlestick.
Cassia
A spice bark like cinnamon.
Castanets
Pairs of small wooden shells clicked together in the hand, as in Spanish dance.
Celluloid
An early plastic.
Centaur
In Greek mythology, a creature with the head and upper body of a man and the body and legs of a horse.
Chandelier
A branched hanging light.
Chattels
Movable possessions.
Cherubim
Winged angelic beings. In art they are often shown as chubby winged children. The singular is cherub.
Combers
A nautical term for long, curling waves that roll in and break on a beach or reef.
Constitutional
A walk taken regularly for the sake of one’s health.
Corporeal
Having a body; physical.
Corset
A close-fitting undergarment, stiffened with whalebone or steel and laced tight, worn to shape the waist.
Counterpane
A bedspread.
Curdled

Delusive

Denuded

Dope sheet
A racing sheet giving information and tips on the horses running.
Dory

Emissary

Festering

Figurehead
A carved figure, often a woman, mounted on the bow of a sailing ship. See On the figurehead and intuition (Ch 40).
Firmament

Fly-specked
Spotted with the tiny marks left by flies.
Forecastle
The forward part of a ship below the deck, where the crew lived. Pronounced “FOHK-sul.”
Forelock
A lock of hair over the forehead.
Gargoyle
A carved grotesque figure on a building, often serving as a waterspout.
Gelding
A castrated male horse.
Genealogy
A record of a family’s descent.
Goldeneye
A diving duck with bright yellow eyes, called a whistler for the sound of its wings.
Gregarious
Fond of company; sociable.
Griffin
A mythical beast with the head and wings of an eagle and the body of a lion.
Helm
The wheel or tiller that steers a ship.
Hock
The joint in the hind leg of a horse, between the knee and the fetlock.
Homespun
Simple and plain; originally, cloth spun at home.
Hulk
The body of an old ship; a big, clumsy person or thing.
Imploring
Begging earnestly.
Incorporeal
Without a body; not physical.
Inordinately
Excessively.
Invidious

Jeremiad

Laconically

Laggard
Slow; falling behind.
Larboard
The old word for the left side of a ship.
Leeward
On the side sheltered from the wind.
Leviathan
A sea monster in the Bible; anything huge.
Livid
Bluish-gray, the color of a bruise. Also furiously angry.
Lucid
Clear; clear-headed.
Lunar month
The time from one new moon to the next, about 29.5 days.
Mackerel sky
A sky of rippled clouds like the markings of a mackerel.
Mackintosh
A raincoat of rubberized cloth, named for its inventor, Charles Macintosh.
Mandarin
A high-ranking official of imperial China.
Mantle
A loose sleeveless cloak; anything that covers or envelops.
Marcelled

Mica
A mineral that splits into thin, shiny, nearly transparent sheets and makes rock glitter.

A seasonal wind in South Asia that brings months of heavy rain.
Morosely
Gloomily, sullenly.
Mosaic
A picture or pattern made by setting small pieces of colored stone, glass, or tile together.

Myrrh
A fragrant resin used in incense and embalming.

The tide with the smallest difference between high and low water, twice a month at the quarter moons.

The process of going out of use.
Palings
Pointed wooden stakes, or a fence made of them.
Paraphernalia
Personal belongings or equipment.

Inherited from one’s father.
Peaked
Thin and pale, as from illness.
Percale
A fine, closely woven cotton.

Ghostly; like a phantom or an illusion.

A clear piece of glass with flat sides that splits light into the colors of the rainbow.

A small, plump ground bird hunted as game.

Regatta
A series of boat races.
Seine
To fish with a large hanging net.
Spar
A pole used as a ship’s mast, boom, or yard. Spar is also the name for certain shiny, easily split crystalline minerals, such as Iceland spar.

Spray blown from the tops of waves.
Starboard

A horse race over fences, ditches, and water jumps, first run cross-country from one church steeple to another.

Tallow
Animal fat used for candles and soap. Tallow-colored is a dull, yellowish white.

A heavy waterproof cloth for covering things.

A crowded, run-down apartment building.

A loud, confused uproar.

Excessively proud and boastful.

A person’s face or expression.

Large, full, or great in volume.

A weathervane shaped like a rooster; also, a person who changes with every wind.

A railed platform on a coastal roof, from which to watch for ships.

Idle daydreaming.

Chapter 74
