Content note: The Esther Longtree chapters (72 to 81) deal with stillbirth and pregnancy loss, rape, infanticide, racist violence including lynching, and cruelty to children. This chapter is one of the hardest in the novel: Esther describes being raped, three winters running, by the Chicago detective, who found her unconscious in the fields.

Summary

Esther dreads the trial she expects next autumn, when the town’s women will crowd the courthouse to accuse her and she will be unable to produce the three children the Chicago detective says she killed. Her worst mistake, she thinks, was writing to him, a father who was not dying. Three winters, hunting a man who had killed several wives, he found her lying in the frozen fields and took her for a corpse; he felt her pulse, found her heartbeat, and raped her, leaving his eye-glasses, his calling card, a bone button, and a stillborn behind. He came once as a locksmith, once as a soap salesman, once as himself, and told her he was partly wax. When she wrote that she needed an abortion he sent her the name of an abortionist under police protection; now he accuses her of murdering his children. She sets her shame beside a man’s freedom to boast of his bastards, waxes and wanes like the moon, and speaks of the murder of her heart when she was young. A small, warped child’s hand lies across her womb, and her own childhood reproaches her.

Characters present

Esther Longtree · The Chicago Detective · Esther’s Father

Concepts present

Themes: Faith, God, and the Supernatural · Fear and Courage · Grief, Loss, and Mourning · Guilt, Innocence, and Justice · Identity and the Self · Isolation and Connection · Memory and the Past · Motherhood, Pregnancy, and Birth · Society, Class, and Race · Time · Women, Gender, and Marriage

Symbols: Birds · Clothing, Hats, and Skirts · Horses and Carriages · Moon and Stars · Pregnancy, Birth, and Children · Roses and Flowers · Snow, Ice, and Winter · The Sea and Water

Philosophy: Marguerite Young on Her Craft

Allusions: Angels and Archangels · Exploration and the Poles · Fairy Tales and Folklore · Genesis · Greek Mythology · Judaism · Music and Composers · Pregnancy, Abortion, and Midwifery · Revelation and the Apocalypse

Key passages

From the research

  • Esther expresses her dread and isolation as she anticipates a courtroom trial, where she will be accused and misunderstood by a crowd of women who will judge her harshly without truly understanding her. It underscores her loneliness and the societal scrutiny she faces, as well as the impossibility of defending herself against accusations about her maternity and morality.
  • The detective’s repeated, disguised appearances and his cold, investigative demeanor create a haunting, almost spectral presence in Esther’s life. He is both the father of her stillborn children, by rape, and the figure who pursues her in the law, embodying both violation and threat.
  • The narrative of the detective’s rape of Esther is described with a mixture of detached observation and emotional complexity. The experience is both a physical violation and a symbolic act that precipitates her ongoing “pregnancy” with stillborn children, both literal and metaphorical.
  • The motif of being “always pregnant” with stillborn children recurs throughout this chapter. This is also tied to her physical and emotional condition, which isolates her further.
  • Esther contrasts her own suffering and social condemnation as a woman with the freedom and impunity of men, highlighting societal hypocrisy and the loneliness of her position.
  • Esther traces her sorrows to “the murder of her heart when she was young.”
  • Despite the external pressures, accusations, and her own confusions, Esther claims a mysterious, almost radiant identity, self-sufficient and brooding, unwilling to explain herself to anyone.

Questions and observations

Reading closely

  • “She had felt as if a candle burning had raped her.” What does the candle say about a man who calls himself “partly wax”?
  • “He was a Christopher Columbus in the world of the dead.” What does Esther mean?
  • “What would happen would be worse than what would not happen.” What does Esther fear most?

Characters

  • The detective felt her pulse, found her heartbeat, and then raped her. Why does Esther say “She had not felt violated”?
  • “He had solved all life’s mysteries but his own, the one he was creating then.” What is his own mystery?
  • Esther wrote to the detective “as if she had resisted.” Why does she change the story in her letters?

Connections

  • “A man could have gone off whistling after he had done something wrong.” Where else in the novel do men go off whistling?
  • Esther goes on “dragging the stars after her.” How is she like the woman with child in Revelation 12?
  • “A woman abortionist who enjoyed police protection” is offered by the very detective who now accuses Esther of murder. What does that say about the law?

Reflection

  • “Conception was always a secret to the mother, too, as well as to the father.” Is that still true?
  • “Who was innocent? Who was guilty?” How would you answer for Esther?
  • “Her own childhood reproached her.” What might have happened when she was young?

Research: Characters

Esther Longtree

  • The protagonist, a woman who is perpetually pregnant yet burdened with loss and mystery.
  • She is introspective, lonely, and caught between hope and despair.
  • She fears legal prosecution and societal judgment but is also fiercely protective of her own narrative and secrets.

The Chicago Detective

  • The father of Esther’s children: three winters he found her unconscious in the fields, took her for a corpse, felt her pulse, and raped her.
  • He hunts murderers and now accuses Esther of murdering his children, though he himself raped her and sent her the name of an abortionist “who enjoyed police protection.”
  • He represents authority, suspicion, and the complexities of truth and guilt.

Esther’s Father (the Policeman)

  • Symbolizes familial and societal surveillance and judgment.
  • His passive role highlights Esther’s isolation and the inescapability of the small-town environment.

Research: Themes

Motherhood and Loss

See: Grief, Loss, and Mourning · Motherhood, Pregnancy, and Birth

  • Esther experiences repeated pregnancies that result in stillbirths, symbolizing loss, unfulfilled potential, and emotional trauma.
  • Her womb is described as swollen with “empty waters,” a metaphor for hope and despair coexisting.

Societal Judgment and Isolation

See: Isolation and Connection · Guilt, Innocence, and Justice · Society, Class, and Race

  • Esther fears the court trial, anticipating gossip, blame, and misunderstanding from the community.
  • She is alienated and misunderstood, with the jury and townspeople serving as a metaphor for harsh societal judgment.

Mystery and Ambiguity

See: Faith, God, and the Supernatural

  • The narrative blurs reality and memory. Esther’s story is full of mysteries: the paternity of her children, the nature of her pregnancies, and the actions of the detective.
  • The repeated motif of “stillborn” children and the detective’s ambiguous role deepen this theme.

Powerlessness and Defiance

See: Fear and Courage

  • Despite her vulnerability, Esther exhibits moments of defiance, especially against unfair accusations and societal expectations.
  • Her internal world remains rich and complex, even as she is perceived as “crazy” or “mulish.”

The Passage of Time and Memory

See: Memory and the Past · Time

  • The cyclical nature of seasons (autumn, winter, spring) parallels Esther’s repeated pregnancies and losses, symbolizing the persistence of trauma and hope over time.

Gender and Identity

See: Identity and the Self · Women, Gender, and Marriage

  • The text contrasts Esther’s experiences with societal expectations of men and women, highlighting gendered double standards, especially concerning sexuality, motherhood, and blame.

Research: Symbols and Imagery

Stillborn Children

See: Pregnancy, Birth, and Children

  • Symbolize lost potential, grief, and the failure of life to manifest fully.

The Chicago Detective’s Bloody Knife

  • Represents violence, mystery, and perhaps the intrusion of external forces into Esther’s life.

The Old Rosebud

See: Roses and Flowers

  • Placed on Esther’s body, symbolizing innocence, death, or a token of remorse.

The Seasons (Winter and Autumn)

See: Snow, Ice, and Winter

  • Reflect desolation, death, and the cyclical nature of Esther’s suffering.

The Small Warped Hand

  • “A small, warped, mole-colored hand,” a child’s hand, laid across her womb and her mouth; it seems tied to “something cold and small and dead that she had seen when she was much younger.”

Birds (Blackbirds, Sobbing Bird)

See: Birds

  • Represent sorrow, the passage of time, and the fragility of life.

The Shroud with Many Pockets

See: Clothing, Hats, and Skirts

  • Symbolizes the secrets Esther keeps, the hidden aspects of her identity and history.

Research: Resources

  • “Esther Longtree had gone on with her expectations”: Esther Longtree in this chapter is portrayed as a profoundly tragic and complex figure, embodying themes of loss, mystery, maternal suffering, and societal judgment. Her character is marked by an overwhelming burden of perpetual pregnancy and stillbirths, an existence both physically and emotionally laden with pain and unanswered questions. Esther’s situation is unique and unprecedented in the legal realm, as she faces the threat of arrest and trial for the disappearance or death of her children: children who may never have been born or who remain unseen by others. She is caught in a web of suspicion and gossip, misunderstood and condemned by her community and the justice system, yet she remains deeply isolated, bearing her sorrow silently and without defense. This isolation is compounded by her physical condition (repeatedly pregnant yet without the relief of childbirth) and by the haunting presence of her absent children, described metaphorically as her “tears” and “stillborn” who haunt her mind and body. Her relationship with the Chicago detective, who is implicated as the father of her lost children, adds layers of complexity and darkness to her narrative. The detective’s repeated appearances (disguised as various characters) are both invasive and inscrutable. Esther’s encounters with him are marked by violence, mystery, and a sense of inevitability: she is raped by him, yet the experience is described with a strange passivity and detachment, as if she were “sleeping in the grass” and indifferent. This rapist-father figure represents a brutal intrusion into her life, one that leaves physical and psychological scars, but also a tangled mystery of conception, conception without life, and lost pregnancies. Esther’s internal world is rich with symbolism and metaphor: the “stillborn” children, the “broken gooseberry bushes,” the “buzzard hanging rounded like a period” all evoke a landscape of death, loss, and unfulfilled potential. Despite her suffering, Esther is radiant and self-sufficient in a strange way, carrying her burden with a stubborn dignity. She is aware of the social judgments (accusations of insanity, immorality, or deceit) but she resists these with a fierce inner knowledge of her own innocence and the mystery of her condition. Her loneliness and estrangement are deeply felt, yet she remains luminous, a figure of both vulnerability and strength. The chapter also explores Esther’s reflections on gender and societal double standards. She contrasts her own experience as a woman burdened with loss and silence to the freedom a man might have in fathering children without consequence or shame. Her pregnancy and stillbirths are not only physical but symbolic of her emotional and existential state: a life marked by “murder of her heart,” repeated disappointments, and unanswered questions about innocence and guilt. Esther Longtree is a character defined by enigmatic suffering, caught between the natural and the supernatural, the legal and the personal. She embodies a tragic maternal figure whose story is one of loss made visible and invisible, a woman burdened by an unexplainable condition and an unresolvable mystery. Her narrative is steeped in poetic imagery and a haunting sense of inevitability and silence, marking her as both victim and enigma within the novel’s broader themes of reality, illusion, and the passage of time. See Esther Longtree.
    • Esther Longtree symbolizes a complex and tragic history of female suffering, loss, and misunderstood maternity that can be read as an allegory for broader historical and social issues in the United States. Her life, marked by repeated pregnancies, stillbirths, and the mysterious disappearance or loss of her children, reflects the harsh realities faced by many women, especially those marginalized or without social support. Esther’s experiences evoke themes of abandonment, societal judgment, and the silencing of women’s voices, particularly in the context of reproductive rights and maternal health. The narrative describes her perpetual state of pregnancy and loss, the accusations she faces from being called an “old maid” to insinuations of infanticide and her helplessness before the law and community gossip. This represents a history of women’s reproductive experiences often ignored or stigmatized by society and legal systems. Her story also touches on the failures of paternal responsibility, as the Chicago detective (a figure of authority) is implicated in her rape and desertion, embodying male cruelty and neglect. Esther’s repeated encounters with the detective, who is seeking evidence and truth in a cold, clinical way, symbolize the invasive and often hostile scrutiny women face from institutions. Her isolation in a small town, where every movement is known, contrasts with the anonymity she imagines in a big city like Chicago, highlighting the oppressive small-town social surveillance prevalent in American history. Her story, which is full of loss, silence, and the mystery of unacknowledged or stillborn children, can be seen as symbolizing the broader historical experiences of women who have suffered reproductive trauma, been marginalized in legal and social systems, and whose lives have been shaped by forces beyond their control. The imagery of barren family trees, repeated stillbirths, and accusations of guilt without proof evokes the historical struggles with fertility, motherhood, and female agency in the US. Esther Longtree’s history symbolizes the hidden, painful legacies of women’s reproductive lives in American history, including issues of maternity, loss, societal judgment, and the often cruel intersection of personal suffering with institutional authority.
  • “Her menses had stopped so long ago”: Menses, commonly known as a period or menstrual flow, is the monthly shedding of the uterine lining (endometrium) that occurs when a pregnancy does not happen. It is a natural part of the reproductive cycle, typically lasting 2 to 7 days, and is characterized by bleeding from the uterus.
  • “to be let alone outside the pale of law”: The Pale was the English-ruled ground around Dublin; to be beyond the pale was to be outside the law and its protection. The Pale of Settlement (1791 to 1917) was the land at the western edge of the Russian Empire where Jews were forced to live. See Judaism.
  • “All the women would flock to the courthouse in droves”: Andrea Dworkin wrote the book Right Wing Women that examined how women are exploited by right wing, conservative politics. They answer women’s fears about their place in the world with offers of chivalrous protection within the domain and under the control of men through patriarchal structures such as the male head of household. It reassures women that they do not need to change the status quo, but accept it, and take whatever access to power is given, almost exclusively along gender defined norms. When these women see other women flaunting these gender norms, they bond with their fathers, husbands or father-figures to form a power base through misogyny, the enforcement branch of patriarchy, to bring the status quo back in force. Right-Wing Women was published in 1983. See Women, Gender, and Marriage.
  • “an old maid plucking at a daisy’s petals”: “He loves me, he loves me not.” In French the game is effeuiller la marguerite, plucking the daisy, and marguerite is the French for daisy. See Roses and Flowers and Marguerite Young on Her Craft.
  • “a crazy old mule in heat”: See the barren mule in the Chapter 72 resources and the Chapter 73 resources. See Horses and Carriages.
  • “little white faces propped on ice floes”: See Exploration and the Poles.
  • “the captain of a Great Lakes steamer”: The Great Lakes Storm of November 1913, the worst on record, wrecked nineteen ships and sank twelve, several with all hands; about 250 sailors died. See The Sea and Water.
  • “some old preacher or jack-in-the-pulpit”: The jack-in-the-pulpit is a woodland wildflower whose spadix stands under a hooded spathe like a preacher in his pulpit; the Johnny-jump-up is the wild pansy, the four o’clock opens in late afternoon, and shepherd’s purse is named for its heart-shaped seed pods. See Roses and Flowers.
  • “a Chicago detective and specialist in murder mysteries”: The Chicago Detective can be understood symbolically as a representation of a police state or police corruption through several layers of meaning revealed in the novel. See The Chicago Detective.
    • The Chicago Detective appears as an omnipresent, persistent figure who repeatedly pursues Esther Longtree, the woman at the center of a murder mystery involving unknown children and dark accusations. He comes “three times in three different years” looking for evidence and never finds the murderer but consistently finds Esther herself, lying vulnerable and exposed. His repeated visits and obsessive investigations suggest an invasive, overreaching authority typical of a police state that monitors and controls individuals without clear cause.
    • Esther Longtree’s experience with the Chicago Detective is marked by fear and victimization. She is “raped” by him in a mysterious way, leaving behind “evidence, the symptoms, the signs” (his “eye-glasses, his calling card, a bone button, the frozen conception, a thread, and a single spot of brown blood”) which haunts her. This portrayal aligns the detective with a corrupt or abusive power that violates personal boundaries and fabricates or misuses evidence to persecute the vulnerable.
    • The Detective’s attitude toward “white” versus “black” deaths underscores a racial bias, a hallmark of systemic police corruption and institutional racism. In Chapter 77, “he only dealt with the deaths of little white children, for the deaths of the little black children were not his business, there being so many and so unimportant.” This selective interest in victims based on race symbolizes the partiality and injustice within a corrupt police system.
    • The Detective is described as one who “had solved all life’s mysteries but his own” and “crept in among murderers and had gotten their confessions by confessing his own imaginary crimes.” He is trapped in a cycle of investigating crimes, yet he himself is implicated in the system’s violence and injustice. This reflects the idea of a police state where the enforcers are both agents and victims of systemic oppression, unable to escape the machinery they uphold.
    • The detective’s inability to find the true culprit yet his readiness to implicate Esther Longtree highlights the paranoia and miscarriage of justice prevalent in such systems.
    • The detective’s “many murder cases” and obsession with “quiet mysteries” where “there had never been a body” (Chapters 76 and 77) symbolize not only literal crimes but the suppression or erasure of truths inconvenient to those in power. The recurring motif of “quiet, quiet murders” points to systemic silencing and cover-ups typical in corrupt regimes.
    • The detective is associated with “old evidence staring, new evidence, trampled grass,” and “a clue which led nowhere” (Chapters 76 and 68). This suggests the manipulation or fabrication of evidence which is a central tool of police corruption to maintain control or silence dissent.
    • The detective threatened Esther Longtree with legal persecution and exposed her to the scrutiny of a judgmental society. This intertwines with the theme of social control exercised by authoritarian entities that use fear and punishment to maintain order.
    • The Chicago Detective functions symbolically as an embodiment of police state oppression and corruption. He is a figure of invasive surveillance, racial bias, miscarriage of justice, and systemic violence. His relentless pursuit of a vulnerable woman, selective concern for victims based on race, and role in perpetuating a cycle of unending investigation without resolution all reflect the mechanisms by which a police state enforces control through fear, misinformation, and partiality. The Detective’s character exposes the tragic human consequences of living under such a regime, where truth is elusive and justice is compromised.
  • “a man who had killed several wives”: In Perrault’s Bluebeard (1697) a husband murders wife after wife. Chicago had its own: Johann Hoch, the “Stockyard Bluebeard,” married at least 55 women between 1890 and 1905, poisoning many with arsenic, and was hanged in Chicago in 1906. See Fairy Tales and Folklore and Women, Gender, and Marriage.
  • “his eye-glasses, his footprints, too, his calling card”: These are all clues used in famous mystery novels. The Golden Age of Detective Fiction (roughly 1913-1939) was an era between the World Wars defined by polite, “whodunit” puzzle mysteries, primarily featuring British writers like Agatha Christie, Dorothy L. Sayers, Margery Allingham, and Ngaio Marsh. These stories favored intellectual, fair-play clues over violence, often set in closed circles like country houses, focusing on solving the murder rather than dark, psychological grit. The “closed circle” of suspects, “fair play” (all clues provided to the reader), and the focus on the “whodunit” puzzle. Iconic characters from this time period: Hercule Poirot, Miss Marple, Lord Peter Wimsey, Perry Mason, and Philip Marlowe. E.C. Bentley’s Trent’s Last Case (1913) is often cited as the beginning, with Christie’s The Mysterious Affair at Styles (1920) setting the standard. The Detection Club, founded in 1930, established “rules” for the genre, such as no faked clues or supernatural solutions. The stories offered escapism, featuring a return to order after a “sanitized” version of murder, often reflecting a desire to move past the trauma of World War I. While often associated with the British “cozy” style, the era also saw the rise of American “hard-boiled” fiction. American hard-boiled detective fiction is a gritty, unsentimental subgenre emerging in the 1920s-30s, defined by cynical private eyes, urban corruption, fast-paced dialogue, and brutal violence. Pioneered by Dashiell Hammett and perfected by Raymond Chandler, these stories moved away from genteel puzzles to realistic crime, often published in pulp magazines like Black Mask.
    • During the Golden Age of Detective Fiction, eyeglasses generally symbolized intellectualism, keen observation, or a specific social, physical, or moral state. They were used to signify a character’s scholarly status, wealth, or, in some cases, to conceal identity or suggest a hidden, vulnerable, or untrustworthy nature.
    • In the Victorian and Golden Age eras, footprints functioned as vital, often clichéd, forensic evidence used to reconstruct a crime scene in the absence of advanced, systematic fingerprinting. They served as a tangible link between a suspect and the crime, often revealing clues about the perpetrator’s physical characteristics, movement, and identity.
    • A calling card, also known as a visiting card, generally refers to two distinct concepts: a social tool of the Victorian/Edwardian era and a signature item left by a criminal at a crime scene.
    • A thread as a clue refers both to a literal, physical object and, metaphorically, to the clue which guided a detective through the “labyrinth” of a crime, originating from the Greek myth of Theseus and Ariadne.
  • “a moss rosebud brown as a mushroom”: The moss rose, its buds furred with green moss, was a favorite of Victorian gardens. See Roses and Flowers.
  • “ringing, ringing, ringing in his ears”: During Esther’s part in the book the repetition of three words appears as if Esther has a stutter. In rhetoric, epizeuxis is the repetition of a word or phrase in immediate succession, typically within the same sentence, for vehemence or emphasis. A closely related rhetorical device is diacope, which involves word repetition that is broken up by a single intervening word, or a small number of intervening words. As a rhetorical device, epizeuxis is utilized to create an emotional appeal, thereby inspiring and motivating the audience. However, epizeuxis can also be used for comic effect.
  • “He had despoiled the withered flowers”: To deflower and to despoil: Esther was “deflowered” in the graveyard in the Chapter 73 resources.
  • “a bone button, the frozen conception”: A bone button as a clue generally signifies a crucial, mundane, and often overlooked piece of physical evidence that identifies a suspect based on their social standing, clothing, or actions. In the “Golden Age” of detective fiction, such items were used to show how a killer could be convicted by a small, everyday object rather than just fingerprints or bloodstains.
  • “She had felt as if a candle burning had raped her”: The detective is “partly wax,” and later “his fire was burned out, perhaps had never been. Perhaps there was no candle.”
  • “Oh, mother, what have you done with my father?”: Esther’s mother and the passive policeman, “still on their long honeymoon,” appear in the Chapter 72 resources. See Esther’s Father.
  • “an abyss into which she might fall, dragging the stars after her”: “And there appeared a great wonder in heaven; a woman clothed with the sun, and the moon under her feet, and upon her head a crown of twelve stars: And she being with child cried, travailing in birth. . . . And his tail drew the third part of the stars of heaven” (Revelation 12:1-2, 4, KJV). The dragon waits to devour her child. See Revelation and the Apocalypse and Moon and Stars.
  • “This Chicago detective was creating quite a problem even now”: The detective’s suit “was based upon a real case which happened in Chicago,” which Young read about in a New York paper, “and I wove it into my story” (Marguerite Young, interview with Kay Bonetti, American Audio Prose Library, May 1983). See The Chicago Detective and Marguerite Young on Her Craft.
  • “He was a Christopher Columbus in the world of the dead”: Christopher Columbus was an Italian explorer and navigator who completed four Spanish-based voyages across the Atlantic Ocean sponsored by the Catholic Monarchs of Spain, opening the way for the widespread European exploration and colonization of the Americas. His expeditions were the first known European contact with the Caribbean, Central America, and South America. See Exploration and the Poles.
    • On Hispaniola Columbus enslaved the Taíno; in 1495 he shipped some 500 to Spain to be sold, and about 200 died on the voyage. In 1500 he was arrested for his cruelty as governor and sent home in chains. See Society, Class, and Race.
  • “of the babes who were murdered in the woods”: See the Babes in the Wood in the Chapter 72 resources. See Fairy Tales and Folklore.
  • “the poisoned blackbirds falling from the sky”: Blackbird control programs in the US aimed at reducing large roosting populations often involved, albeit with limited success, the use of toxic baits in open or plowed fields. These efforts often caused accidental mortality of non-target wildlife species. See Birds.
  • “Where was her lost girlhood?”: On the one hand this can be symbolic and on the other men do perpetrate the majority of the violence against women and other men probably due to men and boys being socialized to accept masculine stereotypes that reinforce violence toward others and themselves. The most dangerous time for a woman is when she is trying to leave an abusive relationship. Gendered thinking about women is that they are supposed to be mysterious and cultivate feminine aspects to be appealing to men. This is sexist in that one would not apply the same statement to men as it is applied to women. Women are not mysterious or impossible to understand but rather there is so little actual data collected and used scientifically, socially or historically about women. It is understandable in this context that men can feel that way since they never hear anything different than the baseline of men applied to everything. See Women, Gender, and Marriage.
  • “she had lost her toxic condition”: Toxemia of pregnancy, now called preeclampsia, brings high blood pressure, swelling, and sometimes convulsions (eclampsia); before modern prenatal care it was one of the great killers of mothers. See Pregnancy, Abortion, and Midwifery.
  • “the mark of the gavel on his forehead”: “And the LORD set a mark upon Cain” (Genesis 4:15, KJV). See Genesis.
  • “a shroud with many, many pockets”: “Shrouds have no pockets”: what is hidden in life cannot be carried into death. An Italian proverb in English print since 1854, it is also a Yiddish saying. See Judaism and Clothing, Hats, and Skirts.
  • “The birth veil had perhaps never been lifted from her face”: A child born with the caul, the birth membrane, over the face was said to have second sight and never to drown; sailors bought cauls as charms. See Fairy Tales and Folklore.
  • “Conception was always a secret to the mother”: In many cultures, the discussion of all sexual issues has traditionally been considered taboo, and adolescents were not given any information on sexual matters. Such instruction, as was given, was traditionally left to a child’s parents, and often this was put off until just before their marriage. However, in the late 19th century, the progressive education movement led to the introduction of sex education as social hygiene in North American school curricula and the introduction of school-based sex education. Despite early inroads of school-based sex education, most of the information on sexual matters in the mid-20th century was obtained informally from friends and the media, and much of this information was deficient or of dubious value, especially during the period following puberty, when curiosity about sexual matters was the most acute. This deficiency was heightened by the increasing incidence of teenage pregnancies, particularly in Western countries after the 1960s.
  • “some old pecan trees that were brought here from the old world”: The pecan is native to North America, growing wild along the Mississippi and its rivers; “pecan” is an Algonquian word. In the Chapter 72 resources Esther speaks of “the pecan trees that were brought from the old Jerusalem.”
  • “a woman abortionist who enjoyed police protection”: Abortion was a crime in Illinois from 1867 until 1973. In Chicago, the historian Leslie J. Reagan found, the state prosecuted chiefly abortionists, most often after a woman had died, and police questioned dying women about their abortionists and lovers to obtain “dying declarations.” Reagan, When Abortion Was a Crime (1997). See Pregnancy, Abortion, and Midwifery and Women, Gender, and Marriage.
  • “she had done much lying but no laying”: Young seems to at least in part use Esther to explore the sexual double standard where men who have many sexual experiences are considered studs, while women who have many sexual experiences are considered sluts. A double standard is the application of different sets of principles for situations that are, in principle, the same. Research has found that casual sexual activity is regarded as more acceptable for men than for women. Double standards between men and women can potentially exist with regards to: dating, cohabitation, virginity, marriage/remarriage, sexual abuse/assault/harassment, domestic violence and singleness. See Women, Gender, and Marriage.
  • “she was only a silent piano with dusty keys”: In the Chapter 72 resources Esther insists, “I am a white piano.” See Music and Composers.
  • “God, she was not mulish!”: Esther insisted that she was not “mulish.” Being mulish means to be stubborn. See Horses and Carriages.
  • “A man could have gone off whistling after he had done something wrong”: He “could have bragged about this in a railroad station, how many bastards he had had.” See Women, Gender, and Marriage.
  • “as if she had resisted”: She was “sleeping in the grass” and “unresponsive except to memory”; consent cannot be given asleep or unconscious. See Guilt, Innocence, and Justice.
  • “this rape of a sightless child, for this was only one of many”: Esther lay with “her sightless brown eyes staring fixedly at the grey, hovering winter sky.” She calls herself a sightless child, and this rape “only one of many.” See Women, Gender, and Marriage.
  • “She guessed it had all been over too soon”: Young may be referring to rape culture in which rape is pervasive and normalized due to societal attitudes about gender and sexuality. Behaviors commonly associated with rape culture include victim blaming, slut-shaming, sexual objectification, trivializing rape, denial of widespread rape, refusing to acknowledge the harm caused by sexual violence, or some combination of these. Men and women who are victims of sexual violence may not report the assault because of shame, the stigma, not being believed and the criminal justice system. Traumatic memories since there is a heightened emotional response often are remembered as specific details about the event as opposed to false memories. Research shows that forgetting, not thinking about, and even misremembering an assault may be both necessary and adaptive to help survivors cope with their reality. See Women, Gender, and Marriage.
  • “Like the slow moon itself”: Esther, “waxing, waxing, never waning” in the Chapter 73 resources, now “waxed, reddish in wind,” like “a scarred, dead, cold, bald planet.” See Moon and Stars.
  • “Her own childhood reproached her”: This section may refer to the death of Esther’s baby when she was young and how that traumatized her even now. Rape has been used as a plot device in literature and other media. It has been criticized for using rape as a metaphor that displaces the actual, violent and traumatic act of rape. It is considered misogynistic in the way female rape victims continue to be cast as collateral damage and the assault and rape of women is used as a plot point in a narrative that is fundamentally about men. Young is making this about Esther and showing how things would be different if she were a man. Young makes many references to mythology. The struggle to escape from sexual pursuit is one of the most popular motifs of Greek mythology: Persephone, Callisto, Daphne, Europa, Io, etc. Greek mythology depicts women as vulnerable to assault, able to escape only through death, or metamorphosis like Daphne who becomes a laurel tree. The consequence of fleeing sexual violence is another type of force on the body, the loss of the human form where women who survive sexual violence become pregnant, and when gods as the rapists, produce a hero child. The Chicago detective takes Esther for a corpse, then feels her pulse, finds her heartbeat, and rapes her. Chione in Greek mythology was said to be so beautiful that she was the object of a thousand men’s desire. Hermes put Chione into a deep sleep with his wand and proceeded to rape her. Since Young has said Esther is the mother of us all and Mr. Spitzer as the father of us all, these could be archetypes for Adam and Eve and possibly Lilith. In On the Origin of the World, part of the Nag Hammadi Library, the rulers of the world rape the earthly Eve, and she bears their children. In the midrash Pirkei de-Rabbi Eliezer, Samael, riding the serpent, seduces Eve and fathers Cain; later Kabbalah makes Lilith, Adam’s first wife, Samael’s bride. The Talmud says that in the years Adam was apart from Eve he fathered spirits, demons, and lilin (Eruvin 18b). See Greek Mythology, Genesis, and Angels and Archangels.

chapter-28:
Chapter 28

← Chapter 27 · Home · Chapter 29 →

Content note: This chapter mentions the suicide of Mr. Spitzer’s twin brother, Peron. Vera’s mother, Catherine Cartwheel, is addicted to opium.

Summary

Mr. Spitzer admits that he may be only another of Catherine’s hallucinations, and that he truly lives only during these evenings in her room. Peron, who loved “the wastrel wheels of chance,” had no patience “for the caterpillar to become the butterfly.” Mr. Spitzer recalls the butterfly collecting he gave up two or three years after Peron’s death, his correspondence with fellow collectors, and the births and deaths of butterflies he watched. If one were called away at the crucial moment, he observes, one could never tell whether one had seen a beginning or an end.

Characters present

Joachim Spitzer · Peron Spitzer · Catherine Cartwheel · Vera Cartwheel

Concepts present

Themes: Death and Mortality · Dreams and Imagination · Fate and Chance · Identity and the Self · Illusion and Reality · Memory and the Past · Motherhood, Pregnancy, and Birth · The Search for Meaning · Time

Symbols: Birds · Butterflies and Moths · Lamps, Candles, and Light · Mirrors and Reflections · Opium · Pregnancy, Birth, and Children · Twins and Doubles

Philosophy: Kant and Hegel · Plato and Platonism · Taoism and Zhuangzi

Allusions: Exploration and the Poles · Fairy Tales and Folklore · Gambling and Playing Cards · Genesis · Greek Mythology · Romantic Poets · The Bible

Key passages

From the research

  • The opening passage describes Mr. Spitzer’s nightly visits as a kind of faithfulness, drawing “him each evening here as to a brilliant star,” despite his life feeling like a “dark and empty plain” except for these “delusive evenings.” This passage highlights the blurred boundary between his corporeal reality and the narcotic, hallucinatory world of Catherine. He is portrayed as a “living ghost” caught between life and death, reality and fantasy, which underscores the chapter’s exploration of existence, memory, and identity. The imagery of “the vastness of this trembling flesh enclosing his feeble spirit like a flame” poignantly captures the fragility of his being.
  • There is a significant reflection on Mr. Spitzer’s dead twin brother, who had a very different approach to life. While Mr. Spitzer was thinking “only of the impossible future,” his brother “had loved the cruelty of actual life” and seemed to live only in the present moment. The brother’s death profoundly affected Mr. Spitzer, dividing his soul almost to lunacy. This contrast illuminates themes of mortality, memory, and the divergent ways individuals confront existence and loss. It also sets up a tension between rationality and passion, foresight and immediacy.
  • Mr. Spitzer’s passion for collecting butterflies is portrayed not merely as a hobby but as a meditative and symbolic pursuit. The butterflies are described with poetic richness. This imagery conveys a mystical quality, indicating that these ephemeral creatures represent moments of beauty, transformation, and perhaps spiritual truth. His care for butterflies is contrasted with Catherine’s visions of “imaginary sea bishops,” “mermaids,” and other fantastical figures, suggesting a shared yet distinct engagement with the invisible or transcendent world.
  • The chapter notes that after Peron’s “devastating funeral,” many aspects of Mr. Spitzer’s life ended, including his butterfly collecting and his “own capacious heart.” Peron’s pragmatic, earthly interests are contrasted with Mr. Spitzer’s more spiritual and impersonal passions. This marks a turning point, emphasizing loss not only of a person but of a way of life and a kind of inner vitality. Peron’s skepticism about the afterlife and the significance of spiritual phenomena positions him as a foil to Mr. Spitzer’s contemplative nature.
  • The closing passage reflects on the indistinguishability of birth and death moments: “if one were suddenly called away in the midst of these proceedings, one should never know whether it was death or birth, beginning or end.” This philosophical observation encapsulates a central motif of the chapter, the fluid boundary between beginnings and endings, life and death, seen through the metaphor of the butterfly’s emergence and expiration. It also explains the impetus for Mr. Spitzer’s studies: the search for meaning in “impalpable butterflies,” or elusive spiritual truths.

Questions and observations

Reading closely

  • “He might well have been… among my mother’s irresponsible hallucinations.” Why does the thought not frighten him?
  • Why does Mr. Spitzer find “his only sense of his unbroken continuity” in a room where “no chair had changed its place for years”?
  • “One should never know whether it was death or birth.” What does the butterfly teach him?

Characters

  • Peron had no patience “to wait for the caterpillar to become the butterfly.” What did he love instead?
  • Mr. Spitzer gave up his butterflies after Peron’s death. Why give up the thing that consoled him?
  • Catherine sees “all these beauties which he could no more see than if he were a mole.” What does each of them see that the other cannot?

Connections

  • The butterfly on the flower was “as identical to the flower as twin to twin.” How does that echo the twins?
  • In Chapter 24, Catherine imagined “a unicorn wearing a necklace.” Here the unicorn is “enclosed by a picket fence.” What has changed?
  • The “painted ladies fluttering through the darkness” are butterflies and street women at once. Where else does Young let one word carry two worlds?

Reflection

  • Is a beginning ever distinguishable from an end?
  • What do we collect, and why?
  • Does the dead person return “except in our thoughts”?

Research: Characters

Joachim Spitzer (Peron’s twin brother)

  • The central figure of this chapter, haunted by his brother’s death and Catherine’s narcotic-induced visions.
  • A collector and contemplator of butterflies, symbolizing his search for meaning and beauty.
  • A man of solitude, haunted by existential questions about life and identity.
  • He may be, he admits, “among my mother’s irresponsible hallucinations,” and only in her room is he “still renewed.”
  • He gave up his butterflies “two or three years after his brother’s irrational death,” and much else ended “on the day of Peron’s devastating funeral.”
  • He finds “his only sense of his unbroken continuity in life” in her room, “perhaps because no chair had changed its place for years.”

Peron Spitzer (Joachim’s twin brother)

  • A loudmouthed, pragmatic man who embraced the cruelty of actual life and seemed indifferent to spiritual or afterlife concepts.
  • His untimely death deeply affects Mr. Spitzer’s psyche and way of life.
  • He loved “the wastrel wheels of chance, the games of loaded dice, the croupiers, the billiard hall artists… the drugged horses.”
  • He “would most certainly have seen no value, no unearthly significance as to butterflies or any other spirits.”

Catherine Cartwheel (Vera’s mother)

  • A figure whose narcotic dreams create the enchanted, surreal world Mr. Spitzer visits each evening.
  • Her “obtuse faith that he would always return” and her hallucinations sustain Mr. Spitzer’s sense of renewal and continuity despite his personal losses.
  • She sees “all these beauties which he could no more see than if he were a mole under the ground,” even when her eyes are closed.

Research: Themes

The Intersection of Life and Death

See: Death and Mortality

  • Mr. Spitzer exists in a liminal space, described as “this living ghost,” caught between corporeal reality and spiritual or hallucinatory realms.
  • The chapter reflects on how death and memory interact, emphasizing that the dead do not return except in the thoughts of the living.
  • The novel suggests a tenuous grasp on identity after death or loss, especially in relation to Mr. Spitzer’s dead twin brother, whose absence profoundly impacts him.

Memory and Identity

See: Memory and the Past · Identity and the Self

  • Mr. Spitzer’s struggle to understand “the actual man he was” highlights the elusive nature of self-knowledge and the effect of loss on personal identity.
  • Memory serves as a bridge to the past and as a means to preserve continuity, especially through his recollections of his brother.
  • The chapter suggests that memory may be deceptive or limited, with “things not possible” entering the mind through “the deceived memory of the unknown.”

The Role of the Narcotic and Hallucinatory World

See: Dreams and Imagination · Opium

  • Mr. Spitzer is drawn each evening to a place shaped by Catherine’s narcotic dreams, a surreal, enchanted world filled with fantastical figures (e.g., Russian bishops, lighthouse keepers, moon-faced duchesses) and imagery (snow owls, serpents, music boxes).
  • This dreamlike space is where, though “still denied and turned away,” he is “still renewed,” suggesting a complex relationship between reality and illusion.

Butterflies as a Symbol

See: Butterflies and Moths

  • Butterflies serve as a powerful metaphor for fleeting beauty, transformation, and the ephemeral nature of life and memory.
  • Mr. Spitzer’s passion for collecting butterflies reflects his attempt to capture and preserve moments of beauty and meaning amid loneliness and loss.
  • The novel details the vividness and variety of butterflies he treasured, symbolizing spiritual messengers or incarnations of beauty in various realms.
  • His butterfly collection and memories also contrast with the pragmatic and mundane approach of his brother Peron, who dismissed such ethereal concerns.

Contrast Between Mr. Spitzer and His Brother Peron

See: Twins and Doubles · Peron Spitzer

  • Peron is portrayed as a man focused on the immediate, material world, indifferent to spiritual or afterlife concepts, and unconcerned with the delicate beauty Mr. Spitzer values.
  • Peron’s death, “by accident or suicide,” marks a turning point for Mr. Spitzer, leading to the end of many of his pursuits and a deepening of his introspection.

Philosophical Reflections on Birth, Death, and Time

See: Death and Mortality · Time · Motherhood, Pregnancy, and Birth · The Search for Meaning

  • The chapter explores the ambiguity between birth and death, suggesting moments in life where beginning and end are indistinguishable.
  • Mr. Spitzer muses on how one could never be sure if a certain moment signifies death or birth, reflecting on the cyclical and interconnected nature of existence.
  • This ambiguity first set him on his study of the “impalpable butterflies,” symbolizing ineffable and transient moments in life.

Research: Symbols and Imagery

Butterflies

See: Butterflies and Moths

  • Represent transformation, beauty, and the fleeting nature of life.
  • Emblematic of Mr. Spitzer’s desire to preserve ephemeral moments amid existential uncertainty.

The Enchanted Dream World

See: Illusion and Reality · Fairy Tales and Folklore

  • Filled with fantastical figures and surreal imagery (e.g., snow owls with human faces, headless horsemen, mermaids).
  • Symbolizes the blurred line between reality and illusion, life and death, sanity and madness.

The Candle Flames and Venetian Mirrors

See: Mirrors and Reflections · Lamps, Candles, and Light

  • Reflect the delicate, transient nature of perception and memory.

The Ambiguity of Birth and Death

See: Pregnancy, Birth, and Children

  • The duality of beginning and end, highlighting the cyclical nature of existence.

Research: Resources

  • “perhaps the Antarctic Queen Maud Mountains”: The Queen Maud Mountains are a major group of mountains in the Antarctic. Roald Amundsen named them in 1911 for Queen Maud of Norway, on his way to the South Pole. See Exploration and the Poles.
  • “perhaps Queen Charlotte Islands in a storm”: The Queen Charlotte Islands, now called Haida Gwaii, are an archipelago off the coast of British Columbia in Canada. Captain George Dixon named them in 1787 after his ship, the Queen Charlotte, which was named for George III’s queen.
  • “perhaps the headless horseman fording a brook”: Washington Irving’s headless horseman. See the Chapter 26 resources.
  • “that spindle of creative flame which is said to sleep in the eternal darkness, weaving our bodies”: Weaving plays a significant role in the mythologies of various cultures, often symbolizing creation, destiny, and even the weaving of life itself. In many stories, weaving is attributed to deities or individuals who control fate or have supernatural abilities. For example, the Greek Moirae (Fates) spin, measure, and cut the thread of human lives, and the Norse goddess Frigg is associated with weaving and seiðr magic, which involves weaving destiny. Greek mythology: Athena, Arachne, Moirae (Fates), Penelope, Philomela. Norse mythology: Frigg, The Norns. Other mythologies: Neith, Laima, Päivätär and Kuutar, Spider Woman, Arianrhod. In Plato’s Myth of Er (Republic 10), the Spindle of Necessity turns the spheres on the knees of Necessity, and her daughters, the Fates, spin each life. In the chapter the “spindle of creative flame” weaves bodies, souls, and dreams, so that identity is woven like a tapestry from many threads of experience and memory, made of many intertwined selves rather than one. See Plato and Platonism, Fate and Chance, and Greek Mythology.
  • “deserts suddenly flowering”: “The desert shall rejoice, and blossom as the rose” (Isaiah 35:1). See The Bible.
  • “no patience to wait for the caterpillar to become the butterfly”: The Greek psychē means both “soul” and “butterfly.” In Apuleius’s The Golden Ass (2nd century AD), Psyche is the soul who marries Cupid. See Greek Mythology and Butterflies and Moths.
  • “as of the great shell of Venus”: Botticelli’s The Birth of Venus (c. 1485), the goddess rising from the sea on a scallop shell. See Greek Mythology.
  • “a booming sound like that of the loud sea bittern”: The bittern, a marsh heron, is known for its deep, booming call. See Birds.
  • “these candle flames reflected in dark Venetian mirrors”: The mirror-makers of Murano, near Venice, held the secret of fine glass mirrors from the sixteenth century. See Mirrors and Reflections.
  • “the Hesperides like spirit messengers”: Hesperides in Greek mythology are nymphs of the evening. They guarded the golden apples at the western edge of the world. The skippers, a family of butterflies, are the Hesperiidae, named for them. See Butterflies and Moths.
  • “brimstone-colored butterflies”: The brimstone (Gonepteryx rhamni), a sulphur-yellow butterfly. Its butter color is one guess at the origin of the word “butterfly.”
  • “bejeweled butterflies as precious to him as the most precious jewels or mosaic emperors”: The emperors are butterflies too, among them the Purple Emperor (Apatura iris).
  • “more precious than the cuckoo singing as it flies”: Wordsworth’s “To the Cuckoo” (1807): “No bird, but an invisible thing, / A voice, a mystery.” See Romantic Poets and Birds.
  • “the griffins flying over the roof-tops”: The griffin, with an eagle’s head and wings and a lion’s body, guarded gold in Greek legend (Herodotus, Histories 3.116). See Greek Mythology.
  • “the imaginary sea bishops with mitre-shaped heads and vestments of silver scales”: The Sea Bishop, a fish-man in a bishop’s mitre, was said to have been caught off Poland in 1531. It is pictured in Conrad Gesner’s Historia animalium (1558). See Fairy Tales and Folklore.
  • “walking in the cool of the evening shade”: “They heard the voice of the Lord God walking in the garden in the cool of the day” (Genesis 3:8). See Genesis.
  • “the mermaids feeding their infants at their breasts”: Mermaids nursing their young. See Fairy Tales and Folklore.
  • “the milk-white unicorn enclosed by a picket fence”: The Unicorn in Captivity, the last of the Unicorn Tapestries (c. 1495-1505), shows the unicorn inside a round wooden fence. It hangs at The Cloisters in New York. See the Chapter 24 resources.
  • “as she had cared for things invisible made visible to her”: “For the invisible things of him from the creation of the world are clearly seen” (Romans 1:20). See The Bible.
  • “the wastrel wheels of chance, the games of loaded dice, the croupiers”: Roulette (“little wheel”), whose croupier spins it. See Gambling and Playing Cards, Fate and Chance, and Peron Spitzer.
  • “the harlequins, the painted ladies fluttering through the darkness”: Harlequin was the patched, masked trickster of the commedia dell’arte. The Painted Lady (Vanessa cardui) is a butterfly, and “painted lady” was also slang for a woman of the streets. Young lets both meanings fly at once. See Butterflies and Moths.
  • “a large correspondence with other meditative butterfly hunters”: The great collectors corresponded and traded specimens. Vladimir Nabokov, novelist and lepidopterist, worked on butterflies at Harvard’s Museum of Comparative Zoology (1942-48).
  • “the phenomenal world of the butterfly in all its illusive manifestations”: For Kant, the phenomenal world is the world as it appears to us, as against the thing in itself (Critique of Pure Reason, 1781). See Kant and Hegel and Illusion and Reality.
  • “the butterfly perching upon the flower had seemed as identical to the flower as twin to twin”: Zhuangzi (c. 300 BC) dreamed he was a butterfly, and woke to write: “Now I do not know whether I was then a man dreaming I was a butterfly, or whether I am now a butterfly, dreaming I am a man” (trans. Herbert Giles, 1889). See Taoism and Zhuangzi and Twins and Doubles.
  • “watching the amazed birth of a butterfly, the first tremblings of the feeble, dew-lit wings”: The emergence of the butterfly from the chrysalis is called eclosion. See Butterflies and Moths.

chapter-60:
Chapter 60

← Chapter 59 · Home · Chapter 61 →

Summary

Mr. Spitzer wonders whether he is really a musician or only a gambler like Peron, who read nothing but the sporting page, never went to a concert, and could never have imagined silence. A gambler would know how to call moose, and Mr. Spitzer remembers practicing moose calls on an empty city street at dusk until a great purple moose answered him through the fog; ever since, he has only whispered. A gambler would know duck calls too, and once, absent-minded in a windy avenue, Mr. Spitzer must have made one, for a flight of wild ducks came down and rushed past him, or through him, while he stood still like a lighthouse. He decides they were mandarin ducks blown far off course, exotic pilgrims to this shore. Their honking follows him for days or years, and he concludes that he need not write his elegy after all: the wild duck’s horn is his elegy.

Characters present

Joachim Spitzer · Peron Spitzer

Concepts present

Themes: Death and Mortality · Dreams and Imagination · Identity and the Self · Memory and the Past · Music, Sound, and Silence · Nature, the Sea, and the Cosmos

Symbols: Birds · Cards, Games, and Chance · Clothing, Hats, and Skirts · Horses and Carriages · Lamps, Candles, and Light · Moon and Stars · Music and Instruments · The Bus and the Journey · The Umbrella

Allusions: American Writers · Angels and Archangels · Astronomy · Gambling and Playing Cards · Greek Mythology · Music and Composers · Romantic Poets · The Bible

Key passages

From the research

  • The chapter opens with a profound reflection on whether the protagonist, Mr. Spitzer, is truly a musician or merely a gambler who has deluded himself into believing in a lost musical career. This internal conflict is central where he is haunted by the “germinal music in his head,” yet increasingly obsessed with gambling. The imagery of cards (ace of clubs, spots on dice) and horse races evokes a chaotic, chance-driven world contrasted with the ordered art of music. The passage poses the question of identity and authenticity and whether his essence is musical or rooted in worldly, mundane obsessions like gambling. This sets the tone for the chapter’s exploration of perception and self-delusion.
  • The chapter imagines the gambler Mr. Spitzer might have been, who is really Peron: a man who read only the sporting page, ignored international, financial, and high society news, and never attended a concert in his life. Measuring himself against that man, Mr. Spitzer tests whether his own music is real. The gambler’s ignorance of “the value of a sand dollar or a Boston dollar or an English pound sterling” sets the world of the track against the world of money and high culture.
  • There is a symbolic and surreal moment where Mr. Spitzer practices moose calls in the city at dusk, only to hear the answering call of an actual moose which is an extraordinary, almost hallucinatory experience. The moose’s antlers are described as “looming like tree boughs through the blowing purple fog,” blending natural imagery with urban and cosmic elements (traffic lights, the Pleiades). This encounter blurs the boundary between reality and imagination, the natural and the supernatural, highlighting Mr. Spitzer’s liminal state between sanity and hallucination, music and noise, life and death.
  • The climax of the chapter is the vision of the wild ducks flying overhead: exotic “beautiful Asiatics” with crested heads and golden eyes, described in luminous, almost otherworldly colors. Mr. Spitzer perceives their honking calls as a “wild sonata,” a natural music that becomes his elegy. The ducks’ flight is metaphorically linked to transcendence, migration, and perhaps the soul’s journey. He imagines himself metamorphosed into wings, a silent observer caught between earth and sky. The passage conveys a sense of awe, mystery, and the dissolution of boundaries between self and nature, music and silence, sound and chaos.
  • Near the end, the chapter suggests that Mr. Spitzer’s elegy (the music he cannot write or remember) may be embodied in the calls of the wild ducks. This is a powerful metaphor for artistic creation as something wild, natural, and perhaps uncontrollable, rather than composed or intellectual. The elegy is not just a lament but an acceptance of the wild, untamed forces that accompany him “through the long reaches of the silence.”

Questions and observations

Reading closely

  • Mr. Spitzer wonders whether he “had merely deceived himself by his pretensions to a lost musical career.” Why does he test himself against the gambler Peron?
  • “Sound shared the silence, but his dead brother could not have imagined the silence.” What does silence mean to Mr. Spitzer that it could not mean to Peron?
  • Young calls music “a path dividing sound from chaos.” How does the chapter’s own long first sentence find its way through chaos?

Characters

  • Peron never read “the obituary columns listing himself.” What does it mean to imagine a dead man who does not know he is dead?
  • After the moose answers, Mr. Spitzer “had only whispered for fear the great purple moose might be anywhere and answer.” What does this comic episode show about him?
  • Mr. Spitzer stands “like the burning of the lighthouse on the distant rock.” Who in his life has been the lighthouse, and who the birds?

Connections

  • The “great flutist who had caused the avalanche” returns from Chapters 58 and 59. Why does Young keep calling him back?
  • Mr. Spitzer hears “the starter’s music” again. How do horse racing and music twine together through the Spitzer chapters?
  • In Chapter 59 Mr. Spitzer could not finish his elegy; here “his elegy was this wild duck’s horn.” What has changed?

Reflection

  • The birds “have mistaken the lighthouse for the light, the reflection of a star.” What lights do people mistake for stars?
  • The wings roar “not so much past him as through him.” What would it mean for music to pass through a person rather than past?
  • Mr. Spitzer rebuilds the ducks from a few gleams, “even as a dead man might build the world.” How much of any memory is rebuilt this way?

Research: Characters

Mr. Spitzer

  • Torn between his identity as a musician and as a gambler, Mr. Spitzer experiences profound self-doubt and alienation.
  • His focus on gambling and his distracted thoughts reveal a fragmented psyche, obsessed with trivial and profound matters simultaneously.
  • Despite his urban surroundings, he has a deep affinity for natural sounds, which evoke powerful emotional and spiritual responses.
  • Memories of his dead twin brother and lost musical compositions haunt him, reflecting a sense of unfinished business and loss.
  • Mr. Spitzer embodies the human struggle to find meaning through art, memory, and connection, even when confronted with mortality and oblivion.

Peron Spitzer

  • Peron appears as the gambler Mr. Spitzer measures himself against: a man who read only the sporting page, never attended a concert in his life, and could not have imagined silence.
  • He would have known how to call moose and wild ducks, and would have recognized the ducks’ horns “even if he had been in his grave.”

Research: Themes

Identity and Self-Perception

See: Identity and the Self

  • Mr. Spitzer is uncertain about whether he is truly a musician or merely a gambler who has deceived himself.
  • His self-questioning reveals a deep internal conflict and a search for meaning in his life.
  • The duality of musician versus gambler serves as a metaphor for the struggle between art and chance, order and chaos.

Music and Sound as Metaphor

See: Music, Sound, and Silence

  • Music is portrayed as a transcendent, intellectual force that shapes reality and the imagination.
  • The “music of the world” and the “music of the track” symbolize different aspects of life, artistic creativity versus raw, primal existence.
  • Mr. Spitzer reflects on musical composition, the clef, bar, and rhythm as pathways dividing sound from chaos, highlighting sound as a spiritual and intellectual phenomenon.

Memory, Imagination, and the Unconscious

See: Dreams and Imagination · Memory and the Past

  • The text weaves memories, hallucinations, and dreams, blurring boundaries between past and present, real and imagined.
  • Mr. Spitzer’s recollections of his dead brother and the imagined music he never wrote suggest themes of loss, regret, and the elusive nature of artistic creation.

Nature and the Wild

See: Nature, the Sea, and the Cosmos

  • Calls of moose and wild ducks serve as recurring motifs, connecting Mr. Spitzer to the natural and primal world.
  • These animal calls symbolize communication beyond human language, evoking mystery and transcendence.
  • The vivid description of the wild ducks conveys a mystical beauty and the theme of otherworldly visitation.

Silence and Sound

See: Music, Sound, and Silence

  • Silence is portrayed as unimaginable to the dead brother, emphasizing the importance of sound as life and presence.
  • Sound and silence share a complex relationship, where sound moves “like the human spirit through heavens of imagined silence,” suggesting spiritual continuity beyond death.

Death and Transcendence

See: Death and Mortality

  • References to death, such as “the sleep of the dead,” “bones in an old bone-box,” and the leveling effect of death, permeate the text.
  • Mr. Spitzer’s experiences of hearing moose calls and wild duck honkings border on the supernatural, indicating a liminal state between life and death.

Research: Symbols and Imagery

The Ace of Clubs / Playing Cards

See: Cards, Games, and Chance

  • Symbolize chance, fate, and the gamble of life.
  • The falling ace and the spots on cards evoke the randomness and structure of existence.

The All Black Harpsichord and Instruments

See: Music and Instruments

  • Represent lost artistic potential and the melancholic beauty of forgotten music.
  • The “all black keys” and “viola da gamba” suggest a somber, elegiac tone.

Moose Calls and Antlers

See: Nature, the Sea, and the Cosmos

  • Symbolize primal communication and a connection to a wild, untamed world.
  • The moose’s antlers “looming like tree boughs” create a haunting, majestic image of nature’s power.

Wild Ducks

See: Birds

  • Represent migration, passage, and the ephemeral beauty of life.
  • Their “crested heads and veiled gold eyes” suggest exoticism and a mystical presence.
  • Their flight and honking are likened to a “wild sonata,” connecting nature with music.

Traffic and Cityscape

See: The Bus and the Journey

  • The contrast between natural sounds and the urban environment highlights the tension between civilization and nature.
  • The “old cars” and “traffic streams” serve as a backdrop to the surreal, almost supernatural events.

Stars and Heavens

See: Moon and Stars

  • Stars are symbolic of eternity, guidance, and mystery.
  • The merging of all stars into “one great star” suggests unity and transcendence beyond earthly existence.

Research: Resources

  • “the pedal note prolonged and crying above a choir”: A pedal note, or pedal point, is a long-held note, usually in the bass, sounding on while the harmonies above it change; on the organ it is played with the feet. See Music and Instruments.
  • “the ace of clubs falling like a swallow from his sleeve”: A card sharp hides an ace up his sleeve, the source of the phrase for a secret advantage. See Gambling and Playing Cards.
  • “seeing the cubistic dream player melt upon the trembling air”: Cubism shows an object from several viewpoints at once, broken into planes. The “cubistic dream player” is Mr. Spitzer seen the same way, a self of many disjointed parts that will not form one picture. See On the cubistic dream player.
    • The Cubist art movement, pioneered by Pablo Picasso and Georges Braque in the early 20th century, revolutionized art by rejecting traditional single-point perspective and instead depicting subjects from multiple viewpoints simultaneously. This approach resulted in paintings and sculptures that appear fragmented into abstract, geometric forms, emphasizing the flat, two-dimensional surface of the canvas. Notable women Cubist artists are:
    • Marie Laurencin: A French painter who met Georges Braque as a fellow student at the Académie Humbert and developed a distinct style with soft, pastel colors and graceful, flowing figures. Her work offered a lyrical and feminine counterpoint to the more traditional Cubist aesthetic.
    • María Blanchard: A Spanish painter who moved to Paris and became a significant figure in the Cubist movement. Despite being an important painter, she was often overlooked in historical accounts of the era, which were dominated by male artists.
    • Sonia Delaunay: While also known for her work in Orphism, Delaunay’s style was heavily influenced by Cubism and she was a key figure in the avant-garde.
    • Natalia Goncharova: A Russian avant-garde artist who, along with her partner Mikhail Larionov, was a founder of the Rayonist movement. Her work engaged with many modernist styles, including Cubism.
    • Lyubov Popova: A leading figure of the Russian avant-garde, Popova’s work moved through various phases of modernism, including Cubo-Futurism.
    • Aleksandra Exter: Studied art in Kiev and became a prominent avant-garde artist whose work became increasingly radical, mixing Cubist influences with other modernist ideas.
    • Mainie (Mary Harriet) Jellett (1897-1944): An Irish painter who studied with André Lhote and Albert Gleizes in Paris; her Decoration (1923) was among the first abstract paintings shown in Ireland.
    • The central idea of Cubism was to show objects as the mind comprehends them in their totality, rather than from a single, fixed viewpoint. This involved breaking down and reassembling objects into an abstract form to suggest their three-dimensional structure and their movement through time and space. Artists reduced figures and objects to fundamental geometric shapes such as cubes, spheres, and cones. This fragmentation of forms challenged traditional naturalistic representation. Cubists rejected the illusion of depth created by traditional perspective, instead highlighting the flatness of the canvas. Background and foreground often merge in their compositions. Cubism was significantly influenced by the late work of Post-Impressionist painter Paul Cézanne, who simplified nature into geometric forms, and by the abstract, stylized forms of African masks and Iberian sculpture.
    • Compare Paul Cézanne’s Card Players (1890s) and Pablo Picasso’s Card Player (winter 1913-14, Museum of Modern Art), in which the player and his cards break into flat, overlapping planes. See Gambling and Playing Cards.
  • “the wild fool, the solitary player playing on and on”: The joker, the fool of the deck, is often played wild; a card game for one is solitaire, or patience. See the joker in euchre in the Chapter 59 resources. See Cards, Games, and Chance.
  • “the starter’s music awakening him after so many years of sleep”: See the “Call to the Post” in the Chapter 59 resources.
  • “the value of a sand dollar”: A sand dollar is a flat, round sea urchin whose bleached skeleton washes up on beaches like a coin.
  • “golden shekels, talents, florins, drachmas”: The talent was the largest weight of money in the ancient world; in the parable, the servant who buried his one talent in the earth lost it (Matthew 25:14-30, KJV). The florin was first struck in gold in Florence in 1252. See The Bible.
  • “the writings of Boston music critics”: Boston’s critics were famous for severity: John Sullivan Dwight ran Dwight’s Journal of Music (1852-1881), and Philip Hale wrote the Boston Symphony’s program notes from 1901 to 1933.
  • “had never sat in a diamond horseshoe”: See the Diamond Horseshoe in the Chapter 48 resources.
  • “dresses of bone lace or bird-cages”: Bone lace is bobbin lace, worked on a pillow with bobbins once carved from bone. A bird-cage was the hooped steel crinoline of the 1850s and 1860s. See Clothing, Hats, and Skirts.
  • “whether they carry black umbrellas or white umbrellas”: See The Umbrella.
  • “that death which levels all”: “Sceptre and crown / Must tumble down, / And in the dust be equal made / With the poor crooked scythe and spade” (James Shirley, “Death the Leveller,” from The Contention of Ajax and Ulysses, 1659). See Horace’s pale Death in the Chapter 59 resources. See Death and Mortality.
  • “some poor old tramp who slept under the El”: The El is an elevated railway. New York’s Sixth Avenue El came down in 1939 and its Third Avenue El in 1955-56; Boston’s Washington Street Elevated ran from 1901 to 1987, a date after 1964.
  • “whistle like Mozart in the silent hours”: See Mozart in the Chapter 55 resources. At fourteen Mozart heard Allegri’s Miserere in the Sistine Chapel and wrote it out from memory (1770). See Music and Composers.
  • “Why should he think he was an authority on the harpsichord?”: The harpsichord plucks its strings with quills rather than striking them with hammers like the piano. See Music and Instruments.
  • “He would have known more about calling moose”:
    • Hunters called moose with a horn of rolled birch bark. In Thoreau’s “Chesuncook” (The Maine Woods, 1864), the Penobscot guide Joe Aitteon “imitated the call of the moose,—ugh-ugh-ugh, or oo-oo-oo-oo.” See American Writers.
    • A bull moose’s antlers can spread five or six feet, wider than Young’s “four-foot spread.”
  • “causing the northern light beams to rustle”: People of the far North have long said the aurora rustles or crackles. Finnish researchers led by Unto Laine recorded such sounds in 2012 (after 1964). See Nature, the Sea, and the Cosmos.
  • “the dim clusters of the Pleiades”: The Pleiades, the Seven Sisters, are a star cluster in Taurus; “Canst thou bind the sweet influences of Pleiades, or loose the bands of Orion?” (Job 38:31, KJV). See Astronomy and Greek Mythology.
  • “sound being an intellectual thing”: Compare William Blake: “For a Tear is an Intellectual Thing” (“The Grey Monk,” c. 1803, and Jerusalem). See Romantic Poets.
  • “the great gold-eyed snow owl”: The snowy owl of the Arctic has yellow eyes; in some winters snowy owls come south in numbers to fields, shores, and airports. See Birds.
  • “old owl car bumping down the dusk”: An owl car was a streetcar that ran through the night; late-night transit is still called owl service.
  • “passing the horse fountains”: Between 1902 and 1915 Hermon Lee Ensign’s National Humane Alliance gave about 125 granite watering troughs to American cities, for horses, dogs, cats, and people. See Horses and Carriages.
  • “that great flutist who had caused the avalanche”: The “great flutist who had caused the avalanche” may refer to the god Kokopelli. Kokopelli is the humpbacked flute player of the rock art of the American Southwest, a bringer of fertility and rain. See On Kokopelli. See also Amphion in the Chapter 58 resources.
  • “the all black harpsichord with the all black keys”: Many old harpsichords reverse the piano’s colors, with black natural keys and white sharps; Young’s is black throughout. See Chopin’s “Black Key” Étude in the Chapter 58 resources. See Music and Instruments.
  • “the viola da gamba”: The viola da gamba, or viol, is the “viol for the leg,” held between the knees and bowed underhand. It has frets and usually six strings. The viols are a separate family from the violins; they flourished in the Renaissance and Baroque and were revived in the twentieth century. See On the viola da gamba and Music and Instruments.
  • “lute with an angel’s head as screw”: Old viols and lutes often end in a carved head in place of a scroll, a lion, a woman, or an angel.
    • A “lute with an angel’s head” is not a specific type of musical instrument. Angels, cherubs, and putti playing the lute are also a common motif in Renaissance and Baroque art.
  • “tortoise-shell violin”: In the Homeric Hymn to Hermes, the newborn god makes the first lyre from a tortoise shell, stretching strings of sheep gut across it. See Greek Mythology and Music and Instruments.
  • “the polysyllabic horns of the wild ducks”: Young’s “polysyllabic horns” are the ducks’ calls of many syllables, which hunters imitate with wooden duck calls. See Birds.
  • “like an unfinished fugue running through his mind”: A “fugue” has two main meanings: a complex musical composition where a theme is repeated and interwoven by multiple voices, and a temporary mental state of amnesia and wandering, often associated with dissociative disorders. Musically, it involves a single theme being introduced by one voice and then imitated by others in a structured, imitative style. Psychologically, a dissociative fugue is a condition where an individual forgets their past and may travel, only to have no memory of the period later. Bach’s Art of Fugue breaks off in its last fugue; he died in 1750 before finishing it. See On fugue and Music and Composers.
  • “for he had forgotten many fugues”: Lethe is both a river in the Greek underworld and the personification of forgetfulness and oblivion. Souls who drank from the River Lethe would forget their past lives, and this concept of forgetfulness is used in a broader, metaphorical sense as well. See On the River Lethe and Greek Mythology.
  • “many antiphonies”: “Antiphonies” are a type of responsive singing or music between two groups, creating a “call and response” effect. The term can also refer to a verse sung before and after a psalm or hymn, often used in religious services. See On antiphonies and Music and Composers.
  • “many winding horns”: “Winding horns” are a type of wind instrument, historically made from animal horns or metal, used for signaling over long distances in activities like hunting, battle, and ceremonies. Also known as blowing horns or war horns, they produce a single note, and different meanings are conveyed through rhythms and speed. See Music and Instruments.
  • “the old Locomobile, circa 1912”: Locomobile, circa 1912 may refer to the Locomobile Company of America which was one of the earliest manufacturers of cars before the assembly line.
    • The Locomobile Company of America made steam cars from 1899, then luxury gasoline cars; its racer “Old 16” won the Vanderbilt Cup in 1908.
  • “skipped a beat like a trip hammer”: A trip hammer is a heavy power hammer lifted by a cam and dropped again and again, used in forges and mills.
  • “almost angelic wings”: Compare the cherubim of Solomon’s temple: “the wing of the one touched the one wall, and the wing of the other cherub touched the other wall; and their wings touched one another in the midst of the house” (1 Kings 6:27, KJV). See Angels and Archangels and The Bible.
  • “a flight of mandarins driven by non-adventitious winds far off their usual course”: The mandarin duck of East Asia is the most brilliantly colored of ducks, the drake crested and with orange “sails” on his back. In China a pair of mandarin ducks stands for faithful married love. See Birds.
  • “the dappled light cast by a dying dolphin”: See Byron’s dying dolphin in the Chapter 56 resources. See Romantic Poets.
  • “those poor birds of passage who, with their eyes blinded by the light”: Lighthouse keepers reported hundreds of migrating birds killed against the lantern in a single foggy night; the light draws night migrants, above all in fog. See Birds and Lamps, Candles, and Light.
  • “exotic Pilgrims to this shore”: The “exotic Pilgrims” are the mandarin ducks, the “beautiful Asiatics” with gold-tipped wings, travelers from far lands arriving like pilgrims on a strange shore.
    • The capital P recalls the Pilgrims who landed at Plymouth in 1620, and the chapter’s Boston dollars and Boston critics point toward New England.
  • “his elegy was this wild duck’s horn”: Compare Henrik Ibsen’s The Wild Duck (1884), whose wounded duck, kept in a garret, comes to stand for lives sustained by illusion.

Vocabulary

Happening by chance; not essential or built in.

Singing or playing in alternation between two groups, as of a divided choir.
Basso profundo
The deepest bass voice.
Bone lace
Bobbin lace, made with bobbins once carved from bone.
Clef
A sign at the start of a staff fixing the pitch of the notes.
Drachma
A silver coin of ancient Greece.
Elegiac
Mournful, like an elegy, a poem of lament for the dead.
Elegy
A poem or song of mourning.

A fine thread or fiber.
Florin
A gold coin first struck in Florence in 1252; later a British two-shilling piece.
Foghorn
A deep horn sounded to warn ships in fog.
Fugue
A composition in which one theme is taken up in turn by several voices; also a flight from one’s own identity.

A keyboard instrument, ancestor of the piano, whose strings are plucked rather than struck.

Hieroglyphics
