  • The chapter opens with a complex metaphorical description of mystery, time, and identity. Mr. Spitzer reflects on the suffragette’s lost love and her elusive, shadowy identity, “No name, no face told him her identity in cloud fusions as none told him who he was now.” This sets the tone of searching for meaning in a life shrouded in ambiguity.
  • Mr. Spitzer sees himself as connected to her through shared duplicity and duality, unable to condemn her without condemning himself. He describes himself as “one already dead in the midst of life” and the “locksmith in a street of dreams where there was neither key nor lock.” This reflects the theme of lost identity and the search for self in a confusing world.
  • Cousin Hannah is portrayed as a figure who chased a lost love, symbolized by the lost skirt on a mountain peak, a metaphor for incomplete or thwarted love: “the old suffragette had returned without her love who had gone to retrieve her skirt, surely no dog would ever find.” This image resonates through the chapter as a motif of longing and unattainable fulfillment.
  • Mr. Spitzer’s research reveals her as a woman of many paradoxes and adventures: a mountain climber, balloonist, flyer, traveler through deserts and Holy Lands, who lived beyond time and space: “She had gone to Holy Lands as to Death’s seraglio guarded by eunuchs black and white where were locked so many beautiful girls with their faces veiled.” Her life is portrayed as almost mythical, full of contradictions and mysteries.
  • The chapter meditates on the nature of time, memory, and existence. Cousin Hannah’s life is described as one without clear chronology, “with little relationship to chronology, for hers were the chronologies of all dead loves, lost loves, doomed efforts.” This connects to the idea that love, life, and death are intertwined in a timeless dance.
  • Mr. Spitzer’s physical search through her estate, opening trunks, examining keys, finding wedding gowns, veils, and other artifacts, symbolizes an attempt to unlock the mysteries of her life and, metaphorically, the mysteries of love and existence itself. The trunks with “hinges sealed by rust, the lids which had been seemingly soldered by great flames,” and the abundance of bridal gowns and veils suggest the elusive and fragile nature of identity and memory.
  • Mr. Spitzer questions not only her identity but his own, reflecting on the blurred lines between reality and illusion, living and dead: “He questioned who he was as he questioned who she was, and doubtless this would always be the case.” This highlights the existential uncertainty permeating the chapter.
  • The suffragette is likened to a bride who has hidden away or been lost, a figure of unfulfilled destiny and love: Perhaps “she had abandoned the bridegroom at the church door.” This symbolizes the elusiveness of love and the human condition of searching for something lost or unattainable.
  • There is a recurring tension between what is real and unreal, the dream and reality, memory and oblivion. Mr. Spitzer reflects that “Perhaps the unreal and the real were one—or there was only this mask of the stars, and there was no face behind the stars.” This blurring of boundaries questions the nature of existence itself.
  • The chapter closes with a meditation on the limits of language and knowledge: “He was not certain of the book’s title now when all writing had faded… no language contained truth, for the truth was that which could not be expressed.” This encapsulates the chapter’s theme of the ineffability of the greatest mysteries of life and love.

Questions and observations

Reading closely

  • “Should doubt move mountains which faith had not moved, or should doubt be joined with faith when the mountains moved?” What does Mr. Spitzer come to believe, and when?
  • “Yes, there was an external world, he knew now as it departed.” Why does he believe in her adventures only after her death?
  • “There was always one lid more than there was a key, one key more than there was a lid.” What does the leftover key or lid stand for?

Characters

  • Mr. Spitzer leaves the wedding gowns out of his inventory. What does that choice say about him as a lawyer and as a mourner?
  • “She reminded him of his duplicity and his duality so that he could not condemn her unless he condemned himself.” How does Cousin Hannah mirror Mr. Spitzer and his dead twin?
  • Cousin Hannah preached against marriage and urged ladies to “divest themselves of excess luggage,” yet she kept forty trunks of bridal gowns. Was she the bride or the bridegroom, and does it matter?

Connections

  • The Swiss drew up a bill of claims against her for the League of Nations. How does Young turn one woman’s freedom into a threat to a nation’s mountains?
  • She chained herself to a lamp-post to protest “that woman was a chattel, a thing, a possession, a mere skirt.” How do coverture and the vote shape her story and her secret?
  • Why might Young end the chapter with Eloise and Abelard, Tristram and the white Yseult, “lovers never mated”?

Reflection

  • “How much more successful she had been in her failure than if only one door had opened to her knock.” Can failure leave a life larger than success?
  • “No language contained truth, for the truth was that which could not be expressed.” Is there truth beyond words?
  • He was “her only mourner among men—and he was mourning for himself.” Is all mourning partly for oneself?

Research: Characters

Mr. Spitzer

  • A reflective, almost spectral figure, the investigator of the old suffragette’s estate. He embodies duality and duplicity, often questioning his own identity and existence, blurring lines between life and death, reality and dream. His role is to manage and close the estate of the old suffragette, but his journey is deeply philosophical and metaphysical.

Cousin Hannah

  • A mysterious woman shrouded in symbolism; she is a traveler, a rebel, and a figure of lost love and elusive identity. Known for her suffrage activism, she is also depicted as a wanderer through physical and metaphysical realms of mountains, deserts, and clouds. She carries the paradox of being both bride and bridegroom, representing the complex intersections of gender, love, and death.

Peron Spitzer

  • Mr. Spitzer’s dead twin is present in every list he makes, for he is “mindful always that he was two persons, himself and his dead brother, and that what appeared in one column should appear in the other.” His greatest fear is “that there might be no differing counterpart.”

Catherine Cartwheel

  • Recalled as “the opium lady” who entertains only imaginary guests, when Mr. Spitzer finds a golden teapot circled by twelve tiny golden cups as if Cousin Hannah had been entertaining someone.

Research: Themes

Mystery and Identity

See: Identity and the Self

  • The chapter is permeated with questions of identity, both Mr. Spitzer’s and the suffragette’s. Mr. Spitzer struggles to know who he is or whether he is a ghostly twin. The suffragette’s identity remains veiled, indicated by symbols like veils, masks, and cloud fusions.

Love and Loss

See: Love · Grief, Loss, and Mourning

  • Central to the narrative is the motif of lost love, symbolized by the suffragette’s lost skirt and her search for love that may never be found or may be forever elusive. Love is portrayed as inseparable from death, an eternal quest that transcends time.

Life, Death, and the Afterlife

See: Death and Mortality

  • The chapter explores the boundaries between life and death, suggesting that death may multiply uncertainties and dissolve distinctions, such as gender roles and personal identities. Death is not an end but a continuation or transformation, with echoes of the past and shadows of lost loves lingering.

Time and Timelessness

See: Time

  • Time is fluid and ambiguous; events are reported out of chronological order, and the notion of “when” is elusive. The suffragette’s life and death exist in a timeless realm where beginnings and ends blur.

The External and Internal Worlds

See: Illusion and Reality

  • The suffragette’s adventures traverse both external landscapes (mountains, deserts, clouds) and internal, psychological realms. Reality and dream intertwine, with the external world mirroring internal emotional and spiritual states.

The Search and the Unattainable

See: The Search for Meaning · Keys, Doors, and Locks

  • Mr. Spitzer’s search through the suffragette’s estate, her memories, and her secrets is a metaphor for the human quest for meaning, often futile and always incomplete. The imagery of keys, trunks, and locked doors symbolizes mysteries that cannot be fully unlocked.

Women, Gender, and Marriage

See: Women, Gender, and Marriage · Women’s Suffrage

  • Cousin Hannah fought “for the overthrow of man” and urged all ladies to “divest themselves of excess luggage,” yet her forty trunks hold only wedding gowns. Mr. Spitzer cannot tell whether she dreamed of being the bridegroom or the bride, and he decides the world need not know.

Research: Symbols and Imagery

Clouds and Snow

See: Clouds and Storms · Snow, Ice, and Winter

  • Represent mystery, concealment, and transformation. They are often described as moving, shifting, and obscuring identity and reality.

Skirts and Veils

See: Clothing, Hats, and Skirts · Weddings and Funerals

  • The suffragette’s lost skirt embroidered with forget-me-nots symbolizes lost love and identity. Veils and skirts also signify the blurred boundaries of gender and self.

Keys, Locks, and Trunks

See: Keys, Doors, and Locks

  • These represent the attempt to unlock secrets, memories, and truths. Mr. Spitzer’s fumbling with keys and trunks underscores the impossibility of fully understanding or revealing the suffragette’s life.

Stars, Moons, and Celestial Bodies

See: Moon and Stars

  • Used to depict guidance, mystery, the unreachable, and the eternal. The moon, often mirrored or sunken, symbolizes reflection and illusion.

Birds and Butterflies

See: Birds · Butterflies and Moths

  • Symbols of transformation, fleeting beauty, and the soul’s journey. The butterfly sailing out of the ear (a door) suggests escape or transcendence.

Music and Silence

See: Music, Sound, and Silence

  • Music represents life’s rhythm, emotion, and unspoken realities; silence and muteness indicate death, absence, or the ineffable.

Mountains

See: Mountains

  • Her mountains move, skip like rams, turn into clouds, and change with every climber: “Never were both the unchanging mountain and the unchanging mountain-climber.” They are her lost love’s grave and the stage of her legend.

Research: Resources

  • “Perhaps she should be the husband and not the bride”: The woman might take the role traditionally assigned to the husband. Death, which offers “no firm foundation stone or unchanging lintel,” unsettles fixed roles, including those of gender, so that husband and bride, beginning and end, life and death become unstable, and the woman may take on strength, authority, and active agency in the face of life’s precariousness.
  • “that old jack of all trades who was the master of none”: The saying “Jack of all trades, master of none” grew from older forms; in 1592 Robert Greene sneered at the young Shakespeare as a Johannes factotum, a Jack of all trades. See Shakespeare.
  • “those feathered goose barnacles”: Medieval naturalists believed that the barnacle goose hatched from the goose barnacle, a stalked shellfish that clings to driftwood, because no one had seen the geese nest; they breed in the Arctic. Gerald of Wales described the birds hanging from timber by their beaks in his Topographia Hibernica (1188), and John Gerard pictured geese dropping from a barnacle tree in his Herball (1597).
  • “Should doubt move mountains which faith had not moved”: Mr. Spitzer inverts the saying that faith can move mountains: “If ye have faith as a grain of mustard seed, ye shall say unto this mountain, Remove hence to yonder place; and it shall remove; and nothing shall be impossible unto you” (Matthew 17:20). The suffragette’s search for a lost skirt, which leads to the death of her lover, suggests the absurdity of human pursuits, as in existentialist thought. She cries “Long live woman! Vive la femme! Viva la donna!” in many languages, “perhaps even in Sanskrit which was the language written upon a silent snowflake,” yet there are “secret languages never to be translated into words.” Her decision to dress as a man asserts her freedom against social norms, and her practical clothing against the other climbers’ finery sets materialism against idealism. The footman cutting a golden stairway from a frozen lake to the mountains of the moon may recall the ascent from Plato’s cave toward the light, and her climbing the Transcendentalist journey beyond the material world. See Plato and Platonism.
  • “like the sea giving up its dead”: “And the sea gave up the dead which were in it; and death and hell delivered up the dead which were in them: and they were judged every man according to their works” (Revelation 20:13, KJV). See Revelation and the Apocalypse.
  • “the rescuer, might be the rescued”: Mr. Spitzer, so often the protector, confronts the possibility that he himself needs saving. His near-turning “to her” shows a yearning for connection beneath his reserve and sense of duty.
    • This mimics the damsel in distress trope in which one or more men must rescue a woman who has either been kidnapped or placed in general peril. Kinship, love, or lust gives the male protagonist the motivation or compulsion to initiate the narrative. The female character herself may be competent, but still finds herself in this type of situation. The helplessness of these fictional females is linked to views outside of fiction that women as a group need to be taken care of by men. What changes through history is the attacker, not the damsel: in popular media the attacker’s role goes to whichever group best meets a culture’s collective fears. This trope does not necessarily involve the male protagonist getting the female as a reward, but may be combined with other tropes where the female character becomes the male character’s reward at the end of the story. (Wikipedia)
  • “the greatest St. Bernard who ever lived”: Barry (1800-1814), the most famous of the rescue dogs kept by the Augustinian canons of the Great St. Bernard Hospice in the Swiss Alps, is said to have helped rescue forty people, and the canons and their dogs saved more than two thousand travellers over two centuries. His mounted body is in the Natural History Museum of Bern, which notes that the stories of his carrying a child on his back and of his death at the hands of a soldier who took him for a wolf are legends (Natural History Museum of Bern, “Barry”). Later Cousin Hannah sleeps in shepherds’ huts with “an old St. Bernard sleeping at her feet, a Red Cross dog who had not retrieved her”; the Red Cross was founded in Geneva in 1863.
  • “It was a white skirt embroidered with forget-me-nots”: Forget-me-nots are charming, low-growing plants, known for their small, delicate blue flowers with yellow or white eyes. They typically bloom in the spring and are often found in gardens and natural settings. Forget-me-nots are widely associated with true love, remembrance, and enduring friendship. They are often given as gifts or used in remembrance ceremonies. The name “forget-me-not” is derived from a German legend about a knight who, while picking the flowers for his beloved, fell into a river and drowned, tossing the flowers to her with the cry “Vergiss mich nicht!” (Forget me not).
    • Young told Studs Terkel that she found the skirt in “the history of British mountain climbing”: one of the original bloomer girls and her companion climbed an Alpine peak to shout “Vive la femme,” took off their skirts at the top where no one could see them, and on the way down the younger, “the acolyte as I call her,” went back for the skirt she had left on the other side of the peak and never returned. Cousin Hannah “is haunted all her life by the ghostly rustle of the skirt” (Marguerite Young, interview with Studs Terkel, WFMT radio, 1965). In the novel the girl is her “apostle.” In 1858 Julia Archibald Holmes, a suffragist, climbed Pikes Peak in Colorado in a bloomer costume, the first recorded ascent by a woman. See Women’s Suffrage.
  • “All might have been imaginary in this life as in this death”: This relates to philosophical discussions about the nature of reality, perception, and the extent to which experience is shaped by the mind. The search through the suffragette’s belongings is a search for truth and understanding, but the paragraph suggests that this search may be futile. “Surely her entire life could not have been a game of hide-and-seek, for although she was hiding—who was seeking for her?” This touches on the philosophical problem of epistemology, or how anyone can know what is true, and whether objective truth is even attainable. Mr. Spitzer reflects on the suffragette’s death and its meaning. He wonders if death might be a “miracle,” and questions whether she has found her love in death. This aligns with philosophical inquiries into the nature of death, the possibility of an afterlife, and the meaning of existence in the face of mortality. The paragraph suggests that time may not be linear or objective, but rather a subjective experience. “All might have been an indeterminate moment or one beyond this calendar of days, hours, years. And what calendar was ever kept in the long night?” This idea relates to philosophical discussions about the nature of time, its relationship to consciousness, and whether time is an objective reality or a human construct. The paragraph also presents love as a paradox, questioning whether it can ever be fully realized or understood. It is filled with dualities and opposing forces: life and death, reality and imagination, love and loss, male and female. This relates to philosophical concepts of duality, dialectics, and the idea that reality is composed of opposing forces that are constantly interacting. It questions the value of individual experience and the search for meaning. This aligns with philosophical discussions about existentialism, individualism, and the search for meaning in a seemingly absurd world.
  • “the water hen which was the Pleiades”: The Pleiades, or Seven Sisters, are a cluster of stars in the constellation Taurus. Many old European names picture them as a hen with her chicks: the Vikings called them Freyja’s hens, and the old Hungarian name Fiastyúk means “a hen with chicks.” (Wikipedia) See Astronomy.
  • “had thought of satyrs and garlanded fawns”: Satyrs in Greek mythology are male nature spirits, companions of Dionysus, with the ears and tail of a horse or goat; the Roman fauns, half goat, followed the god Faunus. Both stand for unbridled desire, which may be why Mr. Spitzer feels disloyal thinking of them in the house of the suffragette. See Greek Mythology.
  • “some who were the beardless boys”: Many young people served as soldiers in the Civil War, with estimates suggesting that around 10% of Union soldiers were under 18. Some were as young as 10 years old, and many served as musicians, messengers, or even in combat roles. While the official minimum enlistment age was 18, many boys lied about their age to join the military, and some were even encouraged by recruiters. William Black: At age 12, he was wounded in battle, making him the youngest known wounded soldier, according to Nashville.gov. Johnny Clem: He joined the Union Army at age 10 and became a drummer boy. Johnny Cook: He was 15 when he volunteered as a cannoneer at the Battle of Antietam and received the Medal of Honor for his bravery, according to the National Park Service. Young soldiers faced the same dangers and hardships as older soldiers, including combat, disease, and imprisonment. See The Civil War.
  • “the great weaver weaving upon this loom”: Weaving is used as a metaphor in many cultures for understanding the workings of the universe and a person’s place in it. Through the physical process of weaving, people have tried to explain or gain a better understanding of this world and how human beings are woven into it. See the weaving goddesses in the Chapter 28 resources.
  • “like the infant Moses sleeping in his little boat among the reeds”: “And when she could not longer hide him, she took for him an ark of bulrushes, and daubed it with slime and with pitch, and put the child therein; and she laid it in the flags by the river’s brink” (Exodus 2:3, KJV). Pharaoh had ordered every Hebrew son cast into the river (Exodus 1:22), and three women, his mother, his sister, and Pharaoh’s daughter, saved him. See The Bible.
  • “I might fish up a minor prophet”: The twelve Minor Prophets of the Bible, Hosea through Malachi, are called minor for the shortness of their books, not their importance. Their message is judgment and salvation, social justice and the treatment of the poor, and concern for divine judgment in the future. One of them was fished up indeed: “And the LORD spake unto the fish, and it vomited out Jonah upon the dry land” (Jonah 2:10, KJV). See The Bible.
  • “His faith came at that moment which should have most justified his lack of faith”: This paragraph uses the figure of Mr. Spitzer, a lawyer and musician, to explore the fragile boundary between faith and doubt, reality and illusion, life and death. His faith, unexpectedly strengthened by loss, parallels the fate of his music: unheard, incomplete, and destined to fade. The woman’s life and identity are similarly elusive, caught in endless cycles and transformations like the horses on a carousel or the turns of a planetary wheel. The paragraph reflects on how truth often comes too late, and how identity, art, and existence are marked by impermanence and mystery.
  • “pivoted on nothingness like the dancer over the abyss”: Zarathustra tells the crowd, “Man is a rope stretched between the animal and the Superman—a rope over an abyss,” and a tightrope walker falls to his death before them (Friedrich Nietzsche, Thus Spake Zarathustra, Prologue 4, trans. Thomas Common, 1909). See Nietzsche.
  • “the experiments of Marconi”: Guglielmo Marconi was an Italian inventor and electrical engineer, known for his creation of a practical radio wave-based wireless telegraph system. On 12 December 1901 he received the first transatlantic wireless signal, the letter S in Morse code, at St. John’s, Newfoundland, sent from Poldhu in Cornwall.
  • “like the breasts of pigeons, perhaps those who were already extinct”: The passenger pigeon, once the most numerous bird in North America, was hunted to extinction; the last one, Martha, died at the Cincinnati Zoo on 1 September 1914. See Martha the Passenger Pigeon.
  • “the snows as old as the kingdom of Charlemagne”: Charlemagne was a ruler who united the majority of western and central Europe. He was crowned emperor in Rome on Christmas Day, 800.
  • “Who heard the knock of her dead heart?”: “Behold, I stand at the door, and knock: if any man hear my voice, and open the door, I will come in to him, and will sup with him, and he with me” (Revelation 3:20, KJV). Here the knock comes from within, and no one opens. See Revelation and the Apocalypse.
  • “in an old Ford”: The Ford Motor Company is an American multinational automobile manufacturer. Henry Ford’s Model T (1908-1927) put America on wheels; more than fifteen million were sold.
  • “in cloud cuckoo lands”: In Aristophanes’ comedy The Birds (414 BC), two Athenians persuade the birds to build Nephelokokkygia, Cloud-Cuckoo-Land, a city in the air between gods and men. The name now means any absurd dream world.
  • “Mr. Spitzer had trembled like a gambler”: The opening lines immediately establish a world governed by chance. Mr. Spitzer trembling “like a gambler” suggests a life where outcomes are unpredictable and determined by forces beyond individual control. This aligns with existentialist themes of the absurdity of existence and the lack of inherent meaning. The “faceless card” and “star of no known number” symbolize the limits of human knowledge. No one can fully grasp the forces shaping a life, and there will always be elements of the unknown. This resonates with the existentialist emphasis on the limits of reason. The line “Yes, there was an external world, he knew now as it departed” is crucial. It indicates a loss of faith in an objective reality. The world is not fixed but is constantly slipping away, emphasizing the subjective experience. “He gave his belief when there was no reason for his belief” highlights a rejection of rationalism. Spitzer’s faith is not based on evidence or logic but on something deeper, perhaps a Kierkegaardian “leap of faith” into the absurd. “For he reserved his credulity for the grand occasions eliciting the skepticism of others. Their skepticism was his faith” is a complex statement. It suggests that Spitzer finds meaning in what others reject. This could be interpreted as a form of contrarianism, or as a deeper understanding that truth often lies in challenging conventional wisdom. See Existentialism and Gambling and Playing Cards.
  • “a foot lover might have loved her”: Podophilia, also known as foot fetishism, is a sexual interest or attraction to feet. It is considered a type of paraphilia, where the focus of sexual arousal is on a specific body part or object. While it’s a common form of fetish, it’s only considered a paraphilic disorder if it causes significant distress or impairment in a person’s life.
  • “she could not have worn her heart upon her sleeve”: Iago says in Shakespeare’s Othello, “But I will wear my heart upon my sleeve / For daws to peck at” (1.1). See Shakespeare.
  • “But where was Jill who came tumbling after?”: The nursery rhyme was first printed about 1765 in Mother Goose’s Melody: “Jack and Gill / Went up the Hill, / To fetch a Pail of Water; / Jack fell down / And broke his Crown, / And Gill came tumbling after.” Cousin Hannah is Jack, and no Jill follows.
  • “the white bull garlanded with white flowers”: Zeus took the form of a snow-white bull to carry off Europa, who hung garlands of flowers on his horns before she climbed onto his back (Ovid, Metamorphoses 2). Bulls were also led to the altar garlanded for sacrifice. See Greek Mythology.
  • “a thieving robin redbreast such as accompanies lone travellers”: The robin redbreast of this line is the European robin, which follows gardeners and travellers for the insects they turn up; the American robin is a larger thrush named after it. A children’s poem and a legend explain that the robin’s breast was reddened by fanning the fire to keep the infant Jesus warm in the manger. In the old ballad The Children in the Wood (1595), robins cover the two lost children with leaves when they die in the forest. Many cultures have different meanings for robins, from death to the coming of spring to messengers of the spirits. See Fairy Tales and Folklore.
  • “She had challenged a prime minister to a duel”: Young took the duel from life. She told Studs Terkel that the lawyer Charles Studin, a founder of the NAACP, knew a suffragist “battle axe who spent her entire life fighting against men. She challenged a British prime minister to a duel and the prime minister refused to bear arms against the lady” (Marguerite Young, interview with Studs Terkel, WFMT radio, 1965). No record of the duel itself has turned up. The best-known duel between women is the “petticoat duel” said to have been fought in Hyde Park in 1792 between Lady Almeria Braddock and Mrs. Elphinstone, after Mrs. Elphinstone remarked on Lady Braddock’s age: both missed with pistols, and Lady Braddock wounded Mrs. Elphinstone’s arm with a sword. The story rests on later retellings and may be fiction. Real confrontations with prime ministers were common. In October 1908 fourteen suffragettes were thrown out of a bazaar in Islington for interrupting H. H. Asquith, and Margaret Haig Thomas, later Viscountess Rhondda, was attacked by a crowd after trying to stop the prime minister’s car. She went to prison and hunger struck after trying to set fire to a postbox, and in 1922 she petitioned to take her late father’s seat in the House of Lords; the Committee for Privileges first accepted her claim, then, with its membership changed, rejected it (Viscountess Rhondda’s Claim, [1922] 2 AC 339). Women entered the Lords only in 1958, with life peerages, and hereditary peeresses in 1963.
  • “She had slept among Laplanders”: “Laplander” is an outdated and sometimes considered offensive term for the Sami people, an indigenous group inhabiting the Arctic region of Sápmi, which includes parts of Norway, Sweden, Finland, and Russia. While “Laplander” was historically used to refer to people from the region of Lapland, it’s now more respectful to use the term Sami or the endonym their specific language group uses, such as Northern Sámi. See Exploration and the Poles.
  • “climb these Boston mountains”: There are no mountains in Boston; the Boston Mountains are in Arkansas. Boston itself was first called Trimountaine for the three peaks of Beacon Hill, which were cut down in the late eighteenth and early nineteenth centuries to fill the marshes. Tremont Street keeps the name.
  • “She had chained herself to a lamp-post”: Chaining was a signature suffrage protest. In January 1908 Edith New and Olivia Smith chained themselves to the railings of 10 Downing Street and shouted “Votes for Women!” so that Flora Drummond and Mary Macarthur could slip inside. On 28 October 1908 Muriel Matters and Helen Fox of the Women’s Freedom League chained themselves to the grille of the Ladies’ Gallery in the House of Commons, and the section of grille had to be removed with them still attached. Young’s source, Charles Studin’s suffragist, “chained herself to a lamppost in front of the White House” (Marguerite Young, interview with Studs Terkel, WFMT radio, 1965). Chaining herself to a lamp post, she makes herself a public fixture, visible and accountable, a woman who takes control of her fate even while bound by it. See Women’s Suffrage.
  • “a gerrymandered ward shaped like a salamander”: The word gerrymander comes from a Massachusetts district drawn in 1812 under Governor Elbridge Gerry, which a cartoon in the Boston Gazette pictured as a salamander.
    • Gerrymandering, defined in the contexts of representative electoral systems, is the political manipulation of electoral district boundaries to advantage a party, group, or socioeconomic class within the constituency. The manipulation may involve “cracking” (diluting the voting power of the opposing party’s supporters across many districts) or “packing” (concentrating the opposing party’s voting power in one district to reduce their voting power in other districts). Gerrymandering can also be used to protect incumbents. Wayne Dawkins, a professor at Morgan State University, describes it as politicians picking their voters instead of voters picking their politicians. The word comes from Elbridge Gerry, governor of Massachusetts and later Vice President, who in 1812 signed a bill creating a partisan district in the Boston area; the Boston Gazette compared its shape to a salamander and called it the Gerry-mander. The term has negative connotations, and gerrymandering is almost always considered a corruption of the democratic process. (Wikipedia)
  • “that woman was a chattel, a thing, a possession”: This reflects the brutal reality and social critique regarding the status of women, particularly in the context of marriage and society during the period depicted. To call a woman a “chattel” means to reduce her to the status of personal property or something owned by her husband or father, rather than a person with autonomy and rights.
    • Coverture was a legal doctrine in common law systems where a married woman’s legal existence was subsumed into that of her husband’s, essentially making her a legal non-entity. Under coverture, a married woman (feme covert) had no independent legal rights, meaning she couldn’t own property, enter into contracts, sue or be sued, or control her own earnings. This concept, rooted in the idea that husband and wife were one legal entity, with the husband as that entity, has significantly shaped legal and social landscapes, particularly for women. William Blackstone put it plainly in his Commentaries on the Laws of England (1765): “By marriage, the husband and wife are one person in law: that is, the very being or legal existence of the woman is suspended during the marriage.” This concept formed the core of coverture, asserting that husband and wife were a single legal entity, with the husband as the representative. Coverture has roots in feudal Norman customs and English common law. It was a fundamental aspect of the legal system in early America, shaping social and legal norms. Coverture influenced not only legal practices but also societal expectations and gender roles. As the women’s rights movement gained momentum, coverture was increasingly criticized as oppressive, leading to reforms. The Married Women’s Property Acts, passed in the United States from 1839 (Mississippi) and 1848 (New York) onward, began to modify or dismantle coverture by granting women greater control over their property. Coverture was gradually weakened and eventually eliminated through legislation and legal reforms in the United States. While coverture is no longer in effect, its legacy continues to shape legal and social discussions, particularly concerning gender equality. Some legal scholars argue that vestiges of coverture persist in contemporary legal frameworks, particularly in areas like real estate and tax law. Hannah chains herself to a lamp-post against the denial of political rights, and woman is called “chattel, a thing, a possession, a mere skirt.” Mr. Spitzer thinks all should vote, even the dead. Of the two moons, he inclines to believe the “sunken moon was real because it existed only in men’s dreams,” and “he had stood still as she had progressed”: she is modern and has changed with the times, while he is “stuck in the age of the surrey.” See the Blackstone entry in the Chapter 48 resources.
  • “seals of the old Merovingian kings”: The Merovingian dynasty was the ruling family of the Franks. They were called the long-haired kings, for uncut hair was the mark of their royalty. The gold signet ring of Childeric I, father of Clovis, engraved with his long-haired portrait and the words CHILDIRICI REGIS, was found in his tomb at Tournai in 1653; it was stolen from the royal library in Paris in 1831 and is known today from casts.
  • “Or both changed together”: Neither the mountain, the world, nor the mountain-climber, the person, stays fixed; both change together, and permanence is an illusion.
    • This may refer to Heraclitus, a Greek philosopher, who proposed universal flux and unity of opposites. The universal flux statement is that it is not possible to step twice into the same river, or to come into contact twice with a mortal being in the same state. Unity of opposites statement points to ways things are the same and not the same over time. Things are interconnected but not identical. An example of this is ocean water is fine for fish but undrinkable for man. See Heraclitus and Flux.
  • “come down by angelic, swan-breasted parachute”: Early parachuting was as much a woman’s art as a man’s, and two pioneers fit Cousin Hannah’s daring.
    • Georgia Ann “Tiny” Thompson Broadwick or Georgia Broadwick, previously known as Georgia Jacobs, and later known as Georgia Brown, was an American pioneering parachutist and the inventor of the ripcord. She was the first woman to jump from an airplane, and the first person to jump from a seaplane. (Wikipedia)
    • Katharina “Käthe” Paulus was a German exhibition parachute jumper and the inventor of the first collapsible parachute. At the time, 1910, the parachute was named “rescue apparatus for aeronauts.” The previous parachutes were not able to fit in a case like apparatus worn on the back, thus Paulus’ invention became of paramount importance for the Germans in the First World War and she produced about 7,000 parachutes for the German forces. During the First World War, Paulus created approximately 125 parachutes a week. She was also credited with inventing the “drag ‘chute,” an intentional breakaway system where one small parachute opens to pull out the main parachute. Paulus was an avid aeronaut herself and logged over 510 balloon flights and over 165 parachute jumps in her lifetime. She was the first German to be a professional air pilot and the first German woman aerial acrobat. Despite the fact that hot air balloons are currently known as a sort of tourist attraction, during the final decades of the 19th century these hot air balloons were on the cutting edge of technology, and were popular before the invention of airplanes. (Wikipedia)
  • “parachute slowly down to Skid Row”: Skid Row began as Skid Road in Seattle, where logs were skidded down to Henry Yesler’s mill in the 1850s; the street became a district of cheap lodging, and the name passed to down-and-out districts everywhere.
    • It is an impoverished area, typically urban, in English-speaking North America whose inhabitants are mostly poor people “on the skids.” This specifically refers to people who are poor or homeless, considered disreputable, downtrodden or forgotten by society. A skid row may be anything from an impoverished urban district to a red-light district to a gathering area for people experiencing homelessness or drug addiction. In general, skid row areas are inhabited or frequented by impoverished individuals and also people who are addicted to drugs. Urban areas considered skid rows are marked by high vagrancy, dilapidated buildings, and drug dens, as well as other features of urban blight. Used figuratively, the phrase may indicate the state of a poor person’s life. The term skid road originally referred to the path along which timber workers skidded logs. Its current sense appears to have originated in the Pacific Northwest. Areas in the United States and Canada identified by this nickname include Pioneer Square in Seattle; Old Town Chinatown in Portland, Oregon; Downtown Eastside in Vancouver; Skid Row in Los Angeles; the Tenderloin District of San Francisco; and the Bowery of Lower Manhattan. The term Poverty Flats is used for some Western US towns. (Wikipedia)
  • “one of the first women flyers over the Alps”: Marie Marvingt was a French athlete, mountaineer, aviator, and journalist. She won numerous prizes for her sporting achievements including those of swimming, cycling, mountain climbing, winter sports, ballooning, flying, riding, gymnastics, athletics, rifle shooting, and fencing. Between 1903 and 1910 she was the first woman to climb most of the peaks in the French and Swiss Alps, and she was the first woman to cross the North Sea by balloon (1909) and the English Channel (1914). She was a record-breaking balloonist, an aviator, and during World War I she became the first female combat pilot. She was also a qualified surgical nurse, was the first trained and certified flight nurse in the world, and worked for the establishment of air ambulance services throughout the world. In 1903 M. Château de Thierry de Beaumanoir named her “the fiancée of danger,” which newspapers used to describe her for the rest of her life. It is also included on the commemorative plaque on the façade of the house where she lived at 8 Place de la Carrière, Nancy. (Wikipedia)
  • “like Venus sleeping in her mother-of-pearl shell”: In Sandro Botticelli’s The Birth of Venus (about 1484-1486, Uffizi, Florence), the goddess, born of the sea foam, is blown ashore standing in a scallop shell. See Greek Mythology.
  • “an airplane with canvas wings”: Early airplanes were wooden frames covered with doped canvas. Young’s is a “flying chicken coop buzzing in the snow clouds,” fit for Cousin Hannah, whose daring journeys included balloon ascensions and flights over the Alps.
    • It may refer to the Wright Flyer which made the first sustained flight by a manned heavier-than-air powered and controlled aircraft on December 17, 1903. Invented and flown by brothers Orville and Wilbur Wright, it marked the beginning of the pioneer era of aviation. The aircraft is a single-place biplane design with drooping wings, front double elevator, and rear double rudder. It used a 12 horsepower (9 kilowatts) gasoline engine powering two pusher propellers. Employing “wing warping,” it was relatively unstable and very difficult to fly. The Wright brothers flew it four times in a location now part of the town of Kill Devil Hills, about 4 miles (6 kilometers) south of Kitty Hawk, North Carolina. The airplane flew 852 ft (260 m) on its fourth and final flight, but was damaged on landing, and wrecked minutes later when powerful gusts blew it over. The brothers shipped the wreckage back to Dayton, and the aircraft never flew again. Orville later restored it and displayed it on several occasions. The Flyer joined the Smithsonian Institution’s collection of historic aircraft in 1948 after the end of a long and bitter dispute between Orville and the Institution over its refusal to recognize the Flyer as the first successful airplane. Today, it is on display in a place of honor in the National Air and Space Museum in Washington, D.C. (Wikipedia)
  • “glowed like a Holy Grail”: The Holy Grail is a treasure that is an important motif in Arthurian literature. It is the cup of the Last Supper, sought by the knights of the Round Table and achieved by the pure Galahad.
  • “between the evening star and the morning star”: The evening star (Hesperus) and the morning star (Phosphorus, the light-bringer) are both the planet Venus, seen after sunset and before dawn; the Greeks came to know that the two were one. Gottlob Frege used the pair in “On Sense and Reference” (1892) to show that two names can have different senses yet name the same thing, a question of “the constitution of reality” into which Cousin Hannah never inquired. See Astronomy.
  • “presented to the League of Nations”: The League of Nations was the first worldwide governmental organization whose principal mission was to maintain world peace. Founded in 1920 after the First World War, it had its seat in Geneva, Switzerland, and voted itself out of existence in April 1946, its work passing to the United Nations.
  • “there were many accusations possible”: The Swiss accusations against Cousin Hannah highlight the ethical problem of unintended consequences. Even if her actions were driven by noble intentions, such as seeking her lost love or advancing suffrage, they allegedly resulted in harm to others, such as causing snow-slides or burying trains. This relates to consequentialism, which evaluates actions based on their outcomes. There is a tension between progress and destruction. Cousin Hannah “uncovered some things” but “covered others,” raising questions about whether progress inevitably involves loss or harm. This relates to dialectical thinking, where progress emerges from the conflict between opposing forces. The Swiss fear of Cousin Hannah potentially disrupting the stability of their nation reflects a conflict between individual freedom and the collective good. The Swiss are concerned about their community and way of life. This relates to political philosophy and the social contract. Mr. Spitzer questions the reliability of perception and the possibility of truly knowing anything. The mountains may be clouds, and the clouds may be mountains, highlighting the subjective nature of reality. This relates to skepticism and the questioning of empirical knowledge. The newspaper reports of the suffragette’s adventures are presented as “blurred” and open to interpretation. This emphasizes the role of the observer in shaping reality and the difficulty of establishing objective truth. Mr. Spitzer’s belief “when there was no reason for his belief” and his reservation of “his credulity for the grand occasions eliciting the skepticism of others” suggests a rejection of conventional notions of truth based on empirical evidence or logical reasoning. This relates to philosophical movements like existentialism, which prioritize individual experience and meaning-making. The notion that Cousin Hannah’s actions could cause “reverberations to eternity if not to infinity” implies a belief in the interconnectedness of all things and the far-reaching consequences of even seemingly small actions. This aligns with holistic philosophies that emphasize the unity of existence. The idea that “time and the dream were never married in her” suggests a rejection of linear time and an embrace of a more fluid, dreamlike reality. This relates to philosophies that challenge conventional notions of time, such as those found in process philosophy. Mr. Spitzer considers the possibility that Cousin Hannah might “ferry snow-crowned mountains of passage to another world” and “take all to that world where there was no mourning,” suggesting a belief in transcendence or the possibility of escaping the limitations of earthly existence. These philosophical inferences are not presented as systematic arguments but rather as fragmented reflections that emerge from Mr. Spitzer’s consciousness as he grapples with the legacy of Cousin Hannah.
  • “had uncovered many cantons never marked on any map”: A canton is a subdivision of a country established for political or administrative purposes. Switzerland is a confederation of cantons, each with its own constitution; there are twenty-six today.
  • “The mountains skipped about like rams”: “The mountains skipped like rams, and the little hills like lambs” (Psalm 114:4, KJV). See The Bible.
  • “the airplanes crashing over Switzerland”: During World War II, Switzerland experienced both intentional and accidental airplane crashes. While Switzerland was neutral, its airspace was frequently violated, and some aircraft were forced to land or crash within Swiss territory. Switzerland’s neutrality during World War II meant it was often violated by both Allied and Axis aircraft. These incursions led to aerial engagements, including the Swiss shooting down German planes and being forced to intern some aircraft. One notable incident involved a Swiss Messerschmitt 109 shooting down a German Bf 110, which prompted a retaliatory incursion by 32 Bf 110s, intercepted by Swiss fighters.
    • Swissair, the Swiss national airline, was formed on 26 March 1931 by the merger of Ad Astra Aero (1919) and Balair (1925) under Walter Mittelholzer and Balz Zimmermann. In 1933 it opened the first air route across the Alps, Zurich to Milan, and in 1934 it put Europe’s first flight attendant, Nelly Diener, aboard; she was killed in a crash that July. On 4 September 1963, Swissair Flight 306, a Caravelle bound from Zurich to Rome by way of Geneva, caught fire after takeoff and crashed near Dürrenäsch in the canton of Aargau, killing all eighty people aboard. The farming village of Humlikon lost forty-three of its 217 residents, among them its whole council, all of its school board, and its post office clerk. After 1964: the whole Swissair fleet was grounded for lack of cash on 2 October 2001, and its last flight landed in Zurich on 1 April 2002. (Wikipedia)
  • “mail planes crashing on their way to Italy”: air mail services were disrupted during World War II, particularly in Northern Italy under the Italian Social Republic (RSI). Allied forces banned all Italian air activities, including civilian flights, until the peace treaty was defined. Despite these disruptions, civilian mail was transported by air in Northern Italy from December 1944 until the end of the war, mainly along the Milan-Munich route with connections to Berlin and Vienna.
  • “carried by pigeon post”: During the Prussian siege of Paris in 1870 and 1871, carrier pigeons taken out of the city by balloon flew messages back in, photographed onto film so small that one bird could carry thousands of letters.
  • “a letter written by the Pope to a French queen”: Young makes the anachronism part of the joke: “It was a fourteenth century Pope who had written to a thirteenth-century queen.” Two real cases come close. Philip II of France married Ingeborg of Denmark in 1193 and repudiated her the day after the wedding; Pope Celestine III declared the annulment invalid, and Innocent III placed France under interdict in 1200 after Philip took Agnes of Merania as his wife. Ingeborg, held for years in confinement, wrote that she lacked visitors, a priest for comfort, and even sufficient food and clothing; Philip restored her as queen in 1213. In the fourteenth century Isabella of France, a French king’s daughter and the wife of Edward II of England, went to France in 1325 with the encouragement of Pope John XXII, who called her an “angel of peace,” to mediate between her husband and her brother Charles IV. She refused to go home and from December 1325 lived openly in Paris with Roger Mortimer, and when word came that the pope had spoken against her, her brother ordered her out of France.
    • An example of a Pope intervening in the affairs of the French monarchy regarding morality can be found in the context of the Avignon Papacy. This period happened from 1309 to 1376 during which seven successive popes resided in Avignon (at the time within the Kingdom of Arles, part of the Holy Roman Empire, now part of France) rather than in Rome. The situation arose from the conflict between the papacy and the French crown, culminating in the death of Pope Boniface VIII after his arrest and maltreatment by agents of Philip IV of France. Following the subsequent death of Pope Benedict XI, Philip pressured a deadlocked conclave to elect the Archbishop of Bordeaux as pope Clement V in 1305. Clement refused to move to Rome, and in 1309 he moved his court to the papal enclave at Avignon, where it remained for the next 67 years. This absence from Rome is sometimes referred to as the “Babylonian captivity” of the Papacy. A total of seven popes reigned at Avignon, all French, and all under the influence of the French Crown. In 1376, Gregory XI abandoned Avignon and moved his court to Rome, arriving in January 1377. After Gregory’s death in 1378, deteriorating relations between his successor Urban VI and a faction of cardinals gave rise to the Western Schism. This started a second line of Avignon popes, subsequently regarded as illegitimate. The last Avignon antipope, Benedict XIII, lost most of his support in 1398, including that of France. After five years besieged by the French, he fled to Perpignan in 1403. The schism ended in 1417 at the Council of Constance.
  • “attacked by a golden mountain eagle”: Mistaking her for another bird, the eagle attacked her in the “wasp-colored clouds over Switzerland,” and she “jousted furiously against him,” yet “none knew who had won or who had lost.” The battle stands for the dangers of her long fight for suffrage and liberation.
    • Several groups of World War II aircraft were nicknamed “Eagles.” The Eagle Squadrons (three Royal Air Force squadrons composed of American volunteers), the Aztec Eagles of the Mexican Air Force, and the P-51 Mustang fighter planes nicknamed “Gray Eagles.”
  • “the furies of crinolines”: Mr. Spitzer, as an old man dealing with the complexities and increasing impersonality of the modern world, nostalgically prefers this bygone era with its passionate, theatrical, and perhaps clearer social roles and rituals. It contrasts with his current experience of fading realities, illusions, and the disorienting modernity surrounding him.
    • Crinolines were a popular fashion in women’s clothing during the mid-1850s to the mid-1860s, a period often referred to as the Crinoline Period within the Victorian era. This era is characterized by the widespread adoption of crinolines, which created the voluminous, bell-shaped skirts that defined the fashion of the time. “Crinolinomania” (refers to the widespread adoption and fascination with the crinoline fashion during the mid-19th century) saw the crinoline evolve from a dome shape to a more pyramid shape, and eventually became almost flat in the front. Crinolines emerged as a lighter and more convenient alternative to the numerous petticoats previously used to create fullness in skirts. The mid-1850s to the mid-1860s period marks the height of crinoline popularity, with the style becoming a fashion staple across different social classes. While still worn, crinolines began to evolve, with the silhouette shifting from a bell shape to a flatter front and more fullness in the back. By the 1870s, the crinoline was largely replaced by the bustle, which focused on fullness at the rear of the skirt.
  • “each reporter had worn his own antennae on his head”: Mr. Spitzer looks back to the days before wire services and radio, when each reporter gathered his own news.
    • The 1850s and 1860s in the US were a period of intense national division and conflict, culminating in the Civil War. The central issue was slavery and its expansion, which led to political realignment, violence, and ultimately, secession and war. The decade of the 1850s saw escalating tensions surrounding slavery, with political compromises failing to resolve the issue and the nation moving closer to the brink of war. The Civil War itself, fought from 1861 to 1865, resulted in the end of slavery and Northern victory, but at a tremendous cost in human lives and national unity. Compromise of 1850 attempted to address the issue of slavery in newly acquired territories, but ultimately failed to quell the growing divide. The Kansas-Nebraska Act of 1854 introduced the concept of “popular sovereignty,” allowing residents of territories to decide on slavery, leading to violence and conflict in Kansas (“Bleeding Kansas”). Existing political parties fractured, and new ones emerged, such as the Republican Party, dedicated to preventing the expansion of slavery. The movement to abolish slavery gained momentum, with figures like Harriet Beecher Stowe and her novel Uncle Tom’s Cabin further inflaming anti-slavery sentiment. Dred Scott Decision (1857) where the Supreme Court ruled that enslaved people were not citizens and Congress could not prohibit slavery in the territories, further exacerbating tensions. Abraham Lincoln’s election as president in 1860, without a single Southern electoral vote, led to the secession of several Southern states. The Civil War (1861-1865) was fought between the Union (North) and the Confederacy (South), resulting in immense loss of life and widespread destruction. Major battles like Gettysburg and Vicksburg marked turning points in the war. Emancipation Proclamation (1863) declared enslaved people in Confederate-held territory to be free. New York City draft riots (1863) discontent with the draft laws during the Civil War led to violent protests. The 13th Amendment (1865) officially abolished slavery in the United States. Reconstruction (1865-1877) after the Civil War focused on rebuilding the South and integrating formerly enslaved people into society. This era was marked by successes and failures in achieving true equality. See The Civil War.
    • From 1850 to 1860 American news was dominated by the quarrel over slavery: the Compromise of 1850, the Kansas-Nebraska Act, and the Dred Scott decision. The penny press, led by James Gordon Bennett’s New York Herald, made newspapers a mass medium, and editors like Horace Greeley of the Tribune shaped opinion. Papers were openly partisan. The telegraph sped the news, railroads carried the papers across the country, and the Civil War made the war correspondent. Harriet Beecher Stowe’s Uncle Tom’s Cabin first ran as a serial in The National Era (1851-1852), and the Wide Awakes of the late 1850s organized through the press. (Wikipedia)
    • Samuel Morse sent the first message over his telegraph line from Washington to Baltimore on 24 May 1844: “What hath God wrought” (Numbers 23:23, KJV).
  • “kiss of a frog or by its croak”: In the Grimms’ “The Frog King” (1812) the princess does not kiss the frog but throws him against the wall, and he becomes a prince; the kiss came later. Here the enchantment fails: neither the frog’s kiss nor its croak can wake this beauty.
    • It may refer to The Frog Prince; or, Iron Henry, a German fairy tale collected by the Brothers Grimm and published in 1812 in Grimm’s Fairy Tales. In the forest, a selfish princess accidentally drops her golden ball into a well. A frog offers to retrieve it in exchange for her friendship. She agrees but goes back on her word after getting the ball back and runs to her castle. The next day, she is eating with her father when the frog knocks on the door and requests to be let in. The king tells his daughter that she must keep her promise and she reluctantly obeys. The frog sits next to her and eats from her plate, then desires to sleep in the princess’s bed. She is disgusted at the idea of sleeping with the frog, but her father angrily chastises her for loathing someone who helped her in a time of need. She picks up the frog and places him in the corner of her bedroom, but he hops up to her bed and demands to sleep as comfortably as the princess. Furious, she throws the frog against the wall, but as he falls to the floor he has transformed into a handsome prince. He explains that he was cursed by a wicked witch and the spell could only be broken with the princess’s help. The next day, the two go to the prince’s kingdom where they will be married. In modern versions, the transformation is triggered by the princess kissing the frog (a motif that apparently first appeared in English translations). In other early versions, it was sufficient for the frog to sleep for three nights on the princess’ pillow. The frog prince also has a loyal servant named Henry who had three iron bands affixed around his heart to prevent it from breaking from sadness when his master was cursed. When the frog prince reverts to his human form, Henry’s overwhelming happiness causes the bands to break, freeing his heart from its bonds. (Wikipedia) See Fairy Tales and Folklore.
  • “guarded by eunuchs black and white”: In the Ottoman palace of Topkapı in Istanbul, Black eunuchs under the Kızlar Ağası, the Agha of the Girls, guarded the harem, while white eunuchs guarded the palace gates and the school of pages. Most of the Black eunuchs were enslaved boys taken from Sudan and Ethiopia and castrated on the way north, an operation that killed many of them.
  • “locked at home in an iron chastity belt”: The story that crusaders locked their wives in chastity belts before riding east is a later legend. The earliest known drawing of a chastity belt is in Konrad Kyeser’s military treatise Bellifortis (1405), and most belts in museum collections are now thought to be later fabrications.
  • “this old bloomer girl”: Elizabeth Smith Miller wore loose trousers under a short skirt in Seneca Falls in 1851, and Amelia Bloomer championed the costume in The Lily, her temperance and women’s rights paper, so that it took her name. Elizabeth Cady Stanton and Susan B. Anthony wore it for a time before ridicule drove most women back into long skirts. See Women’s Suffrage.
  • “The Swiss had called her the Black Knight or blackamoor”: The nicknames make her a striking, fearsome figure riding through the Alps in dark clothes and a turban. See the Black Knight of Ivanhoe in the Chapter 43 resources and the blackamoor ballad in the Chapter 35 resources.
    • Saint Maurice, commander of the Theban Legion raised in Roman Egypt, was martyred in the late third century at Agaunum, now Saint-Maurice in the Swiss canton of Valais, for refusing orders to persecute Christians; his historicity is not certain. A statue of about 1240 in Magdeburg Cathedral is the earliest known depiction of him as a Black African knight in armor, and he was venerated across Europe. Black knights could also be called this because of the color of their armor. A black knight is a literary stock character who masks his identity and that of his liege by not displaying heraldry. Black knights are usually portrayed as villainous figures who use this anonymity for misdeeds. They are often contrasted with the knight-errant (white knight). The character appeared in Arthurian literature and has been adapted by various authors, in film and popular culture, and is sometimes associated with death or darkness. See Ancient Egypt.
  • “the white witch sleeping under the snow”: The Alp is both the mountain and, in German folklore, the Alp, a nightmare spirit (below), so the sleeping peak hides a dangerous power.
    • Both are in folklore and literature. The Alp is a supernatural being, often likened to a demon, vampire, or incubus. It can be a spirit summoned by a witch or an evil person or can be a human or animal that transforms into an Alp during the night. Known for shapeshifting, sometimes appearing as a cat, pig, dog, snake, or even a small white butterfly. It wears a magical hat which grants powers like invisibility. The Alp may also possess an “evil eye” that causes illness and misfortune. Primarily known for attacking sleeping victims, causing nightmares and difficulty breathing, similar to sleep paralysis. They may also drink blood or milk from their victims. Can be warded off by placing a broomstick under a pillow, iron horseshoes on the bedpost, or shoes with toes pointing towards the door. Trapping them indoors by plugging holes and keeping a light on at night are also mentioned as protective measures. A White Witch is generally considered a benevolent or sympathetic magic practitioner, focusing on healing and/or helping others. In C.S. Lewis’s “The Chronicles of Narnia,” specifically “The Lion, the Witch and the Wardrobe,” Jadis, the White Witch, is the main antagonist, a powerful and malevolent sorceress who usurped the throne of Narnia. She is not human but rumored to be half-Jinn and half-Giantess. Described as tall with skin “white like snow or paper or icing-sugar,” with a very red mouth. She casts a spell of eternal winter, turns her enemies to stone, and is defeated by Aslan, who stands for Christ. (Wikipedia) See Fairy Tales and Folklore.
  • “Perhaps she was the ladder personality”: “And he dreamed, and behold a ladder set up on the earth, and the top of it reached to heaven: and behold the angels of God ascending and descending on it” (Genesis 28:12, KJV). See The Bible.
  • “he had purchased this new planet”: In Antoine de Saint-Exupéry’s The Little Prince (1943), a businessman spends his days counting the stars because he believes he owns them, though he can do nothing with them; the little prince, who tends a single flower on his tiny planet, finds him absurd.
  • “no old Boston tram”: Boston’s tram or streetcar system has a long and complex history, evolving from horse-drawn cars to electric streetcars and eventually to the modern MBTA’s Green Line and Mattapan Line. The system saw significant expansion in the late 19th and early 20th centuries, with the first subway tunnel (Tremont Street) opening in 1897. Over time, many lines were converted to buses or trackless trolleys, and the system was consolidated under various entities, including the Boston Elevated Railway Company and the Metropolitan Transit Authority, before becoming part of the MBTA. (Wikipedia)
  • “a four-faced cherub one hundred cubits high”: “And every one had four faces, and every one had four wings” (Ezekiel 1:6, KJV). See The Bible.
  • “Every coffin should have its keyhole”: Mr. Spitzer’s wish has a history. The first recorded safety coffin, made for Duke Ferdinand of Brunswick in 1792, had a window for light, a tube for air, and a lid locked rather than nailed shut, with keys to the lid and to the tomb door placed in a pocket of his shroud. Later designs ran cords from the coffin to bells above ground so that someone buried alive could signal. Perhaps every coffin should have its telephone, “now in these days of instruments to deny both space and time, to say that all had been man’s dreams.”
  • “he was not violent like a mad musician”: Young’s mad musician “had reduced a piano to fire wood in three minutes and had even burned the harp.” Mr. Spitzer, who could have hacked open the trunks with an axe, is not violent.
    • Raphael Montañez Ortiz gained recognition for his “Piano Destruction Concerts” in the 1960s, using an ax to chop up pianos as a form of performance art. Flag: after 1964. His piano destructions were performed in London in 1966 at the Destruction in Art Symposium.
  • “that old knight Tancred”: Tancred, a hero of the First Crusade, is the knight of Torquato Tasso’s epic Jerusalem Delivered (1581). He loves the pagan warrior maiden Clorinda and, not knowing her in her armor, kills her in single combat at night, baptizing her as she dies. In Canto 13, when the crusaders need timber from an enchanted forest, Tancred strikes a tall cypress; blood flows from the cut, and Clorinda’s voice cries from inside the tree that he wounds her still. Claudio Monteverdi set the duel as Il combattimento di Tancredi e Clorinda (1624). Clorinda was never Tancred’s wife; Young makes her one. See Music and Composers.
  • “She had been reading a little book opened at page seven when she died”: The book open at page seven marks a life stopped early, its story unfinished; seven, often the number of completeness, here marks the incomplete.
    • The trope of a book left open to a specific page or passage serving as a clue in a mystery novel is a classic device.
  • “Perhaps it was she who was the master of keys”: grapples with the question of what happens after death. Mr. Spitzer contemplates whether the soul (“spirit”) needs a physical exit, like a chimney, if the conventional routes (“doors and passage-ways”) are closed. This reflects philosophical inquiries into the soul’s immortality and its separation from the body. The idea that “death was unknown to those who loved, and death was unknown to those who loved not, and death was unknown to those who died” suggests that death remains an enigma regardless of one’s experiences or beliefs. It’s a state beyond comprehension, aligning with existentialist themes of the unknown and the limits of human knowledge. The paragraph questions whether the senses provide a complete picture of reality. The idea that “Even the closed door was not closed, for should death be better known than love? Not all the senses were ever sealed at once” suggests that there are realities beyond immediate perception. The image of the butterfly escaping through the ear, “even when it was a door of the silence,” implies that even in the absence of sound, there are avenues for experience or existence. The description of Mr. Spitzer as a night watchman in the “starry universe” raises questions about the nature of reality. Is he a real figure, or is he merely a figment of someone’s imagination? His light awakening “other sleepers, those he never knew” suggests the interconnectedness of existence, even unawares. The suggestion that he perhaps “had intended to lock and not to unlock” introduces the possibility that his actions may have unintended consequences, highlighting the limits of human control and the role of chance. The final lines emphasize Mr. Spitzer’s role as the “only mourner among men,” suggesting a profound sense of isolation and the burden of grief. His mourning for himself implies a recognition of his own mortality and the inevitability of loss. This connects to existentialist themes of individual responsibility and the search for meaning in a seemingly meaningless world.
  • “the spirit might go up a chimney flue”: In European folklore chimneys were a liminal space connecting the natural and supernatural worlds. Spirits were widely believed in the fifteenth century to be able to travel through closed doors and walls. An old custom in Britain and Ireland was to open a window or door at a death so the soul could leave, as Mr. Spitzer thinks of leaving “only one aperture through which the spirit might escape.”
  • “Perhaps her butterfly had sailed out of her ear”: The Greek word psyche means both soul and butterfly, and the soul was often pictured leaving the body as a butterfly. See Greek Mythology.
  • “he had always been so remarkably careful in making lists”: Mr. Spitzer’s meticulous accounting and listing is directly tied to his struggle with his identity, particularly his relationship with his deceased brother. He seeks a perfect balance, a mirrored reflection where everything in his life corresponds to his brother’s, suggesting a desire to understand himself through this dualistic lens. The fear of “no differing counterpart” speaks to the existential anxiety of lacking a defined self, relying on another for definition. This resonates with philosophical concepts of identity formation, the “self” versus the “other,” and the influence of external relationships on self-perception. Thinkers like Sartre and Simone de Beauvoir explored similar themes in existentialism. Spitzer’s obsessive listing and indexing of even the most mundane objects (pearl buttons, rusted nail heads, etc.) reflects a deep-seated need to impose order on a chaotic world. He’s trying to find patterns, connections, and a “common denominator” to make sense of existence. This aligns with the philosophical pursuit of metaphysics: trying to understand the fundamental nature of reality. The futility of Spitzer’s efforts mirrors the inherent difficulties in finding absolute order or meaning in a world often perceived as absurd or chaotic (a key theme in existentialism and absurdism). The questions about the sail (“Was the sail unwinding the same as the winding sail?”) touch on the philosophical problem of identity over time. Does something remain the same if its state changes? This is further complicated by the cyclical nature of the tides and the wagon wheels, implying a sense of eternal return or repetition. This connects to Heraclitus’s famous saying, often given as “No man ever steps in the same river twice” (Plato’s version is “you could not step twice into the same river,” Cratylus 402a), emphasizing the constant flux and change in the universe. The paragraph also hints at Nietzsche’s concept of eternal recurrence. Spitzer’s attempts to capture reality through lists and measurements are ultimately limited. His fear that “all the weight, as he had often complained, was on this weightless star” alludes to the disparity between the tangible and intangible, the concrete and abstract. He can list the physical properties of objects, but he cannot capture their essence or meaning. This is related to epistemology, the study of knowledge and its limitations. The paragraph suggests the impossibility of fully knowing or representing reality, as there will always be something missing or lost in translation. The description of Spitzer’s actions creating “division as in division there was creation,” suggests that in every act of creation, there is also an act of destruction. This mirrors the belief that every action has an equal and opposite reaction. This is connected to the concept of the “Tao” which states that everything is composed of two opposites, and that without the other, it cannot exist. See Nietzsche and Taoism and Zhuangzi.
  • “in creation there was division as in division there was creation”: Genesis tells creation as a series of divisions: “and God divided the light from the darkness” (Genesis 1:4, KJV). Life begins the same way: in nearly all animals the fertilized egg, or zygote, splits again and again, a process called cleavage. See The Bible.
  • “Who knew the womb of a snowflake?”: “Hath the rain a father? or who hath begotten the drops of dew? Out of whose womb came the ice? and the hoary frost of heaven, who hath gendered it?” (Job 38:28-29, KJV). See The Bible.
  • “like that old coachman who had lost his passenger long ago”: This may be the opium lady’s black coachman, who drove her through the nights. See The Black Coachman.
  • “where none had moved over the face of the waters”: “And the earth was without form, and void; and darkness was upon the face of the deep. And the Spirit of God moved upon the face of the waters” (Genesis 1:2, KJV). See The Bible.
  • “who should find the doors which held back the sea”: “Or who shut up the sea with doors, when it brake forth, as if it had issued out of the womb?” (Job 38:8, KJV). Young follows it at once: “The sea flowed like the waters from the womb.” See The Bible.
  • “his fingers turning to candles with flames like Mr. Chandelier”: See Mr. Chandelier.
  • “a lost bride who had played a game of hide-and-seek with the bridegroom”: The old romance is “The Mistletoe Bough,” a legend claimed by several English country houses and best known from Thomas Haynes Bayly’s ballad of the 1830s: on her wedding day a bride hides in an old oak chest during a game of hide-and-seek, the lid locks shut, and her skeleton in its wedding dress is found years later. Samuel Rogers told the same tale of the Italian bride Ginevra in his poem Italy (1822). See Fairy Tales and Folklore.
  • “She would be found when she was dust and ashes”: The body is found among the remnants of a life, “the bride who might almost have been the bridegroom,” as if death dissolved the roles that defined her. Lost Atlantis drifts above, its cities “carried away while man slept and woman loved,” and Mr. Spitzer has heard of conceptions by strange means, children “born by the ear of the dead,” “because the wind blew,” and “because another woman had shouted at her”: forces at work beyond the senses. “Dust and ashes” is Abraham’s phrase before God: “I have taken upon me to speak unto the Lord, which am but dust and ashes” (Genesis 18:27, KJV).
  • “being that Lost Atlantis”: Plato tells of Atlantis in the Timaeus and Critias (about 360 BC), an island empire beyond the Pillars of Hercules that “in a single day and night of misfortune” disappeared in the depths of the sea (Timaeus, trans. Benjamin Jowett). See Plato and Platonism.
  • “who were born by the ear of the dead”: In the Christian bible Mary is supposed to be impregnated by the Holy Spirit and not by a mortal man, thus giving birth to Jesus. A medieval belief held that Mary conceived through her ear when she heard the angel’s word, conceptio per aurem, and paintings of the Annunciation sometimes show a ray of light or the dove of the Holy Spirit entering her ear. See The Bible.
  • “a sterile woman had conceived because another woman had shouted at her”: This may echo the barren Hannah of 1 Samuel, whose name Cousin Hannah shares, taunted by her husband’s other wife: “And her adversary also provoked her sore, for to make her fret, because the LORD had shut up her womb” (1 Samuel 1:6, KJV). Hannah prayed at Shiloh, “and the LORD remembered her,” and she bore Samuel (1 Samuel 1:19-20, KJV). In Luke, when the long-barren Elisabeth heard Mary’s greeting, “the babe leaped in her womb” and “she spake out with a loud voice” (Luke 1:41-42, KJV). See The Bible.
  • “like that Spanish don”: It evokes a man whose bride leaves him not for another man but for the convent, to become a bride of Christ. Like the don’s bride, the suffragette left traditional roles for solitary journeys and quests.
    • It may refer to José Zorrilla’s play “Don Juan Tenorio,” Don Juan makes a bet that he can conquer more women than Don Luis. Don Luis challenges Don Juan to conquer a woman about to take her vows as a nun, and an engaged woman. Here is a Spanish don whose bride became a nun. In the play, Don Juan’s target, Doña Inés, is a novice nun whose innocence captivates him and leads him to contemplate redemption.
  • “like a blind man playing dice by Braille”: Louis Braille, blinded as a child, published his system of raised dots for reading and music in 1829. Dice for the blind have raised pips.
  • “searching for he knew not what”: He searches for “he knew not what,” and “magnetic doors” open by themselves, as if knowledge came unsought. The “windowless seraglio or cave or darkened tower” is the mind as a prison, and the “supernumerary love, a wife unknown” a hidden self. The “blind god of love” is love irrational and indiscriminate, and in the turban-winder’s unwinding “there should be no memory and no woman and no man.”
  • “Love knew no age”: Jessica says in Shakespeare’s The Merchant of Venice, “But love is blind, and lovers cannot see / The pretty follies that themselves commit” (2.6). Cupid was sometimes depicted blindfolded; Erwin Panofsky traced the image in “Blind Cupid,” in Studies in Iconology (1939). See Shakespeare.
  • “those knockings which might have come from him”: Modern Spiritualism, popular through the Victorian age, began in 1848 when the Fox sisters of Hydesville, New York, claimed that rappings in their house were messages from the dead; in 1888 Margaret Fox confessed that the knocks were made by cracking her toe joints, though she later took the confession back. In 1920 Thomas Edison told B. C. Forbes of The American Magazine that he was working on an apparatus for communicating with the dead. See Spiritualism and the Occult.
  • “footless like the footless bird of paradise”: Skins of birds of paradise reached Europe from New Guinea with the feet cut off by the traders who prepared them, beginning with those brought home by the survivors of Magellan’s voyage in 1522, and Europeans came to believe the birds had no feet and lived always in the air. Linnaeus named the greater bird of paradise Paradisaea apoda, “footless,” in 1758.
  • “the tree rooted in clouds with its branches growing downward”: The Bhagavad Gita (15.1) and the Katha Upanishad (6.1) describe the eternal ashvattha, the sacred fig, with its roots above and its branches below. See Hinduism.
  • “He had felt as if he were Ali Baba in the cave of forty thieves”: Ali Baba in the cave of forty thieves is a folk tale from the One Thousand and One Nights book where the door to the treasure only opened if a person said the magic word, open sesame. The tale is not in the Arabic manuscripts. Antoine Galland added it to his French translation (1704-1717) after hearing it in 1709 from Hanna Diyab, a young Maronite storyteller from Aleppo.
  • “there had been trunk lid after trunk lid”: Mr. Spitzer finds “so many wedding gowns, sheets of silk and veils of lace,” “many bridal gowns and no bride’s slippers,” “porous silks so thin that the least touch might cause them to fall into nothingness”: the trappings of a ceremony that never came. These are Young’s source story, the sealed trunks of Charles Studin’s suffragist, each holding a bridal trousseau; see the Chapter 31 resources.
    • Which leaves more questions than it answers. Had Cousin Hannah secretly wanted to marry even though it was supposed that she did not support the institution of marriage? Had there been forty suitors who wanted to marry her but she had backed out at the last minute? Had there been forty weddings where Cousin Hannah was rejected at the last minute? There is, of course, a deeper pull in men and women. Human beings are animals with instincts. One of the strongest is to reproduce. Mr. Spitzer has also thought about his lack of progeny to pass on the family since his brother is dead and he did not marry. Mr. Spitzer commented earlier that if Cousin Hannah had wanted to marry he would have married her when they were younger. If she had noticed him.
