A further study of marriage, suffrage and Cousin Hannah can be found in Volume 3 of To All My Darlings.
    • Young took the trunks from life. She told Studs Terkel that Charles Studin’s suffragist went to Europe every year for forty years, “brought back a heavily sealed trunk and had it placed in the basement of her Fifth Avenue house,” and never opened them. “It was his business as a lawyer to open the trunks when she died,” and in each he found a complete bridal trousseau, “showing that after all she had a dream too.” One of Studin’s themes was “that you never know a person really until he is dead” (Marguerite Young, interview with Studs Terkel, WFMT radio, 1965). See the Chapter 30 resources.
  • “He had been trapped by wedding gowns”: The wedding gowns turn into seas, sails, and shrouds, and Mr. Spitzer cannot tell whether there is one moon, many mirrored moons, or none, a world of reflections like Plato’s cave. He fears the census-taker as he fears final knowledge. The old maid who told women to “divest themselves of excess luggage” kept her trunks of wedding gowns, rejecting marriage yet longing for it, and Mr. Spitzer, a “dead man coming to mourn for her,” likens himself to the ferry of Charon, who carried the dead across the Styx.
  • “let the dead bury the dead”: “But Jesus said unto him, Follow me; and let the dead bury their dead” (Matthew 8:22, KJV). See The Bible.
  • “or perhaps a hen crowing if she was right”: An old proverb says, “A whistling woman and a crowing hen are neither fit for God nor men.” See the Chapter 43 resources.
  • “no language contained truth”: The truth “was that which could not be expressed”: the ineffable of the mystics, “the word never written, the name never told.” His mind is “like a sieve,” and he walks on “coming to no end.” She died reading of “lovers never mated,” Eloise and Abelard, and he cannot tell whether she was Tristram or Yseult. The pennies on her eyes, “one in memory of the sun, one in memory of the moon,” close all perception, and he will not wake the dead for fear they might die again.
  • “Eloise et Abelard”: The twelfth-century philosopher Peter Abelard and his student Héloïse secretly married, were parted when her uncle had Abelard castrated, and lived out their lives in the cloister, joined afterward by their letters. Young names them again among parted lovers in Chapter 65; see the Chapter 65 resources.
    • Peter Abelard was a medieval French scholastic philosopher, leading logician, theologian, teacher, musician, composer, and poet. In philosophy he is celebrated for his proposed logical solution to the problem of universals via nominalism and conceptualism and his pioneering of intent in ethics. Often referred to as the “Descartes of the twelfth century,” he is considered a forerunner of Rousseau, Kant, and Spinoza. He is sometimes credited as a chief forerunner of modern empiricism. In Catholic theology, he is best known for his development of the concept of limbo, and his introduction of the moral influence theory of atonement. He is considered (alongside Augustine) to be the most significant forerunner of the modern self-reflective autobiographer. He paved the way and set the tone for later epistolary novels and celebrity tell-alls with his publicly distributed letter, The History of My Calamities and public correspondence. In history and popular culture he is best known for his passionate, tragic love affair and intense philosophical exchange with his brilliant student and eventual wife, Héloïse d’Argenteuil. After they secretly married, Abelard sent Héloïse to the convent at Argenteuil; her uncle and guardian Fulbert, believing she had been cast off, had Abelard ambushed and castrated, and both entered religious life. Roscellinus and others made fun of him. Their son was named Astrolabe. (Wikipedia) See the problem of universals in the Chapter 49 resources.
    • Héloïse d’Argenteuil was a French nun, philosopher, writer, scholar, and abbess. Héloïse was a renowned “woman of letters” and philosopher of love and friendship, as well as an eventual high ranking abbess in the Catholic Church. She achieved approximately the level and political power of a bishop in 1147 when she was granted the rank of prelate nullius. She is famous in history and popular culture for her love affair and correspondence with the leading medieval logician and theologian Peter Abelard, who became her colleague, collaborator, and husband. She is known for exerting critical intellectual influence upon his work and posing many challenging questions to him such as those in the Problemata Heloissae. Her surviving letters are considered a foundation of French and European literature and primary inspiration for the practice of courtly love. Her erudite and sometimes erotically charged correspondence is the Latin basis for the bildungsroman genre and serve alongside Abelard’s Historia Calamitatum as a model of the classical epistolary genre. Her influence extends on later writers such as Chrétien de Troyes, Geoffrey Chaucer, Madame de Lafayette, Thomas Aquinas, Choderlos de Laclos, Voltaire, Rousseau, Simone Weil, and Dominique Aury. She is an important figure in the establishment of women’s representation in scholarship and is known for her controversial portrayals of gender and marriage which influenced the development of modern feminism. When Abelard gave a rationalistic interpretation of the Trinitarian dogma he was charged with heresy. Theologia by Peter Abelard refers to his three treatises on the Trinity, written in the 12th century. These works, titled Theologia “summi boni,” Theologia Christiana, and Theologia “scholarium,” explore the nature of God and the Trinity using dialectical reasoning. Theologia Christiana is considered the most influential of the three. However, Abelard’s Theologia was also controversial, with the first version being condemned as heretical and burned in 1121. Abelard employed logical arguments and philosophical analysis to examine theological concepts, particularly the Trinity. He adopted the Boethian sense of theologia as discourse about the divine nature, according to a study from Oxford Academic. The core of his work revolves around understanding the nature and relationship of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. Abelard’s approach, which emphasized reason and challenged traditional interpretations, led to conflicts with Church authorities. His works were condemned at the Council of Soissons (1122) and the Council of Sens (1141). Abelard proposed that Christ’s death was primarily a demonstration of God’s love, rather than a satisfaction of divine justice. This view is now known as the moral influence theory. Despite the controversies, Abelard’s work had a lasting impact on medieval philosophy and theology, particularly in the development of scholasticism. (Wikipedia)
    • The Letters of Abelard and Heloise are two series of passionate and intellectual correspondences apparently written in Latin during the 12th century. The purported authors, Peter Abelard, a prominent theologian, and his pupil, Heloise, a gifted young woman later renowned as an abbess, exchanged these letters following their ill-fated love affair and subsequent monastic lives. The letters reveal the personal and intellectual relationship between Abelard and Heloise, and provide an intimate glimpse into the societal context of 12th-century Europe. They’ve played a significant role in the development of Western epistolary literature, attracting attention from historians, literary scholars, and general readers alike. The Letters of Abelard and Heloise also serve as primary source documents on questions of medieval gender roles, love, and monastic life. (Wikipedia)
  • “Was she Tristram, or was she the white Yseult?”: Tristram (Tristan) and Iseult (Yseult, Isolde) is a chivalric romance told in many versions since the twelfth century, the tragedy of the illicit love between the Cornish knight Tristram and the Irish princess Iseult, wife of his uncle King Mark. The white Yseult is Iseult of the White Hands, the Breton princess Tristram marries for her name; in the version of Thomas of Britain and many later tellings the marriage is never consummated, so she too is a lover never mated. Matthew Arnold’s Tristram and Iseult (1852) is in three parts, “Tristram,” “Iseult of Ireland,” and “Iseult of Brittany,” and gives the last part to the white-handed wife, whom Arnold, unusually, makes the mother of Tristram’s children.
  • “no physician even to a centaur”: Chiron, the wise centaur, was the healer and teacher of Asclepius, Achilles, and Jason. Wounded by a poisoned arrow of Heracles that would not let him die, he gave up his immortality. See Greek Mythology.
  • “two pennies, one in memory of the sun”: Coins were laid on the eyes of the dead to keep the lids closed, a custom often linked to the Greek obol placed in the mouth of the dead as Charon’s fare across the Styx. Mr. Spitzer has just pictured himself as “Charon’s ferry boat.” See Greek Mythology.

Chapter 70

← Chapter 69 · Home · Chapter 71 →

Summary

In the silence after the doctor’s quarrel, Vera half dreams of Mrs. Hogden, a woman she never saw, whose name slides from Hogden to Logden, Fogden, Dogden, and Bogden. During Vera’s absence Mrs. Hogden arrived at Catherine’s house in four coats, hung with temple bells and packages, carrying an empty bird cage and a basket of wormy apples. She had sold her Dutch windmill on Long Island to become the arithmetic teacher Catherine says she never hired. Lisa Lunde, the would-be physicist who replaced Vera as Catherine’s companion, carries messages between the two women and interprets neither to the other. Lodged in the deserted playroom, Mrs. Hogden explores the house, plays chess alone with an atomizer for the missing bishop, drinks, and at last takes to bed as a rival invalid, dreaming the household’s dreams out loud. Mr. Spitzer offers to restore her windmill and more, and she rides away in the mist. In the empty playroom Vera finds, on the little blackboard, a message in red chalk ending, “and therefore, dear heart, all a’s are c’s. You know me.”

Characters present

Mrs. Hogden · Vera Cartwheel · Catherine Cartwheel · Lisa Lunde

Concepts present

Themes: Decay and Ruin · Illusion and Reality · Isolation and Connection · Madness and Sanity · Order, Chaos, and Discipline · Society, Class, and Race · Time · Women, Gender, and Marriage

Symbols: Birds

Philosophy: Existentialism · Pythagoras and the Music of the Spheres

Allusions: Angels and Archangels · Astronomy · Don Quixote · Judaism · Napoleon and Wellington · Romantic Poets · Shakespeare · Suicide in History and Literature · The Bible

Key passages

From the research

  • Vera describes the mysterious and unsettling arrival of Mrs. Hogden, a corporeal yet ghostly figure who invades Vera’s dreams and memories, contrasting sharply with Miss MacIntosh, the former nursemaid. Mrs. Hogden is portrayed as a confusing and contradictory figure (fat, over-dressed, and intrusive) acting almost like an apparition haunting the household and Vera’s psyche. This passage sets the tone of ambiguity and surrealism, highlighting the blurred lines between reality and dream, presence and absence.
  • Mrs. Hogden arrives unexpectedly, burdened with numerous packages and personal belongings, having sold her Dutch windmill home to take up a position supposedly offered by Vera’s mother. Despite her chaotic appearance and peculiar behavior, she is convinced of her rightful place in the household, promising to teach arithmetic and “reflect my mother’s every mood.” The tension between Mrs. Hogden’s assured intrusion and the household’s skepticism is introduced here, particularly through Lisa Lunde’s suspicion and Catherine’s disbelief and rejection.
  • A key passage details the growing argument between Mrs. Hogden and Vera’s mother, who denies ever inviting her. Despite this, Mrs. Hogden knows intimate details of Catherine’s life, suggesting a mysterious or imagined connection. Catherine’s refusal to accept Mrs. Hogden, calling her a liar and impostor, contrasts with Mrs. Hogden’s unwavering optimism and strange knowledge.
  • Mrs. Hogden’s life in the playroom (a place full of forgotten objects and memories) is described in detail. She is isolated, eccentric, and increasingly despondent yet strangely content with her condition. Her behavior of talking to herself, playing chess alone, drinking secretly, and dressing and undressing depicts a tragic figure clinging to illusions of importance and social connection.
  • As Mrs. Hogden feigns or experiences illness, taking to her uncomfortable bed, Catherine’s revulsion grows. Catherine refuses to tolerate a “rival invalid” and orders her removal through Mr. Spitzer, the lawyer.
  • Eventually, Mrs. Hogden is expelled from the house with a generous financial settlement arranged by Mr. Spitzer. The aftermath reveals the house’s return to emptiness, the closure of the playroom, and the lingering mystery of Mrs. Hogden’s identity and presence. Vera contemplates Mrs. Hogden’s role as both a real and dreamlike figure, a substitute for lost connections, and a symbol of the fragile boundary between memory and imagination.
  • The chapter closes with the image of the little three-legged blackboard left behind by Mrs. Hogden, inscribed with a cryptic message in red chalk: “All a’s are b’s, it read—all b’s are c’s—and therefore, dear heart, all a’s are c’s. You know me.” The syllogism is sound, but “dear heart” and “You know me” turn the logic into a personal claim of recognition from a woman nobody can place.

Questions and observations

Reading closely

  • “She was my mind’s betrayal of my mind.” What does Vera mean by calling Mrs. Hogden a substitute?
  • “If two and two made only four, my mother said, what else was there to talk about?” Why does Catherine want, and then refuse, simple arithmetic?
  • The blackboard reads, “All a’s are b’s, it read—all b’s are c’s—and therefore, dear heart, all a’s are c’s. You know me.” What does “You know me” add to the logic?

Characters

  • Mrs. Hogden “was the least critical human being.” Is that a virtue or a madness?
  • Lisa Lunde “would do nothing to interpret either character to the other.” Why does she enjoy the quarrel?
  • Catherine “would not have a rival invalid in the house.” What is she protecting?

Connections

  • “Her connection with Miss MacIntosh, her predecessor, is only one of a shadow-haunted place, after all.” How are the two women alike and unlike?
  • Mrs. Hogden “dreamed our dreams out loud as if they were hers instead of ours.” Why does that feel like an insult to the household?
  • “Home, James, my good man. Home, James.” Where is home for Mrs. Hogden?

Reflection

  • “Everybody is lonely.” Does the chapter prove it?
  • “She was one of those persons who, disappearing from the earth, would have been missed by nobody at all.” Who in the novel is like her?
  • “Is it possible that any life can be the surface impression only, just no more than it seems to others?” What is your answer?

Research: Characters

Mrs. Hogden/Logden/Fogden/Dogden/Bogden

  • Fat, corpulent, with bleached, plastered curls.
  • Wears multiple coats stacked over each other, eccentric hats, and carries a variety of odd objects (empty birdcage, packages, temple bells).
  • Her face is blandly expressionless except for an aggressive chin and abnormally large, unfocused eyes.
  • Smells of over-ripe apples and is associated with decay and disorder.
  • Wears a water-stained yellow satin nightgown, black fur slippers, and a frilled white night-cap with an aggressive chin bow.
  • Optimistic despite her apparent destitution and displacement.
  • Talks to herself and answers her own questions, which others interpret as madness.
  • Displays a strange serenity and is described as the “least critical human being.”
  • Has an air of maudlin dignity and commands a dubious respect.
  • Exhibits contradictory behavior: vain but neglected, hopeful but delusional.
  • Plays chess alone, often crying over imagined victories or defeats.
  • Has a strong attachment to visual education and arithmetic, though she never succeeds in teaching.
  • Claims to be descended from notable historical figures (Daniel Boone, William the Conqueror, Alexander Graham Bell).
  • Sold a Dutch windmill home to come to Catherine’s house based on a letter of employment that Catherine denies writing.
  • Possibly a shoplifter or of dubious character as viewed by Lisa Lunde, but not confirmed.
  • Mysterious in origin, with no known relatives or friends, disappearing without trace after leaving.

Vera Cartwheel

  • Vera emerges as a deeply introspective, highly imaginative, and somewhat detached individual whose internal world often blurs with external reality.
  • She explicitly states that Mrs. Hogden, a central figure in this chapter, is someone she “never saw,” but rather a “trick of my imagination, this substituting of the one for the other.” Vera acknowledges Mrs. Hogden as a “substitute... for the dream life I wanted” and even calls her “my mind’s betrayal of my mind.” Figures like Mrs. Hogden go “waddling in and out of my dreams.” She can “see” Mrs. Hogden by simply “closing my eyes, by concentrating.” Vera’s consciousness is the lens through which the narrative unfolds, making her a subjective and unreliable narrator.
  • Vera’s character is also deeply shaped by her past and the figures who influenced her upbringing, particularly Miss MacIntosh and her mother. Miss MacIntosh, Vera’s former nursemaid, “brought me up to understand that my mother’s way of life was far from average and was not to be imitated by a good woman such as she saw me becoming, a woman like herself, simple and average and clear-eyed.” This suggests that Miss MacIntosh tried to instill a sense of conventionality in Vera, despite Vera’s inherent imaginative tendencies (night-dreaming, too, “she would have disapproved of, most ardently”). That Vera “escaped from my mother’s house” further indicates a strained relationship with her mother, who is portrayed as eccentric and prone to “frenzied dreaming.” Vera keeps comparing Mrs. Hogden to Miss MacIntosh, even after Miss MacIntosh’s death.
  • Despite her imaginative immersion, Vera demonstrates a keen observational and analytical mind, though often applied to her internal world. She meticulously describes Mrs. Hogden’s outlandish appearance and actions, down to the “smashed hat with a wilted ostrich feather” and the “row of Javanese temple bells.” She also notices the “evidence left by Mrs. Hogden” in the playroom, such as “derelict whiskey bottles, empty coat hangers, withered apple cores, broken egg shells, dead flies,” distinguishing even an “artificial eyelash.” Her philosophical reflections, such as her belief in a “small, warped flower growing... outside the consciousness of God,” reveal a mind that questions universal truths and finds significance in anomalies.
  • Vera also conveys a sense of loneliness and a search for meaning or connection. She explicitly states, “The life I required was the life which required, like his, a lost companion —not merely this self-centered affliction of the right hand loving the left.” Her observation that “Everybody is lonely” suggests a deep, shared human experience she identifies with. Mrs. Hogden, as an imagined companion, could be seen as Vera’s attempt to fill this void, even while acknowledging the illusion.
  • Vera’s identity appears somewhat fluid and permeable. Mrs. Hogden mistakenly supposes Vera to be Lisa Lunde, and Vera herself often blurs the lines between her own experiences, her mother’s dreams, and the fabricated reality of Mrs. Hogden.

Catherine Cartwheel

  • Catherine, Vera’s mother, is a profoundly eccentric, wealthy invalid whose grasp on reality is tenuous and fragmented. Her character is defined by a series of contradictions, delusions, and a self-centered, often manipulative, approach to those around her.
  • Initially, Vera establishes Catherine as an unconventional figure, noting that Miss MacIntosh, Vera’s former nursemaid, raised Vera to understand that her “mother’s way of life was far from average and was not to be imitated by a good woman.” Catherine is also revealed as the “true subject of [Vera’s] dreams,” indicating her deep, almost obsessive, significance to Vera.
  • Catherine’s disconnection from reality is a dominant trait. She “dreamed that she was poor,” contrasting with Lisa Lunde’s mother who “dreamed that she was rich.” Her physical and mental state is described as one of profound invalidism, often sinking into “deeper and deeper coma” and experiencing hallucinations, such as “a huge toad was eating my mother’s face” or “the balloon fish floating over my mother’s head,” and “shadowy figures stepped out of the walls. There were moths with human faces.” She herself admits to having “lost my mind several times” and declares, “I am not responsible for my actions.” Her identity is fluid; she believes she has “killed her former self and that my mother’s former self was walking through the house while my mother lay with her hair streaked out like twilight on a pillow, for my mother was dead—added, subtracted, multiplied, divided.”
  • Despite her profound mental disarray, Catherine exhibits moments of surprising shrewdness and practicality, particularly concerning financial matters. She can display a “shrewd gleam in her eyes, the absolute efficiency with which she inquired into her financial concerns, past and present,” even seeking to collect “Old loans which she had forgotten making” from dead parties. Her instruction to meticulously inspect the house for missing items after Mrs. Hogden’s departure further underscores this trait.
  • Catherine’s interactions with Mrs. Hogden, her newly arrived companion, highlight her manipulative and self-centered nature. Initially, she feigns “profound, glazed astonishment,” denying any knowledge of Mrs. Hogden or having sent an invitation, calling her an “impostor, a liar, a day-dreamer, a thief.” Despite Mrs. Hogden possessing intimate details of Catherine’s life like “the head of Alcibiades was in the drainpipe” or “a whale swimming into my mother’s bedroom” which only Catherine could have divulged, Catherine still refuses to see her. She employs elaborate excuses, claiming to be “gone to Boston to see a podiatrist” or “to the North Pole.” She blames Lisa Lunde for Mrs. Hogden’s presence and attempts to discourage Mrs. Hogden by assigning her an uncomfortable “deserted playroom” and a “hospital cot” that was “too short and too narrow.” Her ultimate directive to Mr. Spitzer to “push her off a high building or throw her into the ocean” to get rid of Mrs. Hogden reveals a cruel and extreme impulse.
  • Catherine’s desire for an arithmetic teacher who would teach “Two and two always making four...over and over again” suggests a yearning for simple, undeniable truths in a chaotic personal reality. However, she rejects Mrs. Hogden’s attempts to teach, deeming her “mad as a loon” for repeating the lesson. She views Mrs. Hogden as a “rival invalid” and a “gross, stinking parody” of her own “distended world of shimmering, loosely woven textures,” indicating a fierce protectiveness over her unique inner world.
  • Catherine’s memory and awareness fluctuate. After Mrs. Hogden’s departure, she is “disappointed now that she had not been taught arithmetic and blamed Lisa Lunde,” even considering hiring another “lonely old woman” to teach her.

Lisa Lunde

  • Lisa Lunde is introduced as Vera’s mother’s “young companion who took my place when, carrying a large suitcase, I escaped from my mother’s house.” This immediately establishes her as a replacement for Vera and suggests a practical, perhaps less privileged, background. Indeed, she is described as a “would-be physicist working for her living in order to help support her mother who was poor and mad and dreamed that she was rich,” highlighting her sense of responsibility and pragmatic drive, contrasting with the opulence and delusion of Vera’s mother’s household.
  • Lisa Lunde is characterized by her analytical, skeptical, and often blunt nature. She “prided herself on seeing immediately through Mrs. Hogden’s pretensions” and quickly assesses Mrs. Hogden as a “very dubious character, a shoplifter or something equally vicious.” Her scientific inclination is evident in her desire to “shatter all illusions at one blow,” as when she cruelly declares “Res Tacamah... is nothing but a drug bottle.” She struggles with Mrs. Hogden’s evasiveness, conceding “she was perhaps not a shoplifter... but she did not look like a school-teacher either—there was something so evasive about her, something that evaded definition.”
  • Despite her initial skepticism and clear-sightedness, Mrs. Hogden’s unwavering self-assurance eventually sways Lisa Lunde, until she “began to believe that she had come because she was invited.” This suggests a slight vulnerability to the pervasive illusions of the house, or perhaps a weariness from constantly battling them.
  • Her role in the conflict between Vera’s mother and Mrs. Hogden is notable. When Vera’s mother blames her for Mrs. Hogden’s presence and demands she “get rid of her,” Lisa Lunde reveals a more complex, almost vindictive side. “Lisa Lunde, revengeful, began to enjoy the embarrassing situation. She ran back and forth with meaningless messages between the two, and she would do nothing to interpret either character to the other.” This shows a passive-aggressive streak, where she derives satisfaction from the escalating absurdity, perhaps as a form of rebellion against her demanding employer or simply a release from her own constrained life.
  • Lisa Lunde also acts as a voice of conventional sanity, remarking that talking to oneself is fine, “but when you get to answering your own questions—then you are crazy as a loon.” This pragmatic, somewhat judgmental perspective contrasts sharply with the eccentricities of Mrs. Hogden and the delusions of Vera’s mother.
  • Lisa Lunde serves as a grounded, albeit sometimes resentful, observer and participant in the surreal events of the household. Vera’s mother, however, consistently blames Lisa Lunde, even for “keeping Mrs. Hogden out of sight.”

Research: Themes

Illusion and Reality

See: Illusion and Reality

  • Mrs. Hogden blurs the line between dream and waking life, reality and hallucination.
  • Her presence challenges the boundaries between sanity and madness.
  • Symbol of the mind’s betrayal of itself, a substitute for lost or desired figures (such as Miss MacIntosh).

Loneliness and Isolation

See: Isolation and Connection

  • Mrs. Hogden is depicted as profoundly lonely, coming from a desolate life in a cold windmill.
  • The Arctic tern’s repeated, inexplicable visits symbolize persistent isolation.
  • Despite her eccentric behavior, she is a figure of tragic solitude.

Decay and Disorder

See: Decay and Ruin · Order, Chaos, and Discipline

  • Her physical smell and appearance evoke decay (rotted apples, dead flies).
  • The disorder she brings contrasts with the previously orderly household.
  • Symbolizes the intrusion of chaos into a controlled environment.

Madness and Sanity

See: Madness and Sanity

  • Mrs. Hogden’s behavior is perceived as madness, yet she retains a shrewd awareness and control.
  • The narrative questions who is truly mad: the woman or those rejecting her.
  • Madness is portrayed both as a social stigma and a complex psychological state.

Time and Permanence

See: Time

  • Mrs. Hogden talks about time running backward and forward, dreams of a motorboat, and eternal social seasons.
  • Her presence represents a temporary permanence, a fixture in a house and life otherwise transient.

Research: Symbols and Imagery

  • Mrs. Hogden herself is a complex symbol. She represents a kind of spectral presence, both corporeal and ghost-like, who invades the household and disturbs the established order. She is described as a “fat, corporeal, moon-eyed” woman who is not beautiful and who waddled “in and out of my dreams.” She embodies the intrusion of chaos and unwanted reality into a fragile, dreamlike world maintained by Vera’s mother and the memory of Miss MacIntosh.
  • Mrs. Hogden is also symbolic of decay and disorder, her physicality is often described in grotesque and unsettling terms, such as “rolling of loose, misshapen flesh,” “wrinkled breasts hanging like bags of whey,” and “a huge mold of greenish, bluish jelly.” She contrasts sharply with the idealized past represented by Miss MacIntosh and the house itself.
  • Miss MacIntosh and Mrs. Hogden, in their stark contrast, explore different facets of the novel’s central themes. Miss MacIntosh, the champion of stark reality, ultimately reveals a hidden life of profound vulnerability and disillusionment, making her a complex figure of “imperfection” that Vera comes to love. Mrs. Hogden, on the other hand, is a figure of superficial optimism and self-deception, a “grotesque parody” who inadvertently reveals the emptiness and shared nature of the very illusions she seems to embody. Through these two women, Young delves into the intricate relationship between outward appearance and inner truth, the nature of human suffering, and the pervasive power of imagination in shaping individual realities. Vera’s journey of understanding and acceptance, particularly regarding Miss MacIntosh, becomes a quest to reconcile the perceived and the concealed, the dream and the truth.
  • The playroom is a central symbolic space. It is “closed for so many years” and filled with “useless or forgotten objects,” old trunks, umbrellas, and boxes. This room represents a liminal space where the past and present collide, and where forgotten memories and decayed hopes reside. Mrs. Hogden inhabiting this space symbolizes the intrusion of decay and madness into the sanctuary of childhood memories and order. The moonlight that “lit her up” and the “silvery walls” that “shone around her like curled water” give the playroom an eerie, otherworldly quality, blurring the line between reality and dream.
  • Mrs. Hogden’s teaching of arithmetic is symbolized by the apples she brings, some of which are wormy, and later by buttons as substitutes. The apples and buttons stand for the attempt to impose order and reason in a chaotic, irrational world. The wormy apples suggest decay and imperfection beneath the surface of seemingly simple truths. Yet Mrs. Hogden’s faith that “two and two still making four” is a “triumph of reason” symbolizes a desperate clinging to logic and clarity amidst confusion.
  • The radio, described as an old cracked instrument producing static, multiple voices, and unintelligible noises, symbolizes the fragmented and unreliable nature of communication and reality in the house. Mrs. Hogden argues with announcers and imagines conversations among them, reflecting her fractured mental state and the fractured reality in which she dwells.
  • Mr. Res Tacamah, revealed to be a drug bottle, symbolizes the presence of medication, altered consciousness, and perhaps addiction or dependency, linking to the theme of mental instability.
  • The Arctic tern that visits Mrs. Hogden annually at her Dutch windmill home symbolizes a kind of haunting persistence and the natural cycle that contrasts with human loneliness and decay. The tern’s repeated visits, and Mrs. Hogden’s perception of being singled out by it, underline themes of isolation and the inexplicability of fate or nature.
  • Mrs. Hogden sitting “under a frieze of gargoyles” and the idea that “if Mrs. Hogden sat under the frieze of gargoyles long enough, she would become a gargoyle herself” symbolizes the transformation between human and stone, animate and inanimate, reality and myth. The statues and gargoyles represent permanence, desolation, and grotesque beauty, mirroring Mrs. Hogden’s own state and the house’s atmosphere.
  • The ivory-handed back-scratcher which Mrs. Hogden steals, symbolizes a small but tangible connection to the past and the household, a personal token in the midst of disorder. It also symbolizes Mrs. Hogden’s claim to the house and her attempt to assert identity and control.
  • Imagery of Mrs. Hogden wearing “a mask of beauty clay, cracking as it dried, only her eyes exposed, her eyes winking” and her multiple coats, diverse objects, and elaborate, sometimes disheveled wardrobe symbolize the layering of identity, the performance of self, and the blurring of appearance and reality. Her “blondish hair,” “bleached face,” and “plastered curls” depict a constructed and fragile persona.
  • Mrs. Hogden playing chess alone with an atomizer substituting for a bishop symbolizes her solitary struggle to impose order and control. The chessboard and the immovable Black King represent strategies, inevitability, and perhaps the futility of control over one’s fate.
  • Throughout the chapter, there is a recurring motif of dreaming: Mrs. Hogden’s presence in dreams, Vera’s mother dreaming, and the confusion between reality and imagination. Dreams symbolize the fragile boundary between perception and reality, memory and forgetting, sanity and madness.

Physical decay is a pervasive image

  • wormy apples, rotted fish-like faces, dirty and torn clothes, dust, dead flies, and foul smells. This imagery creates a sense of entropy and decline, reflecting the mental and physical deterioration of characters and the household.
  • The repeated emphasis on arithmetic, especially “two and two always making four,” functions as a symbol of order, logic, and certainty. Yet it is juxtaposed against the madness and chaos that Mrs. Hogden and the household embody, highlighting the tension between reason and irrationality.
  • Catherine and Mrs. Hogden, though seemingly antithetical, are deeply intertwined through their relationship with illusion and Vera’s perception.
  • Catherine creates illusions to escape a painful reality, while Mrs. Hogden accepts the house’s illusions as her own reality, finding profound happiness within them. Catherine is the “genuine unbeliever” in reality, while Mrs. Hogden is the “least critical human being.”
  • Catherine is a fading, beautiful ghost, a “dead beauty,” while Mrs. Hogden is an overwhelmingly corporeal, even grotesque, presence. Mrs. Hogden’s physical reality is a “stinking parody” of the house’s dreams.
  • Mrs. Hogden acts as a “substitute” for Miss MacIntosh in Vera’s mind and directly mirrors Catherine’s dreams, often speaking them aloud. Catherine even mistakes Mrs. Hogden for her dead Cousin Hannah, highlighting the fluidity of identity within the house’s dreamscape.
  • Mrs. Hogden’s character serves to “universalize” and “vulgarize” the “rare and individual and hidden” aspects of the house’s dreams, making them commonplace through her uncritical embrace.
  • Both characters, in their distinct ways, explore the novel’s central themes of reality, illusion, memory, and identity, offering different facets of a world where the boundaries between the living and the dead, the real and the imagined, are constantly dissolving.

Research: Resources

  • “there was a faceless woman, a Mrs. Hogden”: Mrs. Hogden is a complex, multifaceted figure who embodies disorder, decay, misplaced optimism, and the collapse of old certainties. She is a grotesque presence in the household after Miss MacIntosh’s departure, representing a stark contrast to the grounded, practical, and clear-eyed Miss MacIntosh. Mrs. Hogden is described as corpulent, overburdened with possessions, dressed in layers of ill-fitting clothes, and surrounded by chaos, both physical and mental. She clings to illusions of social status, authority, and control, despite her evident disarray and marginalization. She is simultaneously comic and tragic, a figure who inhabits a liminal space between reality and dream, presence and absence, sanity and madness. Symbolically, Mrs. Hogden could be seen as representing aspects of American society and history, especially those tied to the decline of certain old social orders and the ambiguous transition to modernity. Mrs. Hogden’s sale of her Dutch windmill, her carrying all her worldly goods in a two-door Ford, and her clinging to relics such as the beaded bag, the birdcage, and the Javanese temple bells evoke the image of a once-privileged class now reduced to decay and disarray. She could symbolize the fading of old American aristocracy or the genteel upper-middle class, who struggled to maintain dignity and status in a changing social landscape. Her presence in the house, with its priceless chairs and frozen grandeur, underscores the tension between fading grandeur and the disorder of decline. Mrs. Hogden’s peripatetic arrival, her confusion about places and people (mixing up Mr. Res Tacamah, a drug bottle, with a gentleman visitor), and her life of loneliness parallel the broader social dislocations in America, including the effects of the Great Depression, the migration from rural to urban areas, and the alienation of individuals in modern capitalist society. Her sense of being unwanted yet persisting reflects the experience of many who were left behind by rapid social and economic change. As a middle-aged woman burdened by social pretensions and personal illusions, Mrs. Hogden represents the constrained roles available to women before the feminist advances of the 1960s. Her role as a supposed “teacher of arithmetic” who never fulfills this role and instead devolves into a caricature of herself suggests the limitations and frustrations imposed on women whose identities were often tied to domestic service or caretaking roles, without autonomy or recognition. Mrs. Hogden’s refusal to acknowledge reality fully: her constant smiling despite ruin, her endless dressing and undressing, her imagining social events and parties in an empty house, and her inability to accept her own decline can be read as a metaphor for American society’s denial of its underlying problems. This denial includes racial segregation, economic inequality, and social injustice that persisted before the civil rights movements and social reforms of the 1960s. Mrs. Hogden may symbolize the marginalized individuals who existed on the peripheries of American prosperity, those who were invisible or ignored by mainstream narratives of progress. Her ambiguous identity (Mrs. Hogden, Logden, or Fogden), her lack of family or friends, and the servants’ refusal to acknowledge her expectations all point to a persona that is both part of and apart from society. Mrs. Hogden symbolically represents the decaying remnants of a bygone American social order, burdened by illusions of grandeur and authority, and caught in the liminal space between past certainties and an uncertain modern future.** She embodies the contradictions of persistence and decline, presence and invisibility, sanity and madness, reflecting the complex historical and social transformations experienced in the United States, including the decline of old aristocratic values, the dislocations of modernity, the constrained roles of women, and the societal denial of persistent inequalities. See Mrs. Hogden.
  • “my basting stitches to hold together surf and shore”: Basting stitches are long, temporary stitches used in sewing to temporarily hold fabric layers together, secure pleats, create gathers, or mark pattern lines before permanent stitching, allowing for easy removal and adjustments without damaging the fabric, often done with a machine’s longest stitch or by hand with a loose running stitch. They are crucial for fitting, easing fabric, and managing slippery materials, replacing pins to avoid bulk or shifting.
  • “It was her great desire that I should be brought up as a kindly extrovert”: The line refers to Miss MacIntosh’s strong wish for Vera to grow up as an outgoing, socially engaged person who interacts kindly and openly with others. Miss MacIntosh wants Vera to be a clear-eyed, active participant in life, focusing on reality and kindness toward others rather than retreating into introspection or fantasy, which she sees as less helpful or even harmful.
    • Extroverts gain energy from social interaction, thrive in groups, are often talkative and assertive, and process thoughts externally (thinking out loud). Introverts expend energy in social situations, need solitude to recharge, prefer deep dives into fewer topics, process internally, and are often described as reserved or introspective, though not necessarily shy. Both types exist on a spectrum, with most people being ambiverts, falling somewhere in the middle.
  • “according to Lisa Lunde, my mother’s young companion”: Lisa Lunde is presented as a sharp, young, aspiring physicist who works to support her poor and mentally ill mother. She occupies a role of both practical caretaker and critical observer within the household, particularly when dealing with Mrs. Hogden, whom she suspects of being a dubious character, possibly a shoplifter or deceiver. Lisa Lunde is skeptical, pragmatic, and often harsh in her judgments, especially toward Mrs. Hogden’s self-assured but chaotic presence. She acts as a foil to Mrs. Hogden’s delusional optimism and to the dreamlike, unstable atmosphere surrounding Vera’s mother, Catherine. Symbolically, Lisa Lunde could represent the emerging rational, scientifically minded, and socially aware American woman or intellectual figure in the early to mid-20th century. Lisa is a “would-be physicist,” embodying the growing presence of women entering scientific and intellectual fields in the US, especially during the early 20th century when women increasingly challenged traditional gender roles. Before 1965, women in science were rare and often marginalized, but they symbolized progress, rationality, and a break from the purely domestic roles prescribed to women in earlier eras. Lisa’s role as a breadwinner and caretaker for her mentally ill mother also reflects the increasing visibility of women as both laborers and family anchors in a changing social landscape. Lisa supports her poor and “mad” mother, who dreams of wealth despite poverty, highlighting the contradictions and struggles of many working-class American families during the early to mid-20th century. Many immigrants or second-generation Americans faced such hardships, balancing ambition and survival. Lisa’s pragmatic, no-nonsense attitude may symbolize the ethos of self-reliance and skepticism toward illusions that characterized many striving Americans. Lisa exposes Mrs. Hogden as potentially a shoplifter and ridicules her pretensions, thus acting as a guardian of social order and truth in the face of delusion and fantasy. This can be read as a broader symbolic role of the rational, modern American citizen who resisted charlatanism and false pretenses in a rapidly modernizing society, especially during the post-Depression and post-war years when social realism and pragmatic attitudes gained prominence. Lisa’s critical view of Mrs. Hogden and the fanciful world around Vera’s mother points to the tension between dream and reality, illusion and fact, an important theme in American culture, especially as the country grappled with modernity, the aftermath of the Great Depression, war, and social change. Lisa embodies the scientific, empirical mindset that confronts myth and deception. Lisa’s skepticism toward the older generation’s illusions (including those of Vera’s mother and Mrs. Hogden) may symbolize the younger generation’s disillusionment with the promises of the American Dream, especially in the years before the social upheavals of the 1960s. Her practical, sometimes harsh demeanor reflects a cultural shift toward realism and away from romantic or fanciful ideals that had dominated earlier eras. Symbolically, Lisa Lunde represents the scientifically educated, pragmatic, socially aware young American woman before 1965 who challenges illusions and embodies the tensions of modernity, class struggle, and generational change in the United States. She is a figure of rationality and skepticism standing in contrast to the dreamlike, unstable figures around her, reflecting broader cultural and historical shifts in American society during the early to mid-20th century. See Lisa Lunde.
  • “in a high tower at the ten cent store”: A ten cent store which goes by a variety of other names in the US was first established by Frank Winfield Woolworth who had seen the success in Michigan and western New York of nickel stores, where everything cost five cents. In 1879, Woolworth opened his Great Five Cent Store in Utica, New York, and it was his later success and expansion of that format as the F. W. Woolworth Company that would create the American institution of the five and ten cent store, five and ten, five and dime, or dime store.
  • “such as the old man who stole nothing but egg-beaters”: Kleptomania was named in 1816, and in the nineteenth century it was diagnosed above all in middle-class women caught taking goods from the new department stores, while poor shoplifters were simply called thieves. See Women, Gender, and Marriage.
  • “The life I required was the life which required, like his, a lost companion”: The line conveys a deep sense of longing for a meaningful connection beyond superficial or self-contained relationships. The passage highlights the importance of external bonds and the emotional reality of loss as shaping one’s life experience. It is an expression of the human need for companionship and the pain of its absence, distinguishing authentic relational life from a merely self-referential existence.
  • “Oh, she was a creature compounded of illusions”: Mrs. Hogden strongly embodies Quixotic characteristics through her elaborate self-deception and unwavering optimism in the face of a stark reality. See Don Quixote.
  • “Poor Lisa Lunde, the amateur physicist!”: The line serves as a wry, somewhat ironic commentary on Lisa Lunde’s position and perhaps on the nature of expertise itself. Lisa Lunde is described as a “would-be physicist” who works for her living to support her poor and mentally ill mother. Calling her an “amateur physicist” acknowledges that she is not yet fully established or recognized in her field, implying a sense of struggle or incompleteness. The narrator’s rhetorical question, “But are not all physicists amateurs?” suggests that even those who are formally experts in physics are, in a deeper sense, all amateurs because of the vast unknowns and uncertainties within the field. This comment subtly downplays the distinction between professional and amateur, hinting that no one truly masters the complexity of physics (or perhaps knowledge in general), so everyone works with partial understanding and constant questioning. Applied to Lisa Lunde, this phrase evokes sympathy (“Poor Lisa Lunde”) for her difficult situation but also gently elevates her by implying that her “amateur” status is not a mark of failure since everyone is in some way an amateur, navigating uncertainties.
    • Pioneering female physicists like Marie Curie, Lise Meitner, Irène Joliot-Curie, Maria Goeppert Mayer, and Chien-Shiung Wu made foundational discoveries in radioactivity, nuclear fission, and particle physics, often overcoming significant gender bias to contribute to breakthroughs like the first self-sustaining nuclear reaction and proving parity violation, though some, like Wu, were notably excluded from Nobel recognition for their experimental work. Marie Curie (1867-1934) was the first woman to win a Nobel Prize (Physics, 1903) and first person to win in two different sciences (Chemistry, 1911) for radioactivity research and discovering polonium and radium. Lise Meitner (1878-1968) was the co-discoverer of nuclear fission, though often overlooked, she was a central figure in understanding nuclear processes. Irène Joliot-Curie (1897-1956) was the daughter of Marie Curie, she won the Nobel Prize in Chemistry (1935) for synthesizing new radioactive elements. Maria Goeppert Mayer (1906-1972) was awarded the Nobel Prize in Physics in 1963 for her nuclear shell model, a major achievement in nuclear physics. Chien-Shiung Wu (1912-1997) conducted the crucial “Wu Experiment” that proved parity violation in particle physics, a discovery that earned two men the Nobel Prize in 1957 while she was excluded. Leona Woods Marshall Libby (1919-1986) was the only woman on the team that achieved the first self-sustaining nuclear chain reaction (Chicago Pile-1) in 1942. Marietta Blau (1894-1970) was a pioneer in using nuclear emulsions to study particle tracks, nominated multiple times for the Nobel Prize. Katharine Burr Blodgett (1898-1979) was the first woman to earn a PhD in physics from Cambridge (1926) and a key researcher at General Electric. Many faced discrimination as women and Jews, hindering their academic and professional advancement. Women like Wu and Blau made crucial experimental contributions that challenged theoretical physics. Despite groundbreaking work, several, including Wu and Meitner, were denied Nobel recognition. See Women, Gender, and Marriage.
  • “they had both understood so well that truth is beauty and beauty is truth”: “Beauty is truth, truth beauty,—that is all / Ye know on earth, and all ye need to know” (John Keats, “Ode on a Grecian Urn,” 1819). See Romantic Poets.
  • “one of those European refugees who had come from a town filled with storks”: There are “Stork Villages” such as: Ruhstadt, Germany, Zywkowo, Poland, Pentowo, Poland, Cigoc, Croatia, Alsace France, and Trujillo, Spain. These villages may also refer to the nearly 1000 Jewish Holocaust survivors brought to Fort Ontario in Oswego, New York by President Roosevelt in 1944 as America’s only World War II refugee shelter, known as “guests” offering a temporary sanctuary from Nazi Europe before World War II ended. They lived behind barbed wire, couldn’t work, and had to promise to return to Europe after the war, though most eventually stayed in the US. See Judaism.
  • “She had the almost seraphic look of an old alcoholic”: Seraphic is characteristic of a seraph, one of the seraphim, or an angelic being, regarded in traditional Christian angelology as belonging to the highest order of the ninefold celestial hierarchy, associated with light, ardor, and purity. See Angels and Archangels.
  • “She had sold the Dutch windmill which was her home on upper Long Island”: The old windmills of eastern Long Island, about a dozen still standing, are the largest group in America. Hook Windmill in East Hampton, NY is a historic 1806 gristmill, one of the most complete on Long Island, that operated until 1908 and is open to visitors as the Old Hook Mill. See the windmills in the Chapter 65 resources.
  • “A rose by any other name would smell as sweet”: “What’s in a name? that which we call a rose / By any other name would smell as sweet” (Romeo and Juliet 2.2). Mr. Spitzer answers the same way at the end of the chapter: “What’s in a name?” See Shakespeare.
  • “an Arctic tern with a black-rimmed eye”: The Arctic tern breeds in the Arctic and winters in the Antarctic, the longest migration of any bird, so that it sees more daylight than any other creature. See Birds and Astronomy.
  • “visual education being so progressive”: Visual education, teaching with pictures, lantern slides, films, and objects, was a cause of the progressive schools of the 1920s.
  • “the head of Alcibiades was in the drainpipe”: See the head of Alcibiades in the Chapter 2 resources and the Chapter 40 resources.
  • “droves of peaceful whales committing suicide upon a lonely beach”: Whale beachings were common natural events, often involving sick, old, or disoriented individuals, or sometimes large groups, with historical records showing strandings in places like Nantucket and New Zealand long before modern naval sonar, though documentation was less complete than today; events like a 1927 false killer whale mass stranding in Scotland demonstrate significant incidents, with causes typically attributed to disease, injury, or navigational errors, rather than solely modern human factors. See Suicide in History and Literature.
  • “She was descended from three signers of the Declaration of Independence”: Lineage societies such as the Daughters of the American Revolution (1890) made descent from the founders a mark of status. In 1939 the DAR barred the Black contralto Marian Anderson from singing at its Constitution Hall, and Eleanor Roosevelt resigned from it in protest. See Society, Class, and Race and Women, Gender, and Marriage.
    • Laura Haines Belman is a descendant of three signers: Samuel Chase, William Ellery, and Oliver Wolcott.
  • “She was an American citizen”: Mrs. Hogden can be symbolically interpreted as representing America itself, particularly aspects of its national character, materialism, and a certain kind of pragmatic, often self-deluding, innocence.
    • Mrs. Hogden explicitly identifies herself with the nation’s founding, stating she is “descended from three signers of the Declaration of Independence” and an “American citizen.” This directly links her to the historical origins and self-image of the United States.
    • Her physical description emphasizes her “overladen” state, wearing “at least four coats of seemingly graduated sizes,” burdened with “packages,” “cardboard boxes,” and various “diverse objects” like Javanese temple bells. This chaotic accumulation can symbolize America’s burgeoning consumer culture and materialism, as well as its “melting pot” nature, haphazardly collecting diverse cultural elements. The narrator’s observation that she is surrounded by “useless or forgotten objects” in the playroom reinforces this idea of a nation accumulating without necessarily valuing or integrating its possessions.
    • Her role as an “arithmetic teacher” who insists that “two and two always making four” and her ability to “win every argument” by not hearing it to its close can symbolize a national tendency towards simplistic solutions, a foundational but perhaps superficial understanding of truth, and a stubborn self-assurance that dismisses complexity.
    • Her “permanently adjusted to her temporary situation” mentality and her disregard for fixed schedules or routines, along with her former home being a “Dutch windmill” before her arrival, suggest a nation constantly reinventing itself or moving forward without deep ties to a consistent past, or perhaps a past that is “forgotten” or “cast-off.”
    • Despite her chaotic and often absurd behavior, she “exude[s] contentment” and is “the least critical human being,” believing herself to be the “mistress of the house” and pulling an “imaginary bellrope” to summon servants. This can symbolize a national self-perception of innocence and optimism, even in the face of underlying chaos or delusion, as well as a self-appointed authority. My mother’s perception of Mrs. Hogden as “mad as a loon” and a “parody,” yet one who embodies these American traits, further supports this.
    • Her aversion to James, the chauffeur, for shooting animals and Lisa Lunde’s retort that he went to Alaska “a quarter of a century ago,” dismissing his current reality, can be seen as a symbolic rejection of perceived “outsiders” or inconvenient truths.
    • Mrs. Hogden, with her blend of declared American heritage, material accumulation, simplistic certainty, and oblivious self-satisfaction amidst chaos, serves as a complex and often satirical symbol of the United States.
  • “none of these fish-headed Phoenicians”: Fish-headed Phoenicians may refer to Dagon or Dagan who was a god worshiped in ancient Syria as the father of gods. According to the Hebrew Bible, Dagan was also the national god of the Philistines. “And when they arose early on the morrow morning, behold, Dagon was fallen upon his face to the ground before the ark of the LORD; and the head of Dagon and both the palms of his hands were cut off” (1 Samuel 5:4, KJV). See The Bible.
  • “where was Mr. Res Tacamah, the delightful gentleman”: See Mr. Res Tacamah.
  • “driving a taxi cab in Nome, Alaska”: Nome, Alaska is a historic gold rush town on the Seward Peninsula, known for its Inupiat culture, gold mining history, and as the finish line for the Iditarod Trail Sled Dog Race. In 1925 dog-sled teams carried diphtheria antitoxin 674 miles to Nome in five and a half days, the serum run later remembered by the Iditarod (begun 1973). See James the Chauffeur.
  • “the Greek javelin-thrower with the snow on his shoulders”: The statue may refer to Phayllos of Kroton, famous for his seemingly impossible 55 foot long jump. He was a respected military commander. His discus or javelin throw is supposed to have been 95 feet.
  • “the shivering cherub wrapped in a bath towel”: Cherubim are in the books of Ezekiel and Revelation. They are majestic beings with four faces (man, lion, ox, eagle) representing divine power, majesty, and guardianship of God’s presence. The lion face signifies strength and kinship, the ox represents service, the man wisdom, and the eagle swiftness, with their overall form symbolizing God’s all-encompassing glory and authority. A lion’s skin evokes strength, majesty, and mythic power (recalling, for example, the Nemean lion’s skin worn by Hercules). The uncertain reference “was it a bath towel or a lion’s skin?” suggests a blurring between fragility and pretension, innocence and grandeur, reality and illusion. Applied to Mrs. Hogden, who is described as fat, oddly adorned, and carrying a confusing assortment of objects, this phrase underscores her contradictory character: she tries to present herself with an air of dignity and importance (like a lion’s skin) but is also pathetic and vulnerable (like a cherub wrapped in a bath towel). It reflects the novel’s themes of illusion, identity, and the tension between appearance and reality. The phrase metaphorically captures the complexity and ambiguity of Mrs. Hogden’s presence as part farcical, part tragic, both grand and diminished which highlights her as a figure caught between opposing qualities and uncertain roles within the household and narrative. See Angels and Archangels.
  • “a graduate of the Rhode Island State Teachers’ College”: Rhode Island College was founded in 1854 as the Rhode Island State Normal School.
  • “I have always wanted social security”: Social Security began with the Social Security Act of 1935, signed by President Franklin D. Roosevelt, creating a federal insurance system for old-age, unemployment, and aid for dependent mothers/children, funded by payroll taxes and intended as a safety net against economic hardship, evolving to include disability, Medicare, and automatic cost-of-living adjustments over time. The first monthly benefits were paid in 1940, establishing a cornerstone of American social welfare. This statement reflects Mrs. Hogden’s desire for stability, safety, and assurance in her later years, representing a longing for a dependable and secure life. Mrs. Hogden’s character is portrayed as a disordered, eccentric woman burdened by her past and her current precarious existence. When she says she has always wanted social security, it can be understood both literally and figuratively: 1) Social security here refers to the governmental program providing financial support and benefits to the elderly or disabled. Mrs. Hogden, having sold her home (the Dutch windmill) and brought all her possessions with her, hopes that her new position in Catherine’s house will provide her with a stable income and a secure livelihood for the rest of her life. 2) Beyond financial stability, the phrase encapsulates Mrs. Hogden’s deeper yearning for a place where she belongs, where she is cared for, and where she can live out her days without uncertainty or fear. Her arrival at the house and her insistence on staying, despite Catherine’s resistance, highlight her desperate need for security and acceptance. Mrs. Hogden’s longing for social security contrasts sharply with the instability and decline experienced by Catherine and the surreal, dreamlike atmosphere surrounding the household. It also underscores Mrs. Hogden’s practical, if somewhat delusional, approach to life, differing greatly from Miss MacIntosh’s grounded and clear-eyed presence. Mrs. Hogden’s statement can be seen as a poignant expression of her wish for material and emotional security in a world that has otherwise been unstable and unkind to her. See the Social Security Act in the Chapter 66 resources.
  • “Will the Bishop of Spade be coming?”: There is no such bishop; Mrs. Hogden’s title blends the bishop of the chessboard with the spade of the card deck. It fits a chapter built around a chess set “from which the bishop was missing.”
  • “She was like a mare sticking its head in through the window”: Compare Henry Fuseli’s painting The Nightmare (1781), in which a wild-eyed mare thrusts its head through the curtains above a sleeping woman. The “mare” of nightmare was once a goblin that sat on the sleeper’s chest, not a horse.
  • “if only to ride in a swan boat”: The swan boats of the Boston Public Garden, pedal boats behind great wooden swans, have carried riders since 1877.
  • “going all the way from Odessa to Siberia”: The phrase refers to historical movements, often forced, of people from the Black Sea port of Odessa (in modern Ukraine) to Siberia, particularly during the Russian Civil War and World War II, involving White Army remnants, ethnic Germans deported by Nazis/Soviets, or political prisoners, highlighting themes of exile, conflict, and displacement across vast distances within the Russian sphere of influence.
  • “died just north of Moscow by three departments”: A joke on Napoleon’s Grande Armée, which reached Moscow in 1812 and perished in the retreat across the frozen waste. Mr. Hogden, the floor-walker, dies between kitchenware and bedware. See Napoleon and Wellington.
  • “which she had won by solving a simple puzzle”: Prize puzzles asking readers and listeners to find what was missing from a picture were a craze of the 1930s, in newspapers and on the radio.
  • “It would admit both Jews and Negroes”: Catherine’s hotel “would admit both Jews and Negroes.” Jews and African Americans could not freely stay in hotels in the US until the passage of federal and state laws that banned discrimination in public accommodations, which was enforced with the Civil Rights Act of 1964. The Civil Rights Act of 1964 was a landmark piece of legislation that explicitly prohibited racial discrimination in public places, such as hotels, and this was the first time that Jewish people were also protected from discrimination in public places. The Civil Rights Act of 1964 prohibited discrimination based on race, color, religion, sex, or national origin in public accommodations like hotels, restaurants, and theaters. In the pre-1964 era, many hotels openly discriminated against both African Americans and Jews, often barring them from the premises entirely or requiring them to stay in separate, inferior accommodations. This was particularly true in the South, where discriminatory practices were widespread, even after the Civil War. In 1877 the banker Joseph Seligman was turned away from the Grand Union Hotel at Saratoga Springs because he was a Jew, and resorts advertised themselves as “restricted.” From 1936 Black travelers carried Victor Hugo Green’s Negro Motorist Green Book to find where they could sleep. See Judaism and Society, Class, and Race.
  • “this Mrs. Hogden must be my Cousin Hannah”: See Cousin Hannah, who recurs in Catherine’s dreams, in the Chapter 24 resources. See Catherine Cartwheel.
  • “a descendant of Daniel Boone and William the Conquerer and Alexander Graham Bell”: Daniel Boone was an American pioneer and frontiersman whose exploits made him one of the first folk heroes of the United States. (Wikipedia)
    • William the Conqueror was the first Norman king of England. (Wikipedia)
    • Alexander Graham Bell was a Scottish-born inventor, scientist and engineer who is credited with patenting the first practical telephone. (Wikipedia)
  • “the dolls exhumed from children’s graves”: The phrase refers to a macabre and symbolic assortment of objects that Vera’s father collected. These dolls, taken from children’s graves, are described as part of a collection that is both eerie and futile “useless” because they serve no practical purpose and perhaps because they embody a disturbing link to death and loss. This collection symbolizes the haunting presence of the past and the persistence of memory, even when it is unsettling or unwanted. The dolls, being exhumed from graves, evoke themes of death, childhood innocence lost, and the way memories or remnants of the past are kept alive in physical, but unsettling, objects. It reflects the novel’s broader atmosphere of decay, ghostliness, and the intertwining of life with death and dreams. The dolls are kept in the deserted playroom, which Mrs. Hogden occupies after Miss MacIntosh’s departure. This setting emphasizes the connection between the past (Vera’s childhood and family history), the present disarray, and the spectral or dreamlike quality that permeates the household. The phrase underscores the novel’s blending of reality and dream, and the weight of history and memory carried by seemingly trivial or “useless” objects. The “dolls exhumed from children’s graves” are a metaphorical and literal emblem of haunting memories and the eerie persistence of the past within the domestic space of Vera’s family. See the Chapter 31 resources.
  • “The sleighs had belonged to murdered royal children”: Sleighs suggest Russia: the five children of Tsar Nicholas II were murdered with their parents at Yekaterinburg in July 1918.
    • This may refer to The Princes in the Tower refers to the mystery of the fate of the deposed King Edward V of England and his younger brother Prince Richard of Shrewsbury, Duke of York, heirs to the throne of King Edward IV of England. The brothers were the only sons of the king by his queen, Elizabeth Woodville, living at the time of their father’s death in 1483. Aged 12 and 9 years old, respectively, they were lodged in the Tower of London by their paternal uncle and England’s regent, Richard, Duke of Gloucester, in preparation for Edward V’s forthcoming coronation. Before the young king’s coronation, however, he and his brother were declared illegitimate by Parliament. Gloucester ascended the throne as Richard III. It is unclear what happened to the two princes after the last recorded sighting of them in the tower. It is generally assumed that they were murdered; a common hypothesis is that the murder was commissioned by Richard III in an attempt to secure his hold on the throne. Their deaths may have occurred sometime in 1483, but apart from their disappearance, the only evidence is circumstantial. As a result, several other theories about their fates have been proposed, including the suggestion that they were murdered by their kinsman the Duke of Buckingham, their future brother-in-law King Henry VII, or his mother Lady Margaret Beaufort, among others. It has also been suggested that one or both princes may have escaped assassination. In 1487, Lambert Simnel initially was crowned in Dublin as “King Edward,” but later claimed by others to be York’s cousin the Earl of Warwick. And again several years later, from 1491 until his capture in 1497, Perkin Warbeck claimed to be the Duke of York, having supposedly escaped to Flanders. Warbeck’s claim was supported by some contemporaries, including York’s aunt the Duchess of Burgundy. In 1674, workmen at the Tower of London excavated, from under a staircase, a wooden box containing two small human skeletons. The bones were widely accepted at the time as those of the princes, but this has not been proven and is far from certain. King Charles II had the bones buried in Westminster Abbey, where they remain. These figures symbolize innocence lost amidst political intrigue and violence, fitting the novel’s motif of intertwined histories and personal tragedies.
  • “Louis Quatorze or Louise Quinze”: Louis Quatorze (Louis XIV, the “Sun King”) was France’s longest-reigning monarch (1643-1715) and an icon of absolute monarchy, known for centralizing power, glorifying France through arts and architecture (like Versailles), and establishing French cultural dominance; the term also refers to the ornate, Baroque style of his era.
    • Louis Quinze (Louis XV) refers to both the King of France (reigned 1715-1774) and the opulent French Rococo design style (Louis XV style) that flourished during his long reign, known for its curved lines, asymmetry, shell motifs, and luxurious comfort, marking a shift from the formal grandeur of Louis XIV. The style emphasized nature, intimacy, and craftsmanship, seen in intricate furniture with cabriole legs and elaborate decor, contrasting with the heavy formality of the previous era.
  • “She would squirt an atomizer into her mouth”: The atomizer later stands in for the missing bishop on the chessboard.
  • “like Mr. Spitzer, who could not tell the difference between himself and his dead identical twin”: See Peron Spitzer and Joachim Spitzer.
  • “a most outrageous déshabillé”: Déshabillé means the state of being only partly or scantily clothed.
  • “she would sit looking through a kaleidoscope”: David Brewster invented and named the kaleidoscope in 1816.
  • “famed set of chessmen which had belonged to my father”: The chess set is a symbolic detail connected to Mrs. Hogden’s character and the overall atmosphere of the novel. This chess set, once belonging to Vera’s father, is described specifically as missing the bishop piece. The missing bishop symbolizes an incomplete or disrupted order in the household and in the lives of the characters. Chess, a game of strategy and control, is here rendered imperfect, reflecting the disorder and the fractured reality that permeates Vera’s family and environment. Mrs. Hogden, who occupies the deserted playroom after Miss MacIntosh’s departure, uses this chess set in her solitary activities. She substitutes her atomizer for the missing bishop and continues to play, treating the atomizer as if it were the actual piece. This act highlights Mrs. Hogden’s ability to adapt to disorder and to impose her own illusory order on a fragmented world. It also implies her detachment from reality and her tendency to create her own meaning amid confusion. Mrs. Hogden’s playing chess alone with imaginary partners and her emotional responses to the game, crying when the Black King is checkmated, reflect her inner life and perhaps her longing for control and understanding in a chaotic existence. The missing bishop thus becomes a metaphor for absence, loss, and the incomplete nature of the house’s history and the characters’ lives. The missing bishop is not just a lost piece; it carries a sense of mystery and longing, reflecting perhaps a deeper theme of incompleteness or the search for something lost. Mrs. Hogden, who later occupies the household, even uses an atomizer as a substitute for the missing bishop when she plays chess alone, treating it as if it were the real piece and unable to distinguish between the two. This substitution emphasizes the symbolic nature of the missing bishop and the blending of reality and illusion present in the story.
  • “the Black King can never move from his position”: In chess the Black King is simply the king of the black pieces; Mrs. Hogden sets up problems in which it is checkmated without being able to move.
    • The most famous historical figure called the “Black King” (or Prince) is Edward of Woodstock, the eldest son of King Edward III of England, known as the Black Prince, though the exact reason for the nickname remains debated. An English prince, famous for his military prowess during the Hundred Years’ War, who never became king himself but was heir apparent. His black armor or black shield are potential origins for the name. The chess scenario symbolizes a situation of inevitable defeat or entrapment, reflecting Mrs. Hogden’s own existential and mental state as she navigates her disordered life and surroundings. Mrs. Hogden’s emotional response to this chess game (she sits and cries when the Black King is inextricably checkmated) suggests a deep identification with the helplessness and inevitability embodied by the Black King’s plight. She imagines her chessmen as planets moving under her control, which contrasts with her admission that the universe itself has no intelligence; this intelligence is hers alone.
  • “There is no return but the return of what is different”: Compare Heraclitus: no one steps into the same river twice, for other waters are ever flowing on.
  • “the unheard music of the spheres”: The passage reflects a philosophical meditation on the unavoidability of change, the human compulsion to find or impose meaning, and the possibility that such meaning is not inherent but constructed. It challenges the belief in a fixed cosmic order and suggests that what we perceive as meaningful patterns may be self-deceptions, resonating with existentialist skepticism and the impermanence stressed in ancient and modern philosophies. Pythagoras taught that the planets sound a harmony too perfect for human ears. Compare Keats, in the ode Vera has already echoed: “Heard melodies are sweet, but those unheard / Are sweeter.” See Pythagoras and the Music of the Spheres, Romantic Poets, and Existentialism.
  • “the crowds screaming on the Wilhelmstrasse when Hitler appeared”: Wilhelmstrasse is a major thoroughfare in the central Mitte and Kreuzberg districts of Berlin, Germany. Until 1945, it was recognised as the center of the government. Hitler addressed the cheering crowds on Wilhelmstrasse from a window of a modern chancellery annex building erected in 1930. (Wikipedia)
  • “Information, Please”: Information, Please, the NBC radio quiz (1938-1951), invited listeners to send in questions to stump its panel of experts.
  • “the Irish Catholic maid”: These young women (ages 15 to 24) were a cornerstone of U.S. domestic service from the mid-19th to early 20th centuries, arriving as young, single immigrants seeking economic opportunity after the Irish Famine, providing vital labor in cities, and using their wages to support families back home while facing discrimination but gaining a foothold in American society, often serving as a pathway to education and other professions for their children. In 1871 Harper’s Bazaar published an article named “Bridget” or “Biddy.” Biddy’s refusal to follow orders and her frequent bouts of insubordination compromised the tranquillity and moral calm that the nineteenth-century home and the creation of a domestic space were supposed to promise. An article in Harper’s Monthly noted to its mainly male audience that the result of Biddy’s presence was that ‘the master of the house returns from the cares and vexations of his day’s business, seeking repose in his home, but finds only disquiet’.13 It was the responsibility of Anglo-American women to devise solutions on how to put Biddy in her place, in order to preserve the sanctity of the home. See Women, Gender, and Marriage.
  • “cut on the bias”: The phrase means to cut fabric or food at a 45-degree angle to its grain or edges, not straight across, giving it more stretch, fluidity, and a softer drape. In sewing, it uses the fabric’s diagonal “true bias” for a slinky, body-hugging fit in dresses or skirts, popularized by couturier Madeleine Vionnet.
  • “Home, James, my good man”: “Home, James,” the order of the rich to the chauffeur, became a joke and a song title, “Home, James, and Don’t Spare the Horses” (1934). See James the Chauffeur.
  • “She had left it on the back of a crab at the surf’s edge”: Miss MacIntosh’s wig, not Mrs. Hogden’s. See her walk into the sea in the Chapter 65 resources.
  • “All a’s are b’s, it read”: The message is a syllogism, the first of Aristotle’s forms of valid reasoning (Prior Analytics), which medieval logicians named Barbara: all A is B; all B is C; therefore all A is C. Lewis Carroll filled his Symbolic Logic (1896) with such puzzles. Mrs. Hogden, who said that “Things that confused other people never confused her,” leaves Vera a proof and a riddle.
