Chapter 40

← Chapter 39 · Home · Chapter 41 →

Content note: Vera’s mother, Catherine Cartwheel, is addicted to opium.

Summary

Catherine remembers Cousin Hannah’s voice, a husky baritone like iron bells, and believes Hannah taught her every language of the living and the dead, from Saracen and Provençal to the speech of seals and Platan rails, though Catherine herself had studied nothing but the French of a Peacock Alley menu. In her room she still converses with Alcibiades, Dante, Daniel Boone, and Darius, who answers the kitchen telephone. Her memories come without sequence, the echo before the song, the death before the life. She once greeted every stranger as a cousin and went to bed to escape the embarrassment, and now she introduces the living among the dead, to Mr. Spitzer’s patient wonder. She suspects that Hannah’s adventures, like her own, may have been dreams. She had no faith to lose, and she cannot say whether opium caused her somnolence or her somnolence the opium. She is many selves at once, the horse and the rider, and she believes that a ship’s figurehead knows more than its captain, because it always goes first.

Characters present

Cousin Hannah · Catherine Cartwheel · Joachim Spitzer · The Black Coachman · Vera Cartwheel

Concepts present

Themes: Death and Mortality · Dreams and Imagination · Identity and the Self · Illusion and Reality · Memory and the Past · Music, Sound, and Silence · Order, Chaos, and Discipline · Time · Women, Gender, and Marriage

Symbols: Angels, Devils, and Myth · Birds · Clouds and Storms · Dogs · Horses and Carriages · Mirrors and Reflections · Moon and Stars · Opium

Philosophy: Aristotle · Buddhism · Descartes and Dualism · Hinduism · Nietzsche · Plato and Platonism · Stoicism · Taoism and Zhuangzi

Allusions: American Writers · Ancient Egypt · Astronomy · Dante · Exploration and the Poles · Genesis · Greek Mythology · Judaism · Milton · Music and Composers · Revelation and the Apocalypse · Romantic Poets · Shakespeare · Sir Walter Raleigh · The Bible · The Book of Job

Key passages

From the research

  • The chapter opens with a vivid, almost surreal description of Cousin Hannah’s voice as “a husky baritone, ranging between bass and tenor…as loud, as heavy as iron bells ringing in a leaden-colored northern sky.” This voice is not merely physical but carries an oratorio-like Gothic cathedral weight, symbolizing a profound, almost otherworldly presence. Cousin Hannah is portrayed as a polyglot fluent in “dead languages,” “languages of the dead,” and innumerable tongues, both real and imagined, from “fourteenth-century Saracen or Spanish cavalier” to “Sanskrit from a holy text printed on a snowflake” and “the hieroglyphic language of the drowned Egyptian sailor.” This linguistic breadth represents a connection across time, cultures, and even worlds: living and dead. It suggests a mystical or dreamlike knowledge that transcends normal human experience.
  • The narrative explores the disordered nature of Catherine’s memories and perceptions, emphasizing non-linear time and chaotic mental states. Events do not follow sequentially but occur in a “medley, the imbroglio, Pandemonium, Saturnalia of her deranged imagination.” Time is depicted as fluid, with “a step forward would be a step backward,” and phenomena such as “the after-glow came before the sunset” or “the echo came before the song.” This passage captures the confusion between reality and dream, suggesting a psychological or metaphysical state where logic and chronology dissolve.
  • Catherine is described as “many selves, many beautiful, volatile Psyches wandering about” yet physically “lying in bed, propped up among satin pillows.” This duality between her fragmented inner selves and her physical frailty conveys themes of identity fragmentation and alienation. She greets strangers as friends or relatives, blurring social boundaries, and retreats into solitude to avoid “social embarrassments.” The passage evokes loneliness and the tension between imaginative expansiveness and corporeal confinement.
  • The chapter reflects deeply on death and what follows, with Catherine’s dreams merging “life… and death” into one indistinct realm. The phrase “life was that which, as it had had no beginning, should have no end, not even this death” reveals a mystical vision of existence as continuous and cyclical rather than finite. The suffragette’s struggles are framed as part of a cosmic drama involving light and darkness, “cloud-rack and storm” rather than “eternal darkness.” This suggests hope and transformation rather than finality in death.
  • The closing passages emphasize fluidity and interconnectedness: “All was water. The water flowed over the mooned sand. The sentinels slept at the shifting borderlands.” This dreamlike imagery expresses a world without fixed boundaries, where “there was no place, but there were all places dreaming together, flowing like water into each other.” Catherine’s sense of ubiquity, being in many places at once, or being both rider and horse, symbolizes a dissolution of individual selfhood into a larger, flowing existence.
  • The final metaphor contrasts the figurehead of a ship with its captain, with Catherine believing “the figurehead knew more, the waters roaring at its mouth. For one thing, it always went first.” This image can be read as a symbol of intuition, the unconscious, or the spiritual leading the conscious self through the turbulent seas of life and death.

Questions and observations

Reading closely

  • English was, Catherine says, “the only foreign language to her.” What does she mean?
  • “Perhaps the most important thoughts were those which never found expression.” Why should Hannah have spoken at all, if “silence should have spoken for her”?
  • Had opium caused her somnolence, or had her somnolence been the cause of her taking opium? Which came first?

Characters

  • Hannah “had come not to create but to destroy the last romance on earth.” Why does Catherine remember her as romance itself?
  • Mr. Spitzer waits “all his life here to prove that he no longer lived.” What would such proof look like?
  • Catherine greeted every stranger as “Cousin Jack” or “Cousin Wilbur.” Is her mistake a kind of welcome?

Connections

  • In Chapter 39 Catherine was “the chair… the lamp… Brooklyn Bridge.” Here she is “both the fox-hunter and the fox.” How do her selves multiply?
  • Hannah always whispered, “I am dead.” How does this echo Mr. Spitzer, who in Chapter 36 “had led a single life— knowing he was dead”?
  • The wheels of the coach are “the sleeping seraphim,” as the cherubim were in Chapter 39. Where is this carriage going?

Reflection

  • “If one had no knowledge, should one not have freedom to imagine”?
  • Can a person understand a language she has never learned?
  • Is it better to go first, like the figurehead, or to steer?

Research: Characters

Cousin Hannah

  • A suffragette and member of an old, aristocratic family (“Old Guard”).
  • Portrayed as a spectral, dream-like figure, both vibrant and ghostly.
  • Speaks in multiple languages, including dead and mythical tongues, embodying the “languages of the dead” and those never spoken.
  • Eccentric, passionate, and combative, yet enigmatic in her presence and communication.
  • Her voice is described as powerful and haunting, a “Gothic cathedral weight.”
  • Seems to exist partly in the realm of dreams or memory rather than pure reality.
  • Her voice was “a husky baritone, ranging between bass and tenor and partaking somewhat of the quality of both.”
  • She swore like “an old veteran of the cavalry,” with “zounds,” “egad,” “caitiff,” “craven,” and “tallyho.”
  • “I am dead—had not old Cousin Hannah always whispered, even when she was vitally alive, the beau ideal of suffrage.”

Catherine Cartwheel (Vera’s mother)

  • Reflects on her memories and impressions of Cousin Hannah.
  • Although limited in formal education, she surprisingly understands many languages and voices, real or imagined, symbolizing a deep intuitive or dreamlike comprehension.
  • Lives a life intermingled with dreams, illusions, and layers of time and memory.
  • Struggles to order events or states of being logically, experiencing time and experience as fragmented and fluid.
  • Has an opium habit that blurs reality and dreams, contributing to the fluidity between life and death, reality and imagination.
  • English was “the one language she really knew, the only foreign language to her.”
  • She had greeted every stranger as a cousin, “so that she had gone to bed to save herself from further social embarrassments. Then she had begun to speak where there was no one.”
  • “She had had no faith to lose, so change had followed change, and chance had followed chance.”
  • She was always “the errant somnambulist,” and she believes “the figurehead knew more.”

Mr. Spitzer

  • Embodies a skeptical and analytical perspective amid the swirling dreamlike and often chaotic narrative centered on Catherine and Cousin Hannah.
  • Portrayed as a patient observer who frequently comments on Catherine’s behavior and mental state.
  • He is described as believing himself to be “non-competitive,” a detail that suggests a self-aware, possibly detached attitude toward social or intellectual contests.
  • His habitual gestures like pulling the jowl of his cheek, tapping his teeth with a toothpick which is noted as a “tiny diamond-headed gold walking stick,” add a layer of characterization that conveys both a certain meticulousness and an almost aristocratic fastidiousness. This imagery paints Mr. Spitzer as a man deeply engaged in subtle, perhaps cynical reflection.
  • His observations reveal an inclination toward rational skepticism. For example, he frequently notices Catherine’s “serene unconcern for facts,” and how she “would introduce the living among the dead,” blurring the boundaries between reality and fantasy, life and death. Mr. Spitzer seems to see Catherine’s tendencies as both a kind of madness and a poignant human frailty, noting how she assumes that some living people have already “passed over to the other shore,” thus reflecting her confusion or perhaps her unique perception of existence.
  • He is described as “waiting all his life here to prove that he no longer lived, that he had died long ago,” which imbues his character with a certain existential irony or fatalism.
  • In the context of the chapter’s dreamlike atmosphere, where time is non-linear, identities are fluid, and reality merges with imagination, Mr. Spitzer functions as a grounding figure, representing a rational, if somewhat resigned, viewpoint.

The Black Coachman

  • “She heard the coachman’s whip like the dark tree branches whirling,” and “horses and coach and coachman were one entity passing through the rolling fog.”

Research: Themes

Language and Communication

See: Music, Sound, and Silence

  • Language is a major motif: Cousin Hannah’s polyglot abilities symbolize the bridge between past and present, life and death.
  • Vera’s mother understands languages not through formal study but through mystical or dreamlike insight.
  • The narrative suggests some languages transcend spoken word, being part of an ineffable, universal communication.

Memory, Dream, and Reality

See: Illusion and Reality · Dreams and Imagination · Memory and the Past

  • The chapter blurs the boundaries between what is remembered, what is dreamed, and what is real.
  • Time is non-linear; events and voices intermingle without chronological order, reflecting Catherine’s fragmented memory and dream state.
  • Catherine frequently questions the reality of her experiences, wandering “not only the known world but the unknown world which she knew so very well because no one knew the unknown.”

Death and Immortality

See: Death and Mortality

  • Characters like Cousin Hannah and references to historical or mythical figures suggest a liminal state between life and death.
  • For Catherine, death is not an end but a transformation or continuation of existence in another form: “life was that which, as it had had no beginning, should have no end, not even this death.”
  • The motif of ghosts, spirits, and the “dead languages” reinforces the permeable boundary between the living and the dead.

Identity and Multiplicity of Self

See: Identity and the Self

  • Catherine perceives herself as many selves, reflections, and chimeras, sometimes unable to distinguish her true self from her images or memories.
  • This multiplicity reflects the complexity of identity within the realms of memory, dream, and consciousness.

Time and Order

See: Time · Order, Chaos, and Discipline

  • The chapter challenges conventional notions of time and causality (“the echo came before the song,” “death came before life”).
  • Time is cyclical, layered, and full of “refractions” and “oblique passages,” making logic and sequence unreliable.

Research: Symbols and Imagery

Gothic Cathedral Voice

  • “Her voice had been a Gothic cathedral weight, an oratorio accompanied by many singing, whistling voices.”
  • Symbolizes the weight and grandeur of Cousin Hannah’s presence and communication.

Clouds, Stars, and Celestial Imagery

See: Moon and Stars · Clouds and Storms

  • Frequently used to evoke dreamlike states, mystery, and the vastness of time and space.

Mirrors and Reflections

See: Mirrors and Reflections

  • Suggest duality, multiplicity of identity, and blurred boundaries between self and other.

Angelic and Mythical Figures (e.g., angels, unicorns, griffins)

See: Angels, Devils, and Myth

  • Symbolize transcendence and the mingling of reality and fantasy.

Opium and Somnolence

See: Opium

  • Represent altered states of consciousness, blurring reality and dream.

The Horse and Rider

See: Horses and Carriages

  • Symbolize unity and inseparability of entities, reflecting on identity and consciousness.
  • “Sometimes she thought she was riding on her own back… she did not know whether she was the horse or the rider, the carrier or the carried.”

Research: Resources

  • “Was her vizor up or down”: A vizor, or visor, is the movable front of a helmet, lowered to cover the face in battle.
  • “Silence should have spoken for her”: “Speech is silvern, Silence is golden” (Thomas Carlyle, Sartor Resartus 3.3, 1836).
  • “and the black sunlight”: “Le Soleil noir de la Mélancolie,” “the black sun of Melancholy” (Gérard de Nerval, “El Desdichado,” 1854).
  • “for all was fair in love and war”: “all was fair in love and war” is a proverb generally attributed to John Lyly’s 1578 novel, Euphues: The Anatomy of Wit. Euphues is described as a type of student who is “apt by goodness of wit, and applicable by readiness of will, to learning, having all other qualities of the mind and parts of the body.” Although the exact phrasing used today, “All’s fair in love and war” didn’t appear until Francis Edward Smedley’s 1850 novel, Frank Fairleigh; or, Scenes from the Life of a Private Pupil, a domestic English drama of virtue rewarded and vice getting its just deserts, based on Smedley’s own experiences.
  • “like turreted steeplechase riders”: See the steeplechase entry in the Chapter 35 resources.
  • “which was fourteenth-century Saracen or Spanish cavalier”: Saracen were primarily Arab Muslims, Turks, Persians, or other Muslims according to Christian writers during the Middle Ages in Europe.
    • Cavalier is associated with the Royalist supporters of King Charles I and across Europe as a style of dress during the seventeenth-century.
  • “the language of the Nubian boy”: Nubians are an ethnolinguistic group of people indigenous to what is now present-day Sudan and Egypt. See Ancient Egypt.
  • “the language of Volpone who died an imaginary death”: Volpone is a comedy play by English playwright Ben Jonson. It is a satire of greed and lust.
    • In Act 5 of Volpone (1606) he feigns death to watch his would-be heirs, and is unmasked.
  • “which was Sanskrit from a holy text printed on a snowflake”: Sanskrit is a classical language of South Asia. It is the sacred language of the Vedas. See Hinduism.
  • “which was ancient Eskimo hunter”: Eskimo are the indigenous peoples who live from eastern Siberia, Alaska, Canada, and Greenland.
    • Eskimo is Young’s word. Many Inuit and Yupik people now reject it. See Exploration and the Poles.
  • “the hieroglyphic language of the drowned Egyptian sailor”: Egyptian sailor may refer to the Tale of the Shipwrecked Sailor. The proverbs from this story are: the mouth of a man saves him; do not act arrogant; why give water to a bird before it is slaughtered. It is interpreted as a shipwrecked traveler goes on a spiritual quest through the cosmos and meets a primordial god that provides the traveler with a moral vision to return home with. See Ancient Egypt.
  • “the language of the dead Finnish king with the long heron toes”: Finnish is from Finland and herons are considered the king of the wading birds.
    • See the heron-footed King Canute in the Chapter 35 resources.
  • “third-century Chinese polo players storming over the roofs of Peking”: Polo is a horseback ball game and one of the oldest known team sports.
    • Peking, now known as Beijing, is the capital of the People’s Republic of China.
    • Polo was the passion of the Tang court in China in the seventh and eighth centuries.
  • “which was Provencal, that language of the wandering Troubadour”: Provencal is a language and region of France.
    • Troubadour was a composer and performer of lyric poetry during the High Middle Ages.
    • Jaufre Rudel sang of amor de lonh, love from afar, for a countess of Tripoli he had never seen. His legend says he sailed to her and died in her arms.
  • “which was Greek shepherd singing to his flock”: Greek shepherd may refer to several references listed. The Passionate Shepherd to His Love is a poem by Christopher Marlowe which was responded to by Raleigh in Nymph’s Reply to the Shepherd and later by different poets over the years. See Sir Walter Raleigh.
    • Pan in Greek mythology is the god of the wild, shepherds and flocks, rustic music and impromptus, and companion of the nymphs. He has the hindquarters, legs, and horns of a goat, in the same manner as a faun or satyr. See Greek Mythology.
    • In Greek mythology, Daphnis was a Sicilian shepherd who was said to be the inventor of pastoral poetry.
  • “her furies against archaeologists with pick and spade”: Feminist archaeology employs a feminist perspective in interpreting past societies. It often focuses on gender, but also considers gender in tandem with other factors, such as sexuality, race, or class. Feminist archaeology has critiqued the uncritical application of modern, Western norms and values to past societies. It is additionally concerned with increasing the representation of women in the discipline of archaeology, and reducing a masculine bias within the field. In archaeology this includes: focusing on presumed male roles such as hunter, warrior, chief, and farmers; under-analyzing activities considered to be in the female domain by western tradition; interpreting data from the perspective of middle-age, middle-class, western white men (Margaret W. Conkey and Janet D. Spector, “Archaeology and the Study of Gender,” Advances in Archaeological Method and Theory 7, 1984). See Women, Gender, and Marriage.
  • “like her furies against believers in a future life”: In Chapter 36 Catherine wondered whether Hannah had “gone over from the cross to the crescent.” Here Hannah rages against “believers in a future life or a past life,” as in Chapter 35, where she “had had no faith… in any after-life.”
  • “the French of a Peacock Alley menu”: Peacock Alley was the long corridor joining the Waldorf and Astoria hotels in New York, opened in 1897, where fashionable society strolled to see and be seen. The name moved with the Waldorf-Astoria to Park Avenue in 1931 and lived on in its restaurant.
  • “owls and nightingales and whirling dervishes”: Whirling dervishes or Sufi whirling is a meditation practice performed within a worship ceremony.
    • The whirling dervishes are the Mevlevi order, founded in Konya by the followers of the poet Rumi in the thirteenth century.
  • “chantings of Tibetan monks”: Tibetan monks in Tibetan Buddhism chant mantras which are phrases that protect the mind from negativity. See Buddhism.
  • “cries of Chinese mandarins with great butterfly sleeves”: Chinese mandarins or Mandarins was a bureaucrat scholar in ancient China, Korea and Vietnam. They were officials appointed through the imperial examination system.
  • “screaming contests of Platan rails like the human voice exerted to its utmost pitch”: Young’s source is W. H. Hudson, who describes the giant wood rails, the ypecaha, of La Plata: “This is a tremendous screaming concert,” and “The screams they utter have a certain resemblance to the human voice, exerted to its utmost pitch” (W. H. Hudson, The Naturalist in La Plata, 1892, chapter 19, “Music and Dancing in Nature”). See Birds.
  • “as if it were she who had driven the sun against the clouded net, stopping time”: “And the sun stood still, and the moon stayed” (Joshua 10:13). See The Bible.
  • “who else had talked to so many water carriers in clouds”: The water carrier is Aquarius, the constellation of the zodiac. See Astronomy.
  • “a rider in the great Coffin of Stars”: Coffin of Stars may refer to Delphinus and the main group of stars called Job’s Coffin. See The Book of Job and Astronomy.
  • “voices buzzing like bees in Magellanic Clouds”: Magellanic Clouds are two irregular dwarf galaxies in the Southern Celestial Hemisphere.
    • They are named for Ferdinand Magellan, whose crew recorded them on the first circumnavigation of the world (1519-1522). See Exploration and the Poles.
  • “so many pharaohs in swan boats passing with the sentinel moon”: The pharaohs’ boats recall the solar barque of Ra, which carried the sun god across the sky by day and through the underworld by night. See Ancient Egypt.
  • “or Boston Greek”: Boston Greek: a significant wave of immigration between 1890 and 1921 to the US with many settling in Boston. Greeks entering the country rose from 524 in 1890 to 25,675 in 1910 (Thomas Burgess, Greeks in America, 1913, quoted in George J. Leber, The History of the Order of AHEPA, 1922-1972, Order of AHEPA, 1972). About a hundred Boston Hellenes formed the Plato Society in 1890 to help with life in their new country and to provide religious services. It disbanded after several years for lack of money. In 1899 efforts resumed to bring the Greeks of Boston together, and in 1905 the Hellenic Association of Boston was chartered (Christopher Gussis, “The Historic Boston Greek Cathedral: Reliving 100 Years,” Annunciation Greek Orthodox Cathedral of New England). The Boston community bought a church building, the first owned by Greeks after that of New Orleans, and in 1910 the Pan-Hellenic Union fixed its headquarters in Boston (Leber).
  • “how should she be this human Tower of Babel”: Tower of Babel in Genesis 11 is an origin myth to explain why the world’s peoples speak so many different languages. “Therefore is the name of it called Babel; because the LORD did there confound the language of all the earth” (Genesis 11:9). See Genesis.
  • “just as a thought is changed by speech”: “A thought once uttered is a lie” (Fyodor Tyutchev, “Silentium!,” 1830).
  • “the king of the Medes”: King of the Medes may refer to Darius the Mede who is mentioned in the Hebrew Bible in the Book of Daniel as a King of Babylon but is not known to history. See The Bible.
  • “the language of bawling Alcibiades, that drunken war lord”: Alcibiades was a prominent Athenian statesman, orator, and general.
    • In Plato’s Symposium (212d) Alcibiades bursts in drunk, crowned with ivy and violets, and praises Socrates. See Plato and Platonism.
  • “Alexander the Great, King of Macedon”: Alexander the Great, King of Macedon, was a king in ancient Greece.
  • “the bird king whose head was turned backward upon his shoulders”: In Dante’s Inferno 20 the diviners walk with their heads twisted backward: “For tow’rds the reins the countenance was turned, / And backward it behoved them to advance” (trans. Henry Wadsworth Longfellow, 1867). See Dante.
  • “many who were kings before Christ and many who came afterward”: Young’s list runs from Alexander the Great to Boethius, Balboa, Baldwin, Columbus (“Christolpho Colombo”), Cánovas del Castillo, Hugh Capet, Dante, Diderot, and Harold Harefoot.
  • “Boethius, Balboa, Baldwin”: Boethius or Anicius Manlius Severinus Boethius was a Roman senator, consul, magister officiorum, and philosopher.
    • Balboa or Vasco Nunez de Balboa was a Spanish explorer, governor, and conquistador. In 1513 he became the first European to see the Pacific from the Americas.
    • Baldwin may be Baldwin I, the first crusader King of Jerusalem (1100-1118).
  • “Christolpho Colombo”: Christolpho Colombo or Christopher Columbus was an Italian explorer and navigator who completed four voyages across the Atlantic Ocean. See Exploration and the Poles.
  • “Canovas del Castillo”: Canovas del Castillo or Antonio Canovas del Castillo was a Spanish politician and historian known principally for serving six terms as Prime Minister and instrumental in reinstituting the Bourbon monarchy.
    • He was assassinated by the anarchist Michele Angiolillo in 1897.
  • “Hugh Capet who had arisen from his watery grave”: Hugh Capet was the King of the Franks.
    • He reigned from 987 to 996 and founded the Capetian dynasty.
  • “ageless Dante”: Dante or Durante di Alighiero degli Alighieri was a Florentine poet, writer and philosopher. See Dante.
  • “revolutionary Diderot”: Diderot or Denis Diderot was a French philosopher, art critic, and writer.
    • He edited the Encyclopédie (1751-1772).
  • “Harold Harefoot”: Harold Harefoot or Harold I was King of England.
    • After his death in 1040 his half-brother Harthacnut had his body dug up and thrown into a fen, and it was later buried again (Anglo-Saxon Chronicle).
  • “that she listened for hours to Ahaseuris, the Wandering Jew”: Ahaseuris or Ahasuerus is the name of a king, the husband of Esther, in the Book of Esther from the Bible. A German pamphlet of 1602 gave the same name to the Wandering Jew, and Young follows it. See The Bible and Judaism.
  • “as she preferred to think of him, the Everlasting Jew”: Der ewige Jude, the Everlasting Jew, is the German name of the Wandering Jew. The Everlasting Jew is also the title of a modern collection of the writings of Rabbi Isaac Lichtenstein (1825-1908), ed. D. Thomas Lancaster (First Fruits of Zion, 2013). Lichtenstein who after an encounter with the Gospel became an outspoken disciple of Yeshua (Jesus) of Nazareth, but he remained in his post as district rabbi for several years. Despite pressure from rabbinic authorities, Jewish believers, and Christian leaders, he could not be compelled to renounce Judaism or his devotion to the Torah. He is regarded as a pioneer of the Messianic Jewish movement. See Judaism.
  • “Hebrew parables in palaces of red sandalwood”: Hebrew parables or Mashal/nimshal is a short parable with a moral lesson or religious allegory.
    • Solomon made pillars and harps of almug trees (1 Kings 10:12), often identified as red sandalwood. See The Bible.
  • “tinkling bells and many horns in faraway Cathay”: Cathay is an alternative European historical name for China.
  • “How else could she communicate now so easily with Darius the Magnificent”: Darius the Magnificent is most likely Darius I, the Great, King of Persia (522-486 BC). Another possibility is Dara Shikoh, who was the eldest son and heir-apparent of the Mughal emperor Shah Jahan. He was defeated by his younger brother.
  • “the sleepy voice of Potiphar”: Potiphar is the captain of the Pharaoh’s guard who is said to have purchased Joseph as a slave in the Hebrew Bible and Quran (Genesis 39:1). See Genesis.
  • “Cousin Hannah had also spoken the King’s English”: “Here will be an old abusing of God’s patience and the King’s English” (Shakespeare, The Merry Wives of Windsor 1.4). See Shakespeare.
  • “such words as zounds”: Zounds is short for “God’s wounds,” the wounds of Christ, as egad is for “ah, God.”
  • “defender of the faith”: “Defender of the faith” is a title traditionally held by the British monarch, symbolizing their role as the supreme governor of the Church of England. The title was originally granted by Pope Leo X to Henry VIII in 1521 for his defense of the Catholic Church against Martin Luther. While the title was later revoked by the papacy, it was reestablished by Parliament and continues to be used by the monarch today. Here it is one of Cousin Hannah’s oaths.
  • “Avaunt, villains, knaves, blackamoors, blackbirds, Boanerges”: Avaunt means to move away, depart. Boanerges is a vociferous preacher or orator. A nickname applied by Jesus to James and John in Mark 3. “Boanerges, which is, The sons of thunder” (Mark 3:17). See The Bible.
  • “both the fox-hunter and the fox”: Oscar Wilde called the English fox-hunter “the unspeakable in full pursuit of the uneatable” (A Woman of No Importance, Act 1, 1893).
  • “the medley, the imbroglio, Pandemonium, Saturnalia”: Medley is a varied mixture of people or things.
    • Imbroglio is an acutely painful or embarrassing misunderstanding.
    • Pandemonium is a wild uproar among a crowd of people. John Milton invented the name in Paradise Lost for the capital of Hell. (Paradise Lost 1.756). See Milton.
    • Saturnalia was an ancient Roman festival and holiday in honor of the god Saturn. It was held on December 17th of the Julian calendar and later expanded with festivities through to December 23rd. The Saturnalia reflects the contradictory nature of the deity Saturn himself with joyful and utopian aspects of careless well-being and disquieting elements of threat and danger.
    • The actual date of Jesus’s birth is unknown. A reported correspondence between Cyril of Jerusalem and Pope Julius I, quoted by John of Nikiu in the 9th century, is sometimes given as a source for a claim that, in the fourth century AD, Pope Julius I formalized that the nativity of Christ should be celebrated on December 25th as possibly a way to entice more converts to Christianity. Vestiges of the Saturnalia festivities may still be preserved in some of the traditions now associated with Christmas. The custom of gift-giving at Christmas time resembles the Roman tradition of giving small or gag gifts and the lighting of Advent candles resembles the Roman tradition of lighting torches and wax tapers. Likewise, Saturnalia and Christmas both share associations with eating, drinking, singing, and dancing. (Wikipedia)
  • “occultations as when a star crossed the moon”: An occultation is the passing of one heavenly body in front of another, as when the moon hides a star. Catherine has it the other way round. See Astronomy.
  • “maybe Daniel Boone, wearing his coonskin hat”: Daniel Boone: See the Chapter 70 resources.
    • Boone himself wore a broad-brimmed felt hat. The coonskin cap belongs to the Davy Crockett craze of the 1950s. See American Writers.
  • “the life of the oppossum which, when caught, feigns death”: Playing possum: the opossum, when caught, falls limp and seems dead for minutes or hours.
  • “the ubiquitous pigeons of St. Mark’s Square”: St. Mark’s Square or Plaza San Marco is the principal public square of Venice, Italy.
  • “She was struck by moon blindness”: Catherine claims to have moon blindness even though she knew it affected horses and not humans. Moon blindness or equine recurrent uveitis is the leading cause of blindness in horses with the specific cause unknown. See Horses and Carriages.
  • “She heard the angelus”: See the angelus entry in the Chapter 35 resources.
  • “an emperor’s riding party hunting the unicorn”: See the Unicorn Tapestries entry in the Chapter 35 resources.
  • “balloonists who had not been sighted for years”: S. A. Andrée’s balloon expedition to the North Pole vanished in 1897. The men’s last camp was found on White Island in 1930. See Exploration and the Poles.
  • “lutenists who had known Mozart who had not known them”: By Mozart’s day the lute had nearly fallen out of use. See Music and Composers.
  • “harpists harping on a sea of glass”: “And I saw as it were a sea of glass mingled with fire… stand on the sea of glass, having the harps of God” (Revelation 15:2). See Revelation and the Apocalypse.
  • “what anachronism could there possibly be in the realm of the dead”: Anachronism is a chronological misplacing of persons, events, objects, or customs.
  • “A horse knew what the horseman did not know”: Balaam’s ass saw what Balaam could not: “And the ass saw the angel of the LORD standing in the way, and his sword drawn in his hand” (Numbers 22:23). See The Bible and Horses and Carriages.
  • “combing her hair in a psyche knot”: Psyche in psychology is the totality of the human mind, conscious and unconscious. Psyche knot is a woman’s hair style in which the hair is brushed back and twisted into a conical coil usually just above the nape. See the Psyche entry in the Chapter 38 resources.
  • “who should know when the dream ended”: In philosophy there is the question of dreams by Zhuangzi, Plato, and Aristotle. Descartes asked how he could know that he was not now dreaming (Meditations on First Philosophy, Meditation 1, 1641), which seems to be the same question Catherine is preoccupied with. Descartes’ answer was that we cannot trust our senses in waking life without invoking a benevolent God who would not deceive us. Catherine takes this one step further at the end of Chapter 39 and asks, “who could be right if God was dreaming?” In psychology the question “Is Life a Dream?” is answered with the coherence of the waking world does give evidence that it is not just a figment of our imagination. However, the objects that we perceive as permanent are in reality through the science of quantum physics mostly made up of empty space. In a sense people do live in a dream world that is created by the mind. When people are awake, their minds conform their dreaming to a reliable set of patterns, which they assume to be determined by a reality that exists independently of their experience of it, though they have no way of knowing that reality except through the complex ways in which it affects their dream. There is also reality that is experienced and affected by psychedelic drugs and other altered states of consciousness (Sharon Hewitt Rawlette, “Is Life a Dream?,” Psychology Today, July 31, 2019). See Taoism and Zhuangzi, Plato and Platonism, Aristotle, and Descartes and Dualism.
  • “I am dead—had not old Cousin Hannah always whispered”: Nietzsche’s phrase, “God is dead” (Friedrich Nietzsche, The Gay Science 125, 1882), refers to the demise of traditional religious belief and the moral structures built upon it. He believed this shift opened up new possibilities for humanity to create its own values and meaning. Marcus Aurelius wrote, “Consider thyself to be dead, and to have completed thy life up to the present time” (Marcus Aurelius, Meditations 7.56, trans. George Long, 1862), where one focuses on present experiences and accepts the inevitability of death, rather than clinging to the past or fearing the future. See Nietzsche and Stoicism.
  • “the dust returning always to the dust”: “For dust thou art, and unto dust shalt thou return” (Genesis 3:19). See Genesis.
  • “non angli sei angeli”: Non angli sei angeli (They are not Angles but angels) is attributed to Pope Gregory I after seeing pale-skinned boys at a slave market. The Latin is properly non Angli sed angeli, “not Angles but angels.” Bede tells the story (Ecclesiastical History of the English People 2.1, 731).
  • “lived through easeful death”: See Keats’s “easeful Death” in the Chapter 38 resources. See Romantic Poets.
  • “ignotum per ignotius”: Everything is explained as “ignotum per ignotius” which is explaining the unknown by means of the more unknown. It is not a logical fallacy but rather a criticism that is not useful in a particular context.
  • “a golden mean between extremes”: Aristotle placed virtue at the mean between two extremes, as courage lies between cowardice and rashness (Nicomachean Ethics 2.6). See Aristotle.
  • “a sound mind in a sound body”: “Orandum est ut sit mens sana in corpore sano,” “one should pray for a sound mind in a sound body” (Juvenal, Satire 10.356).
  • “as if the truth were mighty and would prevail”: “Magna est veritas, et praevalet,” “great is truth, and it prevails” (1 Esdras 4:41, Vulgate). See The Bible.
  • “her succumbing to this fatal drug habit by gradual degrees”: Addiction is a complicated phenomenon that overwhelms people and can harm an individual and those around them.
  • “the errant somnambulist”: In Bellini’s opera La Sonnambula (1831), the sleepwalking Amina crosses the high, broken bridge of a mill. See Music and Composers.
  • “the roaring, silent sea of dreams where all should change”: “Nothing of him that doth fade, / But doth suffer a sea-change / Into something rich and strange” (Shakespeare, The Tempest 1.2). See Shakespeare.
  • “Would the sheathbills have told”: Sheathbills are Antarctic shore scavengers, ruddy turnstones are wading shorebirds, and stormy petrels are seabirds of the open ocean. See the petrel entry in the Chapter 39 resources and Birds.
  • “A rider on a bicycle was to her one entity”: “How can we know the dancer from the dance?” (W. B. Yeats, “Among School Children,” 1928).
  • “All was water”: Thales, the first Greek philosopher, held that all things are water (Aristotle, Metaphysics 1.3). See Aristotle.
  • “the long-bodied coach dogs barking at the wheels”: Coach dogs, usually Dalmatians, ran beside carriages to guard the horses. See Dogs.
  • “the turning wheels of spokes which were the sleeping seraphim”: See Ezekiel’s wheels and cherubim in the Chapter 39 resources.
  • “As between the figurehead and the greatest captain of the greatest boat”: Plato’s parable of the ship (Republic 6.488), where a quarrelling crew ignores the true navigator, symbolizes the dangers of a political system not based on expertise. It is often called the Ship of State, where the ship represents a nation or government, with the crew, captain, and passengers symbolizing different social classes or politicians. See Plato and Platonism.
    • The Ship of Fools is Sebastian Brant’s Das Narrenschiff (1494), and Katherine Anne Porter’s novel Ship of Fools (1962).

Chapter 75

← Chapter 74 · Home · Chapter 76 →

Content note: The Esther Longtree chapters (72 to 81) deal with stillbirth and pregnancy loss, rape, infanticide, racist violence including lynching, and cruelty to children. This chapter describes a miscarriage Esther forced by beating her womb, the dead infant thrown into a river, and her dream that her own father fathered it.

Summary

Vera listens to Esther all morning, perhaps through many mornings. Esther wonders whether she carries a child or a benign tumor, and admits that she told the Chicago detective, who raped her and left her to face the disgrace, that he would be a father when the child was already dead. Long ago, young and frightened, she knelt by the river beating the child in her womb; a fisherman who heard her screams helped her wrap the dead baby in a gunny sack and throw it into the river above the dam. Years later it comes back at night, a mud baby bigger in death than in life, a funeral wreath hanging from its navel, and in her dreams it is the policeman’s son: her father was the father. She sets out food on the window sill for a tall child who never comes in, nurses her own hand, and fits two wedding rings on her nipples. The detective now writes that he will prove she murdered his three children. She hopes the coming war, “killing all the men and some of the children,” will make one or two old murders matter less.

Characters present

Esther Longtree · The Chicago Detective · Esther’s Father

Concepts present

Themes: Dreams and Imagination · Faith, God, and the Supernatural · Fear and Courage · Grief, Loss, and Mourning · Guilt, Innocence, and Justice · Isolation and Connection · Memory and the Past · Motherhood, Pregnancy, and Birth · Society, Class, and Race · Women, Gender, and Marriage

Symbols: Birds · Lamps, Candles, and Light · Moon and Stars · Pregnancy, Birth, and Children · Roses and Flowers · Shadows · The Sea and Water · Weddings and Funerals

Allusions: Exploration and the Poles · Fairy Tales and Folklore · Homer’s Epics · Iowa, Indiana, and the Midwest · Pregnancy, Abortion, and Midwifery · Revelation and the Apocalypse · The Bible

Key passages

From the research

  • Early in the chapter, Esther reflects on her condition (her swelling body compared to a “face under water”) and the ambiguity of whether her growth is motherhood or a “benign tumor.” She is simultaneously hopeful and fearful, uncertain whether the growth inside her is a child or a symbol of past trauma and miscarriage.
  • A pivotal passage reveals that Esther was raped by a detective who left her to face disgrace alone. Her complex feelings toward the detective (wanting to deceive him, to mystify the “solver of mysteries,” yet also wanting to express her pain) highlight her isolation and trauma. She acknowledges that the child in her womb was already dead when the detective came, underscoring a sense of hopelessness and despair.
  • Long ago, young and frightened, Esther knelt by the river “beating the child in her womb” until it came, dead; a fisherman who heard her screams helped her wrap it in a gunny sack and throw it into the river above the dam. The fisherman wonders if he is dreaming or sunstruck.
  • Esther’s recurring nightmares of the dead baby who “would come floating back to her” in various forms (mud baby, seed, star) serve as a powerful motif for unresolved grief and memory. The child is both “ugly” and “beautiful,” “bigger in death than it had been in life,” representing how trauma continues to grow and haunt her psyche despite physical absence.
  • The chapter explores Esther’s suspicion that her own father, the policeman, might be the father of the dead child, a deeply disturbing and taboo notion. The imagery of the funeral wreath and the policeman’s whistle evokes a chilling connection between family, authority, and violation.
  • Despite her losses, Esther yearns for motherhood and imagines children flocking around her. She tries to nurture an “eldest son” who never comes indoors, hiding food for him and hoping for his return.
  • Esther’s fear of going to court, accused of murdering her children, is a critical passage that highlights her vulnerability and the social stigma she faces. The detective’s threatening letters and the possibility of being blamed for deaths without physical evidence deepen her anxiety and sense of injustice.
  • The metaphor that once made pregnant by a man, Esther “was always bearing his children ever afterward,” underscores the cyclical and inescapable nature of her trauma.
  • Toward the end, Esther’s stubbornness and refusal to explain herself unless compelled reveal her resilience and complexity. She hopes for a future free of past shadows and miscarriages, longing for the happiness and fulfillment that motherhood might bring, despite the chaotic and painful history she carries.
  • The closing lines reflect on the coming war and its capacity to kill “all the men and some of the children,” suggesting that in the larger scale of human suffering, Esther’s personal tragedies might seem insignificant.

Questions and observations

Reading closely

  • “She had the miscarriages, and other women had the carriages.” What does the pun reveal?
  • Esther says “her tears were her children.” What does she mean?
  • “A woman of her character preferred uncertainty, the great question mark.” Why would she?

Characters

  • In her dream the mud baby “was the policeman’s son, and her father was the father.” Why does this child, alone among the stillborn, keep coming back?
  • The fisherman “was not sure he himself was not dreaming.” Why does he never speak of it again?
  • The tall child is “one who was not dead, one who called her mother.” Who is he?

Connections

  • The mourners enter “through the ivory portals.” In Homer, false dreams pass through the gate of ivory. Is Esther’s dream true or false?
  • The detective’s “wife said that he was sterile.” How does that change his accusation?
  • “If she was made pregnant once by a man, she was always bearing his children ever afterward.” How does this explain the “little detectives”?

Reflection

  • “The only anguish would be the anguish of knowing entirely what was so.” Is uncertainty ever a mercy?
  • “Nothing had been washed away.” What cannot be washed away?
  • “One or two old murders should not have mattered so much” with a war coming. Does a war make private grief smaller?

Research: Characters

Esther Longtree

  • The protagonist of this chapter; a woman burdened by miscarriages, trauma, and social suspicion, yet clinging to hope and faith.

The Chicago Detective

  • A figure of violence and threat; he raped Esther and later accuses her of murder.

The Fisherman

  • A compassionate figure who helps Esther dispose of a stillborn child and never speaks of it again. Fishing with a red geranium for bait, he had just seen “another stillborn, almost exactly like this,” and was “not sure he himself was not dreaming.”

Esther’s Father

  • The night policeman. Esther “loved her father from a distance,” and in her dream the mud baby is his son.

Mud baby

  • The “mud baby” is one of Esther’s stillborn children, soft as a marsh butterfly. Young and frightened, she beat the child in her womb until it came dead; she wanted to bury it in the mud, but the fisherman wrapped it in a gunny sack and put it into the river “so that it would be washed away.” It returns in her dreams “bigger in death than it had been in life,” swollen and covered with mud and brambles, with “awful starlight which was not starlight” on its face. It would “come floating back to her in the roar of dreams” and “spread its fingers wide,” made of “glass, twigs, brambles, mud, sand, starlight.”
  • The mud baby is linked ambiguously to the men in her life, including her father, a policeman, and a detective who raped her. A funeral wreath hangs from its navel, and its male organs are hidden from the moonlight, signs of the secrecy, shame, and societal judgment she faces. She nurses her own hands to soothe pain and fits wedding rings on her nipples, and she lives with a “great question mark.”

Tall Child

  • The tall child is not the mud baby. He is “her other, other, other child, one who whistled at the window, one who wore no funeral wreath, one who was not dead, one who called her mother.”
  • He is “her eldest son, her little boy who would not come in out of the darkness, who would not eat, who said he did not trust his mother.” Each night, even in sub-zero weather, she sets food on the window sill for him: cold cereal, old bones, toast stolen from the restaurant, apples, cheese. “But there was never the print of a tooth.”
  • Her mother scolds her for hiding bread under her pillow and apples everywhere, not knowing whom the food is for.

Research: Themes

Motherhood and Loss

See: Grief, Loss, and Mourning · Motherhood, Pregnancy, and Birth

  • Esther is pregnant but plagued by miscarriages and stillborn children, some of whom return as haunting apparitions in her dreams.
  • The passage frequently contrasts the physical reality of her miscarriages with her emotional and spiritual yearning to be a mother.
  • The idea of motherhood is both a source of hope and despair; she desires motherhood passionately but is tormented by repeated loss.

Grief and Trauma

See: Grief, Loss, and Mourning

  • Esther’s grief is pervasive and seems untethered, wandering like a ghost over a vast emotional landscape.
  • She experiences violent trauma, including rape by a detective, which deepens her sense of disgrace and isolation.
  • Her memories are fragmented and filled with uncertainty, reflecting the trauma’s impact on her sense of reality.

Memory and Uncertainty

See: Memory and the Past

  • The narrative is marked by confusion between what is real and imagined. Esther questions whether the growth in her womb is a benign tumor or a conscience.
  • She struggles with uncertainty about the paternity of her children and the reality of her experiences.
  • The recurring motif of “the little shadow boxer” symbolizes this uncertainty and elusive truth.

The Body and the Supernatural

See: Faith, God, and the Supernatural

  • Esther’s body is a site of suffering and mystery; her miscarriages are described in surreal terms (e.g., “mud baby,” “marble statue,” “ectoplasm”).
  • The dead babies return as ghostly figures, sometimes walking, sometimes lying in boats, symbolizing unresolved grief and the supernatural intrusion into her life.

Justice and Injustice

See: Guilt, Innocence, and Justice

  • Esther faces suspicion and possible accusation of murder regarding her children.
  • The detective who raped her threatens her, accusing her of killing his children, adding a layer of societal judgment and legal peril.
  • Her father being a policeman adds complexity to her relationship with authority and justice.

Isolation and Resistance

See: Isolation and Connection · Fear and Courage

  • Esther is isolated emotionally and socially, with only vague support from a fisherman and conflicted feelings toward her parents.
  • Despite her hardship, she exhibits stubbornness and a refusal to explain or defend herself fully.
  • She clings to hope for motherhood and resists being broken by the accusations and losses.

Research: Symbols and Imagery

The Stillborn Children

See: Pregnancy, Birth, and Children

  • Represent loss, guilt, and the haunting past; they return in dreams as a “mud baby,” a “marble statue,” and ghostly figures.

The Funeral Wreath

See: Roses and Flowers · Weddings and Funerals

  • Symbolizes death and mourning; it appears on the dead baby and connects to Esther’s fears about paternity and legacy.

The River and Water

See: The Sea and Water

  • Associated with cleansing, oblivion, and the passage of time; the river carries away dead babies, symbolizing attempts to escape grief.

The Moonlight and Starlight

See: Moon and Stars · Lamps, Candles, and Light

  • Juxtaposed images representing the mysterious, supernatural, and elusive nature of Esther’s experience.

The Little Shadow Boxer

See: Shadows

  • A mysterious child figure that embodies Esther’s ambiguous feelings about her unborn child and her fractured conscience.

Esther and the Abortion Rights Movement

  • Esther Longtree is a complex, symbolic character whose life and experiences can be analyzed in the context of the abortion rights movement in the US.
  • Esther Longtree is portrayed as a woman burdened by an “everlasting pregnancy,” haunted by multiple stillborn children, miscarriages, and the symbolic weight of unborn or lost children. She is at once maternal and mysteriously barren, pregnant yet never fully delivering living offspring that the world can recognize or accept. Her pregnancies are often described as “clouded,” “mysterious,” or “stillborn,” and she experiences isolation, societal judgment, and legal threats because of her reproductive history.
  • Esther faces accusations, lawsuits, and societal condemnation for the loss or absence of children, implicitly tied to notions of infanticide or abortion. She dreads being brought to court, exposed to public scrutiny, and misjudged by a jury that cannot understand her unique suffering and mystery.
  • Esther’s narrative is filled with ambiguity since she does not always know the fathers of her children, nor can she fully explain the fate of her pregnancies. This ambiguity echoes the clandestine and complex nature of abortion and reproductive control for women of her era, especially those marginalized by society.
  • Despite her “mulish” stubbornness and physical strength, Esther is powerless against the forces governing her body and fate. She is caught between societal expectations, personal despair, and the biological realities of her reproductive health. Her identity as a mother is fraught with loss, secrecy, and yearning.
  • The stillborn children and the “little shadow boxer” under her heart symbolize both the tangible and intangible losses women endure: lost potential lives, societal invisibility, and the emotional and spiritual costs of reproductive control or failure.
  • Esther’s fear of legal entanglement, the threat of arrest, and the impossibility of proving her innocence reflect the harsh realities women faced when dealing with unwanted pregnancies or abortions before legal reform. Her case is described as unprecedented, with no legal precedent to protect her.

Historical Context

  • Abortion was a criminal offense in most states, punishable by fines, imprisonment, and social disgrace. Laws were stringent, and enforcement was often harsh, particularly for poor or marginalized women.
  • Abortions were generally only permitted to save the life of the mother, and even then, access was restricted and dangerous. Women often sought illegal and unsafe procedures.
  • The early abortion rights movement began to take shape in the 1950s and early 1960s, advocating for legal reform to protect women’s health and autonomy. Activists challenged the criminalization and pushed for exceptions and ultimately for the right to abortion itself.
  • Abortion was associated with moral failure and criminality. Women who had abortions or miscarriages were often stigmatized as sinners or murderers, a theme echoed in Esther’s fear of public judgment and legal accusation.
  • Esther’s secretive pregnancies, miscarriages, and the threat of legal action mirror the precarious position of women in the pre-1964 US abortion context. Her fear of exposure, societal condemnation, and her isolation reflect the lack of support or understanding women faced.
  • Esther’s case is described as not being covered by any law, highlighting the legal vacuum and absence of rights for women like her before reform. This underscores the historical reality where women had little recourse and were vulnerable to prosecution.
  • Esther internalizes and externalizes the stigma attached to reproductive failure, much as women were publicly and privately judged harshly for abortions or miscarriages. The accusations of murder, infanticide, or madness parallel societal responses to women’s reproductive choices or misfortunes.
  • The narrative portrays figures such as doctors, detectives, and the legal system as intrusive and judgmental, echoing the control and surveillance women’s bodies were subjected to, especially regarding reproduction and abortion.
  • Esther’s uncertain reproductive history, multiple possible fathers, and the surreal quality of her pregnancies evoke the secretive and often misunderstood nature of abortion experiences before legalization, where women’s stories were fragmented and hidden. Esther Longtree embodies the tragic, mysterious, and socially fraught experience of a woman caught in the web of reproductive loss, societal judgment, and legal peril characteristic of the era before the first abortion rights reforms in the US. Her story, rich in symbolism and emotional complexity, reflects the harsh realities faced by many women: criminalization, stigma, fear, and isolation. Esther Longtree’s character and her narrative can be seen as a poignant, allegorical exploration of the consequences of restrictive reproductive laws and the deep personal and societal costs borne by women in that historical context.

Research: Resources

  • “So I listened to Esther Longtree’s tale of woe”: Esther Longtree in this chapter is portrayed as a deeply tragic and complex figure whose life is marked by sorrow, loss, and an overwhelming burden of maternal suffering. Her narrative is laden with symbolism and a haunting sense of ambiguity between life and death, reality and illusion. Esther is described as a large, swollen woman who is often pregnant or carrying the weight of pregnancies, many of which have ended in miscarriage or stillbirth. She is physically affected by her experiences, with her body growing and swelling “like a face under water” and her heart “roaring” with pain and confusion. This corporeal imagery reflects her emotional turmoil and the heavy burden she carries. Esther is haunted by the memory of her stillborn children, especially a particular “dead baby” who recurs in her dreams and visions. This child appears as a ghostly, mutable figure: sometimes a mud baby, sometimes a star, sometimes walking and whistling like a policeman (her father). This spectral child embodies Esther’s unresolved grief and the mysterious, painful legacy of her reproductive history. The child’s presence symbolizes the inescapable past that “spread its fingers” into her present, confusing her maternal identity and her sense of reality. Esther’s narrative is fraught with uncertainty about the paternity of her children, including both the living and the dead. She suspects her father, the night policeman, might be the father of one child, which adds a disturbing layer of incestuous implication and deepens her psychological conflict. She also grapples with the menace of a detective who raped her and later threatens her with accusations of murder regarding her lost children. Esther’s sense of guilt and fear is compounded by this external pressure, making her situation even more tragic and isolating. Despite the miscarriages and losses, Esther’s yearning for motherhood remains central to her identity. She imagines herself surrounded by children, calling to them, feeling on the verge of “something big.” Yet, she is tormented by doubts, wondering if what she feels is not motherhood but a “benign tumor,” a metaphor for something unnatural or pathological growing inside her. This tension between hope and despair, life and death, defines her tragic longing. Esther is a stubborn, “mulish” woman who resists explanation or confession. She keeps her pain hidden, crying aloud only when she is sure no one is near. She is wary of judgment and the legal consequences she might face, especially from the detective’s accusations. Her isolation is both physical and psychological, as she navigates a world that neither fully understands nor sympathizes with her. The chapter uses rich, poetic imagery to convey Esther’s inner life: the “quail rustling among the purple shadows,” the “marble children,” the “funeral wreath,” and the “mud baby” all evoke the blending of life, death, memory, and dream. The river motif, with the stillborn children thrown into its current, suggests the flow of time and the attempt to wash away pain and guilt, though ultimately unsuccessfully. Esther’s story reflects broader themes of female suffering, reproductive trauma, and social marginalization. Her experiences are not merely personal but speak to the harsh realities faced by many women, especially those who are poor, vulnerable, and victimized. Her connection to various men (the detective, the policeman father, other “dying fathers”) and her ambiguous reproductive history also hint at societal failures and abuses. Esther Longtree is a profoundly tragic character embodying the painful complexities of motherhood, loss, and survival. She is caught between hope and despair, reality and dream, the past and an uncertain future, her life shadowed by death and the haunting presence of lost children. Her narrative is a poignant exploration of grief, guilt, and the human desire for connection and meaning amid suffering. See Esther Longtree.
    • Esther Longtree embodies a deeply tragic and complex symbol of American history, particularly the history of marginalized and dispossessed women who have endured cycles of loss, violence, and erasure. Her story is a series of miscarriages, stillbirths, and pregnancies marked by trauma and abandonment that can be read as an allegory for the broader historical experiences of women in the United States who have borne the consequences of social neglect, patriarchal oppression, and systemic injustice. Esther’s repeated miscarriages and the haunting presence of her dead children symbolize the lost potential and silenced voices of countless women who suffered physical and emotional damage, often in anonymity and without justice. The references to her being raped by a detective, the mysterious paternity of her children including insinuations of incest (her father possibly being the father of one child), and the threat of legal prosecution for supposed murder suggest the historical reality of women victimized by those in power (law enforcement, family patriarchs, and societal structures) that failed or actively oppressed them. Esther’s condition (physically swollen, burdened with grief, and haunted by ghostly children) also metaphorically represents the burden of historical trauma that accumulates over generations. Her narrative touches on themes of women’s reproductive rights denied or controlled, the stigma and silence surrounding miscarriages and stillbirths, and the societal tendency to blame or shame women for such tragedies. Esther’s life reflects the harshness of economic and social hardship, implied by her work as a waitress, her isolation, and the absence of support. Her struggle resonates with the stories of working-class women who faced exploitation and abandonment. Esther Longtree symbolizes the history of American women who have been subjected to violence, reproductive suffering, and social marginalization: a history marked by loss, injustice, and resilience. Through her, Young evokes the silent, painful legacies of many such women, whose experiences are written into the fabric of the nation’s troubled past.
  • “Often, she pondered upon difficult questions”: “...pondered upon difficult questions, some legal, some illegal… often, was raped when there was no one present but a ghostly, mean, mean child… She could not always blame men for her disappointments. Sometimes she blamed the child…” The children ruined her body and “...her raped, wounded sky, the whole world?” During and after pregnancy, a woman’s body undergoes significant changes, including increased blood volume and heart rate, breast enlargement, and skin changes like stretch marks. Postpartum, the uterus shrinks, abdominal muscles may separate (diastasis recti), and some muscles may be weakened, potentially leading to urinary incontinence. Other common after-effects include changes in shoe size, wider hips, and hair loss after an initial period of thicker hair. During pregnancy, organs like the uterus, stomach, and intestines are pushed and shifted by the growing fetus to make room. After pregnancy, these organs gradually return to their pre-pregnancy positions over several weeks or months. Vaginal stretching happens as the baby moves down the birth canal. As the baby’s head descends, it interacts with the vaginal walls and pelvic floor, causing the tissues and muscles to stretch significantly. Computer models show that some pelvic floor muscles can stretch to more than three times their normal resting length. See Pregnancy, Abortion, and Midwifery.
  • “it might be a benign tumor, this growth”: In pseudocyesis, false or phantom pregnancy, a woman believes she is pregnant and her body follows: the menses stop, the belly swells, she feels the child move. Mary Tudor, Queen of England, believed herself pregnant in 1554 and 1555; London rang its bells for a prince who was never born. See Pregnancy, Abortion, and Midwifery and Women, Gender, and Marriage.
  • “she would be pregnant if the stars fell like leaves upon a rotted world”: “And the stars of heaven fell unto the earth, even as a fig tree casteth her untimely figs, when she is shaken of a mighty wind” (Revelation 6:13, KJV). Untimely figs are fruit dropped before it ripens. See Revelation and the Apocalypse.
  • “had not borne witness against herself”: Esther had resisted and not “...borne witness against herself, for it would have been illegal to do so, and her own father was the policeman.” This may refer to the Fifth Amendment in the United States where, Pleading the Fifth, is often used to invoke the self-incrimination clause when witnesses decline to answer questions where the answers might incriminate them. The amendment (1791) says no one “shall be compelled in any criminal case to be a witness against himself.” See Guilt, Innocence, and Justice.
  • “While dangling a red geranium for bait”: A red geranium may be herb Robert (Geranium robertianum), the small wild red cranesbill, also called red robin, stinking Bob, and death-come-quickly; folk magic linked it with luck and fertility. Geranium comes from the Greek geranos, crane, for the beak-shaped seed pods, and in German the plant is Stinkender Storchschnabel, stinking stork’s-bill. Because the stork was already an established European symbol of birth, family, and new babies, people linked the stork’s-bill herb to conception and depicted it alongside storks in folk art. See Roses and Flowers and Fairy Tales and Folklore.
  • “wearing its birth veil like a bridal veil”: See the caul in the Chapter 74 resources. See Fairy Tales and Folklore.
  • “They had thrown the stillborn into the river above the dam”: This may refer to the Mississippi Burning Case on August 4, 1964, FBI agents discovered the bodies of three civil rights workers (James Chaney, Michael Schwerner, and Andrew Goodman) buried in an earthen dam on a farm in Neshoba County, MS. The workers had been murdered by members of the Ku Klux Klan and a local deputy sheriff on June 21, 1964, and their bodies were buried within the construction of the dam. The novel was published in 1965. See Society, Class, and Race.
  • “perhaps clear to the Gulf of Mexico”: From Indiana the Wabash runs to the Ohio, the Ohio to the Mississippi, and the Mississippi to the Gulf of Mexico. See Iowa, Indiana, and the Midwest and The Sea and Water.
  • “Nothing was brought to light that had been hidden”: Esther reverses the Gospel: “For there is nothing hid, which shall not be manifested; neither was any thing kept secret, but that it should come abroad” (Mark 4:22, KJV). See The Bible.
  • “Sometimes it was a mud baby”: Mud baby may refer to Tar-Baby in the second of the Uncle Remus stories published in 1881. It is about a doll made of tar and turpentine used by the villainous Brer Fox to entrap Brer Rabbit. The more that Brer Rabbit fights the Tar-Baby, the more entangled he becomes.The term tar baby has come to refer to a problem that is exacerbated by attempts to struggle with it, or by extension to a situation in which mere contact can lead to becoming inextricably involved. Although the term “tar baby” is documented as coming from a folktale of African origin, its modern meaning in America is different. Many consider tar baby to be a racial term for African Americans. See Fairy Tales and Folklore.
    • Joel Chandler Harris, a white Georgia journalist, took the tales from Black storytellers, some of them enslaved on the Turnwold plantation where he worked as a boy, and put them in the mouth of Uncle Remus, a contented old former slave of white Southern fantasy. See Society, Class, and Race.
  • “through the ivory portals”: In the Odyssey (Book 19) Penelope says that dreams come through two gates: those through the gate of ivory deceive, those through the gate of horn come true. Virgil sends Aeneas back from the underworld through the ivory gate (Aeneid 6). See Homer’s Epics and Dreams and Imagination.
  • “some little windowpeeper”: In the Coventry legend, Peeping Tom, the tailor who looked out at Lady Godiva as she rode naked through the town, was struck blind. See Fairy Tales and Folklore.
  • “hear the lovebirds crying for their mother”: See Esther’s lovebirds in the Chapter 72 resources. See Birds.
  • “She was the Poles, she guessed”: See Exploration and the Poles and the ice floes in the Chapter 74 resources.
  • “she ate geraniums and paper and string”: Pica, the craving to eat things that are not food (clay, chalk, paper, ice, starch), is common in pregnancy and has been described since antiquity; the word is Latin for magpie, the bird that will eat anything. See Pregnancy, Abortion, and Midwifery.
  • “whose little hands had stung like nettles upon her cheeks”: Esther’s mother slapped her as a child. See Esther’s Father and Esther’s parents in the Chapter 72 resources.
  • “Was she a maypole or what”: A maypole is a tall wooden pole erected as a part of various European folk festivals, around which a maypole dance often takes place. The festivals may occur in May or Pentecost, although in some countries it is instead erected at Midsummer. See Fairy Tales and Folklore.
  • “even if there were no corpses derelicti”: Esther’s “corpses derelicti” mangles corpus delicti, “the body of the crime,” the legal rule that a crime must be shown to have happened before anyone can be convicted of it; she mixes in corpses and derelicts. The phrase is often misread to mean that there can be no murder conviction without a body. See Guilt, Innocence, and Justice.
  • “for it was not her business if his wife said that he was sterile”: The detective is married, and he and his wife each say the other is sterile. See The Chicago Detective.
  • “the soap salesman’s soap baby”: The Chicago detective once came “as a soap salesman in the winter meadows” (Chapter 74). See The Chicago Detective.
  • “It was the world of this creation that was wrong, O’Leary said”: See Justice O’Leary.
  • “especially when there was going to be another war soon”: Esther couldn’t understand why anyone would “...bother a poor creature like her… especially when there was going to be another war soon, killing all the men and some of the children, and one or two old murders should not have mattered so much, especially if it was nothing murdered?” This phrase expresses a sense of futility and the overwhelming insignificance of individual tragedies in the face of much larger, impending catastrophes, namely, war and mass death. The “other war” is the Second World War, then coming.
