chapter-72:
Chapter 72

← Chapter 71 · Home · Chapter 73 →

Content note: The Esther Longtree chapters (72 to 81) deal with stillbirth and pregnancy loss, rape, infanticide, racist violence including lynching, and cruelty to children. This chapter centers on pregnancy and stillbirth.

Summary

On an early spring morning Vera walks past the undertaker’s and the beauty parlor, which share one door, and a mule in a crocheted hood, into the Greasy Spoon, its walls painted with hollyhocks and Niagara. There she meets Esther Longtree, the passive policeman’s only daughter, a big, cross-eyed waitress with a growing bald spot and a deformed foot, who believes she is always pregnant, now with “the little shadow boxer.” Setting out seven cups for her stillborn, Esther tells of the children she has lost and hidden under leaves and snow, as many as the autumn leaves, and of their fathers, the salesmen passing through. She tells of wild mares pregnant by the wind on an island off Virginia; of old Dr. O’Leary, who calls her the immortal medical case; of her parents, who think her an old maid; of the lovebirds she keeps to hide the cries she hears at night; and of the layettes she has buried. At last she asks who killed cock robin and answers that all people killed him, never she.

Characters present

Esther Longtree · Justice O’Leary · The Little Shadow Boxer

Concepts present

Themes: Death and Mortality · Faith, God, and the Supernatural · Isolation and Connection · Nature, the Sea, and the Cosmos · Society, Class, and Race · The Search for Meaning · Women, Gender, and Marriage

Symbols: Birds · Butterflies and Moths · Fireflies · Hair, Wig, and Baldness · Horses and Carriages · Music and Instruments · Pearls and Jewels · Shadows

Allusions: American Religious Movements · Astronomy · Ecclesiastes · Fairy Tales and Folklore · Gambling and Playing Cards · Greek Mythology · Iowa, Indiana, and the Midwest · Judaism · Music and Composers · Pregnancy, Abortion, and Midwifery · Revelation and the Apocalypse · Shakespeare · The Bible

Key passages

From the research

  • The chapter opens with a vivid description of an early spring morning in a foggy, desolate town. The undertaker’s hearse, old ghostly automobiles, a grey wagon with a bony mule, and the “Greasy Spoon” restaurant set the scene.
  • Esther is introduced as a robust, vibrant woman whose vitality contrasts with her bleak surroundings. She is perpetually pregnant, known for her “everlasting pregnancy” which is at once a burden and a source of hope. She has ponderous red lips, flowing black hair, a swollen belly, and morning and evening sickness.
  • A central passage concerns Esther’s countless stillborn children, “as many as the autumn leaves,” and the sterile, puny salesmen who fathered them. Esther’s maternal love extends even to these lost children, and her loneliness is compounded by the lack of recognition or mourning from others. The stillborn are described haunting her, whispering and crying.
  • Old Dr. O’Leary’s character provides a counterpoint as a doctor who is senile and confused but insists Esther is a unique “immortal medical case.” He predicts she will never die in childbirth and attributes much to atmospheric, cosmic influences.
  • Esther reflects on her parents’ ignorance and misunderstanding, their teasing, and their failure to comprehend her life and condition. Her parents see her as a failure and an old maid, yet she has lived a secret, wild life full of pregnancies and losses unknown to them.
  • There are various men (salesmen, horn-blowers, detectives, and others) who have passed through her life, many being sterile fathers of her stillborn children.
  • Despite the repeated losses, Esther maintains hope for a living child. She has prepared layettes, toys, and clothes, knitting a little black suit for the child she expects to survive. Her hope is described as “luminescent,” and she embraces her condition with a mixture of strength, sorrow, and resilience. This passage is crucial for understanding her perseverance and the symbolic weight of her pregnancy.
  • The chapter delves into Esther’s psychological and emotional life, her conversations with the stillborn, the lovebirds she raises, and the voices she hears. She is portrayed as deeply connected to the unseen world of the lost children and haunted by their presence. She knits without thread, plays the piano, and cares for her lovebirds.
  • Near the end, Esther poses the question “Who killed cock robin?” She concludes that nobody alone is to blame; the child was killed by “the death that was in him from the time of his birth” and by the forces of nature like the wind, night, day, atmospheric pressure.
  • The last passage reveals Esther’s acceptance of her condition and her defiant hope. She knows she has been “always pregnant,” never the murderer of her children, and she prepares for the winnowing test of childbirth.

Questions and observations

Reading closely

  • “This was not the restaurant. This was the womb. This was the grave.” How can one room be all three?
  • “I am a white piano,” Esther insists. What does the image say about how she has been used?
  • “The stillborn were the most successful.” What does Esther mean by success?

Characters

  • Old Doctor says, “The ebb of reason, he said, is accompanied by the tide of imagination.” Is that a diagnosis of Esther or of himself?
  • “The parents could rid themselves of the child, but the child could never get rid of the parents.” How does this fit Esther, and Vera?
  • The drummer sells Fuller brushes, “always staring beyond the woman to see if he could see that which he sought for as for earthly paradise.” Why does Esther’s heart go out to him?

Connections

  • The mule stands at “the dead-end of creation, being that being from which no mortal issue comes.” What does the mule have to do with Esther?
  • Old Doctor says the world will go on in imagination and “the wild white mothers be fecundated by the wind.” Where did Vera read of such mares in Chapter 71?
  • “Who killed cock robin?” Esther answers, “All people killed him.” Is she right?

Reflection

  • “It is not true that people are either a success or a failure in life. They could be both.” Do you agree?
  • “Her searchings for the truth were noiseless. Only the lie roared.” What lie roars in this chapter?
  • “There is something about all of us, he said, that is unrealized.” What is unrealized in you?

Research: Characters

Esther Longtree

  • Esther is heavily pregnant, with a “bald spot shaped like a large coin” and “long black hair flowing free.”
  • She is described as “plum-colored but square,” with “ponderous red lips” and “lustrous, dull but shining” eyes.
  • Her body is both a source of strength and burden; she experiences morning and evening sickness, swollen breasts, and a deformed foot.
  • Esther is simultaneously robust and vulnerable, embodying vitality and suffering.
  • She is known as the “passive policeman’s only daughter,” indicating a background of isolation and misunderstanding.
  • She broods over her “everlasting pregnancy,” symbolizing continuous loss and hope.
  • Despite her hardships, Esther is compassionate, loving, and hopeful, often talking to herself and her unborn child.
  • Esther’s pregnancy is metaphoric and literal, reflecting repeated stillbirths and lost children.
  • She refers to the “little shadow boxer” inside her, a foetus representing hope, fear, and the unknown.
  • The pregnancy signifies the struggle between creation and destruction, life and death, hope and despair.
  • Salesmen and transient men pass through her life, often fathering her stillborn children.
  • Her parents misunderstand her, seeing her as a failure or beast of burden.
  • She holds a secret inner life that no one fully comprehends, except the “stillborn and the white birds.”
  • Esther experiences loneliness, resilience, and a profound sense of mystery about her condition.
  • She wrestles with feelings of failure and hope, often laughing, crying, and brooding.
  • She fears being discovered by her mother but also finds solace in her secret world, including her lovebirds.

Doctor O’Leary

  • Dr. O’Leary is portrayed as an aging, somewhat senile physician who embodies both a figure of traditional medical authority and a symbol of the limitations of human knowledge and mortality.
  • Dr. O’Leary is described as “drunkenly leaning on his cane,” with “old eyes frozen” and suffering from “hardening of the artery of the brain” a condition that makes him senile and confused. His physical frailty contrasts sharply with the vitality and mysterious condition of Esther Longtree, the central character in this chapter. He is aware of his own decline and admits that he has “retired from practice” because of his confusion and failing faculties.
  • Despite his failing health and failing mind, Dr. O’Leary offers Esther “everlasting hope,” encouraging her that she “will never die in child birth” and that her labor will be “easy” and “like passing a seed.” He calls her “the immortal medical case,” suggesting that her condition, her “everlasting pregnancy” and her strange, continuous fertility is an anomaly beyond his medical understanding. He believes that although she is “over-hopeful and bloated with no form within the form,” her problem will end with her, and her disappointments will “pass away and not be seen again upon the earth.” Yet, he cannot fully explain her condition, reflecting his own limitations as a doctor.
  • Dr. O’Leary once believed in a simple, anatomical understanding of the human body but now sees “the false eyes, the false cartilage, the false heart,” and “false generations,” causing him confusion and leading to his withdrawal from active practice.
  • Dr. O’Leary’s comments on atmospheric pressure, the whirling stars, and the cold ether suggest a more cosmic or metaphysical dimension to Esther’s pregnancy and to human life and death generally. He attributes some medical phenomena to “the unusual atmospheric pressure” and “the thin ether,” implying that natural forces beyond human control or understanding influence human fate.
  • Dr. O’Leary is a tragic yet compassionate figure as an old doctor who has seen many failures and losses but still offers hope and comfort.

The little shadow boxer

  • The “little shadow boxer” is the unborn child Esther carries, “the little shadow boxer who in the waters of her womb had grown and grown and had warded off every blow.” She feels “the little shadow foot that ran and ran” and its accelerated heartbeat under her heart. Shadow boxing is fighting an opponent who is not there, and the child stays hidden, “crouched where I place my hand,” with folded arms and knees drawn up.
  • Old Dr. O’Leary gives Esther “everlasting hope” for its birth, though she has lost many stillborn children. Her “lonely pregnancy” is “ominous and opalescent and unforgiving,” and she carries “two hearts, mine and his,” knitting clothes and collecting toys for the child. Yet the doctor warns that the glaciers are creeping down from the Arctic and “only the dead gave birth.”

Sad father sub-plot

  • The sad father subplot is embodied in the figure of a stout, fat drummer who visits Esther Longtree. This man, once happily married with a business and a good home, has suffered a profound personal tragedy: the death of his wife’s sister’s little girl from scarlet fever. This loss devastates him so deeply that he abandons his business and family to wander the roads as a Fuller brush salesman, haunted by the memory of the child he lost. He stops at Esther’s restaurant, tearful and remorseful, carrying a bag of candy for the little girl he cannot forget.

Research: Themes

Life and Death

See: Death and Mortality

  • The juxtaposition of the beauty parlor and undertaker’s hearse symbolizes the thin line between life and death.
  • Esther’s story is a meditation on the persistence of life despite repeated encounters with death (stillbirths).
  • The motif of stillborn children recurs, emphasizing loss and the fragility of existence.

Hope and Despair

  • Despite her repeated losses, Esther holds onto hope for a living child, representing the human spirit’s endurance.
  • The “little shadow boxer” is a symbol of this hope amidst despair.
  • Old Dr. O’Leary’s encouragement reinforces this theme of hope against all odds.

Isolation and Misunderstanding

See: Isolation and Connection · The Search for Meaning

  • Esther is isolated physically and emotionally, misunderstood by family and society.
  • The metaphor of being “engulfed” and her parents’ ignorance highlight the loneliness of her experience.

Nature and the Cosmos

See: Nature, the Sea, and the Cosmos

  • Imagery involving stars, moons, winds, and atmospheric pressure ties Esther’s personal story to universal forces.
  • The narrative suggests a cosmic scale to human suffering and creation, blurring lines between the earthly and celestial.

Mystery and the Unseen

See: Faith, God, and the Supernatural

  • The unborn child, the stillborn babies, and the hidden layers of Esther’s life symbolize the mysteries of existence and creation.
  • References to shadows, ghosts, and invisible presences underscore this motif.

Research: Symbols and Imagery

The “little shadow boxer”

See: Shadows

  • Represents the unborn child, hope, and the tension of life not fully realized.

Bald spot

See: Hair, Wig, and Baldness

  • Symbolizes the wear and loss Esther has endured.

Fireflies, moths, and butterflies

See: Butterflies and Moths · Fireflies

  • Represent fleeting life, transformation, and the ethereal nature of existence.

The “white piano”

See: Music and Instruments

  • A metaphor for Esther herself as a complex, beautiful, misunderstood person, and played upon by life’s “dreaming fingers.”

The grey mule and manure wagon

See: Horses and Carriages

  • Symbolize burden, endurance, and the dead-end nature of Esther’s existence.

The pearl-like raindrops that never fall

See: Pearls and Jewels

  • Reflect suspended time and unfulfilled potential.
  • Esther Longtree may symbolize the sexual revolution in the United States by considering her character’s embodiment of themes such as fertility, sexuality, societal repression, and the struggle for female autonomy.
  • Esther is depicted as “everlastingly pregnant,” carrying multiple stillborn children, representing an ongoing, unresolved fertility and reproductive issue. She is physically swollen, with symptoms of pregnancy (morning sickness, evening sickness, swollen breasts) but no viable birth occurs. This paradox of constant pregnancy without fulfillment can symbolize the tension in the 1960s between traditional expectations of women centered on motherhood and the emerging desire for sexual freedom and reproductive control. Esther’s “everlasting pregnancy” may reflect the societal burden placed on women to reproduce and the frustration when that role is unfulfilled or controlled by external forces like sterile fathers or societal norms.
  • Esther is described as robustly alive and free in some ways like her hair that flows loose “at whatever cost to sanitation,” and she tosses it regularly as if to preserve her freedom. This image evokes a woman resisting social constraints, symbolic of the sexual liberation movement where women began to assert control over their own bodies and sexuality. Yet, she is also trapped in a “womb” that is both a restaurant and a grave, a liminal space between life and death, fertility and barrenness, reflecting the societal repression of female sexuality and the stigma around pregnancy out of wedlock or outside accepted norms.
  • The numerous stillborn children Esther carries (hidden under leaves, buds, snow, rivers) represent unrealized potential, lost possibilities, and the silencing of female sexual and reproductive expression. The fact that the fathers are “sterile” or “impotent” men, often traveling salesmen or transient figures, can symbolize the failure of patriarchal structures to support or recognize women’s full sexual agency. The stillborns haunt Esther, much like the repressed desires and consequences of sexual control haunt society during the sexual revolution.
  • Esther is simultaneously described as “brilliant but dumb,” “ugly outside... but beautiful inside,” “experienced and sought after” yet also an “old maid” misunderstood by her own parents. This duality reflects the conflicted social status of women during this time who were beginning to break free from traditional roles but still faced judgment, misunderstanding, and marginalization. Esther’s education and cultural refinement contrast with her physical and social marginalization, symbolizing the new woman’s struggle to reconcile intellect, sexuality, and societal acceptance.
  • Esther’s “immortal medical case” status, with the old doctor predicting she will “be pregnant until the stars had fallen,” suggests the ongoing, unresolved nature of women’s sexual liberation. The “everlasting pregnancy” can metaphorically represent the period of social transformation as an era pregnant with possibilities but fraught with struggle, loss, and hope. Her hopefulness despite repeated disappointments mirrors the spirit of the sexual revolution, which challenged existing norms and sought new forms of expression and liberation.
  • Her affinity with natural and mythical elements (wild mares pregnant by the wind, the great skull, the starry heavens, the moon, and the stars) links Esther to a broader symbolic framework of fertility, creation, and cosmic forces. This elevates her personal reproductive tragedy to a universal level, reflecting the countercultural embrace of naturalism, mysticism, and a redefinition of human sexuality as part of a cosmic order or liberation from mechanistic, repressive traditions.
  • Esther Longtree symbolizes the complexities and contradictions of the sexual revolution in America: the tension between fertility and barrenness, freedom and repression, hope and despair, tradition and change. Her character embodies the social anxieties about female sexuality, the quest for autonomy, and the redefinition of womanhood during a period of profound cultural upheaval.
  • Her story encapsulates the bodily, social, and legal struggles over reproduction, economic survival, and patriarchal oppression that shaped the conditions the women’s rights movement sought to change through activism.

Research: Resources

  • “kewpie dolls which I had first thought were children”: Rose O’Neill drew her Kewpies for the Ladies’ Home Journal in 1909, and the dolls were a craze from 1912; she grew rich on them and drew posters for women’s suffrage. See Women, Gender, and Marriage.
  • “being that being from which no mortal issue comes”: The mule, foaled of a male donkey and a mare, is almost always sterile. The mule embodies a threshold or boundary between life and death, fertility and barrenness, creative potential and its cessation. In the broader context of the novel, which often interweaves themes of decay, loss, and the boundaries between reality and dreams, this image can be interpreted as a symbol of stagnation or an end point in the cycle of life. It also resonates with the novel’s attention to characters who are trapped in states of limbo or arrested development, such as the doctor delivering imaginary babies or the hangman haunted by the children of the hanged. The passage conveys a mood of desolation and quiet warning about reaching a place where creation and renewal cease, urging the narrator (and the reader) to recognize the significance of this boundary in the unfolding narrative and in life itself. See Horses and Carriages.
  • “the walls were painted crazily with hollyhocks”: Symbolically, the hollyhocks can be interpreted as representing both vitality and decay. Hollyhocks are traditionally tall, hardy flowers that stand upright and bloom, often symbolizing ambition, fecundity, and the cycle of life and death. However, in the novel, their depiction as dripping paint on cracked walls suggests fragility, impermanence, and the blurring between life and death, reality and illusion. This duality mirrors Esther Longtree’s own condition: she is physically swollen with a seemingly endless pregnancy, embodying fertility and hope, yet she suffers continual loss and stillbirths, embodying sorrow and loss. The hollyhocks’ reach toward the cracked ceiling might symbolize striving for life or transcendence despite the decay and desolation surrounding them, just as Esther, despite her tragic circumstances, maintains hope and resilience. The hollyhocks thus underscore themes of fertility, loss, and the tension between life and death that permeate Esther’s narrative and the novel’s broader atmosphere of haunting liminality.
  • “Niagara booming over jagged rocks”: Niagara refers primarily to the iconic Niagara Falls, a group of three massive waterfalls on the U.S.-Canada border, renowned for their power, beauty, and hydroelectric generation, featuring attractions like the Maid of the Mist and Cave of the Winds. It also refers to the surrounding region, including cities in New York and Ontario, the Niagara River, historical sites like Old Fort Niagara, and the Niagara Escarpment, a significant geological formation. See Niagara Falls in the Chapter 65 resources.
  • “who could have been more robustly alive than she, Esther Longtree”: Esther Longtree emerges as a deeply tragic and complex figure who embodies themes of fertility, loss, unrecognized suffering, and resilience. Physically, she is described as large, swollen, with a deformed foot, a growing bald spot, and marked by signs of repeated pregnancies. Her body is a site of contradiction: robust and vital in some ways, yet burdened by an “everlasting pregnancy” that brings her both strength and sorrow. She is portrayed with vivid imagery (her “ponderous red lips,” “long black hair flowing free,” and swollen breasts like “milky breakers”) highlighting her physicality and her connection to life and creation, even as she suffers repeated stillbirths. Esther’s story is one of repeated loss and unfulfilled motherhood. She has borne many stillborn children, hidden their remains in various natural places, and carries the constant sorrow and haunting memory of these lost lives. Despite this, she harbors a fierce hope and determination to have a living child, the “little shadow boxer” moving inside her, symbolizing persistent life against overwhelming odds. Her repeated pregnancies symbolize both a curse and a source of identity and purpose; she is “always pregnant,” yet always losing the child before birth. This paradoxical state underscores a profound loneliness and alienation from the conventional experiences of womanhood and motherhood. Her relationships with men are fraught and ambiguous. Although she has had many “fathers” of her children (often passing salesmen and transient men) these men are sterile or absent, contributing to her losses and isolation. They remember her and sometimes send tokens or inquiries years later, but their involvement is superficial and transient. Esther’s parents also misunderstand and fail to support her, regarding her as an “old maid” and a failure, unaware of her hidden suffering and the complexity of her condition. Esther also exhibits moments of bright vitality and spirited defiance. She tosses her hair freely “at whatever cost to sanitation,” laughs uproariously despite her pain, and engages in small acts of rebellion such as knitting without thread or playing with lovebirds. These actions underscore her refusal to be wholly defeated by her circumstances, highlighting her strength and courage in face of despair. Psychologically, Esther is haunted by the “little shadow boxer,” a persistent presence and hope that sustains her. She experiences both the physical symptoms of pregnancy and the deep emotional turmoil of loss and expectation. Her mind is described as clear and luminous amid the confusion and sorrow of her body, suggesting a complex inner life where hope and despair coexist. Esther Longtree is a figure of profound maternal tragedy and endurance. She embodies the pain of unrealized potential, the mystery of fertility and loss, and the resilience of the human spirit. Her story is steeped in symbolism: her body as womb and grave, her lost children as ghosts and shadows, her struggle as a metaphor for unfulfilled creation and hope amid desolation. See Esther Longtree.
    • Esther Longtree symbolizes a profound and tragic history of loss, barrenness, and unfulfilled potential that can be read as an allegory for certain aspects of the American experience, particularly in the Midwest and frontier regions. Her story embodies themes of repeated failure and disappointment in birth and creation, despite persistent hope and effort. She is perpetually pregnant yet never successfully gives birth to a living child, instead bearing countless stillborns, symbolizing a cycle of loss and despair. Her condition, an everlasting pregnancy with multiple stillborn children, reflects a history marked by sterile or fruitless attempts at creation and growth. The fathers of her children are often absent, sterile, or incapable, representing the failures of human agency and perhaps the broken promises of American expansion, settlement, or progress. The sterile salesmen, the transient men who pass through her life, can be seen as metaphors for the exploitative, transient nature of early economic ventures and social relationships in certain parts of the country, where hope for new life or renewal often met with harsh realities and repeated disappointments. Esther’s narrative is also deeply tied to the natural and atmospheric conditions of the Midwest or frontier (unusual atmospheric pressure, thinning ether, creeping glaciers, cold starlight, and the harshness of the natural environment) suggesting a land that is difficult to cultivate and sustain life in the traditional sense. This may symbolize the historical hardships endured by settlers and their descendants: the physical challenges of the land, the cold and unforgiving climate, and the spiritual or emotional barrenness that accompanied these struggles. Esther’s lonely, misunderstood existence, her isolation from family and community, and the ignorance of her parents reflect a broader social history of alienation and neglect, possibly alluding to marginalized or overlooked populations in American history, especially women who bore the burdens of fertility and loss in silence. She carries the legacy of these losses quietly yet with a luminous hope, knitting layettes and preparing for a child that might someday be born alive, symbolizing the persistence of hope and renewal in the face of overwhelming hardship and repeated failure. Esther Longtree symbolizes the history of human and environmental struggle in the American Midwest or frontier: the repeated disappointments in birth and renewal, the harshness of the environment, the failures of human connections, and the enduring hope amid loss and barrenness. Her figure serves as a poignant metaphor for the tragic, often unrecognized history of creation and loss that underlies the American experience in these regions.
  • “a braying, sighing sound almost like a mule”: Esther, “the mule woman,” came partly from Marc Chagall’s painting of a pregnant “mule lady” in a bridal veil, which Young “had not seen when I wrote the book,” and partly from Charlie Chaplin. Young remembered a scene in The Gold Rush (1925) in which Charlie invites a beautiful lady to dinner, “instead of that a mule arrives,” and he “entertains the mule as if it were a lady”: “Charlie has been a great inspiration to this book from start to finish” (Marguerite Young, interview with Studs Terkel, WFMT radio, 1965). No such scene appears in the film as released. Steven Moore recalled that Young would have titled the Esther section “Mule” (Steven Moore, “Remembering Marguerite Young,” 1999, in Dalkey Days). See Esther Longtree.
  • “Esther Longtree, the passive policeman’s only daughter”: The passive policeman was W. C. Fields. Young’s editor, Burroughs Mitchell, told her that his favorite character was “the passive policeman in the graveyard that separated couples,” who reminded him of Fields, and she told him that it was Fields (Marguerite Young, interview with Kay Bonetti, American Audio Prose Library, May 1983). See Esther Longtree.
  • “for she was soon to have a sweet, sweet little baby”: The line is spoken by Esther Longtree, a character haunted by endless pregnancies and stillbirths. This line is deeply symbolic and layered with meaning. Esther Longtree has experienced numerous stillbirths and losses of children fathered by various men who passed through her life. The “sweet, sweet little baby” she anticipates is not only a literal unborn child but also represents a profound hope for life and renewal amidst despair and loss. This baby “would cry in her arms” signifies the first living child she might finally hold and nurture, a sign of successful birth after so many failures. The phrase “that would kill them all” is metaphorical and suggests a transformative power of this forthcoming child. It implies that this child will “kill” or end the haunting presence of all the previous dead or stillborn children or the ghosts and memories that have burdened Esther. In other words, the living child will supersede the dead children, symbolically putting to rest the sorrow, loss, and endless cycle of stillbirths that have defined her life. This child could “kill” the past grief and suffering, bringing a new beginning.
  • “We are ships passing in the night and honking”: “Ships that pass in the night, and speak each other in passing, / Only a signal shown and a distant voice in the darkness” (Longfellow, Tales of a Wayside Inn, 1863). This phrase may refer to the poem, Tales of a Wayside Inn by Henry Wadsworth Longfellow.
  • “Johnny-jump-ups springing in her path”: Johnny-jump-ups symbolize the delicate, fragile, and often invisible presence of Esther’s stillborn children and the impermanence of life and hope in the midst of suffering.
  • “Johnny-jump-ups springing in her path”: The Johnny-jump-up, the wild pansy, is also called heartsease; in A Midsummer Night’s Dream it is love-in-idleness, whose juice makes the sleeper love the first creature seen on waking (2.1). See Shakespeare.
  • “those old, puny, sterile salesmen”: American traveling salesmen, or “drummers,” evolved from frontier peddlers carrying wagons of goods to figures selling encyclopedias, sewing machines, and elixirs, becoming cultural icons known for face-to-face pitches, sometimes using exaggerated claims, yet essential in connecting rural America to commerce through their personalized service before mass advertising took over, though they faced suspicion as “con men.” Their journey involved developing systematic sales techniques, using sample cases, and becoming central to American consumer culture, even while being portrayed as both mythic and untrustworthy figures.
    • The salesmen appear recurrently as figures who pass through the town and interact with Esther Longtree, the waitress who is perpetually pregnant but only bears stillborn children. These men represent sterile, ephemeral fathers who contribute to Esther’s endless cycle of conception and loss. They are described variously as “old, puny, sterile salesmen” and are often linked to the notion of futility and failure in reproduction. Despite their repeated presence in Esther’s life, they do not provide the stable, living progeny she longs for. Instead, they are associated with sterile conceptions and the birth of stillborn children who haunt her.
    • The different salesmen, such as the piano-tuner, the horn-blower, the tin roofer, the soap salesman, the rubber salesman, the featherweight, the Chicago detective, and others highlight the diversity yet uniformly disappointing nature of these transient relationships. Each is portrayed as a figure who fails to fulfill the biological or emotional role of a father, symbolizing the sterile, fractured modern world where connections are fleeting and fruitless. Their various professions suggest a broad cross-section of society, emphasizing that this sterility and failure transcend social or occupational boundaries. The salesmen symbolize the broader theme of displacement and rootlessness. They are drifters, passing through, unable or unwilling to form lasting bonds. They also embody the void and the mystery of loss that permeates Esther’s life, as they often write years later to inquire if the child they fathered was ever born, unaware or unwilling to accept the reality of their sterility and the stillbirths.
    • The salesmen collectively symbolize the failure of fertility and the loneliness of human existence in the novel’s landscape. They represent the absent or inadequate father figure and the broader societal and cosmic forces that contribute to Esther’s tragic, endless pregnancy and loss. The salesmen are trapped in cycles of hope and disappointment, mirroring Esther’s own cycles of conception and loss, and underscore the novel’s themes of death, loss, and the haunting presence of what might have been.
  • “the little shadow boxer, him inside, my other heart”: See The Little Shadow Boxer.
  • “Eat grass like the wild ass in the fields”: Of Nebuchadnezzar, driven out in his madness: “his dwelling was with the wild asses: they fed him with grass like oxen” (Daniel 5:21, KJV). See The Bible.
  • “Balaam’s ass beheld an angel”: Balaam’s ass may refer to Balaam’s story in the Bible starting in Numbers 22. God finally permits Balaam to go but with instructions to say only what He commands. Balaam then sets out in the morning with the princes of Moab. God becomes angry that he went, implying that he only used Balaam as a tool to further his will, and sends the Angel of the Lord to prevent him. At first, the angel is seen only by the donkey Balaam is riding, which tries to avoid the angel. After Balaam starts punishing the donkey for refusing to move, it is miraculously given the power to speak to Balaam, and it complains about Balaam’s treatment. At this point, Balaam is allowed to see the angel, who informs him that the donkey’s turning away from the messenger is the only reason the angel did not kill Balaam. Balaam immediately repents, but is told to go on. “And the ass saw the angel of the LORD standing in the way, and his sword drawn in his hand” (Numbers 22:23, KJV). See The Bible.
  • “the winnowing test”: “Whose fan is in his hand, and he will throughly purge his floor, and gather his wheat into the garner; but he will burn up the chaff” (Matthew 3:12, KJV). See The Bible.
  • “face the Ghostly Reaper”: See the Ghostly Reaper in the Chapter 68 resources. See Death and Mortality.
  • “There were as many stillborn as the autumn leaves”: In Esther Longtree’s dialogue, she makes several philosophical and symbolic references that reflect her profound meditation on life, creation, loss, and existence. These references are woven into her reflections on her repeated pregnancies, stillbirths, and her unique condition of “everlasting pregnancy.” Esther speaks repeatedly of her numerous stillborn children as “leaves,” “snowflakes,” and “stars,” emphasizing the natural cycles of birth and death, creation and dissolution. This links to philosophical meditations on impermanence and the transitory nature of existence. She frequently refers to the “void,” the “shadow,” and “the unknown heavens,” reflecting on what is unrealized or invisible in life: an existential contemplation of what lies beyond human perception or understanding. This resonates with themes of mystery and the limits of human knowledge. Esther imagines her pregnancy as connected to cosmic forces: stars, the Milky Way, atmospheric pressure, and the ether. She even recounts a mystical experience on a desert island where she witnessed wild mares pregnant without males, suggesting a mystical or imaginative form of creation that transcends conventional biology. This evokes philosophical ideas about nature’s mysteries and creative power beyond conventional human understanding. She refers to the “bubble,” “foam,” and “afterbirth” as metaphors for creation itself, pondering if all creation might be just these transient phenomena. This metaphor has a philosophical resonance with ideas about the provisional or ephemeral nature of existence and reality. Esther contemplates the mysterious “Who killed cock robin?” question, ultimately concluding that death is a universal, impersonal force: no one is solely to blame, and it is the natural fate of all beings. This reflects a fatalistic or existential acceptance of mortality. She embodies the paradox of being “brilliant but dumb,” “beautiful but misunderstood,” “strong but burdened,” which reflects philosophical tensions between appearance and reality, strength and vulnerability, hope and despair. Esther’s reflections on her lonely, misunderstood condition, her parents’ ignorance, and the many “fathers” who come and go, highlight themes of alienation and the human search for meaning and connection. Esther’s narrative blurs the line between imagination and reality, such as when she speaks of knitting without thread or the foetus swimming beyond ivory cliffs, suggesting a philosophical inquiry into the nature of perception, belief, and the creative power of the mind. Despite her sorrow, Esther expresses a persistent hope that “something will be born,” reflecting a philosophical tension between despair and hope, a fundamental human condition. Esther’s dialogue is rich with philosophical symbolism about life’s mysteries, the burden of fertility and loss, the cosmic and individual scale of existence, and the human confrontation with mortality and meaning. These reflections position her as a tragic yet luminous figure embodying elemental human experiences and mysteries.
  • “off the coast of the Old Dominion”: “Old Dominion” is Virginia’s well-known nickname, given by King Charles II of England to thank the colony for its loyalty during the English Civil War, signifying it as a cherished, longstanding territory of the crown, and it’s also a nod to its status as one of the oldest English overseas dominions. The name reflects Virginia’s early colonial significance and its historical ties to the monarchy, appearing on colonial seals and adopted officially as a state slogan.
    • Wild ponies have run on Assateague Island, off Virginia and Maryland, for centuries; legend makes them survivors of a Spanish shipwreck. Marguerite Henry’s Misty of Chincoteague (1947) made them famous. See Horses and Carriages and Women, Gender, and Marriage.
  • “the wild white mothers be fecundated by the wind”: There are myths about animals, not just mares, being impregnated by the wind. Pliny and Virgil told it of the mares of Lusitania. See the wind-made mares in the Chapter 71 resources. See Horses and Carriages.
  • “a poor mule, or else everlastingly pregnant”: Esther is described as a mule laboring on and on much like the myth of Sisyphus where Zeus punished him for cheating death twice by forcing him to roll an immense boulder up a hill only for it to roll down every time it neared the top, repeating this action for eternity. Through the classical influence on modern culture, tasks that are both laborious and futile are therefore described as Sisyphean. See Greek Mythology.
  • “old Dr. O’Leary had told her only this morning”: See Justice O’Leary.
  • “as if she dropped a handkerchief”: Dropping a handkerchief was also used when describing “...a moment’s passage, was a handkerchief dropped from the hand of God…” by Mr. Spitzer. See the Chapter 50 resources.
  • “all the Fallopian tubes”: Fallopian tubes (in a female mammal) is either of a pair of tubes along which eggs travel from the ovaries to the uterus. They are named for Gabriele Falloppio, the Italian anatomist who described them in 1561. See Pregnancy, Abortion, and Midwifery.
  • “the skies had unrolled like a scroll on the last day”: “And the heaven departed as a scroll when it is rolled together” (Revelation 6:14, KJV). See Revelation and the Apocalypse.
  • “It is probably the medica materia”: Medica materia is a Latin term from the history of pharmacy for the body of collected knowledge about the therapeutic properties of any substance used for healing. The term derives from the title of a work by the Ancient Greek physician Pedanius Dioscorides. In the 20th century it was changed to pharmacology.
  • “had never had to take a stitch”: “The stitch” may refer to a procedure called an episiotomy, also known as perineotomy and is a surgical incision of the perineum and the posterior vaginal wall generally done by a midwife or obstetrician. It was in the 50s in the US called the “husband stitch” because it was believed to return a woman’s vaginal opening to its original size. The routine is no longer recommended for vaginal births except in emergencies. Despite this, it is one of the most common surgical procedures specific to women. See Pregnancy, Abortion, and Midwifery and Women, Gender, and Marriage.
  • “for she had lost no teeth as did most women who, in her condition, lacked the calcium”: It is a myth that women’s teeth become worse during pregnancy since any calcium needed would be taken from the bones and not the teeth. If a pregnant woman’s diet is not sufficient then nutrients for the baby will be leached from the mother. The old saying was “a child, a tooth.”
  • “the General Electric representative”: General Electric or General Electric Company (GE) is an American multinational conglomerate founded in 1892, and incorporated in New York state and headquartered in Boston. (Wikipedia)
  • “the Cumberland Gap”: The Cumberland Gap is a pass through the long ridge of the Cumberland Mountains, within the Appalachian Mountains, near the junction of the U.S. states of Kentucky, Virginia, and Tennessee. It is famous in American colonial history for its role as a key passageway through the lower central Appalachians. (Wikipedia)
  • “the man who was on his way to salty Utah, the Mormon”: “Salty Utah” may refer to Salt Lake City which is the capital and most populous city of the U.S. state of Utah, as well as the seat of Salt Lake County, the most populous county in Utah. (Wikipedia)
    • Mormons are a religious and cultural group, the principal branch of the Latter Day Saint movement started by Joseph Smith in upstate New York during the 1820s. The largest number of members reside in Utah. (Wikipedia) See American Religious Movements.
  • “the W.P.A.”: The W.P.A. may refer to the Works Progress Administration, renamed in 1939 as the Work Projects Administration, which was an American New Deal agency that employed millions of jobseekers, mostly men who were not formally educated, to carry out public works projects.
  • “a little Jehovah’s Witness”: Jehovah’s Witnesses in America, initially Bible Students, grew from the late 1800s under Charles Taze Russell, faced intense persecution during the 1930s & WWII for neutrality, adopted the name in 1931, expanded significantly with organized campaigns and Gilead training, and solidified doctrines like the 1935 “great crowd” redefinition, all while building their distinctive identity through publications, conventions, and door-to-door work, establishing a strong presence despite opposition. See American Religious Movements.
  • “her walnut jewelry”: Walnut jewelry, spanning from historical, hand-polished Chinese health balls (sometimes worn or carried as status symbols) to Victorian-era “fancywork” using shells for keepsakes, signifies a blend of natural, symbolic, and sentimental adornment. It represents durability and connection to nature, often featuring carved shells or polished walnut wood.
  • “her wooden shoes”: Wooden shoes, known as klompen in the Netherlands, originated in the Middle Ages (circa 13th century) as durable, affordable, and waterproof footwear for farmers, fishermen, and laborers across Europe. Carved from alder, willow, or poplar, they provided protection against damp, muddy conditions and sharp objects. While traditional, they became iconic Dutch, Swedish, and European cultural items.
  • “the pecan trees that were brought from the old Jerusalem”: Old Jerusalem, a 5,000-year-old city, has been a central hub of religious and political conflict, serving as the Jewish capital since King David (c. 1000 B.C.) and holding immense significance for Christians and Muslims. The current 0.9-square-kilometer walled city, rebuilt by the Ottomans in the 16th century, is divided into Armenian, Christian, Jewish, and Muslim quarters.
  • “the moon gleamings of pomegranates”: Within the novel’s themes of life, death, and transformation, pomegranates symbolize the richness and complexity of these cycles, fertility, and the mysterious transitions between states of being.
  • “to borrow a nickel for his drink”: Esther asked for Dr. O’Leary’s advice when he came in to get a drink. A nickel then bought a cup of coffee or a glass of beer, and played a record on the jukebox.
  • “for God loves a silent woman”: “A silent and loving woman is a gift of the Lord” (Ecclesiasticus 26:14, in the Apocrypha of the King James Bible); “Let the woman learn in silence with all subjection” (1 Timothy 2:11, KJV). See The Bible and Women, Gender, and Marriage.
  • “watched the marathon skaters”: See the ice-skaters and marathon dancers in the Chapter 71 resources.
  • “was vertiginous”: Vertiginous means dizzy.
  • “her garter snapping”: Garters originated in the Dark Ages as practical, functional bands (leather or ribbon) used by both men and women to hold up stockings, evolving from simple ties to decorative accessories by the 18th century. They became essential, specialized lingerie in the 19th/early 20th centuries before largely disappearing with the advent of elastic, nylon, and pantyhose.
  • “the oldest pinochle player”: Pinochle originated in 19th-century Germany from the French game Bezique, evolving from Binokel, with its name possibly meaning “eyeglasses” (from the Queen of Spades and Jack of Diamonds combo). German immigrants brought it to America, where it became hugely popular in the late 1800s and early 1900s, especially in the Midwest, growing into a beloved game rivaling poker and bridge, featuring unique melding and trick-taking mechanics with a special 48-card deck. See Gambling and Playing Cards.
  • “buried layettes laid out in long white boxes”: Young’s first poem, written at sixteen, “was about preparing a layette for my unborn fatherless baby,” and “it does become the character of Esther Longtree in Miss Macintosh, My Darling, many decades later.” An English teacher told her “that a young girl should not have such thoughts on her mind” (Marguerite Young, interview, WNYC radio, New York). On a train to Chicago a man told her of a cocker spaniel whose false pregnancy was eased only by giving “her toys to play with as if the baby were really there” (Marguerite Young, interview with Studs Terkel, WFMT radio, 1965). See Esther Longtree and Pregnancy, Abortion, and Midwifery.
    • A layette is a curated collection of clothing and essentials for a newborn, traditionally prepared by expectant mothers through sewing or knitting. Originating from the French term for a small drawer or box (laie) in the 17th-19th centuries, it evolved from hand-stitched, essential linens to modern, pre-curated sets, often used in charity programs for mothers in need.
  • “the moon-globed persimmon”: Persimmon, peach, and cherry: these fruit trees, with their blossoms and fallen fruits, are evocative images of the ephemeral nature of life and the enduring sorrow that accompanies it throughout the novel.
  • “a Finnish worker”: Finnish workers in America were primarily part of a large wave of immigrants (1864-1924) employed in heavy labor, particularly mining in Michigan and Minnesota, logging, and farming. Often fleeing poverty and political turmoil, they were known for being hard-working, literate, and settling in tight-knit, often socialist-leaning communities.
  • “She had never eaten ergot”: Ergot is a fungus that in the 1930s companies marketed to women whose pregnancy was not progressing since abortion, drugs that aborted a fetus and birth control devices were illegal. The FTC deemed the pills unsafe and ineffective and stopped their sale. In 1774 it is documented that midwives used ergot to ease delivery of a baby. In 1808 the New York doctor John Stearns published his use of ergot, “pulvis parturiens,” to hasten labor. See Pregnancy, Abortion, and Midwifery and Women, Gender, and Marriage.
  • “breeding lovebirds”: Lovebirds, are small parrots native to Africa and Madagascar, with nine distinct species identified. Known for their intense social bonding and “allo-preening” behavior, they were popularized in Europe during the 1800s as pets. Early records date to the 1600s, though they were extensively trapped and traded in the 19th and 20th centuries. See Birds.
  • “thank you, George Washington”: George Washington was an aggressive surveyor and land speculator who acquired over 50,000 acres, often on indigenous lands, earning him the name “Town Destroyer” (Conotocarious) from the Iroquois. He was a lifelong, large-scale slaveholder, inheriting ten enslaved people at age eleven and later controlling over 300, while navigating brutal, disease-ridden early frontier life. See Society, Class, and Race.
  • “Martin Luther”: Martin Luther was a German priest, theologian, author and hymn writer. A former Augustinian friar, he is best known among Christians as the seminal figure in the Protestant Reformation and as the namesake of Lutheranism. (Wikipedia)
    • In his last years Luther turned on the Jews in On the Jews and Their Lies (1543), a tract the Nazis reprinted. See Judaism.
  • “Beau Geste”: Beau Geste is an adventure novel by British writer P. C. Wren, which details the adventures of three English brothers who enlist separately in the French Foreign Legion following the theft of a valuable jewel from the country house of a relative. Published in 1924, the novel is set in the period before World War I. It has been adapted for the screen several times. (Wikipedia)
  • “she might be dropsical”: Dropsy is an archaic medical term for the swelling of soft tissues due to the excessive accumulation of fluid (edema). Historically used to describe symptoms of underlying diseases like heart failure, kidney disease, or malnutrition, it is now known simply as edema. Symptoms include swollen legs, ankles, or abdomen, and tight, stretched skin.
  • “What if the over-active foetus”: The spelling “foetus” entered English from Late Latin (around the 16th century) as a “hypercorrection” based on Latin words like amoenus, adding the ‘o’ where it wasn’t etymologically correct, though it became common in British/Commonwealth English and medical fields for a time. The true Latin root is fetus, meaning “offspring,” making “fetus” the etymologically correct form, now the standard globally in medicine and preferred in the U.S., while “foetus” persists in non-medical UK usage.
  • “a breech birth”: A breech birth occurs when a baby is positioned feet or bottom down instead of head-down near the end of pregnancy (around 36-37 weeks). While most babies turn head-down, about 3-5% remain in this position, which carries a higher risk for vaginal delivery, often requiring a C-section. See Pregnancy, Abortion, and Midwifery.
  • “the Hoosier Amateur Star-Gazers”: “Hoosier” refers to the U.S. state of Indiana. It is the official nickname for residents of Indiana, used since the mid-19th century, and serves as the state’s official demonym (the name for a person from a specific place). See Iowa, Indiana, and the Midwest.
  • “the maternal pelvis was smaller than the needle’s eye”: “It is easier for a camel to go through the eye of a needle, than for a rich man to enter into the kingdom of God” (Matthew 19:24, KJV). See The Bible.
  • “outside the precincts of the Starry Girdle, the Milky Way”: The Milky Way or Milky Way Galaxy is the galaxy that includes the Solar System, with the name describing the galaxy’s appearance from Earth: a hazy band of light seen in the night sky formed from stars in other arms of the galaxy, which are so far away that they cannot be individually distinguished by the naked eye. (Wikipedia) See Astronomy.
  • “it could pass through as in the twinkling of an eye”: “In a moment, in the twinkling of an eye, at the last trump” (1 Corinthians 15:52, KJV). See The Bible.
  • “the great bubble which precedes creation”: World egg, cosmic egg or mundane egg are mythological motifs found in the cosmogonies of many cultures that are present in Proto-Indo-European culture and other cultures and civilizations. Typically, the world egg is a beginning of some sort, and the universe or some primordial being comes into existence by breaking the shell of the egg, sometimes lain on the primordial waters of the Earth. Eggs symbolize the unification of two complementary principles from which life or existence, in its most fundamental philosophical sense, emerges.
  • “The wailings, the gnashings of teeth”: “There shall be weeping and gnashing of teeth” (Matthew 8:12, KJV). See The Bible.
  • “The jukebox repairman”: The jukebox, a nickel a record, filled the taverns and diners of the 1930s and 1940s. See Music and Composers.
  • “Who killed cock robin?”: Who Killed Cock Robin is an English nursery rhyme. Although the earliest known record of the song is from the mid-eighteenth century, there is some evidence that it is much older. Versions of the story appear to exist in other countries, including Germany. There are a number of theories that have been advanced to explain the meaning of the rhyme. According to Celtic traditions, Lugh, the sun god who dies as the nights get longer after the summer solstice, is marked in the old Celtic pictographic calendar with a bow-and-arrow shape. Lugh was the primary god representing the red sun and was also known in Welsh as Coch Rhi Ben, which when anglicized would mean Cock Robin (coch meaning red, rhi meaning lord, ben meaning leader) This may be a reference to the belief that souls became birds after death. The sparrow who kills him with his bow and arrow may represent Brân the Blessed, the god of winter in the form of a raven. (Wikipedia) Its answer, first printed in Tommy Thumb’s Pretty Song Book (1744), is “I, said the Sparrow, / With my bow and arrow.” Esther’s last words echo it: “Ah, I knew, she saw, who killed him!” See Fairy Tales and Folklore and Birds.
  • “Was there a babe lost in the woods, a babe lost in the snow?”: In the ballad of the Babes in the Wood (1595), two orphaned children, abandoned by their wicked uncle, die in the forest and are covered with leaves by robins. See Fairy Tales and Folklore.
  • “Did not all people come into the world to die, as the preacher sayeth”: “A time to be born, and a time to die” (Ecclesiastes 3:2, KJV). See Ecclesiastes.
  • “had died of scarlet fever”: Before antibiotics, scarlet fever was one of the great killers of children; penicillin made it curable in the 1940s.
  • “selling Fuller brushes from door to door”: Fuller Brushes are high-quality cleaning tools, personal care items, and brushes for various, specialized, and durable household uses, produced by The Fuller Brush Company since 1906. Known for being “built to last,” these products range from brooms, mops, and cleaning supplies to hairbrushes and personal care products. The Fuller Brush Man, going door to door, became an American type.
  • “the darkly shining cheval glass”: Cheval glass is a long mirror, mounted on a swivel in a frame, allowing it to be tilted.

Chapter 61
