Chapter 71

← Chapter 70 · Home · Chapter 72 →

Content note: This chapter contains racist and antisemitic speech, including a racial slur, “the dirty Jew,” and praise of Hitler, and tells of a pregnant woman who hanged herself.

Summary

Morning comes cold and silent after the night of voices. Vera, awake on her papery bed, wonders whether the Christian hangman has hanged himself at last and remembers Marie, cut down in the orchard with her unborn child. She dresses in her mother’s black velvet, the shroud Catherine meant to abandon, with her lace and the real pearls that, Catherine said, multiplied each time they were lost. She recalls the Italian thief her mother once entertained, sent off in a dead man’s white clothes with a promise to finance a Revolution. In Dr. O’Leary’s empty office she finds mateless women’s shoes, birth instruments, a Yale diploma, a calendar twenty years old with Mary Pickford on it, and a library of strange books. On the stairs a widow in curlers accuses her of keeping her awake, then rages against Jews, Catholics, and Black people and praises Hitler. Downstairs the landlady, a vast woman with a goiter, tells Vera in broken, wandering speech of the hotel, its dead watchdog, and Tabitha, the mute chambermaid, who looks up from washing the stones and whispers, “Good-morning.”

Characters present

Mr. Weed · Justice O’Leary · Tabitha · The Tavern Landlady · Vera Cartwheel · Catherine Cartwheel · Simeon the Doctor · The Tavern Landlord · Esther Longtree · Jacqueline White

Concepts present

Themes: Death and Mortality · Decay and Ruin · Illusion and Reality · Isolation and Connection · Madness and Sanity · Memory and the Past · Motherhood, Pregnancy, and Birth · Society, Class, and Race · Women, Gender, and Marriage

Symbols: Clocks and Watches · Clothing, Hats, and Skirts · Dogs · Pearls and Jewels · Weddings and Funerals

Philosophy: Astrology, Alchemy, and Esoterica · Plato and Platonism

Allusions: American Religious Movements · Ancient Egypt · Astronomy · Dante · Fairy Tales and Folklore · Genesis · Iowa, Indiana, and the Midwest · Judaism · Lynching and Racial Violence · Music and Composers · Pregnancy, Abortion, and Midwifery · Romantic Poets · The Bible · The History of Opium

Key passages

From the research

  • The chapter opens with reflections on the “Christian hangman,” his routine duties, and the haunting memory of his wife Marie who hanged herself while pregnant. Mr. Weed fears what he might find in the orchard, and Marie’s children play at hanging themselves, though Mr. Weed himself does not hang himself.
  • Vera reflects on wearing her mother’s necklace of real pearls, an inheritance described as indestructible and eternal, her “lost estate.” The story of the chauffeur, James, who returns thirteen pearls when twelve are lost, introduces the concept of infinity and the shadow of the past (Joachim as the “quiet, yawning twin”).
  • Vera enters the doctor’s bedroom/office, described as chaotic, filled with scattered, unmatched women’s shoes, medical instruments, and broken objects. The doctor delivers imaginary babies in a barren countryside, and there is mention of a “pregnant man.”
  • The interaction between the doctor and a silent crawling woman, Sarah, his “little sister,” is significant. Sarah is both tormentor and companion to the doctor, who screams at her and makes her promises.
  • Vera studies the doctor’s extensive but disordered medical library, filled with eclectic and outdated books ranging from medical texts to children’s primers and political pamphlets. The doctor’s diploma from Yale hangs above the bed.
  • A confrontation with a half-dressed woman in metallic curlers introduces a sharp critique of social tensions: racism, anti-Semitism, political distrust, and the breakdown of community respect. Her tirade includes references to Hitler, Roosevelt, and racial purity, reflecting the deep social divisions and anxieties of the time and place. This passage grounds the surreal elements in harsh social realities.
  • The chapter ends with a description of the hotel lobby and the landlady, a large woman with a goiter, who speaks in a dialect mixing resignation and fatalism. She describes the household’s routines, the landlord, Tabitha the muted chambermaid, and the decay of the place, including the absence of the priest and the death of the old watchdog.
  • The chapter ends with Tabitha kneeling to wash stones on the porch in the “pale spring air,” with her humble greeting, “Good-morning.”

Questions and observations

Reading closely

  • “What thief I might have been of poverty, of beautiful poverty, of deprivation, of nothing.” What does Vera want to steal?
  • “Few fantasies are so externalized, I supposed, as the doctor’s mind.” What does his room show of him?
  • “Yet how many of us, if we expressed our inner lives, would not express disorder?” Would yours?

Characters

  • Catherine believed that the more often she lost her pearls, “the more pearls there were.” What does this tell us about her?
  • The widow says, “Hitler is right, I tell you.” Why does Young give this hatred to a grieving widow who cannot sleep?
  • Tabitha, “muted as a stone in the stream,” speaks at last: “Good-morning.” What does her greeting mean after this night?

Connections

  • Vera wears “the black velvet which had been her abandoned shroud.” Why does she travel in her mother’s clothes?
  • “There are no Negroes in this county, for the sun will not set on a Negro’s head here.” How does this answer the hangman’s Kentucky story in Chapter 68?
  • “Why was Sarah laughing?” Compare Sarah in Genesis, who laughed at the promise of a child. What do the two laughs share?

Reflection

  • “That which I required for my happiness would not be wealth but would be something quite plain and poor and bare.” Has Vera found it?
  • “But oh, I had wished to discover order, as if it were a beautiful island in the midst of life, island I might never reach.” Is order an island?
  • Vera hopes for “people who went about their accustomed business, people who did not think too much.” Does she meet them?

Research: Characters

Mr. Weed (The Christian Hangman)

  • A man who has hanged many murderers but refuses to hang women or those far gone in pregnancy.
  • His wife, Marie, hanged herself during pregnancy, which haunts him deeply.
  • Mr. Weed is portrayed as a tragic figure, burdened by his past and haunted by ghostly children of the hanged.
  • Vera contemplates whether Mr. Weed might hang himself but concludes he waits for dawn to protect his children from danger.

Dr. Justice O’Leary

  • A once-respected doctor, now mad and living in a chaotic state.
  • His office/bedroom is cluttered with mismatched women’s shoes, birth instruments, and medical books, reflecting his mental disarray.
  • He delivers “imaginary babies” in a barren countryside, symbolizing futile or delusional efforts to bring life or hope.
  • He suffers from senility and hallucinations, including the presence of his dead sister Sarah and the chambermaid Tabitha.
  • Despite madness, he retains some medical knowledge and authority.
  • There are rumors of a “pregnant man” patient, blending reality and fantasy.

Tabitha

  • The chambermaid, also mentally unstable (“too crazy to be on relief”).
  • She cares for the doctor at night, hoping to get a baby by him.
  • She represents the marginalized and the caretakers in the chaotic environment.

Tavern Landlady

  • A large, fat woman with a goiter, representing a figure rooted in reality amidst chaos.
  • She speaks of the hotel’s management, the old watch dogs, the landlord, and the lack of interference in the hotel’s strange happenings.
  • Her speech is laced with local dialect and vivid imagery, adding texture to the scene.
  • Symbolically, the Tavern Landlady can be interpreted as representing the fading old America or traditional American society.
  • As a former circus fat lady, she recalls a form of popular entertainment and spectacle that had its heyday in the earlier part of the 20th century and before.
  • The Landlady’s association with the old watch dog, who was a devout Catholic attending church even during harsh weather, who received the Eucharist from the priest and died in the landlord’s arms, indicates a decline of traditional religious and communal values. This suggests a metaphor for the waning influence of organized religion and community cohesion in mid-20th century America.
  • The landlady is resigned to the decay of the hotel and its inhabitants, but she has a quiet intelligence.

Vera Cartwheel

  • An observer and participant, reflecting on the surreal and tragic elements of the setting.
  • Vera, the narrator, emerges as a deeply contemplative and psychologically complex figure, marked by a blend of wakefulness, memory, and a searching, somewhat haunted awareness.
  • Vera is awake in the cold, grey morning, unable or unwilling to sleep despite the silence and stillness around her. Her state is described as “stiff with wakefulness, with ceaseless memory” and “wide awake, alert, watchful,” showing a restless mind that is both physically and mentally active rather than at rest. This wakefulness seems not merely physical but also symbolic, representing a state of consciousness probing the mysteries and uncertainties of her surroundings and her own psyche.
  • Throughout the chapter, Vera’s thoughts drift into rich, imaginative flights and reflections. She muses on the Christian hangman and his tragic personal history, pondering whether he might hang himself or wait for dawn because of his children playing at hanging themselves. Vera also reflects on her mother’s pearls.
  • Vera is portrayed as a traveler or outsider in this strange, desolate Indiana hotel and its surroundings. She is “some time past the ambiguity of dawn,” wearing travel-stained clothes and carrying her mother’s lace and pearls, symbols of a “lost estate” and an unrealized past. Her presence in the hotel is that of someone searching for something: wild flowers of spring, beauty, or perhaps a deeper meaning amid the decay and disorder around her. This sense of quest is tinged with uncertainty and disillusionment, as the landscape and people she encounters are far removed from her expectations or hopes.
  • Vera is a keen observer of the strange and unsettling characters she encounters, especially the doctor, Dr. O’Leary, and the hangman. She notes the doctor’s madness and the surreal disorder of his office and life, filled with instruments, scattered shoes of various types and eras, and imaginary patients. Vera reflects on the blending of reality and fantasy, the doctor’s second childhood, and the presence of “imaginary babies” and a “pregnant man.”
  • Vera listens to the angry widow who confronts her, accusing her of being a “tramp girl” who kept her awake all night, and to Tabitha, the muted chambermaid who quietly carries out her duties. Despite these confrontations and the vivid descriptions of the inhabitants’ misery and anger, Vera seems somewhat detached as an intruder or observer rather than a participant. She tries to explain herself logically but acknowledges the complexity and strangeness of the place and its people.
  • Vera’s narrative voice often becomes poetic and philosophical. She notes how the hotel room expands during sleeplessness into a vast landscape of memory and future, blending space and time.

Catherine Cartwheel

  • Catherine is a figure deeply immersed in a subjective, dream-like reality, detached from the conventional world. Her character is defined by her peculiar philosophies, eccentric habits, and a luxurious but illusory existence that profoundly shapes Vera’s own journey and desires.
  • Catherine is often referred to by Vera as “my sleeping mother,” suggesting a state of perpetual dreaming or detachment from waking life. Her physical presence is limited; she “had not walked for many years because of the birthmark staining her cheek and because of her fear of the wavering floor, the sea sweeping in, and her dead past.” This immobility further anchors her to her internal world, within her great, “sea-blackened house with gold towers and cornices,” which, despite its grandeur, is described as being “gone,” implying its existence is more in memory or illusion than current reality.
  • Her unique philosophical outlook is evident in her beliefs about her “real pearls,” which, she claimed, “could not be lost or stolen or sold. Whatever the human, unhuman situation might be, those real pearls could not really be lost, and I should wear them, for they were her lost estate.” She believed that losing pearls paradoxically led to their multiplication, creating “infinities of pearls,” a concept she explained as “just simple arithmetic, simple addition.” She also held a profound view of existence, stating that it was “probably not... eternity, something everlasting, this being so temporary a world, the world already gone. Only the shadow... ever does come here.”
  • Catherine’s eccentricity is vividly illustrated through her interaction with a thief who broke into her house one winter night. Far from being alarmed, she “smilingly greeted him, extending her ivory-colored hand, asking him how far he had come, and was the world truly dead, and had offered him drugged sherry.” She engaged him in a languorous conversation, “sympathizing with her that she was rich, just as she had sympathized with him that he was poor.” In a grand, yet impractical, gesture, she offered to “finance a Revolution” with a blank check, contingent on the thief naming “an exact sum needed and an exact date,” which, caught in her “shimmering enchantment,” he could not do. Her generosity extended to outfitting the thief in an aristocratic gentleman’s costume, including a “high silk opera hat,” “long white motor coat,” and “white flowers behind his ears,” symbolizing the “coming Revolution” and making him “the melting snowman upon the first day of spring.”
  • Vera carries the tangible and intangible legacy of her mother. She wears Catherine’s “black velvet which had been her abandoned shroud,” her “lace collar and the lace cuffs,” and the “necklace of pearls.” However, Vera’s own desire for “something quite plain and poor and bare” and her search for “order, as if it were a beautiful island in the midst of life” suggest a yearning for a reality distinct from her mother’s opulent, yet ultimately vanished, dream-world.

The Italian Thief

  • The Italian thief appears in Vera’s memories of her mother Catherine’s stories. He breaks into her mother’s sea-blackened house one winter night, expecting it to be empty, but is surprised to find her there. Instead of robbing her, he is charmed by her and ends up talking with her until morning.
  • The thief is easily taken aback by Catherine’s presence and charm. Instead of sticking to his original plan, he is willing to engage in conversation and accept her hospitality.
  • He sympathizes with Vera’s mother being rich, just as she sympathizes with him being poor.
  • He does not name an exact sum or date for the Revolution, and he allows Catherine to outfit him in ridiculous clothes.
  • The thief is ultimately unsuccessful in his original goal of robbing Catherine, and he leaves with nothing of value, only a bizarre costume.
  • He is a figure in Catherine’s dreamlike world, who is transformed from a thief into a “pale, aristocratic gentleman” destined to be “the melting snowman upon the first day of spring.” This suggests that he represents the potential for transformation and the blurring of reality and illusion.
  • The thief, described as wearing an extravagant costume, “a high silk opera hat with a furry rim, a long white motor coat, glass medallions, ribbons, white trousers, white shoes, white flowers behind his ears” is outfitted by Catherine as a “pale, aristocratic gentleman” and is connected symbolically with the coming Revolution and the melting snowman of spring, implying a transition or transformation fraught with sorrow.
  • Catherine’s “Italian thief” is served with luxury and kindness, almost unreal in the snowy, desolate setting, and she offers to finance his Revolution if he can name an exact sum and date, which he cannot.
  • While the text does not explicitly state that the Italian thief represents Italy in World War II, the symbolic elements strongly suggest an allegorical reading. Italy, during and after World War II, was a nation undergoing profound social and political turmoil and revolution, transitioning from fascism toward a new order. The thief’s aristocratic garb and his association with both crime and revolution could metaphorically reflect Italy’s complex role both as a participant in conflict and as a nation facing internal upheaval and rebirth.

The Woman in Curlers

  • The woman in metallic curlers emerges as a striking, intense figure who confronts Vera with anger and a sense of moral indignation. Her appearance and demeanor are vividly described: she is “half dressed,” with her face marked by a contrasting complexion, one cheek lit by a “high red light,” the other ashen which emphasizes her disturbed, volatile state. She approaches Vera blocking her path, “her mouth opening, closing,” and her face “contorted with a cold rage.”
  • This woman accuses Vera of being one of “those tramp girls,” implicating her in keeping a “decent woman awake all night.” Her repeated insistence on Vera’s shamefulness reveals her rigid moral stance and perhaps a fear or resentment of those she perceives as disrupting social order or propriety within the hotel. Her anger is not merely personal but tied to a broader anxiety about the chaos and unrest around her, symbolized by “couples screaming,” “hitch-hikers,” “ice-skaters,” and “marathon dancers” who disturb her peace and the sanctity of “marriage bonds.”
  • The woman reveals her own vulnerable position: she is a widow, isolated and grieving, with a husband who “died before he ever came to bed,” heightening her sense of loneliness and despair. Her bitter outburst against “the other doctor, Simeon...the dirty Jew,” and her invocation of Hitler and racial and religious prejudices reveal her bigoted attitudes and the pervasive social tensions in the community. This further complicates her character, showing how her personal suffering is entangled with broader social fears, xenophobia, and political resentments that color her worldview.
  • Despite her harshness toward Vera and others, the woman’s fury and bitterness also suggest a deep-seated fear of abandonment and loss of control. Her rage can be seen as defensive, a way to assert agency in a situation where she feels powerless. The fact that she knows Vera and quickly labels her indicates a community that is closely knit but fraught with judgment and suspicion.
  • The woman in curlers is portrayed as a complex character embodying anger, fear, loneliness, and prejudice.
  • The woman in metallic curlers who confronts Vera on the stairs of the hotel is depicted with a face “contorted with a cold rage,” half-dressed and aggressively barring Vera’s path. She accuses Vera of being one of the “tramp girls” who keep a decent woman awake all night, and she voices vehemently racist and anti-Semitic views, blaming Jews, communists, and Roosevelt for various social ills, and asserting white supremacist beliefs, including a denial of African Americans (“There are no Negroes in this county... We don’t want mulattoes”). She even endorses Hitler’s ideology, saying “Hitler is right,” and rants about conspiracies involving Jews and communism.
  • Symbolically, this woman can be interpreted as representing a segment of mid-20th century American society characterized by reactionary, xenophobic, and racist attitudes that were prevalent especially in certain rural or less urbanized areas before the Civil Rights Movement culminated in legislative changes by 1964. Her vehement defense of “traditional” social orders, expressed through racial purity, anti-communism, and religious intolerance, echoes the nativist, segregationist, and anti-Semitic sentiments that persisted in parts of the United States, particularly in the South and Midwest, during the early-to-mid 1900s. This character embodies the cultural anxieties and social resistance to change that would be challenged by the movements for civil rights, integration, and social reform leading up to and following 1964.
  • Her role as a gatekeeper figure barring Vera who might symbolize change, outsider perspectives, or marginalized identities underscores the entrenched social barriers and hostility faced by those who threatened the status quo. The woman’s aggressive posture and speech serve as a stark personification of intolerance and oppression in the historical context before the transformative legislation of the Civil Rights Act of 1964.
  • The woman in curlers symbolically represents the reactionary, racist, and xenophobic elements in American society prior to 1964, embodying the cultural resistance to social progress and equality that defined much of U.S. social history before the Civil Rights era reforms.

Simeon the Doctor

  • He is described through the lens of local prejudice and suspicion, particularly voiced by a woman in the hotel who vehemently refuses to go to him for medical care. This woman expresses strong antisemitic views, calling Simeon “the dirty Jew” and accusing Jews of taking everything and running the world. She recounts that “Hitler ran him out of Germany” and refuses to let Simeon “paw all over her.”

Tavern Landlord

  • A figure of quiet authority but also resigned to the hotel’s state.

Esther Longtree and Jacqueline White · Jacqueline White

  • The landlady says the last waitress at the restaurant was “taken of the tuberculosis with her baby in her arms”; this seems to be Jacqueline. Esther Longtree took her place.

Research: Themes

Death and Hanging

See: Death and Mortality

  • Mr. Weed’s profession, the death of his wife, and the children of the hanged symbolize the inescapability of death and guilt.
  • The motif of hanging recurs with symbolic weight: both execution and suicide.

Madness and Reality

See: Illusion and Reality · Madness and Sanity

  • Dr. O’Leary’s madness blurs the lines between reality and hallucination.
  • The presence of imaginary babies and patients reflects the struggle to grasp meaning in a chaotic world.
  • Vera questions her own perception, wondering if she too is dreaming.

Birth, Creation, and Decay

See: Motherhood, Pregnancy, and Birth · Decay and Ruin

  • The doctor’s instruments and imagery of birth contrast with the barrenness of the landscape and the decay in the hotel.
  • The pregnant man rumor symbolizes disruption of natural order, reflecting anxieties about identity and transformation.

Memory and the Past

See: Memory and the Past

  • Vera is haunted by memories, family heirlooms (mother’s pearls), and dreams.
  • The hotel and doctor’s office contain relics of the past (books, calendars, diplomas) that evoke lost order and fading time.

Social and Cultural Tensions

See: Society, Class, and Race

  • The hotel reflects a microcosm of social prejudice and conflict.
  • The widow’s rant reveals anti-Semitism, racism, and political resentment, referencing Hitler, Roosevelt, and local attitudes.

Isolation and Community

See: Isolation and Connection

  • Characters are isolated (mad doctor, hangman, Tabitha) yet bound within the hotel’s strange community.
  • Vera is an outsider trying to understand but remains detached.

Research: Symbols and Imagery

Shoes

See: Clothing, Hats, and Skirts

  • The doctor’s office is littered with mateless women’s shoes from all eras, symbolizing lost or fragmented lives, unfulfilled journeys, and the absence of order.

Pearls

See: Pearls and Jewels

  • Vera’s mother’s real pearls symbolize inheritance, lost estate, and the eternal amidst transience.

The Dogs’ Graveyard

See: Weddings and Funerals · Dogs

  • Represents death, loyalty, and the neglect of forgotten beings, mirroring the hotel’s decay.

The Calendar and Books

See: Clocks and Watches

  • Symbols of time, knowledge, and the passage from order to chaos.
  • The calendar stuck 20 years ago symbolizes frozen time and lost opportunity.

The Green Baize Curtain

  • Separates reality (hotel lobby) from hidden truths (bedroom behind).
  • Symbolizes the thin veil between public and private, seen and hidden.

Research: Resources

  • “had it been the Christian hangman’s fault or fancy that his wife had stolen out of the house”: See Mr. Weed and Marie Weed.
  • “in no state of the union was it legal to hang a woman far gone in pregnancy”: The old common law, from England, forbade executing a pregnant woman until after the birth; a condemned woman could “plead the belly.” See Women, Gender, and Marriage.
  • “the child strangled by the umbilical cord”: Vera pictured Marie hanging and her unborn baby hanging by its umbilical cord. Pregnant Black women were among the many victims of lynching during the era of racial terror in the United States. While the exact number is not known, the case of Mary Turner is one of the most widely documented instances of this particularly brutal violence. In May 1918, a white farmer named Hampton Smith was killed by one of his Black employees, Sidney Johnson, in Brooks County, Georgia. An enraged white mob began a week-long rampage, killing several Black people, including Mary Turner’s husband, Hayes Turner. After her husband was lynched, a grieving Mary Turner, who was eight months pregnant, publicly denounced the murder and threatened to have the mob members arrested. Her statement enraged the mob, which turned its fury on her. On May 19, 1918, a mob of hundreds of people captured Turner and dragged her to Folsom Bridge over the Little River. There, they tied her ankles, hung her upside down from a tree, and set her on fire. While she was still alive, a man cut open her abdomen with a knife, causing her unborn baby to fall to the ground. A mob member then stomped the baby to death. Turner’s body was then riddled with hundreds of bullets. No one was ever held accountable for the murders of Mary Turner and her unborn child. The grotesque nature of her lynching revealed the level of dehumanization and impunity with which Black women were treated during this period. Her case was widely publicized by the NAACP and became a symbol in the anti-lynching movement. The lynching of Black women is a less-documented aspect of racial terror, but historians have uncovered evidence that it was not uncommon. The violence against Black women, especially pregnant women like Mary Turner, served as a tool of white supremacy to terrorize the Black community and suppress any form of dissent. The sexualized and gendered violence inflicted upon women’s bodies was also used to communicate power and control. Many instances of women being lynched were underreported or not documented at all. The details of Mary Turner’s lynching only became widely known because of the investigation by Walter F. White of the NAACP and the subsequent national anti-lynching campaign. The murder of Mary Turner remains a potent and horrific symbol of the racial and gender-based violence that was inflicted upon Black women during the era of racial terror. See Lynching and Racial Violence and Women, Gender, and Marriage.
  • “the necklace of pearls that had been my mother’s”: The pearls are repeatedly connected to Vera’s mother and her legacy. They represent the “lost estate” of her mother, something precious yet intangible that Vera inherits and wears, symbolizing the remnants of the past and the enduring connection to her mother’s life and identity. The pearls are described as “real pearls which... would bring no more than cultivated pearls” in the market, suggesting a contrast between their material and symbolic value. The pearls also symbolize continuity amid loss and the passing of time. Vera’s mother believed that the pearls could not be lost or stolen, and that their number paradoxically increased with loss, implying an infinite or eternal quality beyond physical reality. This suggests a theme of immortality or persistence beyond death, where loss in one sense begets gain in another “the more pearls there were” despite losses in life. The novel often blurs the line between dream and reality, and pearls, like many other images, are part of this interplay. Pearls are associated with the ephemeral and the eternal, with illusions and truths mingling. They appear alongside motifs of opium dreams, ghosts, and phantoms, symbolizing the fragile and shifting nature of existence and memory. The pearls are linked to the theme of identity, as something that persists yet changes, much like Vera’s mother herself, who is simultaneously present and absent, real and dreamlike. The pearls become a metaphor for what remains of a person’s essence when all else has faded or been lost. The imagery of pearls dripping or cascading like tears, linked to the mother’s lifeless but radiant hands, suggests mourning and the cycle of life and death. Pearls are connected to sorrow (“the pity, pity, pity of nothing, of something”), highlighting their role as symbols of grief and the preciousness of what is gone. See Pearls and Jewels and Catherine Cartwheel.
  • “her chauffeur, James, the ideal, the faithful”: See James the Chauffeur.
  • “It was Joachim”: See Joachim Spitzer.
  • “All the clocks in the house having been stopped at a different time”: Compare Miss Havisham in Dickens’s Great Expectations (1861), who stopped every clock in her house at the minute she was jilted. See Clocks and Watches.
  • “she had promised to finance a Revolution”: “Revolution” serves as a metaphor for a transformative change or upheaval Catherine imagines or aspires to finance. It aligns with the novel’s broader themes of disillusionment, social change, and the tension between dreams and reality. The Revolution here can be interpreted as a symbol of radical change (personal, social, or political) that Catherine contemplates amidst her dreamlike, drug-induced state and the decaying world around her. The promise to finance a Revolution is less about a concrete political movement and more about Catherine’s fantasy or symbolic gesture of power, influence, and change in a world she perceives as lost or slipping away. See The History of Opium.
  • “After all, he was an Italian thief”: By specifying that the thief was Italian, Catherine invokes a common ethnic stereotype: at that time and in many literary works, Italians were often portrayed as charming, passionate, and sometimes criminal or roguish figures. The label “Italian thief” carries connotations of romanticism, cunning, and a certain exotic, theatrical flair. In the story, this adds a layer of color and character to the thief, distinguishing him from a generic burglar and situating the encounter within a broader cultural imagination. Catherine’s world is heavily dreamlike and infused with fantasy, illusions, and theatricality. The thief’s Italian identity fits this atmosphere, lending a sense of drama and exoticism to the otherwise quiet, snow-blanketed house. It underscores the surreal quality of the encounter: where a criminal becomes a guest, sipping sherry and talking about revolutions, dressed in the finery Catherine provided. By choosing to highlight the thief’s nationality and by outfitting him as a “pale, aristocratic gentleman” with a silk opera hat, white motor coat, and white flowers behind his ears, Catherine asserts a kind of control and agency over the narrative. She transforms the thief from a mere criminal into a figure of aristocratic elegance and revolutionary potential, playing with identities and expectations. The Italian thief is not just a criminal but a symbol of possibility, subversion, and transformation. Catherine is herself a figure caught between reality and dream, between past grandeur and present decay. The Italian thief episode reflects her tendency to blur lines between fact and fantasy, to rewrite narratives with theatrical embellishments. By stressing “Italian,” she situates the episode in a world of cultural richness and romantic possibility, contrasting with the harsh realities outside her doors. Catherine’s emphasis on “he was an Italian thief” is a deliberate narrative choice to evoke a particular image and mood: that of a charming, exotic, somewhat romanticized figure who becomes part of her dreamlike, theatrical domain. It reflects her complex psychological state and her inclination to infuse her recollections with drama, fantasy, and symbolic meaning, transforming a criminal intrusion into an almost magical encounter.
    • Prejudice against Italian immigrants ran deep: in 1891 a New Orleans mob lynched eleven Italian Americans, the largest mass lynching in American history, and in 1927 Massachusetts executed the anarchists Sacco and Vanzetti after a trial many believed unjust. See Lynching and Racial Violence and Society, Class, and Race.
  • “he should be the melting snowman upon the first day of spring”: The thief’s being dressed up and changed but melting with the spring sounds familiar to the Frosty the Snowman song written by Walter “Jack” Rollins and Steve Nelson, and first recorded by Gene Autry and the Cass County Boys in 1950 and later recorded by Jimmy Durante. A book and short film were also released that year based on the song. A group of children find a hat and place it on Frosty’s head. Frosty laughs and plays with the children until the hot sun threatens to melt him. Frosty says goodbye to the children, reassuring them he’ll be back someday. Although it is generally regarded as a Christmas song, the original lyrics make no mention of the holiday. The song supposedly takes place in White Plains, New York, or Armonk, New York. Armonk has a parade dedicated to Frosty annually.
  • “this was a dogs’ graveyard”: America’s oldest pet cemetery, at Hartsdale, New York, opened in 1896. See Dogs.
  • “the Wabash country”: The Wabash runs across Indiana to the Ohio. Paul Dresser’s “On the Banks of the Wabash, Far Away” (1897) became the state song in 1913. See Iowa, Indiana, and the Midwest and Music and Composers.
  • “There were women’s shoes scattered over the floor”: The scattered women’s shoes, all mateless, are highly symbolic. Shoes generally suggest journeys, paths, or the presence and absence of people, and the fact that these shoes are mateless highlights a sense of incompleteness, loss, or fragmentation. Each shoe appears to come from a different era and place (white canvas tennis shoes, green opera pumps, old women’s laced shoes, buckskin shoes with buttons, gold Grecian sandals) suggesting a collage of many lives, times, and experiences, all disconnected and isolated in this one room. This could symbolize the scattered, fragmented nature of the doctor’s mind or the fragmented realities of the women who come to him: real or imaginary. The shoes’ variety and solitary nature imply absence: where are the wearers? The doctor deals with pregnancies and deliveries, but many of his “patients” are imaginary or unreal, and the mateless shoes evoke the idea of incomplete or failed births, lost children, or the ghostly presence of women who are not fully there. The shoes are remnants or traces, much like the doctor’s practice itself: delivering “imaginary babies” in a “barren countryside where nothing grew.” This barren setting and the doctor’s madness emphasize infertility, loss, and the failure of creation or procreation. The doctor’s clothes hanging alone, despite his complaint of having only one suit, add to the sense of mystery and absence. He has left behind his physical presence, yet his garments remain, like a ghost or a symbol of an absent self. The idea of the doctor “naked as death” going about delivering imaginary babies deepens the theme of the blurring between life and death, reality and hallucination.
  • “forceps, and something which looked like a tuning fork”: Obstetric forceps were invented in the 1600s by the Chamberlen family of London, who kept them a family secret for more than a century. René Laennec invented the stethoscope in 1816. See Pregnancy, Abortion, and Midwifery.
  • “there was also, as I heard later, a pregnant man”: Couvade syndrome, also called sympathetic pregnancy, is a condition in which an expectant father experiences some of the same symptoms and behavior as their pregnant partner.
  • “Sarah, Sarah!”: The name Sarah means “princess” or “noblewoman” in Hebrew, derived from the Hebrew word sar meaning “prince” or “ruler,” with Sarah being the feminine form, signifying a “lady of high rank” or “princess of a multitude.” It’s a significant Biblical name, given to Abraham’s wife and matriarch of the Jewish people, whose original name was Sarai (meaning “my princess”) before God changed it to Sarah. The name has deep roots in Judaism, Christianity, and Islam, maintaining timeless popularity across cultures. “As for Sarai thy wife, thou shalt not call her name Sarai, but Sarah shall her name be” (Genesis 17:15, KJV). See Sarah O’Leary and Genesis.
  • “Why was Sarah laughing?”: “Therefore Sarah laughed within herself, saying, After I am waxed old shall I have pleasure, my lord being old also?” (Genesis 18:12, KJV): the old woman who laughed at the promise of a child. See Genesis and Pregnancy, Abortion, and Midwifery.
  • “a crêpe de Chine nightgown”: Crepe de Chine nightgowns evolved from ancient Chinese silk luxury, gaining global fame in the early 20th century for their delicate, pebbled texture and drape, becoming symbols of elegance in the 1920s-30s with Art Deco styles and Hollywood glamor, eventually transitioning from pure silk to modern synthetic blends, remaining a favorite for comfortable, stylish sleepwear.
  • “There were pictures of embryos to show that one can hardly tell, at a certain stage, the difference between a rat, a bird, and a man”: Ernst Haeckel’s famous plates of embryos (1874) set fish, birds, and men side by side to show their likeness, though he made them more alike than they are.
    • Many embryos (including humans), since they all evolved from a common ancestor, look strikingly alike during the middle of the phylotypic period.
  • “an old steel engraving of Dante wooing Beatrice”: Dante’s “wooing” of Beatrice was not a traditional courtship but an idealized love he expressed through poetry, famously documented in his book Vita Nuova. He fell in love with her at a very young age, and although he encountered her only a couple of times, she became his lifelong muse, representing a spiritual and intellectual ideal. The term “courtly love” was applied to their relationship, a concept involving an idealized and often unattainable love that inspires poetry and virtue. Henry Holiday’s painting Dante and Beatrice (1883), of Dante meeting her on a Florentine bridge, was reproduced in countless engravings. See Dante.
  • “the Yale School of Medicine had given the doctor his diploma”: The Yale School of Medicine was established in 1810 and opened in 1813, making it the sixth-oldest medical school in the United States. Key developments include becoming the Medical School of Yale College in 1884, adopting the name Yale University in 1887, and establishing the “Yale System” of education in the early 1900s, which emphasizes independent study. The school is also associated with the founding of the New Haven Hospital, which merged with another hospital to form the Grace-New Haven Community Hospital.
  • “Mary Pickford, with her long yellow curls”: Mary Pickford or Gladys Marie Smith, was a Canadian-American stage and screen actress and producer with a career that spanned five decades. A pioneer in the US film industry, she co-founded Pickford-Fairbanks Studios and United Artists, and was one of the 36 founders of the Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences. She was called America’s Sweetheart and The Girl with the Curls. (Wikipedia) See Women, Gender, and Marriage.
  • “there was a bean-shooter on his desk”: A “beanshooter” can refer to a simple toy gun or slingshot. In Chapter 67 the children shot at old Doc with their bean-shooters. See the Chapter 67 resources.
  • “Western Union telegraph pads”: Western Union was founded in 1851 as the New York and Mississippi Valley Printing Telegraph Company in Rochester, New York. The company changed its name to the Western Union Telegraph Company in 1856 after merging with several other telegraph companies. The company dominated the American telegraphy industry from the 1860s to the 1980s. (Wikipedia)
  • “boxes of corn plaster”: A corn plaster is a medicated bandage, often with salicylic acid or hydrocolloid, designed to relieve pain and remove painful foot corns by softening the hard skin, cushioning the area, and protecting it from friction. While effective for many, these plasters should be avoided by diabetics or those with circulatory issues, and careful application is needed to protect surrounding healthy skin.
  • “India rubber erasers”: An “India rubber eraser” is a traditional type of eraser, named for the natural rubber (caoutchouc) it’s made from, used to remove pencil and sometimes ink marks, often featuring a dual-sided design with red for pencil and blue for ink.
  • “There was a magazine rack”: These magazines were the reading material for real, expectant mothers in a time when pregnancy was a significant, often anxious waiting period. The narrator Vera notes that these magazines were once symbols of hope or dread, indicating that the women looked to them for comfort or guidance. Now, the magazines are relics in the doctor’s chaotic room, indicating the collapse of that earlier, more hopeful era into one dominated by madness, illusion, and a suspension of time. The dream patients who now thumb through them are part of this eerie limbo, caught between past realities and present fantasies. The magazines represent the intersection of past reality and present illusion, the ordinary and the cosmic, and the fragile hopes of women awaiting childbirth amidst the doctor’s deteriorating mental state and the novel’s broader themes of time, memory, and decay.
  • “a star rushing toward this world, bound to collide with it”: When Halley’s Comet returned in 1910, newspapers warned that the earth would pass through its poisonous tail, and swindlers sold “comet pills.” See Astronomy.
  • “A recipe for hominy croquettes”: Hominy croquettes are savory, deep-fried bites made from cooked hominy mixed with binders like milk, eggs, and flour (or a béchamel sauce), seasoned with butter, salt, and sometimes other flavors like horseradish or herbs, then coated in breadcrumbs and fried until crispy. They’re a comforting, old-fashioned dish where the soft, starchy hominy provides a unique texture against a creamy interior and crunchy exterior.
  • “What shall I do if my husband leaves me?”: Advice columns for women, such as Dorothy Dix’s, begun in 1896 and read by millions, answered such letters for half a century. See Women, Gender, and Marriage.
  • “There were wild mares who, on the coast of Lusitania, were impregnated by the wind only”: Wild mares of Lusitania may refer to The Lusitano, a Portuguese horse breed. The fame of the horses from Lusitania goes back to the Roman Age, which attributed its speed to the influence of the West wind, who was considered capable of fertilizing the mares. Pliny tells it in his Natural History, Book 8, and Virgil in the Georgics, Book 3.
  • “Queen Wilhelmina of Holland was an excellent housekeeper”: Queen Wilhelmina of Holland may refer to Wilhelmina Helena Pauline Maria who was the Queen of the Netherlands from 1890 until her abdication in 1948. She reigned for nearly 58 years, longer than any other Dutch monarch. (Wikipedia) See Women, Gender, and Marriage.
  • “the doctor’s more coherent medical library”: The books symbolize the doctor’s fractured mind and the blurred boundaries between reality, illusion, and madness pervasive in the novel. They reflect Vera’s exploration of a world where order is elusive, and knowledge is scattered, much like the chaotic mental landscapes of the characters she encounters.
  • “The Gazelle Peninsula”: The Gazelle Peninsula is a large peninsula in northeastern East New Britain. It lies on New Britain, an island of the Bismarck Archipelago that now belongs to Papua New Guinea.
  • “The Transvaal from the Inside”: The Transvaal from the Inside may refer to The Transvaal from Within: A Private Record of Public Affairs (1899) by J. P. Fitzpatrick. Fitzpatrick is known for the children’s book, Jock of the Bushveld. The book refers to the Jameson Raid which was a botched raid against the South African Republic, the Transvaal, carried out by British colonial administrator Leander Starr Jameson. The raid was intended to trigger an uprising by the primarily British expatriate workers in the Transvaal but failed to do so.
  • “The Goiter Belt”: The Goiter Belt refers to a chronic low iodine deficiency in the upper Midwest discovered in men during World War I. Iodized salt was introduced to combat this in the US. Michigan began selling iodized salt in 1924. The landlady below, with “A goiter like a melon,” is a native of the goiter belt.
  • “The Diseases of the King Penguins”: The King Penguin is the second largest species of penguin, smaller, but somewhat similar in appearance to the emperor penguin.
  • “Bronchitis”: Bronchitis is inflammation of the large and medium-sized airways in the lungs that causes coughing.
  • “The Causes of Ejaculatory Praecox Among the Great American Elks”: The Causes of Ejaculatory Praecox Among the Great American Elks did not have a reference but ejaculatio praecox means premature ejaculation. The title twits the Benevolent and Protective Order of Elks, the fraternal lodge founded in 1868.
  • “The Diseases of Coal Miners”: The Diseases of Coal Miners may refer to the lung disease pneumoconiosis that miners are at risk of developing because of their exposure to airborne respirable dust.
  • “Bipolar Medicine”: The phrase “bipolar disorder” came into use only in the 1950s and later; in an old doctor’s library the title more likely means medicine of the two poles, Arctic and Antarctic, beside The Diseases of the King Penguins.
    • Bipolar Medicine may refer to Bipolar disorder which is a mood disorder characterized by periods of depression and periods of abnormally-elevated happiness that last from days to weeks each. If the elevated mood is severe or associated with psychosis, it is called mania; if it is less severe, it is called hypomania.
  • “The Three Bears”: The Three Bears is a 19th-century British fairy tale of which three versions exist. The original version of the tale tells of a not-so-polite old woman who enters the forest home of three bachelor bears while they are away. She sits in their chairs, eats some of their porridge, sits down on one of their chairs and breaks it, and sleeps in one of their beds. When the bears return and discover her, she wakes up, jumps out of the window, and is never seen again. The second version replaced the old woman with a little girl named Goldilocks, and the third and by far best-known version replaced the original bear trio with Papa Bear, Mama Bear, and Baby Bear. What was originally a frightening oral tale became a cozy family story with only a hint of menace. (Wikipedia) Robert Southey published the first printed version in 1837. See Fairy Tales and Folklore.
  • “The Cow Who Jumped over the Moon”: The Cow Who Jumped over the Moon is the English nursery rhyme “Hey Diddle Diddle.” There are numerous theories about the origin of the rhyme. James Orchard Halliwell suggested that it was a corruption of ancient Greek, probably advanced as a result of a deliberate hoax. It was connected with Hathor worship. It refers to various constellations (Taurus, Canis Minor, etc.). It describes the Flight from Egypt (the Exodus) or the founding myth of the Israelites. It depicts Elizabeth, Lady Katherine Grey, and her relationships with the earls of Hertford and Leicester. It deals with anti-clerical feeling over injunctions by Catholic priests for harder work. It describes Catherine of Aragon or Catherine I of Russia, the wife of Peter the Great or Canton de Fidèle, a supposed governor of Calais and the game of cat, an old English bat-and-ball game. This profusion of unsupported explanations was satirized by J. R. R. Tolkien in his fictional explanations of “The Man in the Moon Stayed Up Too Late.” Most scholarly commentators consider these to be unproven and state that the verse is probably meant to be simply nonsense. (Wikipedia) See Fairy Tales and Folklore and Ancient Egypt.
  • “Little Tom Thumb”: Little Tom Thumb is a character of English folklore. Tom Thumb may have been a real person born around 1519, as there is a grave purporting to be his. It is set into the floor adjacent to the font of the main chapel in Holy Trinity Church at Tattershall, Lincolnshire, UK. On the tombstone it reads that T. Thumb was 101 years old. He died in 1620 and the grave measures just sixteen inches in length. (Wikipedia) See Fairy Tales and Folklore.
  • “Walks in Rome”: Walks in Rome, by Augustus J. C. Hare, first published in 1871, was the favorite guide of English and American travelers. Walks in Rome was published by George Allen, 1897, London.
  • “Lallah Rookh”: Lallah Rookh is an Oriental romance by Irish poet Thomas Moore, published in 1817. Scholars have stated Moore, a friend of the executed Irish rebel Robert Emmet, depicts in the poem a version of the French Revolution and the Irish Rebellion of 1798. He condemns the French Revolution but justifies the Irish Rebellion. See Romantic Poets.
  • “Tom Swift in the Land of Giants”: Tom Swift in the Land of Giants may refer to a book in the various Tom Swift book series. All books are credited to the pseudonym Victor Appleton while the character was created by Edward Stratemeyer for his book packaging house, the Stratemeyer Syndicate. Tom Swift is the main character of six series of American juvenile science fiction and adventure novels that emphasize science, invention, and technology. The books contain heavy racism, depicting Africans as brutish, uncivilized animals, and the white protagonist as their paternal savior. The Tom Swift books have been credited with assisting the success of American science fiction and with establishing stories focusing on brilliant scientists and inventors as a basic cultural myth. The series uses many adverbs and the phrase Tom Swiftly or Tom Swifty was coined to describe a book that uses many adverbs. Tom Swift’s fictional inventions have apparently inspired several actual inventions. A number of scientists, inventors, and science fiction writers have also credited Tom Swift with inspiring them. See Society, Class, and Race.
  • “Keats’ Ode to the Grecian Urn”: Keats’ Ode to the Grecian Urn was published in 1819. Ode on a Grecian Urn discusses art and art’s audience. The flyleaf’s “died of tuberculosis” is true of Keats, who died of it in Rome in 1821, at twenty-five. See the ode in the Chapter 70 resources. See Romantic Poets.
  • “What’s Wrong with Democracy?”: What’s Wrong with Democracy? Critiques of democracy existed across a wide range of historical periods and came from diverse intellectual and social movements. These arguments addressed everything from the flaws of ancient Greek democracy to the systemic exclusions within American democracy before the Civil Rights era. Philosophers like Plato warned that in a democracy, the masses, driven by ignorance and emotion, could become susceptible to self-serving demagogues. This “rule by the mob” could lead to rash, unjust decisions, such as the execution of Socrates in ancient Athens. Later, thinkers like Thomas Hobbes argued that democracy leads to chaos and civil war, advocating for a strong, singular sovereign to prevent societal collapse. Some classical and 19th-century thinkers, including Plato, Thomas Carlyle, and John Ruskin, argued that society should be led by a knowledgeable elite rather than the common people. This perspective asserted that only a select few possessed the wisdom and virtue necessary to govern effectively, and that the majority of people were ill-equipped for the complexities of statecraft. As democracy expanded during the Industrial Revolution, critics like Carlyle, John Ruskin, and William Lecky argued that it produced anarchy and chaos within modern industrial society. They believed that democratic capitalism prioritized profit and individual self-interest over social stability and the public good. Commentators like Matthew Arnold expressed concern that democracy led to a flattening of culture and a decline in intellectual standards. He feared that the “average” tastes of the masses would displace high culture and that society would suffer from a lack of moral and intellectual leadership. Before the passage of the Civil Rights Act in 1964, critics pointed out the hypocrisy of American democracy, which systematically excluded many of its own citizens. This was particularly evident in the Jim Crow South, where discriminatory laws like poll taxes and literacy tests disenfranchised millions of African Americans and poor whites. The history of American democracy has been marked by periods of deep instability and division. Scholars point to the 1890s and the aftermath of the Compromise of 1877, which ended Reconstruction, as periods of “backsliding” where racial conflict produced significant damage to democratic ideals. This history was built on the foundation of racial exclusion, as some historians note that democratic norms only took hold among white people after racial equality was removed from the agenda. Especially during the Gilded Age (1865-1915), the rise of powerful, and often corrupt, political machines led many Americans to question the health of their democracy. Critiques focused on the manipulation of the voting process, the influence of money in politics, and the resulting feeling that elections were no longer fair or truly representative of the people. The failure of some interwar and post-WWII democratic governments, such as France’s Fourth Republic, was often cited as a failure of democracy itself. Frequent changes in government and a fractured party system led many to conclude that democracy was inherently unstable and inefficient. The Civil Rights Act marks a significant turning point in the realization of American democratic ideals. See Plato and Platonism.
  • “Southern Germany”: Baedeker’s Southern Germany, the red-bound travel guide, went through many editions from the 1870s. Southern Germany’s history involves Celtic and Roman roots, Germanic tribal settlement (Bavarians, Alemanni), and powerful medieval duchies like Bavaria and Swabia, central to the Holy Roman Empire, later becoming key players against Prussia in unification, retaining strong Catholic traditions and distinct Upper German dialects, culturally linked to Austria and Switzerland.
  • “The Salvation Army Exposed”: The Salvation Army Exposed may refer to a book by Jack London, The People of the Abyss. His story contains his first-hand account of several weeks spent living in the Whitechapel district of the East End of London in 1902. London attempted to understand the working-class of this deprived area of the city, sleeping in workhouses or on the streets, and staying as a lodger with a poor family.
  • “White Nights”: White Nights is a short story by Fyodor Dostoevsky, originally published in 1848. The narrator is a young man living in Saint Petersburg who suffers from loneliness. He gets to know and falls in love with a young woman, but the love remains unrequited as the woman misses her lover, with whom she is finally reunited.
  • “Inside Ibsen”: Inside Ibsen may refer to Henrik Johan Ibsen who was a Norwegian playwright and theater director. He is considered one of the founders of modernism in theater and referred to as the father of realism and one of the most influential playwrights of his time. The social questions which concerned Ibsen belonged unequivocally to the 19th century. From a modern perspective, the aspects of his writing that appeal most are the psychological issues which he explored. (Wikipedia)
  • “The President’s Daughter”: There are two books by this name. One published by Nan Britton in 1927 is a memoir, detailing her affair with President Warren G. Harding. The second is Clotel; or, The President’s Daughter (1853) by William Wells Brown, about the enslaved daughters of Thomas Jefferson, the first novel published by an African American. See Society, Class, and Race and Women, Gender, and Marriage.
  • “Poor Richard’s Almanack”: The Poor Richard’s Almanac was a yearly almanac published by Benjamin Franklin, who adopted the pseudonym of Poor Richard or Richard Saunders for this purpose. The publication appeared continually from 1732 to 1758. It sold exceptionally well for a pamphlet published in the Thirteen Colonies in the US. The print runs reached 10,000 per year. “Early to bed and early to rise, makes a man healthy, wealthy, and wise” (Poor Richard, 1735).
  • “There were numerous charts and maps of medical diagnosis cast by astrolabe”: Medical astrology assigned each part of the body to a sign of the zodiac, pictured in the “Zodiac Man” of old almanacs. An astrolabe is an ancient astronomical instrument, a handheld star chart and analog computer used by astronomers, navigators, and astrologers to tell time, determine latitude, find celestial positions, and even survey, serving functions similar to modern GPS but relying on stars and the horizon. Essentially a metal disc with intricate rotating parts and markings for constellations, it helps users calculate the time of day, predict sunrise/sunset, and locate celestial bodies by matching observations to the device’s model of the sky. See Astrology, Alchemy, and Esoterica.
  • “A stiff brochure, fly-specked with age, written by the doctor when he was young, described senility”: Senility is an outdated term for age-related mental decline, often used to describe memory loss and confusion, but it’s not a normal part of aging and is now generally replaced by terms like dementia, which refers to specific diseases (like Alzheimer’s) causing significant cognitive impairment. While some mild cognitive changes can occur with age, severe issues like dementia are caused by brain cell damage from conditions, not just aging itself, and require medical evaluation for proper diagnosis and management. See Justice O’Leary.
  • “it was Tabitha, as everybody knew, crazy Tabitha”: “Now there was at Joppa a certain disciple named Tabitha, which by interpretation is called Dorcas: this woman was full of good works” (Acts 9:36, KJV). When she died, Peter said, “Tabitha, arise,” and she opened her eyes. See Tabitha and The Bible.
  • “who was too crazy to be on relief”: “Relief” was public aid to the poor; the federal relief programs of the New Deal began in 1933. See Tabitha.
  • “the hitch-hikers”: Hitchhiking was a vital, romanticized mode of transport during the Depression and WWII for the jobless and soldiers, evolving from necessity to counterculture symbol.
  • “the ice-skaters”: Sonja Henie, the Norwegian Olympic champion, made figure skating an American craze in the 1930s with her films and touring ice revues.
    • Ice-skaters was defined by the rise of influential figures like Tenley Albright, Carol Heiss, and Dick Button, who established the U.S. as a dominant force in international figure skating. The era, often considered a “Golden Age” of American skating, saw rapid advancements in technical skill, including the popularization of the double Axel and triple jumps. Non-competitive ice skating was primarily characterized by recreational club skating and the rise of professional ice shows, which allowed talented skaters to perform without competing in official ISU events.
  • “the marathon dancers”: Dance Marathons (and walkathons) were a national craze, providing cheap entertainment and survival for the desperate during the Depression, featuring endurance contests often lasting months, with participants dancing or walking for nearly non-stop hours for prizes Horace McCoy’s novel They Shoot Horses, Don’t They? (1935) is set at one.
  • “The other doctor, Simeon”: Simeon is derived from Simeon, son of Jacob and Leah, patriarch of the Tribe of Simeon. The text of Genesis 29:33 argues that the name refers to Leah’s belief that God had heard that she was hated by Jacob, in the sense of not being as favored as Rachel. “Because the LORD hath heard that I was hated, he hath therefore given me this son also: and she called his name Simeon” (Genesis 29:33, KJV). Thousands of refugee doctors fled Nazi Europe for the United States, and many were kept from practice by state licensing rules and by antisemitism. See Simeon the Doctor and Judaism.
  • “Was I a Communist?”: Communism is a far-left philosophical, social, political, and economic ideology and movement whose goal is the establishment of a communist society, namely a socioeconomic order based on the idea of common ownership of the means of production, distribution, and exchange, allocating products to everyone in the society. (Wikipedia)
  • “Did I believe in sharing the wealth?”: Huey Long’s Share Our Wealth movement (1934) promised to cap great fortunes and give every family a homestead and a yearly income.
  • “Hitler ran him out of Germany”: Adolf Hitler was an Austrian-born German politician who was the dictator of Germany from 1933 until his death in 1945. He rose to power as the leader of the Nazi Party. During his dictatorship, he initiated World War II in Europe by invading Poland on 1 September 1939. He was closely involved in military operations throughout the war and was central to the perpetration of the Holocaust, the genocide of about six million Jews and millions of other victims. (Wikipedia) See Judaism.
  • “The Catholics don’t practice birth control because they want to overcome us”: In the encyclical Casti Connubii (1930), Pope Pius XI forbade Catholics to use contraception. See the Comstock Act in the Chapter 68 resources. See Women, Gender, and Marriage.
  • “They want an American Pope”: Vatican conspiracy theories are conspiracy theories that concern the Pope or the Roman Catholic Church. A majority of the theories allege that the Church and its representatives are secretly controlling secular society with a Satanic agenda for global domination. In the 1920s the Ku Klux Klan in Indiana enrolled perhaps a quarter of a million members, preaching against Catholics, Jews, and Black Americans and holding the state government until its leader, D. C. Stephenson, was convicted in 1925 of the rape and murder of Madge Oberholtzer. See Society, Class, and Race, Lynching and Racial Violence, and Women, Gender, and Marriage.
  • “There are no Negroes in this county, for the sun will not set on a Negro’s head here”: Such places were called sundown towns: Black people had to be gone by nightfall or risk violence. Indiana had scores of them. See the Kentucky lynching in the Chapter 68 resources. See Lynching and Racial Violence and Society, Class, and Race.
    • White supremacy or white supremacism is the belief that white people are superior to those of other races and thus should dominate them. The belief favors the maintenance and defense of any power and privilege held by white people. White supremacy has roots in the now-discredited doctrine of scientific racism and was a key justification for European colonialism. It underlies a spectrum of contemporary movements including white nationalism, white separatism, neo-Nazism, and the Christian Identity movement. (Wikipedia)
  • “We don’t want mulattoes”: Indiana forbade marriage between white and Black people from its first years until 1965; the Supreme Court struck down the last such laws in Loving v. Virginia (1967). See Society, Class, and Race and Women, Gender, and Marriage.
  • “There’s a nigger in the woodpile somewhere”: In the English language, negro, is a term historically used to denote persons considered to be of Black African heritage. The word negro means the color black in both Spanish and in Portuguese, where English took it from. The term can be construed as offensive, inoffensive, or completely neutral, largely depending on the region or country where it is used. It has various equivalents in other languages of Europe. In the English language, the word nigger typically is an ethnic slur used against black people, especially African Americans. Because it is considered extremely offensive, even if only mentioned and not used as a slur, it is often referred to by the euphemism, the N-word. It became a racist insult by the 20th century. Accordingly, it began to disappear from general popular culture. Its inclusion in classic works of literature has sparked controversy and ongoing debate. The phrase, meaning a hidden catch, dates from the 1840s and is said to come from fugitive slaves hidden in woodpiles on their way north. See Society, Class, and Race.
  • “It’s all the fault of that Roosevelt in the White House”: “Roosevelt in the White House” refers to Franklin D. Roosevelt, the thirty-second president of the United States and author of the New Deal in response to the Great Depression. See the Chapter 67 resources.
  • “A green baize curtain”: A green baize curtain is typically a heavy, felt-like woolen fabric, traditionally hung in large, old houses to deaden noise and block drafts between servants’ quarters and family areas, symbolizing the dividing line of domestic service.
  • “those three tiny monkeys”: The three wise monkeys are a Japanese pictorial maxim, embodying the proverbial principle “see no evil, hear no evil, speak no evil.” There are various meanings ascribed to the monkeys and the proverb including associations with being of good mind, speech and action. The phrase is often used to refer to those who deal with impropriety by turning a blind eye.
  • “an advertisement by a local preacher of all mortal household goods and furniture for sale”: Compare the Millerites of 1844, who sold their goods to await the end of the world. See the Chapter 65 resources. See American Religious Movements.
  • “A goiter like a melon”: Goiter, a swelling of the thyroid, was common in the iodine-poor soils of the Great Lakes region until iodized salt arrived in the 1920s. See The Tavern Landlady.
  • “Her husbane and she were owners of the hotell”: The Tavern Landlady is speaking with a strong Indiana or rural Midwestern accent, such as: “clombed the stars” for “climbed the stairs,” “bedses” for “beds,” “husbane” for “husband,” “weller and weller” for “better and better,” “axed” for “asked,” and “agone” for “gone.” Her speech reflects a rustic, colloquial manner typical of rural Indiana, with grammatical irregularities and a folksy tone that evoke a local, uneducated speaker from that region.
  • “was given the euchre Christ and the cue by the priest”: The landlady’s “euchre Christ” is the Eucharist, and the priest’s “cue” may be the last rites, given to a watchdog.
  • “were Methodists like her”: Methodist history in the U.S. began with English immigrants and lay preachers in the 1760s, growing rapidly through circuit riders like Francis Asbury, leading to the formation of the Methodist Episcopal Church in 1784 under John Wesley’s guidance to establish independence after the Revolution. It became America’s largest denomination by the 19th century, spreading across frontiers, fostering revivals, birthing Black denominations like AME. See American Religious Movements.
  • “without the dogsology”: Dogsology may refer to doxology which is a short hymn of praises to God in various forms of Christian worship, often added to the end of canticles, psalms, and hymns. The tradition derives from a similar practice in the Jewish synagogue, where some version of the Kaddish serves to terminate each section of the service.
  • “The lieutenant governor of Indiana combed here”: The position of Lieutenant Governor emerged as Indiana became a state, with early officials setting precedents. Ashbel P. Willard served as Lt. Governor (1853-1857) before being elected Governor in 1856, showing a direct path to the top office. Like the governorship, the Lt. Governor’s office saw shifts between Democratic and Republican figures throughout the late 19th and early 20th centuries. The Lt. Governor presides over the Senate and assumes the governorship if the elected governor is unable to serve. See Iowa, Indiana, and the Midwest.
  • “the poor girl kissed the health officer before she died of tuberculosis”: See Jacqueline White.
  • “Esther Longtree got it all cleaned out”: See Esther Longtree.
  • “But Tabidia was muted”: The name appears to echo the Latin tabidus, “wasting away” or “consumptive.” The same passage mentions a waitress taken by tuberculosis, the disease once called consumption.

Chapter 81

Content note: The Esther Longtree chapters (72 to 81) deal with stillbirth and pregnancy loss, rape, infanticide, racist violence including lynching, and cruelty to children. This chapter contains the little toy salesman’s antisemitic raving about a “Jewish conspiracy,” and describes a shipwreck in which women and children drown while he survives.

Summary

On a dark, rainy day Esther tells of the man she has chosen to be the legal father of the little shadow boxer: the little toy salesman, bandy-legged and pot-bellied, with three soft teeth, no tear ducts, and no taste buds, who drinks warm milk from a baby bottle and asks her to rock him to sleep. His mother, a world-famous beauty and spy, stole him from his father, a windowpeeper, and put him to sleep in dresser drawers. He tells her he is a murderer of women and little children because he alone survived a great storm at sea, rocking in a rubber life boat while the German captain conducted with his withered arm and everyone else drowned. Adrift in the calm, a dead child’s hand wearing a gold ring like his clung to his sleeve, a white shark that looked like his mother circled him, and he raved that the sea, the sky, and God were a Jewish conspiracy. He has not come lately. He whispered that the bad men would blow up the world some day of calm just for fun; if they do, Esther will go on pregnant with her dreams, and maybe the dead loved the dead.

Characters present

Esther Longtree

Concepts present

Key passages

From the research

  • Esther is described as “always pregnant,” swelling like a dark tide, carrying a “little shadow boxer” under her heart. This pregnancy is not just physical but symbolic of her hope, expectancy, and also her loneliness. Despite her past of “stillborn” children and losses, she remains hopeful that something real and good will come in the future. She imagines marriage and a legal father for her unborn child, the little toy salesman, who is peculiar yet innocent in his own way.
  • The little toy salesman is portrayed as a fragile, almost childlike man with physical oddities: “only three teeth,” “pale blue eyes,” “bandy-legged,” and “tearless.” He drinks milk from a baby bottle and seems innocent to a fault. His past is mysterious and tragic: his mother was a world-famous beauty and spy, his father a windowpeeper, and he himself was a “bottle baby,” never knowing maternal love. He flirts with Esther, seeks comfort, and longs for a home and normal childhood, which he never had. Esther feels a mix of pity, nervousness, and a maternal instinct to “teach him” how to behave and live a normal life.
  • A pivotal passage reveals that the little toy salesman survived a catastrophic sea storm that drowned all others: captain, crew, women, children, even “the moon, the sun, the stars, the kittens.” He was the “lone survivor,” saved by accident in a rubber life boat. This survival haunts both him and Esther: he is a “murderer” in her eyes for not having drowned with the others, for having lived when so many died. His survival is marked by loss; he has lost memory, taste buds, tear ducts, and reason.
  • Throughout his ordeal, the little toy salesman is haunted by a dead child’s ivory-colored hand, “always uplifted from the slow, swelling waters,” wearing a gold ring like his own. This hand tugs at him, clings to him. It represents the children Esther has lost and hidden, as well as the burden carried by the survivor. The hand is described as luminous and moth-like.
  • After the storm, he is pursued by a great white shark, which he initially mistakes for a woman but recognizes as a predator. Despite delirium and starvation, he clings to the memory of the dead child’s hand and the tokens he carries: the baby bottle, the withered branch, the rosebud, the mourning band. He returns to America a stranger, physically and mentally altered.
  • The chapter closes with Esther’s reflections on the terrible future forewarned by the little toy salesman: a great war, the world blown up, the death of all living things, the end of music, stars, fireflies, and life itself. Yet, in this bleak vision, Esther remains forever “pregnant with her dreams,” nurturing the little shadow boxer, the symbol of hope and continuity. The chapter ends on a note of ambiguous hope and mystery, with Esther wondering who fathered the child and suggesting that “the dead loved the dead” and that this might be how the world goes on.
  • Adrift in the calm, the little toy salesman raves that the ocean, the sky, the sunlight, and God himself are Jewish, “a Jewish conspiracy,” and that “the rubber business belonged to the Jews.” Young puts the oldest antisemitic myth in the mouth of a man who survived by watching women and children drown.

Questions and observations

Reading closely

  • “Maybe the dead loved the dead, and that was the way the world went on.” What does Esther mean?
  • “There was beauty in the heart of death.” Where in the storm does the little toy salesman find it?
  • “What difference would one tear more or less have made in a world of water? All the difference, said Esther Longtree, weeping one tear.” Why does one tear matter?

Characters

  • The little toy salesman “had seemed like a dead child that grew.” Who might he be?
  • He calls himself “a victim of the Jews” and blames a “Jewish conspiracy” for the sea and the sky. What is Young showing about him?
  • Esther calls him a murderer because “he had not drowned when all others drowned.” Is she fair?

Connections

  • He “was always put to sleep in a dresser drawer.” Where was Walter left in Chapter 80?
  • The dead child’s hand “wore a gold ring like his.” How is this hand like the small brown hand across Esther’s womb?
  • The German captain goes down conducting, “his withered arm lifting.” Who might he be?

Reflection

  • “The world needed pity.” Does the little toy salesman deserve any?
  • “Who could beat a dead child’s hand away?”
  • “Great chaos had asked no questions, and great chaos had answered none to man.” What answers does Esther want?
