Research: Resources

  • “a little man wearing a bowler hat”: The bowler hat, or “derby” in the US, is a hard felt hat with a, rounded crown and slightly curled brim, originally designed in 1849 by Thomas and William Bowler for British gamekeepers to provide durable, close-fitting head protection. It became an iconic symbol of 19th-century British, and later American Western, style. See Clothing, Hats, and Skirts.
  • “struck all the silent keys”: See “I am a white piano” in the Chapter 72 resources. See Music and Composers.
  • “the little shadow boxer, he crouched under her heart”: Esther Longtree is portrayed as a deeply complex and tragic figure whose identity is heavily shaped by themes of perpetual pregnancy, loss, and loneliness. The narrative presents her as a woman “always pregnant” with a “little shadow boxer” inside her, symbolizing both hope and despair. This endless state of pregnancy is marked by a haunting series of stillbirths and hidden children buried in various secret places, which underscores a profound maternal suffering and grief. Her body is described vividly as swollen and luminous, with breasts marked by small teeth, signifying the physical and emotional scars of her repeated losses. Esther harbors a desire for a legitimate father for her unborn child, choosing the little toy salesman as the “legal father” not because of love but for the sake of appearance and legality. This man is himself a peculiar and fragile character, described as childish, innocent, and physically weak is an echo of Esther’s own vulnerability. His presence exacerbates her anxiety and sense of fragility, as he is unable to see her obvious pregnancy and the pain it entails. Despite his flaws and oddities, Esther feels maternal towards him and plans to teach him basic emotional responses and social manners, further illustrating her longing for care and order amidst chaos. The little toy salesman is also a symbol of survival and guilt; he is the lone survivor of a great storm at sea in which all others, including children, drowned. Esther’s complex feelings toward him, both pity and accusation, reflect her broader struggle with abandonment, survival, and loss. She calls him a “murderer,” not because of direct harm, but because he survived when others, including many children, did not. His survival represents a painful exception and a haunting reminder of the deaths she has endured. His repeated visits and the spectral presence of a dead child’s hand clinging to him evoke a liminal state between life and death, memory and oblivion. Esther’s inner world is one of continuous tension between hope and despair, reality and dream, maternal love and fatal loss. She imagines a future where she might be married and her child might live, but she remains haunted by the many children who never were. Her relationship with the little toy salesman encapsulates this tension: he is both a source of comfort and a symbol of her grief and unfulfilled desires. The chapter reveals her as a figure caught in an endless cycle of pregnancy and mourning, embodying themes of fertility, death, survival, and the elusive nature of identity and belonging. Esther Longtree is a tragic, almost mythic figure embodying the paradoxes of motherhood: creation shadowed by destruction, hope intertwined with loss within the dreamlike and melancholic atmosphere of the novel. See Esther Longtree.
    • Esther Longtree symbolizes a complex and tragic history of maternal suffering, loss, and the burden of unrealized potential in the United States. Her character embodies themes of repeated loss, loneliness, and the haunting presence of stillborn or hidden children, which can be read as a metaphor for the nation’s troubled past, especially concerning the cycles of hope, despair, and unfulfilled promise. Her “everlasting pregnancy” and the many stillborn children she has buried symbolize the countless hopes and dreams that have failed to come to fruition in American history. The repeated motif of her “children” hidden in various natural places (tree stumps, streams, roots of flowers) suggests a hidden, suppressed history of loss and forgotten lives. This can be interpreted as reflecting the historical erasures and silencing of certain groups and tragedies within the nation. The interaction with the little toy salesman who survived a great storm at sea that drowned all others and who appears as a fragile, infantile man with the burden of survivor’s guilt adds a layer of historical allegory. The storm and the drowning of the many except the lone survivor who “should have drowned” but did not, can be seen as symbolizing catastrophic events in American history (such as mass tragedies, wars, or social upheavals) where many perish or are lost, but some survive carrying the weight of memory and guilt. Esther’s sorrow over the little toy salesman’s survival, her bitter recognition that he is a “murderer” simply because he lived while others died, reflects a historical ambivalence about survival and progress in the US: the idea that some have survived or prospered amid the suffering or destruction of others. Her physical description (large, swollen, always pregnant but marked by small teeth bites on her breasts) further evokes the land or the country itself as fertile yet scarred, nurturing yet wounded, carrying the weight of generations of loss and unrealized futures. Esther Longtree symbolizes the historical experience of America as a land marked by repeated cycles of birth and death, hope and loss, survival and guilt. She embodies the maternal figure of a nation perpetually pregnant with unrealized futures, haunted by its stillborn children, and struggling with the legacy of survival amid widespread tragedy.
  • “bandy-legged”: A bandy-legged man has legs that curve outward at the knees, creating a bow-like shape where the knees are farther apart than the ankles when standing straight. Also known as bow-legged or genu varum, this condition often causes the legs to appear arched. The term refers to a physical, often congenital, alignment where the legs bend outward.
  • “drank his milk from a baby bottle”: Bottle feeding has existed for thousands of years, with archaeological evidence of clay feeding vessels dating back 7,000 years to the Bronze and Iron Ages. Early methods used animal horns, clay pots, and, in the 19th century, dangerous “tube bottles” that often caused fatal bacterial infections. Modern, safer materials like glass and rubber nipples emerged in the late 19th/20th century.
  • “She had been a world spy”: Mata Hari is the most famous female spy in history, known as a WWI-era Dutch exotic dancer accused of passing secrets. Other notable agents include WWII heroes Virginia Hall (Allied spy), Noor Inayat Khan (SOE wireless operator), and Nancy Wake (“The White Mouse”), alongside American Civil War scout Harriet Tubman. See The Civil War and Women, Gender, and Marriage.
  • “he would rather spy upon a woman”: Peeping Tom, the windowpeeper struck blind for looking at Lady Godiva, is in the Chapter 75 resources.
  • “Until the world blew up”: This mirrors Mr. Bonebreaker who is also looking forward to the end of the world. This also may refer to the development of the atomic bomb and its use during WWII. See Mr. Titus Bonebreaker.
  • “bald bays”: “bald bays” Bald spots (or patches) are localized areas on the scalp or body, such as the beard or eyebrows, that have little to no hair growth. Often caused by conditions like alopecia areata (an autoimmune disorder) or stress, these patches can appear suddenly, resulting in small, round, bare areas.
  • “a cold pigeon, a stool pigeon, a fence, a shadow, a dead duck”: “a stool pigeon” is a police informer.
    • “a fence” deals with stolen goods.
    • “a dead duck” means a person or thing that has no chance of success.
  • “had been in the Gobi Desert and in Arabia”: The Gobi Desert is a vast, arid region in northern China and southern Mongolia. It’s known for its dunes, mountains and rare animals such as snow leopards and Bactrian camels. In the Gobi Gurvansaikhan National Park, the Khongoryn Els sand dunes are said to sing when the wind blows. The park also features the deep ice field of Yolyn Am canyon. Dinosaur fossils have been found at the red “Flaming Cliffs” of Bayanzag.
    • The Arabian Peninsula, or Arabia, is a vast, arid region in Southwest Asia, bordered by the Red Sea, Persian Gulf, and Arabian Sea. As the birthplace of Islam and Arab culture, it comprises Saudi Arabia, Yemen, Oman, UAE, Kuwait, Qatar, and Bahrain. The region is historically known for its nomadic Bedouin traditions, significant oil resources, and rapid 20th-century urbanization.
  • “to speak only the English language”: The “English-only” movement in the US was characterized by waves of nativism and forced Americanization, peaking around World War I to target immigrants and minority languages. While English was the dominant language, it was not legally official, but rather enforced through laws, school policies, and cultural assimilation, aiming to eliminate bilingual education and marginalize non-English speakers, particularly German speakers. Although English predominated, early America was multilingual. However, English was established as the primary language of political, economic, and social life. Following a surge in immigration, former President Theodore Roosevelt wrote, in a letter of January 3, 1919, that immigrants should become Americans, not “dwellers in a polyglot boarding house.” World War I sparked intense hostility against German-Americans, leading many states to ban German in public spaces, schools, and even conversations. By 1919, 15 states mandated English as the sole language of instruction. Restrictions extended to foreign-language newspapers and, in some areas, required non-citizens to pay special taxes. By the 1940s, bilingual education had been virtually eliminated due to policies focused on rapid, forced assimilation. Explicit English-only policies were used to systematically eliminate indigenous languages in government-run boarding schools.
  • “he could flash the money, even the Chinese money”: Chinese money evolved from ancient cowrie shells to the world’s first paper currency (7th-15th centuries) and a dual system of copper “cash” and silver. Key developments included the Song dynasty’s invention of paper money, the Yuan dynasty’s reliance on paper notes, and later, the Qing dynasty’s shift toward silver, culminating in modern currency reforms in the early 20th century, culminating in the Renminbi’s emergence.
  • “had been in Bathsheba selling earrings”: Bathsheba is a woman, not a place; he means Beersheba, the desert town of the Negev, where Abraham dug his well (Genesis 21:31). See Genesis.
    • Bathsheba was an Israelite queen consort. According to the Hebrew Bible, she was the wife of Uriah the Hittite and later of David, with whom she had all of her five children. Her status as the mother of Solomon, who succeeded David as monarch, made her the Gebirah of the Kingdom of Israel.
  • “had been in Siberia selling lace table cloths”: Siberia is a massive region covering over 5.2 million square miles (13.5 million square km) across Northern Asia, constituting about three-quarters of Russia’s total territory. Known for its extreme, long, and cold winters, it features vast tundra, coniferous forests (taiga), and major mountain ranges, including the Ural and Altai. It contains Lake Baikal, the world’s deepest lake, and is resource-rich, while being sparsely populated and historically significant for its indigenous communities and Russian expansion.
  • “had been in the Holy Land selling holy water”: The Holy Land is a sacred region in the Southern Levant, primarily located within modern-day Israel and Palestine. It is revered by Jews, Christians, and Muslims as the setting for key biblical events, including the life, ministry, and death of Jesus Christ, as well as the birthplace of the Jewish people.
  • “the whole world turned into salt”: “But his wife looked back from behind him, and she became a pillar of salt” (Genesis 19:26, KJV). See Genesis.
    • This could be a reference to the atomic bomb which was dropped on Japan during WWII.
    • The whole human race “turned into smoke” may also call up the crematoria of the death camps, where six million Jews were murdered. See Judaism.
  • “He would be driving along in the Baby Austen”: Baby Austen may refer to Austin 7 which was an economy car that was produced from 1923 until 1939 in the United Kingdom by Austin. It was nicknamed the Baby Austin and was at that time one of the most popular cars produced for the British market and sold well abroad.
    • In America the American Austin Car Company built its own version of the little car in Butler, Pennsylvania, from 1930.
  • “a cargo of toys and kewpie dolls”: Kewpie is a brand of dolls and figurines that were conceived as comic strip characters by American cartoonist Rose O’Neill. The illustrated cartoons, appearing as baby cupid characters, began to gain popularity after the publication of O’Neill’s comic strips in 1909, and O’Neill began to illustrate and sell paper doll versions of the Kewpies. The characters were first produced as bisque dolls in Waltershausen, Germany, beginning in 1912, and became extremely popular in the early 20th century. See the kewpie dolls in the Chapter 72 resources.
  • “gently rocking in the vasty deep”: “I can call spirits from the vasty deep. / Why, so can I, or so can any man; / But will they come when you do call for them?” (Henry IV, Part 1, 3.1). See Shakespeare.
  • “under his rain-streaked ulster”: An ulster is a long, loose overcoat, often with a cape, first made of rough Irish frieze in Belfast and named for the province. Ulster is one of the four historical provinces of Ireland, located in the north of the island. It traditionally comprises nine counties: six form Northern Ireland (Antrim, Armagh, Down, Fermanagh, Londonderry, and Tyrone), which is part of the United Kingdom, while three (Cavan, Donegal, and Monaghan) are part of the Republic of Ireland. See Clothing, Hats, and Skirts.
  • “a wild, raging storm between the cracking Poles”: The shipwreck described in this chapter is a powerful and symbolic event that carries deep thematic weight. The shipwreck is recounted primarily through the perspective of the little toy salesman, who is portrayed as the lone survivor of a catastrophic maritime disaster during a fierce storm at sea. See The Sea and Water, Revelation and the Apocalypse, and Exploration and the Poles.
    • The storm and subsequent sinking of the ship represent a cosmic upheaval, described as “a wild, raging storm between the cracking Poles,” with the sea rising “in billows to the dark heavens hammering,” and the moon and stars falling like sparks and rain of blood. This imagery evokes an apocalyptic vision of the world’s end, suggesting the collapse of order and the overwhelming power of nature and fate.
    • The little toy salesman survives the wreck, sitting alone in a rubber life boat while all others perish, including the captain, crew, women, children, and even celestial bodies like the moon and stars. His survival is depicted ambiguously; he is both pitied and condemned as a “murderer” because he did not drown with the others and thereby “killed” them by surviving. His survival seems almost accidental or unwilling; he “had wanted to do so,” but was upheld by “swollen bladders” and “heaving breasts.”
    • After the storm, the salesman experiences a prolonged “calm” that is described as worse than the storm itself, filled with loneliness, disorientation, and existential dread. He is surrounded by floating debris and bloated bodies, with a haunting “dead child’s hand” that clings to him, symbolizing his inescapable connection to death and loss. This hand, which wears a gold ring like his own, is a spectral reminder of the dead children and the burden of survival.
    • The little toy salesman loses his memory, taste buds, tear ducts, and reason during the storm and the aftermath, which symbolizes a loss of self and disconnection from reality. His mind “cracking” and being “lost between the Poles like a leaf falling nowhere” reflects the disintegration of identity and the fragility of human existence in the face of overwhelming catastrophe.
    • The narrative critiques human selfishness and cruelty during the disaster: the old German sea captain orders men to jump into the sea while women and children take the lifeboats, reflecting societal and gendered survival biases. The passengers are described as conceited and snobbish, oblivious to their impending doom. The little toy salesman’s survival contrasts with the collective fate, emphasizing themes of exclusion and difference.
    • The shipwreck is accompanied by powerful, almost liturgical imagery: “leaden church bells,” “mourning bands,” “a golden flood of music more beautiful than Bach, Beethoven, or Brahms,” and the captain conducting as he goes down with the ship. This suggests the shipwreck as a kind of requiem or cosmic ritual. The black mourning band in the sky spanning horizon to horizon intensifies the sense of universal mourning.
    • The little toy salesman’s story parallels Esther Longtree’s ongoing “everlasting pregnancy” with the “little shadow boxer,” symbolizing themes of birth, death, and hope amidst despair. The shipwreck and the salesman’s survival underscore Esther’s loneliness and the burden of nurturing life in a world shadowed by loss and uncertainty.
  • “It was all the old German sea captain’s fault”: The little toy salesman blamed the German sea captain because he thought there were more lifeboats when there was only one. This resembles the lifeboat situation on the Titanic. See The Sea and Water.
    • The German sea captain went down with the ship looking up “...bright with rage and love as if he had realized his strength, at last, his weakness.” There was a Gustav Schroder that tried to take 937 German Jews in 1939 to Havana, Cuba to save them from the Nazis. They were turned away from Cuba, Canada and the United States and returned to Europe.
  • “there was only one”: The Titanic (1912) carried lifeboats for only about half of the 2,224 people aboard, and more than 1,500 died; “women and children first” was the order of the night. See The Sea and Water.
  • “The captain was crazy, too”: The captain’s withered arm points to Kaiser Wilhelm II, the German emperor born in 1859 with a withered left arm, who led Germany into the First World War.
    • It may also refer to Wilhelm Furtwängler, a renowned German conductor. Furtwängler was known for his intense and passionate conducting style, though, unlike the captain, he had no withered arm. He was considered one of the greatest conductors of his time. The novel’s reference to him as a “German captain” could also subtly allude to his controversial position during World War II, when he remained in Germany under the Nazi regime.
  • “There were also four ugly gamblers”: May refer to the “Big Four” Allied powers during World War II, who led the fight against the Axis, were the United States, the United Kingdom, the Soviet Union (USSR), and China. These nations formed the core of the alliance, with China fighting Japan since 1937 and the others joining later. See Gambling and Playing Cards.
    • May refer to France who was also a major Allied power, particularly before its occupation and later during liberation.
  • “Saturn stood still in the glassy heavens”: “Sun, stand thou still upon Gibeon; and thou, Moon, in the valley of Ajalon” (Joshua 10:12, KJV). See The Bible.
  • “ten thousand Niagaras”: See Niagara Falls in the Chapter 65 resources.
  • “more beautiful than Bach, Beethoven, or Brahms”: Johann Sebastian Bach was a German composer and musician of the late Baroque period. He is known for his prolific output across a variety of instruments and forms, including the orchestral Brandenburg Concertos; solo instrumental works such as the cello suites and sonatas and partitas for solo violin; keyboard works such as the Goldberg Variations and The Well-Tempered Clavier; organ works such as the Schübler Chorales and the Toccata and Fugue in D minor; and choral works such as the St Matthew Passion and the Mass in B minor. He is known for his mastery of counterpoint, as heard in The Musical Offering and The Art of Fugue. Felix Mendelssohn precipitated the Bach Revival with a performance of the St. Matthew Passion in 1829. Ever since, Bach has been known as one of the greatest composers of classical music. See Music and Composers.
    • Ludwig van Beethoven was a German composer and pianist. One of the most revered figures in the history of Western music, his works rank among the most performed of the classical music repertoire and span the transition from the Classical to the Romantic era. Beethoven’s early period, during which he forged his craft, is typically considered to have lasted until 1802. From 1802 to around 1812, his middle period showed an individual development from the styles of Joseph Haydn and Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart, and is sometimes characterised as heroic. During this time, Beethoven began to grow increasingly deaf. In his late period, from 1812 to 1827, he extended his innovations in musical form and expression. See Deafness and Sign Language.
    • Johannes Brahms was a German composer, virtuoso pianist, and conductor of the mid-Romantic period. His music is noted for its rhythmic vitality and freer treatment of dissonance, often set within studied yet expressive contrapuntal textures. He adapted the traditional structures and techniques of a wide historical range of earlier composers. His œuvre includes four symphonies, four concertos, a Requiem, much chamber music, and hundreds of folk-song arrangements and Lieder, among other works for symphony orchestra, piano, organ, and choir.
  • “his withered arm lifting”: “the German captain went down with the ship” Captain Hans Langsdorff is the most famous German captain who went down with his ship metaphorically in WW2. After ordering his ship, the pocket battleship Admiral Graf Spee, to be scuttled in Montevideo on December 17, 1939, to save his crew, he died by suicide on December 20, 1939, in Buenos Aires. Hans Langsdorff chose to take his own life to prove that he acted with honor, ensuring his crew’s safety after the Graf Spee was trapped by British cruisers. He is often cited for his moral courage and for prioritizing the lives of his crew over the strict, often suicidal, orders of the Nazi regime. See Suicide in History and Literature.
  • “with antiphon between the antipodes”: An antiphon is a short, often scriptural chant or verse sung as a refrain in Christian liturgy, particularly within Catholic Mass (Entrance, Offertory, Communion) and the Liturgy of the Hours (Lauds, Vespers). It acts as a thematic focal point for a specific day or season, usually accompanying psalms or canticles. Historically rooted in early Christian worship and favored by St. Ambrose, they were originally performed in a call-and-response style between two choirs.
    • Antipodes are points on Earth diametrically opposite to one another, representing the maximum distance apart on the globe. Most landmasses have their opposite point in the ocean, as 70% of Earth is water. The US mainland aligns with the Indian Ocean, Australia with the North Atlantic, and New Zealand with Spain/Portugal.
  • “nimbus, aureole”: Nimbus primarily refers to a dark gray rain-bearing cloud (often associated with nimbostratus) or, traditionally, a luminous cloud/halo surrounding a deity or saint. Derived from Latin for “cloud,” it represents an aura, atmosphere, or a specialized cloud type that produces rain.
    • Aureole is a circle of light or brightness surrounding something, especially as depicted in art around the head or body of a person represented as holy.
  • “a victim of the Jews”: May refer to Arthur Miller’s play Death of a Salesman. The play features a character, Willy Loman, who is a failing salesman. While Arthur Miller was Jewish, the play itself is often considered a universal American tragedy about the failure of the American Dream, and Willy’s Jewish identity is a long-debated topic among literary critics. Some productions and analyses have framed Willy as a Jewish character whose assimilation makes him vulnerable to societal pressures. The rubber hose that Willy hides by the gas heater, planning suicide, is a key symbol in the play; in the end he dies in his car. This is also a representation of the character’s antisemitism, prejudiced and paranoid worldview within the fictional narrative. The play opened in 1949.
    • The concept of a “Jewish conspiracy” is an antisemitic myth with roots in medieval Europe that became the foundation for modern political antisemitism. These conspiracy theories falsely allege that Jewish people secretly manipulate institutions, banks, the media, and governments for malevolent purposes, such as achieving world domination. It is a dangerous and debunked fiction used throughout history to justify discrimination, persecution, and violence against Jews. In the Middle Ages, hostility toward Jews was often rooted in religious prejudice and false accusations, which served as a basis for later conspiracy myths. The antisemitic myth of blood libel emerged in the 12th century with the story of William of Norwich. It falsely claimed that Jews ritually murdered Christian children to use their blood for religious rituals, particularly for Passover matzah. This accusation frequently led to violent massacres and expulsions of Jewish communities. During the Black Death in the mid-14th century, Jews were used as scapegoats and falsely accused of poisoning wells to cause the plague. This led to the destruction of hundreds of Jewish communities across Europe. Due to restrictions that prevented Jews from owning land or joining certain trades, many worked as moneylenders. This created resentment and gave rise to stereotypes of Jews as greedy and obsessed with money, which later fueled secular conspiracy theories about Jewish wealth and control. In the 19th century, antisemitic ideas evolved from religious prejudice into modern political and racial theories of antisemitism, giving rise to more elaborate conspiracy narratives. German novelist Hermann Goedsche published Biarritz, which featured a fictional scene of a secret rabbinical cabal meeting in a Jewish cemetery to discuss a plot for world domination. This work was a commercial success and was later plagiarized to create The Protocols of the Elders of Zion (circa 1903), this fabricated document is the most infamous antisemitic text. It was a forgery created by the Russian secret police to stir up antisemitism and deflect from public discontent with the Tsarist regime. The Protocols claim to be the minutes of secret meetings held by Jewish leaders outlining a plan to take over the world. Though repeatedly exposed as a hoax, it continues to circulate and influence conspiracy theories to this day. Antisemitic conspiracy myths played a central role in the rise of Nazism and the Holocaust. Adolf Hitler and the Nazi Party adopted the Protocols as proof of a “Jewish world conspiracy.” They used it to justify their persecution and extermination of six million Jews. They falsely claimed that Jews were behind communism, capitalism, and Germany’s loss in World War I. The American industrialist Henry Ford distributed massive quantities of antisemitic material, including articles based on the Protocols, through his newspaper, The Dearborn Independent. He later retracted and apologized for his publications following a lawsuit, but the damage was already done. Following the Russian Revolution, an antisemitic conspiracy theory known as “Jewish Bolshevism” or Żydokomuna claimed that Jews controlled the Soviet Union and international communist movements. This false notion was promoted by anti-communist factions and heavily used by Nazi propaganda. In the modern era, antisemitic conspiracy theories have adapted to contemporary fears and platforms, continuing to spread hatred. “ZOG” theory (Zionist Occupation Government) theory, promoted by some white nationalists, claims that Jews secretly control Western governments. “Great Replacement” theory is a white nationalist conspiracy theory, which has influenced mass shootings, and claims that Jews are orchestrating a demographic “replacement” of white people through immigration. At the 2017 Charlottesville rally, participants chanted “Jews will not replace us.” The internet and social media have facilitated the widespread dissemination of antisemitic conspiracy theories, with groups like QAnon promoting versions of the myth. These online forums and platforms amplify old lies and connect them to new global events, continuing the cycle of prejudice and misinformation. Antisemitism remains part of American life. On October 27, 2018, a gunman who blamed Jews for immigration killed eleven worshipers at the Tree of Life synagogue in Pittsburgh, the deadliest attack on Jews in American history; another killed a worshiper at the Chabad of Poway synagogue in California in 2019, and in 2022 a gunman held a rabbi and three congregants hostage in Colleyville, Texas. The Anti-Defamation League, which has tracked incidents since 1979, counted a record 9,354 antisemitic incidents in 2024 and 6,274 in 2025, when assaults rose to 203. That year two staff members of the Israeli embassy were shot dead outside the Capital Jewish Museum in Washington, D.C. (May 21, 2025); a firebombing in Boulder, Colorado, killed an 82-year-old woman; and an arsonist set fire to Pennsylvania Governor Josh Shapiro’s residence on the first night of Passover. The FBI counted 1,528 anti-Jewish hate crimes in 2025, 63 percent of all religion-based hate crimes, though Jews are about two percent of the population. Like many forms of prejudice and bigotry in the United States, antisemitism is still being reckoned with. Flag: after 1964, the events from 2017 to 2025. See Judaism.
    • The history of the Jewish rubber business is marked by individual entrepreneurial success, particularly in products like condoms, alongside the forced seizure of Jewish-owned businesses during the Nazi era. A prominent example is Julius Fromm, a Polish-German chemist who developed a way of making seamless rubber condoms and founded a successful rubber products company, only to have his factory stolen by the Nazis before he fled to England in 1939.
  • “old Mongolians churning in the waters”: Mongolians are an East Asian ethnic group native to Mongolia, China (primarily Inner Mongolia), and parts of Russia, numbering around 10 million in total. Known for a historical, enduring, and nomadic pastoralist tradition, they are closely linked to the Mongol Empire founded by Genghis Khan. They primarily speak Mongolian languages and practice Tibetan Buddhism and shamanism. See Buddhism.
  • “In death, all persons were black as Negroes on slabs”: His contempt reaches past the Jews: even the drowned are, to him, “black as Negroes on slabs.” See Society, Class, and Race.
  • “The burning sunlight was blackening his skin”: “The burning sunlight was blackening his skin” may refer to the damage done by a nuclear bomb.
  • “He had dreamed in an everlasting silence”: “He had dreamed in an everlasting silence. He had thought that his mother had killed him…” in the desert. This echoes stories about Cousin Hannah’s travels in desert countries. See Cousin Hannah.
  • “When he recovered consciousness again, he was lying on a shore”: When the stranger, identified as the little toy salesman, recovers consciousness on the shore, the items he sees symbolize America as a landscape of accumulated detritus, lost potential, and the complex interplay of natural decay and human impact.
    • Purple oyster sponges, crab shells, jellyfish like glass, and bones of dead fish: These natural elements represent the raw, indifferent cycles of nature, where life and death are constantly intertwined. The “glassy” jellyfish can also hint at the blurred lines between reality and illusion that permeate. This aspect of America is ancient, untamed, and a vast receptacle for the remnants of countless lives, both human and non-human.
    • “little carcasses of other little children”: This deeply tragic image symbolizes the profound loss of innocence and unfulfilled potential within the American experience. It resonates with Esther Longtree’s story of stillbirth fantasies and lost children, suggesting a hidden sorrow or the casualties of a harsh reality that often goes unacknowledged.
    • “playing cards”: Playing cards in the novel are often associated with chance, fate, and the illusions of control, as seen in scenes with gamblers. Their presence on the shore suggests America as a place where fortunes are gambled, where outcomes are subject to unpredictable forces, and where the remnants of failed risks are left behind.
    • “old junk”: This broad category signifies the accumulation of discarded material, reflecting a society of consumption and the inevitable detritus of progress. It speaks to America as a land that produces and discards, where forgotten objects bear witness to past lives and aspirations.
    • “rubber tires”: As specific man-made discards, rubber tires represent the waste product of modern industry and transportation. They highlight the impact of human activity on the natural landscape, suggesting a departure from a pristine wilderness towards an environment marked by the remnants of ceaseless movement and consumption. This also connects to the little toy salesman’s later identity as a “rubber salesman.”
    • “birth control devices”: The inclusion of these items is particularly striking, pointing to themes of sexuality, control over reproduction, and perhaps the anxieties or deliberate choices related to creating or preventing life. In a novel deeply concerned with motherhood, loss, and the nature of existence, these devices symbolize attempts to manage or deny natural processes, or the consequences of such interventions in the American context. See Pregnancy, Abortion, and Midwifery.
    • Collectively, these items portray America not as a land of simple, idealized dreams, but as a complex, often melancholy landscape where the natural world is inextricably mixed with human-made refuse and the poignant echoes of lives lived and lost. It is a place of stark reality, littered with the tangible evidence of decay, chance, and the profound, sometimes tragic, consequences of human existence, leaving the returning “stranger” with a sense of alienation and a confrontation with a less glamorous truth.
  • “a voice saying to jump from the high places”: “If thou be the Son of God, cast thyself down: for it is written, He shall give his angels charge concerning thee” (Matthew 4:6, KJV), the devil’s temptation on the pinnacle of the temple. See The Bible.
  • “He whispered into her ear that there would be a great war”: Everything would be poisoned and disappear forever. This may refer to the proliferation of nuclear weapons during the Cold War. The Cold War saw a rapid nuclear arms race that saw the U.S. and Soviet Union build massive arsenals, which fueled the proliferation of nuclear weapons to other nations like the UK, France, and China. This escalation was driven by mutual suspicion and doctrines like Mutually Assured Destruction (MAD), but was tempered by arms control efforts such as the Partial Test Ban Treaty and the Non-Proliferation Treaty (NPT). The period is also marked by dangerous standoffs, such as the Cuban Missile Crisis, which underscored the need to prevent nuclear conflict. Little Boy was the codename for the type of atomic bomb dropped on the Japanese city of Hiroshima on 6 August 1945 during World War II. It was the first nuclear weapon used in warfare. Carl Jung had visions and dreams about carnage and thought he was going insane. From his journals it is considered a premonition of World War I. See Freud and Jung.
    • “there would be a great war and that the bad men would blow up the world some day of calm just for fun” may refer to the Cold War. The Cold War was a period of international geopolitical rivalry between the United States and the Soviet Union and their respective allies, the capitalist Western Bloc and communist Eastern Bloc, which began in the aftermath of the Second World War and ended with the dissolution of the Soviet Union in 1991. The Cold War outlasted 1964.
  • “the star, bright star”: “Bright star, would I were stedfast as thou art” (Keats, 1819). See Romantic Poets.
  • “and the red haw”: “red haw” most commonly refers to the Red Hawthorn, a small, thorny deciduous tree or shrub native to North America known for its white spring flowers and bright red fruits. It is also referred to as Downy Hawthorn or Scarlet Hawthorn.
