Chapter 82

← Chapter 81 · Home

Content note: Vera’s mother, Catherine Cartwheel, dies after a lifetime of opium addiction.

Summary

Vera thinks of all she could have confessed to Esther. Her mother is dead. Weaned at last from her drugs, Catherine rose from her bed and walked, and suddenly she was old, so changed that no one would have known her. Riding with her in the old surrey at the sea’s edge, Mr. Spitzer declared his long love and told her he was really Peron, and that it was Joachim who had died, but she had died before he spoke. A great storm then swept away the house with its golden towers and drowned the old clam-digger, leaving chandeliers strewn along the shore; only the string of pearls Vera wears remains. Vera sees Miss MacIntosh anew, “Whatever is average is the dream. Whatever is hidden is the revealed,” and remembers her singing the psalms and hymns of her childhood over the ironing board. At the Tavern Vera hears a man shouting all night to Lucie Bell, a girl who had already left him, and at dawn she meets him, a stone deaf man, deaf since he was fourteen. They become lovers, he whispers that their child will be their ear, and they plan to marry and invite everyone, the flowers and the birds and Esther Longtree. “Esther Longtree would be me.” Esther hangs a misspelled sign in the restaurant window: “Owt to luntsch. bee bak in a whale.”

Characters present

Vera Cartwheel · Esther Longtree · Joachim Spitzer · Catherine Cartwheel · The Old Clam-Digger · The Stone Deaf Man · Lucie Bell

Concepts present

Themes: Death and Mortality · Grief, Loss, and Mourning · Illusion and Reality · Love · Music, Sound, and Silence · Nature, the Sea, and the Cosmos · Society, Class, and Race · Time

Symbols: Birds · Dogs · Eyes and Blindness · Fog and Mist · Horses and Carriages · Lamps, Candles, and Light · Moon and Stars · Music and Instruments · Pearls and Jewels · Silence and Deafness · The Sea and Water

Philosophy: Marguerite Young on Her Craft

Allusions: Angels and Archangels · Astronomy · Deafness and Sign Language · Exploration and the Poles · Greek Mythology · Homer’s Epics · Romantic Poets · The Bible · The History of Opium

Key passages

From the research

  • Early in the chapter, Vera reflects on the death of her mother, Catherine, the destruction of the house with its golden turrets and towers by the sea, and the scattering of chandeliers along the shore. The only remaining possession is a string of pearls worn by Vera. Vera mourns “three deaths” and is “in love with an older love than memory provided.”
  • A significant section meditates on the experience of deafness. Vera compares the deaf to marble statues who perceive much but miss the vital auditory dimension of reality. The silence is described as a cold, alien world, yet it also holds a unique, possibly more beautiful mode of communication beyond speech. Even those who hear do not perceive everything, while the deaf may be haunted by imagined sounds or the absence of words.
  • The narrative details Catherine’s gradual return from a drug-induced dreamlike state to a fragile awareness before her death. Mr. Spitzer, who had loved Catherine secretly and faithfully, waited for a moment to confess his love, which ultimately came too late. Mr. Spitzer holds Catherine in his arms in the old surrey at the sea’s edge, speaking of his long-buried love as the sea and nature respond around them. Catherine dies as he speaks.
  • Mr. Spitzer declares that he is Peron, not the dead brother Joachim, though Young said that he himself does not know which brother he is (Marguerite Young, interview with Kay Bonetti, American Audio Prose Library, May 1983). His grief over Catherine’s death and the loss of the old clam-digger valet is profound. The old clam-digger, a loyal companion, drowned in the storm.
  • The descriptions of the old clam-digger’s habits (burying himself in the sand, being mistaken for part of the landscape, developing nervous tics) serve as a metaphor for the human condition in the face of time and loss. Despite physical preservation, there is a spiritual or intellectual departure, resulting in a “living corpse.” This passage contemplates the nature of life, death, and decay in a subtle, haunting way.
  • Toward the end of the chapter, Vera hears the voice of a stone deaf man who, though unable to hear, speaks and sings in a world of silence. His voice, full of longing, loss, and fragmented thoughts, expresses the paradox of communication without sound. Vera falls in love with this silent traveler.
  • Throughout the chapter, there is a recurring motif of life as a dream, of love preceding words, and of silence having its own language. Vera and the stone deaf man imagine a wedding attended by wildflowers, birds, and nature itself, a symbolic union beyond earthly conventions. The chapter closes on a note of tender acceptance and mystery, with Vera embracing love and silence as intertwined realities.

Questions and observations

Reading closely

  • “Whatever is average is the dream. Whatever is hidden is the revealed.” What has Vera learned about Miss MacIntosh?
  • “My beginning was my end, and my end was my beginning.” How does the novel end where it began?
  • “Perhaps there is always a sense missing, that sense which would make the world real.” What sense is missing in Vera?

Characters

  • Mr. Spitzer tells Catherine he is Peron, but “she was dead, had died at the beginning of his whispers.” Why must the confession come too late?
  • Vera loves the stone deaf man “as a mother might love a child” and as a woman loves a man. Why both?
  • Of Miss MacIntosh: “Her doubt was her own wound.” What else did she keep hidden?

Connections

  • “Esther Longtree would be me.” What does Vera take from Esther?
  • Esther’s sign reads “Owt to luntsch. bee bak in a whale.” Why end the novel with a misspelling?
  • The old horse turns into “the golden mare.” Where else has the novel shown one thing passing for another?

Reflection

  • “There are ways more beautiful than the ear, the eye.” What are they?
  • “Life is imaginary, and this be an imaginary world.” Do you agree?
  • The lovers “would invite everybody to our wedding,” the flowers, the birds, the old mule, and Esther. Who would be at yours?

Research: Characters

Vera

  • Reflective and deeply emotional, Vera grapples with mourning, love, and the nature of existence.

Esther Longtree

  • Mentioned as someone Vera might have confided in but who perhaps would not fully understand or be interested. Represents a contrasting perspective on loss and endurance.

Mr. Spitzer

  • A complex figure who reveals his true identity as Peron, the brother of Joachim. He has waited years to confess his love and to close a chapter on the past. His grief is profound, encompassing the loss of Catherine, the old clam-digger, and his own illusions.

Catherine

  • Once beautiful and dreamlike, she lived in a state between life and death, sustained by drugs and illusions. Her death and the destruction of her home symbolize the dissolution of a dream or an era.

The Old Clam-Digger (Valet)

  • A loyal servant and companion to Mr. Spitzer, embodying endurance and the passage of time. His disappearance in the storm represents another loss for Mr. Spitzer.

The Stone Deaf Man

  • A poignant figure who cannot hear but communicates and experiences the world through other senses. He has a profound inner life and love beyond words. Young said that “the deaf are normal in every way” and that those who lack a sense “develop a hypersensitivity in every other way” (Marguerite Young, interview with Studs Terkel, WFMT radio, 1965). His lost love is Lucie Bell, who “had left him before I ever came”; Vera never saw her.

Lucie Bell

  • Lucie Bell is the deaf man’s lost love, gone before Vera came, so Vera never sees or hears her. He calls her “a little bird girl with such a small, pecking face and such long, thin legs,” fickle, loving a jukebox or a “tired marathon skater” more than him: “You make too much noise. I am going to leave you. Man loves a silent woman.” He hears with his eyes and fingers and longs for a silent love, and Vera comes to love him “for all the tongues of silence speaking the name of love.”

Research: Themes

Loss and Mourning

See: Grief, Loss, and Mourning

  • Vera mourns not only Catherine but also the loss of a dreamlike past, the family estate, and symbolic “pearls.” Mr. Spitzer’s layered grief includes his brother Joachim, Catherine, and the old clam-digger.

Illusion and Reality

See: Illusion and Reality

  • Catherine’s life was sustained by dreams and drugs, blurring the line between waking life and sleep, life and death. Vera questions what is real and what is dream.

Silence and Communication

See: Music, Sound, and Silence

  • Extensive meditation on deafness, silence, and the limitations and beauty of communication beyond words. The stone deaf man represents the world of silence yet full of inner sound and love.

Time and Timelessness

See: Time

  • Time is experienced unevenly, accelerating at moments and suspended in others. Catherine’s slow death, Mr. Spitzer’s long wait, and the clam-digger’s timeless endurance reflect different relationships with time.

Love Beyond Death

See: Death and Mortality · Love

  • Mr. Spitzer’s confession of being Peron and his love for Catherine after her death touches on eternal love transcending mortality.

Nature and the Sea

See: Nature, the Sea, and the Cosmos

  • The sea is a powerful force of destruction and transformation, symbolic of change, loss, and perhaps renewal. It carries away the house and treasures but also represents the boundary between worlds.

Research: Symbols and Imagery

The Sea

See: The Sea and Water

  • Represents overwhelming change, the passage of time, and the erasure of the past. It is both nurturing and destructive.

Pearls

See: Pearls and Jewels

  • The only remaining inheritance of Vera after the storm. Symbolize lost treasures, memories, or purity.

The Old White Horse and Surrey

See: Horses and Carriages

  • Symbolize the passage toward death and the journey between worlds. The horse turning into silver, blue, green, and gold hints at transformation and transcendence.

The Silent Dog and Barking

See: Dogs · Silence and Deafness

  • Represent intuition and knowledge beyond human perception, especially about death.

Music and Silence

See: Music and Instruments · Silence and Deafness

  • Mr. Spitzer’s identity as Peron and his music represent communication beyond words and the connection between the living and the dead.

The Stone Deaf Man

See: Silence and Deafness

  • Symbolizes alternate perception and the power of love and inner sound beyond physical hearing.

Fog and Moonlight

See: Fog and Mist · Moon and Stars · Lamps, Candles, and Light

  • Indicate ambiguity, the boundary between clarity and obscurity, life and death, dream and reality.

Further notes from the text

  • Vera’s mourning begins with the house: the sea has swept over the opium paradise, the divan upheld by dolphins dreams under the flood, and no lawyer will be needed for the estate, because nothing is left to administer.
  • Catherine’s last hours are framed as a paradox Mr. Spitzer understood: she would die if her enchantment continued, and she would die if she rose and walked again. She rises, takes a few steps, and dies.
  • Mr. Spitzer’s declaration, that he was really Peron, comes with his usual rolling periods, as if to assure himself that what he says is true, or not quite true. Vera does not decide which.
  • The old clam-digger, Mr. Spitzer’s valet, used to bury himself in the sand with only a hole for his mouth and nose, so that the herring gulls mistook him for a moss animal or a rock. The storm takes him with the house.
  • Left alone like an old barnacled boat, Mr. Spitzer asks how he will pass his time, and the novel turns to Miss MacIntosh’s creed of the average and the middle way, which Vera now sees anew.
  • The songs and hymns of the chapter gather the book’s images, the Rock of Ages, the lighthouse beam for the wanderer, the waters that have gone over the soul, and repeat its oldest line: my beginning was my end, and my end was my beginning.
  • The stone deaf man’s ears are in his fingertips. His former love, Lucie Bell, left him before Vera came. Vera loves him “as a mother might love a child” and as a woman loves a man, and they plan a wedding to which everyone is invited, Esther Longtree included.

Research: Resources

  • “how my mother, after many years of sleeping, arose from her bed and walked”: So did Weissenbach. She “had been able to get out of bed after many, many years, but this is what killed her, so that she turned old overnight. She had never shown the mark of time.” She died in 1943 in New York, and Young, who kept writing to her, learned of it months later from her daughter: “as long as you kept writing to Mother and I read your letters, I felt as if my mother was somehow alive” (Marguerite Young, interview with Kay Bonetti, American Audio Prose Library, May 1983). See Catherine Cartwheel, Marguerite Young on Her Craft, and The History of Opium.
  • “With Braille, he teaches”: Louis Braille, blinded as a child, published his raised-dot alphabet in 1829. The Seeing Eye, the first American school for guide dogs, was founded in 1929 by Dorothy Harrison Eustis. See Eyes and Blindness.
  • “One drop more of nepenthe”: Nepenthe is a mythical, ancient Greek potion or drug used to induce forgetfulness of pain, sorrow, or grief. In Homer’s Odyssey (Book 4), Helen had it as a gift from Polydamna of Egypt and mixed it into the wine to ease the grief of Menelaus and his guests. See Greek Mythology and Homer’s Epics.
  • “seeming to be scaling like the moon”: Here “scaling” means flaking off in scales, as old paint or skin does: the old white horse is “streaked with grey and scaling, flaking like the moon.” See Horses and Carriages.
    • Scaling refers to the adjustment of size, scope, or intensity, with meanings ranging from enlarging/reducing dimensions in mathematics and design to increasing business operations, or removing deposits from teeth. It fundamentally involves changing the scale of a subject.
  • “if he did not speak now, he might never speak”: Young took the scene from the death of the poet Elinor Wylie (December 16, 1928) as she remembered it: William Rose Benét explained his feelings to her at length, “and then he realized that she was sitting there dead and had never heard a word. She missed his confession” (Marguerite Young, interview with Kay Bonetti, American Audio Prose Library, May 1983). See Joachim Spitzer and Catherine Cartwheel.
  • “the reason no one had heard his music since Peron’s death was that he was Peron”: Young compared Mr. Spitzer’s “great impersonation in this life” to “the Titchborn claimant” (Marguerite Young, interview with Studs Terkel, WFMT radio, 1965), Arthur Orton, who claimed in 1866 to be the lost heir Roger Tichborne and was convicted of perjury in 1874. In her first draft “Mr. Spitzer knew that he was really Peyron the gambler,” which “seemed so tricky to me” that she rewrote it so that he does not know (Marguerite Young, interview with Kay Bonetti, American Audio Prose Library, May 1983). See Joachim Spitzer, Marguerite Young on Her Craft, and Peron Spitzer.
  • “the old nag turning into the golden mare”: Young read about racehorse “ringers” painted to race under false colors: “I read of one marvelous case at Saratoga Springs when it was a rain storm in the midst of the race, and people with absolute horror looked out to see the old nag turning into the speeder, losing the mottled coat.” She also read lives of John W. “Bet-a-Million” Gates and Diamond Jim Brady (Marguerite Young, interview with Studs Terkel, WFMT radio, 1965). See Joachim Spitzer and Horses and Carriages.
  • “for hers would be an urn burial”: Sir Thomas Browne’s Urne-Buriall (1658), a meditation on ancient burial urns, ends: “Man is a Noble Animal, splendid in ashes, and pompous in the grave.” See Death and Mortality.
  • “like a jackdaw picking up sticks”: A jackdaw is a small, highly social bird in the crow family, known for its striking pale-gray eyes and a distinctive silver-gray “shawl” on the back of its head. It is commonly found in urban areas, farmland, and woodlands across Europe, Asia, and North Africa. See Birds.
  • “tatterdemalions”: Tatterdemalion describes a person wearing ragged, torn, or disreputable clothing, or refers to something in a state of decay, filth, or disrepair. Originating in the early 1600s, this term often used for a “ragamuffin” implies a shabby, unkempt appearance. As an adjective, it means ragged or dilapidated.
  • “Snow-breasted gannets and Arctic terns”: Gannets are seabirds, closely related to boobies. They are known as ‘solan’ or ‘solan goose’ in Scotland. A common misconception is that the Scottish name is ‘guga’ but this is the Gaelic name referring to the chicks only. (Wikipedia) See Birds.
    • The Arctic tern is a tern in the family Laridae. This bird has a circumpolar breeding distribution covering the Arctic and sub-Arctic regions of Europe, Asia, and North America. (Wikipedia) See Exploration and the Poles.
  • “beach plum bushes and beach cherry”: On the Atlantic coast the beach plum (Prunus maritima) and the sand cherry (Prunus pumila) grow wild in the dunes.
    • “beach cherry” Eugenia reinwardtiana is a shrub to small tree in the family Myrtaceae. Native to tropical forests in Indonesia, the Australian state of Queensland, and many Pacific Islands, its common names include Cedar Bay cherry, beach cherry, Australian beach cherry, mountain stopper, nīoi, and a’abang. (Wikipedia) This tropical beach cherry does not grow on the Atlantic shore.
    • “eel grass” Zostera is a small genus of widely distributed seagrasses, commonly called marine eelgrass, or simply seagrass or eelgrass. The genus Zostera contains 15 species. (Wikipedia)
  • “Map-makers of the heavenly bodies”: In 1930 the International Astronomical Union adopted the constellation boundaries drawn by Eugène Delporte, dividing the whole sky among 88 constellations so that no star falls outside. See Astronomy.
  • “as if this were the coast of Charon”: Charon ferried the dead across the river Styx into Hades, for a coin laid in the mouth. See Greek Mythology and Death and Mortality.
  • “golden chanticleer”: Chauntecleer is the proud rooster of Chaucer’s “Nun’s Priest’s Tale,” nearly carried off by the fox. See Birds.
  • “Thou hast wrapped me in Thy fleece”: The hymns Miss MacIntosh sings reveal a profound spiritual dimension to her character. While she keeps her doubt to herself (“Her doubt was her own wound”) and will not be “the stumbling block in another’s path,” these songs from her childhood represent an enduring, if conflicted, faith. They expose her inner struggles with vulnerability, physical and emotional wounds, and the existential human condition of being lost and in need of guidance. These moments of singing, even as she performs mundane tasks, highlight the tension between her practical life and her deep, unarticulated spiritual longings, demonstrating that her common sense and brusqueness are often a defense against profound personal suffering and a search for meaning in a chaotic world. See Miss MacIntosh and The Bible.
    • “Lo, she would lift her eyes to the hills from whence cometh help.” This references Psalm 121, often the basis of hymns about looking to the hills for help. “I will lift up mine eyes unto the hills, from whence cometh my help” (Psalm 121:1, KJV).
    • “Thou didst turn Thy face from me, and I was troubled” echoes Psalm 30:7: “thou didst hide thy face, and I was troubled” (KJV).
    • “For Thou art my strong rock and my castle, so also be my guide.” This refers to God as a “strong rock and castle,” a common biblical metaphor used in hymns. In the psalter of the Book of Common Prayer (Coverdale’s translation), Psalm 31:3 reads, “For thou art my strong rock, and my castle: be thou also my guide,” nearly Miss MacIntosh’s very words.
    • “Thou hast covered me, and Thou hast numbered the hairs of my head, and Thou hast closed the wound of my side. Thou hast plucked out the arrows.” These lines evoke biblical imagery associated with God’s protection and healing, reminiscent of hymns about divine care and salvation. “The very hairs of your head are all numbered” (Matthew 10:30); “thou hast covered me in my mother’s womb” (Psalm 139:13); “one of the soldiers with a spear pierced his side” (John 19:34); “thine arrows stick fast in me” (Psalm 38:2, KJV).
    • “Song of the shepherd who would lead all sheep home, losing none in narrow defiles” alludes to the Good Shepherd theme common in Christian hymns. “I am the good shepherd: the good shepherd giveth his life for the sheep” (John 10:11, KJV).
    • “Song of the Rock of Ages cleft for me” directly mentions the famous hymn “Rock of Ages.” Augustus Toplady’s hymn (published 1775): “Rock of Ages, cleft for me, / Let me hide myself in thee.”
    • “Songs of the Rugged Cross” refers to the hymn “The Old Rugged Cross,” focused on the crucifixion. George Bennard wrote it in 1912.
    • Songs “of the shaded valley, of the still stream” evoke traditional hymn imagery of peaceful pastoral scenes symbolizing God’s care. “He leadeth me beside the still waters” (Psalm 23:2, KJV); “As the hart panteth after the water brooks” (Psalm 42:1, KJV).
    • “Songs of those who reel to and fro and stagger like a drunken man, of the lost soul, of the pinioned wings” suggest hymns that address human frailty, being lost, and spiritual struggle. “They reel to and fro, and stagger like a drunken man, and are at their wit’s end” (Psalm 107:27, KJV).
    • Songs “of the lighthouse beam which lights the way to the poor wanderer tossed upon the rolling waves far from any harbor” is a metaphor often used in hymns about guidance and salvation.
    • “Awake, thou lute and harp, she sang. I myself will awake right early.” This is Psalm 57 in the psalter of the Book of Common Prayer: “awake, lute and harp: I myself will awake right early.” The King James has “awake, psaltery and harp: I myself will awake early” (Psalm 57:8).
    • “The waters have drowned us. The stream has gone over our soul.” is Psalm 124 in the psalter of the Book of Common Prayer: “Yea, the waters had drowned us: and the stream had gone over our soul.”
  • “My beginning was my end, and my end was my beginning”: Mary, Queen of Scots, embroidered the motto “En ma fin gît mon commencement” (“In my end is my beginning”); T. S. Eliot’s “East Coker” (1940) opens “In my beginning is my end” and closes “In my end is my beginning.” See Miss MacIntosh.
  • “Little boidies don’t have no tits”: The stone-deaf man was Young’s friend Howard Mitcham, a deaf painter in Greenwich Village. “He used to love to sing this, little boydies don’t have no tits. Little boydies don’t have no umbilical cords,” and “he knew that I was putting him in” (Marguerite Young, interview with Kay Bonetti, American Audio Prose Library, May 1983). For a magazine article on the deaf she interviewed deaf leaders in New York and heard the Lord’s Prayer in sign language at St. Mark’s (Marguerite Young, interview with Studs Terkel, WFMT radio, 1965). See The Stone Deaf Man, Deafness and Sign Language, and Marguerite Young on Her Craft.
  • “Man loves a silent woman”: In Ben Jonson’s comedy Epicoene, or The Silent Woman (1609), Morose, who cannot bear noise, marries a bride for her silence; once wed, she talks without stopping. See Love.
  • “A hand was arisen on the road and spelled out a name for me”: “That was a dream, actual dream of a deaf friend I knew that he solved. He thought he solved a mystery down in Louisiana by the hand speaking to him in a dream” (Marguerite Young, interview with Studs Terkel, WFMT radio, 1965). See The Stone Deaf Man.
  • “like an albatross”: The sailor who shot the albatross wears it around his neck: “Instead of the cross, the Albatross / About my neck was hung” (Coleridge, The Rime of the Ancient Mariner, 1798). See Romantic Poets and Birds.
  • “When the white girls turned their faces away from him”: This sudden inclusion of a Negro woman plays into the Magical Negro trope in cinema, television, and literature. The character often has no past but simply appears one day to help the white protagonist. They usually have some sort of vague magical power. The character is patient and wise, often dispensing various words of wisdom. Racism historians Francisco Bethencourt and John Beusterien trace the trope to the Spanish comedias de negros of the late fifteenth and early sixteenth centuries. The Magical Negro stereotype serves as a plot device to help the white protagonist get out of trouble, typically through helping the white character recognize his own faults, overcome them and teaching him to be a better person. Although the character may have magical powers, their magic is used to help and enlighten a white male character. (Wikipedia) See Society, Class, and Race.
  • “when Gabriel blew his horn”: “For the Lord himself shall descend from heaven with a shout, with the voice of the archangel, and with the trump of God” (1 Thessalonians 4:16, KJV); The Bible does not name the angel who sounds the last trump; the spiritual “Blow Your Trumpet, Gabriel,” printed in Slave Songs of the United States (1867), gives it to Gabriel. See Angels and Archangels and The Bible.
  • “Esther Longtree would be me”: When Vera says, “Esther Longtree would be me,” the line holds deep symbolic and thematic significance. This statement reflects Vera’s identification with Esther Longtree as a representation of a universal, enduring love and connection to all forms of life and experience, especially those that are broken, silent, or marginalized. Throughout the narrative, Vera contemplates profound themes of loss, silence, death, and the complexities of human love and perception. Esther Longtree emerges as a figure who embraces life and love despite her own hardships, embodying a kind of maternal, nurturing spirit who “loved us all and all things hurt or silent or broken or dead or living.” Vera’s final identification with Esther suggests a merging of identities, where Vera aspires to embody Esther’s compassion, endurance, and openness to the multiplicity of loves and sufferings that define human existence. Esther is not presented as a traditional role model in terms of success or societal status but rather as a symbol of the “average,” the “hidden,” and the dream-like qualities of life and love that transcend ordinary perception. Vera recognizes in Esther a power and enchantment beneath the surface that she had been too wrapped up in herself to fully perceive earlier. Esther represents a bridge between the ordinary and the extraordinary, the visible and the hidden, the living and the dreaming. By choosing Esther as her role model, Vera acknowledges the importance of embracing the “average” and the “hidden” aspects of life, which can “crumble into the most phantasmagoric dream that man has dreamed” and that “all the shining waters dream beyond the surface cold and bare.” Esther’s figure embodies the theme that through acceptance of loss, silence, and the unseen dimensions of existence, one can attain a deeper, more inclusive love and one that is not dependent on words or conventional communication but flows through “tongues of silence” and “all our loves.” Vera’s statement is not merely an adoption of Esther’s persona but a profound recognition of the values Esther symbolizes: compassion for the silent and broken, an embrace of the unseen dimensions of reality, and a love that transcends ordinary understanding. It marks a transcendence of Vera’s earlier isolation and mourning toward a more universal, interconnected understanding of love and existence and an acceptance of the dream-like, silent world that Esther inhabits and loves. Vera chooses Esther Longtree as her role model because Esther represents the enduring, silent love that encompasses all life’s contradictions, sufferings, and mysteries, and through this identification, Vera finds a way to affirm her own place in the continuum of love and loss that the novel so poignantly explores. See Esther Longtree and Vera Cartwheel.
    • Vera comes to terms with the other adults in her life:
    • Catherine: Vera’s view of her mother changes drastically by the end of the novel. While Vera used to see her mother as a beautiful lady sleeping in her swan boat, Vera comes to terms with her mother’s death and sees her mother as poor, as if she had been evicted from her house long before she died and wandered like a beggar through the streets. This is vastly different from the beautiful woman Vera once idolized. See Catherine Cartwheel.
    • Mr. Spitzer: Vera learns the truth about Mr. Spitzer’s identity, that he was Peron, not Joachim, and that his life had been a “celestial joke.” She understands his love for her mother, a love hidden and unfulfilled for many years. Vera sees him as someone who has lost everything and is living in the past. She sees that his grief over the loss of the old clam-digger “had seemed far greater than when my mother died.” See Joachim Spitzer.
    • Miss MacIntosh: Vera acknowledges that her love for Miss MacIntosh came late, only when she saw beyond the surface of her character. Vera realizes that Miss MacIntosh’s apparent mediocrity hid a phantasmagoric dream. Vera understands that despite Miss MacIntosh’s seemingly sensible nature, she was drawn to the ocean’s depths and eventually drowned. See Miss MacIntosh.
    • The final chapter marks a significant shift in Vera’s narrative. After recounting the stories of Esther Longtree, Miss MacIntosh, Mr. Spitzer and her mother, Vera turns her attention to her own experiences and a newfound love with a stone deaf man. This signals a move towards personal redemption and finding meaning amidst the chaos and illusions that permeate the novel.
    • Vera’s relationship with the stone deaf man highlights the theme of communication beyond conventional means. Since he cannot hear, their connection relies on visual cues, touch, and unspoken understanding. This echoes the novel’s broader exploration of how people connect despite their individual limitations and the illusory nature of reality.
    • The stone deaf man’s perspective offers a unique insight into the world of silence. He claims that all the waters of creation had smashed against his ears, leaving him stone deaf. He is bombarded by loud noises in his mind, but it is a silent world. Silence allows Vera and her lover to connect on a deeper level, transcending the superficiality of spoken words. The silence also seems to be a way for him to be closer to death.
    • The stone deaf man’s experiences also emphasize the importance of imagination. Having lost his hearing at fourteen, he lives in a world where sounds are memories or creations of his mind. This reinforces the novel’s recurring motif of the power of imagination to shape reality and find beauty in the face of adversity.
    • The relationship between Vera and the stone deaf man shows an acceptance for one another. He accepts that she can hear and she accepts that he cannot. This can be compared to the acceptance that Miss MacIntosh has for death and Vera has for her mother’s opium addiction.
    • The final chapter returns to the novel’s recurring themes.
    • The line between illusion and reality continues to blur in this chapter. The stone deaf man’s perception of the world is shaped by his unique sensory experience, highlighting the subjective nature of reality. He says that life is imaginary and this is an imaginary world.
    • Vera’s loss of everything but the string of pearls she wears symbolizes the shedding of material possessions and the pursuit of deeper meaning. Her relationship with the stone deaf man offers a path towards redemption, as she finds love and connection in unexpected circumstances.
    • The chapter explores different facets of love: maternal love, romantic love, and universal love. Vera’s love for the stone deaf man transcends physical limitations and societal norms, representing a pure and unconditional form of affection. She feels elegiac even before her love arrives.
    • The thought of death, especially Vera’s death, is brought up many times. The stone deaf man cannot hear the silent horn that Gabriel will blow.
    • Some concluding thoughts on the ending follow.
    • The ending remains ambiguous, leaving the reader to ponder the ultimate meaning of Vera’s journey. The novel does not offer easy answers but instead celebrates the complexities and contradictions of human existence.
    • The final chapter reinforces the novel’s celebration of the unconventional and the marginalized. Vera’s choice to embrace a relationship with a stone deaf man challenges societal expectations and highlights the beauty of finding love in unexpected places.
    • The final chapter suggests that the power of imagination and the capacity for love can transcend the limitations of reality. Despite the losses and disillusionments Vera has experienced, she finds solace and meaning in her connection with the stone deaf man, embracing a world where silence speaks volumes and love knows no bounds.
    • Vera and the stone deaf man plan to get married, and they plan to invite everyone. The stone deaf man believes that their procreation will provide life that can transcend his limits. There is hope because the next generation will lead the way.
  • “Owt to luntsch”: The last line was a friend’s idea, about ten years before Young finished: a painter told her to have Esther “hang up a sign in the restaurant window, out to lunch,” “And I said, I’ll do exactly that” (Marguerite Young, interview with Duncan MacDonald, Observation Point, 1965). See Esther Longtree.

chapter-67:
Chapter 67

← Chapter 66 · Home · Chapter 68 →

Summary

The bus reaches the Tavern at the end of its journey and cannot wedge into the space between a leaking milk truck and a hearse. Moses Hunnecker, drunk or so Vera thinks, curses old Doc, the mad Dr. Justice O’Leary, whose invisible ghost buggy, an old Ford full of the children Moses jeers at, he believes is taking the space. He sings scraps of old songs, boasts of the buzzards returning to Rush Creek, and threatens to scatter Doc all over the street. Vera, Madge, and Homer stay in their seats out of infinite weariness, for they have come home to no home. Madge laughs at a misery that is nothing new to her and likens them to people trapped in a crazy house of mirrors with no doors, and Homer wonders which door Jackie found.

Characters present

Moses Hunnecker · Justice O’Leary · Madge Capehorn · Homer Capehorn · Vera Cartwheel

Concepts present

Themes: Death and Mortality · Society, Class, and Race · Women, Gender, and Marriage

Allusions: Ecclesiastes · Music and Composers

Key passages

From the research

  • Moses curses and talks to old Doc, an unseen presence whom children shoot at with bean-shooters. Moses says old Doc should move his “old ghost buggy” to let the bus park, and lectures him on traffic rules: chalk lines, detour signs, slow turns.
  • Moses’s exhaustion is palpable as he drapes himself over the steering wheel, singing softly and lamenting his situation. Homer and Madge are caught in an “infinite weariness,” reluctant to leave the bus, suggesting a deeper existential fatigue or a reluctance to face reality. Moses’s talk of increasing the town’s population by three contrasts with old Doc’s apparent failure to contribute positively, adding layers of irony and social commentary.
  • Moses describes Old Doc’s “old ghost buggy” as an old Ford without essential parts, and accuses Doc of being dead “from the shoulders down.” Moses threatens to scatter “heathen Chinee” inside Doc’s buggy and warns of a “hot time in the old town tonight” with buzzards arriving.
  • Vera briefly contemplates that old Doc might be the undertaker in the hearse, blending the roles of doctor and death. Perhaps, she thinks, the undertaker was “the best doctor,” since after his work there could hardly be a complaint from the corpse.
  • The passengers’ rocking back and forth, Madge’s high, thin laughter, and Homer’s absent-mindedness contribute to a dreamlike, nightmarish atmosphere. Madge describes their stalled situation as being trapped in a crazy house with mirrored walls and no doors, evoking feelings of entrapment and confusion. Homer’s mention of “Jackie” and tuberculosis introduces a note of illness and impending loss, heightening the emotional tension.

Questions and observations

Reading closely

  • “Probably half the conversation in America occurs in this manner.” What kind of conversation does Vera mean?
  • “I’m increasing the population of this town by three, and that is more than you can ever bring.” Who are the three, and what is Moses boasting of?
  • “Perhaps the undertaker, cutting the jugular vein, was the best doctor.” What joke is Vera making?

Characters

  • Moses addresses “old Doc, a grizzled, unseen man.” Who is old Doc, and why can only Moses see him?
  • Madge laughs “at the bus-driver’s misery, Doc’s misery, which was nothing new to her.” Why is it nothing new to her?
  • “He was impatient as well as absent-minded, dreaming of a bride his wife might never know.” What does this tell us about Homer and Madge?

Connections

  • “After all, we had come home to no home.” How does this answer the journey that began in Chapter 1?
  • “The generations of buzzards do go on, honest to God.” Compare “One generation passeth away, and another generation cometh” (Ecclesiastes 1:4). What is Moses saying about old Doc?
  • “Jackie found the door,” Homer says. Which door does he mean?

Reflection

  • “There had to be some traffic rules.” Is Moses talking about traffic?
  • “The past was the past, though. Time waited for no man.” Does this chapter agree?
  • “You felt along the glass, but you did not know how to get out, which mirror was a door.” When has life felt like that?

Research: Characters

Moses Hunnecker, the bus-driver

  • A long-haired, possibly drunk or deeply weary man who curses and talks aloud to “old Doc,” an unseen figure. He embodies frustration, loneliness, and a struggle against an unyielding obstacle.

Old Doc, Dr. Justice O’Leary

  • Old Doc is Dr. Justice O’Leary, the mad old doctor whose imaginary patients are “those pregnant women who were dead and whom old Doc seemed to think were living again.” Only Moses sees him here.
  • Moses sees him in an old “ghost buggy” (car), who occupies a parking space and seems to symbolize obstruction, death, or the past. As a doctor he may represent death or stagnation.

Madge

  • Laughs breathlessly at Moses’s misery, indicating a detachment or acceptance of the surreal situation.

Homer

  • Impatient and absent-minded, dreaming of a bride his wife might never know.

Vera

  • Observes and reflects on the scene, feeling tired and dreamlike.

Research: Themes

  • Loneliness and Communication with the Unseen: Moses talks to old Doc, who is unseen and possibly a ghost or symbolic figure. This “conversation” reflects the human need to vent frustration and to communicate even when no one is listening or present. It highlights isolation and the internal battles people face.
  • The Struggle Between Life and Death: Old Doc’s “ghost buggy” and the hearse symbolize death or the past, while the bus and its passengers represent life moving forward. Moses’s frustration in trying to park reflects the tension between these forces, with death obstructing the path of life.
  • Rules and Order vs Chaos: Moses imagines traffic rules (chalk lines, detours, traffic lights) as metaphors for social order and fairness. The chaotic reality, with obstacles like old Doc’s ghost buggy, represents life’s unpredictability and unfairness.
  • Existential Weariness and Dreamlike Reality: Vera and passengers feel an “infinite weariness,” and the situation is likened to being stuck on a ferris wheel or in a crazy house with mirrored walls and no exits. This surreal imagery evokes the feeling of being trapped in life’s endless struggles and the confusion about how to move forward.
  • The Passage of Time and Memory: Moses references the past (“the past was the past”) and the inevitability of time moving on. Old Doc’s presence and the image of buzzards returning evoke decay and the cyclical nature of life and death.

Research: Symbols and Imagery

  • Moses pleads repeatedly with Doc to move over, symbolizing the desire for obstacles (death, the past, inertia) to yield to life and progress.
  • “I can’t give you anything but love, baby,” sung by Moses, contrasts the harshness of his situation with a tender expression, perhaps hinting at the human capacity for care amid struggle.
  • Moses’s comment about the passengers in old Doc’s buggy suggests confusion or denial about the nature of life, lineage, or reality. “They look like pigs to me one minute and birds the next,” he says. “They don’t look like their mama.”
  • It’s “like being stalled on a ferris wheel at the top of the sky.” Madge’s description captures the surreal, trapped feeling of the moment.

Further notes from the text

  • The bus tries to wedge into the space between a milk truck leaking from its cans and a hearse, birth and death on either side of the passengers. See Comedy in Chapter 67.
  • Moses’s cursing of old Doc becomes a comic theory of marriage and traffic: perhaps there should be a chalk line down the middle of every bed, with signs for detours, narrow shoulders, and steep inclines, or a man might be ditched.
  • He boasts that he is bringing in real business, increasing the population of the town by three, more than Doc can say, and calls Doc’s car an old ghost buggy that could be parked on a postage stamp.
  • His report of the buzzards that have staged a return and brought their relatives, eighty or ninety seen over Rush Creek at sundown, ends with a cheerful jab: the generations of buzzards go on.
  • Vera says the passengers stay in their seats out of infinite weariness: “we had come home to no home,” and perhaps they wished to prolong the journey.
  • Madge’s laughter is high and thin, at the driver’s misery and Doc’s, while Homer dreams of a bride his wife might never know. Vera expects a bird to fly out of the bus-driver’s beard.

Research: Resources

  • “the pregnant girl with the bird upon her hat”: Hats trimmed with whole birds were the fashion around 1900. In 1896 two Boston women, Harriet Hemenway and Minna Hall, founded the Massachusetts Audubon Society to stop the slaughter of birds for the plumage trade, and the federal Lacey Act of 1900 and the Migratory Bird Treaty of 1918 followed. See Madge Capehorn and Women, Gender, and Marriage.
  • “He addressed old Doc, a grizzled, unseen man”: Old Doc is Dr. Justice O’Leary. See Justice O’Leary.
  • “Roosevelt in the White House”: There were two Roosevelt presidents, Theodore and Franklin D. Since Miss MacIntosh talked about not seeing the Golden Gate Bridge which was built in the 1930s it is a good guess and since Moses hates Democrats, he is probably talking about Franklin D. Roosevelt. In Chapter 5 Moses swore that as long as the Democrats were running the country, he would not cut his hair. See the Chapter 5 resources. He was the President of the US from 1933 until his death in April 1945, the only president elected four times.
  • “Move over, Doc”: See Moses Hunnecker.
  • “cretin idiots”: “Cretin” first named people with congenital iodine deficiency, from an Alpine French word for “Christian,” that is, a fellow human being; “water on their brains” is hydrocephalus. Both became insults.
  • “I can’t give you anything but love, baby”: I Can’t Give You Anything But Love, Baby is an American song from 1928. The idea behind the song came during a stroll Fields and McHugh were taking one evening down Fifth Avenue. They saw a young couple window-shopping at Tiffany’s. McHugh and Fields understood that the couple could not afford to buy jewelry from Tiffany’s. They heard the man say, “Gee, honey, I’d like to get you a sparkler like that, but right now, I can’t give you nothin’ but love!” Within an hour McHugh and Fields came up with the song. (Wikipedia) The lyricist was Dorothy Fields, one of the first women to succeed as a Broadway and Hollywood songwriter, with Jimmy McHugh; the song was introduced in the all-Black revue Blackbirds of 1928. See Music and Composers and Women, Gender, and Marriage.
  • “After all, we had come home to no home”: Compare Thomas Wolfe’s novel You Can’t Go Home Again (1940).
  • “How many rabbit tests old Doc had run”: In the Friedman test (1931), a woman’s urine was injected into a female rabbit, whose ovaries were examined a few days later for signs of pregnancy. The rabbit was killed either way, so “the rabbit died” was never the sign. See Women, Gender, and Marriage.
  • “Time waited for no man”: The proverb “Time and tide wait for no man” is centuries old in English.
  • “the one-hoss shay, she ain’t what she used to was”: Moses mixes Holmes’s “One-Hoss Shay” with the folk song “The Old Gray Mare,” who “ain’t what she used to be.”
    • The poem is Oliver Wendell Holmes’s “The Deacon’s Masterpiece; or, The Wonderful One-Hoss Shay” (1858). In the poem, a deacon laments the fact that carriages break down due to weakness at one place or another. The carriages were usually built locally by enterprising villagers. The deacon deduces that if he were to build a one hoss shay using the finest materials from top to bottom, it would have no weaknesses and would therefore endure forever. So the deacon decides to build the most reliable one hoss shay there ever could logically be, in accordance with the Puritan principles that critics of the era believed Oliver Wendell Holmes to be satirizing. Every part of it is equally as strong as every other part. This marvel of logical construction lasts and lasts through a parade of decades and deacons, providing perfect service all the while. But as Holmes says, logic is logic, and eventually it catches up to the shay. Exactly one hundred years to the day that the deacon finished it, the whole thing collapses in a heap of particulates, leaving the parson who was driving it sitting on a rock. (Wikipedia)
  • “Sweet Mary O’Grady”: Moses sings Sweet Mary O’Grady but the famous song is called Sweet Rosie O’Grady. “Sweet Rosie O’Grady” (1896) was written by Maude Nugent, a vaudeville singer, and “down by the old mill stream where I first met you” is from Tell Taylor’s “Down by the Old Mill Stream” (1910); Moses runs the two together. See Music and Composers and Women, Gender, and Marriage.
  • “Why did a doctor have to go on a doctor’s holiday?”: A pun from a busman: a busman’s holiday is a day off spent doing what one does at work.
  • “the junk that was going to Japan”: Through the 1930s the United States sold Japan great amounts of scrap iron and steel, which went into the war in China, until Roosevelt embargoed scrap exports in October 1940. Protesters warned that the junk would come back as bombs.
    • The U.S. sent significant goods and aid to Japan primarily during the post-WWII Occupation (1945-1952) through massive aid packages for reconstruction, and earlier, U.S. trade with Japan began after Commodore Matthew Perry forced open ports in 1853, leading to regular shipments of goods and commodities, with Japan importing more U.S. products than exporting to the U.S. until the mid-1960s.
  • “a case where an invulnerable force met with an invulnerable obstacle”: The old paradox asks what happens when an irresistible force meets an immovable object.
  • “These heathen Chinee”: “The Heathen Chinee” was the popular name of Bret Harte’s poem “Plain Language from Truthful James” (1870). Harte meant to mock the white cardsharps who cheat a Chinese player, but the phrase became an anti-Chinese slur, sung and shouted during the agitation that led to the Chinese Exclusion Act of 1882. See Society, Class, and Race.
    • “A Chinaman’s chance” meant no chance at all. Chinese workers were given the most dangerous work on the railroads and in the mines, and in People v. Hall (1854) the California Supreme Court ruled that a Chinese witness could not testify against a white man. See Society, Class, and Race.
  • “There was going to be a hot time in the old town tonight”: “There’ll Be a Hot Time in the Old Town Tonight” (1896), by Theodore Metz and Joe Hayden, became the marching song of Theodore Roosevelt’s Rough Riders in 1898. See Music and Composers.
  • “They have staged a return and have brought their relatives with them”: Turkey vultures, called buzzards in America, leave the northern states for the winter and return each spring; Hinckley, Ohio, has celebrated their return every March since 1957.
  • “Be a good Boy Scout, Doc”: The Boy Scouts of America, founded in 1910, pledged a good turn daily.
  • “The generations of buzzards do go on”: “One generation passeth away, and another generation cometh: but the earth abideth for ever” (Ecclesiastes 1:4, KJV). See Ecclesiastes.
  • “cutting the jugular vein”: In arterial embalming, fluid is pumped in through an artery, usually the carotid, while the blood is drained out through the jugular vein. See Death and Mortality.
  • “an old Ford with black canvas curtains flapping”: The Ford Model T (1908-1927) was built by the millions; its open touring cars kept out the rain with side curtains of black canvas.
  • “a bird would fly out of the bus-driver’s beard”: Compare Edward Lear’s limerick (1846): “There was an Old Man with a beard, / Who said, ‘It is just as I feared! / Two Owls and a Hen, / Four Larks and a Wren, / Have all built their nests in my beard!’” See Moses Hunnecker.
  • “It was like being stalled on a ferris wheel at the top of the sky”: George Ferris built the first Ferris wheel for the World’s Columbian Exposition in Chicago in 1893.
  • “Jackie found the door”: See Jacqueline White. Before streptomycin came into use after 1944, tuberculosis was the leading killer of young adults, and its patients were sent away to sanatoriums for months or years.

Vocabulary

Bean-shooter
A peashooter or slingshot.
Carapaced
Covered with a hard shell, like a beetle or a turtle.
Casket
A small, often ornate box for jewels or valuables. In American usage, also a coffin, so Young’s “casket containing no jewel” carries both meanings.
Corset
A close-fitting undergarment, stiffened with whalebone or steel and laced tight, worn to shape the waist.
Cretin
A person stunted in body and mind by a lack of iodine from birth; later an insult.
Grandiose
Grand in an exaggerated, self-important way.
Grizzled
Streaked with grey.
Harangue
To lecture loudly and at length.
Invulnerable
Unable to be wounded or harmed.
Jugular
The great vein of the neck.
Luna moth
A large pale green moth of North America with long tails on its hind wings.
Maudlin
Tearfully sentimental, as a drunk can be.
Melodiously
Tunefully.
Monopoly
Sole possession or control of something.
Seesaw
To move up and down or back and forth.
Shay
A light, one-horse carriage; a chaise.
Testimonial
A formal statement given as evidence or proof of something.
Thatched
Covered with straw or reeds, like a roof; of hair, thick and shaggy.
Transfusion
The transfer of blood into a person’s veins.

Chapter 29

← Chapter 28 · Home · Chapter 30 →

Summary

Mr. Spitzer speaks at length about butterflies. He compares the difficulty of telling butterfly from moth to telling brother from brother, and happiness from sorrow. He names species by the hundreds and dwells on the butterfly as psyche, the soul. He gives God many names, from the True Vine to the King of Light “opposed… by the necessary King of Darkness,” and counts the gods who visit Catherine’s bedroom. He describes Peron’s funeral, crowded with gamblers and merry mourners, and the one person who saw his grief, an old lamplighter weeping on a street corner. He wonders whether a sock darned again and again until no original thread remains is still the same sock. The chapter ends with him as a dark atheist who knows more of the life beyond the grave than of this one.

Characters present

Joachim Spitzer · Peron Spitzer · Catherine Cartwheel · Vera Cartwheel · Mr. Chandelier · The Black Coachman

Concepts present

Themes: Death and Mortality · Faith, God, and the Supernatural · Grief, Loss, and Mourning · Identity and the Self · Illusion and Reality · Memory and the Past

Symbols: Angels, Devils, and Myth · Birds · Butterflies and Moths · Lamps, Candles, and Light · Mirrors and Reflections · Music and Instruments · Silence and Deafness · Snow, Ice, and Winter · The Bus and the Journey · Twins and Doubles

Philosophy: Aristotle · Astrology, Alchemy, and Esoterica · Augustine and Christian Theology · Buddhism · Descartes and Dualism · Hinduism · Nietzsche · Plato and Platonism · Pythagoras and the Music of the Spheres · Stoicism

Allusions: American Writers · Ancient Egypt · Angels and Archangels · Astronomy · Dante · Deafness and Sign Language · Exploration and the Poles · Fairy Tales and Folklore · Gambling and Playing Cards · Genesis · Greek Mythology · Homer’s Epics · Judaism · Music and Composers · Napoleon and Wellington · Revelation and the Apocalypse · Romantic Poets · Shakespeare · The Bible · The Book of Job

Key passages

From the research

  • The chapter opens by discussing the difficulty of distinguishing butterflies from moths, creatures that exist on a boundary line, symbolic of the blurred lines between happiness and sorrow, day and night, life and death.
  • Mr. Spitzer’s observations on butterfly and moth behavior are presented as metaphors for life’s uncertainties.
  • The mystery of night-flying butterflies and oceanic migrations suggests the theme of wandering souls or psyches, with butterflies representing spiritual voyagers seeking reunion with immortal love.
  • The transformation of the caterpillar into the chrysalis and then the butterfly is described with deep symbolism: death and rebirth, the chrysalis as a shroud or mummy, and the butterfly as an epitome of immortality within mortality.
  • The enduring and recurring memories of butterflies in Mr. Spitzer’s mind serve as a metaphor for memory, identity, and the persistence of the soul beyond physical death.
  • The chapter elaborates on the spectacular colors of butterflies, which are illusions created by light on scales, not pigmentation, paralleling the illusory nature of life and perception.
  • The idea that male butterflies emit perfumes to attract scentless females introduces a sensual, almost spiritual dimension to the butterfly’s existence, with Mr. Spitzer even imagining he can smell these perfumes as extensions of his own thoughts or memories.
  • Mr. Spitzer reflects on the unknowability of life beyond death, the multiplicity of gods and spirits, and the possibility that butterflies may have originated beyond Earth, highlighting the vast unknown and the limits of human reason.
  • The metaphor of the “bipart soul” and the questioning of selfhood and identity are central to the chapter’s existential inquiries. Who really owns a soul, and can one be alive and dead simultaneously?
  • The death of Mr. Spitzer’s brother Peron and the impact of that loss loom large. The chapter contrasts Peron’s early death and wild life with Joachim’s (Mr. Spitzer’s) long survival marked by grief, memory, and the pursuit of meaning through butterflies.
  • The funeral scene with its bizarre, lively crowd reflects the complexities of social death and memory.
  • Mr. Spitzer’s mental state and his ongoing internal struggle with grief and identity are woven through the reflections on butterflies and memory.
  • Despite his age and diminished faculties, Mr. Spitzer retains and even deepens his knowledge of butterflies, from common species to exotic and mythical varieties, associating them with gods, myths, and celestial bodies.
  • The chapter gives a sense of the butterfly as a cosmic and spiritual symbol, embodying life’s fragility and transcendence.
  • The analogy of Mr. Spitzer’s patched socks and tattered coat illustrates the human condition of decay and endurance, the fragility of identity, and the process of continual repair and reinvention.
  • The regal butterflies, despite their vulnerability, symbolize dignity and persistence amid mortality.

Questions and observations

Reading closely

  • “Just as it might at times be difficult to distinguish between brother and brother.” Why does the chapter begin with butterflies and moths?
  • “Yet butterflies were colorless.” What does that discovery mean to a man who doubts his own reality?
  • Are the darned socks “new socks or old”?

Characters

  • Joachim played Peron’s role to break off Peron’s affairs. What did it cost him to be taken for his brother?
  • At the funeral, only an old lamplighter saw his grief. Why a lamplighter?
  • “This dark atheist, this believer in nothing” says no one can “speak with greater authority than he of the life beyond the grave.” How can both be true?

Connections

  • The butterflies are “wandering psyches” here. In Chapter 28, the butterfly was “as identical to the flower as twin to twin.” How has the image grown?
  • Catherine’s gods include “the goddess with the head of a cat,” and Chapter 26 had the Siamese cats eating from dishes “fit for the dead pharaohs.” What does Egypt mean in this house?
  • Catherine the Great’s amethyst bed returns from Chapter 27. What do the beds of the famous dead share?

Reflection

  • Is happiness always “tinctured by sorrow”?
  • If every thread is replaced, are you the same person?
  • Can a grief be too great to be seen?

Research: Characters

Joachim Spitzer (Peron’s twin brother, who allegedly lived)

  • An old, reflective lawyer and butterfly collector.
  • He embodies melancholy, wisdom, and the quest for understanding life through the metaphor of butterflies.
  • His thoughts are clouded by grief and age, yet his butterfly knowledge grows even in mental decline.
  • His grief after his brother’s death is profound and almost hidden, and it shapes his worldview.
  • He played “Peron’s role” as his brother’s “reluctant go-between,” breaking off Peron’s affairs by seeming to be him.
  • At the funeral he seemed serene, “strange as the phoenix,” but he was “utterly devastated,” and only an old lamplighter saw his tears.
  • He calls himself “this dark atheist, this believer in nothing.”
  • He gave up knitting socks for himself and Peron, for fear of “the ribbing he would get,” and apologizes for the pun.

Peron Spitzer (Joachim’s twin brother, allegedly dead by suicide)

  • A mysterious, volatile figure who lived a fragmented life.
  • His death profoundly impacts Mr. Spitzer, whose mourning colors his worldview.
  • Peron’s character contrasts with Mr. Spitzer’s logical nature; he is seen as a greater mystery.
  • His funeral drew “the merriest mourners who ever were”: dice shooters, vaudeville stars, mountebanks, and “ruined gamblers.”
  • He “airily dismissed Joachim from his mind when a purpose had been served” and would have shown “not a spark of gratitude.”
  • His coffin “had been sealed, and no one had looked upon his dead brother’s shattered face.”

Catherine Cartwheel (Vera’s mother)

  • She believes herself “both living and dead, this animated and bejeweled corpse,” and imagines the migratory beds of the famous dead drifting to her.
  • She is imagined alongside Mr. Spitzer’s butterfly reflections, creating a shared atmosphere of mystery.
  • She “would spend hours, years talking to someone who was not there.”

Research: Themes

Butterflies as Symbols of the Soul and Immortality

See: Death and Mortality · Butterflies and Moths

  • Butterflies represent the psyche or soul, echoing the Greek notion where “psyche” means both soul and butterfly.
  • They symbolize transformation, immortality, and the elusive nature of life and death.
  • Despite their mortality, butterflies are portrayed as perfect images of immortality, transcending their ephemeral physical existence.

The Boundary Between Life and Death

See: Death and Mortality

  • The novel explores the liminal space between life and death through Mr. Spitzer’s reflections.
  • His own existence is depicted as an oscillation between these states, likened to butterflies fluttering between light and darkness.
  • The chapter meditates on memory, loss, and the persistence of the soul or consciousness beyond physical death.

Memory, Loss, and Mourning

See: Memory and the Past · Grief, Loss, and Mourning

  • Mr. Spitzer mourns his dead brother Peron, whose life was full of mystery and volatility.
  • His butterfly memories serve as a means to keep his brother’s essence alive, reflecting the human struggle to grasp and preserve fleeting moments.
  • The grief is profound yet hidden, affecting Mr. Spitzer’s mental state deeply.

The Mystery of Origin and Existence

See: Faith, God, and the Supernatural

  • The chapter speculates on the origins of butterflies and existence itself.
  • Questions arise about whether butterflies predate time and space or came from cosmic or otherworldly realms.
  • This reflects broader metaphysical inquiry into creation, existence, and the nature of the divine.

The Role of God and the Divine

See: Faith, God, and the Supernatural · Augustine and Christian Theology

  • Mr. Spitzer contemplates the nature of God, presenting a multifaceted and paradoxical image of divinity.
  • God is the King of Light, “opposed… by the necessary King of Darkness,” who must “create… bless, absolve, curse, forgive,” and is elusive beyond human comprehension.
  • The divine is intertwined with the symbolism of butterflies and the cosmic order.

Ephemeral Beauty and the Illusion of Permanence

See: Illusion and Reality

  • Butterfly colors are not from pigmentation but the play of light on scales, symbolizing the illusory nature of beauty and permanence.
  • Life’s fleeting moments are compared to bubbles: transient, yet significant.

Butterflies

Winter and Hibernation

Music and Silent Music

On Butterfly and Moth Distinctions and Flight Times (Day versus Night)

Butterflies as Psyche and Their Cosmic Journeys

Mr. Spitzer’s Butterfly Collection as Memory and Identity

See: Butterflies and Moths

Reflections on God and Creation

See: Mirrors and Reflections · Faith, God, and the Supernatural

Butterfly Names and Mythological Associations

See: Butterflies and Moths · Angels, Devils, and Myth

  • Butterflies named after gods (Aphrodite, Apollo, Morpheus, Leto), mythological figures (Io, Atlas), and symbolic concepts.

The Illusion of Reality

See: Illusion and Reality

Multiplicity of the Soul
