Research: Resources

  • “between the ecstasy of happiness and that of sorrow”: In philosophy, happiness and sorrow are intertwined, with sorrow often seen as a necessary component for experiencing the depth of joy and vice versa rather than as simple opposites. It can be viewed in a number of ways: a dialectical relationship (yin and yang-complementary forces where one cannot exist without the other); the contrast highlights the value of positive experiences; a catalyst for growth, introspection, and a deeper understanding of life’s complexities. Philosophical perspectives are found in Buddhism, Christianity, Hinduism, Stoicism, Utilitarianism, Hedonism, Life Satisfaction Theory. Plato and Aristotle’s eudaimonia where flourishing and well-being are achieved by living a virtuous life, not simply experiencing happiness. Nirvana is a state of liberation from suffering and the cycle of rebirth. Equanimity is the ability to remain calm and balanced in the face of both pleasure and pain. Mr. Spitzer finds it as hard to tell butterfly from moth as “to distinguish between brother and brother or between the ecstasy of happiness and that of sorrow,” for “Seldom did happiness and sorrow occur in pure and disrelated states.” See Aristotle, Plato and Platonism, Buddhism, Hinduism, and Stoicism.
  • “a butterfly performed its peregrinations by day”: Butterflies are generally active during the day and are brightly colored.
    • Moths are generally active at night and have more muted colors.
  • “when the trumpets of Jericho were blowing in the windy gardens”: Trumpets of Jericho refers to Joshua 6:1-27 in the Bible. The walls of Jericho fell after the Israelites marched around the city walls once a day for six days and seven times on the seventh day and blew their trumpets. Here the “trumpets” are also flowers blowing in the garden. See The Bible.
  • “clouds of luna moths with moons of passage upon their wings”: Luna moths are found in North America and are commonly known as giant silk moths.
  • “clouds of migratory butterflies had sometimes been observed far out at sea”: Butterflies and moths migrate on all continents except Antarctica. They do not like water or mountains but butterflies have been found across an ocean from where they are normally found and scientists do not know exactly how.
  • “According to the Greek, the butterfly was psyche”: Butterflies feature prominently in mythology across various cultures. They often symbolize the soul, death, rebirth and transformation and, to some, good luck and messengers from the spirit world. Psyche, in Greek mythology a goddess of the soul, is often depicted with butterfly wings, symbolizing her connection to the soul and transformation. See Greek Mythology, Fairy Tales and Folklore, and the Chapter 28 resources.
    • Moths have a rich history in folklore and mythology and are often associated with death, the afterlife, and even messengers from the spirit world as well as good fortune and cleansing. Black moths can symbolize mortality, divinity, and universal secrets. White moths can symbolize death or ill wishes. Brown moths symbolize the need for a purification and the slow, unseen destruction of things. Moths in Matthew 6:19-21 are something that destroys treasures on earth so treasures in heaven should be created instead.
    • Butterflies and moths are considered symbols of the soul. In Europe they are symbols of the dead or the newly dead. In Jacobite symbolism they are rebirth and renewal or the ‘return of the soul.’
  • “achieving immortality within the logic of mortality”: Immortality within the framework of mortality is a philosophical exploration of extending life, potentially indefinitely, while acknowledging the inherent limitations of our biological existence. Collective immortality suggests that while individuals are mortal, their legacy and impact on others can create a form of enduring existence. Some argue that immortality could strip life of its meaning and urgency, while others believe it could offer an opportunity for greater exploration and purpose. Exploring the concept of death and its implications for our understanding of life and existence is central to the discussion of immortality. Mortality can also be a source of meaning and value, as it can make experiences more precious and urgent. Mr. Spitzer, the surviving twin, knows that his brother will never return, “for the dead did not return except in our thoughts,” so that immortality may lie in memory. The “immortal invalid” and the “deathless dead” are beings neither fully alive nor fully dead.
  • “as if there were a frog in his throat”: Nietzsche’s frog is a way to metaphorically understand perspective and belief. Nietzsche believed that all knowledge and values are perspectival, meaning they are shaped by our individual experiences and values. Nietzsche himself borrowed the painters’ term: values may be seen “perhaps from below, ‘frog perspectives,’ as it were” (Beyond Good and Evil, 1886, §2, trans. Helen Zimmern). This is reflected in the idea of a “frog’s perspective,” which can be understood as a belief system that is constantly changing and shifting. The term “frog’s perspective” can also be associated with the idea of narrow-mindedness or being unable to see the bigger picture. Another metaphorical expression, “swallowing the frog” can refer to confronting unpleasant realities or difficult emotions in order to grow or achieve a higher level of understanding. This aligns with Nietzsche’s emphasis on confronting difficult truths and embracing the “unpleasantness” of life. The frog can also symbolize a sense of “being in the muck,” referring to the lower aspects of oneself that need to be overcome in order to reach a higher level of awareness. Frogs appear symbolically connected to themes of life, death, transformation, and communication beyond ordinary human experience. Mr. Spitzer encounters a mute man who uses a frog as a musical instrument, training it to croak and even mimic human speech. The mute grieves the frog’s death, and Mr. Spitzer mourns it as a loss greater than many others. Young’s frog is closer to fragility and loss than to Nietzsche’s perspectives. See Nietzsche.
  • “many mementoes of golden coppers dazzling as sunlight and white admirals”: Golden copper is a small butterfly found in Greece and Asia Minor.
    • White Admiral butterfly is found in Europe (Limenitis camilla) and North America (Limenitis arthemis), and the American one is studied for its evolution of mimicry where the butterfly evolves to resemble another organism.
  • “speckled woods and pearl crescents and mountain ringlets”: The Speckled Wood (Pararge aegeria) and Mountain Ringlet (Erebia epiphron) are European. The Pearl Crescent (Phyciodes tharos) is North American.
  • “black-bordered white handkerchief which he had worn in his breast pocket over his heart ever since his brother’s death”: Black borders on handkerchiefs and letter paper marked mourning. The wider the border, the closer the loss. See Grief, Loss, and Mourning.
  • “The old caterpillar sleeping like the infant Moses in his cradle among the bulrushes”: “She took for him an ark of bulrushes… and laid it in the flags by the river’s brink” (Exodus 2:3). See The Bible.
  • “pearly eyes and eyed browns”: The Northern Pearly-eye and the Eyed Brown, butterflies of North American woods and marshes.
  • “before the sleeping coachman driving his sleeping horses in the long avenue”: The coachman and horses of Chapter 14. See The Black Coachman and the Chapter 14 resources.
  • “the beautiful mourning cloak butterfly hibernating in a hollow tree trunk”: Mourning Cloak butterfly is found across North America and Eurasia, where the English call it the Camberwell Beauty. It lives eleven to twelve months.
    • Some species of adult butterflies do hibernate through the winter.
  • “He remembered many meadow browns”: The Meadow brown butterfly is found in Europe, Asia and North Africa.
  • “the Essex skippers and the Lulworth skippers”: Essex and Lulworth skipper are European butterflies.
    • Chalkhill blue butterflies are found in Eurasia and North Africa.
    • Orange tips are found in Europe and Asia.
    • Large browns (Large wall brown butterfly) are found in Europe and Asia Minor.
    • Bath whites are found in Europe.
    • Pale veined marble butterflies may be the Marbled White (Melanargia galathea), which is found in Europe, not western North America.
    • Pale clouded yellows are found in Europe and Asia.
    • Purple hairstreaks: the Purple Hairstreak (Favonius quercus) is a European butterfly of oak woods.
    • Black hairstreaks are found in Europe and the Far East.
    • White mountain butterflies are only found in the Presidential Zone of the White Mountain National Forest in New Hampshire.
    • Arctic satyrs are found in North America.
    • Monarchs are found in North America and are famous for their multi-generational, long migration from the north to the south, including into Mexico.
  • “regal viceroys and vicereines and small gate-keepers”: The Viceroy (Limenitis archippus) mimics the Monarch, and the Gatekeeper (Pyronia tithonus) haunts the gates and hedgerows of Europe.
    • Red-spotted purples: the Red-spotted Purple is the same species as North America’s White Admiral, Limenitis arthemis.
  • “brilliance as of the jewels of Aaron’s breastplate, colors like Japheth’s enlarged opals”: Aaron’s breastplate (Priestly breastplate) was a sacred breastplate worn by the high priest of the Israelites. Its twelve stones stood for the twelve tribes (Exodus 28:15-21). See The Bible and Genesis.
    • Japheth is one of the three sons of Noah in the Book of Genesis.
    • Joseph’s coat of many colors is from Genesis 37:3 where his father gave him a coat of many colors.
  • “Yet butterflies were colorless”: Butterflies have two ways to display the color of their wings: ordinary and structural. The ordinary color comes from normal chemical pigments that absorb certain wavelengths of light and reflect others. Structural color stems from the specific structure of the butterflies’ wings and explains why some of a butterfly’s colors seem to shift and appear so intense. It happens when light passes through a transparent, multilayered surface and is reflected more than once. The multiple reflections compound one another and intensify colors.
    • Collectively our brain makes up colors to help humans find food and avoid danger.
  • “some of the male butterflies were perfumed”: Both male and female butterflies use pheromones to communicate during the breeding cycle. Many males carry androconia, scent scales, on their wings.
  • “when the heavenly harmonies were established on a surer foundation”: The music of the spheres. See Pythagoras and the Music of the Spheres and the Chapter 26 resources.
  • “when he was divested of desire”: To Buddhists desire is the craving for worldly pleasure, material objects and immortality. Since all these things can never be attained they only lead to suffering. See Buddhism.
  • “to shuffle off these mortal coils”: “When we have shuffled off this mortal coil” (Hamlet 3.1). See Shakespeare and the Chapter 26 resources.
  • “the purple pharaohs in their swan boats, the Irish poets wrapped in bands of fog”: The swan boats are from Chapters 2 and 25. The fog-wrapped Irish poets recall Yeats’s The Celtic Twilight (1893). See the Chapter 25 resources.
  • “the creature of mystical metamorphosis, of many transfigurations and conversions”: Mystical Metamorphosis generally refers to a transformative process that involves a shift or change, often with a mystical or spiritual element. It can be applied to various contexts, including artistic creations, self-discovery, and the transformative nature of life itself. The term can evoke the natural process of metamorphosis, like that of a caterpillar transforming into a butterfly, which is seen as a symbol of change and transformation. It can also be used to describe the mystical journey of self-discovery and spiritual growth.
    • Transfiguration refers to a significant transformation, often involving a shift in understanding, perspective, or even a change in one’s self or the world. In the Gospels Jesus “was transfigured before them: and his face did shine as the sun, and his raiment was white as the light” (Matthew 17:2). Nietzsche viewed transfiguration as an aesthetic process, where individuals can transform their brokenness and misfortune into a form of artistic creation and redemption, calling philosophy itself an art of transfiguration (The Gay Science, preface to the second edition, 1887, §3).
    • The philosophy of conversion explores the concept of a significant and transformative change, often in belief, behavior, or identity. It can be viewed within religious, philosophical, and psychological contexts, examining the nature of this change, its motivations, and its implications for individuals and societies. Religious conversion takes different forms in Christianity, Judaism, and Islam; Hinduism has no formal conversion process. In Plato’s philosophy, the concept of conversion is represented in the allegory of the cave, where a prisoner’s awakening involves turning away from shadows and towards the light of truth. Philosophical conversion can also refer to an existential change in the individual, adopting new moral standards or making a fundamental shift in their understanding of reality. Moral conversion involves a change in an individual’s moral beliefs, values, and actions, often driven by a critical self-reflection and a new understanding of moral principles. Philosophers like Descartes and Husserl are considered to have undergone a form of philosophical conversion in their pursuit of universal science and phenomenology, respectively.
  • “the expanding crystals of Mr. Chandelier”: Catherine’s companion of the candles. See Mr. Chandelier.
  • “a nine days’ wonder at the most”: A proverb in Chaucer: “eek wonder last but nyne nyght” (Troilus and Criseyde, c. 1385).
  • “eyes like the eyes of Argus”: Argus Panoptes was a many-eyed giant in Greek mythology who watched over a heifer-nymph Io. Hera set Argus to guard Io, and after Hermes killed him she set his hundred eyes in the peacock’s tail (Ovid, Metamorphoses 1). Young makes the same link in Chapter 5: “eyes like the eyes of Argus if he had lived, full of eyes like the peacock’s burning tail.” See Greek Mythology.
    • Eyespot mimicry in butterflies is thought to have evolved in order for them to evade predators.
  • “those who could hear the grass grow, those who needed less sleep than a bird”: Heimdall, watchman of the Norse gods, “needs less sleep than a bird” and “hears the grass grow on the earth” (Snorri Sturluson, Prose Edda, c. 1220).
  • “the Happy Isles, the Fortunate Isles, the Isles of the Blessed”: The list runs from the Happy Isles to Aldebaran, Venus, the Garden of the Hesperides, the third and seventh heavens, Valhalla, Nirvana, and the happy hunting grounds, and ends: “God was not God in Himself, Mr. Spitzer believed, but in these pitiful images of God.” See Judaism, Buddhism, Hinduism, and Astronomy.
    • The Happy Isles are the Isles of the Blessed, as in Tennyson’s “Ulysses” (1842): “It may be we shall touch the Happy Isles.”
    • Fortunate Isles or Isles of the Blessed are semi-legendary islands in the Atlantic Ocean in Greek mythology.
    • Garden of the Hesperides is Hera’s orchard where the golden apples grow.
    • The third heaven in Judaism, Islam, Church of the Latter Day Saints and early Christianity is a division of heaven in religious cosmology as either the abode of God or a lower level of paradise (one of seven). (Wikipedia) Paul was “caught up to the third heaven” (2 Corinthians 12:2).
    • The seventh heaven is one of the seven heavens found in various religious and mythological cosmologies.
    • Valhalla in Norse mythology is the majestic hall located in Asgard and ruled by Odin.
    • Nirvana is a concept in Indian religions that is a state of perfect quietude, freedom, highest happiness, liberation from worldly attachment, suffering and an end to existence.
    • The happy hunting grounds is a concept of the after-life attributed to Native Americans in the US and was most likely made up by US settlers.
    • The stars and planets are rich metaphors for the complexity and mystery of life, death, and the soul’s journey. They embody the fluid boundaries between states of being, the transient nature of beauty and reality, and the cosmic scale of human existence.
    • Aldebaran is a giant star in the constellation Taurus.
    • Venus is the second planet from the sun.
  • “God, it had been said, was the True Vine”: The list mixes titles of Christ from the Bible and Christian devotion (the True Vine, the Bread of Life, the Door, the Good Shepherd, the Light of the World, the Man of Sorrows, the Prince of Peace) with the Great Spirit of many Native American traditions, and Young sums it up: “God was many things to many people.” See The Bible, Augustine and Christian Theology, Revelation and the Apocalypse, and Judaism.
    • True Vine: an allegory or parable in John 15:1-5 where Jesus’s disciples are described as branches of himself, who is described as the “true vine” and God the Father as the “husbandman.”
    • Bread of Life: John 6:35, a statement by Jesus signifying that he is the source of spiritual nourishment and eternal life, not just physical sustenance.
    • Gate and Door (John 10:9): words often used metaphorically to represent opportunities and access to God’s presence and salvation, with Jesus himself being referred to as both.
    • Wine symbolizes joy, God’s blessings and provisions, and even the blood of Jesus Christ, but it also warns against the dangers of excessive drinking and intoxication. Can represent the fullness of God’s Kingdom (Isaiah’s prophecy).
    • Mediator: a go-between or intercessor who reconciles two parties, particularly God and humanity, with Jesus Christ being the one and only mediator, bridging the gap between the divine and human. Moses was also a mediator between God and Israel. Kings, priests, and prophets also acted as mediators in the Old Testament, representing God to the people. 1 Timothy 2:5, Hebrews 8:6, Hebrews 9:15. Young’s “Methator” is likely a misprint for Mediator.
    • Only-Begotten: emphasizes the unique relationship and divine nature of Jesus Christ as God’s Son. John 1:14 and John 3:16. The Nicene Creed is a foundational Christian statement of belief that affirms Jesus as the only-begotten Son of God.
    • Anointed: signifies being consecrated or set apart for a special purpose or role, often through the ritual of anointing with oil which symbolizes God’s favor, power, and divine authority. 1 Samuel 10:1 and 16:13, Exodus 28:41 and Leviticus 8:12, 1 Kings 19:16. The Hebrew word for anointed is the root term of Messiah meaning The Anointed One. Psalm 23:5.
    • Word: the Word refers to the concept that Jesus Christ, the divine Son of God, is the Word who existed with God from the beginning and through whom all things were made. John 1:1.
    • Restorer: signifies God’s ability and desire to bring back to their former state, or even to a better state, what has been lost, damaged or broken, whether spiritually, physically, or relationally. The story of Job, Israel, and Jesus are examples.
    • Resurrection: the belief that Jesus rose from the dead on the third day after his crucifixion. In Islam, the resurrection is also a key belief.
    • Great Spirit: in many American Indigenous Nations represents a divine force that created and sustains all life with interpretations varying across different Nations. The Great Spirit emphasizes harmony with nature, communication, and guidance.
    • Light of the World: signifies God’s role as a source of truth, guidance, and salvation, illuminating humanity from spiritual darkness. 1 John 1:5, John 8:12, Matthew 5:14-16, Psalm 119:105.
    • Man of Sorrows or Man of Pains is in Isaiah 53:3-5 which describes Jesus Christ (God’s suffering servant) and his suffering and identification with humanity’s pain, as he bore our griefs and carried our sorrows.
    • Old Man is an image used to describe God (Michelangelo’s Sistine Chapel ceiling) with a long white beard and robes. It is not universal but common in Western religious art and literature. Daniel 7:9, Revelation 1:14.
    • King of Glory Psalm 24 It emphasizes his majesty, power, and sovereign rules over all creation. Jesus is also referred to as the Lord of glory 1 Corinthians 2:8.
    • King of Kings is a title used in Judaism and Christianity to describe God’s supreme authority and power over all earthly rulers and powers. 1 Timothy 6:15, Revelation 17:14, 19:11-16.
    • Prince of Peace Isaiah 9:6 is used to describe Jesus and his role as a bringer of peace and reconciliation between humanity and God, as well as among people. Philippians 4:7.
    • Good Shepherd: Jesus Christ appears as the guide, the protector, the healer and shepherd of his sheep.
    • Narrow Way: Matthew 7:13-14 (narrow gate and broad way), suggesting the path to salvation is difficult and requires effort. Psalm 24:7, John 10:2.
    • Rose or Rose of Sharon refers to Jesus Christ as stated in the Song of Solomon 2:1. The rose in general can symbolize love, beauty, and hope. In Islamic mysticism the rose represents divine beauty, as in Saadi’s Gulistan (The Rose Garden, 1258). The rose of Tawhid means to make one, to integrate, to bring unity to that which is fragmented.
    • Thorn: in 2 Corinthians 12:7 Paul refers to a “thorn in the flesh” given to him by God to keep him humble and dependent on Christ’s power, rather than becoming conceited from his revelations. When Paul prayed to God to remove the thorn, God’s response was to strengthen him in his weakness rather than remove it.
    • Risen: the belief that Jesus Christ through his resurrection demonstrated victory over death and offers hope of eternal life.
    • Immanuel: meaning “God with us,” a title for Jesus Christ highlighting God’s presence and intimate relationship with humanity. Isaiah 7:14 and Matthew 1:23.
    • Word made Flesh: God, who through Jesus Christ is believed to have taken on human form, becoming both fully God and fully human. John 1:14, John 1:1.
    • Advocate: Jesus Christ, who is seen as mediator and intercessor between humanity and God, pleading for forgiveness and reconciliation. 1 John 2:1. The Holy Spirit is also referred to as an advocate for God.
    • Intercessor: Jesus Christ as the ultimate intercessor between God and humanity, always living to intercede for those who come to God through him. Hebrews 7:25, 1 John 2:1, John 1:9, Romans 8:26-28. In Islam Shafa’a is the act of pleading to God by an intimate friend of God for forgiveness. In Judaism Moses is the model of intercessory prayer. In Hinduism the Grand Intercessor symbolizes the Divine Mother’s pivotal role in connecting humanity with God, notably embodied by Shri Lakshmi, called purushakara, the one who intercedes with Vishnu for the devotee, in the Sri Vaishnava tradition.
    • Dove: a prominent symbol of the Holy Spirit. Matthew 3:16, Mark 1:10, Luke 3:22, John 1:32, Genesis 8:8-12. In Judaism the dove is a symbol of the soul. In Greek mythology doves are associated with Aphrodite, the goddess of love.
    • King of Light often describes God symbolizing purity, truth, and divine presence, contrasting with darkness and evil. 1 John 1:5, John 8:12, James 1:17. God is also referred to as The Lord of Light and The Red God.
    • King of Darkness or prince of darkness refers to Satan, the leader of spiritual forces of evil, who opposes God and His kingdom. Ephesians 6:12, John 8:44, Colossians 2:15, 2 Corinthians 11:14.
  • “many other gods, the god of the sun, the goddess of the moon, the judge of the dead, the busy clerk of the underworld”: The gods are Egyptian. Osiris judged the dead, and Thoth, the scribe of the gods, recorded the weighing of the heart (Book of the Dead, spell 125). Young’s list goes on to “the goddess with the head of a cat” (Bastet) and “the jackal god who was the conductor of the dead” (Anubis). See Ancient Egypt.
    • The god of the sun may refer to a solar deity which is a sky deity who represents the Sun, or an aspect of it. Such deities are usually associated with power and strength. Solar deities and Sun worship can be found throughout most of recorded history in various forms. In Egypt, the sun god was Ra. (Wikipedia)
    • The goddess of the moon may refer to a lunar deity and sometimes as a personification. These deities can have a variety of functions and traditions depending upon the culture, but they are often related. Some form of moon worship can be found in most ancient religions. (Wikipedia)
    • The goddess with the head of a cat may refer to Bastet who is a goddess of ancient Egyptian religion, worshiped as early as the Second Dynasty. In ancient Greek religion, she was known as Ailuros.
    • The goddess of wisdom may refer to Ma’at or Isis of Egypt, or to Athena from Greek mythology.
    • The jackal god may refer to Anubis who is the god of death, mummification, embalming, the afterlife, cemeteries, tombs, and the Underworld, in ancient Egyptian religion.
    • The judge of the dead is Osiris, who presided over the weighing of the heart in ancient Egyptian religion. In Christianity, God is the judge of the dead.
    • The busy clerk of the underworld is Thoth, the ibis-headed scribe of the gods, who records the weighing of the heart.
  • “screeching harpies, wailing banshees, salamanders”: In Paracelsus, salamanders are the spirits of fire. See Astrology, Alchemy, and Esoterica.
  • “before the separation of the waters from the land, before the division of light from darkness”: “God divided the light from the darkness… and let the dry land appear” (Genesis 1:4, 9). See Genesis.
  • “Did it come through the strings of the golden lyre of the stars”: The constellations Lyra, Sagittarius (the archer), Argo Navis, and Centaurus. The Small Magellanic Cloud is a dwarf galaxy, named for Magellan’s crew, who described it on the first voyage around the world (1519-22). See Astronomy, Greek Mythology, and Exploration and the Poles.
    • Argo in Greek mythology was a ship built with the help of the gods which Jason and the Argonauts sailed to find the Golden Fleece.
    • The “small cloud of Magellan” is the Small Magellanic Cloud, named for Ferdinand Magellan, the Portuguese explorer. Explorers in general serve as metaphors for the human condition: our navigation through life’s mysteries, the search for meaning, and the inevitable encounter with the unknown and the unknowable.
  • “the Milky Way, the thin stream of stars streaming from the breast of Juno”: Juno was an ancient Roman goddess. In the myth, milk spilled from Juno’s (Hera’s) breast as she nursed the infant Hercules, and became the Milky Way. See Greek Mythology.
  • “had originated not at all upon this planet”: This may refer to the hypothesis of panspermia, first proposed by Anaxagoras in ancient Greece: life exists throughout the universe and is deposited by comets, meteors, space dust, etc. Svante Arrhenius revived the idea in 1903. (Wikipedia)
  • “when one bird should sing for a thousand years”: The medieval legend of the monk who listened to a bird for what seemed a moment and returned to find a hundred years gone, told as the tale of Monk Felix in Longfellow’s The Golden Legend (1851). See American Writers.
  • “flying out of the flame-colored butterfly bushes and elder bushes”: This may refer to actual butterfly bushes. They are found on four continents and attract pollinators.
    • Elder bushes, particularly American Elderberry (Sambucus canadensis), attract butterflies with their vibrant, nectar-rich flowers. Besides elderberry, other bushes that attract butterflies include butterfly bush (Buddleja), lilacs, and rose of sharon.
  • “They had survived the deaths of stars, the cyclic whirlwinds, the ages of fire, the ages of ice”: Each of these has a place in Earth’s long history.
    • Fire has been a part of Earth’s history for at least 420 million years, coinciding with the emergence of terrestrial plants. Fossil evidence of charcoal, a sign of fire, shows its presence in the Late Silurian period. (Wikipedia)
    • Earth has experienced at least five major ice ages throughout its history, with the most recent one starting about 2.6 million years ago and continuing today. These ice ages are characterized by periods of extensive glaciation followed by warmer interglacial periods. The Huronian ice age occurred around 2.4 to 2.1 billion years ago, the Cryogenian ice age from 720 to 630 million years ago, the Andean-Saharan ice age from 460 to 420 million years ago, the late Paleozoic ice age, and the Quaternary ice age, which began about 2.6 million years ago. The last major glaciation peaked around 18,000 years ago and ended about 11,700 years ago. (Wikipedia)
    • Earth has survived the deaths of countless stars in the Milky Way’s past, but this is largely due to the vast distances between stars and the relatively short lifespan of massive stars that undergo supernova explosions. The Sun’s death, although inevitable, is a more gradual process.
    • Earth has survived through periods of intense environmental stress. These events have included massive asteroid impacts, volcanic eruptions, and periods of extreme climate change, all of which have led to mass extinctions and reshaped the planet.
    • Butterflies are estimated to have originated around 100 million years ago, splitting from their moth ancestors during the mid-Cretaceous period. This evolution likely occurred in what is now North or Central America. By the time dinosaurs went extinct 66 million years ago, the six modern butterfly families had already emerged (Akito Kawahara et al., Nature Ecology & Evolution, May 2023).
  • “Only his silent music”: There is such a thing as “silent music” that was done by several musicians as experimental. John Cage’s 4’33” (1952) is an example. Mr. Spitzer “had written only silent music, that which, for many years now, no one else had ever heard.” See Music and Composers.
  • “his failure to win the object of his love”: Catherine, who refused him (Chapter 26). See the Chapter 26 resources.
  • “Perhaps she heard, beyond the wild oceanic gales, a canary twittering”: Catherine’s canary of Chapter 2. See the Chapter 2 resources.
  • “It was his own personal theory that a butterfly could hear”: Science has found membranes on some butterfly wings that allow it to hear. The hearing organ on the wings of some butterflies is called Vogel’s organ, after Richard Vogel, who described it in 1912. His own “dead ear” is from Chapter 25. See Deafness and Sign Language.
  • “even in a dark night of the human soul”: Dark Night of the Soul is a poem written by a Spanish Christian mystic St. John of the Cross (c. 1578). Dark night in Roman Catholic spirituality describes a spiritual crisis in the journey toward union with God. See Augustine and Christian Theology.
  • “eye shell, ear shell, wing shell”: Seashells: ear shells are abalones, wing shells are Pteria, and the “golden mouthed” is the gold-mouth turban shell.
  • “the bipart soul”: Aristotle’s bipartite psychology divides the soul into two main parts: the rational soul and the non-rational soul. The rational soul is responsible for reason, intellect, and higher thinking, while the non-rational soul encompasses emotions, appetites, and bodily functions. Aristotle further subdivided the rational soul into two parts: the calculating and the scientific. He also divided the non-rational soul into vegetative and appetitive (Nicomachean Ethics 1.13, 6.1). Young sets it beside Mr. Spitzer’s divided self. See Aristotle.
  • “thirteen moons in a cloudless sky”: The phrase, 13 moons, often refers to a lunar calendar with 13 months. It is often seen as a way to track the changes in nature and the cycles of life and each moon is associated with specific teaching and practices. Many Indigenous peoples of North America count thirteen moons in a year by the thirteen plates on a turtle’s back, as retold in Joseph Bruchac and Jonathan London’s Thirteen Moons on Turtle’s Back (1992).
  • “the bed of the sleeping beauty who would sleep until she was awakened by the kiss of a fairy prince”: Perrault’s “La Belle au bois dormant” (1697) and the Grimms’ “Briar Rose” (1812). See Fairy Tales and Folklore.
  • “the bed of Charlemagne, the amethyst bed of Catherine the Great”: See Napoleon and Wellington, Ancient Egypt, and the Chapter 27 resources.
    • Charlemagne or Charles the Great, Charles I, was King of the Franks, King of the Lombards, and Emperor of the Romans. (Wikipedia)
    • Catherine the Great was known for favoring amethysts and using them in buttons, earrings, necklaces, and hair ornaments. Amethyst has been a gemstone associated with royalty and has been used in jewelry by various royal families. Amethyst has been associated with humility, modesty, and royalty throughout history.
    • Catherine the Great was empress regnant of Russia, the country’s longest-ruling female leader.
    • Cleopatra was Queen of the Ptolemaic Kingdom of Egypt.
    • Martin Luther was a German professor of theology, priest, author, composer, former Augustinian monk, and seminal figure in the Protestant Reformation.
    • Napoleon (Bonaparte) was a French military and political leader during the French Revolution. He died on his camp bed at Longwood, St. Helena, in 1821.
  • “the beds of Arabs whose beds were tents and shrouds in which they wrapped themselves and quietly stole away”: “Shall fold their tents, like the Arabs, / And as silently steal away” (Longfellow, “The Day Is Done,” 1844). See American Writers.
  • “butterflies of the antipodes”: The antipodes are the far side of the earth.
  • “butterflies in Elysium”: Elysium (Elysian Fields) is the Greek religious and philosophical concept of an afterlife. See Greek Mythology.
  • “He knew Urania Sloanus, Ornithoptera Paradisea, Saturnia Pyri, eyeless whites, green hair-streaks”: Urania Sloanus was a moth from Jamaica last seen in 1895.
    • Ornithoptera Paradisea (Paradise birdwing) is found in New Guinea.
    • Saturnia Pyri (Giant peacock moth) is native to Europe.
    • Eyeless whites may refer to Cabbage White Butterflies or Small White Butterflies. These butterflies are easily recognized by their white wings with small black spots, and are a common sight in many gardens and agricultural areas.
    • Green hair-streaks are small butterflies found in Europe and Asia.
    • Butterflies of the mountain ranges: Himalayas, the Alps, the Andes and Mt. Olympus. Mt. Olympus was the home of the Greek gods.
  • “Homeric butterflies which were like persons who had passed through many unknown forms of being”: Io Vanessa is the Peacock butterfly. The Aphrodite Fritillary and the Apollo (Parnassius apollo) are named for gods. Morpheus, “the fashioner,” shapes dreams in Ovid’s Metamorphoses 11. The Atlas moth is among the largest moths in the world. Papilio homerus of Jamaica is the largest swallowtail in the Americas, and Papilio antimachus is the largest butterfly in Africa. See Homer’s Epics and Greek Mythology.
  • “the last infernal circle of this Divine Comedy”: Divine Comedy (c. 1308-21) is a long Italian narrative poem by Dante Alighieri. It depicts the afterlife according to the Western Church medieval world view of the time. (Wikipedia) Like The Pilgrim’s Progress (1678) it is a journey from sin to heaven. See Dante.
  • “not even a ghostly captain lashed to the mast and wound in a winding sheet of snow”: Longfellow’s “The Wreck of the Hesperus” (1840), where the skipper’s daughter is found “Lashed close to a drifting mast,” with “The salt sea… frozen on her breast.” See American Writers.
  • “the Stygian night”: Stygian refers to the River Styx of the underworld in Greek mythology. See Greek Mythology.
  • “Were these two souls which moved through him”: The soul is the purported immaterial aspect or essence of a living being. It is typically believed to be immortal and to exist apart from the material world. The three main theories that describe the relationship between the soul and the body are interactionism, parallelism, and epiphenomenalism. Anthropologists and psychologists have found that most humans are naturally inclined to believe in the existence of the soul and that they have interculturally distinguished between souls and bodies. In philosophy, the soul has been the central area of interest since ancient times. Socrates envisioned the soul to possess a rational faculty, its practice being man’s most godlike activity. Plato believed the soul to be the person’s real self, an immaterial and immortal dweller of our lives that continues and thinks even after death. Aristotle sketched out the soul as the “first actuality” of a naturally organized body: form and matter arrangement allowing natural beings to aspire to full actualization. (Wikipedia) The chapter’s “two souls” and “three souls or the amalgamations of many souls” reflect the fragmented and overlapping nature of consciousness and existence. See Descartes and Dualism.
    • In Mongolian shamanism every person has three souls, two mortal and one immortal: “the female spirit of flesh and blood, the male spirit of bones and lastly the Heaven spirits,” in the words of the Mongolian scholar Byambyn Rinchen (1965). The mother’s soul of flesh and blood stays in the body until the heart stops, the father’s soul of bone stays until the bones decay, and the immortal soul rises (Otgony Pürev, Mongolian Shamanism). Other Siberian and East Asian peoples hold related beliefs in more than one soul, such as the Chinese hun and po. Aristotle, Plato, Christian theology, and Hinduism also have versions of a three part soul. Aristotle ranks three kinds of soul by what living things can do: the nutritive soul of growth and reproduction, which plants have; the sensitive soul of perception and movement, which animals add; and the rational soul of thought, which belongs to humans (On the Soul, Book 2). Plato divides the human soul into three parts in the Republic, Book 4: the rational (logistikon), which seeks truth; the spirited (thymoeides), which drives emotion and honor; and the appetitive (epithymetikon), which governs bodily desires.
  • “that a new tenant had not taken over an old, empty house”: Spirit possession is an altered state of consciousness and associated behaviors which are purportedly caused by the control of a human body and its functions by spirits, ghosts, demons, angels, or gods. The concept of spirit possession exists in many cultures and religions, including Buddhism, Hinduism, Islam, Christianity, Judaism, Wicca, Haitian Vodou, Dominican Vudú, and Southeast Asian, African, and Native American traditions. Depending on the cultural context in which it is found, possession may be thought of as voluntary or involuntary and may be considered to have beneficial or detrimental effects on the host. (Wikipedia)
  • “the seal of hermetic privacy”: Hermeticism is a philosophical and religious system based on the writings attributed to Hermes Trismegistus, a legendary figure in ancient Greece and Egypt. The core principles are: the belief in a single, transcendent God or cosmic principle, there is a correspondence between the macrocosm (universe) and the microcosm (humans and the world around them) as used in the term “As above, so below,” and, in the modern Hermetic book The Kybalion (1908), seven principles (mentalism, correspondence, vibration, polarity, rhythm, cause and effect, gender). Hermeticism has influenced various religious and philosophical traditions. A “hermetic seal” is airtight, named for Hermes Trismegistus, supposed inventor of the alchemist’s sealed glass. See Astrology, Alchemy, and Esoterica.
  • “even like the midnight rainbow”: A moonbow, a rainbow made by moonlight.
  • “Clearwing Aurora”: Clearwing Aurora may refer to a butterfly found in Mexico and South America.
  • “Did he not remember Croesus, the golden bambino in a golden cradle”: Croesus may refer to one or two different butterflies found in South America and Indonesia. Ornithoptera croesus, Wallace’s golden birdwing, was found by Alfred Russel Wallace in 1859.
    • Croesus and Fate: Croesus is a rich king in ancient Lydia who is quite enamored with his own wealth. When the wise man Solon comes to visit his kingdom, Croesus asks Solon if he had ever seen greater opulence than his own. In Plutarch’s telling, Solon answers that cocks, pheasants, and peacocks are clothed in colors more brilliant than any king’s finery (Life of Solon 27). Croesus disagrees, and he tries to impress Solon with a list of vanquished foes and claimed territories. Solon still disagrees, telling Croesus that the happiest man he had known was Tellus of Athens, who lived in a prosperous city, saw his children and grandchildren grow, and died bravely in battle for his country. Croesus takes this as an insult and Solon leaves. Soon after Solon’s departure, tragedy befalls Croesus. His son Atys is killed in a hunting accident, and then Emperor Cyrus invades. Cyrus’ army is triumphant, and Croesus’ kingdom is ravaged and Croesus himself is captured and ordered to be executed. As Croesus is about to be burned on a pyre, he cries out Solon’s name. Cyrus stops the pyre to hear what Croesus has to say. Croesus relates Solon’s story to Cyrus, and Cyrus is moved by the notion that Fate can bring misery to a rich man and happiness to a poor man. Croesus is freed and the emperor and the king become good friends. (Herodotus, Histories 1.30-45, 1.86-88)
    • “False Greatness” by Isaac Watts: “Thus mingled still with wealth and state, / Croesus himself can never know; / His true dimensions and his weight / Are far inferior to their show.”
  • “out of the whirlwind”: “Then the LORD answered Job out of the whirlwind” (Job 38:1). See The Book of Job.
  • “as the plume of Raphael”: The plume (feather) of Raphael may refer to the archangel. See Angels and Archangels.
  • “as the Venus-comb upon the beach”: The Venus comb murex (Murex pecten), a seashell with long comb-like spines.
  • “the nebulous mass of golden light like hairs surrounding the nucleus of a comet”: “Comet” comes from the Greek komētēs, “long-haired,” for the glowing coma around its nucleus. See Astronomy.
  • “How out of the heart of darkness”: Heart of Darkness (1899) is a novella by Polish-English novelist Joseph Conrad. The novel is widely regarded as a critique of European colonial rule in Africa, while also examining the themes of power dynamics and morality. (Wikipedia)
  • “one rose evoke a garden, one sea shell evoke a sea”: “To see a World in a Grain of Sand / And a Heaven in a Wild Flower” (Blake, “Auguries of Innocence,” c. 1803). See Romantic Poets.
  • “old Beau Brummells who had risen from their graves”: The dandies of Chapter 24. See the Chapter 24 resources.
  • “where the turf meets the surf”: The slogan of the Del Mar racetrack, opened in 1937 by Bing Crosby and Pat O’Brien. Crosby sang “Where the Turf Meets the Surf.” See Gambling and Playing Cards and Peron Spitzer.
  • “merry andrews and fat aldermen”: A merry-andrew was a clown at a fair, and a domino a hooded masquerade cloak.
  • “wild goose chases and pretty chicks… pigs in the poke”: Mercutio’s “Nay, if our wits run the wild-goose chase” (Romeo and Juliet 2.4). A “pig in a poke” is a bargain bought unseen in its sack. See Shakespeare.
  • “strange as the phoenix, the perfumed bird of Arabia arising from its ashes”: Herodotus describes the phoenix that comes from Arabia every five hundred years (Histories 2.73). See Greek Mythology.
  • “an old lamp-lighter”: Lamplighter is a person employed to light and maintain candle, oil, or gas street lights. Very few exist today.
  • “like Jacob with his ladder of dreams”: Jacob’s Ladder is a ladder leading to heaven that was featured in a dream the biblical Patriarch Jacob had during his flight from his brother Esau in Genesis 28:12. The significance of the dream has been debated, but most interpretations agree that it identified Jacob with the obligations and inheritance of the people chosen by God, as understood in Abrahamic religions. (Wikipedia) The King James text reads: “And he dreamed, and behold a ladder set up on the earth, and the top of it reached to heaven: and behold the angels of God ascending and descending on it.” See Genesis.
  • “the similitude of death, its twin brother”: Sleep and Death are twins in Hesiod (Chapter 25), and sleep is “death’s counterfeit” in Macbeth 2.3. See Twins and Doubles and Shakespeare.
  • “the powdery pollen gold freighting the bright wings of transcendental butterflies”: Transcendental butterflies may refer to the Butterfly curve which is a transcendental plane curve discovered by Temple H. Fay (“The Butterfly Curve,” American Mathematical Monthly 96, no. 5, May 1989, 442-443).
  • “the veined leaf green, the milky midnight blue”: The veined leaf green is a butterfly found in Europe and Asia.
    • The milky midnight blue is found in tropical Mexico, Central and South America.
  • “the old Diomedes with planets and half moons”: Diomedes (Deudorix) is a butterfly found in Africa. See Homer’s Epics.
    • Diomedes is a prominent figure in Greek mythology. He is known as a brave and skilled warrior who participated in the Trojan War and is renowned for his exploits in Homer’s Iliad.
  • “the ethereal tortoise-shell”: Tortoise-shell butterflies are found in Europe, Asia, and North America.
  • “the white-veined blacks, the black-veined marble whites”: The white-veined blacks are a common butterfly found in northwest Africa and Asia.
    • The black-veined marble white may be the Black-veined White (Aporia crataegi), a large butterfly of Europe that died out in Britain in the 1920s.
  • “butterflies as big as the wailing lapwing”: Lapwing is a ground nesting bird found in Europe. See Birds and Astronomy.
    • Tropic of Cancer (Northern Tropic) is the most northerly circle of latitude on Earth.
    • The Tropic of Capricorn (Southern Tropic) is the circle of latitude closest to the equator.
    • Aurora Borealis is the northern lights.
    • Aurora Australis is the southern lights.
  • “the emerald, the amethyst, the coxcomb red”: The emerald (Papilio palinurus) butterfly is found in Southeast Asia.
    • The amethyst may refer to the Purple emperor butterfly found in Europe and Asia.
    • The “coxcomb red” most likely refers to the Coxcomb Prominent moth (Ptilodon capucina). This moth is named for the white tuft of scales on its head, which resembles a coxcomb or the crest of a rooster. It’s a fairly common moth in Britain and is known for its camouflaged appearance when at rest, resembling a dead leaf. The moth’s caterpillar is green with two red projections and has a unique defense mechanism of curling its head back when alarmed.
  • “the red admiral of the light-wing fleet”: The red admiral is a butterfly found on five continents.
  • “the old butterfly geographers drawing their maps of this world”: The Piri Reis map (1513), drawn by an Ottoman admiral from older sources.
  • “the uniform of the checkered skipper”: The checkered skipper is a butterfly found in the US.
    • The silver-spotted skipper is a butterfly found in North America.
    • The grizzled and dingy skippers are butterflies found in Europe and Asia.
    • The greylings is a butterfly found in Europe.
    • Adonis blues butterflies are found in Europe and Asia.
    • Wood white butterflies are found in Europe.
  • “Io on one wing and Io on the other wing as if they knew they had two souls”: Io was one of the mortal lovers of Zeus in Greek mythology. See Greek Mythology and Twins and Doubles.
  • “the cabbage-haunting butterflies”: Cabbage white butterflies are found in Europe and North America. See the Chapter 28 resources.
    • The painted lady is a butterfly found on every continent except Antarctica and South America.
    • Swallowtail butterflies are found mostly in tropical regions but are found on every continent except Antarctica.
  • “crowding through his mind in empty hours”: Young is describing a hyperfixation where a person is completely engrossed by something, to the point where it becomes all-consuming and disrupts day-to-day functioning. It gets hard to focus on anything other than the object of hyperfixation. With hyperfixation, passion can turn into obsession. The object of interest takes up so much time, it comes at the cost of personal wellbeing, relationships, and responsibilities. It can even be a symptom of an underlying mental health condition. (Jackie Menjivar, “What Is Hyperfixation, and How Can You Manage It?” I Don’t Mind, March 8, 2022)
  • “the harmless hobby of knitting fine socks”: Knitting’s history traces back to the Middle East and North Africa, with evidence suggesting its origins around the 10th century. It spread to Europe via trade routes and became a widespread craft.
  • “the ribbing he would get”: Ribbing is both the knitted rib of a sock and teasing, and Mr. Spitzer apologizes for the pun. See Comedy in Chapter 29.
  • “to ask himself the philosopher’s question”: Mr. Spitzer has applied the philosophical question of the Ship of Theseus to his socks. Ship of Theseus is a thought experiment that questions if an object that has had all of its components replaced remains fundamentally the same object. There have been three proposed solutions: there is no identity over time, four-dimensionalism, and according to cognitive science it is an example of extreme externalism, the assumption that what is true in our minds is true in the world. In philosophy of mind, the ship is replaced by a person, whose identity over time is called into question. The puzzle is from Plutarch, Life of Theseus 23.
  • “and all the dogs of creation would bark at him”: The nursery rhyme “Hark, hark, the dogs do bark, / The beggars are coming to town; / Some in rags, and some in tags.” See Fairy Tales and Folklore.
  • “butterflies of Byzantium”: The gold mosaics of Byzantine churches, made of small pieces of colored glass and stone, as the next lines say.
  • “purple emperors the wind had blown ten thousand miles from shore”: The Purple Emperor of Chapter 28. See the Chapter 28 resources.
  • “old monarchs with their orange-brown wings”: King butterfly is another name for a Monarch butterfly.
    • Queen butterflies are found in North and South America.
    • Cardinal butterflies are found in Europe and Asia.
  • “He swore that their chant would be almost Gregorian”: Gregorian chant is a form of monophonic, unaccompanied sacred song in Latin of the Roman Catholic Church. (Wikipedia) See Music and Composers.
    • “Palestrina” may refer to Giovanni Pierluigi da Palestrina (c. 1525-1594), the Italian composer of late Renaissance sacred music, best known for his Masses for the Roman Catholic Church.
    • Felix Mendelssohn placed him in the pantheon of the greatest musicians, writing, “I always get upset when some praise only Beethoven, others only Palestrina and still others only Mozart or Bach. All four of them, I say, or none at all.” (Wikipedia)
  • “this dark atheist, this believer in nothing”: Mr. Spitzer considers himself a dark atheist. A negative atheist is someone who does not believe in the existence of deities but does not explicitly assert that there are none. (Wikipedia)

Vocabulary

Amalgamation
A blending into one.
Ambient
Surrounding.
Amorphous
Without a clear shape or form.
Aperture
An opening.
Apocryphal
Of doubtful truth.
Apparition
A ghost, or a ghostlike image of a person.
Attar
A fragrant oil of roses.
Banshee
In Irish folklore, a spirit whose wail foretells a death.
Barnacled
Crusted with barnacles, small shelled sea creatures that cling to rocks, pilings, and the hulls of ships.
Begetting
Fathering; producing offspring.
Bindlestiff
A hobo who carries his belongings in a bundle.
Breastplate
A piece of armor covering the chest.
Burnished
Polished until shining.
Centaur
In Greek mythology, a creature with the head and upper body of a man and the body and legs of a horse.
Chandelier
A branched hanging light.
Chimerical
Imaginary, fanciful, or wildly unrealistic. From the Chimera, the fire-breathing monster of Greek myth made of a lion, a goat, and a serpent.
Coalescence
A growing together.
Cockle
A small saltwater clam with a ribbed, heart-shaped shell. A cockleshell boat is a small, flimsy one.
Conch
A large sea snail with a spiraled shell that can be blown like a horn. Held to the ear, it seems to hold the sound of the sea.
Conformation
The shape and proportions of an animal’s body, especially a horse’s.
Coxcomb
The red crest of a rooster, or the jester’s cap shaped like one; also a vain, foolish man.
Crow’s-nest
A lookout platform high on a ship’s mast.
Deference
Polite respect, or yielding to someone else’s wishes or judgment.
Demented
Out of one’s mind.
Dervish
A member of a Sufi order known for whirling in worship.
Devious
Winding; straying from the direct way.
Diaphanous
Delicate and translucent.
Diminuendo
A gradual softening in music.
Dominoes
A game played with small oblong tiles marked with spots.
Drove
A herd or flock driven or moving together.
Ducal
Belonging to a duke.
Effigy
A sculpture or model of a person, especially one lying on a tomb.
Emanation
Something that flows out from a source.
Empyreal
Of the highest heaven.
Ephemera
Things that last a very short time; the mayflies.
Epitome
A perfect example; a summary.
Ethereal
Light, airy, and delicate, as if not of this world; heavenly.
Evanescent
Quickly fading or vanishing.
Extant
Still existing.
Extempore
Spoken or done without preparation.
Figurehead
A carved figure, often a woman, mounted on the bow of a sailing ship. See On the figurehead and intuition (Ch 40).
Firmament
The sky or the heavens, imagined as a solid dome overhead, as in Genesis 1.
Gannet
A large white seabird that dives for fish.
Gauze
A thin, transparent fabric.
Grizzled
Streaked with grey.
Harpy
In Greek myth, a monster with a woman’s face and a bird’s body.
Headland
A high point of land jutting into the sea.
Heterogeneous
Made of unlike parts; mixed.
Hulk
The body of an old ship; a big, clumsy person or thing.
Ice floe
A sheet of floating ice.
Inane
Silly; empty of meaning.
Incongruent
Not in agreement.
Ineffable
Too great or wonderful to be put into words.
Inviolable
Never to be broken or harmed.
Iridescence
