chapter-09:
Chapter 9

← Chapter 8 · Home · Chapter 10 →

Summary

Vera asks whether she caused Miss MacIntosh’s death simply by opening her eyes. She recalls their life together: drills in geography and history, the Chicago fire and the glaciers, embroidery hoops and hemmed handkerchiefs, Solomon the turtle dragging a geranium pot across the schoolroom, and the silver dollar watch Miss MacIntosh used to remind her that time was passing. Then comes her fourteenth birthday. Mr. Spitzer sends a party dress, but no guests come. Vera dances alone and declares she is dancing with Death, and Miss MacIntosh sternly corrects her. That night Vera lies awake wondering about the man she might marry and whether a true marriage could ever be dissolved.

Characters present

Vera Cartwheel · Miss MacIntosh · Joachim Spitzer · Catherine Cartwheel · Solomon the Turtle

Concepts present

Themes: Death and Mortality · Dreams and Imagination · Grief, Loss, and Mourning · Illusion and Reality · Isolation and Connection · Nature, the Sea, and the Cosmos · Order, Chaos, and Discipline · Women, Gender, and Marriage

Symbols: Birds · Clocks and Watches · Clothing, Hats, and Skirts · Lamps, Candles, and Light · Pregnancy, Birth, and Children · The Sea and Water · Weddings and Funerals

Philosophy: Aristotle · Marguerite Young on Her Craft · Pythagoras and the Music of the Spheres

Allusions: Astronomy · Deafness and Sign Language · Ecclesiastes · Genesis · Greek Mythology · Iowa, Indiana, and the Midwest · Music and Composers · Romantic Poets · Shakespeare · The Bible · The Book of Job

Key passages

From the research

  • The chapter opens with a haunting reflection on a terrible deed, possibly the death of Miss MacIntosh, and Vera’s lifelong torment over whether she was responsible, even as a child. She contemplates whether the death was murder, accident, fate, or suicide, and wrestles with deep remorse and existential questions about life, death, and responsibility. This passage sets the tone of guilt, mystery, and fatalism that permeates the chapter.
  • Vera describes Miss MacIntosh’s upbringing in What Cheer, Iowa, emphasizing her tough, unprivileged childhood and strict, austere personality. Despite her cheerfulness, she is portrayed as a forceful, practical woman who imposes discipline and domestic training on Vera. This passage highlights the tension between Miss MacIntosh’s rigid worldview and Vera’s more dreamlike, rebellious nature.
  • Miss MacIntosh’s insistence on preparing Vera for a traditional female role (domesticity and marriage) is detailed extensively. She emphasizes sewing skills, housekeeping, thriftiness, and moral discipline, reflecting societal expectations of women at the time. Vera’s subtle rebellion against this fate is also revealed. This theme of constrained female roles versus yearning for freedom is central to understanding Vera’s inner conflict.
  • The presence of an ancient turtle named Solomon in their home, which Miss MacIntosh disapproves of, serves as a symbol. The turtle, slow and slothful, contrasts with Miss MacIntosh’s energy and discipline. It may represent endurance, ancient wisdom, or the burdensome nature of their isolated existence. This subtle symbolism enriches the atmosphere of the household.
  • When Vera inquires about Miss MacIntosh’s ovaries and later her eyebrows, Miss MacIntosh evades these personal questions with unrelated historical or geographical lectures. This avoidance illustrates the emotional distance and repression within their relationship, as well as Miss MacIntosh’s discomfort with intimacy and femininity.
  • Vera’s fourteenth birthday is depicted as a moment of transition and tragedy. Despite preparations and the gift of a party dress, there is no real celebration or guests, and Vera dances alone, imagining a partner. Miss MacIntosh’s stern disapproval and the absence of family highlight the loneliness and isolation. This passage symbolizes lost innocence and the beginning of the end in their lives.
  • Vera’s fanciful statement, “I am dancing with Death,” and Miss MacIntosh’s severe response underscore the omnipresence of death and the seriousness with which it is regarded. The discussion reveals their differing attitudes toward life and death, with Miss MacIntosh embodying stern reality and Vera caught between fantasy and despair.
  • In the darkness after the birthday, Vera contemplates the nature of love and marriage, intrigued and troubled by Miss MacIntosh’s assertion that spouses do not truly know each other until after marriage and then it is too late. Vera dreams of a passionate, adventurous union rather than a mundane, poor existence, signaling a deep yearning for meaning and escape from imposed roles.

Questions and observations

Reading closely

  • Vera asks whether she killed Miss MacIntosh “only perhaps by opening my eyes.” What does she mean?
  • Miss MacIntosh answers the question about her eyebrows with the Chicago fire. What is she refusing to say?
  • “The dream was always the lie.” Does the chapter agree with Miss MacIntosh?

Characters

  • Miss MacIntosh calls herself “the land-locked sailor” who “could not swim an inch.” What does her sea talk reveal about her?
  • Vera imagines Miss MacIntosh as a circus ring-master with a mustache and bushy eyebrows. Why give her a man’s face?
  • Mr. Spitzer chooses a dress “too mature” for Vera while thinking “of someone else.” Whom does he see when he looks at her?

Connections

  • Madge called twelve “the age of wisdom” in Chapter 7, and here Miss MacIntosh does the same. What changes for Vera at twelve, and what does not?
  • Vera’s dance with Death echoes Madge’s “dead child dancing” in Chapter 6. Why do the girls in this novel dance with the dead?
  • Miss MacIntosh warns that “no wife ever knows her husband… until after she is married to him.” How does Madge’s marriage prove her right?

Reflection

  • “If I knew Love, I would not dream of Death.” “What makes you think they are not one?” Who is right?
  • Is it kinder to train a child for the life she will probably have, or for the life she dreams of?
  • Vera says she “could have dispensed with her company” for seven years and then loved her in one month. Why do people so often know someone only at the end?

Research: Characters

Vera Cartwheel

  • A young girl on the cusp of adolescence, navigating strict domestic training and her own inner dreams.
  • Exhibits a tension between obedience and rebellion.
  • Yearns for love, adventure, and a meaningful future beyond the mundane expectations set by Miss MacIntosh.
  • Reflects deeply on identity, mortality, and the mystery of human relationships.

Miss MacIntosh

  • Vera’s guardian, strict and practical, embodying discipline and austere values.
  • Holds strong beliefs about women’s roles, marriage, and responsibility.
  • Comes from a harsh, unprivileged background in What Cheer, Iowa.
  • Acts as a maternal figure but also as a controlling authority.
  • Is caring yet unyielding, knowledgeable yet evasive.

Mr. Spitzer

  • Gives Vera her first party dress.
  • He gives Vera an old Roman coin and goes to Buzzards Bay to trace a lost heir “who had died a decade previously and who claimed to be egregiously alive.”
  • Suggests a connection to the past and to Vera’s mother, Catherine.
  • His absence at the party emphasizes Vera’s isolation.

Catherine Cartwheel (Vera’s Mother)

  • On Vera’s fourteenth birthday she lies “in an unearthly coma,” entertaining her dead guests, “the many P’s,” from Pythagoras and Proteus to Pandora and pterodactyls.

Solomon the Turtle

  • Symbolic companion residing in the schoolroom.
  • Represents slowness, wisdom, and perhaps stagnation.
  • Miss MacIntosh disapproves of the turtle, reflecting her disdain for inactivity and sloth.

Research: Themes

Loss and Remorse

See: Grief, Loss, and Mourning

  • Vera grapples with a haunting sense of guilt and loss, possibly linked to Miss MacIntosh’s disappearance or death.
  • Questions of responsibility and fate permeate the narrative.

Discipline and Domesticity

See: Order, Chaos, and Discipline

  • Miss MacIntosh’s rigorous training prepares Vera for the traditional female role of housekeeping and marriage.
  • Emphasis on practical skills (sewing, household chores) contrasts with Vera’s imaginative inner life.
  • The discipline is strict, yet there is an undercurrent of rebellion and dissatisfaction.

Dreams and Reality

See: Illusion and Reality · Dreams and Imagination

  • Vera’s dreams of adventure, romance, and the wider world conflict with Miss MacIntosh’s insistence on practicality and limitation.
  • The metaphor of the circus (ringmaster and bareback rider) illustrates the control Miss MacIntosh exerts over Vera’s life.

Mortality and Death

See: Death and Mortality

  • Vera dances “with Death,” and the inevitability of mortality is discussed seriously by Miss MacIntosh.
  • The chapter contemplates death’s universality and the human responses to it.

Marriage and Gender Roles

See: Women, Gender, and Marriage

  • Marriage is portrayed as the “normal state” and a natural institution sanctioned by God and nature.
  • Miss MacIntosh emphasizes the importance of preparation for marriage and warns against sexual dangers.
  • Vera reflects on the mystery of marriage, love, and the unknown nature of her future husband.

Isolation and Companionship

See: Isolation and Connection

  • Vera and Miss MacIntosh live in relative isolation, with only the ancient turtle Solomon as a companion.
  • Their relationship is marked by authority and tension but also moments of care.

Nature and Nautical Imagery

See: Nature, the Sea, and the Cosmos

  • References to the sea, birds, fog, and weather create a vivid natural backdrop and symbolize change and uncertainty.
  • Nautical language reflects Miss MacIntosh’s character and worldview.

Research: Symbols and Imagery

Sea and Water Imagery

See: The Sea and Water

  • The sea, waves, tides, fog, and shore recur repeatedly as symbols of life’s uncertainty, danger, and transition.
  • The sea represents the unknown, the subconscious, and the boundary between life and death.
  • Miss MacIntosh’s identity as a “land-locked sailor” who “could not swim an inch” but who constantly talks in nautical terms symbolizes a life caught between stability and the wild, uncontrollable forces of nature.

Bird Imagery, Especially Seagulls

See: Birds

  • Seagulls appear as recurring natural motifs connected with care and injury. They may symbolize vulnerability and healing, but also freedom and the natural world.
  • The death of the seagull “when its wound was healed” suggests a paradox of survival and loss, or the cost of recovery.

Embroidery Hoops and Sewing

  • Embroidery hoops and sewing serve as symbols of domesticity, discipline, and the preparation for womanhood and marriage.
  • Miss MacIntosh’s insistence on sewing straight basting stitches and hemming handkerchiefs reflects the imposition of order and control over Vera’s life.
  • The hoops themselves evoke a circus ring and suggest that Vera’s life is a performance under Miss MacIntosh’s strict supervision.

The Turtle Named Solomon

  • The ancient turtle living in the schoolroom functions as a symbol of slow, deliberate life and possibly wisdom or its apparent absence.
  • Miss MacIntosh despises the turtle for its slowness and sees no wisdom in it, associating it with sloth and ignorance.
  • The turtle’s carrying a clay flower pot with a geranium that smells of tobacco suggests a blend of nature and artifice, endurance, and perhaps the burden of life.

Time and Watches

See: Clocks and Watches

  • The silver dollar watch worn by Miss MacIntosh symbolizes the relentless march of time and the pressure of discipline.
  • Miss MacIntosh frequently refers to time as deceptive and insists on punctuality and the urgency of preparing for the future, reinforcing the theme of control versus Vera’s dreams.

Light and Darkness

See: Lamps, Candles, and Light

  • The interplay of light and darkness appears in the descriptions of the house and Vera’s inner world.
  • The rest of the house, Miss MacIntosh says, is overheated and smells of “cold marbles, like a funeral parlor,” emphasizing decay and death.
  • Vera’s dreams and secret thoughts are contrasted with the harsh reality imposed by Miss MacIntosh, symbolizing the tension between imagination and discipline.

Death and Dancing with Death

  • Death is personified as a companion Vera dances with, highlighting a close and intimate relationship with mortality.
  • The dialogue with Miss MacIntosh about Death emphasizes its inevitability and commonality but also Vera’s youthful fascination and defiance.

Marriage and Reproduction Imagery

See: Weddings and Funerals

  • Miss MacIntosh’s lectures on marriage, ovaries, and reproduction are laden with symbolic meaning about societal expectations, femininity, and the passage into adulthood.
  • Miss MacIntosh’s comparison (flowers impregnated only by the wind are colorless, “but with a woman, there must be a man, not merely the wind”) symbolizes the necessity of union and procreation in life, reflecting the cultural norms around marriage and gender roles.

The Party Dress and the Birthday Celebration

See: Clothing, Hats, and Skirts · Pregnancy, Birth, and Children

  • The party dress, described as filmy, sleeveless, and embroidered with seed pearls, symbolizes both Vera’s coming of age and the tension between innocence and emerging sexuality.
  • The empty birthday party and Vera dancing alone highlight loneliness, unfulfilled expectations, and the absence of community or connection.

Natural Elements and Geography

  • Miss MacIntosh’s frequent references to geography, natural phenomena, and history (e.g., Chicago fire, glaciers, grasshoppers, rivers) symbolize the structured, factual world she insists on teaching, contrasting with Vera’s inner dream world and rebellion.

Research: Resources

  • “Was it murder or the key turning of itself in the lock?”: Vera asks the question of Chapters 7 and 8, now of Miss MacIntosh. See the Chapter 7 resources.
  • “Desire be to thy husband”: God tells Eve, “thy desire shall be to thy husband” (Genesis 3:16). See Genesis.
  • “All of us are mortal, and some of us are more mortal than others”: George Orwell’s Animal Farm (1945): “All animals are equal, but some animals are more equal than others.”
  • “What Cheer, Iowa”: A real town in Keokuk County. Its name is said to come from Roger Williams’s greeting to the Narragansett, “What cheer, netop?” See Iowa, Indiana, and the Midwest.
  • “She was just the cross I had to bear”: “Whosoever doth not bear his cross, and come after me, cannot be my disciple” (Luke 14:27). See The Bible.
  • “Opportunity, it has been said, knocks only once at the door”: John James Ingalls’s poem “Opportunity” (1891): “I knock unbidden once at every gate.”
  • “Sit not there dreaming of Triton among the minnows”: Triton is a Greek god of the sea who later evolved into a merman. He is the messenger of his father, the god Poseidon. Wordsworth, in “The World Is Too Much with Us,” would rather be a pagan and “hear old Triton blow his wreathèd horn.” Miss MacIntosh would have none of it. See Greek Mythology and Romantic Poets.
  • “Time marches on”: The March of Time newsreels (1935-1951) closed with “Time marches on!”
  • “naked as in that day when we came from our mothers’ wombs”: “Naked came I out of my mother’s womb” (Job 1:21). See The Book of Job.
  • “Hope dies hard in the human breast”: Miss MacIntosh turns Pope’s “Hope springs eternal in the human breast” (An Essay on Man, 1734).
  • “When, Vera Cartwheel, did the first Viking land upon this bleak New England shore?”: Leif Erikson reached North America about 1000. The Norse site at L’Anse aux Meadows, Newfoundland, was found in 1960, and New Englanders long claimed Vikings had landed there.
  • “can you locate its source?”: The Mississippi rises at Lake Itasca, Minnesota, named its source by Henry Schoolcraft in 1832.
  • “for we were put here to be tested and not found wanting”: The writing on Belshazzar’s wall reads, “Thou art weighed in the balances, and art found wanting” (Daniel 5:27). Miss MacIntosh sees life as a rigorous discipline, where even suffering and failure have their place but must be met with fortitude. The phrase underscores her belief in the necessity of accepting life’s challenges as part of one’s duty and not giving way to despair or weakness. See The Bible.
  • “Charles’s Wain, the Hair of Berenice”: Charles’s Wain is the Big Dipper. Berenice’s Hair is the queen’s hair offered to the gods and set among the stars. Cassiopeia sits in her chair. See Astronomy.
  • “Twelve hours in a day, twelve hours in a night”: “Are there not twelve hours in the day?” (John 11:9). See The Bible.
  • “breaking into two parts like the worm”: Flatworms can be cut in two and each half grows into a whole worm.
  • “a loving couple need not ratify its bond by marriage”: Common-law marriage, by living together as husband and wife, is still recognized in Iowa. See Iowa, Indiana, and the Midwest.
  • “the apple was no sweet mackintosh”: The McIntosh apple, found in Ontario in 1811, carries Miss MacIntosh’s name. Genesis never names the fruit; the apple came from the Latin pun malum, “apple” and “evil.” See Genesis.
  • “God, Who had divided the light from the darkness and created great whales”: “And God created great whales . . . Be fruitful, and multiply, and fill the waters in the seas” (Genesis 1:21-22). See Genesis.
  • “had been found in the mouth of a dead salmon”: In Glasgow’s legend Saint Mungo recovered a queen’s ring from a salmon’s mouth, and Herodotus tells how Polycrates’s ring came back in a fish.
  • “the G which stood for Georgia”: Georgia is a female name from the Greek georgos, farmer, a fitting name for the earthbound Miss MacIntosh. Its masculine form is George.
  • “her bloomers, which were red jersey”: Amelia Bloomer promoted the loose trousers named for her in 1851.
  • “her underclothes had been made of bleached flour bags”: Poor families sewed clothes from flour and feed sacks, and by the 1930s mills printed the sacks in patterns for that use.
  • “the London Tower where the ravens were chained”: Legend says the kingdom will fall if the ravens leave the Tower of London, so their wings are clipped.
  • “the dark Satanic mills”: William Blake’s “Jerusalem” (1804). See Romantic Poets.
  • “The old ship would be entombed in an ice block with its captain still on board”: In the legend of the Octavius, a whaler found in 1775 drifting off Greenland, the captain sat frozen at his log.
  • “all the genealogies of the Moody Bible”: The Moody Bible Institute was founded in Chicago in 1886 by the evangelist Dwight L. Moody. It is a conservative, evangelical Bible college.
  • “the sons of Levi, Judah, Er, Onan, Issachar, the sons of Tola, Phuvah, Zebulun”: Miss MacIntosh makes Vera memorize the Bible’s genealogies for discipline. See The Bible.
    • Levi was the third son of Jacob and Leah in the Bible.
    • Judah was the fourth son of Jacob and Leah.
    • Er was the eldest son of Judah and a Canaanite wife (Genesis 38).
    • Onan was the second son of Judah. He spilled his seed on the ground (Genesis 38:9), an irony in a chapter about ovaries and seeds.
    • Issachar was the ninth son of Jacob.
    • Tola was a son of Issachar (Genesis 46:13), and he had six sons (1 Chronicles 7:2). A later Tola was one of the Judges of Israel (Judges 10:1).
    • Phuvah was another son of Issachar, like Tola. Zebulun was the last son of Jacob and Leah.
  • “the heave shoulder and the breast wave”: “The wave breast and the heave shoulder” are the priests’ portion of the sacrifice (Leviticus 7:34), and Vera turns the phrase around. See The Bible.
  • “Hannibal crossing the Alps with his elephants”: Hannibal crossed in 218 B.C. to attack Rome.
  • “in some legendary preadamite time”: Pre-Adamism is the belief that there were humans before Adam. Isaac La Peyrère argued in 1655 that men lived before Adam.
  • “the whole world on his back”: Vera says the turtle is so old that it might be the “World Turtle.” This myth is found in different parts of the world and different cultures. In Hindu myth the turtle Akupara holds up the world, and the Lenape and Haudenosaunee tell of the earth built on a turtle’s back, Turtle Island.
  • “Solomon, Miss MacIntosh objected, had had too many wives”: Solomon may be named after King Solomon of the Bible, who was regarded as a wealthy and wise king. Solomon “had seven hundred wives, princesses, and three hundred concubines” (1 Kings 11:3), and his temple had tables of gold, lamps, snuffers, and pomegranates (1 Kings 7). See The Bible.
  • “Wall Street or Threadneedle Street”: Wall Street is the banking center of the U.S., and Threadneedle Street is home of the Bank of England, “the Old Lady of Threadneedle Street.”
  • “My twelfth birthday, Miss MacIntosh said, was the dividing line”: Madge named twelve “the age of wisdom” too. See the Chapter 7 resources.
  • “Her red, marcelled hair”: The Marcel wave, set with hot irons, was invented by Marcel Grateau in Paris in 1872.
  • “Ovaries, I knew, were little brown pods filled with seeds”: Vera gives her own explanation of ovaries where there is a comparison to a school book which showed the anatomy of flowers. In a detailed drawing a flower has ovaries that look similar to the human female reproductive organs. In a flower the ovary holds the ovules, which become seeds. The anthers hold pollen.
  • “sixteen bleeding Greek metropolitans”: Greek metropolitans are archbishops who head a province of the Orthodox Church. Some were killed and became martyrs and saints. In 1922, when Smyrna burned, Metropolitan Chrysostomos was handed to a mob and mutilated to death, one bleeding Greek metropolitan the church made a saint.
    • The sixteen metropolitans may refer to the Greek genocide (1914-1922).
  • “the great Chicago fire”: It burned October 8-10, 1871, killed about three hundred people, and was blamed on Mrs. O’Leary’s cow, which shares a name with old Doc, Justice O’Leary.
  • “Where were those showers of grasshoppers?”: Rocky Mountain locusts swarmed the Plains in 1874-1877 in clouds that darkened the sun.
  • “Where were those seven years of lean? Who shall divide the wheat from the tares? Who hid his lantern under a bushel?”: Joseph’s seven lean years (Genesis 41), the parable of the wheat and the tares (Matthew 13:24-30), and the candle under a bushel (Matthew 5:15). See The Bible.
  • “There, but for God’s grace, go I”: “There but for the grace of God” is attributed to John Bradford in reference to a group of prisoners being led to execution. John Bradford was an English Reformer, a prebendary of St. Paul’s, and martyr. He was imprisoned in the Tower of London for alleged crimes against Queen Mary I. He was burned at the stake on July 1, 1555. (Wikipedia) Paul writes, “But by the grace of God I am what I am, and his grace toward me was not in vain” (1 Corinthians 15:10). This meaning fits into the broader themes of the novel around fate, suffering, and the search for meaning amidst human vulnerability.
  • “the thirteen year old son of a Portuguese fisherman”: Portuguese fishermen from the Azores settled New Bedford, Gloucester, and Provincetown.
  • “A blind violinist and a deaf dancer”: There are many blind, deaf, and mute people in the book. This could be a play on the Three Wise Monkeys. The Three Wise Monkeys are a Japanese folk representation of the proverb “see no evil, hear no evil, speak no evil.” They symbolize prudence and purity, and are often seen as a call for discretion or willful ignorance. The three monkeys are Mizaru (see no evil), Kikazaru (hear no evil), and Iwazaru (speak no evil). The concept originates in Japan, with statues of the monkeys found in temples and shrines. The proverb “see no evil, hear no evil, speak no evil” is often interpreted as a way to avoid negative experiences or situations by choosing to ignore them. In Japan, the monkeys are seen as attendants of Koshin, the God of Roads, and their message is used to teach prudence and purity. In the West, the proverb is often used sarcastically to criticize those who deliberately ignore wrongdoing. The idea is rooted in Confucius: “Look not at what is contrary to propriety; listen not to what is contrary to propriety; speak not what is contrary to propriety” (Analects 12.1, trans. James Legge). Some representations include a fourth monkey, Sezaru, who “does no evil.” (Wikipedia) One misses the train by seeing it but not hearing its whistle, the other by hearing but not seeing. See the Chapter 8 resources and Deafness and Sign Language.
  • “for tomorrow was another day”: Scarlett O’Hara’s last line in Gone with the Wind (1936): “After all, tomorrow is another day!”
  • “Early to bed and early to rise makes a man healthy, wealthy and wise”: The proverb praises rising before most others, early and consistently, so as to accomplish more in the day. This method has been recommended since antiquity. The philosopher Aristotle said a phrase very similar to the one Miss MacIntosh used. Within the context of religious observances, spiritual writers have called this practice the heroic minute, referring to the sacrifice which this entails. Benjamin Franklin printed the exact phrase Miss MacIntosh used in Poor Richard’s Almanack (1735). It is a saying that is viewed as a commonsensical proverb. (Wikipedia)
  • “this vale of tears”: “In hac lacrimarum valle,” from the hymn Salve Regina, after Psalm 84:6. See The Bible.
  • “It would be better to celebrate, not the day we were born into this world but the day we were born out of it”: “The day of death than the day of one’s birth” (Ecclesiastes 7:1). See Ecclesiastes.
  • “Was there even a dark angel at the gate? What horseman reining his horse at the door?”: Death rides a pale horse (Revelation 6:8). Lionel Johnson’s poem “The Dark Angel” (1893) is about a tempter who haunts the soul. See The Bible.
  • “Pythagoras who had a golden thigh”: Pythagoras was an ancient Greek philosopher. It is believed his teachings were metempsychosis, that every soul is immortal and after death enters another body, and musica universalis where the planets move according to mathematical equations and create an inaudible symphony of music. Legend says he showed a golden thigh at Olympia as a sign of his divinity. See Pythagoras and the Music of the Spheres.
  • “Proteus who changed from fish to bird before her eyes”: Proteus was an early Greek, shape-shifting sea-god. In the Odyssey Menelaus holds him fast while he turns into a lion, a serpent, a leopard, water, and a tree. See Greek Mythology.
  • “Pandora’s bottomless box”: Pandora was the first woman created and her story is used to explain why there is evil in the world. In Hesiod it was a jar. Erasmus made it a box in 1508. Only Hope stayed inside, and Miss MacIntosh says, “Hope dies hard in the human breast.” See Greek Mythology.
  • “Pythian games”: The Pythian Games were held at Delphi every four years in honor of Apollo, two years after each Olympics. They included music, poetry, and dance, and women could participate in some of the events. See the Chapter 6 resources on laurel.
  • “the canker eats the rose”: “And loathsome canker lives in sweetest bud” (Shakespeare, Sonnet 35). See Shakespeare.
  • “There is vomit at all tables”: “For all tables are full of vomit and filthiness” (Isaiah 28:8). See The Bible.
  • “the ephemera who last but for a day”: Mayflies, order Ephemeroptera, live as winged adults for a day or less.
  • “Died Abner as a fool died”: David’s lament for Abner, murdered by Joab: “Died Abner as a fool dieth?” (2 Samuel 3:33). This phrase is part of a broader meditation in the chapter on the impermanence of human life, the certainty of death, and the idea that all distinctions between people are ultimately erased by death. See The Bible.
  • “One died in his full strength. Another died in bitterness of soul. How died the wise man?”: Job 21:23-25, and “how dieth the wise man? as the fool” (Ecclesiastes 2:16). See The Book of Job and Ecclesiastes.
  • “When thou diest, I shall die with you”: Ruth 1:16-17 reads, “whither thou goest, I will go . . . Where thou diest, will I die.” See The Bible.
  • “Experience, as I have heard, is a much harder teacher”: Franklin: “Experience keeps a dear school, but fools will learn in no other” (Poor Richard, 1743).
  • “What makes you think they are not one?”: Love and death as one is the Liebestod, the love-death of Wagner’s Tristan und Isolde (1865). See Music and Composers.
  • “There are many gay deceivers”: A “gay deceiver” was an old name for a rake or seducer. Gay here could mean happy or may be in reference to homosexuals. The term gay to describe immorality or someone addicted to pleasure was in use in the 17th century. Gertrude Stein in 1922 used the word gay to specifically reference homosexuals. In 1950, the earliest reference found to date for the word gay as a self-described name for homosexuals came from Alfred A. Gross who used it in the June 1950 issue of SIR magazine. In a series of interviews with Susan S. Neville, Marguerite Young said she had lovers both male and female. There was a relationship where she would not marry him but said he could visit her every Tuesday for the rest of her life.
  • “the Islands of the Blessed”: Islands of the Blessed or the Fortunate Isles are the winterless earthly paradise of the heroes of Greek mythology. See Greek Mythology.
  • “the Islands of the Dead”: Arnold Böcklin’s painting Isle of the Dead (1880-1886), a rocky island of cypresses with a white-draped figure arriving by boat, inspired Rachmaninoff’s tone poem (1909). See Music and Composers.
  • “all local habitations and all names”: The poet “gives to airy nothing / A local habitation and a name” (A Midsummer Night’s Dream 5.1). See Shakespeare.
  • “Were not true marriages made in heaven”: “What therefore God hath joined together, let not man put asunder” (Matthew 19:6). See The Bible.

Chapter 78

← Chapter 77 · Home · Chapter 79 →

Content note: The Esther Longtree chapters (72 to 81) deal with stillbirth and pregnancy loss, rape, infanticide, racist violence including lynching, and cruelty to children. This chapter describes a mother’s cruelty to her young child, hitting her, tying her by a rope in the yard, and blaming her all her life for her twin’s stillbirth, and mentions a suicide in the family.

Summary

Esther was called Little Jackass from birth, because she was born kicking and stubborn. She grew up lonely, bullied at school for her deformed foot and crossed eyes, always stung by bees, always falling. Her tiny, cold mother, a pallid descendant of George Washington’s sister, hit her, tied her by a rope to a tree in the yard, and blamed her all her life for the death of her twin, Rosemary, whom Esther had kicked out of the womb months early, stillborn and buried under an unnamed pear tree; Rosemary would have been the perfect daughter. As a child Esther dug for her with a spoon and found only a thimble, beads, a broken doll, the toys of the dead. She loves her father, the passive policeman, who patrols the graveyard whistling to warn off the lovers and whose own mother spilled babies like leaves; she embarrasses her mother by telling that her father has a Negro streak and that her mother’s brother killed himself. She wonders whether she herself is the shadow, the one who never truly lived.

Characters present

Esther Longtree · Esther’s Father · Esther’s Mother · Rosemary

Concepts present

Themes: Guilt, Innocence, and Justice · Identity and the Self · Isolation and Connection · Memory and the Past · Nature, the Sea, and the Cosmos · Society, Class, and Race · Women, Gender, and Marriage

Symbols: Birds · Horses and Carriages · Pregnancy, Birth, and Children · Roses and Flowers · Shadows · Twins and Doubles · Weddings and Funerals

Philosophy: Augustine and Christian Theology

Allusions: Genesis · Iowa, Indiana, and the Midwest · Music and Composers · Pregnancy, Abortion, and Midwifery · Romantic Poets · Shakespeare · The Bible

Key passages

From the research

  • The opening lines explain why Esther was called “Little Jackass” because she was born stubborn, kicking, awkward, and reluctant to be born.
  • Esther’s father is described as a passive, slow, and timid policeman who patrols the graveyard at night to warn off lovers. Despite his loneliness and bad luck, Esther feels pity and love for him. She sees herself as a “chip off the old block,” sharing his nature but contrasting with her mother. This passage contrasts the warmth and vitality Esther inherits from her father with the coldness of her mother.
  • Her mother is portrayed as small, childish, and cold, with a narrow heart and fragile possessions. Everything in the house is built to her size and easily broken. Esther’s awkwardness and physical attributes are contrasted with her mother’s delicate, fragile nature. This passage helps explain Esther’s difficult upbringing and lack of maternal warmth.
  • Esther’s childhood is marked by physical accidents, deformities (like her crippled foot), and social abuse by other children. She is described as always stung by insects. There is the story of the bee flying up her skirts and the buzzing under her skin.
  • There is an important passage about Esther’s father’s mother, who gave birth many times, often without realizing it, and whose children mostly survived. This contrasts with Esther’s own fate, where she is haunted by the loss of her own stillborn children.
  • Central to the chapter is the revelation that Esther had a twin sister, Rosemary, who was born prematurely and dead because Esther had “kicked the other out” of the womb. This accusation, made repeatedly by her mother, defines much of Esther’s shame, guilt, and identity. Rosemary is described as perfect, delicate, and the child the mother would have preferred. Esther’s lifelong feeling of being a murderer and a shadow is tied to this traumatic event.
  • The mother constantly blames Esther for killing Rosemary before birth and accuses her of being ungrateful and awkward. Esther lives with this accusation, which shapes her self-perception as a mulish, sullen child who broke things and was not properly loved or nurtured. This deep maternal rejection is a key to understanding Esther’s emotional struggles.
  • Throughout her life, Esther looks for signs of Rosemary or the “other,” digging in the ground, finding small objects buried under trees, and interpreting shadows and noises as traces of the lost twin.
  • Esther sometimes wonders if she is the shadow and if the other twin was the one truly born. She doubts her own reality and existence, feeling like an elusive being or ghost.
  • The chapter closes with Esther’s reflection on loneliness, the emptiness of life, and the idea that no heart is as great as “non-heart,” no being as beautiful as “non-being.” She sometimes feels like a shadow, never fully found or understood.

Questions and observations

Reading closely

  • Her father says that to miss by an inch “was the same as to miss it by infinity.” What has he missed?
  • “No being so beautiful as non-being. No heart so great as non-heart.” Why would Esther believe this?
  • “The graveyard was the place where life began in this county, not where it ended.” What does she mean?

Characters

  • Her mother says “if the other had been born alive instead of this big creature, her mother would have been happier.” What does a child do with that?
  • “He whistled in the night to warn away the thieves, the lovers. She whistled to let them know when the coast was clear!” How are father and daughter alike?
  • Esther tells “that the father had a Negro streak in him, that the mother’s brother had committed suicide.” Why does she enjoy embarrassing her mother?

Connections

  • In Chapter 76 Esther confessed to killing her twin. Now we learn the charge came from her mother. Whose story is it?
  • Rosemary is for remembrance. What does Esther’s mother keep remembering, and what does she forget?
  • “She had been born instead of the shadow.” How is Esther like Mr. Spitzer, who is never sure which twin he is?

Reflection

  • “The children were wise by comparison with their fathers.” Is that so?
  • “Was she not the shadow?” Have you ever felt like the one who was not wanted?
  • Esther never found Rosemary, only “the toys of the dead creature.” What are we looking for when we dig up the past?

Research: Characters

Esther Longtree

  • She was called “Little Jackass” due to her stubborn, awkward nature and her difficult birth. She was born kicking and fighting against life itself, a symbol of resistance and struggle. Her childhood was lonely, marked by accidents, physical scars, and emotional neglect. She made friends of “her natural enemies, the woodpeckers, the bluejays.”
  • Esther wrestles with her identity, sometimes wondering if she is the “shadow,” the lesser, the one who should not have lived. She is caught between the life she has and the ghost of the twin she lost, a metaphor for the conflict between existence and non-existence, presence and absence.
  • A complex figure embodying strength, stubbornness, and vulnerability. She is deeply affected by her family’s past and her own mysterious shadow, the lost twin. Her physical awkwardness and emotional turmoil underscore her unique resilience and tragic circumstances.

Esther’s father

  • He is a passive policeman, seen as a lonely, timid man whose life is confined and unfulfilled. He patrols the graveyard to warn off lovers to avoid arrests. Her mother is a small, childlike woman with little understanding of life or Esther’s struggles. Their marriage lacks love, and Esther inherits nothing from her mother but much from her father’s robust, natural lineage.

Esther’s mother

  • She blames her for the death of her twin sister, Rosemary, who was born prematurely and dead. Esther is accused of killing this twin by kicking her in the womb, an act that haunts her throughout her life. This accusation shapes Esther’s self-perception as a murderer even before birth and contributes to her lifelong feelings of guilt and alienation.
  • She hit Esther for screaming about the bee, tied her by a rope in the yard, and “had never nursed her at those narrow breasts.”

Rosemary

  • Rosemary represents the idealized child who never lived, who would have been perfect and brought ease to the family. Esther’s mother mourns Rosemary and holds her up against Esther, constantly reminding Esther of what she supposedly destroyed. Esther, in contrast, struggles with this shadow, often questioning her own reality and identity.

Research: Themes

Loneliness and Isolation

See: Isolation and Connection

  • Esther’s life is marked by solitude and misunderstanding, from her childhood nickname to her estranged family relationships and societal alienation.

Identity and Self-Perception

See: Identity and the Self

  • The story explores Esther’s struggle with her own identity. She questions her own existence, haunted by the twin she allegedly killed and by feelings of being an outsider within her own family.

Guilt and Innocence

See: Guilt, Innocence, and Justice

  • Esther is burdened with a guilt she cannot fully understand or escape: accused of infanticide before she was even born. This theme explores the complexity of innocence and culpability.

Family Legacy and Conflict

See: Memory and the Past

  • The contrast between Esther’s parents, her father’s passivity and her mother’s childishness, frames her difficult inheritance and her complicated relationship with familial love and expectations.

Nature and Symbolism

See: Nature, the Sea, and the Cosmos

  • Birds, graveyards, and natural imagery symbolize life, death, and the cycles of existence. The graveyard is paradoxically described as a place of beginning as well as an end, reflecting Esther’s complicated view of life and death.

Research: Symbols and Imagery

The Graveyard

See: Weddings and Funerals

  • A place associated with both death and life, symbolizing the cycle of existence and the blurred line between endings and beginnings.

Birds and Nests

See: Birds

  • Birds (woodpeckers, bluejays, blackbirds) symbolize freedom, nature, and sometimes fragility. The blackbirds’ nest with pale blue eggs and gold hair suggests innocence and the preciousness of life, as well as the shadow of loss.

The Shadow

See: Shadows

  • The twin Rosemary often appears as a shadow figure, representing the unseen, the lost, and the internalized guilt and doubt within Esther.

The Alphabet Book and Toys

See: Pregnancy, Birth, and Children

  • Objects like the alphabet book, beads, and dolls symbolize childhood innocence, learning, and the traces of the lost twin’s existence.

Research: Resources

  • “she had been called by one name, Little Jackass”: Esther Longtree is portrayed in this chapter as a deeply tragic and complex character, burdened by loneliness, loss, and a profound sense of guilt that shapes her entire existence. Esther is introduced as a “mulish,” stubborn, and awkward individual, nicknamed “Little Jackass” because she was born kicking and resisting life from the very beginning. This obstinacy is both physical, shown in her accidents and bruises, and emotional, manifesting in her defiance against her circumstances and her family dynamics. Despite her struggles, Esther tries hard to embrace life, described poetically as a red rose “blooming in the heart of death” or a “white piano in a tinkling stream,” symbolizing her vitality and resilience amid suffering. Her family background is marked by estrangement and emotional coldness. Her father, a passive, slow, and timid policeman with a sad, isolated life, contrasts with Esther’s fiery nature. He patrols the graveyard to warn off lovers rather than arrest them, embodying a gentle but resigned presence. Esther inherits her strength and naturalness from her father’s lineage, which includes Irish, Indian, and possibly Negro ancestry, known for their robust fertility and natural births. In contrast, her mother is tiny, childish, emotionally cold, and narrow-hearted, representing a limiting and oppressive force in Esther’s life. A central element of Esther’s tragic identity is the burden of a lost twin, Rosemary, who was stillborn before Esther’s birth. Esther’s mother accuses her repeatedly, laughing and crying, that Esther “killed” Rosemary by kicking her out of the womb, condemning Esther as a murderer even before she was born. This accusation haunts Esther throughout her life, coloring her self-perception with guilt and shame. She grows up overshadowed by the memory of Rosemary, an idealized “perfect” child who would have been obedient, delicate, and beloved, the daughter her mother longed for. Esther, by contrast, is awkward, large, and defiant, and constantly reminded of her failure to be the child her mother wanted. Esther’s relationship with motherhood and fertility is deeply fraught. She is often pregnant or swollen but has lost many children, described metaphorically as “little birds,” “snowflakes,” or “stillborn,” which reflects the repeated cycle of hope and grief she endures. She carries a secret sorrow for these lost children, which she can never openly mourn or explain, and she battles both physical and emotional pain, including an enlarged heart and a crippled foot, which further symbolize her suffering. Her internal world is haunted by shadows, rustlings, and the presence of the lost children, hinting at a mystical or spectral dimension to her grief. Esther digs holes in the earth, searching for remnants of the past, the “shadow” of her twin, and the lost children, but never fully finds peace or closure. She experiences a profound alienation, sometimes doubting her own reality and identity, wondering if she herself is the shadow or the lesser existence, while Rosemary is the “real” one who should have lived. Despite all this, Esther is not without moments of fierce joy and strength. Her laughter can be loud and powerful, shaking the snow from clouds, and she fiercely protects and claims love for the children she does carry, even if they do not survive. Her stubbornness and vitality make her a figure of tragic endurance, struggling against the “nameless grave” and the weight of familial expectations and curses. Esther Longtree is a figure of intense contradiction: strong yet vulnerable, life-affirming yet haunted by death, natural yet marked by unnatural loss. Her story in this chapter reveals themes of maternal grief, the burden of inherited trauma, and the search for identity amid family secrets and personal suffering. Her character embodies the tragic complexity of fertility and loss, the interplay of life and death, and the painful legacies passed down through generations. See Esther Longtree.
    • Esther Longtree symbolizes a deep and painful history of struggle, loss, and marginalization that can be read as a reflection of certain aspects of American history, particularly those involving the complex legacies of race, family, and survival. Her lineage is described as mixed: “partly Irish and partly Indian and maybe even had a Negro streak in them,” suggesting the multiracial and multicultural heritage that is part of the American fabric, especially in the context of colonial and frontier histories where Indigenous peoples, European settlers, and African descendants intersected. This mixed heritage points to the tangled histories of racial identity and the often painful intersections of different communities in the United States. Esther’s life is marked by hardship, loneliness, and repeated loss: she has borne many children who have died before or shortly after birth, symbolizing the high rates of infant and maternal mortality historically faced by impoverished, marginalized, or rural populations in the US. Her mother’s accusation that Esther “killed a little child before she was ever born,” referring to the death of her twin Rosemary, suggests the tragic fate of many families who suffered such losses quietly and without support. Her father, a passive policeman whose “life was a prison,” represents the ordinary working-class man trapped in a limited existence, disconnected from emotional life and unable to protect or nurture fully. This dynamic echoes the social and economic constraints faced by many in American history, especially in small, insular communities where traditional roles and isolation prevailed. Esther’s story also touches on the theme of women’s experiences of oppression and misunderstanding: her mother’s coldness, the abuse from schoolmates, and her own physical and emotional pain symbolize the harsh realities women have faced, including neglect, judgment, and the burden of reproductive suffering. Esther’s “mulish” nature and stubbornness reflect resistance and survival despite these adversities, embodying the resilience necessary to endure “long trial, long suffering.” Esther Longtree’s narrative can be understood as a microcosm of the American historical experience involving racial mixture, frontier hardship, the struggles of working-class families, the tragedy of loss, and the resilience of women caught in cycles of suffering and survival. Her character embodies the silent histories of pain and endurance that underlie much of the American story.
  • “being a white piano in a tinkling stream”: “I am a white piano,” Esther says in the Chapter 72 resources; in the Chapter 74 resources she is “only a silent piano with dusty keys.” See Music and Composers.
  • “she was the chip off the old block”: When the young William Pitt first spoke in Parliament in 1781, Edmund Burke said he was “not merely a chip of the old block, but the old block itself.” See Esther’s Father.
  • “He showed him the way to the bank”: Indiana’s John Dillinger robbed banks across the Midwest in 1933 and 1934 and broke out of the Crown Point, Indiana, jail with a wooden gun. See Iowa, Indiana, and the Midwest.
  • “The children were wise by comparison with their fathers”: The novel portrays children, especially characters like Esther Longtree and Musidora’s children, as burdened by premature or inappropriate knowledge of sexual realities. This knowledge is often linked to trauma, loss, and the failure of adult protection. Esther Longtree is depicted as a woman who has been “always pregnant,” with many stillborn children and a pervasive sense of loss, loneliness, and burden. She is surrounded by the imagery of children who have suffered or died, and these children represent both literal and symbolic figures of innocence lost and corrupted sexuality. The children are often shown as victims of adult failures, such as unloving or absent parents, societal neglect, and the consequences of adult promiscuity or irresponsibility. They are described as “wise” beyond their years, aware of harsh truths that should be hidden from them, and sometimes as reproachful presences haunting their mothers or the community. Vera, and other characters, like Madge, observe that these children are burdened with knowledge and experiences they cannot comprehend or control, symbolizing a premature confrontation with adult realities. This is reflected in phrases like children “playing at hanging themselves,” or being “mysterious shrouded presences” who cause confusion and suffering. The presence of sexually aware children also ties into the motif of pregnancy and birth, which in the novel is often depicted as fraught with mystery, loss, and sometimes death. The characters’ struggles with conception, stillbirths, and motherhood are interwoven with a cultural critique of the consequences of repressed or mismanaged sexuality. The motif symbolizes the erosion of childhood innocence in a world where adult hypocrisies, failures, and social decay impinge on the young. It reflects a cultural anxiety about the premature sexualization of children and the failure of society to protect them. These children embody the consequences of broken families, absent or irresponsible parents, and a society that neglects its vulnerable members. Their knowledge of sex is not empowering but burdensome, linked to trauma rather than understanding. The novel critiques the social conditions that produce such outcomes: poverty, neglect, and moral confusion. The children represent lost potential and fragmented identities, paralleling the novel’s themes of multiplicity and fractured selves. Their awareness of sex and its consequences contrasts with their powerlessness and the mysteries surrounding birth, life, and death. The motif also connects with the novel’s larger exploration of dreams, illusions, and altered states of consciousness. The children’s premature knowledge is part of a distorted reality, where what is known and unknown, real and unreal, is blurred. Their sexual awareness is part of the complex interplay between truth and illusion that defines the novel’s atmosphere. By highlighting the plight of children burdened with adult knowledge, the novel implicitly critiques the social hypocrisies surrounding sex, marriage, and reproduction. It questions the societal failure to provide clear, honest guidance and protection, instead leaving children to navigate complex, often harmful realities alone. See Women, Gender, and Marriage.
  • “She had been abused by her schoolmates”: Esther Longtree endured significant bullying from her schoolmates and other children during her childhood. She was nicknamed “Little Jackass” because of her stubborn, awkward nature and physical deformities, including a deformed foot and crossed eyes. The children made fun of her for these traits as well as for her “streaming hair” and her mulish head, which she was always sticking into old wasps’ nests, a behavior her mother had criticized as well. Esther was often stung and worried by wasps, bees, and flies, which added to her distress. Her physical awkwardness and accidents (she was always falling, her knees scarred, and her body black and blue) made her a target for ridicule. The children’s cruelty was compounded by Esther’s own suffering and her mother’s lack of understanding or protection, leaving her lonely and often crying in the dark. The bullying was not just verbal but tied to Esther’s physical and emotional isolation, making her childhood unhappy and lonely.
  • “She was the red, red rose”: “O my Luve’s like a red, red rose, / That’s newly sprung in June” (Robert Burns, 1794). See Roses and Flowers and Romantic Poets.
  • “Poor Little Jackass, stinging inside”: See Balaam’s ass and the barren mule in the Chapter 72 resources. See Horses and Carriages.
  • “stealing the food out of the icebox”: An icebox is a compact non-mechanical refrigerator which was a common early-twentieth-century kitchen appliance before the development of safely powered refrigeration devices. Before the development of electric refrigerators, iceboxes were referred to by the public as refrigerators. The terms icebox and refrigerator were used interchangeably in advertising as long ago as 1848.
    • Esther Longtree’s lack of food is described as a persistent and painful condition that has been part of her life even before she was pregnant. She is characterized by an empty stomach because she could not eat enough to give her strength. The chapter notes that even before pregnancy, Esther was always hungry and resorted to stealing food from the icebox when her mother wasn’t looking. This chronic hunger is part of her broader suffering and physical weakness, contributing to her difficult existence marked by accidents, bruises, and a crippled foot. Esther’s experience of hunger and deprivation can be seen as a personal reflection of broader themes of scarcity and struggle that many individuals have faced historically. The narrative situates Esther’s hunger within a familial and emotional context of neglect, poverty, and hardship as her mother’s household is described as small and fragile, with delicate objects easily broken, and her father as a passive policeman with little home life, suggesting an environment of limited resources and emotional deprivation. The history of child hunger in the U.S. includes its public “discovery” in the late 1960s, which led to the creation of federal programs like the Special Food Service Program (now the Summer Food Service Program) and the Supplemental Nutrition Program for Women, Infants, and Children (WIC). The 1980s saw the development of metrics like “food insecurity” to better measure the problem, and despite fluctuations, child hunger remains a significant issue, with families of color and single-parent households disproportionately affected. The federal programs and the 1980s measures postdate 1964.
  • “Her mother used to tie her by a rope”: Vera narrates the harsh and painful parental abuse Esther Longtree endured from a very early age. Esther’s mother is portrayed as a cold, narrow-hearted woman who blamed Esther for the death of her twin sister, Rosemary, even before Esther was born. Her mother repeatedly accused her of having “killed a little child before she was ever born,” labeling her guilty of infanticide in the womb, which created a deep sense of shame and guilt in Esther throughout her life. This accusation was a source of constant reproach and emotional cruelty, with her mother both laughing and crying as she reminded Esther of this supposed crime. The mother also expressed disappointment and resentment toward Esther, comparing her unfavorably to the lost twin, Rosemary, who was idealized as perfect, delicate, and the daughter her mother wished she had. This kept Esther in a state of embarrassment and alienation, burdened by the shadow of the lost child and her mother’s cold judgment. Esther’s mother physically abused her as a child, exemplified when she once hit Esther for screaming about a bee that had flown up her skirts, not believing her and dismissing her cries. Esther was also tied by a rope in the yard under a tree by her mother, indicating neglect and harsh treatment. The mother is described as childish in mentality and size, living in a house too small for both her and Esther, filled with fragile objects that seemed to symbolize the fragile and oppressive environment Esther was subjected to. The emotional abuse extended to lack of nurturing; Esther’s mother never nursed her at the narrow breasts or stayed to comfort her tears. She also mocked Esther’s awkwardness, physical deformities, and stubborn nature, further isolating her emotionally. The mother’s coldness was a constant presence, leaving Esther to grow up lonely and unloved, intensifying her suffering. Esther’s maternal abuse was a complex mixture of emotional cruelty, neglect, physical punishment, and harsh judgment rooted in the tragic loss of her twin and her mother’s inability to love her fully, which deeply affected Esther’s sense of self and her life trajectory. See Esther’s Mother.
  • “partly Irish and partly Indian and maybe even had a Negro streak”: Indiana outlawed marriage between white and Black people for most of its history and repealed the ban only in 1965, two years before Loving v. Virginia (1967) ended such laws everywhere. See Society, Class, and Race and Iowa, Indiana, and the Midwest.
  • “She would turn, bend, spill a baby”: A precipitate labor, three hours or less from the first contractions to birth, can deliver a baby before the mother has time to lie down. See Pregnancy, Abortion, and Midwifery.
  • “that needle’s eye through which the camel shall not pass”: “It is easier for a camel to go through the eye of a needle, than for a rich man to enter into the kingdom of God” (Matthew 19:24, KJV). See also the Chapter 72 resources. See The Bible.
  • “the swaddling clothes which she had buried”: “And she brought forth her firstborn son, and wrapped him in swaddling clothes, and laid him in a manger” (Luke 2:7, KJV). See The Bible.
  • “pallid descendant of George Washington’s sister”: Esther says her mother is a “pallid descendant of George Washington’s sister.” This may refer to Betty Washington Lewis who was the younger sister of George Washington and the only sister that survived childhood. Betty Washington was born into the Washington Family as the first daughter of Augustine Washington and Mary Ball Washington.
    • Elizabeth “Betty” Washington Lewis (1733-1797) was George Washington’s only sister to survive to adulthood and a dedicated patriot. She managed the family estate, Kenmore, in Fredericksburg, Virginia, while her husband, Fielding Lewis, supported the Revolution. She faced financial hardships and managed the household after her husband’s death.
  • “kicking against them all, against the traces”: “It is hard for thee to kick against the pricks” (Acts 9:5, KJV), said of Saul, the persecutor, before he became Paul; the pricks are the goads that drive an ox. See The Bible.
  • “She was not born innocent and stainless”: “Behold, I was shapen in iniquity; and in sin did my mother conceive me” (Psalm 51:5, KJV). Augustine, in the first book of his Confessions, saw sin even in the jealous infant at the breast; the doctrine of original sin holds that every child is born guilty. See The Bible and Augustine and Christian Theology.
  • “Poor, poor little thing, poor little other one who would have loved her mother so much, Rosemary”: “There’s rosemary, that’s for remembrance; pray, love, remember” (Ophelia, Hamlet, 4.5). Esther’s mother remembers Rosemary all her life. See Rosemary, Shakespeare, and Twins and Doubles.
  • “flesh of her flesh”: “This is now bone of my bones, and flesh of my flesh” (Genesis 2:23, KJV). See Genesis.
  • “Her mother had accused her of murder”: Esther’s mothers behavior is a form of severe emotional abuse with devastating psychological consequences for the surviving child. The parent’s actions are often rooted in their own inability to cope with the trauma, grief, and feelings of helplessness surrounding the death. Individuals with narcissistic or antisocial traits may lack empathy and view their children as objects to be used to regulate their own emotions. In this context, blaming the child can serve the parent’s emotional needs rather than the child’s. See Esther’s Mother.
  • “her having killed somebody without shedding of blood”: “And almost all things are by the law purged with blood; and without shedding of blood is no remission” (Hebrews 9:22, KJV). See The Bible and Guilt, Innocence, and Justice.
