Chapter 65

← Chapter 64 · Home · Chapter 66 →

Content note: Mr. Bonebreaker, a missionary, speaks of “the dirty Jew” and the stars he wins for each Jew he converts.

Summary

As August turns to September, Miss MacIntosh, bald and half dressed, plays solitaire and mends a pair of black gloves; Vera reveals that these are the gloves she wore when she walked into the ocean one September morning, leaving her wig, her corset, and her umbrella on the beach. The umbrella was Mr. Bonebreaker’s, and Miss MacIntosh tells the story. Weak after losing her left breast and setting ninepins in a Chicago bowling alley, she was found reeling in the street by Titus Bonebreaker, a vegetarian Gospel salesman from the Ozarks who preached the end of the world through a trumpet and believed his grandmother’s story that he was the true King of Sweden. He called her the little sister who had no breasts, praised the hair she did not have, gave her his watch, and kept postponing their wedding. On the night before it, she stood before him naked and bald under an electric bulb. He fled, leaving his umbrella, and later married a foreign girl to give her child a name. Miss MacIntosh worked among the blind, drifted east, spent her savings in Buffalo on white clothes and an ashen wig, and stood alone among the honeymooners at Niagara Falls.

Characters present

Miss MacIntosh · Mr. Titus Bonebreaker · Richard MacIntosh · John Knox MacIntosh · Mercy MacIntosh · Vera Cartwheel

Concepts present

Themes: Faith, God, and the Supernatural · Identity and the Self · Illusion and Reality · Isolation and Connection · Love · Society, Class, and Race · Time · Women, Gender, and Marriage

Symbols: Angels, Devils, and Myth · Clocks and Watches · Clothing, Hats, and Skirts · Eyes and Blindness · Hair, Wig, and Baldness · The Sea and Water · The Umbrella · Weddings and Funerals

Philosophy: Buddhism · Hinduism · Marguerite Young on Her Craft

Allusions: American Religious Movements · Ancient Egypt · Don Quixote · Ecclesiastes · Exploration and the Poles · Gambling and Playing Cards · Genesis · Greek Mythology · Iowa, Indiana, and the Midwest · Judaism · Music and Composers · Revelation and the Apocalypse · Shakespeare · Suicide in History and Literature · The Bible · The Book of Job

Key passages

From the research

  • Early in the chapter, Vera reflects on Miss MacIntosh’s many moods and the symbolic nature of her baldness. Her bald head, described as a “prism or a flame,” becomes a metaphor for her essential loneliness and mystery, a symbol of life and death intertwined.
  • Miss MacIntosh expresses disdain for “old kings of gold and silver towers,” traditional dreams of grandeur, and religious or royal symbolism such as the King James Bible and king crabs. She values the natural world and simple facts, rejecting illusions and pretenses. This passage highlights her grounded perspective and her rejection of false hopes or societal conventions.
  • A large part of the chapter focuses on Mr. Bonebreaker, the Gospel salesman. His character is described vividly: a man driven by religious zeal, preaching the end of the world, carrying a long black umbrella, and possessing a complex personality filled with contradictions.
  • The narrative details the courtship and engagement of Miss MacIntosh and Mr. Bonebreaker, which is fraught with difficulties. Mr. Bonebreaker’s inability to accept Miss MacIntosh’s physical reality, her baldness and mutilation, is a critical moment. When she reveals herself without her wig and shows her wounds, he reacts with shock and flees, leaving behind his umbrella and Bible literature.
  • Throughout the chapter, Miss MacIntosh contemplates mortality and the nature of existence. She plans simply to live as long as she can and then to die without ceremony (no coffin, no forwarding address) accepting life and death on her own terms. Her quiet strength and acceptance contrast with Mr. Bonebreaker’s fiery religiosity.
  • After Mr. Bonebreaker leaves, Miss MacIntosh supports herself by working with the blind in Chicago, finding some solace among those who cannot see her physical wounds. Eventually, she flees Chicago, drifting eastward with a sense of loneliness and the painful memory of her failed romance. This passage portrays her resilience and the painful solitude she endures.
  • The black umbrella and the luminous watch given by Mr. Bonebreaker serve as symbols of their relationship and of faith and protection. After he flees, she keeps these items, but they are reminders of a lost and failed connection. The umbrella especially symbolizes shelter and salvation that proved illusory.
  • Throughout the text, there is a striking contrast between Miss MacIntosh’s sober, pragmatic view of the world and Mr. Bonebreaker’s apocalyptic and evangelical fervor. He preaches the end of the world, judgment, and salvation, while she quietly endures and accepts life’s hardships, reflecting a tension between religious hope and human reality.
  • Miss MacIntosh’s visit to Niagara Falls, a place of honeymooners and new beginnings, is poignant. She stands alone, no bridegroom or escort, with only her black umbrella. The noise and joy around her contrast sharply with her solitude and lost dreams.

Questions and observations

Reading closely

  • “It was the one and only time a man possessed her, body and soul.” What does “possessed” mean for an embrace that lasts a moment?
  • Mr. Bonebreaker calls her “that little sister who had no breasts.” How does he turn Scripture into a wound?
  • “She was neither sinful nor beautiful.” How does Miss MacIntosh measure herself against his compliments?

Characters

  • Mr. Bonebreaker eats no meat, “but he would eat an egg, never supposing that it was the unborn he ate with such gusto.” What do his inconsistencies show?
  • Miss MacIntosh “could not agree that the Jews should be singled out for the brightest, biggest stars,” and at her mission “People of all races were to be admitted.” Where does she stand apart from him?
  • When she stands before him, “He was like a crazy, snared bird when he saw her.” Why does the man who preached the end of the world flee from one bald woman?

Connections

  • The gloves she mends are “those very black gloves she must have worn” into the sea. How does Vera’s foreknowledge change this chapter?
  • “The sun and the moon shone in the same pearly sky when she walked into the ocean.” Where did Miss MacIntosh foretell this in Chapter 63?
  • On the beach lay “her black umbrella, Mr. Bonebreaker’s umbrella.” How does knowing where the umbrella came from change it?

Reflection

  • “Only in love does one notice these things.” Is that true?
  • “Life is never in accordance with what we think it is.” When has that been true?
  • “There is surely a man somewhere in every woman’s life.” What does Miss MacIntosh, whose one love was Lorena, mean by this?

Research: Characters

Miss MacIntosh

  • A woman of many moods and contradictions, both physically and emotionally marked by her ailments.
  • She is bald, missing a breast, and wears wigs to mask her reality.
  • Profoundly lonely and marked by a sense of loss, she is simultaneously resigned and hopeful.
  • She embodies a “pilgrim’s progress from nowhere to nowhere,” with a simple, austere view of life and death.
  • Her internal conflict centers on her past, her physical condition, and her tenuous relationship with faith and society.
  • She is portrayed as both vulnerable and strong, practical yet mystical.

Mr. Titus Bonebreaker

  • A passionate, zealous Gospel salesman from Missouri, characterized by his fervor and eccentricity.
  • He preaches about the impending end of the world, salvation, and the need for repentance.
  • He is physically gaunt and stoop-shouldered, with distinctive features like a beaked nose and bright eyes.
  • Despite his religious zeal, he is inconsistent and flawed (e.g., his diet, brushes with police, personal hygiene).
  • He represents religious fanaticism and the human desire for meaning and redemption amid decay and despair.
  • His relationship with Miss MacIntosh is complex: he idealizes her, but ultimately fails to accept her fully.
  • His preaching is openly racist and antisemitic: Black men are to be shipped back to Africa as “the sons of Ham,” and each Jew he saves earns him a star twice as bright. Miss MacIntosh disagrees with him, “quite flatly.”
  • His first name may refer to Titus the Roman emperor from 79 to 81 AD, who was also a celebrated military general. He is known for leading the Roman army to victory in the First Jewish-Roman War, which resulted in the destruction of Jerusalem and its temple. His brief reign as emperor is notable for the eruption of Mount Vesuvius and the opening of the Colosseum. Titus is also the companion to whom Paul wrote the Epistle to Titus.

Richard MacIntosh

  • He is Miss MacIntosh’s brother, a primitive Christian bishop from Iowa who went to the Easter Islands to convert the heathen but disappeared, presumably a victim of head-hunters. He represents a failed attempt to impose a particular belief system onto a different culture, and his fate is a source of anxiety for Miss MacIntosh.

John Knox MacIntosh

  • He is Miss MacIntosh’s father.

Mercy MacIntosh

  • She is Miss MacIntosh’s mother.

Research: Themes

Loneliness and Isolation

See: Isolation and Connection

  • Miss MacIntosh’s life is defined by solitude, both physical and emotional.
  • Her baldness and physical wounds symbolize her vulnerability and societal alienation.
  • She finds some solace among the blind, where her own differences are less visible.

Faith, Salvation, and Doubt

See: Faith, God, and the Supernatural

  • The chapter explores the tension between religious fervor, spiritual hope, and personal doubt.
  • Mr. Bonebreaker’s apocalyptic preaching contrasts with Miss MacIntosh’s pragmatic and skeptical attitude.
  • Her rejection of his God and his ultimate flight from her when confronted with her full reality illustrates this tension.

The Body and Physical Affliction

See: Hair, Wig, and Baldness · Women, Gender, and Marriage

  • The physical condition of Miss MacIntosh (her baldness, lost breast, and scars) are central to the narrative.
  • They symbolize both human frailty and inner strength.
  • Her mending of black gloves carries guilt. Young’s psychiatrist friend explained “all the meanings of the word black and gloves in relation to psychology and guilt” (Marguerite Young, interview with Charles Ruas, WBAI radio, New York), and she told Studs Terkel, “I finally understood why it was again a symbol of guilt” (Marguerite Young, interview with Studs Terkel, WFMT radio, 1965).

The End of Time and Apocalypse

See: Time

  • Mr. Bonebreaker’s constant preaching about the “Last Day,” the destruction of Chicago, and the fall of creation permeates the narrative.
  • This apocalyptic vision frames the personal drama within a cosmic scale.

Identity, Appearance, and Reality

See: Illusion and Reality · Identity and the Self

  • Miss MacIntosh’s wearing of wigs and her attempt to hide her baldness reflects issues of identity and societal perception.
  • The contrast between appearances and inner reality is a recurring motif.
  • Mr. Bonebreaker’s idealized view of her contrasts sharply with her own self-perception.

Research: Symbols and Imagery

The Black Umbrella

See: The Umbrella

  • Carried by Mr. Bonebreaker, symbolizes protection, shelter, and religious zeal.
  • When left behind, it signifies abandonment and the collapse of Miss MacIntosh’s hopes.

Baldness and Hairlessness

See: Hair, Wig, and Baldness

  • Represents vulnerability, loss, and the stripping away of pretense.
  • Contrasted with Mr. Bonebreaker’s idealized descriptions of hair and beauty.

Mutilated Crockery and Black Gloves

See: Clothing, Hats, and Skirts

  • Symbols of care, brokenness, and preparation for hardship or death.

Niagara Falls and Honeymooners’ Hotel

See: The Sea and Water

  • Represents the irony of Miss MacIntosh’s solitude amidst joy and new beginnings for others.

The Watch and Biblical Quotations

See: Clocks and Watches · Angels, Devils, and Myth

  • Mr. Bonebreaker’s watch symbolizes time running out, the urgency of salvation, and the inevitability of the end.

Research: Resources

  • “the old King James version which was, in her pale esteem, befogged”: The King James Bible (1611) was made at the order of James I, the Stuart king; Miss MacIntosh objects to it as she objects to all royalty, “even to king crabs, kingfishers, king posts.” See The Bible.
  • “just as she had done to the King of Sweden”: See the King of Sweden in the Chapter 64 resources, and Mr. Bonebreaker below. See Mr. Titus Bonebreaker.
  • “playing solitaire with a pack of the old playing cards”: Solitaire originated in Europe in the late 18th century, likely in Germany or Scandinavia, with early versions potentially used for fortune-telling. The game, also known as Patience, spread to France and England in the 19th century, with the first rule books appearing around the 1870s. See the solitary player in the Chapter 60 resources. See Gambling and Playing Cards.
  • “In Chinese gambling dens”: Vera recounts Miss MacIntosh’s memories and opinions, which include several stereotypes about Chinese people: Miss MacIntosh states, “Did I know that the Chinese are a nearly hairless people, that Chinese men prefer a hairless woman with small breasts?” This perpetuates a stereotype about the physical characteristics of Chinese individuals. Miss MacIntosh mentions Chinese gambling dens where men play solitaire and are watched to prevent cheating the “invisible partner.” This associates Chinese culture with gambling and implies a need for surveillance to ensure fair play. Miss MacIntosh claims to have learned solitaire in San Francisco’s Chinatown, suggesting a connection between the game and Chinese culture.
  • “called by many the Windy City”: Chicago’s nickname mocked its boastful promoters and politicians, its “windy” talkers, as much as its weather. A popular story credits Charles A. Dana of the New York Sun, writing in 1890 while Chicago and New York competed to host the 1893 World’s Columbian Exposition, but his editorial has never been found, and the name was already in print by 1876, when a Cincinnati Enquirer headline, “That Windy City,” joked about both a tornado and Chicago’s speakers (Barry Popik, in Evan Andrews, “Why Is Chicago Called the Windy City?,” History.com). Chicagoans came to wear the name with pride. The lake does bring strong winds to the waterfront, and the cold winter wind is called “The Hawk.” See Iowa, Indiana, and the Midwest.
    • Chicago’s history began with Indigenous peoples, followed by French fur traders and the first permanent settler, Jean Baptiste Point du Sable, in the late 1700s. The city was officially founded in 1837 and grew into a major transportation hub for canals and railroads, becoming an industrial and commercial center by the late 19th century. The city experienced rapid expansion, and key events include the Great Chicago Fire of 1871, which destroyed much of the city but led to a period of robust rebuilding, and the 1893 World’s Columbian Exposition, which boosted the city’s reputation.
    • Chicago’s history spans from Native American roots as Shikaakwa (wild onion place) through its rapid 19th-century growth into a major industrial hub, the Gilded Age’s steel and meatpacking dominance, the devastating Great Fire of 1871, its rise as a cultural center (World’s Fairs, jazz), the Prohibition-era crime, the political machine era under Mayor Richard J. Daley, and its emergence as a modern metropolis, all while grappling with significant immigration, racial tension, and urban development leading up to the turbulent late 1960s.
  • “the old playing cards with the Dutch windmills flying on their backs”: Waddingtons in England, produced playing cards featuring Dutch windmills on the backs, often in sealed, faux-leather boxes, with designs popular in the 1950s and 1960s for their quaint, scenic appeal. See Gambling and Playing Cards.
  • “Chasing windmills—Miss MacIntosh had always been chasing windmills”: Miss MacIntosh told Vera she had been chasing Dutch windmills. Another character, Mrs. Hogden, claims to have lived in a Dutch windmill. Moses Hunnecker, the bus driver of Chapter 1, is also imagined as “some mad Don Quixote chasing windmills.” Windmills in the Dutch style stand in the United States too, among them the Fabyan Windmill outside Chicago and the two in San Francisco’s Golden Gate Park (1903, 1908), the two cities of Miss MacIntosh’s solitaire. Tilting at windmills is an idiom for attacking imaginary enemies from the novel Don Quixote by Miguel de Cervantes. It is a founding book in Western literature and is labeled the first modern novel. Antonio Rivas of Dickinson College called it “a very good reminder of why we read, why we watch movies, why we need fiction and imagination” (“Chasing Windmills,” Dickinson College, April 21, 2015). According to Mark Aldrich of Dickinson College, in a video for the novel’s 400th anniversary (Dickinson College, 2015, YouTube), Don Quixote is the story of an older man who has lost his mind over his obsession with literature and decides to go and live these adventures of time past. Little by little through his friendship with his companion he recovers his mind. It is ultimately the journey of one man finding out who he really is. Quixote is the highest aspirations of human beings. It pits the world of imagination against the terrible reality of modern life. It highlights the challenges of understanding one’s identity. There is a parallel between Don Quixote and Miss MacIntosh My Darling in that it is not a book of issues but of tissues, like an onion, you find layer after layer upon subsequent rereadings. Don Quixote stands for change and renovating society. He wants to help the poor and the oppressed. See On tilting at windmills, Don Quixote, and Moses Hunnecker.
  • “her brother Richard who had disappeared among the islands of Oceania”: Oceania is a vast geographical region in the Pacific Ocean, encompassing Australia, New Guinea, New Zealand, and thousands of smaller islands, traditionally divided into Melanesia, Micronesia, and Polynesia, plus Australasia (Australia/NZ). It’s defined by the ocean, featuring diverse climates and landforms, from large continental islands like Australia to tiny coral atolls, with cultures shaped by unique island isolation and later European colonization. See On Richard MacIntosh and the Easter Islands.
    • Richard MacIntosh is Miss MacIntosh’s brother.
    • “Polynesian head-hunters”: Polynesian headhunting, particularly prominent in places like the Solomon Islands (Melanesia, often grouped with Polynesian cultures in historical accounts) and among the Māori of New Zealand, wasn’t just about violence; it served deep cultural, spiritual, and economic purposes, often tied to ancestor worship, capturing soul matter, avenging deaths, enhancing warrior status, and controlling land, with practices evolving and often intensifying or changing due to European contact and the trade in preserved heads (mokomokai).
  • “in old San Francisco’s old Chinatown”: Chinatown, San Francisco is the oldest in North America and was founded in the 1840s by Chinese immigrants seeking opportunity during the Gold Rush but found refuge from discrimination. It grew into a tight-knit community that preserved Chinese culture and provided mutual support, despite facing prejudice that led to events like the 1882 Chinese Exclusion Act. The neighborhood was rebuilt after the 1906 earthquake and has since become a vibrant cultural hub, officially renamed “Chinatown” by the press in 1853.
  • “just before the Golden Gate was built”: Miss MacIntosh claims to have been there right before the Golden Gate Bridge was built. This would place her there before the bridge opened in 1937; construction began in 1933. She also claims it may have been foggy so she didn’t see it.
  • “And the Arabs had their topknots by which God might fish for them”: The topknot hairstyle has ancient origins in various cultures, often symbolizing status, maturity, or spiritual significance. Historically, it was adopted by samurai in Japan for practical reasons, such as securing their helmets, while in ancient China it was worn by scholars and nobility. In South Asian traditions, it holds religious meaning, and in Korean society, it was used to signify adulthood. Many Muslim men in Egypt once shaved the head but left a small tuft, the “shoosheh,” on the crown; Edward William Lane was told it was kept so that a Muslim slain by an unbeliever would not have his head carried in an unclean way (An Account of the Manners and Customs of the Modern Egyptians, 1836). The belief Miss MacIntosh repeats, that God would draw the faithful up to heaven by the tuft, is folk belief rather than Islamic teaching; the hadith forbid qaza’, shaving part of the head and leaving the rest (Sahih al-Bukhari, Book of Dress).
    • Western travelers told of Muslim men, Turks especially, who shaved the head but for one lock by which they would be drawn up into paradise; Young gives the belief to “the Arabs.”
  • “that there is a great hole at the North Pole”: In 1818 John Cleves Symmes Jr. announced that the earth is hollow and open at the poles. In the 1880s Cyrus Teed’s Koreshan Unity in Chicago taught the reverse, that we live on the inside of a hollow earth. See Exploration and the Poles.
  • “No matter how many explorers draw how many maps of the Himalayas”: The Himalayas are Earth’s highest and youngest mountain range, forming a massive arc across Asia, known as the “Abode of Snow,” containing Mount Everest and over 110 peaks over 24,000 feet, creating a major climatic barrier and source of major rivers like the Ganges and Brahmaputra, vital to billions in India and beyond. Formed by the collision of the Indian and Eurasian tectonic plates, the range features three main parallel ranges (Great, Lesser, Outer) and supports unique ecosystems, with glaciers providing water to billions.
  • “my fourteenth year”: Vera is fourteen in this last month with Miss MacIntosh.
  • “she walked into the roaring ocean on a cold September morning”: Miss MacIntosh died or disappeared sometime in September. Vera tells it here, before Miss MacIntosh has finished her story. See Suicide in History and Literature.
  • “her old Admiral Dewey corset was found draped over a rock”: See the Admiral Dewey corset in the Chapter 63 resources.
  • “The sun and the moon shone in the same pearly sky when she walked into the ocean”: In Chapter 63 Miss MacIntosh foretold that “the sun and the moon will shine in the same sky, and yet the earth will not be lighted.” See the Chapter 63 resources.
  • “her work in the bowling alley where, every evening, it was her duty to set ninepins up”: Bowling alleys evolved from ancient games, gaining indoor structure in 19th-century America, particularly among German immigrants, shifting from nine-pin to ten-pin to circumvent gambling bans, and transforming into modern entertainment venues with automatic pinsetters and widespread media appeal, especially after the 1950s, though they’ve always been associated with socializing and gambling. Pinsetters began as young boys and girls (“pinboys”) manually resetting pins and returning balls, a common, low-paying job in early 20th-century alleys, often enduring harsh conditions. It was hard, hot work, requiring speed and agility to avoid fast-moving balls and pins, as recounted by both men and women who did the job. See ninepins in the Chapter 64 resources.
  • “to wrestle with the dark angel of death”: “And Jacob was left alone; and there wrestled a man with him until the breaking of the day” (Genesis 32:24, KJV). See Genesis.
  • “Mr. Bonebreaker, a Gospel salesman, saw her reeling”: The surname Bonebrake is an Americanized version of the German name Beinbrech and means “bone break.” The original Beinbrech family lineage began in Switzerland in the 17th century, and the name evolved through various spellings before becoming Bonebrake in America. The name likely served as a metonymic occupational name for a herbalist, possibly referring to medicinal plants. See On the name Bonebreaker. Titus Bonebreaker.
  • “for whom the Lord loveth, the Lord chasteneth”: “For whom the Lord loveth he chasteneth, and scourgeth every son whom he receiveth” (Hebrews 12:6, KJV). See The Bible.
  • “A man, said he, shall be as the shadow of a great rock in a weary land”: “And a man shall be as an hiding place from the wind… as the shadow of a great rock in a weary land” (Isaiah 32:2, KJV). See The Bible.
  • “as dead leaves are cast forth and burned”: “If a man abide not in me, he is cast forth as a branch, and is withered; and men gather them, and cast them into the fire, and they are burned” (John 15:6, KJV). See The Bible.
  • “as the sheep from the goats, as the wheat from the tares”: “And he shall separate them one from another, as a shepherd divideth his sheep from the goats” (Matthew 25:32, KJV); the wheat and the tares are in Matthew 13:24-30. See Revelation and the Apocalypse and The Bible.
  • “Mr. Bonebreaker was born in Missouri, in the Ozark foothills”: The Missouri Ozarks begin with Native American tribes like the Osage, followed by French claim and Spanish jurisdiction. Significant white settlement started in the 1800s, driven by settlers from the Appalachian region, and the area was a major destination during the Trail of Tears. Throughout the 19th century, industries like lead mining and farming flourished. See Iowa, Indiana, and the Midwest.
    • “I come from a country that raises corn and cotton, cockleburs and Democrats… I’m from Missouri. You have got to show me,” said Congressman Willard Duncan Vandiver in 1899, and Missouri became the Show-Me State.
  • “his work as a clerk in a St. Louis shoe store”: St. Louis, Missouri, was founded by French fur traders in 1764 at a strategic location on the Mississippi River. It became the “Gateway to the West” after being purchased by the United States in the Louisiana Purchase of 1803 and was the starting point for the Lewis and Clark Expedition. The city grew into a major trade center, fueled by its river and railroad access, and hosted the 1904 World’s Fair and Olympics. Key historical moments include its 1823 incorporation, its strategic importance during the Civil War, and the famous Dred Scott case at the Old Courthouse.
    • St. Louis’s history spans from a French fur trading settlement in 1764, becoming a crucial Mississippi River hub, booming during the steamboat era, hosting the 1904 World’s Fair, growing into a major industrial city, experiencing rapid suburbanization and population shifts post-WWII (seeing a peak then decline), and navigating racial tensions and social changes leading up to the mid-1960s, all while evolving from “Mound City” (ancient earthwork mounds of the Illini Confederacy) to a significant American metropolis.
  • “that which eye has not seen and ear has not heard”: “Eye hath not seen, nor ear heard, neither have entered into the heart of man, the things which God hath prepared for them that love him” (1 Corinthians 2:9, KJV). See The Bible.
  • “and the numbers of the hairs in her head, and the least sparrow”: “But the very hairs of your head are all numbered” (Matthew 10:30, KJV), said to a woman who has none. See The Bible and Hair, Wig, and Baldness.
  • “lest we likewise perish”: “Except ye repent, ye shall all likewise perish” (Luke 13:3, KJV). See The Bible.
  • “Weep not, Hagar, for thy little son”: According to the Bible, Hagar was the Egyptian slave of Sarah, Abram’s wife. Sarah had been barren for a long time and sought a way to fulfill God’s promise that Abram would be father of many nations, especially since they had grown old, so she offered Hagar to Abram to be his concubine. Hagar bore Abraham’s son, Ishmael. “What aileth thee, Hagar? fear not” (Genesis 21:17, KJV). Where the King James has “he will be a wild man” (Genesis 16:12), the Hebrew reads “a wild ass of a man,” as Mr. Bonebreaker has it; see Ishmael in the Chapter 62 resources. See Genesis and Ancient Egypt.
  • “and she hath no breasts”: “We have a little sister, and she hath no breasts: what shall we do for our sister in the day when she shall be spoken for? If she be a wall, we will build upon her a palace of silver” (Song of Solomon 8:8-9, KJV). Mr. Bonebreaker makes the palace a tower. See The Bible and Women, Gender, and Marriage.
  • “What is the perishing meat of this world?”: “Labour not for the meat which perisheth” (John 6:27, KJV). See The Bible.
  • “old Masonic banners”: Freemasonry, a fraternal order descended from the stonemasons’ guilds, was one of the largest social institutions in America, and lodges often met in hotels and public halls hung with their banners. American membership peaked at about four million around 1959.
  • “when God prepared the heavens and set a compass upon the face of the depth”: “When he prepared the heavens, I was there: when he set a compass upon the face of the depth” (Proverbs 8:27, KJV). See The Bible.
  • “the ravens of the valley shall pluck us”: “The eye that mocketh at his father… the ravens of the valley shall pick it out” (Proverbs 30:17, KJV). See The Bible.
  • “Man is but a frail reed in the wild storm”: Compare Pascal: man is but a reed, the weakest in nature, but a thinking reed (Pensées, 1670).
  • “Unfruitful are the works of darkness”: “And have no fellowship with the unfruitful works of darkness” (Ephesians 5:11, KJV). See The Bible.
  • “One woe is past”: “One woe is past; and, behold, there come two woes more hereafter” (Revelation 9:12, KJV). See Revelation and the Apocalypse.
  • “Men shall be crushed before the moth”: “Them that dwell in houses of clay… which are crushed before the moth” (Job 4:19, KJV); “For what is your life? It is even a vapour” (James 4:14, KJV). See The Book of Job.
  • “we who are saved are not like to whited sepulchres”: “Ye are like unto whited sepulchres” (Matthew 23:27, KJV). See The Bible.
  • “man caught as a wild bull in a net”: “As a wild bull in a net” (Isaiah 51:20, KJV); God speaks “out of the whirlwind” in Job 38:1. See The Book of Job.
  • “To hoar hairs will I carry you”: “And even to hoar hairs will I carry you” (Isaiah 46:4, KJV). Miss MacIntosh cannot say that she has none. See The Bible and Hair, Wig, and Baldness.
  • “in old China the wise men wore horsehair hats”: The horsehair hat was the mark of the scholar-gentleman in Korea, where it is called the gat.
  • “where the canker cannot touch us”: “Lay not up for yourselves treasures upon earth, where moth and rust doth corrupt” (Matthew 6:19, KJV). See The Bible.
  • “She had been a poor creature, yes, with wide blue eyes”: We get another detail about Miss MacIntosh’s appearance.
  • “for his bones were out of joint”: “I am poured out like water, and all my bones are out of joint” (Psalm 22:14, KJV). This biblical reference is consistent with Mr. Bonebreaker’s character, who is deeply religious yet flawed and struggling, using scripture to make sense of his life and to assert his role as a preacher of impending judgment and salvation. The phrase encapsulates both his physical frailty and his spiritual earnestness in a poetic, scriptural metaphor. “I may tell all my bones” (Psalm 22:17, KJV).
  • “where there were black marble beds”: In Mr. Bonebreaker’s heaven, which will take Miss MacIntosh only if she weeps, the beds are black marble, the stone of tombs and monuments.
  • “since in heaven nobody remembers anybody”: Mr. Bonebreaker tells Miss MacIntosh that in heaven he would not remember her or her face. His heaven erases earthly bonds and memory, a bleak promise to a woman already alone. “For in the resurrection they neither marry, nor are given in marriage” (Matthew 22:30, KJV). See On since in heaven nobody remembers anybody.
  • “our fathers have eaten sour grapes, that the worm is mother of us all”: “The fathers have eaten sour grapes, and the children’s teeth are set on edge” (Ezekiel 18:2, KJV); “to the worm, Thou art my mother, and my sister” (Job 17:14, KJV). See The Book of Job.
  • “the Egyptians were spoiled”: “And they spoiled the Egyptians” (Exodus 12:36, KJV): the Israelites, leaving Egypt, carried off the Egyptians’ silver and gold. See The Bible and Ancient Egypt.
    • “the Egyptians were spoiled” implies that the Egyptians, once a mighty and revered people, became corrupt or morally ruined in his religious worldview. This phrase is part of Mr. Bonebreaker’s sweeping religious rhetoric about the decline of the world and the need for salvation before the Last Day.
  • “Babylon was sunken into the sea”: In Revelation Babylon is the great city of sin, thrown down by divine judgment, and Mr. Bonebreaker uses its fall as a sign of the coming end of the world. “And a mighty angel took up a stone like a great millstone, and cast it into the sea, saying, Thus with violence shall that great city Babylon be thrown down” (Revelation 18:21, KJV). See Revelation and the Apocalypse.
  • “he had dwelled for a long time in the Land of Ham”: In the Psalms the land of Ham is Egypt: “Israel also came into Egypt; and Jacob sojourned in the land of Ham” (Psalm 105:23, KJV). See The Bible and Ancient Egypt.
  • “She was fruit he had plucked from the Dead Sea”: The Dead Sea, also known by other names, is a landlocked salt lake bordered by Jordan to the east, the Israeli-occupied West Bank to the west and Israel to the southwest. It lies in the endorheic basin of the Jordan Rift Valley, and its main tributary is the Jordan River. (Wikipedia)
    • Dead Sea fruit, the apples of Sodom, were said to look ripe but to dissolve into smoke and ashes in the hand (Josephus, The Jewish War, Book 4).
    • “Do men gather grapes of thorns, or figs of thistles?” (Matthew 7:16, KJV). See The Bible.
  • “God gave snow like wool”: “He giveth snow like wool: he scattereth the hoarfrost like ashes” (Psalm 147:16, KJV). See The Bible.
  • “her hands were the pureness”: “Consider the lilies of the field, how they grow; they toil not, neither do they spin” (Matthew 6:28, KJV). See The Bible.
  • “She had gone down into the valley of the shadow to get him”: “Yea, though I walk through the valley of the shadow of death” (Psalm 23:4, KJV). See The Bible.
  • “Her head was filled with dew, he said”: Mr. Bonebreaker courts her with the Song of Solomon: “my head is filled with dew” (5:2), “thy hair is as a flock of goats” (4:1), “Thy neck is as a tower of ivory” (7:4), “Many waters cannot quench love” (8:7), and Job’s “eyelids of the morning” (41:18), all KJV. Every compliment is to her hair or her beauty. See The Bible and Hair, Wig, and Baldness.
  • “Georgia MacIntosh, who was born in a snowstorm”: Her full name is Georgia; her brothers called her George. See her name in the Chapter 63 resources.
  • “John Knox MacIntosh, her father”: John Knox MacIntosh and Mercy MacIntosh are Georgia MacIntosh’s parents. See On John Knox MacIntosh.
    • John Knox was a Scottish minister, Reformed theologian, and writer who was a leader of the country’s Reformation. He was the founder of the Church of Scotland.
    • Young claimed descent from John Knox on her mother’s side. While writing the novel she “discovered that the Macintoshes, this really astonished me, were descendants from a prince, a bald prince, who was washed up on the shores of Scotland,” so that “Miss Macintosh is really a bald prince, disguised with a red wig and the woman’s gear” (Marguerite Young, interview, WNYC radio, New York). See John Knox MacIntosh, Miss MacIntosh, and Marguerite Young on Her Craft.
  • “the mountains full of horses”: “The mountain was full of horses and chariots of fire” (2 Kings 6:17, KJV). See The Bible.
  • “Miss MacIntosh was the brightest star in his crown”: Revival hymns promised the soul-winner a star in his crown for each soul saved, as in Eliza Hewitt’s “Will There Be Any Stars in My Crown?” (1897), after “they that turn many to righteousness as the stars for ever and ever” (Daniel 12:3, KJV). See American Religious Movements.
    • “The star of the Turk” most likely refers to the crescent and star on the Ottoman flag and emblems. It could also recall the Gallipoli Star (Ottoman War Medal), a WWI Turkish military decoration for bravery, or the famous Mechanical Turk, an 18th-century chess-playing automaton.
  • “the star of the dirty Jew”: “Dirty Jew” is a widely recognized and offensive antisemitic slur with historical roots in hate speech and discrimination. The term is a standard antisemitic taunt used in real-world attacks and verbal abuse against Jewish people. During the Holocaust, the yellow Star of David identification marker that Jews were forced to wear encouraged people to use slurs like “dirty Jew” and to harass them. The phrase draws on ancient anti-Jewish themes that falsely associated Jews with filth or spreading disease. Miss MacIntosh objects, “quite flatly,” that the Jews should not be singled out. See Judaism.
  • “the neighborhoods of Old Jewry”: “Old Jewry” in London was the center of England’s medieval Jewish community, thriving from the Norman Conquest (1066) through the 13th century as financiers and merchants, but faced increasing persecution, discriminatory laws like the 1275 Statute of Jewry, and accusations (e.g., coin clipping), culminating in King Edward I’s expulsion of all Jews from England in 1290, ending centuries of Jewish life in that area until their readmission under Cromwell in 1657.
    • In Chicago the Jewish neighborhood around Maxwell Street on the Near West Side was known from the 1880s as the ghetto. See Judaism.
  • “Why should the black men, the railroad porters, the shoe-shiners”: The history of returning enslaved people to Africa, known as the Back-to-Africa Movement, involved efforts by groups like the American Colonization Society (ACS) in the 19th century to send freed slaves to colonies like Liberia and Sierra Leone, aiming to create homelands for Black people in Africa. While supported by some, including President Lincoln at times, it faced strong opposition from many African Americans who saw it as racist and a way to strengthen slavery, with thousands settling in Liberia before the Civil War despite harsh conditions and high mortality. Founded in 1816 by white elites, the ACS established Liberia (settled 1822) as a colony for freed U.S. slaves, modeled partly on British efforts in Sierra Leone. Paul Cuffee was an early proponent who, in 1815, transported free Black people to Sierra Leone, envisioning trade and immigration. The British settled formerly enslaved people in Sierra Leone starting in the late 1780s, a model the ACS followed. See Society, Class, and Race.
    • In the Bible, Ham, one of Noah’s three sons, had four sons: Cush, Mizraim, Phut, and Canaan, who became ancestors of peoples in Africa and the Middle East, particularly Ethiopia, Egypt, Libya, and Canaan (modern Israel/Palestine). The story in Genesis details how Ham saw his father Noah naked while drunk, leading Noah to curse Ham’s son, Canaan, rather than Ham himself, a narrative known as the Curse of Ham. After the Flood, Noah became drunk and lay uncovered in his tent. Ham saw his father’s nakedness and told his brothers, Shem and Japheth. Shem and Japheth, however, respectfully covered Noah without looking. Noah, upon waking, cursed Canaan (Ham’s son) to be a “servant of servants” to his brothers (Genesis 9:25, KJV), a passage later misused to justify slavery. In the American South the Curse of Ham was preached as God’s own warrant for enslaving Africans, and Mr. Bonebreaker still calls Black men “the sons of Ham.” See Society, Class, and Race.
  • “a narrow-hearted man like all Missourians”: Miss MacIntosh perceives Mr. Bonebreaker has a narrow or limited heart because of his rigid and sometimes judgmental religious views, his intolerance towards certain groups, and his conservative attitudes. This narrow-heartedness implies a lack of broad compassion or understanding beyond his own particular worldview.
  • “the Justice of the Peace”: A Justice of the Peace is a local public officer handling minor legal matters like small claims, traffic violations, and misdemeanors, and performing administrative duties such as officiating marriages, administering oaths, and witnessing signatures; they are often laypersons (not required to be lawyers) trained in local law, serving as accessible community judicial figures in many common law jurisdictions. Their powers are limited, focusing on local, less serious disputes and essential civic functions, acting as a first point of contact with the legal system.
  • “the great, loud-ticking watch, luminous and waterproof”: Luminous dials were painted with radium paint from the 1910s. The young women who painted them, the Radium Girls, were poisoned by pointing their brushes between their lips; in Ottawa, Illinois, the Radium Dial Company’s painters won their case in 1938, and their fight helped establish workers’ right to compensation for occupational disease. See Clocks and Watches and Women, Gender, and Marriage.
  • “first the sermon and then the soup”: Rescue missions such as Chicago’s Pacific Garden Mission (1877) fed the poor after the sermon, not before. The Salvation Army promised “soup, soap, and salvation,” and Joe Hill’s union song “The Preacher and the Slave” (1911) mocked the arrangement as “pie in the sky.” See American Religious Movements.
  • “It was most deranging. The yoke of God”: “Take my yoke upon you” (Matthew 11:29, KJV).
  • “All the old mansions on the Lake Michigan front”: Old mansions lined the Lake Michigan front, especially in affluent areas like Chicago’s North Shore and Michigan’s Grosse Pointe, showcasing Gilded Age opulence with grand architecture (Italian Renaissance, French-inspired), extensive grounds, luxurious interiors (parquet floors, wood paneling, ballrooms), and historic significance, with examples including the historic David Adler Mansion.
  • “the barren who had borne seven times”: “So that the barren hath born seven” (1 Samuel 2:5, KJV); “Rejoice, thou barren that bearest not” (Galatians 4:27, KJV). See The Bible.
  • “relapse into the language of baseball”: The language of baseball, or “baseballese,” was rich with colorful, evocative slang like “banjo hitter” (soft contact) or “daisy cutter” (hard grounder), alongside foundational terms such as “ace” (pitcher) and “dish” (home plate). It featured unique terms for plays like “around the horn” (infield relay) and players like “baller” or “hurler,” reflecting a simpler, more traditional game before extensive media exposure amplified modern jargon. In the late 19th and early 20th centuries some Christian leaders saw the sport as a moral threat. Many communities had laws that banned baseball games on Sundays to encourage church attendance and prevent “rowdy behavior” often associated with saloons and alcohol consumption. State laws even forced some professional teams, like the Boston Red Sox, to play Sunday games at different fields away from churches. Some religious groups viewed baseball as a frivolous activity that distracted from intellectual and spiritual pursuits. Debates emerged about whether good Christians should play or watch baseball, especially on the Sabbath. Individual Jewish players, notably Hank Greenberg (in the 1930s) and Sandy Koufax (in the 1965 World Series), gained national attention and became heroes to many in their community by choosing not to play on the Jewish high holiday of Yom Kippur, a public declaration of faith that highlighted the choice between religious observance and professional demands. Simultaneously, baseball became a powerful cultural force in America, developing many characteristics that paralleled religious institutions. The game was given a deliberate creation myth in the early 1900s, attributing its invention to Abner Doubleday in Cooperstown, NY, which became a “sacred” origin site (now the home of the Baseball Hall of Fame). The sport developed its own rich repository of legends, rituals, and traditions (e.g., the seventh-inning stretch song “Take Me Out to the Ball Game,” the “Curse of the Bambino” (a phrase from 1990), the “infield fly rule”) that fostered a sense of continuity and shared experience. Iconic players like Babe Ruth were treated with reverence, their personal artifacts (bats, uniforms, gloves) becoming the “relics” of modern-day fandom, housed in the “shrine” of the Hall of Fame. The shared experience of fandom, with fans gathering in stadiums or living rooms, created strong bonds of community and belonging, much like a religious congregation. See Christopher H. Evans and William R. Herzog II, eds., The Faith of Fifty Million: Baseball, Religion, and American Culture (2002). Flag: after 1964, Koufax (1965) and the “Curse of the Bambino” (1990).
  • “He was on the baseball diamond again”: Compare Billy Sunday, who played outfield for the Chicago White Stockings, was converted at Chicago’s Pacific Garden Mission in 1886, and became the most famous revival preacher in America, preaching in the slang of the ballpark. See American Religious Movements.
  • “Chicago was as fat as grease”: “Their heart is as fat as grease” (Psalm 119:70, KJV); “What ailed thee, O thou sea, that thou fleddest?” (Psalm 114:5, KJV). See The Bible.
  • “Selah, Selah”: “Selah” is a Hebrew word of uncertain meaning, probably a musical or liturgical direction, often read as a call to pause and reflect. It appears seventy-one times in the Psalms and three times in Habakkuk.
  • “Love lifted me”: The hymn “Love Lifted Me,” written by James Rowe in 1912 with music by Howard E. Smith, tells a story of salvation using the biblical account of Peter walking on water (Matthew 14) as a metaphor for being pulled from sin by Jesus’s love, with Smith composing the melody despite severe arthritis, creating a powerful testament to divine rescue and devotion. See On Love Lifted Me and Music and Composers.
  • “In his father’s house were many mansions”: “In my Father’s house are many mansions” (John 14:2, KJV). See The Bible.
  • “the French beaver kings”: St. Louis was founded in 1764 by the fur traders Pierre Laclède and Auguste Chouteau, and the Chouteau family grew rich on beaver pelts.
    • “French Beaver Kings” may refer to French fur traders, known as coureurs de bois, established a significant presence around Chicago from the late 17th century, using the vital portage connecting the Great Lakes and Mississippi River for the lucrative beaver trade, leading to French outposts, missionary work (like Marquette’s), early forts (Fort Chicago), and enduring French-Indigenous Métis communities, with figures like Jean Baptiste Point du Sable and Antoine Ouilmette becoming key figures in this fur-driven economy, long before Chicago became a major American city.
  • “the German beer kings”: St. Louis’s “German Beer Kings” were immigrant brewers like Eberhard Anheuser, Adolphus Busch, the Lemp family, and the Griesediecks, who built brewing empires in the mid-19th century by introducing lager beers and leveraging St. Louis’s German population and unique limestone caves for brewing, transforming local businesses into national brands like Anheuser-Busch (Budweiser) and creating a rich brewing heritage.
  • “the locusts have no king”: “The locusts have no king, yet go they forth all of them by bands” (Proverbs 30:27, KJV). See The Bible.
  • “many slaughter yards”: Chicago’s Union Stock Yards, opened in 1865, became the world’s largest meatpacking center, transforming America’s food system by centralizing livestock processing through rail, making Chicago the “hog butcher for the world,” attracting waves of immigrant labor, and spurring related industries, but its reign ended in 1971 due to industry shifts, leaving behind legacy sites like its famous entrance gate and a lasting impact on Chicago’s economy and immigrant communities. Carl Sandburg called Chicago “Hog Butcher for the World” (“Chicago,” 1914). Flag: after 1964, the closing of the stock yards in 1971.
  • “As in water, face answers to face”: “As in water face answereth to face, so the heart of man to man” (Proverbs 27:19, KJV). See The Bible.
  • “a great Chicago hotel fire”: “great Chicago hotel fire” may refer to the near-destruction of the Grand Pacific Hotel during the massive 1871 Great Chicago Fire, which destroyed much of the city, and later, tragic incidents like the 1946 LaSalle Hotel Fire.
  • “the bar sinister”: The bar sinister, properly a bend or baton sinister, is popularly taken as the heraldic mark of illegitimate birth. Mr. Bonebreaker believes it shut him out from a throne, and decides that all the kings who sit on thrones are crossed by it as he is. See Mr. Titus Bonebreaker.
  • “Almanach de Gotha”: Almanach de Gotha is a directory of Europe’s royalty and higher nobility. It was published from 1763 to 1944.
  • “he could take the Hapsburgs by storm, sweep the Stuarts off their feet”: The Habsburgs were a powerful German royal dynasty that ruled vast European territories for centuries, rising from Swiss origins in the 10th century to dominate the Holy Roman Empire and control Spain, Austria (as Austria-Hungary), and extensive colonies through strategic marriages and shrewd politics, eventually ending with World War I. Their empire peaked under Charles V, uniting Spain, the Netherlands, and Austria, but the dynasty’s vast reach and complex succession eventually led to internal strains, culminating in the dissolution of their empire after WWI.
    • The Stuart dynasty ruled Scotland from the late 14th century and later England, Scotland, and Ireland from 1603 to 1714, unifying the crowns under James VI of Scotland (James I of England) and overseeing a turbulent era of civil war, religious conflict, plague, and the Great Fire of London, ultimately ending with Queen Anne and leading to the Hanoverian succession, establishing England as a constitutional monarchy.
  • “his was the shield of the unicorn”: In medieval art, unicorns were tamed only by virgins, making them symbols of purity, often featured on shields alongside figures like the Virgin Mary. The unicorn, often chained and rearing, appears in heraldry, notably with the lion in the British Royal Arms and Canadian symbols, representing royal power.
  • “I have put away childish things”: Mr. Bonebreaker tells his street audience, “I have put away bicycles, billiards, card playing, smoking, drinking, the things of my childhood.” Yet there was “a child in Mr. Bonebreaker as in us all, according to Miss MacIntosh, a child, a human frailty.” His dream of a heavenly crown, his backsliding, his brushes with the law and occasional violence, and his wild, scattered preaching show the child still there. “When I was a child, I spake as a child… but when I became a man, I put away childish things” (1 Corinthians 13:11, KJV). See The Bible.
  • “like a shadow running backward”: The shadow on the sundial of Ahaz went back ten degrees as a sign to King Hezekiah (2 Kings 20:10). See The Bible.
  • “He was poor as Tobit’s dog”: In the Book of Tobit, found in the Apocrypha of the 1611 King James Bible and in Catholic and Orthodox Bibles, a dog faithfully accompanies Tobias, Tobit’s son, and the angel Raphael on their journey: “So they went forth both, and the young man’s dog with them” (Tobit 5:16, KJV). In Christianity, dogs represent faithfulness. See The Bible.
  • “What of her crown of patience?”: In Stoicism, patience is a key virtue for achieving inner tranquility and living a good life; Epictetus summed up his teaching as “bear and forbear” (Aulus Gellius, Attic Nights 17.19). In Hindu thought, patience is viewed as the capacity to wait, endure opposites, and act calmly without anxiety, anger, or resentment; in the Bhagavad Gita, Krishna tells Arjuna to endure heat and cold, pleasure and pain, which come and go (2:14). “Patience is bitter, but its fruit is sweet,” often credited to Aristotle, comes from Rousseau’s Julie, or the New Heloise (1761), Part 1, Letter 46. Miss MacIntosh’s patience is active endurance, practical and unsentimental, daily perseverance in place of dreams and self-pity. See the Chapter 40 resources. See Hinduism.
  • “the day he figured would be the day after the world would end”: Compare the Millerites, who followed William Miller’s prophecy that Christ would return in 1843 or 1844; when October 22, 1844, passed, they called it the Great Disappointment. The Seventh-day Adventists, who grew out of them, also urged a meatless diet, as Mr. Bonebreaker keeps. See American Religious Movements.
    • Religious food restrictions, seen across Judaism (Kashrut), Islam (Halal/Haram), Hinduism (no beef), Jainism (strict vegetarianism, no roots), and early Christianity (abstain from idol-sacrificed food, blood), have ancient roots, often linked to divine command, health/sanitation (pork, blood), ecological reasons, or cultural identity, evolving over time from specific scriptural interpretations (like Jesus declaring all foods clean) to broader ethical principles like non-violence, shaping practices from what to eat to how it’s prepared. Religions emphasizing vegetarianism include Jainism (which mandates it for non-violence), Buddhism and Hinduism (strong traditions rooted in Ahimsa or non-violence), and certain Christian denominations like the Seventh-day Adventists, alongside practices in Sikhism, some Jewish traditions, and Eastern Orthodox Christianity during fasts. The core principles often involve compassion for animals, spiritual purity, and minimal harm (Ahimsa). Vegetarians, and vegans especially, must find other sources for nutrients most plentiful in animal foods, such as vitamin B12, iron, zinc, and omega-3 fats. Some anthropologists hold that eating meat, and later cooking, fueled the growth of the human brain (Richard Wrangham, Catching Fire: How Cooking Made Us Human, 2009). Flag: after 1964, Wrangham (2009). See Buddhism and Hinduism.
  • “Instead of a girdle, there would be a rent”: “And it shall come to pass, that instead of sweet smell there shall be stink; and instead of a girdle a rent; and instead of well set hair baldness” (Isaiah 3:24, KJV). See The Bible and Hair, Wig, and Baldness.
  • “He himself had often said, quoting the Bible, that the wife should stand forth before her husband”: “Whose adorning let it not be that outward adorning of plaiting the hair, and of wearing of gold… But let it be the hidden man of the heart” (1 Peter 3:3-4, KJV). See The Bible and Hair, Wig, and Baldness.
  • “God loves the shorn lamb”: “God tempers the wind to the shorn lamb” (Laurence Sterne, A Sentimental Journey, 1768). See Sterne in the Chapter 55 resources.
  • “You, too, can be washed as white as the new-fallen snow”: “Though your sins be as scarlet, they shall be as white as snow” (Isaiah 1:18, KJV). See The Bible.
  • “See Chicago and live”: A joke on the proverb “See Naples and die.”
  • “Chicago will roll back the waters”: In 1900 Chicago reversed the flow of the Chicago River, turning its sewage away from Lake Michigan toward the Mississippi.
  • “a future contender with the Hapsburgs, Medicis, Bourbons, Navarres”: The Medici were a powerful Italian banking family and political dynasty that ruled Florence and Tuscany for centuries, becoming synonymous with the Italian Renaissance through their vast wealth, strategic political maneuvering, and unparalleled patronage of arts and sciences, sponsoring figures like Michelangelo and Leonardo da Vinci and producing four Popes before their dynasty ended in 1737. Starting as wool merchants, they built a massive bank, used financial power to gain political control, and fostered an explosion of Florentine culture, making Florence the heart of the Renaissance.
    • The House of Bourbon is a major European royal dynasty, originating from France as a branch of the Capetians, ruling France from 1589 to 1792 and again from 1814-1848, and later providing monarchs for Spain (since 1700, with interruptions, and currently), Naples, Sicily, and Parma. Key figures include France’s Henry IV, the Sun King Louis XIV, and the ill-fated Louis XVI, whose execution ushered in the French Revolution, ending Bourbon rule in France until the restoration. Their legacy is tied to absolute monarchy, French cultural dominance, and widespread European influence, continuing today in Spain and Luxembourg.
    • The history of the Navarres involves the ancient, powerful Kingdom of Navarre in the Pyrenees, which produced French royalty like Henry IV of France, and distinct lines of American families, notably the French-Canadian Navarres who settled in Michigan (like Robert Navarre in Detroit) and the Potawatomi Navarre family in Kansas/Indian Territory, tracing back to early settlers like Pierre Navarre in Indiana.
  • “she was herself the Argus-eyed”: Argus had a hundred eyes, some always awake; Hera set him to watch Io (Ovid, Metamorphoses, Book 1). See Greek Mythology.
  • “much like the blind leading the blind”: “And if the blind lead the blind, both shall fall into the ditch” (Matthew 15:14, KJV). See Eyes and Blindness.
  • “Shuffling off to Buffalo”: Shuffle Off to Buffalo is a song from the 1933 musical film 42nd Street. The lyrics talk about traveling by train to Niagara in a sleeper car for a honeymoon.
  • “Love is blind”: The saying, meaning that love overlooks faults, is ancient; Plato wrote that the lover is blind about the beloved (Laws 731e). In English, Chaucer has “For love is blynd alday, and may nat see” (“The Merchant’s Tale”), and Shakespeare’s Jessica says, “But love is blind, and lovers cannot see / The pretty follies that themselves commit” (The Merchant of Venice, 2.6). See Love and Eyes and Blindness.
  • “The blind would rub noses like the Chinese”: People from cultures like the Inuit (using the kunik), Māori (the hongi), and peoples in some Persian Gulf countries (like the UAE and Saudi Arabia) use nose rubbing as a greeting, often to exchange breath or scents, signifying affection, respect, or a spiritual connection, rather than a Western-style kiss, with different cultural meanings attached.
  • “drifting, rudderless in the state of Ohio”: Ohio’s history spans from its Native American roots, through European exploration and settlement (leading to statehood in 1803, though officially recognized later), its crucial role in the Civil War as a Union state with significant anti-slavery sentiment, rapid industrialization in the late 19th century fueled by cities like Cleveland and Akron, its identity as the “Mother of Presidents,” and into the mid-20th century, solidifying its industrial might and diverse cultural influences from New England, New York, and the South.
  • “why should she not see Niagara Falls”: Niagara Falls, near Buffalo, New York, was a favorite honeymoon destination. The falls formed about 12,000 years ago as the glaciers retreated and the water of Lake Erie poured over the Niagara Escarpment toward Lake Ontario, carving the seven-mile Niagara Gorge. The first inhabitants were the Neutral and other Iroquoian-speaking peoples, and the name is believed to come from the Iroquoian “Onguiaahra,” meaning “thundering noise.” The Jesuit Louis Hennepin wrote the first European eyewitness account in 1678. After the Erie Canal (1825) and the railroads, tourists and honeymooners came in crowds; legend makes Jérôme Bonaparte, Napoleon’s brother, the first honeymooner, in 1804. Commercial exploitation led Frederick Law Olmsted and others to campaign for New York’s Niagara Reservation, the first state park in the U.S., and Ontario’s Queen Victoria Niagara Falls Park, both established in 1885. In 1896 Niagara power reached Buffalo, more than twenty miles away, proving long-distance alternating current, with Nikola Tesla as a consultant to Westinghouse. In 1901 Annie Edson Taylor became the first person to go over the falls in a barrel. In 1848 an ice jam stopped the flow for up to 40 hours, and in 1969 the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers turned off the American Falls to study erosion. Flag: after 1964, the 1969 dewatering. See On Niagara Falls and honeymooners.
    • The Maid of the Mist has carried visitors in oilskins to the foot of the falls since 1846.
  • “so many Aphrodites and Apollos”: See Aphrodite in the Chapter 42 resources.
    • Apollo is one of the Olympian deities in Greek mythology. Apollo has been recognized as a god of archery, music and dance, truth and prophecy, healing and diseases, the Sun and light, poetry, and more. (Wikipedia)
  • “Romeo and Juliet, Paul and Virginia, Eloise and Abelard, Tristram and the white Yseult”: Romeo and Juliet is a tragedy written by William Shakespeare early in his career about two young Italian star-crossed lovers whose deaths ultimately reconcile their feuding families. (Wikipedia) See Shakespeare.
    • Paul and Virginia is a novel by Jacques-Henri Bernardin de Saint-Pierre, first published in 1788. The novel’s title characters are friends since birth who fall in love. It records the fate of a child of nature corrupted by the artificial sentimentality of the French upper classes in the late eighteenth century. (Wikipedia)
    • Eloise and Abelard refers to Heloise who was a French nun, philosopher, writer, scholar, and abbess. She is famous in history and popular culture for her love affair and correspondence with the leading medieval logician and theologian Peter Abelard, who became her colleague, collaborator and husband. (Wikipedia) More in the Chapter 52 resources.
    • Tristan and Iseult or Yseult is a chivalric romance told in numerous variations since the 12th century. The tale is a tragedy about the illicit love between the Cornish knight Tristan (Tristram) and the Irish princess Iseult (Isolde, Yseult). (Wikipedia)
  • “handing out cards promising quick and easy divorces”: In 1931 Nevada cut its residency for divorce to six weeks, and Reno became the divorce capital. See Weddings and Funerals.
  • “a Moody’s Bible chained to a post”: Young’s “Moody’s Bible” recalls Dwight L. Moody, the Chicago evangelist whose Bible Institute opened in 1886; the Gideons began placing Bibles in hotel rooms in 1908. See American Religious Movements.
  • “the serpent bite without enchantment”: “Surely the serpent will bite without enchantment” (Ecclesiastes 10:11, KJV). See Ecclesiastes.
