Chapter 18

← Chapter 17 · Home · Chapter 19 →

Content note: This chapter strongly suggests that the young Vera has been sexually assaulted, and it shows an adult frightening a child into silence.

Summary

Through the rest of the night, Miss MacIntosh holds Vera and talks, in two voices: the familiar one of proverbs and geography lessons, and a raw, grieving one that cries for the left breast “already gone,” for her hair, and for “one kiss,” all she ever asked. A red wig hangs on the chair post. She insists nothing happened, that it was all a dream. She covers Vera’s head with a pillow, leaves “the heavy, claw-shaped mark of her hand” upon her forehead “to teach you… charity,” and swears she will kill Vera if she ever tells. By dawn she is quizzing her on Michigan’s industries and the Battle of Shiloh, and promising that all will be as it was. As Vera falls asleep, Miss MacIntosh whispers that she lost her hair in Vera’s service, that she once had a pale gold mane, and that she is not as old as Vera thinks. Vera carries the secret as her sin, and ever after tries to be charitable.

Characters present

Vera Cartwheel · Miss MacIntosh · The Old Blind Sheep Dog · Catherine Cartwheel · Falada · Joachim Spitzer

Concepts present

Themes: Death and Mortality · Duality and Doubles · Fear and Courage · Identity and the Self · Illusion and Reality · Memory and the Past · Nature, the Sea, and the Cosmos · Order, Chaos, and Discipline · The Search for Meaning · Women, Gender, and Marriage

Symbols: Birds · Dogs · Hair, Wig, and Baldness · Horses and Carriages · Mirrors and Reflections · Roses and Flowers · The House · The Sea and Water · Weddings and Funerals

Philosophy: Buddhism · Freud and Jung · Hinduism · Taoism and Zhuangzi · Wittgenstein

Allusions: American Writers · Angels and Archangels · Astronomy · Edgar Allan Poe · Exploration and the Poles · Fairy Tales and Folklore · Gambling and Playing Cards · Genesis · Iowa, Indiana, and the Midwest · Napoleon and Wellington · Shakespeare · The Bible · The Book of Job · The Civil War

Key passages

From the research

  • Vera confronts “the phantom of change,” a figure that embodies both the fixed and true, yet also the unsettling reality beneath illusion. This passage explores the idea that what we take as reality is often a self-deception, with the “curtain of illusion” stripped away, revealing the naked truth that each person wears a mask, pushing them into “the imperial darkness.” This emphasizes human vulnerability and the elusive nature of identity and reality.
  • Miss MacIntosh, initially a “red-headed, plain nursemaid,” becomes a complex, almost demonic figure: bald, naked, and both terrifying and intimate. The lover who emerges is described as neither man nor woman but an “angelic demon,” symbolizing the secret, hidden aspects within each person, the “other self” that is always present yet unreachable. This passage reveals the interplay of identity, gender, and inner conflict.
  • Miss MacIntosh’s bald, furrowed head “looming above me in the foggy darkness,” with her “false teeth clicking, clicking like old bones or dice in the wind,” represents a haunting presence of mortality and decay. Her voice moans about ephemerality and the transient nature of life, blending imagery of death, loss, and cosmic insignificance. This creates a powerful atmosphere of dread and existential despair.
  • Miss MacIntosh delivers a harsh reflection on mortality, sin, and human frailty: “One leak sinks a ship, and one sin sinks a sinner,” and “God pity us all,” underscoring the inevitability of death and the universal vulnerability of humanity. Her admonitions and proverbs touch on themes of fate, loss, and the futility of resistance, adding a somber philosophical layer to the narrative.
  • Despite the terrifying nocturnal revelations, Miss MacIntosh insists that everything will “be all right” in the morning, that the night’s horrors are but a dream, and life will resume its “fixed schedule.” This tension between nightmare and waking life reflects Vera’s struggle to reconcile the profound encounter with the mundane reality of everyday existence.
  • Baldness here symbolizes a stripping away of pretense and beauty, a harsh exposure to the raw truth beneath appearances. Vera’s painful awareness of Miss MacIntosh’s “essential baldness” represents a loss of innocence and the confrontation with the unvarnished realities of life and human nature.
  • In the closing passage, Miss MacIntosh, holding Vera, reflects on her lost hair as a metaphor for the passage of time and aging. She poses a poignant question about the nature of age itself, “Alas, when shall I grow old?” suggesting the elusive and paradoxical quality of time and existence.
  • “I have lost my hair in your service.” The nursemaid who threatened to kill Vera if she told turns, in the last lines, into a woman confessing what her service cost her: “When I came here, I had all my own hair, a thick mane of it, pale gold hanging down my back.”

Questions and observations

Reading closely

  • “Memory sometimes provides the one flower more than ever blossomed. Memory sometimes omits the only flower there really was.” Which does Vera’s memory of this night do?
  • “Perhaps, however, the lack of deception is always another deception.” What deception is left when the wig is off?
  • Miss MacIntosh insists, “Nothing that you think is happening is happening!” Why does she need Vera to believe it?

Characters

  • She marks Vera’s forehead “to teach you… charity.” What lesson does Vera take?
  • “If ever I told what I had seen, she would kill me.” How does the threat change what Vera remembers?
  • “I have lost my hair in your service.” What else has Miss MacIntosh given up?

Connections

  • The “claw-shaped mark” echoes the “claws upon her forehead” Vera imagined in Chapter 10. What has passed from one woman to the other?
  • The quiz questions of Chapter 13 (“Where is North Dakota?”) return here at dawn. What are they for?
  • Vera’s dream made Miss MacIntosh the bridegroom (Chapter 10). How does that dream come back here?

Reflection

  • What does a child lose when she learns an adult’s secret and cannot unlearn it?
  • Is a secret kept under threat still one’s own?
  • Can tenderness and harm come from the same person on the same night?

Research: Characters

Vera Cartwheel

  • Questioning reality, memory, and self-identity.
  • Experiences a profound revelation and confrontation with hidden truths.
  • Shows vulnerability, fear, and eventual resolve to accept and understand.
  • She carries “the heavy, claw-shaped mark” of Miss MacIntosh’s hand and resolves to be charitable, “as a retribution for my cruelty.”

Miss MacIntosh

  • Initially perceived as a plain, red-headed nursemaid.
  • Transforms into a bald, frightening figure symbolizing raw truth and loss.
  • Acts as a guide or interlocutor, mixing sternness with intimacy.
  • Represents both nurturing and harsh realities of life, death, and change.
  • Embodies themes of charity, mortality, and the limits of human understanding.
  • Her red wig hangs on the chair post, and she mourns the left breast “already gone.”
  • She threatens to kill Vera if she tells, then says she lost her hair in Vera’s service.

The Phantom Lover and the Secret Man

  • A spectral figure representing the hidden aspects of self.
  • Neither fully man nor woman; embodies the duality of human nature.
  • Symbolizes the unrecognizable parts of identity and love.

The Old Blind Sheep Dog

  • The old blind sheep dog appears only briefly and indirectly. It may function as a potent symbol of failing protection, limited perception, and the human struggle to confront elusive and overwhelming existential truths. Its presence underscores the chapter’s meditation on vulnerability, loss, and the elusive nature of reality and memory.
  • Vera hears him barking “perhaps at a spar, perhaps at the last falling star… or some danger greater than any I could have imagined.”

Research: Themes

The Phantom of Change and Illusion versus Reality

See: Illusion and Reality

  • Vera encounters a “phantom of change” (something fixed, undeniable yet elusive in understanding).
  • Illusion is portrayed paradoxically as “the only reality,” with self-deception being the “only rose” (symbol of beauty and pain).
  • The external world is likened to “a mad man’s dream,” emphasizing the fragility and elusiveness of perceived reality.

Memory and its Limitations

See: Memory and the Past

  • Memory is depicted as incomplete, evolving, and surrounded by the unknown.
  • Vera questions the accuracy of remembered events, hinting that memory may omit or alter essential details.
  • The idea that “the dream is never complete” and that new realities arise from what is missing in memory.

Duality of Human Nature: The Secret Man and Woman

See: Duality and Doubles

  • The concept that within every woman is a secret man, and within every man, a secret woman.
  • This duality is visualized through the phantom lover who is neither fully man nor woman but an “angelic demon” representing the hidden self.

Fear, Vulnerability, and the Mask of Identity

See: Identity and the Self · Fear and Courage

  • Vera experiences fear and confusion confronting Miss MacIntosh’s bald, naked, and terrifying form, symbolizing raw truth stripped of pretense.
  • The “mask” everyone wears shields them from their true selves, leading to isolation and existential loneliness.

Mortality and the Inevitability of Death

See: Death and Mortality

  • Dialogue and imagery emphasize transience and mortality: “Oh, how ephemeral are we!” and “The brief candle goes out.”
  • The inevitability of death and the futility of resistance are central, with Vera urged to “be silent as the corpse” and accept loss.

Charity and Understanding

See: The Search for Meaning

  • Despite cruelty and misunderstanding, Vera resolves to be charitable toward others, especially toward Miss MacIntosh, recognizing her essential vulnerability and “baldness.”

Return to Normalcy and the Persistence of Routine

See: Order, Chaos, and Discipline

  • Miss MacIntosh insists that the strange night is a dream and that normal life will resume with the morning.
  • The repeated references to daily routines, domestic tasks, and practical lessons reflect the human need to cling to order amid chaos.

Research: Symbols and Imagery

Baldness of Miss MacIntosh

See: Hair, Wig, and Baldness

  • Represents the stripping away of illusion, revealing raw and uncomfortable truth.
  • Symbolizes mortality, vulnerability, and the loss of pretense.

Curtains Blowing, Shutters Banging, Weathercocks Creaking

See: The House

  • Create an atmosphere of instability and eerie music; symbolize the chaotic forces of change and the unknown.

The Sea, Waves, and Tides

See: Nature, the Sea, and the Cosmos · The Sea and Water

  • Evoke transience, the unconscious, and the relentless movement of life and death.

False Teeth Clicking

See: Death and Mortality

  • Symbolize decay, mortality, and the eerie persistence of mortality’s reminder.

Feather Pillow

See: Birds

  • Used by Miss MacIntosh to cover Vera’s head, symbolizing an attempt to induce forgetfulness, sleep, or escape from harsh realities.

The Brief Candle

See: Shakespeare

  • Classic metaphor for the fragility and brevity of life.

The Rider and the Horse

See: Falada · Horses and Carriages

  • Metaphor for the unity of self and illusion, indicating the inseparability of dream and dreamer.
  • Vera wonders if she has “become Falada,” with Miss MacIntosh now the rider.

Research: Resources

  • “some angelic demon”: Young may be referring to the Nephilim. In Genesis 6:4, they are born when “the sons of God came in unto the daughters of men.” Later legend made them the children of fallen angels and mortal women, at once angelic and demonic. See Genesis and Angels and Archangels.
  • “That night, the curtain of illusion had been stripped away”: Vera is describing what others in literature have said. Sarah Dessen writes, “You can’t unlearn something, even if you want to. You know what you know” (Along for the Ride, 2009). Arundhati Roy writes, “The trouble is that once you see it, you can’t unsee it” (Power Politics, 2001).
  • “Would that my lover had been a man!”: Vera’s realizations this night seem to be described again as a sexual act, something very intimate and physical. See Women, Gender, and Marriage.
  • “such a man as is hidden in the woman”: Jung named the woman within the man the anima, and the man within the woman the animus. See Freud and Jung and Duality and Doubles.
    • Young may also be drawing from the Chinese philosophy of Yin and Yang which is a concept of dualism, describing how obviously opposite or contrary forces may actually be complementary, interconnected, and interdependent in the natural world, and how they may give rise to each other as they interrelate to one another. (Wikipedia)
  • “one who combs her long gold hair upon the rock”: Heine’s Lorelei (1824), the Rhine siren who combs her golden hair on the rock and draws boatmen to their deaths. Clemens Brentano first told of her in a ballad of 1801. The body “scaled with silver scales” that follows is the mermaid’s. See Fairy Tales and Folklore.
  • “Who was that old rapist if not Miss MacIntosh”: Imagery in this chapter hints that either physically, emotionally, or psychologically a rape took place. Vera because of her age and experience does not have the words to fully explain what has happened to her. See Miss MacIntosh.
  • “Oh, how ephemeral are we!”: Ephemeral means something is short-lived or temporary, and it can be used to describe the nature of life and relationships.
  • “Watchman, what of the night? Who goes there?”: “Watchman, what of the night?” (Isaiah 21:11), and the opening of Hamlet, “Who’s there?” See The Bible, Shakespeare, and the Chapter 43 resources.
  • “Dead men tell no tales”: An old proverb, in print by 1664. See Death and Mortality.
  • “wrapped in this house of clay”: “How much less in them that dwell in houses of clay, whose foundation is in the dust” (Job 4:19). See The Book of Job.
  • “Thus did sparrows fall”: “Are not two sparrows sold for a farthing? and one of them shall not fall on the ground without your Father” (Matthew 10:29). It is a poetic way to express the transience of life and the shared fate of all creatures within the vast cycle of existence portrayed in the novel. See The Bible.
  • “The left breast is already gone”: Miss MacIntosh talks about losing her left breast. William Halsted performed his first radical mastectomy in New York in 1882 and described the operation in 1894. There is no clear record of how earlier women survived the operation, or for how long. See Miss MacIntosh, Women, Gender, and Marriage, and the Chapter 17 resources.
  • “Oh, bear the sinner up! Oh, wash our sins away and leave us white as snow!”: “Though your sins be as scarlet, they shall be as white as snow” (Isaiah 1:18). Compare 1 Peter 2:24, Psalm 38:4, Galatians 6:2, and Lamentations 5:7. It is a plea for cleansing and forgiveness. Just before, “Oh, plunge me in the purple flood” echoes William Cowper’s hymn: “And sinners, plunged beneath that flood, / Lose all their guilty stains” (1772). See The Bible and the Chapter 3 resources.
  • “Oh, where’s What Cheer, Iowa”: Miss MacIntosh’s hometown. See Iowa, Indiana, and the Midwest and the Chapter 9 resources.
  • “that hers was that knob where the breast was missing”: In the AMC series Dietland (2018), based on Sarai Walker’s novel, the character Julia (Tamara Tunie) reveals to Plum that she has had a double mastectomy, after a life of wearing “a mask,” as Tunie put it: “the hair, the makeup, the clothes.” See Miss MacIntosh.
  • “This earth is but the poor testing ground”: “The testing ground” of Chapter 15. See the Chapter 15 resources.
  • “and all oxen are our brothers”: “Thou shalt not see thy brother’s ox or his sheep go astray” (Deuteronomy 22:1). The phrase underscores the theme of humility before life’s challenges and the interconnectedness of all beings in their vulnerability and strength. See The Bible.
  • “Only the worm is clothed, and the worm is our little brother”: “I have said to corruption, Thou art my father: to the worm, Thou art my mother, and my sister” (Job 17:14). See The Book of Job.
  • “Where is Issachar”: Jacob’s sons, the tribes of Israel Vera learned to recite in Chapter 9. See The Bible and the Chapter 9 resources.
    • Issachar was a son of Jacob and Leah.
    • Reuben was Jacob’s firstborn son, by Leah. (The Flemish painter is Rubens.)
    • Nabal is in 1 Samuel 25, a story where he insults David and “the Lord smote Nabal, that he died.” His name means “fool” (1 Samuel 25:25), set beside “No fool like an old fool.”
  • “No fool like an old fool”: John Heywood’s proverb (1546). See the Chapter 10 resources.
  • “Out, out, brief candle!”: “Out, out, brief candle! / Life’s but a walking shadow” (Macbeth 5.5). See Shakespeare.
  • “Man was but a shadow and a breath”: “Man is like to vanity: his days are as a shadow that passeth away” (Psalm 144:4). It echoes the novel’s sense that a human life is as insubstantial as a shadow and as brief as a breath. See The Bible and the Chapter 15 resources.
  • “greaves of brass upon her legs, a target of brass between her shoulders, her spear like a weaver’s beam”: Goliath “had greaves of brass upon his legs, and a target of brass between his shoulders. And the staff of his spear was like a weaver’s beam” (1 Samuel 17:6-7). See The Bible.
  • “One leak sinks a ship, and one sin sinks a sinner”: Franklin’s Poor Richard (1745) has “A small leak will sink a great ship,” a warning against neglecting small expenses. Miss MacIntosh turns it from money to sin, where one small fault can sink a soul.
    • John Bunyan is credited with the saying “One leak will sink a ship: and one sin will destroy a sinner.”
  • “when the roll was called up yonder”: “When the Roll Is Called Up Yonder” is a popular Christian hymn that speaks of being ready for the day when God’s chosen ones gather in heaven. The song was written by James Milton Black in 1893 and has been translated into multiple languages and sung by various artists. (Wikipedia) The song’s lyrics are often interpreted as a reflection on the concept of the Book of Life and the promise of eternal life in heaven. It encourages believers to live a life of faith and service so that they will be among those who are called up yonder. Here the hymn becomes part of Miss MacIntosh’s shipwreck lament, where “God Himself should not know us, and our own parents should not know us.” The phrase underscores the idea that life and death, beginnings and ends, are intertwined and that ultimately, all must face a final accounting beyond earthly existence.
  • “we are sinned against more than we are sinning”: “I am a man / More sinned against than sinning” (King Lear 3.2). See Shakespeare.
  • “Clubs are trumps”: The cards of Chapter 14. See Gambling and Playing Cards and the Chapter 14 resources.
  • “Luck is for the few, but death is for the many”: The line echoes an Arabic proverb, “Misfortune is for everyone, but good fortune is for a few” (al-bala yaʿumm wa al-rahma takhuss; Al-Ahram, “Proverb of the day”). The phrase is a somber reminder of human mortality and the limits of worldly success, fitting into the novel’s larger themes of illusion, inevitability, and the search for meaning in the face of death.
  • “Never married, never buried. An old man’s love is a young maid’s sorrow”: Both lines are old proverbs, often found in folk traditions and songs, particularly in the context of warnings against marrying old men, as in the ballad “Maids When You’re Young Never Wed an Old Man” (Ballad Index). John Heywood’s Proverbs (1546) has the other side: “Better to be an old man’s darling than a young man’s warling.”
  • “The bald head is soonest shaved”: Miss MacIntosh turns old jokes about baldness on herself, here and in “No grass grows on a busy street.” See Hair, Wig, and Baldness.
  • “a fool’s paradise”: The phrase is Middle English, and the earliest known use is in the Paston Letters of 1462. In Romeo and Juliet, the Nurse warns Romeo not to “lead her into a fool’s paradise” (2.4). Miss MacIntosh tells Vera she was “living in a fool’s paradise, and now you know there is no answer.” See Shakespeare.
  • “Heaven’s nets are woven very wide”: The Tao Te Ching, chapter 73, in one common translation: “Heaven’s net is vast; though its meshes are wide, nothing slips through.” Miss MacIntosh finishes the thought, “but none shall escape them.” Indra’s Net appears in the Atharva Veda, and Huayan Buddhism made it the image of a world where each jewel in an endless net reflects every other. It means that the net of divine grace or judgment is extensive and all-encompassing, offering no easy escape from one’s spiritual destiny. It underscores themes of universality, inevitability, and the encompassing nature of divine authority in the novel. See Taoism and Zhuangzi, Hinduism, and Buddhism.
  • “this life was all a dream”: The idea runs through many works:
    • Pedro Calderón de la Barca’s Life Is a Dream (first performed 1635, published 1636) is a famous play that uses the metaphor of life as a dream to explore themes of free will, fate, and the nature of reality. The play’s central character, Segismundo, is imprisoned in a tower and then released, experiencing both pleasure and suffering before being told it was all a dream. (Wikipedia) See the Chapter 2 resources.
    • Prospero’s “We are such stuff / As dreams are made on, and our little life / Is rounded with a sleep” (The Tempest 4.1) compares life to a dream.
    • Edgar Allan Poe’s “A Dream Within a Dream” explores the cyclical nature of dreams and the illusion of reality, further reinforcing the idea of life as a dream. See Edgar Allan Poe.
    • Ludwig Wittgenstein wrote in a diary entry of the early 1930s: “We are asleep. Our life is like a dream. But in our better hours we wake up just enough to realize that we are dreaming.” See Wittgenstein.
    • In Indian philosophy, Maya, literally “illusion” or “magic,” has many meanings; in later Vedic texts it connotes a “magic show, an illusion where things appear to be present but are not what they seem.” (Wikipedia) See Hinduism.
  • “her fishnet bag with her Pilgrim’s Progress”: Miss MacIntosh’s Bunyan again. See the Chapter 3 resources.
  • “the last rose of the last summer on earth”: “The Last Rose of Summer” is a poem by the Irish poet Thomas Moore, published in 1813 and written while staying at Jenkinstown Castle in County Kilkenny, Ireland, where he was said to have been inspired by the China rose ‘Old Blush.’ (Wikipedia) It poignantly represents the final vestiges of youth, vitality, and love, standing on the brink of disappearance, much like the characters grappling with mortality and the fading of dreams. See Roses and Flowers and the Chapter 6 resources.
  • “There is no God”: “The fool hath said in his heart, There is no God” (Psalm 14:1). Diagoras of Melos, a fifth-century BC poet, was called “the Atheist” in antiquity. He was said to have mocked the Eleusinian Mysteries and was condemned at Athens. This phrase marks a moment of profound questioning or a crisis point in the narrative where the comforting presence of God is deeply questioned or felt to be absent, confronting the characters with the mystery of existence and the silence in the face of suffering. See The Bible.
  • “the true love is that which does not alter when it alteration finds”: Shakespeare wrote, “Love is not love / Which alters when it alteration finds… O no! it is an ever-fixed mark / That looks on tempests and is never shaken” (Sonnet 116). Young follows with “The true love wears an old shirt and is familiar.” See Shakespeare and the Chapter 6 resources.
  • “as if I myself had become Falada”: Vera’s pony of Chapter 16, named for the horse in the Grimm tale. See Falada, Horses and Carriages, and the Chapter 16 resources.
  • “the heavy, claw-shaped mark of her hand upon my forehead”: In Chapter 10, Vera imagined “claws upon her forehead like the claws of a lobster.” Now the claw marks Vera. See Miss MacIntosh and the Chapter 10 resources.
  • “I have tried to be charitable”: “And now abideth faith, hope, charity, these three; but the greatest of these is charity” (1 Corinthians 13:13). See The Bible.
  • “hold with the hounds while she ran with the hares”: John Heywood’s proverb (1546). See Fairy Tales and Folklore.
  • “a house divided”: “If a house be divided against itself, that house cannot stand” (Mark 3:25), and Lincoln’s speech of 1858. See The Bible and The Civil War.
  • “to stand with one foot in the sea and one foot on the shore”: “Men were deceivers ever, / One foot in sea and one on shore, / To one thing constant never” (Much Ado About Nothing 2.3). See Shakespeare.
  • “all flesh, she said, is as the burned grass”: “For all flesh is as grass, and all the glory of man as the flower of grass. The grass withereth, and the flower thereof falleth away” (1 Peter 1:24). This metaphor, spoken by Miss MacIntosh during a moment of intense revelation and struggle with Vera (the narrator), equates human flesh with grass that has been burned. Something once living and vibrant but now scorched, fragile, and destined to wither away. It conveys the stark reality that human life, no matter how vibrant or full, is ultimately fleeting and fragile, much like grass that is scorched by fire and will not regrow. It invites reflection on mortality and the importance of facing life’s truths with courage and acceptance. See The Bible.
  • “every heart is married to death who is the bridegroom and the bride”: Death as the bridegroom, as in Chapter 15. It means that human life is fundamentally intertwined with death. Death is not an external threat but a constant, intimate presence in life. It emphasizes the tragic and inevitable nature of mortality that defines and shapes human existence, love, and relationships. This theme is woven throughout the novel, in the narrator’s reflections on life, death, and illusion. See Weddings and Funerals, Death and Mortality, and the Chapter 15 resources.
  • “the king of rags and patches”: Hamlet calls his uncle “A king of shreds and patches” (Hamlet 3.4). See Shakespeare.
  • “Better be stung by a nettle than pricked by a rose”: An old proverb. The nettle’s sting is sharp but plain, while the rose, beautiful and seemingly gentle, wounds in hiding.
  • “He who covers us with his wings will bite us with his bill”: The first half echoes Psalm 91:4, “He shall cover thee with his feathers, and under his wings shalt thou trust.” It is a vivid metaphor expressing the ambivalence and potential cruelty in relationships, especially those involving protection or intimacy. This line suggests that the one who seems to protect or shelter us (covering us with wings, like a bird shielding its young) can also cause harm or betrayal (biting us with his bill). It captures the paradox that those closest to us, who may offer care and safety, can also inflict pain and disappointment. The imagery implies vulnerability and the complicated nature of love and trust with those who protect have the power to hurt as well. The phrase conveys the idea that protection and harm are often intertwined in human relationships, emphasizing the complexity and sometimes painful duality of intimacy. See The Bible.
  • “Better go to hell with rags than to heaven with embroidery”: The old proverb runs the other way: “Better go to heaven in rags than to hell in embroidery.” Miss MacIntosh turns it around.
  • “the crooked way of the crab”: Aesop’s crab, who cannot walk straight. See Fairy Tales and Folklore and the Chapter 15 resources.
  • “Why bark if one keeps a dog?”: “Why keep a dog and bark yourself?” (1583). See Dogs.
  • “the chief industry of northern Michigan”: Iron and copper mining and lumber on Michigan’s Upper Peninsula.
  • “Where was Egg Harbor?”: Egg Harbor is a village in Door County, Wisconsin. There is also an Egg Harbor in New Jersey.
  • “Where was Aldebaran?”: Aldebaran is a giant star in the zodiac constellation Taurus. See Astronomy.
  • “Where was the lost star?”: Traditionally the lost star is the Lost Pleiad, Merope, said to have dimmed for shame at marrying a mortal. See the Chapter 11 resources.
  • “Where was Tobias Smollett?”: Tobias Smollett (1721-1771) was a Scottish author known for his picaresque novels. Miss MacIntosh names him in her dawn quiz, among places, battles, and stars.
  • “it was all a dream through which I had lived”: Miss MacIntosh and Vera’s mother Catherine seem to agree that whether a person decides to fill their head with factual knowledge or live in an imaginary world, it is all a dream of living and dying. Human beings ultimately go through life not knowing why they are here or not wanting to know.
  • “where was Skagerrak”: The Skagerrak is a strait between Denmark, Norway, and Sweden, “an arm of the North Sea,” as Miss MacIntosh says, “which should be south of Norway.”
  • “the Battle of Shiloh”: The Battle of Shiloh (April 1862) was fought in the Western Theater of the American Civil War. See The Civil War.
  • “the Society Islands”: The Society Islands, which include Tahiti, are an archipelago in the South Pacific Ocean.
  • “the Easter Islands”: Easter Island is a remote volcanic island in Polynesia. See the Chapter 3 resources.
  • “who spoke only with a whistling language”: Whistled languages exist in Spain, Turkey, France, Mexico, South America, India, Nepal, New Guinea, and West Africa. The best known is the Silbo Gomero of La Gomera, in the Canary Islands.
  • “where was Shakespeare?”: William Shakespeare was an English playwright, poet and actor. See Shakespeare.
  • “the Palace of the Doges”: The Palace of the Doges was built in the Venetian Gothic style in Venice. See the Chapter 16 resources.
  • “Where was Ratisbon?”: Ratisbon is the old name of Regensburg, in Bavaria, which Napoleon stormed in 1809. Browning’s “Incident of the French Camp” (1842) begins, “You know, we French stormed Ratisbon.” See Napoleon and Wellington.
  • “Where was Paul Revere?”: Paul Revere was an American silversmith, engraver, early industrialist, and Patriot of the American Revolution. (Wikipedia) Longfellow’s “Paul Revere’s Ride” (1861) begins, “Listen, my children, and you shall hear / Of the midnight ride of Paul Revere.” See American Writers.
  • “Where were the Pyrenees?”: The Pyrenees are a mountain range that separates the Iberian Peninsula from the rest of Europe.
  • “old proverbs plucked from the World Almanac or farmers’ journals”: The World Almanac has been published since 1868. The Farmer’s Almanac appears in Chapter 15. See the Chapter 15 resources.
  • “the joker is that card which has no face but is the highest card when it is used in euchre”: The joker was added to the deck for euchre in 1860s America as the “best bower,” the highest card, just as Miss MacIntosh says. See Gambling and Playing Cards.
  • “most men are conceived in the night and die with the ebbing of the tide”: In Dickens’s David Copperfield (1850), Mr. Peggotty says of the dying Barkis, “People can’t die, along the coast, except when the tide’s pretty nigh out.” Falstaff died “ev’n at the turning o’ th’ tide” (Henry V 2.3). See Shakespeare.
  • “Where were her red jersey bloomers?”: Amelia Bloomer’s reform dress. See Women, Gender, and Marriage and the Chapter 9 resources.
  • “an un-Christian institution for the sports of kings and fools”: The Roman circus was the arena for chariot racing, the greatest being the Circus Maximus, which held well over 150,000 spectators. Early Christian writers such as Tertullian, in On the Spectacles (around 200 AD), condemned the games as pagan idolatry, and tradition linked the arenas with the martyrdom of Christians.
  • “or were they angels in the furnace fire?”: The fourth figure in the fiery furnace, “like the Son of God” (Daniel 3:25), and Daniel in the lions’ den (Daniel 6). See The Bible.
  • “winter is summer’s heir”: The proverb of Chapter 15. See the Chapter 15 resources.
  • “The tallow is burning low. We have no oil.”: The foolish virgins of the parable say, “Give us of your oil; for our lamps are gone out” (Matthew 25:8), and miss the bridegroom. See The Bible and Weddings and Funerals.
  • “the rose at the North Pole is the rose immortal”: In a spiritual sense it signifies the coexistence of death and eternal life, the presence of enduring beauty and essence in a world otherwise marked by loss, coldness, and transience. It evokes a mystical, almost sacred dimension beneath the surface of harsh reality or an eternal “rose” blooming in the frozen heart of the North Pole. See Exploration and the Poles.
    • A compass rose, sometimes called a rose of the winds, is the diagram of directions on maps and nautical charts, and medieval mariners were expected to name all 32 of its points. It is also the emblem of the worldwide Anglican Communion. (Wikipedia) There are two North Poles, magnetic and true.
  • “What if the whole world should turn to salt?”: Lot’s wife “became a pillar of salt” (Genesis 19:26). See Genesis.
  • “A good husband makes a good wife”: Miss MacIntosh in this case is taking on the role of the groom in molding Vera to be the bride. See Women, Gender, and Marriage.
  • “robbing Peter to pay Paul”: or other versions that have developed over the centuries such as “to borrow from Peter to pay Paul” and “to unclothe Peter to clothe Paul” are phrases meaning to take from one person or thing to give to another, especially when it results in the elimination of one debt by incurring another. (Wikipedia) Within the context of the chapter, it emphasizes the frustration with life’s compromises and the lack of genuine progress or resolution in their difficult circumstances. It conveys the sense of being caught in a cycle of compromises and sacrifices that do not truly improve the situation but merely shift burdens around, reflecting the broader themes of futility, suffering, and the search for meaning in the novel.
  • “we must prepare to go into the winter solstice”: Chapter 15 sets this night in “the hot August night,” so Miss MacIntosh is looking ahead to winter. “Solstice” comes from the Latin sol and sistere, “the sun stands still,” which Young spells out: “when the sun should apparently stand still.”
  • “triple-crowned kings”: The triple crown is the papal tiara. See the Chapter 16 resources.
  • “the Anatolian coast”: Anatolia is the peninsula of Western Asia that makes up most of Turkey.
  • “the Bay of Biscay”: The Bay of Biscay is a gulf south of the Celtic Sea.
  • “the Shetland Islands”: The Shetland Islands are an archipelago in Scotland.
  • “and Archangel”: Archangel, or Arkhangelsk, is a Russian port on the White Sea.
  • “Archimedes”: Archimedes was a Greek mathematician, physicist, engineer, inventor, and astronomer. (Wikipedia) In the chapter he is a representation of reason, science, and the human quest for comprehension amidst the mystical and often inscrutable realities that Vera confronts in her dreamlike journey. His figure anchors the narrative’s oscillation between the mystical and the rational, the historical and the personal. See the Chapter 15 resources.
  • “fuss and feathers”: “Old Fuss and Feathers” was the nickname of General Winfield Scott, known for his love of uniform and ceremony.
  • “O, temporal O, mores!”: Cicero’s “O tempora, o mores!” (“Oh, the times! Oh, the customs!”), from his speech Against Catiline (63 BC), garbled by Miss MacIntosh.
  • “for he is unworthy to live who lives only for himself and not somewhat in others”: The wording has not been traced to Luther. His On the Freedom of a Christian (1520) closes on a like thought, that a Christian “lives not in himself, but in Christ and in his neighbor.” The line expresses a moral and philosophical viewpoint about the nature of a meaningful life. It suggests that a person who lives solely for their own self-interest, without regard or connection to other people, lacks true worth or dignity. This idea aligns with Miss MacIntosh’s practical and no-nonsense worldview, emphasizing selflessness, community, and service to others as fundamental values. She believes that life’s purpose is found in caring for and contributing to the well-being of others (the poor orphans of this world) and that the “fool’s paradise” of self-indulgence and isolation is not the way to live a good or worthy life. The phrase means that a life confined within selfishness and isolation is considered lacking, and true worth comes from empathy, love, and living in connection with other souls. It underscores one of the novel’s recurrent themes about the importance of shared humanity and moral responsibility toward others.
  • “if ever I told what I had seen, she would kill me”: A person who rapes another often threatens their life or the life of someone they care about in order to ensure they will never tell anyone what happened.
  • “She had never seen it herself except in a mirror”: Until this night, only a mirror had seen her baldness. See Mirrors and Reflections.
  • “a man’s bedroom was a man’s castle”: “A man’s house is his castle” (Sir Edward Coke, 1628). See Women, Gender, and Marriage.
  • “She had tried to woo me away from my mother, believing I was more nearly her child than my mother’s”: Young told Studs Terkel that the novel began with “a famous court case” in which “a rich girl… declared publicly that she loved her nursemaid more than her mother”: “that is actually where the idea of the book came from” (Marguerite Young, interview with Studs Terkel, WFMT radio, 1965). Young did not name the case. Coral Russell, searching for the case Young may have meant, identified the most likely match as the 1934 Vanderbilt custody trial, in which ten-year-old Gloria Vanderbilt clung to her nurse, Emma Sullivan Keislich, “Dodo,” and the newspapers called her the “poor little rich girl.” See Vera Cartwheel and Miss MacIntosh.
  • “Common sense was the rarest jewel, more precious than rubies”: Wisdom “is more precious than rubies” (Proverbs 3:15), and “the price of wisdom is above rubies” (Job 28:18). See The Bible and The Book of Job.
  • “I needed a father to guide me”: Miss MacIntosh believes Vera should have had a father and this might refer to a husband since in earlier marriages a daughter is passed from her father to her husband as her guardian. See Women, Gender, and Marriage.
  • “tempus fugit”: Tempus fugit is Latin for “time flies.” It comes from Virgil’s Georgics (3.284), “fugit inreparabile tempus,” time flies, never to be regained.
  • “Age is the most difficult thing to achieve”: Life expectancy in the United States in 1900 was 47 years and in 1950 rose to 68 years. Neil deGrasse Tyson has said, “The fact that you and I are alive is against stupendous odds. One day we will die, and that’s sad, but there are people who will never die because they were never born. We’re the lucky ones, we get to die” (in conversation with Vikas Shah, Thought Economics, January 13, 2023). Miss MacIntosh whispers the line as Vera falls asleep, just after “Alas, I was several years younger then than I am now, for tempus fugit.” To achieve age is to endure loss, hardship, and change, not simply to count the years.
    • Society shapes human health because social factors like income, education, stress levels, access to healthcare, neighborhood environment, social support networks, and cultural norms significantly influence people’s health behaviors, prevailing marketing around lifestyle choices, and overall health outcomes, essentially determining the level of health an individual can achieve within a given community. The World Health Organization calls these the social determinants of health, “the conditions in which people are born, grow, work, live, and age.”

Chapter 50

← Chapter 49 · Home · Chapter 51 →

Summary

Everything seems off key and out of course to Mr. Spitzer, the universe tacking like the wild white snow bird and every room doubling, so that when he sees two golden chairs in the clouds he does not know which is the dream. He steps lightly, breathes softly, and pauses before every door lest it open on the void, for he believes he is living his life after death and may be the one dreamer who dreams not. It was not from the opium lady, “the invalid lady flourishing on the enchantment of nightshade,” who waits for him as for his dead self and mistakes life for death, that he learned that all that happened happened only once. Life is a moment’s fading luminosity, and he is not the Holy Writ but the flyleaf stuck between the testaments, ground between the zenith stone and the nadir stone, leaving no water-mark, no signature, no name. His little firefly is his key of gold and perhaps all there is. He walks like the tide, advancing as he retreats. He learned much from the old suffragette captain, for whom the hyphen in her name was more important than the two names it joined; she died before he came, and for her he wrote this nocturne.

Characters present

Catherine Cartwheel · Joachim Spitzer · Cousin Hannah

Concepts present

Themes: Death and Mortality · Identity and the Self · Illusion and Reality · Society, Class, and Race · The Search for Meaning

Symbols: Butterflies and Moths · Fireflies · Keys, Doors, and Locks · Lamps, Candles, and Light · Mirrors and Reflections · Moon and Stars · The Sea and Water · Twins and Doubles

Philosophy: Astrology, Alchemy, and Esoterica · Descartes and Dualism · Heraclitus and Flux · Hinduism · Plato and Platonism · Pythagoras and the Music of the Spheres · Taoism and Zhuangzi

Allusions: Alice in Wonderland · American Writers · Ancient Egypt · Astronomy · Exploration and the Poles · Genesis · Greek Mythology · Music and Composers · Revelation and the Apocalypse · Romantic Poets · The Bible · Women’s Suffrage

Key passages

From the research

  • The chapter opens with Mr. Spitzer lamenting how “everything seemed off key and out of course,” and how the universe “tack[ed] like the wild white snow bird away from central fires of jewels.” This passage introduces the core theme of disorientation and the impossibility of fixed maps or certainties in this universe. The imagery of drifting moons, vanished stars, and shifting mirrors sets the tone for a world where nothing is stable or fully knowable.
  • Mr. Spitzer contemplates seeing “two golden chairs in the clouds” and not knowing which is real or if both are illusions. This metaphor reflects his deeper fear of indistinguishable realities and the collapse of boundaries between dream and reality, self and other. His caution about touching the “strings of the constellation Lyre” for fear of interacting with imaginary elements highlights his existential uncertainty.
  • A significant passage is Mr. Spitzer’s reflection that he is living his “after-life, his life after death,” questioning when he had ever lived before death. He is cautious and uncertain, “continually checking, rechecking” his impressions as he navigates this liminal state. His wildness and caution are balanced by his awareness that he may be the one who “dreamed not,” forced to live by the dreams of others, symbolizing a profound detachment from conventional experience and identity.
  • Although Mr. Spitzer spends much time with the opium lady, he did not learn from her the sense of mortality or the failure of the sensorium (his perception). She is “the invalid lady flourishing on the enchantment of nightshade,” who lived so immersed in imagination that she blurred the lines between life and death, day and night. Her failure to distinguish these states contrasts with Mr. Spitzer’s heightened awareness of the ephemeral nature of existence.
  • Mr. Spitzer recognizes that “all that happened happened only once” and that life is a “moment’s fading luminosity.” He mourns the impossibility of going back, the non-recurrence of events, and the uniqueness of every moment. This awareness adds a tragic beauty and pathos to life’s fleeting nature. The metaphor of a train derailed in grass or a star derailed captures his sense of displacement and loss.
  • The chapter explores places that are neither: land nor water, one nor the other, ambiguous or undefined regions. This reflects existential ambiguity and the difficulty of defining states of being, identity, or even reality itself. Mr. Spitzer identifies with these liminal spaces, drifting and lost like sailors or farmers swallowed by the earth.
  • Mr. Spitzer sees himself as a “mere flyleaf stuck between two passages or testaments,” not the main text of life or death but a transient, fragile presence. The imagery of silver and gold illuminations shining through him like candle flames evokes a faint spiritual light, but ultimately one that is transient and delicate. He reflects on the absence of any lasting mark or memory of his passage, emphasizing mortality and the erasure of individual existence.
  • Among all the vast and complex imagery, the motif of the “little firefly” stands out as Mr. Spitzer’s “key of gold,” his soul, and the light he reads by. This small light represents the essence of life or consciousness amid the vast silence and uncertainty. It suggests that perhaps all that remains or matters is this fragile inner light.
  • Mr. Spitzer’s movement is described as a tide advancing and retreating, embodying hesitation, uncertainty, and the interplay of opposites. This rhythm of contradictory motion captures the existential tension he experiences, the constant questioning and the inability to find firm ground or certainty.
  • Towards the end, Mr. Spitzer recalls lessons from an old suffragette captain whose hyphenated name symbolizes the joining of opposites and the importance of connection (“the hyphen was all”). Her life was solitary, and her death represented a pause in a broken melody, suggesting unresolved narratives and the persistence of longing or unfinished business beyond death.

Questions and observations

Reading closely

  • “He was often at a loss when he saw two golden chairs in the clouds to know in which chair to sit.” Why is choosing a chair so dangerous?
  • Mr. Spitzer is “not the Holy Writ but was the mere flyleaf stuck between two passages or testaments.” What does it mean to live between the testaments?
  • “His little firefly was his key of gold.” What is the firefly?

Characters

  • “Perhaps among dreamers he was the one person who dreamed not.” How can someone who dreams not live “by the dreams of others”?
  • The opium lady “waited for him as for his dead self whom she had loved or thought she loved.” Who does she think Mr. Spitzer is?
  • For the old suffragette captain “the hyphen was all.” What does the hyphen join?

Connections

  • In Chapter 49 Mr. Spitzer could not tell whether he was one or two. Here “he feared that one should be one.” Why is being one more frightening?
  • Mr. Spitzer places Hannah “with her head pointing North and her feet pointing South.” How does this echo the poles and reversals of earlier chapters?
  • The chapter closes with a nocturne. How does night music close what came before?

Reflection

  • “All that happened happened only once.” Does this make life more precious or more terrible?
  • “Because he took so much for granted, it might seem that he took nothing for granted.” Is caution a form of faith?
  • “There would be no star of this world in memory of him.” What would you want to leave behind?

Research: Characters

Mr. Spitzer

  • Mr. Spitzer is a liminal figure, caught between life and death, reality and dream, certainty and doubt.
  • He exhibits caution born of experience, aware of the fragility of perception and existence, yet he also harbors a “wildness” that contrasts with his cautiousness.
  • His relationship with other characters reveals his search for meaning through others’ dreams and experiences, though he himself “dreamed not.”
  • His journey is symbolic of human consciousness confronting mortality and the unknown beyond.

Catherine Cartwheel

  • The opium lady “waited for him as for his dead self whom she had loved or thought she loved,” and “she had always lived by such indirections and evasions that she would never know when he was gone.”

Cousin Hannah

  • The old suffragette captain, “for whom the hyphen was more important than the two names it joined… for the hyphen was all.”
  • “So solitary her life had been. How could death be different or provide any great change for her? Her mind had died before her heart had died.”

Research: Themes

The Fluidity and Ambiguity of Reality and Identity

See: Illusion and Reality · Identity and the Self

  • Mr. Spitzer experiences a world where “everything seemed off key and out of course” and where familiar structures (rooms, stars, chairs) multiply or dissolve, making it impossible to distinguish reality from dream or hallucination.
  • The doubling of images and uncertainty about which chair to sit on symbolize the instability of identity and the multiplicity of existence. The text questions whether one can trust the senses or even oneself: “one chair might be only the dream, and one might be real.”

Death and the Afterlife as Continuums, Not Endings

See: Death and Mortality

  • The text portrays death not as a final cessation but as a passage to another form of existence or consciousness. Mr. Spitzer’s “life after death” is a realm where time, space, and form are mutable and indistinct.
  • There is a tension between the desire for continuity (to find a “way-station” or star where love and identity persist) and the fear of absolute dissolution (“he feared that one should be one, both the dream and the reality”).

The Limits of Knowledge and Perception

See: The Search for Meaning

  • Mr. Spitzer is cautious, “continually checking, rechecking, altering his impressions,” recognizing that perceptions themselves alter and deceive.
  • The text explores the idea that some beings or states (“cells which knew not death or life”) may exist beyond human comprehension.

The Transience and Uniqueness of Life

  • Life is portrayed as a fleeting moment, a “moment’s fading luminosity,” never repeating or returning (“there was nothing twice the same”).
  • This impermanence imbues life with pathos and beauty, likened to snowflakes melting or fireflies flickering.

Philosophical and Existential Questions

See: The Search for Meaning

  • What is reality if perceptions and identities are unstable or illusory?
  • Is death an end or a transformation?
  • Can one separate the self from the dream or the other?
  • What is the nature of time and experience if moments never repeat and life is a singular event?
  • How does one live in the face of uncertainty and impermanence?

Research: Symbols and Imagery

Stars and Moons

See: Moon and Stars

  • Represent shifting phases of identity and reality, the unreachable or illusory nature of truth (“locked moons with tangled horns,” “vanished stars”).

Mirrors and Prisms

See: Mirrors and Reflections

  • Symbols of reflection and distortion, suggesting fragmented perception and the multiplicity of selves.

Fireflies and Light

See: Fireflies · Lamps, Candles, and Light

  • Recurring symbols of the soul or consciousness, fragile and transient, yet illuminating the darkness.

Doors and Thresholds

See: Keys, Doors, and Locks

  • Emblems of transition and uncertainty, with repeated imagery of doors opening, closing, or leading to voids.

Water and Tides

See: The Sea and Water

  • Represent flux, the movement between life and death, progress and retreat, echoing the ebb and flow of existence.

Research: Resources

  • “where the snowflakes whirled big as cartwheels”: The snowflakes are “big as cartwheels,” and later the fire medusas are “big as cart wheels”: Young plays on the Cartwheel name of Vera and her mother. See Catherine Cartwheel and Vera Cartwheel.
  • “trembling mirages piling up like mountainous waves”: The castles that appear and vanish over the water recall the Fata Morgana, the mirage of towers and castles seen above the Strait of Messina and named for Morgan le Fay. See The Sea and Water.
  • “the same in his end as in his beginning”: “In my beginning is my end,” and “In my end is my beginning” (T. S. Eliot, “East Coker,” 1940), after the motto of Mary, Queen of Scots, En ma fin est mon commencement.
  • “prisms breaking mirrors which should have looked upon eternity”: “Life, like a dome of many-coloured glass, / Stains the white radiance of Eternity” (Percy Bysshe Shelley, Adonais, stanza 52, 1821). See Romantic Poets and Mirrors and Reflections.
  • “One might disappear like the Water Carrier”: The chairs vanish like constellations at dawn. See Astronomy and Astrology, Alchemy, and Esoterica.
    • The Water Carrier is the constellation Aquarius. The water carrier is Ganymede, cupbearer to Zeus.
    • Cassiopeia’s Golden Chair or Cassiopeia’s chair is a constellation in the northern sky. The vain queen Cassiopeia was set among the stars on her throne.
    • The Crib is Praesepe, the Manger, the Beehive Cluster in Cancer; the Virgin is the constellation Virgo.
    • The Hair of Berenice is an ancient group of stars in the northern sky. Queen Berenice II of Egypt cut off her hair as an offering for her husband’s safe return from war, and the astronomer Conon declared it had been set among the stars (Callimachus, “The Lock of Berenice,” translated by Catullus, poem 66).
    • The constellation Lyre or Lyra is a small one in the northern sky. It is the lyre of Orpheus; see Lyra in the Chapter 49 resources. See Greek Mythology.
  • “a lyre without strings”: The Chinese poet Tao Yuanming (365-427) kept a qin without strings and would stroke it when he drank, saying that one who understood the instrument had no need of the sound of its strings (Book of Jin, biography of Tao Qian). See Taoism and Zhuangzi.
  • “or dice without markings”: “I, at any rate, am convinced that He is not playing at dice” (Albert Einstein, letter to Max Born, December 4, 1926, in The Born-Einstein Letters, trans. Irene Born, 1971).
  • “a dog without a bark”: “The dog did nothing in the night-time.” “That was the curious incident,” remarked Sherlock Holmes (Arthur Conan Doyle, “Silver Blaze,” 1892).
  • “Should a demoniac butterfly appear”: A demoniac butterfly may refer to a restricted demon or grass demon butterfly found in Asia. The Greek psyche means both soul and butterfly, and the butterfly rising from the fire is the soul leaving the body. See Butterflies and Moths and Greek Mythology.
  • “His breath was his spirit”: Spirit comes from the Latin spiritus, breath. “And the LORD God formed man of the dust of the ground, and breathed into his nostrils the breath of life; and man became a living soul” (Genesis 2:7). See Genesis.
  • “dream dreamed by another dreamer”: A dream dreamed by another dreamer points to multiple levels of perception and existence where the boundaries between dream and reality blur. Tweedledee tells Alice that the Red King is dreaming her: “You’d be nowhere. Why, you’re only a sort of thing in his dream!” (Lewis Carroll, Through the Looking-Glass, 1871, chapter 4). See Zhuangzi’s butterfly in the Chapter 49 resources. See Alice in Wonderland and Taoism and Zhuangzi.
  • “never again would he leave his calling card”: Victorian callers left engraved cards on a silver tray in the hall; a card with a corner turned down meant one had come in person.
  • “the Golden Horn”: The Golden Horn is a major waterway and an inlet of the Bosphorus in Istanbul, Turkey. The schooners round it to reach the opium lady’s bedside. See Catherine Cartwheel.
  • “she saw the human-sized blackbird at the door”: See the human-sized blackbird of Weissenbach’s dreams in the Chapter 33 resources. See Catherine Cartwheel.
  • “Come in, Blackamoor”: Blackamoor is an old, racist English word for a Black African. Figures of Black servants in livery and turbans, called blackamoors, were fashionable decorations in European and American houses; the opium lady greets the human-sized blackbird with it. See Society, Class, and Race.
  • “the invalid lady flourishing on the enchantment of nightshade”: Nightshade is belladonna; see “this bella donna” in the Chapter 47 resources.
  • “the lighthouse dolphin flashing its dying colors”: “Parting day / Dies like the dolphin, whom each pang imbues / With a new colour as it gasps away, / The last still loveliest” (Lord Byron, Childe Harold’s Pilgrimage, canto 4, stanza 29, 1818). The dolphin fish changes color as it dies. See Romantic Poets.
  • “butterfly was sequestered like this mourning cloak”: The mourning cloak butterfly, dark with a pale border, sleeps through the winter as an adult hidden in bark and crevices. See Butterflies and Moths.
  • “There was no twin star to this”: The twin star is the lost brother; see Peron, who “would not live” beyond Mr. Spitzer. See Twins and Doubles.
  • “threads wrapped around a spindle”: In Plato’s myth of Er the heavens turn on the Spindle of Necessity, and “on the upper surface of each circle is a siren, who goes round with them, hymning a single tone or note. The eight together form one harmony” (Republic 10, 617b, trans. Benjamin Jowett, 1871). See Plato and Platonism and Pythagoras and the Music of the Spheres.
  • “the door of truth which was covered with a golden disc”: “The door of the True is covered with a golden disk. Open that, O Pûshan, that we may see the nature of the True” (Isa Upanishad 15, trans. F. Max Müller, 1879). See Hinduism and Keys, Doors, and Locks.
  • “the ambient surrey top with its fringes”: See the fringe-topped surrey in the Chapter 49 resources.
  • “perhaps the poles themselves had flown”: A geographic pole is either of the two points where Earth’s axis of rotation meets its surface, the North Pole in the Arctic Ocean and the South Pole in Antarctica. The poles wander by a few meters over a few years, partly from the Chandler wobble, a free oscillation with a period of about 433 days, but for maps they are taken as fixed, the points where the lines of longitude meet. (Wikipedia) See the reversals of the magnetic poles in the Chapter 42 resources. See Exploration and the Poles.
  • “an empire enduring a thousand years”: The Nazis called their state the Thousand-Year Reich; it lasted twelve years, 1933 to 1945. In Revelation the saints reign with Christ “a thousand years” (Revelation 20:4). See Revelation and the Apocalypse.
  • “the blind astronomer”: Galileo, who first turned the telescope on the heavens in 1609, was blind by 1638. See Astronomy.
  • “a flying sand grain might grow to be a star”: See Blake’s “To see a World in a Grain of Sand” in the Chapter 46 resources. See Romantic Poets.
  • “begot this pearl with the light burning within”: A pearl forms when an oyster coats an irritant with layer upon layer of nacre; the grain of sand of legend is rarely the cause, more often a parasite or a bit of tissue. “The kingdom of heaven is like unto a merchant man, seeking goodly pearls: Who, when he had found one pearl of great price, went and sold all that he had, and bought it” (Matthew 13:45-46). See The Bible.
  • “there was neither starboard nor larboard”: Larboard, the left side of a ship, was replaced by “port” because it was too easily confused with starboard; the Royal Navy made the change official in 1844. See The Sea and Water.
  • “false signal lights luring him out of his depths”: Wreckers of Cornish legend were said to show false lights on the cliffs to lure ships onto the rocks for plunder. See The Sea and Water.
  • “to know that there was nothing twice the same”: Young reverses Heraclitus, “The way up and the way down is one and the same,” here “the way up was not the way down,” and follows him in “You cannot step twice into the same rivers; for fresh waters are ever flowing in upon you” (Heraclitus, fragments 69 and 41, in John Burnet, Early Greek Philosophy, 1892). T. S. Eliot set the first as an epigraph to “Burnt Norton” (1936). See Heraclitus and Flux.
  • “many pages of the book of life had been transparent”: “And I saw the dead, small and great, stand before God; and the books were opened: and another book was opened, which is the book of life” (Revelation 20:12). See Revelation and the Apocalypse.
  • “old, skull-faced surrey-driver”: See The Black Coachman.
  • “that earth which swallows the horse and the rider”: “The horse and his rider hath he thrown into the sea” (Exodus 15:1), and “the earth opened her mouth, and swallowed them up” (Numbers 16:32). See The Bible.
  • “many an old mariner chartlessly drifting over the body of his sleeping wife”: “O my America! my new-found-land” (John Donne, Elegy 19, “To His Mistress Going to Bed,” written in the 1590s, published 1669), the lover’s body mapped as a new world.
  • “the Big Dipper and the Little Dipper”: See Ursa Major and Ursa Minor in the Chapter 49 resources. See Astronomy.
  • “bird never to break through the shell of night”: In Hermann Hesse’s Demian (1919) the bird must fight its way out of the egg, which is the world, in order to be born.
  • “not even the book of death”: The Egyptian Book of the Dead, the Book of Coming Forth by Day, was a collection of spells written on papyrus and buried with the dead from about 1550 BCE to guide them through the underworld. See Ancient Egypt.
  • “a handkerchief dropped from the hand of God”: “Or I guess it is the handkerchief of the Lord, / A scented gift and remembrancer designedly dropt” (Walt Whitman, “Song of Myself,” section 6, Leaves of Grass). See American Writers.
  • “a light upon the water”: “Who layeth the beams of his chambers in the waters: who maketh the clouds his chariot: who walketh upon the wings of the wind” (Psalm 104:3). See The Bible and The Sea and Water.
  • “the mere flyleaf stuck between two passages or testaments”: In the King James Bible of 1611 the Apocrypha, books such as 2 Esdras that are outside the Hebrew canon, were printed between the Old and New Testaments; Mr. Spitzer, who “was not of this margin, canon, text” but “the apocryphal firefly,” is that leaf between. See The Bible.
    • Holy Writ is a synonym for the Bible.
  • “between the patriarch and the cloud or water bird”: “Also he sent forth a dove from him, to see if the waters were abated from off the face of the ground” (Genesis 8:8). See Genesis and The Bible.
  • “stuck between the millstone above him and the millstone below him”: “No man shall take the nether or the upper millstone to pledge: for he taketh a man’s life to pledge” (Deuteronomy 24:6), and “Though the mills of God grind slowly, yet they grind exceeding small” (Henry Wadsworth Longfellow, “Retribution,” 1846). See The Bible and American Writers.
  • “fleets of nautiluses turning their sails”: “This is the ship of pearl, which, poets feign, / Sails the unshadowed main” (Oliver Wendell Holmes, “The Chambered Nautilus,” 1858), the shell built “chamber after chamber,” as Young writes here. See American Writers.
  • “no minaret which had written him spiral after spiral”: The spiral minaret of the Great Mosque of Samarra in Iraq, the Malwiya, built between 848 and 852, winds upward in a single ramp.
  • “no water-mark, no signature, no name”: Keats asked that his grave bear no name, only “Here lies One Whose Name was writ in Water” (Protestant Cemetery, Rome, 1821). See Romantic Poets.
  • “His little firefly was his key of gold”: See the firefly lamplighter in the Chapter 48 resources. See Fireflies, Lamps, Candles, and Light, and Keys, Doors, and Locks.
  • “the great huntsman passing at the far zenith of the glassy sky”: Orion hunts with his two dogs, Canis Major and Canis Minor; see the frozen constellations in the Chapter 49 resources. See Astronomy and Greek Mythology.
  • “those gleaming cells which knew not death or life”: Mr. Spitzer imagines the smallest units of life existing beyond the human definitions of living and dead, not knowing or aware of them. “Perhaps no messages had ever arrived”: they may be cut off from any experience that would mark them as alive or dead in a conscious sense. Life and death may be limited concepts, and existence at a deeper level may transcend them.
    • There is an actual case. Henrietta Lacks, a Black woman treated for cervical cancer at Johns Hopkins in 1951, had cells taken without her knowledge or consent; they became HeLa, the first immortal human cell line and an important source of medical data. Neither she nor her family was compensated, and the family did not learn of the cell line until the 1970s (Rebecca Skloot, The Immortal Life of Henrietta Lacks, 2010). Its use for medical research and for commercial purposes continues to raise concerns about privacy and patients’ rights; in 2023 her estate settled a lawsuit against a company that had sold the cells. See Society, Class, and Race.
  • “like the scarlet pimpernels folding at the first approach of rain”: The scarlet pimpernel closes its flowers when the sky clouds over, so it was called the poor man’s weatherglass. Baroness Orczy took it for the sign of her hidden hero in The Scarlet Pimpernel (1905).
  • “sea urchins who knew not whether they lived or were dead”: The sea urchins stand for creatures caught between life, death, and sleep, uncertain of their own condition, and for the mutual ignorance of all beings: even if the urchins know their state, humans cannot know it, nor can the urchins know what humans understand. Much of existence is enveloped in layers of unknowing; “Perhaps all human beings were also mystified, even as Mr. Spitzer was.”
    • It is hard to tell whether a sea urchin is dead or alive, and the red sea urchin may live 200 years. Scientists now hold that humans are not the only beings with the neurological substrates that generate consciousness: “Non-human animals, including all mammals and birds, and many other creatures, including octopuses, also possess these neurological substrates” (The Cambridge Declaration on Consciousness, 2012).
    • Dualism was defended by Descartes who believed that the mind and body were separate and only humans had a mind. Many modern philosophers maintain that the mind is not separate from the body. See Descartes and Dualism.
  • “perhaps at that very time she had lost her love”: The phrase conveys Cousin Hannah’s experience of losing the actual love or connection she once had, yet still being defined or constrained by the formal tie that remains: a poignant reflection on the nature of identity, love, and loss in the story. See Cousin Hannah.
    • Hyphenated double surnames began among the British aristocracy as a way to keep a family name and inheritance alive when there was no male heir, and spread to the Victorian upper middle class. In the United States wives took their husbands’ names; the suffragist Lucy Stone kept her own at her marriage in 1855, and the Lucy Stone League, founded by Ruth Hale in 1921, urged women to do the same. Second-wave feminists of the 1960s and 1970s made the hyphenated name a common choice, and states removed barriers to keeping a birth name on passports, bank accounts, and other documents. For the old suffragette captain “the hyphen was all.” (Wikipedia) See Women’s Suffrage.
  • “without paying a toll”: See Charon’s fare in the Chapter 46 resources. See Greek Mythology.
  • “So he had written this nocturne”: The Irish composer John Field published the first nocturnes in 1812, and Chopin made the form his own. The chapter closes on this night music. See Music and Composers.

Vocabulary

A large sea snail with a spiraled shell that can be blown like a horn. Held to the ear, it seems to hold the sound of the sea.

Fluted

Gentian

Holy Writ

The shining, rainbow-colored lining of some shells, used for inlay.

The lowest point.
Nautilus
A sea creature with a spiral shell. The paper nautilus is a small octopus whose female makes a thin, papery shell.

Content note: This chapter is a long meditation on suicide, which Mr. Spitzer wonders might be “the most creative act.”

Summary

Mr. Spitzer wanders the foggy city tossing coins to street musicians, never sure who is poor or rich, living or dead. One old horn-blower he pitied for years turns out to play in a great symphony orchestra and to be richer than he is. Another, a pale cavalier in white silks outside the old Opera House, turns out to be an usher waiting for his cue; Mr. Spitzer’s gold coin lands in his horn, and soon the whole street is tossing coins. He hears bells, horns, and the cries of migratory birds, and writes his silent music on his shirt cuff where Peron once kept his horse scores. He wonders whether Peron’s suicide was a creative act, a reach for life beyond the grave. He grows convinced that the skeleton inside him is not his own, that body, soul, and spirit may have been exchanged, and that he might even be Peron. What he fears most is a third body that is neither brother. At last he suspects that one fact would explain everything: he is already dead.
