Chapter 35

← Chapter 34 · Home · Chapter 36 →

Content note: Vera’s mother, Catherine Cartwheel, is addicted to opium.

Summary

Catherine imagines Cousin Hannah returning from the dead for a long winter of cards in the empty house, with Mr. Spitzer banished so that he cannot remind her that he outlived her. Mr. Spitzer, who cannot tell a heart from a spade, has always believed Hannah a card cheat and death “itself a great deceiver.” Catherine reviews Hannah’s suffrage campaigns through deserts, emirates, and harems, the bribes she refused, the stained glass window she declined, and her lack of time for courtly graces, small talk, or the dance. Hannah could never have been made to confess that “she had yearned for marriage, or she had loved a man,” for the suffrage movement was “her awesome husband.” Catherine admires in Hannah the “splendid unity of character” she lacks in her own fragmented selves, and wonders who brought the faded rose Hannah clutched when she died in bed. Hannah once told of a eunuch who became a father and was strangled for love. The chapter ends on Catherine’s distrust of anything predictable and her habit, as Mr. Spitzer says, of taking the opposite view.

Characters present

Cousin Hannah · Joachim Spitzer · Catherine Cartwheel · Vera Cartwheel · Peron Spitzer

Concepts present

Themes: Death and Mortality · Duality and Doubles · Fear and Courage · Freedom and Escape · Identity and the Self · Isolation and Connection · Light and Darkness · Memory and the Past · Women, Gender, and Marriage

Symbols: Birds · Butterflies and Moths · Cards, Games, and Chance · Dogs · Fireflies · Horses and Carriages · Lamps, Candles, and Light · Mirrors and Reflections · Moon and Stars · Mountains · Music and Instruments · Snow, Ice, and Winter

Allusions: Astronomy · Ecclesiastes · Exploration and the Poles · Gambling and Playing Cards · Genesis · Greek Mythology · Music and Composers · Napoleon and Wellington · Revelation and the Apocalypse · Romantic Poets · Shakespeare · The Bible · The Book of Job · The Civil War · The History of Opium · Women’s Suffrage

Key passages

From the research

  • Early in the chapter, the narrative contrasts Cousin Hannah’s fiery spirit and audacity with Mr. Spitzer’s cautious, prideful, and somewhat pitiable nature. Mr. Spitzer is portrayed as ignorant of cards, jealous, embittered by failures and losses, and unable to compete or engage fully in life’s “games.” Cousin Hannah, in contrast, is described as a lively, dashing, and indomitable player who “had out-witted every mistaken strategy” of Catherine’s and had “played a mean game of cards,” which metaphorically represents her boldness in life and politics.
  • The chapter extensively praises Cousin Hannah’s life and character. She is portrayed as a “great pioneer” and “great captain” in the suffrage movement, a woman who had no time for trivialities or passive existence. Her life was devoted to overthrowing male domination and advocating for women’s rights on every front, domestic and foreign, and even in unknown territories. The metaphorical imagery of her riding horseback through vast deserts, confronting dragons and minotaurs, and facing physical dangers portrays her as an almost mythic figure whose courage and commitment transcended ordinary limitations.
  • Cousin Hannah’s rejection of typical feminine roles and sentiments, as Catherine sees it, is a key passage. She had no time for “feminine wiles,” “the halo of self-pity,” or a “moment of intimate and unexpected revelation.” Unlike the romantic or domestic aspirations often associated with women of her era, she was married to the suffrage movement itself.
  • Catherine imagines Cousin Hannah returning as a ghost or spirit, invited to stay in the large, empty house with its many vacant rooms and servants. The passage contrasts Cousin Hannah’s vivid, active presence with Mr. Spitzer’s “vacant face” and absence, underscoring the symbolic displacement of vitality by inertia and jealousy.
  • The chapter reflects on the idea that Cousin Hannah is “more vivid in death than she had been in life,” having “escaped this wide-meshed net of years.” The chapter contrasts the enduring flame of her character with the fading presence of others, including Mr. Spitzer.
  • Vera’s mother, Catherine, sees herself as fragmented with multiple partial selves and vague thoughts, compared to Cousin Hannah’s remarkable unity of character and steadfastness. This passage offers insight into the psychological complexity and self-reflection of Vera’s mother, emphasizing themes of identity, coherence, and internal conflict.
  • The chapter describes Cousin Hannah’s “hardy temper,” her unflinching courage in the face of threats, dangers, and opposition, and her refusal to compromise or surrender. Her willingness to face “greater dangers than most men know” and to cross forbidden boundaries symbolizes her heroic stature and her commitment to her cause.
  • Towards the end, Catherine is portrayed as “beautifully obtuse,” often taking contrary views, bewildered by familiar surroundings, and suffering from claustrophobia even when thinking of vast cosmic spaces. This reflects her emotional and mental state as conflicted and detached, yet proud of Cousin Hannah. The mention of their “day” being her “night” and their “winter” her “summer” encapsulates the theme of opposites and contrasts running through the chapter.

Questions and observations

Reading closely

  • Mr. Spitzer believes that death “was itself a great deceiver.” Is he speaking of Hannah or of himself?
  • Hannah was “unforgettable even when she was forgotten.” How can both be true?
  • Catherine “would forget that it was she who might have been the dream visitor bearing the rose in her hand.” Why might she forget?

Characters

  • Hannah could never have been made to confess that “she had yearned for marriage, or she had loved a man.” What does Catherine need Hannah to be?
  • Mr. Spitzer was “an excellent dancer” and Catherine “the most marvelous dancer.” Why can Hannah not dance?
  • Catherine admires Hannah’s “splendid unity of character which she herself had never achieved.” Is Hannah as whole as Catherine believes?

Connections

  • In Chapter 34 Hannah called marriage “the death of a woman’s soul.” Here the suffrage movement is “her awesome husband.” Has she escaped marriage?
  • The old maid with “ivory-boned knitting needles” recalls Miss MacIntosh. Is Hannah her opposite or her double?
  • King Canute “could not command the waves to stand still.” How does he fit the sea that invades this house?

Reflection

  • “If a thing was predictable, my mother at that moment ceased to believe in it.” Do you trust what you can predict?
  • Can a cause become a marriage?
  • “The extremities of faith in anything might always beget… its opposite.” Have you seen this happen?

Research: Characters

Cousin Hannah

  • A formidable, spirited woman and a leader in the suffrage movement.
  • Described as a “great captain,” “old New England suffragette,” “stone horseman,” and a pioneer who had traveled extensively and fearlessly.
  • Known for her strength, courage, and refusal to conform to traditional feminine roles.
  • She is remembered as someone who never sought pity or protection and who had no time for courtly graces or domestic bliss.
  • Her life was devoted to overthrowing man’s dominance, both socially and domestically.
  • She represents emancipation, freedom, and unyielding resolve.
  • Even in death, she remains vivid and influential, symbolized by images of snowy mountains and celestial journeys.
  • Refused memorial tributes like stained glass windows, showing her disdain for conventional commemoration.
  • “She had believed in no image, neither the living nor the dead.”
  • She died in bed, “clutching in her withered hand like a claw a faded rose.”
  • She told Catherine “there was nothing so cold as the heart of a woman who had never been awakened.”
  • Domestic couples “had whispered their secrets to her—usually the reasons for their separations.”
  • She is “this proud cousin on the male side, not on the distaff side,” with “the glittering eye, the pointed silver beard, the lifted sword.”
  • She once told Catherine of “a eunuch who had become a father.”

Mr. Spitzer

  • Portrayed as cautious, timid, and jealous; he lacks the boldness and dynamism of Cousin Hannah.
  • He is ignorant of cards, suspicious of Cousin Hannah, and bears grudges linked to personal failures and family misfortunes.
  • His presence is seen as an obstacle to Cousin Hannah’s legacy and spirit.
  • Mr. Spitzer is described as “corporeal, fat, soft-jowled, many-valved, sleepy-eyed,” symbolizing inertia and lack of willpower.
  • He is contrasted sharply with the fiery and active Cousin Hannah.
  • He “had always believed that Cousin Hannah was a card cheat.”
  • “Death, he had no doubt, was itself a great deceiver.”
  • In his youth he had been “an excellent dancer, taking every step with mincing precision.”
  • Catherine believes Mr. Spitzer should no longer linger in the house or in memory, making room for Cousin Hannah’s continued influence. “From every sphere, Mr. Spitzer should be missing.”
  • Catherine thought him “embittered by his own sense of failure in music.”
  • He thought Hannah “quite gloomy with her project to organize all ladies to rebel.”

Catherine Cartwheel (Vera’s mother)

  • Catherine holds a complicated view of both Cousin Hannah and Mr. Spitzer.
  • She is reflective, sometimes “unreasonably proud” of Cousin Hannah and often alone, conversing with shadows and memories.
  • Her own life is described as fragmented, filled with multiple selves and illusions.
  • She contrasts with Cousin Hannah’s unity of character and decisiveness.
  • Catherine blends admiration, doubt, and longing.
  • Before she went to bed she had been “the most marvelous dancer.”
  • “She had always seemed to give her attention to those who were not there.”
  • “If a thing was predictable, my mother at that moment ceased to believe in it.”
  • She is “always in her swan boat,” talking to “grotesque shadows on a wall.”
  • She carries on “long conversations with triple-crowned, heron-footed King Canute.”
  • “She suffered from claustrophobia even when she thought of the moon, the sun, the stars, the pathless places.”

Peron Spitzer

  • Unlike Joachim, he “had always had an ace in the hole.”
  • His “astronomical gambling losses” kept Joachim “in a state of colossal bankruptcy for years.”
  • “Peron would never have lingered here.”

Research: Themes

Freedom and Emancipation

See: Freedom and Escape · Women, Gender, and Marriage · Women’s Suffrage

  • Cousin Hannah embodies the fight for women’s rights and freedom from traditional roles.
  • Her life is a metaphor for breaking boundaries: social, geographic, and existential.
  • The suffrage movement is portrayed as her husband, her master, and her true love.

Memory and Legacy

See: Memory and the Past

  • The chapter meditates on how people are remembered after death.
  • Cousin Hannah remains vivid in memory, more alive in death than in life.
  • Mr. Spitzer’s legacy is one of bitterness and inertia, suggesting that memory favors the bold.

Conflict and Opposition

See: Fear and Courage

  • The tension between Cousin Hannah and Mr. Spitzer symbolizes broader conflicts: between courage and timidity, action and passivity, truth and deception.
  • Mr. Spitzer’s jealousy and bitterness contrast with Cousin Hannah’s fearless spirit.

Isolation versus Connection

See: Isolation and Connection

  • Catherine’s isolation contrasts with Cousin Hannah’s active engagement with the world.
  • Despite physical distance and death, Cousin Hannah communicates and influences across time and space.

Death and Immortality

See: Death and Mortality

  • For Catherine, death is not an end but a transformation.
  • Cousin Hannah’s death elevates her to a symbolic, almost mythic status.
  • Mr. Spitzer’s survival past her death is seen as a burden.
  • Mr. Spitzer “looked for no improvement on the other side,” and Hannah “had had no faith… in any after-life.”

Unity and the Fragmented Self

See: Identity and the Self · Duality and Doubles

  • Catherine is “this fragmented ego, these fragmentations of partial selves, of splintered mirrors and partial images.”
  • Her selves include “the look-out in the crow’s-nest… the lady in the phaeton, the figurehead in the foam.”
  • Hannah seemed never to have “divided herself… into opposing factions, warring camps, the battle raging in her own breasts.”
  • “Yet the extremities of faith in anything might always beget, my mother knew, its opposite.”
  • Mr. Spitzer acknowledges “at all times, two truths, neither of which should be true.”

Research: Symbols and Imagery

Cards and Games

See: Cards, Games, and Chance · Gambling and Playing Cards

  • The metaphor of cards and poker reflects strategy, risk, and deception.
  • Cousin Hannah is a “mean game” player; Mr. Spitzer distrusts her, believing she cheats.
  • This imagery symbolizes life’s gambits and the characters’ differing approaches to fate and challenge.

Nature and the Elements

See: Snow, Ice, and Winter

  • Frequent references to snow, stars, deserts, mountains, and storms symbolize the harshness and grandeur of Cousin Hannah’s life.
  • Snow and ice often signify coldness, isolation, and purity.
  • The natural imagery links Cousin Hannah to timeless, elemental forces.

Music and Dance

See: Music and Instruments

  • Music is associated with Mr. Spitzer. It represents internal worlds and subtle emotional states.
  • His “quavering harp strings” reach “through clouds to catch the wind music where there was no wind.”
  • Cousin Hannah rejects courtly graces and formal dances, symbolizing her rejection of conventional femininity and societal constraints.
  • She “could never have taken her place in the pattern of a minuet,” and “she had escorted, it had seemed, no lady to the dance.”

Light and Darkness

See: Lamps, Candles, and Light · Light and Darkness · Moon and Stars

  • Light (stars, jewel reflections, candles) contrasts with darkness (shadows, fog, cosmic darkness).
  • Cousin Hannah is connected with shining stars and blazing eyes, symbolizing her enduring spirit.
  • Darkness often surrounds Mr. Spitzer and Catherine’s fragmented self.
  • “Like a shooting star which probably knows not its destination when it starts… she would have overshot her mark.”

Horses and Riders

See: Horses and Carriages

  • “She would have ridden naked through the gale. She would have ridden through the storm of years.”
  • She “had ridden horseback through many distant capitals already evacuated and was like a great stone horseman with a stone helmet.”
  • Mr. Spitzer thought “the fearful captain of the horse quite gloomy.”

Mirrors

See: Mirrors and Reflections

  • Catherine’s selves are “these many, beautiful, waxen ladies parading in a room of mirrors and phantoms, each but the partial portrait of the other.”
  • Hannah’s life “had seemingly included no such multiple mirror images and imaginary loves.”
  • Catherine asked “that the ice-breakers should go ahead of her and clear a way, break the mirrors, break the ice.”

Research: Resources

  • “unlike his brother, who had always had an ace in the hole”: In stud poker the hole card is dealt face down. An ace in the hole is a hidden winning card, and by the early 1900s the phrase meant any hidden advantage. See Cards, Games, and Chance and Peron Spitzer.
  • “he had not entered the lists”: The lists were the fenced field of a medieval tournament. To enter the lists is to accept a challenge.
  • “swifter in the race”: “The race is not to the swift, nor the battle to the strong… but time and chance happeneth to them all” (Ecclesiastes 9:11). See Ecclesiastes.
  • “even a British prime minister to quail”: Young’s source for Cousin Hannah, a suffragist “battle-axe” described by Charles Studin, a founder of the NAACP, “challenged a British prime minister to a duel and the prime minister refused to bear arms against the lady” (Marguerite Young, interview with Studs Terkel, WFMT radio, 1965). See Cousin Hannah and Women’s Suffrage.
  • “room for one who had crossed dark waters”: Charon ferried the souls of the dead across the river Styx into Hades, for a coin placed with the corpse. Later Hannah is one who “would have ridden to the sable shores of Hades or even farther.” See Greek Mythology.
  • “with troops of singing stars”: “When the morning stars sang together, and all the sons of God shouted for joy” (Job 38:7). See The Book of Job.
  • “the blind moth fluttered with jewels upon its wings”: “The desire of the moth for the star, / Of the night for the morrow” (Percy Bysshe Shelley, “One word is too often profaned,” 1821). See Butterflies and Moths and Romantic Poets.
  • “and no Western Union messengers”: Western Union, an American company established in 1851, was the leader of the telegraphy industry.
    • Its uniformed messengers, many of them boys on bicycles, delivered telegrams by hand.
  • “She would have ridden naked through the gale”: By the legend in Roger of Wendover’s thirteenth-century chronicle, Lady Godiva rode naked through Coventry, covered only by her hair, so that her husband Leofric would lift a heavy tax.
  • “in no drugged moments outside of time such as the opium lady might indulge in”: The opium lady is Catherine herself. Young drew her from Minna K. Weissenbach, “the opium lady of Hyde Park” (David O. Dowling, “The Guru,” in A Delicate Aggression: Savagery and Survival in the Iowa Writers’ Workshop, Yale University Press, 2019). See the Chapter 2 resources and The History of Opium.
  • “that dark captain of the light-footed brigade”: The phrase may echo Tennyson’s “The Charge of the Light Brigade” (1854): “Into the valley of Death / Rode the six hundred.”
  • “the Crusader whose cap was covered with shells of mother-of-pearl”: The scallop shell was the badge of pilgrims to the shrine of St. James at Santiago de Compostela. Pilgrims home from Jerusalem carried palm fronds and were called palmers.
  • “the triumph of woman over man, even of beauty over strength”: Joan Smith’s Misogynies discusses the pervasive nature of hatred and discrimination against women in society, exploring cultural, social, and psychological roots of misogyny (Joan Smith, Misogynies: Reflections on Myths and Malice, Faber and Faber, 1989). The novel vividly portrays the suffering, marginalization, and complex interior lives of women like Catherine, Esther Longtree, and Mrs. Hogden, who each embody different facets of women’s oppression and resilience. The presence of misogyny is implicit in their isolation, the betrayals they endure, and their struggles to assert identity and selfhood. Miss MacIntosh’s pragmatic, no-nonsense character challenges the illusions and fantasies that trap women like Catherine, reflecting resistance to the roles imposed by a misogynistic society. Her disdain for frivolity and self-pity contrasts with the more vulnerable or victimized female figures, highlighting the varied responses to misogyny. Smith emphasizes how misogyny permeates both public and private spheres, a theme echoed in the novel’s blending of intimate psychological struggles with broader social critiques, such as the suffrage movement represented by Cousin Hannah and the economic hardships faced by characters like Esther Longtree. See Women, Gender, and Marriage.
  • “She had not been merely another old maid dreaming with her ivory-boned knitting needles”: Cousin Hannah is contrasted with Miss MacIntosh, whose “knitting needles of ivory bone” click in Chapter 1. Young’s old maid, with her balls of grey yarn and her looks at the alarm clock, lives in “empty servitude.” Cousin Hannah is the opposite: she journeyed to far and dangerous places and fought for women’s rights and freedom.
  • “one who had seen the burning bush”: “And he looked, and, behold, the bush burned with fire, and the bush was not consumed” (Exodus 3:2). See The Bible.
  • “pitched her tents in strange lands from which no living man returns”: “The undiscover’d country from whose bourn / No traveller returns” (Shakespeare, Hamlet 3.1). See Shakespeare.
  • “this old hunter with the glittering eye”: “He holds him with his glittering eye” (Samuel Taylor Coleridge, “The Rime of the Ancient Mariner,” 1798). The eye returns later, when Hannah is “this old New England suffragette with the glittering eye.” See Romantic Poets.
  • “She had wished to overthrow man, both as to the marital state”: The suffrage movement did not oppose marriage. The anti-suffrage movement opposed suffrage because it feared that women would be “masculinized” and that this in turn would “feminize” men. Under coverture, after marriage the man and woman became one legal unit that the man controlled. Women in many cases were not allowed to own property, sign contracts, earn a salary, or enter education without their husbands’ permission. See Women’s Suffrage and Women, Gender, and Marriage.
  • “paternal domination, the regnancy of the past and of the future”: Kate Millett’s Sexual Politics is a foundational feminist text analyzing the ways patriarchal power operates through sexual and social relationships, emphasizing how gender roles and power imbalances shape personal and political dynamics (Kate Millett, Sexual Politics, Doubleday, 1970). The novel portrays complex gender dynamics, especially through Vera’s mother Catherine and Miss MacIntosh. Catherine inhabits a world of illusion and decay, surrounded by hallucinations and dominated by male absences and betrayals. Miss MacIntosh, by contrast, embodies a practical, no-nonsense counterpoint to Catherine’s dreamlike passivity, and she strongly critiques illusions and instability. This tension reflects the gendered power struggles Millett describes, though in a symbolic and psychological mode. Cousin Hannah, the suffragette figure in the novel, represents a militant, radical feminist presence, dedicated to overthrowing patriarchal domination, which aligns with Millett’s critique of male control over women’s bodies and lives. Cousin Hannah’s battles for women’s freedom and her rejection of traditional feminine roles resonate with Millett’s political feminism. The novel’s exploration of pregnancies, stillbirths, and female suffering (notably through Esther Longtree’s story) touches on the control of women’s sexuality and reproduction, key concerns in Sexual Politics. See Women, Gender, and Marriage.
  • “a dream retreating at cockcrow”: Hamlet’s father’s ghost “faded on the crowing of the cock” (Shakespeare, Hamlet 1.1). See Shakespeare.
  • “why so many great Antarctic explorers had left home”: Richard E. Byrd named Marie Byrd Land in Antarctica for his wife, Marie, in 1929. See Exploration and the Poles.
  • “riding in a desert place with her Mahound”: Mahound, a medieval European corruption of the name Muhammad, was used by Christians to depict him as a god worshipped by pagans or a demon who inspired a false religion.
  • “the memorial art which Mr. Spitzer practiced”: Memorial art has evolved from ancient civilizations’ elaborate tributes to the deceased to modern expressions of remembrance and commemoration, reflecting cultural beliefs and societal values across different eras.
    • Mr. Spitzer’s own memorial art is music, the “memorial music sobbing as he sobbed” of Chapter 54. See Joachim Spitzer.
  • “a stained glass window in memory of her”: Memorial windows were a fashion of American churches from the 1880s into the 1930s, many of them made by the studios of Louis Comfort Tiffany.
  • “the emperor and the unicorn”: The emperor and the unicorn may refer to The Unicorn Tapestries (about 1495-1505) at The Cloisters, part of the Metropolitan Museum of Art, in New York City. The imagery is thought to represent “the beloved tamed,” with fertility imagery.
    • The Lady and the Unicorn, six tapestries of about 1500, hang in the Musée de Cluny in Paris.
  • “the lady and the blackamoor”: The pairing may recall a seventeenth-century broadside, “A Lamentable Ballad of the Tragical End of a Gallant Lord and a Virtuous Lady, with the Untimely End of Their Two Children, Wickedly Performed by a Heathenish Blackamoor Their Servant” (printed by A. Milbourn, London, about 1686-1693). The ballad casts its Black servant as a monster, a racist stock figure of the period.
  • “great gold-eyed white ptarmigans”: Ptarmigans are medium-sized game birds in the grouse family. See Birds.
    • They turn white in winter, all but the black of the tail.
  • “even like Queen Maud Mountains”: Roald Amundsen named the range for Queen Maud of Norway in November 1911, as his party climbed the Axel Heiberg Glacier toward the South Pole. See Exploration and the Poles and Mountains.
  • “expecting Madame DuBarry with her Persian hound”: Madame du Barry, the last royal mistress of Louis XV of France, was guillotined in 1793 during the French Revolution.
    • The Persian hound is likely the saluki, also called the Persian greyhound. See Dogs.
  • “a plague of fiery locusts, those who have no king”: “The locusts have no king, yet go they forth all of them by bands” (Proverbs 30:27). The locusts of Revelation do have one: “they had a king over them, which is the angel of the bottomless pit” (Revelation 9:11). See The Bible and Revelation and the Apocalypse.
  • “he never stepped on terra firma without assuming that it was terra incognita”: Terra incognita means unknown or unexplored territory. Terra firma means firm land or solid earth.
  • “the dance of the hours”: In Greek myth the Horae, the Hours, were goddesses of the seasons and of order. Ponchielli’s ballet “Dance of the Hours,” from his opera La Gioconda (1876), shows the hours of dawn, day, evening, and night. See Greek Mythology and Music and Composers.
  • “the pattern of a minuet”: The minuet, a slow French court dance in triple time, was the fashion at the court of Louis XIV.
  • “as Sherman marching to the sea”: Sherman marching to the sea was a military campaign of the American Civil War through Georgia. See The Civil War.
    • It ran from Atlanta to Savannah, November 15 to December 21, 1864.
  • “Napoleon at the gates of Moscow”: Napoleon at the gates of Moscow may refer to Moscow being occupied in 1812 by French Emperor Napoleon Bonaparte’s army during the Napoleonic Wars. See Napoleon and Wellington.
    • The city burned, and the retreat through the Russian winter destroyed his army.
  • “heron-footed King Canute”: King Canute or Cnut the Great was the king of England, Denmark, and Norway.
    • Henry of Huntingdon tells that he set his chair on the shore and commanded the tide not to rise. When it wet his feet, he said, “Let all men know how empty and worthless is the power of kings” (Henry of Huntingdon, Historia Anglorum, about 1130, trans. Thomas Forester, 1853).
    • Three kingdoms made him “triple-crowned.”
  • “she had yearned for marriage, or she had loved a man”: Young’s source for Cousin Hannah, Charles Studin’s suffragist “battle-axe,” fought men all her life, yet for forty years brought home sealed trunks that proved at her death to hold “a complete bridal trousseau” each. “She had a dream too” (Marguerite Young, interview with Studs Terkel, WFMT radio, 1965). See Cousin Hannah and the Chapter 31 resources.
  • “Or she had yearned for a homunculus”: A homunculus is the tiny man the alchemists claimed they could grow in a flask, as in De natura rerum (1537), attributed to Paracelsus. The “dwarf” symbolizes a small, subservient male figure, a “gentleman’s gentleman,” who would serve her but not stand as an equal or partner. It contrasts with her grandeur and strength. Catherine believes Hannah could never have been made to confess such a wish, but Young’s source for Hannah kept a secret dream of marriage. See the entry above. The house later offers its own gentleman’s gentleman, “his head a steaming silver teapot, to wait on her.”
    • A gentleman’s gentleman is a valet, a phrase made famous by P. G. Wodehouse’s Jeeves, who first appeared in 1915.
  • “For hers was, indeed, this buried life”: “But often, in the world’s most crowded streets, / But often, in the din of strife, / There rises an unspeakable desire / After the knowledge of our buried life” (Matthew Arnold, “The Buried Life,” 1852).
  • “the infinite steeplechase stretching between two leaning steeples”: The first recorded steeplechase was run in County Cork in 1752, when Cornelius O’Callaghan and Edmund Blake raced from the church at Buttevant to the steeple of St. Leger church at Doneraile, about four and a half miles.
  • “the great battle of the white eunuchs with the black eunuchs”: In the Ottoman palace, white eunuchs, mostly from the Balkans and the Caucasus, served the inner palace under the Chief White Eunuch, while black eunuchs, enslaved in Africa, guarded the harem. From the late sixteenth century the Chief Black Eunuch outranked him (Jane Hathaway, The Chief Eunuch of the Ottoman Harem: From African Slave to Power-Broker, Cambridge University Press, 2018). A eunuch is a man who has been castrated. Throughout history, castration often served a specific social function. The earliest records for intentional castration to produce eunuchs are from the Sumerian city of Lagash in the 2nd millennium BCE. Over the millennia since, they have performed a wide variety of functions in many different cultures: courtiers or equivalent domestics, for espionage or clandestine operations, castrato singers, concubines, or sexual partners, religious specialists, soldiers, royal guards, government officials, and guardians of women or harem servants. Eunuchs would usually be servants or slaves who had been castrated to make them less threatening servants of a royal court where physical access to the ruler could wield great influence. In control of both the Harem and a net of spies among the black eunuchs, the Chief Eunuch was involved in almost every palace intrigue and thereby could gain power over either the sultan or one of his viziers, ministers, or other court officials. One of the most powerful Chief Eunuchs was Beshir Agha in the 1730s, who played a crucial role in establishing the Ottoman version of Hanafi Islam throughout the Empire by founding libraries and schools (Wikipedia). Cousin Hannah’s eunuch “had become a father,” though a great sheik had used him to guard, “in supposedly perfect safety,” his “black veiled love.” This eunuch, “dying for love,” was strangled and left in a desert courtyard.
  • “gates guarded by minotaurs and dragons and speaking birds”: The Minotaur, half man and half bull, was kept at the center of the Cretan labyrinth until Theseus killed it. See Greek Mythology.
  • “Had she not crossed into Mesopotamia”: Mesopotamia is a historical region of Western Asia within the Tigris-Euphrates river system.
    • Young said she “had read the histories of mountain climbers, of suffragette captains, of travelers to the Middle East” (Ellen G. Friedman and Miriam Fuchs, “A Conversation with Marguerite Young,” Review of Contemporary Fiction 23, no. 1, Spring 2003 (1989 original)).
    • Gertrude Bell crossed these deserts and helped draw the borders of Iraq in 1921, yet by 1909 she was honorary secretary of the Women’s National Anti-Suffrage League. See Women’s Suffrage.
  • “Had she not crossed over into Transjordania”: Transjordania, the Emirate of Transjordan, was a British protectorate established in 1921.
  • “Did she not know Felix Arabia”: Felix Arabia, properly Arabia Felix, “fortunate Arabia,” was the Roman name for the fertile southwest of the Arabian Peninsula, roughly today’s Yemen.
  • “She had wished to rescue the slave, not only the economic slave but also the slave of love”: Cousin Hannah’s struggle is presented in terms of gender emancipation and suffrage activism. The economic slavery she aims to end is linked to the patriarchal and marital structures. Her battle is against male dominance and the social and domestic oppression of women. See Women’s Suffrage.
  • “She had caused many a flutter in many a dovecote”: “Like an eagle in a dove-cote, I / Flutter’d your Volscians in Corioli” (Shakespeare, Coriolanus 5.6). See Shakespeare.
  • “until he heard the angelus”: The Angelus is a Catholic devotion commemorating the Incarnation or the Annunciation.
    • It is announced by the Angelus bell, rung morning, noon, and evening. Jean-François Millet painted two peasants pausing in a field at its sound in The Angelus (1857-1859).
  • “great wentletraps reaching to mother-of-pearl clouds”: Wentletraps are small, often white, very high-spired sea snails.
    • The name comes from the Dutch wenteltrap, a winding staircase, which is why they stand beside the “intricate mother-of-pearl circular stairways.”
  • “thin as the deceptive Pleiades”: The Pleiades, the Seven Sisters, also Messier 45, is an open star cluster. See Astronomy and Greek Mythology.
    • Most eyes see only six stars, and the myth of a lost Pleiad grew to explain the missing seventh.
  • “fireflies like fragments of dead souls”: In Japan, “Any firefly may be a ghost— who can tell?” Two kinds are “popularly named Genji-botaru and Heike-botaru,” and “a legend avers that these fireflies are the ghosts of the old Minamoto and Taira warriors” (Lafcadio Hearn, “Fireflies,” in Kottō, Macmillan, 1902). See Fireflies.
  • “an organizer of chaos”: Amanda Vajskop reads the Babylonian Enuma Elish and the Genesis creation story, in which male creators take over woman’s part in bringing forth life and women are cast as destabilizing and dangerous, a fear that patriarchy uses to keep women subordinate (Amanda Vajskop, “Finding Patterns in the Chaos: Woman as Chaos Agent in Creation Myths,” Denison Journal of Religion 5, article 7, 2005). Vera’s narrative continuously navigates between dreamlike confusion and the search for meaning or “ultimate harmony.” Miss MacIntosh represents order and common sense amid the chaos of Catherine’s opium-induced visions and the fragmented lives of other characters. The novel portrays characters with fragmented selves: Vera’s own complex consciousness, Miss MacIntosh’s evolving physical and psychological state (including her baldness and amputated breast), and the multiple personae like Cousin Hannah and Mrs. Hogden. The novel’s intense focus on female embodiment, sexuality, motherhood, loss, and survival complements critical perspectives on misogyny and sexual politics. Cousin Hannah, “an organizer of chaos,” takes up the part these myths assign to woman and turns it against the order men have made. See Genesis and Women, Gender, and Marriage.
  • “of Stygian night which knew no time”: Stygian refers to the River Styx in the underworld of Greek mythology. See Greek Mythology.
  • “toppling cloud-topped towers”: “The cloud-capp’d towers, the gorgeous palaces, / The solemn temples, the great globe itself, / Yea, all which it inherit, shall dissolve” (Shakespeare, The Tempest 4.1). See Shakespeare.

Chapter 80

← Chapter 79 · Home · Chapter 81 →

Content note: The Esther Longtree chapters (72 to 81) deal with stillbirth and pregnancy loss, rape, infanticide, racist violence including lynching, and cruelty to children. This chapter describes an infanticide, a man fleeing a lynching, and a stranger who has sex with Esther, then a young girl, while she sleeps.

Summary

On a rainy afternoon in the dark restaurant, Esther tells Vera about Walter, her first-born. When she was a young girl, a stranger found her asleep in the summer fields, and she woke with him already inside her; at dawn she saw that he was a Black man, his face scarred where a white mob in the South had tried to hang him because he smiled at a white old maid’s rooster. He fled north for fear the white people would kill him. Hardly knowing what was happening to her body, she hid the pregnancy, went south, and gave birth alone in a dirty hotel room, where she pressed her thumb on the newborn’s throat, wrapped him in a sporting page, left him in a dresser drawer, and fled by train and bus. Yet she believes Walter lives, a Boy Scout raised by kind white people, and he follows her everywhere, asking why she killed him and where his father is. She sets out crumbs for the spirits, knits with invisible thread, and waits for the little shadow boxer to make up for the first.

Characters present

Esther Longtree · Walter

Concepts present

Themes: Death and Mortality · Faith, God, and the Supernatural · Guilt, Innocence, and Justice · Identity and the Self · Memory and the Past · Motherhood, Pregnancy, and Birth · Society, Class, and Race · Time · Women, Gender, and Marriage

Symbols: Horses and Carriages

Philosophy: Freud and Jung · Spiritualism and the Occult

Allusions: American Religious Movements · Greek Mythology · Lynching and Racial Violence · Pregnancy, Abortion, and Midwifery · The Bible · The Civil War

Key passages

From the research

  • Esther is deeply affected by the presence of spirits and the memory of her dead children. She engages in rituals like making little clothes for no one, setting out bread crumbs for spirits, and building a little house of straw in a tree for the spirit to come home to. This shows her ongoing connection to the lost children and her attempt to reconcile with the past.
  • Esther discusses her impending marriage but insists she will not marry until the child comes. She contemplates the future of her progeny, hoping for strength and happiness despite her doubts.
  • A central and deeply moving passage details Esther’s first-born, Walter, who she believes she “killed” but who lives on in some form, haunting her conscience and mind. Walter represents both her guilt and her love, a child she tried to kill at birth by pressing her thumb on his throat and then abandoned, yet whose presence continues to torment her.
  • Walter accuses Esther of killing him and questions her about his father. Esther’s guilt is palpable as she tries to reconcile her actions with her love for Walter, describing him as a “black mystery” and acknowledging the painful burden he places on her.
  • Esther distinguishes Walter from her many stillborn children, emphasizing that he was born alive and continues to grow.
  • The chapter provides a detailed narrative of how Walter was conceived by a “stranger,” a Black man, in a night of love and how Esther was unprepared and frightened by the pregnancy. This passage is important as it contextualizes Esther’s fear, shame, and the social consequences she faced, especially regarding race and societal judgment.
  • Throughout the chapter, Esther is described as perpetually pregnant, symbolizing her ongoing burden of guilt, loss, and hope. This “everlasting pregnancy” is a metaphor for her emotional state: caught between life and death, hope and despair.
  • Esther admits to having pressed her thumb to still Walter’s birth cry, effectively killing him, but not without enduring lifelong remorse. She also recounts how she hid the body and fled to avoid detection. This revelation is crucial as it underlines the secret that haunts her and explains her psychological torment.
  • The chapter closes with Esther reflecting on her many miscarriages and stillborn children, the idea that life is filled with loss and unfinished stories. Despite everything, she clings to the memory of Walter.

Questions and observations

Reading closely

  • “Who murdered me? Who married me?” Why does Esther put the two together?
  • “Some might have put on mourning after such loss. She had put on pregnancy.” What does she mean?
  • “Where is black white—where is white black—where is the dead child living—where is the live child dead?” Can these questions be answered?

Characters

  • Esther says Walter’s father “had awakened her with his body already in hers,” yet she calls that night “the snowy peak of her existence.” How can both be true?
  • The white mob tried to hang Walter’s father, though he “had only smiled at a white old maid’s white rooster.” What does Young expose here?
  • Walter tells her, “mother, I go to a fine school with the white children now!” Why does Esther imagine him raised white?

Connections

  • “Hee, haw, my darling,” Esther cries. Where else do we hear “my darling”?
  • Walter is “my black mystery whom the white detective will not find.” How does this answer Chapter 77?
  • Walter confuses her “much like a limb that hurts after the limb is cut away.” What is he to her?

Reflection

  • “Truly, she was guilty, but she was not guilty of what people thought.” Of what is she guilty?
  • “Could she have killed him for his difference?”
  • “In life, we always must lose something of ourselves, long before we die.” Do you agree?

Research: Characters

Esther Longtree

  • Esther is complex, embodying resilience, confusion, sorrow, and hope.
  • She is aware of her societal marginalization and her own perceived “madness” but embraces her unique perspective.
  • Her character oscillates between despair and defiance, as she laughs at her barrenness and mourns her losses simultaneously.
  • Her first-born child, Walter, both haunts and defines her. He symbolizes her greatest loss and source of emotional torment.
  • Walter’s Father is a black man whose identity and fate are shrouded in mystery and racial tension.
  • Many transient men appear in her life, symbolizing fleeting connections and failed attempts at establishing lasting family bonds.

Walter

  • Walter is a profoundly complex and symbolic character. He is Esther Longtree’s first-born child, a figure who embodies both literal and metaphorical dimensions of life, death, guilt, and memory.
  • Walter is described as a child whom Esther had “killed,” yet paradoxically, he “lived.” Esther hears his cries, feels his accusations, and wrestles with the burden of her guilt and regret that he represents. Walter’s persistent questioning, “Mother, why have you killed me?” and “Where is my father?,” haunts Esther’s conscience.
  • Walter acts as a relentless accuser who confronts Esther with her past actions and their consequences. His presence keeps her working (“He keeps me working”), making her scrub floors and endure long hours in the restaurant. His accusations are unanswerable, and he seems to have a cruel, hard heart, adding to Esther’s suffering.
  • Walter is portrayed with specific physical features, “black as my true love, black as my heart,” reflecting his mixed racial heritage, which complicates Esther’s feelings toward him. His blackness symbolizes difference and alienation, as well as the social challenges unresolved in Esther’s life. The fact that his father was black and a “prince of Africa” adds layers to Walter’s identity, evoking themes of race, social stigma, and forbidden love.
  • Walter represents the “beloved obstacle” to Esther’s life and future. His existence and the guilt attached to him prevent her from fully embracing motherhood and happiness. Esther’s many stillborn children and miscarriages contrast with Walter’s unique status as the one child who lived but remained emotionally inaccessible. Walter is both the cause of her endless pregnancies and the reason for her emotional isolation.
  • Walter is inseparable from Esther’s memories, a persistent shadow in her mind.
  • Walter is not merely a character but a symbolic force representing Esther’s guilt, lost motherhood, racial complexity, and the unresolved past that haunts her. He is a living accusation and a ghostly memory, a child who should have died but has instead become an eternal presence in Esther’s life, shaping her identity and destiny.

Walter’s father

  • The white people of his Southern town tried to hang him “from a white-blossoming tree,” though he “had only smiled at a white old maid’s white rooster”; the rope broke, and he walked away from the scene of his own death and stumbled on Esther asleep in the fields. He “had awakened her with his body already in hers.”
  • Walter’s father is portrayed primarily through Esther Longtree’s memories, feelings, and the symbolic weight he carries rather than through direct characterization or actions.
  • Walter’s father is described as a black man, “as black as the ace of spades,” a “Negro, a Negro, a Negro,” who came into Esther’s life unexpectedly and left an indelible mark upon her. He is portrayed as a “stranger,” a “poor fellow,” “a tramp,” “a fugitive,” or even a “prince,” which indicates Esther’s ambivalence and the mystique surrounding him. This man came into her life in the darkness of a summer night, in an act that was “half of sleeping and half of waking,” suggesting a blend of innocence, confusion, and inevitability in their union.
  • His blackness is significant in the narrative: Esther did not initially realize the racial difference at the moment of conception because “his face had been white” in the moonlight, and only “at dawn... she had seen that he was black.” This racial difference introduces a complex dynamic of love, fear, and societal judgment. Esther’s heart turns “black with the years,” and she recognizes her bond to him as something that makes her a “slave to his memory.” His departure is framed not as Esther leaving him, but as him fleeing “for fear the white people would see him and kill him,” underscoring the racial tensions and dangers of the time.
  • Walter’s father is not depicted as a traditional or nurturing figure in Esther’s life. He is absent after the conception, and Esther carries the burden of his memory, the pregnancy, and the consequences largely alone. Despite this absence, his presence haunts Esther, symbolizing both the origin of her deepest grief and the source of a love she treasured but could not fully realize. His identity as a black man in a racially divided society adds a layer of tragedy and alienation to the story.
  • Walter’s father is a mysterious, absent figure whose racial identity and sudden disappearance shape Esther’s life and psyche profoundly. He embodies the forces of love, loss, societal exclusion, and the lingering pain of an unfinished past that Esther cannot escape.

Research: Themes

Motherhood and Pregnancy

See: Motherhood, Pregnancy, and Birth

  • Esther is perpetually pregnant, both literally and metaphorically. Her body swells with pregnancies that often end in stillbirths or miscarriages, yet she carries an enduring hope for a living child.
  • The physical and emotional toll of her pregnancies is immense; she experiences nausea, swelling, and an overwhelming sense of waiting and expectation.
  • Pregnancy is symbolic of life, death, and the cyclical nature of existence. It is her “widow’s weeds,” representing loss and continual renewal.

Guilt and Redemption

See: Guilt, Innocence, and Justice

  • Esther harbors deep guilt over her first-born son, Walter, whom she believes she “killed” by pressing her thumb on his throat at birth and abandoning him.
  • Despite her guilt, Walter is alive in her memories and visions, accusing her of her sins and questioning her about his father.
  • Her attempts to redeem herself manifest in her ongoing pregnancies and her hope that the new child will compensate for the past losses.

Race and Identity

See: Identity and the Self · Society, Class, and Race

  • Walter’s father was a black man, described metaphorically as “the prince of Africa” and “as black as the ace of spades.”
  • Esther’s shock and societal stigma over this interracial relationship and child profoundly impact her life.
  • Walter’s blackness is a symbolic and literal source of conflict, shame, love, and fear for Esther, reflecting broader themes of racial tension and identity.

Life, Death, and the Supernatural

See: Death and Mortality · Faith, God, and the Supernatural

  • The narrative blurs boundaries between life and death, as Esther communicates with spirits and imagines an “other world” parallel to this one.
  • Her miscarriages and stillborn children are depicted as ghostly presences and delicate entities like moths, feathers, and snowflakes.
  • Walter exists both as a living child and a spectral presence haunting her conscience.

Memory and Time

See: Memory and the Past · Time

  • Esther’s memory is fragmented, cyclical, and tinged with confusion as she recalls her past pregnancies, loves, and losses.
  • Time is fluid; events from years ago feel present and immediate, especially as she contemplates the “unfinished murder” of Walter.
  • The narrative explores how memory shapes identity and the persistence of past trauma.

Research: Symbols and Imagery

  • Pregnancy is a central symbol representing creation, hope, and the possibility of life. However, in Esther’s case, it also symbolizes loss, failure, and the burden of guilt, as she has experienced many stillbirths and miscarriages. Her “everlasting pregnancy” is not just physical but metaphysical, carrying the memory and shadow of her first child who died but also “lived” in a spiritual or haunting way. This duality of birth and death intertwined in her pregnancy reflects her conflicted emotions and the complexity of motherhood.
  • Walter, Esther’s first-born, is a powerful symbol of both guilt and unresolved trauma. He is described as both dead and alive; he haunts her as a ghostly presence, accusing her of killing him, yet he “lives” and grows outside her. Walter’s contradictory existence symbolizes Esther’s inner turmoil, remorse, and the inescapable consequences of past actions. His blackness, in contrast to the white imagery surrounding Esther, also symbolizes otherness, racial difference, and social alienation.
  • The interplay of black and white is a recurring symbol throughout the chapter. Esther herself is dark-skinned, and her lover and child are black, while many surrounding images are white: white butterflies, white snow, white moonlight, white flowers, and the white detective. This contrast symbolizes racial difference, purity versus guilt, life versus death, and the blending or conflict of identities. The “black as the ace of spades” and white moonlight imagery evokes a sense of fate, mystery, and the intersection of love and tragedy.
  • Nature is used extensively to symbolize the cycle of life and death, the presence of spirits, and the passage of time.
  • Butterflies and moths symbolize fragile, ephemeral life and transformation.
  • Leaves stirring and falling evoke the whispering of spirits and the inevitability of decay.
  • Rain and umbrellas suggest cleansing, sorrow, and the connection between this world and the “other world” where spirits reside.
  • The moon and stars symbolize mystery, the unconscious, and the eternal presence of life beyond death.
  • Esther’s connection to nature signifies her role as a “go-between,” mediating between life and death, reality and spirit.
  • The “Little Shadow Boxer” is a metaphor for the unborn child she carries now, representing hope and continuity but also uncertainty. The child is called a “shadow,” indicating something not fully realized or tangible and a continuation of her past mistakes but also a potential for redemption. This image underlines the tension between reality and illusion, life and death.
  • Esther is described as “always knitting the invisible,” a metaphor for her attempts to create and sustain life out of intangible dreams and memories. This symbolizes her efforts to reconcile with her past and to give form to what has been lost or broken. The invisible thread also suggests the fragile connections between generations, memory, and identity.
  • The Chicago Detective and Salesmen recurring characters symbolize societal judgment, surveillance, and the external pressures Esther faces. The white detective’s suspicions and the sterile salesmen represent the social forces that have failed to understand or accept her, adding to her isolation and guilt.
  • The knocking and Esther’s answering represent her confrontation with her past, her guilt, and the spirits of her children; both born and unborn. It symbolizes the inescapable nature of memory and conscience, and her role as the mediator between the living and the dead.
  • Walter is described as the “beloved obstacle” preventing her from moving fully into new relationships or new conceptions. This symbolizes how past trauma and guilt can block future happiness and freedom.
  • The “Cloud,” “Shadow,” and “Reflection” images symbolize ambiguity, duality, and the blurred boundaries between reality and imagination, life and death. Esther often reflects on these, questioning where the living and the dead reside, and suggesting her mental state blurs these distinctions.
  • The “small brown hand” laid across the womb is a potent symbol of the legacy of her first child’s death and haunting presence. It represents both the physical and psychological obstruction preventing her from fully moving on, and the lasting impact of her guilt and loss.
  • The “white bird upon the ice floe” evokes both beauty and isolation, symbolizing the fragile hope and distance between Esther and what she desires or has lost. It suggests the elusiveness of her dreams and the coldness of her reality.

Research: Resources

  • “She had answered every knocking”: Modern Spiritualism began with knockings: in 1848 the Fox sisters of Hydesville, New York, said the rappings in their house were spirits answering. See Spiritualism in the Chapter 79 resources. See American Religious Movements and Spiritualism and the Occult.
  • “Hee, haw, my darling”: “My darling” is the novel’s own phrase, the call of its title, Miss MacIntosh, My Darling; Esther brays it to herself. See Esther Longtree.
  • “But I will not marry him until the child comes”: Esther Longtree is portrayed as a profoundly tragic and complex figure, embodying themes of maternal loss, guilt, and longing. Her character is suffused with a haunting sense of grief that permeates her existence, shaped by repeated pregnancies, stillbirths, and a particularly painful memory of her first-born child, Walter. Physically, Esther is described as a large, cross-eyed waitress who is perpetually pregnant or swollen, a physical manifestation of her inner burden and continuous state of expectation and sorrow. Her pregnancy is not merely biological but symbolic: it represents her ongoing attempt to atone for past mistakes and losses and to reclaim a maternal identity fractured by tragedy. A central aspect of Esther’s character is her relationship with Walter, her first-born, who, despite being “killed” in a sense, has lived on outside her awareness. Walter is both a ghostly presence and a source of endless accusation and sorrow. He haunts her conscience, asking why she killed him and where his father is, embodying Esther’s unresolved guilt and the burden of an unfinished murder. Walter’s existence outside her, his growth and vitality, contrasts sharply with the stillborn children and miscarriages that have otherwise defined her reproductive life. Her narrative reveals a deep, ambivalent love and a tragic recognition of her own limitations and mistakes as a mother, compounded by her youth, ignorance, and fear at the time of Walter’s birth. Esther’s story exposes the intersection of race and identity: Walter’s father was a black man, a “prince” from Africa, who was a fugitive and victim of racial violence. This adds layers of social and personal complexity to Esther’s grief, shame, and isolation. Her memories of this man are filled with shock and surprise, reflecting the racial tensions and prejudices surrounding her. Esther’s heart turning black metaphorically expresses her internalization of this complex legacy. Esther is shown as a woman caught between two worlds: the physical, harsh reality of her life as a waitress and the spiritual, shadowy world of her lost and unborn children, as well as the memory of Walter. She acts as a “go-between,” navigating the liminal space between life and death, presence and absence, reality and dream. This is symbolized by her making a little house of straw for the spirit to come home to, answering every knocking, and feeding the spirits as if to soothe her conscience. Her repeated pregnancies and stillbirths symbolize not only personal tragedy but also a universal theme of loss and unfulfilled potential. Esther’s life is a continual cycle of hope and despair, birth and death, presence and absence. Her laughter, sometimes convulsive or mule-like, reflects a bitter acceptance of her fate, mingled with stubborn resilience. Esther Longtree is a figure of profound maternal suffering and endurance. She is marked by a deep, unresolved guilt and grief linked to her first child, Walter, whose living presence she both mourns and fears. Her story is one of tragic memory, racial and social complexity, and the haunting persistence of loss. She is a living embodiment of the liminal space between life and death, the seen and unseen, the known and the unknowable, and her narrative richly explores themes of motherhood, identity, and redemption within the novel. See Esther Longtree.
    • Esther Longtree symbolizes a deep and tragic history of racial and social injustice in the United States, particularly relating to the legacy of slavery, interracial relationships under oppressive conditions, and the ongoing consequences of systemic racism. Her story reflects the painful history of a black father, described as a “Negro, a Negro, a Negro, poor young fellow, black as the black bough, the ace of spades,” who was a fugitive, possibly an ex-convict, victimized by white supremacy: “the white people there had tried to kill him because he was black and had wanted to sleep with a white woman... they had tried to hang him from a white-blossoming tree for revenge, but the rope had broken.” This narrative evokes the historical reality of lynching and racial violence in the American South. Esther’s pregnancy with this black man’s child, her subsequent abandonment of the child, and her lifelong torment symbolize the fraught and often violent intersections of race, gender, and power in America. Her child, Walter, who is black and whom she both loved and feared, becomes a haunting presence in her life: a symbol of the legacy of interracial unions condemned and punished by society, and the personal and social consequences of such relationships. The repeated motif of Esther being “always pregnant,” carrying the memory and burden of lost or stillborn children, reflects the cycles of trauma and loss imposed on black and mixed-race families by systemic racism and social rejection. Her incarceration in the “Greasy Spoon” restaurant, her social marginalization, and her sense of isolation also symbolize the economic and social disenfranchisement experienced by many African Americans and women in American history. Esther’s struggle with guilt and the haunting presence of her first child, who lives outside her physically but not emotionally, represents the unresolved historical wounds of slavery’s legacy: the unacknowledged and hidden suffering passed down through generations. Esther Longtree embodies the history of racial violence, forbidden and punished interracial love, maternal suffering, social exclusion, and the enduring scars of America’s racial past. Through her narrative, Young confronts the complexity of identity, memory, and historical trauma in the United States.
    • Esther Longtree’s character carries symbolic weight that can be interpreted in relation to the abortion debate in the U.S., although the symbolism is complex, multifaceted, and embedded within the novel’s rich, dreamlike narrative. Esther Longtree is portrayed as a woman who is “everlastingly pregnant,” carrying many stillborn children, miscarriages, and unfulfilled pregnancies over the years. She is described as both “brilliant but dumb,” “mulish,” “big-footed,” and “pregnant with doubtfulness,” yet also maternal, loving, and burdened by her mysterious, repeated losses. Her pregnancies are often linked to a haunting mystery involving many absent or sterile fathers and the ambiguous presence of children who are never fully born or recognized. The narrative suggests that Esther has tried repeatedly to give birth to a “child who lived” but is also surrounded by countless stillborn, ghostly children, and shadows: symbolizing loss, grief, and the elusive nature of life and creation. In this light, Esther Longtree can be seen as embodying the tensions surrounding abortion debates: the conflict between life and death, fertility and sterility, birth and loss, hope and despair. Her “everlasting pregnancy” and the repeated miscarriages may symbolize the ongoing societal struggle over reproductive rights, the moral and emotional complexity of abortion, and the societal judgment and silence that often surround it. The ambiguity about the paternity of her children, the legal threats she faces, and her isolation also reflect the politicized and often stigmatized dimensions of abortion in American society. Esther’s story touches on themes of bodily autonomy, societal control, guilt, and secrecy. She is pursued by a detective who accuses her of murder, threatened with legal action, and yet she remains evasive, protective of her secret “pregnancies,” and burdened by the consequences of societal judgments. This can be interpreted as symbolic of the legal and moral scrutiny women face in abortion debates, where personal agency conflicts with external control and societal norms. The novel frames Esther’s experiences within a broader cosmic and existential context, blurring lines between life and death, reality and dream, and individual and universal experiences. This deepens the symbolism, suggesting that the abortion debate is not simply a social or political issue but also a profound human and metaphysical dilemma about creation, destruction, and the meaning of existence. Esther Longtree may symbolize the abortion debate in the U.S., the detailed portrayal of her character’s perpetual pregnancies, miscarriages, societal judgment, and emotional complexity strongly suggests an allegorical reflection on the themes central to abortion discourse. Her story embodies the profound personal and societal conflicts surrounding reproductive rights, loss, and the nature of life itself.
  • “But if one takes the first step downward”: “Easy is the descent to Avernus,” the Sibyl tells Aeneas, but to climb back up to the air is the labor (Virgil, Aeneid 6). See Greek Mythology.
  • “she had been swallowed by the earth”: “And the earth opened her mouth, and swallowed them up” (Numbers 16:32, KJV); “and it vomited out Jonah upon the dry land” (Jonah 2:10, KJV). See The Bible.
  • “Now the first would not be the last”: “So the last shall be first, and the first last” (Matthew 20:16, KJV). See The Bible.
  • “a Boy Scout and could recite the Declaration of Independence”: The Boy Scouts of America was founded in 1910; a Scout of Walter’s age would have been in grammar school in the 1930s. See Walter.
  • “Some sins, if they were sins, had left no stains”: “Though your sins be as scarlet, they shall be as white as snow” (Isaiah 1:18, KJV). See The Bible.
  • “pregnant only with the yeast of her own dreams”: There are two famous pseudocyesis cases (phantom pregnancies): Mary Tudor, Queen of England, experienced a well-documented false pregnancy, where she showed physical symptoms, and her doctors and court prepared for a birth, even drafting announcement letters with blanks for the date and sex. Anna O, the patient of Freud’s colleague Josef Breuer, experienced a false pregnancy where she believed she was in labor with her therapist’s child. Anna O was Bertha Pappenheim, who went on to found the League of Jewish Women (1904) and fought the trafficking of women. See Pregnancy, Abortion, and Midwifery and Freud and Jung.
  • “much like a limb that hurts after the limb is cut away”: The Philadelphia neurologist Silas Weir Mitchell named the “phantom limb” in 1871, after treating Civil War amputees who still felt pain in the arms and legs they had lost. See The Civil War.
  • “the featherweight champion—the bantam, the flyweight”: See Joe Goldberg, the featherweight champion, in the Chapter 73 resources.
  • “The thousand nipples, the Milky Way”: In Greek myth the Milky Way is milk spilled from Hera’s breast when she pulled away from the infant Heracles. See Greek Mythology.
  • “A bee flying up her skirt had never made such difference”: See the bee that flew up little Esther’s skirt in the Chapter 78 resources.
  • “as black as the ace of spades”: “Negro” was the standard, accepted, and often respectful term for people of African descent in the U.S., evolving from slavery-era usage to a self-identifying term supported by leaders like W.E.B. Du Bois. It was used by the U.S. Census from 1950, though it later became associated with Jim Crow, declining in favor of “Black” by the late 1960s. “Negro” was used by the U.S. Census for much of the twentieth century. See Society, Class, and Race.
  • “He had fled for fear the white people would see him and kill him”: Interracial marriage in the United States has only been legal since the 1967 U.S. Supreme Court decision Loving v. Virginia that held anti-miscegenation laws were unconstitutional by the 14th Amendment established in 1868. The court’s landmark decision has been commemorated and celebrated every year on the Loving Day, June 12th. The number of interracial marriages in 1967 was three percent. The first interracial marriage in what is today the United States was that of Pocahontas, who married tobacco planter John Rolfe in 1614. The first ever law prohibiting interracial marriage was passed by Maryland in 1691. The Quaker Zephaniah Kingsley married, outside the US, a black enslaved woman that he bought in Cuba. He also had three black common-law enslaved wives. He freed all four. They had to flee Florida for Haiti when it became a US territory. The prospect of black men marrying white women terrified many Americans before the Civil War. It was magnified into the greatest threat to society. The first legal black-white marriage in the United States was that of African-American professor William G. Allen and a white student, Mary King, in 1853. When their plans to marry were announced, Allen narrowly escaped being lynched. Their marriage was secret, and they left the country immediately for England, never to return. In 1957 actor Sammy Davis Jr. faced backlash for his relationship with a white woman, actress Kim Novak. In 1958, Davis briefly married a black woman, actress and dancer Loray White, to protect himself from mob violence. See Society, Class, and Race and Lynching and Racial Violence.
  • “He had gone farther North”: In the Great Migration, some six million Black Southerners moved north and west between 1910 and 1970, fleeing lynching and Jim Crow. See Society, Class, and Race and Lynching and Racial Violence.
  • “they had tried to hang him from a white-blossoming tree”: Jo Reed was an African American man who was lynched in Nashville, Tennessee, on April 30, 1875, where he was taken by a white mob from the county jail after being arrested for killing a police officer in a confrontation. He was hanged from a suspension bridge but, after the rope broke, Reed survived the attempted lynching, escaped via the river, and left Nashville to go West. A reference to part of the history of lynching in America is included at the end of this chapter. In 1955 the brutal lynching of fourteen year old Emmett Till for allegedly flirting with a white woman was a catalyst for the Civil Rights Movement after his mother permitted an open casket and photographs were published nationwide. See Lynching and Racial Violence.
  • “Where is black white”: “Woe unto them that call evil good, and good evil; that put darkness for light, and light for darkness” (Isaiah 5:20, KJV). See The Bible.
  • “mother, I go to a fine school with the white children now”: In Brown v. Board of Education (1954) the Supreme Court struck down segregated public schools; in the 1930s a Black child like Walter was barred from white schools across the South and kept out of many in the North. See Society, Class, and Race.
  • “She had gone to the South where the black people were”: In the US the South consists of sixteen states along the bottom part of the country from Texas to Maryland.
  • “and she had pressed her thumb because she could not really kill herself”: Esther in admitting to killing or wanting to kill her children is considered infanticide. In most modern societies the practice is considered immoral and criminal. It still takes place in the Western world usually because of the parent’s mental illness or violent behavior, in addition to some poor countries as a form of population control, sometimes with tacit societal acceptance. Female infanticide, a form of sex-selective infanticide, is more common than the killing of male offspring, especially in cultures where male children are more desirable. In the book Genome, Matt Ridley explains that there may be a genetic factor involved as well. The book Genome was published in 1999. See Guilt, Innocence, and Justice.
    • Esther fits the pattern later called neonaticide: a young, unmarried mother who does not recognize or denies her pregnancy, gives birth alone, and kills the newborn in panic within the first day. The psychiatrist Phillip Resnick named it in 1970. See Pregnancy, Abortion, and Midwifery and Women, Gender, and Marriage.
  • “an old sporting page that had to do with the Kentucky race-horses”: “Kentucky racehorses” Horse racing in Kentucky predates statehood (1792), with organized racing occurring in Louisville as early as 1783. All Kentucky thoroughbreds trace their lineage back to three foundation sires: the Darley Arabian, the Godolphin Arabian, and the Byerly Turk. On May 17, 1875, the first Kentucky Derby was held at Churchill Downs (then the Louisville Jockey Club). It was won by Aristides, trained by Ansel Williamson and ridden by Black jockey Oliver Lewis. In the first 28 runnings of the Derby, Black jockeys won 15 times. Notable jockeys included Isaac Murphy (three-time winner) and the aforementioned Oliver Lewis. Key winners included Vagrant (1876), the first gelding winner, and Hindoo (1881). In 1902, a syndicate led by Col. Matt Winn took over Churchill Downs, transforming it into a premier racing venue. In 1919, Sir Barton became the first horse to win the Kentucky Derby, Preakness, and Belmont Stakes, though the term “Triple Crown” was not commonly used until 1930 with Gallant Fox. Exterminator (1918) was a fan favorite who won despite being a last-minute substitute. Calumet Farm became the dominant force in American racing, with winners like Whirlaway (1941), Pensive (1944), Ponder (1949), and Hill Gail (1952). Often considered one of the greatest horses of all time, Citation won the Triple Crown and became the first horse to win $1 million. See Horses and Carriages.
    • Black jockeys were driven from the track after 1900; Jimmy Winkfield, who won the Derby in 1901 and 1902, was the last Black jockey to win it. See Society, Class, and Race.
