Chapter 17

← Chapter 16 · Home · Chapter 18 →

Content note: Miss MacIntosh warns Vera of a lurking rapist, and the chapter leads into the events of Chapter 18.

Summary

In the moonlight Miss MacIntosh stands by the window, and Vera sees that she is bald, “bald as the egg or as the rock where nothing grows,” with “only one breast.” Vera knows her only by her broken nose. Terrified and wildly triumphant at having always pictured her with a mustache and cast her as the bridegroom, Vera screams, “Miss MacIntosh, you are a man!” A struggle follows, told in the language of the boxing ring. Vera is knocked down, her mouth covered by “his hoary hand,” and laid on the bed, and she wonders whether her attacker is a fallen angel, a gladiator, the sandbag dummy come to life, or the angel Jacob wrestled. She calls it the work of someone “who should take advantage of a poor, ignorant girl, only fourteen years old.” She calls for her mother and for Mr. Spitzer, but no one comes. In the morning her braids are exactly braided, and the only scratches on her cheeks could have come from leafless branches.

Characters present

Miss MacIntosh · Vera Cartwheel · Falada · Catherine Cartwheel · Joachim Spitzer

Concepts present

Themes: Death and Mortality · Fear and Courage · Identity and the Self · Illusion and Reality · Madness and Sanity · Memory and the Past · Society, Class, and Race · Women, Gender, and Marriage

Symbols: Clothing, Hats, and Skirts · Hair, Wig, and Baldness · Horses and Carriages · Lamps, Candles, and Light · Mirrors and Reflections · Moon and Stars · Weddings and Funerals

Allusions: Ancient Egypt · Dante · Fairy Tales and Folklore · Genesis · Greek Mythology · Revelation and the Apocalypse · Shakespeare · The Bible · The Book of Job

Key passages

From the research

  • Miss MacIntosh is portrayed almost as a spectral, otherworldly figure standing by the tall windows with blowing curtains. Her corset stays resemble quills of a porcupine or rays of moonlight, and her head is replaced by a “cold and dented” moonlike dome. This surreal image evokes a sense of alienation and transformation, suggesting that she is no longer fully human or recognizable. The metaphor of her body being “more angular than curved” and “ready to meet with the opponent at a single move” sets the tone of confrontation and tension.
  • The silence, the white curtains blowing like wings, and the “faint tappings of a spectral branch” create an eerie atmosphere, hinting at supernatural or psychological disturbance. This passage is important because it introduces the unsettling and uncanny presence of Miss MacIntosh, foreshadowing the dramatic events to follow.
  • A key moment is the revelation that Miss MacIntosh is bald “as the egg or as the rock where nothing grows,” her face “absolutely impersonal and expressionless.” This stark image symbolizes loss of identity, vitality, and femininity. Vera is horrified by this transformation, seeing her as a “monster” or a “phantasmagoric being,” a “bald pretender” who deceives the senses.
  • The contrast with the memory of her “red, shining hair, tawny as an August sunset,” her eyeglasses, and umbrella underscores the dramatic change, suggesting that this is either a ghostly apparition or a symbolic representation of death, decay, or betrayal.
  • Vera reflects on proverbs and parables, such as “the mountains shall never meet with the mountains,” “you shall praise the bridge that carried you,” and “man is not born to happiness.” These reflections highlight the philosophical and existential underpinnings of the chapter, emphasizing themes of inevitability, loss, and the fragile nature of human happiness.
  • Vera struggles with the notion that either Miss MacIntosh has changed or she herself has changed, questioning the nature of reality and perception. This self-doubt and questioning of identity deepen the psychological tension and ambiguity.
  • This extended passage details a physical and symbolic struggle between Vera and the bald figure (Miss MacIntosh or a phantom). The fight is described in vivid, almost cinematic terms, with references to boxing moves (“left jab,” “straight right,” “rabbit punch”) and wrestling.
  • Vera experiences disorientation, pain, and a sense of duality (“my body seemed divided as if now there were two of us”). The imagery of stars falling “like dried seed pods,” “dark horsemen,” and a black “cloud extending from pole to pole” evokes apocalyptic or mythic grandeur.
  • Importantly, Vera questions the identity of the attacker, wondering if it is a “fallen angel,” a “Christian knight,” or merely a “sandbag dummy come to life.” This uncertainty blurs the line between reality, dream, and hallucination.
  • Vera describes being overpowered, feeling hair pulled out “by handfuls,” yet experiencing no pain but a speculative wonder about being “snatched bald.” This loss of hair symbolizes a profound loss of beauty, femininity, and power, likened to a “terrible mistake, God’s error.”
  • Despite this, Vera notes that “the next morning, of course, my long braids were exactly braided down my back,” suggesting the experience may have been a dream, vision, or hallucination, blurring reality and illusion.
  • “She was only this old man who had only one breast and no hair and no future prospect.” Chapter 19 confirms that one breast was amputated. The novel’s clues to Miss MacIntosh’s illness, the lobster’s claws upon her forehead in Chapter 10 and the blue lips in Chapter 12, come to this.
  • Vera’s account of the struggle, her mouth covered, laid on “the bed of death or something which might be worse,” the work of someone “who should take advantage of a poor, ignorant girl, only fourteen years old,” is the language of assault. That the morning shows no trace leaves open what happened, not whether Vera was harmed.

Questions and observations

Reading closely

  • “I refused to accept the simple explanation which I myself proposed, refused to believe that she had not changed, that only I had changed.” Which is true?
  • “What shall we do when, fleeing from illusion, we are confronted by illusion?” How does Vera answer?
  • Her “body seemed divided as if now there were two of us, one who fought, one who lay still and watched it all.” What does that division tell us?

Characters

  • Vera laughs and feels “no pity for her but only a kind of wild triumph.” Why?
  • Vera calls Miss MacIntosh “the bald pretender” who “had been pulling the wool over my eyes.” Who has been deceived?
  • She knows Miss MacIntosh “by her broken nose.” What does it mean to know someone by a wound?

Connections

  • Vera has pictured Miss MacIntosh with a red mustache (Chapter 9) and as the bridegroom (Chapter 10). How does that prepare for “you are a man”?
  • The sandbag dummy of Chapters 12 and 15 comes “to life.” What has Vera been training for?
  • Falada’s head speaks after death in Chapter 16. What does Miss MacIntosh’s bare head say?

Reflection

  • Why might a child react with cruelty when someone she trusted is suddenly exposed?
  • Can a person be harmed by an event she cannot be sure happened?
  • How does illness change how others see a body?

Research: Characters

Miss MacIntosh

  • Initially described as a familiar and trusted figure, a nursemaid, a guardian.
  • Transforms into a bald, expressionless, ghostly figure, described as “bald as the egg or as the rock where nothing grows,” symbolizing loss, change, or an unsettling void.
  • Portrayed with contradictory imagery: both fragile and monstrously strong, spectral yet physically violent.
  • Vera struggles to reconcile this apparition with the Miss MacIntosh she knew, suspecting deception and a hidden identity.
  • Symbolizes a “bald pretender,” a false self, or a shadowy force challenging Vera.
  • She has “only one breast,” and Vera knows her only “by her broken nose” from the Spokane bus (Chapter 9).

Vera Cartwheel

  • On the night of her fourteenth birthday, caught between terror and fascination.
  • Experiences a physical and psychological battle with the transformed Miss MacIntosh.
  • Reflects on memories, identity, and the nature of illusion versus reality.
  • Shows moments of wild laughter, despair, and confusion, indicating a complex emotional state.
  • Vera’s perception is unreliable or dreamlike, blending corporeal reality with surreal visions.
  • She screams, “Miss MacIntosh, you are a man!” and feels “a kind of wild triumph,” though “I should have cried.”

Research: Themes

Identity and Transformation

See: Identity and the Self

  • Miss MacIntosh’s sudden baldness and altered demeanor symbolize a profound change, calling into question the stability of identity.
  • Vera’s inability to accept this change reflects a struggle with understanding the self and others.
  • The motif of hair loss as a loss of femininity or vitality is potent and unsettling.

Illusion versus Reality

See: Illusion and Reality

  • The chapter blurs the lines between waking life, dream, and hallucination.
  • Vera questions what is real, what is illusion, and the nature of perception.
  • The fight with the “bald opponent” may also be symbolic, reflecting an internal conflict or a confrontation with an aspect of the self.

Fear and Madness

See: Madness and Sanity · Fear and Courage

  • The setting at midnight, the eerie descriptions, and the “zero hour” evoke a sense of dread.
  • Vera’s fear escalates into a violent struggle, suggesting a descent into madness and trauma.
  • The chapter explores how strange events can “leave us mad” or shatter sanity.

Power and Vulnerability

See: Fear and Courage · Women, Gender, and Marriage

  • Miss MacIntosh’s physical power contrasts with her ghostly, fragile appearance.
  • Vera, though young and vulnerable, refuses to be defeated quietly.
  • The battle becomes a metaphor for the fight between opposing forces within or external threats.

Memory and Perception

See: Memory and the Past

  • Vera recalls past moments with Miss MacIntosh, contrasting them with the present terrifying vision.
  • There is an awareness that memory and perception can deceive or change over time.
  • Vera’s reflections on proverbs and parables hint at larger philosophical questions.

Research: Symbols and Imagery

Baldness

See: Hair, Wig, and Baldness

  • Represents loss, emptiness, exposure, and transformation.
  • Compared to “the egg,” “the rock where nothing grows,” “the rose stripped of all its petals,” and “bare as the winter winds,” emphasizing barrenness and desolation.

Moonlight and Darkness

See: Moon and Stars · Lamps, Candles, and Light

  • The moonlight creates a cold, distant atmosphere.
  • The interplay of light and shadow symbolizes the tension between knowledge and ignorance, reality and illusion.

Corset and Armor

See: Clothing, Hats, and Skirts

  • Miss MacIntosh’s metallic corset is described like a battleship or wrestler’s gear, symbolizing restraint, protection, and conflict readiness.

Animal Imagery

See: Horses and Carriages

  • Falada, Vera’s old pony, a present from Mr. Spitzer, represents loyalty and alertness but is powerless.
  • Vera’s comparison of Miss MacIntosh to a “codfish swept up upon a barren shore” and “old man” adds to the grotesque transformation.

Physical Combat

See: Fear and Courage

  • The fight is depicted with detailed boxing terminology (rabbit punch, jab, left hook), emphasizing the visceral and brutal nature of the struggle.
  • The encounter may also symbolize internal psychological conflict or a battle with one’s fears or identity.

Style

  • The narration flows with intense, fragmented, and poetic sentences reflecting Vera’s emotional turmoil.
  • The imagery is often dreamlike, blending the real with the fantastical.
  • The tone fluctuates between terror, disbelief, wild laughter, and despair.

Use of Parables and Philosophical Reflections

See: Fairy Tales and Folklore

  • Vera contemplates proverbs and existential questions, adding depth and universality.

Further notes from the text

  • Miss MacIntosh first appears as a silhouette: corset stays sticking out like the quills of an angry porcupine, and in place of a head another moon, an ivory ball “such as perhaps a god should play with.”
  • The baldness arrives as a litany of similes, bald as the egg, as the rock where nothing grows, as the rose stripped of its petals, and then as a list of missing things: her red hair, her eyeglasses, her black umbrella, her Pilgrim’s Progress.
  • Vera’s first response is laughter and “a kind of wild triumph” at having been right all along in imagining Miss MacIntosh with a red, curled mustache and in casting her as the bridegroom, a direct callback to the dream wedding in Chapter 10.
  • The figure Vera fears is the lurking rapist Miss MacIntosh had warned her about, the drunken sailor reeling out of the fog. The protector and the danger she warned against have become one figure in the dark.
  • The struggle is told in boxing language: the left jab, the straight right, the rabbit punch, the left hook, the southpaw. It is the sandbag dummy of Chapters 12 and 15 come to life, and also, Vera thinks, the angel with whom Jacob wrestled at Peniel.
  • Vera calls for help that cannot come: her mother, and Mr. Spitzer, who “was gone from Boston to Boston.” She says she will be asking the questions of this night long years afterward, when she is old and grey.

Research: Resources

  • “her corset stays sticking out like the quills of an angry porcupine”: The Ghost tells Hamlet his tale would make “each particular hair to stand on end, / Like quills upon the fretful porpentine” (Hamlet 1.5). A few lines later, “My hair crawled,” and soon Vera’s hair stands “on end.” See Shakespeare and Clothing, Hats, and Skirts.
  • “a figure of a tomb”: She stands “her hands crossed against the flatness of her breasts,” the pose of a tomb effigy. See the Chapter 16 resources.
  • “that zero hour, the hour of midnight when strangest things do often happen”: “Zero hour” was the soldiers’ name for the hour of attack in the First World War. “’Tis now the very witching time of night, / When churchyards yawn” (Hamlet 3.2). See Shakespeare.
  • “as if I were entombed in fields of everlasting ice”: At the bottom of Dante’s Hell, the traitors are frozen in the ice of Cocytus (Inferno 32-34). Vera is about to feel betrayed. See Dante.
  • “she was bald. She was bald as the egg”: Alopecia, the total loss of hair, was popularly blamed on “some sudden shock or amazement or illness.” The hair passage of Chapter 12 prepared for this, and in Chapter 19 Vera finds Miss MacIntosh’s red wig. See Hair, Wig, and Baldness, Miss MacIntosh, and the Chapter 12 resources.
  • “a great mirror where one should see one’s self if one looked closely”: Her bald head as a mirror. See Mirrors and Reflections.
  • “I knew her by her broken nose”: The broken nose from the Spokane bus. See Miss MacIntosh and the Chapter 9 resources.
  • “many a game of battledore and shuttlecock”: Battledore and shuttlecock is the old paddle game, the ancestor of badminton.
  • “the mountains shall never meet with the mountains”: “Friends may meet, but mountains never greet,” an old proverb. See Fairy Tales and Folklore.
  • “you shall praise the bridge that carried you”: “Praise the bridge that carries you over,” an English proverb. See Fairy Tales and Folklore.
  • “man is not born to happiness and is a bubble”: Homo bulla, “man is a bubble,” and “man is born unto trouble, as the sparks fly upward” (Job 5:7). See The Book of Job and the Chapter 15 resources.
  • “old pharaohs voyaging to heaven upon clouds of incense”: The Pyramid Texts tell of the king rising to heaven on the smoke of incense. See Ancient Egypt.
  • “where was her Pilgrim’s Progress?”: Miss MacIntosh’s Bunyan. See the Chapter 3 resources.
  • “Better it had been King Magnus, the fleshless being!”: It is not clear which Magnus Young means. Magnus the Good (1024-1047), an illegitimate son of St. Olaf, became king of Norway and Denmark. St. Magnus of Orkney, an earl and martyr, whose skull, split by an axe, was found hidden in a pillar of Kirkwall Cathedral in 1919, would fit “the fleshless being.”
  • “who knows not the grinning skull?”: Yorick’s skull: “Where be your gibes now?… Not one now, to mock your own grinning?” (Hamlet 5.1). See Shakespeare, Death and Mortality, and the Chapter 7 resources.
  • “some Irish hooligan or drunken sailor”: “Hooligan” came into use in 1890s London, said to be from a rowdy Irish family named Houlihan. The word carries the era’s contempt for the Irish poor. See Society, Class, and Race.
  • “visualizing her with a red, curled mustache, that I had been right in assigning to her the role of the bridegroom”: The red mustache of Chapter 9 and the wedding dream of Chapter 10. See Weddings and Funerals, the Chapter 9 resources, and the Chapter 10 resources.
  • “this old man who had only one breast”: Halsted’s radical mastectomy (1894), which removed the breast and the muscles beneath it, was the standard treatment for breast cancer for most of the twentieth century. Chapter 19 confirms the loss. In Chapter 10, Vera imagined “claws upon her forehead like the claws of a lobster,” and cancer takes its name from the crab. See Miss MacIntosh, Women, Gender, and Marriage, and the Chapter 10 resources.
  • “It was a horse ballet, a Spanish carousel with many mirrors”: Baroque courts staged horse ballets, and the carrousel was first a tournament of horsemen, like Louis XIV’s Grand Carrousel of 1662. See Horses and Carriages and the Chapter 16 resources.
  • “the moon which draws the waves in its wake and has no life of its own”: The moon raises the tides and shines only by reflected sunlight. See Moon and Stars.
  • “she was the ring-master”: The circus of Vera’s bareback dream in Chapter 16 returns, Miss MacIntosh with her “steel embroidery hoops.” See the Chapter 16 resources.
  • “one rose which canker shall not eat”: “And loathsome canker lives in sweetest bud” (Shakespeare, Sonnet 35). See Shakespeare.
  • “one door which shall not open to our knocking”: An inversion of “Knock, and it shall be opened unto you” (Matthew 7:7). See The Bible.
  • “the left jab which annoys, hurts, and stings, the straight right”: The fight follows boxing under the Marquess of Queensberry rules (1867). The rabbit punch, a blow to the back of the neck named for the way hunters killed rabbits, is illegal. The Sunday punch is a fighter’s best blow, and a southpaw fights left-handed. The little shadow boxer returns as a character in Chapter 72. See The Little Shadow Boxer.
  • “The stars fell like dried seed pods upon a dark and barren plain”: “And the stars of heaven fell unto the earth, even as a fig tree casteth her untimely figs” (Revelation 6:13). See Revelation and the Apocalypse.
  • “Myriads of dark horsemen thundered against a sky”: The four horsemen of Revelation 6. See Revelation and the Apocalypse.
  • “was it some fallen angel, some livid creature of the deep, or was it the angel of light”: “For Satan himself is transformed into an angel of light” (2 Corinthians 11:14). See The Bible.
  • “Where was Mr. Spitzer? He was gone from Boston to Boston.”: The preacher’s words in the dream of Chapter 10: “from Boston to Boston.” See Joachim Spitzer and the Chapter 10 resources.
  • “some ancient Sumerian or Greek wrestler or Roman gladiator”: In the Epic of Gilgamesh, from ancient Sumer and Babylon, Gilgamesh wrestles the wild man Enkidu, who becomes his friend. See Greek Mythology.
  • “someone who wore a jumbo corset whale-boned”: Corsets were stiffened with whalebone, the baleen from the mouths of whales. See Clothing, Hats, and Skirts.
  • “even that holy angel with whom Jacob struggled at Peniel”: Genesis 32:22-32 and Hosea 12:3-5: “And Jacob was left alone; and there wrestled a man with him until the breaking of the day” (Genesis 32:24). See Genesis and the Chapter 6 resources.
  • “the sandbag dummy come to life”: The sandbag dummy Vera was made to box in Chapters 12 and 15, now “the shadow boxer moving with such rapidity that his blows were impossible to block.” The little shadow boxer returns as a character in Chapter 72. See The Little Shadow Boxer, the Chapter 12 resources, and the Chapter 15 resources.
  • “my wailings and gnashings of teeth”: “There shall be weeping and gnashing of teeth” (Matthew 8:12). See The Bible and the Chapter 10 resources.
  • “the anesthesia provided by nature before she strikes her final blow”: David Livingstone, mauled by a lion, wrote that the shock “caused a sort of dreaminess, in which there was no sense of pain nor feeling of terror” (Missionary Travels, 1857).

chapter-27:
Chapter 27

← Chapter 26 · Home · Chapter 28 →

Content note: This chapter mentions the suicide of Mr. Spitzer’s twin brother, Peron. Vera’s mother, Catherine Cartwheel, is addicted to opium.

Summary

Vera grows exasperated with the adults who circle their problems endlessly. Mr. Spitzer carries calling cards and an old passport so that, if he is found dead, he will be identified as himself and not his brother. He wears Peron’s accurate wristwatch, and has lately rediscovered his own identical watch, broken and stopped near the time of Peron’s death, and wears it too. He fears nothing so much as the loss of his dignity, yet he is proud of walking through a glass wall and of being declared dead. He is always too early or too late, and always caught between streams of traffic. A stranger once asked him on a crowded street whether he wanted to die. He said no while nodding yes, and was led safely across.

Characters present

Joachim Spitzer · Catherine Cartwheel · Vera Cartwheel · Peron Spitzer · Mr. Chandelier

Concepts present

Themes: Death and Mortality · Dreams and Imagination · Identity and the Self · Illusion and Reality · Isolation and Connection · Memory and the Past · Music, Sound, and Silence · Time

Symbols: Birds · Clocks and Watches · Clothing, Hats, and Skirts · Horses and Carriages · Mirrors and Reflections · Music and Instruments · Opium · Roses and Flowers · Silence and Deafness · The Bus and the Journey · The Sea and Water · Twins and Doubles

Philosophy: Pythagoras and the Music of the Spheres

Allusions: Astronomy · Fairy Tales and Folklore · Greek Mythology · Romantic Poets · Shakespeare · The Bible · The History of Opium

Key passages

From the research

  • The chapter opens with Vera’s exasperation at “these ancient people,” forever turning upon the same spiral problems, and at her mother’s habit of living in an imaginative, surreal world rather than facing reality. Catherine imagines herself as historical or fantastical figures (e.g., Catherine the Great) and engages in imagined dialogues, addressing absent entities. This highlights her detachment from actual life and the dreamlike, opium-induced nature of her thoughts. It sets the tone for understanding her as a figure caught between illusion and reality, embodying a perennial lack of faith that paradoxically makes everything possible for her.
  • In contrast to Catherine, Mr. Spitzer is portrayed as being more aware of his difficulties and realities. Yet, he is burdened by his isolation, preferring neutrality and distance from the competitive world. His existence is described as “intermittent,” marked by memory lapses and confusion, symbolized by the possibility of walking “through a wall of shimmering glass” or forgetting destinations. This motif emphasizes his fragile grasp on reality and self-identity, as well as his struggle with time and memory.
  • The chapter deeply explores the symbolism of time through the motif of watches. Mr. Spitzer wears his dead brother’s fine, accurate watch, contrasting it with his own broken and rusted timepiece. The brother’s watch marks “the course of the inaccurate planets.” Timing the breakers with it becomes “his elegiac music in memory of his brother.” This duality of watches reflects the tension between order and chaos, memory and loss, and the elusive nature of time itself. The mention of the brother’s death and Mr. Spitzer’s confusion about timing around this event underscores the theme of temporal dislocation and the impossibility of fully grasping or controlling time.
  • Mr. Spitzer reflects on the artifice of time, comparing it to Catherine’s opium dreams and the “great coffin of stars” that might contain “the body of her love.” This passage philosophically questions the reality of time, suggesting it is an artificial construct. The image of Peron “jumping headlong into time with screaming stars” conveys a sense of fatalism and the overwhelming force of existence that defies human control.
  • Despite his solemn reflections, Mr. Spitzer is conscious of his external dignity, fearing ridicule and the loss of respect. The passage describing the humor in a “fat man slipping on a banana peel” humanizes him, showing his vulnerability and self-awareness. His concern with maintaining dignity despite physical and mental frailty illustrates a profound human struggle against decline and absurdity.
  • The motif of musical discord parallels the confusion and disorder in Mr. Spitzer’s life. This metaphor extends to his experience of reality, where signals, timing, and order are unreliable. The image of being caught between two traffic streams or crossing streets at wrong lights symbolizes his dislocation in time and place. The stranger who asks if he “wanted to die” and then guides him through chaotic traffic encapsulates his precarious existence, teetering between life and death, clarity and confusion.

Questions and observations

Reading closely

  • “It was this lack of faith which made all things possible to her.” What does Catherine’s unbelief give her?
  • Why does Mr. Spitzer carry calling cards, an old passport, and his silent music?
  • “Almost any fool, including himself, could tell him that there was no time.” Then why does he wear two watches?

Characters

  • Peron’s watch is accurate, and Joachim’s own is broken. Which brother keeps time?
  • Mr. Spitzer is “proud” of walking through glass and of being told he was dead. Why?
  • Asked if he wanted to die, he said no “at the same time shaking his head in the affirmative.” Which answer is true?

Connections

  • Miss MacIntosh’s “silver-dollar watch” is the kind Mr. Spitzer says “should have done for” Peron. What does the plain watch say about each of them?
  • The false signal lights, “the red where there should be the green,” return from Chapter 24. Who sees them first?
  • His brother “had not been Mr. Spitzer,” and the desk clerk said Mr. Spitzer was dead (Chapter 25). How does a man prove who he is?

Reflection

  • Does time heal all wounds, “even the wounds of time”?
  • Why is a fat man slipping on a banana peel funny, and to whom?
  • What would you carry so that the world would know who you were?

Research: Characters

Mr. Spitzer

  • A man burdened by his awareness of his difficulties and haunted by memories and illusions.
  • He is isolated, secretive, and struggles to reconcile his inner world with external reality.
  • His interactions with Catherine and his own sense of time and self are central.
  • Mr. Spitzer rarely leaves his home except for business and is burdened by his fragmented memory and difficulties.
  • He wears his deceased brother’s watch, and under his cuff on his left wrist his own broken one, as a memento and a symbol of time and loss.
  • Mr. Spitzer experiences dislocation in time and space: arriving early or late, encountering sudden weather changes, and experiencing shifts in scenery.
  • Mr. Spitzer struggles with the notion that life, time, and events are illusions, yet he continues to strive for dignity and order in his existence.
  • Mr. Spitzer’s clothes are always described, and he carries things that were Peron’s, above all Peron’s accurate watch.
  • He carries calling cards, an out-dated passport, and his silent music, so that if he is found in a city morgue, “all men should know that he had not been his brother.”
  • He fears “the loss of his dignity” above all, yet is proud of walking through glass and of the clerk who “insisted that he was dead,” “thinking of the joke he had played.”

Peron Spitzer (Joachim’s twin brother)

  • A man of “blatant tastes” who “had worn loud checks” and preferred “low company, lapsed souls, void characters, dice-rattlers.”
  • He “laughed at Mr. Spitzer’s silence,” yet left a fine, accurate watch, which he seems to have “most thoughtfully removed” before he jumped.
  • The twins “had always suffered, except for this final accident, the same accidents, one not falling unless the other fell.”

Catherine Cartwheel (Vera’s mother)

  • A woman lost in opium dreams and fantasies, disconnected from reality.
  • She imagines herself in surreal, historical, or symbolic roles, often interrupting conversations with remarks addressed to absent figures.
  • Her lack of faith paradoxically makes “all things possible” for her.
  • Catherine insists on assigning significant interpretations to minor details and ignores major events, suggesting her detachment from reality.
  • She enjoys “her present sense of omniscience” about Mr. Spitzer’s goings and comings, yet ignores him “in favor of God knew whom.”

Research: Themes

Isolation and Alienation

See: Isolation and Connection

  • Mr. Spitzer prefers solitude and neutrality, finding the competitive world burdensome.
  • Catherine is isolated in her opium-induced fantasies and mental state.
  • Both characters exhibit a disconnection from ordinary social interactions and time.

Perception of Reality and Imagination

See: Illusion and Reality · Dreams and Imagination

  • Catherine confuses or replaces reality with elaborate fantasies (e.g., imagining herself as Catherine the Great).
  • Mr. Spitzer’s reality is complicated by his own fragmented memory and sense of identity.

Time and Memory

See: Memory and the Past · Time

  • Time is portrayed as fluid, unreliable, and artificial.
  • Mr. Spitzer’s broken and inherited watches symbolize the fractured nature of time and memory.
  • The struggle with remembering and forgetting is a persistent motif, especially in relation to Mr. Spitzer’s brother’s death.

Death and Existence

See: Death and Mortality

  • The idea of death is ever-present, especially concerning Mr. Spitzer’s brother.
  • Mr. Spitzer contemplates his own mortality and the notion of life as an illusion or transient state.

Dignity and Self-Image

See: Identity and the Self

  • Mr. Spitzer is deeply concerned with preserving his dignity and avoiding ridicule.
  • His physicality (notably his size) and the fear of losing control over his image are recurring concerns.

Music and Harmony

See: Music, Sound, and Silence

  • Mr. Spitzer finds solace in musical metaphors: the “Pythagorean harmonies,” “music of the silent spheres,” and the discordant experiences of life.
  • Music represents both order and chaos, reflecting the tension in Mr. Spitzer’s internal state.

Research: Symbols and Imagery

Watches

See: Clocks and Watches · Time

  • Mr. Spitzer wears both his own watch and his brother’s. Miss MacIntosh also has a watch, her “old dollar watch which was given to her by her dead love” (Chapter 22).
  • The brother’s unbroken, elegant watch contrasts with Mr. Spitzer’s broken, dust-clogged timepiece.
  • Watches symbolize the passage and distortion of time, memory, and connection between the brothers.

Opium Dreams and Fantasies

See: Opium

  • Catherine’s opium-induced visions illustrate altered perception and escapism.
  • These dreams blur the line between reality and imagination.

Phantasmagoric Facts

See: Illusion and Reality

  • Catherine’s interpretation of Mr. Spitzer’s life is described as “phantasmagoric,” highlighting the surreal and distorted nature of her view.

Invisible Glass Wall

See: Mirrors and Reflections · Chapter 25 resources

  • Metaphor for Mr. Spitzer’s barriers between himself and the external world, also referencing an incident where he “walked through a wall of invisible glass,” symbolic of his fragile state.

Traffic and Crossings

See: The Bus and the Journey · Chapter 24 resources

  • Recurring images of Mr. Spitzer being caught in dangerous or confusing traffic symbolize his existential confusion and vulnerability.

Calling Cards and Passport

See: Identity and the Self

  • His calling cards, out-dated passport, and scroll of silent music are what he carries so that the world will know him from his brother.

Further notes from the text

  • The chapter opens with Vera’s exasperation at “these ancient people,” forever turning on the same spiral problems, and at her mother imagining she is Catherine the Great in a bed with pillars of twisted amethyst rather than facing the living sunlight.
  • Mr. Spitzer objects less to Catherine’s “phantasmagoric facts” about his life than to her interpretation of them: she insists that minor details matter most and major events not at all.
  • His life, which should be continuous, is “intermittent.” He takes the wrong train, gets off at the wrong city, “the wrong station, the wrong star,” though he is painfully accurate and covered with exact reminders to himself.
  • Almost any fool, he admits, including himself, could tell him there is no time, that it is all artifice like Catherine’s opium dreams, and yet Peron’s watch is a convenient timepiece for a poor lawyer and musician.
  • Peron’s watch was made for clocking horses. Mr. Spitzer now uses it to time the breakers coming in with their foaming manes and tails, thinking of the long horse race of life.
  • His fear of losing his dignity runs alongside a frank admission that a fat man slipping on a banana peel is the funniest thing there is. See Comedy in Chapter 27.

Research: Resources

  • “perhaps Catherine the Great sleeping in a bed with pillars of twisted amethyst”: Catherine II, Empress of Russia (reigned 1762-96). Catherine Cartwheel shares her name. See Catherine Cartwheel.
  • “her mind distilled by the juices of languorous poppy flowers”: Opium is the dried latex of the opium poppy, Papaver somniferum. See The History of Opium and Opium.
  • “it was this lack of faith which made all things possible to her”: It inverts Mark 9:23, “All things are possible to him that believeth.” See The Bible.
  • “the Pythagorean harmonies, the muffled planetary voices, the music of the silent spheres”: The music of the spheres. See Pythagoras and the Music of the Spheres and the Chapter 26 resources.
  • “even the company of Mr. Chandelier”: Catherine’s companion of the candles. See Mr. Chandelier.
  • “likely to walk through a wall of shimmering glass”: The glass wall of Chapter 25. See the Chapter 25 resources.
  • “his high silk hat and black necktie and rosebud with maidenhair”: Maidenhair fern (Adiantum) was the usual green set behind a buttonhole rose. See Clothing, Hats, and Skirts and Roses and Flowers.
  • “unfinished epithalamiums and dirges and vast recessionals”: Epithalamiums are songs that celebrate a marriage, while dirges are a lament for the dead. Spenser wrote his “Epithalamion” (1595) for his own wedding, and Kipling’s “Recessional” (1897) is remembered for “Lest we forget!” See Music, Sound, and Silence.
  • “for the tongue-less nightingales”: Philomela, whose tongue Tereus cut out, became the nightingale (Ovid, Metamorphoses 6). See Greek Mythology and Birds.
  • “in a city morgue among the drowned women and the fallen men”: It reverses the “fallen woman” drowned in Thomas Hood’s “The Bridge of Sighs” (1844): “One more Unfortunate, / Weary of breath.” See the Chapter 26 resources.
  • “time healing, he believed, all wounds”: The proverb is old. Chaucer has “As tyme hem hurt, a tyme doth hem cure” (Troilus and Criseyde, c. 1385).
  • “storks’ nests on the roof-tops”: In northern Europe a stork’s nest on the roof brought luck, and storks brought babies. Hans Christian Andersen’s “The Storks” (1838). See Birds and Fairy Tales and Folklore.
  • “Any old silver-dollar stop watch should have done for him”: Miss MacIntosh’s “silver-dollar watch,” which she always wears (Chapters 3, 9, and 22). Ingersoll’s Yankee (1896), sold for a dollar, was “the watch that made the dollar famous.” See Clocks and Watches and Miss MacIntosh.
  • “the course of the inaccurate planets”: “Planet” is from the Greek planētēs, “wanderer.” See Astronomy.
  • “searching through time for that which was already lost”: Proust’s In Search of Lost Time (À la recherche du temps perdu, 1913-27).
  • “her dream of some great coffin of stars”: “The table might easily be a coffin of stars” (Chapter 25). See the Chapter 25 resources.
  • “the groupings of beats or pulses into equal measures, accelerated or delayed”: Meter and tempo: accelerando and ritardando. See Music and Instruments.
  • “they had always suffered, except for this final accident, the same accidents, one not falling unless the other fell”: The twins, like Castor and Pollux in Chapter 25. See Twins and Doubles and the Chapter 25 resources.
  • “when not one wind would blow through the sails of a ship stuck at the far horizon”: “As idle as a painted ship / Upon a painted ocean” (Coleridge, “The Rime of the Ancient Mariner,” 1798). See Romantic Poets.
  • “the great breakers coming in with their foaming manes and tails”: Poseidon was god of the sea and of horses, and breaking waves are still called “white horses.” See Greek Mythology, Horses and Carriages, and The Sea and Water.
  • “more accurate than the sundials in the windy gardens”: The sundial motto “Horas non numero nisi serenas,” “I count only the sunny hours.” See Clocks and Watches.
  • “had died a thousand deaths”: “Cowards die many times before their deaths; / The valiant never taste of death but once” (Julius Caesar 2.2). See Shakespeare.
  • “the old desk clerk had insisted that he was dead”: The end of Chapter 25. See the Chapter 25 resources.
  • “there is nothing funnier than a fat man slipping on a banana peel”: Henri Bergson’s Laughter (1900): “A man, running along the street, stumbles and falls; the passers-by burst out laughing.” We laugh, he argued, at “something mechanical encrusted upon the living.” The banana-peel fall was a vaudeville and silent-film staple. See Comedy in Chapter 27.
  • “his elephantine avoirdupois”: Avoirdupois is a system of weights based on a pound of 16 ounces. The word comes from Old French aveir de peis, “goods of weight.”
  • “these loud noises ringing in his dead or deafened ear”: His “dead ear” of Chapter 25. See Silence and Deafness.
  • “the holding over of one or more tones of a chord into the following chord”: In music, a suspension is a note held over from one chord into the next. It clashes, then resolves, and here the resolution never comes. See Music and Instruments.
  • “caught ponderously in a revolving door”: Theophilus Van Kannel patented the revolving door in 1888.
  • “just when the red light turned to green”: The first electric traffic signal was installed in Cleveland in 1914. See the Chapter 24 resources.

Chapter 73

← Chapter 72 · Home · Chapter 74 →

Content note: The Esther Longtree chapters (72 to 81) deal with stillbirth and pregnancy loss, rape, infanticide, racist violence including lynching, and cruelty to children. This chapter describes stillbirths and the hidden remains of infants.

Summary

Esther Longtree, everlastingly pregnant, has given birth so often to nothing that she remembers her stillborn only as fragments, “an eye, an ear, a long gold hair, a fingernail, a cobweb,” hidden in hollow stumps, streams, and snowdrifts, and the undertaker complains that she brings him no business. Dying fathers, salesmen and insurance agents, write to ask whether their children lived, and on old Doctor’s advice she says nothing. The strongest of them, Joe Goldberg, the Jewish featherweight champion now wasting from tuberculosis in the Colorado mountains, writes of the night he raped her among the tombs of a hillside graveyard and calls her the greatest victory of his life; she remembers the graveyard but not him. An old grey mule, barren, stands by at every love. She fears a trial for murder, for the old Chicago detective, another of the fathers, is hunting proof that she killed his three. She remembers a labor alone under a barren dwarf apple tree, summer turning to winter in a single night, and the birth of nothing, the hardest birth to bear, while a white feather drifted down from some Arctic bird.

Characters present

Esther Longtree · Joe Goldberg · Justice O’Leary · The Chicago Detective · Phoebe · Coleman Bluebough · Abigail Porter

Concepts present

Themes: Death and Mortality · Duality and Doubles · Society, Class, and Race · Women, Gender, and Marriage

Symbols: Birds · Horses and Carriages

Allusions: Ancient Egypt · Angels and Archangels · Astronomy · Fairy Tales and Folklore · Greek Mythology · Iowa, Indiana, and the Midwest · Judaism · Pregnancy, Abortion, and Midwifery · Romantic Poets · Shakespeare · The Bible

Key passages

From the research

  • The chapter opens and repeatedly returns to the motif of Esther’s “everlasting pregnancy,” a state in which she is perpetually carrying children who are never fully born or who are stillborn, described as fragments like “an eye, an ear, a long gold hair, a fingernail, a cobweb.” She has a swollen womb and “the whistle of the stillborn in her ears.”
  • Throughout the chapter, the narrative emphasizes the letters sent to Esther by several dying men, “the fathers,” who inquire about the children they supposedly fathered with her. These men seek reassurance that their progeny live, clinging to hope at the moment of death. Esther keeps silent, as her old, drunken doctor advises, to preserve their vanity and peace. She cannot confirm their hopes because, in fact, the children are “snowflakes,” “marsh butterflies,” or other insubstantial forms.
  • A particularly poignant and detailed passage concerns Joe Goldberg, the champion featherweight boxer who wrote long, anguished letters to Esther as he wasted away from tuberculosis. He remembered her as the “peak of his existence,” the greatest “victory” among his battles, and begged for remembrance and forgiveness. Esther, however, cannot recall him clearly as his image is “lost in clouds” and like “the weight of a feather” in her mind, unlike the weaker men whose memories linger more distinctly.
  • Joe Goldberg’s memory of meeting Esther in a graveyard on a foggy, windy night is recounted in detail. It was rape. He “had taken her against her will,” he “had held her pinioned in his arms,” and he “had knocked off the nose of an angel as they struggled,” yet he remembers it as the greatest victory of his life. The graveyard setting ties the crime to death and decay, reinforcing the chapter’s motifs of mortality and the ambiguity of life and conception.
  • Repeatedly, the narrative returns to Esther’s silence and her solitary endurance of her condition. She neither confirms nor denies the existence of the children to the fathers and has no answers for the legal or emotional claims made upon her. Her silence is portrayed as a form of protection for herself and the dying men and as a reflection of the “imponderable answer” she cannot find.
  • One of the most emotionally charged passages describes a labor in which Esther endures all the pains of childbirth but delivers “nothing.” In this “birth of nothing” her body is broken and her labor intense, but no child emerges.
  • The chapter uses the image of an old mule, barren and mournful, as a recurring symbol of sterility and loneliness that stands by whenever Esther is with a lover. Similarly, the white feather that drifted down as she staggered across the snow after the birth of nothing is interpreted as a possible “message from the silence,” a sign of hope amid despair. These symbols deepen the thematic exploration of fertility, loss, and the fragile boundary between life and death.
  • Esther faces the threat of legal inquiry and possible trial for “murder” because her stillborn children have disappeared: the old Chicago detective is hunting proof, and the undertaker complains that she has not brought business to the graveyard. This introduces a grim social dimension to her plight, where her mysterious condition could be criminalized, adding to her burden of silence and secrecy.
  • Throughout, Esther struggles with memory: she cannot recall all the fathers or children, especially the strong featherweight champion, despite his vivid letters and pleas.

Questions and observations

Reading closely

  • “The birth of nothing was the hardest birth to bear.” Why would it be harder than any other?
  • “Her lack of any feeling was her deepest feeling now.” How can an absence be the deepest feeling?
  • “A woman’s faith was her pregnancy.” What does faith mean for Esther?

Characters

  • Joe Goldberg calls the night he raped Esther the “peak of his existence.” What does it say about him that he counts her among his victories?
  • “The strongest men were the weakest.” Is this true of Joe Goldberg?
  • Old Doctor tells Esther to say nothing to the dying fathers. “Supreme knowledge was always the last cruelty.” Is her silence kindness or cruelty?

Connections

  • Joe comes of a family of fighters “beginning with those who had fought the angels.” How is his last bout, with God on a peak above the clouds, like Jacob’s?
  • The salesman thinks his wife and her twin are two women “like the evening star and the morning star,” but Esther knows “the evening star and the morning star were one star.” Where else in the novel are two people one?
  • The old mule, “the barren animal who could not be mated,” stands by at every love. Why does it follow Esther?

Reflection

  • “Why were the sterile fathers never blamed?” Who is blamed for a lost child, then and now?
  • “Time would heal all wounds but hers.” Are there wounds that time does not heal?
  • The graveyard children were “cut down in the flower of their youth” and given funerals, while Esther’s had none. Why do some deaths get mourned and others hidden?

Research: Characters

Esther Longtree

  • Big-boned, slow-moving waitress, cross-eyed, with a deformed foot and swollen womb.
  • Maternal, compassionate, yet burdened by a mysterious, continuous pregnancy with stillborn children.
  • Silent and evasive when questioned by fathers, embodying endurance, sorrow, and resilience.
  • Symbolizes fertility, loss, and the complex intersection of memory and identity.

Joe Goldberg (Champion Featherweight)

  • A once-powerful boxing champion, now frail and dying of tuberculosis.
  • Writes long, emotional letters to Esther, hoping to be remembered and to claim his child.
  • Represents strength, vulnerability, and the tragic human fight against death.
  • He raped Esther in a graveyard and remembers it as the “peak of his existence”; she remembers the graveyard but not him.

Old Doctor

  • A drunken, disillusioned physician who advises Esther to maintain silence with dying men.
  • Offers a philosophical perspective on death, illness, and the illusions surrounding conception and fertility.

The Fathers (Traveling Salesmen, Sterile Men)

  • Many are weak, sterile, or self-centered men who impregnated Esther but never took responsibility.
  • They symbolize failure, disappointment, and the social stigma attached to Esther’s condition.

The Chicago detective

  • A symbolic figure representing societal judgment, scrutiny, and the external pressures faced by Esther Longtree. Though he appears only indirectly through Esther’s thoughts and fears, his presence is significant and multifaceted.
  • The detective symbolizes the potential legal and moral condemnation that Esther fears. She imagines a scenario where she might be arrested, tried, and accused of murder for the stillborn children she has carried and lost over the years. The detective’s investigation represents society’s attempt to impose order and assign blame on Esther for the tragic outcomes of her pregnancies, despite her innocence in her own mind.
  • The detective is “old” and “worm-ridden,” and he is himself one of the fathers, “another old, sterile father,” hunting proof “that she had killed his three whom she had never borne or who were born without eyes.” He stands for the many fathers who impregnated Esther and took no responsibility for the children. The detective’s search for proof and evidence reflects a broader theme of male absence and desertion, with Esther bearing the burden alone.
  • Esther fears the detective’s inquiries, which might lead to public exposure of her condition and the stillborn children. She worries about appearing before a jury while visibly pregnant, the social humiliation involved, and the invasive nature of such an investigation. This fear adds to her isolation and suffering, emphasizing the harshness of societal judgment towards women in her position.
  • The detective’s efforts to find evidence of murder or wrongdoing are ultimately futile, as Esther has hidden the stillborn children in natural places (streams, fields, under snowdrifts) making proof elusive.
  • Esther’s silence and refusal to answer inquiries, partly motivated by kindness to the dying fathers and partly by self-preservation, contrast with the detective’s probing.

Phoebe

  • Phoebe is mentioned in the context of a graveyard, specifically as “the old washwoman’s grave” with a statue that has a bulbous nose, warts, wrinkles, and a sunbonnet. Joe Goldberg names her statue in his letters as proof that he was in the graveyard with Esther.
  • Phoebe’s statue symbolizes one of the many tombs in the graveyard, representing the past and the presence of the dead in the narrative. She is part of the imagery of mortality and memory that permeates the story.
  • Phoebe is a symbolic figure within the narrative, evoking themes of death, memory, and the passage of time.

Coleman Bluebough

  • Coleman Bluebough is mentioned in the context of Esther Longtree’s story as a figure associated with old deaths and graves, named on a tombstone in the graveyard where Joe Goldberg raped Esther.
  • Esther Longtree recalls the name Coleman Bluebough, who died at the age of three, and his place is marked among other graves and memorials in the narrative.
  • The mention of Coleman Bluebough helps underscore themes of death, stillbirth, and loss that pervade Esther Longtree’s life and experiences, particularly her repeated pregnancies and the stillborn children she mourns.
  • Coleman Bluebough represents one of the many children who have died young or were stillborn, figures that are part of Esther Longtree’s troubled memories and grief.

Abigail Porter

  • Abigail Porter is referenced as a person whose grave is marked in the graveyard, and she is among the many figures evoked in the narration that surrounds Esther Longtree’s story.
  • The graveyard where she rests is described as a place filled with various symbolic elements like crosses, rustling owls, winged beings, inscriptions, and old statues. Abigail Porter is part of a broader meditation on death, memory, and loss within the narrative.

Research: Themes

  • Esther Longtree is a woman perpetually pregnant, carrying the memory and burden of many stillborn children: fragments such as an eye, ear, fingernail, cobweb, or snowflake rather than whole babies. This condition is both literal and symbolic, representing loss, unfulfilled motherhood, and isolation. Her pregnancy is a metaphor for enduring sorrow and hope intertwined.
  • Esther struggles to remember the fathers of her many lost children and even the details of conception, while the dying fathers vividly recall her and their supposed children. The featherweight champion Joe Goldberg, one of the few who wrote her, haunts her memory, but she cannot fully recall him, symbolizing the elusive and fragmented nature of memory.
  • Despite her perpetual pregnancy and maternal instincts, Esther is isolated, misunderstood, and burdened with silence. She mothered many children who never lived, and she bears the emotional weight alone, rarely responding to inquiries from dying fathers, protecting their illusions and her own fragile peace.
  • The novel explores the boundary between life and death, conception and loss. The children are often invisible and symbolized as feathers, snowflakes, or shadows which highlight the ephemeral nature of existence and the impossibility of closure or concrete answers.
  • Joe Goldberg represents a powerful figure in Esther’s life and the narrative: strong and victorious in his prime, yet reduced to a frail, dying man battling God. His letters to Esther reveal his longing for remembrance and his hopes for their child, underscoring themes of memory, regret, and the human desire for legacy.
  • Esther faces potential accusations, including murder of her stillborn children, reflecting societal judgment and misunderstanding of her condition. She fears trial and public humiliation, but she remains protective of her silence and her unborn “little shadow boxer.”

Research: Symbols and Imagery

  • Stillborn Children as Snowflakes, Feathers, Cobwebs: These fragile, ephemeral images represent the children that Esther carries but never fully births. They highlight invisibility, loss, and the intangible nature of her motherhood.
  • The Graveyard: The location of Esther’s encounter with Joe Goldberg symbolizes death, the boundary between life and afterlife, and the haunting memory of their union.
  • The Old Mule: Represents sterility, loneliness, and the persistence of life without fruition. It is Esther’s constant companion symbolizing the barrenness surrounding her fertility.
  • The Little Shadow Boxer: The unborn child she feels under her heart, symbolizing hope, continuation, and the enduring mystery of life and death.
  • Blood-Stained Clothes and Bruises: Signify the pain, violence, and social stigma Esther endures during her labors and life. They also underscore the physical and emotional toll of her condition.

Research: Resources

  • “said Esther Longtree, a big-boned, slow-moving waitress”: Esther Longtree emerges as a profoundly tragic and complex figure burdened by perpetual pregnancy and the sorrow of countless stillborn children. Her character is marked by an overwhelming maternal instinct intertwined with mystery, loneliness, and a haunting sense of loss. Esther is described as a “big, dumb-headed waitress,” slow-moving and physically altered by her condition: one foot is deformed, her womb swollen, and her body constantly expanding with what she perceives as an “everlasting pregnancy.” This physical state symbolizes her ceaseless burden and the weight of her unresolved grief. Her dark hair often drifts before her eyes, symbolizing both a literal and metaphorical veil between her and the world around her, emphasizing her isolation and internal confusion. Despite the numerous pregnancies resulting only in stillborns or incomplete births (“an eye, an ear, a long gold hair, a fingernail, a cobweb”) Esther remains intensely maternal. She has mothered everything from her childhood thumb and big toe to a bullfrog, underscoring her nurturing nature even in the face of continual loss. This maternal impulse is paradoxical; she is both the source of life and a witness to death and absence, which causes her embarrassment and deep sorrow. Many men, termed “fathers,” have impregnated her, yet none seem to have produced a living child. These men are generally weak, sterile, or dying, and several write to Esther as they face death, seeking acknowledgment of their supposed offspring. Esther, however, rarely answers these inquiries. She prefers to maintain silence to preserve the dignity and hope of the dying fathers, fearing the cruelty that truth would impose. This silence also protects her from the pain of confronting the truth about her stillborn children and the uncertain paternity of her current perpetual pregnancy. A significant figure in Esther’s narrative is Joe Goldberg, the champion featherweight boxer, who wrote to her desperately in his dying days. He remembers their encounter in a graveyard: he raped her there, “had taken her against her will,” “deflowered her,” and “had knocked her out, stone cold.” Despite his vivid memories and longing for recognition, Esther cannot recall him clearly, only the graveyard and the circumstances of their meeting. This failure to remember symbolizes her fragmented and overwhelmed state of mind. Joe represents the strongest of the fathers who becomes weak and ephemeral like a feather, and Esther’s inability to anchor him in her memory contrasts sharply with her vivid remembrance of the weaker men. Esther’s narrative is steeped in symbolic imagery: the stillborn children as snowflakes, feathers, cobwebs, and shadows; the old mule representing sterility and loneliness; the graveyard setting for the conception of Joe Goldberg’s child; and the recurring motif of silence as both protection and sorrow. Her “everlasting pregnancy” could be read as a metaphor for enduring grief, unfulfilled potential, and the human condition of bearing loss silently. Her story is riddled with ambiguity about reality versus memory, truth versus illusion, and life versus death. Esther is socially isolated, working alone in a restaurant with fewer and fewer customers, burdened by her physical state and the mystery of her pregnancies. There is an undercurrent of potential accusation against her, from a Chicago detective who suspects her in a forgotten murder of stillborn children to the threat of a public trial. This looming social judgment contrasts with Esther’s own self-view as a suffering, unselfish mother who has never demanded support or recognition from the fathers. Despite her suffering and the enormity of her loss, Esther exhibits resilience. She continues “waxing, waxing, never waning,” embodying a strange, almost supernatural endurance. Yet there is also resignation and confusion: she cannot fully grasp her own condition, cannot remember many fathers, and exists in a liminal space between hope and despair, life and death. Esther Longtree is a figure of tragic maternal devotion, loss, and mystery. Her physical and emotional existence is defined by an endless cycle of pregnancy and stillbirth, a heavy silence toward the men who impregnated her, and a haunting ambiguity about what is real and remembered. Her story explores themes of fertility, death, memory, and the human tendency to shield others from harsh truths through silence. She stands as a poignant embodiment of suffering and endurance. See Esther Longtree.
    • Esther Longtree symbolizes a complex and tragic history of loss, abandonment, and the elusive promise of fertility and continuity that can be read metaphorically as reflecting aspects of American history. Her character embodies the sorrow of countless lost hopes and unfulfilled potential: she is “everlastingly pregnant” yet only ever gives birth to stillborn children: fragments like “snowflakes,” “cobwebs,” “little feet,” or “golden hair.” These stillborns are the children of many fathers, most of whom are sterile or absent, and who only awaken a sense of conscience or responsibility at their deathbed, asking about the children they never knew. Esther’s silence toward these dying fathers symbolizes the unanswerable questions of lineage, legacy, and accountability in a fragmented, transient society where promises remain unfulfilled and where the past cannot be fully reconciled with the present. This condition can be interpreted as symbolic of the broader American experience, particularly the history of displacement, broken promises, and the elusiveness of the American Dream. Esther’s endless pregnancies with no living offspring reflect the cycles of hope and disappointment in a land marked by migration, loss, and the failure of paternal or institutional responsibility. The many “fathers” who impregnate her but then disappear or fail to support her children can be related to the many waves of settlers, immigrants, and transient individuals who have contributed to the making of America but whose legacies are uncertain or incomplete. The fact that Esther hides her stillborns “everywhere,” in streams, under snow, in tree stumps, and yet is threatened with accusations of murder, can be seen as a metaphor for the buried or forgotten histories of marginalized people and the silenced suffering that underlies American progress. The undertaker’s complaint that she brings no business because she hides the evidence of death symbolizes the societal reluctance or failure to confront these hidden tragedies. Her life is also connected to a landscape marked by graveyards, broken fences, and natural elements like wind, snow, and autumn leaves, evoking the American frontier and the harsh realities faced by those living on its margins. Esther Longtree’s tragic and ambiguous history symbolizes the haunted, fragmented, and often unacknowledged history of America itself: a land of many fathers but few fulfilled legacies; a place where life and death, hope and despair, fertility and barrenness coexist; and where the true stories of loss and endurance are obscured by silence and the passage of time. Esther Longtree stands as a profound metaphor for the unresolved burdens and contradictions in American history (the tension between promise and loss, presence and absence, birth and death) that shape the nation’s identity.
  • “his long practice of medica materia”: Materia medica (It encompasses ancient and medieval knowledge of remedies, with a foundational text being Dioscorides’ De Materia Medica) refers to the comprehensive body of knowledge, historically cataloging the origins, properties, and preparation of substances used to treat diseases. These remedies are derived from natural sources, primarily plants, but also animals and minerals, and are considered precursors to modern pharmacology.
  • “too, too solid for his tastes”: “O, that this too too solid flesh would melt, / Thaw and resolve itself into a dew!” (Hamlet, 1.2). Dew falls all through this chapter. See Shakespeare.
  • “worse than the Chaldeans”: In the Bible the Chaldeans are the Babylonians of Nebuchadnezzar, who burned the Temple and carried the people of Judah into captivity (2 Kings 25). Habakkuk calls them “that bitter and hasty nation” (Habakkuk 1:6, KJV), and in Daniel they are the king’s astrologers: “the magicians, and the astrologers, and the sorcerers, and the Chaldeans” (Daniel 2:2, KJV). For a Jewish fighter, no people could be worse. See The Bible and Judaism.
    • Chaldeans may refer to Chaldean Catholics who are adherents of the Chaldean Catholic Church, which originates from the historic Church of the East. The Chaldean community originates from groups of adherents of the Church of the East that entered into communion with the Roman Catholic Church in the 16th and 17th centuries. They were indigenous to the regions of northern Iraq, southeastern Turkey, northeastern Syria and northwestern Iran, many have migrated to Western countries including the United States, Canada, Mexico, Australia, Sweden and Germany. Many of them also live in Lebanon, Egypt, Palestine, Israel, Jordan, Iran, Turkey, and Georgia. (Wikipedia)
  • “the salesmen, the insurance agents”: American traveling salesmen (or “drummers”) were vital, iconic agents of commerce, bridging manufacturers with rural and small-town retailers throughout the 19th and early 20th centuries. They drove expansion by selling everything from textiles and machinery to household goods via rail and later automobiles, often utilizing direct-to-consumer, persuasive tactics before declining due to urbanization. Salesmen used personal charm and sometimes exaggerated pitches to move goods, often operating under a “caveat emptor” (buyer beware) market. They introduced items like sewing machines, pots, encyclopedias, and personal care products.
  • “In her vast super-fecundation”: In medicine, superfecundation is the fertilizing of two or more eggs from one cycle in separate acts of intercourse, so that twins may have different fathers. See Pregnancy, Abortion, and Midwifery.
  • “the brave little Jew, hard as rock”: Jewish fighters ruled American boxing in the first half of the twentieth century: twenty-six Jewish world champions between 1910 and 1940, most of them wearing the Star of David on their trunks. Abe Attell held the featherweight title from 1906 to 1912 (he first claimed it in 1901) and was later tied to the fixing of the 1919 World Series. Benny Leonard was lightweight champion from 1917 to 1925, and Barney Ross, raised in Chicago, held titles in the 1930s. See Joe Goldberg and Judaism.
  • “Tuberculosis, God’s hand”: Tuberculosis was a leading cause of death in the US in the early 1900s, thriving in crowded, unsanitary, and poverty-stricken urban areas. Before effective antibiotics (streptomycin in 1944, isoniazid in 1952), treatment focused on sanatoriums, fresh air, and surgery. Mortality fell from 194 per 100,000 in 1900 to 40 by 1945 due to public health initiatives.
  • “Joe Goldberg, the golden cock”: The surname Goldberg is of German/Yiddish origin, meaning “gold mountain,” formed from the German words Gold (gold) and Berg (mountain/hill). It’s a common Ashkenazi Jewish surname, used both as a habitational name from places named Goldberg and as an artificial or ornamental name, often adopted for its sound or association with wealth. Joe, the gold mountain, dies in the mountains and calls Esther the “peak of his existence among the snowy peaks.” See Joe Goldberg.
  • “an Indiana waitress said to be everlastingly pregnant”: Indiana’s history spans from prehistoric Native American mounds to becoming the 19th state in 1816 and establishing itself as “The Crossroads of America” by 1937. Key milestones included significant Civil War participation, pioneering professional baseball in 1871, and becoming a manufacturing and agricultural hub. See Iowa, Indiana, and the Midwest.
  • “in Chicago or St. Louis or Kansas City”: Chicago, founded in 1833 and incorporated in 1837, grew from a small trading post at the mouth of the Chicago River into a major industrial, rail, and manufacturing hub by the mid-20th century. Key eras included rapid growth after the 1871 fire, pioneering skyscraper architecture (1880s-90s), and becoming a postwar, segregated city by the 1950s.
    • Founded in 1764 by French fur traders, St. Louis grew from a strategic Mississippi River trading post into a major 19th-century industrial and transportation hub. Following its 1876 separation from the county, the city boomed as a manufacturing center, peaked in population around 1950, and began facing suburban flight and modernization, including early planning for the Gateway Arch.
    • Kansas City was founded in the 1830s as a Missouri River trading post, evolving from a frontier river town into a major 19th-century railroad hub and cattle center. Known as a wide-open “Paris of the Plains” during Prohibition, the city grew significantly through the mid-20th century, developing a strong jazz scene, a thriving downtown, and expanding its physical footprint significantly by 1960.
  • “a man dying in the Colorado mountains”: Colorado’s history was defined by Native American habitation, Spanish exploration, and a rapid transition from a mining frontier to a 38th state (1876). The 1858-59 Pike’s Peak Gold Rush sparked major settlement, while the late 19th-century economy shifted to ranching and farming.
    • Doctors sent consumptives west for the dry, high air, and Denver filled with them. National Jewish Hospital for Consumptives opened there in 1899 under the motto “None may enter who can pay, none can pay who enter” (University of Denver Libraries, “Chasing the Cure”), and the Jewish Consumptives’ Relief Society opened at Lakewood in 1904. See Judaism.
  • “married to a twin whose identical twin was married to no one”: Twins who change places in the night echo the Spitzer twins, Joachim and Peron, one never sure which of the two he is. See Joachim Spitzer, Peron Spitzer, and Duality and Doubles.
  • “the evening star and the morning star were one star”: The evening star and the morning star are both the planet Venus, called Hesperus at dusk and Phosphorus at dawn; the Greeks credited Pythagoras or Parmenides with discovering they were one. In 1892 the philosopher Gottlob Frege made “the morning star is the evening star” his famous example of two names with one meaning. See Astronomy and Duality and Doubles.
  • “high above the tree-line where no birds sang”: “The sedge has withered from the lake, / And no birds sing” (Keats, “La Belle Dame sans Merci,” 1819). See Romantic Poets.
  • “the pygmies, the Egyptians, the Irish, whoever they were”: Fight posters billed boxers by nation and race, and Irish-American fighters such as John L. Sullivan, heavyweight champion from 1882 to 1892, ruled the American ring before the Jewish fighters rose. “Whoever they were” shows how little his opponents meant to Joe.
    • Pygmies are among Africa’s oldest inhabitants, with ancestors diverging from other populations roughly 60,000 to 100,000 years ago, inhabiting Central African rainforests as hunter-gatherers. They are characterized by short stature (often under 5 feet) and traditionally live in intimate, symbiotic relationships with neighboring Bantu farming communities.
    • In 1904 the St. Louis World’s Fair put Ota Benga, a Mbuti man from the Congo, on display in its anthropology exhibit, and in 1906 the Bronx Zoo caged him in its monkey house until Black ministers forced his release. He died by suicide in Lynchburg, Virginia, in 1916. See Society, Class, and Race.
    • Ancient Egyptian civilization, emerging around 3100 B.C. after the unification of Upper and Lower Egypt, thrived for over 3,000 years along the Nile River. Known for pharaohs, hieroglyphs, and monumental architecture like the pyramids. This advanced society was sustained by the Nile’s predictable floods. The history is divided into Old, Middle, and New Kingdoms. See Ancient Egypt.
    • Irish history spans from prehistoric hunter-gatherer settlements around 10,000 BCE to a modern, independent nation. Defined by Celtic (Gaelic) culture, it endured Viking raids, Norman conquests (1169), and English colonization, leading to the 17th-century Penal Laws, the Great Famine (1845-1851), and 20th-century independence.
  • “Battling Joe, champion featherweight, golden cock”: “Battling” was a popular ring name in the early twentieth century, carried by fighters such as Battling Nelson and Battling Siki. The featherweight class, set at 126 pounds, sits just above bantamweight.
    • Historical weight classes for boxing are: heavyweight at 200+ pounds, light heavyweight at 168-175 pounds, middleweight at 154-160 pounds, welterweight at 140-147 pounds, lightweight at 130-135 pounds, featherweight at 122-126 pounds, bantamweight at 115-118 pounds, flyweight at 108-112 pounds.
  • “a fighter in the Jewish family, beginning with those who had fought the angels”: “And Jacob was left alone; and there wrestled a man with him until the breaking of the day” (Genesis 32:24, KJV). The man renamed him Israel, “for as a prince hast thou power with God and with men, and hast prevailed” (Genesis 32:28, KJV); Hosea says “he had power over the angel, and prevailed” (Hosea 12:4, KJV). Joe’s last bout, with God on a peak above the clouds, is Jacob’s, and he is losing it. See The Bible, Angels and Archangels, and Judaism.
  • “the birth control devices littering the bare ground”: Before 1965, birth control in the US relied on barriers, withdrawal, and, later, hormonal methods, with access heavily restricted by the Comstock Act of 1873. Common methods included condoms (vulcanized rubber by 1839), diaphragms, spermicides, and dangerous, ineffective douches marketed as “feminine hygiene.” The first oral contraceptive pill was approved in 1960. See Pregnancy, Abortion, and Midwifery and Women, Gender, and Marriage.
  • “old Phoebe’s statue”: Old Phoebe was a washwoman, and the Phoebe of the Bible was a servant of the church: “I commend unto you Phebe our sister, which is a servant of the church which is at Cenchrea” (Romans 16:1, KJV; the King James spells her name Phebe). The Greek word translated “servant” is diakonos, deacon, and she is the only woman so named in the Bible; Paul trusted her to carry his letter to Rome. Where modern translations of 1 Timothy 3:11 speak of women deacons, the King James Version has “Even so must their wives be grave, not slanderers, sober, faithful in all things.” In Greek mythology Phoebe was a Titaness, grandmother of Apollo and Artemis; the name means bright. See Phoebe, The Bible, Women, Gender, and Marriage, and Greek Mythology.
  • “Ephemeral all die at sunset”: Mayflies belong to the order Ephemeroptera, from the Greek ephemeros, “lasting a day”; the adults live from a few hours to a day or two. Aristotle wrote of a creature on the river Hypanis that lives a single day. See Death and Mortality.
  • “Coleman Bluebough, dead at the age of three”: See Coleman Bluebough.
  • “Mrs. Abigail Porter, who folded up her tent and crept silently away”: “And the night shall be filled with music, / And the cares, that infest the day, / Shall fold their tents, like the Arabs, / And as silently steal away” (Longfellow, “The Day Is Done,” 1844). See Abigail Porter.
  • “there had been thirty rounds”: Glove fights once ran long: on July 4, 1910, in Reno, Jack Johnson, the first Black heavyweight champion, knocked out Jim Jeffries, the “Great White Hope,” in the fifteenth round of a fight scheduled for forty-five. Riots broke out in some two dozen places, most of them white mobs attacking Black Americans; between 11 and 26 people were killed, among them a Black man lynched in Wheeling, West Virginia, for driving an expensive car (Wikipedia). New York’s Walker Law of 1920 capped bouts at fifteen rounds. See Society, Class, and Race and Joe Goldberg.
  • “cut down in the flower of their youth”: “He cometh forth like a flower, and is cut down: he fleeth also as a shadow, and continueth not” (Job 14:2, KJV). See The Bible and Death and Mortality.
  • “taken by the Ghostly Reaper’s sickle”: The Grim Reaper originated in 14th-century Europe, evolving from medieval personifications of death during the Black Death pandemic. Representing the inevitability of mortality, this figure is typically depicted as a skeleton in a dark robe carrying a scythe to harvest souls. It blends ancient mythologies, such as the Greek figure Cronus, with a profound, culturally pervasive fear of the unknown. See the Ghostly Reaper in the Chapter 68 resources. See Death and Mortality.
  • “The old grey mule had stood with head hanging over a fence”: See the barren mule in the Chapter 72 resources. See Horses and Carriages.
  • “under the frozen cranberry marsh”: A cranberry marsh (or bog) is a specialized wetland habitat where cranberries grow on low-running vines in acidic soil, typically in Wisconsin, Massachusetts, and other northern regions. Contrary to popular belief, they do not grow in water year-round, but are flooded in autumn for harvest, as the berries float, and in winter for frost protection.
  • “Something under the green quince”: In the US, green quince are typically under-ripe, hard, and extremely tart, often covered in a fuzzy coating that disappears as they turn golden-yellow in late fall. Primarily grown in California and imported from Chile, these fragrant fruits are available from August through December in specialty, Latin American, or Middle Eastern markets.
  • “the old Chicago detective was trying to find the proof”: England’s Act to Prevent the Destroying and Murthering of Bastard Children (1624) presumed that an unmarried mother who hid the death of her newborn had murdered it, unless she could prove “by one witness at the least” that the child was born dead; the penalty was death. It stood until 1803. In Massachusetts Hannah Piggen was reportedly the last woman hanged for concealing a birth, in 1785 (Wikipedia). Concealment of birth is still a crime in many states. See The Chicago Detective, Women, Gender, and Marriage, and Pregnancy, Abortion, and Midwifery.
  • “the flowering horse chestnut, the bloody flower”: The horse chestnut, introduced to the US from Europe in the 1700s, is a popular, large ornamental shade tree featuring showy white spring flowers, palmately compound leaves, and inedible, shiny brown nuts enclosed in spiky, green husks. Common in urban landscapes, parks, and the Midwest, these trees thrive in zones 3-7.
  • “dead robin redbreast under a ten-foot snowdrift”: See “Who killed cock robin?” and the Babes in the Wood, covered with leaves by robins, in the Chapter 72 resources. See Fairy Tales and Folklore and Birds.
  • “she might endure the birth of nothing”: “We have been with child, we have been in pain, we have as it were brought forth wind” (Isaiah 26:18, KJV). See The Bible and Pregnancy, Abortion, and Midwifery.
  • “a white feather of some far-flying Arctic bird”: To show the white feather is to show cowardice, from the cockpit, where a white feather in a gamecock’s tail was taken as the mark of a poor fighter. The feather falls for the featherweight, the golden cock. See Birds and Joe Goldberg.
