Chapter 46

← Chapter 45 · Home · Chapter 47 →

Summary

Mr. Spitzer comes to understand that Cousin Hannah had also been a secret mountain climber, perhaps the greatest ever known among ladies, of the Matterhorn, Mont Blanc, and mountains of consciousness, though she was ashamed of it and spoke of it only when dying. When she died, the room grew colder than the Arctic Alps. As her executor he takes her alpenhorn for his collection of instruments, and on the foggy beach he blows a few notes like a ghost calling his lost love. A ram steps out of the fog, and sheep follow him, and ever after lost men follow him through the grey cities. Her dying has brought him to reality and taught him the power of a dead love. He wanders the fog-bound city asking strangers whether they have seen her, and people take him for mad, until an old steeplejack lurches out of the fog and answers him in paradoxes: “I live because I am dead.” The chapter ends with Hannah’s last cry to the bright star of her love.

Characters present

Cousin Hannah · Joachim Spitzer

Concepts present

Themes: Death and Mortality · Identity and the Self · Love · Memory and the Past · Music, Sound, and Silence · Nature, the Sea, and the Cosmos

Symbols: Birds · Clocks and Watches · Fog and Mist · Horses and Carriages · Lamps, Candles, and Light · Moon and Stars · Mountains · Music and Instruments · Pearls and Jewels · Snow, Ice, and Winter · The Umbrella

Philosophy: Augustine and Christian Theology

Allusions: Astronomy · Fairy Tales and Folklore · Gambling and Playing Cards · Genesis · Greek Mythology · Judaism · Revelation and the Apocalypse · Romantic Poets · Shakespeare · The Bible · The Book of Job · Women’s Suffrage

Key passages

From the research

  • The chapter opens by portraying Cousin Hannah not merely as a suffrage leader but as a “valiant wanderer” who climbed “formidable mountains and supernumerary peaks” beyond physical realms such as mountains “greater than mountains,” rising “Alp above Alp through consciousness” even after death. This metaphor suggests her spirit transcends earthly limits, linking her struggles and love to the eternal and the sublime. Her life is framed as an ascent beyond mortal boundaries, symbolizing a quest for immortal love and freedom.
  • Mr. Spitzer, acting as Cousin Hannah’s executor, finds and appropriates her alpenhorn, a heavy musical instrument twice her height. This alpenhorn is symbolic: though it cannot literally evoke the Alps in the lowlands, it serves as a poignant emblem of her spirit and the mountains she climbed. Mr. Spitzer reflects on how music arises from chaos and how the instruments of earth are linked to the heavenly realm, though none are truly “strung in paradise.” This passage explores the tenuous relationship between art, memory, and transcendence.
  • The novel muses on how ghosts in dreams never appear naked but are always clothed in some form implying that all of life and death is a form of “mask” or “clothing.” This metaphor conveys the idea that identity, beauty, and existence are layered, elusive, and perhaps illusory. Mr. Spitzer’s own music is described as a form of elegy or aubade that cannot quite awaken the dead but hints at the dreamlike quality of life and death.
  • A deeply philosophical passage appears as Mr. Spitzer contemplates the “power of a dead beauty, a dead love,” and the “sterility which begets... all beautiful things.” He asserts that no one truly knows the present moment because it is always “freighted with the past,” suggesting that beauty and existence are ghosts of themselves, transitory and elusive. The cloud over beauty is beauty itself, so the veil of mystery remains intact. This suggests an acceptance of ambiguity and the unknowable as essential to human experience.
  • Despite her achievements, Cousin Hannah is described as being ashamed of her mountain-climbing accomplishments, preferring oblivion over fame. Mr. Spitzer reflects on how many famous people value a moment of oblivion more than lasting glory, as oblivion is paradoxically both what they flee from and what they seek. This passage reveals a tension between public success and private vulnerability, heroism and cowardice, and the human desire for both recognition and escape.
  • A haunting voice from an old steeplejack (a tall, church-like figure) speaks to Mr. Spitzer, embodying contradictions like “I live because I am dead,” “I love because I love not,” and the idea that all who have loved have died and drowned. Time is depicted as a cloud crossing a clock face that tells no time. This passage powerfully captures the theme of existence as filled with paradox, where life and death, love and loss are inseparable, and where time itself is an illusion.
  • After Cousin Hannah’s death, Mr. Spitzer wanders the fog-bound city asking strangers if they have seen her, despite being perceived as mad. This quest symbolizes the human search for meaning, connection, and remembrance in a world of loss and forgetting. It also reflects on how memory is fragmented and how one can be simultaneously lost yet followed suggesting the persistence of influence beyond death.
  • The chapter closes with Cousin Hannah’s dying cry, calling for a “bright star of my love” to find the “lightless star,” signaling the mysterious journey beyond death. The imagery of mountains resurrecting before “the last great cataclysm” and her love “going down” evokes a cosmic, cyclical view of life and death, blending mythic and personal dimensions.

Questions and observations

Reading closely

  • “Never yet had he been present at a climax.” Why does Mr. Spitzer always come before or after?
  • “The cloud upon the face of beauty was beauty itself. So never would he lift the cloud.” Why does Mr. Spitzer refuse to lift it?
  • “For that of which she should have been proud, she was ashamed.” Why would Hannah hide her greatest achievement?

Characters

  • Mr. Spitzer says Hannah “had brought him, by her dying, to reality.” What has he learned from her?
  • The men who call Hannah “a charlatan, a mere poseur, a mountebank” forget “her motive which had been her love.” Does knowing her motive change her deeds?
  • Who is the steeplejack, “tall as a church steeple,” who “fell the night she fell”?

Connections

  • In Chapter 44 Hannah’s love was lost in the mountains. How does knowing she was a great climber change that story?
  • Mr. Spitzer is “like an obsessed census-taker” who always finds “one missing,” as in Chapter 42. Who is the missing one now?
  • The steeplejack says, “All who have loved have drowned.” Where else in the novel do lovers drown?

Reflection

  • “It was oblivion from which they had fled, and yet it was oblivion toward which they fled.” Why might the famous long for oblivion?
  • “For who had ever known the present moment?” Is the present always freighted with the past?
  • Is a great deed lessened if no one remembers it?

Research: Characters

Cousin Hannah

  • A complex figure; a suffragette, a mountain climber, a symbol of liberation and love’s endurance, “perhaps the greatest mountain-climber unknown to history, surely the greatest ever known among ladies.” She is proud yet ashamed of her achievements, embodying contradictions of strength and vulnerability. Her death is portrayed almost mythically, with imagery of frost, mountains, and alpenhorns signaling her passage to another realm.

Mr. Spitzer

  • Witness and executor of Cousin Hannah’s estate, an old musician who is deeply introspective and symbolic. He is both observer and participant, grappling with loss, memory, and the meaning of life and death. His inquiries after Hannah’s death reveal his obsession and his quest for understanding the mysteries she embodied.

The Steeplejack

  • A steeple jack is a skilled tradesperson who works at great heights, primarily on tall structures like church steeples, chimneys, and towers, to perform repairs, maintenance, or construction. The profession has historical roots in the maintenance of ecclesiastical buildings.
  • This “old steeple-headed steeplejack or steeple jill” is the only one who remembers Hannah and says “that she was beautiful.”

Research: Themes

Death and Immortality

See: Death and Mortality

  • Cousin Hannah’s death is described with vivid cold and frozen imagery, suggesting a transition into an eternal, timeless state, but one that still holds mystery and significance. There is an ongoing meditation on what it means to die and what survives beyond death, particularly love and memory.

Love Beyond Mortality

See: Death and Mortality · Love

  • Hannah’s message is that love transcends mortal bounds, aiming for an immortal love. This idea recurs as Mr. Spitzer contemplates the power and persistence of love even after death, and the paradox that those who have loved have also died, and vice versa.

The Mountain as a Symbol

See: Nature, the Sea, and the Cosmos

  • Mountains symbolize challenges, spiritual ascension, and the unknown. Cousin Hannah is portrayed as an unparalleled mountain climber not just of physical peaks like the Matterhorn or Mont Blanc, but of metaphorical mountains of consciousness and existence.

Memory and Oblivion

See: Memory and the Past

  • The chapter addresses how history, fame, and memory are fleeting. Cousin Hannah, despite her great achievements, is largely forgotten by the world, illustrating the tension between individual legacy and collective memory.

Music and Silence

See: Music, Sound, and Silence

  • Mr. Spitzer, a musician, reflects on music as a metaphor for life and death, where silence and sound intermingle. Music arises from chaos and holds a kind of ephemeral power, much like life itself.

Identity and Masks

See: Identity and the Self

  • The motif of masks and clothing in dreams suggests that identity is always layered, never fully naked or transparent. Ghosts and memories are always clothed in some form, and this applies to living beings as well.

Research: Symbols and Imagery

Alpenhorn

See: Music and Instruments

  • Represents a call to lost love and memory; a connection to the mountains and the past. Its presence in a flat coastal landscape symbolizes the displacement of memory and the difficulty of preserving legacy in an unresponsive world.

Mountains and Snow

See: Snow, Ice, and Winter · Mountains

  • Mountains stand for the ultimate challenges and heights of spirit and consciousness. Snow and ice symbolize purity, death, and timelessness, as well as the coldness and isolation that often accompany great achievements or sacrifices.

The Dead Moon

See: Moon and Stars

  • A recurring symbol of deathless love and the eternal, especially in a world where stars have faded or fallen. It suggests a cosmic, timeless love that persists beyond human life.

Music and Bells

See: Music and Instruments

  • Music, especially the unplayed or unheard music, represents the ineffable aspects of life and death. Bells ringing without clear cause evoke mystery, transition, and the presence of the unseen.

Fog and Darkness

See: Fog and Mist · Lamps, Candles, and Light

  • Fog represents uncertainty, loss, and the blurring of reality and memory. The drifting fog and shadows evoke the liminal space between life and death and the difficulty of grasping truth.

Research: Resources

  • “that Troubadour with her flaming message”: See Jaufré Rudel and the troubadours in the Chapter 40 resources and the Troubadour’s love for the dead love in the Chapter 44 resources.
  • “she would have won her laurels and her spurs”: A squire won his spurs when he was knighted for valor. At Crécy in 1346 Edward III is said to have refused to send help to his son the Black Prince: “let the boy win his spurs” (Froissart, Chronicles).
  • “the mountains which were greater than mountains”: See Mountains.
  • “that great Matterhorn”: Matterhorn is a mountain of the Alps on the border between Italy and Switzerland. Edward Whymper’s party first climbed it in 1865, and four of the seven died on the descent.
  • “Mt. Rosa”: Monte Rosa is a massif of the Pennine Alps on the Swiss-Italian border. Its Dufourspitze is the highest summit in Switzerland.
  • “Mt. Blanc, Moensch”: Mt. Blanc is the highest mountain in the Alps. Moensch, or Monch, is a mountain in the Bernese Alps. See Mont Blanc in the Chapter 44 resources.
  • “Wetterhorn”: Wetterhorn is a peak in the Swiss Alps. Alfred Wills’s ascent in 1854 is often taken as the start of the golden age of alpinism.
  • “rising Alp above Alp”: “Hills peep o’er hills, and Alps on Alps arise!” (Alexander Pope, An Essay on Criticism, 1711).
  • “the same flowers may be found, white on white”: The same Arctic-alpine plants, such as mountain avens and moss campion, grow both in the far north and on the high Alps, left behind on the mountaintops when the Ice Age glaciers withdrew. See Snow, Ice, and Winter.
  • “like the asphodel in fields of paradise”: See the meadow of asphodel in the Chapter 42 resources. See Greek Mythology.
  • “the mirrors were rheumed with frost”: In Jewish mourning, and in many Victorian houses, the mirrors were covered after a death. See Judaism.
  • “to play the ranz des vaches”: The ranz des vaches is the call of the Swiss herdsmen to their cattle. Rousseau wrote that it was forbidden to sing it near Swiss soldiers in foreign service, since it made them so homesick that they deserted or died (Dictionnaire de musique, 1768). Rossini set it in the overture to William Tell (1829). See Music and Instruments.
  • “the alpenglow”: Alpenglow is the rosy light on high peaks just after sunset or before sunrise, when the valleys are already in shadow. See Mountains.
  • “the smuggler Charon’s boat”: Charon ferries the dead across the Styx for the coin placed in the mouth of the dead. See Greek Mythology.
  • “like statues upholding the rain-falling roofs”: Statues of women that hold up a roof are caryatids, as on the Porch of the Maidens of the Erechtheion in Athens.
  • “all those lutes played by the angels of heaven”: Painters gave heaven the instruments of earth, as in the music-making angels of Fra Angelico’s Linaioli Triptych (1433). See Music and Instruments.
  • “the enormous shadow of his black cape on the soughing fog”: A walker’s shadow thrown huge upon mist or fog, often ringed with a halo, is the Brocken spectre, named for the Harz mountain where it was first described. Coleridge’s rustic “Nor knows he makes the shadow he pursues!” (“Constancy to an Ideal Object,” 1828). See Fog and Mist and Romantic Poets.
  • “ghosts have seldom or never appeared naked in men’s dreams”: Hamlet’s father appears “in complete steel” on the battlements and later “in his habit as he lived” (Hamlet 1.4, 3.4). See Shakespeare.
  • “The great couturier has snipped his last thread.”: Atropos, the third of the Fates, cuts the thread of life. See Greek Mythology.
  • “his aubade for the evening star”: Aubade is a morning love song or song/poem about lovers separating at dawn. John Donne’s “The Sun Rising” scolds the dawn: “Busy old fool, unruly sun” (1633).
    • Venus is both the morning star and the evening star, called Phosphorus and Hesperus by the Greeks. Gottlob Frege used the two names, one object with two senses, in “On Sense and Reference” (1892). See Astronomy.
  • “the silver sheep’s bell which had once rung to the lost sheep”: “What man of you, having an hundred sheep, if he lose one of them, doth not leave the ninety and nine in the wilderness, and go after that which is lost, until he find it?” (Luke 15:4). See The Bible.
  • “lost like the Dog star”: Sirius, the Dog Star, rises with the sun in late summer, the dog days. See “before the day of the dog,” below. See Moon and Stars.
  • “a ram had stepped out of the fog”: “And Abraham lifted up his eyes, and looked, and behold behind him a ram caught in a thicket by his horns” (Genesis 22:13). See Genesis.
  • “he had been followed by men in the grey cities”: Like the Pied Piper, the musician is followed first by beasts and then by men. See the Chapter 6 resources. See Fairy Tales and Folklore.
  • “For who had ever known the present moment?”: Augustine found that the present has no extent: “the present hath no space” (Confessions 11.15, trans. E. B. Pusey, 1838). See Augustine and Christian Theology.
  • “The cloud upon the face of beauty was beauty itself.”: The fourteenth-century Cloud of Unknowing teaches that God is known not by thought but by love, through a cloud that is never lifted in this life: “By love may He be gotten and holden; but by thought never” (chapter 6).
  • “If he knew not her omega, then how did he know her alpha?”: “I am Alpha and Omega, the beginning and the ending, saith the Lord” (Revelation 1:8). See Revelation and the Apocalypse.
  • “the age of Hugh De Capet”: Hugh Capet was King of the Franks from 987 to 996 and founded the Capetian dynasty.
  • “remembered in no stud book of mountain-climbing”: The General Stud Book, begun by James Weatherby in 1791, records the pedigree of every English thoroughbred. See Horses and Carriages.
  • “some old Roman emperor who had minted too many coins”: In the third century, emperors paying their armies debased the coinage until the silver “antoninianus” held less than five percent silver.
  • “by no winged horse’s head or harp”: The silver coins of Corinth bore Pegasus, the winged horse, and Irish coins the harp. See Greek Mythology.
  • “Alpine holy grass”: Holy grass, sweet with the scent of vanilla, was strewn before church doors on saints’ days in northern Europe.
  • “surely the greatest ever known among ladies”: Real suffragists climbed too. Annie Smith Peck made the first ascent of Huascarán’s north peak in 1908 and planted a “VOTES FOR WOMEN” flag on Coropuna in Peru in 1911. Fanny Bullock Workman of Massachusetts was photographed in the Karakoram about 1912 holding a newspaper headed “Votes for Women.” See Women’s Suffrage and Mountains.
  • “Oblivion was ever at the heart of fame.”: “But the iniquity of oblivion blindly scattereth her poppy, and deals with the memory of men without distinction to merit of perpetuity” (Thomas Browne, Hydriotaphia, or Urn-Burial, 1658, chapter 5).
  • “her granite was but a façade”: See Woolf’s “granite-like solidity” in the Chapter 44 resources.
  • “She was like a dead planet wandering.”: Planet comes from the Greek planētēs, wanderer, for the stars that moved among the fixed stars. See Astronomy.
  • “the croakings of frogs”: The chorus of Aristophanes’s The Frogs (405 BC) sings “Brekekekex koax koax.”
  • “before the day of the dog”: The Day of the Dog is a 1904 comic novel by George Barr McCutcheon, in which a Chicago lawyer, Crosby, sent to get the widow Mrs. Delancy to sign estate papers, is trapped with her in a barn by a bulldog named Swallow, and a romance follows. McCutcheon also wrote Brewster’s Millions (1902), which has been filmed many times.
    • “The cat will mew, and dog will have his day” (Hamlet 5.1). The dog days of late summer are named for Sirius, the Dog Star, which appears earlier in this chapter. See Shakespeare.
  • “I am thine only love”: The phrase suggests a deep, exclusive bond or connection, likely representing the intense and often elusive nature of love in the novel. It could be interpreted as the voice of love itself speaking to a beloved, emphasizing that despite all the illusions, losses, and fragmented experiences of life, there remains one true and abiding love that transcends time and circumstance.
    • The voice is a sand grain: “Because of me there grew this great pearl.” A natural pearl grows when an oyster coats an irritant with nacre, more often a parasite than a grain of sand. See Pearls and Jewels.
  • “apples of Hesperides”: The golden apples of the Hesperides, guarded by a dragon at the edge of the world, were Heracles’s eleventh labor. See Greek Mythology.
  • “like the light-winged cranes”: Pliny wrote that cranes “ballast themselves with coarse sand” before crossing the Black Sea, choose a leader, and post sentinels that each hold “a little stone in its claw” (Natural History 10.30, trans. John Bostock and H. T. Riley, 1855). See Birds.
  • “flying like a Chinaman’s cue”: The queue, a long braid, was forced on Han Chinese men by the Qing dynasty from 1645 as a sign of submission. “Chinaman” is now considered a slur.
  • “go back for a lost leader”: “Just for a handful of silver he left us” (Robert Browning, “The Lost Leader,” 1845).
  • “Have you seen my lady—or my lord?”: “I will rise now, and go about the city in the streets, and in the broad ways I will seek him whom my soul loveth… The watchmen that go about the city found me: to whom I said, Saw ye him whom my soul loveth?” (Song of Solomon 3:2-3). See The Bible.
  • “This is but the shadow of a man.”: “For we are but of yesterday, and know nothing, because our days upon earth are a shadow” (Job 8:9). See The Book of Job.
  • “for time passes not, and only man passes”: See Austin Dobson’s “Time goes, you say? Ah no! / Alas, Time stays, we go” in the Chapter 12 resources.
  • “an old steeple-headed steeplejack”: “Steeple jill” is Young’s joke on Jack and Jill.
  • “I fell when stars fell from the clouds”: On the night of November 12-13, 1833, the Leonid meteor storm filled the American sky with tens of thousands of shooting stars, and it was long remembered as “the night the stars fell.” See Astronomy.
  • “ladies scudding under white umbrellas”: See the white umbrellas of the spa in the Chapter 39 resources. See The Umbrella.
  • “dead as the balloonist shrouded in the garden”: See Sophie Blanchard, who died when her balloon caught fire over Paris, in the Chapter 42 resources.
  • “There is a negress in the belfry.”: The phrase plays on “bats in the belfry.” “Negress” is now considered offensive.
  • “I live because I am dead”: The steeplejack’s line echoes the mystics:
    • Teresa of Ávila: “Vivo sin vivir en mí, / y tan alta vida espero, / que muero porque no muero,” “I live without living in myself, and I hope for so high a life that I die because I do not die.”
  • “the surveyor with his plummet line”: “The Lord stood upon a wall made by a plumbline, with a plumbline in his hand” (Amos 7:7). See The Bible.
  • “Some were killed by a rain drop”: The steeplejack’s litany recalls Richard II: “let us sit upon the ground / And tell sad stories of the death of kings: / How some have been depos’d; some slain in war” (3.2). See the Chapter 3 resources. See Shakespeare.
  • “Eternity was but a moment.”: “To see a World in a Grain of Sand, / And a Heaven in a Wild Flower, / Hold Infinity in the palm of your hand, / And Eternity in an hour” (William Blake, “Auguries of Innocence,” about 1803). See Romantic Poets.
  • “The great steeplechase is over.”: The first steeplechase was run in Ireland in 1752, from the church steeple at Buttevant to the steeple at Doneraile, by Cornelius O’Callaghan and Edmund Blake. Here it is run by the clock’s “tall jockey” and “short jockey.” See Horses and Carriages and Clocks and Watches.
  • “much like the fly in the spider’s web”: “‘Will you walk into my parlour?’ said the Spider to the Fly” (Mary Howitt, “The Spider and the Fly,” 1829).
  • “All was not over so long as there was one card out”: See the ace of spades and the ace of hearts in the Chapter 42 resources. See Gambling and Playing Cards.
  • “he would have had his twin at his last hour”: To see one’s double was an omen of death. Shelley told of meeting his double weeks before he drowned in 1822.
  • “Ah, bright star of my love”: This may refer to John Keats’s sonnet “Bright star, would I were stedfast as thou art” (1819). See Romantic Poets.

Vocabulary

Acme
The highest point of something; the peak.
Alpenglow
The rosy light on high peaks just after sunset or before sunrise.
Alpenhorn
A long wooden horn of the Alps.
Ambivalence
Mixed or contradictory feelings.

To find out for certain.

A lily-like flower that, in Greek myth, covers the meadows of the underworld where ordinary souls go after death.

Having to do with the stars.

Heavy material, such as stones, carried low in a ship to keep it steady.

Crusted with barnacles, small shelled sea creatures that cling to rocks, pilings, and the hulls of ships.

Fathering; producing offspring.

A bell tower, or the room in a tower where the bells hang.

A soldier in the Crusades, the Christian military campaigns to take the Holy Land, fought between 1096 and 1291.

A man who has been castrated. Eunuchs were employed for centuries to guard harems and to serve as officials in royal courts in the Middle East, China, and Byzantium. See The eunuch (Ch 35).

A plucked string instrument with a rounded back shaped like half a pear, popular in Europe from the Middle Ages through the 1700s.

Chapter 37

← Chapter 36 · Home · Chapter 38 →

Content note: Vera’s mother, Catherine Cartwheel, is addicted to opium.

Summary

Vera describes the heaven Catherine expects, as disordered as this world: drifting mirrors, ceilings that become floors, clocks striking inept hours. Catherine has always said that order is “a mad man’s dream,” and that Mr. Spitzer, “wishing to be agreeable, had made a false report as to what might be upon the other side.” Drugged and nearly inert, she cannot tell life from death, and asks who the dreamer is. She sees the reversals of dream: man becoming woman, God become dog, trees with their roots in the sky. Mr. Spitzer insists that Hannah is dead and buried, gone where there is no consciousness and no memory, but Catherine cannot admit her extinction. What she fears is a grey land where none makes reply, and she stays horizontal on her mother-of-pearl boat bed so as not to take that step. She recalls Hannah’s adventures in the harems, unveiling her bearded face to a sheik who went mad, and bowing to a sheik who proved to be a beautiful woman. The riderless horse has already come, and Hannah will not return.

Characters present

Catherine Cartwheel · Joachim Spitzer · Cousin Hannah · Vera Cartwheel · Peron Spitzer · The Black Coachman

Concepts present

Themes: Death and Mortality · Dreams and Imagination · Fate and Chance · Fear and Courage · Identity and the Self · Illusion and Reality · Memory and the Past · Order, Chaos, and Discipline · Society, Class, and Race · Women, Gender, and Marriage

Symbols: Angels, Devils, and Myth · Birds · Butterflies and Moths · Clouds and Storms · Eyes and Blindness · Fog and Mist · Horses and Carriages · Mirrors and Reflections · Roses and Flowers · Snow, Ice, and Winter · The Sea and Water

Philosophy: Aristotle · Astrology, Alchemy, and Esoterica · Descartes and Dualism · Empiricism (Locke, Berkeley, Hume) · Epicureanism · Existentialism · Freud and Jung · Hinduism · Nietzsche · Plato and Platonism · Pythagoras and the Music of the Spheres · Schopenhauer · Stoicism · Taoism and Zhuangzi · Time, Physics, and Chaos Theory · Wittgenstein

Allusions: Alice in Wonderland · American Writers · Astronomy · Dante · Don Quixote · Edgar Allan Poe · Gambling and Playing Cards · Genesis · Greek Mythology · Romantic Poets · Shakespeare · Suicide in History and Literature · The Bible · The Book of Job · The History of Opium

Key passages

From the research

  • The chapter opens with a surreal vision of a world where mirrors drift, the ceiling becomes a fluid floor, clocks strike inept hours, and dolphins bark unusually. This sets up the motif of a “mistaken dream” with no clear boundaries between heaven and hell, life and death. The question “But who was the dreamer?” introduces the existential uncertainty that pervades the chapter.
  • Vera recounts a discussion with her mother, Catherine, and Mr. Spitzer about the nature of order and chaos. Her mother insists that “Order… was a mad man’s dream,” a “suicidal plan omitting the irrational elements,” emphasizing the complexity and irrationality of life and the universe. This passage challenges the human desire for simple, orderly explanations.
  • Catherine is portrayed as someone living under the “pervasive influence of opium,” caught in a half-conscious dream state where time is an illusion. For Catherine, death is not an end but an “immeasurable extension” of this dream, blending life and death indistinguishably. Catherine’s inability or refusal to awaken to this knowledge symbolizes human denial of mortality and oblivion.
  • The chapter describes numerous surreal reversals highlighting the instability of identity and perception. This underscores the theme that nothing is fixed or certain, not even one’s own self or reality.
  • Cousin Hannah, a strong suffrage figure, is presented as having passed beyond death in a way Catherine cannot accept. Her adventures contrast with Catherine’s passive existence. Hannah’s death is final and unescapable, symbolizing the inevitability of mortality despite human pride and strength.
  • Catherine fears complete extinction, that “land of infinite greyness,” without memory, ego, or voice. This fear keeps her “horizontal,” an invalid clinging to life’s illusions rather than facing the void. This passage poignantly captures human dread of nothingness and the unknown beyond death.
  • The chapter closes with the recognition that no matter Catherine’s plotting or longing, Cousin Hannah will not return. Death has “throttled her,” and the echoes of life and struggle fade into silence. Mr. Spitzer’s metaphor of hearing silence after the last requiem symbolizes acceptance of death’s ultimate finality.

Questions and observations

Reading closely

  • Catherine asks who the dreamer is, “astonished that she was not the dreamer.” Who dreams her?
  • “In every lie was a grain of horrible truth—and in every truth was a beautiful lie.” Which kind does Mr. Spitzer tell?
  • Catherine stays “horizontal” to avoid one step. What step is it?

Characters

  • Mr. Spitzer was “that mourner who had felt no grief, no grief but his lack of grief.” Is that a kind of grief?
  • Why does Catherine plan “a future card game” with the dead?
  • One sheik went mad at Hannah’s bearded face, and another proved to be “a beautiful lady.” What do the two stories say about disguise?

Connections

  • In Chapter 34 Catherine was married by a St. Bernard who spoke church Latin. Here “God was dog,” and birds speak “ecclesiastical Latin.” What links them?
  • The riderless horse first came through the window on the day Hannah died, in Chapter 32. Why does it return here?
  • In Chapter 35 Mr. Spitzer called Hannah a card cheat. Here she is “one whose last card long ago was played.” Who won the game?

Reflection

  • Is order “a mad man’s dream”?
  • If life was always a dream, “how should death be different from life”?
  • Can a person be “her own dark lover”?

Research: Characters

Catherine Cartwheel

  • Central figure whose fragmented consciousness and philosophical musings drive much of the chapter.
  • She is an invalid, sedated with opium, caught between life and death, dreaming yet partially aware.
  • She embodies the existential struggle with meaning, identity, and the fear of oblivion.
  • She is “this horizontal invalid upon her mother-of-pearl boat bed.”
  • Her opinions, “even as to the simplest matters such as whether it was night or day,” “were always divided.”
  • “How many years since she had seen the sea which she could have seen at any time if she had ever allowed the shutters to be opened?”
  • “She would be crazed by dreams she had not dreamed.”

Mr. Spitzer

  • A morose figure who provides a skeptical or pessimistic counterpoint.
  • He lies and deceives but also embodies an anguished search for truth.
  • His reflections on death and memory contribute to the chapter’s philosophical depth.
  • “Mr. Spitzer, wishing to be agreeable, had made a false report as to what might be upon the other side.”
  • He longs for “some single point of view which would be at all times constant and unchanging.”
  • At Hannah’s burial he was “that mourner who had felt no grief, no grief but his lack of grief.”
  • He plucks “at his dead ear,” and “heard the silence.”

Cousin Hannah

  • A symbol of strength and defiance in the face of mortality.
  • Her story is a narrative of resistance, a woman who cannot be possessed or ruled.
  • Her death and burial represent the finality Catherine tries to avoid accepting.
  • She is “this daughter of the codfish aristocracy, her silver helmet gleaming, her scimitar uplifted like a new moon.”
  • “Death had been, at last, her bridegroom.”
  • Mr. Spitzer thought “she had been her own dark lover.”
  • She unveiled her “great, gaunt, bearded face” to a sheik who “had gone stark, staring mad,” and bowed to another sheik who was “a beautiful lady with large liquid eyes.”

Peron Spitzer

  • “Peron had been right—and Joachim had been wrong.”
  • Hannah is “gone where poker-faced Peron was.”

The Black Coachman

  • Catherine sees “perhaps the black coachman, the diffused radiance of the carriage lamps in the fog.”
  • No one should see Hannah again, “not even when the black coachman came, and he was dead.”

Research: Themes

Reality versus Dream, Illusion versus Truth

See: Illusion and Reality · Dreams and Imagination

  • The chapter questions what is real and what is dream, emphasizing the fluidity and uncertainty between the two.
  • Catherine and others seem trapped in an ongoing dream where time and space lose meaning.
  • The idea that life itself may be a mistake or dream without end is prominent, and Catherine sees death as an immeasurable extension of this dream.

Death and Life: Blurred Boundaries

See: Death and Mortality

  • The chapter repeatedly blurs the line between living and dead; the living are those who have already died, and the dead are still living in some form.
  • For Catherine, death is not a clear-cut event but an ongoing state or transformation, sometimes portrayed as madness or a mountebank (a deceiver). “Death was madness. Madness ruled supreme.”
  • Catherine fears oblivion, the total extinction of self, and clings to life despite its illusions.

Identity and Transformation

See: Identity and the Self

  • Identity is unstable and mutable, with images of people changing genders, faces, or even species. “One saw that God was dog.”
  • This theme questions the essence of self, suggesting that we might be composites of many selves or none at all.
  • The recurring motif of masks, doubles, and shifting forms highlights the fracturing or multiplicity of identity.

Memory and Oblivion

See: Memory and the Past

  • Catherine fears the loss of memory and self-awareness.
  • There is a contemplation of a “land of infinite greyness” where nothing remains: no memory, image, or ego.
  • This fear underlies her refusal to fully surrender to death or oblivion.

Order and Chance

See: Order, Chaos, and Discipline · Fate and Chance

  • “Order, had she not always said, was a mad man’s dream, the maddest dream of all.”
  • She asks “how should we live except by accident, for were we not already dead.”
  • The music shakes “the enamelled heavens and the earth like a dice box,” and she sees “stars marked like dice.”

Feminine Power and Resistance

See: Women, Gender, and Marriage · Fear and Courage

  • Cousin Hannah, a suffrage captain, symbolizes strength, resistance, and an indomitable spirit.
  • Her death and burial contrast with her bold life, and her story reflects the struggle for identity and agency beyond traditional roles.
  • Cousin Hannah’s adventures in exotic lands and her defiance of powerful men underscore themes of female empowerment and autonomy.

Research: Symbols and Imagery

Mirrors and Reversals

See: Mirrors and Reflections

  • The recurring image of mirrored realities (ceiling as floor, trees growing upside down) suggests the instability of perception and reality.

Sea and Waves

See: The Sea and Water

  • The sea is a motif for transformation, fluidity, and the unconscious.

Eyes and Faces

See: Eyes and Blindness

  • Eyes symbolize perception and identity; the theme of masks and hidden skulls suggests mortality beneath appearances.

Fog and Clouds

See: Fog and Mist · Clouds and Storms

  • These represent uncertainty, the unknown, and the boundary between states of being.

Black Snow / Sable Snow

See: Snow, Ice, and Winter

  • Symbolizes corruption, darkness, and the inversion of purity.

The Cross and Rose

See: Roses and Flowers · Angels, Devils, and Myth

  • Symbolize transformation and the intertwining of suffering and beauty, life and death.

The Hawk and Birds

See: Birds

  • Represent death, predation, and perhaps the inevitability of mortality. “Her head was eaten by great birds. Great birds had plucked out her eyes.”

The Black Coachman

See: Horses and Carriages

  • A symbol of death or transition. In Chapter 14 Catherine likens the coachman to “her dead consciousness fantastically dreaming.”

The Riderless Horse and Conch Trumpet

See: Horses and Carriages

  • Symbolize death’s arrival and the end of an era or life. The horse comes “to signify that the great postilion was dead.”

Cards and Dice

See: Gambling and Playing Cards

  • The snow falls “black as the ace of spades.”
  • The dead dice-throwers rattle “old bones under dimmed street lamps, and their skulls were their dice cups.”
  • Hannah is “one whose last card long ago was played.”

Research: Resources

  • “or there should be these reversals”: Aristotle names reversal (peripeteia) and recognition as the turning points of tragedy (Poetics 11). Baudrillard’s Principle of Reversal examines how oppositions and differences can be overturned, leading to new forms of understanding and meaning (Jean Baudrillard, Symbolic Exchange and Death, 1976). Vera’s “his night was his day” passage is in Chapter 61. See the Chapter 61 resources. Young’s reversals include “there should be these somersaultings as when the ceiling was the mirroring floor, trees of enormous crystal growing with their roots in the clouded sky, their branches under the earth,” and “Love might wear the face of death, the grinning skull, as death might wear the face of love.” See Aristotle.
    • Aristotle calls the reversal peripeteia and the recognition anagnorisis, and finds them together in Oedipus (Poetics 11).
  • “this mistaken earth which was perhaps its counter-earth”: The Pythagorean Philolaus set a counter-earth, the Antichthon, beyond the Earth, always hidden from it, to bring the heavenly bodies to ten (Aristotle, On the Heavens 2.13). See Pythagoras and the Music of the Spheres and Aristotle.
  • “But who was the dreamer”: “You’re only a sort of thing in his dream!” Tweedledee tells Alice of the sleeping Red King (Lewis Carroll, Through the Looking-Glass, 1871). See Alice in Wonderland.
    • Zhuangzi dreamed he was a butterfly and woke not knowing “whether I am now a butterfly, dreaming I am a man” (Chuang Tzŭ, trans. Herbert A. Giles, 1889). See Taoism and Zhuangzi.
  • “Was he a domino or a man”: A domino is a masquerade cloak worn with a half mask.
  • “no silent music like the music of the spheres”: See the Chapter 36 resources and Pythagoras and the Music of the Spheres.
  • “For each face hid the grinning skull”: In Hans Holbein’s The Ambassadors (1533) a stretched skull lies across the floor, seen whole only from the side, a memento mori hidden in the picture. See Death and Mortality.
  • “How should she know when she had crossed the invisible line of demarcation”: Descartes’ dream argument: He used the experience of dreaming to question the certainty of our perceptions and beliefs. He argued that if we cannot definitively distinguish between waking and dreaming, then our sensory experiences, which are the foundation of our knowledge, might be illusions. There is philosophical skepticism because the possibility of dreams may be genuine or a fabrication. It leads one to question the validity of knowledge of the external world. Freud believed dreams are a symbolic representation of unconscious thoughts and desires. Jung expanded on Freud’s ideas that dreams can also reveal universal, archetypal patterns in the human psyche. Some theories suggest dreams are a natural byproduct of the brain’s activity during sleep, possibly involving memory consolidation, emotional processing, or the clearing out of mental clutter. Zhuangzi asked the same question when he woke from dreaming he was a butterfly; see the Chapter 8 resources. See Descartes and Dualism and Freud and Jung.
    • “There are no certain indications by which we may clearly distinguish wakefulness from sleep” (René Descartes, Meditations on First Philosophy 1, 1641, trans. Elizabeth S. Haldane, 1911).
  • “for there was no time. There was the illusion of time”: Time, perception versus reality, distorted time perception, and time as a mental construct is described as an emergent property in physics. Einstein wrote that “the distinction between past, present and future is only a stubbornly persistent illusion” (Albert Einstein, letter to the family of Michele Besso, March 21, 1955). Carlo Rovelli proposes that time is not a fundamental aspect of reality, but rather an emergent phenomenon (Carlo Rovelli, The Order of Time, Riverhead Books, 2018). He suggests that time may be a complex network of events, and our perception of its flow is a projection onto this network. See Time, Physics, and Chaos Theory.
  • “There would be suddenly a whirling windmill”: The whirling windmill may recall the windmills that Don Quixote takes for giants (Cervantes, Don Quixote 1.8, 1605). See Don Quixote.
  • “How should death be different from life, my mother asked”: Life as a state of experience and potential: Socrates thought death might be a dreamless sleep or passage to another realm where one can converse with the dead. Existentialism believes death is an inevitable aspect of human existence and that it can lead to a heightened sense of self-awareness and responsibility. Epicureanism argues death cannot harm a person, as it’s either not yet experienced (while alive) or not experienced at all (once dead). Death is defined as the loss of the capacity to engage in vital activities and the cessation of consciousness. Wittgenstein wrote that death is not an event in life, for we do not live to experience it (Tractatus Logico-Philosophicus 6.4311). Schopenhauer believed that understanding death as the ultimate end of life can provide a perspective on the meaning of life itself. Freud thought the life instinct (Eros) and the death instinct (Thanatos) are fundamental forces in human behavior. See Plato and Platonism, Existentialism, Epicureanism, Wittgenstein, Schopenhauer, and Freud and Jung.
    • “Death, therefore, the most awful of evils, is nothing to us, seeing that, when we are, death is not come, and, when death is come, we are not” (Epicurus, Letter to Menoeceus, trans. Robert Drew Hicks, 1925).
    • “Death is not an event of life. Death is not lived through” (Ludwig Wittgenstein, Tractatus Logico-Philosophicus 6.4311, trans. C. K. Ogden, 1922).
    • Freud wrote of the death drive in Beyond the Pleasure Principle (1920). The name Thanatos came from his followers.
  • “Death was this dream’s immeasurable extension”: The meaning of life in relation to death: Stoicism emphasized that facing death can lead to a deeper understanding of life’s meaning and the ephemeral nature of earthly possessions. Nietzsche used the thought experiment of eternal return (recurrence) to encourage individuals to examine the meaning and value of their lives, given the possibility of living them again and again. See Stoicism and Nietzsche.
    • Nietzsche’s demon asks, “This life as thou livest it at present, and hast lived it, thou must live it once more, and also innumerable times” (Friedrich Nietzsche, The Joyful Wisdom 341, 1882, trans. Thomas Common, 1910).
  • “One had laughed one’s self to death”: The Stoic Chrysippus is said to have died laughing at a donkey eating his figs (Diogenes Laertius, Lives of the Eminent Philosophers 7.185). See Stoicism.
  • “Death was a mountebank”: Mountebank is a person who deceives others, especially in order to trick them out of their money.
    • The word comes from the Italian montimbanco, one who mounts a bench to sell quack remedies.
  • “her face darkening and contorted like the face of a drowning woman”: Opium slows breathing. Signs of an overdose include slow or stopped breathing, blue or purple lips and face, and pinpoint pupils. See The History of Opium.
  • “aware of the earth which, viewed from another celestial body, would seem like a dead moon”: Seen from the Moon, the Earth goes through phases, full when the Moon is new. See Astronomy.
  • “to death’s-head moths”: The death’s-head hawkmoth, Acherontia atropos, bears a skull on its thorax and is named for the Fate who cuts the thread of life. See Butterflies and Moths.
  • “which shook the enamelled heavens and the earth like a dice box”: Einstein wrote to Max Born on December 4, 1926, that he was convinced God does not throw dice. See Time, Physics, and Chaos Theory.
  • “the dream which had dreamed the dreamer”: “With relief, with humiliation, with terror, he understood that he too was a mere appearance, dreamt by another” (Jorge Luis Borges, “The Circular Ruins,” 1940, trans. James E. Irby, in Labyrinths, 1962).
  • “as man became woman with her heaving breasts”: Gender as a social construct refers to the socially created roles, behaviors, expressions, and identities associated with being a woman, man, boy, or girl. It’s not inherently determined by biology, but rather shaped by cultural norms, societal expectations, and historical contexts. This means gender is not fixed and can vary across cultures and time. In short, it is not a biological reality: it is socially created, varies across cultures, is dynamic and fluid, and is distinct from biological sex. Philosophical thought on gender goes back to ancient Greece, where Pythagoras’s table of opposites set male against female (Aristotle, Metaphysics 1.5) and Plato argued that women could be guardians (Republic 5). Later came John Locke, Jean-Jacques Rousseau, Judith Sargent Murray (“On the Equality of the Sexes,” 1790), and Mary Wollstonecraft (A Vindication of the Rights of Woman, 1792). The chapter and novel present gender as a fluid and changeable construct rather than a rigid, innate fact, using metaphorical and dreamlike language to question fixed dichotomies between male and female, self and other, life and death. See Women, Gender, and Marriage, Plato and Platonism, Aristotle, and Empiricism (Locke, Berkeley, Hume).
    • “One is not born, but rather becomes, a woman” (Simone de Beauvoir, The Second Sex, 1949, trans. H. M. Parshley, 1953).
  • “one’s father who gave birth to the dead child”: Zeus bore Athena from his head and Dionysus from his thigh. See Greek Mythology.
  • “seeing that he was a stag”: Actaeon, who saw Diana bathing, was turned into a stag and torn apart by his own hounds (Ovid, Metamorphoses 3). See Greek Mythology.
  • “trees of enormous crystal growing with their roots in the clouded sky”: The Bhagavad Gita (15.1) speaks of an eternal fig tree, the ashvattha, with its roots above and its branches below. See Hinduism.
  • “For the living were those who had already died, and the dead were the living”: Heraclitus: “Mortals are immortals and immortals are mortals, the one living the others’ death and dying the others’ life.” See Heraclitus and Flux.
  • “this daughter of the codfish aristocracy”: The codfish aristocracy were New England families grown rich on the cod fishery. The Sacred Cod, a carved wooden fish, has hung in the Massachusetts State House since the eighteenth century.
  • “the footless messengers”: Birds of paradise were believed to have no feet and never to land, because their skins reached Europe with the feet cut off. Linnaeus named the greater bird of paradise Paradisaea apoda, “footless,” in 1758. See Birds.
  • “birds who could speak ecclesiastical Latin”: Ecclesiastical Latin was developed to discuss Christian thought.
    • In Chapter 34 Catherine was married by a St. Bernard who spoke church Latin. See the Chapter 34 resources.
  • “the floor of the Lost Atlantis”: Atlantis can be a metaphor for something that is no longer attainable. It is a fictional island used as an allegory for the hubris of nations in Plato’s Timaeus and Critias (about 360 BC). It has had a large influence on literature, arts, and culture. See Plato and Platonism.
    • Plato tells the story in the Timaeus and the Critias.
  • “The cross had turned into the immortal rose”: The rose upon the cross is the emblem of the Rosicrucians, announced in the Fama Fraternitatis (1614). Yeats wrote “To the Rose upon the Rood of Time” (1892). See Astrology, Alchemy, and Esoterica.
  • “a cross upon a crossroad”: In England suicides were buried at crossroads, sometimes with a stake through the body, until the Burial of Suicide Act of 1823 ended the practice. See Suicide in History and Literature.
  • “Her head was eaten by great birds”: “The eye that mocketh at his father, and despiseth to obey his mother, the ravens of the valley shall pick it out, and the young eagles shall eat it” (Proverbs 30:17). See The Bible.
  • “that which was void and without form”: “And the earth was without form, and void; and darkness was upon the face of the deep” (Genesis 1:2). See Genesis.
  • “that eternal point where all lines converge”: Nicholas of Cusa taught that in the infinite all opposites coincide, so that an infinite circle would be a straight line (De docta ignorantia 1.13, 1440). See the Chapter 36 resources.
  • “land of infinite greyness”: “A land of darkness, as darkness itself; and of the shadow of death, without any order, and where the light is as darkness” (Job 10:22). See The Book of Job.
  • “Death had been, at last, her bridegroom”: “Because I could not stop for Death – / He kindly stopped for me –” (Emily Dickinson, 1890). Death comes as a suitor in his carriage. See American Writers.
  • “Had she not gone to the court of the emperor worm”: Poe’s “The Conqueror Worm” (1843) ends, “And its hero, the Conqueror Worm.” Wallace Stevens wrote, “The only emperor is the emperor of ice-cream” (1922). See Edgar Allan Poe and American Writers.
  • “the tormented whirlwinds turning upon spindles”: “The infernal hurricane that never rests / Hurtles the spirits onward in its rapine” (Dante, Inferno 5, trans. Henry Wadsworth Longfellow, 1867), the circle of the lovers. See Dante.
  • “evolving from pearls in the womb of time”: “There are many events in the womb of time which will be delivered” (Shakespeare, Othello 1.3). See Shakespeare.
  • “She had crept into a seraglio among a great shiek’s wives”: Seraglios: See the Chapter 36 resources.
  • “she had lifted her veil”: In Thomas Moore’s “The Veiled Prophet of Khorassan,” from Lalla Rookh (1817), the prophet Mokanna hides his face behind a silver veil, and when he lifts it, it is hideous. See Romantic Poets.
  • “not even, as Mr. Spitzer sometimes remarked, a Chinaman’s chance”: A “Chinaman’s chance,” no chance at all, is a racist American phrase of the late nineteenth century. California’s Supreme Court had ruled in People v. Hall (1854) that Chinese people could not testify against whites, and the Chinese Exclusion Act of 1882 barred them from the country. See Society, Class, and Race.
  • “Had not the riderless horse already come”: A riderless horse with boots reversed in the stirrups follows the coffin in a military funeral, as Black Jack did at John F. Kennedy’s funeral in November 1963. In Chapter 32 a riderless horse “white as snow came through the window” the day Hannah died. See Horses and Carriages.
  • “The last conch trumpet had already blown”: Triton blew his conch to call back the waters of the flood (Ovid, Metamorphoses 1). “In a moment, in the twinkling of an eye, at the last trump: for the trumpet shall sound, and the dead shall be raised incorruptible” (1 Corinthians 15:52). See Greek Mythology and The Bible.

chapter-19:
Chapter 19

← Chapter 18 · Home · Chapter 20 →

Summary

“That was the false dawn, surely.” Vera wakes in Miss MacIntosh’s bed, sure that the night was a dream for which no one was responsible. Before she opens her eyes, she goes over things she never thought to question: the missing eyebrows, the face that changes color, the baseball cap in the mornings, the green ribbon in the evenings, the veils over the whaler’s hat, the black umbrella carried even indoors. Her mother calls herself “the horizontal person.” Miss MacIntosh is “perpendicular.” Then Vera looks. The bald head lies on the pillow next to hers, “cold as marble,” and the red wig is perched on the hat rack “like a rare tropical bird.” The room is bare and broken: a bust of Martin Luther, cherubim with no wings, a Bible chained to a table, false teeth in a glass, the deuce of clubs turned up, seaweed hanging on the barred door, the umbrella open on the floor. Then Vera observes “what I must surely have always known.” One breast has been amputated, and “what was left was no bigger than a baby’s.”

Characters present

Miss MacIntosh · Vera Cartwheel · Catherine Cartwheel

Concepts present

Themes: Decay and Ruin · Dreams and Imagination · Faith, God, and the Supernatural · Illusion and Reality · Isolation and Connection · Society, Class, and Race · Women, Gender, and Marriage

Symbols: Angels, Devils, and Myth · Cards, Games, and Chance · Clothing, Hats, and Skirts · Eyes and Blindness · Hair, Wig, and Baldness · Keys, Doors, and Locks · Roses and Flowers · The House · The Sea and Water · The Umbrella

Philosophy: Augustine and Christian Theology

Allusions: Angels and Archangels · Fairy Tales and Folklore · Gambling and Playing Cards · Music and Composers · Shakespeare · The Bible

Key passages

From the research

  • The chapter opens with a meticulous depiction of Miss MacIntosh’s largely bare and austere bedroom. The room contains very few ornaments: a bust of Martin Luther, a large seashell used as a doorstop, and crumbling cherubim heads around a blackened fireplace, covered by cheese-cloth drapery. The room is described as “plain,” “barely furnished,” and showing signs of decay which metaphorically reflects Miss MacIntosh’s own physical and perhaps spiritual condition. This setting evokes a sense of austerity, fragility, and impermanence, mirroring the character’s struggle with her own vulnerabilities.
  • Vera observes Miss MacIntosh’s physical traits with a mix of curiosity and tenderness. Notable is the absence of her eyebrows, the rapid changes in the color of her skin, her habitual wearing of old caps or a baseball cap, and the ever-present whistle around her neck. The description of her headgear and her old black umbrella carried like a shield even indoors suggests a defensive posture against the world or perhaps her own frailty. These details hint at a woman who is both physically fragile and psychologically guarded, living with an awareness of her own vulnerability.
  • A striking image is that of Miss MacIntosh’s bald head lying next to Vera’s pillow, “cold as marble” and “seldom touched by sunlight.” This evokes a sense of mortality and the harsh reality of illness or aging. Her red wig, compared to a “rare tropical bird,” is carefully placed within reach, symbolizing a constructed identity or a protective mask she wears in public. The presence of her worn clothing, her corset stained and draped over a chair, and other personal belongings scattered around the room reinforce the theme of physical deterioration and survival. Vera’s detailed observation of these items underscores a deep intimacy and respect for Miss MacIntosh’s resilience despite her hardships.
  • Among the personal items is a set of translucent playing cards with Dutch windmills, with the upturned card being the deuce of clubs, described as “the test of tears” and “the omen of death.” This is particularly poignant given Miss MacIntosh’s critical view of gambling as “the crafty Devil’s handiwork.” The card’s presence symbolizes fate, mortality, and perhaps the inevitability of death. It also highlights the duality in Miss MacIntosh’s beliefs between her Christian faith, her honesty, and her rejection of “double motions” or duplicity in the heart. This passage deepens the psychological complexity of her character and sets a somber, reflective tone.
  • The description of the room’s decay continues, with cracked walls, stained ceilings, barred doors with seaweed and barnacles, mud tracks, grains of sand, and salt gleamings. These vivid natural and physical details evoke a sense of isolation, imprisonment, and the passage of time, suggesting that Miss MacIntosh’s life is enclosed, weathered by external elements and internal struggles. The imagery of the umbrella, still opened on the floor as if for protection during the night, reinforces the motif of defense and vulnerability. Vera’s discovery that one of Miss MacIntosh’s breasts has been amputated is a stark and intimate revelation, symbolizing loss and suffering, yet also the survival and endurance of the woman.
  • “I observed what I must surely have always known, the fact that one breast had been amputated. What was left was no bigger than a baby’s.” The revelation is something Vera half knew all along.

Questions and observations

Reading closely

  • “That was the false dawn, surely.” What is false about this morning?
  • Miss MacIntosh’s bedroom has “no dust-catchers,” yet Vera finds it crowded with saved things. Which details give the woman away?
  • The upturned card is “the deuce of clubs, that card which signifies the test of tears.” Why does Young place it within reach of her hand?

Characters

  • Catherine is “the horizontal person,” and Miss MacIntosh is “perpendicular.” What does each posture protect?
  • Vera wants to ask her questions “with studied detachment as if one were considering a land one had not visited and would never visit.” Why that distance?
  • “She was no turncoat,” and “she knew not… of these dualities in one heart.” What does the room say about that claim?

Connections

  • The red wig on the chair post in Chapter 18 is “perched like a rare tropical bird” here. How has Vera’s view of it changed overnight?
  • Chapter 18 heard her talk of the breast “already gone.” What changes when Vera sees it?
  • The seaweed on the door and the open umbrella look ahead to the sea. Where has the novel already told how Miss MacIntosh will die?

Reflection

  • “What I must surely have always known.” Can a person know something and not know it?
  • What do the things a person saves “for a rainy day” say about her?
  • Is there tenderness in looking closely at someone who is asleep, or is it a trespass?

Research: Characters

Miss MacIntosh

  • Bald head cold as marble, veined limbs, a missing breast (amputated), thin, ascetic mouth with “not one soft fuzz of hair upon the upper lip,” red wig resembling a tropical bird, gnarled hands.
  • Wears a baseball cap or old caps in the morning and a green ribbon in the evenings.
  • Always carries a whistle around her neck.
  • Wears a veil-tied hat outdoors, sometimes layered with heavy veiling.
  • Carries an old black umbrella indoors and outdoors, like a shield.
  • Sleeps lightly, alert to the slightest noise.
  • Yet this morning she sleeps on with “a kind of abandon,” “singularly unaware of my scrutiny.”
  • Has a strong Christian faith, critical of gambling, “the crafty Devil’s handiwork.”
  • Exhibits physical and emotional contradictions: shifting skin color, blushing for no apparent reason, and trying to resist external forces (“bucking against the broncho wind”).
  • The playing cards, especially the “deuce of clubs,” symbolize fate, death, or a trial by tears, despite her rejection of gambling.
  • Her patched clothing and worn items reflect hardship and resilience.

Vera Cartwheel

  • She describes her mind as “lucid as day” but simultaneously reveals a hesitation or reluctance to fully open her eyes and confront reality directly. This tension between clarity and avoidance suggests an internal conflict or a fragile psychological state. She seems caught between the realms of dream and waking, reality and imagination, as shown by her uncertainty about whether she is truly awake despite the vividness of the dawn light and surroundings.
  • She meticulously catalogues the objects and conditions in Miss MacIntosh’s bedroom, from the “crumbling heads of cherubim” to the “red wig, almost purple,” and the “jeweled water glass” holding false teeth. This detailed observation indicates a careful, almost forensic attention to detail, suggesting a mind that seeks to understand and piece together the significance of the environment and the person within it.
  • There is a tone of gentle curiosity in Vera’s internal questioning about Miss MacIntosh’s peculiarities: her missing eyebrows, the changing colors of her skin, her habitual wearing of hats and a whistle, and the careful way she avoids showing vulnerability (the umbrella carried “like a shield uplifted where there was no gale”). These questions are posed with “studied detachment,” as if Vera is trying to maintain emotional distance while simultaneously probing deeply into the character of Miss MacIntosh.
  • Despite this detachment, Vera’s sensitivity is apparent in her awareness of the “quiver of wind upon the high cheek bones,” the “thin, ascetic mouth,” and the “wet and stained” pillow. She notices intimate, tender details such as the fact that “one breast had been amputated,” describing what remains as “no bigger than a baby’s,” which evokes a sense of vulnerability and loss. This reveals an underlying empathy and a recognition of Miss MacIntosh’s suffering and resilience.
  • Vera recalls Miss MacIntosh’s sayings that “the Devil’s cards are marked” and that she “knew not… of these dualities in one heart, these double motions.”
  • Vera’s detailed description of Miss MacIntosh’s room (with its broken, bare, and patched furnishings, barred door, and scattered personal effects) reflects a broader sense of isolation, hardship, and complexity. She seems attuned to this atmosphere of loneliness and endurance, which may mirror her own inner state or the broader themes of the narrative.

Research: Themes

Reality versus Dream

See: Illusion and Reality · Dreams and Imagination

  • Vera questions the boundaries between waking and sleeping, dream and reality, underscored by the “false dawn” and the dreamlike quality of the observations.

Decay and Brokenness

See: Decay and Ruin

  • The imagery of broken cherubim, cracked walls, a fallen alabaster rose, and worn clothing reflects themes of impermanence, loss, and the passage of time.

Isolation and Protection

See: Isolation and Connection

  • Miss MacIntosh’s habits (umbrella indoors, veils, barred door) suggest a need for defense against external threats and a guarded, solitary existence.

Faith and Morality

See: Faith, God, and the Supernatural

  • Her Christian beliefs, criticism of gambling, and chained Bible contrast with the ominous presence of the cards and other symbols of fate, indicating internal conflicts or tensions between belief and fate.

Physical and Emotional Vulnerability

See: Women, Gender, and Marriage

  • The amputated breast and the varying skin colors symbolize physical trauma and emotional sensitivity.

Research: Symbols and Imagery

Red Wig

See: Hair, Wig, and Baldness

  • A mask or false identity, “perched like a rare tropical bird on the hat rack… within easy reach of her gnarled hand,” ready but separate from her true self.

Playing Cards (Deuce of Clubs)

See: Cards, Games, and Chance

  • Represents the “test of tears” and omen of death; a paradox considering her moral stance against gambling.

Umbrella

See: The Umbrella

  • A shield or protective barrier, even when unnecessary.
  • “The heavy-ribbed black umbrella, opened, was on the floor where it had rolled as if, during the night, she might have upheld it for her protection.”

Barred Door with Seaweed

See: Keys, Doors, and Locks

  • Symbolizes isolation and self-imposed confinement.
  • “A clump of blackened seaweed… much like some other wig, barnacles clinging to it.” The sea is already hanging on her door.
  • The door was “barred from the inside.” Whatever happened, she shut them in together.

Broken Cherubim and Fallen Alabaster Rose

See: Angels, Devils, and Myth · Roses and Flowers

  • Fragments of lost innocence or beauty.

Chained Bible

See: The Bible

  • Firm but restrained faith; tethering spirituality to reality.

Miss MacIntosh’s Bedroom

See: The House

  • A large, sparsely furnished chamber, described as “barely furnished” with no dust-catchers, no hanging tapestries, no floating angels, reflecting a deliberate plainness.

Decor

See: The House

  • Broken cherubim heads around a blackened fireplace, a bust of Martin Luther on a pedestal, a large sea shell used as a door stopper, cracked walls, and stained ceiling with broken cornices.

Atmosphere

See: Dreams and Imagination

  • The dawn light is described as “moon-washed,” filled with “pristine light,” “tremblings,” and “washings” that create a liminal space between night and day, dream and reality.

Details

See: The House

  • Objects are scattered about her room: her red wig on a hat rack, a whale-boned corset, a silver-dollar watch pinned to a curtain, false teeth in a jeweled water glass, stockings, patches, knitting, a porcelain chamber pot, an empty picture frame, a broken ship’s compass, a chained Bible, and a Pullman towel.

Research: Resources

  • “That was the false dawn, surely”: FitzGerald’s note to the Rubáiyát of Omar Khayyám (1859): “The False Dawn; Subhi Kázib, a transient light on the Horizon about an hour before the Subhi sádik, or True Dawn.” In Chapter 18, “the first light of the first dawn… seemed a falsehood.” See the Chapter 18 resources.
  • “the bust of Martin Luther”: Martin Luther (1483-1546) was a German professor of theology, priest, Augustinian monk, and hymn writer, and the central figure of the Reformation. (Wikipedia) His “A Mighty Fortress Is Our God” (c. 1529) is still sung in Protestant churches. Luther himself opposed the image-breakers of 1522, but the Reformation he began stripped many churches bare, as Miss MacIntosh strips her room. Miss MacIntosh quoted a line attributed to him at dawn in Chapter 18. See Augustine and Christian Theology, Music and Composers, and the Chapter 18 resources.
  • “the crumbling heads of cherubim”: In the Bible, cherubim are fierce guardians, set “at the east of the garden of Eden… to keep the way of the tree of life” (Genesis 3:24). The winged child heads of decoration are the putti of Renaissance art. These have “already lost their wings.” See Angels and Archangels and Angels, Devils, and Myth.
  • “the acanthus leaves in the molding”: Acanthus is one of the most common plant forms for foliage ornaments and decoration. (Wikipedia) The Roman architect Vitruvius tells that the sculptor Callimachus saw acanthus growing around a basket left on a young girl’s grave and carved it into the first Corinthian capital (On Architecture 4.1).
  • “my sleeping mother who called herself the horizontal person”: Catherine, who lives lying down, “never walked except in her imagination.” Miss MacIntosh is “perpendicular.” See Catherine Cartwheel.
  • “the cap of a sleeping car porter”: After the Civil War, the Pullman Company hired Black men, many of them formerly enslaved, as sleeping car porters. They worked long hours for low pay and tips, and passengers called every one of them “George,” after George Pullman. A. Philip Randolph organized the Brotherhood of Sleeping Car Porters in 1925, and in 1937 it won “the first major labor agreement between a Black union and a corporation” (Smithsonian Magazine, February 18, 2025). See Society, Class, and Race.
    • “There was a Pullman towel”: Pullman towels were stamped with the company name, and travelers carried them home.
  • “jigsaw puzzles which always turned out to be the faces of presidents or the maps of foreign countries”: The first jigsaw puzzles were “dissected maps,” cut by the London mapmaker John Spilsbury in the 1760s to teach geography.
  • “playing tiddlywinks”: The game was patented in England by Joseph Fincher in 1888 as “Tiddledy-Winks” and became a craze in the 1890s.
  • “my strange bedfellow”: “Misery acquaints a man with strange bedfellows” (The Tempest 2.2). See Shakespeare.
  • “Her red wig, almost purple”: The wig Vera saw “upon the carven chair post” in Chapter 18. See Hair, Wig, and Baldness and the Chapter 18 resources.
  • “Her whale-boned, salmon-colored corset”: The “salmon-colored monstrosity” of Chapter 18, stiffened with whalebone. See Clothing, Hats, and Skirts and the Chapter 17 resources.
  • “my grandmother’s rocking chair”: The blind grandmother of the garden of the blind. See Eyes and Blindness and the Chapter 12 resources.
  • “Her silver-dollar watch”: This may be a dollar watch, like the Ingersoll pocket watch of 1896, which sold for one dollar and was the first watch most Americans could afford.
  • “a grey fedora”: The fedora takes its name from Victorien Sardou’s play Fédora (1882), in which Sarah Bernhardt wore a soft, creased, brimmed hat. It was a woman’s hat first, and then a man’s. See Clothing, Hats, and Skirts.
  • “the convict’s garb”: Striped prison uniforms began at New York’s Auburn Prison in the 1820s, so a prisoner could be seen anywhere. Most prisons gave them up in the early twentieth century.
  • “a pair of white fur ear muffs”: Chester Greenwood of Farmington, Maine, invented earmuffs at fifteen, in 1873, and patented them in 1877.
  • “her dim mackintosh”: The Scottish chemist Charles Macintosh patented his rubberized waterproof cloth in 1823, and the raincoat took his name. It is her name, too. See Miss MacIntosh.
  • “a world’s almanac”: The World Almanac of Chapter 18. See the Chapter 18 resources.
  • “a broken ship’s compass”: The compass rose of Chapter 18, now broken. See the Chapter 18 resources.
  • “a Moody’s hotel Bible. I noted that she had chained it to a table”: The Gideons placed their first hotel Bible in 1908, in Iron Mountain, Montana. In 1538, Thomas Cromwell ordered every church in England to set up “one book of the whole Bible of the largest volume in English” where parishioners could read it. It came to be called the Chained Bible, because it was fastened so it could not be taken away. Miss MacIntosh chains hers. See The Bible.
  • “an Atlantic City paperweight”: Atlantic City, New Jersey, built its Boardwalk in 1870 and became the great seaside souvenir town of the East.
  • “the lashless eyelids”: Alopecia universalis is the loss of all hair on the body, including the brows and lashes. See Hair, Wig, and Baldness and the Chapter 17 resources.
  • “the deuce of clubs, that card which signifies the test of tears”: Cartomancy reads fortunes in ordinary playing cards. Young gives the deuce of clubs its meaning herself. Clubs were trumps the night before. See Gambling and Playing Cards and the Chapter 18 resources.
  • “the Devil’s cards are marked”: The Puritans called playing cards “the Devil’s books.” The American historian of cards Mrs. John King Van Rensselaer titled her book The Devil’s Picture-Books (1890). See Gambling and Playing Cards.
  • “beauty is as beauty does, and beauty is more than skin deep”: Miss MacIntosh bends two proverbs. “Handsome is that handsome does” is Mrs. Primrose’s in Goldsmith’s The Vicar of Wakefield (1766). “Beauty is but skin deep” goes back to Sir Thomas Overbury’s poem “A Wife” (1613): “All the carnall beautie of my wife, / Is but skinne-deepe.” See Fairy Tales and Folklore.
  • “it’s an ill wind that blows nobody good”: John Heywood’s proverb (1546). Falstaff’s man Pistol says, “Not the ill wind which blows no man to good” (Henry IV, Part 2 5.3). See Shakespeare.
  • “a clump of blackened seaweed hanging on a nail on the door”: “much like some other wig.” Miss MacIntosh will be lost to the sea. See The Sea and Water and the Chapter 6 resources.
  • “her red jersey bloomers”: The bloomers Miss MacIntosh asked for at dawn in Chapter 18. See Women, Gender, and Marriage and the Chapter 18 resources.
  • “one breast had been amputated”: The Halsted operation of Chapters 17 and 18. See Miss MacIntosh, Women, Gender, and Marriage, and the Chapter 17 resources.
