chapter-21:
Chapter 21

← Chapter 20 · Home · Chapter 22 →

Summary

Vera promises herself that tomorrow she will look only at the red hair “like shining armor” and go on as before: “Daylight should cover us.” Her “good intention” is to deceive Miss MacIntosh into believing herself “but a usual being in the light.” Yet she remembers Miss MacIntosh’s own warnings, that the road to Hell “is paved with bones and good intentions,” that the Devil “does not always wear horns” and can quote Scripture. Pity wakes in her: “It was only the beginning of pity. It was not the end.” Vera takes a last long look at the sleeping body, the scar, the stalk of the cut-away breast, the wad of cloth in the brassiere, the green ribbon looped over the bust of Martin Luther. Then she falls asleep. When she wakes, Miss MacIntosh stands at the foot of the bed, fully dressed, her red hair shining, in remarkably good humor. She says Vera has been very sick, scolds her for dancing at “your first birthday party, even though no guest came,” and holds up the party dress Mr. Spitzer gave her. Vera can see no tear in it. Miss MacIntosh declares it cannot be mended: “Into the ash bin it goes.”

Characters present

Vera Cartwheel · Miss MacIntosh · The Old Blind Sheep Dog · Joachim Spitzer

Concepts present

Themes: Death and Mortality · Faith, God, and the Supernatural · Grief, Loss, and Mourning · Illusion and Reality · Love · Women, Gender, and Marriage

Symbols: Angels, Devils, and Myth · Clothing, Hats, and Skirts · Dogs · Hair, Wig, and Baldness · Lamps, Candles, and Light · Pearls and Jewels · The Sea and Water · Weddings and Funerals

Philosophy: Aristotle · Augustine and Christian Theology

Allusions: Angels and Archangels · Greek Mythology · Homer’s Epics · Milton · Revelation and the Apocalypse · Shakespeare · The Bible · The Book of Job

Key passages

From the research

  • This opening passage is crucial because it establishes Vera’s conscious perception of Miss MacIntosh in her usual, seemingly strong and formidable state. The language (“shining armor,” “scaled vizor,” “rugged individualist,” “triumphant”) creates an image of someone powerful, decisive, and perhaps intimidating, contrasting sharply with the vulnerability revealed later. It sets up the central theme of appearance versus reality and the layers of disguise or perception that Vera navigates. The detail about the evening walk and the old dog grounds this potentially abstract description in a concrete, if slightly surreal, daily ritual.
  • The revelation of Miss MacIntosh’s baldness is a pivotal moment. Vera contrasts this “palpable disguise of the average man” with a sense of hidden “dead and vanished glory.” The image of the “great baldness as of the moon sunken” is striking and suggests something vast, desolate, and perhaps beyond reach. Crucially, Vera interprets this physical revelation not as a simple lack, but as something that reveals a deeper truth about reality: that strength is intertwined with fragility, illusion, and disorder. This passage shifts the narrative from external observation to deep internal reflection on the nature of identity, love, and perception.
  • Vera’s complex motivation is articulated after witnessing Miss MacIntosh’s vulnerability. The “good intention” is to maintain a facade of normalcy for her sake, even if it requires Vera to “deceive her” about her own profound realization. Vera seems to want to protect her from the implications of the “glory” or “chaos” she perceived, wishing instead for her to see herself as ordinary, stable, and authentic. This reveals Vera’s protective instinct but also highlights the inherent tension in their relationship and the burden of Vera’s newfound knowledge. It introduces the theme of deliberate self-deception or mutual deception as a way to cope with difficult truths.
  • Miss MacIntosh’s sayings about the Devil, while seemingly a digression, reinforce the chapter’s themes of appearance versus reality, disguise, and the difficulty of discerning truth. They emphasize that evil can be deceptive, appearing in attractive forms (“charming,” “handsome,” “fine dancer,” “God’s ape”). This mirrors Vera’s experience of seeing Miss MacIntosh’s seemingly strong exterior peeled away to reveal a hidden reality, suggesting that what appears “normal” or even “good” might conceal something else entirely. It adds a layer of theological or philosophical depth to the personal revelation, implying that the struggle to understand her is part of a larger human struggle to understand complex, hidden realities. It also gives voice to Miss MacIntosh’s own worldview.
  • This extended description is incredibly powerful and visceral. It moves beyond the initial shock of baldness to reveal a body marked by age, illness, and labor (the missing breast, scar, gnarled hands and feet). The imagery is both starkly realistic (“mouth open and toothless”) and metaphoric (“Alpine frozen slopes,” “wintry field,” “polished marble,” “barnacles”). The repetition of “pity” underscores Vera’s overwhelming emotional response. The description emphasizes vulnerability, loss, and a stripping away (“denudement”) of layers both physical and perhaps metaphysical. The comparison of this reality to something “less substantial than the wildest, saddest dream” suggests a profound disorientation for Vera, blurring the lines between waking life and nightmare, and making the revealed reality seem almost unbelievable despite its physical presence.
  • After the intense, detailed description of the vulnerable, sleeping figure, Miss MacIntosh is abruptly presented as the familiar, formidable “Miss MacIntosh,” fully dressed and appearing exactly as she did the previous evening, complete with her shining red hair. Vera notes her lack of astonishment, highlighting how quickly the mind can revert to familiar perceptions, even after a profound revelation. She finds herself in Miss MacIntosh’s brass bed and not her own, “something which had never happened before,” and does not ask how. This passage reinstates the “disguise” or preferred appearance and raises questions about which reality is dominant or “true”: the vulnerable sleeping figure or the robust, familiar Miss MacIntosh.
  • This dialogue shifts the focus away from Miss MacIntosh’s physical state to Vera’s apparent illness of the night before. Miss MacIntosh’s tone is parental (“sick and unusually stubborn,” “mild reproach”), emphasizing their caregiver-dependent relationship. The mention of the “first birthday party” and the torn dress introduces a specific past event, possibly symbolic of a loss of innocence or a failed attempt at celebration. Most significantly, the passage presents a clear discrepancy: Vera sees no tear in the dress, but Miss MacIntosh insists it is irreparably damaged and must be discarded. This highlights a potential unreliability in the narrative, either on the part of Miss MacIntosh (perhaps deliberately misrepresenting the dress’s condition) or Vera (perhaps unable to see the damage, literal or symbolic). The torn dress becomes a symbol of something broken or lost that cannot be fixed, but the disagreement about its state complicates its meaning and adds to the chapter’s layers of uncertain reality. Miss MacIntosh’s repetition of the “road to Hell” saying connects this conversation back to the earlier philosophical digression, grounding it in her practical, somewhat fatalistic worldview.
  • “It was only the beginning of pity. It was not the end.” Vera’s pity starts here and keeps deepening through the novel.

Questions and observations

Reading closely

  • “Daylight should cover us.” What does Vera expect daylight to do?
  • “The pity, pity, pity of nothing, of something, for nothing is always something.” What is the “something”?
  • Vera “could not see a hole in it,” yet Miss MacIntosh says the dress “cannot be mended.” What is torn?

Characters

  • Miss MacIntosh tells Vera, “You have been very sick.” Whose story of the night is this?
  • She is in “a remarkably good humor.” Why now?
  • Vera’s “good intention” is to deceive her. What does Vera know about good intentions, from Miss MacIntosh herself?

Connections

  • In Chapter 9, Miss MacIntosh disliked the dress’s low neck and bare arms, and Mr. Spitzer promised “Fair as a bride I should be.” Why does she throw it away now?
  • “That love is love which… does not alter” echoes Sonnet 116, as in Chapter 18. What is Vera promising?
  • The Devil “might appear as the angel transfixed by light.” Where has Vera already met an angel of light (Chapter 17)?

Reflection

  • Is it kinder to pretend not to know?
  • “Evil has many forms, and the good has only one.” Is that true?
  • What does a person throw away when she throws away a dress?

Research: Characters

Vera Cartwheel

  • She is introspective, empathetic, and deeply affected by Miss MacIntosh’s state.
  • She wrestles with her feelings of pity and the desire to shield Miss MacIntosh from harsh truths.
  • She reflects on love, the nature of identity, and the meaning of suffering, indicating a philosophical and emotional depth.
  • Her “good intention” is “that I should deceive her into accepting herself as but a usual being in the light.”

Miss MacIntosh

  • Portrayed as a strong yet vulnerable figure, marked physically by baldness, scars, and loss, which symbolize deeper suffering.
  • Despite her condition, she maintains a robust and kind demeanor, showing resilience. She is depicted with vivid details like her red hair, green ribbon, and practical attire.
  • She embodies the tension between appearance and inner reality, strength and vulnerability.
  • Her sayings on the Devil: he “does not always wear horns,” can “quote his Scriptures,” and is “God’s ape.”

Research: Themes

Love as Eternal and Unchanging

See: Love · Shakespeare

  • “That love is love which… does not alter with the changing circumstance” echoes Sonnet 116, as in Chapter 18.
  • Vera emphasizes that true love remains constant despite changing circumstances. Love “does not ebb, does not wane,” symbolizing an ideal of permanence in an impermanent world.
  • This eternal love contrasts with the physical and emotional struggles depicted, underscoring a spiritual or emotional steadfastness.

Appearance versus Reality

See: Illusion and Reality

  • There is a tension between outward appearances and inner realities. Vera observes Miss MacIntosh’s bald head, a stark and raw image that strips away pretense and illusion.
  • The “palpable disguise of the average man” and the “inarticulate mediocrity” hint at the masks people wear to hide deeper truths.
  • Vera’s intention to let Miss MacIntosh believe she is “a usual being” shows a desire to protect her from harsh truths.

Suffering and Pity

See: Death and Mortality

  • The chapter conveys deep pity for Miss MacIntosh’s condition, symbolized by her baldness and the physical aftermath of illness or trauma (e.g., the missing breast, scar, and hairlessness).
  • The imagery of “valley of dry bones” and “the road to Hell… paved with bones and good intentions” suggests the harshness of life and the prevalence of suffering masked by well-meaning actions.

The Devil and Deception

See: Faith, God, and the Supernatural

  • The narrative includes reflections on evil’s many forms, warning against being deceived by charming appearances (“The Devil does not always wear horns”).
  • The Devil is described metaphorically as “God’s ape,” emphasizing the complexity of good and evil and the danger of superficial judgments.

Research: Symbols and Imagery

Bald Head

See: Hair, Wig, and Baldness

  • Symbolizes raw truth, vulnerability, and the stripping away of superficial identity.

Sea and Light

See: The Sea and Water · Lamps, Candles, and Light

  • The sea light covering the scene suggests mystery, change, and the vastness of life’s experience.

Valley of Dry Bones

See: The Bible

  • Represents death, decay, and the desolation of existence, yet also possibly hints at resurrection or hope in a biblical sense.

The Devil as “God’s Ape”

See: Angels, Devils, and Myth

  • Illustrates the deceptive nature of evil and the difficulty in distinguishing it from good.
  • This metaphor warns against being deceived by appearances, a central theme in the chapter.

The Party Dress

See: Clothing, Hats, and Skirts

  • Represents innocence and celebration. Miss MacIntosh declares it beyond mending, though Vera “could not see a hole in it” or “a seed pearl which was not in its place.”
  • The destruction of the dress symbolizes the loss of innocence and the inevitability of change.

Love and Identity

See: Love

  • Highlights Vera’s struggle to reconcile ideal love with the imperfect reality of human beings.

Pity and Reality

See: Grief, Loss, and Mourning

  • The repetition of “pity” emphasizes the deep sorrow felt for Miss MacIntosh’s condition, portraying her as an incomplete and tragic figure.

Miss MacIntosh’s Morning Appearance

See: Hair, Wig, and Baldness

  • Miss MacIntosh’s appearance contrasts sharply with the earlier portrayal of vulnerability, showing her resilience and normalcy despite suffering.

Research: Resources

  • “the scaled vizor of my rugged individualist”: Herbert Hoover praised “the American system of rugged individualism” in his campaign speech of October 22, 1928.
  • “the old, blind sheep dog running ahead of us on three legs”: The dog still “guarding the pasture which was no more against the thief who would not come.” See The Old Blind Sheep Dog and Dogs.
  • “that love is love which is love forevermore and unchanging, which does not alter with the changing circumstance”: “Love is not love / Which alters when it alteration finds” (Sonnet 116), as in Chapter 18. See Shakespeare and the Chapter 18 resources.
  • “this great head which was the secret pearl”: The merchant “who, when he had found one pearl of great price, went and sold all that he had, and bought it” (Matthew 13:46). See The Bible and Pearls and Jewels.
  • “one who had not built her house upon shifting sands”: “A foolish man, which built his house upon the sand” (Matthew 7:26). See The Bible.
  • “evil has many forms, and the good has only one”: Aristotle writes that “it is possible to fail in many ways… while to succeed is possible only in one way,” and quotes the line “men are good in but one way, but bad in many” (Nicomachean Ethics 2.6). See Aristotle.
  • “the road to Hell, as she had often grimly said, is very broad and very wide and is paved with bones and good intentions”: “Wide is the gate, and broad is the way, that leadeth to destruction” (Matthew 7:13). Samuel Johnson said “Hell is paved with good intentions” (Boswell’s Life of Johnson, 1775). Miss MacIntosh repeats it at the end of the chapter: “the highway to Hell is paved with more good intentions than shining cobblestones.” See The Bible.
  • “life is this valley of dry bones”: “The hand of the Lord… set me down in the midst of the valley which was full of bones… Can these bones live?” (Ezekiel 37:1-3). See The Bible.
  • “The Devil does not always wear horns”: In Goethe’s Faust (1808), Mephistopheles tells the witch that the devil has given up his horns, tail, and claws to keep up with the times. See Angels, Devils, and Myth.
  • “fine feathers which make fine birds”: An old proverb, in print by the sixteenth century.
  • “the Devil wore a red coat and a pair of green breeches”: Folklore often makes the Devil a gentleman and a dancer. In Burns’s “Tam o’ Shanter” (1791), “auld Nick” plays the pipes for the witches’ dance. See Angels, Devils, and Myth.
  • “The Devil could quote his Scriptures, too, chapter and verse for his purpose”: “The devil can cite Scripture for his purpose” (The Merchant of Venice 1.3). In the temptation, Satan quotes Psalm 91 to Christ (Matthew 4:6). See Shakespeare and The Bible.
  • “once he sat at the right hand of the throne of God and was a favorite son of Heaven”: “How art thou fallen from heaven, O Lucifer, son of the morning!” (Isaiah 14:12). Milton’s Satan was “of the first, / If not the first Archangel, great in power” (Paradise Lost 5.659-660). See Milton and Angels and Archangels.
  • “some there are who still confuse the brothers, he who fell”: Both are called the morning star: Lucifer, “son of the morning” (Isaiah 14:12), and Christ, “the bright and morning star” (Revelation 22:16). See The Bible.
  • “The Devil, she had said when opening her black umbrella in the sunlight, is God’s ape”: The devil as God’s ape, simia Dei, who mocks God by imitating Him, is an old Christian saying, often traced to the Church Fathers and used by Luther. Medieval bestiaries made the ape the devil’s creature: “As the devil poorly imitates the Lord, so do apes poorly imitate us” (Samiksha Chopra, “Book of Beasts,” Getty Iris). See Augustine and Christian Theology and Angels, Devils, and Myth.
  • “God’s crown which is a crown of stars”: Compare the woman clothed with the sun, “upon her head a crown of twelve stars” (Revelation 12:1). See Revelation and the Apocalypse.
  • “better the Devil you know than the Devil you will never know”: The proverb is “Better the devil you know than the devil you don’t.” Miss MacIntosh makes the unknown devil one you will “never know.”
  • “He might appear as the angel transfixed by light or as the angel of darkness”: “For Satan himself is transformed into an angel of light” (2 Corinthians 11:14), as in Chapter 17. See The Bible and the Chapter 17 resources.
  • “The greatest sorrows were those not described”: Seneca’s Phaedra has “Curae leves loquuntur, ingentes stupent” (“Light griefs speak, great ones are struck dumb”). Malcolm tells Macduff, “Give sorrow words: the grief that does not speak / Whispers the o’er-fraught heart and bids it break” (Macbeth 4.3). See Shakespeare.
  • “The King James version of the Bible was not to be trusted because made for the vanity of earthly kings”: The King James Version of the Bible was not the first English language version of the Bible, but the culmination of extensive translation activity (some illegal!) in the 1500s. This began with the work of William Tyndale and the printing of the first English New Testament in 1526. Following a tumultuous 75 years, James VI of Scotland became James I of England in 1603, joining the two crowns. Three main English Bibles were in use: the Bishops’ Bible (Church of England), the Geneva Bible (Protestants), and the Rheims New Testament (1582, Roman Catholic Church), causing much confusion and dissension. To settle disagreements over reforms in the Church of England and respond to pressure from the Puritans, King James in 1604 approved a new translation of the Bible, primarily because he knew that it would reinforce his image as a political and spiritual leader. He approved six companies of translators, 54 men in all, of whom 47 are known to have worked on it, to prepare the new translation, using previous English Bible translation work, and using the best Hebrew, Greek, and Latin texts and manuscripts. The completed King James Version was first published in 1611. These first editions were large pulpit Bibles (folios) to be read in churches, but were followed within a year by the printing of smaller versions (quartos) for personal use. Though slow to be adopted in the English-speaking world and to replace the more popular Geneva Bible, from the mid-1600s to the late 20th century, the King James Version was the Bible of the English-speaking church (Encyclopaedia Britannica). The translators’ dedication addresses “the most high and mighty Prince James,” the kind of flattery Miss MacIntosh distrusts. See The Bible.
  • “A man who is a pig is still a man”: Circe turns Odysseus’s men into swine, but “their minds were as before” (Odyssey 10). See Homer’s Epics and Greek Mythology.
  • “the darkness and the whirlwind”: “Then the Lord answered Job out of the whirlwind” (Job 38:1). See The Book of Job.
  • “the tissues like a baby’s fist”: Here the text has “a baby’s fist.” Chapter 19 has “no bigger than a baby’s.” See the Chapter 19 resources.
  • “a brassiere with a wad of cloth which had been Concealed”: The “breast pad” Vera imagined in Chapter 20. After a mastectomy, women padded the brassiere with cloth. Young’s capital “Concealed” is in the text. See Women, Gender, and Marriage and the Chapter 20 resources.
  • “her Irish green hair ribbon looped over the bust of Martin Luther”: The bust of Chapter 19. See the Chapter 19 resources.
  • “Dancing is never to be encouraged by this old lady”: Miss MacIntosh vividly expresses sexism through her character by highlighting her pragmatic, no-nonsense attitude toward the limitations imposed on women, her rejection of illusions, and her critical view of the societal roles prescribed to women. Miss MacIntosh’s insistence on practicality and self-reliance reflects a critique of traditional sexism by underscoring how women are often expected to conform to narrow roles, suppressing their individuality and desires. Miss MacIntosh’s harshness can be read as internalized sexism, reflecting how women may police themselves and others to survive within a patriarchal system that offers them limited agency. This portrayal critiques the constraints sexism imposes on women’s lives, identities, and dreams by grounding Miss MacIntosh as a figure of practical wisdom and resilience who nonetheless embodies the burdens of gendered limitations. It sums up how Miss MacIntosh has internalized sexism where she takes sexist behaviors and attitudes about women and projects them onto herself and Vera in the form of fear, envy, jealousy, suspicion, resentment, rage, anxiety, lack of self-esteem and confidence. Miss MacIntosh’s greatest fear is that Vera will become and get to do everything society expects a ‘normal’ woman to be and do, something Miss MacIntosh will never achieve. See Women, Gender, and Marriage.
  • “as when Mr. Spitzer had taken it out of its long white box”: The dress of Chapter 9. Mr. Spitzer promised, “Fair as a bride I should be,” and Miss MacIntosh complained of its low neck and lack of sleeves. See Joachim Spitzer, Weddings and Funerals, and the Chapter 9 resources.

Chapter 14

← Chapter 13 · Home · Chapter 15 →

Content note: This chapter deals with suicide: Mr. Spitzer’s twin brother Peron killed himself, perhaps, Mr. Spitzer thinks, in order to kill the other twin.

Summary

Vera comes to the grave of the black coachman, who drove the carriage and four white horses for her grandfather, his blind mother, his unmarried sister, and his blind wife, and outlived them all. Catherine, who had not visited the grave for years, perhaps never, cannot stop asking Mr. Spitzer about it: whether the coachman was buried, as she ordered, with the carriage and horses so that he could go on driving her in death, and in his livery. She insists the arrangement was his idea, though he had no wages for years and she cannot remember his name. Her questions turn on Mr. Spitzer himself. His twin Peron, the quick, brilliant gambler, fell from a tall building, and Joachim lives on in his brother’s shadow, finding his cigarette still burning in a coat pocket and an ace dropping from his sleeve, and being taken for him in the street. Catherine counts four Mr. Spitzers, mocks his train journeys, and accuses him of losing the coachman. She talks on after he has gone and, at dawn, asks for the grave of “the slow one, the sick musician she had always loved,” reversing which twin she lost.

Characters present

Catherine Cartwheel · Joachim Spitzer · Peron Spitzer · The Black Coachman · The Old Clam Digger · Mr. Chandelier · Mr. Res Tacamah

Concepts present

Themes: Death and Mortality · Duality and Doubles · Fate and Chance · Guilt, Innocence, and Justice · Identity and the Self · Illusion and Reality · Memory and the Past · Order, Chaos, and Discipline · Society, Class, and Race

Symbols: Birds · Cards, Games, and Chance · Clothing, Hats, and Skirts · Dogs · Horses and Carriages · Roses and Flowers · Snow, Ice, and Winter · The Sea and Water · Twins and Doubles · Weddings and Funerals

Philosophy: Aristotle · Astrology, Alchemy, and Esoterica · Augustine and Christian Theology · Descartes and Dualism · Hinduism · Kant and Hegel · Phenomenology · Plato and Platonism · Pythagoras and the Music of the Spheres · Time, Physics, and Chaos Theory

Allusions: American Writers · Astronomy · Dante · Gambling and Playing Cards · Greek Mythology · Music and Composers · Revelation and the Apocalypse · Shakespeare · The Bible · The Book of Job · The Civil War · The History of Opium

Key passages

From the research

  • The chapter opens with Vera’s reflection on the grave of the black coachman, a figure who drove the family carriage with four white horses. Catherine, in her illness and hallucinations, obsessively wonders about the black coachman’s grave and whether he was buried with the carriage and horses as she had instructed, by the sea where one might still hear the sounds of hooves and carriage wheels. This passage sets the tone of uncertainty and haunting memory, questioning the final resting place and fate of the coachman and symbolizing the fragile boundary between life, death, and memory.
  • Catherine believes in “two Mr. Spitzers,” referencing a duality or doubling that permeates the narrative. Mr. Spitzer himself is portrayed as a figure caught between realities as possibly the survivor of a tragic loss, burdened by his brother’s death and his own diminished existence. His silence about the black coachman and other mysteries reflects his internal conflict and the blurring of identities, especially between himself and his deceased brother.
  • The narrative delves deeply into Mr. Spitzer’s troubled life: his failed law practice, his haunted memories, and the confusion between himself and his brother. He is pursued by people who mistake him for his dead brother, and he carries the burden of that mistaken identity. His life is marked by a sense of loss, failure, and existential ambiguity, symbolized by repeated motifs such as the playing cards (four aces), the silent music he composes, and his futile attempts to make sense of his past and present.
  • Catherine’s hallucinations and visions serve as a counterpoint to Mr. Spitzer’s silence. She imagines vast, surreal scenes (funeral gondolas, angels, floating faces, and shifting landscapes) reflecting her mental state and the dissolution of clear boundaries between reality and illusion. Her insistence on the black coachman’s significance and her questioning of Mr. Spitzer highlights the themes of memory, loss, and the search for meaning in chaos.
  • The idea of multiple Mr. Spitzers (four in total) and the tragic fate of one brother killing himself to erase the other introduces a metaphysical layer about identity, fate, and the cosmic balance between opposites (life and death, presence and absence, order and chaos). The chapter explores the instability of self and the universe, where even laws (human and divine) seem uncertain or contested.
  • Throughout the chapter, both Catherine and Mr. Spitzer grapple with what is real and what is illusion. Catherine challenges Mr. Spitzer on his stories of travel, on the whereabouts of the black coachman, and on the nature of the world around them, pointing out contradictions and impossibilities, suggesting that much of what is accepted as real is mutable and uncertain. Mr. Spitzer’s evasiveness and Catherine’s accusations of his lying deepen this uncertainty.
  • The description of the brother’s funeral, with its symbolic white roses and horse racing imagery, stands out as a poignant moment that crystallizes the theme of mourning and the loneliness of the surviving Mr. Spitzer. The image of the corpse as the only mourner is a powerful metaphor for isolation and the burden of memory.
  • Mr. Spitzer’s retreat into composing “silent music,” music not heard by living ears but meant for the dead, symbolizes his withdrawal from the world and the limits of communication between the living and the dead, between reality and dream. This motif ties into the overarching theme of failed communication and the ineffability of certain experiences.
  • “Her body was the carriage, and her soul, now it seemed, was the passenger, and her horses were her will, and the coachman was her conscience.” Catherine’s own map of herself is the ancient chariot of the soul.
  • Catherine orders her Black servant buried with her carriage to serve her in death, claims it “had been the coachman’s idea, not hers,” cannot recall his name, and admits he “had had no wages for years.” She is the mistress who will not let even death end his service.
  • At dawn she asks for “the grave… of the other Mr. Spitzer, the slow one, the sick musician she had always loved.” The living twin is now the dead one.

Questions and observations

Reading closely

  • “If she could find him, she could perhaps find herself, the bewildered passenger.” Why does everything depend on the coachman?
  • “He could not say no unless he should say yes.” What does this say about Mr. Spitzer’s silence?
  • “The loser was the victor.” Who won the game between the twins?

Characters

  • “What, my mother would ask, had been that black coachman’s name? … but what was a name?” What does Catherine’s forgetting reveal?
  • Joachim lets strangers believe he is his brother: “Thus his brother lived.” Is this love, guilt, or something else?
  • Catherine “was very much confused by clarities.” What is she clear about?

Connections

  • Mr. Spitzer’s “dead ear” from Chapter 13 has moved from right to left. Why does Catherine keep changing which ear is dead?
  • The life-sized chessmen and invisible players of Chapter 13 become the Devil playing “with man for man’s soul.” Who is playing here?
  • Rhadamanthus judged Mr. Spitzer in Chapter 11, and now Catherine tries “Spitzer versus Spitzer.” What is the charge?

Reflection

  • Can a person go on serving someone past death? Should anyone be asked to?
  • Is it possible to live another person’s life to keep him alive?
  • “One understands the mystery only by proposing the greater mystery.” Is that true?

Research: Characters

Catherine Cartwheel (Vera’s Mother)

  • Ailing and often delirious, she is obsessed with locating the black coachman and understanding the fate of her family’s legacy.
  • She experiences visions and hallucinations, blurring the line between reality and fantasy.
  • She is deeply distrustful of Mr. Spitzer and concerned that her last wishes have been ignored or betrayed.
  • In “codicil after codicil” she left the coachman first one thing and then “everything,” even her old, empty gowns, though he was dead or unpaid.

Joachim Spitzer

  • Joachim Spitzer is depicted as one of two Mr. Spitzers (twins or doubles) each reflecting and haunting the other. The chapter explores the idea that there were “four Mr. Spitzers,” due to reflections and mirrored images, and that the boundaries between them blur, creating a complicated identity crisis.
  • This duality extends to the notion that one Mr. Spitzer is “vacant and slow and smiling,” while the other had died by suicide, attempting to “kill the Mr. Spitzer who was the pale reflection in his own heart.”
  • The surviving Spitzer is burdened by his brother’s shadow, the “dark counterpart running through all his nights and days,” which disrupts his peace and confounds his existence.
  • Joachim is portrayed as a man who has not achieved conventional success.
  • He is described as a “failure,” living “the most retired, the most unassuming life” in the shadow of his brother’s more colorful and gregarious personality.
  • Despite his literal-mindedness and conservative habits, he is haunted by self-doubt and confusion, often unsure of his own actions and memories.
  • Instances such as finding his brother’s belongings in his coat pockets, or the mysterious “second cup of coffee” he supposedly drank but cannot explain, illustrate his fragmented sense of self and reality.
  • Joachim’s relationship with Vera’s mother is complex. He is her lawyer, executor, and companion in her illness, yet she doubts his trustworthiness and resents his evasiveness and silence.
  • Catherine’s obsession with the black coachman (a symbolic figure representing continuity, memory, and conscience) serves as a foil to Joachim’s own failures and ambiguities.
  • She accuses him of neglecting or betraying the black coachman and the family’s legacy, suggesting that he may have “cheated the black coachman out of his employment and inheritance” and failed to honor her dying wishes.
  • Joachim’s inability or unwillingness to answer her questions about the black coachman and other matters deepens the tension and highlights his evasive nature.
  • Joachim is a man of silence and restraint, in contrast to his brother’s vibrant life.
  • He has ceased composing “oral music” and instead writes “silent music, a dirge for a dead clam,” symbolizing his withdrawal from active life and communication.
  • This self-imposed silence and his “utter self-forgetfulness and selflessness” suggest a man resigned to obscurity and loss, attempting to protect himself and others from the chaos that surrounds him.
  • His life is overshadowed by the death of his brother, an event that has left him “hopelessly benumbed” and struggling to keep up with time and reality.
  • He is pursued by people who mistake him for his deceased brother, and he attempts to shield his brother’s memory, sometimes maintaining the illusion that the brother still lives.
  • This haunting presence causes him distress but also a certain pride in having “preferred the last footstep, the last doorway,” indicating a preference for quiet endurance over dramatic exit.
  • Joachim is enveloped in mystery and ambiguity. His actions and whereabouts are uncertain; he is sometimes imagined wearing the black coachman’s livery, sometimes unable to explain trivial facts like train journeys.
  • His existence blurs the line between the living and the dead, the real and the illusory.
  • He is “a man who did not know himself” and whose life is marked by “minor but palpable discrepancies” and “things which did not add up.”
  • Joachim’s character is embedded in a cosmic framework where ordinary human concerns intersect with metaphysical questions.
  • He and Catherine speak of “the music of the spheres,” “the silent music,” and the “lawless image of the dream,” suggesting a man grappling with the ultimate nature of reality and existence.
  • His legal work, particularly the “case of Spitzer versus Spitzer,” symbolizes his internal conflict and the unresolved tensions of his identity.
  • Joachim shows a degree of faithfulness and compassion, toward Catherine.
  • He visits Catherine regularly, tries to please her, and protects her interests “to the best of his present legal ability.” However, his “slumberous inertia” and evasiveness frustrate her, revealing a gap between his intentions and her expectations.
  • Joachim Spitzer’s life is inextricably linked to the death of his brother Peron. The brother’s suicide or accidental death seems to have precipitated a crisis in Joachim’s identity and existence.
  • He is described as having taken up his brother’s mantle in some respects: wearing his brother’s cufflinks, carrying his cane, and even being mistaken for him by acquaintances. Yet he is also deeply burdened by the consequences, trying to protect his brother’s reputation while simultaneously being haunted by his brother’s unresolved, chaotic life.
  • This complicated relationship fuels Joachim’s feelings of inadequacy and deepens his tendency toward silence and withdrawal.

Peron Spitzer

  • The quick, brilliant twin, a gambler “in the horse circles,” who “had fallen from a tall building.”
  • Catherine calls him the one “loved by her, yet never loving her,” yet at dawn she mourns “the slow one, the sick musician,” confusing which twin she lost.

The Old Clam Digger

  • The clam-digger is Mr. Spitzer’s manservant.
  • He swears Mr. Spitzer drank the second cup of coffee himself.

The Black Coachman

  • A symbolic and somewhat mythical figure associated with the family’s carriage and horses.
  • Represents continuity, memory, and the link between life and death.
  • Catherine’s wish was for the black coachman to be buried with the carriage and horses so that she might continue to “go driving” even after death.
  • His actual fate and whereabouts are uncertain, and this uncertainty fuels much of Catherine’s anguish.
  • Catherine has also defined the Black Coachman as her conscience.
  • Catherine insists the burial was “the coachman’s idea, not hers,” that “money had meant nothing to him,” though he had no wages for years, the old excuses of those who kept Black servants unpaid.
  • She cannot remember his name, only his “white, rolling eyes.”

Research: Themes

Memory, Identity, and Duality

See: Memory and the Past · Identity and the Self · Duality and Doubles

  • The chapter explores fractured identities, especially through the figure of Mr. Spitzer and his deceased brother.
  • Catherine perceives multiple overlapping realities and versions of Mr. Spitzer, reflecting her confusion and the blurred boundaries of life and death.
  • The motif of “four Mr. Spitzers” suggests layered selves and mirrored images, raising questions about selfhood and existence.

Death and the Afterlife

See: Death and Mortality

  • Catherine’s visions often revolve around death, funerals, and the journey beyond life.
  • The black coachman and the family carriage symbolize passage and continuity after death, and also her conscience and her body.
  • There is a persistent questioning of what happens after death and whether true peace or harmony exists beyond.

Illusion versus Reality

See: Illusion and Reality

  • Catherine’s hallucinations and the shifting perceptions of Mr. Spitzer’s reliability highlight the tension between what is real and what is imagined.
  • Mr. Spitzer’s evasiveness and Catherine’s accusations create a dynamic where truth is elusive and layered with doubt.

Law and Order versus Chaos

See: Guilt, Innocence, and Justice · Order, Chaos, and Discipline

  • Mr. Spitzer embodies legal order but is portrayed as overwhelmed by the disorder of life and his own ghosts.
  • Catherine’s world is chaotic, filled with shifting images, ghosts, and memories that resist neat categorization.

Family Legacy and Betrayal

See: Memory and the Past

  • Catherine suspects Mr. Spitzer of betraying the black coachman and mishandling her will and the family estate.
  • There is a theme of lost inheritance, broken promises, and the failure of caretakers to uphold traditions.

Race and Servitude

See: Society, Class, and Race

  • The black coachman is unpaid, nameless, and ordered to serve in death.
  • He is described by the minstrel-show stereotype of “white, rolling eyes.”
  • Catherine’s slip, “the carriage and the white coachman and the four black horses, what had become of the color line?” turns the whole arrangement inside out.

Research: Symbols and Imagery

The Black Coachman and the Family Carriage

See: Horses and Carriages

  • Symbolizes continuity beyond death, the passage of time, and the family’s legacy, Catherine’s conscience and body.
  • The mystery of his grave and whether he was buried with his horses signifies Catherine’s fear of disruption and loss.

White Horses (King, Queen, Prince, Spade)

See: Horses and Carriages

  • These horses have personified names and represent stability and tradition.
  • Their fate is ambiguous, mirroring the uncertainty in the narrative.

Mr. Spitzer’s Hat and Garments

See: Clothing, Hats, and Skirts

  • The black cape, high silk hat, silver buttons evoke the image of the coachman, suggesting blurred identities and roles.

Playing Cards (Aces)

See: Cards, Games, and Chance

  • The four aces that drop from Mr. Spitzer’s sleeve symbolize the four Mr. Spitzers and the layered selves.
  • The cards also represent fate, chance, and the game of life and death.

The Funeral and the Graveyard

See: Weddings and Funerals

  • The funeral scenes, especially Mr. Spitzer’s brother’s funeral, symbolize mourning, loss, and the passage of time.
  • Catherine’s absence from funerals and the details of the mourning rituals emphasize her detachment and the fragmented nature of her existence.

Imagery of Water, Snow, and Night

See: The Sea and Water · Snow, Ice, and Winter

  • Recurring references to water, foaming seas, snowflakes, and darkness evoke a liminal, otherworldly atmosphere.
  • These natural elements symbolize change, decay, and the boundary between life and death.

Research: Resources

  • “the four white horses”: White horses in mythology are often associated with the sun chariot, warrior-heroes, fertility, and an end-of-time savior. The white horses symbolize the solemn, mystical journey of the soul from life into death and beyond, carrying Catherine through the shifting landscapes of memory, dream, and existence by her will. They are a powerful emblem of transition, purity, fate, and the ethereal nature of mortality in the novel. In Revelation, “behold a white horse: and he that sat on him had a bow; and a crown was given unto him” (Revelation 6:2). See Horses and Carriages and Revelation and the Apocalypse.
  • “the barkings of spotted coach dogs running beside the wheels”: Dalmatians were bred to run beside carriages, clearing the road and guarding the horses. See Dogs and Horses and Carriages.
  • “a dark porte-cochere”: A porte-cochere is a covered entrance where a carriage stops so its passengers can step down out of the weather.
  • “Nothing should be missing from the chaos, not one leaf that ever fell”: “Are not two sparrows sold for a farthing? and one of them shall not fall on the ground without your Father” (Matthew 10:29). See The Bible.
  • “her Seeing Eye dogs”: The Seeing Eye, the first American guide dog school, was founded in 1929. See Dogs and the Chapter 2 resources.
  • “she had asked, long, long ago, that the black coachman be buried with the carriage and the white horses”: Chariot burials are tombs in which the deceased was buried together with their chariot, usually including their horses and other possessions. An instance of a person being buried with their horse (without the chariot) is called horse burial. (Wikipedia)
    • In the royal tombs of Ur, Leonard Woolley found (1920s) grooms, attendants, and oxen buried with their masters’ carts, servants sent to serve in death.
  • “himself the food of worms”: “Your worm is your only emperor for diet” (Hamlet 4.3). See Shakespeare and the Chapter 10 resources.
  • “but what was a name?”: “What’s in a name? That which we call a rose / By any other word would smell as sweet” (Romeo and Juliet 2.2). Catherine says it of a servant whose name no one kept. See Shakespeare and The Black Coachman.
  • “King and Queen, Prince and Spade”: The horses are named like playing cards, and the aces fall later in the chapter. See Horses and Carriages and Gambling and Playing Cards.
  • “The black coachman had had no wages for years”: The history of domestic work in the United States is deeply intertwined with the exploitation of Black women, men, and immigrant laborers through systemic racism, limited economic opportunities, and discriminatory labor practices. Enslaved Black women performed essential, unpaid domestic labor before emancipation, with conditions often leading to sexual abuse and the work continuing in a similar vein after abolition. For both Black and immigrant workers, this path was one of few available options, resulting in low pay, long hours, and a lack of protections, while modern policies continue to perpetuate a cycle of vulnerability. See The Black Coachman and Society, Class, and Race.
  • “the black coachman with the white, rolling eyes”: The “white, rolling eyes” are the stock caricature of minstrel shows and early films, which made Black servants figures of fear and comedy. See The Black Coachman and Society, Class, and Race.
  • “instead of a winding sheet”: A winding sheet is a cloth to wrap a body with for burial. The winding sheet here serves as a powerful symbol of the inevitable mortality that envelops all, including the black coachman and the other characters intertwined in the narrative’s exploration of life, death, and memory. It is a reminder of the mortality underlying the novel’s dreamlike and sometimes surreal atmosphere. See Death and Mortality.
  • “in codicil after codicil”: A codicil is an amendment added to a will.
  • “she had not been unduly influenced or coerced, and she had been possessed of all her mental faculties”: The language of a will: “being of sound mind,” free of “undue influence.” A will can be overturned if its maker lacked capacity or was coerced.
  • “the twelve moons shining over Jupiter”: Galileo found four of Jupiter’s moons in 1610. The twelfth was found in 1951, so twelve was the count when Young wrote. See Astronomy.
  • “Did his right hand know what his left hand did”: “But when thou doest alms, let not thy left hand know what thy right hand doeth” (Matthew 6:3). See The Bible.
  • “the law of gravity defied and golden apples falling upward”: Newton’s falling apple, and the golden apples of the Hesperides. See Greek Mythology.
  • “the excellent clam-digger”: Mr. Spitzer’s manservant, who swears Mr. Spitzer drank the second cup of coffee himself. See The Old Clam Digger.
  • “the Manchurian or some other conflict”: Manchuria is a region of northeast China. The conflict is likely Japan’s seizure of it in 1931, or the Russo-Japanese War of 1904-05, fought there.
  • “suits for heart’s balm”: Breach-of-promise and alienation-of-affection suits, which many states abolished in the 1930s.
  • “their cosmic union in the womb of time”: “There are many events in the womb of time which will be delivered” (Othello 1.3). See Shakespeare, Twins and Doubles, and the Chapter 5 resources.
  • “the plural melody which was not Mr. Spitzer’s composition or choice”: His “melody moving or attended by one or more related but independent arrangements of sounds” is nearly the dictionary definition of polyphony, or counterpoint, several independent melodies sounding at once. See Music and Composers.
  • “he had spoken to her out of the whirlwind”: “Then the Lord answered Job out of the whirlwind” (Job 38:1). See The Book of Job.
  • “There should be the same divisions and multiplications”: Multiplicity is a philosophical concept developed by Edmund Husserl and Henri Bergson from Riemann’s description of the mathematical concept. Bergson distinguished two kinds: a countable multiplicity of distinct parts, and a qualitative one whose parts interpenetrate. (Wikipedia)
  • “the Battle of the Roses”: The Wars of the Roses (1455-1487) were a series of civil wars in England between the houses of York, with its white rose, and Lancaster, with its red. See Roses and Flowers.
  • “the funeral gondola with the corrugated angel at its helm”: Venice carries its dead by black gondola to the cemetery island of San Michele. Liszt wrote “La lugubre gondola” (1882) foreseeing Wagner’s death in Venice, and Wagner’s body left by gondola in 1883. See Weddings and Funerals and Music and Composers.
  • “the golden cock perched at the foot of her bed, that it was really Pythagoras shedding his golden feathers”: In Lucian’s dialogue “The Dream, or the Cock,” a cobbler’s rooster reveals that it is Pythagoras reborn. Pythagoras was said to have a golden thigh. Rimsky-Korsakov’s opera The Golden Cockerel (1909), from Pushkin’s tale (1834), has a golden cock that warns a tsar. See Pythagoras and the Music of the Spheres, Birds, and the Chapter 11 resources.
    • The teaching most securely identified with Pythagoras is the “transmigration of souls” or metempsychosis, which holds that every soul is immortal and, upon death, enters into a new body. He may have also devised the doctrine of musica universalis, which holds that the planets move according to mathematical equations and thus resonate to produce an inaudible symphony of music. (Wikipedia)
    • Alectryomancy is a form of divination involving roosters and a method of seeking answers or predictions by observing the behavior of roosters.
    • Weissenbach saw such a bird. Young was with her “when the golden bird, which was the spirit of Heraclitus, came and perched upon the bedpost” (Marguerite Young, interview with Charles Ruas, WBAI radio, New York), and remembered “a beautiful golden cockerel perched at the foot of her bed, sometimes emitting messages in the Greek language” (Marguerite Young, interview, WNYC radio, New York).
  • “Isabella of Spain”: Isabella I of Castile backed Columbus, established the Spanish Inquisition, and expelled Spain’s Jews in 1492.
  • “imaginary street Arabs”: “Street Arab” was the Victorian name for homeless children, a slur drawn from the image of Arabs as rootless wanderers. See Society, Class, and Race.
  • “a palimpsest of many hieroglyphic writings”: A palimpsest is a parchment scraped and written over, the old text still faintly showing. Thomas De Quincey called the human brain one in “The Palimpsest of the Human Brain” (1845). See The History of Opium.
  • “the appearance beyond the appearance”: Plato’s Allegory of the Cave, in which prisoners take the shadows on a wall for reality. See Plato and Platonism and the Chapter 12 resources.
  • “knew that the dog was Socrates”: Socrates was a Greek philosopher who wrote no texts of his own but is credited as one of the founders of Western philosophy. In the work Republic, written by Plato, there is a Socratic dialogue. In it Socrates argues that the dog is very much like a philosopher because the dog distinguishes the face of a friend and of an enemy only by the criterion of knowing and not knowing. (Wikipedia) Socrates swore “By the dog, the god of the Egyptians” (Gorgias 482b). See Plato and Platonism and Dogs.
  • “she had a third eye in her forehead”: The third eye is a mystical and esoteric concept of an invisible eye on the forehead that provides perception beyond ordinary sight. In Indian spiritual traditions it is the ajna, or brow, chakra, and Buddhists regard it as the “eye of consciousness.” (Wikipedia) The third eye symbolizes a mystical insight and a deeper understanding of the unseen worlds as an insight that both enlightens and alienates Catherine from ordinary human experience. Descartes placed the soul’s seat in the pineal gland, which some have called the third eye. See Descartes and Dualism, Hinduism, and the Chapter 43 resources.
  • “a skeleton with an hour-glass in his hands”: Death’s figure in the Dance of Death, carrying the hourglass of a life’s measured time. See Death and Mortality and the Chapter 6 resources.
  • “her peacocks”: Aristotle referred to the peacock’s vain reputation. The Roman poet Ennius, following the Pythagorean teaching of rebirth, dreamed that Homer’s soul had passed into a peacock and then into himself. See Birds.
  • “Mrs. Astor could not go, and Mrs. Vanderbilt would not be seen”: Mrs. Astor is Caroline Schermerhorn Astor, a famous American socialite who led the Four Hundred, the list of New York society in the Gilded Age. Mrs. Vanderbilt is likely Grace Graham Wilson Vanderbilt, another American socialite of the Vanderbilt family. In 1883 Alva Vanderbilt’s costume ball forced Mrs. Astor to call on the Vanderbilts, a famous defeat for old society. See Society, Class, and Race.
  • “Czar Kolokol, the King of the Bells”: It is known as the Tsar Bell. It is the largest bell in the world that has never rung. It was cast in 1733-35 and cracked in the Kremlin fire of 1737 when cold water struck the hot metal. (Wikipedia)
  • “Was it before or after the Revolution”: The Russian Revolution of 1917 refers to two distinct revolutions that occurred in that year, ultimately leading to the end of the Tsarist regime and the rise of Bolshevik rule in Russia. The first, the February Revolution, overthrew the Czar Nicholas II, while the second, the October Revolution, saw the Bolsheviks seize power. February Revolution (March 1917): Widespread strikes and protests in Petrograd (St. Petersburg) against food shortages and World War I led to the Tsar’s abdication and the establishment of a provisional government. October Revolution (November 1917): The Bolsheviks, led by Vladimir Lenin, seized control of the government, ending the provisional government and paving the way for a socialist state (Encyclopaedia Britannica). The Bolsheviks’ seizure of power ignited a civil war with anti-communist forces, ultimately resulting in the Bolshevik victory and the establishment of the Soviet Union. The United States did not recognize the Soviet Union until 1933, the point of Catherine never breaking “her diplomatic relations with Moscow.”
  • “the coachman was her conscience”: The Katha Upanishad: “Know the Self as the lord of the chariot, the body as the chariot, the intellect as the charioteer, the mind as the reins, and the senses as the horses.” In Plato’s Phaedrus, the soul is a charioteer driving two horses. See Hinduism, Plato and Platonism, and Horses and Carriages.
    • G. I. Gurdjieff likened a person to a horse and carriage: the horse is the emotional body, the carriage the physical body, and the driver the mind. (“Horse-and-buggy,” not “horse and carriage,” is the idiom for something outdated.) Funerals were traditionally drawn by horse and carriage before being replaced by automobiles. Even in the present day they are still used by the wealthy, for a famous person or significant death, or by someone wanting a special funeral procession.
    • A conscience is a cognitive process that elicits emotion and rational associations based on an individual’s moral philosophy or value system. In common terms, conscience is often described as leading to feelings of remorse when a person commits an act that conflicts with their moral values. (Wikipedia)
  • “the case of Spitzer versus Spitzer”: A case in which he “must appear as both the defender and the accuser.” See Joachim Spitzer, Peron Spitzer, and Twins and Doubles.
  • “Which was alpha, and which was omega?”: “I am Alpha and Omega, the beginning and the ending, saith the Lord” (Revelation 1:8). See Revelation and the Apocalypse and the Chapter 8 resources.
  • “a papal divorce from her dead husband”: The Church grants annulments, not divorces, and a husband’s death already ends a marriage.
  • “a fundamental human weakness which was the desire to be deceived”: “The world wants to be deceived, so let it be deceived.” Mundus vult decipi, ergo decipiatur. The saying is first found in Sebastian Franck (1534).
  • “the financial bubbles”: The South Sea Bubble of 1720, when shares in the South Sea Company soared and collapsed and ruined thousands.
  • “the Admiralty Law, the Lords Justices, the Vice-Chancellors, the Masters of the Rolls”: These are offices of the English courts: Admiralty law governs ships and the sea, the Vice-Chancellors sat in the Court of Chancery, and the Lords Justices and the Master of the Rolls sit in the Court of Appeal. Gilbert and Sullivan satirized this world of wigs and titles in Iolanthe (1882), which features the Lord Chancellor as a leading comic character.
  • “the pettifoggers”: A pettifogger is a lawyer whose methods are petty, underhanded, or disreputable.
  • “what had become of the color line?”: W. E. B. Du Bois: “The problem of the twentieth century is the problem of the color-line” (The Souls of Black Folk, 1903). Catherine has just turned the coachman white and the horses black. See Society, Class, and Race and The Black Coachman.
  • “the stone fleet manned by stone figures”: In 1861 the Union sank old New England whaling ships, loaded with stone, to block Charleston harbor. They were known as the Great Stone Fleet. See The Civil War.
  • “the antinomies, both true, each contradicting the other”: Kant set out four antinomies in the Critique of Pure Reason (1781). An antinomy is a real or apparent contradiction between two conclusions, both of which seem justified. It is a term used in logic and epistemology, particularly in the philosophy of Immanuel Kant. Kant’s antinomies are four: two “mathematical” and two “dynamical.” They are connected with (1) the limitation of the universe in respect of space and time (whether the universe has a beginning or is infinite), (2) the theory that the whole consists of indivisible atoms (whereas, in fact, none such exist), (3) the problem of free will in relation to universal causality (free will vs determinism), and (4) the existence of a necessary being. The first two antinomies are dubbed “mathematical” antinomies, presumably because in each case the concern is the relation between what are alleged to be sensible objects (either the world itself, or objects in it) and space and time. The second two are dubbed “dynamical” antinomies, presumably because the proponents of the thesis are not committing themselves solely to claims about spatio-temporal objects. (Wikipedia) See Kant and Hegel.
  • “the octave, the eighth day of the week”: Early Christians called Sunday “the eighth day,” the day of the resurrection. A liturgical octave is a feast kept for eight days.
  • “a delusion and a snare”: From Lord Denman’s judgment in O’Connell v. The Queen (1844): “a mockery, a delusion, and a snare.”
  • “driving a coach and six through a legal statute”: Attributed to the Irish judge Stephen Rice in the 1680s: “I will drive a coach and six through the Act of Settlement.” See Horses and Carriages.
  • “a short life but a merry one”: “A merry life and a short one,” the motto of the pirate Bartholomew Roberts (1720s).
  • “a long weekend in Newport”: Newport, Rhode Island, where Gilded Age families summered in marble “cottages.” See Society, Class, and Race and the Chapter 10 resources.
  • “Mr. Spitzer had attended Mr. Spitzer’s funeral”: Tom Sawyer and Huck Finn watch their own funeral from the church gallery (The Adventures of Tom Sawyer, 1876). See American Writers.
  • “a horseshoe of white roses”: Floral horseshoes and saddles of roses honored racing men. Since 1932 the Kentucky Derby winner has worn a garland of roses. See Roses and Flowers, Horses and Carriages, and the Chapter 43 resources.
  • “the Phoenician fleet”: The Phoenicians, a seafaring people of the eastern Mediterranean, were the great sailors of the ancient world. Herodotus reports that Phoenician sailors went around Africa for Pharaoh Necho (c. 600 BC).
  • “the Thirty Years’ War”: The Thirty Years’ War (1618-1648) was fought in Central Europe by different countries and included fighting between Catholics and Protestants.
  • “Dr. Galen”: Galen was a Greek doctor in the Roman Empire. See the Chapter 13 resources.
  • “Copernicus, the author of that great celestial revolution”: Nicolaus Copernicus formulated a model of the universe that placed the Sun rather than Earth at its center. (Wikipedia) His findings triggered the Copernican Revolution. His book was De revolutionibus (1543). Freud named Copernicus, with Darwin and psychoanalysis, as one of three blows to human pride (“A Difficulty in the Path of Psycho-Analysis,” 1917). See Astronomy.
  • “He had dreamed that he had climbed a tensile rope to heaven”: The Indian rope trick, in which a rope rises into the air and a boy climbs it out of sight, and Jacob’s dream of a ladder “set up on the earth, and the top of it reached to heaven” (Genesis 28:12). See The Bible and the Chapter 2 resources.
  • “the music of the spheres, the silent music”: Boethius was a Roman senator, consul, magister officiorum, polymath, historian, and philosopher of the Early Middle Ages. He sought to reconcile the teachings of Plato and Aristotle with Christian theology. He broke logic into three parts: that which defines, that which divides, and that which deduces. There are three types of arguments: those of necessity, of ready believability, and sophistry. In De Musica there are three classifications: Musica mundana, Musica humana, Musica instrumentalis. In Dante’s Divine Comedy, the spirit of Boethius is pointed out by Saint Thomas Aquinas and is mentioned further in the poem. In his book De Institutione Musica (Fundamentals of Music) his drawings appear striking and may be an inspiration for the organization of Young’s novel. Musica universalis or music of the spheres or harmony of the spheres is a Greek philosophical concept founded by Pythagoras. This metaphysical principle stated that mathematical relationships could produce ‘tones’ of energy that could produce, among other things, sounds. Pythagoras proposed that the celestial bodies all have their own unique hum based on their orbital revolution. This idea influenced many scholars until the end of the Renaissance. Johannes Kepler, a German astronomer from the 1600s wrote extensively on the subject. (Wikipedia) Later astronomy set it aside. Boethius wrote The Consolation of Philosophy in prison awaiting execution, with its Wheel of Fortune. See Pythagoras and the Music of the Spheres and Dante.
  • “one understands the mystery only by proposing the greater mystery”: The Latin obscurum per obscurius, explaining the obscure by the more obscure.
  • “paper-backed dream books sold by fortunetellers”: Dream books matched dreams to numbers for the policy, or numbers, game played in poor neighborhoods, as in Aunt Sally’s Policy Players’ Dream Book (1889). See Gambling and Playing Cards.
  • “They placed the planets forty degrees off their course”: Because of the precession of the equinoxes, the signs of Western astrology have drifted from their constellations by nearly a whole sign since antiquity. See Astrology, Alchemy, and Esoterica.
  • “The playing card dropping from his sleeve each morning had nearly always been an ace”: The “ace up the sleeve” is the cardsharp’s hidden card. In most fortune-telling, the ace of spades is the death card. See Gambling and Playing Cards and Cards, Games, and Chance.
    • In fortune telling the Ace of Hearts when among hearts implies love, friendship, and affection; with diamonds, money and news of distant friends; with clubs, festivities, and social or domestic rejoicing; with spades, disagreements, misunderstandings, contention, or misfortune; individually, it stands for the house; Ace of Diamonds means a ring or paper money; Ace of Clubs means wealth, a peaceful home, industry, and general prosperity; Ace of Spades means love affairs, or conveys a warning that troubles await the inquirer through bad speculations or ill-chosen friends (P. R. S. Foli, Fortune-Telling by Cards, 1915).
    • The mystical meaning of cards for fortune telling are the fifty-two cards in the pack correspond with the fifty-two weeks in the year. The thirteen cards in each suit symbolize the thirteen lunar months, and the thirteen weeks in each quarter. There are four suits, as there are four seasons in the year. There are twelve court cards in the pack, just as there are twelve calendar months and twelve signs of the Zodiac. Counting ace as one and king as thirteen, the four suits add up to 364, and with the joker, 365, the days of the year (P. R. S. Foli, Fortune-Telling by Cards, 1915; Manly P. Hall, The Secret Teachings of All Ages, 1928).
  • “the Devil plays with man for man’s soul”: Moritz Retzsch’s painting The Chess Players (1831) shows Satan playing chess with a young man for his soul while an angel watches. See Fate and Chance.
  • “The club, which was trifoliate, might be transformed into the sign of the cross”: The club suit is a trefoil, and the shamrock was said to teach the Trinity. See Gambling and Playing Cards.
  • “There were many transformations, many butterflies”: Steven Shaviro writes of the novel, “The difficulty of interpretation in this novel is that in a certain sense, there is nothing to interpret, since everything is right there; but the difficulty comes in grasping and holding onto just how these entirely clear phrases metamorphose into one another, intensify or double one another, contradict one another, derail one another, and so on” (Steven Shaviro, “Lost Chords and Interrupted Births: Marguerite Young’s Exorbitant Vision,” Critique: Studies in Contemporary Fiction, 1990).
  • “a place set for the dead”: The “dumb supper,” a folk custom of setting a place at table for the dead. See Death and Mortality.
  • “a horse doctor talking as if he were an argumentative centaur”: Chiron, the wise centaur, was a healer and teacher of heroes. See Greek Mythology and the Chapter 2 resources.
  • “at shrouded parimutuel windows”: The parimutuel, a betting pool shared among the winners, was invented by Joseph Oller in Paris in 1867. See Gambling and Playing Cards and Peron Spitzer.
  • “incongruent harpers harping congruously”: “I heard the voice of harpers harping with their harps” (Revelation 14:2). See Revelation and the Apocalypse.
  • “changed trains at Hartford”: The New York, New Haven and Hartford Railroad electrified its lines from 1907. Hartford was “the insurance capital,” home of Aetna and Travelers, and Wallace Stevens worked there as an insurance executive. See the Chapter 13 resources.
  • “Queen Victoria was dead”: She died January 22, 1901.
