Chapter 20

← Chapter 19 · Home · Chapter 21 →

Summary

In the full light of dawn, Vera studies the sleeping woman. It is “the light which had already killed the heart of Miss MacIntosh,” stripping her “bare as roses of their petals”: no “crowning glory of woman’s hair,” no single hair “to suggest a possibility of future growth,” and the “narrow and intolerable vacancy” where the other breast should be. Vera wonders who robbed her of her hair, and when, whether hair by hair or all at once, whether a broken heart caused it, whether she was “deserted at the altar by her bridegroom or her bride.” Then she makes her resolve. She will go on “as if I had never seen her,” iron the shirts with new alacrity, learn the Hebrew measures, coins, months, and the stations of the Exodus, and “protect her from the knowledge of herself.” The old routine is already “the elegiac past,” and she will “hold to every moment as if I lived with a dying man.” Near the end Vera asks, “Was God bald, too,” in a litany of the Bible’s images for God, and she closes knowing she has come “close to something which none should see and live to relate.”

Characters present

Miss MacIntosh · Vera Cartwheel · Catherine Cartwheel

Concepts present

Themes: Death and Mortality · Decay and Ruin · Faith, God, and the Supernatural · Grief, Loss, and Mourning · Identity and the Self · Light and Darkness · The Search for Meaning · Women, Gender, and Marriage

Symbols: Angels, Devils, and Myth · Hair, Wig, and Baldness · Lamps, Candles, and Light · Mirrors and Reflections · Weddings and Funerals

Philosophy: Augustine and Christian Theology · Kant and Hegel

Allusions: Ancient Egypt · Astronomy · Dante · Ecclesiastes · Exploration and the Poles · Fairy Tales and Folklore · Gambling and Playing Cards · Genesis · Judaism · Revelation and the Apocalypse · Shakespeare · Suicide in History and Literature · The Bible · The Book of Job

Key passages

From the research

  • The chapter opens with a vivid depiction of dawn which paradoxically serves as both illumination and a force that has “already killed the heart of Miss MacIntosh” before her actual death. The light reveals wounds and deprivations that “would not heal with time,” suggesting an exposure of deep, irrevocable suffering and loss.
  • A striking passage focuses on the physical absence of hair on Miss MacIntosh’s head which symbolically represents a loss of feminine identity, vitality, and perhaps a history of mourning or trauma. Vera reflects on the significance of hair as beauty or terror and wonders about the circumstances of her hair loss, whether gradual or sudden, linking it to emotional or existential devastation.
  • Vera experiences a powerful tension between the recognition of Miss MacIntosh’s vulnerable, altered state and a desire to revert to ignorance for the sake of “common sense” and routine. There is a determined resolve to “go on as if I had never seen her,” to protect her from the knowledge of herself, and to maintain the illusion of normalcy despite the stark reality of her condition.
  • The passage detailing Vera’s imagined daily routines contrasts sharply with the internal, almost mystical knowledge of Miss MacIntosh’s profound deprivation. Vera contemplates learning ancient measures, weights, and biblical geography, suggesting a search for meaning or order amid chaos and personal loss.
  • Toward the end, Vera muses deeply about mortality, identity, and divinity. The baldness and missing breast become metaphors for the exposed realities of life and death, while Vera questions the nature of God with rich biblical imagery, reflecting on God’s multifaceted definitions as friend, refuge, crown, and shadow. This passage underscores the theme of confronting harsh truths and the limits of human understanding.
  • The final lines evoke a solemn recognition of the “image of life failing before his eyes,” highlighting Vera’s acute awareness of mortality and the profound emotional weight of witnessing the decline of a once vibrant individual.
  • “I should hold to every moment as if I lived with a dying man, and I should protect her from the knowledge of herself.” Vera’s resolve turns the daily routine into an elegy.

Questions and observations

Reading closely

  • “It was surely the light which had already killed her.” What does the dawn take from Miss MacIntosh?
  • “I should have been less surprised to have found her with a red beard than with no hair at all.” Why would a beard surprise Vera less?
  • Vera promises to learn the digit, the cubit, the gerah, and Nisan and Elul. Why does she turn to measuring now?

Characters

  • Miss MacIntosh was “not endowed… with intuitive imagination.” How does Vera use that to keep the secret?
  • “It would be easy to deceive her.” What has Vera learned about deception overnight?
  • “Was she her only lover?” What does Vera suspect about her past?

Connections

  • Chapter 10’s dream made Miss MacIntosh the bridegroom. Here Vera asks if she was “deserted at the altar by her bridegroom or her bride.” How do the two scenes speak to each other?
  • The Israelites wander from Egypt to Canaan, and “some die… on their way.” How does that journey match Vera’s?
  • In Chapter 15, Miss MacIntosh said “none should ever see it and live.” How does Vera come “close to something which none should see and live to relate”?

Reflection

  • Can keeping someone’s secret be a way of loving them?
  • “Grey hair does not signify a necessary wisdom.” What does?
  • Is pretending that we are simple ever simple?

Research: Characters

Miss MacIntosh

  • A figure of strength and common sense, yet marked by profound physical and existential deprivation.
  • Described as “hale and hearty, a red-headed nursemaid” in the past, yet now revealed in a state of vulnerability and loss.
  • Her condition is a mystery to Vera, who struggles to reconcile her external robustness with the internal and physical ravages revealed by the light.
  • She embodies the tension between resilience and suffering, denial and revelation.
  • Vera resolves to “protect her from the knowledge of herself.”
  • She had never wished to travel or see the world, “for she had seen enough of it,” and she was “cryptic as to any forlorn romance of the past.”

Vera Cartwheel

  • Exhibits complex emotions: pity, love, denial, and a protective instinct toward Miss MacIntosh.
  • Is philosophical and reflective, wrestling with large existential questions prompted by Miss MacIntosh’s condition.
  • Exhibits a desire to maintain normalcy and routine to shield both herself and Miss MacIntosh from harsh truths.
  • She plans to deceive Miss MacIntosh, as she “had often done before,” and to pretend “that it was someone else I dreamed of.”

Research: Themes

Light as a Revealing and Destructive Force

See: Light and Darkness

  • Dawn and light symbolize both revelation and destruction. Vera suggests that light has “already killed the heart of Miss MacIntosh” before her physical death, exposing wounds that cannot heal and deprivations that are eternal.
  • The light strips away illusions, revealing the “fearful forehead” and the “bald and naked, cloudless summit” of Miss MacIntosh’s head, symbolizing a harsh unveiling of truth and vulnerability.
  • There’s also a paradoxical beauty in the light, described as “diamond dawn” and “celestial aureole,” which offers hope for redemption and healing, yet simultaneously exposes harsh realities.

Loss and Absence

See: Grief, Loss, and Mourning

  • Miss MacIntosh’s baldness is a potent symbol of loss: loss of hair as a “crowning glory,” loss of feminine nature, and the missing breast as a “door knob,” a stark reminder of what is absent.
  • Vera questions the cause and timing of this loss: was it gradual or sudden? Was it caused by heartbreak, mourning, or some unknowable trauma?
  • This absence is not just physical but metaphysical, representing the stripping away of identity and vitality.

Mortality and the Inevitability of Decay

See: Death and Mortality · Decay and Ruin

  • Vera reflects on mortality, decay, and the “wounds in our sides” that light will bind up to prevent death like “Saul or Solomon or Sennacherib.”
  • There is a tension between the desire to protect Miss MacIntosh from the knowledge of her own condition and the inevitability of facing harsh truths.
  • The novel grapples with the idea that despite external appearances or the passage of time, some wounds and losses are timeless and unhealable.

Identity and Self-Perception

See: Identity and the Self

  • Miss MacIntosh’s lack of “intuitive imagination” and her common sense shield her from the deeper, visionary truths Vera perceives; she is “content with things just as they were” and would deny or not suspect the “empty vision” beyond the commonplace.
  • Vera’s internal conflict involves a desire to pretend normalcy to protect both Miss MacIntosh and herself from confronting the full reality of her condition.
  • There is also a complex emotional dynamic, where Vera simultaneously sees her as an “obstacle” to her happiness and as someone deeply significant, a secret lover or cause of her “vain pursuits.”

Spiritual and Existential Questions

See: Faith, God, and the Supernatural · The Search for Meaning

  • The narrative moves toward existential and spiritual reflection, pondering God’s nature, the problem of creation, and the place of suffering and imperfection in the divine order.
  • Vera likens the “baldness” and loss to a profound experience, possibly greater than mere mortal wisdom or aging, invoking biblical and mythological imagery.
  • The chapter closes with a meditation on life failing before one’s eyes and the idea of seeing something no one “should see and live to relate.”

Research: Symbols and Imagery

Hair and Baldness

See: Hair, Wig, and Baldness

  • Hair symbolizes beauty, identity, and vitality; baldness represents loss, vulnerability, and exposure.
  • Absence of hair is described as a “barren, impoverished landscape without flower or bush or hedge.”

Light and Dawn

See: Lamps, Candles, and Light

  • Dawn is both “diamond” and “many-prismed,” a metaphor for clarity, revelation, but also a harsh revealer of truth.
  • The “Aurora Borealis” in her sparsely furnished bedroom suggests a surreal, otherworldly illumination, the “first experience of light” upon uncreated things.

Missing Breast

See: Women, Gender, and Marriage

  • The missing breast is a stark physical symbol of loss and incompleteness, described as “like a door knob,” emphasizing its unnatural absence.

Biblical and Mythological References

See: The Bible · Angels, Devils, and Myth

  • References to biblical figures (Saul, Solomon, Sennacherib) and ancient measurements, calendars, and places (Nisan, Jyar, Wady Feiran, Egypt to Canaan) ground the narrative in a spiritual and temporal history.
  • Quotes and allusions to Ovid and Greek perspectives on beauty and hair enhance the classical depth of the novel.

Research: Resources

  • “shall bind up the wounds in our sides”: “He healeth the broken in heart, and bindeth up their wounds” (Psalm 147:3). The wounds “in our sides” recall the wound in Christ’s side (John 19:34), which Thomas was told to touch (John 20:27). See The Bible.
  • “that we shall not die like Saul or Solomon or Sennacherib in the midst of our corruption”: Saul fell on his own sword (1 Samuel 31:4). Solomon “slept with his fathers” (1 Kings 11:43) after his wives “turned away his heart after other gods” (1 Kings 11:4). Sennacherib was killed by his sons while he worshipped in the house of his god Nisroch (2 Kings 19:37). See The Bible and Suicide in History and Literature.
  • “celestial aureole”: An aureole is a radiant light around the head or body of a representation of a sacred personage.
  • “when we shall put on our shining armor”: “Let us put on the armour of light” (Romans 13:12), and “Put on the whole armour of God” (Ephesians 6:11). See The Bible.
  • “those who dwell in hidden caves beneath the overhanging, moss-grown rocks”: The kings and great men “hid themselves in the dens and in the rocks of the mountains; And said to the mountains and rocks, Fall on us” (Revelation 6:15-16). See Revelation and the Apocalypse.
  • “dark as the ace of spades”: The ace of spades has long been called the death card. The deuce of clubs was “the omen of death” in Chapter 19. See Gambling and Playing Cards and the Chapter 19 resources.
  • “haunted rays of Aurora Borealis”: The northern lights. The Latin name, “northern dawn,” joins Aurora, the Roman goddess of the dawn, and Boreas, the north wind, and is usually credited to Galileo (1619). See Astronomy and Exploration and the Poles.
  • “the experimental light of the first day of crazed creation”: “And the Spirit of God moved upon the face of the waters. And God said, Let there be light: and there was light” (Genesis 1:2-3). See Genesis.
  • “celebrating his triumphs over the Devil and the flesh”: The Litany in the Book of Common Prayer (1549): “From all the deceits of the world, the flesh, and the devil, Good Lord, deliver us.”
  • “less surprised to have found her with a red beard”: The red mustache Vera gave her in Chapter 9. See the Chapter 9 resources and the Chapter 17 resources.
  • “There was no crowning glory of woman’s hair”: “If a woman have long hair, it is a glory to her: for her hair is given her for a covering” (1 Corinthians 11:15). See The Bible, Hair, Wig, and Baldness, and Women, Gender, and Marriage.
  • “Ugly is a field without grass, a plant without leaves, a head without hair, according to Ovid”: Ovid, The Art of Love (3.249-250): “Turpe pecus mutilum, turpe est sine gramine campus, / et sine fronde frutex, et sine crine caput” (“Ugly is a hornless bull, ugly a field without grass, a bush without leaves, and a head without hair”). The lines come in his advice to women on hiding the loss of hair, which includes buying false hair. See Hair, Wig, and Baldness.
  • “Hair adds beauty to a good face and terror to an ugly one, according to the Greek”: Plutarch’s Life of Lycurgus (22) explains that the Spartans wore their hair long, remembering a saying of their lawgiver Lycurgus “that a fine head of hair made the handsome more comely still, and the ugly more terrible.” See Hair, Wig, and Baldness.
  • “the wheels within wheels”: Ezekiel’s vision: “their work was as it were a wheel in the middle of a wheel” (Ezekiel 1:16). See The Bible.
  • “Calvinistic rigors and denials and aggressions”: John Calvin (1509-1564) taught predestination, that God has chosen from eternity who will be saved. Calvinism shaped the Puritans and the Presbyterian and Reformed churches. Young sets its rigor against a woman’s “vague evasions and whimsicalities.” See Augustine and Christian Theology.
  • “Had some old crow plucked each hair away?”: In Aesop’s fable, a middle-aged man had two sweethearts. The young one plucked out his grey hairs, the old one his dark ones, until he was bald. See Fairy Tales and Folklore.
  • “Was she deserted at the altar by her bridegroom or her bride?”: Compare Miss Havisham in Dickens’s Great Expectations (1861), jilted on her wedding day, who stopped every clock and wore her wedding dress ever after. See Weddings and Funerals.
  • “this which was like sackcloth and ashes”: Mordecai “put on sackcloth with ashes” (Esther 4:1), and Christ says the cities “would have repented long ago in sackcloth and ashes” (Matthew 11:21). See The Bible.
  • “the existence which is the phenomenal beyond which we do not inquire”: Kant’s Critique of Pure Reason (1781) separates the phenomenal world, things as they appear to us, from the noumenal, things as they are in themselves, which we cannot know. See Kant and Hegel.
  • “recite the genealogies and names of those who fled into a desert”: The genealogies of Chapter 9. See the Chapter 9 resources.
  • “the digit or fingerbreadth, the tophach or handbreadth, the cubit, the fathom, the reed, the foot”: Miss MacIntosh’s lessons follow the tables of measures, weights, months, and Exodus stations printed in the back of many old Bibles. See Judaism.
    • The digit, or fingerbreadth, was about three-quarters of an inch.
    • The tophach, or handbreadth, was four fingers, about three inches. The table of the tabernacle has “a border of an hand breadth” (Exodus 25:25).
    • The cubit ran from the elbow to the fingertip, about eighteen inches. The long, or royal, cubit was about twenty inches.
    • The fathom is six feet, the span of outstretched arms. Paul’s sailors “sounded, and found it twenty fathoms” (Acts 27:28).
    • The measuring reed of Ezekiel’s temple vision was “six cubits long” (Ezekiel 40:5), about nine to ten feet. John is given “a reed like unto a rod” to measure the temple (Revelation 11:1).
    • A foot is a unit of measurement for length that is equal to 12 inches.
  • “the value of the Attic drachma, the gerah, the beka, the maneh, the talent”: The coins and weights of the Greeks and Hebrews, part of humanity’s effort to impose order and meaning on life. See Judaism.
    • The Attic Drachma was a silver coin and monetary unit of ancient Athens. It was one of the world’s earliest coins and was used from the 6th century BC until the Roman period. It had the head of Athena on one side and an owl on the other. (Wikipedia)
    • A gerah was an ancient Hebrew unit of weight and currency, the smallest the Hebrews used: “a shekel is twenty gerahs” (Exodus 30:13). The gerah also appears in Leviticus 27:25, Numbers 3:47 and 18:16, and Ezekiel 45:12.
    • The beka was a unit of weight equal to half a shekel: “A bekah for every man, that is, half a shekel” (Exodus 38:26). It was used as a counterweight for the silver half shekel brought to the temple each year. Abraham’s servant gave Rebekah “a golden earring of half a shekel weight” (Genesis 24:22).
    • In the Bible, maneh is a unit of weight that is sometimes translated as “pound.” It appears in Ezekiel 45:12, 1 Kings 10:17, Ezra 2:69, and Nehemiah 7:71-72. A maneh is estimated to weigh around 2.5 or 3 pounds.
    • In the Bible, a talent was a unit of weight and money and it also appears in the parable of the talents. A talent weighed about 75 pounds (34 kilograms), or 3,000 shekels (“Bekahs, Shekels, and Talents,” Ensign, August 1987). The Israelites used 29 talents of gold to build the tabernacle (Exodus 38:24). A talent was worth 20 years of labor. The parable of the talents (Matthew 25:14-30) is about a master who entrusts his wealth to three servants while he goes away on a journey. The parable is often interpreted as a lesson on the responsible use of one’s abilities, resources, and gifts.
  • “I would learn the Jewish calendar”: The Jewish calendar is a lunisolar calendar, which means it’s based on both the moon and the sun. It has 12 months, with each month containing either 29 or 30 days. To keep it in step with the solar year, a leap month is added seven times in every 19 years, the Metonic cycle. The months are Nisan, Iyar, Sivan, Tammuz, Av, Elul, Tishrei, Heshvan, Kislev, Tevet, Shevat, and Adar. In leap years, Adar becomes Adar II and another month, Adar I, is added before it. (Wikipedia) The civil year begins on Rosh Hashanah, but Nisan is the first month of the religious year: “This month shall be unto you the beginning of months” (Exodus 12:2). “Jyar” is an old spelling of Iyar. The calendar’s structure ensures that Jewish holidays take place in the correct season. It is significant as a motif of disciplined learning, historical consciousness, and the search for order in a world otherwise marked by instability and dreamlike disorientation. See Judaism.
  • “the names of the antediluvian patriarchs”: The antediluvian patriarchs are the individuals listed in Genesis 5 who lived before the Noachian flood: Adam, Seth, Enosh, Kenan, Mahalalel, Jared, Enoch, Methuselah, Lamech, and Noah. (Wikipedia) They represent the lineage of humanity before the Great Flood. Methuselah lived “nine hundred sixty and nine years” (Genesis 5:27). See Genesis.
  • “the itinerary of the children of Israel from Egypt to Canaan”: The Israelites’ journey from Egypt to Canaan involved a circuitous route through the wilderness, lasting approximately 40 years. The Israelites’ long journey is often attributed to their disobedience, doubt, and lack of faith in God’s leadership. God led them by a longer route to protect them from enemies and allow them time to develop their faith and trust: “God led them not through the way of the land of the Philistines, although that was near; for God said, Lest peradventure the people repent when they see war” (Exodus 13:17), and “your children shall wander in the wilderness forty years” (Numbers 14:33). See Ancient Egypt and The Bible.
    • In the Bible, Rameses refers to a city in Egypt and a pharaoh’s name. The city was a treasury city built by the Hebrews in Egypt. It was the Israelites’ departure point from Egypt (Exodus 12:37; Numbers 33:3).
    • Succoth was the Israelites’ first camp after leaving Rameses (Exodus 12:37; Numbers 33:5). Another Succoth, in Canaan, is where Jacob built booths (Genesis 33:17), and the feast of Sukkot celebrates the Israelites’ time in the desert.
    • In the Bible, Etham was a place where the Israelites camped after leaving Egypt and before turning back to Pi-hahiroth. It was a significant stop on their journey to the Promised Land (Exodus 13:20; Numbers 33:6-8).
    • Pi-hahiroth is the fourth station of the Exodus mentioned in Exodus 14:2. The biblical books Exodus and Numbers refer to Pi-hahiroth as the place where the Israelites encamped between Migdol and the sea, opposite Baal Zephon, while awaiting an attack by the Pharaoh, prior to crossing the Red Sea. (Wikipedia) Marah and Elim come after the crossing, in the wilderness of Shur.
    • Marah is a place where the Israelites found bitter water after crossing the Red Sea. The word “Marah” is Hebrew for “bitterness” (Exodus 15:22-27).
    • In the Bible, Elim was a place where the Israelites camped after leaving Egypt. It was the second stop after crossing the Red Sea, where there were “twelve wells of water, and threescore and ten palm trees” (Exodus 15:27; Numbers 33:9; Exodus 16:1).
  • “Where was the mouth of Wady Feiran?”: Wadi Feiran or Wadi Faran is Sinai’s largest and widest wadi (an Arabic term referring to a river valley or wet riverbed). It is an intermittent stream and rises from the mountains around Saint Catherine’s Monastery, at 2500 m above sea level. It is one of the alleged sites of Rephidim, a station of the Exodus where Moses struck a rock causing it to spring water, allowing his people the Hebrews to drink. (Wikipedia) “Wady” is the old spelling of wadi.
  • “Where was the desert of El-Tih?”: El-Tih, Arabic for “the wandering,” is the high limestone desert of central Sinai, named for the Israelites’ forty years of wandering.
    • The poem El Tih (1859) was written by Frederick Stewart, 4th Marquess of Londonderry, who signed his dedication only “L.” Its two cantos, written during a journey by Lake Como and through the Alps, “are called El Tih, or ‘The Wandering’” (El Tih and Other Poems, London, 1859), borrowing the Arabic name of the Sinai desert for the poet’s own wandering.
  • “Should some die… on their way from Egypt to Canaan”: “Your carcases shall fall in this wilderness” (Numbers 14:29). A whole generation died on the way, and Moses saw the land from Mount Nebo but did not enter it (Deuteronomy 34:4-5). See The Bible.
  • “a face which should break all mirrors”: The old saying is of a face that would crack a mirror. See Mirrors and Reflections.
  • “sent shivering like ghosts at dawn”: The ghost in Hamlet “faded on the crowing of the cock” (Hamlet 1.1). See Shakespeare.
  • “a busy Etruscan seaport. A place where the dead came and went”: The Etruscans of ancient Italy built great cities of the dead, the necropoleis of Cerveteri and Tarquinia, and Populonia was one of their seaports. See Catherine Cartwheel.
  • “Not that she would ever really die, of course!”: Her disappearance into the sea is told in Chapter 6. See Miss MacIntosh and the Chapter 6 resources.
  • “What was old age?”: Chapter 18 ends with her line “Age is the most difficult thing to achieve.” See the Chapter 18 resources.
  • “Better were two heads than one”: “Two heads are better than one,” in John Heywood’s proverbs (1546), and “Two are better than one” (Ecclesiastes 4:9). See Ecclesiastes.
  • “grey hair does not signify a necessary wisdom”: “The hoary head is a crown of glory, if it be found in the way of righteousness” (Proverbs 16:31), but “great men are not always wise: neither do the aged understand judgment” (Job 32:9). See The Book of Job.
  • “a babe cast into purgatory”: Catholic tradition placed unbaptized infants not in purgatory but in limbo, at the edge of Hell, where Dante puts the virtuous unbaptized (Inferno 4). See Dante.
  • “the dead tree of life”: “The tree of life also in the midst of the garden” (Genesis 2:9). See Genesis.
  • “the missing breast like a door knob”: The “knob where the breast was missing” of Chapter 18. See Miss MacIntosh and the Chapter 18 resources.
  • “Was God bald, too”: Children mocked Elisha, “Go up, thou bald head” (2 Kings 2:23), and the Ancient of Days has “the hair of his head like the pure wool” (Daniel 7:9). See The Bible and Hair, Wig, and Baldness.
  • “What was God, defined in so many terms”: Young’s litany gathers images of God and of Christ from across the Bible. The descriptions emphasize the profound mystery of divinity, the coexistence of opposites within the divine, and the limited capacity of human beings to grasp the full nature of God. See The Bible.
    • “as a fuller’s soap, as a refining fire”: “He is like a refiner’s fire, and like fullers’ soap” (Malachi 3:2). A fuller cleaned and whitened cloth.
    • “as the light of the morning when the sun arises, even as a dawn without clouds”: “As the light of the morning, when the sun riseth, even a morning without clouds” (2 Samuel 23:4).
    • “as rivers of water in a dry place, as a hiding place from the wind”: “A man shall be as an hiding place from the wind… as rivers of water in a dry place, as the shadow of a great rock in a weary land” (Isaiah 32:2).
    • “as a stone of grace”: Proverbs 17:8 reads “a precious stone” in the King James Version and “A stone of grace” in Young’s Literal Translation (1862).
    • “a friend that sticketh closer than a brother” (Proverbs 18:24).
    • “a brother born for adversity” and “a friend that loveth at all times” (Proverbs 17:17).
    • “a root out of a dry ground” (Isaiah 53:2).
    • “a nail fastened to a sure place”: “I will fasten him as a nail in a sure place” (Isaiah 22:23).
    • “as the tender grass by clear shining after the rain” (2 Samuel 23:4).
    • “as a casket”: In older English a casket is a small box for jewels, not a coffin. Compare “in that day when I make up my jewels” (Malachi 3:17).
    • “as an ark”: In the Bible, the Ark of the Covenant was a symbol of God’s presence and a holy place where God dwelt with his people. Noah’s ark carried life through the Flood (Genesis 6-8).
    • “as a crown of glory, as a diadem of beauty”: “In that day shall the Lord of hosts be for a crown of glory, and for a diadem of beauty” (Isaiah 28:5).
    • “as a belt of stars”: Orion’s Belt: “Canst thou bind the sweet influences of Pleiades, or loose the bands of Orion?” (Job 38:31). See Astronomy and The Book of Job.
    • “as the shadow of a great rock in a weary land” (Isaiah 32:2).
    • “Was there the plant not planted by God?”: “Every plant, which my heavenly Father hath not planted, shall be rooted up” (Matthew 15:13).
    • “Were there the strayed sheep?”: the parable of the lost sheep (Matthew 18:12; Luke 15:4).
    • “Was there the relapsing demoniac?”: the unclean spirit that returns with “seven other spirits more wicked than himself” (Matthew 12:43-45).
  • “something which none should see and live to relate”: “There shall no man see me, and live” (Exodus 33:20), as in Chapter 15. See The Bible and the Chapter 15 resources.

Vocabulary

Chapter 3

← Chapter 2 · Home · Chapter 4 →

Content note: Vera’s mother, Catherine Cartwheel, is addicted to opium.

Summary

After Catherine took to her bed, Mr. Spitzer hired Miss Georgia MacIntosh of What Cheer, Iowa, to raise Vera. Vera paints her in full: marcelled red hair, a broken nose, a black umbrella, a tight corset, sensible shoes, long walks along the shore in any weather, strict schedules, and a deep suspicion of anything imaginary. She is everything Catherine is not, the practical Middle West in one person. Vera recalls how Miss MacIntosh dealt with an Australian bushman, a head-hunter who visited Catherine’s bedside and was obsessed with the nursemaid’s head, and she mentions Miss MacIntosh’s brother, a missionary bishop lost among the islands. Then Vera returns to the loss. Miss MacIntosh’s clothes were found on the beach and her purse held two pennies. Her body was never found, and Vera blames herself. Mr. Spitzer always insists that she was a good and dependable woman who never wavered.

Characters present

Miss MacIntosh · Vera Cartwheel · Joachim Spitzer · Catherine Cartwheel

Concepts present

Themes: Death and Mortality · Faith, God, and the Supernatural · Illusion and Reality · Isolation and Connection · Light and Darkness · Nature, the Sea, and the Cosmos · Order, Chaos, and Discipline · Society, Class, and Race

Symbols: Birds · Cards, Games, and Chance · Clothing, Hats, and Skirts · Fireflies · The Sea and Water · The Umbrella · Twins and Doubles

Philosophy: Augustine and Christian Theology · Freud and Jung · Heraclitus and Flux · Marguerite Young on Her Craft · Plato and Platonism · William James and Pragmatism

Allusions: American Religious Movements · American Writers · Ancient Egypt · Fairy Tales and Folklore · Greek Mythology · Iowa, Indiana, and the Midwest · Milton · Revelation and the Apocalypse · Romantic Poets · Shakespeare · Suicide in History and Literature · The Bible · The Civil War · The History of Opium

Key passages

From the research

  • Miss MacIntosh is described as a “truer than the North star” guide to the bewildered child, Vera, someone who is steadfast in her moral principles and practical in her approach to life. She rejects fantasies, illusions, and the “phantoms thickening in the air” around others, especially Vera’s mother, Catherine’s hallucinatory environment. Her quick temper and no-nonsense attitude symbolize a force that dispels the fanciful and unreal.
  • The detailed imagery of Miss MacIntosh’s red hair shining like fire or sparks, her robust health sustained by sunlight and physical exercise, and her preference for outdoor life even in inclement weather emphasize her grounded, vigorous nature. She uses physical activity and connection with natural elements to keep herself strong and unclouded by fantasy or despair. This connection also reflects her philosophy that life is about facing realities, not escaping them.
  • Miss MacIntosh disdains fanciful dreams, luxury, and illusions such as the “golden apples” or “pearls” that Catherine dreams of. She insists on simplicity, honesty, and the acceptance of life’s hardships: “Life was made up, in short, of the necessary deprivations.” She believes in fulfilling one’s duties, avoiding self-pity, and not chasing impossible ideals. Her practical mindset is embodied in her tasks like mending clothes, preparing meals, and maintaining order.
  • Miss MacIntosh holds a stark, unromantic view of death as a final, dreamless sleep without illusions of heaven or afterlife grandeur. She rejects “six-winged seraphim” and “golden towers” as fanciful nonsense, insisting that if there is a heaven, it should be plain and unfurnished. This reflects her consistent rejection of fantasy and her focus on the tangible realities of mortal life.
  • Miss MacIntosh is brusque, solitary, and does not encourage intimacy or pity. Her past is largely unknown, and she has no friends, embodying a figure who compensates for others’ losses in a practical way. She has little patience for mental or emotional sorrows that lack physical cause, emphasizing courage in the face of actual trials. Her interactions with the Australian head-hunter highlight her disdain for affectation and false pretenses.
  • The Australian head-hunter serves as a foil to Miss MacIntosh’s grounded realism. She despises his semi-civilized, erratic behavior, his ambitions, and his inappropriate intimacy, seeing him as a symbol of confused and corrupt aspirations that contrast with her straightforward, honest life. Her reactions to him underscore her rejection of fantasy, deceit, and social pretense.
  • The chapter ends with the mystery of Miss MacIntosh’s disappearance, leaving behind her clothes and personal effects on the beach as if she had walked into the sea. Mr. Spitzer’s reflections underscore her enigmatic presence and the lasting impact she had on those around her. Despite her ordinariness, she was a “pearl of light” in a world of shadows and illusions, and her absence leaves an unresolved question about her fate.
  • Miss MacIntosh believes in honest work, self-discipline, and the acceptance of life’s hardships. She foresees a necessary revolution to overthrow the “powers of darkness” and strip away illusions and luxury. Her philosophy is one of immediate action and responsibility to others, emphasizing that life is short and should not be wasted in “the vain expectation of that which might never happen” or on “graven images.” This reflects a deep existential and moral seriousness.

Questions and observations

Reading closely

  • The chapter opens with adults “like the shadows of grotesque puppets dancing on a wall,” and “The puppeteer they dreamed of did not exist although he moved the strings.” How does this image prepare for a nursemaid who believes only in what she can see?
  • Miss MacIntosh “could endure nothing that took its time,” and her days are filled with mending, hammering, sweeping, and running. What is she outrunning?
  • She and Vera “swept our footprints away from the sands before the waters crept over” them. Why might someone so committed to the present want to leave no trace?
  • Miss MacIntosh makes a lamp of fireflies when they are lost in the dark, “carrying the lamp up high like a lighthouse.” How does this moment complicate her refusal of anything fanciful?

Characters

  • Miss MacIntosh is “so usual” that her ordinariness becomes strange in Catherine’s house. Yet she has a broken nose, a receding brow, a past no one knows, and a cheek that throbs when her hand is touched. What clues does the chapter plant that she is not what she seems?
  • Mr. Spitzer remembers hiring “the shawled figure” he took for a brunette, whose “eyebrows were dark and beetling cliffs.” Why might the novel let him misremember the one person he chose so quickly?
  • The head-hunter tells Miss MacIntosh that she “had a greater imagination than anyone who lived.” Why does this compliment offend her more than any insult?
  • Miss MacIntosh preaches common sense, but her own sayings are full of contradictions: there is no heaven, yet God is a harness-maker; the sins committed are worse than those of omission, yet God has forgotten things. How does she hold her faith together?

Connections

  • In Chapter 2 Catherine lives only in dreams. In Chapter 3 Miss MacIntosh insists “If she dreamed, she would dream that she was running.” What does Vera inherit from each of these two mothers?
  • Miss MacIntosh believes in revolution, “the whole bird,” not the left wing or the right. How do her politics grow out of her years in “the dregs of the city”?
  • The chapter ends with clothes on the beach, two pennies under a rock, and a body never found. How does this loss reshape everything Vera has said about Miss MacIntosh up to that point? See The Search for Life, for Love, for Truth That Does Not Fail.

Reflection

  • “Who but I had killed her?” Vera asks. Why do children so often blame themselves for the losses of the adults around them?
  • Miss MacIntosh says “we knew now all we would ever know . . . of misery or happiness.” Is living wholly in the present a kind of courage, a kind of hiding, or both?

Research: Characters

Miss (Georgia) MacIntosh

  • A nursemaid who embodies practicality, common sense, and moral certainty.
  • Described physically with “marcelled red hair,” “greyish, greenish eyes,” and a robust constitution.
  • She is a symbol of stability, reality, and groundedness amidst chaos and confusion.
  • Rejects illusions, fantasies, and idle dreams; values labor, discipline, and the present moment.
  • Wears simple, durable clothing; disdains luxury and extravagance.
  • Has a brusque, rough demeanor, often compared to an old sailor.
  • She is industrious, always busy, and advocates physical exercise and self-forgetfulness.
  • Holds a strict moral code, emphasizing honesty, self-control, and acceptance of life’s hardships.
  • Originates from What Cheer, Iowa, a simple town, and contrasts sharply with the opulent, dreamlike environment of the household.
  • Maintains distance from others, avoids intimacy, and does not indulge in self-pity.
  • Ultimately disappears under mysterious circumstances, leaving behind only her clothes and belongings on the beach.
  • Mentions her brother, who went out as a missionary bishop to the Easter Islands and never returned.

Vera Cartwheel

  • A child who has escaped from her mother’s “opium paradise.”
  • Looks up to Miss MacIntosh as a guide and protector.
  • Observes and reflects on the strange atmosphere and characters around her.

Mr. Spitzer

  • Employer who hired Miss MacIntosh without much inquiry.
  • Holds a fondness and respect for her practical nature.
  • Believes Miss MacIntosh might have returned to the city’s “dregs” after disappearance.
  • Is uncertain about her fate but respects her memory and legacy.

The Head-Hunter (Australian Bushman)

  • An unwelcome visitor who comes each afternoon in a black-curtained cab to sit at Catherine’s bedside.
  • Seen by Miss MacIntosh as deceitful, semi-civilized, and culturally alien.
  • His presence and behavior clash sharply with Miss MacIntosh’s values.
  • Fascinated by Miss MacIntosh’s head, which he wants to sculpt, but she rejects his advances.

Catherine Cartwheel

  • Living in a surreal, opium-induced environment with grand illusions and fantasies.
  • Contrasted with Miss MacIntosh’s grounded reality.

Research: Themes

Reality and Illusion

See: Illusion and Reality

  • Miss MacIntosh represents the harsh reality of life, while Catherine’s world is filled with dreams, illusions, and hallucinations.
  • The nursemaid’s disdain for luxury, fantasy, and self-pity underscores the value of facing life’s truths directly.

Discipline, Labor, and Practicality

See: Order, Chaos, and Discipline

  • Life is portrayed as a testing ground requiring discipline, hard work, and acceptance of necessary deprivations.
  • Miss MacIntosh’s emphasis on practical tasks (mending clothes, building fires) and physical exercise reflect this ethos.

Mortality and Transience

See: Death and Mortality

  • Frequent imagery of time running low, life’s brevity, and the inevitability of death.
  • The nursemaid’s disappearance and the uncertainty surrounding her fate emphasize the fragile nature of existence.

Isolation and Independence

See: Isolation and Connection

  • Miss MacIntosh is a solitary figure who keeps to herself, avoids intimacy, and values self-reliance.
  • Her rejection of social pretenses and false hopes highlights her independence.

Nature and the Elements

See: Nature, the Sea, and the Cosmos

  • The natural world (sea, wind, light, sand) is a constant presence and source of strength for Miss MacIntosh.
  • She prefers exposure to natural elements over sheltered luxury or confinement.

Social Order and Class

See: Society, Class, and Race · Order, Chaos, and Discipline

  • Miss MacIntosh rejects aristocratic airs and illusions of grandeur.
  • She advocates for the dignity of simple people and honest labor.

Faith and Doubt

See: Faith, God, and the Supernatural

  • While Miss MacIntosh acknowledges God, she does not believe in extravagant religious fantasies or promises of an afterlife.
  • She sees life itself as a sufficient test and believes in accepting one’s lot without illusions.

Research: Symbols and Imagery

Black Umbrella

See: The Umbrella

  • Miss MacIntosh’s shield and sword against the elements and the unknown.
  • Represents her protection from illusions and external threats.

Fireflies in a Jar

See: Fireflies

  • Symbolize hope and guidance in darkness.
  • The moment when Miss MacIntosh uses them as a lamp suggests her role as a beacon of reason amid confusion.

Sea and Surf

See: The Sea and Water

  • Represent the uncontrollable forces of nature and time.
  • The beach is the boundary between worlds and the place where Miss MacIntosh’s disappearance occurs.

Two Pennies

See: Cards, Games, and Chance · Twins and Doubles

  • Found in her purse, symbolizes her humility and the little she possessed.
  • Also a poignant reminder of her mortality and disappearance.

Corset

See: Clothing, Hats, and Skirts

  • Represents discipline and the necessary constraints of life.
  • Miss MacIntosh’s tight corset is a physical embodiment of her moral and mental self-control.

Research: Resources

  • “like the shadows of grotesque puppets dancing on a wall”: In the allegory of the cave in Plato’s Republic, prisoners chained in the dark see only shadows thrown on a wall by figures carried past a fire, like a puppet show, and take the shadows for the whole of reality. Vera’s adults are the shadows, and “The puppeteer they dreamed of did not exist although he moved the strings.” See Plato and Platonism.
  • “Miss MacIntosh, my darling, truer than the North star”: Polaris, the North Star, stays nearly fixed above the North Pole while the other stars wheel around it, so sailors steered by it. Shakespeare’s Julius Caesar boasts, “I am constant as the northern star.” In Chapter 1 she was “the dead steersman.” See Moon and Stars.
  • “not even a game of chess as chess was the game of kings”: Chess has long been called “the royal game” and “the game of kings.” Its pieces are a feudal court, with the king who must be protected at all costs and the pawns who are sacrificed, which is why Miss MacIntosh finds the game undemocratic.
  • “her marcelled red hair fitting close like a helmet”: Marcelled hair is set in deep, regular waves with heated tongs, a method introduced by the Paris hairdresser Marcel Grateau in 1872 and most fashionable in the 1920s. See Marcelled hair (Ch 3).
  • “imaginary nightingales or turrets of ivory”: The Song of Solomon says, “Thy neck is as a tower of ivory” (7:4), and “Tower of Ivory” became a title of the Virgin Mary. By the nineteenth century an ivory tower meant a place of dreamy retreat from the world, which Miss MacIntosh will not allow. The nightingale is the bird of the Romantic poets, as in Keats’s “Ode to a Nightingale.”
  • “flower-crowned satyrs and moon-eyed minotaurs”: A satyr is a male nature spirit of Greek myth with the ears and tail of a horse, a follower of Dionysus given to wine, music, and dancing. Later Roman art gave satyrs the legs of goats, like Pan.
  • “giant periwinkle shells filled with mystic roarings”: The roar heard when a shell is held to the ear is not the sea but the sounds of the room around it, caught and amplified as they echo inside the shell’s spiral.
  • The problem with God and his attributes of omniscience (God’s complete and perfect knowledge, knowing everything past, present, and future), omnipotence (God’s unlimited power and ability to do anything), omnipresence (God is present everywhere at all times, not limited by space or time), and also added by some omnibenevolence (God has perfect or unlimited goodness) are that they create fallacies: god cannot be omnibenevolent and omnipotent in a universe in which evil exists (i.e., his creation suffers). Can god not prevent evil? Then he is not omnipotent. Does he not want to prevent evil? Then he is not omnibenevolent. If god can prevent evil, and god wants to prevent evil, then evil would not exist. Can god defy the laws of physics (create a rock so heavy even he can’t lift it? destroy himself? create a square circle? make himself not omnipotent?) If god is omniscient, then he has always known every single choice every human has ever and will ever make. Therefore, from his perspective, free will is impossible because there was only ever one choice any person who has ever or will ever exist could make. Any argument made from free will with an omniscient god is logically unsound. Any god that forces his followers to adopt illogical arguments to defend his existence in a universe very clearly explicable by logic is a malicious god, not a benevolent god.
  • “God had been her harness-maker, that He had hung her harness with tinkling bells so that it might always be known where she was”: The robe of the Hebrew high priest was hung at its hem with golden bells and pomegranates, “and his sound shall be heard when he goeth in unto the holy place” (Exodus 28:33-35). Miss MacIntosh’s bells ring on through the chapter: “her bells ringing so that I might know, through fog and mist and darkness, where she was.”
  • “labor was man’s lot upon this earth”: The Protestant work ethic, the Calvinist Work Ethic, or the Puritan Work Ethic is a work ethic concept in theology, sociology, economics and history that emphasizes that hard work, discipline, and frugality are a result of a person’s subscription to the values espoused by the Protestant faith, particularly Calvinism. The phrase was coined by the sociologist Max Weber in his book The Protestant Ethic and the Spirit of Capitalism (1904 to 1905). Weber asserted that Protestant ethics and values along with the Calvinist doctrine of asceticism and predestination gave birth to capitalism. (Wikipedia) See The Protestant Work Ethic (Ch 3) and The Protestant Ethic.
  • “If at night I heard the wings of time like angelic wings roaring faster and faster”: Andrew Marvell’s “To His Coy Mistress” says, “But at my back I always hear / Time’s wingèd chariot hurrying near.”
  • “the sleep of the innocent should be deep and dreamless”: Macbeth, after murdering the sleeping king, thinks he hears a voice cry that he has murdered sleep, “the innocent sleep, / Sleep that knits up the ravell’d sleave of care.” See Shakespeare.
  • “almost Tyrian purple in certain lights”: Tyrian purple is a reddish-purple dye made from the glands of murex sea snails, first in the Phoenician city of Tyre. Thousands of snails were needed for a single garment, so the color was worth more than gold, and in Rome it was reserved for emperors.
  • “knocking down ninepins and the old kingpin who should be leveled like the old king of Bulgaria”: Ninepins, the old form of bowling, is the game the ghostly crew plays in the mountains in Washington Irving’s “Rip Van Winkle.” The kingpin stands at the center. Bulgaria’s kings fell one by one: Tsar Ferdinand abdicated after defeat in the First World War in 1918, his son Boris III died suddenly in 1943, and in 1946 the monarchy was abolished and the boy king Simeon II sent into exile.
  • “no hawk’s-wing sea shell with a broken wing or broken great keyhole limpet or star sea shell dragging its broken foot”: Limpets are sea snails with simple cone-shaped shells that cling to rocks. The keyhole limpet has a small opening at the top of its shell, and the hawk-wing conch and star shells are other sea snails of warm waters. Miss MacIntosh “could endure nothing that took its time.”
  • “not venturing to do what the wisest man had failed to do”: When the oracle at Delphi said that no one was wiser than Socrates, Socrates concluded that his only wisdom was knowing that he knew nothing (Plato, Apology). The wisest man in the Bible, Solomon, ends Ecclesiastes with the same humility: “of making many books there is no end.”
  • “I should make a useful contribution to human society, which was composed of simple people”: The Greek word aretē means excellence or virtue, the fulfillment of something’s purpose, and for people the act of living up to one’s full potential. For Miss MacIntosh excellence means usefulness: a person lives up to her potential by serving “simple people.”
  • Miss MacIntosh’s philosophy could be compared to the Amish, Quakers, or Shakers. The Amish have a significant population in the Middle West and are known for simple living, plain dress, and reluctance to adopt many conveniences of modern technology. They educate their children up to the eighth grade and then they are apprenticed to work.
  • “these unusual luxuries which tempted no honest face”: The Theory of the Leisure Class (1899) is a treatise on economics and a detailed, social critique of conspicuous consumption. Its author, Thorstein Veblen, coined the phrase “conspicuous consumption” for the spending of money on and acquiring of luxury goods and services to publicly display economic power in order to attain or maintain social status.
  • “as if she were trying to placate it”: An old story told by the chronicler Henry of Huntingdon has King Canute set his throne on the shore and command the tide to stop, to show his flattering courtiers that even a king cannot rule the sea.
  • “rolling pea-souper”: A pea-souper was a thick, yellowish fog, named for its likeness to pea soup, especially the coal-smoke fogs of London. See Fog and Mist.
  • “wearing her salt-streaked mackintosh of almost faded plaids”: The mackintosh, the rubberized raincoat, is named for the Scottish chemist Charles Macintosh, who patented his waterproofing process in 1823, and Miss MacIntosh wears her name. See Charles MacIntosh (Ch 3).
  • “useful work for the benefit of others and strenuous physical exercise and self-forgetfulness prolonged one’s useful life”: In his speech “The Strenuous Life,” given in Chicago on April 10, 1899, Theodore Roosevelt said, “I wish to preach, not the doctrine of ignoble ease, but the doctrine of the strenuous life.” He advocated for a life of effort, hardship, and struggle over ease and idleness, arguing that it was essential for both individual character and national greatness. He believed that facing challenges, whether physical or moral, was the only way to achieve true success and national power in the coming century. The speech also reflected his views on American expansionism and the “strenuous” duty of the nation to take an active role in the world. Miss MacIntosh warns against “slothful ease.”
  • “on this old terra firma which was certainly no cloud”: Terra firma is Latin for “firm land,” dry ground as opposed to the sea.
  • “One should mind his own knitting”: Miss MacIntosh’s answer to fate is to mind one’s own knitting: to live in the present and attend to one’s work rather than chase impossible dreams. She neither denies suffering nor yields to despair, and finds the true expression of human will in labor, self-forgetfulness, and service to others. Against this the novel sets Vera’s thought that “The individual is the one illusion,” bound by circumstance, time, and fate. See the free will entry in the Chapter 38 resources.
  • “there was not much room for the individual, for those who should lift up their heads”: A Japanese proverb says, “the nail that sticks out shall get hammered down.”
  • “the mischief caused by those who did not work and yet were restless”: The saying that the devil finds work for idle hands is often thought to be biblical, but it comes from Isaac Watts’s hymn for children “Against Idleness and Mischief” (1715): “For Satan finds some mischief still / For idle hands to do.” Proverbs 16:27 has a similar thought: “An ungodly man diggeth up evil.”
  • “no time for the luxury of idle tears”: The phrase recalls Tennyson’s song from The Princess (1847): “Tears, idle tears, I know not what they mean, / Tears from the depth of some divine despair.”
  • “the dark prince charming who should carry me away and rescue me from this dark tower”: The dark prince is a symbolic figure representing an imaginary or idealized rescuer, a figure of hope and escape for Vera.
  • “this dark tower”: The phrase recalls Robert Browning’s “Childe Roland to the Dark Tower Came” (1855), whose title comes from a line in King Lear. In Chapter 30 Catherine’s search for her lost husband ends where “Childe Roland had blown his horn before a dark tower.” See Childe Roland to the Dark Tower Came.
  • “Like the princess, I would let down my hair, and he should climb it as if it were a rope”: The image is Rapunzel’s, from the Grimm brothers’ tale of 1812: “Rapunzel, Rapunzel, let down your hair.” The Grimms took the story from Charlotte-Rose de La Force’s French tale “Persinette” (1698). Many scholars have interpreted “Maiden in the Tower” stories, which Rapunzel is a part of, as a metaphor for the protection of young women from premarital relationships by overzealous guardians. Scholars have drawn comparisons of the confinement of Rapunzel in her tower to that of a convent, where women’s lives were highly controlled and they lived in exclusion from outsiders. Scholars have also noted the strong theme of love conquering all in the story, as the lovers are united after years of searching in all versions after Persinette and are ultimately happily reunited as a family. The “Maiden in the Tower” archetype has drawn comparisons to a possible lost matriarchal myth connected to the sacred marriage between the prince and the maiden and the rivalry between the maiden, representing life and spring, and the crone, representing death and winter. See Fairy Tales and Folklore.
  • “We should not nurture our grief at the breast of sorrow”: Miss MacIntosh allows no time for grief. Elisabeth Kübler-Ross later described five stages of grief in On Death and Dying (1969): denial, anger, bargaining, depression, and acceptance. See Grief, Loss, and Mourning.
  • “God, moving in His mysterious ways”: “God Moves in a Mysterious Way” is a Christian hymn written in 1773 by the English poet William Cowper, first titled “Light Shining out of Darkness.” The poem is the likely source for the phrase “God moves in mysterious ways,” although the first line of the poem actually runs “God moves in a mysterious way.” Cowper wrote it at Olney, and it is often said to have been his last hymn, written as he felt a period of deep depression coming on. (Wikipedia)
  • “Apples fell downward, not upward”: The best-known falling apple is Isaac Newton’s. Newton told his friend William Stukeley that the fall of an apple in his mother’s orchard at Woolsthorpe set him thinking about gravity, the force that keeps the moon in its orbit. Miss MacIntosh’s law of gravity is moral as well as physical: “All that fell upward were bound to fall downward.”
  • “not even should there be those golden apples of which my mother dreamed”: Catherine dreamed of the golden apples of the Hesperides in Chapter 2. Miss MacIntosh sets practicality against such dreams.
  • “the macintosh apple and the crab apple and the pippin and the russet”: The McIntosh apple grew from a seedling that John McIntosh found on his farm in Ontario in 1811. Pippins and russets are old English apple varieties; a russet has rough, brownish skin. The nursemaid named MacIntosh lists her own apple first.
  • “the path of the brave was narrow and girt about by thorns, and it was lonely, there being great solitude, for man was seldom good”: The passage turns on Matthew 7:13-14: “wide is the gate, and broad is the way, that leadeth to destruction, and many there be which go in thereat: Because strait is the gate, and narrow is the way, which leadeth unto life, and few there be that find it.”
  • “of fleshly pleasures and fleshpots of luxury, of dancing girls and headless men”: The fleshpots come from Exodus 16:3, where the Israelites in the wilderness long for Egypt, “when we sat by the flesh pots, and when we did eat bread to the full.” The dancing girl and the headless man recall Salome and John the Baptist from Chapter 2.
  • “none finding a celestial city”: The Celestial City is the goal of the pilgrim Christian in Bunyan’s Pilgrim’s Progress, the heavenly Jerusalem at the end of his road. Miss MacIntosh’s travelers on the path of virtue never reach it.
  • “chasing a will-o’-the-wisp, a false light”: The will-o’-the-wisp, or ignis fatuus, “foolish fire,” is a faint light seen at night over marshes, probably caused by burning marsh gas. In folklore it lures travelers off the path and into the bog.
  • “no slug with its shell rudimentary and often buried in the mantle or wanting entirely”: The phrase reads like an entry from an old natural history or dictionary, which defined slugs as mollusks whose shell is small and hidden in the mantle or wanting altogether. Miss MacIntosh wants no child without a shell to carry.
  • “my house would be well kept, and I should make my husband happy”: There has been important feminist criticism of marriage including: the effect that marriage has on individual liberty, equality between the sexes, the relation between marriage and violence, philosophical questions about how much control can a government have over its population, the amount of control a person has over another, the financial risk when measured against divorce/separation, and the questioning of the necessity to have a relationship sanctioned by government or religious authorities. There is also the emotional labor and management of the house that has been and is the unpaid work of mostly women.
  • “the numbers of tons of coal mined by coal-miners in distant mines”: Coal mining labor history in the United States is marked by dangerous work, exploitation, and the struggle for workers’ rights, driven by waves of immigration, the Civil War, and industrialization. Early laborers were diverse, including enslaved and free African Americans, and later, large numbers of immigrants from Great Britain, Ireland, and Eastern and Southern Europe were drawn to the industry by recruiters. The United Mine Workers of America (UMWA) was founded in 1890 to fight for better wages, safer conditions, and benefits, leading to significant labor conflicts and hard-won reforms like the eight-hour workday and pensions. The coal industry was marked by a series of violent conflicts and massacres, often stemming from labor disputes between striking workers (many of whom were immigrants) and mine owners who hired private security forces or leveraged local law enforcement to suppress union organizing efforts.
    • Lattimer Massacre (September 10, 1897): In Lattimer, Pennsylvania, a sheriff’s posse opened fire on a march of unarmed striking immigrant anthracite miners, mostly of Polish, Slovak, Lithuanian, and German descent. At least 19 miners were killed, and many more were wounded. The sheriff and his deputies were later tried but acquitted.
    • Battle of Virden (October 12, 1898): In Virden, Illinois, a gun battle erupted when the Chicago-Virden Coal Company attempted to bring in African-American strikebreakers with armed guards. Eight striking miners and at least four guards were killed.
    • Ludlow Massacre (April 20, 1914): During a major strike in Colorado, the Colorado National Guard and guards from the Colorado Fuel & Iron Company attacked a tent colony of 1,200 striking miners and their families. The assault resulted in the deaths of approximately 21 people, including women and children, many of whom were burned to death when the camp was set on fire.
    • Matewan Massacre (May 19, 1920): A deadly shootout occurred in Matewan, West Virginia, between Baldwin-Felts detective agency guards (hired by mine owners to evict striking workers from company-owned housing) and local residents, including the mayor and police chief, who supported the miners. Ten people died in the clash (seven detectives, two miners, and the mayor).
    • Battle of Blair Mountain (August/September 1921): The culmination of the West Virginia Mine Wars, this was the largest armed insurrection in U.S. history since the Civil War. Thousands of union miners fought against local law enforcement and company-hired forces. Federal troops were eventually sent in by President Harding to quell the uprising, which involved the use of airplanes to drop bombs. Estimates of the dead vary widely.
    • Herrin Massacre (June 21-22, 1922): In Herrin, Illinois, a violent confrontation occurred between union miners and strikebreakers at a strip mine. After a gunfight and a surrender under the promise of safe passage, union miners killed the mine superintendent and 19 strikebreakers and guards, and three union miners also died. The incident is considered one of the most violent labor disputes in U.S. history.
    • Columbine Mine Massacre (November 21, 1927): In Serene, Colorado, striking miners were met with machine-gun fire from the Colorado Rangers and guards from the Rocky Mountain Fuel Company during a strike, resulting in the deaths of six miners.
    These events, part of the broader “Coal Wars” (roughly 1890-1930), were pivotal in the struggle for better wages, safer working conditions, and the right to unionize in the U.S. coal industry.
  • “We dealt with the unjust circumstances under which Negroes were employed”: Miss MacIntosh’s lessons show her concern with social movements, the working class, and inequality, and she is repeatedly described as left-leaning. “Negro” was the standard term of the time. See Society, Class, and Race.
    • Ta-Nehisi Coates’ “The Case for Reparations” is a 2014 essay arguing that the U.S. owes African Americans compensation for centuries of systemic injustices, from slavery and Jim Crow laws to modern discrimination like redlining. The essay uses historical examples and personal accounts, like that of Clyde Ross, to trace how a legacy of stolen labor, land, and wealth created an enduring racial wealth gap. Coates argues that acknowledging and addressing this “moral debt” is necessary for both African Americans and the nation’s spiritual and economic healing.
    • The 1619 Project reframes American history by centering the consequences of slavery and the contributions of Black Americans, arguing that the country’s founding can be understood as beginning with the arrival of enslaved people in 1619. It explores how slavery has shaped modern America, including its economy, healthcare, and music, and challenges traditional narratives of American exceptionalism. The project originated as a New York Times Magazine special issue and has since expanded into a book and podcast series.
  • “the injustices done to the Africans working in diamond mines”: Diamond mining in Africa began in 1867 with the discovery of alluvial diamonds in South Africa, leading to a large-scale rush and the founding of De Beers Consolidated Mines by Cecil Rhodes in 1888. Subsequent discoveries of diamonds in kimberlite pipes enabled the transition from small-scale digging to industrial mining, which eventually consolidated into a monopoly by De Beers. Diamond mining then expanded to other countries, including Namibia, Botswana, Angola, and Sierra Leone, though its history is also marked by exploitation and conflict, such as the issue of “blood diamonds” which were sold to finance civil wars.
  • “We pitied the lighthouse keepers who had no union and no organization”: Lighthouse keepers lived for months at isolated stations, keeping the lamps lit and the lenses clean through every storm. In 1939 the United States Lighthouse Service was merged into the Coast Guard, and most lights were later automated.
  • The history of U.S. labor is a story of evolving unions fighting for worker rights, from the first trade unions in the late 18th century to the formation of national organizations like the National Labor Union and American Federation of Labor. Key events include the Great Railroad Strike of 1877, the Haymarket bombing, the Pullman strike, and the Triangle Shirtwaist factory fire, which led to significant safety reforms. The movement saw a peak in power between the late 19th century and mid-20th century, especially with the passage of protective legislation like the National Labor Relations Act during the New Deal, but has since faced a decline in membership while new organizing efforts continue.
    • 1794: The Federal Society of Journeymen Cordwainers (shoemakers) is formed in Philadelphia, marking the start of sustained trade union organization in the U.S.
    • 1866: The National Labor Union is founded, making the first national call for an 8-hour workday.
    • 1869: The Knights of Labor is established, becoming a major force in organizing skilled and unskilled workers.
    • 1886: The American Federation of Labor (AFL) is formed, focusing on a coalition of craft unions.
    • 1892: The Homestead strike occurs at a Carnegie Steel plant, and the Pullman strike takes place in 1894, highlighting the intense conflicts between labor and big business.
    • 1909: The New York shirtwaist strike, the “Uprising of the 20,000,” highlights the role of women in the labor movement.
    • 1911: The tragic Triangle Shirtwaist factory fire leads to a national outcry and a push for significant workplace safety reforms, inspired by eyewitness accounts and activism.
    • 1914: The Ludlow Massacre is a violent confrontation between coal miners and company guards, leading to further calls for reform.
    • 1920s: The rise of new industries leads to new labor-management challenges.
    • 1932: The Norris-LaGuardia Act is passed, limiting the power of courts to block strikes and other union activities.
    • 1933: The Wagner-Peyser Act creates a nationwide system of public employment offices.
    • 1935: The National Labor Relations Act (Wagner Act) is signed into law, giving workers the right to organize, bargain collectively, and strike.
    • 1937: A sit-down strike against General Motors in Flint, Michigan, results in the company recognizing the United Auto Workers (UAW).
    • Post-WWII: Labor unions begin to see a decline in membership and political influence, though they remain powerful in some sectors.
    • Late 20th Century: Globalization and a changing economy lead to further challenges for organized labor.
    • 2014: The Bureau of Labor Statistics reported that 11.1 percent of U.S. wage and salary workers belonged to unions, down from 20.1 percent in 1983, the first year of comparable figures.
  • “the united brotherhoods of the sleeping car porters”: The Brotherhood of Sleeping Car Porters (BSCP) was founded in 1925 by A. Philip Randolph and other porters to fight for better wages and working conditions against the Pullman Company. After a long and difficult struggle involving company opposition, the Great Depression, and internal community division, the BSCP gained recognition from the Pullman Company in 1937. It became the first African-American labor union to receive a charter from the American Federation of Labor (AFL) and went on to become a vital training ground for civil rights leaders and a significant force in the broader civil rights movement.
  • “the truck-drivers driving their trucks all night long”: The history of U.S. trucking labor is marked by early exploitation and the rise of powerful unions. Early drivers faced dangerous conditions and long hours, leading to the formation of the International Brotherhood of Teamsters (IBT) in 1903 to fight for better wages and conditions. In 1938 the federal government set the first limits on how many hours a truck-driver could drive, because tired drivers like the ones Miss MacIntosh pities were falling asleep at the wheel. The Federal-Aid Highway Act of 1956, which created the National Interstate and Defense Highways, spurred the industry’s growth.
  • “The shadow created the light, but the light created the shadow”: Miss MacIntosh, the practical nursemaid, sides with the light and with facts faced plainly. Vera finds her “far too clear to be seduced by the soporific luxury” of her mother’s dreams, and she holds it best never to dream of “those things which the conditions of this mortal frame could not simply provide.” Darkness belongs to dreams, memory, and death, the twilight where Vera’s mother lives among shadows and hallucinations. Young’s sentence makes each the maker of the other, so the light is never pure and the darkness is never simply absence. See Light and Darkness.
  • “the light which came from within was the only light by which to steer our way”: The Quakers teach that every person holds the Inner Light, the light of God within, a surer guide than any outward authority. George Fox, who founded the Society of Friends in the 1650s, spoke of “that of God in every one.” See American Religious Movements.
  • “made a lamp by filling it with fireflies”: A firefly’s light comes from a chemical reaction between luciferin and the enzyme luciferase, and nearly all its energy is given off as light rather than heat, which is why it is called cold light. See Fireflies.
  • “This flat-footed Middle Westerner”: “Middle Westerner” encapsulates Miss MacIntosh’s essential nature as a pragmatic, strong, and no-nonsense woman, deeply rooted in the values and environment of the American Midwest. The term “Middle Westerner” emerged in the late 19th century, solidifying a regional identity for the area between the American East and West. This region, often called the “Midwest,” evolved through westward expansion and the development of transportation networks, particularly railroads. It became a distinct area with its own cultural and economic characteristics, influenced by both rural and urban landscapes. The Midwest, initially known as the “Northwest,” played a key role in westward expansion following the Louisiana Purchase. As the frontier moved further west, the term “Middle West” gained traction to define the area between the Northwest (Great Lakes region) and the Southwest (Oklahoma and Texas). The development of railroads significantly shaped the Midwest’s growth, facilitating trade and connecting disparate areas. A literary movement in the late 19th century focused on realistic depictions of Midwestern life, particularly in small towns and rural areas. The Midwest has been a significant force in American history, contributing to movements like the Granger movement (The Granger movement, also known as the Patrons of Husbandry, was a 19th-century agrarian movement that aimed to address the economic hardships faced by farmers, particularly those related to railroad and grain elevator monopolies. Founded in 1867 by Oliver Hudson Kelley, the movement grew rapidly in the 1870s, fueled by economic instability and the perceived exploitation of farmers by powerful industries.), the Progressive movement (The Progressive Movement was a period of widespread social and political reform in the United States, spanning roughly from the 1890s to the 1920s. It aimed to address the negative consequences of rapid industrialization, urbanization, and political corruption, seeking to improve society and government through various reforms.), and the development of industries and architecture. The Midwest uniquely combines urban industrial power with the conservatism of its rural hinterland. Miss MacIntosh’s Iowa was Granger country: in the 1870s Iowa had more Granges than any other state, farmers banding together against the railroads, which fits her concern for “those who were not the children of fortune.” The Midwest typically includes the following 12 states: Illinois, Indiana, Iowa, Kansas, Michigan, Minnesota, Missouri, Nebraska, North Dakota, Ohio, South Dakota, and Wisconsin.
  • “all those Romish graven images”: Graven images come from the Ten Commandments: “Thou shalt not make unto thee any graven image” (Exodus 20:4). Romish is an old, hostile Protestant word for Roman Catholic, and Miss MacIntosh distrusts the statues of saints.
  • “the whirling dervishes”: The whirling dervishes of the Mevlevi Order, founded by followers of the thirteenth-century poet Rumi in Konya, Turkey, are a Sufi order that practices whirling as a form of dhikr or remembrance of God.
  • “those sorrows bringing our grey hairs”: Jacob, fearing the loss of his youngest son, says his sons would “bring down my gray hairs with sorrow to the grave” (Genesis 42:38). See Genesis.
  • “this life being so short, so earnest, so full of woe”: Henry Wadsworth Longfellow’s “A Psalm of Life” (1838) declares, “Life is real! Life is earnest! / And the grave is not its goal,” and promises that great lives leave “Footprints on the sands of time.” Miss MacIntosh sweeps her footprints away. See American Writers.
  • “one should not place his faith in earthly things”: Colossians 3:2 reads, “Set your affection on things above, not on things on the earth.”
  • “She dismissed the insubstantial fabric of the dream”: The phrase echoes Prospero in Shakespeare’s The Tempest: “And, like the baseless fabric of this vision, . . . this insubstantial pageant faded, / Leave not a rack behind. We are such stuff / As dreams are made on.” See Shakespeare.
  • “those green pearls which had been manufactured by the secretive ear oyster”: The ear shell is the abalone, a sea snail named for its ear-shaped shell. Its rare pearls are green, blue, and violet like the shell’s lining.
  • “those pink pearls formed by the winged stromb”: Strombs are the conchs, sea snails whose shells flare into a wide lip, or wing. The queen conch of the Caribbean produces rare pink pearls with a shimmering, flame-like pattern. Like all natural pearls, they form around an irritant, which is why Miss MacIntosh says they “belonged to the sick oysters.”
  • “pearls of greater price, a pearl as big as her head”: Jesus compares the kingdom of heaven to a merchant who, “when he had found one pearl of great price, went and sold all that he had, and bought it” (Matthew 13:46). See Pearls and Jewels.
  • “those already rich as Croesus for whom all things had turned to gold, even his bed and his bread”: Croesus was the king of Lydia, in Asia Minor, in the sixth century B.C., renowned for his wealth. The golden bed and bread belong to another king, Midas, whose wish that everything he touched would turn to gold left him unable to eat. Croesus is significant as a metaphor for the fragile and illusory nature of material wealth and earthly glory, reinforcing the novel’s meditation on mortality, loss, and the contrast between external appearances and deeper truths.
  • “coats of golden fleece”: The Golden Fleece, the hide of a golden ram, was the prize Jason and the Argonauts sailed to Colchis to win. See Greek Mythology.
  • “the black-winged angels of mortality falling into the burning sea”: Revelation 8:8 tells how “a great mountain burning with fire was cast into the sea,” and Revelation 12:9 how Satan and his angels were cast out of heaven. See Revelation and the Apocalypse.
  • “she was in the middle passage, as she would always say”: Miss MacIntosh means the middle of life’s voyage, the place Dante begins the Divine Comedy: “Midway upon the journey of our life” (Inferno 1.1, trans. Henry Wadsworth Longfellow, 1867). The Middle Passage also named the crossing of the Atlantic by slave ships from Africa, the deadliest leg of the slave trade, a darker meaning in a chapter about injustice.
  • “these end-of-the-world visions staining the atmosphere”: Miss MacIntosh notes that the Bible’s visions of the end “had appeared in the end and not in the beginning,” in the Book of Revelation, “and they had not been intended for daily life.” The philosophy of the end of the world, or “apocalyptic philosophy,” explores the concept of the world’s end, often involving catastrophic events, societal collapse, or human extinction, and examines its implications for ethics, meaning, and the understanding of existence. Philosophers have considered various end-of-world scenarios, from natural disasters to societal collapse, prompting reflection on human mortality, the nature of time, and the value of life.
  • “The sands of time . . . were running low”: The phrase “sands of time” is an idiom that refers to the passage of time, often emphasizing its relentless and irreversible nature. It originates from the imagery of an hourglass, where sand steadily flows from one chamber to another, symbolizing the continuous movement of time from past to future. The idiom is used to convey that time marches on, and moments are fleeting and irretrievable.
  • “Man was but a breath, a puff of smoke, and quickly gone. Time was short, growing always shorter just like a candle burning in the wind”: The Psalms say, “Man is like to vanity: his days are as a shadow that passeth away” (Psalm 144:4), and James asks, “For what is your life? It is even a vapour, that appeareth for a little time, and then vanisheth away” (James 4:14). Macbeth cries, “Out, out, brief candle!”
  • “we knew now all we would ever know, it was her opinion, of misery or happiness, all we would ever need to know. We must not waste our lives in the vain expectation of that which might never happen and had never happened and was impossible and would not be good for us if it did happen”: Matthew 6:34 counsels, “Take therefore no thought for the morrow: for the morrow shall take thought for the things of itself. Sufficient unto the day is the evil thereof.” The passage encourages embracing what is real and immediate rather than being consumed by hopes that lead to despair or distraction.
  • “To kiss the rod”: To kiss the rod means to accept punishment meekly, like a child kissing the rod that beat it. Shakespeare uses it in The Two Gentlemen of Verona.
  • “than to imagine we were free and our own architects, building heaven”: In John Milton’s Paradise Lost, Satan, newly fallen into hell, declares, “The mind is its own place, and in itself / Can make a Heaven of Hell, a Hell of Heaven.” The line suggests that one’s inner state can transform the worst outward circumstances. Miss MacIntosh distrusts any such architecture of the mind. See Milton.
  • “We were the nestless birds”: Jesus says, “Behold the fowls of the air: for they sow not, neither do they reap” (Matthew 6:26), and also, “The foxes have holes, and the birds of the air have nests; but the Son of man hath not where to lay his head” (Matthew 8:20).
  • “all these fine-feathered birds of paradise”: The birds of paradise of New Guinea reached Europe in the 1500s as trade skins with their feet removed, and naturalists concluded that they had no feet and lived their whole lives in the air, feeding on dew, until they fell to earth at death. Linnaeus named one species Paradisaea apoda, “footless.” See Birds.
  • “six-winged seraphim with crowns of gold”: In Isaiah’s vision of the throne of God, “each one had six wings; with twain he covered his face, and with twain he covered his feet, and with twain he did fly” (Isaiah 6:2). See Angels and Archangels.
  • “God was not a harlequin with a shaven head and a masked face and parti-colored tights and a sword of lath”: Harlequin is the acrobatic servant of the Italian commedia dell’arte, in a black half mask and a costume of colored diamonds, carrying a wooden bat or slapstick, the “sword of lath.”
  • “God was rather an old harness-maker or an old harpooner or a simple carpenter”: In Mark 6:3 the people of Nazareth ask of Jesus, “Is not this the carpenter, the son of Mary?” Miss MacIntosh can imagine God only as a working man.
