  • “the hard way which closed behind us, which had provided no way of turning back, of walking twice in the same path, of living once again in memory”: This is a take on the saying credited to Heraclitus that no man ever steps in the same river twice, for it is not the same river and he is not the same man. See “No man ever steps in the same river twice” (Ch 3).
    • The philosophy of impermanence or becoming, panta rhei, is best known in Western philosophy from the writings of Heraclitus. Panta Rhei is translated as everything flows. Heraclitus was famous for his insistence on ever-present change as being the fundamental essence of the universe. “No man ever steps in the same river twice.” See Heraclitus and Flux.
  • “we were given our opponent in order that we might struggle with him”: The struggle recalls Jacob, who wrestled through the night with a mysterious stranger and would not let him go until he was blessed (Genesis 32:24-30).
  • “She believed… in accepting the plain reality as it was, not in self-indulgence and these corrupting dreams of incorruptibility”: 1 Peter 1:23 speaks of being “born again, not of corruptible seed, but of incorruptible.” The statement emphasizes Miss MacIntosh’s practical, no-nonsense approach to life that values facing facts honestly and living with integrity, rather than indulging in self-delusion or fanciful ideals that deny human frailty and mortality.
    • Philosophical realists hold that the world exists independently of anyone’s mind and can be known as it is. Critics reply that even realists see through their own assumptions and biases. Miss MacIntosh’s realism is closest to the common-sense philosophy of the Scottish thinker Thomas Reid, who held that ordinary people know the world directly through their senses and that common sense is the foundation of all reasoning. American colleges taught his philosophy throughout the nineteenth century. In Chapter 1 she declares, “Common sense is the finest sense.” See Common Sense and American Pragmatism.
  • “those who died but once, those who could not afford to die twice”: Julius Caesar says in Shakespeare’s play, “Cowards die many times before their deaths; / The valiant never taste of death but once.” See Shakespeare.
  • “these lute-players strumming in fields of asphodel above the stars”: The Asphodel Meadows were the part of the ancient Greek underworld where ordinary souls were sent to live after death.
  • “Her feet were too big a size, number eights, long and narrow, pointed outward”: In the 1940s the average shoe size for men was size eight like Miss MacIntosh. Women’s shoes were about half that size.
  • “this stout Admiral Dewey corset”: George Dewey was Admiral of the Navy, the only person in United States history to have held the rank. He is best known for his victory at the Battle of Manila Bay during the Spanish-American War, in 1898, where the American side lost only a single man. (Wikipedia) His name was given to streets, towns, products, and babies across the country, and Young’s corset, with its “girders as of a ship made to cut the Arctic ice,” is built like a battleship.
  • “the glassy shore covered with comb jellyfish like a mirror”: Comb jellies are not true jellyfish but ctenophores, clear sea animals that swim by beating rows of tiny hairs, the combs, which scatter light into moving rainbows.
  • “the chambered nautilus”: The nautilus builds its spiral shell one chamber at a time, sealing off each old room as it grows. In Oliver Wendell Holmes’s poem “The Chambered Nautilus” (1858), the shell becomes a lesson for the soul: “Build thee more stately mansions, O my soul.” See American Writers.
  • “Woman’s heart was folly”: Proverbs 9:13 says, “A foolish woman is clamorous: she is simple, and knoweth nothing.” The line can be interpreted as a recognition of the emotional vulnerability and the sometimes irrational nature of the human heart, especially as experienced through the female characters in the novel, caught between dreams and reality, love and loss.
  • “This earth was the testing ground even for God, often making His own mistakes which had perhaps been unavoidable as He had wished to leave man free”: Augustine, in On Free Choice of the Will, argued that God gave human beings free will, though they could misuse it, because a world with freedom is better than one without. This free-will defense remains one of the main answers to the problem of evil. See Augustine and Christian Theology.
  • “the argument as to how many angels might stand on a needle’s point”: The question of how many angels can stand on a needle’s point is a philosophical and theological one, often used to illustrate the difference between physical and spiritual beings. If angels are understood as immaterial beings, an infinite number could potentially occupy the space of a needle’s point. However, if angels are considered to have physical bodies, then the number would be limited by the physical space available. It is also used as a metaphor for wasting time, debating topics of no practical value, or questions whose answers hold no intellectual consequence, while more urgent concerns accumulate. Medieval scholastics such as Thomas Aquinas did ask whether angels occupy space, but the needle’s point seems to come from later mockery of them; the English writer William Chillingworth asked in 1638 “whether a million of angels may not sit upon a needle’s point.”
  • “whether a camel shall enter through the needle’s eye or a rich man through the gates of heaven”: The image is a metaphor used in both the Bible and the Quran. It emphasizes the difficulty, or even impossibility, of a wealthy person achieving salvation through their own means. The phrase uses the image of a camel, a large animal, being unable to pass through the tiny eye of a needle to illustrate the immense challenge for a rich person to enter heaven. The saying appears in the Gospels of Matthew, Mark, and Luke, often in the context of Jesus speaking to a rich young man who is unwilling to give up his possessions to follow him. The Quran also uses this metaphor in Surah Al-A’raf (7:40), stating that those who reject God’s signs will not enter Paradise until a camel passes through the eye of a needle.
  • “we should rather be concerned with the anatomy of the clouds”: In 1802 the English chemist Luke Howard gave the clouds the Latin names still used today, cirrus, cumulus, and stratus, and Goethe wrote a poem in his honor. See Clouds and Storms.
  • “opportunity knocked but once at the door of the sleeper”: The proverb “opportunity knocks but once” was common by the nineteenth century, and John James Ingalls’s sonnet “Opportunity” gave it its best-known form: “I knock unbidden once at every gate! / If sleeping, wake.” The word “opportunity” comes from the Latin ob portum, “toward the harbor,” and the phrase uses personification to describe opportunity as something that comes to a person’s door.
  • “these empty husks”: In the parable of the prodigal son, the son who has wasted his inheritance “would fain have filled his belly with the husks that the swine did eat” (Luke 15:16).
  • “We were to be proved, and the truth was better than the lie, even should the lie seem truer than the truth, every lie containing a seed of truth in it, no doubt, but ours was the freedom to make a choice between the truth and the lie and the truth and the truth, to do what was good and right, leaving no uncertainty”: The passage underscores that while lies may be seductive and intertwined with truth, it is the conscious choice to pursue what is good and true that defines human freedom and moral integrity. Many cultures and thinkers have expressed the belief that, despite the potential pain or discomfort of truth, it ultimately offers a more beneficial and sustainable foundation than deception. A Swahili proverb says, “Kweli chungu si uwongo mtamu,” a bitter truth is better than a sweet lie, and a West African variant runs, “The truth may be bitter, but it lasts longer than a lie.” (Wikipedia) This highlights the idea that even if the truth is difficult to hear, it is ultimately more valuable than a comforting falsehood. Writers and thinkers like Tolstoy have emphasized the importance of truth for moral clarity and authentic relationships. They argue that while lies might offer temporary comfort, they ultimately lead to unsustainable situations and undermine trust. Miss MacIntosh, who “could not endure a bare-faced lie or even the equivocal statement hovering between two truths,” would agree.
  • “a lighthouse for the blind”: The Lighthouse, founded in New York in 1905 by the sisters Winifred and Edith Holt as the New York Association for the Blind, gave its name to “lighthouses for the blind” across the country, agencies that trained blind people for work.
  • “a home for old sailors on shore leave”: Sailors’ Snug Harbor on Staten Island opened in 1833 as a home for “aged, decrepit and worn-out sailors,” paid for by the estate of the shipowner Robert Richard Randall.
  • “crack nuts on a rusted flatiron”: A flatiron was a heavy iron for pressing clothes, heated on the stove before electric irons. Upturned between the knees, it made a good anvil for cracking nuts.
  • “passing through the garden of the blind”: The garden is the one Catherine’s father planted for his blind wife in Chapter 2, with “neat and circling paths where was no obstacle.” See Eyes and Blindness.
  • “wallowing in a Slough of Despond, almost the gutter itself”: The Slough of Despond is a deep bog in John Bunyan’s allegory The Pilgrim’s Progress, into which the protagonist Christian sinks under the weight of his sins and his sense of guilt for them. It signifies a dark, painful phase in Miss MacIntosh’s life, highlighting both her resilience and the harsh realities she has faced before becoming Vera’s steadfast moral guide. See Miss MacIntosh in Intertextuality in MMMD.
  • “before, at last, I knew her, before I saw her plain”: The phrase echoes Robert Browning’s “Memorabilia”: “Ah, did you once see Shelley plain, / And did he stop and speak to you?” To see someone plain is to see the person as they really are, which no one in the house has done with Miss MacIntosh.
  • “a phosphorous light playing upon the darkened waters”: The glow sailors called phosphorescence in a ship’s wake is bioluminescence, light made by tiny plankton such as Noctiluca, “night light,” when the water is disturbed.
  • “She was neither a high brow nor a low brow but just . . . a plain middle brow”: The terms come from phrenology, which judged intelligence by the shape of the skull. Highbrow and lowbrow were in use by the 1900s, Van Wyck Brooks wrote “Highbrow and Lowbrow” in 1915, Virginia Woolf wrote an essay, “Middlebrow,” around 1932, and Russell Lynes’s “Highbrow, Lowbrow, Middlebrow” appeared in Harper’s in 1949.
  • “trying to steer her middle course between these jangling rocks”: Odysseus had to steer between Scylla, the six-headed monster, and Charybdis, the whirlpool, and the Argonauts passed through the Clashing Rocks that crushed ships between them. See Homer’s Epics.
  • “her British tan oxfords, her grey fedora”: The fedora, a soft felt hat with a creased crown, took its name from Victorien Sardou’s play Fédora (1882), whose heroine wore one, and was later taken up by men. Miss MacIntosh wears the men’s hat.
  • “armored always by her silver dollar watch”: Dollar watches were cheap, sturdy pocket watches. The Ingersoll company sold one for a dollar from 1896 and called it “the watch that made the dollar famous.” See Clocks and Watches.
  • “she could not see the purple hairstreak moths among the evening flowers”: The purple hairstreak is in fact a small butterfly, not a moth, that lives high in the tops of oak trees, where it is easily missed. See Butterflies and Moths.
  • “her good pin-striped grey serge with the shining elbows”: Serge is a type of twill fabric that has diagonal lines or ridges on both sides, made with a two-up, two-down weave. This choice of material aligns with Miss MacIntosh’s practical, no-nonsense character, emphasizing her plain, robust, and durable style of dress suited to her hardworking and sensible nature.
  • “made up of the bare necessities, as she would say, and no more”: Miss MacIntosh’s wardrobe is simple living in practice, with “not even a trimming of braid or a fichu of lace or an unnecessary button, for if there were an unnecessary button, it would be only one more button to lose.” Simple living encompasses a number of different voluntary practices to simplify one’s lifestyle. These may include: reducing one’s possessions, generally referred to as minimalism, or increasing self-sufficiency. Simple living may be characterized by individuals being satisfied with what they have rather than want.
  • “its pockets sagging because she had carried so many rocks, perhaps as ballast”: The novelist Virginia Woolf drowned herself in March 1941 by filling her pockets with stones and walking into the River Ouse, a few years before Young began writing this novel. See Virginia Woolf walked into the River (Ch 3) and Suicide in History and Literature.
    • “I had been inspired as to the means of Miss MacIntosh’s suicide by Virginia Woolf’s suicide,” Young said, and she learned only later that Woolf had “carried her walking stick with her clear to the tide’s edge,” as Miss MacIntosh leaves her umbrella (Marguerite Young, interview with Studs Terkel, WFMT radio, 1965); (Marguerite Young, interview with Duncan MacDonald, Observation Point, 1965).
  • “the known facts I had memorized as to the deaths of kings”: Shakespeare’s Richard II, facing his own fall, says, “For God’s sake let us sit upon the ground / And tell sad stories of the death of kings.” Miss MacIntosh thinks the deaths of kings “far less important than instructions in navigation.”
  • “Pilgrim’s Progress which she preferred to even the Word of God”: The Pilgrim’s Progress from This World, to That Which Is to Come is a 1678 Christian allegory written by John Bunyan. It is commonly regarded as one of the most significant works of Protestant devotional literature and of wider early modern English literature. It has been translated into more than 200 languages and has never been out of print. It appeared in Dutch in 1681, in German in 1703 and in Swedish in 1727. The first North American edition was issued in 1681. It has also been called the first novel written in English. According to literary editor Robert McCrum, “there’s no book in English, apart from the Bible, to equal Bunyan’s masterpiece for the range of its readership, or its influence on writers as diverse as William Hogarth, C. S. Lewis, Nathaniel Hawthorne, Herman Melville, Charles Dickens, Louisa May Alcott, George Bernard Shaw, William Thackeray, Charlotte Bronte, Mark Twain, John Steinbeck and Enid Blyton.” The lyrics of the hymn “To be a Pilgrim” are based on the novel. See John Bunyan’s Pilgrim’s Progress (1678) (Ch 3) and Pilgrim’s Progress.
  • “the Word of God was that which should be taken with a grain of salt”: To take something with a grain of salt, cum grano salis, goes back to Pliny the Elder, who described an antidote to poison to be taken with a grain of salt.
  • “the winds and their antiphon reminding me of all who had died”: An antiphon is a short chant in Christian ritual, sung as a refrain.
  • “an Arctic tern stopping upon the rocks”: The Arctic tern makes the longest migration of any animal, flying each year from its Arctic breeding grounds to the Antarctic and back, and so sees two summers and more daylight than any other creature. See Birds.
  • “The sins we committed were worse than those of omission”: Christian teaching distinguishes sins of commission, wrongs done, from sins of omission, good left undone, as in the general confession of the Book of Common Prayer: “We have left undone those things which we ought to have done; And we have done those things which we ought not to have done.” Miss MacIntosh ranks the first as worse, yet elsewhere she speaks of “those things God in His haste had forgotten,” as if God, too, had sins of omission.
  • “What is the best time to plant corn? Which part of the ship is abaft the main-mast?”: Old farm lore says to plant corn when the oak leaves are as big as a squirrel’s ear, when the soil has warmed. Abaft means toward the stern, and starboard is the right-hand side of a ship facing forward.
  • “two pennies with which, she used to say, her eyes would be closed when she was dead”: Charon’s obol is the term for the coin placed in or on the mouth of a dead person before burial. Greek and Latin literary sources specify the coin as an obol, and explain it was used as a payment or bribe for Charon, the ferryman who conveyed souls across the river that divided the world of the living from the world of the dead. (Wikipedia) In later custom, coins were laid on the eyelids of the dead to keep them closed.
  • “that I would see America first”: The slogan returns from Chapter 1, where Miss MacIntosh’s advice sends Vera into the Middle West. See the Chapter 1 resources.
  • “better than all the principalities, all the powers of darkness”: Ephesians 6:12 reads, “For we wrestle not against flesh and blood, but against principalities, against powers, against the rulers of the darkness of this world.”
  • “What Cheer, Iowa, a small town like any other”: What Cheer is a real town in Keokuk County, Iowa, of about six hundred people. Its name is an old English greeting; the Narragansett people are said to have greeted Roger Williams in 1636 with “What cheer, netop?” (“What cheer, friend?”). In an interview Young said she had no idea there was a real town by the name of What Cheer, Iowa. She thought she had made it up. See What Cheer (Ch 3) and Iowa, Indiana, and the Midwest.
  • “Few ever saw Miss MacIntosh”: Social invisibility here signifies the overlooked yet vital presence of Miss MacIntosh, whose plainness and refusal to engage in illusion cause her to be unseen or ignored, representing those who labor quietly and faithfully without acknowledgment in a world filled with illusions and distractions. It also emphasizes themes of isolation, unrecognized labor, and the contrast between appearance and reality. Social invisibility occurs when a group or individual is consistently overlooked or excluded from social, political, or economic participation. Catherine’s visitors “cared not to inquire who the active servant was.”
  • “her admirer was a head-hunter. He was an Australian bushman”: In Australian English a bushman is someone at home in the outback, usually a white settler skilled in bush life, and the Bushmen contingents were Australian volunteers who fought in the Boer War in 1900. The word did not usually mean Aboriginal people. There is little evidence of head-hunting on the Australian mainland. He is a foil to Miss MacIntosh, who rejects him, and the chapter treats his presence in the invalid’s house as a scandal. Young gives him a “wild mien and calculated, incalculable eloquence,” a “flow of broken rhetoric” with “imitations of a lyre bird.”
    • Miss MacIntosh’s head-hunter is a mixture. He is called an Australian bushman, a “wild, half-naked man of Borneo,” and a recent arrival from New Mexico, and her brother was lost in the Easter Islands. A bushman is easily confused with a bushranger, an outlaw of the bush; the most famous, Ned Kelly, was hanged in 1880, and some saw him as a champion of poor farmers against large landowners.
    • Head-hunting was practiced in the Torres Strait Islands, between Australia and New Guinea, including on Badu, where taking heads was tied to warfare and ceremonies honoring the dead. It was also practiced by the Dayak peoples of Borneo and in New Guinea, and the Māori of New Zealand preserved the tattooed heads of ancestors and enemies.
    • Of the bushman Young said, “I was thinking of the Easter Islands and those distant places where they worshipped the great stone heads” (Marguerite Young, interview with Studs Terkel, WFMT radio, 1965).
  • “his dreams . . . were that he might go over to Rome”: To “go over to Rome” was the English phrase for converting to Roman Catholicism, used of John Henry Newman and others in the Oxford Movement of the 1840s.
  • “nor was he even a good Presbyterian or Free Methodist or Shouting Baptist or Jehovah’s Witness”: Miss MacIntosh lists the plain Protestant churches of the Middle West. The Free Methodist Church was founded in New York in 1860 in protest against pew rents and slavery, and “shouting” describes the loud, ecstatic worship of revival meetings. See American Religious Movements.
  • “nor did he believe in total immersion, for he believed in sprinkling”: Churches have long divided over baptism. Baptists and many revival churches baptize adults by total immersion, while Catholics, Presbyterians, and Methodists usually baptize by sprinkling or pouring. Anabaptist groups are established in Iowa, including the Amish, the Mennonites, and the Old Order River Brethren, who baptize by immersion.
    • Baptism for especially early Christians was like being buried so that a person could rise to a new life. According to Paul, full immersion under water represents the believer’s death and burial in a watery grave with Christ, and the rising out of the water represents resurrection to a new life (Romans 6:3-4). Drownings during baptism have occasionally happened, and in the 1500s drowning was used as a punishment against the Anabaptists themselves: Felix Manz was drowned in Zurich in 1527, a mocking “third baptism.”
  • “as if he might even some day become the Pope wearing turrets of gold”: The papal tiara was a beehive-shaped crown of three tiers. Pope Paul VI was crowned with one in 1963 and then gave it away, and no pope since has worn it.
  • “walls of bones in beautiful designs like lace”: In the Capuchin Crypt beneath the church of Santa Maria della Concezione in Rome, the bones of some 3,700 friars are arranged in arches, rosettes, and chandeliers.
  • “the dead burying the dead until there were no more to bury”: Jesus tells a would-be follower who first wants to bury his father, “Follow me; and let the dead bury their dead” (Matthew 8:22).
  • “the primitive Christians of great works and little faith, not of great faith and little works”: The old quarrel between faith and works runs through Christianity. James 2:17 says, “faith, if it hath not works, is dead,” and Martin Luther, who taught salvation by faith alone, called the Epistle of James “an epistle of straw.”
  • “stopping to admire a broken Apollo”: Apollo is an Olympian deity in classical Greek and Roman religion and mythology.
  • “a dreaming Psyche”: The story of Psyche, told by Apuleius in The Golden Ass, is about the overcoming of obstacles to the love between Psyche and Cupid/Amor. Psyche in this context embodies the spiritual and psychological dimensions of human life, the inner reality behind outward appearances, and the continual transformation inherent in the human condition.
  • “a fat-stomached cupid with grapes in its hair and its nose broken when it had fallen from a Roman roof”: Roman palaces and churches lined their rooflines with stone statues of saints, gods, and cupids, so a broken cupid might well have fallen from a Roman roof. The roofs themselves were made of overlapping clay tiles, flat tegulae with curved imbrices covering the joints, a durable design still used across the Mediterranean.
  • “the wooden huntresses in ruined gardens”: Diana is a goddess in Roman and Hellenistic religion primarily considered a patroness of the countryside, hunters, crossroads, and the Moon. She is equated with the Greek goddess Artemis.
  • “in his native bush among bush-whackers”: In Australia a bushwhacker is someone who lives in the bush or clears it. In the United States the word meant a guerrilla fighter, especially in the Civil War. See The Civil War.
  • The Catholic Church had an assimilation policy (as in many other colonized countries) which was used to break the spiritual and cultural identity of Aborigines (and indigenous cultures worldwide) by removing tens of thousands of children from their parents. They apologized to Aborigines for the “stolen generation.” Recently Canada (2008), Pope Francis (2022) and the United States (2024) have also apologized for this practice.
  • “the love songs of a lyre bird who had fallen in love with an Australian spinster and had built a tower of earth to her window”: The lyrebird is a ground-dwelling Australian bird famous for mimicking natural and artificial sounds, even chainsaws and camera shutters. The male builds mounds of earth on which he dances and sings to court the female. Rural Australia also has its Bachelors and Spinsters Balls, country dances where single men and women meet.
  • “an old Ritz menu . . . an Etruscan mirror and an ivory comb”: César Ritz opened the Hôtel Ritz in Paris in 1898 with the chef Auguste Escoffier, whose French menus set the standard of luxury dining. Etruscan mirrors were polished bronze hand mirrors, engraved on the back with scenes from myth.
  • It is interesting that the Head-hunter focuses on her head given what follows in later chapters. This also highlights a man’s feeling that he has the right to interrupt, surprise, and corner a woman when he is interested in her no matter how the woman is feeling. In feminist literature this behavior can be identified as a man who feels he is entitled, deserving, and owed a woman’s attention regardless of her feelings. He is the “hunter,” and she is his “prey.”
  • “he might still revert to the noble savage”: The phrase “noble savage” first appears in English in John Dryden’s play The Conquest of Granada (1672). It is often credited to Jean-Jacques Rousseau, who never used it, though he praised humanity in a natural state.
  • “the wild, half-naked man of Borneo”: “The Wild Man of Borneo” was a stock attraction of nineteenth-century freak shows, and P. T. Barnum exhibited men under that name.
  • “memories of Eskimos”: Eskimos are the Indigenous peoples who have traditionally inhabited the northern region from eastern Siberia to Alaska, Canada, and Greenland. Many now prefer their own names, such as Inuit and Yupik.
  • “cherubim, many-faced angels with plumes of gold”: In Ezekiel’s vision the cherubim each have four faces, of a man, a lion, an ox, and an eagle (Ezekiel 1:10).
  • “Charon on his great ferry boat crossing the dark river Styx”: In Greek and Roman mythology Charon is the ferryman of Hades who carries souls of the newly deceased across the river Styx and Acheron that divided the world of the living from the world of the dead.
  • “the ghost of Cheops”: Cheops is the Greek name of the Egyptian pharaoh Khufu, who built the Great Pyramid of Giza around 2560 B.C. See Ancient Egypt.
  • “St. Simeon the Stylite and what he had thought of this lower world”: St. Simeon the Stylite was a Syriac ascetic saint who achieved notability for living thirty-seven years on a small platform on top of a pillar near Aleppo. (Wikipedia)
  • “Daniel encompassed by sleeping lions”: Daniel 6:22 tells how Daniel is saved from lions by the God of Israel. Symbolically, this reference typically evokes themes of courage, faith, endurance, and survival in the face of danger or adversity.
  • “the Appian Way and houses of the dead”: The Appian Way, begun in 312 B.C., is one of the earliest and most important roads of the Roman Republic. Its first miles outside Rome are lined with tombs, the “houses of the dead.”
  • “St. Augustine in the city of God”: The City of God is a book of Christian philosophy written in Latin by Augustine of Hippo after the sack of Rome in 410. (Wikipedia) The mention of St. Augustine’s “City of God” serves as a profound symbol of the contrast between earthly decay and spiritual aspiration, reflecting the characters’ inward struggles with faith, reality, and the hope for salvation or ultimate truth beyond the ephemeral world. See Augustine and Christian Theology.
  • “Georgian architecture”: Georgian architecture is the name given in most English-speaking countries to the set of architectural styles between 1714 and 1830, the reigns of the first four King Georges.
  • “Spode chinaware”: Spode is the English pottery founded by Josiah Spode in Stoke-on-Trent in 1770, famous for its blue-and-white transfer-printed ware.
  • “of Delft, of silver urns”: Delftware is the blue-and-white tin-glazed pottery made in the Dutch city of Delft from the seventeenth century, in imitation of Chinese porcelain.
  • “He could not digest the golden steeples and streets of gold”: The heavenly Jerusalem of Revelation has gates of pearl, “and the street of the city was pure gold, as it were transparent glass” (Revelation 21:21). See Revelation and the Apocalypse.
  • “these gaping cannibals”: Thomas Baker was a Methodist missionary in Fiji and is the only missionary in that country to be killed and eaten.
  • “Her own dear brother had gone out as a primitive Christian bishop from Iowa”: A bishop is an ordained member of the Christian clergy who oversees other clergy. See Richard MacIntosh.
  • “to convert the heathen of the Easter Islands”: Easter Island is an island and special territory of Chile in the southeastern Pacific Ocean. It is famous for its nearly 1,000 statues called moai. Its people are the Rapa Nui. Recent research has challenged the old story that an ecological collapse drove the islanders to war and cannibalism.
  • “the ladies mentioned by Plutarch”: Plutarch was a Greek Middle Platonist philosopher, biographer, and essayist, and a priest at the Temple of Apollo at Delphi, best known for his Parallel Lives of famous Greeks and Romans. (Wikipedia) Plutarch functions as a symbol of the mother’s intellectual and cultural anchoring amidst her drifting consciousness, representing a link to enduring human wisdom and the complexities of love, fate, and history that permeate her visionary world.
  • “the Protestant graveyard where Keats and Shelley slept and who after only one week in Rome had died of the marsh fever”: Keats and Shelley are buried in Rome’s Non-Catholic Cemetery near the Pyramid of Cestius. Marsh fever, or Roman fever, was malaria, whose name comes from the Italian mal aria, “bad air.” In Henry James’s “Daisy Miller” (1878), an American girl dies of Roman fever after a night visit to the Colosseum. See Romantic Poets.
  • “the best hotel would be the Quirinale”: The Quirinal Palace in Rome was a papal palace, then the royal palace, and is now the home of the president of Italy. It has housed thirty Popes, four Kings of Italy and twelve presidents of the Italian Republic. Rome also has a Hotel Quirinale, on the Via Nazionale.
  • “if he should not be admitted there, then he should try the Pantheon”: The Pantheon, completed about 125 A.D., was a temple to all the gods. Since 609 it has been a Catholic church, Santa Maria ad Martyres, and it holds the tombs of the painter Raphael and two kings of Italy, a strange hotel.
  • “mummery and flummery and junk”: Mummery is empty ritual or play-acting, from the masked mummers of folk plays. Flummery is a soft pudding, and so empty flattery or nonsense.
  • “For herself, she asked nothing”: Saint Teresa Margaret of the Sacred Heart, an eighteenth-century Carmelite nun of Florence, gave this counsel: “Always receive with equal contentment from God’s hand either consolations or sufferings, peace or distress, health or illness. Ask nothing, refuse nothing, but always be ready to do and to suffer anything that comes from His Providence.”
  • “even as the canker eats the rose, as gold and silver rust”: Shakespeare’s Sonnet 35 says “loathsome canker lives in sweetest bud,” the canker being a worm or blight. James 5:3 warns the rich, “Your gold and silver is cankered; and the rust of them shall be a witness against you,” and Matthew 6:19 speaks of treasures on earth “where moth and rust doth corrupt.”
  • “a dead lobster or broken hermit shell or lion’s mane”: The lion’s mane is the largest known jellyfish, with a reddish bell and masses of long, stinging tentacles like a mane.
  • “There must be, in fact, a revolution”: In political science, a revolution is a fundamental and relatively sudden change in political power and political organization which occurs when the population revolts against the government, typically due to perceived oppression or political incompetence. (Wikipedia) Miss MacIntosh cannot wait for gradual change, “no more than for a glacier moving in the night,” and socialists of her time argued the same question, whether society should change by slow reform or by revolution.
  • “What had this Darwinian evolution ever done for anybody?”: Darwinian evolution, set out in Charles Darwin’s On the Origin of Species (1859), is a theory of biological evolution stating that all species of organisms arise and develop through the natural selection of small, inherited variations that increase the individual’s ability to compete, survive, and reproduce.
  • “God’s was the strength of the unicorn”: Numbers 23:22 and 24:8 say of God that “he hath as it were the strength of an unicorn.” The King James translators used “unicorn” for the Hebrew re’em, probably the wild ox. The phrase may be interpreted as a poetic way of emphasizing the ineffable, incorruptible power of the divine, which stands apart from the fragile, chaotic human condition depicted throughout the novel.
  • “were we not still in Egypt, the waste-howling wilderness”: Miss MacIntosh’s speech is a weave of scripture. God led Israel out of Egypt, and Deuteronomy 32:10 says he found Jacob “in the waste howling wilderness.” “I was shapen in iniquity” is Psalm 51:5, “the mystery of iniquity” is 2 Thessalonians 2:7, “the joy of the hypocrite but for a moment” is Job 20:5, and “In the sweat of thy face shalt thou eat bread” is Genesis 3:19. See The Bible.
  • “Honesty was surely, and it had always been, the best policy”: The proverb has been attributed to Sir Edwin Sandys, who used it in 1599, and it was later quoted by Benjamin Franklin and Thomas Jefferson.
  • “never to hide one’s head in the desert sands like the poor ostrich”: The belief that the ostrich hides its head in the sand goes back to Pliny the Elder. Ostriches actually lie low with their necks along the ground, or turn their eggs in the nest with their beaks.
  • “our good works should not live after us”: Miss MacIntosh reverses Mark Antony in Shakespeare’s Julius Caesar: “The evil that men do lives after them; / The good is oft interred with their bones.” See Shakespeare.
  • “not the left wing . . . not the right wing . . . but something more immense, an honest point of view, the whole bird”: Centrism is a political outlook or specific position that involves acceptance or support of a balance of a degree of social equality and a degree of social hierarchy, while opposing political changes which would result in a significant shift of society strongly to either the left or the right. Centrism has a specific meaning within the Marxist movement, referring to a position between revolution and reformism. (Wikipedia) Miss MacIntosh’s centrist position is a firm, pragmatic, and sober approach to life, emphasizing common sense, self-discipline, and the rejection of illusions as the best way to navigate a harsh and uncertain world. Miss MacIntosh’s centrism is not merely a political or social stance but a fundamental worldview that privileges order, clarity, and practical wisdom in a world otherwise engulfed by confusion and chaos. Catherine’s list in Chapter 2 included “the left-wing political movement, the right wing of the dove.”
  • “another sea-swept spar which, clothed with feathery goose barnacles”: Goose barnacles hang from driftwood on fleshy stalks, their feathery feeding legs looking like plumes. Medieval writers such as Gerald of Wales believed that barnacle geese hatched from them, since no one had seen the geese nest.
  • “without the dead body, there could be no proof of death in a legal sense”: In the common law, a person who has been missing without word for seven years may be presumed dead, but without a body or that long wait, a death cannot be proved.
  • “or even a lamp-lighter”: A lamplighter lit and tended candle or gas street lamps at dusk. Maria Susanna Cummins’s novel The Lamplighter (1854) was one of the great bestsellers of its century, and the lamplighter on his tiny planet in Antoine de Saint-Exupéry’s The Little Prince (1943) lights and puts out his lamp every minute. The lamplighter stands as a symbol of hope, constancy, and the pursuit of clarity in a world engulfed by darkness, illusion, and uncertainty.
  • “The wait-and-see policy had always been his”: “Wait and see” became a political catchphrase in 1910, when the British prime minister H. H. Asquith used it repeatedly in Parliament, and his critics made it his nickname.
  • “no man knew, unless it was Mr. Spitzer, the hour of his death”: “Watch therefore, for ye know neither the day nor the hour wherein the Son of man cometh” (Matthew 25:13).
  • “He had always preferred a dark lady”: The phrase recalls the Dark Lady of Shakespeare’s Sonnets, the dark-haired, dark-eyed woman of Sonnets 127 to 152, so unlike the fair beloved of convention. Miss MacIntosh, the redhead Mr. Spitzer remembers as a brunette, is the novel’s own dark lady.
  • “at the doors of an employment agency which was turning away the unemployed”: During the Great Depression, unemployment in the United States reached about a quarter of the workforce in 1933, and lines of jobless men waited outside employment offices and soup kitchens.
  • “under the sign of three golden balls of a pawn shop like golden apples”: The pawnbroker’s sign of three golden balls is often traced to the Medici of Florence, whose coat of arms bore balls, and to Saint Nicholas, patron of pawnbrokers, who gave three bags of gold to save three poor girls.

Chapter 10

← Chapter 9 · Home · Chapter 11 →

Summary

Unable to picture her own wedding, Vera imagines other weddings and drifts into a dream of one. Mr. Spitzer is the veiled bride and Miss MacIntosh the bridegroom. The preacher’s marriage vows slide into a funeral service before he vanishes. Vera laughs at the dream, then is ashamed of it. She realizes she has been thinking unkindly of Miss MacIntosh as colorless and unwanted, and she feels pity for a woman who gave her life to duty. She is hungry and wants to go to her, but Miss MacIntosh must not be disturbed without good reason, and Vera has been warned not to wander by the sea at night.

Characters present

Vera Cartwheel · Joachim Spitzer · Miss MacIntosh · Solomon the Turtle

Concepts present

Themes: Death and Mortality · Dreams and Imagination · Identity and the Self · Illusion and Reality · Isolation and Connection · Society, Class, and Race · Women, Gender, and Marriage

Symbols: Clothing, Hats, and Skirts · Roses and Flowers · The House · Twins and Doubles · Weddings and Funerals

Philosophy: Augustine and Christian Theology · Plato and Platonism

Allusions: Angels and Archangels · Astronomy · Fairy Tales and Folklore · Greek Mythology · Judaism · Milton · Music and Composers · Romantic Poets · Shakespeare · The Bible · The Book of Job

Key passages

From the research

  • Vera dreams or hallucinates a surreal wedding ceremony in which Mr. Spitzer and Miss MacIntosh are paired, but the roles and identities are confused and inverted. The preacher’s words blur distinctions between man and woman, human and beast, and even marriage rites and funeral rites become intertwined. This dream culminates in an eerie meditation on death and the fleeting nature of life. The preacher’s speech shifts seamlessly from wedding vows to funeral liturgy, emphasizing the inseparability of marriage and death, union and dissolution. The dream ends with the unsettling image of Mr. Spitzer as the bride and Miss MacIntosh as the bridegroom, highlighting ambiguous identities and roles.
  • Following the dream, Vera reflects on Miss MacIntosh’s situation, age, and prospects for marriage. She is portrayed as a somewhat colorless, ordinary woman, past the prime of youth, who has resigned herself to loneliness. Yet Vera also feels a budding pity and empathy for her, contemplating the pain of being old and unloved and recognizing her human frailty.
  • Throughout the chapter, there is a strong undercurrent of existential melancholy. The preacher’s speech invokes biblical imagery about the brevity of life, decay, and the inevitability of death. This generalizes human fate and questions the permanence of social institutions like marriage.
  • Vera’s hunger, both literal and metaphorical, is evident as she contemplates the absence of celebration and the lack of meaningful connection. She regrets not visiting Miss MacIntosh, wishing to reconcile and share intimacy, yet respects her privacy and limitations, underscoring themes of isolation and the human need for companionship.
  • The chapter is rich in symbolism. The wedding and funeral imagery combined suggests the cyclical nature of life and death. Mr. Spitzer’s twin iron bedsteads symbolize duality or fractured identity; the snow and ice evoke coldness and isolation; the locked bedroom door represents the boundaries of privacy and emotional distance. The preacher’s litany names biblical and mythic figures (Lucifer, Beelzebub, Gorgons, Hydras, Chimeras) and cosmic events, creating a vision of a chaotic universe where human rituals struggle for meaning.

Questions and observations

Reading closely

  • The preacher does not seem “to know who was woman and who was man and who was beast and who was bird.” What does the dream undo?
  • Mr. Spitzer nods “negatively as he replied affirmatively.” What is he really saying?
  • When the stars light the scene, “this error was the error of the dream which had begotten nothing.” Whose error is it?

Characters

  • Vera gives Miss MacIntosh a waxed mustache and a silk hat, as she did in Chapter 9. What does Vera keep seeing in her?
  • Mr. Spitzer would marry “no one now but his brother worm.” What holds him to his dead brother?
  • Vera calls Miss MacIntosh “the most colorless” person in the world, then feels “the first embryonic emotion of pity.” What changes in one night?

Connections

  • Madge’s wedding was a funeral in Chapter 6, and here the preacher slides from one service to the other. Why does the novel keep joining weddings and funerals?
  • Miss MacIntosh’s locked bedroom door returns to the locked doors of Chapters 7 and 8. What is behind it?
  • The preacher recites the tribes of Israel as Miss MacIntosh made Vera recite them in Chapter 9. Why does the dream use her lessons?

Reflection

  • “One who could know us and yet love us was undoubtedly the truest love this world has ever seen.” Is it possible to be fully known and still loved?
  • “What would it be like to be old and unloved?” Is it harder to be young and unloved, or old?
  • Vera laughs at the dream, then feels ashamed. When does laughing at someone become wronging them?

Research: Characters

Vera Cartwheel

  • She is the central consciousness reflecting on marriage, dreams, and the strange events unfolding.
  • She is introspective, sensitive, and somewhat confused by the surreal experiences.

Mr. Joachim Spitzer

  • An older man, melancholic and resigned to his fate.
  • He is described with an old-fashioned elegance, symbolized by his clothes and the twin beds he shares (in memory) with his deceased brother.
  • His identity is ambiguous, shifting between bride and groom in the dream.

Miss MacIntosh

  • An older woman, practical and resigned to a life without love or marriage.
  • She is portrayed as colorless, ordinary in appearance, yet capable and domestically inclined.
  • In the dream, she assumes the role of bridegroom, further blurring gender and identity.

The Preacher

  • A mysterious figure who recites ritualistic and apocalyptic language blending wedding rites with funeral orations.
  • His speech is symbolic and confusing, reflecting the instability of the event.
  • His words come almost entirely from the Book of Common Prayer, the marriage service sliding into the Order for the Burial of the Dead, with verses from Job, Psalms, Corinthians, Jude, and Revelation spliced in.

Solomon the Turtle

  • He can be interpreted as a symbol of longevity, endurance, and ancient wisdom.
  • Turtles traditionally embody qualities such as patience, stability, and a slow, deliberate approach to life.
  • In the context of this chapter, where Vera confronts themes of mortality, the fleeting nature of existence, and the confusion between life’s ceremonies (weddings) and rites of passage (funerals), Solomon may represent a counterpoint to human transience and folly.
  • The turtle’s slow, deliberate presence contrasts with the chaotic, disordered, and surreal wedding-funeral rites, emphasizing the tension between the ephemeral and the enduring.
  • The turtle’s name, “Solomon,” evokes the biblical King Solomon, renowned for his wisdom and judgment. This further amplifies the symbolic weight of the turtle as a figure of insight and contemplation amidst the chaos and absurdity Vera perceives around her.
  • Solomon’s silent witness role amidst this disarray may suggest the presence of a wise, patient observer within Vera’s subconscious, hinting at a deeper understanding or acceptance of life’s contradictions and mysteries.

Research: Themes

Marriage and Identity

See: Identity and the Self · Women, Gender, and Marriage

  • The confusion and inversion of roles in the dream wedding hint at fluidity in gender and societal roles.
  • Marriage is portrayed ambiguously, blending union and separation, life and death.
  • The preacher’s confusing vows suggest the complexity and sometimes absurdity of social rituals.

Mortality and Impermanence

See: Death and Mortality

  • The wedding turns into a funeral, reflecting the inseparability of life and death.
  • Biblical and apocalyptic references underscore the transient nature of human life.
  • The preacher’s speech highlights human frailty and the inevitability of death.

Loneliness and Human Connection

See: Isolation and Connection

  • Miss MacIntosh’s character symbolizes the loneliness of aging and societal neglect.
  • Vera feels pity and empathy, recognizing the shared human condition.
  • The dream’s isolation (few guests, symbolic objects) stresses the solitude underlying social ceremonies.

Dream versus Reality

See: Illusion and Reality · Dreams and Imagination

  • The blurred line between dream and waking life shows the instability of perception.
  • Vera’s hallucinatory experience reflects inner turmoil and existential questioning.

Social Roles and Expectations

See: Society, Class, and Race

  • Miss MacIntosh’s resignation to a life without marriage and Vera’s reflections reveal societal pressures on women.
  • The notion that “none would have her” contrasts with Vera’s hope for unexpected companionship.

Research: Symbols and Imagery

Twin Iron Bedsteads

See: The House · Twins and Doubles

  • Represent memory, duality, and the coexistence of past and present selves (Mr. Spitzer and his deceased brother).

Wedding/Funeral Ceremony

See: Weddings and Funerals

  • Symbolizes the intertwined nature of beginnings and endings, union and separation.

Veil and Mustache

See: Clothing, Hats, and Skirts

  • Play with gender roles and identity, challenging traditional expectations.

Turtle Solomon

  • Symbolizes wisdom and endurance.

Red Geranium

See: Roses and Flowers

  • Might symbolize life, vitality, and domesticity.

Old Empty Shoe

See: Clothing, Hats, and Skirts

  • Could represent emptiness, absence, or abandonment.

Research: Resources

  • “some other bride blushing like a red, red rose”: Robert Burns, “O my Luve’s like a red, red rose” (1794). See Romantic Poets.
  • “live happily ever after as in an old fairy tale”: The fairy-tale ending, “and they lived happily ever after.” See Fairy Tales and Folklore.
  • “his brother worm who was under the ground”: Job says “to the worm, Thou art my mother, and my sister” (Job 17:14), and Hamlet says, “Your worm is your only emperor for diet” (Hamlet 4.3). See The Book of Job and Shakespeare.
  • “pots and pans jangling in my ears”: A shivaree, or charivari, was the old custom of banging pots and pans outside newlyweds’ windows on their wedding night. See Weddings and Funerals.
  • “it was a funeral march which was played at a perfect wedding”: Chopin’s Funeral March (Piano Sonata No. 2, 1839) in place of Mendelssohn’s Wedding March (1842) or Wagner’s “Here Comes the Bride” (Lohengrin, 1850). See Music and Composers.
  • “we are gathered here in the sight of God and of this company to join man and woman together”: The Book of Common Prayer opens the marriage service, “Dearly beloved, we are gathered together here in the sight of God, and in the face of this congregation, to join together this man and this woman in holy matrimony.” See Weddings and Funerals.
    • The marriage vows and priestly blessing in the prayer book came from the Sarum rite, the medieval service of Salisbury Cathedral.
    • The canons long known as the Fourth Council of Carthage (398) are now called the Statuta Ecclesiae Antiqua, a collection compiled in southern Gaul between 476 and 485, probably by Gennadius of Marseille. One canon has the bride and groom presented to the priest for a blessing by their parents or by their attendants, the paranymphs, a custom the Schaff-Herzog Encyclopedia of Religious Knowledge traces to “the Fourth Synod of Carthage (398).”
  • “for the end of the world draweth nigh”: This echoes “The end of all things is at hand” (1 Peter 4:7) and “your redemption draweth nigh” (Luke 21:28). “Lightnings and thunderings and voices” come from Revelation 4:5, and “in the twinkling of an eye” from 1 Corinthians 15:52: “we shall all be changed, in a moment, in the twinkling of an eye.” See The Bible.
  • “when there shall be many gnashings of teeth, many wailings”: Matthew 8:12 reads, “there shall be weeping and gnashing of teeth.” This phrase underscores themes of mortality, judgment, and the sorrow that accompanies human existence, blending the sacred with the tragic in Vera’s experience of the marriage ritual. See The Bible.
  • “a mighty hurricane is blowing in from the Canary Islands or Hebrides”: Atlantic hurricanes are born off West Africa, near the Canary and Cape Verde Islands. The Hebrides lie in the cold north of Scotland, where no hurricane begins.
    • The Canary Islands are a Spanish archipelago off the coast of northwestern Africa.
    • The Hebrides are an archipelago comprising hundreds of islands off the northwest coast of Scotland.
  • “this life is very short and full of mortal sorrow”: Job 14:1 reads, “Man that is born of a woman is of few days, and full of trouble.” This phrase serves as a sobering meditation on human finitude, the inevitability of death, and the sorrow that colors a brief life. See The Book of Job.
  • “Porpoises shall eat the drowned sailor. The waters of this world shall close over his head”: The preacher gives the bride and groom a sailor’s burial at sea. Milton’s “Lycidas” (1638) mourns a friend drowned in the Irish Sea, and Ariel sings of a drowned father in The Tempest: “Full fathom five thy father lies.” The line foreshadows Miss MacIntosh lost in the waves. See Milton, Shakespeare, The Sea and Water, and the Chapter 6 resources.
  • “Do either of ye know of an impediment to this marriage”: The phrase is from the Book of Common Prayer, which drew on the Sarum rite. It reads, “I require and charge you both, as ye will answer at the dreadful day of judgment when the secrets of all hearts shall be disclosed, that if either of you know any impediment . . . ye do now confess it,” and calls on anyone who knows a cause to “speak, or else hereafter for ever hold his peace.” See Weddings and Funerals.
  • “St. Michael and of all the holy angels”: The list comes out of Milton’s Paradise Lost, which gives Hell “Gorgons and Hydras, and Chimaeras dire” (2.628) and seats Chaos as umpire with “high arbiter Chance” who “governs all” (2.907-910). See Milton and Angels and Archangels.
    • St. Michael is an archangel, a spiritual warrior in the battle of good versus evil.
    • Lucifer “who was the brightest and is fallen farthest” is the name of different figures in folklore associated with the planet Venus. “How art thou fallen from heaven, O Lucifer, son of the morning!” (Isaiah 14:12). See the Chapter 7 resources.
    • Beelzebub is Baal-zebub, “lord of the flies,” god of the Philistine city of Ekron (2 Kings 1:2), and in the Gospels the prince of devils (Matthew 12:24).
    • Chaos is the void before the forming of the universe in Greek mythology.
    • Gorgons are creatures in Greek mythology. Medusa and her sisters had a gaze that turned men to stone.
    • Hydras are serpentine water monsters in Greek and Roman mythology. Heracles killed the many-headed Hydra as his second labor.
    • Chimeras are monsters made of different parts of animals in mythology. Bellerophon killed the Chimera, part lion, part goat, part serpent.
    • In Aristotle’s Physics, chance (automaton) works in nature and luck (tyche) in human affairs.
  • “the dreadful Day of Judgment”: The Day of Judgment belongs to eschatology, the part of theology that deals with the ultimate destiny of humans. It is found in Judaism, Christianity, Islam, and Zoroastrianism. The golden thrones and “the sea shall turn to glass” come from Revelation 4:4-6: “a sea of glass like unto crystal.” See The Bible.
  • “Unadvisedly or lightly, marriage should not be entered in”: The prayer book says marriage is “not by any to be enterprised, nor taken in hand, unadvisedly, lightly . . . but reverently, discreetly, advisedly, soberly.” See Weddings and Funerals.
  • “none shall take a wife of whoredoms”: God tells the prophet Hosea, “Go, take unto thee a wife of whoredoms” (Hosea 1:2). See The Bible.
  • “to have and to hold from this day forward”: The prayer book vows: “to have and to hold from this day forward, for better for worse . . . in sickness and in health, to love, cherish, and to obey.” Mr. Spitzer nods “negatively as he replied affirmatively.” See the Chapter 6 resources on “love, honor, and obey.”
  • “all corporeal and incorporeal hereditaments”: Appurtenances are accessories or other items associated with a particular activity or style of living. The preacher slips into the language of property deeds, which pass “hereditaments and appurtenances,” everything that can be inherited or that goes with an estate.
  • “Man that is born of woman”: The burial service opens, “Man, that is born of a woman, hath but a short time to live, and is full of misery.” The preacher adds the swollen stomach, from the trial of the jealous husband’s wife in Numbers 5:27. See The Book of Job.
    • “Her belly shall swell, and her thigh shall rot” (Numbers 5:27). This phrase encapsulates the complex interplay of physical condition and the spiritual or emotional state likely reflecting on the human condition’s heaviness and vulnerability as portrayed throughout the novel.
  • “the rites for the burial of the dead”: Funeral rites originated from Jewish and Roman customs. The Order for the Burial of the Dead in the Book of Common Prayer is the service the preacher slides into. See Weddings and Funerals.
  • “He cometh up, and he is cut down”: Job 14:2 reads, “He cometh forth like a flower, and is cut down: he fleeth also as a shadow, and continueth not.” This phrase serves as a poignant reminder within the narrative of life’s impermanence and the inescapable presence of death even at moments of joy and union. The preacher quotes the burial service word for word: “He cometh up, and is cut down, like a flower; he fleeth as it were a shadow, and never continueth in one stay.” See The Book of Job.
  • “He has gone from Newport to Mystic, from Wellfleet to Buzzards Bay”: The preacher lists the coast of Rhode Island, Connecticut, and Cape Cod, the New England shore where Vera grows up.
  • “May God forgive us, for we know not who or where we are”: “Father, forgive them; for they know not what they do” (Luke 23:34). See The Bible.
  • “Spare us, Lord most holy, God most mighty, holy and merciful Savior”: The burial service prays, “spare us, Lord most holy, O God most mighty, O holy and merciful Saviour.”
  • “the archangel trumpeting the last trump”: “For the Lord himself shall descend from heaven with a shout, with the voice of the archangel, and with the trump of God” (1 Thessalonians 4:16). See Angels and Archangels.
  • “Why stand we in jeopardy every hour?”: Paul asks it in 1 Corinthians 15:30. The phrase conveys a broader theme in the novel of the tension between life and death, the known and the unknown, and the profound uncertainties that define human experience. It is a rhetorical question that underscores the fragile, often perilous journey of life that the characters navigate throughout the narrative. 1 Corinthians 15 is the lesson read at the burial service. See The Bible.
  • “Nothing thou hast brought into this world”: “For we brought nothing into this world, and it is certain we can carry nothing out” (1 Timothy 6:7), one of the burial service’s opening sentences. See The Bible.
  • “Gold and silver rust”: “Your gold and silver is cankered; and the rust of them shall be a witness against you” (James 5:3). See The Bible.
  • “What is man but a poor, two-legged animal?”: Plato defined man as a featherless biped, and Diogenes answered with a plucked chicken. Lear calls man “such a poor, bare, forked animal” (King Lear 3.4). See Plato and Platonism and Shakespeare.
  • “His beauty consumeth away, like as if it were a moth fretting a woolen garment”: “Thou makest his beauty to consume away, like as it were a moth fretting a garment” (Psalm 39:12, as the burial service gives it). See The Bible.
  • “In the morning it is green and groweth up, but in the evening it is cut down, withered”: “In the morning it is green, and groweth up; but in the evening it is cut down, dried up, and withered” (Psalm 90:6, in the burial service). See The Bible.
  • “All hearts shall melt to water”: “The hearts of the people melted, and became as water” (Joshua 7:5). See The Bible.
  • “The weak are the strong”: Paul writes, “for when I am weak, then am I strong” (2 Corinthians 12:10). See The Bible.
  • “Selah, selah, selah”: In the Bible, the word “selah” typically signifies a pause, a time for reflection, or a musical interlude. It appears most often in the Psalms and Habakkuk, suggesting a moment to stop and consider what has just been said or sung.
  • “Where is Nepthalin? Where is Reuben who begot a horde? Where is Manasses?”: Nephthalim and Manasses are the King James spellings of Naphtali and Manasseh in Revelation 7:6, where twelve thousand of each tribe are sealed. See the Chapter 9 resources on the genealogies.
  • “Oh, death, where is thy sting? Oh, grave, where is thy victory?”: Paul’s words in 1 Corinthians 15:55, read at the burial service. The phrase encapsulates the struggle to find meaning beyond death and the hope or belief that death may not be the ultimate end. It reflects a yearning for transcendence, where death’s “sting” (its pain and finality) and the “victory” of the grave (the end of life) are questioned or denied. See The Bible.
  • “thy womb of morning”: “From the womb of the morning” (Psalm 110:3). See The Bible.
  • “Can these bones live?”: God asks Ezekiel in the valley of dry bones (Ezekiel 37:3). See The Bible.
  • “earth to earth, ashes to ashes, dust to dust”: The burial service reads, “Forasmuch as it hath pleased Almighty God . . . to take unto himself the soul of our dear brother . . . we therefore commit his body to the ground; earth to earth, ashes to ashes, dust to dust.” The preacher’s “brother to brother, deep calling to deep” adds Psalm 42:7. See the Chapter 1 resources.
  • “As it was in the beginning, is now, and ever shall be, world without end”: The Gloria Patri, the doxology sung at the end of the psalms.
  • “Where is Philemon?”: Philemon was a Christian of Colossae to whom Paul wrote his letter about Onesimus, a runaway slave, asking forgiveness for him. In Ovid, Philemon and Baucis are the old married couple who asked to die at the same hour and were turned into two trees, an oak and a linden. See The Bible and Greek Mythology.
  • “Where is Zipporah, a little bird?”: Zipporah was the wife of Moses. Her name means “bird” in Hebrew. See The Bible.
  • “Where are those wandering stars to whom is reserved the blackness of darkness forever?”: The preacher recites Jude 1:12-13: “clouds they are without water, carried about of winds; trees whose fruit withereth, without fruit, twice dead, plucked up by the roots . . . wandering stars, to whom is reserved the blackness of darkness for ever.” See The Bible.
  • “Strike up the music! On with the dance”: Byron’s “On with the dance! let joy be unconfined,” from the ball on the eve of Waterloo (Childe Harold’s Pilgrimage, Canto III). See Romantic Poets.
  • “the turtle Solomon and the red geranium and an old, empty shoe”: An old shoe was thrown after the bride or tied to the carriage for luck. See Weddings and Funerals.
  • “Her face was certainly not her fortune”: The nursery rhyme’s milkmaid answers, “My face is my fortune, sir, she said.” See Fairy Tales and Folklore.
  • “She had stopped it only once, and that was in Spokane”: Miss MacIntosh’s broken nose from a bus in Spokane, from Chapter 9. See the Chapter 9 resources.
  • “the oldest fool was the greatest fool”: “There is no fool like an old fool” (John Heywood, 1546).
  • “she could be the helpmeet”: “I will make him an help meet for him” (Genesis 2:18). See The Bible.
  • “their numbers were legion”: “My name is Legion: for we are many” (Mark 5:9). See The Bible.
  • “Familiarity breeds contempt”: Chaucer’s Tale of Melibee has “over-greet hoomlynesse engendreth dispreisynge,” too much familiarity breeds contempt. The Latin proverb “Nimia familiaritas parit contemptum” is credited to Publilius Syrus and repeated by Thomas Aquinas (Hoyt’s New Cyclopedia of Practical Quotations, 1922), and the English wording first appears in Richard Taverner’s Garden of Wysdome (1539). In Hindu tradition the Srimad Bhagavatam (Bhagavata Purana) teaches the same lesson in Canto 6, Chapter 7: Indra, king of the demigods, grows so used to the daily presence of his spiritual master, Bṛhaspati, that he takes him for granted and fails to rise when Bṛhaspati enters the assembly. A. C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupada draws the moral in his purport: “Familiarity sometimes breeds contempt, but one should be very careful in one’s dealings with the acarya” (Srimad-Bhagavatam 6.7.15, purport).
  • “One who could know us and yet love us was undoubtedly the truest love this world has ever seen”: Psalm 139 begins, “O Lord, thou hast searched me, and known me.” The line suggests that the deepest and most genuine form of love is not blind or naive, but rather one that fully comprehends all aspects of a person (their strengths, weaknesses, flaws, and complexities) and loves them in spite of, or even because of, that complete knowledge. This statement highlights the theme of authentic love as acceptance and compassion for the whole person, including their imperfections and vulnerabilities. It contrasts with superficial or idealized love, which might only appreciate a partial or idealized image. The “truest love” is grounded in reality, acknowledging the full truth of the beloved. In the context of the chapter, Vera (the narrator) reflects on the nature of love and marriage, and the idea that true love involves a deep understanding and acceptance of the other person. Miss MacIntosh, who values common sense and reality, would likely agree with this view, emphasizing love based on truth rather than illusion or fantasy. The phrase captures a central insight into the nature of love as something that embraces the whole self (the light and the dark, the certain and the uncertain) and that this kind of love is the most meaningful and enduring.
  • “to waste one’s sweetness in the desert air”: Thomas Gray’s Elegy: “Full many a flower is born to blush unseen, / And waste its sweetness on the desert air.” See the Chapter 5 resources.
  • “The sands of time were always running low”: The hourglass, and the hymn “The sands of time are sinking” (Anne Ross Cousin, 1857).
  • “claws upon her forehead like the claws of a lobster”: The pain from shoulder to hand and the crab’s claws may foreshadow what Vera learns of Miss MacIntosh’s body. Cancer takes its name from the crab, the Greek karkinos.
  • “whirling dervishes”: The Mevlevi Sufis, followers of the poet Rumi, worship by whirling.
  • “good, true, beautiful”: Plato’s three highest ideas, the Good, the True, and the Beautiful. See Plato and Platonism.

Vocabulary

Harsh and jarring in sound.
Chimera
A monster of Greek myth, part lion, part goat, part serpent; any wild, impossible fancy.

Archaic for consumes; wastes away.

A member of a Sufi order known for whirling in worship.

In a scattered, spread-out way.

Doubtful.

Unpredictably; irregularly.

A record of a family’s descent.
Gorgon
In Greek myth, one of three snake-haired sisters whose gaze turned men to stone.
Helpmeet
A helper and companion, especially a wife.
Hereditament
Property that can be inherited.
Hydra
A many-headed serpent of Greek myth.
Impoverished
Made poor.
Incorporeal
Without a body; not physical.
Indetermination
Indecision.
Inscrutable
Impossible to understand or interpret.

A vast number.

Many and various.

Marriage.

One who calls up the dead.

Sad and mournful in sound.

Pain and stiffness in the joints and muscles.

A Hebrew word in the Psalms, perhaps a pause.
