chapter-08:
Chapter 8

← Chapter 7 · Home · Chapter 9 →

Summary

The bus pushes through a cloudburst with a broken windshield wiper, the road barely distinguishable from the flooded fields. It stops at a fork near a hill of old tombstones, beside Beatrice Fitzgerald’s tin house in a yard of mud and wreckage. Madge calls Beatrice a common prostitute. Homer defends her: a hard worker who lost an eye to a boy’s arrow, whose son, rumored to be old Doc’s, joined the Navy. Lost in thought of drowning, Vera cries out for Miss MacIntosh. Moses brings word that old Josh Hathaway is dead and calls it murder, whoever turned the key. Moses delivers a long, dark meditation on death and medicine, insisting that not even the best doctor could help Jacqueline. The bus enters a village at night. Its houses look like coffins under a skull-like moon, and Vera wonders whether she has arrived in a land of eternal night or a dream within a dream.

Characters present

Vera Cartwheel · Moses Hunnecker · Madge Capehorn · Homer Capehorn · Beatrice Fitzgerald · Jacqueline White · Miss MacIntosh · Justice O’Leary

Concepts present

Themes: Death and Mortality · Faith, God, and the Supernatural · Isolation and Connection · Madness and Sanity · Memory and the Past · Society, Class, and Race · Time

Symbols: Birds · Keys, Doors, and Locks · Lamps, Candles, and Light · The Bus and the Journey · The House · The Sea and Water · Weddings and Funerals

Philosophy: Aristotle · Augustine and Christian Theology · Descartes and Dualism · Kant and Hegel · Plato and Platonism · Schopenhauer

Allusions: Dante · Don Quixote · Edgar Allan Poe · Fairy Tales and Folklore · Genesis · Greek Mythology · Iowa, Indiana, and the Midwest · Milton · Music and Composers · Shakespeare · The Bible · The Book of Job

Key passages

From the research

  • The chapter opens with a vivid description of passing through violent weather: cloudbursts, thunder, rain like a deluge, darkness without illumination, the broken windshield wiper, and the road as a river. This stormy journey symbolizes a transition, perhaps even a metaphor for the passage from life to death or from one state of existence to another. Vera reflects, “Perhaps it was the beginning of creation. Perhaps we had said farewell to earth.” This sets a tone of mystery and existential reflection, indicating a crossing into an unknown or liminal space.
  • The bus stops at a place where the road divides near a graveyard hill, with old tombstones bearing faded names. One branch leads downward to an obscure village described as a “land of promise through eternity,” where time ceases, and life is eternal, “where the children would dance, where the young would not grow old, where the old would never die.” This passage contrasts the realm of death (graveyard) with the idealized vision of eternal life, emphasizing themes of mortality, hope, and the human yearning for immortality.
  • On the other side of the road is a decrepit tin house in a flooded yard, described in grim detail: mud, refuse, broken furniture, and wreckage. Here lives Beatrice Fitzgerald, an old woman shrouded in mystery and local gossip. The dialogue about her reveals the community’s harsh judgments, mingling myth and fact: she is called a “common prostitute,” yet also described as “royal,” with “blue blood” due to her name’s prefix “Fitz-.” Her tragic story includes losing an eye and having a son who joined the Navy and travels the world but still remembers her. This passage reflects themes of social ostracism, the complexity of human identity, and the enduring bonds of family amid decay and despair.
  • Moses delivers a long, rambling, and philosophical monologue about “old Doc,” a once-practicing physician now dismissed as mad and irrelevant. He talks about the futility of medical science against death and decay, expressing skepticism about doctors, cures, and even the existence of God or heaven. His words are laced with dark humor and bitterness: “There’s no hell, and there’s no heaven, and there’s no doctor.” He wrestles with mortality, the inevitability of death, and the human desire to resist it, but ultimately acknowledges the helplessness everyone faces. This passage is a meditation on aging, illness, and the limits of human control over life and death.
  • Moses’s speech includes vivid, symbolic imagery: “Alpha and Omega, beginning and end! Trunk, bole, hulk, skeleton,” and references to biblical and mythological figures: Leviathan, Julius Caesar, Hercules, and Charon. These evoke the grand, inescapable cycle of life and death, reinforcing the theme that no one escapes mortality. The passage blends the mundane and the cosmic, illustrating the universal human condition through both everyday and mythic lenses.
  • The chapter concludes with a haunting description of arriving at a village at night, described as “spectral,” with “upright houses like coffins,” “a pale, dented moon like a skull,” and “great spaces yawning between.” The imagery evokes death, emptiness, and silence, filled only with the voices of the past and the dead. Vera questions whether this place is real or a dream, a “dream within the dream,” underscoring the elusive nature of reality and the boundary between life and death.

Questions and observations

Reading closely

  • The road divides at the graveyard: one branch climbs to the tombstones, the other descends to the village of “promise through eternity.” Which branch does the bus take?
  • Madge leaves the light on so a man “cannot say he did not know,” while Beatrice puts the lights out. What does each woman want to be seen, or not seen?
  • Moses rattles off strings of words: “Barmy . . . screw loose, unhinged, off his head.” What is he trying not to say?

Characters

  • Homer calls Beatrice “royal,” and Madge calls her “the oldest prostitute in all this country.” What makes each of them see her as they do?
  • Moses says of old Doc, “you can’t help giving him your hand when he gives his hand to you.” Why can’t Moses let Doc go?
  • Beatrice’s son “never forgot her” and sends postcards from the world’s great ports. What has he escaped, and what has he kept?

Connections

  • Moses repeats “the key turned by itself” and Madge’s charge of murder from Chapter 7. Why does the novel keep returning to the locked door?
  • Vera wonders whether she relives “another’s” life, as the drowning are said to do. Whose face is “pillowed upon the oozy tides of time”?
  • The chapter ends on “that dream within the dream.” How has the whole journey come to feel like one?

Reflection

  • “You can’t prove it’s murder . . . you can’t prove it’s not, so you are right, whichever way you look at it.” Can a town live by that logic?
  • “There’s no hell, and there’s no heaven, and there’s no doctor.” What is left to Moses if he believes this?
  • “To come to a village at night may be never to know it.” What do people miss when they first meet a place, or a person, in the dark?

Research: Characters

Vera Cartwheel

  • Her descriptions are richly metaphorical and poetic, often blending natural imagery with existential or mythic overtones.
  • She imparts a sense of transition or passage not just through physical space but through states of being or time.
  • She frequently distances herself from the events, perceiving them as if in a vision or dream.
  • She is grappling with realities that are elusive, fragmented, or overwhelming.
  • She contemplates mortality, memory, and identity. This reflects an engagement with themes of impermanence and the unknowability of ultimate fate.
  • While observing others on the bus, Vera remains somewhat apart, bearing witness to their stories and conflicts without fully participating.
  • Her grief and confusion suggest a loneliness or estrangement, emphasized by the eerie, almost spectral description of the village and its inhabitants.
  • Vera is positioned on the edge of the known and unknown, the living and the dead, the earthly and the eternal.
  • The stopping of the bus at a fork, one path leading to a graveyard hill and the other to a mysterious village of promise, serves as a potent symbol for her liminal condition. This reflects an internal or spiritual threshold, not merely a physical one.
  • Her tone is somber, contemplative, and at times skeptical or cynical, especially in the bus-driver’s monologue on medical science, mortality, and social decay. She absorbs this skepticism without endorsing it outright, contributing to a complex, layered narrative voice.

Moses Hunnecker (The Bus Driver)

  • An experienced, somewhat cynical man who knows the terrain well and sees the storm as routine.
  • He stops the bus at a graveyard hill, signaling a crucial moment in the journey.
  • He is skeptical of medical science and doctors, especially “old Doc,” whom he sees as out of touch and ineffective.
  • The bus-driver’s long monologue reveals his mistrust in institutions, the inevitability of death, and a complex view of life, health, and mortality.

Madge Capehorn

  • Madge condemns Beatrice Fitzgerald as “the oldest prostitute in all this country.”
  • Madge is outspoken and somewhat judgmental, suggesting that Beatrice tries to hide in darkness because of her ugliness and reputation.
  • Madge’s perspective contrasts with Homer’s more sympathetic view.

Homer Capehorn

  • Offers a more nuanced and sympathetic view of Beatrice Fitzgerald, describing her as hardworking, loyal, and even “royal” because of her name’s lineage.
  • He recounts stories of her past hardships and suggests a tragic background, including the loss of an eye and a son who joined the Navy.

Beatrice Fitzgerald

  • Described by some characters as an “old dirty thing,” “the ugliest old hag for miles,” and a “common prostitute,” highlighting the harsh judgment and stigma she endures.
  • Madge’s disdainful remarks emphasize how Beatrice is viewed through a lens of moral condemnation and social ostracism.
  • This negative perception is powerful enough that Beatrice is said to hide because she “puts out the lights” so “they won’t see her,” suggesting that she is conscious of her social invisibility and perhaps the shame imposed upon her by the community.
  • Contrasting with the harsh judgments, Homer provides a more sympathetic and respectful view of Beatrice. He notes that she “brings my mother’s laundry” and “washes the clothes so clean,” and that “no one ever worked so hard,” illustrating her role as a diligent, if marginalized, member of society.
  • The image of her pulling a little red sled over snow, with “Her face turns blue,” evokes a sense of endurance and hardship borne quietly.
  • This portrayal complicates the one-dimensional negative stereotype and suggests that beneath social condemnation lies a person who struggles to survive and maintain dignity.
  • Beatrice is noted to be “nearly blind” and losing “the other eye,” a physical manifestation of her vulnerability and decline.
  • This detail adds a layer of pathos to her character, symbolizing not only physical deterioration but also perhaps the metaphorical blindness of society toward her suffering.
  • The loss of her eye is somberly attributed to a childhood incident, where “a little boy shot at her with his bow and arrow,” an event she dismissed lightly, indicating either denial or stoic acceptance of suffering.
  • Homer refers to Beatrice as “royal,” citing her surname Fitzgerald and the idea that names beginning with “Fitz” are linked to royal bastardy (“the bar sinister”).
  • This rumor of noble blood contrasts sharply with her low social standing, suggesting a tragic fall from grace or a life marked by lost potential.
  • The community’s suspicion and gossip about her lineage add to the aura of mystery and complexity surrounding her identity.
  • Homer also speaks of a son Beatrice supposedly had with “old Doc,” a figure who “never claimed him.”
  • This son, who joined the Navy and travels the world, symbolizes a link to a life beyond the village and possibly a hope or legacy that Beatrice clings to.
  • The son’s absence and the fact that “no one ever worked so hard” to survive in the village underscore themes of abandonment and endurance.
  • The chapter uses Beatrice as a symbol of those who exist on the margins of society, invisible and judged yet enduring.
  • Her existence amidst “wreckage” and a “flooded yard oozing with mud and refuse” reflects her precarious social and material condition.
  • The bus-driver’s need to “change horses” at her house metaphorically suggests a pause or shift in the journey, highlighting Beatrice’s role as a waypoint in the narrative of this community’s life and death struggles.

Jacqueline White

  • Jacqueline is described as a “poor little Jacqueline” who evokes a poignant emotional response from the old bus-driver. The bus-driver reflects on her with a mixture of sympathy and sorrow, noting that “Death never entered her head” and calling her “kind of infatuated with life.”
  • He observes that she is “prettier now than she ever was,” and there is a hopeful anticipation that she will go “to see us all next Christmas, going to dance the light fantastic.”
  • This imagery conveys a youthful vitality and innocence, an almost naïve optimism or denial of mortality in the face of impending death.
  • Jacqueline is portrayed as vibrant and spirited, someone who clings to life and the joys it holds, despite the dark, foreboding atmosphere that envelopes much of the chapter.
  • The bus-driver’s reflection on Jacqueline contrasts with the grim and fatalistic tone that permeates his monologue about death, illness, and the futility of medical science.
  • He laments that “the best doctor couldn’t help her,” and that “Old Doc certainly couldn’t,” implying Jacqueline is suffering from an incurable condition.
  • This adds a tragic dimension to her character; she is full of life and hope, yet doomed by forces beyond her control.
  • The bus-driver’s lament underscores the helplessness felt by those who witness her decline and the inevitability of death, which no amount of medical intervention or human will can prevent.
  • Jacqueline’s brief mention is also thematically significant. Her character embodies the tension between life and death, hope and despair, youth and decay that runs throughout the chapter.
  • The contrast between her vitality and the decay and ruin described elsewhere in the chapter highlights the fragility of life and the relentless passage of time.
  • Jacqueline represents a fleeting glimpse of beauty and life amidst a landscape marked by death, desolation, and resignation.

Research: Themes

Mortality and Death

See: Death and Mortality

  • The graveyard hill, the bus-driver’s reflections, and the references to death throughout the dialogue emphasize the theme of mortality.
  • The bus-driver’s long rant on death, medical science’s limitations, and the inevitability of going “when the tide goes” frame death as an unavoidable reality.

Memory and the Passage of Time

See: Memory and the Past · Time

  • Vera reflects on the idea that drowning people relive their lives in moments before death, but here the memories seem fragmented and possibly belong to others.
  • The blending of past and present, and the uncertainty of reality and memory, permeate the narrative.

Isolation and Mystery

See: Isolation and Connection · Faith, God, and the Supernatural

  • The setting (a spectral village at night, broken fences, a flooded yard with refuse, and a mysterious woman who hides from strangers) creates a sense of isolation and secrets.
  • The village itself appears ghost-like, with empty streets, wooden geese, and flickering lights, symbolizing a place suspended between life and death.

Skepticism Toward Institutions

See: Society, Class, and Race

  • The bus-driver’s distrust of “old Doc,” politicians, and even the concept of God highlights disillusionment with traditional authorities and systems.
  • Medical science is portrayed as outmoded and helpless in the face of mortality.

Social Stigma and Reputation

See: Society, Class, and Race

  • Beatrice Fitzgerald’s character embodies themes of social judgment, stigma (being called a prostitute), and resilience.
  • The conflicting opinions of Madge and Homer reveal the complexity of social roles and the harshness of gossip.

Research: Symbols and Imagery

The Broken Windshield Wiper and Flooded Road

See: The Sea and Water · The Bus and the Journey

  • Symbolize vulnerability and the overwhelming forces of nature or fate that the characters cannot control.

The Graveyard Hill

See: Weddings and Funerals

  • Represents the boundary between life and death, a literal and figurative crossroads on the journey.

The Old Tin House and Flooded Yard

See: The Sea and Water · The House

  • The dilapidated house and refuse-strewn yard symbolize decay, neglect, and the harsh realities hidden behind appearances.

Light and Darkness

See: Lamps, Candles, and Light

  • The dimming and raising of lights in the house reflect attempts to hide or reveal truth, beauty, and identity.
  • Madge’s insistence on keeping the light on contrasts with Beatrice’s hiding in darkness.

Names on Tombstones

See: Weddings and Funerals

  • Names like Stonecipher, Longtree, Thistlewaite, Chesterfield, and others evoke lineage, memory, and the passage of generations, underscoring the permanence of death. Longtree is the last name of Esther, a character at the end of the novel.

The Locked Door and the Turning Key

See: Keys, Doors, and Locks

  • Suggest mysteries, secrets, or supernatural forces at play.
  • The locked door that “just locked by itself” hints at unseen powers or fate.

Birds (Woodpeckers, Bluejays, Mockingbirds)

See: Birds

  • Birds appear repeatedly, symbolizing nature, communication, and, perhaps, the persistence of life amid decay.

Research: Resources

  • “where the cape of the glacier had reached”: The last ice sheets covered northern and central Indiana and left behind the flat, rich till plains. See Iowa, Indiana, and the Midwest.
  • “a white carbon lamp like a moon”: Carbon-arc lamps lit streets and grounds with a harsh white light from the 1880s into the 1920s.
  • “Stonecipher, Longtree, Thistlewaite, Chesterfield, Dalton, Grebe, Thomas, Whitehill”: The graves carry names of stone, tree, thistle, and hill, as Chapter 7’s dead carried names of stone. Longtree is the surname of Esther, who appears late in the novel.
    • Stonecipher means stone, swampy creek.
    • Longtree refers to the parish they came from in England.
    • Thistlewaite means thistle meadow.
    • Chesterfield means Roman fort, open country.
    • Dalton means from the valley town.
    • Grebe means digger of ditches or graves or engraver of seals.
    • Thomas is a common name meaning twin.
    • Whitehill is a Scottish name meaning white hill.
  • “a realm of visionary hypothesis or uncertain speculation”: Representationalism, or indirect realism, is the philosophical theory that argues that the mind perceives only mental images (representations) of the external world, not the world itself. It is opposed to direct realism, which holds that “physical objects are after all themselves directly or immediately perceived” (Laurence BonJour, “Epistemological Problems of Perception,” Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy). In his philosophy, Kant distinguishes between intuitions (immediate, sensory representations) and concepts (general, mediate representations). He also distinguishes between appearances (things as they appear to an observer) and things-in-themselves (the world as it is independently of anyone’s perception).
  • “I got to change horses”: Stagecoaches changed horses at stations along the road. Moses’s “last stage” is also a phrase for dying.
  • “that same old one-eyed Beatrice”: Beatrice is a name derived from the French name Béatrice, which came from the Latin Beatrix, which means “she who makes happy.” The popularity of the name spread because of Dante Alighieri’s poetry about the Florentine woman Beatrice Portinari. Dante presents Beatrice as being worthy of speaking for God, making her a holy individual. Beatrice “Bice” di Folco Portinari was an Italian woman who has been commonly identified as the principal inspiration for Dante Alighieri’s Vita Nuova, and is also identified with the Beatrice who acts as his guide in the last book of his narrative poem the Divine Comedy, Paradiso, and during the conclusion of the preceding Purgatorio. Within the Comedy, Beatrice is symbolic of divine grace and theology. (Wikipedia) Young’s Beatrice, a one-eyed washerwoman called a whore, is the opposite of Dante’s guide to heaven. Yet she too lives where the road divides, the graveyard on one side and the village of “promise through eternity” on the other. See Dante.
  • “Everything that begins with Fitz is royal in this country”: There is the belief that the last name Fitzgerald and every name that begins with Fitz is from royalty except that it is a bastard line in England. This belief is because of Charles II, who named his bastard son Fitzroy and the Duke of Clarence, later William IV, whose children by the actress Dorothea Jordan were named FitzClarence. Fitz comes from the Norman French fils, “son,” so Fitzgerald means son of Gerald. The Fitzgeralds were Norman lords in Ireland, the Earls of Kildare.
  • “It’s the bar sinister”: Bar sinister is the popular and erroneous term for bend sinister. Bend sinister is a diagonal stripe on a shield said to be a sign of bastardy.
  • “That’s where they learned to toboggan, too”: Toboggan is a sled. The word comes from the Mi’kmaq, and Madge uses it as a sly euphemism.
  • “See no evil”: The three wise monkeys are carved over a stable at the Tōshō-gū shrine in Nikkō, Japan (1636).
  • “Borneo, Singapore, Japan, the China Sea, the Rock of Gibraltar”: In the 1920s and 1930s the U.S. Navy’s Asiatic Fleet patrolled the China coast and its rivers, so a sailor could truly send postcards from these ports.
    • Borneo is the third largest island in the world.
    • Singapore is a sovereign island city-state.
    • Japan is an island country in East Asia.
    • The China Sea is the East and South China Seas, the waters off the coast of China.
    • The Rock of Gibraltar is a monolithic limestone promontory located in the British territory of Gibraltar, near the southwestern tip of Europe on the Iberian Peninsula. (Wikipedia) Its name is Arabic, Jabal Tariq, for Tariq ibn Ziyad, the Muslim general who landed there in 711 to invade Spain. The Prudential Insurance Company made the Rock its emblem in 1896, which is Homer’s “life insurance ad.”
  • “was it really true that one relived, in three minutes, all one’s life as the drowning are said to do”: Life review: In 1790, British naval officer Francis Beaufort nearly drowned and reported experiencing a life review. In 1847, a letter by Beaufort recalling the incident was published in the autobiography of Sir John Barrow, 1st Baronet. Wrote Beaufort: “Thought rose after thought with a rapidity of succession that is not only indescribable, but probably inconceivable, by any one who has not been in a similar situation. The course of those thoughts I can even now in a great measure retrace... our last cruise - a former voyage, and shipwreck - my school - the progress I had made there, and the time I misspent - and even all my boyish pursuits and adventures. Thus travelling backwards, every past incident of my life seemed to glance across my recollection in retrograde succession; not, however, in mere outline, as here stated, but the picture filled up with every minute and collateral feature. In short, the whole period of my existence seemed to be placed before me in a kind of panoramic review, and each act of it seemed to be accompanied by some reflection on its cause, or its consequences; indeed, many trifling events which had been long forgotten then crowded into my imagination, and with the character of recent familiarity. The length of time that was occupied by this deluge of ideas, or rather the shortness of time into which they were condensed, I cannot now state with precision, yet certainly two minutes could not have elapsed from the moment of suffocation to that of my being hauled up.” (Wikipedia) Vera finds herself remembering not her own life but “another’s ultimate face,” and she cries out for Miss MacIntosh, who was lost in the sea.
  • “I was sinking for the first, the second, the third time”: An old belief held that a drowning person rises three times before going down for good.
  • “Where was Miss MacIntosh, my darling, now aloud I cried?”: The novel’s title may echo the old ballad “Oh My Darling, Clementine,” whose Clementine is lost beneath the water. See Music and Composers.
  • “You can’t prove it’s murder”: A logical fallacy is a flaw in reasoning, “a form of argument that seems to be correct but which proves, upon examination, not to be so” (Irving Copi, quoted in Hans Hansen, “Fallacies,” Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy). It’s an error in logic that can weaken or even defeat the conclusion of an argument. Fallacies can be either formal (related to the structure of the argument) or informal (related to the content or premises of the argument). Knowing them helps a reader spot weak or flawed arguments, argue more persuasively by avoiding them, and weigh information more critically. Moses commits the argument from ignorance: what cannot be proved false is taken as true.
  • “Who killed the old horse? Who killed the sparrows?”: The nursery rhyme asks, “Who killed Cock Robin? / I, said the Sparrow.” See Fairy Tales and Folklore.
  • “the influenza epidemic that struck us shortly after the Armistice”: The influenza pandemic of 1918 peaked as the war ended on November 11, 1918, and killed about 675,000 Americans. It reached the United States through Boston, and rumors blamed German agents for spreading it, hence Moses’s “German germs washed up in Boston Harbor.”
  • “Delirium tremens, mocking birds, snakes”: The shaking delirium of alcohol withdrawal often brings visions of snakes and crawling things. See Madness and Sanity.
  • “snatch me from the jaws of living death”: Tennyson’s “The Charge of the Light Brigade” (1854): “Into the jaws of Death, / Into the mouth of Hell.”
  • “me hanging by a thread”: The sword of Damocles hung over him by a single horsehair. In Chapter 5 Moses hangs on to life by “a single hair that would never break, a hair hanging between him and a star.” See the Chapter 5 resources.
  • “me trusting to a broken reed”: “Thou trustest in the staff of this broken reed, on Egypt” (Isaiah 36:6). See The Bible.
  • “going to dance the light fantastic”: John Milton’s poem L’Allegro (The Happy Man), written about 1631 and published 1645, has the lines “Come, and trip it as ye go / On the light fantastic toe.” It is a pastoral poem, which has from its first appearance been paired with the contrasting pastoral poem, Il Penseroso (The Melancholy Man), which depicts a similar day spent in contemplation and thought. (Wikipedia) L’Allegro is the poem of the happy man, and Moses gives its dance to the dying Jacqueline. See Milton.
  • “Barmy, old Doc is, screw loose, unhinged, off his head”: Moses’s strings of synonyms, mad words here and later “Trunk, bole, hulk, skeleton,” read like the lists in Roget’s Thesaurus (1852). See Madness and Sanity.
  • “Mad as a March hare”: Hares run wild in their March mating season. Lewis Carroll’s March Hare (1865) keeps the mad tea party. See Madness and Sanity.
  • “that old knight errant curing them all”: Don Quixote, the mad knight errant who rides out to help people who never asked to be rescued. See Don Quixote.
  • “A clean bill of health!”: A ship’s certificate that no disease was aboard when it left port.
  • “Galloping consumption, that churchyard cough”: Moses names Jacqueline’s tuberculosis. See the Chapter 6 resources.
  • “horse feathers”: 1920s slang for nonsense, and the title of a Marx Brothers film (1932).
  • “You got to go when the tide goes”: In Dickens’s David Copperfield, Barkis “goes out with the tide,” since, as Mr. Peggotty says, people along the coast “can’t die . . . except when the tide’s pretty nigh out.”
  • “Shallows, rocks, crossing the bar”: Tennyson’s “Crossing the Bar” again. See the Chapter 7 resources.
  • “Greatest kings have died. A turtle falling on your head”: The story goes that the playwright Aeschylus, father of tragedy, died when an eagle dropped a tortoise on his bald head. See Greek Mythology.
  • “three sheets to the wind”: Sailors’ slang for drunk. The sheets are the ropes that, let loose, leave a ship staggering.
  • “Yet you can’t help giving him your hand when he gives his hand to you”: Schopenhauer places compassion as the foundation of his ethical system, arguing that it is the only truly moral motive because it is based on a genuine concern for the well-being of others. He sees indifference as the opposite of this, something to be overcome in order to live a moral life. Compassion allows individuals to transcend their self-centeredness and act for the benefit of others, whereas indifference is a form of egoism that hinders moral conduct. Moses mocks old Doc and still pities him: “It kind of makes your heart give.” See Schopenhauer.
  • “Was old Lethe roaring, making you forget?”: Lethe means oblivion, forgetfulness, or concealment. Lethe is the river of forgetfulness in Hades, from which the dead drank to forget their lives. See Greek Mythology.
  • “How was old Charon that rowed the boat?”: Charon is the ferryman of Hades (the underworld). See the Chapter 5 resources and Greek Mythology.
  • “My age, my change of life!”: The change of life is menopause. Moses claims it for himself, as in Chapter 5 he would not be “my mother’s daughter.”
  • “Alpha and Omega, beginning and end!”: “I am Alpha and Omega, the beginning and the end” (Revelation 22:13). See The Bible.
  • “Man of straws where?”: A man of straw is a weak argument set up to be knocked down, another fallacy for Moses.
  • “bone of my bone”: Adam says of Eve, “This is now bone of my bones, and flesh of my flesh” (Genesis 2:23). See Genesis.
  • “Render unto Caesar the things that are Caesar’s!”: “Render therefore unto Caesar the things which are Caesar’s; and unto God the things that are God’s” (Matthew 22:21). Moses turns it into “Render unto Doc.” See The Bible.
  • “Canst thou draw out leviathan with a hook?”: Moses recites God’s speech on Leviathan from Job 41:1-21 nearly word for word, then adds his own line, “He roareth like a great locomotive.” See The Book of Job.
    • “Or his tongue with a cord which thou lettest down?” (Job 41:1). This phrase metaphorically questions how one might access or influence the hidden, powerful depths of existence: whether within the self, nature, or the cosmos.
  • “What happened to Julius Caesar?”: Julius Caesar was a Roman general and statesman. He was stabbed in the Senate in 44 B.C. by conspirators including Brutus, his friend, and Shakespeare gave him the words “Et tu, Brute?” See Shakespeare.
  • “Hercules, what happened to Hercules?”: Hercules is a half-god in Greek and Roman mythology famous for his strength and adventures. He died through his wife, Deianira, who gave him a shirt soaked in the centaur Nessus’s poisoned blood, believing it a love charm. Burning with it, he built his own funeral pyre, a death by a wife and by fire, like old Josh’s. See Greek Mythology.
  • “Wormwood, dust, ashes”: The burial service commits the body “earth to earth, ashes to ashes, dust to dust” (Book of Common Prayer).
  • “Hewers of wood and drawers of water!”: The Gibeonites were made servants of Israel (Joshua 9:21). See The Bible.
  • “Was I not made to be the king of the earth?”: Genesis 1:26 reads, “let them have dominion over the fish of the sea, and over the fowl of the air.” This question is a poignant expression of human aspiration confronted by existential despair and the limitations imposed by mortality and circumstance. It highlights themes of lost potential, the transience of life, and the universal confrontation with death that pervades the novel. See Genesis.
  • “No partridges in these mountains”: David says Saul hunts him “as when one doth hunt a partridge in the mountains” (1 Samuel 26:20). See The Bible.
  • “Roosevelt in the White House?”: Moses asks whether old Doc thinks he is Roosevelt, who seemed never to leave the White House. In Chapter 5 Moses swore not to cut his hair until Roosevelt was gone. It may also refer to the New Deal and Social Security as well as other programs. See the Chapter 5 resources.
  • “Don’t believe in free silver”: William Jennings Bryan ran for president in 1896 on free silver and his “Cross of Gold” speech, and Republicans held to the gold standard.
  • “Upon a thin steeple, a fish weather vane”: The fish, ichthys in Greek, was an early Christian sign for Christ.
  • “Cyclops, men whose heads do grow beneath their shoulders”: Othello tells of “the Anthropophagi, and men whose heads / Do grow beneath their shoulders” (Othello 1.3). The Cyclops is the one-eyed giant of the Odyssey, like one-eyed Beatrice. See Shakespeare and Greek Mythology.
  • “dead souls”: This may echo Gogol’s Dead Souls (1842), whose hero buys up the names of dead serfs.
  • “that dream within the dream”: This may refer to Edgar Allan Poe’s poem “A Dream within a Dream” (1849), which says, “All that we see or seem / Is but a dream within a dream.” The first stanza ends with that statement, and the last stanza turns it into a question: “Is all that we see or seem / But a dream within a dream?” This dream within a dream is a recurring theme throughout the book. The idea that life is a dream goes back to Zhuangzi, who dreamed he was a butterfly and woke not knowing whether he was a man who had dreamed he was a butterfly or a butterfly dreaming he was a man (Zhuangzi, chapter 2, 4th century BCE), and to Plato, Aristotle, and Descartes. See Edgar Allan Poe and Taoism and Zhuangzi.

Chapter 69

← Chapter 68 · Home · Chapter 70 →

Content note: This chapter deals with executions by hanging and tells of a “mad butcher” who sold human beings as meat.

Summary

Vera’s room is marked Fire Escape: a corn-husk mattress, a “Forget me not” picture of a church steeple, and a slop jar beside someone else’s blonde hair combings. On the stairs the tattooed landlord, once a magician, a ventriloquist, a sailor, a soldier in the Intelligence, and a hunter of wild animals for Hagenbeck’s, now married to the former circus fat lady who owns the hotel, tells her that the hangman’s talk came from his shadow and that Mr. Weed is in truth a prosperous dairy farmer paid for his work. Her neighbors include Tillie, a very young girl who is also an old woman keeping turkey buzzards, or canaries, in chains, and a legless newspaper man who rides a sled with rusted sleigh bells. All night, through the thin wall, old Dr. Justice O’Leary rages at Sarah, a silent woman who may be his little sister, dead at the age of one, or the love who ran off with a travelling salesman. He lists every disease he knows and speaks of his strangest case, a woman always pregnant with an imaginary baby. At last Vera screams at Sarah to go.

Characters present

Vera Cartwheel · The Tavern Landlord · Mr. Weed · Justice O’Leary · Sarah O’Leary

Concepts present

Themes: Death and Mortality · Decay and Ruin · Faith, God, and the Supernatural · Illusion and Reality · Isolation and Connection · Madness and Sanity · Memory and the Past · Society, Class, and Race · Women, Gender, and Marriage

Symbols: Birds · Clocks and Watches · Clothing, Hats, and Skirts · Fire · The House

Allusions: Alice in Wonderland · Ecclesiastes · Genesis · Revelation and the Apocalypse · Romantic Poets · Shakespeare · The Bible · The Book of Job

Key passages

From the research

  • The chapter opens with a vivid description of the protagonist’s room marked “Fire Escape,” featuring a narrow bed stuffed with corn husks, a picture of a silver church steeple with the words “Forget me not,” and unsettling details such as a slop jar with sediment and blonde hair combings. Only her eyes are reflected in the warped mirror, and a rocking chair creaks.
  • The landlord is depicted as a colorful, loquacious man with tattoos, a rich past, and contradictory traits: strong yet faded in color, worldly yet tied to this dilapidated hotel. His monologues reveal a layered personality and provide backstory on Mr. Weed and other characters like Moses and “Tillie,” a young girl who knits baby hoods. The landlord’s tales weave together local myths, histories, and the odd coexistence of the living and dead in the hotel.
  • The landlord’s comments about Mr. Weed and his “shadow” who speaks for him reveal a symbolic duality. Mr. Weed himself is cautious and reserved, while his shadow is outspoken and more intriguing. This duality might represent the tension between public persona and hidden truths, or between the living and the spectral. Mr. Weed’s reputed success in his enterprises and his role in the local community add complexity to his character.
  • The most emotionally intense passages are the doctor’s anguished soliloquies and interactions with “Sarah,” a ghostly, haunting figure who disrupts his life. The doctor mourns the loss and disgrace Sarah represents; he curses her (“God damn it, Sarah!”), sees her as a “baby” and “senile,” with cold breath and sores, and agonizes over his professional failures.
  • The room is marked “Fire Escape,” and the hotel is “a good enough port for a man in a storm.”

Questions and observations

Reading closely

  • “Whose hair, I wondered as I undressed in the red-streaked dark—whose hair?” Why does a stranger’s hair matter to Vera?
  • The landlord speaks of Tillie, young and old, “always of one person —for as if in ocean depths, the two were one.” How can one woman be both?
  • The landlord says it was “the hangman’s shadow, who got loose after every hanging and said the things the hangman never would have said.” Which is the real Mr. Weed?

Characters

  • “God had never been in the hotel business.” What does the landlord know that God does not?
  • “I am the only one who remembers you, Sarah,” the doctor says, and then, “I have forgotten you.” Which is true?
  • “Many a woman was brought to child-bed against her will.” What does the old doctor reveal about the women of the town?

Connections

  • Over Vera’s bed are the words “Forget me not,” and the doctor tells Sarah “that is why your eyes are blue forget-me-nots.” What links them?
  • The doctor cries, “My God! Why hast thou deserted me?” What does he change from the words on the cross?
  • The doctor’s strangest case is “a woman who was always pregnant with an imaginary baby.” How does she echo Vera’s stone child in Chapter 68?

Reflection

  • “Who could endure the sight of his love when his love was old?” Who in the novel has?
  • He tells Sarah to go so that “she would seem beautiful, beautiful because distant and forgotten.” Is love easier from a distance?
  • “Go, Sarah!” Vera screams. Why does she join the doctor’s quarrel?

Research: Characters

Vera

  • A reflective observer who notices the eerie attributes of the room and the unfolding drama next door.

The Landlord

  • A loquacious, colorful figure with a tattooed, lion-like chest, who shares stories of Mr. Weed, the hotel’s history, and his own varied past as a sailor, performer, and soldier. He is knowledgeable but somewhat cynical, providing a bridge between reality and the supernatural elements.
  • His wife, a former circus fat lady, owned the hotel. He tells of being a candy merchant at ten, a magician, a ventriloquist, a sailor, a soldier in the Intelligence, and a hunter of wild animals for Hagenbeck’s, and of having killed, “very reluctantly, against his will,” “a very little black man who had no tongue but had swallowed a diamond.”

Mr. Weed and His Shadow

  • Mentioned as mysterious figures, Mr. Weed is a man of few words, while his shadow is more outspoken and unsettling. The landlord distinguishes between the two, adding layers to the mythos of the hotel.
  • The landlord says Mr. Weed is in truth “a prosperous farmer and the soul of respectability” with a model dairy farm, and that “The reason he tied the knot was that he got paid to tie it.”

Dr. Justice O’Leary

  • An aging, embittered physician who is haunted by “Sarah,” a ghost or symbolic figure representing death, disgrace, and the burden of his past. He is portrayed as mad, desperate, and filled with sorrow and rage.

Sarah O’Leary

  • A ghostly, troubling figure who haunts Dr. O’Leary’s room and mind. She is described variously as a dead woman, a baby, and a spiteful presence.

Other Figures

  • The bus driver, Imadaisy (Imadaisy appears only here; asked who she was, the landlord answers, “Nobody.” The name reads as “I’m a daisy,” old American slang for someone first-rate.), and various clients of the doctor add depth to the setting’s community. Tillie is a young girl who lives in the hotel where the narrator, Vera, is staying. The landlord describes her as “a very young girl” who will knit a baby hood for Vera. He mentions her casually while showing Vera the corridors of the hotel, specifically pointing to the door opposite Vera’s room. But the landlord insists that she and the old woman who keeps canaries as big as turkey buzzards are one person: “as if in ocean depths, the two were one.”

Research: Themes

Death and Haunting

See: Death and Mortality

  • The omnipresence of death is felt through the spectral figure of Sarah, Mr. Weed’s shadow, and the decaying hotel environment.
  • Dr. O’Leary’s confrontation with Sarah is a meditation on mortality, loss, disgrace, and the persistence of the past.

Memory and Forgetting

See: Memory and the Past

  • Dr. O’Leary claims to be the only one who remembers Sarah, highlighting the tension between remembrance and societal forgetting.
  • The landlord’s stories and Mr. Weed’s shadow serves as conduits for local history and legend, preserving memory in a decaying place.

Decay and Corruption

See: Decay and Ruin

  • Physical decay (the mattress, the slop jar, Sarah’s sores) mirrors moral and psychological decay, especially in the doctor’s life and the hotel’s atmosphere.

Isolation and Madness

See: Isolation and Connection · Madness and Sanity

  • The doctor’s madness and isolation are emphasized through his anguished monologues and the strange, disruptive presence of Sarah.
  • The landlord and Vera observe these events as somewhat detached witnesses, enhancing the sense of alienation.

The Supernatural and Reality

See: Illusion and Reality · Faith, God, and the Supernatural

  • The narrative blurs lines between reality and the supernatural with ghostly figures, haunted rooms, and symbolic presences.
  • The landlord’s tall tales and Mr. Weed’s shadow complicate the story’s realism.

Research: Symbols and Imagery

Fire Escape Room

See: Clothing, Hats, and Skirts · The House · Fire

  • Symbolizes escape but also confinement, a place between safety and danger.

Slop Jar

  • Filled with sediment and blonde hair, represents decay and the remnants of life.

Silver Church Steeple Picture

  • A hopeful or nostalgic image contrasting with the room’s decay, with the phrase “Forget me not” symbolizing memory and longing.

Sarah

  • Embodies death, disgrace, lost innocence, and the inescapability of the past.

Mr. Weed’s Watch

See: Clocks and Watches

  • A “world within a world,” symbolizing time, fate, or the inevitability of death.

Turkey Buzzards/Canaries

See: Birds

  • Represent death and the grotesque in the everyday world.

Research: Resources

  • “was marked Fire Escape”: Fire escapes emerged in the U.S. from the 1800s, driven by deadly urban fires, initially as simple ladders and later evolving into complex external stair systems, with Anna Connelly’s 1887 patent for a bridge-like design becoming foundational; they became common after laws following disasters like the Triangle Shirtwaist Factory fire but faded in new construction after the 1960s as modern sprinklers, alarms, and improved firefighting equipment made them less essential, though they remain iconic features in older cityscapes.
  • “the mattress stuffed with corn husks”: Corn husks were used from the Colonial era to the 19th century.
  • “Forget me not”: The forget-me-not is the flower of remembrance. In the German legend a knight, gathering the flowers for his lady by a river, was dragged down by his armor and threw them to her as he drowned, crying “Forget me not.” See Death and Mortality.
  • “There was a slop jar with big handles like ears”: Slop jars were used along with a pitcher and basin in hotels until the 1950s.
  • “as loquacious as the hangman”: Loquacious means talkative or tending to talk a great deal.
  • “as many colors as Joseph’s coat”: Joseph’s coat of many colors is from the Book of Genesis. It was a special, richly decorated robe given to him by his father Jacob, symbolizing his favoritism, which fueled his brothers’ jealousy, leading them to sell Joseph into slavery and present the bloody coat to Jacob as proof he was dead. The garment, likely a regal tunic with long sleeves, signified Joseph’s special status and set him apart, though it also provoked envy, highlighting themes of favoritism, betrayal, and God’s guiding purpose through hardship. “Now Israel loved Joseph more than all his children… and he made him a coat of many colours” (Genesis 37:3, KJV). See Genesis.
  • “the landlord’s wife who had been a circus fat lady”: The “fat lady” in the U.S. circus was a prominent sideshow attraction from the 19th to mid-20th centuries, embodying spectacle, curiosity, and sometimes exploitation, with famous figures like Lottie Whitlock, billed as the original “Fat Lady,” and later stars like Alice from Dallas and Celesta Geyer (Dolly Dimples) who gained fame and fortune before some dramatically lost weight, highlighting societal views on size and health. These performers, part of the “freak show” tradition, used their size to build successful careers, often achieving celebrity status within the circus world, though facing exploitation and objectification. See Women, Gender, and Marriage.
  • “He had seen lamer ducks than the hangman”: A lame duck is an official (especially the president) in the final period of office, after the election of a successor; an ineffectual or unsuccessful person or thing.
  • “Barnum’s seven wonders of the universe”: Phineas Taylor Barnum was an American showman, businessman, and politician, remembered for promoting celebrated hoaxes and founding the Barnum & Bailey Circus with James Anthony Bailey. Barnum went on to create America’s first aquarium and to expand the wax figure department of his museum. His Seven Grand Salons demonstrated the Seven Wonders of the World which claimed 850,000 curiosities. (Wikipedia) His circus was billed as the Greatest Show on Earth.
  • “old people with hardening of the arteries”: Hardening of the arteries, or atherosclerosis, is a widespread issue in the U.S., a slow-developing disease where plaque (fat, cholesterol) narrows arteries, significantly contributing to heart attacks and strokes, the leading causes of death, affecting roughly half of Americans aged 45-84, often silently until serious events occur, with risk factors including high blood pressure, smoking, high cholesterol, and diabetes.
  • “If you hear sleigh bells ringing”: More than four thousand American soldiers came home from World War I as amputees. The rusted sleigh bells Vera dreaded in Chapter 68, jingling all night in the corridors, are his. See the Chapter 68 resources.
  • “He was coming home on a furlough during the Last War”: The landlord’s Last War is World War I: he remembers the Marne and the Lusitania, steps on the face of a “Hun,” and goes hunting for Hagenbeck’s after it ends.
  • “Maybe I was surprised by the hangman’s confessions”: The passage explores themes of death, violence, and respectability, highlighting the banality and repetitiveness of horror, and the unsettling coexistence of brutality and normalcy in the hangman’s life. The gruesome crimes serve as a backdrop to the hangman’s enigmatic identity and the eerie atmosphere of the setting.
  • “the mad butcher who sold human beings as hams”: Compare Fritz Haarmann, the “Butcher of Hanover,” executed in 1925 for murdering young men and long suspected of selling their flesh as black-market meat.
  • “a model dairy farm”: The modernization of model dairy farms started in 1879 and continued to World War II.
  • “a very little black man who had no tongue but had swallowed a diamond”: At the Kimberley diamond mines in South Africa, from 1885 Black miners were locked in closed compounds, searched naked, and held and dosed with purgatives before they left, to recover any diamonds they had swallowed. See Society, Class, and Race.
  • “I was in the Intelligence during the Last War”: In World War I the United States built its first real intelligence services: the Army’s Military Intelligence Division (1917), its Corps of Intelligence Police, and MI-8, Herbert Yardley’s codebreakers.
  • “I can say parlez vous to little Frenchies”: “Frenchies” is an informal and sometimes derogatory term used describing French people. American soldiers in France sang “Mademoiselle from Armentières,” with its refrain “Hinky dinky, parlez-vous.”
  • “Remember the Marne”: The Marne was the river of two great battles of World War I. In 1914 the French and British stopped the German advance on Paris there, and in 1918 American troops held the line at the Second Battle of the Marne. “Remember the Lusitania” was a recruiting cry of 1915.
    • Remember the Marne may refer to Remember the Maine! To hell with Spain! after the USS Maine. It was a United States Navy ship that sank in Havana Harbor on February 15, 1898, contributing to the outbreak of the Spanish-American War in April 1898. Although the USS Maine explosion was not a direct cause, it served as a catalyst that accelerated the events leading up to the war.
  • “His sacred pictures were on his back”: Sailors’ lore held that a crucifixion tattooed across the back would stay the hand of an officer ordering a flogging.
  • “a supposedly dead Hun”: “Hun” was the Allied name for German soldiers in World War I, revived in World War II, linking them to the barbaric, nomadic Huns of antiquity known for cruelty under Attila, especially after Kaiser Wilhelm II’s 1900 speech encouraging similar savagery in China; Allied propaganda effectively used this to portray Nazis as barbaric, though terms like “Fritz” or “Jerry” (British) and “Heinie” (American) were also common for German soldiers.
  • “Hagenbeck’s out of Berlin”: Hagenbeck’s out of Berlin may refer to The Tierpark Hagenbeck zoo in Stellingen, Hamburg, Germany. The collection began in 1863 with animals that belonged to Carl Hagenbeck Sr., a fishmonger who became an amateur animal collector. The park itself was founded by Carl Hagenbeck Jr. in 1907. It is known for being the first zoo to use open enclosures surrounded by moats, rather than barred cages, to better approximate animals’ natural environments. Among his collections, however, were also human beings whom he exhibited in “human zoos.” The private zoo is still run by the Hagenbeck family. Hagenbeck’s was based in Hamburg, not Berlin. From 1874 it exhibited Sámi, Nubians, Inuit, and other peoples in its “ethnological shows.” See Society, Class, and Race.
  • “had seen elephants copulating”: The belief is not from the Bible but from Pliny, who wrote that elephants mate in secret, out of modesty (Natural History, Book 8), and from the medieval bestiaries that followed him.
  • “Sarah, you are dead, this town’s little sister”: See Sarah O’Leary.
  • “a canker in the rose immortal”: “And loathsome canker lives in sweetest bud” (Shakespeare, Sonnet 35). Compare Blake’s “The Sick Rose” (1794), destroyed by “The invisible worm.” See Shakespeare and Romantic Poets.
  • “We must put away our childish loves”: “When I was a child, I spake as a child… but when I became a man, I put away childish things” (1 Corinthians 13:11, KJV). See The Bible.
  • “He was as mad as a March hare”: “Mad as a March hare” is an idiom meaning extremely silly, eccentric, or crazy, originating from the frenzied, unpredictable behavior of European hares during their spring breeding season (March), which includes frantic chases, high leaps, and “boxing” matches where females swat males away to discourage unwanted advances. This phrase was popularized by Lewis Carroll’s Alice’s Adventures in Wonderland, featuring the eccentric March Hare at the Mad Hatter’s tea party, though the behavior itself is a real, albeit misunderstood, part of hare mating rituals, not actual madness. See Alice in Wonderland.
  • “Dr. Justice O’Leary, for so he called himself”: In Chapter 67, Moses believed old Doc dead at the wheel of his ghost buggy. See the Chapter 67 resources and Justice O’Leary.
  • “He had blown his breath into the mouths of dead men”: “And he went up, and lay upon the child, and put his mouth upon his mouth… and the flesh of the child waxed warm” (2 Kings 4:34, KJV), Elisha raising the Shunammite woman’s son. See The Bible.
  • “he had seen something steal out of the room”: Compare Dr. Duncan MacDougall of Haverhill, Massachusetts, who in 1907 weighed six dying patients and claimed that the soul weighed about twenty-one grams.
  • “The outside of the cup was shining”: “For ye make clean the outside of the cup and of the platter, but within they are full of extortion and excess” (Matthew 23:25, KJV). See The Bible.
  • “a wormwood”: Culturally wormwood has been used in the Christian Bible to connote something incredibly bitter. In the Book of Revelation it is used as the name of the star. In Hamlet, he uses the word wormwood to describe the situation he believes is going on with his family. “And the name of the star is called Wormwood” (Revelation 8:11, KJV). See Revelation and the Apocalypse and Shakespeare.
  • “Let this cup pass from him”: From Matthew 26:39 where Jesus is asking God if he has to go through with this. This moment is part of a larger, surreal and symbolic interaction filled with themes of death, memory, disgrace, and the passage of time, as the doctor grapples with his own mortality and the ghostly reminders of a troubled past. “O my Father, if it be possible, let this cup pass from me” (Matthew 26:39, KJV). See The Bible.
  • “Better a stone cherub than a baby now”: Compare Vera’s stone child, “a marble statue in your womb,” in the Chapter 68 resources.
  • “For God knew he was no abortionist”: By 1900 abortion was a crime in every state. In 1930 abortion was the recorded cause of death of nearly 2,700 American women, almost one in five maternal deaths. See Women, Gender, and Marriage.
  • “as God is not the great physician”: “They that are whole have no need of the physician, but they that are sick” (Mark 2:17, KJV); revival hymns hailed Jesus as “The Great Physician.” See The Bible.
  • “Why hast thou deserted me?”: From Psalm 22, according to the Gospels, Jesus spoke these words during the Crucifixion, after he had suffered on the cross for three hours. It is a cry of abandonment and despair, reflecting Dr. O’Leary’s inner turmoil as he confronts death, loss, and the haunting past. The King James reads, “My God, my God, why hast thou forsaken me?” (Psalm 22:1; Matthew 27:46). The doctor makes it “deserted.” See The Bible.
  • “Could anyone get blood out of a turnip”: The phrase refers to the idiom, “You can’t squeeze blood from a turnip,” meaning you can’t get something from someone or something that doesn’t have it to give, like trying to get money from someone with no money, or forcing an impossible result. It’s similar to “You can’t get blood from a stone” and signifies the futility of demanding something unavailable.
  • “Jerusalem, Jerusalem”: “O Jerusalem, Jerusalem, thou that killest the prophets” (Matthew 23:37, KJV). See The Bible.
  • “Mayo, Mayo!”: Mayo Clinic originated with the medical practice of William Worrall Mayo, M.D. who immigrated to the United States in 1846. He had two sons. The Mayo brothers were financially successful and professionally prominent. The Mayo Clinic is still in the US and has opened branches in several countries. The clinic grew from St. Marys Hospital in Rochester, Minnesota, which Mother Alfred Moes and her Sisters of St. Francis built after the tornado of 1883 and opened in 1889, with the Mayos as its doctors. See Women, Gender, and Marriage.
  • “a woman who was always pregnant with an imaginary baby”: The doctor says his strangest case is a woman who believes she is always pregnant with an imaginary baby and suffers from many miscarriages. This woman seems to refer to Esther Longtree who will be prominent towards the last chapters of the novel. See Esther Longtree.
  • “that penny he stole off a dead man’s eyes”: Coins were laid on the eyes of the dead to keep them closed, and in Greek custom a coin was left for Charon, the ferryman of the dead. See Death and Mortality.
  • “his house was his Englishman’s castle”: “The house of every one is to him as his castle and fortress” (Sir Edward Coke, Semayne’s Case, 1604).
  • “naked, we come into this world, and naked, we go out of it”: The line comes from the Bible, found in both Ecclesiastes 5:15 and Job 1:21. The phrase reflects the inevitability of human vulnerability at birth and death, stripping away all pretenses or material concerns, which is a poignant theme running through the novel’s exploration of mortality, identity, and human frailty. “Naked came I out of my mother’s womb, and naked shall I return thither” (Job 1:21, KJV). See The Book of Job and Ecclesiastes.
  • “Oh, my Lady Gonorrhea!”: Gonorrhea was first documented in ancient Greece by Galen, who used the term from the Greek words gonos (semen) and rhoia (flow) to describe what he mistakenly called an “involuntary ejaculation of semen.” The name “the clap” emerged in the 1500s, originating from the French “les clapiers,” a term for brothels where the disease was common. While medieval and early modern records describe symptoms, the specific bacterium, Neisseria gonorrhoeae, wasn’t identified until 1879 by Albert Neisser, though the connection to women’s health was sometimes misunderstood.

Chapter 1

← Introduction · Home · Chapter 2 →

Content note: Vera’s mother, Catherine Cartwheel, is addicted to opium.

Summary

Vera Cartwheel rides a Grey Goose bus through the mist of the American Midwest. The driver, Moses Hunnecker, has long bushy hair. He whistles, drinks openly from a whiskey bottle, calls on God and the angels, and drives erratically. Vera imagines a wife and children waiting for him at home, then wonders whether she has invented them. The only other passengers are a sleeping couple, Madge and Homer Capehorn. Madge is pregnant and seems to resent it, and Homer sleeps in placid innocence. Along the roadside Vera sees a moving van piled with furniture and a double-headed man staring into nothing. These sights lead her to reflect that individuality is an illusion and every soul is joined to every other. She explains why she is traveling. She is searching for Miss MacIntosh, the plain, red-haired nursemaid from What Cheer, Iowa, who disappeared or died. She was the one solid presence in Vera’s childhood, in a house by the New England sea ruled by her mother’s opium dreams.

Characters present

Vera Cartwheel · Miss MacIntosh · Moses Hunnecker · Madge Capehorn · Homer Capehorn

Concepts present

Themes: Illusion and Reality · Isolation and Connection · Memory and the Past · Nature, the Sea, and the Cosmos · The Search for Meaning

Symbols: Clothing, Hats, and Skirts · Fog and Mist · The Bus and the Journey · The House · The Umbrella · Twins and Doubles

Philosophy: Freud and Jung · Kant and Hegel · Marguerite Young on Her Craft · Phenomenology · William James and Pragmatism

Allusions: American Religious Movements · Deafness and Sign Language · Don Quixote · Greek Mythology · Iowa, Indiana, and the Midwest · American Writers · Suicide in History and Literature · The Bible

Key passages

From the research

  • The opening depiction of the bus-driver, his erratic driving, and his imagined family life introduces a sense of instability mixed with hopeful human connection. Vera speculates about the bus-driver’s wife and children, highlighting a longing for established human relationships and happiness that seems almost mythical or legendary. The bus-driver’s erratic driving amid heavy mist and his open drinking juxtaposed with calls upon God and angels create a complex character who embodies both chaos and faith.
  • The detailed description of Madge contrasts sharply with Homer’s blissful innocence and placid smile. This passage explores themes of denial, despair, and innocence amidst difficult circumstances. Madge’s appearance and behavior suggest a deep inner conflict and suffering, while Homer’s peaceful sleep offers a counterpoint of hope or oblivion.
  • Vera’s descriptions of the landscape create an atmosphere of desolation, otherworldliness, and existential uncertainty. This setting evokes a sense of isolation and the fading of reality into illusion, emphasizing Vera’s internal struggles and sense of alienation.
  • The image of the double-headed man standing by the roadside, staring into nothingness, symbolizes the fragmented self and the elusive nature of reality. Vera reflects on the “organization of illusion” and the interconnectedness of all souls, suggesting that individuality is an illusion and that deeper unity might exist beyond appearances. This philosophical meditation on identity and connection is central to the chapter’s thematic core.
  • Vera’s long and restless search for Miss MacIntosh, an old red-headed nursemaid who was a moral guide and symbol of truth and constancy, represents a quest for stability, love, and truth in a world of illusions and loss. Miss MacIntosh embodies simple virtues, common sense, and a grounded view of life, contrasting with Vera’s experience of chaos and dreams. This passage reveals Vera’s deep loneliness and yearning for a meaningful human connection.
  • Miss MacIntosh’s rejection of illusions and adherence to “truth to nature” underscores the tension between the dream world and reality. Her practical, no-nonsense attitude highlights Vera’s struggle to reconcile the dreamlike, illusory aspects of existence with the desire for concrete, simple truth. This tension is a major thematic element of the chapter.
  • The closing passage emphasizes Miss MacIntosh’s practical strength and sensibility amidst desolation. Her rejection of luxury and illusion in favor of plainness and resilience serves as a counterpoint to Vera’s journey through a world of fading images and lost souls. This passage reinforces themes of endurance, reality, and the search for meaning in a harsh world.

Questions and observations

Reading closely

  • Vera imagines the bus-driver’s wife and children, then wonders whether his family life is “an emanation of my over-active imagination.” What does it suggest that the novel opens with its narrator inventing other people’s lives and then doubting her inventions?
  • The pregnant girl is covered from head to toe in charms, sports, butterflies, and a stuffed canary, “discursive details which should not focus attention, yet drew attention to her.” What is she hiding, and what does the hiding reveal?
  • The flat road becomes “the first creation when only the spirit of God had moved upon the deep,” and then “There was now no landscape but the soul’s.” How does the chapter turn an Indiana highway into an inner landscape?
  • A man with a child on his shoulders becomes “a double-headed man.” Why might this passing image stay “forever engraved on memory’s whirling disc”?

Characters

  • Miss MacIntosh’s religion is “truth to nature,” and she insists that “Common sense is the finest sense.” Yet Vera remembers her as “the dead steersman” and “the heart of all hearts.” How does the plainest person in the book become its most mythic figure?
  • Vera says the years of Miss MacIntosh’s death “had added to her stature, making her seem almost vague.” How does memory both enlarge and blur the people it keeps?
  • Vera gave up architecture “because I could not plan a house if there was one soul which could not live in it,” and later typed “mortality rates through a blur of tears.” What do these jobs reveal about her?
  • The blind juggler asks, “When shall the light, Peter, enter my soul?” Why does Vera hear his question “like my own”?

Connections

  • “Every heart is the other heart. Every soul is the other soul. Every face is the other face. The individual is the one illusion.” How does this claim prepare for the novel’s wheel of characters turning around Miss MacIntosh at the hub? See The Wheel and the Spokes.
  • Vera comes from a house by the sea and enters the Midwest because Miss MacIntosh told her to “see America first.” How does the chapter set the ocean of the Cartwheel house against the plain interior of the country?
  • Don Quixote and Tantalus both appear in the chapter’s first pages. What do a knight who fights imaginary enemies and a man forever reaching for what recedes have in common with Vera?
  • The Cartwheel garden is full of statues, cupids, psyches, and the Apollo Belvedere, “sculptured by man dreaming that he was other than he was.” Why does Miss MacIntosh distrust them?

Reflection

  • “All my life I had been reaching for the tangible, and it had evaded me.” What in ordinary life seems most solid and turns out hardest to hold?
  • Vera’s quest is “the search for life, for love, for truth that does not fail.” Is a truth that does not fail possible, or is the search itself the point?

Research: Characters

Vera Cartwheel

  • Vera, the narrator and seeker, deeply introspective and philosophical, haunted by loss and the search for truth.

Miss Georgia MacIntosh

  • Vera’s lost companion and moral anchor, embodying simplicity, truth, and steadfastness.
  • Young saw this common sense as a disguise: “Her whole life is an impersonation. She’s by no means sensible. It’s just her verbalism that makes her seem sensible” (Marguerite Young, interview with Duncan MacDonald, Observation Point, 1965). “Miss Macintosh was the one illusionist in her assumption that there was a simple foundation of truth” (Marguerite Young, interview, WNYC radio, New York).

Moses Hunnecker (The Bus Driver)

  • A complex figure mixing spiritual invocation with reckless behavior, embodying ambiguity.

Madge Capehorn (born Edwards) and Homer Capehorn

  • Symbols of innocence and conflict, youth and resistance to natural processes.

Research: Themes

The Bus Journey and Characters

  • The story begins with a bus driver whistling and driving erratically through heavy mist in a rural, indistinct part of interior America. The bleak, mist-shrouded landscape evokes a feeling of desolation and uncertainty.
  • Moses Hunnecker (The Bus Driver) is described as a large-headed man with bushy hair, who drinks whiskey openly and calls upon God and angels, suggesting a complex mix of spiritual longing and reckless behavior. His family life is ambiguous, possibly a projection of Vera’s desires.
  • A sleeping young couple (Madge and Homer) joins the bus at a pottery town. The girl is pregnant but resists her condition, described in vivid detail with a mix of artificiality and natural growth, symbolizing conflict and alienation. The boy contrasts her with innocence and blissful stolidity.
  • The bus brushes against a moving van carrying an array of household items, including a feathered hat bobbing in the mist like a bird, evoking a surreal atmosphere where everyday objects gain symbolic weight.
  • The journey progresses into a formless, oceanic-like mist-covered plain with no distinct landmarks, symbolizing the dissolution of the familiar world and the encroachment of the unknown or the subconscious.

Philosophical Reflection on Illusion and Connection

See: Illusion and Reality · Isolation and Connection · The Search for Meaning

Vera reflects on the nature of memory, illusion, and the human soul

See: Illusion and Reality · Memory and the Past · Nature, the Sea, and the Cosmos

  • The idea that individuality is an illusion and that every heart, soul, and face is interconnected.
  • The metaphor of ships passing in the night, representing fleeting human connections.
  • Vera’s lifelong search for tangible truth and connection, which has often evaded her, leaving only illusions and disconnected images.

Vera Cartwheel’s Personal Quest and History

See: Memory and the Past · The Search for Meaning

  • Vera reveals herself as searching for a lost companion, Miss MacIntosh, an old nursemaid who symbolized stability, truth, and moral guidance in Vera’s life.
  • Miss MacIntosh is described as a simple, practical woman with a broken nose and red hair, who rejected illusions and fanciful dreams in favor of truth to nature. She was a grounding figure during Vera’s turbulent childhood amid a family haunted by opium and dreams.
  • Vera has wandered through various cities, employment, and social strata, always searching for Miss MacIntosh who had disappeared or died. This search is both literal and symbolic of Vera’s deeper quest for meaning, love, and truth.
  • Vera contrasts the opulent but empty grandeur of her mother’s house, filled with ghosts and illusions, with the plain, unpretentious life Miss MacIntosh led by the sea. This contrast highlights the theme of reality versus illusion in the narrative.
  • Vera contemplates the ephemeral nature of life, the inevitability of death, and the elusive quest for light and meaning in a world filled with darkness and dreams that fail.
  • Vera’s journey is both physical and spiritual, seeking a reality not distorted by illusion.
  • The narrative questions what is real, suggesting individuality and perception may be illusory.
  • The human condition is described as one of alienation, with fleeting and often failed attempts at connection.
  • The past haunts the present, and memory is both a source of pain and a guide.
  • Miss MacIntosh’s simple life contrasts with grand illusions, suggesting truth lies in everyday reality.

Research: Symbols and Imagery

The Bus

See: The Bus and the Journey

  • A vessel moving through uncertain, misty landscapes, symbolizing the journey of life and the search for meaning.

Mist and Grey Landscape

See: Fog and Mist · Clothing, Hats, and Skirts

  • Representing ambiguity, the unknown, and the dissolution of familiar reality.

Household Items on the Moving Van

See: The House

  • Everyday objects gaining symbolic, almost surreal significance.

The Double-Headed Man

See: Twins and Doubles

  • A mysterious figure by the roadside symbolizing fragmented identity or duality.

Miss MacIntosh’s Whaler’s Hat and Umbrella

See: The Umbrella · Clothing, Hats, and Skirts

  • Symbols of groundedness and practicality against the backdrop of illusion.

The Opulent but Empty House

See: The House

  • Represents illusion, decay, and the failure of grandeur without truth.

Research: Resources

  • Jehovah’s Witnesses is a millenarian (the belief by a religious, social, or political group or movement in a coming fundamental transformation of society, after which “all things will be changed”) restorationist (is the belief that Christianity has been or should be restored along the lines of what is known about the apostolic early church, which restorationists see as the search for a purer and more ancient form of the religion) Christian denomination with nontrinitarian (is a form of Christianity that rejects the mainstream Christian doctrine of the Trinity: the belief that God is three distinct hypostases or persons who are coeternal, coequal, and indivisibly united in one being, or essence) beliefs distinct from mainstream Christianity. Jehovah’s Witnesses are best known for their door-to-door preaching, distributing literature such as The Watchtower and Awake!, and for refusing military service, refusal to salute state symbols and blood transfusions. They consider the use of God’s name vital for proper worship. They reject Trinitarianism, inherent immortality of the soul, and hellfire, which they consider to be unscriptural doctrines. They do not observe Christmas, Easter, birthdays or other holidays and customs they consider to have pagan origins incompatible with Christianity. They prefer to use their own Bible translation, the New World Translation of the Holy Scriptures, although their literature occasionally quotes and cites other Bible translations. Adherents commonly refer to their body of beliefs as “The Truth” and consider themselves to be “in the Truth.” They consider “human society” to be morally corrupt and under the influence of Satan, and most limit their social interaction with non-Witnesses. Congregational disciplinary actions include disfellowshipping, their term for formal expulsion and shunning, a last resort for what they consider serious offenses. Baptized individuals who formally leave are considered disassociated and are also shunned. Disfellowshipped and disassociated individuals may eventually be reinstated if deemed repentant. (Wikipedia) The movement grew out of the Bible Student movement that Charles Taze Russell began in the 1870s, and it took the name Jehovah’s Witnesses in 1931.
  • The “Grey Goose” bus: “Gray Goose” became American slang for a prison bus, often a converted Greyhound painted grey, used to move prisoners between jails, courts, and prisons, always migrating like geese from one prison to another. Green’s Dictionary of Slang first records the term in 1976, after the novel was published, so it is a later echo rather than Young’s source, but read that way the bus suggests displacement and a loss of freedom, movement without arrival. The name also recalls the old song “Go Tell Aunt Rhody,” whose old grey goose is dead, which the bus-driver sings in Chapter 5. See On the bus (Ch 1) and Go Tell Aunt Rhody (Ch 5).
  • Harold Bloom says Don Quixote is the first modern novel, and that the protagonist is at war with Freud’s reality principle, which accepts the necessity of dying. Bloom says that the novel has an endless range of meanings, but that a recurring theme is the human need to withstand suffering. Edith Grossman, who wrote and published a highly acclaimed English translation of the novel in 2003, says that the book is mostly meant to move people into emotion using a systematic change of course, on the verge of both tragedy and comedy at the same time. Grossman has stated: “The question is that Quixote has multiple interpretations [...] and how do I deal with that in my translation. I’m going to answer your question by avoiding it [...] so when I first started reading the Quixote I thought it was the most tragic book in the world, and I would read it and weep [...] As I grew older [...] my skin grew thicker [...] and so when I was working on the translation I was actually sitting at my computer and laughing out loud. This is done [...] as Cervantes did it [...] by never letting the reader rest. You are never certain that you truly got it. Because as soon as you think you understand something, Cervantes introduces something that contradicts your premise.” The novel’s structure is episodic in form. The full title is indicative of the tale’s object, as ingenioso (Spanish) means “quick with inventiveness,” marking the transition of modern literature from dramatic to thematic unity. The novel takes place over a long period of time, including many adventures united by common themes of the nature of reality, reading, and dialogue in general. Although burlesque on the surface, the novel, especially in its second half, has served as an important thematic source not only in literature but also in much of art and music, inspiring works by Pablo Picasso and Richard Strauss. The contrasts between the tall, thin, fancy-struck and idealistic Quixote and the short, stout, world-weary Panza is a motif echoed ever since the book’s publication, and Don Quixote’s imaginings are the butt of outrageous and cruel practical jokes in the novel. Even faithful and simple Sancho is forced to deceive him at certain points. The novel is considered a satire of orthodoxy, veracity and even nationalism. In exploring the individualism of his characters, Cervantes helped lead literary practice beyond the narrow convention of the chivalric romance. He spoofs the chivalric romance through a straightforward retelling of a series of acts that redound to the knightly virtues of the hero. The character of Don Quixote became so well known in its time that the word quixotic was quickly adopted by many languages. Characters such as Sancho Panza and Don Quixote’s steed, Rocinante, are emblems of Western literary culture. The phrase “tilting at windmills” to describe an act of attacking imaginary enemies (or an act of extreme idealism), derives from an iconic scene in the book. It stands in a unique position between medieval romance and the modern novel. The former consists of disconnected stories featuring the same characters and settings with little exploration of the inner life of even the main character. The latter are usually focused on the psychological evolution of their characters. In Part I, Quixote imposes himself on his environment. By Part II, people know about him through “having read his adventures,” and so, he needs to do less to maintain his image. By his deathbed, he has regained his sanity, and is once more “Alonso Quixano the Good.” (Wikipedia) Vera wonders whether the bus-driver is “some mad Don Quixote chasing windmills.” See On Don Quixote (Ch 1).
  • “his bushy hair grew almost to his shoulders”: The bus driver came from life. “And I met such a bus driver on my way perhaps to New Harmony,” Young said (Marguerite Young, interview with Kay Bonetti, American Audio Prose Library, May 1983). The novel “takes place at that time when Republicans were threatening to let their hair grow until Roosevelt got out of the White House” (Marguerite Young, interview with Studs Terkel, WFMT radio, 1965). See Moses Hunnecker, the Chapter 5 resources, and Marguerite Young on Her Craft.
  • “an emanation of my over-active imagination”: Blaise Pascal thought imagination was powerful but often led people astray. In his Pensées he called it “that deceitful part in man, that mistress of error and falsity, the more deceptive that she is not always so” (Pensées 82, trans. W. F. Trotter). Vera, doubting the bus-driver’s family as her own invention, fears the same trick of the mind. He also argued that believing in God is more beneficial than not believing in God, which is known as Pascal’s wager.
  • Madge is a traditional nickname for Margaret, which comes from the Greek word for “pearl.” Margaret’s French form is Marguerite, the author’s own name. The girl on the bus wears “ten cent store pearls” dripping from her ears.
  • Madge’s maiden name is Edwards. John Edwards, an eighteenth-century Welsh translator and poet, put the second and third parts of Bunyan’s Pilgrim’s Progress into Welsh in the 1760s.
  • Homer means hostage, pledge. It is also the name of the poet of the Iliad and the Odyssey.
  • Capehorn is a French occupational name for a robe-master or maker of hoods. It also suggests Cape Horn, the stormy southern tip of South America, where many sailing ships were lost rounding the Horn.
