Chapter 49

← Chapter 48 · Home · Chapter 50 →

Summary

In a frozen cosmos where ice covers the rivers, the boats, the archer, and the constellations, Mr. Spitzer lives when he is dead and wakes only when he sleeps. He weeps for others who do not weep for him, and above all for Martha, the last passenger pigeon, whose death he dates to September 14, 1918, “in a war-torn world” (she died September 1, 1914). He arrived too late to see her alive, rode all night on the train that carried her body to Washington, and begged the old caretaker of the Washington Museum to set a mirror before her so that she would not know she was alone; the caretaker refused, saying she had no soul and that it was the incapacity to be deceived which caused extinction. Mr. Spitzer would have indicted America before the Senate for what it had done to the pigeons and to the Indians, but he would have been threatened with the Federal pen. He remembers meeting an old sailor, the sole survivor of a shipwreck, and telling him that the greatest shipwreck is to sink when there is no storm. He comes to trust only the false, the blind, and the deaf, all who have lost, and walking through the rain among the pigeons he cannot tell whether he is one or two, or which brother he is.

Characters present

Joachim Spitzer · Martha the Passenger Pigeon · Peron Spitzer

Concepts present

Themes: Death and Mortality · Faith, God, and the Supernatural · Guilt, Innocence, and Justice · Identity and the Self · Isolation and Connection · Memory and the Past · Nature, the Sea, and the Cosmos · Society, Class, and Race · Women, Gender, and Marriage

Symbols: Birds · Butterflies and Moths · Fireflies · Keys, Doors, and Locks · Lamps, Candles, and Light · Mirrors and Reflections · Moon and Stars · Music and Instruments · Shadows · Snow, Ice, and Winter · The Sea and Water

Philosophy: Aristotle · Augustine and Christian Theology · Buddhism · Descartes and Dualism · Empiricism (Locke, Berkeley, Hume) · Hinduism · Kant and Hegel · Marguerite Young on Her Craft · Plato and Platonism · Spinoza · Taoism and Zhuangzi · The Problem of Universals · Time, Physics, and Chaos Theory · William James and Pragmatism

Allusions: Alice in Wonderland · American Writers · Ancient Egypt · Angels and Archangels · Astronomy · Deafness and Sign Language · Don Quixote · Gambling and Playing Cards · Genesis · Greek Mythology · Homer’s Epics · Judaism · Music and Composers · Revelation and the Apocalypse · Romantic Poets · Shakespeare · Sir Walter Raleigh · Suicide in History and Literature · The Bible

Key passages

From the research

  • Mr. Spitzer experiences a profound disorientation where he “was disoriented by his great experience of living when he was dead, waking only when he was sleeping, sleeping in a watery grave or in an ice hole.” This passage encapsulates the paradoxical state of existence and non-existence, blurring the boundaries between life and death, wakefulness and sleep.
  • The imagery of landscapes and continents being lost or carried away like feathers or lace handkerchiefs symbolizes the transient, fragile, and mutable nature of reality itself.
  • Mr. Spitzer contemplates vast cosmic elements: “Ice had frozen so hard that it was like a dome or like the shell of an egg… Ice was frozen into shapes of frozen roofs over the winding rivers and the seas and the lakes… ice piled up like weird spires and minarets and bell towers.” This grand imagery conveys a frozen, timeless cosmos, a metaphor for stasis, death, or suspended animation of existence.
  • The passage also reflects on the impossibility of finding solid ground or stable meaning in a world dominated by illusions and transformations.
  • Mr. Spitzer mourns the death of Martha, the last passenger pigeon, noting the poignant historical moment: “Martha, who expired September 14, at one o’clock in the afternoon just as the clock was tolling one, 1918, A.D., at the Cincinnati zoo” (Young’s date; Martha died September 1, 1914). This event symbolizes the extinction of a species and, metaphorically, the loss of innocence, beauty, and connection to nature.
  • His grief for Martha becomes a symbol for his own loneliness and the universal sorrow at loss and disappearance: “He wept for others who wept not for him.”
  • The novel frequently questions the nature of the self: “He knew not whether he was himself or an image contained within an image… one of whom no unitary statement could be made.” This reflects a fragmented identity, the multiplicity of selves, or even the illusion of a stable self.
  • The motif of doubling and mirrored selves recurs: “how often he had nearly collided with himself though this would seem impossible.” This evokes existential ambiguity and the fluidity of personal identity across time and space.
  • Mr. Spitzer embraces a paradoxical philosophy: So he had come “to trust only the false… For why… should he trust the truth which had already failed him if the false would never fail.” This reflects a deep skepticism about knowledge, reality, and the reliability of perception or memory.
  • The passage suggests that constancy is found only in inconstancy, and that faith in truth is always tentative and fraught.
  • The chapter emphasizes the unreliability and fragmentation of memory: “His memory… had omitted so much, perhaps the whole content of mortal life, of certain death.”
  • Time is portrayed as fluid, uncertain, and perhaps even illusory: “Perhaps there was no time… What calendar keeps the sea of the months flowing into the months…?.”
  • Reality is likened to a dream or a fog: “the fog concealed the barnacle, the rose, the wing, the star… obliterated the obvious differences between the living and the dead.”
  • Mr. Spitzer reflects on the interrelatedness of life’s opposites: “He died through sickness, died through health… died through happiness which should have saved him, died through sorrow, sorrow by which he lived, died by not dying, died by living, lived by dying.”
  • Love is depicted as immortal and paradoxical: “when love lived, it died—but having died, it lived and could not die.”
  • The text repeatedly returns to Mr. Spitzer’s profound loneliness and his longing for understanding and communion: “He trusted those who had lost… all those who were dispossessed and wandering through the storm of years as he was. They drew him nearest to the city. They were all his loves because he could not love or could love only by indirection.”
  • His existential isolation is underscored by the metaphor of walking “through the rain of the city where the rain of the city drummed upon the dark or golden porches and roofs” and feeling himself “oblivious to them.”
  • Water, ice, and the sea are pervasive symbols throughout the chapter, representing both life and death, fluidity and stasis, memory and oblivion: He was like a shipwreck, “his hull broken… paying out more water than the seas contained.” The rising waters symbolize overwhelming forces beyond control and the engulfing nature of death and oblivion.
  • Near the end, Mr. Spitzer is described as “the living lighthouse at that one moment when he saw his light, moment when he was dying… his own light shining, shining from him.” This image captures the simultaneous presence of life and death, light and darkness, as well as the enduring, though fragile, spark of consciousness amid cosmic dissolution.

Questions and observations

Reading closely

  • “There was nothing he feared so much as the light of the sun.” Why does Mr. Spitzer live by fog and shadow?
  • “Greatest shipwreck is this… to sink when there is no storm.” What is a shipwreck in calm water?
  • Mr. Spitzer’s paradox is “to trust only the false.” How can falsehood be more faithful than truth?

Characters

  • The old caretaker says “It was this incapacity to be deceived which caused extinction.” Why does Mr. Spitzer want a mirror placed before Martha?
  • Mr. Spitzer would indict America for “what America had done to passenger pigeons… and had done to Indians in their lonely tepees.” Why does he join the two?
  • “He trusted all persons suffering some fatal defect.” Why are the blind and the deaf his loves?

Connections

  • Young dates Martha’s death to 1918, “in a war-torn world,” though she died in 1914. Why might the date move to the last year of the war?
  • In Chapter 48 Mr. Spitzer imagined himself a stowaway on a ship that went down; here he is the shipwreck itself. How has the image changed?
  • “He did not know which brother he was, and this was the crux of his mystery.” How does this chapter answer Chapter 48’s question of whether the twins are one and the same?

Reflection

  • “Rarely had there been known in the annals of time the date of the death of the last member of an entire species.” What does it mean to be the last of one’s kind?
  • “Perhaps perfect silence was the perfection of love.” Is it?
  • “He was forgotten now, so should he be remembered then?” What makes a life remembered?

Research: Characters

Mr. Spitzer

  • A complex figure symbolizing the human struggle with mortality, memory, and meaning.
  • Described metaphorically as a shipwreck, a shadow, a lighthouse, a phantom, and a musician whose music is unheard.
  • His physical ailments (e.g., irregular pulse, short breath) parallel his metaphysical disintegration and confusion.
  • He functions as a “mourner” and witness to extinction, loss, and the fading of worlds.
  • Mr. Spitzer’s paradoxical existence of alive yet dead, remembering yet forgetting makes him a liminal, almost mythical figure.

The Old Caretaker

  • Represents skepticism, finality, and the harsh reality of extinction.
  • His views on Martha the passenger pigeon emphasize the finality of death and the absence of spiritual continuation.
  • “It was this incapacity to be deceived which caused extinction, the old caretaker had announced.”

Peron Spitzer

  • “His brother could never have accepted an ineluctable reality such as Mr. Spitzer feared. His brother had thought that there was something he could do to change things, to make for greater hope or greater hopelessness.”
  • “They were born together.” Mr. Spitzer “did not know which brother he was, and this was the crux of his mystery.”

Martha (Passenger Pigeon)

  • Symbolizes lost beauty, extinction, and irretrievable loss.
  • Her death is mourned as the death of a species, a cosmic event, and a personal loss for Mr. Spitzer.

Research: Themes

Life, Death, and Immortality

See: Death and Mortality

  • Mr. Spitzer’s state blurs the boundary between living and dead. He lived “when he was dead, waking only when he was sleeping.”
  • Death is portrayed as a paradox: he “died at his zenith because he was at his nadir, died at his nadir because he was at his zenith.”
  • The text questions the reality of death and life, suggesting both may be illusions: “He knew there was no death because there was no life.”
  • The theme of immortality is paradoxical, with Mr. Spitzer’s spirit existing in a liminal state, neither fully present nor gone.

Memory and Forgetfulness

See: Memory and the Past

  • Mr. Spitzer struggles with remembering and forgetting, his past and identity constantly shifting.
  • His “forgetfulness veiling his forgetfulness” and “oblivion hiding behind his oblivion” illustrate layers of fading consciousness.
  • He questions the reliability of memory, pondering if he ever truly lived or if life was just a “mistaken dream.”

Identity and Self-Perception

See: Identity and the Self

  • There is a profound ambiguity regarding Mr. Spitzer’s identity, “He knew not whether he was himself or an image contained within an image.”
  • The motif of doubling, shadows, and reflections recurs, contributing to his fragmented self-understanding.
  • He often quarrels with himself or his shadow, suggesting an internal conflict and fractured self.

The Natural World and Extinction

See: Nature, the Sea, and the Cosmos

  • The extinction of the passenger pigeon, Martha, serves as a poignant symbol of loss and mourning.
  • Nature is depicted as vast, mystical, and fragile all subject to decay and disappearance.
  • The natural world mirrors the human condition as being both transient, vulnerable, and caught in cycles of life and death.

The Cosmic and the Mystical

See: Faith, God, and the Supernatural · Nature, the Sea, and the Cosmos

  • The cosmos, stars, and celestial imagery permeate the text, emphasizing vastness, mystery, and the unknowable.
  • Mr. Spitzer imagines his existence woven into universal patterns, yet feels lost and disoriented within them.
  • The narrative contemplates the idea of multiple dimensions, alternate realities, and the eternal recurrence of life and death.

Isolation and Connection

See: Isolation and Connection

  • Despite being surrounded by crowds, Mr. Spitzer experiences profound solitude and alienation.
  • His relationships are ambiguous since he mourns lost loves, mourns a lost species, and even quarrels with his own shadow.
  • The idea of failed communication and the search for understanding pervade, especially in his interactions with the blind and deaf.

Research: Symbols and Imagery

Water and Ice

See: The Sea and Water · Snow, Ice, and Winter

  • Recurring images of frozen waters, ice domes, and watery graves symbolize stasis, death, and the frozen moment between life and death.
  • Water also represents fluidity, dream states, and the passage between worlds.

Stars and Celestial Bodies

See: Moon and Stars

  • Stars represent memory, the soul, and cosmic order, yet are also fading, crumbling, or melting snowflakes.
  • The interplay of light and shadow among stars mirrors the ambiguities of life and death.

Shadows and Reflections

See: Mirrors and Reflections · Shadows

  • Shadows emphasize duality, absence, and the elusive nature of identity.
  • Reflections question reality versus illusion, with Mr. Spitzer sometimes chasing shadows or reflections rather than reality.

Birds (Pigeons, Blackbirds, Fireflies)

See: Birds · Fireflies

  • Birds symbolize life, freedom, and the passage of souls.
  • The extinction of the passenger pigeon is a metaphor for loss and the fragility of existence.
  • Fireflies and moths symbolize faint, fragile light, hope, memory, or the soul’s flicker.

Music

See: Music and Instruments

  • Music is a metaphor for existence, memory, and communication.
  • Mr. Spitzer’s music is “unspoken,” “unheard,” and a “barcarolle” rocking on waves, symbolizing the elusive nature of his life and thoughts.

Research: Resources

  • “It was never reveille in this windy world”: Reveille is a signal sounded especially on a bugle or drum to wake personnel in the armed forces. The old drummer drums taps instead; see Taps in the Chapter 47 resources.
  • “perhaps only one grace note”: A grace note is a musical ornament, a brief note that precedes and embellishes the main note in a musical passage. See Music and Composers.
  • “my mother’s coach”: See the coach of Part One and its driver. See The Black Coachman and Catherine Cartwheel.
  • “butterfly which had seemed one butterfly but was always two butterflies conjoining”: The two butterflies that seem one are the twins in little, “one with its image.” See Zhuangzi’s butterfly, below. See Taoism and Zhuangzi.
  • “fringe-topped surrey lumbering under Alpha and the long-necked horses flying under Omega”: A surrey is a light four-wheeled, two-seated carriage; the fringe-topped surrey recalls Rodgers and Hammerstein’s “The Surrey with the Fringe on Top” (Oklahoma!, 1943). Alpha and Omega are the first and last letters of the Greek alphabet, so the slow, earthly surrey lumbers under the beginning while the horses fly under the end: a journey from the beginning to the end, from the earthly to the cosmic.
    • Alpha and Omega in the New Testament is used as a Christian symbol. “I am Alpha and Omega, the beginning and the ending, saith the Lord” (Revelation 1:8); it means that Christ has existed for all eternity and that God is eternal. See Revelation and the Apocalypse.
    • Among the frozen stars that follow, the surrey may also be the Wain, the old English name for the Big Dipper seen as a wagon, driven by the herdsman Boötes, whose brightest star is Arcturus.
  • “Ice had formed over Arcturus”: The ice covers the constellations one by one. See Astronomy.
    • Arcturus is the brightest star in the northern constellation of Boötes.
    • The Great Ram with its long horn is the constellation Aries, the ram of the golden fleece (see the Chapter 47 resources), and the many-stringed Lyre is Lyra, the lyre Mercury (Hermes) made from a tortoise shell. A ram is also one of Mercury’s symbols. See Greek Mythology.
    • The Huntsman with his glittering belt may refer to the Orion constellation. See Orion in the Chapter 48 resources.
    • The Dog Star is another name for the brightest star in the night sky, Sirius. See the Chapter 48 resources.
    • The Little Goat is another name for Capella, the brightest star in the constellation Auriga. In mythology, Capella depicted the goat Amalthea that suckled Zeus.
    • The Wild Swan is the Cygnus constellation in the northern hemisphere which includes the Northern Cross. Zeus came to Leda as a swan.
    • The polar stars are Polaris in the north and Sigma Octantis, Polaris Australis, in the south.
    • The sub-polar stars or Circumpolar stars never set below the horizon and are always visible because of the proximity to the polar stars.
  • “the twelve Apostles in their long white robes and the thirteenth Apostle”: The twelve Apostles are Jesus’s apostles. The thirteenth Apostle may refer to Judas Iscariot, who was replaced after his suicide when lots were drawn and Matthias was chosen (Acts 1:23-26). Paul, called apart from the Twelve, is often named the thirteenth apostle, and Mary Magdalene was called “the apostle to the apostles.” The emperor Constantine had himself buried among memorials to the Twelve in his Church of the Holy Apostles and was called the thirteenth apostle. See The Bible.
  • “the wine dark sea”: Homer’s sea is oinops pontos, “wine-faced,” the wine-dark sea, in the Iliad and the Odyssey. See Homer’s Epics.
  • “the archer with the arrow in his breast”: may refer to Eros or Cupid who both shot gold-tipped arrows to make gods and humans fall in love. The archer may also be Sagittarius among the frozen stars, or Cupid, who in Apuleius says he “wounded myself with my own weapon” when he fell in love with Psyche (The Golden Ass, book 5). See Greek Mythology.
  • “the cat miaowed”: “Miaow” is the older spelling of the cat’s cry; earlier forms miaow, miau, and meaw date from the 1630s, and “meow” is recorded from 1842 (Online Etymology Dictionary). It is miau in Spanish and German and miaou in French. Cats in Ancient Egypt were called mau, after their cry. See Ancient Egypt.
  • “as if the sea gave up its dead”: “And the sea gave up the dead which were in it” (Revelation 20:13). See Revelation and the Apocalypse.
  • “He died because of a road not taken”: “The Road Not Taken” (Robert Frost, 1916). The road returns throughout the chapter, in “the way taken and the way not taken” and “a road many-branching like a chandelier.” See the Chapter 47 resources. See American Writers.
  • “a many-forking road like Mr. Chandelier”: See Mr. Chandelier and his many-branched lights. See Mr. Chandelier.
  • “Aurora Borealis and Aurora Australis”: Aurora Borealis and Aurora Australis are the lights visible in high northern and southern latitudes (Northern and Southern lights). See Astronomy.
  • “a minority representing a majority, a hidden majority like those sleeping in the churchyard”: Mr. Spitzer is the self-appointed advocate of unpopular and overlooked causes. He speaks for those society does not openly support or acknowledge, who may be a great silent majority, the marginalized, ignored, and forgotten, like the dead in the churchyard who lie without public recognition. No one chose or asked him; he took the role from conviction. Later in the chapter he would present his indictment to the Senate for the passenger pigeons and the Indians. See Guilt, Innocence, and Justice.
  • “His was this barcarolle heard not by the singer”: A barcarolle is a Venetian gondolier’s song in a rocking rhythm, like Offenbach’s Barcarolle in The Tales of Hoffmann (1881); he “had rocked them on the waves.” See Music and Composers.
  • “whether Ursa Major or Ursa Minor”: Ursa Major and Ursa Minor are constellations in the northern sky also known as Great Bear and Little Bear. Zeus set the nymph Callisto and her son Arcas among the stars as the two bears (Ovid, Metamorphoses 2). See Astronomy and Greek Mythology.
  • “the great archangel Uriel”: Uriel, “God is my light,” is an archangel of Jewish and Christian tradition, named in 1 Enoch and in the Apocrypha: “the angel that was sent unto me, whose name was Uriel, gave me an answer” (2 Esdras 4:1). He represents knowledge and wisdom. See Angels and Archangels.
  • “But why should any man weep if the heavens wept for him?”: In the Bible God grieves and Jesus weeps: “it grieved him at his heart” (Genesis 6:6); “Oh that my head were waters, and mine eyes a fountain of tears” (Jeremiah 9:1); “Jesus wept” (John 11:35). In the Book of Moses of the Latter-day Saints, “the God of heaven looked upon the residue of the people, and he wept” (Moses 7:28). The Quran says of Pharaoh’s drowned people, “And the heaven and the earth wept not for them” (44:29, trans. Marmaduke Pickthall, 1930), and the Egyptians said the Nile rose with the tears of Isis for Osiris (Pausanias, Description of Greece 10.32.18). See The Bible, Judaism, and Ancient Egypt.
  • “He wept for others who wept not for him”: “Daughters of Jerusalem, weep not for me, but weep for yourselves, and for your children” (Luke 23:28). To weep for himself seems an excess to Mr. Spitzer, who is already “dead or dying to this world, this world dying,” so he turns his sorrow outward to others who do not mourn him in return: a solitary, unreciprocated mourner and witness caught between life and death. See The Bible.
  • “Halloo, halloo! Is there anybody at home?”: “Halloo!” is the cry used to urge on dogs in a hunt. Mr. Spitzer knocking at empty houses recalls Walter de la Mare’s “The Listeners” (1912): “‘Is there anybody there?’ said the Traveller, / Knocking on the moonlit door.”
  • “Is thy light shining, or hast thy spirit departed upon the evening wind?”: “Neither do men light a candle, and put it under a bushel, but on a candlestick… Let your light so shine before men” (Matthew 5:15-16). Mr. Spitzer asks whether the inner light, the vital spirit, still shines or has already departed upon the evening wind, the approach of darkness and death. See The Bible.
  • “the golden spokes of light”: See Young’s wheel, Miss MacIntosh at the hub and the characters as “the spokes,” in the Chapter 43 resources.
  • “There was nothing he feared so much as the light of the sun”: The prisoner led out of Plato’s cave is dazzled and pained by the sun (Republic 7, 515e-516b), and La Rochefoucauld wrote that “Neither the sun nor death can be looked at steadily” (Maxims 26, 1665). “For life was itself this indirection”: “Tell all the truth but tell it slant — / Success in Circuit lies” (Emily Dickinson, written about 1868, published 1945). See Plato and Platonism and American Writers.
  • “the griffin with its wings of gold”: Griffins were said to guard the gold of the far north (Herodotus 3.116). “The smallest worm will turn being trodden on” (Henry VI, Part 3, 2.2), but this worm never turned. See Greek Mythology and Shakespeare.
  • “the mermaid giving milk to her young”: Manatees and dugongs, which nurse their young at the breast, are often named as a source of mermaid legends. Columbus saw three “mermaids” off Hispaniola in January 1493 and wrote that they “were not so beautiful as they are painted.” See The Sea and Water.
  • “He knew not whether he was himself or an image contained within an image”: Mr. Spitzer cannot tell the true self from its reflections or copies; he may be a reflection or shadow within layers of perception, “like a boatman in a boat or an image without, a ripple, a stir.”
  • “he being many countries, many times, many dimensions”: “Do I contradict myself? / Very well then I contradict myself, / (I am large, I contain multitudes.)” (Walt Whitman, “Song of Myself,” 1855). See American Writers.
  • “one of whom no unitary statement could be made”: The problem of universals in philosophy concerns the nature and existence of universals, qualities or properties that can be shared by multiple particular things, and how they relate to particulars. In this chapter, there are multiple reflections on identity, existence, perception, and the nature of reality that offer a profound literary meditation of this “Problem.” See The Problem of Universals, Aristotle, and Buddhism.
    • Problem of Universals: The problem of universals is an ancient question from metaphysics that has inspired a range of philosophical topics and disputes. “Should the properties an object has in common with other objects, such as color and shape, be considered to exist beyond those objects? And if a property exists separately from objects, what is the nature of that existence?” The problem of universals relates to various inquiries closely related to metaphysics, logic, and epistemology, as far back as Plato and Aristotle, in efforts to define the mental connections a human makes when they understand a property such as shape or color to be the same in nonidentical objects. Universals are qualities or relations found in two or more entities. As an example, if all cup holders are circular in some way, circularity may be considered a universal property of cup holders. Further, if two daughters can be considered female offspring of Frank, the qualities of being female, offspring, and of Frank, are universal properties of the two daughters. Many properties can be universal: being human, red, male or female, liquid or solid, big or small, etc. Philosophers agree that human beings can talk and think about universals, but disagree on whether universals exist in reality beyond mere thought and speech. (Wikipedia)
    • There are many philosophical positions regarding universals (also found in Indian and Buddhist philosophy): Platonic realism is the view that universals or forms in this sense, are the causal explanation behind the notion of what things exactly are which is that universals are real entities existing independent of particulars. Aristotelian realism is the rejection of extreme realism. This position establishes the view of a universal as being that of the quality within a thing and every other thing individual to it which is that universals are real entities, but their existence is dependent on the particulars that exemplify them. Anti-realism is the objection to both positions. Anti-realism is divided into two subcategories; (1) Nominalism and (2) Conceptualism. (Wikipedia)
    • Realism: Realists tend to argue that universals must be posited as distinct entities in order to account for various phenomena. A common realist argument said to be found in Plato’s writings, is that universals are required for certain general words to have meaning and for the sentences in which they occur to be true or false. Take the sentence “Djivan Gasparyan is a musician” for instance. The realist may claim that this sentence is only meaningful and expresses a truth because there is an individual, Djivan Gasparyan, who possesses a certain quality: musicianship. Therefore, it is assumed that the property is a universal which is distinct from the particular individual who has the property. (Wikipedia)
    • Nominalism: Nominalists assert that only individuals or particulars exist and deny that universals are real. Four major forms of nominalism are predicate nominalism, resemblance nominalism, trope nominalism, and conceptualism. One with a nominalist view claims that one predicates the same property of/to multiple entities, but argues that the entities only share a name and do not have a real quality in common.Nominalists often argue this view by claiming that nominalism can account for all the relevant phenomena, and therefore, by Occam’s razor, and its principle of simplicity,nominalism is preferable, since it posits fewer entities. Different variants and versions of nominalism have been endorsed or defended by many. (Wikipedia)
    • Conceptualism: Conceptualism is a position that is meshed between realism and nominalism. Conceptualists believe that universals can indeed be real, but only existing as concepts within the mind. Conceptualists argue that the “concept” of universals are not mere “inventions but are reflections of similarities among particular things themselves.” For example, the concept of ‘man’ ultimately reflects a similarity amongst Socrates and Kant. (Wikipedia)
    • Taking “beauty” as example, each of these positions will state the following. Platonic realism: Beauty is a property that exists in an ideal form independently of any mind or description. Aristotelian realism: Beauty is a property that exists only when beautiful things exist. Conceptualism: Beauty is a property constructed in the mind, so exists only in descriptions of things. (Wikipedia)
    • Porphyry of Tyre was a Neoplatonic philosopher born in Tyre, Roman Phoenicia during Roman rule. He edited and published the Enneads, the only collection of the work of Plotinus, his teacher. He wrote original works in the Greek language on a wide variety of topics, ranging from music theory to Homer. His Isagoge or Introduction, an introduction to logic and philosophy, was the standard textbook on logic throughout the Middle Ages in its Latin and Arabic translations. Porphyry was, and still is, also well-known for his anti-Christian polemics. Through works such as Philosophy from Oracles and Against the Christians (which was banned by Constantine the Great), he was involved in a controversy with early Christians. Important works and philosophy attributed to him. His Isagoge set the question for the Middle Ages, whether genera and species exist in reality or only in the mind. (Wikipedia) See Plato and Platonism.
    • William James: Though James certainly agreed with Peirce and against Berkeley that general ideas exist as a psychological fact, he was a nominalist in his ontology: “From every point of view, the overwhelming and portentous character ascribed to universal conceptions is surprising. Why, from Plato and Aristotle, philosophers should have vied with each other in scorn of the knowledge of the particular and in adoration of that of the general, is hard to understand, seeing that the more adorable knowledge ought to be that of the more adorable things and that the things of worth are all concretes and singulars. The only value of universal characters is that they help us, by reasoning, to know new truths about individual things.” (William James, The Principles of Psychology, 1890, chapter 12). There are at least three ways in which a realist might try to answer James’ challenge of explaining the reason why universal conceptions are more lofty than those of particulars: the moral-political answer, the mathematical-scientific answer, and the anti-paradoxical answer. Each has contemporary or near-contemporary advocates. (Wikipedia) See William James and Pragmatism.
    • Charles Sanders Peirce was an American scientist, mathematician, logician, and philosopher who is sometimes known as “the father of pragmatism.” According to philosopher Paul Weiss, Peirce was “the most original and versatile of America’s philosophers and America’s greatest logician.” Bertrand Russell wrote “he was one of the most original minds of the later nineteenth century and certainly the greatest American thinker ever.” Pragmatism as a philosophical movement originated in 1872 in discussions in The Metaphysical Club among Peirce, William James, Chauncey Wright, John Fiske, Francis Ellingwood Abbot, and lawyers Nicholas St. John Green and Joseph Bangs Warner (1848-1923). He outlined four methods, ordered from least to most successful in achieving a secure fixation of belief: tenacity, sticking to one’s first belief; authority; the a priori method, which settles on “what is agreeable to reason”; and the method of science, the only one that tests, criticizes, corrects, and improves itself (“The Fixation of Belief,” 1877) (Wikipedia)
    • Peter Abelard, the twelfth-century philosopher who argued the problem of universals against his teachers Roscellinus and William of Champeaux, is in the Chapter 52 resources, with Héloïse and their letters. See Descartes and Dualism, Kant and Hegel, and Spinoza.
    • Roscellinus was born in Compiègne, France. Little is known of his life, and knowledge of his doctrines is mainly derived from Anselm and Abelard. He studied at Soissons and Reims, was afterwards attached to the cathedral of Chartres and became canon of Compiègne. As a monk of Compiègne, he was teaching as early as 1087. He had contact with Lanfranc, Anselm, and St. Ivo of Chartres. Roscellinus’s exposition of Nominalist doctrines, and especially his application to the dogma of the Trinity, attracted broad attention. He maintained that the three persons of the Trinity were not referred to as three substances or Gods only by convention, arguing that if they were really one substance then God the Father and the Holy Spirit would have become incarnate along with God the Son. Roscellinus cited Lanfranc and Anselm in support of this doctrine. According to Otto of Freisingen, Roscellinus “was the first in our times to institute the theory of words,” but the chronicler of the “Historia Francia” mentions before him a “magister Johannes,” whose personality is much discussed and who has not yet been definitively identified. The “sententia vocum” was one of the anti-realist solutions of the problem of universals accepted in the early Middle Ages. In accordance with a dichotomy set out by Porphyry, the first medieval philosophers regarded genera and species either as things or as having no existence. The philosophers described this using terminology drawn from Boethius, referring to such abstract concepts as either things or words. Nominalists held that only the individual exists and that universals are merely words. (Wikipedia)
    • In Roscellinus’s theory, the universal is merely an emission of sound, in conformity with Boethius’ definition. Because Roscellinus did not discuss the philosophical concepts of genus and species, he is sometimes considered a pseudo-nominalist, or a moderate realist. However, because of his position as the first medieval philosopher to challenge medieval Realism, he has also been invoked as a forefather of modernity. Roscellinus was also taken to task by Anselm and Abelard for the less clear idea which he gave of the whole and of composite substance. According to Anselm, he maintained that colour does not exist independently of the horse which serves as its support and that the wisdom of the soul is not outside of the soul which is wise. (Wikipedia)
    • In this chapter Mr. Spitzer lives the problem of universals rather than explaining it. He is “many countries, many times, many dimensions,” with no unitary self; there is “no stone which was not a cloud”; music “was ever approximate and not actual,” and “none should live to hear its completion”; signs and gestures have “many and indeterminate meanings.” The imagery leans toward nominalism or conceptualism, with universals as shadows and reflections, yet a mystical unity remains: “He lived between the golden spokes of light. He lived between the spokes of darkness.” Young does not solve the problem; she builds a world where its terms dissolve. For more, see The Problem of Universals, Platonism and nominalism in the Chapter 2 resources, Abelard, Roscellinus, and William of Champeaux in the Chapter 52 resources, and Marguerite Young on Her Craft.
  • “the place where all good pigeons go when they die”: “Good Americans, when they die, go to Paris,” as Thomas Gold Appleton said, quoted by Oliver Wendell Holmes in The Autocrat of the Breakfast-Table (1858). See American Writers.
  • “the last passenger pigeon known to earth”: Martha died at the Cincinnati Zoo on the afternoon of September 1, 1914, a month after the First World War began, alone since her last companions died in 1910. Young gives the date as September 14, 1918, the last year of the war, at one o’clock. Mr. Spitzer mourns her as the last of her kind: once something is lost, whether a species, a person, or a moment, it cannot be recovered, and mourning for her is mourning for all that is irretrievably gone. Aldo Leopold wrote for the monument to the pigeon at Wyalusing State Park in Wisconsin: “We have erected a monument to commemorate the funeral of a species. It symbolizes our sorrow” (“On a Monument to the Pigeon,” 1947). See Martha the Passenger Pigeon and Birds.
    • Mr. Spitzer cried when he thought of the last passenger pigeon named Martha. It was named after First Lady Martha Washington. Records have her dying at the Cincinnati zoo at one o’clock in 1914. It is still on display and is a symbol of the threat of extinction.
    • The passenger pigeon or wild pigeon is an extinct species of pigeon that was endemic to North America. Its common name is derived from the French word passager, meaning to pass by, due to its migratory habits. Passenger pigeons were hunted by Native Americans, but hunting intensified after the arrival of Europeans, particularly in the 19th century. Pigeon meat was commercialized as cheap food, resulting in hunting on a massive scale for many decades. There were several other factors contributing to the decline and subsequent extinction of the species, including shrinking of the large breeding populations necessary for preservation of the species and widespread deforestation, which destroyed its habitat. A slow decline between about 1800 and 1870 was followed by a rapid decline between 1870 and 1890. The last confirmed wild bird is thought to have been shot in 1901. The last captive birds were divided in three groups around the turn of the 20th century, some of which were photographed alive. Martha, thought to be the last passenger pigeon, died on September 1, 1914, at the Cincinnati Zoo. The eradication of the species is a notable example of anthropogenic extinction or extinction of species directly due to human activity. (Wikipedia)
    • Pigeons embody the fragile boundary between life and death, presence and absence, and the haunting nature of what has vanished but is not forgotten.
  • “trapped by nets like the fishes of the sea”: Netters lured whole flocks with a captive pigeon tied to a perch or stool, the origin, it is said, of “stool pigeon.” At the last great nesting near Petoskey, Michigan, in 1878, hunters killed an estimated 50,000 birds a day for nearly five months, netting, shooting, and smothering them with burning sulfur, and shipped them to city markets. See Birds.
  • “The great key-maker had thrown away the key”: See Cousin Hannah’s forty keys and “no master key” in the Chapter 48 resources. See Keys, Doors, and Locks.
  • “The great candle-snuffer had snuffed out this flame”: See “out, out of this life” and Macbeth’s “brief candle” in the Chapter 48 resources. See Lamps, Candles, and Light.
  • “She was embalmed and put upon a train to be sent to Washington”: Mr. Spitzer says Martha was embalmed, but her body was frozen in about 300 pounds of ice and sent by fast train to the Smithsonian Institution in Washington, where it was made into a taxidermy mount and an anatomical specimen; the mount has been displayed there and lent to other museums. See Martha the Passenger Pigeon.
  • “only an old night porter riding with her”: Pullman sleeping-car porters were almost all Black men, many of them formerly enslaved or the sons of the enslaved; passengers called every porter “George,” after George Pullman, and they worked long hours for low pay and tips until they organized the Brotherhood of Sleeping Car Porters under A. Philip Randolph in 1925. “Black as the ace of spades” was a common racist simile; see the ace of spades in the Chapter 42 resources. See Society, Class, and Race and Gambling and Playing Cards.
  • “How precious then was life”: Life is a brief, precious moment, and much that sustains it, the dreamer and the dream, may be “illegal” in the grand scheme of things. Political authority, legal systems, and the great powers oppress, limit, and destroy individual lives, as they destroyed the pigeons. The passage holds both the preciousness of life in its fragility and the dreamlike quality of existence itself. See Guilt, Innocence, and Justice.
  • “Should not the slayer be the slain?”: “If the red slayer think he slays, / Or if the slain think he is slain, / They know not well the subtle ways / I keep, and pass, and turn again” (Ralph Waldo Emerson, “Brahma,” 1857), after the Bhagavad Gita 2.19. See American Writers and Hinduism.
  • “If there were no pigeons, could there be people”: Here pigeons stand for life, presence, and continuity, bound up with dawn and twilight, the passage between night and day, life and death. The mottled “pigeon-colored dawn” is complex and uncertain rather than a clear moment, and “He had lost all sense of the hour”: his time is fractured like his identity, and even the dawn is indistinct to him. See Birds.
  • “several times passing Lincoln’s Monument”: The Lincoln Memorial was begun in 1914 and dedicated in 1922, so in 1914 there was no monument yet to pass. Grant’s Tomb (1897) and Cleopatra’s Needle (set up in Central Park in 1881) are in New York, not Washington.
  • “a Roman head”: The coin left unpaid for the staring cab-driver is the ferryman’s fare; see Charon in the Chapter 46 resources. See Greek Mythology.
  • “he had come to the Washington Museum”: Martha, the last known passenger pigeon, died at the Cincinnati Zoo on September 1, 1914. Her body was frozen in a block of ice and sent to the Smithsonian Institution in Washington, where she was mounted and displayed, so Mr. Spitzer’s visit is a pilgrimage to her remains.
  • “She had surely died without benefit of clergy”: Benefit of clergy was the medieval privilege by which clergy accused of crimes were tried in church courts; “without benefit of clergy” came to mean without the rites of the church. Rudyard Kipling took it for a story title (1890).
  • “had no soul, the old caretaker said”: John James Audubon painted a pair of passenger pigeons for The Birds of America (plate 62, 1827-1838), and Mark Catesby before him in The Natural History of Carolina, Florida and the Bahama Islands (1731-1743). See Birds.
  • “for Martha was no more, and Mark was no more”: Mark is Martha’s mate, for “it took two to make a bargain”; her last companions at the Cincinnati Zoo died in 1910. It may also refer to Mark Catesby, who painted pictures of animals including the passenger pigeon, for Mr. Spitzer asks, “What good did Mark ever do… for all the pigeons.” See Martha the Passenger Pigeon.
  • “three trinitarian minutes”: The old caretaker times Martha’s death to “three minutes after one… three trinitarian minutes. Father, Mother, Son.” The Christian Trinity is the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit; Young puts Mother in the Spirit’s place, joining the sacred triad to family, birth, death, and spiritual passage. See Augustine and Christian Theology.
  • “She is melted in the fiery furnace of man’s disbelief”: Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego were cast “into the midst of the burning fiery furnace” and walked out unharmed (Daniel 3:23-27). Martha is not spared. See The Bible.
  • “These dying species multiplied not like the fishes of the sea”: “I will multiply thy seed as the stars of the heaven, and as the sand which is upon the sea shore” (Genesis 22:17). See Genesis.
  • “whistle all the way from here to Labrador”: The Labrador duck, last recorded in 1878, was the first North American bird known to go extinct after European settlement. See Birds.
  • “not even watery Venus”: Under its unbroken clouds Venus was long imagined as a warm, wet world; Svante Arrhenius pictured it as swamp and jungle (The Destinies of the Stars, 1918). Mariner 2 found its surface scorching hot in December 1962. See Astronomy.
  • “the dove of God like that which flew up through Mary’s skirts”: The Holy Spirit descends “in a bodily shape like a dove” (Luke 3:22), and in paintings of the Annunciation a dove brings the conception to Mary. See the three trinitarian minutes, above. See The Bible and Augustine and Christian Theology.
  • “only the female endures”: “So God created man in his own image, in the image of God created he him; male and female created he them” (Genesis 1:27); Mr. Spitzer’s “female and female created He them” rewrites it. Women are often depicted as enduring various forms of hardship, including prolonged stress and instability, without succumbing to their circumstances. Some believe that societal expectations and responsibilities, like caregiving, can contribute to women developing a strong ability to persevere through difficulties. This concept is reflected in literature and cultural narratives, where women are often portrayed as resilient characters who face challenges with strength and fortitude. While men often dominate in shorter, more intense endurance events, women demonstrate strong performance in longer distances, particularly ultra-endurance activities. This is partly attributed to potential physiological advantages, such as efficient fat utilization and greater fatigue resistance in women during prolonged exercise. Psychological factors like strong mental resilience and consistent pacing strategies are also believed to contribute to women’s success in these events. It is important to acknowledge that the experiences of endurance and resilience differ based on individual circumstances and intersectional factors like race and culture. For instance, Black women in horror narratives are described as “Enduring Women” (Kinitra D. Brooks, “The Importance of Neglected Intersections: Race and Gender in Contemporary Zombie Texts and Theories,” African American Review 47, no. 4, 2014) who face different and more persistent threats than the traditional “Final Girl” (Carol J. Clover, Men, Women, and Chain Saws, 1992), highlighting the complexities of navigating misogynoir and societal challenges. It is crucial to recognize the importance of understanding resilience within the context of women’s lived experiences and the societal factors that influence their well-being. See Genesis and Women, Gender, and Marriage.
  • “Every Martha must have her Mary”: “Martha, Martha, thou art careful and troubled about many things: But one thing is needful: and Mary hath chosen that good part” (Luke 10:41-42); the sisters of Lazarus appear again in John 11. Martha is associated with active service and worldly duties, Mary with contemplative devotion and the inner life. For every Martha bearing the burdens of the world there is a Mary who embodies grace and hope; here Mary is “that snow-white pigeon with the red-rose breast who used to come to her through miles of clouds.” The pairing holds loss, maternal suffering, spiritual yearning, and the interplay of outer and inner life. See The Bible.
  • “had done to Indians in their lonely tepees”: The United States has never been held legally to account for genocidal acts against its Indigenous peoples, though many historians and academics describe the Mystic massacre (1637), the Trail of Tears (1838-1839), the Sand Creek Massacre (1864), and the Mendocino War (1859) as genocidal. Roxanne Dunbar-Ortiz states that U.S. history, as well as inherited Indigenous trauma, cannot be understood without dealing with the genocide the United States committed against Indigenous peoples (An Indigenous Peoples’ History of the United States, 2014). From the colonial period through the founding of the United States and into the twentieth century, it entailed torture, terror, sexual abuse, massacres, systematic military occupations, removals of Indigenous peoples from their ancestral territories, the forced removal of Native American children to military-like boarding schools, allotment, and a policy of termination. During Pontiac’s War, General Jeffery Amherst wrote to Colonel Henry Bouquet, “You will Do well to try to Innoculate the Indians by means of Blanketts, as well as to try Every other method that can serve to Extirpate this Execrable Race” (July 16, 1763), part of a broader genocidal attitude displayed toward Native Americans during the colonization of the Americas. Under the Indian Vaccination Act of 1832, Secretary of War Lewis Cass ordered that no surgeon be sent higher up the Missouri than the Mandans, leaving the upper Missouri nations unvaccinated, and when smallpox swept the northern plains in 1837 it killed thousands of Mandans, Hidatsas, Arikaras, Assiniboines, Crees, and Blackfeet (J. Diane Pearson, “Lewis Cass and the Politics of Disease: The Indian Vaccination Act of 1832,” Wicazo Sa Review 18, no. 2, 2003). The United States has to date undertaken no truth commission and built no memorial for the genocide of Indigenous people, and it does not acknowledge or compensate for the historical violence of westward expansion. American museums such as the Smithsonian Institution do not dedicate a section to the genocide; in 2013 the National Congress of American Indians passed a resolution to create a space for a National American Indian Holocaust Museum inside the Smithsonian, but it was ignored (Wikipedia). After the Family Planning Services and Population Research Act of 1970, the Indian Health Service sterilized thousands of Native American women, many without informed consent: a 1976 General Accounting Office report found 3,406 sterilizations in just four of its twelve areas from 1973 to 1976, and by some estimates a quarter or more of Native American women of childbearing age were sterilized (Jane Lawrence, “The Indian Health Service and the Sterilization of Native American Women,” American Indian Quarterly 24, no. 3, 2000). In 1977 Marie Sanchez, chief tribal judge on the Northern Cheyenne Indian Reservation, told a United Nations conference on the Indigenous peoples of the Americas in Geneva that Native American women suffered involuntary sterilization, which she equated with modern genocide. See Society, Class, and Race.
  • “the whooping crane and the lute bird”: By 1941 only about twenty whooping cranes were left in the world, the wild flock wintering at Aransas on the Texas coast. The lute bird may be the lyrebird of Australia, named for the lyre shape of the male’s tail and famous for imitating any sound. See Birds.
  • “would have been threatened with the Federal pen”: The Federal pen is the federal penitentiary. For “giving a voice to all those beauties which never should have been expressed,” the old pigeon lobbyist would be accused of anarchy and sedition. In 2013 the programmer and activist Aaron Swartz, facing federal charges that carried up to thirty-five years in prison for downloading academic articles, died by suicide. The “beauties” are the elusive, perhaps forbidden, aspects of life and art, hidden truths and deep emotions beyond ordinary perception or social acceptance; to expose them would bring punishment from legal or governmental authority, the power of law enforcement or censorship to suppress such revelations. See Suicide in History and Literature and Guilt, Innocence, and Justice.
  • “Boston, the Great Hub”: “The Hub” is a nickname derived from Oliver Wendell Holmes’s “Boston State-House is the hub of the solar system” (The Autocrat of the Breakfast-Table, 1858). See American Writers.
  • “He heard a bell tolling far inland”: Mr. Spitzer hears a bell tolling. “And therefore never send to know for whom the bell tolls; it tolls for thee” (John Donne, Devotions upon Emergent Occasions, Meditation 17, 1624).
  • “trust only the blind”: “In the Country of the Blind the One-eyed Man is King,” the proverb H. G. Wells turned inside out in “The Country of the Blind” (1904), where the sighted man is the one who cannot find his way.
  • “in that realm the father carried the young”: Among seahorses the male carries the eggs in a brood pouch and gives birth to the young.
  • “the fisherman was caught in his net”: It is a metaphor reflecting the idea of being trapped by one’s own actions or fate. Here, the fisherman, who is usually the one capturing fish with a net, ironically becomes the one ensnared in his own net, symbolizing a reversal of roles or the inevitability of being caught by the consequences of one’s own deeds. “For man also knoweth not his time: as the fishes that are taken in an evil net, and as the birds that are caught in the snare; so are the sons of men snared in an evil time” (Ecclesiastes 9:12).
  • “chessmen who had walked on squares of black and gold”: See the life-sized chessmen of Through the Looking-Glass in the Chapter 13 resources. See Alice in Wonderland.
  • “the Pleiades flying like birds”: See Orion and the Pleiades in the Chapter 48 resources. See Greek Mythology.
  • “the black eunuch and the white”: In the Ottoman palace the harem was guarded by Black eunuchs under the Kızlar Ağası, their chief, and the outer palace by white eunuchs. See Society, Class, and Race.
  • “the black coachman in his pearl-lined grave”: See The Black Coachman. See The Black Coachman.
  • “the star might be drawn by the moth”: Young reverses Shelley: “The desire of the moth for the star, / Of the night for the morrow” (Percy Bysshe Shelley, “One word is too often profaned,” 1824). See Romantic Poets and Butterflies and Moths.
  • “as if he, too, had been to Holy Lands”: Pilgrims came home with shells on their hats, the scallop badge of St. James at Santiago de Compostela: “Give me my Scallop shell of quiet, / My staffe of Faith to walke upon” (Sir Walter Ralegh, “The Passionate Man’s Pilgrimage,” 1604). See Sir Walter Raleigh.
  • “I am that man who was always on his way to a wedding and came to a funeral”: Coleridge’s Ancient Mariner stops one of three on their way to a wedding feast to tell of the ship whose crew all died but him: “Alone, alone, all, all alone, / Alone on a wide wide sea!” (“The Rime of the Ancient Mariner,” 1798). Here the old sailor is the sole survivor and Mr. Spitzer the guest. See Romantic Poets.
  • “You drown in your own drowning”: This conversation mirrors the tales of the Tavern landlord in the later chapters.
  • “how shall I perceive there what was not perceived here?”: Mr. Spitzer seems to be struggling with the philosophical question, if a tree falls in a forest, which asks about the possibility of unperceived existence. Can something exist without being perceived by consciousness? Can the unobserved world function the same as the observed world? There is a division between perception of an object and how an object really is. What does existence mean and what is the difference between perception and reality? George Berkeley held that for things to exist is for them to be perceived, esse est percipi (A Treatise Concerning the Principles of Human Knowledge, 1710, section 3), and the riddle took its familiar form in a physics textbook: “When a tree falls in a lonely forest, and no animal is near by to hear it, does it make a sound?” (Charles Riborg Mann and George Ransom Twiss, Physics, 1910). See Empiricism (Locke, Berkeley, Hume).
  • “It is possible that we are illusions in the light-streaked fog”: Human beings, their identities and experiences, may be insubstantial and transient, like shapes seen in a fog lit only for a moment by streaks of light. The fog is the ambiguity surrounding existence: perceptions, memories, and realities are not fixed but shifting and elusive, and what seems substantial may be ephemeral or constructed by the mind.
  • “Often he could be heard talking to himself”: Mr. Spitzer is exhibiting two psychological issues: 1) internalized conflict which often involves rehearsing disagreements, replaying past interactions, or formulating responses to potential future arguments. This can stem from unresolved conflicts, a need to feel in control, or a tendency to project negative feelings onto others. These mental arguments can be a way to process emotions, prepare for potential conflicts, or even act out suppressed anger or frustration. 2) self-talk is a common and often beneficial behavior as a form of cognitive processing, aiding in problem-solving, decision-making, and memory recall. It can also be a way to regulate emotions, manage stress, and even practice social interactions. Both, of course, taken to excess, could be a mental health condition.
  • “For why, as he might often ask himself, should he trust the truth”: This passage encapsulates Mr. Spitzer’s existential uncertainty and the paradoxes he faces: the instability of what is usually trusted (truth, constancy, solidity) and the endurance of what is usually mistrusted (falsehood, change, fragility).
  • “Why should he suppose his musical murmur should remember him when he was gone?”: Mr. Spitzer doubts he will be remembered after death, since he already feels forgotten in life. His “musical murmur” is his life’s work and presence, subtle, ephemeral, barely noticed, and he expects to be forgotten after death as before.
  • “the dream of the dream”: Zhuangzi’s “Butterfly Dream” is a famous philosophical anecdote about a dream where the philosopher Zhuangzi transforms into a butterfly and then questions whether he is now a man who dreamed of being a butterfly or a butterfly dreaming he is a man. “Once upon a time, I, Chuang Tzŭ, dreamt I was a butterfly, fluttering hither and thither, to all intents and purposes a butterfly… Now I do not know whether I was then a man dreaming I was a butterfly, or whether I am now a butterfly, dreaming I am a man” (Chuang Tzŭ, trans. Herbert A. Giles, 1889, chapter 2). See Taoism and Zhuangzi.
    • Relativity of Reality: The story suggests that the distinction between dreaming and waking reality might not be as clear-cut as it seems.
    • The Fluidity of Self: It questions the fixed nature of identity, implying that the self might be more fluid and transformative than it is usually taken to be.
    • The Unity of All Things: Some interpretations connect the story to the Daoist concept of the “Transformation of Things,” suggesting that all things are interconnected and constantly changing.
    • Beyond Duality: The story can be seen as an invitation to transcend dualistic thinking (e.g., self versus other, dream versus reality) and embrace a more holistic view of existence.
  • “Their yesterday was a pointing backward over the shoulder”: Young seems to use actual ASL sign language gestures but some seem to have changed over time. In American Sign Language time runs along the body: the past is signed behind, over the shoulder, and the future ahead. See Deafness and Sign Language.
  • “What cenotaph was there for him”: Mozart was buried in 1791 in a common grave at St. Marx in Vienna whose place was soon lost; a memorial stands near the likely spot, and a monument was raised to him in Vienna’s Central Cemetery in 1891. See Music and Composers.
  • “the porphyry clouds”: Porphyry, from the Greek porphyra, purple, is an igneous rock with large crystals set in a fine-grained matrix, the mark of two-stage cooling. The purple porphyry of Egypt was prized by Rome and Byzantium for imperial sculpture and architecture, since purple was the color of royalty, and a Byzantine emperor’s child born in the palace’s porphyry chamber was porphyrogenitus, “born in the purple.” See Porphyry of Tyre, above. See Ancient Egypt.
  • “he had seen the other side of the tapestry”: “Translating from one language into another… is like looking at Flemish tapestries on the wrong side; for though the figures are visible, they are full of threads that make them indistinct” (Miguel de Cervantes, Don Quixote, Part II, chapter 62, trans. John Ormsby, 1885). The chapter ends with Mr. Spitzer as the weaver woven into his own tapestry. See Don Quixote.
  • “He was this old fan-tail fanning his tail”: Darwin bred fancy pigeons and opened On the Origin of Species (1859) with them: the fantail with thirty or forty tail feathers spread upright and the pouter with its swollen crop. Mr. Spitzer is “pouter-breasted” too. See Birds.
  • “or perhaps he was the third”: “Who is the third who walks always beside you? / When I count, there are only you and I together” (T. S. Eliot, The Waste Land, 1922). See Peron Spitzer.
  • “the turf meets the surf”: Del Mar racetrack, founded by Bing Crosby with William Quigley, opened on July 3, 1937; “Where the Turf Meets the Surf,” written in 1938 by James Monaco and Johnny Burke with Crosby, is still played at the track.
  • “Venus shell”: In Botticelli’s The Birth of Venus (about 1485) the goddess rises from the sea standing on a scallop shell; “Was he rising from the sea, or was he sinking?” See Greek Mythology.
