This passage explores themes of duality, identity crisis, and grief. The indistinguishability of the brothers and the shifting realities emphasize the fragile nature of selfhood and the impact of loss.
  • Mr. Spitzer wanders through a city resembling Boston but constantly changing, with streets moving, buildings appearing and disappearing, and landmarks like the Flatiron Building or the Fishback Building misplaced. The city becomes a metaphor for Mr. Spitzer’s mental landscape: uncertain, unstable, and haunted by memory and illusion. This shifting environment reflects his inner confusion and his search for meaning and connection.
  • Mr. Spitzer meets various figures (derelicts, disguised persons, forgotten heirs, and those who have lost their identity or status) such as the old cancer specialist who does not know his own greatness, or the old woman who had been Lady Macbeth but now wanders as a man. These encounters highlight themes of loss, forgotten greatness, and the fragility of identity. They also underline Mr. Spitzer’s role as a mediator attempting to restore lost connections or identities, reflecting his own struggle with self and memory.
  • Mr. Spitzer is agitated and fearful over a missing jewel from a rajah’s crown, an incident he is somehow implicated in but does not remember clearly. This episode symbolizes the elusive nature of truth and guilt, and the burden of unremembered or misunderstood events. The jewel itself can be seen as a metaphor for something precious lost or perhaps time, identity, or reality.
  • Mr. Spitzer seeks out “lost heirs,” “forgotten legacies,” and “persons who had forgotten their bank accounts,” trying to restore what has been lost. He helps the poor and forgotten, buying clothes and necessities for those in need. This portrays Mr. Spitzer as a figure of compassion and redemption, despite his own suffering and confusion. It also reflects the broader theme of searching for and reclaiming lost fragments of identity and memory.
  • Mr. Spitzer is described as a composer who carries his musical notes on scraps of paper, composing an elegy that is fragmented and incomplete, with motifs of mistake and truth intertwined. The music represents life’s ephemeral and fragmented nature, the interplay of creation and error, memory and loss. Mr. Spitzer’s music is his means of making sense of his existence and grief, even as it remains unresolved.
  • The chapter repeatedly returns to Mr. Spitzer’s grief for his dead brother and his own fractured existence, caught between life and death, reality and dream, certainty and doubt. The imagery of snow, fog, shadows, and shifting streets reinforce this pervasive melancholy and ambiguity. This is the emotional core of the chapter, emphasizing the universal human experience of loss and the difficulty of finding meaning in a world that is constantly changing and often incomprehensible.
  • The chapter closes with Mr. Spitzer, alone, his elegy scattered like music fluttering away in the wind, a figure both present and absent, caught in a liminal space beyond human knowledge. This ending encapsulates the chapter’s meditation on mortality, artistic creation, and the transience of life and memory. Mr. Spitzer’s elegy symbolizes his enduring yet fading presence in a world indifferent to individual existence.

Questions and observations

Reading closely

  • “Perhaps, indeed, every man must know two worlds.” Which world does each brother belong to?
  • “He preferred glass jewels for the reason that glass jewels were glass, but real jewels were real and, therefore, of no value to him.” Why?
  • “Sometimes he thought the best part of him was his mistake.” What seed of truth can a mistake hold?

Characters

  • The sound effects man could “create the illusion of the city where no city was.” Why does he stir Mr. Spitzer’s “unwilling envy”?
  • The thief’s description “was the description of himself.” What has Mr. Spitzer stolen, if only “the jewel of time”?
  • Peron’s obituary shows that “his brother had been better thought of than he had known.” What does Mr. Spitzer learn about Peron, and about himself?

Connections

  • His “greater work” is “to reunite a man with himself.” How is every lost heir he seeks a version of his search for Peron?
  • The greatest Lady Macbeth now wanders “dressed as a man,” like the ward-heeler of Chapter 53. Why does Young keep returning to lives lived in disguise?
  • On his compass “all four points were North.” Where else in the novel do maps and directions fail?

Reflection

  • “Each man was a deposed king, surrounded by his own fallen glory.” Is Mr. Spitzer right never to challenge another person’s illusions?
  • “There was ineffable beauty in this grief… for it illuminated him.” Can grief illuminate?
  • His elegy blows away down a dark street. Is music lost if no one hears it?

Research: Characters

Mr. Spitzer (Joachim Spitzer)

  • The protagonist, an aging, reflective man struggling with his brother’s death and his own sense of self. He is a man of order and logic but is overwhelmed by grief and uncertainty, experiencing shifting realities and identities. Mr. Spitzer is profoundly lonely and disoriented, caught between madness and sanity.
  • He experiences shifting identities with Peron, unsure of who he is or whether he is alive or dead.
  • His grief is pervasive, touching on universal themes of loss and the search for meaning.
  • He is meticulous but uncertain, often doubting his perceptions and memories.
  • Despite his despair, he displays moments of kindness and creative impulse, especially through his music.

Peron Spitzer

  • Mr. Spitzer’s deceased brother, described as wild, gregarious, and reckless, almost the opposite of Joachim. Peron’s life and death haunt Joachim, and his presence is felt as a contrasting force driving Joachim’s reflections and wanderings.

Sound Effects Man

  • A mysterious figure associated with Peron, capable of producing chaotic, mimicry-like sounds symbolizing the noise and madness of life. He represents the opposite of Spitzer’s silence and order.

Research: Themes

Duality of Identity and Madness

See: Identity and the Self · Duality and Doubles · Madness and Sanity

  • Mr. Spitzer oscillates between his own identity and that of his brother, sometimes confused about who he truly is. The chapter explores the thin line between sanity and madness, with Joachim embodying order and Peron chaos, yet both are reflections of each other.

Life, Death, and the Unconscious

See: Dreams and Imagination · Death and Mortality

  • The narrative blurs the boundaries between the living and the dead. Mr. Spitzer’s experience suggests he might be dead or in a liminal state (“he was dead”), emphasizing the ambiguity of existence and the unconscious mind’s role in understanding life.

Memory, Time, and Reality

See: Illusion and Reality · Memory and the Past · Time

  • Time is fluid and non-linear. Newspapers are dated years ago but read as current; streets and cities shift; memories and experiences overlap. This challenges the concept of objective reality and highlights the fragility of memory.

Isolation and Grief

See: Isolation and Connection · Grief, Loss, and Mourning

  • Joachim’s profound loneliness is expressed through his endless wandering and failed attempts to find connection or meaning after Peron’s death. His grief touches on universal sorrow, described as a “precious grief” that illuminates him despite its pain.

The Search for Meaning

See: The Search for Meaning

  • Mr. Spitzer’s journey is a metaphorical search for self-understanding, love, and redemption, yet it is fraught with failures, illusions, and ambiguities.

Music and Creation

See: Music, Sound, and Silence

  • Music symbolizes order, creativity, and the attempt to impose meaning. Mr. Spitzer is described as a composer of life’s elegy, writing fragments of music on his clothing, representing his fragmented perception and desperate attempt to create coherence.

Research: Symbols and Imagery

The Sea and Water Imagery

See: The Sea and Water

  • The sea symbolizes the unconscious, the fluidity of reality, and the passage between life and death. Underwater fountains, sea’s burning gold, and submerged cities evoke a dreamlike state and loss.

Mirrors and Reflections

See: Mirrors and Reflections

  • Mirrors symbolize identity and illusion. Mr. Spitzer sees his shadow or reflection change or move independently, emphasizing his fractured self.

The Black Cape and High Silk Hat

See: Clothing, Hats, and Skirts

  • These identify Mr. Spitzer’s figure as a ghostly, almost theatrical presence, marking him as an outsider and a man out of time.

Jewels and Coins

See: Pearls and Jewels

  • Gems and coins appear repeatedly, symbolizing value, loss, and illusion. Mr. Spitzer refuses real jewels, preferring glass ones which is a metaphor for preferring illusion over reality.

The Sound Effects Man

  • Represents chaos and the intrusion of noise into Mr. Spitzer’s ordered world, symbolizing the inescapability of life’s dissonance.

The Compass and Directions

  • The compass always pointing North symbolizes disorientation and the impossibility of finding a true direction or meaning.

Research: Resources

  • “He could whistle like the calliope”: In Greek mythology, Calliope is the name of the Muse of epic poetry, known for her eloquence and beautiful voice. Calliope can also refer to a musical instrument, a steam-powered organ with whistles, often associated with circuses and riverboats. See Greek Mythology.
  • “an old-fashioned Maxwell automobile”: Maxwell was an American automobile manufacturer which ran from 1904 to 1925. The present-day successor to the Maxwell company was Chrysler, now Stellantis North America, which acquired the company in 1925.
  • “had he been Peter, he would have betrayed Christ every five minutes”: The Denial of Peter refers to the three acts of denial of Jesus by the Apostle Peter as described in all four Gospels of the New Testament. “Jesus said unto him, Verily I say unto thee, That this night, before the cock crow, thou shalt deny me thrice” (Matthew 26:34, KJV). See The Bible.
  • “his old, gilded Venetian billfold”: A “Venetian billfold” likely refers to a slim, leather wallet, often bi-fold, designed to hold bills and cards, inspired by the style and craftsmanship associated with Venice. The term “Venetian” often suggests a connection to Italian craftsmanship and quality.
  • “a Venetian doge”: Venetian doge was elected for life by the city-state’s aristocracy.
  • “he had never been to Siam”: Siam was the old name for Thailand.
  • “last year’s Grand Steeplechase”: Grand Steeplechase is in Paris, France and is a race for horses five years old and older.
  • “a lead nickel which had been given to him by a blind beggar”: A lead nickel was a counterfeit coin cast in lead, so a “lead nickel” came to mean anything worthless. The real United States nickel, first struck in 1866, is 75 percent copper and 25 percent nickel.
  • “a golden shekel or talent or florin”: A shekel is an ancient Mesopotamian coin, usually of silver. A shekel was first a unit of weight and became currency in ancient Tyre, Carthage and Hasmonean Judea.
    • The Attic talent, also known as the Athenian talent or Greek talent, is an ancient unit of weight equal to about 26 kilograms (57 lb), as well as a unit of value equal to this amount of pure silver. A talent was originally intended to be the mass of water required to fill an amphora, about one cubic foot.
    • The Florentine florin was a gold coin struck from 1252 to 1533 with no significant change in its design or metal content standard during that time. It had 54 grains (3.499 grams, 0.1125 troy ounces) of nominally pure or ‘fine’ gold. The name of the coin comes from the Giglio bottonato, the floral emblem of the city, which is represented at the head of the coin.
  • “the ferry boatman when he had crossed the dark and many-branching and many-flowing Styx”: See Charon and his fare in the Chapter 52 resources. See Greek Mythology.
  • “had seen Red Grange kicking the red football”: Red Grange was an American football player for the University of Illinois, the Chicago Bears, and the New York Yankees.
  • “some school children kicking a skull over a playing field”: Children kicking a skull over a playing field treat death as a plaything, the young careless of mortality and of the past, as the gravediggers toss skulls in Hamlet (5.1).
    • It may refer to the Mesoamerican ballgame where human sacrifice was practiced. There is speculation that human heads were used as the ball. This is also similar to the story of Mr. and Mrs. Tidings in the later chapters.
  • “the Church of the Golden Cockerel”: See the Cockerel Church, Boston’s New Brick Church on Hanover Street, named for Shem Drowne’s gilded rooster weathervane of 1721, in the Chapter 53 resources.
  • “Peron had been mad as a mad hatter”: Hatters were said to go mad from the mercury used to cure felt, which poisons the nerves; Lewis Carroll’s Hatter in Alice’s Adventures in Wonderland (1865) made “mad as a hatter” famous. See Alice in Wonderland.
  • “the Aurora Borealis was the Aurora Australis”: Aurora Borealis and Aurora Australis are the northern and southern lights seen around the Arctic and Antarctic sky. See Astronomy.
  • “whether it was the North Pole or the South Pole”: The North Pole and the South Pole are the northernmost and southernmost points of the Earth. See Exploration and the Poles.
  • “this music of Inferno”: Inferno is the first part of Italian writer Dante Alighieri’s 14th-century narrative poem The Divine Comedy, followed by Purgatorio and Paradiso. The Inferno describes the journey of a fictionalized version of Dante himself through Hell, guided by the ancient Roman poet Virgil. In the poem, Hell is depicted as nine concentric circles of torment located within the Earth; it is the “realm [...] of those who have rejected spiritual values by yielding to bestial appetites or violence, or by perverting their human intellect to fraud or malice against their fellowmen.” As an allegory, the Divine Comedy represents the journey of the soul toward God, with the Inferno describing the recognition and rejection of sin. See Dante.
  • “Sound of the hurdy-gurdy in a dark street”: Hurdy-gurdy is a string instrument that produces sound by a hand-crank-turned wheel rubbing against the strings.
  • “one imaginary Napoleon and another imaginary Napoleon”: Napoleon was a French military and political leader. See Napoleon and Wellington.
  • “one murdered archduke and another murdered archduke”: Murdered archduke may refer to Archduke Ferdinand of Austria whose assassination was one of the events leading up to World War I.
  • “one bishop and another bishop if both were wearing the mitre and the alb”: A Bishop wearing the mitre and the alb are the Pontifical vestments worn by bishops celebrating or presiding over liturgical functions in the Roman Catholic, Eastern Orthodox, Eastern Catholic, Anglican, and some Lutheran churches.
  • “Captain Cook and Admiral Perry”: Captain Cook was a British captain in the British Royal Navy famous for three voyages between 1768 and 1779 in the Pacific Ocean and to Australia. Admiral Perry is probably Robert E. Peary, the Arctic explorer who claimed to have reached the North Pole in 1909 and was made a rear admiral in 1911; Commodore Matthew Perry, who opened Japan to American ships in 1854, never sailed to the ends of the earth. See Exploration and the Poles.
  • “the Northern Cross or the Southern Cross or Charing Cross”: The Northern Cross is the cross-shaped pattern of bright stars in the constellation Cygnus, and the Southern Cross is the constellation Crux, seen from the Southern Hemisphere. Charing Cross is a junction in London named for the Eleanor cross Edward I raised there in memory of his queen; Young slips an earthly cross among the stars. See Astronomy.
  • “At the South Pole of the moon”: “At the South Pole of the moon, there were more mountains than at the North Pole of the moon” is not entirely accurate. The Lunar south pole of the moon has more craters that are not reached by sunlight because of the tilt of the moon’s axis. See Astronomy.
  • “matter has ever a tendency to drift downward”: “matter has ever a tendency to drift downward” is due to friction, gravity, and air resistance which slows an object down. This would be Newton’s laws of motion.
  • “the pearl-mantled Arctic tern”: The Arctic tern: see Chapter 82, Resources, for the full entry.
  • “so many droshkies and troikas”: “droshkies” is a term used for a four-wheeled open carriage used especially in Russia. The vehicle has a long bench on which the driver or passengers sit as if on a saddle, either astride or sideways. The name probably derives from droga, the pole that connects the front and rear axles. “troikas” is a traditional Russian harness driving combination, using three horses abreast, usually pulling a sleigh.
  • “the unfamiliar pleasures of a penny arcade”: Penny arcades, precursors to modern video game arcades, were entertainment venues featuring coin-operated amusement machines that typically cost a penny to operate. These arcades, popular from the late 1800s to the mid-20th century, offered a variety of mechanical games and novelty devices.
  • “an old gramophone honking”: A phonograph, later called a gramophone, and since the 1940s a record player, or more recently a turntable, is a device for the mechanical and analogue reproduction of sound. The sound vibration waveforms are recorded as corresponding physical deviations of a helical or spiral groove engraved, etched, incised, or impressed into the surface of a rotating cylinder or disc, called a record. To recreate the sound, the surface is similarly rotated while a playback stylus traces the groove and is therefore vibrated by it, faintly reproducing the recorded sound. In early acoustic phonographs, the stylus vibrated a diaphragm that produced sound waves coupled to the open air through a flaring horn, or directly to the listener’s ears through stethoscope-type earphones. The phonograph was invented in 1877 by Thomas Edison; its use would rise the following year. Alexander Graham Bell’s Volta Laboratory made several improvements in the 1880s and introduced the graphophone, including the use of wax-coated cardboard cylinders and a cutting stylus that moved from side to side in a zigzag groove around the record. In the 1890s, Emile Berliner initiated the transition from phonograph cylinders to flat discs with a spiral groove running from the periphery to near the center, coining the term gramophone for disc record players, which is predominantly used in many languages. Later improvements through the years included modifications to the turntable and its drive system, stylus, pickup system, and the sound and equalization systems. The disc phonograph record was the dominant commercial audio distribution format throughout most of the 20th century, and phonographs became the first example of home audio that people owned and used at their residences. In the 1960s, the use of 8-track cartridges and cassette tapes were introduced as alternatives. By the late 1980s, phonograph use had declined sharply due to the popularity of cassettes and the rise of the compact disc. However, records have undergone a revival since the late 2000s.
  • “St. Sophia’s Dome, the Kremlin Wall, thirteen minarets, twelve Greek crosses”: St. Sophia’s Dome or Hagia Sophia is a place of worship in Istanbul. The Kremlin Wall or Moscow Kremlin Wall is a defensive wall that surrounds the Moscow Kremlin. Thirteen minarets may refer to the type of tower built around a mosque. There are typically only one to six minarets. Twelve Greek crosses may refer to the Greek cross which predates the Latin cross. It was used in ancient Babylon for the god Shamash. It has an esoteric meaning for the four directions, the four evangelists, the twelve apostles, the twelve zodiac signs and the basic element of many alchemical symbols. See Astrology, Alchemy, and Esoterica.
  • “he had stopped to use a public pay phone”: A public payphone is a coin-operated telephone located in high-traffic areas. They were maintained and operated from 1889 to 1999 where most were discontinued because of the advent of cell phones.
  • “had nearly put a drachma into the slot”: In ancient Greece, the drachma was an ancient currency unit issued by many city-states during a period of ten centuries, from the Archaic period throughout the Classical period, the Hellenistic period up to the Roman period. The ancient drachma originated in Greece around the 6th century BC. The coin, usually made of silver or sometimes gold, had its origins in a bartering system that referred to a drachma as a handful of wooden spits or arrows. The drachma was unique to each city state that minted them, and were sometimes circulated all over the Mediterranean. The coinage of Athens was considered to be the strongest and became the most popular.
  • “she had gone to the Golden Horn”: Golden Horn is a major urban waterway in Istanbul, Turkey.
  • “suing the Boston telephone company”: “Boston telephone company” may refer to the New England Telephone and Telegraph Company formed in 1878.
  • “his wife had cuckolded him”: A cuckold is the husband of an adulterous wife (or partner for unmarried companions); the wife of an adulterous husband is a cuckquean. In biology, a cuckold is a male who unwittingly invests parental effort in juveniles who are not genetically his offspring. A husband who is aware of and tolerates his wife’s infidelity is sometimes called a wittol or wittold. The slang term bull refers to the dominant man who has relations with the cuckold’s partner. See Shakespeare.
  • “A large Colonial boot hanging out over a long grey street”: Colonial boots, while not a specific style like modern cowboy boots, represent the footwear worn during the colonial period in America, primarily by men. They were typically made of leather, with styles ranging from simple, low-cut shoes to taller riding boots, and often featured buckles. The construction and materials reflected the available technology and the wearer’s social status and needs.
  • “the old Flatiron Building”: The Flatiron Building is a triangular landmark in New York City.
  • “from the starboard side to the portside”: Portside is the left side of a vessel, when facing the front (bow). It’s one of the two sides of a ship, the other being starboard (right side). The term “port” replaced “larboard” because it was easily confused with “starboard.”
  • “a wooden policeman in the fog, a traffic robot”: There is one article that mentions a wooden policeman in Marysville, Washington in 1917 that was in the middle of the street with a sign in order to direct the increasing automobile traffic.
    • “traffic robot”: Early automatic traffic signals were often called robots, a name South Africa still uses for traffic lights. The first electric traffic lights went up in Salt Lake City in 1912 and Cleveland in 1914. Garrett Augustus Morgan, an African American inventor, patented a three-position traffic signal in 1923, a T-shaped signal with a position that stopped traffic in every direction, and sold the rights to General Electric. (Wikipedia) Morgan’s work is celebrated during Black History Month as an example of African American innovation.
  • “the grasshopper weathervane on old Faneuil Hall”: The grasshopper weathervane on Faneuil Hall is a famous landmark in Boston. Peter Faneuil commissioned Shem Drowne to make the grasshopper weathervane. In 1755 an earthquake knocked it down and Drowne’s son was commissioned to repair it. He put a note in the grasshopper’s belly. From time to time it has been repaired and more historical documents have been placed inside the grasshopper’s belly. In 1974 it was stolen and recovered and a lock was placed on it so it could not be stolen again.
  • “Sometimes the lights went out on Griffin’s Wharf”: Griffin’s Wharf in Boston is where, on December 16, 1773, colonists disguised as Mohawks dumped 342 chests of East India Company tea into the harbor in the Boston Tea Party. The wharf was later buried by landfill, and its site now lies inland.
  • “Beacon and Charles Streets still crossed”: Beacon and Charles Streets are major thoroughfares in Boston, Massachusetts. Beacon turns into a one way street when it crosses Charles Street.
  • “Once on Copp’s Hill”: Copp’s Hill is an elevation in the historic North End of Boston, Massachusetts.
  • “that old, dour Mather”: “old, dour Mather” may refer to Cotton Mather who was a New England Puritan clergyman and writer. Increase, Cotton, and Samuel Mather lie in the Mather family tomb on Copp’s Hill. See Augustine and Christian Theology.
  • “a ragged news-hawk crying”: A newshawk was a newsboy hawking papers in the street, crying the headlines; the word also meant a reporter.
  • “President Wilson had not died in office”: President Wilson did not die in office. He was the twenty-eighth President of the United States, a Democrat and the leading architect of the League of Nations. His successor President Harding died in office in August 1923, about six months before ex-President Wilson died in February 1924.
    • The League of Nations was an international organization founded in 1920 after World War I to maintain world peace and promote international cooperation. It was headquartered in Geneva, Switzerland, and aimed to prevent future conflicts through diplomacy and collective security. While it achieved some successes in areas like disease eradication and refugee protection, its effectiveness was ultimately limited by factors like the lack of participation from major powers like the United States, and its inability to prevent the outbreak of World War II. The League was formally dissolved in 1946, handing over its assets and responsibilities to the newly formed United Nations.
  • “binomial equations”: Binomial equations may refer to the binomial theorem which describes the algebraic expansion of powers.
  • “He had met the fellow who carried the lantern for Paul Revere”: Paul Revere was an American silversmith, military officer and industrialist who played a major role during the opening months of the American Revolutionary War in Massachusetts, engaging in a midnight ride in 1775 to alert nearby minutemen of the approach of British troops prior to the battles of Lexington and Concord. Born in the North End of Boston, Revere eventually became a prosperous and prominent Bostonian, deriving his income from silversmithing and engraving. During the American Revolution, he was a strong supporter of the Patriot cause and joined the Sons of Liberty. His midnight ride transformed him into an American folk hero, being dramatized in Henry Wadsworth Longfellow’s 1861 poem, “Paul Revere’s Ride.” He also helped to organize an intelligence and alarm system to keep watch on the movements of British forces. Revere later served as an officer in the Massachusetts Militia, though his service ended after the Penobscot Expedition, one of the most disastrous American campaigns of the American Revolutionary War, for which he was absolved of blame. Following the war, Revere returned to his silversmith trade. He used the profits from his expanding business to finance his work in iron casting, bronze bell and cannon casting, and the forging of copper bolts and spikes. In 1800, he became the first American to successfully roll copper into sheets for use as sheathing on naval vessels.
    • Two men are believed to have carried the lanterns to the steeple of Old North Church, Robert Newman and Captain John Pulling.
    • The woman who rode with Paul Revere to warn colonists about the British was Sybil Ludington. She was only 16 years old when she rode 40 miles on April 26, 1777, to alert the militia about the British attack on Danbury, Connecticut. While Paul Revere is famous for his “midnight ride,” Sybil Ludington’s ride was even longer and took place during a rainstorm. Her ride was crucial in mustering the militia, who were able to drive the British out of Ridgefield after the attack on Danbury.
  • “a tri-cornered hat”: Tri-cornered hat or tricorne was a style of hat popular in the 18th century.
  • “the British Red Coats were coming”: British Red Coats were the British infantrymen who fought in the American Revolution.
  • “Constitution Wharf”: Constitution Wharf in the North End stands on the site of Edmund Hartt’s shipyard, where the frigate USS Constitution, Old Ironsides, was built and launched in 1797. Constitution Wharf may refer to the USS Constitution or Old Ironsides which is retired at Pier 1 at one end of Boston’s Freedom Trail.
  • “time for the stirrup cup”: A stirrup cup is a “parting cup” given to guests, especially when they are leaving and have their feet in the stirrups. It is also the traditional drink (usually port or sherry) served at the meet, prior to a traditional foxhunt. It is mentioned in the poem “The Stirrup-Cup” by the nineteenth-century American poet, Sidney Lanier.
  • “running yesterday at Suffolk Downs”: Suffolk Downs is a former Thoroughbred race track in East Boston, Massachusetts.
  • “the Renaissance gilded chairs, the Louis XIII and the Louis XIV and the Louis XV”: The Renaissance is a period in European history marking the transition from the Middle Ages to modern times. Louis XIII was the King of France from 1610-1643. Louis XIV was King of France from 1643-1715. Louis XV was the King of France from 1715 to 1774.
  • “the Duke of Wellington stepped out of the fog”: Duke of Wellington was one of the leading military and political figures of 19th-century Britain. See Napoleon and Wellington.
  • “the old Fishback Building”: The Fishback Building may refer to the Fishback Company Building which was located on McCarty and Delaware streets in Indianapolis, Indiana. Frank Fishback started his coffee roasting business in the late 1880s and, by the 1910s, also sold Virginia Sweet brand foods including coffee and pancake flour. The Fishback Company closed during the 1930s. Young grew up in Indianapolis. See Iowa, Indiana, and the Midwest.
  • “the Steinway Building”: Steinway Hall, the piano maker’s building at 109 West 57th Street in Manhattan, opened in 1925 with a concert hall and showroom. Flag: after 1964, the supertall Steinway Tower (2021) was built over and around it.
  • “an old uncle in Paradiso”: Paradiso is the third and final part of Dante’s Divine Comedy, following the Inferno and the Purgatorio. It is an allegory telling of Dante’s journey through Heaven, guided by Beatrice, who symbolizes theology. In the poem, Paradise is depicted as a series of concentric spheres surrounding the Earth, consisting of the Moon, Mercury, Venus, the Sun, Mars, Jupiter, Saturn, the Fixed Stars, the Primum Mobile and finally, the Empyrean. It was written in the early 14th century. Allegorically, the poem represents the soul’s ascent to God. See Dante.
  • “the foot of Boylston Street”: Boylston Street is a major east-west thoroughfare in Boston, Massachusetts.
  • “nearly knocked down by a lady cyclist”: The bicycle craze of the 1890s gave women a new freedom, and new clothes to ride in. Susan B. Anthony told Nellie Bly in 1896, “Let me tell you what I think of bicycling. I think it has done more to emancipate women than anything else in the world” (New York World, 2 February 1896). See Women’s Suffrage.
  • “the statue of Aristides the Just”: The statue of Aristides the Just is in Boston’s Beacon Hill neighborhood is in Boston, Massachusetts. Aristides was an Athenian statesman. His nickname was The Just and he was called the best and most honorable man in Athens.
  • “Exchange Street”: Exchange Street is in Boston, Massachusetts.
  • “the sentinel Indian on the cupola”: The Province House, the royal governors’ residence in Boston, was crowned by Shem Drowne’s copper weathervane of an Indian archer (1716), his arrow turning with the wind; it is now in the collection of the Massachusetts Historical Society.
  • “a pack of little brown Cubans for the dead”: Brown Cubans may refer to Cuban cigars which come in a variety of colors from pale brown to black.
  • “his dies in faustus”: Dies in faustus may mean dies faustus which means lucky day.
  • “a long dim street of cigar store Indians”: The cigar store Indian or wooden Indian is an advertisement figure, in the likeness of a Native American, used to represent tobacconists. The figures are often three-dimensional wooden sculptures measuring from several feet tall up to life-sized. They are still occasionally used for their original advertising purpose, but are more often seen as decorations or advertising collectibles, with some pieces selling for hundreds of thousands of dollars.
  • “an Indian stockade”: During the forced removal of the Cherokee people, also known as the Trail of Tears, stockades were built to hold them captive before their westward journey to Indian Territory. These stockades were often overcrowded, lacked adequate sanitation and food, and were plagued by disease. A stockade camp at Rattlesnake Springs in Tennessee held many Cherokees awaiting relocation, and it was the site of the final Cherokee council before their departure. The Treaty of Greenville, which concluded a period of conflict between the United States and Native American tribes in the Ohio region, was signed at a large stockade in Greenville, Ohio. See Society, Class, and Race.
  • “Indian massacre!”: “Indian massacre” The phrase eventually became commonly used to also describe mass killings of American Indians. Killings described as “massacres” often had an element of indiscriminate targeting, barbarism, or genocidal intent. According to historian Jeffrey Ostler, “Any discussion of genocide must, of course, eventually consider the so-called Indian Wars, the term commonly used for U.S. Army campaigns to subjugate Indian nations of the American West beginning in the 1860s. In an older historiography, key events in this history were narrated as battles. It is now more common for scholars to refer to these events as massacres. This is especially so of a Colorado territorial militia’s slaughter of Cheyennes at Sand Creek (1864) and the army’s slaughter of Shoshones at Bear River (1863), Blackfeet on the Marias River (1870), and Lakotas at Wounded Knee (1890). Some scholars have begun referring to these events as “genocidal massacres,” defined as the annihilation of a portion of a larger group, sometimes to provide a lesson to the larger group.” In The Wild Frontier: Atrocities during the American-Indian War from Jamestown Colony to Wounded Knee, lawyer William M. Osborn compiled a list of alleged and actual atrocities in what would eventually become the continental United States, from first contact in 1511 until 1890. His parameters for inclusion included the intentional and indiscriminate murder, torture, or mutilation of civilians, the wounded, and prisoners. His list included 7,193 people who died from atrocities perpetrated by those of European descent, and 9,156 people who died from atrocities perpetrated by Native Americans. In An American Genocide, The United States and the California Catastrophe, 1846-1873, historian Benjamin Madley recorded the numbers of killings of California Indians between 1846 and 1873. He found evidence that during this period, at least 9,400 to 16,000 California Indians were killed by non-Indians. Most of these killings occurred in what he said were more than 370 massacres (defined by him as the “intentional killing of five or more disarmed combatants or largely unarmed noncombatants, including women, children, and prisoners, whether in the context of a battle or otherwise”). See Society, Class, and Race.
  • “the lovely Indian maiden Pocahontas”: Pocahontas also known as Matoaka and Rebecca Rolfe was a Native American woman belonging to the Powhatan people, notable for her association with the colonial settlement at Jamestown, Virginia. She was the daughter of Wahunsenacawh, the paramount chief of a network of tributary tribes in the Tsenacommacah (known in English as the Powhatan Confederacy), encompassing the Tidewater region of what is today the U.S. state of Virginia. Pocahontas was captured and held for ransom by English colonists during hostilities in 1613. During her captivity, she was encouraged to convert to Christianity and was baptized under the name Rebecca. She married the tobacco planter John Rolfe in April 1614 at the age of about 17 or 18, and she bore their son, Thomas Rolfe, in January 1615. In 1616, the Rolfes travelled to London, where Pocahontas was presented to English society as an example of the “civilized savage” in hopes of stimulating investment in Jamestown. On this trip, she may have met Squanto, a Patuxet man from New England. Pocahontas became a celebrity, was elegantly fêted, and attended a masque at Whitehall Palace. In 1617, the Rolfes intended to sail for Virginia, but Pocahontas died at Gravesend, Kent, England, of unknown causes, aged 20 or 21. She was buried in St George’s Church, Gravesend; her grave’s exact location is unknown because the church was rebuilt after being destroyed by a fire. Numerous places, landmarks, and products in the United States have been named after Pocahontas. Her story has been romanticized over the years, many aspects of which are fictional. Many of the stories told about her by the English explorer John Smith have been contested by her documented descendants. She is a subject of art, literature, and film. Many famous people have claimed to be among her descendants, including members of the First Families of Virginia, First Lady Edith Wilson, American actor Glenn Strange, and astronomer Percival Lowell.
  • “one hundred First Preferred shares of the Grand Union Pacific Railway”: Grand Union Pacific Railway may refer to the Union Pacific Railroad which is a freight-hauling railroad that is the second largest in the United States. Its tracks met the Central Pacific’s at Promontory Summit, Utah, where the golden spike was driven on 10 May 1869.
  • “a Civil War silver dollar”: “Civil War silver dollar” may refer to the Seated Liberty Dollar. The Civil War caused widespread hoarding of the coins due to their value. They were made of 90% silver. This led to a coin shortage in 1862. The government issued paper Demand Notes and later minted silver dollars which were stored in a vault for future use. The Seated Liberty Dollar was the design in use for U.S. silver dollars before and during the Civil War. A law in 1865 allowed the motto “In God We Trust” to be added to coins, and it was placed on the Seated Liberty dollar in 1866. The Seated Liberty dollar was the first coin struck at the Carson City Mint in Nevada, beginning in 1870, with thousands of these coins stored in Treasury vaults. See The Civil War.
  • “a plush-lined parlor car”: A railroad parlor car is a luxury train car designed for comfort and relaxation, offering amenities superior to standard coach cars, such as plush seating, individual tables, and lounge areas. Historically, these cars served a wealthy clientele, providing a comfortable, exclusive space that conveyed status, and they remain a feature on some modern luxury and heritage railroads for passengers seeking a premium travel experience.
  • “a veritable Midas with the Midas touch”: Midas was the most famous King in Greek mythology for his ability to turn everything he touched into gold. See Greek Mythology.
  • “En passant”: En passant may refer to a special pawn capture that can only occur immediately after a pawn makes a move of two squares from its starting square and provided that it could have been captured by an enemy pawn had it advanced only one square. The opponent captures the just-moved pawn “in passing” through the first square.
  • “he had been offered, at various times, various railroads”: American railroads began in the 1830s with lines like the Baltimore and Ohio. The Pacific Railway Act of 1862 led to the first transcontinental railroad, completed in 1869, and land grants built four more, opening the West and feeding the industry of the Northeast. Rail mileage peaked in 1916; the Interstate Commerce Act of 1887 brought the first federal regulation, and Wilson nationalized the railroads from 1917 to 1920. The automobile and the airplane brought decline. (Wikipedia)
    • Railroad stock: In the nineteenth century railroads were the leading American investment. Their need for capital filled the New York Stock Exchange, drew money from overseas, and gave rise to modern accounting and finance, but also to watered stock, bribery, and boom and bust, as in the panics of 1837, the 1870s, and the 1880s. (Wikipedia)
    • The Panic of 1901 was the first stock market crash on the New York Stock Exchange, caused in part by struggles between E. H. Harriman, Jacob Schiff, and J. P. Morgan/James J. Hill for the financial control of the Northern Pacific Railway. The stock cornering was orchestrated by James Stillman and William Rockefeller’s First National City Bank financed with Standard Oil money. After reaching a compromise, the moguls formed the Northern Securities Company. As a result of the panic, thousands of small investors were ruined. (Wikipedia)
    • Panics and crashes before 1964: 1819, 1837, 1857, 1866, 1873 (followed by the Long Depression, 1873-1896), 1882-1885, 1884, 1890, 1893, 1896, 1901, 1907, 1910-1911, 1914, the recession after the First World War and of 1920-1921, the Wall Street crash of 1929 and the Great Depression (1929-1939), and the recessions of 1937-1938, 1949, 1953, 1958, and 1960-1961. The United States has experienced some of the most globally famous and heavily documented systemic stock market crashes and corrections.
  • “the old Interurban”: The Interurban is a streetcar-like electric self propelled rail car that runs within or between cities.
  • “the old Hartford Electric”: Hartford Electric may refer to the now defunct electrical company that was in Hartford, Connecticut.
  • “the old Mohawk Owl Train”: The Mohawk Owl Train may refer to the New York Central steam locomotive that followed the Mohawk River.
  • “the Iroquois Flyer”: Iroquois Flyer may refer to the Canadian SS Iroquois steamboat ferry.
  • “the Grand Montezuma Railway”: The Grand Montezuma Railway may refer to the steam engine Montezuma or a railroad operated on part of the Rio Grande Southern Railroad by the Montezuma Lumber Company.
    • The tomb of Montezuma may refer to two Aztec Emperors in Mexico.
    • Montezuma’s treasure is a legendary treasure that can be found in the southwest United States and Mexico.
  • “the Andean Special”: The Andean Special may refer to an earlier train than the current Belmond Andean Explorer that runs between Cusco and Puno, Peru.
  • “the Great Siberian”: The Great Siberian may refer to the Trans-Siberian Railway that connects Western and Eastern Russia.
  • “the Oriental Express”: The Oriental Express was a long-distance passenger train service that ran across continental Europe and into western Asia.
  • “never riding in a sleeping car”: The concept of dedicated sleeping cars dates back to the 1830s, with George Pullman’s Pullman Palace Car Company becoming famous for their widespread use beginning in the late 1860s. These cars revolutionized first-class rail travel, offering a level of comfort and privacy previously unavailable.
  • “the Taj Mahal”: The Taj Mahal is an ivory-white marble mausoleum in Agra, India.
  • “the Polo Grounds”: The Polo Grounds was a series of three ballparks in Upper Manhattan, New York City, named for its origin as a polo field in 1876 and later serving as the home for several professional baseball and football teams, most notably the New York Giants and the Yankees, before being demolished in 1964 to make way for apartments. The final Polo Grounds stadium, built after a 1911 fire, featured unique, “bathtub” dimensions with very short foul lines and a deep center field, a design that was unusual for baseball but well-suited for football. Today, the Polo Grounds site is occupied by the Polo Grounds Towers apartment buildings. The unique, “bathtub” shaped field with short foul lines and deep center field became a famous, albeit quirky, part of baseball lore.
  • “Somebody had offered him a lodestar”: See Lodestar in the vocabulary.
  • “tried to sell him a sextant”: A sextant is a doubly reflecting navigation instrument that measures the angular distance between two visible objects.
  • “the Customs House”: The Customs House was traditionally a building housing the offices for government officials. Boston’s Custom House, with its tower added in 1915, was for decades the tallest building in the city.
  • “the Fishermen’s Wharf”: The Fishermen’s Wharf may refer to the famous Fisherman’s Wharf in San Francisco, California. Boston’s own fishing fleet landed at T Wharf and, from 1914, at the Boston Fish Pier.
  • “the Green Dragon Tavern”: The original Green Dragon Tavern in Boston was a central meeting place for American revolutionary leaders like Paul Revere and Samuel Adams, earning it the nickname the “Headquarters of the Revolution.” Located in the North End, it hosted secret gatherings of the Sons of Liberty, Boston Committee of Correspondence, and Boston Caucus, where they planned resistance against British rule, including the Boston Tea Party. The original tavern was destroyed in the 1800s, but the current Green Dragon, opened in the 1990s, continues the legacy with its historical ties and revolutionary-themed restaurant.
  • “several China clippers”: China clippers may refer to the first four-engine flying boats built for Pan American Airways. The name first belonged to the fast sailing clippers of the China tea trade, many built in Boston by Donald McKay.
  • “half of Brooklyn Bridge for half price”: may refer to George C. Parker (1860-1936) and the phrase “If you believe that I have a bridge in Brooklyn to sell you.” Mr. Parker, a native New Yorker, “became famous for selling New York City landmarks of all kinds ranging from Madison Square Garden to the Statue of Liberty. He also sold the Metropolitan Museum of Art and even Grant’s tomb as the general’s grandson! He would set up fake sales offices and forge documents to support his cons. One of his most popular places for spotting rubes or victims was Ellis Island where some of the immigrants came with money to invest in new enterprises. Out-time out-of-town tourists on their first visit to New York comprised another favorite target. His greatest con was selling the Brooklyn Bridge. Legend claimed that he sold it at least twice a week. He did sell it several times including at least once for $50,000! The new owner would discover he was the victim of a con when the New York police officers would stop the “new owners” from setting up toll booths in the middle of the bridge. The Brooklyn Bridge had been a toll bridge that pedestrians had to pay a penny to cross when it opened for business in 1883. Tens of thousands crossed the bridge every day on the way to work from Brooklyn to Manhattan. When the Brooklyn Bridge first opened, it cost a penny to cross by foot, 5 cents for a horse and rider and 10 cents for a horse and wagon. Farm animals were allowed at a price of 5 cents per cow and 2 cents per sheep or hog. Under pressure from civic groups and commuters, the pedestrian toll was repealed in 1891. The roadway tolls were then rescinded on July 19, 1911 with the support of New York Mayor William J. Gaynor, who declared, “I see no more reason for toll gates on the bridges than for toll gates on Fifth Avenue or Broadway.” On Columbus Day, 1892 a quarter of a million people walked across the bridge in celebration of the quadrennial. At one point, George Parker earned the title as “the greatest con man” but he kept on getting caught. Finally, in 1928 upon his third conviction for conning people, Brooklyn Judge Alonzo G. McLaughlin sentenced him to mandatory life imprisonment to Sing Sing Prison, where he died.”
    • Brooklyn Bridge is a bridge in New York City spanning the East River between Manhattan and Brooklyn.
    • Emily Warren Roebling was an engineer known for her contributions over a period of more than 10 years to the completion of the Brooklyn Bridge after her husband Washington Roebling developed caisson disease (a.k.a. decompression disease) and became bedridden. For the decade after Washington was confined to his sick bed, Roebling was dedicated to the completion of the Brooklyn Bridge. She took over much of the chief engineer duties, including day-to-day supervision and project management. Emily and her husband jointly planned the bridge’s continued construction. She dealt with politicians, competing engineers, and all those associated with work on the bridge, to the point where people believed she was behind the bridge’s design. In 1882, Washington’s title of chief engineer was in jeopardy because of his extended illness. To allow him to retain his position, Roebling lobbied for him in meetings with engineers and politicians to defend her husband’s work. To the Roeblings’ relief, the politicians responded well and permitted Washington to remain chief engineer of the Brooklyn Bridge. The Brooklyn Bridge was completed in 1883. In advance of the official opening, carrying a rooster as a sign of victory, Emily Roebling was the first to cross the bridge by carriage. At the opening ceremony, Roebling was honored in a speech by Abram Stevens Hewitt, who said that the bridge was “...an everlasting monument to the sacrificing devotion of a woman and of her capacity for that higher education from which she has been too long disbarred.”
  • “the leaning Chrysler Building”: Chrysler Building is an Art Deco skyscraper on the East Side of Manhattan.
  • “the Brooklyn Dodgers”: The Brooklyn Dodgers were a Major League Baseball team from 1884 to 1957.
  • “by the Big Leagues”: The Big Leagues are the two highest US baseball leagues.
  • “the old Boston Red Stockings”: The Boston Red Stockings are now known as the Atlanta Braves.
  • “the old Baltimore Orioles”: The Baltimore Orioles are an American professional baseball team based in Baltimore.
  • “the Robins and the Cincinnati Woodpeckers and the St. Louis Browns”: The Brooklyn team was called the Robins from 1914 to 1931, after its manager Wilbert Robinson, and was otherwise the Dodgers until it moved to Los Angeles in 1958. The Cincinnati Woodpeckers may refer to a minor league baseball team. St. Louis Browns were a Major League Baseball team that originated in Milwaukee, Wisconsin as the Milwaukee Brewers.
  • “had been able to effect numerous reconciliations”: Forcible and systemic separation of children from their parents has a long and painful history in the US, affecting Native Americans, enslaved Black people, and immigrants. Beyond these large-scale injustices, poverty, war, and the shortcomings of child welfare policies have also led to family separations. From 1819 until the 1970s, the US government and churches ran a system of over 500 boarding schools designed to culturally assimilate Native American children. The policy’s stated goal was to “Kill the Indian, Save the Man.” Children were forcibly taken from their families and communities and sent to distant schools. In 1891, the government began withholding rations and annuities from parents who refused to send their children. Upon arrival, children’s hair was cut, their traditional clothing was replaced with uniforms, and they were assigned new English names. They were forbidden from speaking their native languages and punished for observing cultural practices. In addition to the trauma of forced separation and cultural repression, students often endured physical, sexual, and emotional abuse. Many died from disease or injuries and never returned home. Separating enslaved Black families was a common and profitable practice from the 16th to the 19th centuries. It was also an intentional tool used by enslavers to control and punish. At auction, enslaved children were sold separately from their parents and siblings, sometimes at young ages. Enslavers regularly threatened to sell off family members to prevent enslaved people from escaping or rebelling. Historical evidence suggests that between one-third and two-thirds of Black children were separated from their families during slavery. After emancipation, many formerly enslaved people spent years searching for lost family members. Between 1854 and 1929, the Children’s Aid Society and other charities sent an estimated 200,000 children from Eastern cities on “orphan trains” to be placed with families in the Midwest. While framed as a humanitarian effort for orphans, most children on the trains were not parentless. The program primarily targeted the children of impoverished immigrant families, particularly Irish Catholics. Many of the children were not placed in loving homes but rather treated as a source of indentured labor. Mixed reviews and the rise of foster care as a preferred method for placing dependent children led to the end of the program. During World War II, Executive Order 9066 led to the forcible removal and incarceration of over 120,000 Japanese Americans in internment camps. The forced removal resulted in the separation of families and shattered communities. Although most children remained with their parents in the camps, some families were separated, and others were put under intense emotional strain. The trauma of incarceration and displacement created lasting intergenerational trauma. Even after the closure of orphanages, children continue to be separated from their families through the modern child welfare system. Social workers often conflate poverty with neglect, disproportionately removing children from low-income families, especially those of color. In 2022, a Human Rights Watch report highlighted how poverty, rather than genuine unfit parenting, is frequently the basis for family separation. Black children, in particular, are nearly twice as likely as white children to be investigated by child services and separated from their families. In recent decades, US border and immigration policies have led to the widespread separation of migrant families. Under the Trump administration, a “zero tolerance” policy criminally prosecuted all adults crossing the border without authorization. This led to thousands of children being taken from their parents, often with no system in place to track or reunite families. Even after a court order ended the official policy, separations continued due to inconsistent record-keeping and a failure to protect asylum seekers. In total, more than 5,500 children were separated from their families. Researchers have documented severe and lasting psychological harm to the children and parents affected by these forced separations.
  • “a process similar to parthenogenesis”: Parthenogenesis is a natural form of asexual reproduction in which growth and development of embryos occur without fertilization by sperm.
  • “had once ridden with Napoleon almost to the gates of Moscow”: Napoleon’s invasion of Russia in 1812 reached Moscow, only to end in a winter retreat in which most of the Grande Armée was lost. To have ridden with him is to have shared an epic, doomed undertaking.
    • This is called the French invasion of Russia under Napoleon and is one of the most studied wars with an exceptional number of troop deaths. See Napoleon and Wellington.
  • “cashiered from the Army or the Navy or both”: Cashiering is a ritual ceremony where the individual is dismissed for some form of misbehavior. Military veterans have historically been cashiered for misconduct related to gambling debts, though not typically for the debt itself. Instead, it is the dishonorable failure to pay, fraudulent acts to acquire gambling money, or other offenses undermining military discipline that lead to dismissal or cashiering.
  • “the greatest Lady Macbeth”: Lady MacBeth is a leading character in Shakespeare’s play, MacBeth. Lady Macbeth goads her husband into committing regicide, after which she becomes queen of Scotland. After Macbeth becomes a murderous tyrant, she is driven to madness by guilt over their crimes, and commits suicide offstage. See Suicide in History and Literature.
    • Lord Banquo is a character in Shakespeare’s play MacBeth. He is at first an ally of Macbeth and they meet the Three Witches together. After prophesying that Macbeth will become king, the witches tell Banquo that he will not be king himself, but that his descendants will be. Later, Macbeth in his lust for power sees Banquo as a threat and has him murdered by three hired assassins. See Shakespeare.
  • “a Wall Street broker who had not known he was a Wall Street broker”: The history of Wall Street brokers traces the evolution of securities trading from informal outdoor dealings to the high-tech, regulated global financial markets of today. The profession has shifted from being a specialized service for the wealthy to a digitized industry, leading traditional brokers to focus on financial advising rather than trade execution. In the late 1700s, merchants and speculators met on Wall Street to trade U.S. government bonds and shares of early banks. Business was initially conducted informally, often taking place under a buttonwood tree outside 68 Wall Street or in nearby coffeehouses. To formalize their business and edge out the auctioneers who had previously dominated securities trading, 24 brokers signed the Buttonwood Agreement in 1792. This established a fixed commission rate and required them to give preference to each other in negotiations. This agreement became the foundation of what would later be the New York Stock Exchange (NYSE). As the market grew, trading split between the formal NYSE and an informal “curb” market for riskier stocks. For much of the 19th century, brokers who traded stocks for small, new, or speculative companies operated in the streets of lower Manhattan. These “curbstone brokers” specialized in securities for emerging industries like railroads, mining, and oil. The Open Board of Stock Brokers, founded in 1864 by former curb brokers, competed with the NYSE before merging with it in 1869. In 1921, the curb market moved indoors and eventually became the American Stock Exchange (AMEX). The introduction of the stock ticker in 1867 brought real-time stock prices to brokerage offices, a vast improvement over pneumatic tubes and runners. The “Roaring Twenties” and the crash of 1929 saw an explosion in brokerage activity and a dramatic increase in public participation in the market. Leaders of firms like Merrill Lynch began encouraging middle-class Americans to invest in common stocks, fueling market growth. Brokers aggressively promoted speculative investments and margin trading (borrowing money to buy stocks) to boost their commissions. This pushed stock prices to unsustainable levels. The stock market crash of 1929, triggered by panic selling after prices began to fall, led to widespread broker bankruptcies and financial ruin for many clients. In the aftermath, government regulation was introduced to prevent such events in the future. After the crash, the industry faced greater oversight and eventually underwent a technological transformation. The Securities Exchange Act of 1934 created the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) to regulate the securities industry and protect investors. New York’s municipal slave market, established by a Common Council law on 30 November 1711, stood on Wall Street between Pearl and Water Streets and auctioned enslaved people of African ancestry until 1762; enslaved workers, including people of Native American ancestry, were also hired out there as day laborers (NYC Parks historical marker, 2015). Miss MacIntosh visits the Stock Exchange to “make some imaginary money” in Chapter 66; see the Chapter 66 resources.
  • “the Chase National Bank”: The Chase National Bank of New York was founded in 1877 by John Thompson and named for Salmon P. Chase, Lincoln’s Secretary of the Treasury; by 1930 it was the largest bank in the world. In 1955 it merged with the Bank of the Manhattan Company, which Aaron Burr had founded in 1799 under a charter to supply New York with clean water, to form the Chase Manhattan Bank.
  • “the City Morgue”: The City Morgue is a hospital or place where human corpses wait for identification or burial.
  • “My kingdom for a horse”: “A horse! a horse! my kingdom for a horse!” cries Richard at Bosworth (Shakespeare, Richard III 5.4). See Shakespeare.
  • “the king of Cracow”: may refer to Krakus, also known as Krak or Grakch, a legendary Polish prince and the presumed founder of Kraków. He is also credited with building Wawel Castle and slaying the Wawel Dragon. The first written mention of Krakus, under the name Grakch, dates back to 1190 in the Chronica seu originale regum et principum Poloniae.
  • “a carbuncle from a maharajah’s crown”: is an obsolete term for a deep red, cabochon-cut almandine garnet, named after its resemblance to a glowing coal or a fire. Though originally applied to various red gemstones, the name most commonly referred to almandine garnets cut in a smooth, rounded fashion rather than faceted. Historically, carbuncles were valued for their beauty and were believed to possess magical and healing properties, with mentions in ancient texts and prominent use in Victorian jewelry.
  • “the Tower of London and the ravens”: The ravens of the Tower of London are a group of at least six captive ravens (nine in 2021) resident at the Tower of London. Their presence is traditionally believed to protect the Crown and the Tower; a belief holds that “if the Tower of London ravens are lost or fly away, the Crown will fall and Britain with it.” Some historians, including the Tower’s official historian, believe the “Tower’s raven mythology is likely to be a Victorian flight of fantasy.” The earliest known reference to captive ravens at the Tower is an illustration from 1883.
  • “januis clausis”: means the doors have been closed, behind closed doors, in secret.
  • “crossing Rittenhouse Square”: Rittenhouse Square is in Philadelphia, Pennsylvania and one of the most popular outdoor parks and is the center of the eponymous Rittenhouse neighborhood. The square is one of the five original open-space parks planned by William Penn and his surveyor Thomas Holme during the late 17th century. Together with Fitler Square, the Rittenhouse neighborhood and the square comprise the Rittenhouse-Fitler Historic District. In the early 19th century, as the city grew steadily from the Delaware River to the Schuylkill River, Rittenhouse Square became a highly desirable address. James Harper, a merchant and brick manufacturer who had recently retired from the United States Congress, was the first person to build on the square, buying most of the north frontage, erecting a stately townhouse for himself at 1811 Walnut Street. Having thus set the patrician residential tone that would subsequently define the Square, he divided the rest of the land into generously proportioned building lots and sold them. Sold after the congressman’s death, the Harper house became the home of the exclusive Rittenhouse Club, which added the present facade. From 1876 to 1929, Rittenhouse Square was home to several wealthy families including Pennsylvania Railroad president Alexander Cassatt, real estate entrepreneur William Weightman III, department store founder John Wanamaker, Philadelphia planning commission director Edmund Bacon.
  • “leaving the Grand Central Station”: Grand Central Station or Grand Central Terminal is a commuter rail terminal in New York City. Grand Central Terminal’s history began with railroad mergers creating the need for a central hub, evolving from the Grand Central Depot in 1871 to the current structure that opened in 1913, designed by Warren and Wetmore. After facing demolition threats in the 1970s, Jacqueline Kennedy Onassis helped secure its landmark status, and a significant restoration project in the 1990s brought the terminal back to its former glory. (Wikipedia)
  • “outside the old opera house”: The Boston Opera House on Huntington Avenue opened in 1909 and was demolished in 1958.
  • “walking along Pinckney Street”: Pinckney Street is in Boston, Massachusetts. Pinckney Street is a historic residential street in Boston’s Beacon Hill neighborhood, known for its Federal-style architecture and its connection to a significant African American community that emerged in the area before the Civil War. One of the oldest homes on the street, the George Middleton House, was built in the late 1780s and is a testament to the street’s long history. The area is notable for its role as a center for free Black residents and, later, as a place where people like Louisa May Alcott lived and wrote. See American Writers.
  • “in the casbah”: The casbah is the walled citadel of many North African cities.
  • “The Canadian Mounties”: The Canadian Mounties are the federal and national police service of Canada.
  • “the Eskimo hunter”: Eskimo is a term used to refer to two closely related indigenous peoples: the Inuit and the Yupik of Siberia and Alaska.
  • “the doorman at the Ritz”: The Ritz hotels, now a symbol of luxury, originated from the vision of Swiss hotelier César Ritz in the late 19th century. He partnered with chef Auguste Escoffier to create the first Ritz hotel in Paris in 1898, followed by the Ritz in London. These hotels redefined luxury hospitality, emphasizing personalized service and elegant accommodations, including en-suite bathrooms and telephones in every room, which were revolutionary at the time. In 1911, Albert Keller acquired the rights to franchise the Ritz name in North America, leading to the first Ritz-Carlton in New York City. The Ritz-Carlton brand, born from this expansion, continued to build upon Ritz’s original vision of refined elegance and impeccable service, establishing hotels in various locations.
  • “the land of Catherine the Great”: Catherine the Great (1729-1796), born Sophie of Anhalt-Zerbst, ruled Russia from 1762 to 1796 after a coup against her husband, Peter III. She corresponded with Voltaire and other Enlightenment thinkers, reformed the law and the administration, founded schools, began the Hermitage collection, and took Crimea and much of Poland, making Russia a great European power. (Wikipedia)
  • “Grand Russian Imperial stocks and bonds”: Grand Russian Imperial stocks and bonds were issued by Russia before the revolution. In 1918 they became useless. They are collectors items now.
  • “the Wall Street Stock Exchange”: Wall Street Stock Exchange is the leading US money center for international financial activities.
  • “old soap coupons”: B.T. Babbitt, a soap manufacturer, initiated a promotion where customers could send in 25 wrappers from his Sweet Home Laundry Soap to receive a set of color lithographs. This encouraged customers to buy and collect more bars of soap, establishing a connection between purchasing a product and receiving a premium, which is a precursor to modern couponing. Coupons for various products, including food and personal care items, began to appear in newspapers and magazines. During the 1930s, the coupon saw a surge in popularity as people looked for ways to save money.
  • “some old Bolshevik”: Bolsheviks were a far-left, revolutionary Marxists faction founded by Vladimir Lenin.
  • “a blind flower girl at a bridge”: In Charlie Chaplin’s City Lights (1931), the Tramp spends his last coin on a flower from a blind flower girl, who takes him for a rich man.
  • “a mare clausum”: is a term used in international law to refer to a sea, ocean or other navigable body of water under the jurisdiction of a state that is closed or not accessible to other states. Mare clausum is an exception to mare liberum (Latin for “free sea”), meaning a sea that is open to navigation to ships of all nations. In the generally accepted principle of international waters, oceans, seas, and waters outside national jurisdiction are open to navigation by all and referred to as “high seas” or mare liberum. Portugal and Spain defended a Mare clausum policy during the Age of Discovery. This was soon challenged by other European nations.
  • “Pinkerton’s men”: The Pinkerton National Detective Agency was founded about 1850 by Allan Pinkerton in Chicago and became the largest private law enforcement firm in the world; its emblem, an open eye over “We Never Sleep,” gave us the private eye.
  • “though he had stolen only the jewel of time”: Foreshadowing of who Mr. Spitzer really is and the theft of “the great rajah’s jewel.” The jewel itself may refer to The Moonstone by Wilkie Collins in 1868. It is considered the first modern detective novel, and established many of the ground rules of the genre. A major theme of the novel is the intrusion of imperialism on everyday English life. Lynn Pykett argues that “the main narrative of The Moonstone concerns the disruption of the tranquility and order of genteel English life by a colonial legacy.” The events of the plot are set into motion by Colonel John Herncastle’s unlawful theft of the Moonstone in India, and, in leaving the diamond to Rachel Verinder in his will, he is perpetuating his crime. It is only when the diamond is returned to its rightful owners that the ‘curse’ can be lifted. Pykett also comments that the contradictory forces of feminine passion and silence provide the conflict of the novel, Sergeant “Cuff is defeated by the silence of women (Rachel and Rosanna), by feminine reticence (Lady Verinder), and the failure of individual women to conform to dominant stereotypes of femininity.”
  • “a Channel swimmer had reached the other coast”: Captain Matthew Webb first swam the English Channel in 1875. Gertrude Ederle was the first woman to swim it, in 1926, nearly two hours faster than any man before her.
  • “the interment of Peron Spitzer”: See Peron Spitzer.
  • “a famous sportsman had been laid away”: Young told Studs Terkel that she “had such fun with the gambling part of the book, especially the gambler’s funeral, because Mr. Spitzer provided a marvelous funeral for his brother.” Terkel was reminded of Jack Teagarden singing “Gambler’s Blues,” a version of “St. James Infirmary” (Marguerite Young, interview with Studs Terkel, WFMT radio, 1965). See Gambling and Playing Cards.
  • “his brother’s mocking bird psychology”: The mockingbird mimics the songs of other birds, so a “mocking bird psychology” is a self made of borrowed voices, an echo without an original, fitting for twin brothers who mirror each other.
    • The mockingbird’s history in the US involves its initial decline due to the caged bird trade in the 19th century, its subsequent expansion northward after the trade ceased, and its cultural symbolism as a fighter for its home, its use in literature, and its adoption as state bird in several Southern states. English colonists brought the tradition of caging songbirds to America, and the Northern Mockingbird’s skill at mimicry made it a highly prized pet, leading to heavy trapping and population decline in the 19th century. Despite its diminishing numbers, it became a prominent symbol of the American South, celebrated in music and literature. After the cessation of the caged bird trade, the Northern Mockingbird population recovered and expanded its range northwards. The Northern Mockingbird is the official state bird of Arkansas, Florida, Mississippi, Tennessee, and Texas. Texas, in 1927, officially adopted it as the state bird due to its “fighter for the protection of his home” nature. In Hopi and other Pueblo tribes, the mockingbird is credited with teaching people to speak and serves as a diplomat in the Native American culture. (Wikipedia)
  • “Pay to the bearer, with each box of Ivory soap flakes”: In 1840, the J.B. Williams Company in Glastonbury, Connecticut, manufactured soap under the name Ivorine. Williams decided to focus on its shaving soap and sold Ivorine to Procter & Gamble, which later developed Ivory. In 1879, James Norris Gamble, son of Procter & Gamble co-founder James Gamble and a trained chemist, developed an inexpensive white soap. The name Ivory was created by Harley Procter, the other founder’s son, who was inspired by the quote “[a]ll thy garments smell of myrrh and aloes and cassia out of the ivory palaces,” from Psalm 45 of the Bible. In September 1879, Procter & Gamble trademarked “Ivory” as the name of its new soap product. As Ivory is one of P&G’s oldest products it is sometimes called “Ivory Towers,” and its factory and research center in St. Bernard, Ohio, is named “Ivorydale.” Ivory’s first slogan, “It Floats!,” was introduced in 1891. The product’s other well-known slogan, “99+44⁄100% Pure,” which was in use by 1895, was based on the results of an analysis by an independent laboratory that Harley Procter hired to demonstrate that Ivory was purer than the castile soap available at the time. The original Ivory bar soap was whipped with air in its production and floated in water, although P&G discontinued this version of the soap in 2023, and the new version no longer floats. According to an apocryphal story, later discounted by the company, a worker accidentally left the mixing machine on too long, and the company chose to sell the “ruined” batch because the added air did not change the basic ingredients of the soap. When appreciative letters about the new, floating soap inundated the company, P&G ordered the extended mix time as a standard procedure. However, company records indicate that the design of Ivory did not come about by accident. In 2004, over 100 years later, the P&G company archivist Ed Rider found documentation that revealed that James N. Gamble, who was a chemist, had discovered how to make the soap float and noted the result in his writings.
    • “American soap flake king” may refer to Procter & Gamble (P&G), founded by William Procter and James Gamble. They were a pivotal force in the American soap industry and its transition to soap flakes. While British manufacturer Lever Brothers were the first to produce flakes commercially, P&G popularized the product in the U.S., particularly with its Ivory soap brand. The American Civil War provided a major boost to P&G’s fortunes when the company secured contracts to supply the Union Army with soap and candles. After the war, returning soldiers created nationwide demand for P&G products. In the 1910s, P&G created Ivory Flakes, a shredded form of their popular Ivory soap. Unlike the harsh laundry soap of the era, the mild, pure Ivory Flakes were marketed for washing delicate items like baby clothes, silks, and nylons. The product’s success cemented P&G’s dominance in the market.
  • “Gold Dust Scouring Twins”: were fictional, racially stereotypical black children who served as mascots for Fairbanks’ Gold Dust washing powder from the 1890s until 1960. Created by the N.K. Fairbanks Company, the twins, “Goldie” and “Dusty,” were depicted doing household chores and promoting the slogan “Let the Gold Dust Twins do your Work.” They were a highly successful, albeit controversial, marketing tool, appearing on packaging, in print, and eventually on a popular radio show, becoming as famous as other racially insensitive brands. See Society, Class, and Race.
  • “majolica pavements”: is a type of tin-glazed pottery characterized by its thick white background glaze, on which colorful images are painted before firing to create a durable, vibrant, and often glossy finish. Originating in the Middle East and becoming famous in Italy during the Renaissance, the term “majolica” can also refer to colorful, naturalistic 19th-century earthenware, which was produced in England. The technique involves applying a tin oxide glaze to low-fired earthenware, then painting decorative designs onto the glaze before a second firing, which fuses the colors into the surface.
  • “all four points were North upon this compass”: At the South Pole every direction is north. See Exploration and the Poles.
  • “Bye, bye, blackbird”:
    • It is an American song published in 1926, with music by Ray Henderson and lyrics by Mort Dixon. Gene Austin’s recording topped the charts, and Josephine Baker’s 1927 recording in Paris made it popular in Europe. During World War II the German propaganda band Charlie and His Orchestra set new words to it to demoralize Allied troops, and some segregationists later played it to harass civil rights marchers. It returned in the films The Eddie Cantor Story (1954) and Pete Kelly’s Blues (1955), and Miles Davis’s 1956 recording on ’Round About Midnight made it a jazz standard; Peggy Lee, Ringo Starr, and Paul McCartney recorded it too. (Wikipedia) See Music and Composers.
  • “some old doodle bug writing in the sand”: The doodlebug is the larva of the antlion, which wanders through loose sand leaving winding trails like scribbles before it digs its pit trap.
  • “unpopular with Red Caps”: A Redcap is a train station porter and helps passengers carry their luggage.
  • “his high silk opera hat”: An opera hat is a top hat variant that collapses with a spring system if a man went to the theater or the opera since it was usually five inches tall.
