Chapter 76

← Chapter 75 · Home · Chapter 77 →

Content note: The Esther Longtree chapters (72 to 81) deal with stillbirth and pregnancy loss, rape, infanticide, racist violence including lynching, and cruelty to children. This chapter deals with infant death and abortion; Esther says she once tried to kill herself, and tells of a girl made pregnant by the police in a jail.

Summary

Esther wonders whether her successful conceptions were her worst mistakes. She tells of the Chicago detective, who wears disguises and solves every mystery but his own, above all the “quiet, quiet mysteries” where no bodies are missed; he writes that he will track her to her grave if she does not produce his living children. He is still hunting the “bleeding rapist” whose handiwork he found in Esther, and now she says he “had never touched her.” Her stillborn children hover and applaud whenever she lies with a salesman, and a small brown hand closes her womb. She would rather face trial for mass infanticide than for one murder, says she once tried to kill herself, and confesses that in her mother’s womb she murdered her twin by kicking it out too early. Cupid has missed her, though her heart is broken by experience. Fired from teaching school on false charges, she knits and unravels a black hood for a child to be born white as snow, and she is tired of all the men and all the fathers.

Characters present

Esther Longtree · The Chicago Detective

Concepts present

Themes: Guilt, Innocence, and Justice · Isolation and Connection · Love · Memory and the Past · Motherhood, Pregnancy, and Birth · Society, Class, and Race · Women, Gender, and Marriage

Symbols: Birds · The Sea and Water · Twins and Doubles

Philosophy: Astrology, Alchemy, and Esoterica · Freud and Jung

Allusions: Ancient Egypt · Angels and Archangels · Astronomy · Fairy Tales and Folklore · Genesis · Greek Mythology · Homer’s Epics · Iowa, Indiana, and the Midwest · Music and Composers · Pregnancy, Abortion, and Midwifery · Shakespeare

Key passages

From the research

  • Early in the chapter, Esther contemplates her past life, realizing that her “successful conceptions” might have been her worst mistakes: her “unfulfilled abortions” and “many births.” This passage reveals her conflicted feelings about motherhood, conception, and the pain intertwined with creation and loss. She is puzzled by her “last triumphant pregnancy” and the “diffused radiance” she feels despite her troubles. This sets the tone for her psychological and emotional state throughout the chapter.
  • The Chicago detective is portrayed as a relentless figure, always uncovering “murders, murders everywhere,” yet unable to solve his own mysteries. He pursues crimes both “quiet” and “loud.” He represents external pressure on Esther, threatening exposure for her alleged crimes concerning his children.
  • The Chicago detective’s fascination with “quiet mysteries” or murders “where no bodies were missed” parallels Esther’s own experience with stillborn children and miscarriages. The notion that murder and loss can be silent, unrecorded, and unseen reflects Esther’s hidden suffering and the societal invisibility of her pain.
  • A poignant passage details how Esther perceives her numerous stillborn children as “robed, bloodless,” hovering between life and death, sometimes applauding her “act of intercourse.”
  • Esther’s thoughts on being accused, tried, and perhaps imprisoned reveal her resignation and complex acceptance of her circumstances. She contemplates the “mass infanticide” she might be charged with and paradoxically finds a form of comfort in the vastness of her “cosmic” evidence: her body, nature, and memories.
  • Towards the end, Esther wonders why Cupid, the god of love, has “missed her,” even though her heart is broken.
  • The closing passages describe Esther’s daily life bound by routine yet wild and free in spirit, marked by visions of birth and death, presences and evidence everywhere she goes. Despite her hardships and the looming threat of trial, she holds onto a flicker of hope and purpose, knitting and unraveling a black hood symbolizing night and birth.

Questions and observations

Reading closely

  • “There were always two ways of cruelty.” What are the two?
  • “She was always knitting and unravelling the black hood for one who would be born as white as melting snow.” Why black, and why unravel it?
  • “Her children were snowflakes drifting in eternity, were leaves, were tears.” What do the three images share?

Characters

  • Now Esther says the detective “had never touched her” and “was no more than a mistaken father.” How does this square with Chapter 74?
  • The detective hunts “the bleeding rapist” and finds “his handiwork, Esther Longtree.” Whose handiwork?
  • “She had tried to kill herself.” Why does Esther say it so quietly, between other thoughts?

Connections

  • Esther “had murdered her twin by kicking it out early.” How does this echo the Spitzer twins?
  • Like Penelope at her loom, Esther is “knitting and unravelling.” What is she waiting for?
  • “Who had not killed cock robin among the fallen autumn leaves?” How has Esther’s answer changed since Chapter 72?

Reflection

  • “There were some little boys who were murderers, too, and killed their mothers, but it was only because their mothers had already killed them.” Is that fair to the mothers?
  • “Her heart had been broken by experience.” Can experience break a heart as love does?
  • “She was guilty of some kind of crime.” Why does Esther feel guilty even where she is innocent?

Research: Characters

Esther Longtree

  • A complex woman, described as pregnant and burdened with past conceptions that were either miscarriages or stillbirths.
  • She is reflective, brooding on her life’s mistakes and her uncertain relations with the detective and the many men (salesmen) she encounters.
  • Esther is maternal yet haunted, caught between hope and despair, and struggles with her identity and the accusations she faces.

The Chicago Detective

  • An enigmatic figure who has solved countless murders, both loud and quiet, often using disguises and undercover tactics.
  • He is relentless and invasive, unable to avoid uncovering dark secrets wherever he goes.
  • His interest in Esther is personal, as he believes she has his children.
  • He is still hunting “the bleeding rapist” and says he found “his handiwork, Esther Longtree with her clothes torn and her mouth foaming”; yet in Chapter 74 Esther says the detective raped her, and here that he “had never touched her.”
  • His presence represents judgment, law, and the relentless pursuit of truth.

Research: Themes

Motherhood and Infanticide

See: Motherhood, Pregnancy, and Birth

  • Esther’s experience with pregnancy is fraught with loss, as she has many stillborn or miscarried children, which the detective calls “quiet mysteries.”
  • The concept of murder is extended metaphorically to include unborn or unconceived children, highlighting complex feelings of guilt and responsibility.

Memory and Guilt

See: Memory and the Past · Guilt, Innocence, and Justice

  • Esther is haunted by memories of past events, including her twin’s death in utero, her own repeated losses, and her interactions with men.
  • These memories induce a sense of guilt, self-accusation, and uncertainty about truth and justice.

Justice and Investigation

See: Guilt, Innocence, and Justice

  • The detective’s role symbolizes the pursuit of truth and justice, but also the intrusion and exposure of private pain.
  • His tireless search uncovers “quiet murders” that society ignores, reflecting on the nature of crime and detection beyond the obvious.

Isolation and Alienation

See: Isolation and Connection

  • Esther’s internal world is lonely and bleak. She feels persecuted by both the detective and her memories.
  • Her physical environment (a messy bedroom, empty cradle) mirrors her emotional and psychological state.

The Feminine and the Unseen

See: Women, Gender, and Marriage

  • The narrative explores the unseen aspects of womanhood (miscarriage, stillbirth, and the emotional landscape tied to pregnancy and motherhood) often ignored or silenced in society.

Research: Symbols and Imagery

  • Pregnancy and Birth: Symbolizes creation, life, and hope, but in Esther’s case, it also represents loss, failure, and mystery. Her “last triumphant pregnancy” is tinged with both anticipation and dread.
  • Stillborn Children / Silent Murders: Represent the quiet tragedies that go unnoticed. They haunt Esther and serve as metaphors for lost potential and hidden guilt.
  • The Detective’s Disguises: His changing appearance symbolizes the fluidity of identity, the hidden truths beneath surfaces, and the persistent nature of truth-seeking.
  • Nature (Leaves, Autumn, Flowers, Moths): Recurring natural imagery symbolizes cycles of life and death, decay and renewal, and Esther’s connection to a cosmic order beyond human understanding.
  • The Empty Cradle and Wedding Rings: The empty cradle signifies lost children and unfulfilled motherhood, while wedding rings on Esther’s nipples but not her fingers suggest a distorted or incomplete domestic/marital identity.

Research: Resources

  • “Poor Esther Longtree, who might be killed by little Johnny-jump-up”: Esther Longtree emerges in this chapter as a deeply tragic and complex figure, embodying themes of fertility, loss, sorrow, and marginalization. Her character is portrayed with a rich, symbolic density that reveals much about her internal struggles and her relationship to the world around her. Esther is described as physically large, often pregnant or swollen, with features like a long nose and crossed eyes, evoking a somewhat grotesque yet poignant image. She is burdened by repeated pregnancies, many of which end in stillbirths or miscarriages. This physical condition mirrors her emotional state: she is exhausted, confused, and isolated, caught in a cycle of hope and despair. Her body and mind are both “clouded” and “indistinct,” reflecting her fragmented sense of self and history. Esther’s experience of pregnancy and motherhood is fraught with sorrow and complexity. She carries numerous “stillborn children,” described almost as ghostly presences hovering around her, watching her with innocent smiles and applause, yet also causing her pain and distraction during intercourse. These spectral children symbolize her lost potential for motherhood and the deep trauma of repeated loss. She does not reject these children but claims them as hers, showing a profound maternal attachment despite the pain they bring. However, this attachment is intertwined with guilt and confusion, as she contemplates the nature of her past conceptions and births. Esther is entangled with a Chicago detective who is aggressively pursuing proof of his paternity of her children. This detective symbolizes the harsh, intrusive forces of society, law, and judgment. Esther fears his investigations, seeing them as threats that could expose her to legal and social punishment. Yet at the same time, she contemplates the possibility of the trial with a strange blend of hope and resignation, almost welcoming the exposure as a form of acknowledgment of her suffering and existence. This ambivalence highlights her isolation and the precariousness of her position as a woman burdened by reproductive tragedy and societal scrutiny. The chapter frequently returns to motifs of birth and death, conception and miscarriage, seen both literally and metaphorically in Esther’s story. She is described as knitting and unravelling a black hood, symbolizing the night and mystery surrounding her existence. Her pregnancies are “clouded,” and her children are often invisible or spectral, linking her personal tragedy to broader cosmic or existential mysteries. Esther’s life is likened to an “empty coffin on the water,” merging images of life and death, presence and absence. This symbolism situates her story within larger themes of loss, fate, and the unknowable forces shaping human experience. Despite her suffering, Esther exhibits a kind of wildness and defiance. She runs, she laughs, she knits, she endures. She is “wilder than people thought,” living a life bounded by routine but also marked by moments of freedom and rebellion. Her laughter in the face of the detective’s threats and the looming trial shows a resilience and complexity that defy simple victimhood. Esther’s narrative is one of survival amid despair, of a woman caught between social condemnation and her own intricate inner world. Esther’s experience is deeply intertwined with natural imagery: autumn leaves, winter bees, snowflakes, mists, rivers, and stars. These elements emphasize the cosmic scale of her suffering and the universality of her predicament. Her children are likened to “snowflakes drifting in eternity” and “robed” children and “old cherubim,” linking personal loss to the eternal cycles of life and death. This connection to nature and the cosmos reinforces the mystical and tragic dimensions of her character. Esther Longtree is a richly drawn figure whose story encapsulates themes of loss, fertility, maternal anguish, societal judgment, and existential mystery. She is at once vulnerable and resilient, tragic and wild, caught in a liminal space between life and death, hope and despair. The chapter paints her not merely as a victim but as a complex woman grappling with profound personal and cosmic questions, embodying the novel’s broader exploration of human suffering and endurance. See Esther Longtree.
    • Esther Longtree symbolizes a deeply tragic and complex history of fertility, loss, and maternal suffering that can be read as a metaphor for the burdens borne by many women across American history, particularly those marginalized or caught in cycles of neglect and violence. Her character embodies the pain of countless stillbirths, miscarriages, and unfulfilled pregnancies, reflecting a history of loss not only of children but of potential, hope, and future generations. Esther’s experience of repeated pregnancies resulting in stillborn or unconceived children, her reflections on the silent, “quiet mysteries” of death without visible bodies, and her haunted sense of guilt and accusation evoke a history of women’s reproductive struggles often ignored or misunderstood in society. She is portrayed as carrying the weight of many unborn or lost children “snowflakes drifting in eternity,” “leaves,” “tears” symbolizing not only personal loss but perhaps collective losses related to the harsh realities of life for women who have been abandoned, mistreated, or rendered invisible by legal and social systems. Esther’s sense of persecution, threatened by a detective’s pursuit to uncover her “children,” parallels the historical scrutiny and moral judgment women have faced regarding their reproductive lives, particularly those who have suffered trauma or have been entangled in social and legal conflicts about motherhood and fertility. Her uncertainty, her tangled memories, and the spectral presence of her many lost children evoke a history marked by silence, stigmatization, and the often invisible consequences of violence, both physical and societal, against women. Esther Longtree symbolizes the historical narrative of reproductive suffering and the silenced tragedies of many American women, embodying themes of loss, survival, and the complex interplay between personal history and broader social forces in the United States. Her story reflects a history of pain and resilience, maternal sacrifice, and the haunting presence of what is lost or denied in American society.
  • “her pupa, her Little Tom Thumb”: Little Tom Thumb may refer to Tom Thumb, a character in English folklore. The History of Tom Thumb was published in 1621 and was the first fairy tale printed in English. Tom Thumb may have been a real person born around 1519, as there is a grave purporting to be his. The grave measures just 16 inches in length. See Fairy Tales and Folklore.
  • “to bring life into this sad, mistaken world”: This is a deeply personal, philosophical, and biological question. Despite widespread anxiety about environmental issues, political instability, and suffering, many women continue to choose motherhood. Many believe that creating new life is an act of defiance against despair, bringing love, joy, and potential for positive change into the world. They may believe they can raise children who will contribute to fixing the world’s mistakes, acting as agents of change. Humans are biologically programmed to reproduce, with hormonal and physiological influences often reinforcing the desire to have children. This desire is frequently described as a powerful, instinctual urge. Having children is often seen as a way to find purpose, share love, and create a deeper, lasting connection with a partner. Women are recognized for their immense resilience and capacity to act as “backbones of communities,” even in difficult circumstances, by nurturing the next generation. Some argue that while the world contains suffering, it also holds immense beauty and joy, and that experiencing life, including its challenges, is worthwhile. Despite the trend toward smaller families, significant social, religious, and familial pressures still exist, urging women to conform to the traditional expectation of having children. For many, the desire to experience motherhood and the unique bond with a child outweighs the perceived risks of the world. See Women, Gender, and Marriage.
  • “thin as a comma sleeping in the womb of time”: “There are many events in the womb of time which will be delivered” (Iago, Othello, 1.3). See Shakespeare.
  • “He had solved the quiet, quiet mysteries”: Young talked about a section of the book that expanded on Mr. Spitzer’s story where whatever he wanted, even if he did not want it, came to him. It was advised that she remove it from the novel and she did. It seems the story of the Chicago detective has that same pattern. See Joachim Spitzer.
    • The Chicago detective may refer to a French detective from the 1880s, Robert Ledru, who was famous for solving crimes until a murder he was helping to investigate led to proof that he was, in fact, the murderer. Through an experiment conducted by the police it was determined that he suffered from stress and while sleepwalking, if he had access to a weapon, would shoot and kill a person.
  • “There were always two ways of cruelty”: The idea that “Nothing could ever seem to happen by itself in one cruel, conclusive way” implies that events, especially traumatic or violent ones, are not simple or linear. Psychologically, this aligns with systemic views of behavior, where one action is often a response to another, and causes are multifaceted. The recognition of “two ways of cruelty” acknowledges that hurt and harm are often reciprocated or that one form of cruelty begets another, reflecting the complexity of human interactions and the difficulty of assigning singular blame.
  • “there were some little boys who were murderers, too”: The belief that “some little boys who were murderers, too, and killed their mothers, but it was only because their mothers had already killed them, in quick ways and slow ways” suggests a psychological interpretation of violence as a symptom or consequence of earlier trauma, specifically maternal harm or neglect. This resonates with psychoanalytic and developmental psychology concepts about how early childhood experiences, especially those involving caregivers, profoundly shape emotional regulation, attachment, and later behavior. Children who experience harm, whether physical, emotional, or symbolic (such as neglect or abandonment), may internalize and later reenact these patterns, sometimes violently. The phrase “mothers had already killed them, in quick ways and slow ways” can be interpreted both literally and metaphorically. Psychologically, “killing” here may represent not only physical harm but also emotional or psychological damage such as: rejection, neglect, or emotional unavailability. This “kills” parts of the child’s spirit, identity, or sense of safety. This damage can manifest later in destructive behaviors, including violence towards others, even those closest to the child. The passage underscores the difficulty in attributing simple blame in situations of cruelty and violence. It suggests a cycle where victims may become perpetrators, and cruelty can be both cause and effect. This aligns with psychological understandings of the “cycle of abuse,” where patterns of trauma perpetuate across generations or within family dynamics, making it challenging to identify clear origins or solutions. The sentence carries an existential weight, reflecting on the ambiguity and complexity of human suffering. It challenges the reader to see cruelty not as a straightforward moral failing but as part of a tangled web of pain and reaction. Psychologically, this can be related to the concept of moral injury or the struggle to reconcile acts of harm within relationships that are also sources of love and care. See Freud and Jung.
    • Historical context: Mothers are often blamed for their children’s lives due to historical gender roles that place the burden of child-rearing primarily on them, a phenomenon called mother blaming. This can be seen in societal beliefs, professional fields like medicine and social work, and media, where mothers are assumed to be the cause of their children’s problems, from developmental issues like autism to behavioral problems. This practice overlooks external factors and other contributors to a child’s life and well-being, leading to guilt, shame, and a failure to address underlying issues appropriately. Blaming mothers for their children’s problems, despite gender inequality and lack of support, is a long-standing issue rooted in misogyny and societal expectations. Unequal gender roles assign mothers the bulk of childcare and emotional labor, creating a standard of perfection that is impossible to meet and leaves them vulnerable to blame.
  • “the hangman’s noose or the electric chair”: The electric chair was first used at Auburn Prison, New York, on William Kemmler in 1890; the execution took two jolts and eight minutes. See Guilt, Innocence, and Justice.
  • “not like Cleopatra”: Cleopatra may refer to Cleopatra VII Philopator who was Queen of the Ptolemaic Kingdom of Egypt and its last active ruler. Her death in 30 B.C., by the bite of an asp smuggled in a basket of figs as Plutarch tells it, is history’s most famous unsolved case of murder or suicide. See Ancient Egypt.
  • “a sunken ship of leaden sails and stone hull and stone bells”: See Debussy’s Sunken Cathedral and the drowned city of Ys, whose bells ring under the sea, in the Chapter 59 resources. See The Sea and Water and Music and Composers.
  • “the death of the moth”: Virginia Woolf’s essay “The Death of the Moth” (1942) watches a day moth die at a window: “O yes, he seemed to say, death is stronger than I am.”
  • “Some new crime would break, loud and noisy”: “Some new crime would break, loud and noisy, and the quiet mysteries would remain quiet forever if that was so.” The U.S. news cycle evolved from a slow, partisan, and highly local system in the early 18th century to a fast-paced, nationalized, and professionalized industry dominated by newspaper chains, radio, and the emergence of network television by the early 1960s. Early Colonial to Early 19th Century: Early journalism focused heavily on international news, which was often weeks or months old by the time it arrived by ship. Newspapers in the 18th and early 19th centuries were often subsidized by political parties or factions, acting as propaganda tools rather than objective information sources. Initially, newspapers were expensive and tailored to political and mercantile elites. Mid-19th Century: The launch of The Sun in 1833 revolutionized news by making it affordable (one cent) and focused on human-interest stories, crime, and gossip, targeting a mass audience. The invention of the telegraph and high-speed steam-powered printing presses in the 1840s enabled news to travel instantly, facilitating the growth of national news stories. The mid-19th century saw the rise of the Associated Press (AP), which allowed for the standardization of national news reporting. Late 19th to Early 20th Century: Publishers like Joseph Pulitzer and William Randolph Hearst engaged in sensationalized, scandalous, and often inaccurate reporting to boost circulation. In response to yellow journalism, the early 20th century saw a shift toward, and demand for, objective, “informed” journalism, exemplified by the New York Times under Adolph Ochs. By 1900, massive newspaper chains, such as the Hearst organization, dominated the landscape. 1920s to 1950s: In the 1920s and 1930s, radio introduced the first “instant” news updates, with major expansion during World War II. The Radio Act of 1927 and the Communications Act of 1934 (creating the FCC) brought standards and licensing to the airwaves. By the 1950s, daily television news began to displace radio and newsreels as the dominant medium, with the “Big Three” networks (NBC, CBS, ABC) dominating the airwaves. The news cycle was defined by the daily morning or evening newspaper and the nightly 15-to-30 minute evening news broadcast (e.g., CBS Evening News with Walter Cronkite). Audiences relied on a few trusted figures to interpret major events, such as the Cold War, the Civil Rights movement, and the Kennedy assassination. The 1960 Kennedy-Nixon debate, televised to 70 million viewers, highlighted the shift toward image-driven, nationalized media, setting the stage for the intense, image-focused coverage of the mid-1960s.
  • “who hovered at the ivory gates between life and death”: See the gates of horn and ivory in the Chapter 75 resources. See Homer’s Epics.
  • “little policemen with funeral wreaths, little windowpeepers with blinded eyes”: The mud baby with its funeral wreath, “the policeman’s son,” and the little windowpeeper are in the Chapter 75 resources.
  • “Even when the ejaculation of the male organ had fallen upon the empty air”: “And Onan knew that the seed should not be his; and it came to pass, when he went in unto his brother’s wife, that he spilled it on the ground” (Genesis 38:9, KJV). The LORD slew him for it. See Genesis.
  • “to other little salesmen”: The salesmen characters in the novel may symbolically reflect various aspects of capitalism in the US through their behaviors, roles, and the social contexts they inhabit.
    • The salesmen appear repeatedly throughout the novel in different guises, selling a wide range of goods, from everyday objects like brooms, bird cages, and toys, to more abstract commodities like stocks and bonds. Their omnipresence symbolizes the reach of capitalist commerce into every facet of life, even into the most personal and intimate spaces of the characters. They reflect the diversity and saturation of market interactions in American life.
    • The salesmen often embody the pressures, anxieties, and instabilities caused by the capitalist system. Many salesmen in the novel are depicted as transient, struggling, or lost figures, highlighting the precariousness and alienation experienced by those caught in the capitalist economy. They symbolize the vulnerability of individuals within a capitalist society.
    • The salesmen also represent the commodification of human relations and the alienation inherent in capitalism. They sell not only material goods but also intangible things like securities and futures, connecting to themes of speculation and the illusion of wealth. This commodification extends to human relationships, as seen in the metaphor of the salesmen interacting with stillborn children or lost souls, symbolizing how capitalism can reduce human value to market transactions and speculative interests.
    • The novel hints at exploitation and inequality through the salesmen’s interactions and the socio-economic backdrop. The salesmen, as agents of this system, are both participants in and victims of such exploitation.
    • The salesmen’s activities also symbolize the illusory and unstable nature of capitalist wealth. The novel repeatedly emphasizes the ephemeral quality of money and possessions: stocks that may be worthless, jewels that may be fake, and transient fortunes. The salesmen’s persistent presence amidst loss, deception, and uncertainty reflects capitalism’s inherent volatility and the elusiveness of material success.
    • The salesmen embody human desires fueled by capitalism: desire for wealth, security, social status, and belonging. However, these desires are often unfulfilled or lead to suffering, as seen in the characters’ personal tragedies and the broader social critiques embedded in the narrative. The salesmen’s relentless selling and the characters’ interactions with them suggest the endless cycle of desire and consumption characteristic of capitalist societies.
    • The salesmen in Miss MacIntosh, My Darling symbolize capitalism in the US by representing its ubiquity, its impact on individuals, the commodification of human relations, capitalist exploitation and inequality, the illusory nature of wealth, and the insatiable human desires it engenders. They serve as embodiments of the economic forces shaping the characters’ lives and the social environment of the novel, reflecting both the promise and the perils of capitalist society.
  • “no rubber corporation or Wall Street corporation”: Esther means she never used a condom. Rubber condoms followed Goodyear’s vulcanization of rubber (1844); thinner latex condoms came in the 1920s. Under the Comstock Act of 1873 mailing contraceptives or information about them was a federal crime. See Pregnancy, Abortion, and Midwifery and Women, Gender, and Marriage.
    • Major firms like U.S. Rubber (1892), Goodyear (1898), and Firestone (1900) emerged to supply tires for the booming automotive industry. The industry has been defined by intense monopolization, the 20th-century shift to synthetic rubber, and, historically, brutal exploitation during the Amazonian boom.
    • In King Leopold II’s Congo Free State (1885 to 1908), villagers who failed to meet rubber quotas were flogged, held hostage, and killed, and soldiers cut off hands as proof of the bullets they had used. See Society, Class, and Race.
    • Wall Street originated from a 17th-century Dutch stockade in New Amsterdam, evolving into the center of American finance after 24 brokers signed the Buttonwood Agreement in 1792 to formalize securities trading. It became the nation’s financial hub by the late 1800s, growing through industrial expansion, the creation of the NYSE in 1863, and the establishment of the Federal Reserve Bank of New York in 1914.
  • “old men like old cherubim with bald, flat heads and pot bellies and winged penises”: “The flying penis” refers to the ancient Roman and medieval symbol of the winged phallus, known as fascinus, which was used as a protective charm against evil, infertility, and the evil eye. See Astrology, Alchemy, and Esoterica and Angels and Archangels.
  • “wearing wedding rings upon her nipples but none upon her fingers”: Esther’s wedding rings on her nipples reflect the tension between societal expectations of womanhood and Esther’s actual lived experience: a poignant and poetic symbol of her complex identity and suffering.
  • “He would be happier in his ignorance than in his wisdom”: “Where ignorance is bliss, / ’Tis folly to be wise” (Thomas Gray, “Ode on a Distant Prospect of Eton College,” 1742).
  • “the perineal tears, the ossified bones”: Perineal tears are common to some extent during childbirth. Tears can also occur inside the vagina or other parts of the vulva, including the labia.
    • Most simply, the “enlarged birth ring” is the birth canal stretched by many births. It may also refer to a Bandl’s ring, a rare and dangerous complication of obstructed labor that appears as a constriction at the junction between the upper and lower segments of the uterus. In contrast, a normal birth involves the cervix (a ring of muscle at the base of the uterus) dilating to allow a baby to pass through. While the cervix normally enlarges and opens during a vaginal birth, a Bandl’s ring is an abnormal, pathologic ring of thickened muscle that obstructs the birth process.
    • The labia minora are the inner folds of skin of the female external genitalia, located between the labia majora and surrounding the clitoris and vaginal and urethral openings. They vary significantly in size, shape, and color, and their functions include a sexual one, as they engorge with blood during sexual arousal. The appearance of the labia minora can change throughout a person’s life due to factors like genetics, hormones, aging, and weight fluctuations.
    • The labia majora are the two outer, fleshy folds of skin that form the “lips” of the vulva, protecting the other external genitalia. They are located on the mons pubis and extend down to the perineum, and contain sweat and sebaceous glands. These folds enclose and protect the vaginal and urethral openings and can change in appearance due to factors like aging, childbirth, and hormonal shifts.
  • “the lost music of the lost echo of the lost chord”: “Seated one day at the organ, / I was weary and ill at ease, / And my fingers wandered idly / Over the noisy keys” (Adelaide Anne Procter, “A Lost Chord,” 1858). Arthur Sullivan set it in 1877 as “The Lost Chord,” one of the best-selling songs of the century. See Music and Composers.
  • “She had heard of a girl who was made pregnant by the police in a jail”: Indiana opened the first separate prison for women in the United States in 1873, after the Quaker reformers Rhoda Coffin and Sarah J. Smith exposed the sexual abuse of women prisoners by male guards at the state prison. See Iowa, Indiana, and the Midwest and Women, Gender, and Marriage.
  • “she had put her head into a silvery hornets’ nest”: The idiom to stir up a hornet’s nest means to make trouble or start a commotion.
  • “fools rush in where angels fear to tread”: The saying, fools rush in where angels fear to tread, is from An Essay on Criticism, one of the first major poems written by the English writer Alexander Pope. “For fools rush in where angels fear to tread” (1711).
  • “She was always knitting and unravelling the black hood”: Penelope, waiting twenty years for Odysseus, wove a shroud for his father by day and unravelled it by night to put off her suitors (Odyssey, Book 2). See Homer’s Epics and Women, Gender, and Marriage.
  • “the membrane like a shimmering bridal veil hanging from barren trees”: See the caul in the Chapter 74 resources.
  • “by Cupid, the blind god of love”: In classical mythology, Cupid is the god of desire, erotic love, attraction and affection. “And therefore is wing’d Cupid painted blind” (A Midsummer Night’s Dream, 1.1). See Greek Mythology, Love, and Shakespeare.
  • “drifting like a cloud with a silver lining”: “Was I deceiv’d, or did a sable cloud / Turn forth her silver lining on the night?” (Milton, Comus, 1634).
  • “She had tried to kill herself”: Esther says it once, in passing, and goes straight on to Cock Robin. See Esther Longtree.
  • “who had not killed cock robin”: Who Killed Cock Robin is an English nursery rhyme. The earliest record of the rhyme is in Tommy Thumb’s Pretty Song Book. A number of theories have been advanced to explain the meaning of the rhyme: a mythological event, such as the death of the god Balder from Norse mythology, or the ritual sacrifice of a king figure; a parody of the death of King William II, who was killed by an arrow while hunting, and who was known as William Rufus, which means red; the fall of Robert Walpole’s government in 1742, since Robin is a diminutive form of Robert and the first printing is close to the time of the events mentioned. Some folklore readings make the rhyme a seasonal myth, with the red-breasted robin as Lugh, the Irish god of light, skill, and kingship, killed at the turn of the year by winter. In Celtic studies Lugh is often paired with Brân the Blessed, the Welsh giant-king whose name means “Raven” and who was “crowned king over this Island” (Britannica). See the Chapter 72 resources. See Fairy Tales and Folklore and Birds.
  • “What twin accused his twin whom he had murdered”: This seems to refer to Joachim and Peron Spitzer and here Esther is saying that Peron killed Joachim and took his identity. See Joachim Spitzer, Peron Spitzer, and Twins and Doubles.
    • One set of twins in mythology where one is divine and the other mortal are Castor and Pollux, known as the Dioscuri. The pair are an example of heteropaternal superfecundation. The Dioscuri were regarded as helpers of humankind and held to be patrons of travelers and of sailors in particular, who invoked them to seek favorable winds. Their role as horsemen and boxers also led to them being regarded as the patrons of athletes and athletic contests. They characteristically intervened at the moment of crisis, aiding those who honored or trusted them. See superfecundation in the Chapter 73 resources.
    • The dioscuri had two twin sisters: Helen of Troy and Clytemnestra.
  • “had murdered her twin by kicking it out early”: Physicians have long known that one twin may die early in pregnancy and be shed or reabsorbed. With ultrasound in the 1970s this “vanishing twin” proved far more common than anyone had guessed. See Twins and Doubles and Pregnancy, Abortion, and Midwifery.
  • “swimming around Cape Horn”: Cape Horn is the southernmost headland of southern Chile and marks where the Atlantic and Pacific Oceans meet.
    • See Homer Capehorn.
  • “or maybe he had got to Capricorn”: Capricorn is the tenth astrological sign in the zodiac originating from the constellation of Capricornus, the horned goat. The Tropic of Capricorn, the southern line of the sun’s farthest reach, takes its name from the sign. See Astrology, Alchemy, and Esoterica and Astronomy.
  • “the school trustees who would now be the jury had not fired her on false charges”: Esther once taught school. Rural school boards hired and fired teachers at will, and a woman teacher could be dismissed for marrying, for paint and powder, or for gossip. See Women, Gender, and Marriage.

chapter-57:
Chapter 57

← Chapter 56 · Home · Chapter 58 →

Content note: This chapter mentions the suicide of Mr. Spitzer’s twin brother, Peron.

Summary

A polite, threatening bill keeps arriving from Peron’s tailor for the black funeral suit Mr. Spitzer is sure he paid for in cash, without receipts. In a recurring dream he journeys to pay it twice and finds no tailor, only empty lofts, and wakes from seeing himself in Peron’s brown derby. Awake, he searches Boston for the tailor’s shop, turning left for right because dreams go by opposites. At the Public Library he combs city directories and old newspapers and finds Peron’s death notice and his own name in the society columns, but no tailor and no street. Beside him a man argues with a dead man about the soul, and a young man who cannot be older than twenty swears he took a bullet at Appomattox, where the South won. Outside, at twilight, Mr. Spitzer watches the clouds become a skull, a hand, a bird, and a rose, and wishes for a rose named for both brothers, red and white on a single bush.

Characters present

Joachim Spitzer · Peron Spitzer · The Great Tailor

Concepts present

Themes: Death and Mortality · Dreams and Imagination · Identity and the Self · Illusion and Reality · Memory and the Past · Society, Class, and Race · Time

Symbols: Birds · Butterflies and Moths · Cards, Games, and Chance · Clocks and Watches · Clothing, Hats, and Skirts · Clouds and Storms · Horses and Carriages · Roses and Flowers · Twins and Doubles · Weddings and Funerals

Allusions: American Writers · Ancient Egypt · Gambling and Playing Cards · Greek Mythology · Judaism · Music and Composers · Romantic Poets · Shakespeare · The Bible · The Civil War

Key passages

From the research

  • The recurring motif of the great tailor, possibly mad or non-existent, who supposedly tailored the black funeral suit and sends an incessant bill to Mr. Spitzer, symbolizes Mr. Spitzer’s unresolved debts, guilt, and identity crisis. Despite having paid the funeral expenses, Mr. Spitzer is haunted by the tailor’s persistent demand, which can be interpreted as a metaphor for the burdens of the past that Mr. Spitzer cannot escape. The fact that the suit is associated with his dead brother (Peron) who wore it at the funeral adds layers of grief and identity confusion, as Mr. Spitzer wonders if he himself might be the dead man or the other way around. This passage reveals the theme of blurred boundaries between life and death, self and other, reality and dream.
  • Mr. Spitzer repeatedly dreams of searching for the tailor’s shop, traveling through confusing, shifting streets and cities that resemble a storm-tossed sea or a surreal landscape. This endless, futile search reflects his psychological torment and the elusive nature of truth and memory. The tailor’s shop is described as empty or nonexistent, reinforcing the idea that what Mr. Spitzer pursues may be an illusion or a part of himself lost in time and space. The dream imagery (revolving doors, escalators, pigeons, and contradictory directions) emphasizes disorientation and the fractured nature of his existence.
  • Mr. Spitzer consciously allows for distortions, reversals, and opposites in his search, knowing that dreams operate by opposites: dark is fair, life is death, man is woman. This recognition of duality and the unreliability of sensory impressions underscores the philosophical meditation on reality’s instability and the fluidity between contradictory states. This theme is crucial for understanding Mr. Spitzer’s predicament; he is caught between worlds, identities, and states of being.
  • The scenes in the library reading room, where Mr. Spitzer consults city directories and old newspapers, highlighting his attempt to anchor himself in reality through facts and records, but his efforts are futile, no tailor or street exists. The presence of eccentric characters debating immortality and reconstructing alternate histories (such as the Confederate soldier who claims the South won the Civil War) adds to the surreal atmosphere and reflects Mr. Spitzer’s own existential doubts and confusion about time, history, and death.
  • Mr. Spitzer’s inner desire for absolute certainty and immortality contrasts with his awareness of doubt and confusion. His longing to interrupt the argument about the soul’s existence but refraining out of fear of rejection reveals his loneliness and the human desire for definitive answers about life after death, which remain elusive. This passage deepens the existential questioning central to the chapter.
  • Toward the end of the chapter, Mr. Spitzer’s observation of the twilight sky filled with colorful clouds and shapes (skulls, hands, birds) culminates in the image of a rose that changes from red to white. This rose symbolizes constancy, memory, and perhaps reconciliation of the living and the dead (the two brothers). Mr. Spitzer’s wish for a rose named after him and his brother encapsulates his yearning for remembrance, identity, and peace amid the instability of his existence.
  • Throughout the chapter, Mr. Spitzer struggles to distinguish his dreams from his waking life. He encounters impossible events (dropping a handkerchief in Pisa despite never having been there) and perceives his reflection as a shadow or a pigeon’s murmur. This ambiguity highlights the chapter’s central concern with the fluid boundary between life and death, memory and forgetting, reality and illusion.

Questions and observations

Reading closely

  • “The great tailor was dead, or he was obviously mad.” Who is the great tailor?
  • Mr. Spitzer goes by the rule “that dreams go by opposites.” How does the rule lead him astray?
  • “There had been greater mysteries then than now, Mr. Spitzer believed.” Why does he miss the world before the telegraph?

Characters

  • Mr. Spitzer fears “that he had clothed the wrong man.” Which brother did he bury?
  • A young man insists that “The South had won over the North.” Why does Mr. Spitzer, “a Boston Abolitionist,” only nod?
  • Mr. Spitzer learned that “most people do not want the argument to be settled.” Why does he want certainty when others prefer doubt?

Connections

  • The old librarian “always looked through the wrong pair” of spectacles. Where else in the novel do people see through the wrong lens?
  • Mr. Spitzer dreams of “a red rose and a white rose growing on a single bush.” How does this rose answer the red and white roses of Chapter 56?
  • “So many things had happened to Mr. Spitzer which could not possibly have happened to him.” How does the novel treat memories that cannot be true?

Reflection

  • Mr. Spitzer hopes that “if he waited long enough, there might be no problem.” Do debts to the dead ever expire?
  • He “had yearned for absolute certainty and had wished to be immortal.” Are the two wishes the same?
  • “For how should he be remembered?” What makes a fitting memorial?

Research: Characters

Mr. Spitzer

  • Mr. Spitzer is grappling with grief, guilt, and confusion after his brother’s death. He is introspective, haunted by recurrent dreams, and obsessed with settling an ambiguous tailor’s bill related to his brother’s funeral suit. He represents the struggle between reality and illusion, life and death.

Peron

  • Peron, Mr. Spitzer’s deceased brother, is described as a gambler and a man of dignity in death. Peron’s identity is intertwined with mystery and symbolic imagery (black suit, red rose, bright red necktie), representing a life ended but still profoundly present in Mr. Spitzer’s mind.

The Great Tailor

  • The Great Tailor may have made the black funeral suit for Peron. He symbolizes unresolved debts, both financial and psychological, and the elusive nature of truth and memory.

Strangers in the Library

  • Various strangers and characters Mr. Spitzer encounters, including a Confederate soldier who claims contradictory historical facts, a librarian, and others who contribute to the dreamlike, surreal atmosphere.

Research: Themes

Identity and the Double

See: Identity and the Self · Twins and Doubles

  • Mr. Spitzer’s identity is fluid and fragmented. He sometimes confuses himself with his brother, dreams of being the tailor, or living a double existence. His struggle to reconcile these selves reflects the complexity of human identity, especially after trauma or death.

Debt and the Past

See: Memory and the Past

  • The persistent tailor’s bill symbolizes the unpayable debts of the past and the burden of memory. Mr. Spitzer’s attempts to pay or deny the debt represent his inability to move beyond grief and the past.

Dream and Waking

See: Dreams and Imagination · Illusion and Reality

  • The narrative blurs the line between waking life and dream, with Mr. Spitzer experiencing continuous, overlapping realities. The chapter questions what is real and what is illusion, emphasizing the instability of perception.

The Soul and Immortality

See: Death and Mortality

  • Discussions on the soul, the afterlife, and the persistence of the dead in memory permeate the text. Mr. Spitzer’s desire for certainty about immortality contrasts with others’ doubts, highlighting existential uncertainty.

Time and History

See: Time

  • The chapter reflects on the passage of time, both personal and historical, with references to changing cities, lost histories, and the impossibility of retracing steps exactly. Time is portrayed as fluid and unstable.

Research: Symbols and Imagery

The Black Funeral Suit and Tailor’s Bill

See: Clothing, Hats, and Skirts · Weddings and Funerals

  • Symbolizes unresolved debts, both literal and metaphorical. The suit represents Peron’s dignity and the past that Mr. Spitzer attempts to honor and settle.

The Penny with Heads on Both Sides

See: Cards, Games, and Chance

  • A talisman of luck and uncertainty, symbolizing Mr. Spitzer’s gamble with fate and his desire for control in an uncontrollable world.

The Rose (Red and White)

See: Roses and Flowers

  • Represents memory, fidelity, and duality. Mr. Spitzer imagines a rose named after himself and his brother, red and white together, symbolizing their intertwined fates and memories. The symbolism of red and white flowers together generally represents unity, harmony, and the balance of opposing concepts like passion and purity. This meaning is most common in Western traditions and varies significantly depending on the cultural context and the specific flowers chosen. The Tudor rose joined the red rose of Lancaster and the white rose of York after the Wars of the Roses, two houses in one flower, as Mr. Spitzer joins himself and his brother.

Dream Imagery

  • Recurring images of clouds, city streets, pigeons, skull-shaped clouds, giant hands, and birds evoke the ephemeral and mutable nature of existence.

Timepieces (Two Wrist Watches)

See: Clocks and Watches · Twins and Doubles

  • Represent duality and the conflicting measures of time, cosmic and earthly, highlighting Mr. Spitzer’s fractured perception of time.

Research: Resources

  • “a psychic armor no one now investigates”: The psychoanalyst Wilhelm Reich called the rigid habits of posture and manner that people build against feeling their “character armor” (Character Analysis, 1933).
  • “an insistently polite, threatening note from his brother’s tailor”: See The Great Tailor, Chapter 55 resources, and Clothing, Hats, and Skirts.
  • “for the table was always set for the wanderer”: Compare the old custom of setting an extra place at the table for the unexpected guest or wanderer, kept in Poland on Christmas Eve, and the cup poured for the prophet Elijah at the Passover seder. See Judaism.
  • “alert interest and baited breath”: Young’s spelling puns on the usual phrase, from Shylock: “With bated breath and whispering humbleness” (William Shakespeare, The Merchant of Venice, 1.3). Bated means held back, abated. See Shakespeare.
  • “those old Floradora girls”: Floradora girls may refer to the musical Florodora which ran in London and Broadway in the early 1900s. It was famous for its chorus line of Florodora girls. Bella donna means beautiful woman in Italian. The belladonna plant is poisonous but drops were used by women to dilate their pupils which made them look attractive. The plant’s name, beautiful lady, comes from that use.
  • “horse-hair wigs”: Horsehair has a long history of use in wigs, particularly in 17th-century Europe, with King Louis XIII and Charles II popularizing them as a status symbol and to conceal hair loss or skin conditions. The wigs were initially made of black horse and goat hair but were problematic due to their coarse texture and tendency to attract lice, leading to the development of white horsehair wigs in the late 18th century as a more manageable alternative. Horse-hair wigs will play a role in Miss MacIntosh’s story in the following chapters as we learn more about her background.
  • “The debt, even if there had been a debt which he had forgotten to pay, would be outlawed by time”: A debt no one sues on within a set number of years is barred by the statute of limitations; in Massachusetts the limit for a contract is six years.
  • “to bet with a penny which had heads upon both sides”: The two-headed coin is the oldest of gamblers’ tricks: whoever calls heads cannot lose. See Gambling and Playing Cards.
  • “the same Grand Central Station”: New York’s Grand Central Depot opened in 1871, became Grand Central Station in 1900, and was rebuilt as Grand Central Terminal in 1913.
  • “and he only dreamed that he was dreaming”: “All that we see or seem / Is but a dream within a dream” (Edgar Allan Poe, “A Dream Within a Dream,” 1849). See American Writers.
  • “like his being caught in a revolving door”: Theophilus Van Kannel of Philadelphia patented the revolving door in 1888.
  • “passing himself on an escalator going up as he was going down”: Jesse Reno built a moving inclined stairway at Coney Island in 1896, and the Otis Elevator Company showed its first “escalator” at the Paris Exposition of 1900.
  • “the music of the hurdy-gurdy”: The true hurdy-gurdy is a stringed instrument sounded by a cranked wheel; in America the name went to the barrel organs of street musicians. See Music and Composers.
  • “or perhaps he was the measuring worm”: The measuring worm, or inchworm, is the caterpillar of the geometer moths, whose name means earth-measurers; it moves by looping, as if measuring the ground. See Butterflies and Moths.
  • “Ah, how many gargoyles under the eaves!”: A gargoyle is a carved waterspout, from the French gargouille, throat; the water runs out through its mouth.
  • “well knowing that dreams go by opposites”: The folk saying that dreams go by contraries is old; Freud gave it a theory in The Interpretation of Dreams (1900), where a dream may turn a thing into its opposite. See On dream logic and the logic of the opposite and Dreams and Imagination.
  • “the three golden apples hanging in the air”: The three golden balls of the pawnbroker, which Young calls golden apples, come from the arms of the Medici and the Lombard bankers and are also said to stand for the three bags of gold Saint Nicholas gave as dowries to three poor sisters.
    • In Greek myth the golden apples grew in the garden of the Hesperides, and Eris’s golden apple, inscribed “to the fairest,” began the Trojan War. See Greek Mythology.
  • “Jews’ harps”: Jews’ harps is a small musical instrument, also known as a jaw harp or mouth harp, that produces sound by the vibration of a flexible metal or bamboo tongue attached to a frame. The player places the frame against their teeth or lips and plucks the tongue, while changing the shape of their mouth to create different pitches and melodies. Despite the name, the instrument has no connection to Jewish people or Judaism and most likely originated in Asia thousands of years ago.
  • “corsets”: Are structured garments designed to alter the body’s silhouette, evolved from Minoan-era forms to the rigid 16th-century stays of French courts and later the Victorian era’s extreme hourglass shape. Used by both men and women for centuries, corsets became associated primarily with women, shaping the waist and supporting the bust. Materials progressed from boning to whalebone, steel, and later synthetic options, while the garment’s role shifted from an undergarment to a symbol of social constraints and, in modern times, a symbol of empowerment or rebellion.
  • “bird-cages”: Date to antiquity, first appearing in Mesopotamia, Egypt, and China for symbolic, religious, and wealth display purposes, with the term “bird cage” emerging in late 15th century Europe. During the 16th and 17th centuries, exotic birds became status symbols, leading to ornate, expensive cages in Europe, a trend that peaked in the Victorian era with elaborate designs. The use of birds in cages has also served practical functions, such as navigation by sailors and safety checks in mines, though their primary role shifted from food source to domestic pets and decorative objects.
  • “knowing, also, that dark is fair, that fair is dark”: “Fair is foul, and foul is fair” (William Shakespeare, Macbeth, 1.1). See Shakespeare.
  • “the great blimp like a silver whale”: Goodyear flew its first passenger blimp, the Pilgrim, in 1925, and its blimps became a fixture over American cities.
  • “Chinese kites with their long ribbons streaming in the seventh heaven”: In Jewish and Islamic tradition there are seven heavens, and the seventh is the highest, nearest God.
  • “bridges of blackbirds”: In the Chinese legend of the Cowherd and the Weaver Girl, magpies form a bridge across the Milky Way once a year, on the seventh day of the seventh month, so the lovers can meet.
  • “the ferris wheels reflected on a horizontal sea of clouds”: George Ferris built the first Ferris wheel, 264 feet high, for the World’s Columbian Exposition in Chicago in 1893, as America’s answer to the Eiffel Tower.
  • “how many funeral gondolas there were”: Venetian gondolas are black by a law of 1562 against display, and funeral gondolas carried the dead across the lagoon to the cemetery island of San Michele.
  • “how many black swans following the white midnight”: Europeans long used the black swan as a byword for the impossible, after the Roman poet Juvenal’s “rara avis in terris nigroque simillima cygno,” a bird as rare on earth as a black swan (Satires 6.165), until the Dutch explorer Willem de Vlamingh found black swans in western Australia in 1697. See Birds.
  • “mare clausum”: The sea that is under the jurisdiction of a particular country The phrase comes from John Selden’s Mare Clausum (1635), written against Hugo Grotius’s Mare Liberum (1609), the free sea.
  • “He had dropped his handkerchief in Pisa”: Galileo’s pupil Vincenzo Viviani told the story that Galileo dropped balls of different weights from the Leaning Tower of Pisa to show that they fall together.
  • “He had gone, after several days, to the Public Library reading room”: The history of American public libraries began with early private collections and subscription libraries like Benjamin Franklin’s in 1731. The first entirely tax-supported public library was established in Peterborough, New Hampshire, in 1833, followed by the large Boston Public Library in 1854. The late 19th century marked a boom with Andrew Carnegie’s philanthropy, which funded the construction of over 1,600 libraries, and the establishment of the American Library Association (ALA) in 1876 to advocate for their services. Public libraries have since evolved to offer a wide array of services beyond book lending, including educational programs and internet access, becoming a cornerstone of American civic life. Public libraries in the US are open to all and are known as one of the last open places where the people can come in and stay as long as they do not cause a distraction. This has led to vulnerable populations taking shelter there. See On the Boston Public Library as sanctuary.
  • “consulted the city directory”: Boston’s city directories, published from 1789, listed residents and businesses by name and street year by year.
  • “bustles, corsets, shrouds and stays and canvas sails and masts”: Young puns on rigging: shrouds are the ropes that brace a mast from the sides and stays the ropes that brace it fore and aft, so the shrouds and stays of the dead and of the corset sit beside the sails and masts of the ships.
  • “landaus, barouches, phaetons like great sea shells”: A landau is a four-wheel luxury carriage with a roof that can be let down. See Horses and Carriages.
    • Barouches are large, luxurious, four-wheeled carriages.
    • Phaetons were a sporty open carriage. See Phaethon in the Chapter 56 resources.
  • “the one-horse shay”: One-horse shay or one-hoss shay is a light, covered, two-wheeled carriage. It was made famous by American writer Oliver Wendell Holmes Sr. He memorialized the shay in his satirical poem “The Deacon’s Masterpiece or The Wonderful One-Hoss Shay.” In the poem, a fictional deacon crafts the titular wonderful one-hoss shay in such a logical way that it could not break down. The shay is constructed from the very best of materials so that each part is as strong as every other part. In Holmes’ humorous, yet “logical” twist, the shay endures for a hundred years and then “went to pieces all at once,— / All at once, and nothing first,— / Just as bubbles do when they burst” (Oliver Wendell Holmes, “The Deacon’s Masterpiece,” in The Autocrat of the Breakfast-Table, 1858). See American Writers.
  • “rumors of ships which had gone down far from any human eye and might rise silently, ghost ships”: The brigantine Mary Celeste was found in 1872 sailing the Atlantic with no one aboard, her cargo intact and her crew never seen again; the Flying Dutchman is the legend’s ghost ship, doomed to sail forever.
  • “a string of spectacles attached to her bosom, one above the other, one for every kind of distance”: Benjamin Franklin, tired of changing spectacles, had two pairs cut in half and joined, the first bifocals, which he described in a letter of 1785. See Benjamin Franklin and Poor Richard’s Almanack.
  • “it might have been Bedlam”: Is a word referring to a scene of uproar, chaos, and confusion, or an asylum for the mentally ill, derived from the name of London’s Bethlem Royal Hospital, which was a famous psychiatric institution. The hospital’s historical association with treating the mentally ill led its name to become a common term for a madhouse and, by extension, any place of extreme disorder and madness.
  • “the reading room was an Automat”: Is a restaurant where food is purchased from a wall of individual, coin-operated dispensers and retrieved through small, glass-windowed compartments. The concept originated in Europe with the Quisisana restaurant in Berlin and was brought to America by Joseph Horn and Frank Hardart. Automats were popular in cities like New York and Philadelphia in the early to mid-20th century, symbolizing efficiency and speed. They became less popular with the rise of fast food and changing dining preferences but are now remembered with nostalgia. See On the Automat.
  • “whether it is an elixir, a substance, a speck, a dot, a little man”: Philosophers and doctors tried them all: Descartes placed the soul’s seat in the pineal gland, and in 1907 the Massachusetts doctor Duncan MacDougall weighed six dying patients and claimed the soul weighs twenty-one grams.
  • “the musical stars sang”: “When the morning stars sang together, and all the sons of God shouted for joy” (Job 38:7, KJV). See The Bible.
  • “reconstructing the Civil War—the Battle of Appomattox”: The Battle of Appomattox Court House, fought in Appomattox County, Virginia, on the morning of April 9, 1865, was one of the last battles of the American Civil War. It was the final engagement of Confederate General in Chief, Robert E. Lee, and his Army of Northern Virginia before they surrendered to the Union Army of the Potomac under the Commanding General of the United States Army, Ulysses S. Grant. (Wikipedia) Lee did not surrender in a tent but in the parlor of Wilmer McLean’s house at Appomattox Court House. See On the Confederate soldier and alternative history and The Civil War.
  • “the flags of the Confederacy”: Refers to several flags used by the Confederate States of America during the Civil War (1861-65), with the most recognizable being the Battle Flag of the Army of Northern Virginia. It was created for battlefield use to distinguish it from the Union flag and later became a symbol for the Lost Cause narrative of Southern heritage, though its use also became tied to white supremacy and racist groups. The flag’s controversial meaning, representing both Southern heritage and a symbol of racism and slavery, has led to ongoing public debates and the removal of official displays. See The Civil War.
  • “the flags of the Grand Union Army”: Young’s Grand Union Army is the Union army of the Civil War, whose veterans formed the Grand Army of the Republic in 1866. The Grand Union Flag, by contrast, was the first flag of the Continental Army, flown from 1775 until the Stars and Stripes was adopted in 1777. See The Civil War.
  • “would always be a Boston Abolitionist”: Boston abolitionists, active from the 1830s to the Civil War, included prominent figures like William Lloyd Garrison, Wendell Phillips, and Lewis Hayden, who formed societies like the New England Anti-Slavery Society and published the anti-slavery newspaper The Liberator. These activists, both Black and white, organized and rallied against slavery, often facing violent opposition from anti-abolitionist mobs in the city. They also supported the Underground Railroad, assisted fugitive slaves, and pushed for social justice within their communities, eventually contributing to the eventual end of slavery. See Society, Class, and Race.
  • “opposed even to the slavery of the moth to the star”: “The desire of the moth for the star, / Of the night for the morrow” (Percy Bysshe Shelley, “One word is too often profaned,” 1821). See Romantic Poets.
  • “these were clouds without water”: “clouds they are without water, carried about of winds” (Jude 1:12, KJV). See The Bible and Clouds and Storms.
  • “Delicate as mountain laurel”: Is a flowering plant native to the eastern United States. Its range stretches from southern Maine to northern Florida, and west to Indiana and Louisiana. Mountain laurel is the state flower of Connecticut and Pennsylvania.
  • “a Sphinx had settled on his coat sleeve”: This sphinx is a sphinx moth, or hawk moth, named for the caterpillar’s habit of rearing up its head like the Great Sphinx. See The Life of the Sphinx Moth in the Chapter 55 resources. See Butterflies and Moths and Ancient Egypt.
  • “He had seen a cloud like a great skull”: Compare Hamlet teasing Polonius: “Do you see yonder cloud that’s almost in shape of a camel?” (William Shakespeare, Hamlet, 3.2). See Shakespeare and Clouds and Storms.
  • “there should be a red rose and a white rose growing on a single bush”: Young’s hybrid exists. The York and Lancaster rose, a damask rose grown since the sixteenth century, bears pink and white flowers on the same bush and is named for the red rose of Lancaster and the white rose of York, whose Wars of the Roses ended when Henry VII joined the two in the Tudor rose. See On the red rose and white rose and Roses and Flowers.
