Chapter 30

← Chapter 29 · Home · Chapter 31 →

Content note: Vera’s mother, Catherine Cartwheel, is addicted to opium.

Summary

Catherine and Mr. Spitzer discuss unreal persons as if they were real, especially Eustace, an invisible visitor who takes many shapes. Then Cousin Hannah Freemount-Snowden enters through memory. She was a Boston suffragette, archer, duelist, climber, and traveler who crossed deserts disguised as an Arab king, and she seemed to foresee assassinations. She is now dead and buried. She never cared for the Spitzer twins. Hannah once rode in Arab disguise against Spanish soldiers to defend a caravan of Riffs, and she was dedicated to “the overthrow of the dream and of the dreamer.” Catherine longs for her company and imagines sending her to search the Alps for Jock, Catherine’s husband, who vanished while mountain climbing.

Characters present

Catherine Cartwheel · Eustace · Joachim Spitzer · Cousin Hannah · Jock Cartwheel · Vera Cartwheel

Concepts present

Themes: Death and Mortality · Faith, God, and the Supernatural · Freedom and Escape · Grief, Loss, and Mourning · Illusion and Reality · Memory and the Past · Nature, the Sea, and the Cosmos · Society, Class, and Race · Women, Gender, and Marriage

Symbols: Butterflies and Moths · Clothing, Hats, and Skirts · Moon and Stars · Mountains · Snow, Ice, and Winter · The Sea and Water

Philosophy: Augustine and Christian Theology · Marguerite Young on Her Craft

Allusions: Ancient Egypt · Angels and Archangels · Astronomy · Dante · Exploration and the Poles · Fairy Tales and Folklore · Gambling and Playing Cards · Greek Mythology · Napoleon and Wellington · Shakespeare · The Bible · The Book of Job · Women’s Suffrage

Key passages

From the research

  • The chapter opens with Catherine and Mr. Spitzer endlessly discussing unreal persons, treating the dead as if they were alive and present. Catherine converses with an invisible figure named Eustace, who takes on many forms symbolizing the fluidity and multiplicity of identity, and the suspension of natural laws in her mental state. This passage highlights her detachment from the tangible world and immersion into a dreamlike or hallucinatory realm.
  • Catherine imagines inviting ancient relatives and historical personages to play card games. Cousin Hannah, a figure of vast duplicity and adventurous spirit, is considered an ideal partner. This fantasy reflects Catherine’s desire for companionship and the bridging of past and present through imagination, as well as her yearning for connection beyond loneliness.
  • A substantial portion of the chapter is devoted to a vivid, expansive biography of Cousin Hannah. She is depicted as a fearless, resourceful, and mercurial adventurer who defied conventional limits of gender and geography. Her life spans numerous cultures and eras symbolically: an archer, dueler, mountain climber, yachtsman, and traveler through remote deserts and cities. Her knowledge of global politics, secret whispers, and historical assassinations underscores a mystical or prescient quality. Importantly, Cousin Hannah embodies a rebellious spirit dedicated to overthrowing dreams and illusions, including those of Catherine.
  • Despite facing numerous mortal dangers, Cousin Hannah survives through her prescience and determination. The narrative contrasts her survival with the fate of others lost to the elements or violence. Her life is portrayed as a continuous journey through perilous lands, reinforcing themes of resilience and the confrontation of fate.
  • Catherine romanticizes and mourns her lost husband, Jock Cartwheel, imploring Cousin Hannah to search for him in the Alps and other remote places. This longing underscores Catherine’s refusal to accept finality and death, blending memory, fantasy, and hope. The imagery of snow-capped peaks, dark valleys, and silent towers evokes a haunting atmosphere of loss and the persistence of love beyond death.
  • Catherine imagines herself sailing two ships simultaneously, one for the living and one for the dead, symbolizing a liminal existence between life and death, consciousness and unconsciousness. The dialogue with the star watchman, reflecting on stars, tides, and the nature of shore and shorelessness, deepens the metaphysical dimension of the chapter, contemplating the mysteries of existence, transition, and the cosmos.

Questions and observations

Reading closely

  • “The real persons were apparently the only persons who were unreal to my mother.” Who is real in Catherine’s room?
  • Cousin Hannah was “dedicated to the overthrow of the dream and of the dreamer.” Why does Catherine admire her?
  • “Because of the loss of a skirt… her entire life had been perhaps an act of sorrow and redemption.” What might that loss have been?

Characters

  • Hannah “had never cared for the Spitzer boys” and called both brothers “profligates.” Is she right?
  • Hannah rides against the Spanish soldiers, “forgetting that she was a stockholder of American firearms.” What does that detail say about her?
  • Catherine asks of one “not likely to respond,” “Have you seen my husband?” What does she refuse to accept?

Connections

  • Catherine tried to telephone Cousin Hannah on a number “disconnected long ago” (Chapter 24). How does this chapter answer that call?
  • The blackamoor messenger returns from Chapter 24, now “in a fringe-topped surrey.” What do these servants of her dreams have in common?
  • Catherine sails “one ship for the living, one for the dead.” Where else has a ship carried the dead in this novel?

Reflection

  • Can a life of adventure be its own kind of escape?
  • What does it mean to be “an emancipated extension” of someone else?
  • “Watchman, where is the shore?” To whom do we put that question?

Research: Characters

Catherine Cartwheel (Vera’s mother)

  • Portrayed as a figure lost between reality and fantasy.
  • Engages in conversations with unreal or invisible persons such as “Eustace” who changes forms and identities.
  • She seems to live in a dreamlike state, haunted by memories and by the presence of the dead.
  • Experiences sudden emotional outbursts and imagines elaborate scenarios involving historical and mythical figures.
  • Wishes for company and distraction, often imagining card games with ghostly or imaginary partners.
  • Struggles with loss, particularly the absence of her husband, and clings to hope that he might still be found or returned.

Eustace

  • An invisible, multi-faceted figure in Catherine’s mind.
  • Takes on various guises: a mocking bird, an old woman, an old bearded man, a Venetian valet, a murdered gentleman, a blind astronomer, even Wellington.
  • Represents the fluidity of identity and the suspension of natural laws in Catherine’s opium dreams.

Mr. Spitzer

  • A companion to Catherine, often silent and seemingly unable to anchor her in reality.
  • His presence is uncertain, described as an abstraction yawning like cosmic ideas.
  • Catherine often ignores or addresses him tentatively.
  • He “seemed to indulge, often through his silence, her every mood, even her ignoring him.”

Cousin Hannah Freemount-Snowden

  • In stark contrast to Catherine, she is a robust, adventurous, and mercurial woman.
  • Known for her vast, almost mythical experiences across the globe, including deserts, mountains, and ancient cities.
  • Has a reputation for prescience, having foreseen many historical assassinations and events.
  • Skilled in various martial and survival arts: archery in Persia, dueling in France, mountain climbing, horseback riding, balloon ascensions.
  • Has traveled extensively in disguise, infiltrated hostile territories, and defied dangers.
  • Represents a force of action, clarity, and determination, dedicated to overthrowing dreams and illusions.
  • Symbolizes a bridge between myth and history, reality and fantasy, embodying strength and resilience.
  • She rode in Arab disguise against Spanish soldiers to defend a caravan of Riffs, for “her proud heart could not endure injustice of any kind in this world.”
  • She is buried in a New England churchyard, “her jeweled sword at her side,” in “her old grey army coat” worn in “wars for the emancipation of woman.”
  • Young built her from two true stories: Charles Studin’s suffragist “battle-axe,” “one of the original bloomer girls,” whose sealed trunks held “a complete bridal trousseau” each, and two bloomer girls on an Alpine summit, the younger lost going back for her skirt (Marguerite Young, interview with Studs Terkel, WFMT radio, 1965).
  • She “had never cared for the Spitzer boys,” predicted they “would come to no good end,” and called both brothers “profligates.”
  • Catherine sees her as “an emancipated extension of herself,” who might “rescue my mother from the opium dreams of her dead loves.”

Jock Cartwheel

  • Late husband of Catherine who is described as a philanderer who enjoyed dogs, sailing, and mountain climbing.
  • He disappeared while mountain climbing.
  • Catherine imagines him “lifting a beautiful lady’s skirts in clouds and winds,” “philandering,” or “racing dogs through snow clouds.”

Research: Themes

Reality versus Illusion

See: Illusion and Reality

  • Catherine’s conversations with invisible and shifting figures highlight the tension between what is real and imagined.
  • The suspension of natural laws around Eustace suggests the fluidity of identity and reality within opium dreams.
  • Cousin Hannah’s practical and adventurous life contrasts with Catherine’s dreamlike existence, yet even Hannah’s life borders on legend.

Memory and the Past

See: Memory and the Past

  • The narrative dwells on historical figures and events (e.g., Russian czar’s murder, archdukes’ assassinations, Saladin, Solymon the Magnificent).
  • Cousin Hannah’s knowledge spans centuries and cultures, emphasizing the weight of history and memory.
  • Catherine’s longing for her lost husband and her imaginary invitations for card games with ancestors suggest an attempt to connect with the past.

Death and Immortality

See: Death and Mortality

  • Catherine imagines the dead as still living and interacting.
  • Cousin Hannah’s death is ambiguous, with no clear date, emphasizing the elusive nature of mortality.
  • Catherine’s hope that her husband still exists somewhere reflects denial of death and the desire for immortality.

Adventure and Escape

See: Freedom and Escape

  • Cousin Hannah embodies the spirit of adventure, traveling to forbidden places and surviving countless dangers.
  • Her life serves as a counterpoint to Catherine’s static, opium-induced dreaming.
  • The recurring imagery of ships, deserts, and mountains emphasizes journeys both physical and metaphysical.

The Feminine and the Skirt

See: Women, Gender, and Marriage

  • Repeated references to skirts, including the loss of a skirt as symbolic sorrow and redemption.
  • Cousin Hannah’s life is linked metaphorically to skirts, suggesting themes of femininity, identity, and transformation.
  • “Cousin Hannah’s entire history, it seemed now, had been a history of skirts.”

The Cosmic and the Mystical

See: Faith, God, and the Supernatural · Nature, the Sea, and the Cosmos

  • Frequent cosmic imagery: stars, planets, moons, constellations, and celestial events.
  • Catherine’s dialogue with cosmic elements (stars, waves, tides) reflects a mystical quest for meaning beyond the earthly.

Research: Symbols and Imagery

Eustace

See: Eustace

  • Shape-shifting figure symbolizing the mutable nature of identity and reality.

Skirts and Whispers

See: Clothing, Hats, and Skirts

  • Symbolize femininity, mystery, loss, and redemption.

Mountains and Deserts

See: Mountains · Exploration and the Poles

  • Represent challenges, isolation, and spiritual journeys.

Ships and Seas

See: The Sea and Water

  • Metaphors for passage between life and death, reality and dream.

Stars and Celestial Bodies

See: Moon and Stars

  • Symbols of guidance, mystery, and the infinite.

Sword of Ice

See: Snow, Ice, and Winter

  • Represents Cousin Hannah’s ruthless clarity and decisive action cutting through illusions.

Research: Resources

  • “She would rather address her solicitous remarks to Eustace”: Eustace is a name of Greek origin that means fruitful or abundant in grain. It can also mean steadfast or stable. (Wikipedia) Eustace may be Saint Eustace since she mentions “golden-antlered stags.” St. Eustace converted to Christianity while out hunting after seeing a cross between the deer’s antlers and hearing the voice of God. The golden-antlered stags also recall the Ceryneian Hind with golden antlers, Heracles’ third labor. See Eustace and Greek Mythology.
  • “an old man bearded like the cypress”: The cypress is the tree of graveyards. In Ovid, the boy Cyparissus, grieving a pet stag he killed, becomes a cypress, the tree of mourning (Metamorphoses 10). See Grief, Loss, and Mourning.
  • “Wellington riding at the head of his troops”: Arthur Wellesley, first Duke of Wellington, was a famous military leader and political figure in 19th century England. See Napoleon and Wellington.
  • “Sometimes he was a Venetian gentleman’s murderous valet”: A Venetian gentleman’s murderous valet may refer to Lord William Russell who was a British aristocrat and murdered by his valet, Francois Benjamin Courvoisier (1840).
  • “He was a blind astronomer”: Galileo went blind in 1638. See Astronomy.
  • “Eustace, Eustace! Oh, is it you, Eustace dear”: At Iowa (1955-57), Young “would pause to greet Henry James at the door” of her classroom (David O. Dowling, “The Guru,” in A Delicate Aggression: Savagery and Survival in the Iowa Writers’ Workshop, Yale University Press, 2019). She kept portraits of dead writers on her walls. Catherine greets the invisible Eustace the same way. Young also told Studs Terkel of a friend in a New York hospital who overheard “one of the richest ladies in America,” dying, greet guests who were not there: “Eustace, turn to the left. Oh, isn’t that Mr. Henry James? How do you do, Mr. James?” (Marguerite Young, interview with Studs Terkel, WFMT radio, 1965). See Marguerite Young on Her Craft.
  • “a game of whist or loo or poker”: Whist, whose rules Edmond Hoyle published in 1742, and loo, the gambling game of Pope’s age. See Gambling and Playing Cards.
  • “a satrap clothed in Saturnian gold or a wild, bearded Cossack”: A satrap was a Persian provincial governor. Saturn ruled the golden age.
  • “who had gone to join her fathers long ago”: “So David slept with his fathers” (1 Kings 2:10). See The Bible.
  • “never worn the white plume of cowardice”: This is a reference to the White Feather Campaign of World War I, begun in August 1914 by Admiral Charles Fitzgerald, in which women in Britain handed white feathers to men in civilian dress to shame them into enlisting before conscription came in 1916. The symbol came from cockfighting, where a white feather in a gamecock’s tail was taken as a sign of poor breeding and a poor fighter. It is the subject of A. E. W. Mason’s 1902 novel The Four Feathers, whose hero receives white feathers when he resigns his commission before his regiment goes to war. (Wikipedia) Henry of Navarre’s white plume, by contrast, was a sign of courage: “Rally to my white plume” (Ivry, 1590). See Women, Gender, and Marriage.
  • “blowing like Gabriel’s skirts”: Gabriel, the archangel of the Annunciation (Luke 1:26). The Bible does not name the angel of the last trumpet; the spiritual “Blow Your Trumpet, Gabriel,” printed in Slave Songs of the United States (1867), gives it to Gabriel. See Angels and Archangels.
  • “Cousin Hannah Freemount-Snowden, the jolly old soul”: “Old King Cole / Was a merry old soul” (nursery rhyme, in print by 1708). See Fairy Tales and Folklore.
  • “the suicidal butterfly-chaser chasing himself with his butterfly net”: Mr. Spitzer’s butterflies of Chapters 28 and 29. See Joachim Spitzer and Butterflies and Moths.
  • “She had known of the murder of the Russian czar and royal family”: The murder of the Russian czar and royal family may refer to the execution of the Romanov family (1918).
  • “the murder of the archduke at Sarajevo”: The murder of the archduke at Sarajevo may refer to the assassination of Archduke Franz Ferdinand which started World War I (June 28, 1914).
  • “great sultans of the past such as Saladin”: Young’s list runs from Saladin, “the opposer of the Crusaders,” to “Solymon the Magnificent” (Suleiman the Magnificent, 1494-1566, the Ottoman sultan), Sardanapalus, and the Seleucid kings of Syria.
    • Salah ad-Din Yusuf ibn Ayyub or Saladin was the founder of the Ayyubid dynasty. Hailing from a Kurdish family, he was the first sultan of both Egypt and Syria. He was an important figure of the Third Crusade. At the height of his power, the Ayyubid realm spanned Egypt, Syria, Upper Mesopotamia, the Hejaz, Yemen, and Nubia. (Wikipedia) See Ancient Egypt.
    • Suleiman the Magnificent was the Ottoman sultan between 1520 and his death in 1566. Under his administration, the Ottoman Empire ruled over at least 25 million people.
    • Sardanapalus was, in Greek legend, the last king of Assyria, a decadent who died in a pyre of his own treasures. The name is probably a corruption of Ashurbanipal (reigned 669-c. 631 BC). He is the subject of Byron’s play Sardanapalus (1821) and Delacroix’s painting The Death of Sardanapalus (1827).
    • Seleucus I Nicator was a Macedonian Greek general, officer and successor of Alexander the Great. He went on to found the Seleucid dynasty.
    • Seleucus II Callinicus was a ruler of the Hellenistic Seleucid Empire. His reign was a time of great turmoil and fragmentation of the Seleucid Empire.
    • Seleucus III Ceraunus was the eldest son of Seleucus II Callinicus and Laodice II and for a few years was king of the Seleucid Empire. He was assassinated in Asia Minor by courtiers during a campaign against Attalus I of Pergamon.
    • Seleucus IV Philopator was a ruler of the Hellenistic Seleucid Empire. He was assassinated by Heliodorus, one of his leading bureaucrats. He is mentioned in 2 Maccabees in the Old Testament.
    • Seleucus V Philometor was the ruler of the Hellenistic Seleucid kingdom. The epithet Philometor means “mother-loving” and in the Hellenistic world usually indicated that the king’s mother acted as co-regent; here it was his mother, Cleopatra Thea. He was killed by his mother in order to advance his younger brother, Antiochus VIII, to the throne. (Wikipedia)
  • “many Bengal lancers”: The Bengal Lancers were cavalry of British India. The phrase is from Francis Yeats-Brown’s memoir The Lives of a Bengal Lancer (1930), filmed in 1935.
  • “Cousin Hannah had known the politics of all those nations”: Most of the main characters recite or list facts, real or imaginary. This may be a critique of school learning or rote memorization or The three Rs. The three Rs are three basic skills taught in schools: reading, writing and arithmetic. The phrase appears to have been coined at the beginning of the 19th century. The skills themselves are alluded to in St. Augustine’s Confessions where students learn to read, and write, and do arithmetic. (Wikipedia) See Augustine and Christian Theology.
  • “conversations over the telephone which had nearly always rung in an empty house”: Catherine’s calls to Cousin Hannah in Chapter 24. See the Chapter 24 resources.
  • “by a blackamoor in a fringe-topped surrey”: See the Chapter 24 blackamoor. The phrase recalls “The Surrey with the Fringe on Top” (Oklahoma!, 1943). See the Chapter 24 resources.
  • “She had been a great archer in Persia, a great dueler in France, an expert with sword and gun in Rumania”: Cousin Hannah takes up sports and roles reserved for men in her time: archer, dueler, mountain climber, yachtsman, explorer. She is a suffragette and adventurer who defies conventional female roles through her militant activism and boundary-crossing journeys, a contrast to the passive, isolated femininity of other characters, and her vitality counterbalances the decay and dream states that afflict them. See Women, Gender, and Marriage.
    • Persian women fought and were warriors until the Arab conquest of Persia in 651. A great archer of Persia may have been Banu, wife of Babak who fought alongside her husband against the Arab Caliphate for 23 years until they were betrayed. (Wikipedia) The Shahnameh has its own woman warrior, Gordafarid, who rode out in armor against Sohrab and fought him with bow and sword (Ferdowsi, Shahnameh, c. 1010).
    • A great dueler in France may be Julie d’Aubigny (c. 1670-1707), the opera singer known as Mademoiselle Maupin. Her father taught her academic subjects and also trained her in fencing since the age of 12 where she competed successfully against men. She became an assistant to fencing master Seranne. Because she is said to have had relationships with men and women, some modern-day sources refer to her as bisexual or queer. (Wikipedia)
    • An expert with sword and gun in Romania may be Ecaterina Teodoroiu (1894-1917), who fought on the front and died in World War I and is regarded as a heroine of Romania. She initially worked as a nurse but decided to be a front-line soldier partly influenced by the death of her brother. (Wikipedia)
    • There were famous female sailors: Lagertha, Jeanne de Clisson, Sayyida al Hurra, Lady Mary Killigrew, Grace O’Malley, Mary Read and Anne Bonny, Jeanne Baret, Zheng Yi Sao, Anne Jane Thornton, Mary Lacy, Grace Darling, Mary Patten.
    • Women sailors from New England: Mary Louisa Brewster, Martha Smith Brewer Brown, Mary Chipman Lawrence, Eliza Azelia Williams, Clara Clifford Kingman Wheldon.
    • A great Swiss mountain climber may refer to Lucy Walker (an Englishwoman climbing in the Swiss Alps, who reached the top of the Matterhorn in 1871) and Hettie Dyhrenfurth (who took part in two major expeditions to the Himalayas in 1930 and 1934).
    • Lucille Mulhall (1885-1940), the first woman called a “cowgirl,” could rope and tie a steer with the best of the men. There were so many famous cowgirls it is impossible to list them all here.
    • A great Chinese horsewoman may refer to Hua Mulan, a legendary warrior who disguised herself as a man to join the army.
    • A tall Tibetan jockey may refer to Ani Pachen (Nun Big Courage). She was a Tibetan nun who inherited her father’s position as clan chieftain and led her people in armed resistance against Chinese rule.
  • “a marksman who could shoot with unwavering aim through the ace of hearts at a distance of twelve paces”: Annie Oakley (1860-1926) shot through playing cards tossed in the air. A free pass punched with holes came to be called an “Annie Oakley.”
  • “She had made many balloon ascensions”: Famous female balloonists: Sophie Blanchard, Elisabeth Thible, Nellie Thurston, Wilhelmine Reichard, Jeannette Piccard, who flew to the stratosphere in 1934.
  • “Because of the loss of a skirt”: Young told Studs Terkel that this came from an Alpine story in which two bloomer girls shed their skirts at a summit, and the younger, going back for hers, was lost: “the lady lost her life for a skirt” (Marguerite Young, interview with Studs Terkel, WFMT radio, 1965). See the Chapter 31 resources. See Cousin Hannah, Clothing, Hats, and Skirts, and Women’s Suffrage.
  • “where slept the white-pronged unicorn”: The unicorn of the tapestries. See the Chapter 24 resources and the Chapter 28 resources.
  • “a Captain Derring-Do”: Derring-do is an old-fashioned word meaning boldness or daring, often with a hint of showiness or foolishness. It’s a noun for the quality of a person’s actions, though Young makes it a name, “Captain Derring-Do.” The word began as Chaucer’s “dorring don,” “daring to do,” misread by Spenser and made popular by Scott’s Ivanhoe (1819) (Online Etymology Dictionary).
  • “She had collided with many icebergs”: It recalls the Titanic, sunk by an iceberg in 1912. Here, “the iceberg had moved to allow her passage.”
  • “chauffeurs blew the horns of old Renaults”: Renault was founded in France in 1899 by the brothers Louis, Marcel, and Fernand Renault, and its cars were prized imports in American cities before the First World War. Renault taxis became famous in 1914, when hundreds of them carried French troops to the front at the First Battle of the Marne. (Wikipedia)
  • “the genealogies of Beacon Hill”: Beacon Hill is one of Boston, Massachusetts’s most picturesque areas. It is the home of Boston’s old families, the Lowells and Cabots of Chapter 24. See the Chapter 24 resources.
  • “the mountains of the moon”: Ptolemy’s Mountains of the Moon, the fabled source of the Nile.
  • “her poor husband, who was lost while walking between two frozen mountain peaks”: Catherine’s husband. See Jock Cartwheel.
  • “the elephants crossing the Alps with Hannibal”: Hannibal was a general and statesman of Carthage in what is now Tunisia. He crossed the Alps in 218 BC. See the Chapter 24 resources.
  • “where snows had not melted since the death of Charlemagne”: Charlemagne died in 814. See the Chapter 29 resources.
  • “where Childe Roland had blown his horn before a dark tower”: Childe Roland is a character in a poem by Robert Browning. The character Roland in the poem makes a journey to the Dark Tower much like the journey of Pilgrim’s Progress and the Divine Comedy. The name Child Roland comes from the Shakespeare play King Lear Act 3 Scene 4 Lines 195-197. Browning’s poem is “Childe Roland to the Dark Tower Came” (1855), and it ends with the horn: “Dauntless the slug-horn to my lips I set, / And blew. ‘Childe Roland to the Dark Tower came.’” The horn also recalls Roland of The Song of Roland, who blew his horn Oliphant at Roncevaux (778). See Shakespeare and Dante.
  • “marked only with the sign of the codfish”: The “codfish aristocracy” was a derisive name for New England families grown rich on the cod trade; in Salem, Colonel Pickman’s house had gilded codfish on its stair ends. Donna Seger writes: “New England cod fed both enslaved Africans and free Europeans and thus created great wealth in New England, but the derisive use of the term ‘Codfish Aristocracy’, in reference to the ostentatious and vulgar display of that wealth, comes later, in the 1840s and 1850s, and most prominently in the debate over slavery” (Donna Seger, “Codfish Aristocracy,” Streets of Salem, April 2, 2019). In 1850 Senator Andrew Pickens Butler of South Carolina, a leading pro-slavery voice, mocked the idea of being kept in order by “a codfish aristocracy” on the Senate floor. Some argued that the codfish aristocracy’s economic interests in the slave trade and the sugar trade were intertwined with their wealth.
    • The Sacred Cod is a four-foot-eleven-inch carved-wood effigy of an Atlantic codfish, painted realistically and hanging in the House of Representatives chamber of Boston’s Massachusetts State House. The one in the House chamber today was installed in 1784.
  • “so many foreign and domestic wars for the emancipation of woman”: The white women’s suffrage movement, primarily organized and led by middle-class educated white women, focused on gaining voting rights for white women, culminating in the passage of the 19th Amendment in 1920. The movement came out of the abolitionist movement with leaders being: Elizabeth Cady Stanton, Susan B. Anthony, Alice Paul, Carrie Chapman Catt, and Sojourner Truth (who played a significant role in the movement’s background). Suffragists employed various tactics, including lobbying, organizing marches and parades, and civil disobedience. After decades of activism, the 19th Amendment to the US Constitution was ratified in 1920 granting some women the right to vote. On paper the 19th Amendment covered all women. In practice it did not secure the vote for women of color. Black women in the South were kept from the polls by poll taxes, literacy tests, and terror. Native American women were not citizens until 1924. Asian immigrant women could not become citizens until 1952. It wasn’t until the Voting Rights Act of 1965 until all women’s voting rights were protected. See Women’s Suffrage.
    • A white skirt often symbolizes purity, innocence, mourning (in some cultures), new beginnings, versatility, symbol of femininity. Suffragettes wore white as a symbol of the movement to represent purity and unity. See Clothing, Hats, and Skirts.
  • “disguised as an Arab king”: There were female explorers in the Middle East: Gertrude Bell (a British explorer, archaeologist, and writer) and Freya Stark who was another British explorer and writer. Other explorers: Isabella Bird, Lady Anne Blunt, Lady Hester Stanhope. Isabelle Eberhardt (1877-1904) rode the Sahara dressed as an Arab man, and Lady Hester Stanhope lived among the Arabs in men’s dress. See Exploration and the Poles.
  • “she had been disguised as a lazar ringing his bell”: A lazar is a person afflicted with a repulsive disease like leprosy. The word comes from Lazarus, the beggar “full of sores” (Luke 16:20). Lepers carried bells or clappers to warn others away. See The Bible.
  • “the ruins of Persepolis”: Persepolis was the ceremonial capital of the Achaemenid Empire. It was burned by Alexander the Great in 330 BC.
    • Darius the Great was the third Persian King of Kings of the Achaemenid Empire.
    • Isfahan is a city in central Iran.
    • Shiraz is in the southwest of Iran.
  • “asked her if she had seen Darius the Great but had gotten only a negative reply”: Darius died in 486 BC, so the “negative reply” is a joke. See Comedy in Chapter 30.
  • “over the red hills of Moab and over the Dead Sea”: Moab, the biblical kingdom east of the Dead Sea, land of Ruth (Ruth 1:4). See The Bible.
    • The Dead Sea is a salt lake bordering Jordan, Israel, and the West Bank.
  • “inside Arabia Deserta”: Travels in Arabia Deserta (1888), by Charles Montagu Doughty, was admired by T. E. Lawrence (Lawrence of Arabia).
  • “where she had heard an archangel blowing a ram’s horn three times”: In Islamic tradition, the archangel Israfil will sound the trumpet of Judgment. The shofar is the ram’s horn of Jewish worship. See Angels and Archangels.
  • “and she had slept in Babylon, Nineveh, Crete”: Babylon was the ancient capital city of the Babylonian empire.
    • Nineveh was an ancient Assyrian city of Upper Mesopotamia.
    • Crete is the largest island in Greece.
  • “Her white horse was named El-Burraq”: Buraq (Young’s “El-Burraq”) is a creature in Islamic tradition that provides transport for certain prophets. In tradition, Muhammad tethered Buraq at the Western Wall on the Night Journey.
  • “a caravan of lonely Riffs”: Riffs are members of a number of Berber tribes around Er Rif. They fought the Rif War (1921-26), in which Abd el-Krim’s Republic of the Rif fought Spanish and French colonial armies.
    • The town of the Third Market Day may refer to the Rif War or one of the Spanish colonial wars in Morocco. Moroccan market towns are named for their market day. Souk el-Tleta is “the market of the third” day.
  • “upon the coasts of incense”: The incense coasts of southern Arabia, Arabia Felix, where frankincense and myrrh were traded.
  • “pirate ships flying black flags with skulls and bones”: The Jolly Roger.
  • “Charon’s empty boat drifting on the midnight tide”: Charon, ferryman of the dead across the Styx. See Greek Mythology.
  • “Moroccan pirates returning from raids upon the sleeping coast of Spain with beautiful captive girls”: The Barbary corsairs of Salé and Algiers raided the coasts of Europe and sold captives into slavery. See Society, Class, and Race.
  • “sailing in the six months’ darkness”: The polar night, when the sun does not rise for months near the poles. See Exploration and the Poles.
  • “Watchman, where is the shore”: “Watchman, what of the night?” (Isaiah 21:11). See The Bible.
  • “Arcturus, Andromeda, rainy Hyades”: Job’s “Arcturus, Orion, and Pleiades” (Job 9:9), and Tennyson’s “Ulysses” (1842): “Thro’ scudding drifts the rainy Hyades / Vext the dim sea.” See Astronomy, The Book of Job, and Greek Mythology.
    • Arcturus is the brightest star in the constellation of Bootes.
    • Andromeda is the daughter of King Cepheus and Queen Cassiopeia in Greek Mythology. The constellation is named for her.
    • Hyades is the nearest open star cluster.
  • “the argosy of the moving stars”: Argosy is a large merchant ship. The word comes from Ragusa (Dubrovnik), the merchant city.
  • “or are they the eyes of a peacock”: After Argus was killed, Hera set his hundred eyes in the peacock’s tail (Ovid, Metamorphoses 1). See Greek Mythology and the Chapter 29 resources.
  • “winter-rimed Orion”: Orion is a prominent constellation located on the celestial equator.

Vocabulary

Alpenhorn
A long wooden horn of the Alps.
Ambient
Surrounding.
Apprised
Informed.
Argosy
A large merchant ship, or a fleet of them.
Blackamoor
An old term for a Black African or any dark-skinned person, common in European art and in decorative figures of Black servants. It is now considered offensive.
Blunderbuss
A short gun with a flared muzzle.
Brigand
A bandit of the hills.
Cavalcade
A procession on horseback.
Codfish
A large food fish of cold northern seas.
Crusader
A soldier in the Crusades, the Christian military campaigns to take the Holy Land, fought between 1096 and 1291.
Deign
To condescend.
Derelict
A person or thing abandoned; a homeless outcast.
Duplicity
Double-dealing.
Emancipated
Set free.
Genealogy
A record of a family’s descent.
Grazier
One who grazes cattle. Here it means the herds.
Imploring
Begging earnestly.
Inscrutable
Impossible to understand or interpret.
Lazar
A diseased beggar, especially one with leprosy.
Leeward
On the side sheltered from the wind.
Loo
An old card game played for stakes.
Mercurial
Quick and changeable in mood. From the swift Roman messenger god Mercury and the liquid metal named for him.
Minaret
A tall, slender tower of a mosque, from which the call to prayer is given.
Mirage
An optical illusion, common in deserts, in which hot air bends light so that distant water or cities seem to appear.
Muezzin
The man who calls Muslims to prayer.
Nocturnal
Of or happening in the night.
Oblivion
The state of being forgotten, or of being unaware of everything.
Peaked
Thin and pale, as from illness.
Pinnacle
The highest point; a tall, pointed mountain peak or the slender spire on a building.
Prescience
Knowledge of events before they happen.
Problematical
Doubtful; hard to settle.
Profligate
A reckless, immoral spendthrift.
Sangfroid
Coolness in danger.
Satrap
A Persian provincial governor.
Solicitous
Anxious and attentive.
Stanchly
Firmly; loyally.
Surrey
A light four-wheeled horse-drawn carriage with two seats, often with a fringed canopy on top.
Taloned
Having talons, the sharp claws of a bird of prey.
Tentative
Hesitant; not certain.
Tethered
Tied with a rope or chain.

A small tower on a building or castle.
Whist
A card game for four players in pairs.

Chapter 32

← Chapter 31 · Home · Chapter 33 →

Content note: Vera’s mother, Catherine Cartwheel, is addicted to opium.

Summary

Catherine remembers Cousin Hannah as a storm of a woman, a suffrage captain with a saber scar and burning eyes who rode through deserts and snowfields. She died not in battle but in bed, after years of frostbite and semi-invalidism, confessing that “the greatest battles were fought in the domestic wars by those who had never left home.” Catherine visited her deathbed only in a dream, and she knew the day Hannah died when a riderless white horse came through the window. Rumor said Hannah once left a suitor at the church door. At Catherine’s own wedding she beat the bridegroom with her white umbrella and tried to carry the bride away. Catherine had married a phantom whose face she never saw: “For weddings are funerals, and funerals are weddings.” She always wanted to die while travelling, for “Death is that which is caused by our partial knowledge.”

Characters present

Cousin Hannah · Catherine Cartwheel · Joachim Spitzer · Vera Cartwheel · Jock Cartwheel · The Black Coachman

Concepts present

Themes: Death and Mortality · Dreams and Imagination · Illusion and Reality · Women, Gender, and Marriage

Symbols: Birds · Clothing, Hats, and Skirts · Horses and Carriages · Lamps, Candles, and Light · Opium · Pearls and Jewels · Snow, Ice, and Winter · The Bus and the Journey · The Umbrella · Weddings and Funerals

Philosophy: Plato and Platonism

Allusions: Astronomy · Ecclesiastes · Exploration and the Poles · Fairy Tales and Folklore · Genesis · Greek Mythology · Homer’s Epics · Romantic Poets · Shakespeare · The Bible · Women’s Suffrage

Key passages

From the research

  • The opening lines immediately establish Cousin Hannah as a dominant, unyielding figure: “Cousin Hannah, a lady who had forcefully expressed herself, a lady who had never drawn in the reins or paused to hear another person’s nugatory opinion…” This sets the stage for her powerful presence.
  • Her dedication is described in almost mythical terms: she “had fought against vanquished competitors when there were none except those of my mother’s drugged dreams… For this consanguineous relative had been interested in her overwhelming suffrage battles for woman on every front, her conquests which could never have been satisfied by temporary victories or the overthrow of man in this world.” This passage is crucial because it introduces her primary cause (woman’s suffrage) but simultaneously casts doubt on the reality of her battles, linking them to Catherine’s internal, dreamlike state. It also suggests her ambitions were absolute, perhaps even unattainable or self-defeating (“the ultimate victory would have been the ultimate defeat”).
  • The novel explicitly contrasts Cousin Hannah with Catherine: “Cousin Hannah, unlike my mother with her superfluity of bewildering pretenses… was not one to drag her standards in the dust… Cousin Hannah had preferred to take the offensive, to advance by open hostilities.” This highlights Cousin Hannah’s directness, unwavering principles, and aggressive approach, standing in stark opposition to the mother’s evasiveness, dissimulation, and passive nature.
  • Vera questions if Cousin Hannah could be a “misogynist” or “woman hater” despite describing herself as a “high-souled lover of woman, whom she had come to rescue from slavery to man.” This paradox is explored through her opposition to traditional feminine “frivolities” like elaborate hats, silks, veils, and parasols.
  • A significant passage describes her urging women to adopt a more combative stance. She “had urged woman to use her parasol as her sword or her shield, her greatest weapon of offense or defense,” and “to take off her great hoop skirts flounced with ribbons and lace, to show her little bird feet, to fly her skirts as her banners in her war against tyrannical man.” This passage vividly illustrates her radical vision of female empowerment, demanding a rejection of conventional femininity and an adoption of martial imagery and action.
  • Catherine’s perception of Cousin Hannah is key: “My mother believed that Cousin Hannah had been the image of that past which never was, that future which might never be realized. She had been extemporal, sudden and abrupt… brief and meteoric, hastening through this life as if it were a journey one should make with the utmost quickness and dispatch.” This portrays Cousin Hannah as existing outside normal time and reality, a fleeting, powerful force that appears and disappears unpredictably, emphasizing her almost mythical status in Catherine’s mind.
  • Her association with storms and cold further emphasizes her disruptive power: “She was certainly the greatest courier of every storm… The barometer dropped when she came… colder than a sea of the icebergs.” Her presence is linked to dramatic, chilling environmental changes, underscoring the profound, unsettling impact she had on Catherine’s world.
  • The description of Cousin Hannah’s death is perhaps the most important passage, as it drastically re-frames her life. My mother believed “that Cousin Hannah’s should have been a hero’s death.” But “she had died in no foreign war… She had suffered for years from frostbite. She had died after many years of semi-invalidism… The greatest battles were fought in the domestic wars by those who had never left home… It was always an unequal battle, for woman reigned supreme.” This passage subverts the heroic narrative built throughout the chapter. The mighty warrior dies quietly after years of decline, revealing a profound shift in her understanding of life’s true conflicts. The declaration that domestic wars are the greatest and that woman reigns supreme within them is a startling conclusion from the champion of public, external battles.
  • The possibility that Catherine’s visit to the dying Cousin Hannah occurred only in a dream, or even after death, is stated explicitly: “my mother had visited her only in a dream when she was riding in her carriage driven by the dead black coachman… Perhaps a visit was all the reality there was… One was dead, and one was dying… He certainly hoped that my mother’s visit had not occurred after she was dead.” This passage dissolves the boundary between reality and Catherine’s internal landscape, suggesting that the most significant interactions, including the deathbed confession, may have occurred entirely within her mind or dreams, reinforcing the subjective and possibly unreliable nature of the narrative.
  • The chaotic wedding scene where Cousin Hannah intervenes is highly symbolic: “Cousin Hannah, beating with her white umbrella upon the bridegroom, screaming like ten thousand demons in the cold midnight air, had tried to cause havoc, a riot… She had tried to intrude, to carry my mother away as the robber bridegroom carries the swooning bride.” This passage portrays the wedding as a battleground, where Cousin Hannah attempts to rescue (or abduct) Catherine from a phantom marriage, using her signature white umbrella as a weapon. It encapsulates her lifelong fight against Catherine’s entanglement with (or illusion of) men and traditional roles.

Questions and observations

Reading closely

  • “Perhaps, in fact, the ultimate victory would have been the ultimate defeat.” What would Cousin Hannah have lost by winning?
  • Catherine visited Hannah “only in a dream.” Why does Mr. Spitzer hope the visit “had not occurred after she was dead”?
  • “For weddings are funerals, and funerals are weddings.” What dies at a wedding?

Characters

  • Hannah confesses that “the greatest battles were fought in the domestic wars by those who had never left home.” Is she renouncing her life or seeing it clearly?
  • Catherine says she married “merely in order to proclaim her independence, to defy Cousin Hannah.” Can a marriage be an act of independence?
  • Hannah left her suitor “at the church door with a white bouquet in his hands,” and afterward he “subscribed heavily to the suffrage movement.” What did he understand about her?

Connections

  • Hannah urges women “to fly her skirts on tallest mountain peaks.” How does this echo the lost skirt of Chapters 30 and 31?
  • Catherine’s husband is “that great traveller who never would return,” and Catherine wants “to die while travelling.” How does this connect to Vera’s bus journey in Chapter 1?
  • Mr. Spitzer’s epitaph in Chapter 31 says Hannah was “not fallen in a foreign field.” Here she dies “while sleeping, perhaps while dreaming.” How do the two chapters tell her death?

Reflection

  • Are the hardest battles fought at home?
  • What do you know only in part?
  • Can you fight for someone who does not want to be rescued?

Research: Characters

Cousin Hannah

  • Cousin Hannah is portrayed as a powerful, uncompromising woman who never concedes or softens her standards, even for strategic reasons. She advances by open hostility and brandishes her symbolic sword like a cane, even when there is no opponent.
  • She is deeply committed to the cause of women’s suffrage and liberation from male oppression. Cousin Hannah fights against man as the cruelest oppressor of beauty and womanhood, advocating for women to use their own “weapons” such as parasols and skirts as symbols of resistance.
  • She is described as a swift, meteoric figure, always on the move and engaged in battles and journeys that span deserts, mountains, and foreign lands. She is likened to a great courier of storms and a weathervane signaling change.
  • Despite her vigor, Cousin Hannah is also seen as ancient, worn by time, and somewhat removed from the natural cycles of life and love. She is described as never having fully experienced youth, romance, or the mating seasons of life.
  • She dies not on a distant battlefield but in obscurity after years of frostbite and semi-invalidism. Her deathbed confession reveals a shift in belief that the greatest battles are fought domestically, in the struggles between man and woman at home.
  • She left her suitor at the church door with a white bouquet in his hands, and “it was said that after that he had subscribed heavily to the suffrage movement.”
  • She had “ravaged, burning eyes, a saber wound upon her cheek, a grizzled chin.”

Catherine (Vera’s mother)

  • Catherine is described as bedridden, veiled in white lace and surrounded by an atmosphere of drifting snowflakes, candle flames, and reflections. She is physically confined and vulnerable, a “creature of such fragility” who is easily overwhelmed by the presence of Cousin Hannah and the harshness of reality. Her bed is a “floating swan bed in a dazzling cloud,” which evokes both fragility and an ethereal, almost otherworldly quality.
  • Catherine’s essential loneliness and isolation is emphasized. She is abandoned by the “mysterious bridegroom” and all her loves are imaginary: pharaohs, captains, and other ethereal figures who “had left her, and they had never been.” This abandonment extends to emotional desolation, as no one, “not even Cousin Hannah,” has ever truly touched her “cold heart,” which is “cold and hard as the mountain rock.” This coldness suggests an emotional deadness or protective numbness born from pain.
  • Catherine lives largely in a world of dreams, illusions, and shifting realities. She imagines weddings to phantoms, sailboats, stars, and icebergs, reflecting a detachment from conventional life and relationships. Her marriage is portrayed as an ambiguous event, possibly symbolic or imaginary, rather than a concrete historical fact. The wedding imagery (“blushing behind her billowing wedding veils,” “married to a phantom”) conveys a sense of being caught between life and death, reality and fantasy.
  • Catherine’s mental state is described as “changeful and capricious,” with a wandering attention and vague memories. She is inconsistent in her accounts and perceptions, which may be interpreted as a symptom of her illness, age, or psychological state. This instability contrasts strongly with Cousin Hannah’s forceful and direct manner, highlighting Catherine’s passivity and internal turmoil.
  • Catherine’s relationship with Cousin Hannah reveals much about her character. Hannah is vigorous, militant, and confrontational, while Catherine simulates emotions she does not feel and “dissemble her feelings” when Hannah visits. Catherine’s indifference masks inner panic and vulnerability. Whereas Hannah is a symbol of active struggle and outward battle, Catherine is an embodiment of internal retreat and quiet suffering. Yet, Catherine admires Hannah’s energy and persistence, even as she is overshadowed by it.
  • Catherine is associated with death-like sleep. The novel suggests that she is “already dead” in a metaphorical sense, living in a “pretense of death.” Her life is marked by a profound stasis, and she may be seen as a “sleeping lady” awaiting awakening or final rest.
  • Catherine’s marriage and attitude toward men are ambiguous. She married “that great traveller who never would return,” possibly to defy Cousin Hannah’s militant feminism or to assert independence, but the marriage was doomed. Her symbolic wedding to various natural and mystical entities rather than a man suggests rejection or transcendence of traditional romantic or marital relationships.
  • Catherine is depicted with a strong aesthetic sensibility: her fingers wear jewels that “gleaming like northern lights,” and her surroundings are rich in poetic symbolism (flutes, harps, snowflakes, candle flames). She is a “beautiful femme fatale,” but her beauty is cold and distant, more a vision than a presence.

Mr. Spitzer

  • Mr. Spitzer serves as the “only go-between” between Cousin Hannah and Catherine, facilitating communication during times when direct contact was difficult or impossible. This intermediary role is underscored by his musical whispering (“musically whispering as he had thought what to say, what not to say”) which suggests a careful, delicate handling of sensitive matters and emotions. His interactions hint at an awareness of the emotional and existential weight carried by these women, especially Cousin Hannah nearing the end of her life.
  • Mr. Spitzer appears as a figure who exists somewhat on the threshold between life and death, reality and dream. The chapter notes that Catherine had visited Cousin Hannah only in a dream, riding a carriage driven by a “dead black coachman,” evoking an otherworldly atmosphere.
  • There is a tone of respect and perhaps even reverence in Mr. Spitzer’s attitude toward Cousin Hannah. He “certainly hoped that my mother’s visit had not occurred after she was dead,” indicating his sensitivity to timing and propriety in moments of transition between life and death. His role is not intrusive but rather one of discreet support and careful facilitation.
  • While Cousin Hannah and Catherine are enmeshed in their struggles (whether political, personal, or metaphysical) Mr. Spitzer’s character represents a connection to the external, practical world. His visits to the mansion, his knocking and waiting in the vestibule, contrast with the dreamlike, shifting realities inhabited by the women.
  • He questions the visit “vaguely as if he were not himself” and wonders whether “a visit was all the reality there was.”

Jock Cartwheel

  • Catherine “had married that great traveller who never would return.”
  • She “had never seen his face.”

The Black Coachman

  • On Catherine’s dream visit to Cousin Hannah, he is “the dead black coachman driving the black horses who wore black plumes and knew the way.”

Research: Themes

  • The novel explores the feminist theme through Cousin Hannah’s militant suffrage activism and her advocacy for women to wield traditional symbols of femininity as weapons in their fight for freedom.
  • Catherine’s life is marked by dreams, illusions, and a sense of unreality, contrasted with Cousin Hannah’s dramatic, tangible battles. The blurred line between dream and reality is emphasized by descriptions of ghostly visits, fading cities, and spectral imagery.
  • Both women embody different aspects of solitude: Cousin Hannah through her relentless battles and eventual physical decline, and Catherine through her emotional coldness and unfulfilled romantic desires.
  • The imagery that weddings are funerals and funerals are weddings suggests a cyclical transformation between life and death, union and separation. Catherine’s ambiguous marriage to a phantom reflects this theme.
  • Cousin Hannah is seen as ancient and time-worn, while Catherine’s memory of her is vague and fleeting. The passage of time is also symbolically represented by the changing weather, candle flames, and shifting landscapes.
  • The confession that the greatest battles are fought at home between man and woman reframes the traditional idea of heroism and war, placing emphasis on personal and domestic struggles rather than grand military conquests.
  • Swords, battles, sieges, and military metaphors are used extensively to describe Cousin Hannah’s activism and life philosophy.
  • Snowflakes, winter winds, desert storms, and mating birds symbolize the passage of time, change, and emotional states.
  • Candle flames, reflections in mirrors, and the interplay of light and dark underscore the theme of illusion and the duality of the characters.
  • Journeys to foreign lands, the Pony Express metaphor, and references to faraway cities emphasize Cousin Hannah’s restless spirit and Catherine’s longing for escape or transformation.
  • Catherine’s wedding veils, billowing skirts, and parasols symbolize both concealment and empowerment, linking femininity with both fragility and strength.

Research: Symbols and Imagery

Cousin Hannah as a Warrior and Adventurer

See: Women’s Suffrage

  • Cousin Hannah is depicted as a forceful, uncompromising woman, a “great captain” who went “brandishing her sword like a cane even when there was no one” and preferred “the strident clash of arms, the pitched battle against man.”
  • Her sword symbolizes her militant feminism and unyielding fight against patriarchal oppression. The sword, usually a weapon of war and honor, here is also described metaphorically as a cane, suggesting both her authority and perhaps a certain defiance despite solitude. The image of her as a “veteran of so many winter campaigns, desert marches through burning sands” evokes the harshness of her battles, both literal and metaphorical.

Winter, Snow, and Cold Imagery

See: Snow, Ice, and Winter

  • The persistent references to coldness, snow, frostbite, and icicles create a chilling atmosphere that underlines both Cousin Hannah’s harshness and isolation and the emotional coldness surrounding the characters. For example, the barometer dropping “colder than a sea of the icebergs,” and the “great icicles hanging from the ceiling” on the day she died symbolize the emotional frost and the chilling impact she has on Catherine.
  • Snow and ice also symbolize purity, whiteness, and unattainable beauty, reflecting Cousin Hannah’s idealized vision of womanhood as “unsullied honor” and beauty “as white as virginal snow.”

The Riderless White Horse and Rider Imagery

See: Horses and Carriages

  • The image of a riderless white horse “white as snow” coming through the window, bringing snow and cold with it, is a powerful symbol of death or the passing of Cousin Hannah.
  • The white horse traditionally symbolizes a harbinger of death or a psychopomp figure in literature, and here it represents the transition from life to death for this warrior woman.

The Veils, Parasols, and Skirts as Symbols of Femininity and Defense

See: The Umbrella · Clothing, Hats, and Skirts

  • The chapter richly describes feminine accouterments like “great garden hats decked with billowing plumes,” “secretive veils,” “frilled parasols,” and “great hoop skirts flounced with ribbons and lace.” These symbolize traditional femininity, societal expectations, and also the subtle weapons and shields women use in social and gender conflicts.
  • Cousin Hannah’s urging for women to wield their parasol “as her sword or her shield” and to “fly her skirts as her banners in her war against tyrannical man” transforms these delicate objects into instruments of rebellion. The parasol becomes a metaphor for female agency in a world dominated by men.

The Journey and the Northwest Passage

See: The Bus and the Journey

  • Cousin Hannah’s life is described in terms of vast, almost mythical journeys through “desert cities,” “impregnable Asiatic fortresses,” “the great Wall of China,” “Manitoba, Hudson’s Bay,” and “ten thousand singing islands of snow and ice.”
  • The reference to the “Northwest Passage” metaphorically represents the ultimate, elusive goal of life or freedom or “that which cannot be found.” It connotes a spiritual or existential journey, echoing themes of quest and discovery.

The Contrast Between Cousin Hannah and Catherine

  • Catherine is portrayed as fragile, veiled in lace and illusions, “bed-ridden,” “cold heart, cold and hard as the mountain rock,” and largely passive. In contrast, Cousin Hannah is active, combative, and direct. This contrast is symbolized by Catherine’s white umbrella and lace, symbols of delicacy and retreat, versus Cousin Hannah “beating with her white umbrella upon the bridegroom” like a weapon.
  • Catherine’s world is one of dreams, illusions, and absence, while Cousin Hannah’s is one of harsh realities and confrontations.

Death as a Wedding and Wedding as Death

See: Weddings and Funerals

  • The narrative blurs the boundaries between life milestones and death: “weddings are funerals, and funerals are weddings.” This imagery underscores the theme of transformation and loss inherent in marriage and life.
  • Catherine’s vague, elusive descriptions of her marriage (to a phantom, a porpoise, a star, an iceberg) symbolize the illusory or absent nature of her union and love. Marriage here is a symbolic death of the self or an eternal separation, while death is the final union.

The Ethereal and Dreamlike Atmosphere

See: Illusion and Reality · Dreams and Imagination

  • The chapter often blurs reality and dream: visits occur “only in a dream,” and there are “ambient ghosts of all dead loves.”
  • The use of mirrors, candle flames, flickering stars, and shifting reflections invokes a dreamscape where time and space are fluid. This imagery conveys the fragile mental and emotional state of Catherine and the elusive, almost mythical nature of Cousin Hannah.

The Military and Siege Imagery

  • Cousin Hannah’s life is described metaphorically as a “long siege” with strategic withdrawals and renewed assaults. This symbolizes her relentless struggle for women’s rights and independence, never defeated but always adapting.
  • The castle symbolizes societal structures opposed to her, and the sea eroding the shore suggests slow but inevitable change wrought by persistent effort.

The Symbolism of Light and Darkness

See: Lamps, Candles, and Light

  • Cousin Hannah is described as “standing in a beam of sudden light,” a figure of revelation and defiance.
  • Yet the chapter also has Mr. Spitzer’s “dark cape,” the ladies’ “already shadowed snow-white faces,” and Catherine’s “clouded looks,” symbolizing mystery, obscurity, and the unknown. This interplay of light and dark reflects the duality of the characters and the ambiguous outcomes of Cousin Hannah’s battles.

Research: Resources

  • “to invite her enemy to a banquet, to ease his suspicions with goblets of wine”: Judith feasted with Holofernes until he lay drunk, then “smote twice upon his neck with all her might, and she took away his head from him” (Judith 13:8, Apocrypha, King James Version). See The Bible.
  • “the misogynist, the woman hater”: A misogynist is a person who dislikes, despises, or is strongly prejudiced against women. Female misogynists (internalized sexism/oppression) are characterized by exalting the feminine ideal, favoring traditional gender roles, looking down on women who are not feminine, self-loathing, and a belief that she is superior to other women or in constant competition with them. There is a three-tiered system for patriarchy. Patriarchy is the system of social organization that favors and empowers men. Sexism is the code of conduct or rules that are established for women. Misogyny is the policing or enforcement of these rules on women (Kate Manne, Down Girl: The Logic of Misogyny, Oxford University Press, 2017). Thus women can be misogynist if they are helping to police or enforce what women can and cannot do. Looking at all of this it can be determined that no, Cousin Hannah was not misogynist for wanting women to have independence or the right to vote. See Women, Gender, and Marriage.
  • “worse than enchantment by an Eastern drug or spiritous liquor or witches’ brew”: The Eastern drug is opium, Catherine’s own enchantment. The witches’ brew is the cauldron of Macbeth: “Double, double toil and trouble; / Fire burn and cauldron bubble” (4.1). See Opium and Shakespeare.
  • “to fly her skirts on tallest mountain peaks”: Young’s Alpine story of the two bloomer girls who shed their skirts on a summit, one lost going back for hers. See the Chapter 30 resources, the Chapter 31 resources, and Women’s Suffrage.
  • “should have been employed by the old Pony Express”: Relays of riders carried the mail between St. Joseph, Missouri, and Sacramento, California, from April 1860 until the telegraph replaced them in October 1861. See Horses and Carriages.
  • “She should have brought the message to Garcia”: A Message to Garcia is an essay by Elbert Hubbard about the value of individual initiative and conscientiousness in work. Published in 1899, it praised Lieutenant Andrew Rowan, who in 1898 carried President McKinley’s message to the Cuban general Calixto García.
  • “colder than the Weddell Sea”: The Weddell Sea is part of the Southern Ocean off Antarctica. It is named for the sealer James Weddell, who sailed into it in 1823, and its pack ice crushed Shackleton’s Endurance in 1915. See Exploration and the Poles.
  • “colder than the lunar sea”: The dark plains of the moon are dry basalt. They were named seas, maria, by Giovanni Riccioli on his map of 1651. See Astronomy.
  • “Her face had not been attractive, certainly”: Miss MacIntosh and Cousin Hannah are both depicted as not attractive or feminine and virgins.
  • “as my mother could have endured no beautiful or potent rival”: In this chapter the rivalry mirrors Madge Capehorn at the beginning of the book because she could not tolerate Jacqueline White. See the Chapter 6 resources.
  • “be she even a dead bride with her face covered by a veil of snowflakes”: It recalls the lost companion of Chapter 31, “a body covered by the snow.” See the Chapter 31 resources.
  • “challenger of Foreign Legions”: The French Foreign Legion was founded in 1831 for foreign volunteers.
  • “as she had lived by the sword, should have died by one sharp blow”: “All they that take the sword shall perish with the sword” (Matthew 26:52). See The Bible.
  • “had slain minotaurs”: Theseus killed the Minotaur in the Labyrinth of Crete. Here Death, who “had overthrown great kings,” is given the hero’s deeds. See Greek Mythology.
  • “the black horses who wore black plumes”: Victorian hearses were drawn by black horses wearing tall plumes of black ostrich feathers. See The Black Coachman and Horses and Carriages.
  • “the walls might crumble at a lonely trumpet’s sound”: “When the people heard the sound of the trumpet, and the people shouted with a great shout, that the wall fell down flat” (Joshua 6:20). See The Bible.
  • “as Boston faded into fog and water from which it came”: Much of Boston stands on made land. The Back Bay was filled from tidal flats between 1857 and the 1880s.
  • “a riderless horse white as snow came through the window”: A riderless horse follows the coffin in state funerals. Lincoln’s horse, Old Bob, was led behind his hearse in Springfield in 1865, and Black Jack followed John F. Kennedy’s coffin in 1963. See Horses and Carriages.
  • “No one had awakened the sleeping lady to life and love”: This characterization of Catherine resembles the folktale of Sleeping Beauty which is a classic fairy tale about a princess who is cursed to sleep for a hundred years by an evil fairy, to be awakened by a handsome prince at the end of that time. The good fairy, realizing that the princess would be frightened if alone when she awakens, uses her wand to put every living person and animal in the palace asleep, to awaken when the princess does. The early versions, Giambattista Basile’s “Sun, Moon, and Talia” (1634) and Charles Perrault’s “The Sleeping Beauty in the Wood” (1697), involve rape, cannibalism, and Sleeping Beauty giving birth to children while she is asleep (similar to noncanonical books, as in the Gnostic Hypostasis of the Archons, in which the rulers of the world rape Eve). No one wakes Catherine. See Fairy Tales and Folklore.
    • In Giambattista Basile’s “Sun, Moon, and Talia” (1634), a king rapes the sleeping Talia, she bears twins without waking, and his wife later orders the children cooked.
  • “the limelight of publicity which was so very different from the light of a halo”: Limelight, a block of lime heated white-hot in a gas flame, was developed by Thomas Drummond in the 1820s and lit theater stages from 1837.
  • “picketing in a cold, sleet rain in front of a skirt factory”: The Silent Sentinels of the National Woman’s Party picketed the White House in all weathers from January 1917, and many were jailed. In the 1912 Lawrence, Massachusetts, “Bread and Roses” strike, women mill workers marched through the New England winter. Charles Studin’s suffragist, Young’s source for Cousin Hannah, “chained herself to a lamppost in front of the White House” (Marguerite Young, interview with Studs Terkel, WFMT radio, 1965). See Women’s Suffrage.
  • “challenging the conductor to a duel”: Studin’s suffragist “challenged a British prime minister to a duel and the prime minister refused to bear arms against the lady” (Marguerite Young, interview with Studs Terkel, WFMT radio, 1965). See Cousin Hannah and Women’s Suffrage.
  • “these hollow men, these advocates of lost causes, these men of straw, these things of naught”: “But hollow men, like horses hot at hand, / Make gallant show and promise of their mettle” (Shakespeare, Julius Caesar 4.2). Matthew Arnold called Oxford the “home of lost causes” (Essays in Criticism, 1865), and “a thing of naught” is Flute’s phrase in A Midsummer Night’s Dream (4.2). See Shakespeare.
  • “less than poor street Arabs”: “Street Arab” was a Victorian term for homeless street children, likening them to wandering Bedouin.
  • “the valleys of dry bones”: “The valley which was full of bones… O ye dry bones, hear the word of the LORD” (Ezekiel 37:1, 4). See The Bible.
  • “the sleepy myrmidons who did my mother’s bidding”: The Myrmidons were the soldiers Achilles led to Troy in Homer’s Iliad. Ovid tells that Zeus made them from ants for King Aeacus (Metamorphoses 7). The word came to mean a follower who obeys without question. See Homer’s Epics and Greek Mythology.
  • “the centaurs laying great golden eggs like moons upon the grass”: It recalls Aesop’s fable “The Goose That Laid the Golden Eggs.” See Greek Mythology.
  • “Had she come from Outer Mongolia, the great Wall of China, the kingdom of Prester John”: Three of Cousin Hannah’s far places.
    • Outer Mongolia was a territory of the Qing dynasty. It declared independence in 1911 and was the Soviet-backed Mongolian People’s Republic from 1924.
    • The great Wall of China is a series of fortifications built across the northern borders of Imperial China. Most of the wall that stands today was built under the Ming dynasty (1368-1644).
    • Prester John was a legendary Christian patriarch, presbyter, and king. The legend began with a forged letter that circulated around 1165.
  • “Had she come from Manitoba, Hudson’s Bay, Cape Reprieve, the Laurentian Shield”: The Canadian Far North. See Exploration and the Poles.
    • Manitoba is a province in Canada.
    • Hudson’s Bay is a large body of saltwater in northeastern Canada. The Hudson’s Bay Company was chartered in 1670 to trade furs there.
    • The Laurentian Shield (Canadian Shield/Laurentian Plateau) is a large area of exposed Precambrian igneous and high-grade metamorphic rocks that forms the ancient geologic core of the North American continent.
  • “sapphires which turned to rubies, rubies which turned to sapphires”: Ruby and sapphire are the same mineral, corundum. A trace of chromium turns it red, and that red stone is ruby. See Pearls and Jewels.
  • “Had she found the Northwest Passage”: Northwest Passage is the sea route between the Atlantic and Pacific oceans through the Arctic Ocean. Sir John Franklin’s expedition was lost seeking it in 1845, and Roald Amundsen first sailed through it in the Gjøa, 1903-1906. See Exploration and the Poles.
    • Northwest Passage (1937) is a novel by Kenneth Roberts. “On every side of us are men who hunt perpetually for their personal northwest passage, too often sacrificing health, strength, and life itself to the search; and who shall say they are not happier in their vain but hopeful quest than wiser, duller folks who sit at home, venturing nothing and, with sour laughs, deriding the seekers for that fabled thoroughfare?”
  • “Did she bring a message from a great king to a great khan”: Kublai Khan sent the Polo brothers to the Pope with a letter asking for a hundred learned men, and they set out back to him in 1271 with the young Marco Polo, reaching his court about 1275.
  • “the seed-times and the golden seasons”: “While the earth remaineth, seedtime and harvest, and cold and heat, and summer and winter, and day and night shall not cease” (Genesis 8:22). See Genesis.
  • “the stately mating dance of the whooping cranes”: Whooping cranes court with leaps, bows, and wing-flapping. By 1941 only about fifteen wild birds remained. See Birds.
  • “She had left him at the church door with a white bouquet in his hands”: Young told Studs Terkel that when Cousin Hannah “abandons the bridegroom at the church door,” “she goes to a numerologist who advises her as to how she should spell her name in the future and adds the hyphen just at the time when she dramatically becomes a hyphenated personality” (Marguerite Young, interview with Studs Terkel, WFMT radio, 1965). The hyphen is the one in Freemount-Snowden. See Cousin Hannah and Women, Gender, and Marriage.
  • “She had been the veteran of so many winter campaigns”: It recalls the painting Liberty Leading the People (Eugène Delacroix, 1830).
  • “like that faint heart which never won fair lady”: An old proverb, which Gilbert and Sullivan made a song, “Faint heart never won fair lady,” in Iolanthe (1882).
  • “she had been married on the tennis court”: Tennis and archery were among the first sports open to women. Charlotte Cooper won the first women’s Olympic title, in tennis, at Paris in 1900.
  • “as the robber bridegroom carries the swooning bride”: In the Grimms’ “The Robber Bridegroom” (1812), a bride discovers that her bridegroom murders young women. Eudora Welty retold it as a novel, The Robber Bridegroom (1942). See Fairy Tales and Folklore.
  • “weird huntsmen and barking dogs”: The Wild Hunt of European folklore, a ghostly troop of huntsmen and hounds riding the storm at night. See Fairy Tales and Folklore.
  • “her wedding gown had been torn to shreds by brambles”: In the Grimms’ “Little Briar Rose,” a hedge of thorns grows around the sleeping castle, and princes who try to pass die caught in it. See Fairy Tales and Folklore.
  • “For weddings are funerals”: In this chapter the idea of weddings and funerals mirrors Madge Capehorn at the beginning of the book because of her situation. In Chapter 6 “she had no bridal trousseau, no negligee ribbons, no clothes to come to child-bed with, no dance programs, no suitors, no husband.” See Weddings and Funerals and the Chapter 6 resources.
  • “this uninvited wedding guest”: In the Grimms’ “Little Briar Rose” (1812), the thirteenth wise woman, not invited to the feast, curses the child. Coleridge’s Ancient Mariner also stops a Wedding-Guest at the door. See Fairy Tales and Folklore and Romantic Poets.
  • “that pale cavalier who, with disheveled locks, with foaming mouth, is driven by the mare”: In Plato’s Phaedrus the soul is a charioteer with two horses, one noble and one unruly, who must master the wild one with the bit. See Plato and Platonism.
  • “Death is that which is caused by our partial knowledge”: “For we know in part, and we prophesy in part. But when that which is perfect is come, then that which is in part shall be done away” (1 Corinthians 13:9-10). See The Bible, Ecclesiastes, and Death and Mortality.
    • “For in much wisdom is much grief: and he that increaseth knowledge increaseth sorrow” (Ecclesiastes 1:18). The paradox of knowledge challenges the common belief that knowledge is always a positive thing. It acknowledges that wisdom, while valuable, might also bring greater awareness of the problems, and limitations of human existence.

Chapter 13

Summary

On the night of her fourteenth birthday, Vera says farewell in advance to her last certainty. After this night Miss MacIntosh, the one person who never seemed to change, will be a stranger Vera has lived with for seven years. Vera compares herself to the rider who crossed frozen Lake Constance in the dark and dropped dead when he learned where he had been. She bids farewell to the old moralities, the rote questions and answers, and What Cheer, Iowa, all of which now seem a lie. She wanders through her mother’s imagined gardens, where Galen, Harvey, Goldsmith, and Ben Jonson stroll at a perpetual garden party and life-sized chessmen move on a board of light and fog, until she reaches the garden of the deaf. There, as Catherine would tell Mr. Spitzer, the ear is dead. Catherine insists the dead ear is his, though he hears a roaring in his right ear that does not come from this world, and that this is why his music is silence.
