Key passages

From the research

  • The chapter opens with a poignant farewell to Miss MacIntosh, a figure who had seemed ordinary and unchanging but is now revealed to be mysterious and complex. Vera reflects on having taken her for granted, washing and ironing her clothes without understanding who she truly was. This passage symbolizes the moment of awakening to the deeper, often hidden realities beneath familiar aspects. The metaphor of the weary traveler crossing the frozen but never fully frozen Lake Constance powerfully conveys the shock of realizing that what seemed solid and known is actually fragile and deceptive. The traveler’s death upon comprehending the impossible crossing parallels Vera’s own transformation in perception. This passage marks the loss of innocence and the beginning of a more complex understanding of life and people.
  • Following the initial farewell to Miss MacIntosh, Vera bids farewell to the stability of past certainties: the “old moralities,” “proverbial wisdom,” and the “fabric of self-deception” that both she and Miss MacIntosh had lived by. This passage underscores a profound existential rupture where the past, reason, purpose, and future become unreliable, even illusory. The imagery of cherry blossoms, peach orchards, and dusty lanes as if they were lies evokes a sense of disillusionment with the world as it was once understood. This farewell is not just to a person but to an entire worldview, highlighting the theme of awakening to a more ambiguous and unsettling reality.
  • Vera wanders through a surreal, neglected garden that is described as “the garden of the deaf,” a place where “the ear is dead.” On the way she passes through Catherine’s “immortal gardens,” where Dr. Galen and Dr. Harvey stroll among the guests. The garden of the deaf is filled with vivid, ghostly images: statues, flowers that fly away like moths, and chessmen moving invisibly. The garden symbolizes a realm where sound and communication are absent, reflecting a profound isolation. The metaphor of the “deaf ear” extends into the relationship between Vera’s mother and Mr. Spitzer, emphasizing themes of silence, unhearing, and the inability to connect or be heard. Catherine’s insistence that the ear is dead and the world is soundless captures the tragic condition of isolation and the fading of meaningful communication.
  • The exchanges between Vera’s mother and Mr. Spitzer are significant for illustrating the tension between reality and perception. Mr. Spitzer represents a figure trying to engage with the world, arguing the possibility of sound and communication despite Catherine’s firm belief in their absence, even as he hears a roaring in his right ear that “did not come from this world.” Their dialogue about whose ear is dead (literal or metaphorical) introduces the theme of death not only of the physical ear but also of the heart and spirit. This passage deepens the motif of silence and the loss of voice, highlighting human suffering and the struggle to maintain connection amid internal and external voids.
  • Throughout the chapter, there is a recurring motif of things appearing familiar but becoming “increasingly unfamiliar,” such as the Venus statue “bearded by patriarchal fog,” flowers that fly away when touched, and shadows cast by barnacle-formed cherubim faces. These images evoke the fragility of memory and the instability of reality as perceived by Vera, underscoring how the past and present intertwine in confusing ways. The luminous yet ghostly descriptions of the garden and the figures within suggest a world where the boundaries between life and death, reality and dream, presence and absence blur.

Questions and observations

Reading closely

  • The rider “dropped dead with the shock of the after-knowledge.” Why is knowing worse than the danger itself?
  • Vera says her “ignorance had been perhaps my salvation.” Is it?
  • “One should see the bird and the shadow of the bird, but one should not hear the song.” What does Catherine lose by choosing silence?

Characters

  • Miss MacIntosh walked through cloudbursts with “her lips blue,” her face “twisted with unuttered pain.” What was Vera not seeing?
  • Catherine “feigned death because it was an enchantment greater than fleeting existence.” What does she gain by it?
  • Mr. Spitzer is “trying to learn not to turn his head every time he heard a traffic horn.” What is he trying not to hear?

Connections

  • Chapter 12 ended in the garden of the blind, and this chapter ends in the garden of the deaf. What does each garden take away?
  • The life-sized chessmen stood in the garden in Chapters 1, 2, and 3. Who are the invisible players?
  • Mr. Spitzer’s “music was the silence.” How does that answer Chapter 2’s “silent music”?

Reflection

  • Is it better not to know where one has been?
  • Can a person live with someone for seven years and not know her?
  • Which would be harder to lose, sight or sound?

Research: Characters

Vera Cartwheel

  • She begins with a poignant farewell to the “last certitude,” including the tender moment of her fourteenth birthday and the figure of Miss MacIntosh, who had been a constant presence for seven years.
  • This farewell symbolizes a significant psychological and emotional shift: a departure from innocence and an acknowledgement that the familiar is no longer certain or reliable.
  • Vera admits to having taken Miss MacIntosh for granted, thinking her the most ordinary person, only to realize she was mysterious and unknowable. This signals an awakening to the complexity and ambiguity of human beings and relationships.
  • She compares her previous ignorance to a weary traveler crossing a frozen lake under unbearable conditions, unaware that the ice beneath is treacherous and that survival was against all odds.
  • This metaphor vividly captures the precariousness of Vera’s former worldview: one that was sheltered and unknowing, yet preserved her from the shock of truth.
  • The crossing into awareness is described as a moment of death and rebirth, forever altering perception: “Everything . . . would be different . . . the simplest gesture having a different meaning.”
  • Following this awakening, Vera experiences a profound fragmentation of reality, where the familiar world loses its coherence and reliability.
  • The surrounding environment, including natural elements like moons, stars, and waters, fails to provide reassurance.
  • Vera explicitly bids farewell to “old moralities,” “proverbial wisdom,” and “the past and its illusion,” highlighting a rejection of previously accepted truths and a plunge into existential uncertainty.
  • Her farewell to the past is not simple nostalgia but a confrontation with the past as a “dream” that must be “laid bare like a corpse.”
  • This suggests a critical and almost forensic examination of memory, recognizing that the past is layered with deception as well as unexpected truths. Vera anticipates surprise and shock in discovering the absence of qualities once assumed and the presence of others previously unrecognized.
  • Vera’s reflections are imbued with elaborate, poetic imagery. These images evoke a dreamlike, liminal space between reality and illusion, life and death, sound and silence.
  • The “garden of the deaf,” where “the ear is dead,” becomes a powerful symbol of isolation, silence, and possibly the failure or refusal of communication.
  • Her environment is suffused with paradox and ambiguity, reflecting Vera’s inner turmoil and the collapse of conventional understanding.
  • Vera wrestles with themes of presence and absence, sound and silence, life and death.
  • Throughout the chapter, Vera’s tone is melancholic, marked by a sense of loss, estrangement, and an almost mournful awareness of change.
  • The farewell to Miss MacIntosh and the past, the dissection of memory, and the surreal descriptions of the garden convey a profound alienation from the world once known, both external and internal.

Miss MacIntosh

  • Miss MacIntosh, once a fixed star in Vera’s life, becomes like a “perfect stranger.”
  • Lips blue and face “pale and twisted with unuttered pain,” she walked through cloudbursts on her constitutional.
  • Her rote questions: “Where is North Dakota, and what is a monsoon, and what is a mirage, Vera Cartwheel?”

Catherine Cartwheel

  • The recurring motif of the “dead ear,” especially in relation to Mr. Spitzer and Catherine, underscores a world where communication fails and the essence of existence is isolated from meaning.
  • Catherine’s insistence that “the ear was dead” and that “there was not a sound to be heard” suggests a bleak vision of human experience as disembodied from relational and sensory engagement.
  • Catherine is depicted as a woman caught between life and a kind of suspended existence.
  • Catherine is enveloped in a self-imposed or circumstantial state of near-death or withdrawal from reality, an enchantment that protects her but also alienates her from the world around her.
  • The “garden of the deaf” is a powerful metaphor for Catherine’s mental and emotional state.
  • This deafness is not just literal but symbolic of a disconnection from the external world and from meaningful human interaction.
  • In this garden, “one should see the bird and the shadow of the bird, but one should not hear the song,” encapsulating Catherine’s experience of perceiving the world without fully engaging with it or being able to communicate effectively.
  • Her interactions with Mr. Spitzer, an old friend and legal professional, further reveal her state of mind.
  • Despite his efforts to speak and argue, Catherine insists that the “ear was dead,” and that no sound truly reaches them. This exchange highlights her detachment and the barrier she has erected between herself and others, emphasizing her internal silence and the futility of communication.
  • Mr. Spitzer’s “subdued roaring” in his ear, a noise which “did not come from this world,” parallels Catherine’s own internal condition, suggesting shared but differently manifested forms of alienation.
  • Catherine’s fear of the silence “unbroken by the sound” and her particular dread “when a frog screamed” indicate deep psychological distress. The silence is oppressive, a void that she cannot endure, and the rare disruptive sounds become sources of terror rather than comfort. This paradox of fearing both silence and sudden noise points to a troubled mind caught between extremes, fragile and haunted.
  • Throughout the chapter, images of decaying flowers, fading colors, and ghostly sounds surround Catherine, reinforcing the themes of impermanence and dissolution.
  • She is part of a world slipping away from life into something spectral or unreal. This imagery parallels her mental state which is caught in a liminal space between reality and illusion, life and death.
  • Despite her distance, Catherine remains a focal figure in Vera’s consciousness. Her presence is felt strongly even as she withdraws, indicating Catherine’s paradoxical role as both a source of life and a symbol of loss and mystery.

Mr. Spitzer

  • Mr. Spitzer is described as “pompous” and “beclouded,” suggesting a man who carries a certain self-importance or authority, yet his thoughts and arguments are somewhat confused or unclear. He is “many-valved,” implying layers or complexities in his personality or reasoning, which are not easily penetrable.
  • He is a lawyer who argues cases and makes decisions, which indicates a rational, structured mind accustomed to logic and human argument. Yet this external rationality contrasts sharply with the surreal, silent garden environment where “the ear is dead.”
  • The repeated motif of deafness is central to his character. While Mr. Spitzer physically experiences a kind of internal “roaring” in his right ear, a noise which “did not come from this world,” he is metaphorically deaf to true communication or sound in the broader existential sense described by Catherine.
  • The conversations with Catherine underline Mr. Spitzer’s role as a symbol of human limitation and isolation. Despite his attempts to speak and reason, he is trapped in a world where “there was no sound” and “he could not hear another’s voice, not even his own voice speaking.” This frames him as a figure caught between the rational world of law and argument and a deeper, more profound silence that challenges or negates those faculties.
  • Their interaction reveals a tension between denial and acceptance of this silence and deafness. Mr. Spitzer tries to argue against the idea that his ear is dead, pointing out that, if she means his dead brother’s ear, his brother was not buried anywhere on the estate, yet Catherine remains insistent that “the ear was dead,” emphasizing a metaphysical or symbolic deafness beyond just physical hearing.
  • Mr. Spitzer’s character embodies the tragic human predicament of isolation and the failure of communication. The novel suggests that even in his legal profession, where voice and argument are paramount, his voice is unheard in the cosmic or existential sense. This heightens the pathos of his character as someone who functions in society but is fundamentally cut off from true connection or understanding.

Research: Themes

Transformation and Loss of Certitude

See: Grief, Loss, and Mourning

  • The chapter begins with a farewell to the last certainty Vera held, symbolized by the tender memory of her fourteenth birthday and the figure of Miss MacIntosh.
  • Vera realizes that Miss MacIntosh, once considered an ordinary and stable presence, is in fact mysterious and unknowable. This realization marks a profound change in her perception of reality.
  • The metaphor of crossing a frozen Lake Constance, an impossible feat, symbolizes the transition from ignorance to knowledge and the shock of awakening to a new reality that alters all previous understandings.

Illusion versus Reality

See: Illusion and Reality

  • Vera describes the world and past experiences as fabrications or illusions, comparing the past to a corpse laid bare to reveal its true nature, which often contradicts prior assumptions.
  • This theme is emphasized through the farewell to familiar places, routines, and moralities that now seem deceptive or false.

Memory and Change

See: Memory and the Past

  • Miss MacIntosh, once a familiar figure, will henceforth be seen as almost a stranger due to Vera’s new awareness.
  • Vera anticipates that all memories and familiar objects will be differently understood, weighted with new meanings.
  • This reflects the theme that memory is mutable and that new knowledge reshapes how the past, and people once thought known, are perceived.

The Garden of the Deaf

See: Music, Sound, and Silence

  • Vera wanders gardens where, in Catherine’s visions, historical and literary figures stroll at a perpetual garden party, a symbol of the mind’s landscape where past and present, life and death intermingle.
  • The garden is where the “ear is dead,” meaning silence reigns and sound is absent, which symbolizes isolation, the limits of communication, and the finality of death.
  • The dialogue between Catherine, who insists on the silence, and Mr. Spitzer, who argues against it yet cannot escape it, dramatizes the struggle to find meaning or connection in a silent, soundless world.

Life, Death, and Silence

See: Death and Mortality · Music, Sound, and Silence

  • The chapter frequently reflects on mortality and the disappearance of sound, which metaphorically represents the death of communication and presence.
  • The silence is described as pervasive and absolute, underscoring the theme of existential isolation and the ineffability of certain experiences.

Miss MacIntosh

See: Miss MacIntosh

  • Initially a symbol of stability and ordinariness, she transforms into a mysterious figure, representing the unknowability of others and the fragile nature of relationships.

Research: Resources

  • “my fourteenth birthday”: The birthday party that never happened, in Chapters 10 and 12. See the Chapter 10 and Chapter 12 resources.
  • “a perfect stranger I had lived with for seven years”: “From my seventh to my fourteenth birthday” (Chapter 9). See Miss MacIntosh and the Chapter 9 resources.
  • “the weary traveller who rode over Lake Constance”: The legend is Gustav Schwab’s ballad “Der Reiter und der Bodensee” (The Rider and Lake Constance, 1826), later set to music by Robert Schumann. A horseman crosses the frozen lake in a snowstorm without knowing it and, told on the far shore where he has been, drops dead of fright. See Snow, Ice, and Winter.
    • Lake Constance is made up of three bodies of water on the Rhine at the foot of the Alps.
    • The lake seldom freezes over. It froze in 1830, 1880, and the winter of 1962-63.
  • “terra firma”: Latin for “solid ground.”
  • “a trembling sea of glass”: “And before the throne there was a sea of glass like unto crystal” (Revelation 4:6). See Revelation and the Apocalypse and the Chapter 10 resources.
  • “Where is North Dakota, and what is a monsoon, and what is a mirage”: Schoolbooks of the time taught by rote question and answer, as the catechism did.
  • “fixed like the North star”: “But I am constant as the northern star, / Of whose true-fix’d and resting quality / There is no fellow in the firmament” (Julius Caesar 3.1). See Shakespeare and Moon and Stars.
  • “my mother feigned death”: Juliet drinks the Friar’s potion to lie as if dead (Romeo and Juliet 4.1). See Shakespeare and the Chapter 12 resources.
  • “farewell to What Cheer”: What Cheer, Iowa, Miss MacIntosh’s hometown. See Iowa, Indiana, and the Midwest and the Chapter 9 resources.
  • “immortal gardens”: In Plato’s Apology, Socrates looks forward to death as a chance to converse with Orpheus, Homer, and Hesiod. See Plato and Platonism.
  • “Dr. Galen”: Galen (129-c. 216), born Aelius Galenus, was a Greek physician, surgeon, and philosopher. He was one of antiquity’s most influential medical researchers, making significant contributions to anatomy, physiology, and pharmacology, among other fields. His work, based on animal dissections and detailed observations, dominated Western medicine for more than 1,300 years. His anatomy stood until Andreas Vesalius published De humani corporis fabrica in 1543, and in 1242 the Arab physician Ibn al-Nafis had already described the pulmonary circulation Galen missed. Galen saw himself as both physician and philosopher, as he wrote in That the Best Physician Is Also a Philosopher. (Wikipedia) He built his theory of temperament on the four humors. He taught that the liver makes blood and the body uses it up, which Harvey overturned.
  • “Dr. Harvey”: William Harvey was the first known physician to describe in detail the human circulatory system, in De Motu Cordis (1628).
    • “sublunar mysteries”: Aristotle divided the cosmos into the changing, mortal world below the moon and the unchanging heavens above it.
  • “Oliver Goldsmith”: Oliver Goldsmith was an Irish writer, poet, playwright, and novelist known for works like the novel The Vicar of Wakefield and the play She Stoops to Conquer. He was a versatile author who also achieved success as a poet. The Deserted Village is a poem by Goldsmith published in 1770, a lament for a lost country village, as Vera bids farewell to What Cheer. It is a work of social commentary that condemns rural depopulation and the pursuit of excessive wealth. (Wikipedia)
  • “Ben Jonson”: Ben Jonson was a significant early modern English poet and playwright, known for his satirical comedies, masques, and poetry. He was a contemporary of Shakespeare, received a royal pension in 1616, which has led some to call him England’s first Poet Laureate, and is celebrated for plays like Volpone (a dark comedy about greed and corruption) and The Alchemist (a satire about fraud and human folly). “To Celia,” also known as “Drink to me only with thine eyes,” is a famous love song by Ben Jonson, first published in his 1616 collection The Forest. (Wikipedia) See Shakespeare.
  • “a perpetual garden party omitting the tragic spirit”: The Epicureans met in the Garden, the school Epicurus founded in Athens. See Epicureanism and Marguerite Young on Her Craft.
    • Marguerite Young loved Anatole France’s writing and read him widely, in French as well as in English. When her grandmother died, her first thought was that “now she can tell Anatole France that she has a little granddaughter on Earth who adores him” (Marguerite Young, interview with Charles Ruas, “The Art of Fiction No. 66,” The Paris Review 71, Fall 1977). Anatole France was a French author, poet, and critic who won the Nobel Prize for Literature in 1921. His short story “Marguerite” first appeared in book form in Paris in 1920, with woodcuts by Siméon, and in J. Lewis May’s English translation in 1921 (Project Gutenberg edition of the John Lane translation, 1921). France had socialist sympathies and was an outspoken supporter of the 1917 Russian Revolution, and in 1920 he backed the newly founded French Communist Party. (Wikipedia)
    • The Garden of Epicurus by Anatole France is a book of short essays and reflections (1894) that explores the nature of happiness, the pursuit of knowledge, and the struggle for personal freedom. France doubts that anyone can be known, even to himself: “What a foolish phrase, the ‘know thyself’ of the Greek philosopher! Why, we can never know either ourselves or others.” No one, he says, has ever told everything: “It would be so profoundly interesting to listen to a confession that was absolutely sincere! Yet since the world began, nothing of the kind has ever been heard.” The past, too, comes to us shaped by art: the historian presents facts “stripped of almost all the individual peculiarities that constitute them facts,” for “History is not a science, it is an art,” and “Beauty undraped is no beauty, and what we love the best is always the unknown” (The Garden of Epicurus, trans. Alfred Allinson, 1908, pp. 67, 93-94, 123-124, 128). One of his favorite periods was the transition from paganism to Christianity (Catharine Savage Brosman, Dictionary of Literary Biography). His English publisher called him “a pagan, but a pagan constantly haunted by the preoccupation of Christ” (John Lane, 1908).
    • The Epicurean “fourfold remedy,” handed down by Philodemus: Don’t fear the gods. Don’t worry about death. What is good is easy to get. What is terrible is easy to endure.
  • “anti-masks and masks”: The antimasque, a grotesque comic dance before the stately masque, was Ben Jonson’s invention in The Masque of Queens (1609).
  • “the life-sized chessmen”: In Lewis Carroll’s Through the Looking-Glass (1871), Alice crosses a countryside laid out as a chessboard with living pieces. The chessmen have stood in this garden since Chapter 1. See Alice in Wonderland, Cards, Games, and Chance, and the Chapter 2 resources.
  • “as if played by invisible players who could perceive an order in multiple confusions of movements and sounds, a secret plan”: “’Tis all a Chequer-board of Nights and Days / Where Destiny with Men for Pieces plays” (Edward FitzGerald’s Rubáiyát of Omar Khayyám, 1859). Heraclitus wrote, “Time is a child playing draughts,” and “The hidden harmony is better than the obvious.” See Fate and Chance and Heraclitus and Flux.
    • Heraclitus taught the unity of opposites: “The straight and the crooked path of the fuller’s comb is one and the same”; “The way up is the way down”; “Beginning and end, on a circle’s circumference, are common”; and “Thou shouldst unite things whole and things not whole, that which tends to unite and that which tends to separate, the harmonious and the discordant; from all things arises the one, and from the one all things.” “Mortals are immortals and immortals are mortals, the one living the others’ death and dying the others’ life”; “As the same thing in us is living and dead, waking and sleeping, young and old. For these things having changed around are those, and those in turn having changed around are these”; and “Cold things warm up, the hot cools off, wet becomes dry, dry becomes wet.” Diogenes Laërtius summarizes Heraclitus’s philosophy as follows: “All things come into being by conflict of opposites, and the sum of things (‘the whole’) flows like a stream.” (Wikipedia) His river fragment has survived in three different forms:
      • “On those who step into the same rivers, different and different waters flow” (Arius Didymus, quoted in Stobaeus)
      • “We both step and do not step into the same river, we both are and are not” (Heraclitus Homericus, Homeric Allegories)
      • “It is not possible to step into the same river twice” (Plutarch, On the E at Delphi)
    • Heraclitus said “strife is justice” and “all things take place by strife.” He called the opposites in conflict “strife,” and theorized that the apparently unitary state, “justice,” results in “the most beautiful harmony.”
  • “the Venus was bearded by patriarchal fog”: Velázquez’s Venus at Her Mirror (1647-51), the Rokeby Venus, hangs in the National Gallery, London. On March 10, 1914, the suffragette Mary Richardson slashed it with a meat cleaver. “I have tried to destroy the picture of the most beautiful woman in mythological history as a protest against the Government for destroying Mrs Pankhurst, who is the most beautiful character in modern history. Justice is an element of beauty as much as colour and outline on canvas. Mrs Pankhurst seeks to procure justice for womanhood, and for this she is being slowly murdered by a Government of Iscariot politicians. If there is an outcry against my deed, let every one remember that such an outcry is an hypocrisy so long as they allow the destruction of Mrs Pankhurst and other beautiful living women, and that until the public cease to countenance human destruction the stones cast against me for the destruction of this picture are each an evidence against them of artistic as well as moral and political humbug and hypocrisy.” (Mary Richardson’s statement, The Times, London, March 11, 1914). See Women’s Suffrage.
    • The bearded Venus of Cyprus, a double-sexed Aphrodite, is described by Macrobius (Saturnalia 3.8).
  • “The mist flowers drooped their purple, langorous heads”: Mistflower, a real wildflower of the American South, blooms in soft purple heads in late summer. See Roses and Flowers.
  • “flew away like luna moths”: The pale green luna moth lives about a week as an adult and has no mouth to eat with. See Butterflies and Moths and the Chapter 2 resources.
  • “I had come to the garden of the deaf”: The companion to the garden of the blind in Chapter 12. See Silence and Deafness and the Chapter 12 resources.
  • “A frog screamed”: Frogs scream when seized by a predator. Bashō’s haiku (1686): “An old pond / a frog jumps in / the sound of water.”
  • “It was not even so much as a straw blowing in the wind”: “They are as stubble before the wind, and as chaff that the storm carrieth away” (Job 21:18). See The Bible.
  • “not even the creaking of starlight”: Aristotle reports the Pythagorean answer: the spheres do make music, and people do not hear it because they have heard it since birth (On the Heavens 2.9). Lorenzo tells Jessica, “Such harmony is in immortal souls; / But whilst this muddy vesture of decay / Doth grossly close it in, we cannot hear it” (The Merchant of Venice 5.1). See Pythagoras and the Music of the Spheres, Aristotle, and Shakespeare.
  • “his brother had not been buried anywhere on this vast, amorphous estate”: Peron Spitzer, Joachim’s twin, lies elsewhere and is not among Catherine’s dead guests. See Peron Spitzer and Twins and Doubles.
  • “a subdued roaring, a noise which came from the head only”: Tinnitus, a ringing or roaring in the ears with no outside source. Beethoven described it in the Heiligenstadt Testament (1802). See Joachim Spitzer, Deafness and Sign Language, and the Chapter 4 resources.
  • “his music was the silence”: John Cage’s 4′33″ (1952) is a piece of silence, in which the audience hears only the sounds of the room. Mr. Spitzer has written “only silent music” (Chapter 2). See Joachim Spitzer, Music, Sound, and Silence, and the Chapter 2 resources.
  • “One should see the bird and the shadow of the bird, but one should not hear the song”: Wallace Stevens, “Thirteen Ways of Looking at a Blackbird” (1917): “The blackbird whistling / Or just after.” See Birds.
  • “never hear his voice speaking farewell”: The chapter that opened “Farewell to the last certitude” closes on a farewell no one hears.

Summary

At breakfast the morning after her dream, Vera tries to see Miss MacIntosh as she always has: the Rock of Ages, the plain, red-haired nursemaid of common sense who scolds the tide, hates the Emperor Constantine for changing the calendar, and rails against Benjamin Franklin and the electric lights that have robbed the poor of the dark. But Vera has seen her bald in the night. She strikes the table and demands the truth: Miss MacIntosh wears a wig and has neither eyebrows nor eyelashes. Miss MacIntosh answers in grief and wild humor, by way of Canute and Constantine, Jonas Hanway and the umbrella that made every man his own coachman, and the brothers who called her George, and at last she lifts off her red wig. She is bald, her left breast is gone, and she was broke when she first came, which is why they saved the electric lights. Vera promises always to love her. Miss MacIntosh tells her to eat her breakfast, that people are never quite what they seem, that nobody knows anybody, and that she suffers especially when there are rainbows.

Key passages

From the research

  • Early in the chapter, Miss MacIntosh is described as a figure of unwavering common sense and moral clarity amid chaos and illusion. She is portrayed as the “Rock of Ages in a land where all things crumbled,” the “surefooted Pilgrim,” and the “one person never dreaming where all might dream.” This passage highlights her steadfastness and practical nature, contrasting with the fog and illusions surrounding them.
  • A substantial and vivid passage details Miss MacIntosh’s intense dislike for electric lights, reflecting her preference for natural darkness and simplicity. She associates electric lights with loss of privacy, artificiality, and moral decay. This passage also reflects her nostalgia and resistance to the encroachment of modern technology and the disruption of natural rhythms.
  • A critical dialogue occurs between Vera and Miss MacIntosh, where Vera confronts her about the “hollow pretense” of their living situation and demands honesty about the nature of their relationship. Vera accuses Miss MacIntosh of deception and questions whether they are truly bound to each other, expressing a desire to understand what she wants and lacks. This exchange is charged with emotional intensity and existential questioning.
  • One of the most poignant moments is when Miss MacIntosh removes her wig, revealing her baldness, which she describes as a source of deep personal embarrassment and symbol of her vulnerability and the “burned wig” shielding her from life’s harsh elements. This act strips away illusion and forces a confrontation with bare reality, emphasizing themes of identity, appearance versus essence, and mortality.
  • Miss MacIntosh offers a bleak yet humorous meditation on life’s disappointments, the inevitability of death, and the “system of mutual deception” that love often entails. She speaks with a mixture of bitterness and dark humor about her past, the failures of God and creation, and the futility of illusions.
  • Miss MacIntosh discusses the umbrella as a symbol of equality and protection, tracing its history from the Orient to England and its social implications. She also mentions the raincoat as a practical item for the poor, underscoring her concern for everyday realities and the working classes. This passage blends historical anecdotes with social commentary.
  • Toward the end of the chapter, despite all the darkness and despair, Miss MacIntosh exhorts Vera to “be of good cheer,” acknowledging that “we are pilgrims” with a long day ahead. She urges living each day as if it were the last, knitting body and soul together even as they unravel. This passage encapsulates the chapter’s tension between despair and endurance, illusion and reality.
  • In the final lines, Miss MacIntosh offers a sober reflection that “people are never quite what they seem” and “nobody knows anybody,” underscoring the chapter’s themes of uncertainty, deception, and the limits of human understanding.

Questions and observations

Reading closely

  • Vera calls Miss MacIntosh “the Rock of Ages in a land where all things crumbled.” How does the opening portrait prepare for its own undoing?
  • “I would have loved the imperfection because I could not love perfection.” What does Vera discover about love?
  • Miss MacIntosh says love “is a system of mutual deception.” Is she bitter, or honest?

Characters

  • “Most especially, for reasons never quite known, the Emperor Constantine was anathema to her.” Why might Miss MacIntosh hate the emperor who made Christianity the empire’s faith?
  • “My elder brothers called me George.” What does the chapter suggest about how Miss MacIntosh has lived between the roles given to women and to men?
  • Vera says, “I will always love you, and I will never part from you.” Miss MacIntosh answers, “Though I be parted from myself.” What is she telling Vera?

Connections

  • Vera is still thinking of “Miss MacIntosh’s marriage to Mr. Spitzer in that vasty deep.” How does the Spitzer dream carry into this breakfast?
  • Miss MacIntosh hides “the missing breast which gave her the pain over which she long ago had triumphed simply by ignoring the pain.” How does her body tell a history the novel has kept hidden?
  • “I was broke, and that was why we saved the electric lights.” How does this line change the rant against electric lights that came before?

Reflection

  • “Nobody knows anybody.” Is it true?
  • The umbrella, Miss MacIntosh says, “did more, over night, to bring equality than half a dozen revolutions.” Can an ordinary object change a society?
  • Vera says, “We all have to assume a great many things are true when they are not true.” What do people live by that they know is not true?

Research: Characters

Miss MacIntosh

  • Miss MacIntosh is described as the “Rock of Ages” in a crumbling world, a symbol of stability, clarity, and common sense.
  • She embodies straightforwardness, rejecting illusions and fantasies, and insists on living within a “framework” of reality.
  • Her physical appearance symbolizes her internal struggle: her ruddy hair like a “sunset burning with bees,” a broken nose, and eventually revealed baldness, all reflecting her life’s hardships and resilience.
  • The black umbrella she carries indoors and out is, in Young’s words, “a kind of canopy between her and reality. You don’t get too close to her” (Marguerite Young, interview with Studs Terkel, WFMT radio, 1965). It “always casts a shadow around her and forbids intimacy” (Marguerite Young, interview, WNYC radio, New York).
  • Miss MacIntosh is a moral mentor and nursemaid figure who values practicality over imagination.
  • She is skeptical of dreams, illusions, and modern distractions, such as electric lights, which she believes disturb natural life rhythms and privacy.
  • She is combative and sharp, not hesitating to scold even divine figures like Emperor Constantine or God Himself for what she sees as excess or failure.
  • Despite her stern exterior, she has a deep, incorruptible sense of humor and reveals moments of vulnerability, especially when discussing her baldness and personal losses.

Vera Cartwheel

  • Vera narrates. Having seen Miss MacIntosh bald in the night, she wakes still half in the dream and for once rebels, striking the table so the cups jump and demanding the truth.
  • Her cruelty turns at once to tenderness: once the wig is off she promises, “I will always love you, and I will never part from you,” and she feels she will suffer all her life “the blows of conscience.”

Research: Themes

Reality versus Illusion

See: Illusion and Reality

  • Miss MacIntosh represents a rejection of illusions, emphasizing the importance of common sense and “just what was immediate and near.”
  • Vera struggles with this perspective, feeling trapped between dreams and the harshness of reality.
  • The fog surrounding them symbolizes ambiguity, confusion, and the shifting nature of perception.
  • The electric lights symbolize modern artificiality, disturbing natural darkness and the “dreamless sleep” necessary for authentic living.

Mortality and the Human Condition

See: Death and Mortality

  • The chapter grapples with death, impermanence, and the fragility of life. Miss MacIntosh openly discusses her own mortality, symbolized by her baldness and physical deterioration.
  • She speaks candidly about the “burned-out wick” and the “empty breast,” metaphors for loss and the fading of vitality.
  • The idea that “life is very short” and “the spirit dwells not long in any place” underscores a sense of existential urgency.
  • Vera’s confrontation with Miss MacIntosh about their relationship and existence reflects a deeper search for meaning and honesty in the face of death.

Isolation and Connection

See: Isolation and Connection

  • Despite Miss MacIntosh’s role as a caretaker, there is a profound emotional distance and complexity in their relationship.
  • Vera demands honesty and openness, revealing a desire for genuine connection beyond social roles and appearances.
  • Miss MacIntosh’s admission of her past struggles and loneliness highlights the theme of isolation in human experience.

Research: Symbols and Imagery

The Wig and Baldness

See: Hair, Wig, and Baldness · Identity and the Self · Women, Gender, and Marriage · Marguerite Young on Her Craft

  • Miss MacIntosh’s wig symbolizes the facade of social norms and appearances, which she ultimately reveals as a protective but deceptive covering. Young described the wig as the illusion itself, “the dream by which she lived” (Marguerite Young, interview with Studs Terkel, WFMT radio, 1965), and the hair it replaces as “the symbol of the dream and of the feminine in life that she never had” (Marguerite Young, interview with Duncan MacDonald, Observation Point, 1965).
  • Her baldness, exposed in a moment of vulnerability, represents raw truth, mortality, and the stripping away of illusions.

The Umbrella

See: The Umbrella

  • The umbrella protects her “sand-colored skin.” Being hairless, Miss MacIntosh, Young said, “is very exposed to colors, to lights, which burn her skin. That’s why she always carried, even on sunny days, that black umbrella” (Marguerite Young, interview, WNYC radio, New York). It also keeps others at a distance: “You don’t get too close to her” (Marguerite Young, interview with Studs Terkel, WFMT radio, 1965).
  • It also symbolizes autonomy and control, as she “scolded a wave” or would defend herself against phantoms.

Electric Lights versus Natural Darkness

See: Lamps, Candles, and Light

  • Electric lights symbolize modernity, artificiality, and the loss of privacy and natural rhythms.
  • Miss MacIntosh longs for the natural darkness, the “night of six months,” and the simple light of the moon or candle, reflecting a desire for authenticity and peace.

The Fog

See: Fog and Mist

  • The fog is a recurring image symbolizing ambiguity, uncertainty, and the elusive nature of truth and identity.
  • Miss MacIntosh insists that “never would she yield to the fog,” asserting her steadfastness and clarity.

Research: Resources

  • “as the Rock of Ages in a land where all things crumbled”: Rock of Ages is a Christian metaphor for God or Jesus, representing stability, strength, and a place of refuge from sin and the storms of life. The phrase originates from the Bible and is famously used in the hymn “Rock of Ages,” by Augustus Toplady in 1775.
    • In the King James Bible the margin of Isaiah 26:4 gives “rock of ages” for “everlasting strength.” Toplady’s hymn begins, “Rock of Ages, cleft for me, / Let me hide myself in thee.” See The Bible.
  • “as the surefooted Pilgrim”: A person on a spiritual journey who remains firm and resolute in their beliefs despite hardships or adversity. This interpretation aligns with the idea of a pilgrim drawing on faith to overcome challenges and continue on their path.
    • Later Vera calls their life “a Pilgrim’s Progress from nowhere to nowhere,” after John Bunyan’s allegory The Pilgrim’s Progress (1678).
  • “the simulacrum, the graven image of truth”: Simulacrum is a representation, imitation, or copy of a person or thing. In a postmodern context, it refers to a copy without an original, or a copy that has become detached from reality. (Jean Baudrillard’s Simulacra and Simulation, 1981, is after 1964.)
    • “Thou shalt not make unto thee any graven image” (Exodus 20:4, KJV). See The Bible.
  • “She scolded a wave, a drifting sail, an old board brought in by the tide”: Compare William F. Buckley Jr. in 1955: “A conservative is someone who stands athwart history, yelling Stop, at a time when no one is inclined to do so, or to have much patience with those who so urge it.” See King Canute below.
  • “the Emperor Constantine who had changed the calendar”: Constantine the Great, the first Christian emperor, legalized Christianity and in 321 made Sunday, “the venerable day of the Sun,” the day of rest. Miss MacIntosh scolds him for changing the calendar and for an institutional Christianity that, in her view, set imposed order in place of natural rhythms and common sense. See On Emperor Constantine and Augustine and Christian Theology.
    • In 321 Constantine ordered that “the venerable day of the Sun” be a day of rest for city courts and workshops, the first Sunday law.
  • “her old silver-dollar watch”: Compare the Ingersoll “dollar watch” (1896), sold for a dollar as “the watch that made the dollar famous.”
  • “It would be impractical for the infernal spirits to conceive their own damnation”: “The mind is its own place, and in itself / Can make a Heav’n of Hell, a Hell of Heav’n” (John Milton, Paradise Lost, 1.254-255, 1667). See Milton.
  • “the fog that wrapped around us like the principle of ambiguity itself”: Ambiguity runs through the novel’s structure and style as well as its fog. Mrs. Hogden is both vulgar and strangely serene; Miss MacIntosh, the figure of common sense, has a hidden past; Mr. Spitzer cannot tell himself from his twin. Vera’s narration, prone to hallucination and dream, keeps objective truth out of reach, and motifs return with slight variations. Young offers no final truths. See Fog and Mist and Illusion and Reality.
  • “Because of Benjamin Franklin who should have known better”: Miss MacIntosh views Benjamin Franklin as a well-intentioned but ultimately disruptive figure whose innovations, especially electric lighting, have intruded on natural life, privacy, and morality, reflecting her deep-seated preference for simplicity, natural order, and skepticism toward modernity.
    • Franklin flew his kite into a thunderstorm in 1752 to show that lightning is electricity, and invented the lightning rod.
  • “there were the Elevated above us and the Subway beneath us”: “Elevated” in U.S. transportation refers to elevated railways (or “els”), which are train systems built on steel, concrete, or brick structures high above city streets to avoid surface traffic, with Chicago’s iconic “L” (short for “elevated”) being the most famous example, alongside systems in NYC (largely removed), Philadelphia, and parts of others like Boston and LA, providing crucial, congestion-free urban transit.
    • “Subway” is an urban, high-capacity, electric railway system, often underground (hence the name), moving large numbers of people; it’s also called metro, rapid transit, or sometimes “the L” (elevated) or “the Tube,” operating on exclusive tracks separate from roads, with major examples in NYC, Chicago, DC, and Boston. Boston opened America’s first subway, under Tremont Street, in 1897.
    • “Grand Central Station” is a commuter rail terminal at 42nd Street and Park Avenue in Midtown Manhattan, New York City. Grand Central is the southern terminus of the Metro-North Railroad’s Harlem, Hudson and New Haven Lines, serving the northern parts of the New York metropolitan area. The present Grand Central Terminal opened in 1913.
  • “God Who brings the blackness of the day”: “Wilt thou break a leaf driven to and fro?” (Job 13:25, KJV); “and maketh the day dark with night” (Amos 5:8, KJV). See The Book of Job.
  • “she preferring either the light of the Apocalypse or of Genesis”: “And God said, Let there be light: and there was light” (Genesis 1:3, KJV); “And the city had no need of the sun, neither of the moon, to shine in it: for the glory of God did lighten it” (Revelation 21:23, KJV). See Genesis and Revelation and the Apocalypse.
  • “she would tell Thomas Edison”: Thomas Edison was an American inventor, businessman, and manufacturer who is considered one of history’s greatest inventors. He was responsible for more inventions than any other inventor, acquiring 1,093 patents in his lifetime. Edison’s inventions, including the light bulb, phonograph, and alkaline storage batteries, revolutionized the world and had a profound impact on everyday life. His first lasting carbon-filament bulb burned in 1879.
    • “War of the Currents” was a bitter commercial and technical battle in the late 1880s and early 1890s between the direct current (DC) system championed by Thomas Edison and the alternating current (AC) system promoted by George Westinghouse and Nikola Tesla. Edison launched a public misinformation campaign, including publicly electrocuting animals with AC, to portray it as dangerous and inferior to protect his DC patents and market share. This was not a public revolution against all electricity, but rather a corporate and technological battle that fueled public anxiety.
  • “Death came like a thief in the night”: “For yourselves know perfectly that the day of the Lord so cometh as a thief in the night” (1 Thessalonians 5:2, KJV). See The Bible.
  • “the electric lights are a monopoly”: Electric utilities are often considered natural monopolies due to massive infrastructure costs (power plants, grid), making it inefficient to have competing lines to every home, leading to government-regulated monopolies for distribution, though generation and retail markets have seen increasing competition, challenging the traditional model. While the infrastructure (wires) remains largely monopolistic, the industry structure is evolving, with debates around breaking up these monopolies for better consumer benefits.
    • Stockholders (or shareholders) are individuals or entities that own shares, representing partial ownership, in a corporation, gaining rights like voting and dividends but limited liability for company debts. They profit from company success through stock appreciation and dividends, while facing risks like investment loss if the company performs poorly. Common stockholders vote on directors, while preferred stockholders get dividends first, and their influence varies by ownership percentage. Criticisms of stockholders often center on shareholder primacy, arguing it fuels short-termism, excessive executive pay, increased inequality (benefiting the wealthy), and can lead companies to neglect other stakeholders (employees, environment, community) for profit, creating agency problems where managers serve themselves or short-term gains rather than long-term value.
  • “We will return to bayberry candles”: New England colonists boiled the waxy berries of the bayberry shrub to make fragrant green candles that burned without smoking. See Lamps, Candles, and Light.
  • “even Eskimos in igloos”: “Eskimo” is a broad, controversial term for the Indigenous peoples of the Arctic (Inuit, Yupik, Iñupiat, Kalaallit) across Greenland, Canada, Alaska, and Siberia, but it’s often considered offensive, with most preferring their specific names meaning “real people,” like Inuit or Yupik. These cultures traditionally thrive in harsh Arctic environments through hunting and fishing, sharing ancient roots from Asia and unique adaptations to the cold, though many now live in modern settlements and practice various faiths.
  • “poor Polynesians in boats”: Polynesians are indigenous peoples from the vast “Polynesian Triangle” of the Pacific (Hawaii, New Zealand, Easter Island), known for incredible ocean voyaging, unique double-hulled canoes, and sophisticated star/swell navigation, originating from Austronesian seafarers who settled the islands over 3,000 years ago, developing shared languages, cultures, and traditions, with major groups including Maori, Samoans, Hawaiians, Tongans, and Tahitians. They are celebrated for their epic migrations, rich oral traditions, art (like Moai statues), and deep connection to the sea, though colonial impacts have affected their traditional ways.
  • “Electric lights, indeed, and great X-rays!”: X-rays began in 1895 with German physicist Wilhelm Conrad Rontgen’s accidental discovery of a mysterious, invisible radiation while experimenting with cathode rays, which he named “X-rays” due to their unknown nature. This breakthrough quickly revolutionized medicine, allowing doctors to see inside the body for the first time without surgery, leading to rapid adoption for diagnosing fractures, though the dangers of radiation weren’t understood early on. Over time, safety measures, digital imaging, and advanced techniques like CT scans evolved, building on this foundational discovery to create modern radiology.
  • “There were all these bright lights of Broadway”: Broadway’s history began with Dutch settlement, named for its width, evolving from a trade route to New York’s entertainment heart, moving uptown with the city, embracing vaudeville, and exploding into a musical powerhouse during its Golden Age (1940s-60s) with Rodgers & Hammerstein, then revitalizing in the 1990s with mega-musicals and Disney, cementing its global fame for polished, diverse productions today, notes Dance Informa Magazine. (The 1990s revival is after 1964.) Broadway’s electric signs made it the Great White Way by about 1902.
  • “all these bright lights of Skid Row”: Skid Row originated from Seattle’s logging days as “skid roads” where logs were dragged (skidded) down hills to mills, evolving into a term for impoverished urban areas where transient, often unemployed men (“down-and-outs”) congregated due to cheap lodging, cheap liquor, and missions, especially during the Great Depression, with Los Angeles’s Skid Row becoming famous for its massive homeless population, cheap hotels, and social services. The history reflects shifts from resource extraction to urban poverty, the impact of economic crises, and evolving policies towards the homeless, becoming synonymous with large concentrations of unhoused people, addiction, and mental health challenges.
  • “the old naphtha flares of the old lamp-lighters”: Naphtha is a flammable liquid hydrocarbon mixture, a key intermediate in petroleum refining, used widely as a solvent, cleaner, and feedstock for gasoline, jet fuel, and petrochemicals, derived from crude oil or natural gas, varying from colorless to reddish-brown with a gasoline-like odor, and known for its volatility and potential health risks like irritation and CNS effects with overexposure. See Lamps, Candles, and Light.
  • “this, the missing breast which gave her the pain”: The Edwin Smith Papyrus, an Egyptian surgical text of about 1600 BC copying older sources, describes bulging tumors of the breast and says there is no treatment. See Ancient Egypt and Women, Gender, and Marriage.
    • In 1804 a Japanese surgeon is recorded as having performed a mastectomy. The surgeon was Hanaoka Seishū, who operated under a general anesthetic of his own making.
    • In 1811 the novelist Frances Burney had a mastectomy in Paris without anesthesia and wrote her sister the most famous account of it (1812). See Women, Gender, and Marriage.
    • In 1882, William Halsted performed the first modern mastectomy. His radical mastectomy, which also took the chest muscles, stayed standard for most of the next century and left many women disfigured and disabled.
  • “Diogenes, in broad daylight, had carried a lantern”: Diogenes of Sinope, also known as Diogenes the Cynic, was a controversial ancient Greek philosopher and founder of the Cynic school of thought. He lived a life of asceticism, rejecting societal norms and material possessions in favor of nature and simple pleasures. Diogenes was known for his provocative actions and sharp wit, which aimed to expose hypocrisy and greed in society and intellectual circles. The story of the lantern comes from Diogenes Laërtius, Lives of the Philosophers (third century). See Lamps, Candles, and Light.
  • “perhaps a man had married a man, and perhaps a woman had married a woman”: Compare the “Boston marriage,” the nineteenth-century name for two women who made a home together, as in Henry James’s The Bostonians (1886); and the life of Murray Hall, a New York Tammany politician who lived as a man for decades, married twice, and was found at death in 1901 to have been assigned female at birth. See Women, Gender, and Marriage.
  • “certainly the Franklin stove”: The Franklin Stove, invented by Benjamin Franklin in 1742, was a revolutionary cast-iron heating device designed to be a more efficient, less smoky alternative to open fireplaces, using less wood to provide more heat by circulating air and radiating warmth in all directions, functioning as an early furnace for its era’s climate crisis and wood shortage. It worked by drawing smoke and heat through a hollow baffle and an “inverted siphon” to extract more warmth before exiting, though it was sometimes difficult to draft and required less wood for better comfort.
  • “he had opposed the domination of George III”: George III was King of Great Britain and Ireland from 25 October 1760 until his death in 1820. The Acts of Union 1800 unified Great Britain and Ireland into the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland, with George as its king. George III is often accused of obstinately trying to keep Great Britain at war with the rebels (American Revolution), despite the opinions of his own ministers.
  • “Poor Richard’s Almanack”: Poor Richard’s Almanack was a popular annual publication by Benjamin Franklin (under the pseudonym “Richard Saunders”) from 1732 to 1758, known for its calendar, weather forecasts, and witty proverbs promoting thrift, industry, and self-reliance, which became a cornerstone of American culture and values. It was a bestseller in the American colonies, selling around 10,000 copies yearly, and served as a vehicle for Franklin’s practical wisdom for the common people.
    • “Early to bed and early to rise, makes a man healthy, wealthy and wise” (Poor Richard, 1735).
  • “he had also tampered with God’s nest egg”: Benjamin Franklin “tampered with God’s nest egg and most private creation keeping us up all day and half the night” metaphorically refers to Franklin’s experiments with electricity, which Miss MacIntosh blames for electric lighting. Miss MacIntosh expresses a strong aversion to electric lights, which she sees as an unnatural and disruptive force in human life.
  • “the carriage and the four white horses and the black coachman”: See The Black Coachman.
  • “No old lamp-lighters wanted”: These jobs have evolved or declined significantly due to technological advancements, mass production, changes in consumer habits, and modern logistics.
    • Ship chandlers are specialized suppliers for the maritime industry, providing everything from food (provisions) and cleaning supplies to technical equipment, safety gear, and deck stores (ropes, anchors) for ships and their crews, acting as crucial logistical partners to keep vessels operational and crews supplied globally.
    • An ironmonger (British English) is a retailer or shop that sells hardware, tools, household items, and metal goods, like hinges, locks, pans, and garden tools, essentially a traditional hardware dealer in American English.
    • Many umbrella repairmen, or “mush-fakers,” were mobile, going from house to house or setting up on streets to mend umbrellas. They would often make one good umbrella out of parts scavenged from several broken ones. A popular song in 1938, “The Umbrella Man” recorded by the Kay Kyser Orchestra, highlighted this common occupation. Frankford Umbrellas started in 1898 in the U.S. as a door-to-door repair service and grew into a manufacturing and repair company in Philadelphia. They repaired various types of umbrellas, including patio and beach umbrellas as well as rain umbrellas. Beehler Umbrella Factory was located in Baltimore, Maryland, this was the first umbrella factory in the U.S., founded in 1828. Baltimore became a hub for umbrella manufacturing, shipping over 1.5 million umbrellas annually by the early 20th century. Uncle Sam Umbrella Shop was a New York City staple, founded in 1866, provided sales and repairs for decades, serving notable figures like Charlie Chaplin and President Franklin D. Roosevelt. Umbrella repair was a necessary trade when umbrellas were durable, often made with quality materials like whalebone (early on) and later steel ribs, designed to last and be repaired. The “throwaway society” eventually led to the decline of the repair business, as mass-produced, inexpensive umbrellas made it easier for people to buy a new one rather than fix an old one. (Frankford Umbrellas is a business still running after 1964.)
    • Tin roofers specialized in installing tin-plated iron/steel sheets, a popular, affordable, fire-resistant material that rose in the 19th century with the Industrial Revolution, evolving from imported tinplate to domestically produced, corrugated, and galvanized sheets (tin over iron/steel) for homes, barns, and factories, offering better durability and ease of installation than older methods, though often called “tin” roofs, they were actually steel coated in tin.
    • Rag pickers (or rag-and-bone men) were vital urban scavengers, primarily poor immigrants in the 19th/early 20th centuries, who gathered discarded textiles, bones, metal, and glass from streets and dumps to sell to middlemen for processing into new materials, forming an essential, albeit low-status, part of early recycling and industrial supply chains, especially for paper and textiles, surviving on meager earnings from this dirty work.
  • “What is a monsoon?”: The questions Miss MacIntosh poses about monsoons (a rainy period in South and Southeast Asia between May and September), mackerel skies (a sky filled with rows of high-altitude cirrocumulus or mid-level altocumulus clouds that form a rippling, wavy pattern, resembling the scales of a mackerel fish. This formation indicates moisture and atmospheric waves, often signaling approaching weather changes, leading to the old saying, “Mackerel sky, not twenty-four hours dry”), the Bering Strait (is a narrow waterway separating Asia (Russia) from North America (Alaska), connecting the Pacific Ocean’s Bering Sea to the Arctic Ocean, famous as the site of the Ice Age land bridge (Beringia) for human migration and currently a vital wildlife corridor with a US-Russia boundary, known for cold, stormy waters and the time-bending Diomede Islands), and Hyperborean lights (refers to the poetic or mythical descriptions of the sun and continuous daylight in the legendary land of Hyperborea, a paradisiacal realm in Greek mythology) are a test of practical knowledge. She asks whether Vera has learned geography, arithmetic, navigation, and household management, for without them one is condemned to “darkest ignorance,” unfit to be a poor man’s wife once the wedding feast is over. See the mackerel sky in the Chapter 62 resources.
  • “Where are the Hyperborean lights?”: See the Hyperboreans in the Chapter 62 resources. See Greek Mythology.
  • “she with her fire red hair gleaming like the lights in a fiery furnace”: The three young men thrown into Nebuchadnezzar’s fiery furnace came out unharmed: “nor was an hair of their head singed” (Daniel 3:27, KJV). See The Bible and Hair, Wig, and Baldness.
  • “a kind of fool’s paradise”: “If ye should lead her into a fool’s paradise” (William Shakespeare, Romeo and Juliet, 2.4). See Shakespeare.
  • “She surely could not expect me to be interested in the ramifications of the Stock Exchange”: Vera cannot share Miss MacIntosh’s interest in the practical world: bull and bear markets, high finance, Australian shipping, cup racing, the marriage of salmon, the buoys of the harbor. Her own world is “the world within,” and she trembles “at the threshold of life” while these things make her “ears roar with distant reverberations.”
  • “Australian shipping or cup racing”: The America’s Cup, the oldest trophy in international sport, has been raced for since the schooner America won it off the Isle of Wight in 1851.
  • “the antiquated structure of Brooklyn Bridge”: The Brooklyn Bridge opened in 1883, then the longest suspension bridge in the world; Emily Warren Roebling saw it through after her husband, its engineer, was disabled by caisson disease. See Women, Gender, and Marriage.
  • “the spar buoys which have a spar attached”: Young’s list of buoys is exact: the spar buoy is a floating pole, the nun buoy a cone, the whistling buoy blows with the swell, and the bell buoy rings with the waves.
  • “and if ever the golden bowl is broken, or the wheel at the cistern”: “Or ever the silver cord be loosed, or the golden bowl be broken, or the pitcher be broken at the fountain, or the wheel broken at the cistern” (Ecclesiastes 12:6, KJV). Miss MacIntosh breaks off and adds, “The Bible exaggerates.” See Ecclesiastes.
  • “How does it happen that you have no hair along your skin?”: Alopecia universalis is considered an autoimmune disease where the person does not grow any hair on any part of their body but is otherwise healthy. See On alopecia universalis and Hair, Wig, and Baldness.
  • “Are you a salamander that you sit there burning in your own light?”: Since Pliny, the salamander was said to live in fire unharmed; Paracelsus made it the spirit of the element of fire.
  • “some ventriloquist had tricked me into being his wooden dummy”: Compare Edgar Bergen and his dummy Charlie McCarthy, stars of American radio from 1937.
  • “There was, I noticed for the first time, a crescentic white marking on her upper right eyelid”: Compare vitiligo, the loss of skin color in white patches, an autoimmune condition often found with alopecia.
  • “Heaven preserve you from a beardless man”: Miss MacIntosh warns against a beardless man and a hairy woman, and asks Vera to “Consider well, my dear, if you mean what you are saying, if this is your infinite desire for nothing.” A screech owl, the old omen of death, flies by. Her prophecy echoes the darkened sun and moon of Revelation: “The sun and the moon will shine in the same sky, and yet the earth will not be lighted but will be wrapped in darkness like the night.” No birds will sing, “There shall be bare and ruined choirs,” as in Shakespeare’s Sonnet 73. “The flower will perish while it is still in the seed. The tides will not return what the tides take out.” At the end, “There will be only, my dear, the dream.”
    • Old proverbs in several languages warn against both a beardless man and a bearded woman.
  • “A screech owl flew by just then”: The screech owl’s cry was long taken for an omen of death. See Birds.
  • “The sun and the moon will shine in the same sky”: “The sun shall be turned into darkness, and the moon into blood, before the great and the terrible day of the LORD come” (Joel 2:31, KJV). See Revelation and the Apocalypse.
  • “There shall be bare and ruined choirs”: “Bare ruined choirs, where late the sweet birds sang” (William Shakespeare, Sonnet 73). See Shakespeare.
  • “ours is a Pilgrim’s Progress from nowhere to nowhere”: See the surefooted Pilgrim above.
  • “Nonsense, oh, nonsense which kills us”: Miss MacIntosh answers Vera’s dreaming: “imagination is nothing. The life is what counts.” She refuses false comfort, will not let anyone “turn the spade over the living heart,” and says “I shall surely disappear as surely as the sun sets,” her own choice and beyond Vera’s control. Her riddles point to fate beyond arithmetic: “What are two and two but one? What are four and four but three? Who holds the cards?” Constantine and Canute stand for human limits against time and the sea. Vera, trembling, wishes she could take back her words.
  • “Shall I tear my hair?”: See mourning that tears the hair in the Chapter 61 resources. See Hair, Wig, and Baldness.
  • “the Emperor Constantine or King Canute or Crispin or Clarence or Cuthbert”: King Canute, or Cnut, ruled England, Denmark, and Norway. Miss MacIntosh invokes him against those who “waste our lives in the vain expectation of that which might never happen,” dreaming of “what was not, of what would never be.” Catherine names Canute too, in her opium dreams, and Miss MacIntosh insists the “opium paradise was never God’s way of life.” The story of Canute setting his throne on the shore and bidding the tide stand still, to show his courtiers that no king commands the sea, comes from Henry of Huntingdon (twelfth century). See On King Canute and The History of Opium.
    • Crispin or Saints Crispin and Crispinian are the Christian patron saints of cobblers, curriers, tanners, and leather workers. They were beheaded during the reign of Diocletian. “And Crispin Crispian shall ne’er go by” (William Shakespeare, Henry V, 4.3).
    • Clarence may refer to the Duke of Clarence which is a substantive title traditionally awarded to junior members of the British Royal Family. George, Duke of Clarence, was drowned in a butt of malmsey wine in the Tower in 1478, as Shakespeare shows in Richard III.
    • Cuthbert may refer to Cuthbert of Lindisfarne who was an Anglo-Saxon saint of the early Northumbrian church in the Celtic tradition. He was a monk, bishop and hermit, associated with the monasteries of Melrose and Lindisfarne in the Kingdom of Northumbria, today in north eastern England and South Eastern Scotland.
  • “My head swaying like harebells in the wind”: Campanula rotundifolia, the harebell or common harebell, Scottish bluebell, or bluebell in Scotland, is a species of flowering plant in the bellflower family Campanulaceae.
  • “It certainly seems a No Man’s Land”: “No Man’s Land” is the disputed ground between the front lines or trenches of two opposing armies.
    • Miss MacIntosh speaks of a “No Man’s Land” where she has been killed again and again, mourning others rather than herself, a skeleton wandering through endless waters. Her worst enemy is the “invisible assassin,” one’s own heart. With the wig gone her head is “naked of all its illusion of planetary glory,” and life a “vain, shallow pretense.” “Time moves us when we move not.” She feels “rooked” by God, “God’s poorest and lowest.” Then she turns practical, telling the history of the umbrella from royal privilege to common protection, and calls for “celestial navigation” to carry on with life’s “mournful business.”
  • “killed by the oldest preacher, he with the flaming hair”: “Vanity of vanities, saith the Preacher; all is vanity” (Ecclesiastes 1:2, KJV). See Ecclesiastes.
  • “Long hair is short wisdom”: An old German proverb said of women, “Lange Haare, kurzer Sinn,” long hair, short sense; the bald Miss MacIntosh turns it back. See Women, Gender, and Marriage and Hair, Wig, and Baldness.
  • “it’s a wise child who knows his own father”: Shakespeare turns the proverb around: “It is a wise father that knows his own child” (The Merchant of Venice, 2.2). See Shakespeare.
  • “Here’s the livid skull that might be any fool’s or king’s”: “Alas, poor Yorick! I knew him, Horatio” (William Shakespeare, Hamlet, 5.1). See Shakespeare.
  • “a plague, a plague, a light, a light!”: Compare “A plague o’ both your houses!” (Romeo and Juliet, 3.1) and the king’s cry “Give me some light. Away!” (Hamlet, 3.2). See Shakespeare.
  • “Ursa Major, Charles’ Wain, Charybdis! Scyllal”: Ursa Major is also known as the Great Bear and is a constellation in the northern sky, whose associated mythology likely dates back into prehistory. See Astronomy.
    • Charles’ Wain is the Big Dipper. A folk etymology holds that this derived from Charlemagne, but the name is common to all the Germanic languages and the original reference was to the men’s wagon, in contrast to the women’s wagon, the Little Dipper.
    • Scylla and Charybdis are sea monsters in Greek mythology. To be “between Scylla and Charybdis” therefore means to be presented with two opposite dangers, the task being to find a route that avoids both. Odysseus passes between them in the Odyssey, Book 12. See Greek Mythology.
  • “Where’s my hair, that woman’s glory?”: “But if a woman have long hair, it is a glory to her: for her hair is given her for a covering” (1 Corinthians 11:15, KJV). See The Bible, Hair, Wig, and Baldness, and Women, Gender, and Marriage.
  • “Drape all the mirrors with black”: Mirrors in a house of mourning were covered, by Jewish custom during shiva and in Victorian homes, so the soul of the dead would not be caught or the living distracted by vanity. See Mirrors and Reflections and Weddings and Funerals.
  • “a Mr. Jonas Hanway”: Jonas Hanway was an English merchant, writer and philanthropist. He was the first male Londoner to carry an umbrella and was a noted opponent of tea drinking. Hanway created seventy-four printed works, mostly pamphlets, on a wide variety of subjects. Of literary importance is the Historical Account of British Trade over the Caspian Sea, with a Journal of Travels, etc. (London, 1753). He is also cited frequently for his work with the Foundling Hospital in London, particularly his pamphlets detailing the earliest comparative “histories” of the foundation versus similar institutions abroad. See On the umbrella’s history and The Umbrella.
    • Hanway also campaigned for the boy chimney sweeps, and the Chimney Sweepers Act of 1788 followed.
  • “the mackintosh raincoat”: Charles Macintosh of Glasgow patented his waterproof cloth, rubber sandwiched between two layers of fabric, in 1823; Miss MacIntosh carries the coat’s name.
  • “Some may be like Jonah”: Jonah from the Book of Jonah was swallowed by a large fish where he prays to God for three days. He is then released. The story of Jonah in the Bible teaches about God’s universal mercy and grace, showing that his compassion extends to all people, not just the Israelites. It also highlights the dangers of disobedience and prejudice, as the prophet Jonah attempts to flee God’s command to preach to the hated city of Nineveh. “Now the LORD had prepared a great fish to swallow up Jonah. And Jonah was in the belly of the fish three days and three nights” (Jonah 1:17, KJV). See The Bible.
  • “but some may be like Noah wanting to come up”: Noah is the last of the pre-flood patriarchs of the Book of Genesis. He builds an ark and takes pairs of animals in order to survive the great flood. The biblical story of Noah’s Ark signifies a profound message about divine judgment, mercy, and salvation. It illustrates that God judges wickedness and sin but also provides a way for salvation for those who are righteous, like Noah, and those who have faith. The story highlights themes of God’s faithfulness through the covenant of the rainbow, and in Christian theology, the ark is often seen as a foreshadowing of Christ as the ultimate source of salvation. The dove came back with “an olive leaf pluckt off” (Genesis 8:11, KJV). See Genesis.
    • The runner who brought Athens the news of Marathon (490 BC) is said to have cried “Rejoice, we conquer!” and died. Wimbledon has played lawn tennis since 1877.
  • “Upon a primrose bank I lie”: Her farewell, “if ever that may be which is not,” ends with a casual “cheerio.” She has slept in doorways and been broke, and saved on electric lights. Her baldness, missing breast, and crooked wig are the marks of her losses, and taking off the wig is her honesty. Words cannot “harness the winds,” and love is “a system of mutual deception.” Had she been a man, “I could have slipped unnoticed through the crowds,” and “No one would have laughed.” “Life brings many blows”; we knit our bones together “though they unravel faster than we knit,” and “people are never quite what they seem. Nobody knows anybody.” She suffers most “especially when there are rainbows.”
  • “I was broke, and that was why we saved the electric lights”: Poverty is a form of stress that research has shown alters a person’s behavior and development. The Great Depression would have been recent history for the characters in this story and Marguerite Young herself. The average American family lived by the Depression-era motto: “Use it up, wear it out, make do or do without.” Many tried to keep up appearances and carry on with life as close to normal as possible while they adapted to new economic circumstances. Households embraced a new level of frugality in daily life. They kept kitchen gardens, patched worn-out clothes and passed on trips. See On the Great Depression.
  • “Fine words butter no parsnips”: An English proverb of the seventeenth century: talk alone feeds no one.
  • “My elder brothers called me George”: Compare George Sand (1804-1876) and George Eliot (1819-1880), women who wrote as George. See Women, Gender, and Marriage and Identity and the Self.
  • “My sisters had long ropes of hair. A man could climb them”: “Rapunzel, Rapunzel, let down your hair” (Brothers Grimm, 1812). See Fairy Tales and Folklore and Hair, Wig, and Baldness.
  • “It is woman who makes man’s life so short and robs him of his hair”: “And she made him sleep upon her knees; and she called for a man, and she caused him to shave off the seven locks of his head” (Judges 16:19, KJV). Delilah’s shears took Samson’s strength. See The Bible and Hair, Wig, and Baldness.
  • “this old Admiral Dewey corset”: After Admiral George Dewey’s victory at Manila Bay in 1898, everything from corsets to cigars was sold under his name.
  • “Oh, my poor Columbine with the broken nose!”: Columbine is the clever maidservant of the Italian commedia dell’arte, sweetheart of Harlequin.
  • “Purple emperor!”: The purple emperor is a butterfly of European oak woods; imperial purple, dyed from Tyrian shellfish, was the color of emperors such as Constantine. See Butterflies and Moths.
  • “beauty is as beauty does”: Compare the proverb “Handsome is that handsome does,” as Oliver Goldsmith gives it in The Vicar of Wakefield (1766).
  • “We must sweep the waves back”: Compare Sydney Smith’s Mrs. Partington, who in a great storm of 1824 tried to mop the Atlantic out of her house: “She was excellent at a slop or a puddle, but she should not have meddled with a tempest” (speech at Taunton, 1831). See King Canute above. See The Sea and Water.
  • “Nobody knows anybody”: See On nobody knows anybody and Isolation and Connection.
  • “I suffer especially when there are rainbows”: “I do set my bow in the cloud, and it shall be for a token of a covenant between me and the earth” (Genesis 9:13, KJV), God’s promise after the flood. See Genesis.
