Chapter 16

← Chapter 15 · Home · Chapter 17 →

Summary

On the night of her fourteenth birthday, Vera rides her old black pony, Falada, bareback through the moonlit grounds, laughing, imagining herself a circus rider in pink tights, and whispering her secrets into his ear: that she is an orphan, that Miss MacIntosh is “an old witch who kept me enchained in a dark tower.” Mr. Spitzer gave her the pony, which had been sent to him by an admirer of his dead brother, and he named its pedigree: the horse that inspired merry-go-rounds and Queen Anne chair legs, and the speaking head of an old fairy tale. Vera rides Falada into the house, past the doge’s lions, the funeral gondola, and the tapestries of angels healing the blind and the deaf. She does not dare enter her mother’s room, for fear Catherine would know they were real. She rides on to Miss MacIntosh, who would. The door, usually barred from inside, swings open. In the moonlight Miss MacIntosh stands by the window, “unbelievably not herself,” and yet Vera knows her at once.

Characters present

Vera Cartwheel · Miss MacIntosh · Falada · Joachim Spitzer · Catherine Cartwheel

Concepts present

Themes: Death and Mortality · Dreams and Imagination · Freedom and Escape · Identity and the Self · Illusion and Reality · Isolation and Connection · Memory and the Past · Women, Gender, and Marriage

Symbols: Birds · Dogs · Eyes and Blindness · Horses and Carriages · Moon and Stars · Silence and Deafness · The House · The Sea and Water · Weddings and Funerals

Philosophy: Freud and Jung

Allusions: Angels and Archangels · Fairy Tales and Folklore · Greek Mythology · Shakespeare · The Bible

Key passages

From the research

  • The chapter begins with a powerful, almost dreamlike description of Vera Cartwheel riding her black pony, Falada, on the night of her fourteenth birthday. This passage captures the fierce pride and exhilaration of youth, the connection between rider and horse, and the blurring of reality and fantasy. The pony, though old and worn, moves with a spirit and grace that transcends its physical limitations, symbolizing both endurance and the imagination’s power to transform the mundane into the magical. This sets the tone for the chapter’s exploration of innocence, freedom, and escape.
  • As Vera and Falada ride through the dark allees, the narrative paints a haunting picture of the estate: burned trees, untended gardens, broken statues, faded tennis courts, gargoyles, and fountains. This imagery evokes decay, neglect, and the passage of time, contrasting with Vera’s youthful vitality. The path circles “like an eye through the garden of the blind,” the real garden the grandfather planted for his blind wife in Chapter 12.
  • Vera’s intimate bond with Falada is a central passage. She confides her deepest secrets to the horse about her orphanhood, her view of Miss MacIntosh as “an old witch who kept me enchained in a dark tower,” her hopes for the future. This reveals Vera’s vulnerability and longing for understanding and companionship. The horse is not just a companion but almost a confidant and extension of her inner world. The symbolic act of tying blue ribbons on Falada’s tail and whispering secrets reflects her need for connection and expression.
  • Another significant passage is the explanation of Falada’s pedigree and the importance Mr. Spitzer places on names. Falada is linked to what Mr. Spitzer calls “an old Arabic fairy tale which had its parallels in many countries, in many ages,” best known in the West as the Grimms’ “The Goose Girl,” whose horse’s head spoke oracles after death, and also to historical influences on furniture design. This passage layers the narrative with mythic and historical resonance, emphasizing the power of names and stories to shape identity and legacy. It also ties the horse, and by extension Vera, to a continuum of cultural memory and symbolism.
  • Vera and Falada’s passage through the shadowy, cavernous house filled with marble statues, mosaics, and relics creates a surreal atmosphere, blending dream and reality. The house is described as a tomb or underwater castle, with muted sounds and mysterious forms, evoking themes of death, memory, and entrapment. Vera’s hesitation to confront her mother, who may be lost in her own dreams or visions, underscores the emotional distance and isolation within the household. This passage poignantly captures the tension between presence and absence, life and death, reality and fantasy.
  • The chapter reaches an emotional climax when Vera and Falada enter Miss MacIntosh’s bedroom. The door opens creakily, the pony whinnies, and Vera observes Miss MacIntosh standing by the window, bathed in moonlight. The description of Miss MacIntosh as changed and “unbelievably not herself,” yet instantly recognizable, suggests a profound, possibly unsettling transformation. This moment encapsulates the themes of recognition, change, and possibly impending confrontation or revelation. Vera’s reflection that this recognition affirms an older shock buried beneath layers of time adds a layer of mystery and foreshadowing.
  • Falada’s head speaks after death from above the gate. Vera’s pony carries her to the door behind which Miss MacIntosh is about to be revealed bald, in Chapter 17.

Questions and observations

Reading closely

  • “I often did not know what I thought until I heard myself speaking the words.” What does Vera learn by telling Falada her secrets?
  • “He seemed to be my head, my intelligence. I was the headless rider.” Who is leading whom?
  • “Water knew no echo.” Why is the house so silent?

Characters

  • Vera tells Falada that Miss MacIntosh is a witch, yet rides to her because she “would know that we were real.” What does Vera need from her?
  • Mr. Spitzer believes “all things were in their names.” How does that fit a man who is mistaken for his brother?
  • Falada came from someone who “had not known… that Mr. Spitzer’s brother was dead.” What else in Mr. Spitzer’s life comes from Peron?

Connections

  • Falada’s head, nailed above a gate, speaks after death, and the sea returned “a strange marble head” for Saul in Chapter 15. Why do heads keep speaking in this novel?
  • The tapestries show angels who “restored sight to the blind and hearing to the deaf,” after the gardens of the blind and the deaf in Chapters 12 and 13. What is being healed?
  • Vera is “the headless rider,” after the headless horsemen of Chapter 12. What is she riding toward?

Reflection

  • Is a secret real before it is spoken?
  • Why might someone fear that being real would frighten another person more than being a phantom?
  • What is the first moment someone you knew became a stranger?

Research: Characters

Vera Cartwheel

  • Vera, the protagonist, a fourteen-year-old girl.
  • She is imaginative, free-spirited, and deeply connected to her pony, Falada.
  • She reflects on her orphaned status, her struggles, and her dreams.
  • Mr. Spitzer gave her Falada and looked carefully into the pony’s pedigree.
  • She whispers to Falada that she is an orphan who never knew her father, that pink is her favorite color, and that she will have “seven stairstep children with long blonde hair.”
  • She dares not visit her mother, fearing Catherine “might die of shock” if she knew horse and rider were real.

Miss MacIntosh

  • Miss MacIntosh is her caretaker, described as an “old witch” by Vera, who holds a controlling influence over Vera’s life.
  • Her door, “usually locked and barred from the inside,” opens of itself, and she stands by the window, “greatly changed… unbelievably not herself.”

Falada

  • Vera’s old black pony, described with affection, mythic qualities, and a symbolic presence.
  • Falada is both a real animal and a figure of imagination and myth.
  • Old, wind-broken, with “dish eyes” and a “diseased, withered mane,” sent to Mr. Spitzer by an admirer of his dead brother.

Research: Themes

Imagination and Childhood Freedom

See: Dreams and Imagination · Freedom and Escape

  • Vera’s ride on Falada is a metaphor for freedom and escape from her restrictive life.
  • The imaginative descriptions of the pony’s capabilities and their adventures reflect the boundless nature of a child’s mind.

Memory and Identity

See: Memory and the Past · Identity and the Self

  • Vera reflects on her orphanhood, her lack of parents, and her future hopes.
  • She shares her secrets aloud, many of which she herself is only understanding as she speaks.

Reality versus Fantasy

See: Illusion and Reality · Dreams and Imagination

  • The chapter blurs the line between what is real and what is imagined.
  • Falada transitions from a tired old horse to a mythical creature.
  • The house is both a physical place and a surreal, dreamlike environment.

Death and Legacy

See: Death and Mortality · Memory and the Past

  • The imagery of marble statues, tombs, and silent fountains suggests mortality and the passage of time.
  • Falada’s pedigree connects him to historical and mythical lineage, suggesting the persistence of memory and identity beyond death.

Isolation and Connection

See: Isolation and Connection

  • Vera’s solitary ride and whispered secrets highlight her isolation.
  • Her bond with Falada offers companionship and understanding.
  • Themes of childhood, freedom, memory, death, and identity are intricately woven through poetic language and symbolism.

Research: Symbols and Imagery

Falada

See: Horses and Carriages

  • Falada, the little black pony given to Vera by Mr. Spitzer, carries rich symbolic meaning that intertwines with Vera’s inner world and her journey.
  • Falada is described as an old, tired, wind-broken pony, light as a spirit, with a sagging back, a scrappy mane, and a knotted tail. Despite his physical frailty and advanced age, Falada moves with grace and seems almost magical, responding to Vera’s desires as if he were her own intelligence or head. The pony is said to be descended from a horse that inspired the jewel-studded horses of merry-go-rounds and carousels, connecting him to themes of childhood innocence and the cyclical nature of life and dreams.
  • Falada embodies a loyal, gentle companion who carries Vera through her internal struggles and the uncertain landscapes of her life. His responsiveness to her unspoken commands suggests an intimate connection between Vera’s mind and her means of navigating reality and illusion.
  • Although Falada is physically frail, he continues to carry Vera with grace and resilience. This mirrors Vera’s own vulnerability and strength as she faces the challenges of growing up and understanding complex realities.
  • Falada’s origin as a model for carousel horses evokes childhood fantasy and cyclical repetition, resonating with Vera’s oscillation between dream and reality. His presence blurs the lines between the tangible and the imaginary, reflecting the novel’s themes of perception and illusion.
  • Given by Mr. Spitzer, Falada also symbolizes a connection to a past that is both real and mythical, and perhaps a hope for guidance and stability amid chaos. His lineage to historical and artistic forms evokes continuity and the search for meaning.
  • Falada is described as seeming like Vera’s head or intelligence, suggesting that the pony is an extension or manifestation of her self-awareness and agency, her “headless rider” identity where the horse seems to guide the rider as much as the rider guides the horse.
  • Falada is a potent symbol of Vera’s complex inner life: her innocence, her challenges, her search for identity and direction, and the interplay between dream and reality that defines her experience in the novel.

The Moonlit Ride

See: Moon and Stars

  • The ride through the dark garden, past statues, fountains, and old tennis courts, symbolizes a journey through memory and imagination, a “circle like an eye through the garden of the blind.”

The House as a Tomb and Water Castle

See: The Sea and Water · Weddings and Funerals · The House

  • The grand house is described with imagery of tombs, water, and underwater life, creating a sense of mystery and timelessness. The references to the phoenix and musical tomb further emphasize themes of death and rebirth.

Miss MacIntosh’s Bedroom Scene

See: The House

  • Vera charges in on horseback, and Miss MacIntosh stands silent by the window, changed. This scene contrasts the fantastical ride with a stark moment of reality.

The Night and the Grounds

See: Moon and Stars

  • The story is set at night, under the moonlight, creating a dreamlike atmosphere.
  • The surroundings include dark allées, stunted trees, an old stable, gardens, fountains, statues, and a large, mysterious house with marble pillars, tapestries, and grand stairways.
  • The moonlit garden resembles a “garden of the blind,” and the house is described like a “water castle” with sea motifs and underwater imagery.
  • The atmosphere is eerie yet magical, with references to stars, fireflies, and phantoms.
  • Rich sensory descriptions evoke visual, tactile, and auditory experiences.

Other Motifs

See: Horses and Carriages

  • Falada represents freedom, imagination, and the link between past and present.
  • Moon and Stars are symbols of mystery, guidance, and the unconscious.
  • Marble Statues and Tombs are symbols of death, memory, and permanence.
  • Water and Sea Motifs represent transition, silence, and the unknown.
  • The entire ride is a metaphor for Vera’s inner journey. The horse is described as “almost only an idea,” and the house is likened to a tomb and an underwater castle.
  • References to historical furniture styles (Queen Anne, Chippendale), mythological creatures (phoenix, Triton), and fairy tales (the fairy tale of Falada, which Mr. Spitzer calls Arabic) enrich the novel’s layers.
  • The setting is a magical, moonlit garden and a grand, mysterious house filled with symbolic statues and motifs.

Research: Resources

  • “The fierce, exultant pride that was mine”: In “What Is It with Women and Horses?” (Intelligent Horsemanship, 2019), Dr. Rosie Jones-McVey, drawing on her PhD research among British horsewomen, writes: “In Victorian novels, as well as in the more modern genre of pony-girl books, it is often aboard a horse that girls find their wings, often proving some snot-nosed boy wrong in the process, or enabling them to escape various romantic dramas and find solace in the barn. Just like the pony-girl books, many of my participants’ life stories entwined horseyness with coming-of-age stories. Horses were the means through which many women first acted in a truly independent way, often pursuing equestrian endeavours despite/without their parents, or else, proudly taking up adult-like responsibilities in being the teacher, pilot, and carer of their ponies, rather than the one being looked after and told what to do.” She argues that horses give many women a space for independence and self-assertion that their everyday lives do not. See Freedom and Escape, Women, Gender, and Marriage, and Horses and Carriages.
  • “riding my black pony, Falada”: In the Brothers Grimm fairy tale “The Goose Girl” (1815), a princess is sent off to marry with her magical horse Falada, who can talk, and a waiting maid. The maid forces the princess to change places with her and, once she is the bride, has the prince kill Falada so he cannot tell. The princess has the horse’s head nailed under the dark gateway, and each morning it speaks to her as she passes: “Alas, young Queen, how ill you fare! / If this your tender mother knew, / Her heart would surely break in two.” In the end the king learns the truth and the false bride is punished. Falada means “spoken” in Portuguese. See Falada and Fairy Tales and Folklore.
    • Mr. Spitzer calls it “an old Arabic fairy tale which had its parallels in many countries, in many ages,” and tells of the head that “had spoken oracles and parables to the people passing through the gates.”
  • “following the movements of an imaginary polo ball”: Polo came to England from India with British cavalry officers in the 1860s, and Vera wears her “polo hat cocked back at a jaunty angle.” See Horses and Carriages.
  • “a path that made a circle like an eye through the garden of the blind”: The grandmother’s garden of the blind. See Eyes and Blindness and the Chapter 12 resources.
  • “It was a steeplechase, and we would jump over all the church steeples”: The first steeplechase (1752) was a race across Irish country from one church steeple to the next. See Horses and Carriages.
  • “I was a bareback rider, wearing a plume, a pair of pink tights”: Philip Astley’s London circus (1768) began as trick riding in a ring, and the bareback equestrienne in tights became the star of American circuses. See Horses and Carriages.
  • “Falada could dance on his hind feet”: The levade and capriole of the Lipizzaners of Vienna’s Spanish Riding School, where horses rear and leap on command. See Horses and Carriages.
  • “Miss MacIntosh was an old witch who kept me enchained in a dark tower”: Rapunzel, locked in a tower by a witch. See Fairy Tales and Folklore, Miss MacIntosh, and the Chapter 3 resources.
  • “served as a model for merry-go-round horses because of his grace in keeping all fours off the earth at once”: In 1878 Eadweard Muybridge photographed Leland Stanford’s horse Sallie Gardner and proved that a galloping horse lifts all four hooves at once, though not stretched out, as on carousel horses. See Horses and Carriages.
  • “had been sent to Mr. Spitzer by someone who had admired Mr. Spitzer’s brother”: Peron, the gambler of the horse circles (Chapter 14). See Peron Spitzer, Joachim Spitzer, and the Chapter 14 resources.
  • “the cabriole, the furniture of good Queen Anne’s day, whole forests of Chippendale”: Queen Anne furniture stands on curved cabriole legs, shaped like an animal’s leg. The name comes from the French cabriole, a goat’s leap. In dressage, the capriole is the horse’s leap with all four feet off the ground. Thomas Chippendale published his Director in 1754. See Horses and Carriages.
  • “the legs of a chair were referred to as the limbs”: The story comes from Captain Frederick Marryat’s Diary in America (1839), where an American lady was shocked by the word “leg,” and piano legs were said to wear frilled trousers.
  • “a rose by any other name would smell as sweet”: Romeo and Juliet 2.2. Catherine forgot the coachman’s name in Chapter 14, while Mr. Spitzer believes “all things were in their names.” See Shakespeare and the Chapter 14 resources.
  • “the sleeping marble lions which had once guarded the palace of a Venetian doge”: The winged lion of St. Mark is the emblem of Venice, ruled by its doges for a thousand years.
  • “the mosaic emperors like the faces of old playing cards”: The Byzantine mosaics of Justinian and Theodora at San Vitale in Ravenna (547).
  • “the kings with the triple crowns”: The triple crown is the papal tiara. See the Chapter 3 resources.
  • “the black funeral gondola”: Venice’s black funeral gondolas. See Weddings and Funerals and the Chapter 14 resources.
  • “the great mother-of-pearl mollusk which might have contained the form of Venus”: Botticelli’s The Birth of Venus (c. 1485) shows the goddess rising from the sea on a scallop shell. See Greek Mythology and The Sea and Water.
  • “I should be the umbrella medusa rising to the surface”: The jellyfish’s bell is called its umbrella, and its free-swimming stage is the medusa. See The Sea and Water.
  • “the phoenix rising from those cold ashes of the dream”: The phoenix, which dies in fire and rises from its own ashes. See Birds and the Chapter 7 resources.
  • “the effigy of a sleeping marble boy lying on his tomb”: Medieval tomb effigies often rest their feet on a dog, the sign of fidelity. See Dogs and Death and Mortality.
  • “angels who restored sight to the blind and hearing to the deaf”: “Then the eyes of the blind shall be opened, and the ears of the deaf shall be unstopped” (Isaiah 35:5). The gardens of the blind and of the deaf were Chapters 12 and 13. See Angels and Archangels, Eyes and Blindness, Silence and Deafness, and The Bible.
  • “the stuffed lute birds”: The lyrebird of Australia, named for its lyre-shaped tail. See Birds and the Chapter 3 resources.
  • “the shell which was the great turbaned Turk, the phaeton, the winding stairway”: These are real shells. The turban shell is one, and the wentletrap takes its name from the Dutch for “winding staircase.” See The Sea and Water.
  • “there would be a ding and a dong and a bell through all the rooms”: The nursery rhyme “Ding, dong, bell, / Pussy’s in the well,” and Ariel’s song in The Tempest. See Fairy Tales and Folklore, Shakespeare, and the Chapter 6 resources.
  • “I was the headless rider”: “The Legend of Sleepy Hollow” again. See Fairy Tales and Folklore and the Chapter 12 resources.
  • “as many husbands as Solomon had wives”: “And he had seven hundred wives, princesses, and three hundred concubines” (1 Kings 11:3). See The Bible and the Chapter 9 resources.
  • “the shock of this knowledge was but the affirmation of some older shock which had been forgotten”: Freud’s “The Uncanny” (1919) describes the uncanny as something long familiar and forgotten that returns as strange. See Freud and Jung.

Vocabulary

Allée
A walk or path lined with trees or tall hedges. Young writes “allees.”
Ascertain
To find out for certain.
Bareback
Riding a horse without a saddle.
Bellrope
A rope pulled to ring a bell, such as one that summons a servant.
Brackish
Of water: slightly salty, as where a river meets the sea.
Cabriole
A curved furniture leg shaped like an animal’s leg, from the French for a goat’s leap.
Canter
A horse’s easy three-beat gait, between a trot and a gallop.
Carousel
A merry-go-round. Earlier, a tournament in which horsemen performed exercises and displays.
Centaur
In Greek mythology, a creature with the head and upper body of a man and the body and legs of a horse.
Cherubim
Winged angelic beings. In art they are often shown as chubby winged children. The singular is cherub.
Cheval glass
A tall mirror swung in a frame so that it can be tilted.
Chippendale
Furniture in the style of the English cabinetmaker Thomas Chippendale (1718-1779).
Cuirass
Armor for the chest and back.
Dank
Unpleasantly damp and cold.
Divan
A long, low couch without a back or arms.
Doge
The elected ruler of Venice.
Effigy
A sculpture or model of a person, especially one lying on a tomb.
Equine
A horse; of horses.
Ethereal
Light, airy, and delicate, as if not of this world; heavenly.
Exultant
Triumphantly joyful.
Gable
The triangular upper end of a wall under a pitched roof.
Gargoyle
A carved grotesque figure on a building, often serving as a waterspout.
Jaunty
Lively and self-confident; set at a rakish angle.
Livid
Bluish-gray, the color of a bruise. Also furiously angry.
Lute
A plucked string instrument with a rounded back shaped like half a pear, popular in Europe from the Middle Ages through the 1700s.
Marquee
A large tent or awning.
Medusa
A jellyfish in its free-swimming, bell-shaped stage, named for the Gorgon of Greek myth whose hair was snakes.
Mollusk
A soft-bodied creature, such as a snail or clam, usually with a shell.
Mosaic
A picture or pattern made by setting small pieces of colored stone, glass, or tile together.
Mother-of-pearl
The shining, rainbow-colored lining of some shells, used for inlay.
Oracle
A message from the gods; a source of prophecy.
Paddock
A small field where horses are kept.
Pallbearer
One who helps carry a coffin at a funeral.
Parable
A short story that teaches a lesson.
Pedigree
The recorded line of descent of an animal or person.
Peruke
A powdered wig of the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries.
Phaeton
A light, open, four-wheeled carriage; also a name for some seashells.
Phosphorescent
Glowing faintly in the dark.
Portico
A porch with a roof supported by columns.
Prism
A clear piece of glass with flat sides that splits light into the colors of the rainbow.
Scalloped
Edged with a series of curves like the rim of a scallop shell.
Steeplechase
A horse race over fences, ditches, and water jumps, first run cross-country from one church steeple to another.
Tapestry
A heavy cloth woven with pictures, hung on walls.
Tendon
A tough cord that joins muscle to bone.
Triton
A sea god of Greek myth, half man and half fish, who blows a conch shell.
Turret
A small tower on a building or castle.
Whinny
A horse’s gentle neigh.
Wind-broken
Of a horse: short of breath from damaged lungs.

Chapter 23

← Chapter 22 · Home · Chapter 24 →

Summary

The breakfast continues. Miss MacIntosh denounces vain man, the Emperor Constantine, and Caesar, declares that history lies, and professes her faith in common sense and the middle way. Then she settles on Benjamin Franklin, whose experiments with lightning led to electric light and the end of privacy. Darkness, she argues, once protected marriage and the poor and the ugly. Vera realizes what the tirade is for: a woman who was just seen without her wig is arguing that no one should have to be seen. She talks of igloos and ice floes, of winter’s blast, of anything but herself. The chapter ends with Miss MacIntosh quoting Job and crying that the stars have always lit the heavens.

Characters present

Miss MacIntosh · Vera Cartwheel · Joachim Spitzer · Catherine Cartwheel

Concepts present

Themes: Death and Mortality · Illusion and Reality · Isolation and Connection · Light and Darkness · Memory and the Past · Nature, the Sea, and the Cosmos · Order, Chaos, and Discipline · Society, Class, and Race · Time · Women, Gender, and Marriage

Symbols: Lamps, Candles, and Light · Moon and Stars · Snow, Ice, and Winter

Philosophy: Aristotle · Descartes and Dualism · Empiricism (Locke, Berkeley, Hume) · Epicureanism · Plato and Platonism · Stoicism · William James and Pragmatism

Allusions: American Writers · Dante · Exploration and the Poles · Fairy Tales and Folklore · Genesis · Greek Mythology · Homer’s Epics · The Bible · The Book of Job

Key passages

From the research

  • The chapter opens with a profound meditation on the futility and vanity of human aspirations, as expressed through Miss MacIntosh’s reflections on Emperor Constantine and the “Slough of Despond.” The metaphor of life as a marshland filled with brambles and weeds sets a somber tone about the human condition and the closing of the heart from within, emphasizing internal barriers to understanding or connection.
  • This passage questions history and knowledge, asserting that “history lies, and geography is uncertain,” underscoring the unreliability of accepted truths and the elusive nature of identity in modern times.
  • Miss MacIntosh expresses a strong belief in common sense as the “middle brow,” the middle way, and the average life, asserting it as a rare and valuable quality. This passage reveals an internal tension between embracing ordinary life and the cosmic or remote issues that also preoccupy her.
  • The comparison of dwarves dreaming they are giants and giants dreaming they are dwarves illustrates the relativity of perception and ambition, hinting at the complexity of human identity.
  • One of the most extended and important passages is the critique of electric lights, attributed ironically to Benjamin Franklin, who paved “the way for electric lights” and thereby disrupted natural rhythms of day and night. Miss MacIntosh laments how electric illumination invades privacy, disturbs sleep, and ruins traditional human experiences such as marriage by exposing flaws that darkness once concealed.
  • This passage deeply mourns the loss of darkness, which once provided refuge and mystery, and contrasts it with the artificial brightness that keeps us “up all night like Roman soldiers,” contributing to social ills like divorce and loneliness.
  • The nostalgia for “bayberry candles” and natural starlight versus intrusive modern electric lights highlights a tension between technological progress and preservation of human dignity and natural order.
  • Miss MacIntosh reflects on the role of darkness in protecting the sacredness and mystery of marriage, allowing spouses to be “modest” and sheltered from immediate judgment. The electric light, by exposing all, undermines this protective veil, leading to disillusionment and social problems.
  • This meditation extends to a broader social commentary on how modern illumination disrupts traditional human relationships and perceptions.
  • Miss MacIntosh’s practical, unadorned manner of dress and demeanor symbolize her serious approach to life, rejecting frivolity, dreams, and illusions. She lives fully in the present reality, “for no other life,” and is skeptical of sentimental or metaphysical distractions.
  • This passage highlights her grounded nature and possibly her resistance or inability to engage with deeper or more cosmic concerns that transcend ordinary experience.
  • Vera reflects on how Miss MacIntosh’s frequent evocations of cosmic phenomena (creation, tides, stars) serve to mask her own human limitations and inner absences. These grand themes conceal what she does not wish to reveal about herself.
  • This passage suggests a tension between the vastness of universal mysteries and the intimate realities of human life.
  • The chapter ends with a meditation on the coming of winter, the changing of seasons, and the narrowing spectrum of colors in the natural world, symbolizing transition, loss, and endurance. The imagery of crystalline snow, dimmed colors, and the “luminous colors of the winter sea” evokes both harshness and beauty in nature’s cycles.
  • This passage metaphorically connects the natural world’s rhythms to human experience, emphasizing acceptance and preparation for inevitable change.
  • The concluding words question why light should be given to those in misery and darkness, affirming the enduring value of natural starlight and rejecting artificial electric light. Miss MacIntosh’s exclamation, “Electric lights, fiddlesticks! The stars have lighted the heavens from pole to pole,” reaffirms a preference for natural order over human tampering.
  • “These were dreams, impersonal and vast, and these did cover, as is said in gambling circles, her hand, for they did conceal her own limitations, the fact that there was something missing from the essential human, something she did not want me to see.” This is where Vera sees what the talk is for.

Questions and observations

Reading closely

  • “The heart, my dear, was locked from the inside.” Whose heart?
  • “How should I know what is true unless I know what is false?” How does Miss MacIntosh answer her own question?
  • Why does she blame Franklin and Edison, of all people, this morning?

Characters

  • “She would say that she snored, not that she loved.” What is Vera beginning to understand?
  • “Of herself, of herself alone, what had she ever said that was personal and sad and revelatory?” What has she said instead?
  • She speaks of winter “now in the August sunlight.” Why skip the autumn?

Connections

  • Chapter 19’s door was “barred from the inside.” What else is locked from the inside here?
  • She blamed Constantine for confusing the days (Chapter 22) and now blames Franklin for confusing the nights. What is she defending?
  • “A man had married a man, and a woman had married a woman, and no one had been the wiser.” How does that line speak to the night of Chapters 17 and 18?

Reflection

  • Is there a right to be unseen?
  • Does darkness protect love, or hide it?
  • What do we talk about so that we don’t have to talk about ourselves?

Research: Characters

Miss MacIntosh

  • Miss MacIntosh is portrayed as fiercely grounded in what she calls “common sense,” valuing the “middle brow,” the “middle way,” and the “average life,” a disposition she prides herself on as her “greatest love,” even if others despise it.
  • This common sense coexists with a pervasive skepticism toward accepted truths such as history, geography, and law, which she dismisses as unstable, uncertain, or outright falsehoods.
  • She challenges grand narratives, like that of Caesar crossing the Rubicon or the veracity of historical figures, suggesting that time has neither accumulated nor taught wisdom.
  • This skeptical realism reveals a character who questions the foundations of knowledge and human pretensions but does so without despair; rather, she seems to accept human limitations with a certain weary humor and irony.
  • Miss MacIntosh’s discourse centers on her criticism of modern inventions, especially electric lights. She associates electricity, notably Benjamin Franklin’s experiments, as a disruptive force that has destroyed natural rhythms, privacy, and the quietness of night. She laments electric lights for erasing darkness, which she sees as essential for sleep, privacy, and even mystery in human relationships, particularly marriage. Electric lights, she argues, expose flaws and imperfections that were once safely hidden in darkness, thereby damaging marriages and social harmony.
  • Her detailed critique extends to “electric trains,” “electric irons,” “fluorescent lamps,” and “two-way lighting systems” as unnatural intrusions into life’s natural order.
  • This stance encapsulates her resistance to tampering with “old, damaged creation” and her preference for simpler, older ways such as “bayberry candles,” “snuffers,” and natural starlight. Her view is that the modern world’s brightness is a form of extravagant excess that impoverishes human experience and dignity.
  • Miss MacIntosh’s practical nature is emphasized by descriptions of her appearance and habits. She dresses plainly, in worn, practical clothing: a grey baseball sweater with a ravelling sleeve, stout shoes, and a patched salt-and-pepper tweed coat.
  • She carries her “rigging” everywhere, including an old black umbrella likened to a sail and a whale-boned ice-breaker corset, symbolizing her preparedness and no-nonsense approach to life on a “rough shore.”
  • She rejects frivolities such as filmy dresses or adornments, even on significant occasions like weddings or funerals, signaling her seriousness and focus on the immediate, tangible world rather than on dreams or illusions.
  • Despite her talk of cosmic and remote issues like glaciers, submerged continents, and the first days of creation, Miss MacIntosh reveals little of her personal emotions or vulnerabilities.
  • She claims her consciousness ceases during sleep and that she cannot remember dreams, not even her own, suggesting a detachment from inner emotional life or a guardedness.
  • Her conscience “kept guard” as a “lonely vigil,” indicating solitude and perhaps a self-imposed emotional isolation.
  • She evades personal disclosures and remains impassive, almost austere, in her demeanor.
  • This emotional reserve contrasts with the vastness of the cosmic themes she invokes, highlighting a tension between the grand and the personal.
  • Miss MacIntosh’s reflections often shift from the mundane to the cosmic and from daily life and societal critiques to the “first starfish upon the first beach” and “the first moon drawing the first tide.” This oscillation suggests that she perceives human life as part of a vast, impersonal natural order that transcends immediate existence.
  • She uses cosmic imagery to mask what she does not want to reveal: her fears, losses, or inner life.
  • This duality makes her a somewhat enigmatic figure, connecting the earthly and the universal while remaining personally elusive.
  • Miss MacIntosh’s thoughts about the coming winter, the colorlessness of the world under snow and ice, and the need to prepare with warm clothing and supplies reveal a keen awareness of mortality and the cycles of life.
  • Winter symbolizes death or hardship, and her sober preparation indicates acceptance rather than fear. Yet, she also acknowledges the subtle beauty of winter’s muted colors, reflecting a nuanced appreciation of life’s phases and transitions.
  • Her concern with time’s passing, the loss inherent in change, and the persistence of “dimmed colors” in hardship underscore a mature, grounded philosophy.
  • Throughout her discourse, Miss MacIntosh repeatedly condemns human vanity, illusions of grandeur, and false hopes.
  • She refers to “vain man” in multiple historical and contemporary contexts, from Emperor Constantine and Caesar to Benjamin Franklin, pointing out the futility of human pretensions to immortality or mastery.
  • She warns against illusions, falsehoods that may mask other truths, and the human tendency to stumble blindly in the “broad daylight which God has lighted.”
  • Her repeated invocation of vanity and illusion underscores a theme of human limitation and the importance of humility and realism.

Vera Cartwheel

  • Notes that Miss MacIntosh never speaks personally or reveals sadness or revelation about herself.
  • Senses that the grand themes Miss MacIntosh talks about serve to conceal her own limitations and personal absence.
  • Wonders and questions Miss MacIntosh’s answers.
  • Realizes for the first time that Miss MacIntosh has not shared any personal history with her.
  • Questions Miss MacIntosh’s insistence on learning about the past and “common sense” and that it might all be false, imaginary, and not real.

Research: Themes

Illusion and Reality

See: Illusion and Reality

  • Miss MacIntosh opens with a critique of “vain man” and the illusions that humans harbor, such as the belief in immortality or the certainty of history.
  • She questions the reliability of history and geography, suggesting that what we accept as truth may be unstable or false.
  • The idea that truth cannot be known without understanding falsehood is emphasized.

Common Sense and the Middle Way

See: Order, Chaos, and Discipline

  • She values common sense and the “middle brow,” the average life, as a guiding principle.
  • Despite her philosophical musings on vast, cosmic issues, she prides herself on practicality and sensibility.

Critique of Modern Technology: Electric Lights

See: Light and Darkness

  • A significant portion of the chapter is devoted to a critical view of electric lighting and its consequences.
  • Miss MacIntosh blames Benjamin Franklin for pioneering electricity, which has disrupted natural cycles of day and night.
  • Electric lights are portrayed as a destroyer of privacy, natural rhythms (sleep and work), and even marital harmony.
  • She laments the loss of darkness, which she sees as essential for personal privacy and the natural order.
  • The chapter contrasts the artificial glare of electric lights with the natural, gentle light of stars and candles used by ancestors.

Historical and Cultural Reflections

See: Memory and the Past · Society, Class, and Race

  • References to historical figures such as Emperor Constantine, Benjamin Franklin, and President Garfield serve as symbols of human folly or misguided progress.
  • The chapter also evokes images from ancient times and myths (e.g., Helen of Troy, Ulysses) to illustrate timeless human experiences affected by modern changes.

Human Relationships and Privacy

See: Isolation and Connection

  • The darkness once allowed spouses to be ignorant of each other’s full appearance or flaws, preserving marital bliss.
  • Electric lighting exposes all imperfections, potentially leading to divorces and the breakdown of relationships.
  • This theme extends to a broader loss of innocence and the protective veil of ignorance.

Nature and the Cosmic Order

See: Nature, the Sea, and the Cosmos · Order, Chaos, and Discipline

  • The novel references natural phenomena such as glaciers, tides, northern stars, and the changing seasons.
  • Miss MacIntosh’s talk about ice floes, winter preparations, and the Arctic environment symbolizes the fragility and impermanence of existence.
  • There is a tension between the cosmic, the remote, and the immediate, everyday life.

Mortality and the Passage of Time

See: Death and Mortality · Time

  • The inevitability of winter and death is anticipated, reflecting on the cycles of life.
  • Despite the harshness of winter, there is beauty in its muted colors and quiet persistence.
  • The chapter ends with a meditation on light and darkness as metaphors for life, suffering, and divine presence.

Research: Symbols and Imagery

Electric Lights

See: Lamps, Candles, and Light · Light and Darkness

  • Symbolize modernity’s intrusion into natural human rhythms and privacy.

Darkness and Light

See: Lamps, Candles, and Light

  • Represent privacy, natural order, sleep, and the divine versus exposure, artificiality, and disturbance.

Winter and Ice

See: Snow, Ice, and Winter

  • Metaphors for death, hardship, and the passage of time.

Stars and Natural Light

See: Moon and Stars · Lamps, Candles, and Light

  • Symbolize the eternal, natural order, and the divine presence.

Historical References

See: Memory and the Past

  • Serve to question accepted narratives and human progress.

Research: Resources

  • “a Slough of Despond this life is”: “The slough of Despond,” where Christian sinks under the weight of his sins in Bunyan’s The Pilgrim’s Progress (1678). Slough of Despond is an area in the book Pilgrim’s Progress that Miss MacIntosh reads more than the Bible. See the Chapter 3 resources.
  • “The heart, my dear, was locked from the inside”: Madge and Homer argued about Josh being locked in the closet and dying at the beginning of the book (Chapter 7). Old Josh, the barkeeper, died in a coat closet that Madge insisted “was locked from the outside.” Miss MacIntosh’s heart is locked from the inside. See Madge Capehorn, Homer Capehorn, and the Chapter 7 resources.
  • “great Caesar crossing the Rubicon”: The phrase “crossing the Rubicon” is an idiom that means “passing a point of no return.” Its meaning comes from an allusion to the crossing of the river Rubicon from the north by Julius Caesar in early January 49 BC. (Wikipedia) It symbolizes a critical turning point or a decisive act that cannot be undone.
  • “Who knows that he crossed the Rubicon or that there was a Caesar?”: Richard Whately’s satire Historic Doubts Relative to Napoleon Buonaparte (1819) argued, with the same logic, that Napoleon could not be proved to have existed.
  • “Ignorance of the law is no excuse”: The Roman maxim “ignorantia juris non excusat.”
  • “We make mountains of molehills”: In print by 1548 (Nicholas Udall). See Fairy Tales and Folklore.
  • “We stumble in the broad daylight which God has lighted”: “We stumble at noon day as in the night; we are in desolate places as dead men” (Isaiah 59:10), and “God said, Let there be light” (Genesis 1:3). It encapsulates a moment or idea of transcendence, an acknowledgment that even in the bleakest moments of human experience or the “darkness” of suffering and death there is a possibility of divine light or spiritual awakening. It is a poetic way of expressing hope, mystery, and the complex interplay of life and death that Vera contemplates. See The Bible.
  • “these falsehoods which, though false, may be the face of another truth”: Even though something is demonstrably false, it can still hold a certain level of truth or reveal a deeper underlying reality, often by acting as a metaphor or symbolic representation of a complex idea, even if the literal details are inaccurate. This concept is often explored in art and literature where fictional narratives can convey profound truths about human nature or society.
  • “Poor mortals all and blind as bats in a cave”: This may echo Plato’s prisoners of the cave, who take shadows for the real (Republic 7). See Plato and Platonism.
  • “Deliver not my soul to a turtle or a crab”: “O deliver not the soul of thy turtledove unto the multitude of the wicked” (Psalm 74:19). Young turns the turtledove into a turtle. See The Bible.
  • “Am I my brother’s keeper?”: Genesis 4:9. Miss MacIntosh asks what Mr. Spitzer might. It resonates with his struggle with his sense of duty, guilt, and responsibility for his brother’s legacy and the lives entangled in their shared history. It asks whether one is truly responsible for the fate, suffering, or salvation of another, particularly a close other like a brother, and by extension, for others in one’s life or society. See Genesis and Joachim Spitzer.
  • “One can be an epicure”: Epicurus lived chiefly on bread and water: “Send me a little pot of cheese, that when I like I may fare sumptuously” (Diogenes Laertius 10.11). See Epicureanism.
  • “One can enjoy too much one’s poverty, in fact, and make a great business of it”: Seneca warns against showy poverty, “a rough cloak, unkempt hair, a slovenly beard” (Letters to Lucilius 5). Seneca was a leading Roman Stoic. The school was founded by Zeno of Citium around 300 BC. Seneca’s works discuss both ethical theory and practical advice, and Seneca stresses that both parts are distinct but interdependent. Seneca regards philosophy as a balm for the wounds of life. The destructive passions, especially anger and grief, must be uprooted, or moderated according to reason. He discusses the relative merits of contemplative life and active life, and he considers it important to confront one’s own mortality and be able to face death. One must be willing to practice poverty and use wealth properly, and he writes about favours, clemency, the importance of friendship, and the need to benefit others. The universe is governed for the best by a rational providence, and this must be reconciled with acceptance of adversity. See Stoicism.
  • “Dwarves may dream that they are giants”: Gulliver is a giant in Lilliput and a dwarf in Brobdingnag (Swift, Gulliver’s Travels, 1726).
  • “What was so rare a thing as common sense”: Thomas Paine’s polemical pamphlet Common Sense (1776) has been described as the most influential political pamphlet of the 18th century, affecting both the American and French revolutions. Today, the concept of common sense, and how it should best be used, remains linked to many of the most perennial topics in epistemology and ethics, with special focus often directed at the philosophy of the modern social sciences. (Wikipedia) See Aristotle, Empiricism (Locke, Berkeley, Hume), Descartes and Dualism, and William James and Pragmatism.
    • The philosophy of common sense is a set of beliefs that challenge skepticism and subjective idealism. It’s based on the idea that there is a basic ability to perceive and judge that most people share. Aristotle first used the term, for the faculty that joins the five senses (On the Soul, Book 3). It was also followed by John Locke, Thomas Reid, and G. E. Moore. Basic tenets are sensations are more than just ideas or subjective impressions; beliefs are based on common sense and reason; people of all levels of education can use common sense; starting off on the wrong path can lead to absurdities.
    • Nous is a concept from classical philosophy, sometimes equated to intellect or intelligence, for the faculty of the human mind necessary for understanding what is true or real.
    • Thomas Reid wrote common sense works as such: If all men observe an item and believe the same qualities about that item, then the knowledge of that item is universally true. It is common knowledge, which without explanation is held true by other people; so, what is universally seen is universally believed. Charles Sanders Peirce later wrote (“Some Consequences of Four Incapacities,” 1868), “The real, then, is that which, sooner or later, information and reasoning would finally result in, and which is therefore independent of the vagaries of me and you. Thus, the very origin of the conception of reality shows that this conception essentially involves the notion of a community, without definite limits, and capable of a definite increase of knowledge.” The combination of the same ideas, of a thing, by multiple people, is what confirms the reality of an object. Reid also believes that the philosophers of his time exaggerated what is truly real. Where most philosophers believe that what we see is not fully what that thing is, for example, Descartes, Reid counters this argument simply by stating that “such a hypothesis is no more likely to be true than the common-sensical belief that the world is much the way we perceive it to be.” (Wikipedia) Reid’s own book is An Inquiry into the Human Mind on the Principles of Common Sense (1764).
  • “the middle brow, the middle way”: “Middlebrow” was new in Young’s day. Russell Lynes’s “Highbrow, Lowbrow, Middlebrow” ran in Harper’s in 1949. The middle way is Aristotle’s mean, virtue as the middle between two extremes (Nicomachean Ethics 2.6). See Aristotle.
  • “Vain man, Benjamin Franklin!”: Benjamin Franklin’s philosophy was practical, optimistic, and focused on self-improvement. He believed that a republic could only succeed if its people were virtuous and had the right temper: “only a virtuous people are capable of freedom. As nations become corrupt and vicious, they have more need of masters” (letter to the Abbés Chalut and Arnoux, April 17, 1787). His ideas included: practicality, through hard work and self-discipline and improving their character through effort and self-control; optimism, as a supporter of the Enlightenment and the power of reason and scientific discovery people could improve their lives through education, community service, and virtuous living; self-improvement, people could improve their character through effort and self-control and that people should strive to live virtuous and purposeful lives; political philosophy, the importance of freedom of the press, religion, education, pragmatism, and the republic would flourish if the freedoms were secured by the US Constitution combined with wisdom and virtue. His lightning rod (1752) drew the heavens’ fire down a wire into the ground. See American Writers.
  • “old President Garfield had seen well enough without them”: Garfield is mentioned in the context of a “time” when people saw well enough without electric lights, implying that even a prominent historical figure like Garfield did not require such artificial illumination to live effectively or happily. The White House was wired for electricity in 1891, under Benjamin Harrison, ten years after Garfield died of an assassin’s bullet.
  • “Even Skid Row”: The name comes from Seattle’s Skid Road (1850s), where logs were skidded down to the mill. It came to mean the poor quarter of any city.
  • “About the only advantage is midnight baseball”: The first major league night game was played in Cincinnati on May 24, 1935. President Roosevelt pressed a button in Washington to turn on the lights.
  • “it was he who had written that early to bed makes us wise”: “Early to bed and early to rise, makes a man healthy, wealthy, and wise” (Poor Richard, 1735), as in Chapter 15. See American Writers and the Chapter 15 resources.
    • While Benjamin Franklin is often mistakenly credited with inventing daylight saving time, he actually penned a satirical essay in 1784 suggesting Parisians wake up earlier to save on candles, not proposing a change to clocks. In 1784, while serving as an American envoy in Paris, Franklin wrote a satirical essay titled “An Economical Project” published in the Journal de Paris. The essay suggested that Parisians could save money on candles and lamp oil by waking up earlier and making the most of the natural daylight. Franklin’s proposal was about changing sleep schedules, not changing the time on clocks, which is what modern daylight saving time involves. Because of this essay, Franklin is often mistakenly credited with inventing daylight saving time, but he was only suggesting a change in sleep habits, not the time itself (Franklin Institute, “Did Ben Franklin Invent Daylight Saving Time?”). The modern concept of daylight saving time, which involves changing clocks, originated later, with some attributing the idea to George Hudson, an entomologist from New Zealand, in 1895. The concept of daylight saving time gained traction during World War I as a way to conserve energy, and it was formally adopted in the US in 1918.
  • “had always brought gold in their mouths”: The German proverb “Morgenstunde hat Gold im Munde,” “the morning hour has gold in its mouth.” See Fairy Tales and Folklore.
  • “Bayberry candles were good enough for our fathers to see by”: The bayberry custom is to burn a candle on Christmas Eve or New Year’s Eve to bring good luck, wealth, and health. It is said to have originated in Colonial America. “A bayberry candle burned to the socket brings food to the larder and gold to the pocket.” See the Chapter 15 resources.
  • “Was Helen of Troy ever disturbed by electric lights”: Helen of Troy in Greek mythology was said to be the most beautiful woman in the world. “Was this the face that launched a thousand ships?” (Marlowe, Doctor Faustus, 1604). Young makes it “caused a thousand ships to sail.” See Greek Mythology.
  • “Ulysses, if ever he had seen Penelope under electric lights”: Ulysses is the Roman name for Odysseus, a hero in ancient Greek literature. Penelope is the wife of Ulysses and is an example of a faithful wife because she waits for her husband to return and tricks suitors who wish to marry her. Penelope wove a shroud by day and unwove it by night to put off her suitors (Odyssey 2). See Homer’s Epics.
  • “of marriage, the sacred union”: Women’s rights in the US were restricted during marriage: married women were legally subordinate to their husbands; they could not own property, keep their own wages, or enter into contracts; they had no rights to their children. Under coverture, “the husband and wife are one person in law” (Blackstone, 1765). New York’s Married Women’s Property Act came in 1848. See Women, Gender, and Marriage.
  • “an ugly woman was safe in her husband’s arms”: Only women are called ugly, because the feminine beauty ideal in every country holds that beauty is a woman’s most important asset. See Women, Gender, and Marriage.
  • “all these dreadful fluorescent lamps”: Fluorescent lamps went on sale in 1938 and were shown at the New York World’s Fair of 1939, which helps date this breakfast.
  • “What business had he flying a kite”: Franklin’s kite experiment of June 1752 showed that lightning is electricity. See American Writers.
  • “to meddle and tamper with creation the way God left it last Saturday”: Miss MacIntosh’s creation week of Chapter 22, when God “had stopped” on Saturday. See the Chapter 22 resources.
  • “The wisest men are never married”: Most philosophers were in fact childless and/or never married. They did not have progeny or like Descartes, had an infant that died. To the current day philosophers are 75% men and 25% women.
    • There are women philosophers who have made significant contributions to the field: Gargi Vachaknavi, who questions the sage Yajnavalkya in the Brihadaranyaka Upanishad (3.6 and 3.8); Ban Zhao, author of Lessons for Women (c. 106 CE); Hypatia of Alexandria (d. 415); Mary Wollstonecraft (A Vindication of the Rights of Woman, 1792); Simone de Beauvoir (The Second Sex, 1949); Hannah Arendt (The Human Condition, 1958); and G. E. M. Anscombe (Intention, 1957). They represent a wide range of eras and philosophical fields, from ancient Greece to modern philosophy, covering topics like politics, ethics, and metaphysics.
  • “A fine thing, she would say to Thomas Edison”: In the US there was a serious debate about which to use, AC or DC current, and that may be what is referred to in the novel. The war of the currents was a series of events surrounding the introduction of competing electric power transmission systems in the late 1880s and early 1890s. It grew out of two lighting systems developed in the late 1870s and early 1880s: arc lamp street lighting running on high-voltage alternating current (AC), and large-scale low-voltage direct current (DC) indoor incandescent lighting being marketed by Thomas Edison’s company. In 1886, the Edison system was faced with new competition: an alternating current system initially introduced by George Westinghouse’s company that used transformers to step down from a high voltage so AC could be used for indoor lighting. Using high voltage allowed an AC system to transmit power over longer distances from more efficient large central generating stations. As the use of AC spread rapidly with other companies deploying their own systems, the Edison Electric Light Company claimed in early 1888 that high voltages used in an alternating current system were hazardous, and that the design was inferior to, and infringed on the patents behind, their direct current system. In the spring of 1888, a media furor arose over electrical fatalities caused by pole-mounted high-voltage AC lines, attributed to the greed and callousness of the arc lighting companies that operated them. In June of that year Harold P. Brown, a New York electrical engineer, claimed the AC-based lighting companies were putting the public at risk using high-voltage systems installed in a slipshod manner. Brown also claimed that alternating current was more dangerous than direct current and tried to prove this by publicly killing animals with both currents, with technical assistance from Edison Electric. The Edison company and Brown colluded further in their parallel goals to limit the use of AC with attempts to push through legislation to severely limit AC installations and voltages. Both also colluded with Westinghouse’s chief AC rival, the Thomson-Houston Electric Company, to make sure the first electric chair was powered by a Westinghouse AC generator. By the early 1890s, the war was winding down. Further deaths caused by AC lines in New York City forced electric companies to fix safety problems. Thomas Edison no longer controlled Edison Electric, and subsidiary companies were beginning to add AC to the systems they were building. Mergers reduced competition between companies, including the merger of Edison Electric with their largest competitor, Thomson-Houston, forming General Electric in 1892. Edison Electric’s merger with their chief alternating current rival brought an end to the war of the currents and created a new company that now controlled three quarters of the US electrical business. Westinghouse won the bid to supply electrical power for the World’s Columbian Exposition in 1893 and won the major part of the contract to build Niagara Falls hydroelectric project later that year (partially splitting the contract with General Electric) (Wikipedia, “War of the currents”).
  • “keeping us up all night like Roman soldiers”: The Roman army divided the night into four watches.
  • “a man had married a man, and a woman had married a woman, and no one had been the wiser”: Womanless marriages were staged as community events and fundraisers. It is a “most unique and attractive entertainment,” the Houston Post reported on May 27, 1917. “Some of the most prominent men in the city will be in it. It is filled with fun from beginning to end and every city or town in which it has been given there have been record breaking audiences, even standing room being at a premium.” In nineteenth-century New England, two women living together as a couple were said to be in a “Boston marriage.” See Women, Gender, and Marriage.
  • “is Baffin Bay?”: Baffin Bay is located between Baffin Island and the west coast of Greenland. It is named for William Baffin, who charted it in 1616. See Exploration and the Poles.
  • “It’s always well”: An igloo (Inuktitut iglu, “house”) is built of snow blocks. See Exploration and the Poles and Snow, Ice, and Winter.
  • “a new broom sweeps clean”: John Heywood’s proverb (1546). See Fairy Tales and Folklore.
  • “fourteen tall white candles”: The candles of Vera’s fourteenth birthday. See the Chapter 9 resources.
  • “where the dead souls wandered like flames”: This may recall Dante’s flames, each wrapping a soul, among them Ulysses (Inferno 26). See Dante.
  • “the latitude and longitude in which may be located the Austral Islands, ice-locked Baffin Bay or the Magnetic Pole”: The Austral Islands are in French Polynesia. James Clark Ross reached the North Magnetic Pole in 1831. See Exploration and the Poles.
  • “dancing like mad dervishes”: The Mevlevi, the whirling dervishes of Turkey, pray by turning.
  • “in the August sunlight”: A clue to the time of these events: August.
  • “no Indian summer like the Indian summer of the human soul”: “Indian summer,” a warm spell after the first frost, is an American phrase, in print by 1778.
  • “no time for the migrations of passenger birds”: The passenger pigeon, once counted in billions, died out with Martha, the last of them, in 1914.
  • “winter wore its coat of many colors”: Joseph’s “coat of many colours” (Genesis 37:3). See Genesis.
  • “be given to a man who is in misery and whose way is darkness and whom God hath hedged in”: “Wherefore is light given to him that is in misery” and “Why is light given to a man whose way is hid, and whom God hath hedged in?” (Job 3:20, 23). See The Book of Job.
    • The last paragraph may refer to the time Miss MacIntosh worked in a house for the blind.

Vocabulary

Aberration
A departure from what is normal or expected.
Astral
Having to do with the stars.
Bayberry
A shrub of the Atlantic coast whose waxy berries were boiled to make fragrant candles.
Corset
A close-fitting undergarment, stiffened with whalebone or steel and laced tight, worn to shape the waist.
Crystalline
Clear and sparkling, like crystal.
Cuttlefish
A sea creature related to the squid that can change color and squirt ink.
Dervish
A member of a Sufi order known for whirling in worship.
Drove
A herd or flock driven or moving together.
Epicure
One who takes refined pleasure in food and drink.
Festering
Rotting and oozing; growing more corrupt.
Fluorescent
Giving off light through a glowing gas in a tube.
Fuliginous
Sooty; dusky.
Glow-worm
A beetle whose wingless female and larvae give off a greenish light.
Ice floe
A sheet of floating ice.
Igloo
An Inuit house built of snow blocks.
Inscrutable
Impossible to understand or interpret.
Iridescence
A rainbow shimmer of colors that change with the angle of view.
Lugubrious
Mournful; gloomy.
Mauve
A pale purple.
Middlebrow
Of conventional, middling taste.
Monsoon
A seasonal wind in South Asia that brings months of heavy rain.
Mossback
An old-fashioned person; literally, an old turtle with moss on its back.
Oblivion
The state of being forgotten, or of being unaware of everything.
Phantasmagoric
Like a phantasmagoria, a shifting series of dreamlike or nightmarish images. A phantasmagoria was an eighteenth-century magic-lantern ghost show.
Precipitous
Very steep; headlong.
Rubicon
A small river in northern Italy. Julius Caesar crossed it with his army in 49 BC, starting a civil war, so “crossing the Rubicon” means passing a point of no return. See Crossing the Rubicon (Ch 23).
Salt-and-pepper
Of cloth or hair: flecked with black and white.

A scissor-like tool for trimming or putting out a candle.

An evergreen tree of northern forests.
